Keys and kingdoms
Animals and plants are so numerous that people need to classify them into groups and then into smaller groups 
to be able to talk about them. The groups are written in order of size, with the largest group first: Kingdom, 
Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
There are four main reasons for classifying into groups:
Communication – 
 
»
So I can say to you the word ‘marsupial’ and you will know I mean a furry, warm, 
pouched mammal.
Conservation 
 
»
– If we know how many there are of a group and we see the numbers declining, we can take 
action to make sure they survive into the future.
Ordering – 
 
»
This happens so we know which ones came first and we can find things, like all the books in a 
library or all the files on your computer.
Relationships – 
 
»
These show which organisms are related to each other. For example, the platypus and 
echidna are both monotreme mammals.

Kingdoms can be used to classify organisms
List the five main kingdoms.



Identify which of the kingdoms has the smallest number of known species.


Identify which of the kingdoms consists of unicellular organisms.


Provide an example of an organism that would be classified as unicellular.





Select an organism from the kingdoms Monera or Protista to research. Record its scientific name and common name (if it has one), where it is found, the size of the organism, how it reproduces, plus one interesting fact about the organism.








Explain how members of the Kingdom Plantae differ from all other life forms.



Members of Kingdom Animalia are unable to create their own food from sunlight. How do they gain energy to survive?




Which of the kingdoms could be considered the most successful form of life on Earth? Provide reasons to justify your answer.




Extend your understanding
Bacteria (Kingdom Monera) are the smallest living organisms on Earth. They are so small that a microscope is needed to see them, and they come in all shapes and sizes. Each type of bacteria causes different diseases, so it is important that medical scientists can correctly identify them.
Spherical bacteria are called cocci.
Spiral-shaped bacteria are called spirillum.
Longer rod-shaped bacteria are called bacilli.
Comma-shaped bacteria are called vibrio.
A doctor sent a sample of bacteria found in a sore throat to the laboratory for testing. The scientist used a microscope to look at the sample and found cocci. Draw a picture of what the scientist saw down the microscope.

Why was it important that the scientist identified the type of bacteria for the doctor?



There are two main types of spherical-shaped bacteria that could cause a throat infection: Staphylococci and Streptococci. Scientists must use a special stain called a Gram stain to tell these two types apart. Staphylococci stain a purple colour with this stain and are called Gram positive; Streptococci do not stain purple and are called Gram negative.
Why do scientists sometimes need to stain bacterial cells?



Staphylococci aureus (also known as Golden Staph) is often resistant to some bacterial treatments such as antibiotics. Why is it important for hospitals to correctly identify this bacterium?



How are bacterial cells different to cells in Kingdom Animalia?

Kingdoms can be used to classify organisms
Key terms
Amoebaa type of single-celled organism belonging to the Protista kingdom
Bacteriaunicellular organisms that have a cell wall but no nucleus
Cell walla structure that provides support around the cell in some organisms, such as plants and fungi
Multicellularconsisting of two or more cells
Nucleusa membrane-bound structure in cells that contains most of the cell’s genetic material
Planktonmicroscopic organisms that fl oat in fresh or salt water
Taxonomista scientist who classifies living things into groups
Unicellularconsisting of only one cell; an example is bacteria
The largest groupings in the classification system are the kingdoms. Features such as body form, type of cells and methods of obtaining nutrients are used to classify living things into groups.

Explain why the classification of living things is important to science.

In the late 1800s, two palaeontologists, Edward Cope and Othniel Marsh, were competing to see who could discover the most dinosaurs. Marsh discovered most of the fossil remains of a new dinosaur, but its skull was missing. In his haste to take credit for the discovery, he substituted the skull of another dinosaur and named the creature “Brontosaurus”.
Propose what evidence the palaeontologists at the time had to produce to claim that a dinosaur they had discovered could not be classified as an already-discovered dinosaur.




Assess the impact that Marsh’s actions could have had on scientific thinking at the time. Identify whether you think he was acting ethically or not.

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian CurriculumName:

Living organisms have characteristics in common
Classification history
In the 4th century, the Greek philosopher Aristotle classified all living things into two groups: plants and animals. His collection of “animals” included giraffes, dragonflies and sharks. He divided these animals into three new groups based on how they moved: walking (land), flying (air) or swimming (water).

Name two animals that would fit into the following groups:
walking

flying

swimming

In which of Aristotle’s groups would a duck belong? Explain why.




In which of Aristotle’s groups would a frog belong? Explain why.




According to Aristotle, both bats and birds would be classified into the “flying” group. Suggest a reason why these two animals should not be classified into the same group.






Carolus Linnaeus designed the current system of classification in the 18th century.
What changes did Linnaeus make?






Draw, label and illustrate a classification key that shows how Aristotle classified living things.

iversity of ecology is the range of different

8f Losing Our Biodiversity
• Clearing of native vegetation for either 
housing, forestry, mining or farmland 
encourages erosion and reduces the quality 
of the soil. In eastern NSW and Victoria 
over 90% of native vegetation has been 
removed.
• Introduced species can become 
competitors, predators or parasites on 
native wildlife. Many introduced micro-
organisms cause diseases to which native 
wildlife has no natural immunity.
• Poaching and the illegal trade in native 
wildlife is the modern-day equivalent of 
hunting. This can cause the destruction of 
large numbers of the most spectacular and 
rare of native species, birds and reptiles in 
particular.
• Pollution of the environment can destroy 
native plants or make it easier for 
introduced species to thrive. Either way the 
original native organisms are placed under

Ecology

Look at my tree house

Ecology
Look at my tree house

se Allin an ant’s day - a narrative

There once lived a small colony of ants in a nice comfortable nest under the ground, hidden by the leaf litter of a
big gum tree. They were always @ busy group going on with their day-to-day business in an orderly manner. Like any
other day, this day the ants started by receiving a message, a signal giving them the location of a new stash of food.
Many juicy mites had been located high up in their big eucalyptus tree extracting nourishing sap from new leaves.
Quickly the ants made their way out of the nest and up along the trunk of the tree.

Along their journey they met several insect borers munching away on some bark. A stick insect curiously moved
towards the ants but suddenly stopped. It camouflaged itself on the bark of the tree by staying very still, so it
looked like a leafless branch. The surprised ants suddenly understood why the stick insect interrupted its journey
when a magpie swooped down and snatched the stick insect for its breakfast. There was not much the ants could
do but to continue their journey, wondering whether the stick insect had enjoyed a last meal of fresh leaves.
Continuing their expedition, the ants noticed a young possum enjoying the sweet taste of the tree blossoms. But
the possum was rudely interrupted by a cat climbing up towards the branches, hoping to score a possum meal!
The possum hurried off, scaring the magpie away from its nest, leaving her young chicks to the fate of the cat or
the tree snake that lay absolutely still amongst the branches. ‘What an advantage it is being tiny’ thought the
ants as they continued to scurry along their path.

It wasn't long till they reached the juicy but clumsy mites. The ants skilfully surrounded the mites and together
in their gangs started to carry the mites down the tree. ‘Such strength and determination!’ thought a flying fox,
hanging upside down enjoying the fruits of the tree. It didn’t take long for a wagtail bird to notice the colourful
mites being hauled down the tree and it flew near the ants to investigate. ‘What a great meal”, and with its sharp
beak the bird grabbed and swallowed about three mites, along with the ants that had held them. The rest of the
ants took one more look at the incoming beak and decided to get out in a hurry ~ even if that meant losing the
mites. Tired and hungry, the surviving ants made their way down the tree towards their nest, only to find it was
blocked by some droppings from the flying fox.

The ants retreated into the bark of the tree, where the borers had been previously, to shield themselves from the
cold evening. Watching their nest from the safety of the tree and hoping the dung beetles would hurry up and
eat the droppings before it got too dark, the ants saw an echidna making its way towards their nest. It all
happened so frighteningly fast: the echidna found their nest, pushed its snout into the nest and with its long
sticky tongue scooped up every last ant. The ants in the tree could not help but think how lucky they were this
time and resolved never to complain again about another flying fox or its droppings! They set off together to
start another colony under another tree.

Activity sheet – Classifying living things
Other ways of grouping organisms
There are all sorts of features that can help us organise groups of living things. Organisms 
can be grouped by biological classification, but they can also be grouped by where 
they live (habitat), what they eat or how they behave. For example, the blue-billed duck 
(Oxyura australis) is grouped with other birds in the Class Aves (Birds), but it could also be 
grouped with Australian wetland creatures. 
Many different types of organisms can live together in the same habitat. Some 
organisms that share the same living area depend on each other for their survival. For 
example, organisms that live on coral reefs are interdependent, which means that they 
all need each other to survive. Some organisms are food for others, while some provide 
shelter or protection to other species.
+ 1 Read the passage and underline all the plants and animals mentioned.
 
A coral reef is home to many different types of life. Reefs contain lots of different 
species of fish. These fish eat the seaweed and grasses that grow on the coral. It 
is important that there is a rich supply of food for all the reef’s creatures. Sharks 
and other predators eat large fish, which in turn eat smaller fish. All sorts of plants 
and animals live in tropical reef habitats. They include eels, crabs, prawns, sea stars, 
seahorses, plankton, seaweed, anemones, clownfish, angelfish, coral polyps, sea turtles, 
jellyfish, dolphins, dugongs and whales.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Ecosystems
33
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Photosynthesis and ecosystems
Green plants produce their own food using photosynthesis. This food helps them grow.  
As the plant grows, more leaves, fruit and flowers are made available for other living  
things to eat. In this way, photosynthesis helps an ecosystem to thrive. 
Plants use carbon dioxide, water and the sun’s energy to make a sugary food called 
glucose. When the plant is eaten by a consumer, some of the energy stored in the glucose 
is released and used by the consumer. The rest of the energy is released as heat. When 
consumers and producers die, decomposers break down their remains into tiny parts 
called nutrients. These nutrients go into the soil or the atmosphere. A new plant uses 
these nutrients to begin the energy transfer process all over again.

Plants from the dinosaur age
In 1994, a bushwalker in Wollemi National Park (just north of Sydney) noticed some large trees that he thought were different from any others he had seen before. He carefully removed a small branch and took it to a friend who was a botanist (an expert in the study of plants). Initially, the botanist thought the branch looked like leaves that could be found on a fern and was surprised to be told it was from a tree that was 40 metres tall.
Careful studies of the tree revealed that it was very similar to the types of trees that existed millions of years ago. The tree was named Wollemi nobelis after Wollemi National Park (where it was found) and Mr William Nobel (the bushwalker who discovered it).
Pine trees belong to a group of plants called conifers. What characteristics can be used to identify these plants?



One of the distinguishing characteristics of the Wollemi pine tree is its bark, which was once described as looking like it was “covered in Coco Pops”. Use more scientific terms to describe what this might look like.


The Wollemi pine has large seeds that have been described as “wings”.






How might these seeds be spread into new areas?



Why would it be an advantage for the Wollemi pine to have seeds that are like wings?





A Brachiosaurus is pictured.








How might the Brachiosaurus help with the dispersal of the Wollemi pine seeds? Hint: The seeds pass through the Brachiosaurus undigested.



What might the Brachiosaurus provide to help the Wollemi pine seeds grow? Hint: Think about what we add to plants to give them nutrients to help them grow.



Why is it important for seeds to move away from the parent tree before growing?

Draw two diagrams: one of a monocot plant and one of a dicot plant. Label any key characteristics that would help you identify which category of flowering plant each would belong to.

Activity sheet – Food and ecosystems 
Producers, consumers and decomposers
All the organisms in an ecosystem can be grouped into one of three types, depending on 
what they eat. 
 
●Producers are living things that make (or produce) their own food from inorganic 
(non-living) ingredients. Examples of producers are green plants.
 
●Consumers are organisms that cannot make their own food. They either eat or 
use food products made by producers or other living things that eat producers. 
Examples of consumers are insects and snakes.
 
●Decomposers break down organic matter (dead plants and animals) by making it 
rot or decay, releasing nutrients, and then absorb the nutrients as food. Examples 
of decomposers are bacteria and fungi. Many decomposers are microscopic 
organisms, called microorganisms.

6.5 | Scientific names

Science as a human endeavour | *

STANDARD

When scientists discover a new plant or animal, they describe it and give it a name. Scientific
naming of living things uses Latin and Greek. Melaleuca viridiflora is the scientific name for a
plant with broad leaves. It is a paperbark tree native to the woodlands, swamps and streams of
northern Australia. The first name (genus name) is a combination of two words: mela (black)
and leuca (white). The bark of the Melaleuca is white with black areas. The second name
(species name) is a combination of virid (green) and flora (flower). So Melaleuca viridiflora is a
tree with green flowers that belongs to a larger group of trees that have white and black bark.

Naming animals

In Table 6.5.1 there is a small selection of words used in naming animal species. When words
are combined, the last letter may be dropped. Sometimes letters such as ‘e’, ‘i’ or ‘o’ have to be

Scientific naming of living things uses Latin and Greek. When scientists discover a new
organism, they describe it and give it a name. They need to understand the meaning
of Latin and Greek words so that the name they give describes the organism in some
way. For example, Melaleuca viridiflorais the biological name for the broad-leaved
paperbark—a small tree native to woodlands, swamps and streams of monsoonal
northern Australia. The first name (genus name) is a combination of two words: mela
meaning black and Jeuce meaning white. The bark of the Melaleuca is white with
black areas. The second name (species) is also a combination of two Latin terms: virid
meaning green and flora meaning flower, So Melaleuca viridiflorais a tree with green
flowers that belongs to a group of trees that have white and black bark.

searchText: ﻿Mercy College Year Eight Science Slime Mould Investigation What are Slime Moulds? Slime moulds are a group of small encrusting moulds consisting of over 500 species. Slime moulds are normally found in cool shady moist places on rotting logs, leaf litter or moist organic soils. They can grow to a few 100 millimetres in size and are often brightly coloured. They feed on bacteria, decaying/rotting organic matter and other microscopic organic material. The group has in the past been regarded as “of uncertain origin” and also classified as both a fungus and an animal. It is now considered as a member of the Kingdom Protista. Its life cycle starts as a spore cell (like a fungus), which can be distributed widely by air and water, and this develops into a .single celled multinucleate plasmodium (or large bag of cytoplasm). This stage can travel by a process of protoplasmic streaming towards food sources, which it then engulfs and consumes. The rate of movement/growth can be as much as 30mm/hour. The plasmodium grows best in moist areas with temperatures below 25C. If environmental conditions deteriorate (too cold, hot, or dry) they will move into an irreversible spore-forming reproductive stage. This investigation will use the slime mould Physarum polycephalum, as it easy to grow on agar plates. It is harmless to humans; but the specimen and agar should not be touched as this will introduce other microbes to the agar medium and possibly ruin the experiment. Oat flakes (think porridge) have been used as the basic food source to grow the specimens. Remarkably the slime can “sense” where the food is and move towards it (like an animal). Instructions for the Investigation The aim of the investigation is to determine what factors affect the growth of the mould. Food types, food quantity, distance of food from the initial specimen, and light intensity may all affect the speed and strength of growth. Note: The agar provides constant moisture conditions and varying the temperature is likely to result in the specimen stopping any further growth. In bench groups (of 3-4 students) plan what is to be tested (rate of growth, type of food etc) and complete the Planning Section. Each student will then get a sample of slime mould growing on an agar plate in a Petri dish. Depending on what they are testing they can also get different types of food. Measurements should then be taken over a couple of days to record the growth rate and observe the directions etc. Specimens can be taken home to record the growth over a period of several hours. Measurements should be taken to the nearest ½ mm with a clear ruler. Data should be collected in tabular form and can then be processed and displayed on graphs or using Excel spreadsheet charts. Evaluations can then be completed onto a final copy sheet for assessment. The Planning process is a group activity, but the Conducting of the experiment (all measurements) and Processing (plotting) should be individual work. In evaluating the investigation you can refer to the results of other group members to compare and contrast growth. A final copy of the investigation can then be written-up for handing in and assessment. 5.15 Science in context: Taxonomists classify new species
5.15 Test your skills and capabilities
Primary and secondary data
There are two sources of data that can be used in scientific research such as taxonomy. Primary data is data directly collected by the scientist. Secondary data is the data that has already been collected by other scientists. When naming a new organism, the primary data includes the drawings and descriptions of newly discovered organisms. This is then compared with the secondary data, such as other samples that are stored by the CSIRO in the National Research Collections Australia. However, not all secondary sources of information are as trustworthy as the CSIRO.
Identify a source of information located on a website and answer the following questions.
Identify who wrote the information or gathered the data. Did they make their observations or measurements in a fair manner, or were they biased (had already decided what they wanted to observe)? (2 mark)



Is the source of information a primary source (did the authors make the measurements themselves) or a secondary source (reporting on other people’s observations)? (1 mark)


When was the information generated? How old is the data? Is it still relevant to your needs? (2 marks)



Why did the author write the information or gather the data? Did they want to convince the reader of their view of the world? Does the author gain anything from publishing the data? (1 mark)

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Differentiation worksheet (C) 
The first Australian scientists classified their environment
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander medicines
In the same way that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples classified their environment, they also classified and built up a thorough knowledge of bush medicine – recognising the characteristics of different plants and understanding how they could be used to treat illnesses. When European scientists arrived in Australia, they learnt many things from the traditional landowners.

Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia)
The oil or paste from the bark or leaves of the tea tree can be used to kill some fungal or bacterial infections.

Kakadu plum (Terminalia ferdinandiana)
This fruit has 50 times more vitamin C than an orange. A lack of vitamin C can result in weakened bones and a weakened immune system.

Emu bush (Eremophila sp.)
Pastes made with the leaves of this plant have been used to wash cuts and scrapes by First Nations communities in the Northern Territory. Recent research suggests that emu bush has antimicrobial properties.

Eucalyptus (Eucalyptus sp.)
Kino is a red-coloured sap or gum produced by eucalypts that has been tested by scientists for its ability to kill bacteria. First Nations communities have used kino to treat burns, eye infections and toothache.
When testing a plant for the first time, early Australian scientists did not put it in their mouth. Instead, they would rub a small amount on their skin. Suggest one reason why they tested plants in this way.


Suggest a modern application of the way that early Australian scientists tested plants. When might people use a small amount of an item to test it?


Suggest ways that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples may have classified the organisms they encountered.



Two ways that some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have classified plants and animals are “edible” vs “inedible” and “venomous” vs “non-venomous”. What is the significance of classifications like this?



Why might scientists prefer to use the scientific names for plants rather than their traditional (or common) names?



Suggest two advantages and two disadvantages of traditional medicines.



Extend your understanding
Research one plant used by local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples for food or medicine that is found on the land on which your school is located (e.g. Yorta Yorta in northern Victoria or Jardwadjali in western Victoria).
Create a poster that explains where the organism is found, what parts are used and how it is prepared.
Include a map of where in Australia this plant can be found. Discuss how the locations where the plant is available may influence how it is classified by different groups of people.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Living things

The hierarchy of biological 
classification
The biological classification system has seven ranks or levels. The groups in the higher 
levels are larger and broader. They group living things that have just some things in 
common. The groups in the lower levels are smaller and more specific. They group living 
things that have many more things in common. The organisation of these groups is called 
the hierarchy of classification. Scientists sometimes disagree with the way others group 
organisms. For example, some scientists use only five kingdoms.
Level
Kingdom
There are six kingdoms in the classification system: animal, plant, protista 
(single-celled organisms including amoebae), fungi, bacteria, archaebacteria 
(microorganisms also called extremophiles).
Phylum
There are more than 30 phyla in the Animal Kingdom and 10 in the Plant Kingdom. 
For example, Phylum Chordata includes humans, birds, fish and all other animals 
with a backbone. 
Class
Each phylum is divided into classes. For example, Phylum Chordata includes the 
classes of amphibians, birds, mammals, reptiles and fish.
Order
An order is a subcategory of a class. 
Family
Families are smaller groups within orders.
Genus
Species that share certain characteristics may be closely related, so they are 
grouped together in a genus. 
Species
A species is a group of living things that can breed to produce fertile offspring.

Human reproduction
Humans reproduce in the same way as other mammals. After sexual intercourse, a single 
sperm cell fertilises the female’s ovum (egg). Usually, one egg is released from the

cells continue to grow for nine months inside the female’s womb. The human baby is born

The importance of plants in ecosystems
Plants are a very important part of ecosystems for a number of reasons. One reason is that 
they are producers, which means they make their own food from inorganic (non-living) 
ingredients, and other living things consume this food. Another important reason is that 
as they are making food they take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. 
Green plants take in carbon dioxide gas through their leaves. Carbon dioxide, 
water and sunlight are used during a process called photosynthesis to help the plant 
produce a sugary food called glucose. When the plant breaks down water during 
photosynthesis, one of the waste products is oxygen. The plant releases the oxygen 
through its leaves. Most animals, including humans, need oxygen in the air they 
breathe for respiration.
The word equation for photosynthesis is:  
carbon dioxide + water (+ light energy) = glucose + oxygen
The chemical formula for carbon dioxide gas is CO2 (one part carbon and two 
parts oxygen).
The chemical formula for water is H2O (two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen).

follow these steps

your list of possibilities.

the notes on the properties of some possible objects provide the information you need for this. Read these and 
then deduce which of the listed objects it is most likely to be. Write your answer on the report sheet.

you have made an incorrect choice in step 3 above, the quality of your reasoning is still important.

The platypus – a case study
8
IntroductIon
Scientists’ thoughts on the platypus have changed over the past 200 years as new information and technologies became 
available. Early descriptions of the platypus seemed far fetched to those who had not seen it. When the first preserved 
specimen reached England in 1798, it was initially thought to be a hoax. It seemed that someone had stuck together the 
bill of a duck, the skin of a mole and the tail of a beaver. Closer examination and the arrival of further specimens proved 
that the platypus did indeed exist.
Aim 
To increase students’ appreciation of how scientists gain knowledge of a species.
Information
The original name for the platypus was Platypus anatinus, which means ‘flat-footed and duck-like’. This was later changed 
to Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The platypus is a member of the order Monotremata. The only other monotremes are 
echidnas. The order Monotremata means ‘one hole’ – there is a single opening serving the digestive, excretory and 
reproductive systems.
The platypus confused early taxonomists because:
• 
it was an endotherm (warm blooded) 
• 
its body temperature is lower than that of most mammals
• 
it has fur
• 
it has a tail like a beaver
• 
it has feet like an otter
• 
it has mammary glands
• 
it lays eggs
• 
its bill is similar to that of a duck
• 
the male produces venom in spurs on its legs.

The seven levels of classification
Traditionally, when classifying organisms, scientists sort them into groups on seven 
levels. This is known as a hierarchical system. Each level classifies the organism in more 
detail. The first, and highest, of these levels is Kingdom. Organisms can be in either the 
animal or plant kingdom, or in other kingdoms such as fungi and bacteria. 
+ 1 What kingdom would you place the following organisms in?
platypus   carrot   frog   rose  
Next, organisms are sorted by their structure. This refers to whether an animal 
has a backbone (chordata), or a soft body or a hard outer shell. This level is called the 
Phylum. 
Organisms are then sorted by Class, then Order, Family, Genus and Species. Each 
level goes into more detail about the structure, shape and other characteristics of the 
organism. The group names are in Latin or Greek, but they are often similar to common 
English names. For example, Class mammalia means mammals.

Carnivores and the rest
Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


1   Organisms can be classified according to what they eat. One classification
    is into three groups: carnivore; omnivore and herbivore. Write the term
    that matches the definition.
                      Definition                              Term
     Consumer that eats only plants.
     Consumer that eats only animals.
     Consumer that eats both plants and animals.

2   Read the description and then classify each organism as a carnivore, an
    omnivore or a herbivore.
                      Description                        Classification

a   Bears in Canada are often photographed
    catching fish as the fish try to jump up
    waterfalls on their way to breed upstream.
    Bears are also seen picking berries from low
    bushes. Campers have to place all their food
    and rubbish in sealed containers or bears will
    steal it from them.
b   There are many different goannas and their
    diets vary. Their prey includes insects, snakes,
    smaller lizards, birds and birds’ eggs. Some
    giant goannas will kill a young kangaroo or
    even attack a dog. Goannas are attracted by
    the smell of rotting meat and feed off the
    bodies of dead animals.


c   Desert hopping mice live in very harsh
    environments with little rain. To survive they
    have to eat what is available to them and have
    a varied diet of seeds, leaves, shoots, roots
    and insects.



d   The common brushtail possum has adapted
    to living in cities and suburbs. In its natural
    habitat a brushtail possum eats mainly leaves
    and flowers. A particular favourite is fresh gum
    tips. Possums occasionally eat insects, eggs
    and meat. In urban areas they hunt through
    open compost bins to see what they can find.


e   Dugongs are large sea creatures that feed on
    sea-grass beds on the bottom of the ocean
    floor. They use their flippers to uproot the sea-
    grasses and then the dugongs chew and crush
    their food. If sea grasses are not available,
    dugongs will eat algae. Scientific studies have
    identified the remains of worms and shellfish in
    the waste produced by dugongs. Scientists are
    not sure if these are eaten accidentally with the
    sea grasses or if the dugongs eat them
    intentionally.

f   The diet of yellow-footed rock wallabies is
    similar to most other wallabies. They eat grass,
    plants and shrubs, which they chew with flat
    teeth at the back of their jaw.

Using a circular key                                                Name: ___________________________


Occasionally keys used to identify organisms are arranged a little differently from chart
keys or table keys. The key below is a circular key for Australian birds. Start from the
centre of the circle and work out making a choice at each stage.




The first choice has three options: Greater than one metre long; greater than or equal to
500 millimetres long; and less than 500 millimetres long. The remaining choices have
only two choices, as in a normal dichotomous key.

	
  

Example:
	
  
                                  This bird is 280–320 mm in length. It has a distinctive black head
                                  with a white collar. The eyes are dark brown, the bill blue-grey with
                                  a hooked tip, and the legs are black.
                                  To identify this bird, start in the middle. Its length is less than 500 mm.
                                  The next choice is whether the legs are black or not. This bird has black
                                  legs.
                                  The choice for birds with black legs is whether the beak is hooked or not.
                                  This bird has a hook on the end of the beak. It is a butcher bird.

What is a decomposer?
A decomposer is a living thing that works to break down organic materials into smaller 
parts. For example, a decomposer breaks down fruit on a forest floor by making it rot or 
decay. The decomposer absorbs the nutrients from the remains and also releases some 
nutrients into the soil. 
Fungi and moulds are decomposers. They decompose plant waste, including 
vegetables. Some small organisms from the animal kingdom are also decomposers, 
including worms, slugs, millipedes and termites, which break down logs and sticks. Other 
decomposers, like maggots and flies, help to break down dead animal carcasses (bodies). 
Dung (animal droppings) is broken down by dung flies and beetles. Microorganisms, 
including various bacteria, break down all kinds of substances, including milk, eggs and 
meat products.

16 Current workplace issues 
Even if you have a job, you should still follow current issues related to the workplace. The daily 
newspapers and television news and current affairs programmes are full of workplace-related stories.  
It is worthwhile to stay aware of the relationship between employment and the state of the  
Australian economy.
The economy and work
Whether you have studied Economics at school or not, you will probably understand that the level of 
economic activity in a country will fluctuate from time to time. The economy tends to operate in cycles, 
as you can see in the graph above. When the economy is booming, there tends to be an increase in 
retail sales, a rise in business confidence and a consequent fall in unemployment. This is good news for 
job seekers as there is a feeling that there are plenty of jobs to go around. 
On the other hand, when economic activity is slowing down with a drop in retail sales, there is a 
consequent lowering of business confidence. Employers are more likely to lay off workers or not employ 
new workers. This can be very frustrating for new job seekers or people wanting to enter the workforce 
or change jobs. As you can see on the graph, terms such as ‘boom’ and ‘bust’ are used to describe mild 
swings in the cycle. Terms such as ‘inflation’ and ‘recession’ or even ‘depression’ are used to describe 
more severe swings. It is the task of the Federal government and the Reserve Bank of Australia to 
manage economic activity by trying to limit these excessive swings.
The state of the economy can be measured using economic indicators. These indicators can include 
retail sales figures, new housing approvals, wage and income levels and employment figures. They are 
readily available on the website of the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Unemployment  
The level of unemployment is the result of several factors. One is the level of economic activity and 
there are other factors, indicated by the main types of unemployment.
Structural unemployment –
s� Occurs as a result of structural changes in industry. Modern machinery 
and computer technology are putting some people out of work. There is a need for people 
displaced to retrain in different jobs.
Frictional unemployment –
s� Occurs when workers are in the process of changing jobs, or are 
having difficulty finding a new job after they’ve left the previous one. There will always be a degree 
of frictional unemployment.
Cyclical unemployment –
s� Occurs when the economy is slowing down. When economic activity is 
on the rise, unemployment is likely to fall.
Seasonal unemployment –
s� This is the result of seasonal changes, such as summer fruit picking, the 
shearing season, Christmas sales. 
One of the aims of the Federal government is to maintain full employment. However, this is a difficult 
task given the types of unemployment described above. Sometimes target rates are set so that an 
unemployment rate of 5% or 4% may be considered acceptable.
Long term unemployment
This can be a serious issue for some people, especially those coming from migrant backgrounds with 
poor language skills. A person who wants a job and can’t get one after a long period of time spent 
trying can suffer from loss of pride, loss of self confidence and self esteem. This can lead to social 
problems. People can get help from the Federal government through its Centrelink agency  
(www.centrelink.gov.au).

Starting out on your own in a new business is very challenging. You may succeed or you may fail; 
you may make a modest living or you may become a millionaire. Often people go into business

Club documents

Club office-bearers
The following is a list of the typical office-bearers of a club:
• President: chairs meetings and acts as the club spokesperson.
• Vice president: assists president and acts on his or her behalf if absent.
• Secretary: records minutes of meetings and handles correspondence.

Meeting procedures
Accepted meeting procedures involve the right of members to present a motion (a proposal put

either by a show of hands or a written secret ballot, then vote on the motion. If a majority of members

18 Learning at work 
Once you have a job, it is a mistake to ‘rest on your oars’. Learning is a life-long business, and you 
should never become complacent. Job security is not the same today as it was in the past, when 
employees could expect a safe job for life. Today there are no guarantees. On-the-job training is 
therefore an increasingly important aspect of workplaces today. 
Learning at work may take many forms. It can be as simple and informal as group or branch meetings, 
one-on-one interviews with supervisors or discussions with mentors. Or it can involve additional courses 
at a TAFE college or a university to upgrade qualifications. You need to keep updating your skills and 
your qualifications, especially if you are in a job where there is strong competition.
Success in your career
Here are ten tips to help you enjoy success in your career through good workplace habits.
1 
 Create a life plan – Success can be achieved if you know where you 
are going and have made a life plan. It doesn’t have to be written 
down, although this helps to clarify goals and recognise achievements 
as they happen. A life plan involves outlining the direction you wish to 
take, what steps you have to achieve along the way and what barriers 
might delay or prevent success. A life plan can be flexible, depending 
on your personal circumstances, but even so it will provide you with a 
focus for your plans.
2 
 Act responsibly – Be professional in all your dealings with people, 
whether they be work colleagues, supervisors or customers/clients.
3 
 Work efficiently and effectively – Try to avoid time wasting. 
Focus on outcomes.
4 
 Make yourself irreplaceable – Some people’s work is so 
efficient and at such a high standard that they make themselves 
irreplaceable or indispensable. Aim to show your supervisor that 
no one can do your job better than you.
5 
 Be part of a network – It is hard to work in isolation. You need 
to have people around you, contacts you can call on for help and 
people who show a positive attitude to their work. It doesn’t have 
to be the ‘old school tie’ type of network – it can take any form 
and there is much you can learn from others.
6 
 Give credit where it is due – Always acknowledge the good work 
of colleagues. Then they are more likely to acknowledge your 
good work.
7 
 Update your skills – You may come to a job with a set of skills, 
but it is important that you not only maintain these skills but 
improve them. The world is constantly changing and so is the 
workplace. You need to stay on top of the possible effects of these 
changes. Keep on learning new things.
8 
 Upgrade your qualifications – These are more formal in nature 
and involve courses at a TAFE college or a university. There is an 
ever-growing number and variety of courses available so look for 
the one that suits you best in your career.
9 
 Strike a balance between promoting yourself and boasting 
about your accomplishments – This takes care, judgement and 
experience. It is good to talk to others, such as a mentor, about 
this.
10  Anticipate barriers – There will always be times when things 
don’t go your way, despite your best efforts. When this happens, act sensibly, not emotionally. 
Above all, do not lose your focus. Always remember that you can learn from your mistakes.

Advertising is part of the marketing and promoting

Living and Work Literacy 3
Being an effective manager of a business, whether large or small, involves certain skills and abilities. 
There are many personal qualities required, such as courtesy, ability to relate to people, ability to 
handle stress, capacity for hard work and willingness to accept responsibility.
Working hard is one thing but it is perhaps more important to work smart. There are some 
important skills and abilities which are either required or at least desirable.
Creativity – Creativity is one of the most important qualities in a successful businessperson. The 
whole essence of entrepreneurship is creating a new business. Creative ideas are limited only by 
one’s imagination and creative ability.
Leadership – What is leadership? Is it important in a business? There are different leadership styles. 
By examining the two emails below, from two different sales managers, you may get a clue as to 
which leadership style is the most effective.
10	Managing	a	business
Memo to all staff
 From: Malachi Berkin
To: All staff
Subject: Monthly sales figures
I have just examined the monthly sales 
figures and they are down on the previous 
month. I can only conclude that people are 
not working hard enough. In future I want 
everyone to cut back on their lunch hours, 
stop wasting time and get on with the work 
that has to be done. Failure to obey this 
directive will lead to severe consequences.
Organisational	skills
Two of the most important organisational skills one can have are:
Time management – when you consider there are 24 hours in a day and you allow some hours 
for sleeping and eating, the question is how to spend the hours available. This is why schedules, 
lists and timetables will help you organise your day and your week. Work hard by all means, but 
work smart. Balancing work and leisure time is also important.
Delegation – Delegation means asking other people to do specific tasks or take responsibility for 
specific areas of the business. One person cannot physically do everything, so he or she has to 
delegate. Knowing what to delegate and to whom is an art. You need to know the capacity or 
ability of the people you are delegating tasks to and the likely success that person will have of 
doing the task. Supportive supervision is also important. On the next page are examples of two 
methods of delegation and the likely response from staff. 
Evaluation - In managing your business you need to evaluate progress from time to time, to see 
if there are any problems, bottlenecks or better ways of doing things. You can learn from mistakes 
and put in place new or better procedures.

Living and Work Literacy 3
What are the necessary qualities of a successful businessperson? Sometimes luck plays a part, but 
other factors are much more important. The checklist below is a useful guide to the qualities that a 
good businessperson should have.  
Qualities	checklist	–	the	top	ten
2	Qualities	of	a	good	businessperson
Matthew	and	Andrew	Italia	–	Terrafirma	Technologies
Even when he was at primary school Matthew Italia helped his teachers to fix computers and solve 
their IT problems. So it wasn’t a surprise when Matthew started up his own small IT business as a 
teenager. Later he went on to register and operate the business in busy, central Geelong as a 21-year-
old. Starting as a sole trader, Matthew later went into partnership with his younger brother, Andrew, 
who showed the same IT problem-solving capabilities. 
Their business, Terrafirma Technologies, provides IT-related services. They targeted the small business 
sector and home users.
“We source and provide software and hardware at competitive prices, and advise people so they can 
get the most out of their IT system. A lot of people with small home offices also use our services as 
they lack the backup of an IT specialist that a bigger company can offer,” Matthew said.
“We also rectify computer faults, update computer security systems, and I have provided advice in 
networking, Internet connections, telecommunications systems and mobile phone systems.”
Matthew has a degree in Internet computing from R.M.I.T. while Andrew is currently studying a 
Bachelor of Information Technology, majoring in computer security and fraud detection. 
“I had always fixed computers for friends and family, but the turning point for me came in Year 10, 
when I completed work experience at a local computer store,” Matthew said.
“I realised I could explain difficult concepts about technology in ways that people without much IT 
knowledge and experience could understand. The work experience gave me the confidence to take the 
step towards starting my own small business.”
Matthew likes working with his brother as he finds they complement each other’s skill sets. “It's great 
bouncing ideas off each other about how to improve our business, and know that we will be the ones 
who reap the benefits of working hard together.” 
“We respect each other’s knowledge and opinions, but feel comfortable to challenge each other as 
well,” Andrew said.
“Our families have always been in small business and we have an uncle who mentors us and provides 
us with advice and feedback.”
Most of their initial business was generated through word-of-mouth, but they still needed to expand 
their client base to support themselves in full-time jobs. They have found that advertising their 
business through well-known computer journals and in local newspapers has helped to attract new 
clients.
“It’s very demanding running your own business and you have to have a wide range of skills besides 
just knowing a lot about IT. You need accounting and marketing skills as well as knowing how to 
provide great customer service,” Andrew says.
“We aren’t sure what our next step in the business will be – whether to open retail premises or employ 
staff – there is always a lot of planning and ‘thinking ahead’ in small business, and that’s what we 
love.”

17 Technology and communication 
The world is changing quickly in the development and use of technology. This 
is especially so in the workplace. The main advances have been in information 
and communications technology. Technology is changing the way people 
communicate, and the way that workplaces operate.
The Internet
The Internet is a worldwide network of computers linked by global 
telecommunications. It allows computers around the world to link and share 
information and resources. Growth in Internet use since the late 1990s has been 
spectacular. In Australia today there are six million subscribers. The Internet has 
enormous potential for use in the workplace. Business has become so reliant on 
the Internet that speed of access is now an important factor. 
Office emails
The use of electronic mail or email has become a widespread means of communication for educational 
and personal purposes as well as workplaces. Email has advantages over regular postal mail in that it is 
delivered very quickly into the recipient’s mailbox for them to read and reply to at their convenience. It 
is a very quick, easy and efficient way to communicate, despite the number of spam emails that clutter 
inboxes. Spam filters and antivirus packages can prevent this from getting out of hand and infecting 
computers, slowing things down and potentially causing damage to files.
Unlike a business letter, an email is informal and often uses informal language. It also has the capacity to 
attach documents which can be opened by the recipient.
Some differences between formal language and email language are listed below.

Brownian Motion and the Particle Theory of Matter

In 1827 Scottish botanist, Robert Brown, used a microscope to examine pollen grains
floating on water. He noticed that the pollen grains did not sit still but were constantly
moving in random directions, as shown in Figure 6.2.1. This random motion was later
called Brownian motion. It describes the motion of many things in nature including

At the time, Brown’s observations provided the most direct evidence
for the Particle Theory of Matter as his findings showed that the water
particles were interacting with the grains of pollen to cause the
observed random movement.

Maximising Exam Marks in Senior Chemistry – Book 1
Chromatography is the process of separating small amounts of substances from mixtures by the relative speeds at 
which they move through or along a medium. Chromatography was first used by Mikhail Tsvet in 1901 to separate 
plant pigments. 
1 
Give another term for pigment.
There are many chromatographic techniques, but they all rely on the components of a mixture being carried by a 
mobile phase over (or through) a stationary phase (the medium) at different rates. The molecules in the mixture will 
have different interactions with the stationary phase. The greater the interaction, the slower the substance will move 
through the stationary phase. 
Chromatography is used to identify dyes, additives, pharmaceuticals and many other organic compounds. 
Chromatography is especially useful in forensic chemistry.
2 What is forensic chemistry? 
Paper chromatography uses a liquid solvent as the mobile phase and 
paper as the stationary phase – strictly speaking, it is water absorbed 
by the paper that is the stationary phase. The mixture to be separated 
is dissolved in the minimum amount of a solvent. This is placed on the 
surface of the paper. A second solvent flows across the sample, carrying it 
through the paper. (See figure 1.) Radial chromatography and ascending 
chromatography are the two most common examples.
Figure 2 shows the sequence followed in a simple radial 
chromatography procedure.

                                        ANSWER KEY
                       Deep Thoughts on Matter

1.   Since you can pour sand into a cup, why isn't it a liquid?


     Each particle of sand has a definite shape and volume. When billions of grains of sand are put
     together, they can be poured because they are so small.


2.   You can't usually see gases in the air. How can you observe gases without seeing them?


     You can feel the wind blow. You can observe air movement, such as a waving flag or a turning
     windmill. You can also observe temperature and humidity changes in the air. You can also
     smell many types of gases.


3.   Can you feel water in the air? Explain.


     Yes, you can feel humidity in the air. You would notice that the air is different on a damp or
     muggy day then on a dry day. Some people can even feel it in their joints. Some people might
     think things feel more “sticky” in a very humid environment.


4.   Does air have mass? Explain.


     Yes, air has mass. Since it is lighter than liquids and solids, it tends to rise above them. One easy
     experiment to test this would be to find the mass of an empty balloon and an inflated balloon.
     The inflated balloon should be heavier. Also, you might notice that an empty air tank (propane,
     for example) weighs less than a full air tank.

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian Curriculum  Name:
Extending science worksheet
Degrees expandium
As liquids absorb heat energy, they expand and take up more space. Humans have used this property for over 300 years to measure temperature using a thermometer.
Thermometers have two main elements: a liquid that changes volume based on the temperature, and a numerical scale that measures how much volume change has occurred.
Measurement scales are a purely human convention, created to assign a value to things that are not automatically numeric. Quite often, completely different scales are devised by different people to measure exactly the same thing, demonstrating how arbitrary they can be.
There are many different scales that have been developed to measure temperature. The three most common ones used today are degrees Celsius (°C), degrees Fahrenheit (°F) and degrees Kelvin (K). For example: 25 °C = 77 °F = 298.15 K.
In this task, you will create your own basic thermometer and your own temperature scale using the expanding properties of matter.
Step 1: Create your thermometer
Materials: 
a clear straw
water
rubbing alcohol
food colouring
a small plastic water bottle
modelling clay
Method:
Add equal parts water and ethanol to the water bottle until it is around one-third full.
Add a few drops of food colouring into your bottle and swirl gently to mix it in.
Insert the straw into the bottle, making sure one end is in the liquid and the other end is sticking out of the top of the bottle. Do not let your straw touch the bottom of the bottle, and leave as much of it as possible sticking out of the top.
Mould the clay around the straw at the bottle opening to hold it in place. Make sure the clay seals around the straw tightly so that air to flow only in or out of the bottle through the straw.
This water bottle contraption will act as a basic thermometer.
Step 2: Create your scale
Materials: 
a fine-nibbed permanent marker
a ruler
Method:
Your thermometer will measure temperature in degrees “Expandium” (°E). You will create your own definition of degrees Expandium by creating a temperature scale on your straw.
Using a permanent marker and a ruler, draw marks on the part of your straw sticking out of the bottle at 5 mm intervals.
Now, decide on the number scale you will assign to your intervals. You can assign any number scale you like as long as it increases in a regular way. For example, your scale could start at 0°E and increase by 5°E with each tick mark, or it could start at 50°E and increase by 1°E with each tick mark.
Choose a number scale and indicate it on your straw.
Step 3: Take some measurements
Materials: 
your bottle thermometer
a real thermometer
a bowl
water of different temperatures (hot water, lukewarm water, tap water, ice water)
Method:
Place your bottle thermometer into the bowl.
Add the hot water to the bowl and wait a few minutes for the water to expand and rise in your straw.
Once the water level in your bottle thermometer has stabilised, measure the temperature in degrees Expandium using the intervals marked on your straw. Record the temperature in degrees Expandium in the Data and results section.
Use the real thermometer to measure the temperature of the water in the bowl in degrees Celsius. Record the temperature in the Data and results section.
Repeat this process with water of different temperatures in the bowl and record your results.

Using your results table (or the trend line on your graph), try to predict the approximate degrees Expandium you would expect for the following degrees Celsius. searchText:
Dry Ice: Simply Sublime!
Background:

Dry Ice is frozen carbon dioxide, a gas which makes up
about .04% of our atmosphere. As a gas, it is colorless and
odorless, and is released when living organisms respire. It
is also 1.5 times the density of air, (which is 78% nitrogen,
21% oxygen, and less than 1% argon.) Carbon dioxide
(CO2 ) gas turns to dry ice when the temperature drops
below 78.5° C. It turns to vapor directly from the solid state, never passing
through a liquid phase. This change, from a solid to a gas, is called
"sublimation."

Dry ice is largely used for refrigeration. Look in your Yellow Pages to find a
local vendor. A couple of blocks about 2 inches by 10 inches by 7 inches
cost about $10 in my area. Place it in an ice chest and keep it there,
taking out only what you need. It is a good idea to wear gloves when
handling the dry ice.

Students are familiar with water ice. Dry ice gives you a chance to
challenge their expectations, and force them to create some new models
to account for their observations. Observation and experimentation of dry
ice sheds light on two concepts: changes of state, and the behavior (or
even existence!) of gases. Here are some steps you might follow to guide
your students in uncovering the properties of dry ice in particular, and
matter in general.

Step One: What is a Solid?

Experiment with water ice to establish melting point and boiling point. It is
useful for students to graph the temperature as ice is heated, melted,
then boiled. They will observe a graph which looks levell for a while, then
reflects the temperature of the water rising, and then levels off again
when it reaches the boiling point.

The water stays at 0° C as long as there is ice left to absorb the heat by
melting. The liquid water warms to boiling, then again holds steady, so
long as water remains in the liquid phase, absorbing heat by turning to
vapor. Activities which do this are widely available, so I will not repeat
them. It might be useful to relate the idea of solids melting to other
materials they are familiar with. Water ice is one solid which melts. Others
include metals, chocolate, wax, and plastic. Water melts at 0° C, mercury
melts at 39° C, gold at 1064°C.

Step Two: Discovering Sublimation

Give the kids a chunk of dry ice, one to two inches square. Warn about
possibledanger from contact. (Since dry ice is so cold, it will quickly freeze
skin if it is in contact for more than a few seconds. The result is similar to
a burn, though no heat is involved) Give them also a styrofoam cup, and a
 piece of plastic wrap. Have them cover the cup, and observe. As the ice
sublimes, it will swell the plastic, and may even pop it, if they can
maintain a tight enough seal. They should record their observations.

Note: This will look more dramatic with water in the cup, but I have found
that the kids often mistake the vapor for steam, and get the idea that the
ice is actually "boiling" the water, a wrong idea, since the bubbles coming
up are mainly CO2, not water vapor. If students blow into the cup, they
will see even more white vapor. Why is that? Isn't it the same as hot
steam? No, it isn't. The dry ice vaporizes into a clear, colorless gas. The
white vapor we see is actually water in the air which is condensing. Our
warm, moist breath cools quickly when in contact with the dry ice, and as
it cools, the moisture condenses into tiny, fog-like droplets. It is like
steam, in that it is water vapor, but it is not the product of heated water.

Water ice will sublime as well. Ice cubes will shrink when left in the
freezer, frozen foods will become desiccated.

Step 3: What is this gas?

After they have experienced sublimation without water, and you have
established that the dry ice is indeed turning into a gas, you could explore
what the gas is. They may notice that the vapor coming off their cup goes
down, unlike hot steam, which rises. This is due both to the temperature
difference, and the inherent density of CO2 gas. If the kids place a lit
candle on the table, they can then "pour" the CO2 gas from their
styrofoam cup onto the flame. It should go out. This is evidence that you
have a gas, heavier than air, and that it is a gas which does not provide
oxygen for combustion. CO2 fire extinguishers are quite common.

You might point out that this gas is the same one which living things
respire (breathe out). In high concentrations, it is poisonous to life, as well
as to fire. It is also the gas released by Alka Seltzer and the gas in the
bubbles of soda pop.

Note: The kids have to "pour" very cautiously, as a slight breeze will blow
the CO2 away

Step 4: Experimenting with Dry Ice and Water.

Give them water and a thermometer. Tell them not to stick the
thermometer right on the dry ice, and not to get it stuck in the water ice
which forms.

You have established that the dry ice is shrinking, and turning into a gas.
What happens when you add water? They will see a high rate of bubbling
at first. They

34
© Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2010
Maximising Exam Marks in Senior Chemistry – Book 1
Many organic molecules have charges or become electrically charged when dispersed in a fluid. If electrodes are 
placed in a fluid containing these molecules then the charged particles will move towards the opposite charges. 
Electrophoresis is the movement of electrically charged particles through a fluid or gel under the influence of an 
external electrical field.
Figure 1 shows the major components used in the 
technique of paper electrophoresis. The mixture is 
spotted onto moist paper, the end of which is dipped into 
buffer solution. A high voltage is applied, causing anions 
and cations to migrate. This type of electrophoresis is best 
suited to the analysis of small molecules.
1 
Define anion. 
2 Define cation. 
3 Why must the paper be moist in paper electrophoresis? 
Gel electrophoresis uses a gel as the stationary medium.  
The gel is porous and smaller particles move through it  
more easily than larger particles do. 
Gel electrophoresis can be carried out either horizontally 
or in columns. It is commonly used to separate and identify 
DNA mixtures. 
Figure 2 shows two views of a typical apparatus used in gel 
electrophoresis. Holes (sample wells) are cut into the gel and 
the mixtures of for example DNA fragments are placed in 
them. Often a dye is added so the progress of the process can 
be observed. Molecular markers, which are mixtures of DNA 
with known molecular masses, are also sometimes added. 
Then a current is applied. 
Because the DNA molecules have a negative charge, they 
are attracted to the positive anode. The greater the charge, 
the greater the attraction. The DNA then has to be treated 
chemically before it can be observed.
4 What is the role of the buffer solution in the apparatus shown in figure 2? 
5 Why do large molecules lag behind when separation starts? 
6 Identify a factor other than size that could cause DNA fragments to move at diff

© Janine Haeusler and Blake Education 2014
Activity sheet – Separating mixtures
Evaporation and crystallisation
Filtration cannot be used to separate substances that have been dissolved in a solvent, 
because the particles are too small and pass through the filter paper. Heat can be used 
to separate a liquid from a solution, leaving the solute behind. This process is called 
evaporation.
+ 
1 Circle the correct option from each pair in brackets.
Filtration is used to remove (soluble/insoluble) substances from a liquid.
Evaporation is used to remove (soluble/insoluble) substances from a liquid.
When you separate a solution using evaporation, you (keep/lose) the solvent.
When you separate a solution using evaporation, you are left with the (solute/solvent).
Evaporating the water from a solution by heating is a quick method of separating the 
solute from the solvent. However, sometimes evaporation is not a suitable method 
because the quantities are too large, or you want large crystals. In these cases, 
crystallisation can be used instead. For example, in the production of commercial salt,  
the sun’s heat is used to evaporate the water. Large salt crystals form because the water  
is evaporated slowly.
2 Decide whether each of the following statements is true or false.
Evaporation allows you to keep the separated solvent and solute.        
Filtration can’t be used to separate the solute and solvent from a solution.        
If you evaporate the liquid quickly, the crystals formed are small.         
Crystallisation occurs when a solution is heated quickly.           
Filtration is used to remove insoluble substances from a liquid.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Gas exchange in amphibians

Introduction

Gas exchange in most organisms involves the absorption of oxygen and the release of carbon dioxide. Gas
exchange is necessary because these organisms undergo aerobic respiration. All animals have moist surfaces
(called respiratory surfaces) through which they can absorb oxygen and release carbon dioxide in a process
called ‘gaseous exchange’. Respiratory surfaces in multicellular organisms are often in or on specialised organs
such as lungs and gills. Adult amphibians (ectothermic animals) have two organs for gas exchange: lungs and a
moist skin.

Maximising Exam Marks in Senior Chemistry – Book 1
In gas–liquid chromatography (GLC), the stationary phase is a liquid coated onto very small particles of inert solid. 
This is packed into a narrow tube which is usually referred to as a column, and is normally coiled to save space and 
made of stainless steel. The mobile phase is an unreactive gas. 
1 
Name two suitable gases that could be used for the mobile phase of GLC. 
A carrier gas (the mobile phase) is allowed to flow through the column until conditions have stabilised. A syringe is 
used to inject the sample into the machine where it is vapourised using a small oven. The carrier gas transports the 
analyte (substance being analysed) mixture through the column. The column is contained in a separate oven, with 
temperatures typically in the range of 50°C to 250°C.
2 Why is the column kept in an oven? 
3 Outline why stainless steel is a good material for making a GLC column. 
The different components of the analyte will interact differently with the stationary phase in the column. This will 
cause each compound to have a different retention time, i.e. the time it spends in the column. These retention times 
are used to identify the substances present. As the components reach a detector, the time of arrival and amount of 
substance is recorded. Levels as low as in the nanogram range can be detected by more sensitive equipment.
4 What is a nanogram?  
GLC cannot always detect 
and conclusively identify the 
components in a mixture, so 
it is often linked to a mass 
spectrometer. The fragmentation 
pattern obtained can be compared 
to others stored in a database.
5 Study figure 1 which shows the major components of a gas-liquid chromatogram.  
Match each part listed below with the correct letter on the diagram.
a carrier gas 
b column 
c column oven 
d detector 
e flow controller 
f injector port
g recorder
6 Outline the purpose of each of the following parts.
a carrier

subject: Science
searchText:
ICE (Ice Cream Experiments) lesson
                               by Norman Brooks
For the first session, students will be given ingredients and instructions for making
ice cream. In subsequent sessions they will bring other ingredients to create new
flavors, improve on recipes, and improve the quality of their ice cream. As the
quality improves, they will want to be able to replicate or produce it consistently.
This will require accurate measurements.
       OBJECTIVES:
       The Beauty of this lesson is that it can be used to reach so many objectives. It
       is most often used as an activity to teach, give practice, or to assess students'
       knowledge of dealing with variables. It also offers exposure to the
       experimental process, forms of matter, changing forms of matter and many
other science concepts and processes.
INGREDIENTS and MATERIALS:
(For a class of 30 students who work in pairs.)
     2-4 bags of party ice
     1 gallon whole milk
     ice chest
     1 box rock salt
     8 oz paper cups (36)
     5 lbs. sugar
     1 gallon zip lock bags (15)
     vanilla extract
     plastic spoons (36)
     1 quart zip lock bags (15)
     paper towels
     two trash cans
     Medicine droppers for extract
     plastic scoops for ice/salt
Trash cans are for disposal of bags, spoons, and cups. Teachers can decide which to
recycle. Doing this activity outside simplifies clean up.
PROCEDURE:
1. Combine Sugar (2-4 tblspoons), Extract ( a few drops), Milk 8 oz. per pair) , in
small zip lock bag and zip it up. This is the S E M bag
2. Combine ice ( 2 cups) and rock salt ( 1/2 cup), in large zip lock bag.This is the S
I bag
3. Insert S E M bag inside the S I bag and zip it up.
4. Each partner takes one end of the S I bag and the two shake until ice cream is
firm.
5. Cups and spoons are then distributed to students for taste testing and eating.
VARIABLES
All ingredients and supplies are VARIABLES and can be varied. The students should
be encouraged to experiment by changing variables for different results. To conduct
an effective experiment, they should only change one variable at a time, and should
keep accurate records of what they have done, and what the results were.
SOME EXAMPLES OF LESSON EXTENSIONS:
     Rubrics for judging results
     History of ice cream
     Different flavors
     Fractions and proportions
     Improving appearance
    Ice cream in different cultures
   What's in commercial ice cream?
   How much fat is in ice creams?
   Changing the consistency
   Economics ( costs)
   Following directions
   Working in pairs
   Changing forms of matter
   Why salt?

One of the common mixtures you will use in Science is the solution. A solution
is a type of mixture containing a solute dissolved in a solvent. A solute is a
solid which will dissolve in a solvent, and the solid is said to be soluble. A
solvent is a substance which will dissolve a solute. For example, when sugar dissolves
in water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent. A substance which dissolves in
another is said to mix evenly into it. A solid which will not dissolve in a solvent is said
to be insoluble. Two liquids which mix evenly in with each other are said to be
miscible. Two miscible liquids are petrol and kerosene. Two liquids which will not
dissolve in each other are called immiscible. Petrol and water are immiscible.

Materials and their uses
The ways a material can be used depend on its properties. 
• A saucepan is usually made out of metal and plastic. Metal is used because it is a good 
conductor of heat. Plastic is used for the handle because plastic is an insulator, or poor 
conductor of heat. This stops you burning your hand when you pick up the saucepan. 
• Electrical cables are often made out of a metal called copper because it is a good 
conductor of electricity and can easily be formed into wires. The copper wire is 
surrounded with a plastic covering so the electrical cable can be handled safely. 
• Ceramic materials are used for lots of different things. Traditional ceramics are used to 
make dishes and tiles because they are hard, do not absorb liquid and are both heat 
and rust resistant. Space shuttles have tiles made from ceramics because they protect 
the shuttle from extreme temperatures. 
Scientists are always trying to design better or smarter materials to develop new 
technology and improve the way objects work. Smart materials are able to respond to 
changes in the environment.

Name: ______________________________



           Why Does Matter Matter?
                                               by Kelly Hashway


       What do trees, air, and water have in common? They all have matter. That means they take up

space. You might be wondering why these things look so different if they all have matter. Everything

found on Earth can be grouped into one of three states of matter: solid, liquid, or gas. In order to figure

out which state of matter an object fits in, we have to examine its properties. The properties we look at

are shape, mass, and volume. Mass is the amount of matter an object has, and volume is the amount of

space the matter takes up.



       Solids are easy to recognize. They have definite shape, mass, and

volume. Trees are solids. They are made up of tiny particles called atoms.

These atoms are packed closely together, and they hold the solid in a

definite shape that does not change. If you look around your house, you

will see lots of solids. Televisions, beds, tables, chairs, and even the food

you eat.



       Liquids do not have definite shape, but they do have definite mass

and volume. Liquids are similar to solids because their atoms are close

together, but what makes a liquid different is that those atoms can move

around. Liquids can change shape by flowing. If you’ve ever spilled a glass

of milk, then you know it spreads out across the floor. It does this because

the milk is taking the shape of the floor. Since liquids do not have a definite

shape of their own, they will take the shape of their containers. This is why

the same amount of milk can look different in a tall glass, a wide mug, or

spread out on your kitchen floor.

                          Super Teacher Worksheets -   www.superteacherworksheets.com
        Gases do not have definite shape or volume. Like liquids, gasses

will take the shape of their containers. If a gas is not in a container, it will

spread out indefinitely. This is because the atoms in a gas are spaced

farther apart than in a solid or a liquid. And being spread out like this

allows them to move around freely. Think about the air you breathe

everyday. That air is spread across the empty space around the earth.

You’ve probably also noticed that you usually cannot see the air. This is

another property of gases. Even though we cannot see them, you

come in contact with them everyday. There’s air in the tires of your

family car and your bicycle. The sun is made up of gases, and the

clouds in the sky are mostly made from water vapor.




When trying to remember the three states of matter, think about

water. If it freezes into a solid, it becomes ice. Its atoms are packed

together keeping its shape. Of course, we know water can also be a

ACHIEVE!   Science understanding – Chemistry for years 7–8
7
© Janine Haeusler and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Matter
Measuring matter
Matter takes up space. This means that it has volume. Volume is one measurement of 
matter. You can use a formula to calculate the volume of regular-shaped objects. You can 
also measure the volume of an object by dropping it in water and calculating the amount 
of water it displaces, or pushes aside. 
Mass is another measurement of matter. Mass describes the amount of matter or atoms 
in a substance. Matter can be measured by finding the weight of an object. An object’s 
weight depends on its mass and how much gravity is pulling on it. For example, an object 
weighs less on the moon than on earth because there is less gravity on the moon. We can 
use a spring balance to measure weight. 
The density of an object depends on both its mass and its volume. Objects with tightly 
packed atoms are very dense. Objects with atoms spaced further apart are less dense. Density 
is measured in grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm3) or kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3).

searchText: ﻿Chapter 7 Elements extra worksheet 2: Mixtures Science understanding Verbal/Linguistic, Visual/Spatial Name: Class: Date: A mixture of two substances can be divided into two components: • the dispersion medium, which makes up most of the mixture • the dispersed phase, which is the substance that is mixed into the dispersion medium. For example, when a teaspoon of sugar is dissolved into a cup of water, the water is the dispersion medium and the sugar is the dispersed phase. Both the dispersion medium and the dispersed phase can be a solid, liquid or gas. For example, when there is a dust storm, the dust is a solid dispersed phase and the air is a gaseous dispersion medium. Questions 1 Complete the following to identify the dispersion medium and dispersed phase for each mixture. Mixture Dispersion medium Dispersed phase a salt water b smoke from a fire c muddy water d fog e whipped cream The type of mixture depends on whether the dispersion medium and dispersed phase are solids, liquids or gases. The table below outlines the names given to various types of mixtures. Dispersion medium Dispersed phase solid liquid gas solid solid solution alloy (for metals) solid sol solution sol suspension solid areosol liquid solution gel liquid solution emulsion aerosol gas solid foam solution foam gas solution 2 Complete the table below to identify one example of each type of mixture. The first one has been done for you. Dispersion medium Dispersed phase solid liquid gas solid e.g. brass alloy liquid gas 3 Draw pictures on the particle level to represent each of the following: a alloy b aerosol c solid foam There are three types of mixtures where a solid dispersed phase is mixed into a liquid dispersion medium. • Solution: solid dispersed phase dissolves into the smallest possible particles, which are invisible to the naked eye • Sol: solid dispersed phase is made up of slightly larger particles that are still invisible to the naked eye but can scatter light • Suspension: solid dispersed phase is made up of even larger particles that may be visible to the naked eye and will settle to the bottom of the dispersion medium if left for long enough 4 Draw diagrams representing each of these types of mixtures inside the beakers:

colloid

emulsion
