You can light a candle without touching the wick.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Secure a candle in a stable position and light it.
2  Strike another match and have it ready.
3  Blow the candle out and immediately hold the burning
match 1–2cm directly above the top of the wick. (The wick
will relight.)
EXPLANATION
Candle wax exists as solid, liquid and gas. Immediately after you have blown out the candle there is still
some paraffin gas near the wick. This gas ignites when a flame is brought near it. 
TO INVESTIGATE
How does the appearance of paraffin change as it turns from a liquid to a solid? (It changes from clear to
white.)
Liquid petrol doesn’t burn — the vapour does. But don’t try to test this because the vapour will always
be there. Safety warning: petrol is extremely dangerous and should never be near a naked flame.
Liquid water is common on earth but is one of the rarest substances in the universe.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Keep tissues dry under water. Crumple a tissue and place
it inside a beaker. Invert the beaker and place it in water.
(The tissue will remain dry because air prevents water from
entering the beaker.)
2  Pour a beaker of air. Add water to a very large beaker until
it is almost full. Hold two small beakers inverted under the
water — the first containing air and the second containing
water. Hold the first beaker directly below the second and
slowly tilt it. (The gas will be transferred to the second
beaker.)

searchText:
The Particle Theory of Matter
Matter

There are thousands of different sorts of materials, all with their own special
characteristics that make them suitable for particular uses. While they are all
different, they all have one thing in common: they are all made of matter.

Matter is defined as anything that has mass (can be weighed) and volume
(takes up space). Objects and materials are matter. Things that are not
matter include time, heat and gravity. A space that does not contain any
matter at all is called a vacuum. Outer space is very close to a perfect
vacuum.

The Particle Theory of Matter

In the particle model, matter is described as being made up of very small
particles which are constantly moving. Scientists have built up this model
by performing investigations and making observations of the behaviour of
different types of matter.

Below are three example of evidence for the particle model.

Brownian Motion

In 1827, Robert Brown first investigated pollen grains in
water. He selected pollen because it is very light. Brown
observed that the pollen grains were constantly moving
around in a random manner. The particle model can be used to explain these
observations. The particles that make up the water are constantly moving and
bump into the pollen grains causing them to change direction. This type of
movement was named Brownian motion, after Robert Brown.

Diffusion

Your nose is very sensitive to particles. Small particles move into your nose
through the air and are detected by sensitive membranes. Being able to smell
                                someone’s perfume or something baking in the
                                oven from a distance are examples of particles
                                moving through the air into your nose. The
                                movement of small particles through a
                                substance, such as air or water, is called
                                diffusion. The particles bump into each other,
                                constantly changing directions and mixing until
                                they are spread out fairly evenly. The figure on
the left shows the diffusion of particles of ammonia in air.

Dissolving
 Substances such as sugar can dissolve when put into water. Dissolving can be
explained in terms of small particles moving through the water particles. This
movement can be sped up by stirring, which forces the particles to move in the
water faster.

1. How would you define matter?

2. What are some examples of things that are not matter?

3. Why did Robert Brown use pollen grains in his experiment?



4. How does Brownian motion show us that particles exist?

   perfume can be smelt at the back of the room. What is this process called
   and describe how it happens.

Sheet 1
Scientists believe that all matter is made of tiny particles and
from this they have developed the Particle Theory of Matter




Matter normally exists in 3 states: solid, liquid or gas.
In solids particles vibrate in fixed positions. Vibrate means to move
backwards and forwards or up and down quickly and repeatedly. The
particle in a solid stay in a fixed space and do not permanently move
away from the particles that they are bonded to.
In liquids particles move by rolling over one another.
In gasses particle move rapidly and randomly.


Why do you think liquids can flow?


Which other state of matter is able to flow?


What happens to the speed of particles in matter if they are
heated?

Key vocabulary

    A solid object has a fixed shape and volume, it cannot be compressed and does not flow. Solid

Chapter 7                                      Elements
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1:                          Properties of water
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                     VERBAL/LINGUISTIC, VISUAL/SPATIAL


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________

Water is one of the most common compounds on Earth. It covers 71% of the Earth’s
surface and makes up over 50% of your body. It is easy to forget that water has
some very special properties that are unlike any other compound. Without these
special properties, life as we know it could not exist.


Melting and boiling points of water
Water is one of the only compounds that you can see as a solid, liquid or gas at
temperatures commonly found on Earth. In your kitchen you can find water as a solid
(ice cubes), liquid (water from the tap) and gas (steam from a kettle or humidity in the
air).

In fact, the melting and boiling points of water were used to define the Celsius
temperature scale. The melting point of water at sea level was used to define 0C in
the Celsius scale. The boiling point of water at sea level was used to define 100C.


Density of water
Another unusual property of water is that its solid form (ice) is less dense than its
liquid form (liquid water). As a result, ice floats in water. This is something you can
see with ice cubes in a drink or icebergs on the ocean. However, this property is
actually quite unusual. Most substances are more dense in the solid form and so sink
to the bottom of the liquid.




        Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Water is most dense at 4C (four degrees above its freezing point). This unusual
property of water is of critical importance to aquatic (water dwelling) plant and animal
life in cold climates. It means that water at 4C sinks to the bottom of a lake and water
at 0C floats to the top. As a result, lakes freeze from the top down. This allows plants
and animals in the lake to continue living, foraging and breeding in the lakebed.


The universal solvent
Water is also very good at dissolving a large range of substances. For this reason,
water is sometimes referred to as ‘the universal solvent’. This term is slightly
misleading because water cannot dissolve all substances (for example, oil, gold,
chalk). Still, water is a very important solvent and is used to make solutions of most
of the compounds you use in the laboratory.

searchText:
Revise change of phase:
Solid to liquid = melting
Liquid to gas = evaporation
Liquid to solid = freezing or solidification
Gas to liquid = condensation
Solid to gas or gas to solid = sublimation

Observing evaporation

Aim: to observe the types of crystals that grow at different rates of evaporation.
Materials:
Alum solution
Bunsen burner
Tripod and gauze mat
2 petri dishes
evaporating basin
heatproof mat
Method:
    1.      Divide the alum solution between the evaporating dish and the two petri
            dishes.
    2.      Place the evaporating dish on the tripod and gauze mat and heat gently
            using the Bunsen burner. (Do not allow the solution to boil rapidly as it
            may start spitting.
    3.      When all the water has evaporated, observe the size of the crystals that
            have formed.
    4.      Place on petri dish in a warm position.
    5.      Place the second petri dish in the refrigerator.
    6.      After three days observe the size of the crystals in the two petri dishes.
    7.      Record your observations in a table with the headings ‘rapid
            crystallisation’, ‘slow crystallisation’, ‘very slow crystallisation’.
    8.      Write a conclusion for your results.


Revise particle model:
All substances are made up of tiny particles which are constantly vibrating.
Heating speeds up the movement of these particles while cooling slows it down.
If movement is speeded up particles move more rapidly and are not held together as
closely as before.

Diffusion – the ‘spreading out’ of a substance. A substance diffuses from an area
where there is more of it to an area where there is less.
Eg. When 2 gases are placed in a container together, the particles of each gas will
spread or diffuse through each other until they are evenly spread out in the container.

Diffusion in a liquid
Aim: To observe what happens when a crystal of potassium permanganate is allowed
to stand in a beaker of water.
Materials:
250mL beaker
spatula
 crystal of potassium permanganate
Method:
    1.      Three-quarters fill a beaker of water and wait for it to be still.
    2.      Carefully lower a crystal of potassium permanganate down the side of the
            beaker.
    3.      Observe what happens immediately, after 20 minutes and after one day.
    4.      Draw a series of diagrams to record your observations.
    5.      In your conclusion, explain what has happened in terms of particle
            movement.


Diffusion of a gas
Release a small amount of perfume in a corner of the room. Have students sitting at
different points of the room with their eyes closed, raise their hands as soon as they
can smell the odour. Two students map the response to show how the odour travels
around the room.

Questions
Why has the odour in this experiment travelled across the room?
Where is the odour the strongest: near the source or on the other side of the room?
Why?

SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                         LOGICAL/MATHEMATICAL                          VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


All the salt produced in Australia is made by using sunlight to evaporate water
from ponds of salt water. Seawater contains about 3.4% of total salts, of which
2.7% is sodium chloride. Sodium chloride is the salt that makes up almost all
of the table salt you buy. The main constituents of seawater are shown in the
table.
       Component                        Percentage (%)
 sodium chloride                               2.68
 magnesium sulfate                             0.22
 calcium sulfate                               0.12
 magnesium chloride                            0.32
 potassium chloride                            0.07
 other salts                                   0.01
 water                                        96.58


The process
Salt water is pumped from the sea into a nearby field consisting of a series of
shallow ponds. In the first pond, the action of the sun and the wind evaporates
some of the water, making the water more concentrated in dissolved salts.
The concentrated salt water is now called brine. As the concentration of the
brine increases, so does its density. The density of the brine is measured
regularly by scientists. Substances such as calcium carbonate crystallise and
settle to the bottom of this first pond.




Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2351 7   Page 1
 When the brine has reached a particular density it is pumped into the next
pond. There it is left to evaporate further. As it evaporates, crystals of gypsum
(calcium sulfate) form and settle to the bottom. The brine is then pumped into
the next pond. Here the remaining water is allowed to evaporate for a long
time. Sodium chloride crystals form and settle to the bottom of the pond. This
is the salt that the producers want to sell. Once most of the sodium chloride
has crystallised, the water is pumped out of this pond and discarded. More
brine is pumped into the pond.




Salt is made by moving sea water through a series of ponds and letting the water
evaporate


The layer of sodium chloride salt is normally harvested once a year. During
harvest, the pond is drained and machines lift the layer of salt from the pond
floor.

Excess brine is removed from the solid salt by a centrifuge. This spins the
brine off, leaving the salt crystals damp but otherwise clean. The remaining
moisture is driven off by heating to just above 110°C to produce dry salt
crystals.

Crushing and sieving to specific size ranges are the final steps in producing
the various salt grades. Sizes vary depending on the use, ranging from very
coarse salt used for pickling and presentation of oysters in restaurant meals,
right down to micro-fine salt used in making butter. In between there is a wide
variety of particle sizes that cater for all needs, from food ingredients to
pharmaceuticals, textiles, stockfeed and swimming pool additives.

Selling The Molecular Kinetic Theory

Edward S. Guzdziol                Worth Junior High
7419 West 109th Place               112th and New England
Worth IL 60482                   Worth IL 60482
(708) 361-4673                   (708) 448-2800

Objectives:                  Grade level: 6-12

   1. To model aspects of the molecular kinetic theory
   2. To observe phenomena influenced by molecular kinetic theory
   3. To present credible evidence for the existence of molecules
   4. To show the effect of pressure on the boiling point of water
   5. To demonstrate how the molecular kinetic theory can explain phase
     change

Materials needed:

   1. Methylene blue dye crystals   7. Wire basket
   2. Two, 600mL beakers           8. Styrofoam balls, (1.5")
   3. Hot and cold water         9. Fire syringe
   4. Ping pong ball and paddle    10. Hair dryer
   5. Syringe, (30cc-50cc)       11. Signs: (solid, liquid, gas, freeze,
   6. Rubber bands                boil, evaporate, melt, condense)

Strategy:

   You will try to convince your students that molecules move. You will
present a variety of activities and demonstrations to help students internalize
concepts associated with the molecular kinetic theory.

    1. Fill one 600mL beaker with 500mL of cold water. Fill the other with
500mL of hot water. Set the beakers aside so that any motion in the water comes
to rest. Now sprinkle equal quantities of methylene blue on the water in both
beakers. Twenty or thirty crystal grains is all that is needed. The blue dye
will diffuse through the hot water faster than it will in the cold water.
Something moves the dye around so it gets spread out evenly throughout both
beakers. However the spreading out, mixing, or diffusing is not done at the
same rate of speed. Hot water gets the mixing done faster than cold.

   2. Take a rubber band and hold it close to your upper lip. Quickly pull
the rubber band apart and immediately place it against your upper lip. It will
feel warm. When you bring the ends back together, and once again hold it
against you lip, the rubber band feels cooler.

    This is where I use the ping pong paddle and ball. Get the ping pong ball
bouncing rythmically between the paddle and the desk top. If you now quickly
lower the paddle you will see and hear a rapid increase in the ping pong ball
collisions. If you, on the other hand, raise the paddle, the number of
collisions will decrease.

   I relate to the students that the ping pong ball and paddle are only a
model of what occurs on a molecular level in matter. If temperature is the
average kinetic energy of moving molecules, then the faster the molecules move
the warmer the substance gets. Conversely, the slower the molecules move the
cooler the substance gets. The rubber band got hotter or cooler depending on
the speed of the molecules that made it up. When we stretched out the rubber
band we decreased the volume for the molecules, (modeled by lowering the
paddle). When we allowed the rubber band to return to its original shape, we
increased the volume for the molecules, (modeled by raising the paddle). When
the volume of the rubber band was decreased, (stretched out), the molecules
moved faster and resulted in the warmer band you felt against your lip. When
 the rubber band returned to its original shape, the molecules had more room.
This is why they slowed and Cooled down.

   3. For the next activity you will use the signs you made. On the board
draw the following diagram showing change of phase from solid to gas and from
gas to solid.

      SOLID" " " " " " " "LIQUID" " " " " " " " " " GAS
              MELTING                   BOILING
                                EVAPORATING


      SOLID$ $ $ $ $ $ $ $LIQUID$ $ $ $ $ $ $ $ $ $ GAS
             FREEZING             CONDENSING

    I like to tell the class that the melting point and the boiling point are
like doors you must go through in order to change the state of matter you're
dealing with. Likewise, condensing and freezing are the same doorways that must
be passed through again but only in the other direction. This helps students
relate heat addition and subtraction as the determining factors in phase change
and that substances have a one of a kind doorway to pass through.

    Let students play with the wire basket, styrene balls and the hair dryer.
The modeling of molecular motion and heat should be readily seen. As we heat a
solid, that solids molecules begin to move. Let the hair dryer gently jostle
the balls. This models the gradual increase in molecular motion through
heating.

   Continue increasing the rate of motion by more directly aiming the air from
the hair dryer on the balls. When you see the balls moving around and about
each other, you have reached the liquid level. Remember this occurred because
you added heat to the molecules. In our model the heat is the air from the hair
dryer but it could have been from a vacuum cleaner or other cool air source.

Separating iron filings from sand
Magnets are used for recycling because they can attract certain types of
metals from the recycling pile.
The metals that magnets attract are iron, nickel, and cobalt. It can also attract
steel because steel has iron in it!
In your investigation, you will use a similar idea in removing iron filings from
sand.

Aim
To investigate how a magnet can extract iron filings from sand and to calculate
the percentage of iron in the mixture.
You will need:
       eye protection
       a bar magnet
       a small plastic bag
       a mixture of iron filings and sand
       a top pan balance
       a calculator
       two small plastic containers
       paper weighing boat.

Method

   1. Measure the mass of the plastic container and record it on the table on
        page 2.
   2. Set the top pan balance to ‘zero’ with the container still on it. If you are
        unsure how to do this ask your teacher.
   3. Weigh out approximately 10 g of the sand and iron filing mixture and
        record the exact mass to 2 decimal points.
   4. Remove the plastic container from the top pan balance.
   5. Put the bar magnet into the small plastic bag and work it through the
        sand and iron filings.
   6. Taking care not to get the iron filings on your fingers, place the iron
        filings removed from the mixture into the other small plastic container.
   7. Repeat steps 5 and 6 until you have removed as many of the iron filings
        from the mixture as you can.
   8. Measure the mass of the sand without the iron filings and record your
        result in the table.

searchText: ﻿Separating mixtures Sedimentation and Decantation These processes can be used to separate an insoluble solid from a mixture of the solid and water. If the insoluble solid is heavy enough it will settle to the bottom of the vessel (sedimentation ) and form a sediment. The clearer water can then be separated from the solid sediment by pouring the liquid off (decantation) This process has a disadvantage in that the process of sedimentation can be very slow. Filtration Filtration can be used to separate an insoluble solid from a mixture of the solid and water. For example, a mixture of sand and water can be separated by filtration. In the filtration process, the mixture is poured through a folded filter paper supported in a filter funnel. The liquid passes through the small holes in the filter paper but the solid is trapped on the filter paper. The liquid that passes through the filter paper is called the filtrate and the solid trapped on the paper is called the residue. Evaporation The change of a liquid to a gas (or vapour) is called evaporation. Evaporation can be used to separate a dissolved solid from its solvent. For example, salt can be obtained from sea water by the process of evaporation. In this process, the solvent is evaporated and the solute is left behind in the container. Distillation

Separation of Rock Salt
 Aim: To obtain pure salt from rock salt.

Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Sample of rock salt
                                                         Hot water – risk of scalds and burns
• Pestle and mortar
                                                         Wear goggles,     take   care   when
• Two 250cm³ beakers                                     heating
• Stirring rod                                           Glassware – risk of cuts if broken
• Filter funnel                                          Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
                                                         immediately
• Filter papers
                                                         Bunsen burner – risk of burns
• Tripod
                                                         Place under cold running water for 10 minutes
• Heatproof mat
                                                         and inform teacher
• Bunsen burner

• Evaporating basin




Method:
Step 1: Carefully grind up the rock salt in the pestle and mortar.

Step 2: Stir the ground rock salt into a beaker of water to dissolve it.

Step 3: Carefully filter the solution through the filter paper in the funnel, into the second beaker.

Step 4: Transfer approximately 10ml of the filtered solution into the evaporating basin and set on the
tripod over the Bunsen burner.



                                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                                                         Separation of Rock Salt


Step 5: Heat the water until it is gently boiling and the water begins to evaporate off.

Step 6: When crystals begin to form on the sides of the basin, turn off the Bunsen burner – you now
have a saturated solution.

Step 7: Leave the equipment to cool and then move the basin to a warm place to evaporate more slowly
(overnight).



                    Rock salt is a mixture of sand and salt. It is also sometimes called grit salt and
                    is used on roads during winter. The sand and salt compounds have different
                    properties and so they can be separated.

Why does this happen?
All matter is made up of particles. In solids, liquids and
gases, the particles behave differently.

Solids
In a solid, the particles are locked into place. Even
though they are locked in place, they are still vibrating.
If you add heat, they vibrate more because they have
more energy.

Liquids
If you heat the solid, the particles will vibrate so much
they can’t stay in their place any more. They start
moving around. The solid has then melted into a liquid.
If you add more heat, they want to move around even
more because they have even more energy.

Gases
 The particles in a gas are free to move around and are not held by any
other particles. Gases have no definite shape.

w.s.38. Solids, liquids and gases. NOte voreeseeseeeseeresisernsee

Everything is made up of particles that are too small to see. The three
states of matter are SOLID, LIQUID and GAS. They all have different
properties due to the arrangement and movement of their particles.

Solids.

The particles are held tightly together by strong
forces. They make small vibrations but they stay
in place. This gives solids a definite shape and
volume. Solids are DENSE (heavy) and they can
not be compressed (squashed) easily because the
particles are already packed closely together.

Liquids.

A liquid can flow because the particles can move
past each other. The particles are still held
closely together by strong forces. Liquids are
DENSE and they can not be compressed easily. A
liquid can change its shape but not its volume.

Gases.

There are only very weak forces between the
particles which are far apart. The particles move
around very quickly and bounce off each other.
Gases have a low density (they are very light)
and they do not have a definite shape or volume.

insoluble in water.

Solutions are defined as homogenous mixtures; they have particles uniformly spread through the mixture. Although 
solutions will pass through filter paper, like most mixtures, the individual components in a solution can be

searchText: States Of Matter I. Introduction The kinetic theory describes matter as a large number of small particles ( atoms or molecules ), all of which are in constant, random motion . The rapidly moving particles constantly collide with each other and /or with the walls of the container. Kinetic theory exp lains properties such as pressure, temperature, viscosity, thermal conductivity, a nd volume . Here are the 4 main ideas of kinetic theory (also known as ‘the particle model’) • Matter is made up of particles which are in c onstant random motion (vibrate, rotate, translate) • The particles are separated by great distances • The particles colli de perfectly elastically • The temperature o f a substance is related to the molecular velocity (speed) . Taboo – solids, liquids, gases

Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any of the
additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.


   1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each team).

   2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto different
      coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have all the cards back at
      the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

   3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

   4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile, and then
      describes the word at the top of the card without using the words below. The rest of
      their team must guess which word is described. Participants are not allowed to say
      ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

   5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the opposing team
      may challenge and the individual must move on to the next word.

   6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as possible to
      the players in their team (a longer time may be required to allow more descriptions
      to take place) before play passes to the next team. There are no penalties for
      wrong guesses.

   7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.
      Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each group.


This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other ways to
describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to reinforcing
the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could research
meanings of new terms.



Extension activity


   1. Each student puts a new vocabulary word at the top of a blank card.

   2. Each student then has to write a further five words which are associated with the
      keyword they have written at the top of the card.

searchText: ﻿The Cloud In The Bottle Overview Students are already interested in the weather and can be made increasingly aware of cloud formation by this rather simple in-class demonstration. Purpose The purpose to this activity is to demonstrate to the students the direct effects of pressure and temperature on cloud formation. Objectives 1. Students will view an illustration of the principles involved in cloud formation. 2. Students will apply these principles to weather maps to predict cloud formation and clearing. 3. Students will observe how nuclei are necessary for the attachment of condensation in order to form clouds. Resources/Materials 1. Wide mouth gallon pickle jar 2. Heavy duty clear plastic bag 3. Rubber bands or masking tape 4. Matches Activities and Procedures 1. Place about 20 ml of water in a wide mouth gallon pickle jar. 2. Place a lit match into the jar. 3. Quickly place a heavy duty clear plastic bag over the mouth of the jar and secure a firm seal by placing a rubber band/masking tape around the top of the jar. 4. Push the bag into the jar quickly, then pull the bag out. Observe! Tying it all Together This activity illustrates how humidity, temperature, and air pressure influence the formation of clouds. The water produces high humidity in the jar and the smoke introduced by the match provides nuclei on which the water vapor can condense. As the bag is pushed into the jar, the pressure and temperature in the jar increase, causing the jar to clear. Upon pulling the bag out, pressure and temperature decrease, allowing water vapor to condense and produce a "cloud" inside the jar. Questions For Further Inquiry 1. Why are smoke and water added to the jar? (They provide moisture and nuclei for cloud formation.) 2. What does pushing and pulling on the bag do to the jar? (They increase/decrease pressure.) 3. How would warming or cooling the jar affect the observations? (They decrease/increase cloud formation.) 4. Relate your findings to weather conditions necessary to produce cloudy/clear skies. For articles, maps, or other media pertaining to this topic, look up the following in Encarta® Encyclopedia: Cloud Meteorology Troposphere For additional online information and media, view the following Encarta articles: Cloud Meteorology Troposphere For additional relevant information, visit the following Web sites: Cloud Catalog http://covis.atmos.uiuc.edu/guide/clouds/html/cloud.home.html

The Particle Theory and States of Matter
 Matter is everything that has mass and takes up space.
 All matter is made up of tiny particles of atoms or molecules.
 The way the particles move and behave depends on the state or
  phase of the matter.
 The particles in matter are in constant motion. This is known as the
  Kinetic Theory.
 The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.

Particles in a Solid
 The particles are packed together tightly, with only small spaces
  between them.
 The particles are held together by strong forces so they cannot move
  freely, but vibrate around fixed positions.
 Solids expand when heated and contract when cooled.
 Solids have a fixed shape and volume.
 Solids cannot be compressed.

Particles in a Liquid
 The particles are packed tightly together, with only small spaces
  between them.
 The particles are held together by weaker forces, but they cannot
  move freely. They are able to roll over each other. This allows liquids
  to flow and be poured.
 Liquids expand when heated and contract when cooled.
 Liquids have no fixed shape but have a fixed volume.
 Liquids cannot be compressed.

Particles in a Gas
 The particles in gases are far apart and only held together with very
  weak forces.
 The particles are able to move freely in all directions.
 Gases have no fixed shape or volume but will fill up the container they
  are enclosed in.
 Gases will expand a lot when heated and shrink when cooled.
 Gases can become liquids if cooled or compressed enough.
 Temperature and Energy
 The temperature of a substance is a measure of the amount of
  internal energy the substance has.
 A substances state of matter is determined by its internal energy or
  temperature.
 Heating matter gives its particles more energy so they vibrate faster
  and move further apart. The matter will expand slightly in volume.
 If enough energy is put into the matter, the particles will have enough
  energy to overcome the forces holding them together and change
  phase.
 Cooling matter takes energy away from the particles so they vibrate
  more slowly and move closer together or shrinks in volume.
 When cooling takes enough energy out of the matter, the particles will
  move more slowly until they condense and change phase.

   temperature?

     a. Solid turns to liquid
     b. Gas turns to liquid
     c. Liquid turns to gas

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian Curriculum  Name:
Extending science worksheets
The solution is the problem …
Hundreds of millions of people around the world do not have access to clean drinking water, a problem that can have serious health consequences. Engineers are continually seeking new and efficient ways to separate contaminants from water, creating devices that can turn a dirty water solution into clean drinking water.
In this task, you will create a water filter with a selection of commonly available filtering materials to separate various contaminants from a dirty water solution. You will then compare your water filters to see if conclusions can be drawn about which filtering materials are effective for which contaminants.
Experiment
Aim: 
To observe how effective different filtering materials are.
Materials:
bucket
water
2 large beakers
2 L plastic bottle with cap
Scissors or Stanley knife
hammer and nail
digital camera
a collection of filter materials, such as: coffee filter paper, crushed activated charcoal, sand, gravel, sponges, cotton balls, pantyhose, mesh or cheesecloth
dirty contaminants, such as: food colouring (chemical contaminant), soil/dirt (top soil contaminant), cooking oil (motor oil contaminant), small pieces of scrap paper (rubbish contaminant)
Method:
As a class, create a large bucket of dirty water solution by adding the dirty contaminants to the water.
In small groups, collect a beaker of at least 200 mL of the dirty water solution, making sure you include a little bit of all the contaminants. Take a photo of this dirty water solution for comparison.
Carefully cut off the bottom of a 2 L bottle using the Scissors or Stanley knife. Your teacher may do this for you.
Remove the bottle cap from your bottle and create a small hole in it using the hammer and nail. Replace the bottle cap on the bottle.
Turn the top half of your bottle upside down and rest it inside the other beaker so the cap with the hole can drain into the beaker.
Select three filtering materials from the options provided and place them in layers in the bottle. Record which materials you choose and in which order they are layered in the Data and results section.
Slowly add the 200 mL sample of dirty water solution to the top of your layered bottle filter.
Once the dirty water has moved through the layered bottle filter, take a photo of the resulting water in the beaker. Record your observations about the quality of this water (how much of the contaminants have been removed) in the Data and results section.
Repeat this process two more times, filtering the same water again. Photograph the resulting water solution each time and note down your observations.
Data and results
Filter materials used (in layer order):






Paste your original dirty water sample photo here:








Filtered water photo
Observations of filtered water
How clean is it? What has been filtered out? What, and how much, still remains?
After first filtration







After second filtration







After third filtration







Discussion and reflection
Join up with another group and compare your filtration results. Make sure the group you compare with used different filtration materials than yours. Record any patterns you see in which of the materials filtered which of the contaminants.




Swap groups and compare your filtration results again. Again, record any patterns you see in which of the materials filtered which of the contaminants.




Discuss your results as a class. Based on your results, describe any conclusions that you made about which materials filtered which contaminants.




Water filters do not remove viruses. Identify a possible reason for this. Describe how you could make water that is contaminated with viruses safe to drink. Do some research to find out!




Extension research activity—Landers Shute Water Treatment Plant
The Landers Shute Water Treatment Plant in Montville, Queensland, is the primary source of drinking water for the Sunshine Coast. Once raw water has been treated, it travels along pipes to homes.
Your task is to find out how the Landers Shute Water Treatment Plant works. Use the following questions to help guide your research:
What are the processes the water goes through from when it enters the plant to when it leaves the plant?
How long do these processes take?
How clean is the water at the end of these processes?
What similarities and differences exist between your plastic-bottle filtration system?

To recycle or to not recycle
Greywater is wastewater generated from washing dishes, laundry and bathing in homes. It makes up
50–80 per cent of residential wastewater. Greywater does not contain chemical and biological
contaminants. Greywater gets its name from its cloudy appearance and from its status as being
neither fresh (whitewater from groundwater or taps) nor heavily polluted (blackwater).
   If collected via a separate plumbing system, greywater can be recycled directly within the home
and garden. Recycled greywater of this kind is never clean enough to drink, but a number of stages
of filtration and microbial digestion can be used to provide water for washing or flushing toilets;
relatively clean greywater may be applied directly from the sink to the garden, because it receives
treatment from the soil and plant roots. Vegetables should not be watered with greywater.

drinking water. Under the plan, wastewater would have been collected and put through a series of
purifying treatments, including ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and oxidation. The treated water would
be pumped into a dam, where it would rest for three to five years — enough time to convince the

Diffusion occurs when particles move from where there are lots of particles (high

X-rays and atomic particles
X-rays
Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895. The rays were called X-rays because they were an 
unknown radiation that came from a vacuum tube. X-rays are produced when a high speed stream of 
electrons strikes the anode in a cathode ray tube. X-rays are the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that has 
wavelengths between 0.3 and 0.03 nanometres. They have very high energy. Many objects in space such as black 
holes, supernova remnants and stars emit X-rays. X-rays are also used to detect broken bones and damaged 
tissues in the body. X-ray detectors collect photons (a unit of electromagnetic radiation) of X-ray light, which is 
useful in astronomy. This collection has to be done in space as the Earth’s atmosphere stops their penetration. 
1 
a in your own words, define x-rays and summarise their uses.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b What can happen if x-rays are absorbed by organisms?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Gamma rays
Gamma rays (γ) have the smallest wavelengths, ranging from 0.03 to 0.003 nanometres, and have the most 
energy of any other wave in the electromagnetic spectrum. Henri Becquerel discovered gamma rays and 
beta particles. Supernova explosions, nuclear fission, nuclear explosions, black holes and pulsars produce 
gamma rays. Because of their short wavelengths, gamma rays can kill living cells. Gamma rays are used to 
sterilise hospital equipment that would be damaged by heat. Both gamma rays and X-rays are part of the 
electromagnetic spectrum.

Understanding the impact of science
In 1967 an Outer Space Treaty that offered a series of guidelines for how countries should explore space was signed by countries in the United Nations. Crater Formation

Background

Impact craters are formed when pieces of asteroids or comets strike the surface of a
planetary body. Craters are found on all the terrestrial planets, on the Earth’s Moon, and
on most satellites of planets. Various geological clues and studies of the lunar rocks
returned by the Apollo missions indicate that about 3.9 billion years ago asteroid-size
chunks of matter were abundant in the solar system. This was a time of intense
bombardment of the young planets, affecting Earth by breaking up and modifying parts of
the crust. Mountain building, plate tectonics, weathering and erosion have largely removed
the traces of Earth’s early cratering period. But the near absence of weathering on the
Moon has allowed the evidence of this ancient time to be preserved.

Impact craters are formed by the transfer of energy from a moving mass (meteorite) to a
stationary body (planet). Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. It is defined as one half
the mass of an object, times the velocity of the object squared (K.E. = ½mv2).

Objects in space move very fast, so this can be a huge amount of energy! In an impact the
kinetic energy of a meteorite is changed into heat that melts rocks and energy that
pulverizes and excavates rock. Simplified demonstrations of this transfer of energy can be
made by creating impacts in powdered materials. If identical objects are impacted into
powdered materials from different heights or using different propulsion systems to increase
velocities, then students can determine the effect velocity has on the cratering process.
The high velocity impact and explosion of an iron meteorite about 30 meters in diameter
could make a crater over one kilometre wide. This is how the Meteor Crater in Arizona was
formed.

Aim: To investigate what happens to the size of craters as the velocity of the impact is
     increased.

   marble
   ruler
   icecream container
   sand

2. Pour sand in the icecream container so that it is approximately one-third filled.
3. Drop the marble from 30 cm above the level of the sand.
4. Measure the depth and width of the crater formed in millimetres.
5. Record measurements in the table provided
6. Level the sand again and repeat steps 3 – 5 another two times.

Earth and space taboo
Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the
keyword on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word
itself or any of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.


   1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each
      team).

   2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto
      different coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have
      all the cards back at the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

   3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

   4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile,
      and then describes the word at the top of the card without using the
      words below. The rest of their team must guess which word is described.
      Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no
      gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

   5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the
      opposing team may challenge and the individual must move on to the
      next word.

   6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as
      possible to the players in their team (a longer time may be required to
      allow more descriptions to take place) before play passes to the next
      team. There are no penalties for wrong guesses.

   7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
      point. Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each
      group.


This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding
other ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary
in addition to reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could
research meanings of new terms.



Extension activity
   1. Each student puts a new vocabulary word at the top of a blank card.


   2. Each student then has to write a further five words which are associated
      with the keyword they have written at the top of the card.

Solar Eclipses

When the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, the Sun
temporarily disappears from the sky. The Sun, the Moon and
Earth are aligned and this is a solar eclipse. The Moon can be seen
blocking the Sun. When the Moon is close enough to Earth, its
disc is sufficiently large enough to hide the Sun. From Earth, a
total eclipse is observed. If the Moon is a little further away from
Earth, an annular eclipse is observed where the Sun's outer edges
remain visible to form a ‘ring of fire”.

Lunar Eclipses

When the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, the Moon is not
lit by the Sun. An equivalent phenomenon causes lunar eclipses.
In this case, Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon. The
Moon is no longer lit up by the Sun. Instead, it turns dark red due
to the deviation of the Sun's rays caused by Earth. This is known
as a lunar eclipse.

EXTRA WORKSHEET 2:                           Martians from Mars
VERBAL/LINGUISTIC                   SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


In 1858, the Italian astronomer Angelo Secchi (1818–1878) reported seeing
channels on the surface of Mars. These observations were confirmed in 1877
by another Italian astronomer, Giovanni Schiaparelli (1835–1910). Although
neither astronomer gave an explanation as to what they were, American
astronomer Percival Lowell (1855–1916) wrote three books (in 1895, 1906
and 1908) that suggested that the channels were canals dug by intelligent
beings (Martians) to move water from the polar caps to irrigate their farms.

Many astronomers, however, couldn’t see the vast network of canals that
Lowell suggested and the channels that could be seen were far too wide to be
dug by anyone. Although the 1910 Encyclopaedia Britannica expressed
serious doubts about them, public imagination was ignited: intelligent Martians
lived (or had lived) on Mars!

Lowell’s canals were not disproved until 1965 when the Mariner 4 space
orbiter sent back the first close-up images of the surface of Mars. Some
channels have been found to be natural canyons while others were an optical
illusion created by lines of craters.

searchText: Measure the Sun’s Size How can you measure the Sun’s real size? Description Make a pinhole viewer, and use it to measure the Sun’s size. You will need a bright sunny day. Age Level: 10 and up Materials • sheet of cardboard (like from a cereal box) • piece of white paper • small piece of aluminum foil, about 3 cm x 3 cm • pin or thumbtack • scissors • tape • ruler • string or yarn (about 60 cm long) • hardcover book (optional) Time Safety Preparation: 5 minutes Never look directly at the Sun! Activity: 20 minutes Cleanup: 5 minutes 1 Cut a square about 1.5 cm x 1.5 cm from the center of the cardboard. Tape the piece of aluminum foil over the square. Carefully use a pin or thumbtack to prick a hole in the center of the aluminum foil. You have now created a pinhole viewer. While you’re outside, hold the piece of white paper behind the pinhole viewer, so that sunlight shines through the hole and projects a circular image on the paper. Try to make the distance between the pinhole and the paper as large as possible. Tip Taping the white paper to a book will help keep the paper upright. 2 While holding the pinhole viewer steady, measure the size of the Sun’s image on the piece of paper in centimeters. Record this measurement below. While still holding the pinhole viewer steady, stretch a piece of string between the pinhole and the piece of paper. Measure that length of string in centimeters. Record this measurement below. Tip It would be useful to have a friend help you with the measuring. Step 6 The equation on the right is used to calculate the Sun’s diameter. Using sun image size (d) and the string length (l) you recorded above, along with the distance from the Sun to Earth (L), calculate the diameter of the Sun. Below is the actual diameter of the Sun. distance from Sun to Earth (L) = 149,600,000 km actual Sun diameter (D) = 1,392,000 km 3 The Sun’s light enters the pinhole and creates an image on the white piece of paper. Because of the geometry of the setup, we can use ratios to solve for the Sun’s real size. The ratio of the Sun’s size (D) to the distance between Earth and the Sun (L) is D/L. This ratio is equal to the ratio of the Sun’s image size (d) to the distance between the pinhole and the image (l) or d/l. Image from a tablet You can also try this measuring activity using the screen of a tablet or smartphone as the “Sun” in a dark room. Cast an image through the same pinhole viewer on a wall or a sheet of paper. If you measure L, l, and d as seen in the image below, you can calcu- late D (the height of your screen) just as you did for the size of the Sun. How close is your measured value to the real size of your tablet or smartphone screen? 4 Learn More For more info and other activities, visit: LawrenceHallofScience.org/do_science_now/diy_sun_science Credits This project was supported by NASA under award number NNX10AE05G. Any opinions, ﬁndings, conclusions or recommenda- tions expressed in this program are those of the author and do not reﬂect the views of NASA. The Moon is the closest celestial body to Earth and so it’s not surprising that it
was the first to be explored. Apart from Earth, the Moon remains the only body
in space that humans have walked upon.


Early exploration
USA and the USSR (Russia) sent roughly 40 missions to the Moon between
1959 and 1969.

The Apollo missions
Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions successfully landed two men
each on the Moon’s surface and brought them safely back to Earth. The
Apollo program, however, started with disaster: a fire raced through the
command module of Apollo 1 during a test of launch procedures, killing all
three astronauts on board. Apollo 13 also suffered disaster: an explosion and
multiple system failures caused its Moon landing to be abandoned and it was
under continued threat of further disaster on its way back to Earth.

 The first human to walk on the Moon was Neil Armstrong, followed shortly by
his crewmate Edwin (Buzz) Aldrin. They spent roughly a day on the lunar
surface, venturing outside of their lunar module for a total of 2½ hours. In
1972, Eugene Cernan was the last person to walk on the Moon. Since then,
the furthest a human has gone into space is into orbit around Earth, a few
hundred kilometres above its surface.

Lunacy
By Ken Kaye, Staff Writer
Sun-Sentinel
(Ft. Lauderdale, FL)




                                                 8|Page
 Aug. 11, 2003, pp. D1

The worst things in the world happen during a full Moon, right? Wrong.

For those given to lore, it might seem likely that a full Moon shone on the sinking of the
Titanic in 1912, the bombing of Pearl Harbor in 1941 or the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist
attacks.

The full Moon, after all, is frequently associated with dark calamities, if not werewolves
and haunted houses.

But that wasn't the case.

Surely, then, the Moon turned full on the day the stock market crashed in 1929, or that
Amelia Earhart vanished in 1937 or President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in 1963,
right?

Nope.

The fact is a full Moon … has been in the sky during very few major world events in the
past century, which would seem to debunk the myth that lunar forces inspire aberrant
behavior or influence the course of history on Earth.

"There are always lots of reports of strange things during a full Moon. But I think if you
look at overall statistics, there's no [link]," says Geoff Chester of the U.S. Naval
Observatory in Washington, D.C., which has kept a careful record of full Moons dating to
1700.

A review of full Moon dates, compiled by the Naval Observatory, shows that most of the
major events of our time took place during some other lunar phase.

For instance, when the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, Japan, on Aug. 6, 1945,
the Moon was in its last-quarter phase. When civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. was
assassinated in April 1968, the Moon was new. President Richard Nixon's resignation in
August 1974 came six days after the full Moon.

Even for humankind's major forays into space, when you might think a full Moon would
be appropriate, it was a no-show.

When Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space in April 1961, the
Moon was in its last-quarter phase. When Neil Armstrong took the first step on the lunar
surface in July 1969, it was during the gibbous waxing Moon.

Some major developments did happen close to a full Moon:

One day after a full Moon, on Feb. 20, 1962, John Glenn became the first American to
orbit the Earth.

                                                                                    9|Page
 Two days after a full Moon, on Jan. 28, 1986, the space shuttle Challenger exploded,
killing seven astronauts, including schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe.

But of the major historic milestones in the past 100 years, only D-Day, June 6, 1944,
when Allied Forces stormed the beaches of northern France to begin the conquest of
Germany in Europe, took place during a full Moon.

And that was deliberate: Military commanders wanted lots of Moonlight so airborne
troops could land near enemy lines and Navy ships could fire on German targets with
precision before dawn…

Strange Things Happen

From a global standpoint, full Moons have seen their share of mayhem:

    On Jan. 16, 1995, a Japan earthquake killed more than 400 people.
    On Nov. 11, 2000, 170 skiers and snowboarders were trapped and killed when their
      cable car caught fire while being pulled through an Alpine tunnel.
    On Jan. 28, 2002, more than 600 were killed in Nigeria, trying to flee explosions at
      an army weapons depot, only to drown.
Did the Moon actually provoke any of these episodes?

No way, astronomers and historians say.

"It's pure coincidence," says Travis Wright, an employee at Buehler Planetarium in Davie.
"I doubt that it has anything to do with the voice of the universe telling people what to
do."

On the other hand, astrologers, or those who think celestial bodies affect the course of
human events, say a full Moon makes people more amorous.

"The Moon affects tides, and since our bodies are mostly water, there probably is a
physical reaction," says Linea Van Horn, an accredited astrologer who works for
Astrology.com, the largest astrological site on the Internet, based in San Francisco.
"When it's big and beautiful in the sky, it does awaken something in us humans."

According to folklore, the full Moon usually has negative connotations, says Christine
Jackson, a professor of humanities at Nova Southeastern University in Davie.

For instance, she says it is believed the full Moon triggers more suicides than usual and
sends more people to mental institutions.

In fiction and film, the Werewolf needed the light of the full Moon to come to life, and
Dracula had to avoid Moonlight to suck blood from his victims.



                                                                                   10 | P a g e
 In the recent movie, Pirates of the Caribbean, moonlight revealed the pirates were half-
dead, nothing but skeletons.

"So the light of a full Moon can sometimes show death," she says

Only a Minute

Astronomically speaking, a full Moon occurs for about one minute, when the Moon and
the Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth. The reason this instant is so short is that all
three bodies are in constant motion.

However, planetarium officials consider the full Moon to occur over a full day and even
more loosely, over three days, says Jack Horkheimer, director of Miami Planetarium.

"The night before a full Moon and night after full Moon look that same to the untrained
eye," he says.

The Moon has four major phases in a month, or more precisely, 29.5 days: New Moon,
first quarter, full Moon, and last quarter.

Those phases are further broken down into waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning
crescent and waning gibbous, based on how much of the lighted surface is visible…

Horkheimer says the myth that the Moon creates strange events arises from ancient
times, when there were few cities and the countryside was extremely dark on Moonless
nights.

The full Moon provided enough light for people to attend festivals and other gatherings
at night. This was when they were most susceptible to thieves, pickpockets and robbers,
he says.

That led to the fear that the full Moon created havoc in people's lives, he says.

Today, police can't say for sure whether crime increases during a full Moon, other than to
say the "freaks" tend to come out. But then, they note such people come out the rest of
[the] time as well.

"In general, in South Florida, it's irrelevant whether the Moon's in or out," says Hollywood
Police Lt. Tony Rode. "We have our fair share of crime either way."

As for that term "lunatics," derived from "Luna," the Roman Moon goddess: Horkheimer
says the light of a full Moon might keep people up at night, and a lack of sleep might
make them cranky, if not crazy.

But does the full Moon inspire werewolves to howl or monsters to come out?

Only in people's imaginations, Horkheimer says.

                                                                                    11 | P a g e
 "People want to believe in the mysterious, in magic and in things beyond their control,"
he said. "So if something happens they can say it must have been the full Moon."

Moon Facts

    The Moon is believed to be 4.6 billion years old, the same age as the Earth.
    It has no atmosphere or water.
    It is comprised of a rocky material that is heavily scarred with craters from
     meteorite impacts.
    The same side is permanently turned toward Earth.
    The gravitational forces between the Earth and the Moon generate two ocean high
     tides per day.
    The word "lunatic" comes from the notion that the Moon's forces could make a
     person go crazy.
    The Moon is moving away from the Earth at a rate of 3.8 centimeters each year.
     When it formed, the Moon was about 14,000 miles from Earth; now it's about
     240,000 miles away.

Moon Nicknames

    January: Wolf Moon
    February: Ice or Snow Moon
    March: Storm or Worm Moon
    April: Growing or Pink Moon
    May: Hare or Flower Moon

Solar system
Our solar system is made up of a medium-sized star called the Sun, eight planets, an asteroid belt and a comet 
belt. The four planets closest to the Sun are made from rock. The other four planets are called gas giants and are 
made up of various gases, but mainly hydrogen, helium, methane and ammonia. Mercury has no atmosphere 
while Venus and Mars have atmospheres made up of carbon dioxide. Earth’s atmosphere is made up of 
nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide and other gases. 
Mercury and Venus do not have moons and Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus do have moons. 
The moons are called satellites because they orbit their planet. All moons rotate. The Sun rotates every 27 days. 
Each planet rotates at a different speed on its own axis. All of the planets orbit the Sun in the same plane and 
their orbits are elliptical. The distance from the Sun to the Earth is 150 million kilometres, which equals  
1 astronomical unit (AU).

searchText:
The Solar System

The Features of our Solar System
The solar system is made up of the Sun, the nine planets that orbit the Sun and various natural satellites (moons),
asteroids, comets and meteors.




The Terrestrial Planets

Terrestrial planets are those planets (and possibly dwarf planets) that are similar to Earth — with bodies largely
composed of rock: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Venus is the planet which is the closest size to Earth but
because of its thick poisonous atmosphere creating extremely hot surface temperatures, Mars is the closest in
environment to Earth.

The Gas Giants

The Gas Giants are planets with a composition largely made up of gaseous material and are significantly more
massive than terrestrials: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Ice giants are a sub-class of gas giants, distinguished
from gas giants by their lack of hydrogen and helium, and a significant composition of rock and ice: Uranus and
Neptune.

 to the other planets and takes it closer to the Sun than Neptune during a portion
 of its orbit. Pluto and its largest satellite, Charon, could be considered a binary
 system because they are closer in size than any of the other known celestial pair
 combinations in the solar system.

 Small Solar System bodies




The large distances between the components of the solar system
Most of the solar system is empty space; distances are so huge it takes a long time to travel between
planets. Travelling at the speed of a fast passenger jet, 1000km, it would take 16 days to reach the Moon
~384,000km away. Astronauts reached the Moon in four days however, as they were travelling much
faster. They needed to reach at least 40,000km to escape Earth’s gravity (called the escape velocity).




Travelling to Mars will take a lot longer, however. Mars is 203 time further away from Earth than the
Moon is. Jupiter is 1635 times further away.

Compared to the large distance between the Earth and the Moon, the distances to the other planets
and the Sun is much greater again. The first four planets are relatively close compared to the outer gas
planets. Because of the vast distances in the solar system we use Astronomical Units. An astronomical
unit is the average distance from the Earth to the Sun.

The changing appearance of the Moon is called its PHASES. The complete cycle from
one new Moon to the next takes 29.5 days even though it only takes the Moon 27.3
days to completely orbit the Earth. The difference between these two times is
because the Earth also slowly changes position as it orbits the Sun.

Gravity on the Moon,
The Moon has a much smaller mass than the Earth. This makes its pull of gravity six

times smaller than the Earth's. This means that if you weigh 600N on Earth you would
only weigh 100N on the Moon. This is why an astronaut feels very light on the Moon
and can jump six times higher than they can on Earth. The bigger the mass of a
planet the bigger its force of gravity.

The Night Sky

Visual objects in the New Zealand night sky include the Southern Cross, and Matariki
(the Pleiades)
People have grouped stars into imagined patterns called constellations since ancient history. The most famous
constellations are those that form the 12 signs of the zodiac (Leo, Aries, and Cancer etc.) but our most well-
known and visible constellation seen only in the Sothern hemisphere is the Southern Cross.




Because of Earth’s rotation the stars are not in the same place throughout the night

As the earth orbits the Sun, we see a different portion of the sky. There are some stars we see at all times of the
year from New Zealand, like the stars that form the constellation the Southern Cross, and others that we never
see, like the North Star.




Constellations are seen as a 2-dimensional view (like seeing them on a flat sheet) of 3-dimensional space – where
stars in a single constellation are at different distances from earth. Different constellations are seen at different
times of the year and from different places on Earth. Stars that make up a constellation may be brighter because
they are closer to Earth and/or they are bigger/brighter stars.
119 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Main constellations in the Southern Night Sky




Matariki

Matariki is the Māori name for a cluster of stars – a seven-star constellation that appears in late May or early
June each year. Each winter the stars of Matariki and Puanga signal the end of one year in Aotearoa and the
beginning of the next.

The rise of Matariki is a time to celebrate and prepare for the Māori New Year. It was a time when crops were
harvested, and seafood and birds were collected – a time of celebration and food, but also a time for preparing
and storing for times of shortage ahead. Matariki was a time to practise manaakitanga – to share kai and present
offerings to others.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
19
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Indigenous Australians were very skilful hunters and gatherers.  
The types of foods they ate varied according to where they lived  
– in deserts, tropical rainforests or mountains, along the coast or near 
rivers. Food sources also varied according to the seasons.
The traditional Indigenous diet has all the vitamins and minerals 
that people need. Indigenous people have a detailed knowledge of the foods in their 
area, and only collected or hunted what they needed and what was in season.

REMEMBER 
The head of government is the leader of the political party in power. Australia’s head of 
state has mainly ceremonial duties and represents the country internationally.
Case study: November 1975
Just how powerful is the head of state? For most of the 20th century it was assumed the 
governor-general had no real power. Little more than a figurehead, the governor-general’s 
duties were traditionally seen as ceremonial. These duties include approving legislation, 
appointing ministers and dissolving the lower house of parliament at election time. By 
convention, the governor-general always acted on the advice of the prime minister.
Even so, the governor-general possesses certain powers that can be exercised without 
the advice of the government. Known as reserve powers, the Queen’s representative has 
the ability to appoint and dismiss a prime minister. Such a tremendous capacity can only 
be exercised in very limited circumstances, for example, if the prime minister loses the 
support of parliament in a ‘no confidence’ vote and then fails to resign.
In November 1975, the Governor-General Sir John Kerr made history by using his reserve 
powers to dismiss Gough Whitlam’s Labor government. The Whitlam government was 
facing a financial crisis. Although the Labor government had a majority in the lower house, 
the Liberal Party had a majority in the upper house. The Liberal Party deferred Supply Bills 
in the upper house, meaning they prevented the government from getting the money it 
needed to run the country. Sir John Kerr broke the deadlock by dismissing Whitlam from 
office. Malcolm Fraser, the leader of the opposition, was appointed caretaker (temporary) 
prime minister and an election was called. The Liberal Party won the election. The Supply 
Bills were passed.

REMEMBER 
Lawmaking powers held only by the Commonwealth are called exclusive powers, 
those held only by the states are called residual powers and shared powers are called 
concurrent powers.
Case study: Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) 158 CLR 1
At first glance, it appears the states have strong legislative powers. However, there are ways in 
which federal laws can override these powers. One way comes straight from the Constitution. 
Section 109 states if there is a clash between a federal and state law, the Commonwealth law 
will prevail and the inconsistent part of the state law will be invalid. 
There are also situations where the Commonwealth may intrude on a state’s residual 
powers and stop the state laws operating. This was shown in the Tasmanian Dams Case. 
The Tasmanian government wanted to increase the state’s capacity to create electricity. It 
passed a law allowing the construction of a hydroelectric dam on the Gordon River, which 
would have flooded part of the Franklin River, an area of great natural beauty. Australia 
has duties under an international agreement to protect areas that are designated World 
Heritage Sites. Responding to public outcry, the Commonwealth passed a law preventing 
construction of the dam.
The Tasmanian government objected, and the case was heard by the High Court. 
The Commonwealth claimed it could override state laws to comply with Australia’s 
international obligations. It claimed it was given this power over external affairs by the 
Constitution. A majority of the High Court agreed and the dam was not built.

REMEMBER 
In Australia, the separation of powers includes:
• legislative or lawmaking power (given to parliaments)
• executive or administrative power (given to the Queen and her representatives – the 
governor-general and state governors; in practice, wielded by government ministers 
and departments)
• judicial power (given to courts and tribunals).

opposition
doctrine
parliament

Westminster
Case study: The power to remove judges
The independence of the judiciary is the most important aspect of the separation 
of powers. Judges cannot be members of either the executive or legislative arms of 
government. Neither can they be controlled or directed by these arms.
But the executive chooses and appoints judges. Governments might select judges that 
have similar values and opinions as their own members. Indeed, several judges were 
once members of parliament. Governments come and go, however, and the judges may 
continue to preside throughout many changes of government.
A greater danger would exist if the executive had the power to dismiss judges if they 
disagreed with their judgements. Is this actually the case? Section 72 of the Australian 
Constitution gives the executive the power to remove judges for ‘proved misbehaviour or 
incapacity’. This nearly happened to a High Court judge.
Justice Lionel Murphy was a radical and outspoken judge who was responsible for many 
reforms. He had once been a member of parliament and he served as attorney-general for 
the federal Labor government in the 1970s.

In the mid-1980s, Murphy was accused of attempting to pervert the course of justice –  
more specifically, to influence a court case in favour of someone he called his ‘little mate’. 
He was eventually found not guilty, and he praised the jury system. His radical judgements, 
however, had upset the conservative factions of the government. Moves were made to 
remove Murphy for misbehaviour by passing a law through parliament.
Sadly Murphy was diagnosed with incurable cancer. The action was dropped. The ability 
of the Commonwealth Parliament to remove a High Court judge has not been finally 
determined.

not directly related to a judge’s work, such as having an extramarital affair? Or should it be 
interpreted more restrictively? If so, how?

29
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Everyday life
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the social structure of 
ancient China.
Background
Everyday life for the ancient Chinese was very 
different to life in Australia today. Although we still 
write, play sports, wear clothes and take medicine, 
in the past these things were done in different ways. 
When playing sports in the past, the focus was not 
on competition but rather on showing your good 
character. It was more important to be a ‘good sport’ 
and behave properly, even when losing, than it was to 
be a physically strong. 
Starter activity
Ask students to draw a picture of the kinds of clothes 
they usually wear. Compare outfits as a class, then 
encourage students to discuss the reasons for their 
chosen outfits. Talk about colours and fashions for boys 
and girls. Are there any differences? Would rich and 
poor people wear different clothes? How might they 
differ? Expand the discussion to consider the clothes 
worn in ancient China and the reasons for these.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘Clothing’ gives students an 
understanding of the clothes worn in ancient China. 
Students draw appropriate clothing onto two 
illustrations to demonstrate their understanding. It 
might be helpful to bring in some pictures of ancient 
Chinese dress for students to refer to. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Medicine’, explores the differences 
between medicine in the past and today. The Resource 
sheet, ‘Writing’, introduces students to Chinese 
writing, and presents a table of pictograms that can 
be used when completing the Activity sheet, ‘Strange 
characters’. The Activity sheet, ‘Sport and recreation’, 
allows students to compare their own experiences 
of sport and recreation to those enjoyed in ancient 
China.
Extension ideas
• Students could draw clothing for all the different 
social groups in ancient China. Encourage them to 
conduct research to ensure that their chosen outfits 
are accurate.
• Have students write a poem or short story about 
living in ancient China. 
• Students could design new clothes for the Emperor 
(encourage them to think about what an emperor 
would wear and why). 
Objectives
• To develop an understanding of everyday life 
in ancient China
• To understand how writing has developed  
over time
• To develop an understanding of the  
similarities and differences between ancient 
and modern life

Writing
Ancient Chinese language was first written over 3500 years ago. It is very different to 
modern Chinese. Chinese writing doesn’t use an alphabet like English does. We use the 
26 letters in our alphabet to make thousands of words. The Chinese use pictograms, or 
‘characters’, instead of letters. A pictogram is a picture used to represent a word. In English, 
‘China’ is written using five letters, but in Chinese it is shown with just one character. 
When the Chinese first developed their written language there were about 3000 
characters. Each character looked like the thing it represented. Over time, the shapes 
slowly changed so they were quicker to write. They ended up looking very different. 
The following table shows how some Chinese characters have changed over time.

the wealthy were the only people in ancient China who were able to read and write.  
They were mostly men, although some wealthy girls or daughters of scholars were also

Activity sheet – Everyday life
Medicine 
Ancient Chinese medicine was very different to today’s Western medicine. The ancient 
Chinese believed that the body was sacred and should not be damaged. This made 
it hard for them to learn about how the human body worked. Today, doctors conduct 
autopsies to examine the human body and learn more about it.
The Chinese mostly used herbs to fix health problems. They also used acupuncture, 
which involves putting lots of thin needles into pressure points in the body to help treat 
illnesses. People still use alternative forms of healing such as these. Sometimes sick people 
will use both Chinese and Western medicine. 
Chinese doctors became very good at diagnosing illnesses. They could sometimes 
work out what was wrong with someone by touching them and checking their pulse. 
Nowadays we use blood tests to find the problem.

Activity sheet – Everyday life
Sport and recreation
The Chinese played many different sports, although the poorer people didn’t get much 
time to play because they were so busy working or farming. The Chinese enjoyed 
playing sports such as boxing, wrestling, polo, archery and shuttlecock. They also 
played a game called Touhu where they tried to throw arrows into a container. Sports 
were mostly played by men, although some women also took part.
+ 
1 Which sports are popular today? Which ones are your favourites?
 
 
 
 
 
 
Martial arts first began in China. This sport involves learning how to defend yourself 
without weapons. Many of the actions look like the movements of animals, which is 
not surprising, given the importance of farming in China.
2  Why might people in ancient China need to defend themselves without weapons? 
Who would have used these skills?
 
 
 
 
 
 
The ancient Chinese were very fond of music and created many musical instruments. 
They had one called a quin, which looked like a box with seven strings on it. They also 
played bamboo flutes and drums. Some people believe that the practice of foot binding 
began when dancers bound their feet to make their movements look light and graceful.
3  List two similarities and two differences between modern music you listen to and the 
music that the ancient Chinese listened to.
