searchText:
What are forces?
A force can be thought of as a push or a pull. Every time you push or pull on
something, you are exerting a force. For instance, when you ride a bike, your legs are
exerting a force by pushing down on the pedals.

Effects of forces

Scientists say that when a force acts on something, a change occurs. Speeding up,
slowing down, changing direction and changing the shape of something are examples
of changes which can be produced by forces.

 Contact Forces occur when one object or person exerts a force through contact with
another object.

Friction

 Friction is an example of a contact force. Friction occurs between any two or more
surfaces that are in contact. The direction of the frictional force is normally opposite to
the movement of the object. Friction is the force that opposes
the movement of one body over another.

The effects of frictional forces can be an advantage or a
disadvantage. Without friction, we would not be able to walk or
hold objects. However, friction also causes moving parts to wear
or can generate significant amounts of heat.

Some ways to reduce the effects of friction are to add a lubricant, make the surface as
smooth as possible or reduce the force pushing the objects together.

Non-contact Forces are forces that act over a distance.

Gravity

Gravity is a pulling force that exists between things that have mass. The strength of
the force of gravity between two objects is determined by their mass. Earth has a
              very large mass so it exerts a large gravitational force on objects close
              to it. The gravitational force of attraction increases as the mass of the
              objects increases or the distance between them decreases.

Weight can be defined as the amount by which an object is pulled downwards by
gravity. It is expressed in newtons (N) and can be measured with a spring balance.
Weight is different to mass. Mass is defined as the amount of matter that makes up
an object and is measured in kilograms (kg).

Electric

Electric forces result from the pulling or pushing effects of electrical charges.
Electrical charges are the result of protons and electrons within atoms. Protons carry
a positive charge and electrons carry a negative charge. When the number of
electrons and protons in an atom are equal, the atom has no charge. If an atom has
unequal numbers of protons and electrons, then it will have an overall charge. More
 electrons than protons gives an atom a negative charge and more protons than
electrons gives it a negative charge.

Objects have a positive or negative charge because the atoms on their surface have
either an overall positive or negative charge. How charged objects affect each other is
governed by the charge law. According to the charge law, objects that have opposite
charges exert pulling forces on each other. These objects attract one another.
Objects that have the same type of charge exert pushing forces on each other. These
objects repel each other.




Magnetic

Magnets can affect one another or attract certain metals without being close to them.
All magnets contain one or more of the metals iron, nickel or cobalt, and magnets will
only affect materials containing these metals. Each end of a magnet is called a pole.
One pole is called north and the other is called south. When the pole of one magnet is
brought close to the pole of another magnet, the two poles either repel or attract one
another. Magnetic poles follow similar rules to those for electric charges. Opposite
poles attract and like poles repel.

   2. What changes can be produced by a force?

   10.       Why is gravity considered to be a non-contact force?
   11.       What factors affect the strength of a gravitational force?
   12.       How is the mass of a pencil different from its weight?
   13.       Would you expect the gravitational force exerted by the moon to be
      smaller or larger than the gravitational force of the earth? Explain your answer.
   14.       How would your weight on the moon compare with your weight on earth?

Ethics is sport
You may have heard the saying “Winning isn’t everything”. This is an example of the ethics in sport, otherwise known as “fair play”. The main goals in an ethical sports competition are fairness, responsibility

Fairness: All participants follow the same rules, and no one is discriminated against on the basis of race, gender or financial capability.
Responsibility: All participants take responsibility for knowing the rules and regulations, and the way they behave (including their performance and emotions).
Respect: All participants show respect for other participants.

Hooke’s Law
 Aim: to observe Hooke’s Law in different materials.


Equipment

Method
Step 1: Set up the retort stand, boss, clamp and spring as
        shown in the diagram.

Step 2: Fully secure the base of the retort stand to the desk
        and check it is firmly secure before continuing.

Step 3: Use the metre ruler to measure and record the original
        length of the spring (at 0g mass).

Step 4: Attach the mass hanger (with no masses on) to the
        spring. (The hanger should have a mass of 100g −
        check with your teacher if you are unsure).

Step 5: Measure the new length of the spring and record.

Step 6: Place a 100g mass onto the mass hanger. Measure
        and record the new length of the spring.

Step 7: Continue to repeat step 6 until you have added 1000g
        (the hanger + 9 masses).

Step 8: Carefully unload the spring and remove from the
        apparatus.

Step 9: Attach the elastic band to the clamp in place of the
        spring and repeat the investigation.

Hooke’s Law states that an object will be stretched or squashed to an extension (e) which is directly
proportional to the force (F) applied. Hooke’s Law only applies within the elastic limit of the object.

                                                   F=k×e

The spring constant (k) varies for different materials. If a spring is stiff (not easily stretched), it will have
a greater value of k.

searchText: teachers guide Forces 1: Introduction to force Components NAME DESCRIPTION AUDIENCE Introduction to force This guide suggests teaching strategies to engage students’ teachers interest in learning about forces and their effects on teachers guide objects. Use the force A ‘Lego-mation’ movie shows different forces in action. students video Thinking about forces Questions about scenarios shown in the video promote class students discussion about forces. presentation Newton explained This background sheet for teachers summarises Newton’s teachers laws of motion and describes some common misconceptions background sheet held by students. Purpose Outcomes This resource is intended to Engage students’ interest Students understand that: in learning about forces and their effects on objects. • forces may change the position or motion of an object; • forces have strength (magnitude) and direction; and • forces may act through contact with objects or at a distance. Activity summary ACTIVITY POSSIBLE STRATEGY Teacher introduces the topic of forces and what they can do to whole class objects, through questions such as: • What forces can you name? (gravity, magnetism, friction …) • What can forces do to objects? (change their position, speed or shape …) • Do forces always have these effects on objects? (No – some forces don’t seem to have any effect on some objects) Teacher explains that students will investigate what forces can do to objects and why. Teacher shows ‘Lego-mation’ video, Use the force. teacher and whole class Students are asked to think about forces that are acting in each scenario included in the video. Teacher-led discussion and summary of forces depicted in the whiteboard summary video and their effects on objects. The presentation, Thinking about forces, contains questions to prompt discussion. Teacher asks students to call out what they want to know more Teacher uses these responses to select about. Responses may include: appropriate exploratory activities. • How do forces affect the motion of objects? • How do forces balance each other? ast0478 | Forces 1: Introduction to force (teachers guide) developed for the Department of Education WA © The University of Western Australia 2013 for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage version 1.0 revised May 2013 page 1 Licensed for NEALS Teacher notes This resource helps develop students’ understanding of Newton’s laws of motion. A summary of these laws is included in the background sheet, Newton explained. The ‘Lego-mation’ video, Use the force, is designed to engage students’ interest in forces and motion, and to elicit their prior knowledge and misconceptions about forces. It is recommended that students view the video all the way through, before examining it in detail to identify forces and their effects in some or all of the scenarios. The presentation, Thinking about forces, contains a series of still shots taken from the video to encourage class discussion. Teachers should decide which, and how many, scenarios to discuss. The following information is provided to assist with the discussion. Scenario 1 Magnetic force 1 Description Luke’s magnet pushes Vader’s magnet away. Vader’s magnet slides and stops. Question Why did Vader’s magnet move away from Luke’s? Answer It moved away because Luke’s magnet repelled it. Magnetic force between like poles (N and N, or S and S) causes magnets to repel one another. slide 2 Notes Magnetism is a force that can act at a distance or through contact. Friction only acts between objects in contact. Question Why did Vader’s magnet stop moving? Answer Friction between the magnet and table stopped his magnet from sliding further. Notes Vader’s magnet stopped sliding when the friction force balanced the magnetic force. Scenario 2 Magnetic force 2 Description The stormtrooper pushes Luke’s magnet towards Vader’s. Vader’s magnet slides and sticks to Luke’s. Luke and Vader fall off. Question What made the magnets slide towards each other? Answer Magnetic force between opposite poles attracts the magnets to each other. Notes When magnets are closer together, attraction is stronger. When slide 3 magnetic force is greater than friction the magnets slide towards each other. Scenario 3 Magnetic force 3 Description The stormtrooper hands Vader a paper clip, which is attached to the ground by a rope. Suddenly Vader is yanked upwards, suspended below a magnet hanging from a crane. Question What is holding Vader and the paper clip up? Answer Magnetic force holds Vader and the paperclip up. Question What other forces are acting on Vader? slide 4 Answer Gravity and tension in the rope are acting on Vader, preventing him from reaching the magnet. Notes Vader and the paper clip remain suspended below the magnet as long as the upward magnetic force balances the downward forces of gravity and tension. Scenario 4 Electrostatic force Description The stormtrooper and Luke hold a charged rod close to a pile of paper. Small pieces of paper jump up and stick to the rod. Question What forces are acting on the pieces of paper? Answer Electrostatic force makes the paper move toward the rod. Gravity is acting on the pieces, pulling them back down. slide 5 Notes When the rod is rubbed it gains (or loses) electrons and becomes electrostatically charged. The charged rod attracts the pieces of paper. The electrostatic force is stronger than gravity, so the pieces of paper move toward the rod. Eventually, charges on paper and rod leak away and the electrostatic force decreases until it is weaker than gravity. At this point the pieces of paper fall to the floor. ast0478 | Forces 1: Introduction to force (teachers guide) developed for the Department of Education WA © The University of Western Australia 2013 for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage version 1.0 revised May 2013 page 2 Scenario 5 Elastic force Description Vader releases the paper clip and jumps onto a weight suspended by elastic. The elastic stretches; then contracts, flinging him off. Questions What made the elastic stretch? What made it spring back? Answer Gravity (Vader’s weight) made the elastic stretch. The more it stretches, the greater the tension in the elastic. Elastic force made the material return to its original length. slide 6 Scenario 6 Tension 1 Description Luke and Vader are engaged in a tug of war. The rope isn’t moving. Questions What forces are acting in the tug of war? Why isn’t the rope moving? Answer The forces are: tension in the rope; friction between Luke’s and Vader’s feet and the ground; gravity; and the ground’s supporting force. Notes The rope isn’t moving because Luke and Vader are pulling in slide 7 opposite directions with an equal amount of force. Forces are balanced. Scenario 7 Tension 2 Description The stormtrooper joins Luke at his end of the rope and together they pull Vader along. Question What forces are acting when the rope starts moving? Answer The forces are: tension in the rope; friction between Luke’s, Vader’s and the stormtrooper’s feet, and the ground; gravity; and the ground’s supporting force. slide 8 Notes Horizontal forces are no longer balanced. Luke and the stormtrooper exert more force than Vader, so they pull him along. Scenario 8 Friction 1 Description Luke and Vader run and slide along the ground. Question What made Luke and Vader stop sliding? Answer Friction between their bodies and the ground stopped them sliding. Notes Friction opposes motion. Because it is strong, they soon stop sliding. The vertical forces (gravity and the ground’s supporting force) have no effect on their motion. slide 9 Scenario 9 Friction 2 Description Luke and Vader repeat their sliding competition, this time on ice. Question What forces are acting on Luke and Vader when they’re sliding along the ice? Answer When they’re sliding at constant speed the only forces acting on them are gravity (down) and the ice’s supporting force (up). Horizontal forces, air resistance and friction, are so small they can be ignored. slide 10 Notes: Vertical forces balance each other. If not, Luke and Vader would sink into the ice. There are no horizontal forces to make them go faster or slower, so they keep sliding at the same speed. Scenario 10 Air resistance Description The stormtrooper drops two pieces of paper at the same time: one flat; the other scrunched into a ball. Questions What forces are acting on the pieces of paper as they fall? Why does the flat piece of paper fall slower? Answer Forces acting on both pieces of paper as they fall are gravity (downwards) and air resistance (upwards). slide 11 Air resistance depends on surface area. The flat sheet has a bigger surface area, which means there’s more air resistance, so it falls slower. Notes If the experiment was repeated in a vacuum, both pieces of paper would fall at the same rate because of absence of air resistance. ast0478 | Forces 1: Introduction to force (teachers guide) developed for the Department of Education WA © The University of Western Australia 2013 for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage version 1.0 revised May 2013 page 3 Technical requirements SPICE resources and copyright The teachers guide requires Adobe Reader (version 5 All SPICE resources are available from the Centre for or later), which is a free download from www.adobe.                                                            Leonardo da Vinci was born in Vinci,
                                                           Italy, in 1452. He was a brilliant
                                                           painter—the Mona Lisa and The
                                                           Last Supper are two of his works. It
                                                           was not until centuries after his
                                                           death in 1519 that people realised
                                                           how many technological designs he
                                                           had created.

                                                           Leonardo da Vinci examined the
                                                           structure of the heart by dissecting
                                                           the bodies of oxen and about 30
                                                           human subjects. He discovered that
                                                           the heart has four chambers, when
                                                           at the time it was only believed to
have two. Many of his observations and designs were recorded in back-to-
front mirror writing in his notebooks because he tried to disguise his ideas
from others.

Leonardo embarked on a quest for knowledge in a wide range of areas,
including geology, optics, acoustics, music, botany, hydraulics, anatomy and
naval armaments. He was said to be handsome, generous and charming, but
also unreliable and vain. He stood out in a crowd as he liked to dress in bright,
striking clothing while other men wore long, dark-coloured robes.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Machines extra worksheet 3: How were the pyramids constructed? Science as a human endeavour Verbal/Linguistic Name: Class: Date: The great pyramid of Giza, near Cairo, Egypt, was constructed some 4500 years ago. It is believed to have been built by more than 20 000 workers, over a period of 20 years. The pyramid consists of approximately 2 million stone blocks with an average mass over 2 tonnes. It was developed to hold a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu, who ruled Egypt from 2589 to 2566 bc. It is a wonder of engineering how ancient pyramid builders cut, shifted and raised the heavy blocks of stone from which this and other pyramids were built. Some people have even suggested that aliens built the pyramids. Most scientists believe that a system of ramps was used to transport these stone blocks. They have not agreed on how these ramps were used, and a number of theories exist to try to provide an explanation. Theory 1 – Single ramp The pyramid of Giza stands almost 150 metres high. If a single ramp was used, it would need to have an incline no greater than 8 per cent, otherwise it would be too steep to use. For a single ramp to reach the top of the pyramid it would need to be more than 1 km long, and would require as much stone to construct as the pyramid itself. This theory seems unlikely. Theory 2 – External spiral ramp Instead of using a single ramp, it is more likely that a ramp may have spiralled around the pyramid. However, this theory means that the outer edges of the pyramid would not have been visible because they would have been covered by the ramp and scaffolding. The pyramid builders would have needed to check the angles of construction to ensure the pyramid came to a point at the top. As a result, this theory is also questioned. Theory 3 – Internal ramps While watching a documentary about the construction of the pyramids in 1999, Henri Houdin, a retired French civil engineer commented that: ‘If I had to build one now, I would build it from the inside out’. His son Jean-Paul, an architect, travelled to Egypt and created detailed 3-D computer models to investigate whether the pyramids could have been constructed using a system of internal ramps. The diagram on the following page outlines the steps in Jean-Paul Houdin’s internal ramp theory. Jean-Paul hopes to gain permission to explore the site to try to find evidence of internal ramps and tunnels in the pyramid over the years to come. As yet, we still don’t know if any of these theories are correct and there is much debate about the issue. As new theories are proposed and tested, we move a little closer to unlocking a long-held secret. 1 State: a how long the pyramid of Giza took to build. b how many builders assisted in the project. c how many stones were used. d the average mass of these stones. 2 If a single ramp was used, explain why it could not be constructed with an incline greater than 8 per cent. 3 Outline the major problem with the single ramp theory. 4 Using a ramp that spiralled around the pyramid also presents a key problem. Outline this problem. 5 Houdin’s theory sprung from a comment his father made while watching a television documentary. Discuss what this tells us about scientific discovery. 6 Use the diagram on the previous page to answer the following questions about Jean-Paul Houdin’s theory. a What was the purpose of the straight ramp used for the first 16 or so years of the pyramid’s construction? b Explain what happened to the limestone blocks that made up this ramp.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 7 Forces extra worksheet 3: Forces produced by ice and steam Science understanding Verbal/linguistic Cracking ice When water freezes, it expands by 9%.This expansion exerts a force on whatever is around the water. In this case, it was glass, which has shattered. Solid gold metal sinks when dropped into a pot of liquid gold. This happens because as a liquid cools, the tiny particles that make it up move more slowly and usually pack together more closely. Being packed more tightly together, solid gold has greater density than liquid gold. At temperatures below 4°C, when liquid water cools to form ice, something unusual happens. Instead of its particles being packed more closely, they become linked in a more open structure as ice crystals. As a result, the particles take up more space as ice than they do as water. The force of this expansion can crack rocks, burst water pipes and damage the foundations of buildings. Full steam ahead! As water particles are heated, they gain energy and break free of their liquid state. In becoming a gas, the particles move freely to fill the available space. If this space is limited, pressure builds up as more steam is produced. Such pressure can exert a large force if it is suddenly released. Steam under pressure can make can make a saucepan lid jiggle up and down on a pot on the stove. On a larger scale, these forces can be used to power a steam engine, as shown below, or to turn the turbines of a power station. Water inside the boiler of the engine is heated to produce steam. Pressure builds inside the boiler and is released by a valve into the engine. The pressure of the steam pushes the piston in one direction. A valve slides across so that the next burst of steam pushes on the other side of the piston. This movement of the valve enables the flow of steam to push the piston back and forth. The piston is connected to the crankshaft, which turns the wheels of the locomotive. 1 State the percentage by which water expands when it is frozen. 2 Propose why the glass bottle shown in the illustration has cracked. 3 Explain why solid gold metal sinks in liquid gold, but ice does not sink in water. 4 When a person is exposed to very cold conditions, their extremities, such as the fingers and toes, and their face can develop frostbite. Propose how the freezing of water to form ice crystals in the skin can damage the body’s tissues. 5 State whether particles of a liquid gain or lose energy as they are heated. 6 In terms of the particle model, explain why gases spread out to fill the container in which they are held. 7 Recall three situations in which the pressure of steam can be used to apply a force. 8 Propose the purpose of the safety valve in the steam engine shown in the illustration. 9 Predict whether a steam engine would work if the steam was not kept under pressure. Justify your response.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Machines extra worksheet 1: Leonardo da Vinci Science as a human endeavour Verbal/linguistic Name: Class: Date: Leonardo da Vinci was born in Vinci, Italy, in 1452. He was a brilliant painter—the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper are two of his works. It was not until centuries after his death in 1519 that people realised how many technological designs he had created. Leonardo da Vinci examined the structure of the heart by dissecting the bodies of oxen and about 30 human subjects. He discovered that the heart has four chambers, when at the time it was only believed to have two. Many of his observations and designs were recorded in back-to-front mirror writing in his notebooks because he tried to disguise his ideas from others. Leonardo embarked on a quest for knowledge in a wide range of areas, including geology, optics, acoustics, music, botany, hydraulics, anatomy and naval armaments. He was said to be handsome, generous and charming, but also unreliable and vain. He stood out in a crowd as he liked to dress in bright, striking clothing while other men wore long, dark-coloured robes. His designs for inventions included a self propelling car (shown below), a crane for emptying ditches, a snorkel for breathing under water, a therapeutic armchair, folding furniture, a type of armoured tank, a bicycle, spinning and weaving machines, various weapons, and even a robot with limbs that could be moved by a series of cables and pulleys. He designed a range of wonderful but unsuccessful flying machines. Some resembled large butterflies with four wings and included pedals, stirrups, harnesses, steering cables and standing platforms. One of his designs could take off vertically and was powered by a rotating blade—it was perhaps the first helicopter ever imagined. The designs he imagined were ahead of his time and are evidence of a great genius. This self propelling car was just one of Leonardo’s designs. He planned for a series of gears and leaf springs to power its motion. 1 Recall when and where was Leonardo born. 2 State what he was most famous for immediately after his death. 3 a Explain what was unusual about the way Leonardo recorded his ideas in his notebooks. b Propose a reason why he may have done this. 4 a Name three of Leonardo’s designs. b Explain why people often comment that Leonardo da Vinci was ahead of his time. 5 a Propose why the desire to fly has fascinated people for so long. b Recall the flying machine that is used today that is similar to a sketch made by da Vinci. 6 Imagine that you are Leonardo da Vinci, alive and well in Australia today. Construct a sketch of an invention that you think may be in use by the end of your lifetime.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Machines extra worksheet 2: Why do you weigh more on shag carpet? Science Understanding Verbal/linguistic Name: Class: Date: Want to gain a few kilograms? Just weigh yourself on shag carpet! People have long realised that if they put their bathroom scales onto carpet, particularly with thick pile, they too pile on the weight. The scales read about 10% more than if the scales were placed on a hard floor. To discover why this happens, we need to look more closely at what is happening inside the scales. Four levers extend inwards from the corners and cross over in its centre. Multiple levers are used to better distribute a person’s weight. When a person stands on the scales, these levers transfer the person’s weight to a spring-loaded metal plate. If we imagine all four levers operating as a single lever, the following illustration shows how they operate inside the scales. Because the distance from the fulcrum to the load is much shorter than the distance from the fulcrum to the effort, the spring experiences a much smaller force through the levers than if these were not used. Using the levers allows the spring to be much lighter in weight. A rack and pinion system converts the motion of the metal plate into the reading on the circular dial. Now we see how a set of scales work, so why do they read differently when placed on shag carpet? On a hard surface, the base of the scales bows downwards by a small amount and the fulcrum tilts in slightly. As a result, the scales record a slightly shorter distance between the load and the fulcrum than they would if the fulcrum was not tilted. On thick carpet, however, this base is supported and stays flat. The corresponding distance between the load and the fulcrum is now slightly increased (see the illustration below). This is increase is translated on the scales as an increase in mass, and the scales register a higher reading. Bathroom scales are actually calibrated on a hard floor, so this is where they give a true reading. So, if you’re ever trying to lose weight, don’t go near shag carpet! 1 State whether the lever in a set of bathroom scales is a first-, second- or third-class lever. 2 Explain why four levers are used instead of a single lever. 3 Describe how using these levers allows a much lighter spring to be used rather than the spring that would be required without the levers. 4 In terms of the distance from the fulcrum to the load and the distance from the fulcrum to the effort, explain why the effort force produced is much smaller than the load force. 5 Describe the role of the rack and pinion gear system in the scales. 6 State whether the distance from the load to the fulcrum is greater when scales are placed on hard floor or shag carpet. 7 Describe the difference this makes to the reading on the scales.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 7 Forces extra worksheet 2: Safer landings Science as a human endeavour Verbal/linguistic Name: Class: Date: Sand playground makes for safer landings Annabel McGilvray In the often high-tech world of modern children's playgrounds, a new study suggests that an old-fashioned solution may be best. Canadian researchers have found that children are nearly five times less at risk of breaking arms, legs or parts of their bodies, if their playground has sand on the ground rather than a wood fibre base. The Toronto team's results are published on the PLoS Medicine website today and may send local councils and planning authorities across Australia scrambling back to their drawing boards. ‘We suspect that the fracture rates are lower on sand because of lower surface friction,’ write the Toronto-based researchers. ‘A lower friction surface allows the hand to slide or sink limiting the bending moment and preventing a fracture.’ ‘Updating playground safety standards to reflect this information will reduce the most common and severe injuries seen on modern playgrounds, without limiting children's access to healthy outdoor play.’ Breaking new ground The researchers describe how they took advantage of a 2003 decision by the Toronto District School Board to resurface the district's school playgrounds. They used the rare opportunity to conduct a randomised controlled trial of the two surfaces. It found that children playing in those playgrounds with wood fibre surfaces were 4.9 times more likely to suffer fractures than the children playing in sand-covered playgrounds. The rate of fractures reported for the sandy playgrounds was 1.9 for every 100 000 student-months of use. Australian playground safety expert and associate professor at the University of Technology, Sydney, David Eager says that it is the first such study comparing surfaces in real world conditions and it is very thorough. ‘It's an excellent study and long-overdue.’ In Australia, a recent study of playground safety found that over a ten-year period there were 106.6 fractures per 100 000 students. Eager attributes the Australian injury rate in part to the fact that many playgrounds around the country are now surfaced with rubber. His recent research has shown that rather than dispersing the energy generated by a fall, rubber rebounds energy back into the falling body. ‘My own opinion is that both sand and wood fibre, or bark, are excellent surfaces for playgrounds and it's the rubber that is the bad surface which causes the rebound and lots more breaks.’ ‘The forces are significantly greater on the rubber than they are on the bark or the sand.’ Sinking to safe depths Adequate maintenance of playground surfaces can also play an important role in safety and may have influenced the impressively small injury outcome in the Canadian study. Any coverings of depth, such as sand or wood fibre, should be maintained at optimum depth to have the desired effect on safety. While no measurements were made, the researchers point out that the playgrounds were well looked after. They add that not only were the surfaces newly laid, but that the supervisors of the participating playgrounds were aware of the research and worked to maintain the grounds. Previous research by the NSW Injury Risk Management Research Centre has demonstrated that the safety benefit of such surfaces is significantly diminished if they are not as deep as required. The Centre suggested that it is one area often overlooked during maintenance. ‘In Australia we have lots of old playgrounds and lots of playgrounds that aren't maintained,’ says Eager. ‘When we do have sand and bark, even if it is put in at the correct depth, at the bottom of slides and climbing poles and other forced movement devices, it all gets pushed away and you're left with something quite hard underneath which is probably where all the injuries are occurring.’ Source: ABC Science website 1 Researchers from Canada found that children who played in playgrounds with a base of sand were at a much lower risk of breaking a bone in a fall than those who played in playgrounds with a wood fibre base. Recall how less likely a break is, according to the article. 2 State the reason why the researchers believe that this is the case. 3 Explain why having an arm or leg being able to slide in the sand would reduce the chance of a break. 4 State the number of fractures that was found over a ten year period out of a total of 100 000 children. 5 Safety expert David Eager criticised the use of rubber surfaces in many Australian playgrounds. Outline his reasons for this view. 6 Explain why it is important that playgrounds are well maintained to prevent injuries.

The Law of Conservation of Energy 
basically says that we can’t obtain energy in 
one situation without losing it in another. 
In other words, we can’t ‘create’ energy. 
This means that simple machines:
a always gain a little energy as they 
operate.
b basically change energy into a more

c make jobs easier by transforming

without any loss.

Perhaps the simplest machine is a lever.  
A lever usually takes the form of:

on a point and seems to make a task 
easier.
b a long steel bar used for prising things.
c a very short, hand-held device that 
assists people without needing a pivot.
d all of the above.

Magnetic Fields
 Aim: To observe magnetic field lines


Equipment:
                                                        Safety Information
• Sheet of white paper                                  Iron filings – rinse hands under cold
• Pair of bar magnets                                   water to remove from skin. Do not
                                                        rub your eyes.
• Small compass

• Iron filings

• Pencil




           Figure 1




           Figure 2




           Figure 3




Method:
Step 1: Set up the bar magnet as shown in figure 1 on the sheet of white paper.

Step 2: Gently scatter iron filings around the bar magnet. Allow them to settle.

Step 3: Draw the pattern of the magnetic field lines on your results sheet.

Step 4: Using the compass, position it at different points around the bar magnet, each time drawing an
arrow on your diagram to show which way the compass is pointing.

Step 5: Repeat steps 1 to 4 for the bar magnet set-ups shown in figures 2 and 3.



                                                Page 1 of 2
                                                                                            Magnetic Fields
Results:




   1




   2




   3




Questions:
 1. Do the magnetic field lines point from north to south, or from south to north around a bar magnet
    (figure 1)?

 2. Where is the magnetic field strength strongest around a bar magnet (figure 1)?

 3. Where is the magnetic field strength weakest around a bar magnet (figure 1)?

 4. Describe the magnetic field line pattern between two opposite poles of bar magnets (figure 2).
    What will the magnets do?

 5. Describe the magnetic field line pattern between two same poles of bar magnets (figure 3). What
    will the magnets do?


                                               Page 2 of 2
 Answers:
1. Magnetic field lines go from the north pole into the south pole.

2. The magnetic field strength is strongest at the poles.

3. The magnetic field strength is weaker the farther it is from the magnet.

4. The magnetic field lines go straight from the north pole of one magnet into the south pole of the
   other magnet. The magnetic field strength is strongest between the poles. The bar magnets will
   attract.

5. The magnetic field lines create a diamond between the poles. The magnetic field strength is
   weakest between the poles. The bar magnets will repel.

LESSON 7 E&C                        MAGIC MAGNETS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
      Investigate how you can make a nail into a magnet using electricity.


        EQUIPMENT



Per Class
    1 jar with some sugar , one leaf and 5 paper clips (iron filings are very useful if
       available)
      1 magnet
      alfoil
      masking tape
      a compass (optional)

Per Group
     2 D batteries
     2 x 15 cm lengths of plastic coated copper wire
     10 paper clips
     1 large nail
     masking tape
     15cm of alfoil
     pop sticks

Preparation
      In a jar mix one teaspoon of sugar, five very small paper clips or pins and a leaf
       cut into tiny pieces

Safety
    Mains electricity must not be used to make magnets.
     BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   An electromagnet is a temporary magnet formed when electric current flows
    through a wire or other conductor.
   Most electromagnets consist of a wire wound around an iron core.
   When an electric current moves in one direction through a wire, a magnetic field
    is created around the wire.
   When the wire is wrapped around an object to form a coil, the magnetic field
    around each wire is aligned right next to the field of the adjacent wires.
   All the coils work together to form a much stronger, single magnetic field.
   Electromagnets are a part of our everyday lives.
   They are useful because they act like magnets when the current is on and lose
    their magnetism when the current is off.
   Some electromagnets we use everyday are in school bells, telephones,
    automatic doors, video and tape recorders.
            LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Show students the jar of sugar, plant material and metal.


                                                     Remove the paper clips with a
  How could you separate these                       magnet.
  items?                                             Add water to dissolve the sugar
                                                     (this could be left on the window
                                                     to evaporate the water).
                                                     The leaves will float on the top
                                                     and can be scooped off.

      Ask a student to attempt to separate the materials. One student could do each
       step.
      Magnets are very useful to separate materials and in this lesson they will make a
       magnet from a nail.


2. Activities and Strategies

      Demonstrate how to make an electromagnet.
          Using the copper wire, begin at the top of the nail head and wrap the wire
          around it (about 15 -20 turns).
         You will need a 5cm wire tail at the top of the nail.
         Wrap the wire tightly trying hard not to leave any spaces.
         When you get near the end of the nail, loop the wire under the previous loop.
         You will need to have another 5cm wire tail at the bottom of the nail.
         Connect each end of the wire to one of the terminals on the battery.

To make an electromagnet, you will need: • A length of wire • A nail 2. Take the wire and straighten it. 3. One end of the wire has a clip attached. Hold the clip in your hand and measure off an arm’s length of wire. This splits the wire into two sections, one much longer than the other. 4. Take the long section of wire and wrap it neatly around the nail. Start wrapping at the flat part of the nail and work your way towards the nail’s point. 5. Wrap the wire around the nail 25 times to build the first electromagnet. Later, you will wrap the wire around the nail another 25 times to make a larger electromagnet. How to use the electromagnet: 1. To test your electromagnet you will need: • A battery pack • Some paper clips 2. There are four different settings on the battery pack. They are labeled 1.5V, 3.0V, 4.5V and 6.0V. The “V” stands for volts. A volt is a unit used to measure the amount of electricity in something, like meters is a unit used to measure the length of something. 3. Your team will test your electromagnet by seeing how many paper clips it can pick up at each voltage. Test each voltage two times. 4. There are two jobs to do: • Power Operator - turns the electromagnet on and off • Crane Operator - dunks the electromagnet into the container of paper clips 5. How do you turn the electromagnet on? Both ends of the wire have to be attached to the battery pack correctly so that electricity can flow: • Clip one end of the wire to the screw on the battery pack labeled TOP • Hold the other end of the wire onto the metal near the voltage label that you want to test REMEMBER: Metal has to touch metal for electricity to flow! Touch the wire to the metal screws, not to the plastic battery case! 6. Once the Power Operator has turned on the electromagnet, the Crane Operator should put the nail in the container of paper clips. Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility - Office of Science Education http://education.jlab.org/ 7. Gently mix the paper clips with the electromagnet. 8. Carefully lift the electromagnet out of the paper clip container and move it to a clean spot over your desk. 9. •     Forces are pushes or pulls.
•     Forces can change the speed of something or change the direction of its movement.
•     Force can also change the shape of something.
•     Force is measured in units called newtons (N).
•     Force can be measured using a spring balance or an electronic force sensor.
Forces only cause movement when the force is bigger in one direction, when the forces are
unbalanced. Look at your books on the table. They are not moving but there are forces
acting on them. Gravity is pulling the books downwards and the table is pushing the books
back up with the same force. The forces on the books are balancing each other out and the
books do not move.
If the leg of the table breaks, the force of gravity will pull the books downwards. The books
move down because the force pulling down is bigger than the force of the table pushing
upwards. The two forces combined result in an overall downward force. This force is called
the net force.

                                        Friction in Everyday Life

                                                     9
 We use friction everyday. Sometimes we need friction, and at other times we try to reduce it.
Need friction? We need it for example when:
         we walk. We use the friction between our feet and the
            ground. Imagine trying to walk if there was no friction.
            This would be like walking on ice!
         we drive a car. You could not stop a car without
            friction. You could not start it moving either – the
            wheels would just spin without the car moving. And
            everybody knows what happens if you go too fast
            around a corner or if the road is slippery.
         we use knots or nails. Friction stops knots from coming
            undone, and holds nails in place.
The list goes on and on.

However, friction can also be a hassle. It opposes motion as we have already mentioned. Friction also
produces heat. This can be useful when you rub a match on the side of a box, but it can also cause an engine
to overheat. Friction also causes wear and tear.




    Friction can be a nuisance.
Reducing Friction
There are five different ways of reducing friction.
1. A rolling object meets with less friction than a sliding one. (eg: moving a car on wheels, Egyptions
   moving huge blocks on rolling logs, ball bearings).
2. Lubricants (LOO-bri-cants) such as oil and grease are often used to reduce friction between moving
   parts to reduce wear and tear and make them slide more easily (eg: in machines, on the bearings in
   bicycle and skate board wheels, between bones in our joints).
3. Surfaces in contact can be polished so that they slide over one another more easily. (eg: hulls in racing
   yachts).
4. If air is blown between two surfaces, the friction becomes very small. This is the principle on which a
   hovercraft works.
5. Air resistance is the friction between a moving object and the air it is moving through, and can be
   reduced by giving the object (eg: car, plane) a more streamlined shape. Streamlining is also important
   for objects moving through water (eg: surfboards, speedboats and fast-swimming fish).

                                                     Friction
Have you ever tried to help someone start a car by pushing it? It is very hard to get the car rolling right at the
 start. If you can get the car to move it seems to be easier to push once it has started to move. The car tyres
have a force working against them. This force is trying to stop the car going forward or is said to be resisting
                                   the movement. This force is called friction.

Friction is all around us. It is because of friction that erasers work for us. There is friction




working against us when we ride a bike or skateboard, roller blade, run, play tennis, cut our
food and use a nail file to shape our nails. These are just a few examples of friction at work.
There are several different types of friction:
• Static friction is the force that stops things from starting to move: think of trying to push a car.
•   Sliding friction happens between moving surfaces such as in downhill skiing.
•   Rolling friction happens when a curved surface rolls over another surface. This happens when the wheel
    of a bike turns in one direction and the bike moves in the other direction.
•   Fluid friction happens between fluids or between fluids and solids. Fluid friction is less than friction
    between solids. Fluids are often used to help movement of two solids by reducing the friction between
    the surfaces. The axle on a bike has oil on it to help the metal axle turn more easily inside the casing.

                                        Measuring weight and mass
If you put a one-kilogram bag of sugar on a set of scales, it is the gravitational pull on the sugar which forces
the scale pan downwards-the scales respond to weight.
Some sets of scales are marked in newtons but most give a reading in mass units such as kilograms or grams
(there are 1000 grams in each kilogram). Readings in mass units present no problem to manufacturers of
scales because an object of large mass also has a large weight on Earth.
As for the one-kilogram bag of sugar: it has a moss of 1 kilogram and a weight on Earth of 9.8 newtons, but
try telling them that at the supermarket!

                                                     Gravity

You can jump in the air but you cannot stay there. You are pulled down by the force of gravity. When you
drop a glass or something falls, it is because gravity pulls the object towards the Earth. This gravitational
force gives objects their weight.

Gravity is the pull of the enormous mass of the Earth on our bodies and any other objects near the Earth’s
surface. It is a non-contact force since it is able to act over a distance, without the objects touching each
other.

There is a small gravitational force that pulls any two objects together. The size of this force depends on:
                the masses of the objects, and
                how far apart they are.

Usually this force is very small, but when one of the objects is the planet Eart, the force is far from small.
This law of gravitation was discovered by Sir Isaac Newton in the seventeenth century.

There is a gravitational pull between the Earth and the moon. This keeps the moon in place and causes tides
on Earth. Similarly, a gravitational pull keeps satellites in orbit around the Earth. The Earth and other planets
are kept in orbit around the sun by a gravitational pull.

Pulleys
Key terms
Block and tackle
a group of pulleys mounted together in a frame or block, which provides significant mechanical advantage
Pulley
a system that changes the direction of the applied force, but not the size
The pictures show pulley systems helping a person lift bigger loads. Fill in the missing information in each picture. Part (a) has been done for you as an example.
the mechanical advantage (M) = the number of pulleys
the force required (F) = mass ÷ M
how far the mass would be raised (D) = L ÷ M
the length of the rope (L) = D × M.
For example, in a single-pulley system, the mechanical advantage is 1 (because there is only 1 pulley). To lift a mass of 100 kg, you have to pull down with a force equivalent to 100 kg. To raise the 100 kg mass 1 m into the air, you have to pull the rope a total distance of 1 m at the other end.

title: Simple Machines - Worksheet - Set 1
subject: Science
searchText: Simple Machines A simple machine is a simple tool that makes work easier. Compound machines have multiple simple machines working together to make work easier. In science, work is defined as force acting on an object to move it across a distance. Pushing, pulling and lifting are all common forms of work. There are 6 simple machines. Inclined Plane An inclined plane is a surface that is set at an angle to the horizontal. It allows objects to be raised with les effort than would be needed to lift it straight up. Ramps are used in shopping centres and other buildings to allow wheelchairs and prams to be raised with less effort. Although smaller effort needs to be made, a greater distance must be travelled. Ramps, hills and slides are examples of inclined planes. Wedge A wedge is made from two inclined planes with their horizontal edges together. The sloped sides of the inclined planes meet to form a sharp edge. This edge can be used to split things apart by reducing the force needed to cut through the object . Knives, axes and nails are examples of wedges. Screw Take an inclined plane and wrap it around a cylinder. Its sharp edge becomes another simple tool: the screw. It is a curved ramp. However, instead of an object being pushed up the ramp, the ramp is pushed down into the object. Car jacks use a large screw to lift huge loads with little effort. Jar lids, jacks, clamps and spiral staircases are examples of screws. Lever Any tool that prises something loose is a lever. A lever is a board or bar that rests on a turning point. This turning point is called the fulcrum. An object the lever moves is called the load. The closer the load is to the fulcrum, the easier it is to move. First-class L evers In a first class lever, the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load. First-class levers are force multipliers. They allow you to move a large load with a small force. Some first-class levers are crowbars and seesaws. Second-class L evers Second-class levers are also force multipliers; however, the load is between the fulcrum and the effort. Some second-class levers are wheelbarrows and nutcrackers. Third-class Levers Levers with the effort between the fulcrum and the load are called third-class levers. This type of lever is not a force multiplier, they are a speed multiplier. Some third-class levers are cricket bats, brooms and tennis racquets. Wheel and Axle The wheel and axle can move objects across distances. The whe el , the turns the axle, a cylindrical post attached to the centre of the wheel, which causes movement. A wheel and axle is a force multiplier. You apply a small effort to the wheel to move a large load with the axle. They can also be used to make things move faster. A ceiling fan is a wheel and axle. A large force is applied to the axle. Each time the axle turns the fan blades move a much greater distance in the same amount of time. Door knobs, gears and clocks and fans are examples of wheel and axles. Pulley s Instead of an axle, the wheel could also rotate a rope or cord. In a pulley, a cord wraps around a wheel. As the wheel rotates, the cord moves. If a hook is attached to the cord, the wheel’s rotation can be used to raise or lower objects. A single, fixed pulley can be used to make lifting a load easier. It does not decrease the amount of force needed to lift the load, but changes the direction of the effort. Using more than one pulley will decrease the force needed to lift the load. Flag poles, blinds and cranes are examples of pulleys. Practical Activities Inclined Planes Aim: To examine the relationship between forces and distance on inclined planes. Equipment: Small stack of textbooks or a dictionary Wooden board Set of slotted masses 5N spring balance Procedure: Place the textbooks in a pile. Place the slotted masses next to the pile of books and use the spring balance to slowly lift the mass so that its base is level with the top of the pile. Record the force measured by the spring balance. Lean the ramp against the pile of books to make a long, gentle slope. Place the slotted masses at the bottom of the ramp and use the spring balance to slowly pull it until its far end reaches the top of the pile. Record the force measured on the spring balance. Turn the wooden board around so it makes a short, steep ramp. Place the slotted masses at the bottom of the ramp and use the spring balance to slowly pull it until its far end reaches the top of the pile. Record the force measured on the spring balance. Change the height of the stack of books and repeat the process with two different heights. Height of books (cm) Length of gentle slope (cm) Length of steep slope (cm) Force used to lift straight up (N) Force used for gentle slope (N) Force used for steep slope (N) Results: Questions: Does it take more force to lift the mass straight up or along the ramp? In which case does the mass have to move further? Which method of raising the mass is better? Why? Look at your measurements of force and distance. Can you see a pattern? Wedges Aim: To observe the action of different wedges in separating wooden blocks. Equipment: 2 blocks of wood 2 elastic bands 2 wooden wedges, one blunt and one sharp Procedure: Use the elastic bands to hold the two blocks of wood together. Try to pull the two blocks of wood apart with your fingers. Now, use the blunt wedge to separate the two blocks. Now, try using the sharp wedge to separate the blocks. Questions: Could you separate the blocks of wood easily with just your fingers? Using the blunt wedge, was it easier or harder to separate the blocks than with just your fingers? Is it easier or harder to separate the two blocks with the sharp wedge than with just your fingers? Which edge made separating the two blocks easiest? Screws Aim: To observe the action of a moving inclined plane, the screw. Equipment: Self-tapping screw Block of wood Screwdriver Procedure: Try to push the screw into the wooden block with your hand. Now use the screwdriver to fix the screw halfway into the wood by turning it Questions: Were you able to get the screw into the wooden block by just pushing it? How does the thread (the inclined plane) on the screw allow you to get the screw in the block? Wheels and Axles Aim: To observe the advantages provided by the wheel and axle. Equipment: Screw embedded in a block of wood Screw driver Procedure: Try to remove the screw from the block of wood by turning the shaft instead of the handle. Remove the screw by using the screwdriver as it is meant to be used, by turning the handle. Questions: Can the screw be removed by turning the shaft of the screwdriver instead of the handle? What difference does using the handle of the screwdriver make to the effort needed to turn the screw? During one full turn of the screwdriver, which moves further – the outside edge of the handle or the outside edge of the shaft? Is a screwdriver a force multiplier or a speed multiplier? Explain your choice. ‘A fan is a speed multiplier.’ Explain what this statement means. Levers Aim: To examine the relationship between forces and distances in first-class levers. Equipment: 30 cm wooden ruler Pencil Blu -tack 8 x 50g masses Procedure: Use the blu -tack to hold the pencil to the bench. Lay the ruler across the pencil so that it balances in the middle (15 cm) . Place three masses 12cm from the fulcrum (on the 3cm mark) . This is the load. Look at the picture below if you are not sure. One at a time place masses on the other end of the ruler until the load is lifted. This is the effort. Record the number masses needed to lift the load. Move the load 4cm closer to the fulcrum and repeat step 4. Move the load another 4 cm closer to the fulcrum and repeat step 4. Load (12 cm from fulcrum) Record your results in the table. Repeat the process for four masses. Effort Fulcrum Results: Load (number of masses) Distance from Fulcrum (cm) Effort (number of masses) 3 12 cm 3 8 cm 3 4 cm 4 12 cm 4 8 cm 4 4 cm Questions: Describe any pattern you can see in the data you have collected. Why is this type of lever called a force multiplier? Would there be any advantage to using this type of lever to raise a light load with a large effort? Explain your answer. Pulleys Aim: To examine the relationships between forces and distances in pulley systems. Equipment: 2 triple pulleys 1 metre length of string Set of slotted masses 5 N spring balance Retort stand Boss head and clamp 2 bricks Procedure: Set up the retort stand, boss head and clamp so that the boss had and clamp is at the very top. Extend the clamp so that it is at the very end. Place the retort stand on the edge of the bench and put the bricks on the base to weigh it down. Attach one pulley to the slotted masses and use the spring balance to find its weight, in newtons. This weight is the load that is to be lifted. Attach the piece of string to the top of the pulley attached to the masses. Thread the string through the lowest pulley at the top. Look at diagram one to help you. Attach the spring balance to the end of the string and pull on the balance slowly so that the load is lifted 10 cm upwards. Record the force on the spring balance. This is the effort. Also record how far you had to pull the string to lift the load. Now arrange the system with 2, 3 and 4 pulleys and record the effort needed to lift the load 10 cm. Use the diagrams to help you thread the systems. One pulley Two pulleys Three pulleys Four pulleys Results: Pulley Arrangement Load (N) Load Distance (cm) Effort (N) Effort Distance (cm) Single pulley 10 cm Two pulleys 10 cm Three pulleys 10 cm Four pulleys 10 cm Questions: The effort needed to lift the load using a single pulley is the same as lifting it straight up. Explain why a single pulley is still useful. Does the effort needed to lift the load increase or decrease when you add more pulleys? Does the distance you need to pull the string increase or decrease when you add more pulleys? Predict the effort that would be needed to lift the load with five pulleys. searchText: Simple Machines Levers Simple machines can change the direction or size of a force by using ‘mechanical advantage’ to multiply force. A lever is balanced on a fulcrum, which allows it to pivot. A load is lifted by placing effort on another part of the lever. A lever involves moving a load around a pivot using effort (or a force). Examples of tools that are classified as levers include scissors, pliers, hammer claws and tongs. Levers are a simple machine that increase force For a tool to be classed as a lever there must be:  a rigid handle  a fulcrum (or pivot) around which the handle rotates  a force increase – caused by the distance from the effort force to the fulcrum being larger than the load force to the fulcrum 124 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Levers are a simple machine that increase force Levers are classified in classes depending on the position of the effort and load in relation to the fulcrum.  Seesaw type Lever (Class 1): A lever where the load force acts on the opposite side of the fulcrum to the effort force. Examples include a Crowbar, Hammer and Tyre iron  Wheelbarrow type lever (class 2): A lever where the load force acts on the same side of the fulcrum as the effort force. Examples include a Wheelbarrow, a Spanner and a Ratchet /tiedown  Inclined Planes An inclined plane is a simple machine and it can be used to reduce the effort required to move a load. If the slope has a small angle, then a person has to push or pull the object over a longer distance to reach a height, but with very little effort. If the slope is steep, with a greater angle, a person must push or pull the object over a very short distance to reach the same height, but with more effort. Mechanical advantage is calculated by length of slope divided by height of the slope. There is a greater mechanical advantage if the slope is gentle because then less force will be needed to move an object up (or down) the slope. 125 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Simple machines Review 1. searchText:
Oxford Science 7 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Differentiation worksheet (C) 
Simple machines decrease the amount of effort needed to do work
The Ancient Egyptians applied their knowledge of forces to develop simple machines to help them build the pyramids.
The two images show some of the methods the Egyptians used. For each image, identify the simple machine and discuss how it was used to increase the amount of force.















Levers allow us to lift and move loads that are heavier than we could pick up using just our body. Diagrams of the three classes of lever are shown. For each diagram:
identify the class of the lever
label the fulcrum, load and the direction of the effort
draw an example (different from those in the textbook) of this type of lever.










Levers allow people to lift and move heavy loads, so they give people a ‘mechanical advantage’. The mechanical advantage can be calculated by dividing the size of the load (in newtons) by the size of the effort (in newtons). For example, if a wheelbarrow contains a 3 N load and it requires 1 N of effort to lift, the mechanical advantage is 3 divided by 1, which equals 3. Work out the mechanical advantage in the following situations:
A boulder has a 10 N load and requires 5 N of effort to move it using a lever. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever?

A nail has a 9 N load of resistance and requires 3 N of effort using a hammer to remove it. What is the mechanical advantage of the hammer?


A washing machine has a 600 N load and requires 200 N of effort to move it using a trolley. What is the mechanical advantage of the trolley?

Extend your understanding 
Research some of the simple machines that were used by the Ancient Romans or Greeks during the construction of their societies. Try to find an example of a first-class, second-class and third-class lever used by these societies.

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian Curriculum   Name:
Extending science worksheet
What a drag!
A helicopter is a type of “rotorcraft” that can take off and land vertically, making it useful to get to dangerous and remote places where there is no runway. The rotors of a helicopter rotate and tilt to create the forces it requires to travel in all directions. When a helicopter is coming down to land, the rotors produce an upward force that stops the helicopter from falling to the ground. This upward force that slows the downward landing movement of the helicopter is called drag. 
Drag can act in any direction, depending on the direction in which an object is moving. Drag is a force that opposes the motion of a moving object. It is always pulling in the opposite direction from the direction of travel. 
Meeting a specification
When engineers have a precise engineering objective, they call it a “specification”. In this task, you have the following engineering specification to meet: 
Specification: A helicopter that will descend 4 metres in exactly 4 seconds.
In a small group, your task is to investigate different helicopter designs to meet this specification as closely as possible. 
First, you will conduct a preliminary experiment to determine the average time a standard helicopter will take to descend 4 metres. Then, you will change or modify the design so that the drag created by your standard helicopter meets the specification.
Preliminary experiment
Aim: 
To determine the descent speed of a standard helicopter for comparison. 
Materials: 
helicopter template attachment
paper clip
staircase/balcony
stopwatch
measuring tape
Method:
Assemble the helicopter template in the attachment as instructed.
Find a safe location with a drop of at least 4 metres (e.g. from a staircase or balcony). Use the measuring tape to measure 4 metres from the ground and mark this as your ‘launching point’. 
Drop the helicopter from the 4 metre launching point and measure the time taken for it to fall to the ground with the stopwatch.
Repeat this process three times.
Record the results in the table below and calculate the average descent time of the standard helicopter.

Modifying the standard design
Using the standard helicopter design as a starting point, your group will now attempt to meet the specification of 4 metres in 4 seconds. You will be asked to think of ways to modify the standard design in order to change the amount of drag generated during the helicopter’s descent, thereby making it faster or slower. 
Before you begin, think about the different tasks that are involved in this problem. You will need people to brainstorm ideas, design and create the helicopter, launch it, time its descent and record the data. Take a few minutes to discuss with your group how you will share these tasks and note this down.




The five steps of the engineering design process below will guide you through this investigation. 
Step 1: Ideate
Identify different ways you could modify the standard helicopter design to increase/decrease the drag forces. Blade dimensions? Type of material? Extra/less weight? What else? Discuss your ideas as a group and write down as many ideas as possible.





Step 2: Design

Step 3: Build

Step 4: Test
Repeat the preliminary experiment with your three modified helicopters, recording their descent time from 4 metres. Record your results in the tables in the “Data and results” section. Did they meet the 4-second specification?
Step 5: Improve

Achieve! Maths – Data, statistics and drawing graphs – 17
Data can be obtained from many sources. It is 
available on the internet and in the media. Often 
you need to conduct a survey or a census to obtain 
the information you need.
A census is taken when you ask everyone to provide 
the information. Every five years, the Australian 
Bureau of Statistics conducts a national census. 
Information is collected from every member of the 
community.
It is not easy to conduct a census every time you 
need data. A survey is conducted using a sample 
from the population. The size of the sample and how 
it is selected can affect the accuracy of the results. 
There are a number of ways to obtain a sample.
•  Random sampling: For example, everyone’s name is placed in a hat.  
The names of 20 people are selected without looking.
•  Systematic sampling: For example, every fifth name on an alphabetical list 
is selected.
• Stratified sampling: For example, equal numbers of girls and boys are selected.

Achieve! Maths – Data, statistics and drawing graphs – 27
Rochelle plays cricket with her school team. Her recent batting scores were  
10, 25, 17 and 40 runs. The coach wanted to calculate her average score.
The term average is used in many situations. For example, batting averages  
in cricket or the average monthly rainfall.
The mean is the mathematical term for the average of a set of scores. 
To calculate the mean we add all the scores and then  
divide the sum by the number of scores.
Mean = the sum of the scores ÷ the number of scores
Calculate the mean of 10, 25, 17 and 40.
The sum of the scores = 10 + 25 + 17 + 40 = 92
The number of scores = 4
Mean = the sum of the scores ÷ the number of scores
 
= 92 ÷ 4 = 23
Rochelle’s average batting score was 23 runs.

Data is the information collected from a

Water travels surprisingly quickly up a celery stalk.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Take a gas jar and pour some red food colouring into it 
(a depth of 0.5cm is enough). Do not dilute the food
colouring.
2  Cut a fresh celery stalk with its leaves still attached and put
the lower end of the stalk into the dye. Place it in a warm
sunny position. Record the time. 
3 Remove the stalk after 3 minutes and progressively cut up
the stalk to see how far the dye has gone. (The dye should
have travelled right up the stem.)
EXPLANATION
The coloured water travels up the xylem vessels in the stalk by adhesive forces (between the water and the
walls of the vessels) and cohesive forces (between the water molecules). Evaporation from the leaves
maintains the flow.
The Australian mountain ash (Eucalyptus regnans) is the
tallest flowering plant in the world. Water travels upwards
over 90 m in some of these trees. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make diet celery. Put about 10 saccharin tablets in 100mL
of water. Stand a celery stalk in the liquid and leave it
overnight. Taste the celery. (The saccharin will  be tasted in
the celery. Humans can taste saccharin at  concentrations
hundreds of times lower than sugar.)
2  Examine the climatic record of your local area. Obtain a
firewood log in which the growth rings are clearly visible.
Count the rings and compare their widths. (Many trees
produce one growth ring each year. Wide rings indicate
years of high rainfall or warm temperatures, with
consequent greater growth.)

An egg will sink in one beaker of water but float in another.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Gently place a fresh egg in a beaker
of tap water. (The egg will sink.)
2  Transfer the egg to a beaker of very
salty water. (The egg will float.)
EXPLANATION
Salt water is more dense than fresh water. The buoyancy force (or upthrust) is greater in fluids of higher
density. In salt water there is enough upthrust for the egg to float.
TO INVESTIGATE
Predict how the weights of equal volumes of the salt water and tap water used in this activity would
compare. Use a volumetric pipette to measure volumes and a digital balance to compare weights;
calculate their densities.
The oceans came from rocks. The space rocks that originally formed the earth contained small amounts of
water chemically combined with minerals in the rocks. When the rocks melted in the interior of the
earth, the water was released as steam, which emerged from volcanoes and eventually formed the oceans. 
When salt water freezes, the salt is forced out, so the ice is fresh water.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make an ice block sink. TEACHER
DEMONSTRATION ONLY — Put one
ice block in water and another one in
methylated spirits. Safety warning: be
careful of fumes. (Water is more dense
than methylated spirits, so the ice will
float in the former and sink in the
latter.)
2  Separate salt water from fresh water. Half fill a beaker
with very salty water then float an egg in it. Slowly and
gently add fresh water to the side of the beaker until it is
full. (The two liquids do not fully mix, so the egg will remain
halfway up the beaker at their interface.)
Some parts of the sea are fresh water. Fresh water and salt water don’t automatically mix, so when the
water from the Amazon River enters the Atlantic Ocean it continues as a body of fresh water for
100 km out to sea.

Static electricity can make confetti take off into the air.

1 Place a handful of confetti on top of the dome of a Van de

Like charges repel. The pieces of confetti become charged with the same charge as the generator, so they
are repelled by the generator and by each other.

into the humidity in the air.

subject: Science
description: Science, Technology and Society. Teaching Guide, Demonstration.
searchText:
It’s easy to tell the difference between gold and fool’s gold.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Rub a piece of white paper on a gold ring. (The gold will
not leave a mark on the paper.)
2  Rub a piece of white paper on some fool’s gold  (iron
pyrites). (A black mark will appear on the  paper.)
EXPLANATION
Iron pyrites (FeS2) is a compound containing iron and sulfur,
so its properties are quite different to those of gold. This
activity is an example of a streak test, in which the colour of a
streak of the mineral can be used to help identify it.
There is no gold in our Australian ‘gold’ coins. One dollar and two dollar coins are 92% copper, 6%
aluminium and 2% nickel. 
There are hundreds of kilograms of gold in each cubic kilometre of seawater, but we have not yet
found a profitable way to extract it.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Model gold panning. Place a mixture of sand and lead shot
in a bowl. Run some tapwater into the bowl. Tip the bowl
slightly to one side and swirl it so that some of the water
and sand leaves the bowl. Repeat this a few times until
there is only lead shot in the bowl. (Lead shot, like gold, is
more dense than sand, so it sinks more rapidly in the
moving water and will thus remain in the bowl.)
2  Model the carat in gold rings. (Twenty-four carat gold is
pure. Other carat numbers indicate the proportion of gold
out of a total of 24. Eighteen carat gold is 18 parts gold and
6 parts copper; 12 carat gold is half gold and half copper.
The copper is added to make the gold harder.) Use lemon
jelly mixture to represent gold and gelatine to represent
copper. For example, a 12 carat mixture would be half jelly
mixture and half gelatine; pure gold would be jelly mixture
only. (The more gelatine in the mixture the harder the jelly
will become.)

searchText:
You can make other colours come out of a spot of black ink.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Cut a thin strip of filter paper about 15cm long.
2  Use a water soluble felt pen to put a spot of black ink about
2cm from one end. Dab the pen several times on the spot
so there is plenty of ink on it. 
3  Position the end of the filter paper in some water in a beaker but make sure the ink spot is not in the
water. (The ink will move upwards and various colours will appear.)
EXPLANATION
Black ink consists of a mixture of several different-coloured pigments. These pigments have differing
solubilities, and the more soluble ones are carried further up the filter paper by the water.
TO INVESTIGATE
What colours would you find in green, pink, orange and brown water-soluble felt pens? Do all black inks
contain the same pigments?
Some pigments can take on more than one colour. Hydrangeas can be pink or blue, depending on the
acidity of the soil. It is the pigment that changes colour in response to pH.
The primary colours of inks and paints are red, blue and yellow, but the primary colours of light are
red, blue and green.

searchText:
Oxford Science 7 Western Australian Curriculum   Name:
Extending science worksheet
Planning a mission: Is it worth it? Cost vs benefit vs risk
Is it worth it? Engineering projects constantly consider this question by weighing up the benefits of each decision in the engineering process against the costs and the risks involved.
The benefit of an engineering decision refers to the positive outcomes the decision will produce. For example, choosing a high-quality material for a moving part can increase the lifetime of a machine.
The cost of an engineering decision refers to the resources that are consumed due to the decision. This could be money or other things that are sacrificed, such as time or space. For example, adding several mechanical arms to a robot could limit the space available for other instrumentation. This lack of space is a cost.
The risk involved in an engineering decision refers to the likelihood that things will not turn out as expected. Risks could relate to safety or the likelihood of a successful result. For example, using a low-quality lubricant in a machine may risk damaging moving parts, causing your machine to stop working.
Space exploration is a field of science and engineering where issues of benefit, cost and risk are really important. In this activity, you will explore these concepts in relation to a mission to space.
Let’s start by considering the benefits, costs and risks of humans exploring space in general. As a class or in small groups, brainstorm some ideas below.
Benefits 
Costs
Risks















With these benefits, costs and risks in mind, let’s go on a mission into space.
Step 1: Create your destination planet
The first step is to figure out which planet your mission will explore. In small groups, decide on the characteristics of a distant planet that may be useful for humans to explore. To do this, choose an option for each planet characteristic below.
For each option, ask yourself what the benefits, costs and risks of studying this planet could be. For example, exploring a planet with violent, windy weather will be very risky, but might bring lots of benefit through finding out about the effects of major weather events.
For each characteristic, select one of the three options provided for your planet:
Planet characteristics
Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
