Give your planet a name, and record the choices you have made. Justify why you selected each option.
Planet name: 
Chosen characteristic
Reason for your choice
Surface

Distance from Earth

Likelihood of water

Surface texture

Temperature

Atmosphere

Weather

Step 2: Decide on a mission type
There are many types of missions possible for space exploration. Discuss in your group which option in the table below best suits the exploration of your particular planet. Circle your chosen option below.
Mission type
Mission characteristics 
Flyby
This mission type involves a spacecraft flying past the planet to observe it for only a short period of time. A flyby mission has limited observations it can make, but it is cheaper and less risky than some other mission types. Often, a single spacecraft can make multiple flyby missions past different planets during the same journey. 
Surface lander 
This mission type involves sending a module to the surface of a planet to explore the planet from the ground. It involves significant cost and risk, but the opportunities to collect information are many. Note that a surface lander would be extremely difficult for a gas planet.
Orbiter
This mission type involves sending a spacecraft designed to orbit a planet, while making observations and studying it from above. It has a lower risk than some other mission types, but it also has restrictions on the variety of observations it can make. 
Underground miner
This mission type combines a surface lander with a type of digging module that can explore beneath the surface of a planet. There are high risks associated with this mission type, but also high levels of observations possible. This is also an expensive mission option. 
Something else?
Can you think of another type of mission that might be suitable for your planet?
Describe the benefits, costs and risks for the selected mission being used to explore your planet.






Step 3: Choose your equipment
Space missions use a wide array of equipment to explore space. Remote-controlled missions beyond Earth (with no people on board) must use automation to navigate to a location, take observations and send data back to Earth for us to analyse.
Choose three to five pieces of equipment from the table below for your mission. Think about the benefits, costs and risks involved with each. Discuss your selection with your group and agree together on what to take.
Equipment category
Option 1
Option 2
Power supplies
Solar panels – This option is moderately expensive and slightly risky, but it provides an endless supply of energy as long as the panels can be exposed to sunlight.
Chemical batteries – This option is reliable, low risk and cheap. However, the energy will run out over time and can’t be replenished.
Image detectors
Light imager – These instruments detect light to provide information about the surface of a planet, such as land features, colour and heat. For this activity, they are considered to be moderately expensive and low risk. 
Imaging radar – These instruments measure radio waves bounced off a planet’s surface to provide 3D images of the surface. For this activity, they are considered to be moderately expensive and low risk.
Element detectors
Gas spectrometer – These instruments can tell us which gases are present in the atmosphere of a planet by detecting how light interacts with the atmosphere. For this activity, they are considered to be moderately expensive and low risk.
X-ray spectrometer – These instruments can tell us what types of rocks exist on a planet by observing how X-rays interact with the surface. For this activity, they are considered moderately expensive and high risk.
Mechanical equipment 
Crusher – These devices measure how hard a rock sample is by crushing it. They are only useful if a surface rock sample can be collected. For this activity, they are considered cheap but high risk. 
Dust detector – These devices can detect when charged particles strike them. They are useful for finding out what particles exist on a planet’s surface. For this activity, they are considered to be expensive but low risk.
Record the equipment you have decided to take. Describe the reason for each decision.
Chosen equipment
Reason for your choice – benefits vs costs vs risks








Discussion and reflection
Some people will suggest that your mission to visit your planet will be risky and not worth the cost. Respond to their argument by explaining the benefits expected from the mission and the costs and risks involved.




Describe how you could change your mission to increase the benefits or decrease costs and risks.






Many people consider the benefits, costs and risks involved in everyday decisions. Identify a decision you made recently. Describe the benefits, costs and risks that you considered when you made your decision. Did one of these factors seem more important (higher priority) than any other factors? Explain why this high-priority factor was more important to you. Would other people make the same decision as you? Why or why not?

If you roll this can away, it will come back to you.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain a can with a lid. Put two nail holes about 1cm apart
on the base of the can, close to the centre. Also do this with
the lid. 
2  Connect the holes with string as shown in the diagram. 
3  Attach a heavy fishing sinker to the centre of the string.
4  Gently roll the can on a hard, level surface. (The can will
roll to a stop about 1m away and then roll back to you.)
EXPLANATION
As the can rolls away from you, the lead weight does not roll,
so the string winds up. In this way, kinetic energy is changed
to potential energy, which is stored as tension in the string
and a slightly higher position of the weight. When the can rolls
back, the potential energy is converted to kinetic energy.
Window glass is highly elastic over short distances because
it always springs back to exactly where it was.

string to the spring lever of the mouse trap, and wind the
other end around the front axle of the car. (As the trap
closes, the potential energy in the spring is converted to
kinetic energy. This movement pulls the string, which is
wound around the axle, so the car will move forward.)

to make a milk carton boat move across a tub of water.

You can watch a snail make waves.
HOW TO DO IT 
1  Put a snail in a dish with a little water to encourage it to
come out of its shell.
2  Put the snail onto a sheet of damp clear plastic (e.g., from
an overhead projector). As the snail is moving across the
plastic sheet, look at it from the underside. (A series of
waves will be flowing forwards along its foot.) Safety
warning: wash your hands after handling specimens.
EXPLANATION
Each time one of the ripples reaches a muscle it contracts and lifts a small part of the foot, which is then
carried forward and set down. In this way the snail is propelled forwards.
TO INVESTIGATE
Can a snail move along the edge of a safety blade without cutting itself?
You should be glad you’re not a snail. A snail’s anus is located just above and just behind its head.
Snails have both male and female sex organs. Before copulation one snail fires a hard calcium ‘love
dart’ into the body of the other snail, then both snails donate sperm.
Our garden snail, Helix aspersa, is considered a delicacy in parts of Europe and the Middle East.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Look a snail in the eyes. Observe what happens to a snail’s
eyes (which are located on the long tentacles) as it emerges
from its shell. (The tentacles extend without the eyes, then
the eyes travel up the tentacles to the tips.)
2  Solve the following problem. Does each snail have a
unique shell pattern? How would you classify the types of
patterns on their shells?
3  Examine other molluscs. Obtain specimens of mussel and
oyster (in their shells), squid and octopus from a fish shop,
and a slug from the garden. What features would you use
to classify them into different groups of molluscs? (Snails
and slugs have a distinct head; mussels and oysters have a
shell in two parts; and cephalopods have several tentacles.)

subject: Science
description: Forensic Science and Evidence. Worksheet, Forensic Skills.
searchText:
Using chromatography to compare inks - .. -- .. acTIviTy 3

Name

The inks found in pens are made from a number of different chemicals.
These chemicals are combined to give the desired colour and consistency
needed to leave a clear line on a page of paper. Different manufacturers
use slightly different combinations of these chemicals to produce their
inks, so each brand of pen has its own unique formula.

The chemicals in different inks can be compared using the simple
technique of chromatography. A sample of the ink is placed about 1 cm
from the bottom of a piece of absorbent paper, which is then stood in a
beaker that contains a small amount of solvent, such as water or
methylated spirits. The solvent slowly soaks up the paper. As it meets the
ink, some of the chemicals in the ink will dissolve and be carried up with
the solvent. This leaves a trail of different colours spread up the paper.

Some of the chemicals consist of very small molecules, and these will be carried furthest up the paper,
especially if they are very soluble. Where the ink chemicals are made of larger molecules that are less soluble,
these will not be carried as fast or as far up the paper. Each ink usually leaves its own unique pattern of
colours, called a chromatogram. If two chromatograms have the same colours in the same order, it is highly
likely that both samples came from a pen of the same type and brand.

Today in the forensic laboratory, chromatography is not used as described above. Instead, scientists use
instruments that measure the exact chemicals found in a mixture. A small sample of the substance is placed
in a chamber where it is heated so that it evaporates as a gas. The types of particles in the gas are identified,
and the scientist can print out a graph that shows the type and amount of each particle in the sample.

This plant can move fast enough to catch insects.

1  Buy a potted Venus flytrap (Dionaea) from a nursery.

EXPLANATION
As venus flytraps are green plants, they produce their food by photosynthesis. However, they are often
found growing in poor soils, so they use their insect prey as a supplementary source of minerals,
especially iron and phosphorus compounds.

If a trap closes without having caught any prey, will it open up faster than one that has caught prey (such

Plants make up about 90% of the mass of all living things

Most of the oxygen in the air is produced by microscopic

A handful of forest litter can conceal a surprising number of these creatures.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
1  Cut away one side of a milk carton to make a rectangular
viewing tray. Put a handful of mixed leaf litter (bits of dry
leaves and bark) in one half of the carton and leave the
other half empty. 
2  Collect 50 healthy woodlice (slaters) from leaf litter or
under paving stones and logs in the garden. Safety
warning: wear sturdy gloves because poisonous spiders also
inhabit these areas.
3  Place all the woodlice on the litter and give them 2 minutes
to hide.
4  Ask the students to observe the box and estimate the
numbers of woodlice inside. (They will usually
underestimate the number.)
EXPLANATION
Woodlice avoid light and open spaces and are sensitive to
slight differences in humidity. This tends to keep them in the
leaf litter, where they are more protected from desiccation.
They feed on decaying plant material.
TO INVESTIGATE
What happens if the woodlice are placed in the bare half of
the box, rather than in the leaf litter?
The giant crab of Japanese waters measures over 3 m from
limb tip to limb tip, and is a cousin of the woodlouse.
Funnel-web spiders can’t kill dogs or cats. In fact, humans
and other primates are the only vertebrates susceptible to
funnel-web toxin.

EI Anaerobic respiration

Science understanding [Founoarion [| stanparD | ADVANCED

Aerobic respiration is the way animals get most of their energy. The muscles of animals usually have
lots of oxygen. However, there are times when oxygen is used at a faster rate than the rate of supply.
The cells of the muscles then have to get their energy by respiring without oxygen. Respiration
without oxygen is called anaerobic respiration.

Glucose is still the source of the energy, but lactic acid (C,H,,O,) is produced instead of carbon
dioxide and water.

Anaerobic respiration in animals can be represented by the chemical equations:
glucose > lactic acid + energy
C.H,,0, > 2C,H,0, + energy

Anaerobic respiration does not produce as much energy as aerobic respiration because some energy
is still stored in the lactic acid molecule.

After an extended period of exercise, a build-up of lactic acid in the muscles can cause muscle
fatigue. Warming down and breathing deeply helps supply oxygen to the muscles. Oxygen helps the
lactic acid break down, releasing more energy.

Respiration in Yeast
 Aim: To observe the process of respiration in yeast


Equipment:

Method:
Step 1: Stretch the balloon out a few times so that the deflated balloon is flexible.

Step 2: Carefully add 1 spatula of dried yeast and 1 of sugar into the boiling tube.

Step 3: Fill the boiling tube, approximately ¼ to ½ full with warm water.

Step 4: Stir gently with spatula for 5 to 10 seconds. Take care not to knock the sides of the boiling tube
and break the glass.

Step 5: With a partner’s help, stretch the neck of the balloon over the mouth of the boiling tube.

Step 6: The yeast mixture will begin to froth. Stand the boiling tube into a rack and observe.

(Optional) Step 7: You may want to take a photograph of the balloon every minute or so as a means of
recording your observations.




                                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                                                        Respiration in Yeast


Questions
 1. What happens to the balloon during the reaction? Explain your answer.

 2. Name the gas that is being produced.

 3. Are the yeast cells respiring aerobically or anaerobically? Explain your answer.

 4. Write the word equation for the anaerobic respiration (fermentation) of yeast.

 5. Name two products in which yeast is used as an ingredient.

 6. Explain how the yeast acts as a raising agent when making bread.




 Extra Challenge
 Write a plan for an investigation to find the optimum temperature of respiration in yeast You will
 need to justify your equipment choices and explain how your method is valid.




                                                Page 2 of 3
                                                                                           Respiration in Yeast

Answers
    1. What happens to the balloon during the reaction? Explain your answer.

      The balloon inflates as it fills with the gas produced during the reaction.
      As the gas cannot escape, it fills and expands the balloon.

    2. Name the gas that is being produced.

      Carbon dioxide

    3. Are the yeast cells respiring aerobically or anaerobically? Explain your answer.

      Initially the yeast cells are respiring aerobically because of the oxygen present in the
      air in the boiling tube. However, as the tube is sealed and no more air can enter, once
      this oxygen has been used up, the yeast cells will carry out anaerobic respiration.

    4. Write the word equation for the anaerobic respiration (fermentation) of yeast.

      glucose carbon dioxide + ethanol + [energy]

    5. Name two products in which yeast is used as an ingredient.

      Bread, beer, wine, pizza dough

    6. Explain how the yeast acts as a raising agent when making bread.

      The respiration of yeast during the baking process produces carbon dioxide gas. The gas builds
      up as bubbles inside the bread dough, forming air pockets, which make the dough expand
      and rise.


    Extra Challenge
    Write a plan for an investigation to find the optimum temperature of respiration in yeast You will
    need to justify your equipment choices and explain how your method is valid.

Angiosperms

IntroductIon
Angiosperms are flowering plants. Like all organisms, they need to reproduce and angiosperms do so sexually. Flowers 
are the sexual organs of these plants and they enable fertilisation to take place. Many, but not all, angiosperms have 
flowers that consist of both male and female parts.
Aim
To investigate pollination and how plants have evolved to ensure it.
Information
The male gametes (sex cells) are the pollen cells and the female gametes are the ovules. The male part of a flower is 
called the stamen and is made up of the filament (a thin stalk) and the anther, which is the source of pollen. The female 
part of the flower (the pistil) is located centrally. At the top is the stigma through which pollen can enter. The pollen then 
proceeds down a tube (the style) to the ovary where the ovules are located. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the 
anther to the stigma and the subsequent fertilisation of the ovule. After pollination has occurred, the fertilised embryo 
develops into a seed, which can develop into a new plant under suitable conditions

To ensure the continuation of the species, plants and animals use two methods of reproduction – sexual and
asexual. Sexual reproduction involves the fusing of two gametes, one from each partner, to form a new being.
Asexual reproduction does not require a second partner. One or more offspring are produced from only one
parent by the process of mitosis.
Vegetative reproduction is the propagation of plants using vegetative tissues such as stems, leaves and
roots. This results in a plant that is genetically identical to the original plant. In some species, stems arch over
and take root at their tips, forming new plants. For example, the horizontal above ground stems (runners or
stolons) of the strawberry produce new daughter plants at alternate nodes. Underground stems such as
rhizomes, bulbs, corms and tubers are used for asexual reproduction as well as for food storage.
Leaves of bryophyllum produce tiny plantlets along the leaf margin. Some plants like dandelion use their roots
for asexual reproduction. Plants can be propagated asexually by taking stem cuttings and by grafting. Animals
also reproduce asexually by various means.
Budding: The offspring develop as a growth on the body of the parent. In some species, such as jellyfish and
many echinoderms, the buds break away and take up an independent existence. In corals, the buds remain
attached to the parent and the process results in colonies of animals. Budding is also common among parasitic
animals such as tapeworms.

             Cells vs cities
             In the city of Keystonia the main industry is the production of keystones. Everyone in
             the town is involved in the production of this one product. The blueprint design for
             keystones is kept in the council chambers. When needed, a photocopy of the design
             is made and then taken to the assembly factory to be made. The keystones are then
             transported along the roads to the post office where they are packaged into special
             boxes and sent out of the town. The energy for the factory is made by a set of solar
             panels. These panels store their energy in batteries until they are needed. To protect
             the city a large wall with a few guarded gates surrounds the town.
             The manufacture of keystones in Keystonia is very similar to how a cell works. Most
             cells are involved in producing special proteins. The nucleus contains the DNA
             instructions to make the protein. Copies of the DNA are made and transported to the
             ribosome where the protein is made. The protein is transported through a series of
             tunnels called the endoplasmic reticulum. The Golgi apparatus/body package up the
             protein and send it out of the cell’s membrane (the structure that surrounds and

A bacterium is a single-celled (unicellular) organism. The plural of bacterium is bacteria. There are many ways to 
classify bacteria, such as by their shape or by the environment in which they are found.

that is each individual cell splits into two 
(identical) ‘daughter’ cells. This type of 
reproduction is ‘asexual’, meaning it doesn’t 
involve males and females, it doesn’t require 
two parents. Because bacteria can reproduce so 
quickly, they can generate large numbers in a  
very short period of time.

Barbara MCGCIINIOCK (1902-1992) 6a

Barbara McClintock was born in 1902 in Brooklyn, New York. As a student, she studied botany at Cornell
Univer graduating with her PhD in 1927. She later taught at Cornell before becoming a Professor at the
University of Missouri in 1936. Between 1942 and 1967, she did research on cytology (study of cells) and
genetics at a research laboratory in Cold Spring Harbour, New York. In 1983, McClintock was awarded the
Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine, one of only six women to have won this.

1 [a) What is genetics?
{b) What is botany?
[c] Explain how someone could study cytology, genetics and botany?

2 [al What type of people would win the Nobel Prize for Medicine and Physiology?

{b) The Nobel Prizes have been awarded since 1901, Why do you think there have been so few
women recipients?

The story so far

Gregor Mendel (1822-1884), the father of genetics, developed ideas on tracing characteristics from parents
to offspring. He was a monk who from 1851 to 1854 studied the characteristics of pea plants in the
monastery vegetable garden. In Australia, the first advances in practical genetics were made by William
Farrer, with the development of wheat strains that could withstand the fungal infection called rust.
3° (al Who was Gregor Mendel?

{b] Why is he called the father of genetics?

{c] What does the word ‘characteristic’ mean?

{d) What are some characteristics of different plants that you know?

le] What are some characteristics of different animals that you know?

4 (a) Why was disease-free wheat so important for Australian farmers?

{b) How could the work of Gregor Mendel help William Farrer?

Other scientists did not notice Mendel’s research results until 1900. In this year, three biologists, Hugo de
Vries from the Netherlands, a German botanist Karl Correns and an Austrian Erich von Taschermak,
separately obtained results similar to Mendel’s while undertaking their own research. Also in the early
1900s, Thomas Hunt Morgan

Insect pollinators and the world food supply

Teaching notes

Make 4 copies of each information sheet.

Give one information sheet to each pair of students. They should read and summarise the
information on their sheet using pictures and a word limit of 12 words. Students then
circulate around the room explaining their poster and finding out about three other threats
to insect pollinators.

During this time keywords/concepts could be added to the questions on the whiteboard.

Finally, students should get into groups of 4 and answer the questions on the group
question sheet.

The extension task questions could be used as part of a group discussion.


Additional teaching notes

This resource can be used as a standalone activity or with the Teachit Science resources
‘Wind or insect pollination’ (22853) and ‘Insect pollinators’ (22854) to make a complete
lesson.

If using the resources together then see below for suggested learning outcomes:
  name four insect pollinators
  outline one consequence of a decrease in the numbers of insect pollinators on our
   food supply
  describe four threats to abundance of honey bees and other insect pollinators
  for two of these threats explain how they could be reduced.

The learning outcomes could be shared with students at the start of the activity and left on
a whiteboard during the activity. Keywords and phrases, ‘memory-joggers’ could be added
by students during the activity.


Background information

http://butterfly-conservation.org/88/biodiversity-action-plans.html
www.bbka.org.uk/learn/general_information/life_in_the_hive
http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-23351215
www.operaresearch.eu
http://www.parliament.uk/briefing-papers/POST-PN-348/insect-pollination-january-2010

                                             Insect pollinators and the world food supply

Suggested answers

Group question sheet
 1.   Our staple foods, wheat, rice etc are wind pollinated. If we lost a large number of insect
      pollinators we would still have plenty to eat but we would lose foods which provide us with
      essential micro-nutrients, vitamins and minerals, antioxidants and variety in our diet.
 2.   Through wind pollination or by insects and other animals.
 3.   Honeybees, bumblebees, hoverflies, butterflies and moths
 4.   The term ‘agricultural intensification’ describes what has happened to farming practices over
      the last 60 years. Only one type of plant is grown in each field. Herbicides are used to kill
      any other plant which may grow on the land. Even when the crop is grass e.g. for silage or
      grazing, only a few species will be found growing in the field and almost no flowering plants.
      For many farmers this is the most efficient method of production.
 5.   Reduced the availability of flowering plants and nesting sites for insects, birds and mammals.
      The UK has lost 97% of its wildflower meadows since the 1930s. The countryside has been
      stripped of the wild flowers which sustained populations of bees, butterflies etc.
 6.   Each farm needs to have natural, wildflower rich areas to support bumblebees, butterflies
      and other insect pollinators when their crops are not in flower. Or, farmers could ‘import’
      honeybees and their hives when they need them.
 7.   Varroa mite
 8.   Colonies of bumblebees should be screened and certified disease free before they are
      imported into this country.
 9.   Bumblebees exposed to these controversial pesticides collect just half the pollen they would
      otherwise harvest, depriving their growing young of their only source of protein.
      It would allow more independent research to be done to ascertain the exact effect these
      pesticides have on wild insect pollinators.
 10. Bees and butterflies are particularly sensitive to wet, cool, windy conditions. Cold wet
     summers can have a detrimental effect on their numbers and breeding success. They may
     move northwards as the climate warms and new species could become established in the
     southern counties.


Suggested answers

Task – extension

 1.   To ensure the results are reliable, unbiased and can be trusted by decision makers and the
      public.
 2.   Farmers/landowners earn their livelihood from the land. Many need to farm intensively to
      make a living. If we value a rich, diverse natural landscape farmers need to be paid to
      maintain it.
 3.   Although at the top of many food webs we are sustained by the organisms below us in that
      web. Damaged habitats/environments cannot always be repaired. We don’t know how
      much damage/loss can be endured before it has a detrimental effect on us.
The natural world is our heritage and we should pass it on to future generations in good order.
People need green spaces.
Extinction is quick; evolution is slow

                                  Information sheet 1

Agricultural intensification
The term ‘agricultural intensification’ describes what has happened to farming practices
over the last 60 years. Only one type of plant is grown in each field. Herbicides are used
to kill any other plant which may grow on the land. Even when the crop is grass e.g. for
silage or grazing, only a few species will be found growing in the field and almost no
flowering plants. For many farmers this is the most efficient method of production.
However, agricultural intensification has reduced the availability of flowering plants and
nesting sites for insects, birds and mammals. The UK has lost 97% of its wildflower
meadows since the 1930s. Such changes affect wild insect pollinators because they are
totally dependent on wild flowers growing in the landscape.
Flowering crops such as oilseed rape produce a super abundance of flowers over a very
short period of time. For there to be enough insects in the environment to pollinate the
flowering oilseed rape each farm needs to have natural, wildflower rich areas to support
bumblebees, butterflies and other insect pollinators when their crops are not in flower.
To overcome this problem in the USA, large numbers of honeybees and their hives are
transported around the country. The bees are taken to orchards as the trees come into
blossom. When the fruit has set the hives are moved to newly flowering orchards. In
recent years many hives in the USA have suffered the devastating colony collapse
disorder (CCD) in which all the adult bees simply disappear from the hive. CCD may be
linked to the practice of transporting bees over large distances or to pesticides.




                                  Information sheet 2

Pests and diseases

Pests and diseases are the main threat to honeybees, particularly an introduced parasitic
mite called Varroa. Varroa infestations can be treated but the mite is beginning to show
resistance to some treatments.
Most beehives in Britain are managed by amateur beekeepers in their spare time.
Beekeeping associations provide training but the quality depends on the expertise of local
volunteers.
The impact of pests and diseases on other pollinating insects has not been well studied,
but is probably less severe than on honeybees as they are particularly exposed to new
dise

Understanding Biology – human and plant life
7
Division of the heart, by a septum, allows for well-organised movement of blood and produces the effect of two 
separate pumps. From this arrangement, two circulation paths have evolved. These paths are called the systemic and 
pulmonary circuits.
Systemic circuit
Once the exchange of carbon dioxide for oxygen has occurred (at the tiny capillaries of the lungs) the flow of blood 
progresses to the four pulmonary veins (one pair per lung). All freshly oxygenated blood begins its journey through 
the circulatory system at the pulmonary veins, which empty freshly oxygenated blood into the left side of the heart. 
This blood flows to the left atrium and into the left ventricle, which sends it through the aorta to the rest of the body.
1 
Why is the cardiac tissue forming the ventricles thicker than that of the atria? 
 
2 
Although the ventricles are thicker than the atria (overall), the muscles on the left side of the heart are often 
thicker than those on the right side of the heart. Suggest why.
 
Pulmonary circuit 
The right side of the heart contains oxygen-poor blood on its way to the lungs. Fully circulated blood (carbon-
dioxide rich, oxygen poor) travels via the inferior vena cava and superior vena cava into the right atrium. From the 
right atrium, it enters the right ventricle. Blood leaves the right ventricle by the pulmonary arteries. Completely 
deoxygenated blood is only found in the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary artery branches into two, directing 
blood to the left and right lungs. At each lung the artery divides 
and divides into ever smaller vessels, which eventually become 
capillaries. All this capillary branching creates a greater surface 
area so larger volumes of blood can efficiently replace carbon 
dioxide with oxygen, by bringing it to the surface of the tissue.

The heart pumps blood around the body in the circulatory system. In the circulatory
system are three types of blood vessels. They each have a different structure that is
related to their function.


Arteries
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. In the arteries, the blood is under high
pressure from the heart beat. As seen in Figure 3.2.1, the walls of the arteries are
strong, thick and elastic to withstand the pressure. Large arteries branch into smaller
and smaller arteries, which spread and carry blood to all parts of the body. Eventually
the branches of the arteries become very fine, and are known as capillaries.

The bodies of animals and humans have billions of cells that are organised into tissues

searchText:
Oxford Sciences 8 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Bone density
Density is the amount of matter in a given space. It is a measure of how tightly packed a material is.
Bone density is the mass of bone per cubic centimetre (the mass per unit volume). It is a measure that tells us about how strong a bone is – the more mass in each cubic centimetre, the less likely it is for the bone to break.
Bone density in humans tends to peak when they are young adults and then starts to decline. However, bone density is positively affected by weight-bearing activities. These are activities where a person uses their muscles to push against the force of gravity. Walking, tennis and weightlifting are all weight-bearing activities. Engaging in weight-bearing forms of exercise will slow down the loss of bone density as a person ages. It will also reduce the chances of developing a medical condition called osteoporosis, which occurs when bones lose too much density. Osteoporosis is typically associated with age as well as hormonal changes, or a deficiency of calcium or vitamin D.
In this task, you will investigate how much force is required to break the bones of different animals with different bone densities. 
Bone density experiment
Aim:
To measure the relationship between bone density and the force required to break a bone
Materials:
Chicken rib bone
Lamb or pig rib bone
Fish rib bone
Kitchen scales
Beaker
Water
Hanging weights secured with fishing line
Retort stands or clamps
Method:
Measure the mass in kilograms of each bone with the kitchen scales and record it in the table in the Data and results section. Be sure to record it in kilograms, not grams. 
Fill up the beaker to a chosen volume that will provide enough water to submerge the bones. 
Submerge each bone, one by one, into the water. Note by how much the volume measurement of the water in the beaker increases when the bone is fully submerged. This is the volume of the bone in millilitres (mL). 
In the table, record the volume of each bone in cm3 (note that 1 mL = 1 cm3).
Use the results to calculate the density of each bone and write it in the table. The density is the mass (kg) divided by the volume (cm3). 
Use the clamps to secure the bones horizontally to the table.
Attach hanging weights to the centre of the secured bone with fishing line. Slowly increase the amount of weight hanging from the bone until the bone breaks. 
In the Data and results section, record the mass of the weights (in kilograms) required to break each bone.
Use these results to calculate the force that was required to break the bones. Force is the mass multiplied by the acceleration due to gravity (which is approximately 9.8 m/s2).
Underneath your results tables, graph the bone density against the force required to break the bone.

Heart disease can develop in different ways. Characteristics inherited from parents 
can play a role in heart problems, but other causes come from the way people choose 
to live. Inactive lifestyles, obesity, the use of anabolic steroids (to increase muscle size) 
and drug use are examples of ‘lifestyle’ causes of heart disease.

What is meant by obesity?  
Smoking is linked to many diseases, including heart disease. A heavy smoker who 
quits will have about half the risk of developing heart disease that a ‘light’ smoker 
who continues does. A person who never smokes is at the least risk of heart disease, 
provided other factors (such as heredity) do not play a role.  
2 
Suggest why people take up smoking or continue smoking even though 
they know it is harmful.
 
Other smoking-related conditions that can indirectly affect the heart include lung cancer, high blood pressure 
and, because of high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) circulating through the blood, cancers developing in major 
organs. A former smoker still has a high chance of developing cancers (though the risks are dramatically reduced 
by quitting) so it is most sensible not to begin smoking in the first place. Many public places are now smoke-free 
because ‘second-hand’ smoke (smoke exhaled by smokers) is highly toxic if inhaled. Constant exposure to second-
hand smoke can lead to cancer developing in a non-smoker.

Cell City Analogy – how a cell is like a city
In a far away city called Grant City, the main export and production product is the steel bolt. Everyone in the
town has something to do with steel bolt making and the entire town is designed to build and export bolts.
The town hall has the instructions for bolt making, bolts come in all shapes and sizes and any citizen of
Grant can get the instructions and begin making their own bolts. Bolts are generally produced in small
shops around the city, these small shops can be built by the carpenter's union (whose headquarters are in
town hall).

In order for a bolt to be exported, the carts take the bolts to the postal office, where the bolts are packaged
and labeled for export. Sometimes bolts don't turn out right, and the "rejects" are sent to the scrap yard
where they are broken down for parts or destroyed altogether. The town powers the bolt shops and carts

Cell division
Cells do not last forever. They grow old and eventually die, so they need to be replaced. 
For example, skin cells in humans get worn out and are replaced continually. The flaky bits 
of dry skin that you scrub away are made of dead skin cells. Underneath this skin, healthy 
new skin cells are ready to replace the lost cells.
Cells also make living things grow bigger or stronger, by producing more of 
themselves. For example, a plant grows taller and gets more leaves as new cells are made.
To make more of themselves, cells separate into two parts that are the same. This is 
called cell division. Its scientific name is mitosis.

Key terms
cell wall
the outer protective and support structure of a plant cell 
chlorophyll
green pigment found inside chloroplasts that absorbs solar energy and uses it in photosynthesis 
chloroplast
organelle found in plant cells that transforms solar energy into chemical energy 
cytoplasm
the jelly-like fluid inside the cell membrane that contains dissolved nutrients, waste products and organelles
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)
a molecule that contains all the instructions for every job performed by the cell; this information can be passed from one generation to the next 
mitochondrion
powerhouse organelle of a cell; the site of energy production (plural: mitochondria) 
nucleus
control centre of a cell that contains all the genetic material (DNA) for that cell 
organelle
smaller part of a cell, each one having a different function 
photosynthesis
chemical process that plants use to make glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water
vesicle
an organelle surrounded by a membrane and used by cells to store materials; a vacuole is a type of vesicle found in plant cells

Understanding Biology  – Ecosystems and living things
5
Cells would not have been discovered without the development of the microscope. Antonie van  
Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723) is often credited with the invention of the microscope. Robert  
Hooke (1635–1703) is the first recorded person to investigate the structure of cells. In 1665 he  
investigated the structure of a section of cork and described the repeating units he saw as cells. 
1 
Why are microscopes essential in the study of cells? 
Hooke stated, ‘... it had a very little solid substance, in comparison of the empty cavity that was  
contained between. Partitions of these pores were near as thin in their proportion to their pores, as those  
thin films of wax in a honeycomb.’ Figure 1 is similar to a section of one of his drawings of cork.  
Hooke didn’t see any of the internal organelles of cells because cork is basically dead wood.
2 
Define cavity. 
3 
Discuss the comparison of cell structure with a honeycomb. 
4 
The interior of a cell is made up of tiny, specialised parts called organelles. What happened  
to the internal organelles of the cork cells Hooke studied? Where did they go?
Intense work on cell theory only started in the first half of the 19th century. It is likely that the lack of improved 
microscopes and a reluctance to take on new ideas caused a delay in research into cells. In 1831 Robert Brown 
(1773–1858), a Scottish botanist, recorded the existence of the nucleus in a range of plant cells. A German botanist, 
Matthias Schlieden (1804–81), stated in 1838 that plants are composed of cells. Theodor Schwann (1810–82), a 
German physiologist, advanced a theory in 1839 that animals were also composed of cells. Schlieden and Schwann 
were not the first people to come up with the concept of cells, but put forward their ideas with clarity and reasoning.

Most plant and animal cells are less than 0.000 02 m in diameter and are not visible to the unaided eye. It has 
taken the development of microscopes to enable the close study of cells in order to support cell theory. In scientific 
method, once a hypothesis is stated (in this case, that all life is made up of cells), it is tested. Scientists have been 
using sophisticated microscopes to look closely at living things for many years. All of their findings have reinforced 
the hypothesis of The Cell Theory.
1 
Define support. 
2 
Define hypothesis. 
Nowadays, two main types of microscopes are used. The light microscope uses  
white (visible) light and glass lenses. The electron microscope uses a beam of  
electrons focused on a fluorescent screen or photographic plate to produce  
an image.
3 
Below are listed the three important attributes of microscopes.  
Define each one.
a magnification 
b resolution 
c contrast 
By the 1880s, microscopes existed that had magnifications in the range of 500  
to 1000 times and very good resolution. Many parts of cells are transparent and  
are difficult to see. 
Scientists developed methods to increase the contrast between parts of cells. 
One method used was to add a dye to a cell. Not all parts of the cell take up the dye to the same extent, and some 
cell structures become coloured more strongly than others.
Staining cells with dye kills the cells, which means that the processes occurring within cells cannot be monitored if 
the cells are stained. Phase contrast microscopy (introduced in 1934 by the Dutch physicist Frits Zernike) increases 
the contrast between living cells and their surroundings, so staining can be avoided. Electron microscopes can 
magnify up to 100 000 times, but cannot be used to study living things because they look at specimens that are in  
a vacuum.

searchText:
A microscope is needed to see cells.

Cells need to be small in order to work efficiently.

The cell is to biology as the atom is to chemistry – cells are the elementary structural unit of all living
organisms.

New cells are formed by the division of living cells.

Cell division produces new cells for growth, repair and reproduction.

We each began life as one cell and now we are make up of 100,000,000,000,000 cells and each
second of our life we make 50,000,000 new cells.



Using the microscope to view cells

        Switch on light or adjust the mirror to get good light.
        Place a small piece of onion epidermis on the glass slide.
        Place a drop of water on the plant tissue.
        Lower the cover slip gently onto the slide to cover the plant tissue.
        Place the slide on the stage of microscope.
        Turn the lowest power objective lens (X4) until it is ‘clicked’ into position.
        Turn the coarse focussing wheel to bring the lens as close to the slide as possible.
        Look through eyepiece and turn coarse focusing knob to slowly move lens away from slide
         until plant tissue is in focus.
        Observe the plant cells and move the slide to scan the tissue.
        Before increasing the magnification, move the area of greatest interest into the very centre of
         your field of view.
        Click the next higher objective lens (X10) into position.
        Only turn the fine focusing wheel to sharpen the image.
        Note the greater detail – draw a labelled diagram of part of the tissue.
        Before increasing the magnification, move the area of greatest interest into the very centre of
         your field of view.
        Click the highest objective lens (X40) into position.
        Only turn the fine focusing wheel to sharpen the image.
        Note the greater detail – draw a labelled diagram of a plant cell.

When finished: click the lowest power objective into position and turn the coarse focusing wheel to
move the objective as far away as possible from the stage.

Iodine may be used to stain plant cells for microscopic examination.

Methylene blue is used to stain animal cells e.g. human cheek cells.



Cell structures

Structures common to plant and animal cells
Nucleus: has DNA, the genetic material; controls cell structure activity.
Chromosomes: made of DNA and protein, found in nucleus.
Gene: a particular section of DNA, which controls a definite inherited trait.
Cell membrane: surrounds the cell keeping all its contents close together; controls movement of
substances in and out of cell keeping its chemistry perfect.
Cytoplasm: a complex sticky solution where many chemical reactions take place.

Structures in plant cells but not in animal cells
Cell wall: made of cellulose, strengthens and supports cell; prevents the cell bursting.
Chloroplast: photosynthesis, present in green plant cells; contains green plant pigment chlorophyll,
which absorbs the light energy needed for photosynthesis.
Vacuole: stores water, food, minerals and waste; plays a support role in the soft non-woody parts of
plants; the liquid of the vacuole is called cell sap.

Note: plant cells are generally much bigger than animal cells; plant cells store excess glucose as
starch.
 Cell types

Plants and animals contain many different types of cells, which are adapted for their function – the
human body has about 300 different types of cells.

Muscle cells: contract to cause movement – move bones, move food along the gut, move blood along
the blood vessels.
Nerve cells: their long fibres carry messages directly and quickly to their target.
Red blood corpuscles: contain haemoglobin to transport oxygen efficiently.
White blood cell: give protection against disease causing organisms and cancer.

Leaf cells: contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Root hair cells: have large surface area to take up water and minerals from soil.
Parenchyma cells: store starch.
Epidermal cells: protect the surface of leaves.



Tissues

A tissue is a group of similar cells specialised to carry out a particular job.

Muscle cells: form muscle tissue for movement.
Nerve cells: form nerve tissue for rapid transfer of information.
Bone: plays an important role in protection, support and movement in the body.
Blood: transports materials throughout the body – can be considered to be a complex tissue as it has
a number of different cell types.

Xylem tissue transports water in a plant.
Phloem tissue transports food in a plant.
Photosynthetic tissue in a leaf produces food for the plant.
Parenchyma is storage tissue and holds food in reserve for later use.



Organs

An organ is a group of tissues working together to carry out a particular job.

Heart: a mixture of muscle and nervous tissue – its job is to pump the blood.
Lungs: their job is to absorb oxygen and excrete carbon dioxide.
Stomach: its job is to digest protein plus absorb water, glucose and minerals.

searchText:
Cells

Scientists have been dissecting plants and animals for centuries to
try and find out how they work, and answer some of the many
questions we have about living things and, more specifically,
ourselves. Over 300 years ago a scientist, Robert Hooke, first used
the term ‘cell’ to describe the tiny building blocks observed in a
piece of cork. We now know that cells are the basic units of all
living things, and although their appearance, shape, size and purpose
may vary, they are responsible for the functions that keep all
organisms alive. So a cell is the smallest part that we can call life.

Give the meaning of the following words:
1. dissecting ________________________________________
2. specifically _______________________________________
3. term ____________________________________________
4. tiny _____________________________________________
5. basic ____________________________________________
6. purpose __________________________________________
7. vary _____________________________________________
8. functions _________________________________________
9. organisms ________________________________________

Which words or phrases can be replaced with the following:
 1. cutting open ______________________________________
 2. function _________________________________________
 3. many years _______________________________________
 4. in particular ______________________________________
 5. very small _______________________________________

 7. differ ___________________________________________

2.   In which century did Robert Hooke first use the term cell?
     _______________________________________________

3.   How do cells vary? _______________________________

4.   What is the function of cells?________________________

Equipment per team (team size 3-4 students)

       cups.

      When a ball lands in a cup, the throwing team answers the question in the cup.

      If they can’t answer the question correctly, they must do the forfeit. The cup is
       then taken away.

      If they answer the question correctly the team scores 4 points. If they do the
       forfeit they score 2 points. If they fail to do either the other team gains 3 points.

      The game ends when a team has had all its cups removed.

      The winning team is the team with most points.

      As a follow up, ask students to keep the questions that they couldn’t answer in
       a pile. They then need to use their notes to find the correct answers. Build up a
       definitive set of answers as a class.

32
Interpreting data in Senior Biology
© Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2010
Chronic heart failure 
15
IntroductIon 
A chronic disease is one that has been present for a long time, e.g. 3 months or more. Chronic heart failure (CHF) is a 
condition in which the heart is no longer able to pump blood efficiently through the body. Although there have been 
advances in treating the disease, it remains a major public health problem in industrialised nations. This disease reduces 
quality of life considerably and has a high mortality rate. Treatments include diet, exercise, pharmaceuticals and surgery 
including heart transplants.
Aim 
To investigate and analyse some causes and treatments of CHF.
data
describing the data
1 
List the risk factors for CHF that are most likely to be related to a person’s lifestyle.
 
 
2 
List three symptoms of CHF.
 
 
3 
State two lifestyle modifications not mentioned in evidence box 3 that could alleviate or help prevent CHF.
 
 
Evidence box 1 
Risk factors include:
• alcohol abuse
• diabetes 
• disease of the heart muscle (cardiomyopathy)
• heart valve disease 
• high blood pressure
• obesity
• previous heart attack (myocardial infarction)
• smoking.
Evidence box 2 
Symptoms include:
• shortness of breath
• impaired kidney function 
• impaired liver function 
• congestion of the lungs
• intestines become less efficient
• eventual death.
Evidence box 3 
Lifestyle modifications include:
• reduced total intake of food, if obese
• reduced intake of sodium and saturated animal fats
• moderate exercise.
These changes are more important in preventing CHF than 
treating it, but can help in most cases.
Evidence box 4 
Pharmaceuticals include:
• ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors, which  
slow the loss of heart pumping ability
• diuretics to reduce excess liquid in body
• digitalis improves strength of heart’s contractions.
Drugs can both improve the quality of life and extend a 
patient’s life. 
Evidence box 5 
Surgical techniques

3. Where are valves found in the circulatory system?
Describe their function. (4)

Valves are found in the heart, where they stop blood
flowing in the wrong direction. They are also found in
blood vessels. In blood vessels, they do exactly the same

5. How does a molecule of oxygen get from the capillaries
in the lungs to a muscle cell in your big toe? (4)

It’s quite easy. The oxygen gets into the blood in the lungs
and then it travels along the arteries to the big toe before
going into a capillary and escaping through its thin walls
into a nearby muscle cell!


*6. Compare the structure and function of veins and
arteries. (4)

Veins take blood into the heart, but arteries take blood
away from the heart. Veins have a big lumen and a thin
wall, and the blood travels through them at low pressure.
Arteries have a thicker wall because they carry blood at
much higher pressures.


7. Compare and contrast the structures and functions of
the two sides of the heart. (6)

Both sides of the heart have two chambers. Each side has
an atrium at the top and a ventricle at the bottom. In the
left atrium, blood enters from the lungs through the
pulmonary vein and then passes through the left ventricle
and out through the aorta. The left side of the heart pumps
blood to the body. The right side of the heart has a very
similar job, but it gets its blood from the body through the
vena cava and sends it to the lungs via the pulmonary
artery. Basically, both sides are pumps but they go to
different places.

He may score one mark for mentioning that they are found in the heart and that they
stop blood flowing in the wrong direction. Although he has correctly said that they are
found in blood vessels, he has not said which type of blood vessel (veins) they are
found in. Also, just saying they do the same job is not sufficient. He again needs to
refer to their function, saying that they stop the backflow of blood.

                                           Circulatory system peer assessment
4) Although Donald’s answer is brief, he would score 2 marks.

He has correctly identified that blood enters at the right atrium. His answer would be
better if he described this as being at the top of the heart and that blood then flows
downwards before being pumped out from the right ventricle. He could gain an extra
mark for mentioning passing valves, or for mentioning the blood vessels that take the
blood in (vena cava) and out (pulmonary artery) of this side.

5) A lot of Donald’s answer repeats what was in the question. He would be lucky to
score even one mark.

Donald needs to recognise that the red blood cells carrying the oxygen go back to the
left hand side of the heart where they are pumped through the aorta into arteries.
They enter capillaries (he may score a mark here) and the oxygen diffuses out to the
muscle cells.

6) Quite a good answer! Donald would likely score three marks.

Donald scores marks for correctly comparing the function of arteries and veins. It is
good to see that Donald has used techniques that he has been taught to remember
the function – it doesn’t matter if the examiners see this! Donald has also correctly
compared much of their structure (e.g. thickness of wall). He could improve the
answer by mentioning that veins have valves. He could also compare the size of the
artery lumen to that of the vein.

7) The content of Donald’s answer is reasonable. He would score 4 marks.

In 6-mark questions, the responses are marked in bands of 1-2, 3-4, 5-6. In each
band, literacy is also considered.

He does give some similarities between the structure of each side (e.g. atria,
ventricles), so he fulfils the requirements for band 1-2.

To get 3-4 marks, differences in structure and function would be expected. Donald
has correctly given detail of each associated blood vessel that supplies the heart or
takes its blood away (e.g. aorta, pulmonary vessels). He has also stated the function
of the left hand side of the heart. However, he does not give the function of the right
hand side, simply stating that it pumps blood elsewhere.

Although Donald does not use capital letters properly, his spelling is very good and he
makes good use of a range of scientific words. Hence, he is awarded 4 marks.

To get 5-6 marks, a full and logical comparison would be expected. For this, the
omission already identified would be expected. Also, the inclusion of oxygenated and
deoxygenated blood would be expected as well as the presence of valves as being a
similar structure in both sides.

Overall, Donald would score (at most) 16 marks.

1 
Read the following passage and write meanings for the 
terms in italics (listed below). 
Asexual reproduction involves only one parent. The parent 
duplicates its own genetic material, followed by the rest of the 
cell contents. The cell then divides to produce offspring known as 
daughter cells, which are genetically identical to the parent. Clones 
can be defined as plants or animals grown from a single cell or 
plants grown from a single multicellular plant. Clones can also be 
defined as a group of organisms that are genetically identical.
Cloning can be used by humans to grow plants when it is difficult 
to get plants to grow ‘normally’, for example, when seeds are 
difficult to obtain, when mass production of genetically identical 
plants is desired and to increase numbers of a plant threatened by extinction. The Wollemi Pine is an example 
of a plant that exists only in minute numbers. Thought to have died out millions of years ago, a small number of 
specimens were discovered in 1994 and since then scientists have been trying to increase its numbers. Seeds have 
been collected, but only a very small percentage of these have proved viable. Scientists have also tried to increase 
the numbers of Wollemi Pine by taking cuttings and by using tissue culture. In tissue culture, a small piece of tissue 
is taken from a growing part of the plant (e.g. a bud or root). This piece of tissue is then cultured in a medium 
containing the required nutrients. The cells in the tissue replicate and a group of cells is formed. These are treated 
with plant hormones and develop into seedlings. These seedlings are clones of the original parent. They can then be 
grown into plants.

extra parts to their digestive systems between the oesophagus and the stomach. These

After eating, the cow rests and ruminates. Rumination involves bringing back the

Because they go through the process of rumination, cows and other animals that chew

The function of the digestive system is to break down food into particles that are small enough to be absorbed

contrast, meat and fleshy fruits and vegetables are generally easier to digest and pass through the digestive

Designed for the job


  Imagine a clear plastic bag, or a balloon or a bubble, filled with water.
  Inside you push a squash ball, a few dried beans and some cling film, all
  scrunched up. You have made a model of a typical animal cell. Add a few
  dried peas, a smaller balloon, squeeze the whole lot into a cardboard box
  and you have a typical plant cell!

  However, most animal and plant cells do not look like typical cells
  because they have special jobs to do. Think of the Olympics and the
  competitors for each sport: a cyclist looks different from a weightlifter; a
  basketball player would not make a very good gymnast!

  Different cells have different jobs. In plants, palisade cells, found in the
  upper part of leaves, are green. The green colour is due to chlorophyll, a
  chemical essential for photosynthesis. The job of a leaf cell is to produce
  glucose from carbon dioxide and water using energy from the sun. A root
  hair cell is long and thin. This gives it a large surface area. Its job is to
  absorb water and minerals from the soil. Stomata are formed from two
  curved cells, rather like your lips. They can move to create an opening
  between them. This enables air to move in and out of the leaf.

  Animals too have a wide variety of cells. Sperm cells resemble tadpoles:
  both have long, lashing tails to help them swim. Sperm cells have plenty
  of mitochondria. Mitochondria provide energy for the long swim to the egg
  cell. The role of a sperm cell is to fertilise an egg. Under a microscope,
  nerve cells look like trees in winter. At one end, surrounding the nucleus,
  are lots of ‘branches’. There is a long, thin ‘trunk’ ending in a cluster of
  ‘roots’.
  The function of a nerve cell is to receive and pass on messages, in the
  form of electrical signals, to different parts of the body. Red blood cells
  are shaped like ‘donut’ peaches. They do not have a nucleus because
  they are designed to carry as much oxygen as possible. They are packed
  with a special, oxygen-carrying molecule called haemoglobin.

Achieve!
Improving cell theory
Scientists improve their theories as new evidence is collected. The idea of cells changed 
over a long time as more evidence was found.
 
l  1665 – Robert Hooke first saw and named cells. Possibly the first theory would have 
begun as: There are some cells in living things.
 
l  1839 – Matthias Schlieden and Theodor Schwann revised the original idea to read: 
All living things are made from cells.
 
l  Soon after, Schlieden and Schwann decided that the theory should be revised to 
include a reference to the materials that cells make, such as bone matrix.
 
l  1858 – Rudolf Virchow added the idea that all cells come from other cells. He is now 
believed to have copied this idea from Robert Remak. 
The theory was then very close to the definition we use today: 
All living things are made from cells and their products. All cells come from other cells.
Science is open to change, but the changes will only be accepted if they are very strongly 
supported and not able to be disproved.

Aim
• To investigate how starch, glucose molecules and water molecules diffuse through a dialysis tubing
which is acting as a differently permeable membrane.
• To observe the process of osmosis when potato cells are placed in hypertonic, hypotonic and
isotonic salt solutions.
Equipment
14
D I F F U S I O N
A N D
O S M O S I S
Diffusion is the passage of molecules from a region of high concentration through a semi-permeable membrane
to a region of low concentration. Osmosis is the passage of water from a region of high water concentration to
a region of low water concentration. Semi-permeable membranes are very thin layers of material which
allow smaller molecules such as water, potassium iodide and glucose to pass through them, but prevent larger
starch molecules from passing through. In a hypertonic solution, the solute concentration is higher than that
in cells. In a hypotonic solution, the solute concentration is below that in cells. In an isotonic solution, the
solute concentration is equal inside and outside the cell.
In this experiment, dialysis tubing is used to demonstrate the action of a differently permeable membrane. When
plant cells are placed in hypertonic solution, they lose water and become flaccid. When plant cells are placed
in hypotonic solution, they gain water and become turgid. In an isotonic solution, cells are unchanged
because the amount of water leaving the cell is equal to the amount of water entering the cell.

Food is digested in the digestive system with the help of digestive enzymes. These enzymes are secreted by
the cells lining the inner surfaces of various glands of the digestive system. Amylase from the salivary glands
and the pancreas digest starch to maltose in the mouth and small intestine. The optimum pH for pancreatic
amylase is 6.7 to 7.0. Proteases are enzymes that break down proteins to polypeptides. Pepsin is secreted in
the stomach and its optimum pH is 2. Trypsin is secreted by the pancreas and its optimum pH is 7–8. Fat is
digested by pancreatic lipase in the intestine into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile from the liver emulsifies fats,
so that lipase has an increased surface to work on. This action takes place in the small intestine. The optimum
temperature for all these enzymes is 37°C.

This is a domino style activity about digestive enzymes and related concepts.
There are 32 cards, allowing it to be used with a whole class. The activity could
also be done individually, in pairs or in small groups to produce a complete
ordered set of cards.

Students may be asked to start by working out the ‘answer’ (left side) on their
card as all vowels are missing – this might be useful as a quick settling activity.
The domino activity can then begin.

To allow for differentiation, some of the harder cards have been shaded
red/pink, whereas the simpler ones are shaded green. To make it more
challenging the gaps showing where the missing vowels are could be removed.

When attempting this activity, students should have already studied the
digestive system (including the roles of the organs, the role of enzymes and
bile and the adaptations of the small intestine).

Find a Friend: The Digestive System Activity

Teacher Instructions

This activity is good for consolidating or checking learning in a plenary or for revision.
Cards can be printed out A4 or A5 and laminated for repeated use.

How to use:
There are 3 types of card:

orange - diagram (with a part labelled as X);
blue - name of a part;
green - description or function of a part.

Give each student in the class one of the cards. This can be random or differentiated by giving easier
cards to weaker students and more tricky cards to higher ability students. Unused cards can be put onto
a table for students to go to if they can't find their ‘friends’. Where there are more students than cards,
give one card to a pair of students.

Students should then move around the room and find their two ‘friends’ with the matching diagram,

searchText:
BOOK 1; CHARACTERISTICS OF LIVING THINGS

The discovery of the cell

The first cell ever observed and illustrated was the empty, dead shell of a once living plant. In 1665 the English
scientist Robert Hooke (1635-1703) used a reasonably new invention, the microscope, to look closely at a thinly
sliced piece of cork. The empty ‘shell’ of what was once living plant matter brought to mind tiny rooms called
cells (from the Latin, cellula, meaning ‘small compartment’). Some books state that Hooke named them after
the celis of monasteries, while others cite the cells of honeycombs, but whatever inspired him, Hooke named
them well.

It took another 170 years before the living contents of cells were discovered, Bohemian physiologist Johannes
von Purkinje (1787-1869) recognised that cells had to be composed of a living matter since they formed a
part of living matter.* He named the matter protoplasm (proto first, plasm form). French scientist Felix
Dujardin (1801-1860) eventually observed the protoplasm. Dujardin called it sarcode, from the Greek sarkos,
meaning ‘flesh’.

* Matthias Schieiden (1804-1881) confirmed this for plants in 1838.

Not long after Dujardin observed the protoplasm, German scientist Theodor Schwann (1810-1882) made the
first really detailed inspection of animal cells. It soon became clear that both plants and animals possess cells,
each with structures that were unique to the group and many that were common to both. It was Schwann who
showed us that every tissue of every organism is made of cells. Prior to this many people recognised that cells
formed a part of an organism, but they did not realise that every structure could be reduced to cellular
components. It was then understood that the husk-like walls, which formed the once living cells of the tree, had
created the cork.

Dissection is a technique used to study the internal organs of a dead animal. It shows the internal structure of
the animal, how the tissues look and feel, and how they are interrelated. All mammals possess similar organs
and systems whether they are small or large in size. To understand the structure and functions of our own
systems, it is helpful to dissect smaller mammals such as rats.
As rats are herbivorous, they have four long, sharp incisors for gnawing and twelve molars for chewing. They
have no canines or premolars. The toothless space between the incisors and molars is called the diastema. Their
digestive system is similar to that of humans except that they have a proportionally longer small intestine, a
large caecum to digest cellulose and no gall bladder. There are no differences between human and rat excretory
systems. The female rats have a V-shaped uterus that can hold many foetuses, whereas the human uterus is
smaller and usually holds only one foetus at a time.

The sheep’s pluck consists of the lungs, heart and liver. The heart is divided into four chambers: right atrium,
right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle. The right side of the heart is separated from the left side by a
thick muscular wall called a septum. The left atrium-ventricle valve is known as the bicuspid or mitral valve.
The right atrium-ventricle valve is known as the tricuspid valve. This valve allows blood to flow only in one
direction: from the atria to the ventricles. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the
superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava. The blood then flows to the right ventricle and from there it
is carried to the lungs by the pulmonary arteries.
The lungs are pale pink in colour and feel firm and spongy. The left lung is divided into two lobes: the upper
lobe and the lower lobe. The right lung is divided into three lobes: the upper lobe, middle lobe and lower lobe.
When humans breathe in, air enters through the nostrils and goes to the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi
and bronchioles and finally to small sacs called alveoli. Exchange of gases takes place by diffusion between
the blood in the capillaries and air in the alveoli. Oxygen rich blood is carried back to the left atrium by the
pulmonary veins. The blood then enters the left ventricle and is pumped out of the heart via the aorta.

Comparing a chemical kinetic reaction with an enzyme catalysed reaction




The graph shows to types of reaction. To explain the difference between these two
types of reaction, we could use the idea of a room with wrapped sweets scattered
across the floor to demonstrate an enzyme-catalysed reaction. Imagine a crowd of
children are released into the room. Their job is not to eat the sweets but to unwrap
them as quickly as possible, leaving the chocolates and wrappers on the floor.

Initially, the more sweets there are in the room the faster they will be unwrapped.
However, there comes a point, quite soon, when the rate of unwrapping begins to level
off despite there being more sweets in the room. This is because the children are
occupied whilst they unwrap a sweet. During this time they cannot move on to
another sweet.

In the more 'usual' chemical reaction the reaction relies on the substrate particles
colliding with one another. The higher the concentration of particles the greater the
chance is of a collision.

Activity 4 - student sheet

Enzymes have all the same properties as chemical catalysts. They lower the amount
of energy needed to get the reaction started (activation energy), as well as increasing
the speed of the reaction once it has started.

However, enzymes are more effective at this than chemical catalysts e.g. the
decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), is accelerated 3 x 104 times in the
presence of ferric ions which act as a catalyst; but it is accelerated 1 x 10 8 times in the
presence of the enzyme catalase.

Chemical catalysts tend to work on a wide range of reactions, whereas enzymes are
usually very selective and only bind to one specific substrate.

Like catalysts, enzymes are not permanently altered by the reaction and can be re-
used. Almost all consist of proteins which are large molecules with a complex
structure. Many catalysts are ions, elements or quite simple inorganic compounds.
Because they are produced by living organisms, enzymes work best at relatively low
temperatures. Catalysts generally require high temperatures or pressure to be
effective.

Catalysts work in two main ways. In one, the reactants stick to the surface of the
catalyst (active site) and move around increasing the chance that they will collide and
so react e.g. platinum catalyst in the catalytic converter of a car. In the second way,
the catalyst combines with a chemical to make a new compound. This is unstable and
quickly breaks down releasing a different new compound and the catalyst. This is also
how many enzymes work. Such a catalytic reaction is responsible for the depletion of
ozone in the atmosphere.

uterus. When this happens, the woman is considered pregnant.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
18
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Single lens to compound microscope
The first microscope was used in the 1500s. Over time, 
microscope technology has steadily improved. As the 
technology improved so did knowledge about microbes – 
living things that are too small to see with the naked eye.
 
l  At first, specimens were magnified with single 
lenses. Some of the scientists involved at the time 
were Sacharias Jansen in around 1595, Robert Hooke 
in 1665 and Antonj van Leeuwenhoek in 1653.
 
l  Hooke and Jansen later used two lenses in a row, 
sometimes inside a barrel. These were the first 
compound microscopes.
 
l  Hooke was the first to try shining a light directly onto the specimen.
 
l  Van Leeuwenhoek was first to see pond life protozoa, spirogyra and sperm of 
many animals.
 
l  Hooke made very thin slices of cork that let light through, and saw little 
compartments, which he named cells.
+ 1 Choose the correct word or phrase in each pair.
Microscopes
The lens of a [microscope/camera] lets only a tiny amount of [light/water] through. Light 
can be blocked by using too much of a specimen or a slice from a specimen that is too 
[wide/thick]. Robert Hooke cut thin slices of cork that let light pass through so he could 
see the cells. He also worked out a way to light up the specimen with a small reflecting  
[lamp/light globe].
Antonj van Leeuwenhoek used tiny lenses made by melting and pulling glass into 
bead shapes. He sometimes used [one/two] lenses – one in each hand – to get a [clearer/
brighter] view. This was like a [compound/simple] microscope without the barrel. 
Improvements in lenses and microscopes over [tens/hundreds] of years show how the 
human endeavours of science and technology develop alongside each other.

7.12 Science in context: Fungal cells can save lives
7.12 Test your skills and capabilities
Communicating with your audience
When you are sick, you visit the doctor. Doctors have many years of training to ask questions, observe disease symptoms, diagnose disease and decide if medication is needed. Doctors need to communicate their critical thinking to patients that do not have the same training or understanding. Doctors change the words about concepts so that their audience understands them.
Use your knowledge of viruses like influenza and how antibiotics kill bacteria to create a brochure that explains why a patient with influenza cannot be treated with antibiotics. Use the following hints to help you.
Before you begin:
Decide the age of the person who will read the brochure. (1 mark)

Describe how much they know about cells and viruses. (1 mark)

1 
Read the following passage and explain what is meant by each term in bold (listed below).  
Australian conditions are not always ideal for the growth of seedlings. There can be prolonged drought, high 
temperatures and bushfires. In order for plants to germinate at the ‘correct’ time, i.e. have the greatest chance 
for the seeds to eventually grow into plants, many seeds remain dormant until special conditions occur. The 
mechanisms that inhibit seed from germination can be a chemical present or a thick seed coat. Often people who 
wish to germinate native Australian seeds have to replicate the conditions of the plant’s natural habitat.
Some seeds have a hard seed coat and this needs to be abraded using a substance such as sandpaper. Seeds with 
their coats treated in this way germinate more quickly than untreated seeds.   
Seeds (such as members of the Acacia species) can also be treated by immersion in boiling water. Many seeds 
from areas that are prone to grass fires may need to experience direct exposure to fire and smoke. Fire-activated 
seeds are particularly interesting. A fire must reach a certain intensity before the seed coat will burst open. The fire 
that achieves this intensity will also have been severe enough to destroy the parent plant. This strategy prevents 
seedlings from competing with parents. It also ensures that the species will survive after a severe fire. 
The chemicals preventing germination can be removed by a process called leaching. Here the seeds are suspended 
in a solution and the chemicals are gradually extracted from the seeds.

CHAPTER 3: Cells

History of the light
microscope
Student: ........................................................................................................ Class: ............................................................

Read the following text and answer the questions that follow.

Before the invention of the microscope, biologists did not know
that living things were made of cells. The first light microscopes
were built from spectacle lenses and tubes by Zaccharias Janssen
and his father Hans in Holland between 1590 and 1610. In 1665,
Robert Hooke used a simple microscope that magnified by 30 to
observe thin slices of cork. He found structures that reminded him
of the boxes or cells of a honeycomb, and so he called them cells.
   Hooke examined other plant tissue in later experiments and
observed that some of these cells contained a fluid. In the 1670s
and 1680s Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using a single lens
microscope, observed cellular life forms (or protozoa) in seawater
and rainwater. He identified microbes such as yeast and bacteria.
His lenses were superior to Hooke’s because he had trained as a
lens grinder and polisher. Magnifications of about 270 were
achieved due to the great radius of curvature of his lenses. (The
radius of curvature of a lens is a measure of how curved it is.)
   It was not until the middle of the nineteenth century that
significant improvements were made to optical microscopes so that
greater magnification and resolution could be achieved. The
American Charles Spencer developed a company that produced
light microscopes with magnification up to 1250. By using blue
light, the magnification was increased to 5000. Throughout the
twentieth century, further improvements in lens manufacture,
improving contrast and the use of specialised dyes to stain tissue
led to improved images of living matter.
