searchText: The Compound Microscope and Calculations The magnifying power of the eyepiece,(a.k.a.: ocular) is (10 x) The magnifying power of the low-power objective is: (40 x) The magnifying power of the medium-power objective is: (100 x) The magnifying power of the high-power objective is: (400 x) Calculations Measuring with the Microscope It is important to know the dimensions of the object being observed under the microscope. 1. To calculate the power of the microscope Multiply the power of the eyepiece, (10x) by the power of the objective lens used (4x, 10x, 40x) Magnifying Power of = Magnifying power of x Magnifying Power Microscope the eyepiece of the objective The Magnifying power of the microscope when the: a. Low power objective is in place = x = b. Medium-power objective is in place = x = c. High power objective is in place = x = Complete the following table: Magnification power of Magnification power of Magnification power of the ocular (eyepiece) the objective the microscope 10 x 4x 10 x 400 x 4x 60 x 15 x 10 x 10 x 100 x 40 x 600 x The Metric System The system of measurement that is used throughout most of the world, including Canada, is La Système international d’unités (SI), commonly called the metric system. This system was developed in France in 1791 and was updated in 1960. The metric system is based on multiples of 10. Each type of measurement (length, mass, volume, energy, and so on) has a base unit. Larger and smaller units are named by adding a prefix to the base unit. For example, the basic unit of length is the metre. The prefix is kilo- means multiplied by 1000, so one kilometer is 1000 metre. The prefix milli- means divided by 1000, so one millimeter is one thousandth of a metre. 1 The table shows the most commonly used metric prefixes. Prefix Symbol Relationship to the Base Unit 9 giga- G 10 = 1 000 000 000 mega- M 106 = 1 000 000 kilo- k 103 = 1000 hecto- h 102 = 100 deca- da 101 = 10 100 = 1 deci- d 10-1 = 0.1 centi- c 10-2 = 0.01 milli- m 10-3 = 0.001 micro- F 10-6 = 0.000 001 nano- n 19-9 = 0.000 000 001 Conversion factors: 1 cm = 10 mm 1 mm = 1000 Fm 1 cm = 10 000 Fm = 10 -2 m = 10 -3 m = 10 -6 m Complete the following conversions: a) 2.7 cm = ___________ mm b) 1.5 mm = ___________ Fm c) 26.1 mm = _______________Fm d) 19.2 cm = ___________ mm e) 0.30 mm = ______________Fm f) 4.2 Fm = ______________ mm g) 30 mm = ______________ cm h) 10 Fm = _______________ cm i) 0.0574 cm = ___________ Fm j) 645 Fm = _______________ mm 2 The circle of light seen through the microscope is called the field of view. It is the area of a slide that you can observe. The distance across the field of view is called the field diameter. The actual measurements for the field diameters of objectives lenses on the microscopes are known, they are listed below on the table: objective lens Field diameter Field diameter (mm) (Fm) 4x 4.5 10 x 1.8 1800 40 x 0.45 2. To calculate the actual size of the object a. Place objects at the edge of the field of view. b. Estimate how many of the objects fit across the diameter of the field of view. c. Record the objective lens that has been used and the diameter of this objective lens (from the table above). Calculate the actual size by using the following formula: Actual Size of Specimen = field diameter # of specimens fitting across the field diameter Example 1: A student was examining strands of his hair under a microscope at medium power, (∴field diameter = 1800 µm ). He estimated that when measured width-wise, 20 strands of his hair would fit across the diameter of the field of view. What is the actual width of each hair strand? Actual Size of Specimen = field diameter # of specimens fitting across the field diameter = 1800 µm 20 = 90 µm ∴ each hair is 90 µm in width Example 2: A cheek cell as observed through the 4x objective lens, (∴field diameter = 4.5 mm ). The number of cheek cell that were estimated to fit across the diameter of field of view were 3.5 Estimate the actual width of the cheek cell. State your answer in mm. (Answer: width of the cheek cell = 1.3 mm) 3 3. To calculate the magnification of a drawing Magnification: the comparison of the actual size of the object with the size of its image is referred to as magnification. To calculate the magnification of a drawing a. Record the actual size of the specimen from the above calculations. b. With a ruler measure the length of the drawing of the specimen in the same direction as you estimated the size of the object. This is the drawing size. c. Calculate the magnification of the drawing using the following formula: Magnification of drawing = width of drawing (measured with a ruler) Actual size of specimen Example 1 (See: Calculation 2, Example 1 above) A student was examining strands of his hair under a microscope at medium power, (∴field diameter = 1800 µm ). Answer: each hair is 90 µm in width. b. Next, the student made a scaled drawing of his hair. He then measured the width of his drawing. It measured 4 mm. What was the magnification of the drawing ? Magnification of drawing = width of drawing (measured with a ruler) Actual size of specimen = 4mm 90 µm = 4000 µm 90 µm = 45 ∴the diagram represents a 45X magnification of the actual specimen 4 Assignment Answer the following questions, showing all the steps. 1. searchText: Microscope Coloring http://www.biologycorner.com/worksheets/microscope_coloring.html Name: ___________________________________________ Color the Microscope Parts The most familiar type of microscope is the standard light microscope. The base (L) and arm (G) are usually one single piece of cast metal. The arm is the correct place to grip the microscope when carrying it while supporting the base with the palm of your other hand. Color the arm green and the base red. The stage (I) is the platform that supports the specimen to be observed. The stage has a hole in its center to allow light to pass through, so specimens must be positioned over the top of this hole. Color the stage blue. You can control how much light goes through the specimen by adjusting the diaphragm (K). It has a range of 1 to 5, with 5 being the most light. Color the diaphragm light green. Since any slight movement of the specimen is magnified many times, the slide is usually held down by a pair of stage clips (J). Color the stage clips gray. Light microscopes use either a bulb or a mirror (M) as their light source. Never use direct sunlight; it may damage your eyes. Color the light source yellow. The switch for this light is usually found on the base of the microscope, and sometimes on the power cord. After the light has passed through the specimen, it enters the objective lens (often called "objective" for short). The shortest of the three objectives is the scanning-power objective lens (N), and has a power of 4X. Color the 4X objective black. The second objective is the low-power objective (F), which is almost always made to produce a magnification of 10 times (10X). Color the low-power objective purple. The high-power objective lens (H) has a magnification of 40X. Draw orange stripes on the high-power objective. The body tube (C) allows the light from the objective to pass upward to form the first magnified image; that image is further magnified by the eyepiece or ocular (A). The eyepiece is usually 10X. Color the body tube brown and the ocular lens orange. The total magnification obtained is the product of the eyepiece times that of the objective lens. You can easily switch objectives by turning the rotating nosepiece (E). Color the nosepiece blue-green. The coarse adjustment knob (B) is the larger on your microscope. You will use this primarily to focus on your specimen. DO NOT USE THE COARSE ADJUSTMENT KNOB ON HIGH POWER (40X), it will crack your slide. Color this knob pink. The fine adjustment knob (D) is also for minute focusing. You use this after you have focused with the coarse adjustment knob. Color this knob tan. The top part of the microscope that supports the ocular lens and the objective lens is not labeled on your image. Color this area to match the base. QUESTIONS: 1. What two structures on the microscope will you use to focus on your specimen? __________________________________________ 2. Why should you never use the coarse adjustment knob on high power? ___________________________________________________________________________________________ 3. What will happen if you use direct sunlight to observe your specimen? ______________________________________________________________________________________ 4. Our microscopes have three objectives. What are their powers?________________________ 5. What is the magnification of the ocular lens? ____________________ 6. What is the shortest objective called? ________________________________________ 7. How do you switch objectives?____________________________________________________________ 8. Which structure controls how much light passes through the specimen?______________________ 9. You should carry the microscope by placing your palm on the _____________________ and gripping the ___________________ with your other hand. 10. How can you prevent your slide from slipping on the stage?________________________________ 1 of 2 8/29/2014 9:19 AM Microscope Coloring http://www.biologycorner.com/worksheets/microscope_coloring.html 2 of 2 8/29/2014 9:19 AM

HANDOUT 5.1-2: FUNCTIONS OF MICROSCOPE PARTS
Ocular: This is the eyepiece lens that usually magnifies by a power of 10. (Note: To determine
the power of the microscope, one multiplies the power of the ocular by the power of the
objective lens being used.)

High-power objective: It is located just above the stage. It is the longer of the objectives. Its
lens has a magnifying power usually of 43.

Low-power objective: It is located just above the stage. It is the shorter objective. Its lens has
a magnifying power usually of 10.

Stage: This is a horizontal platform just below the objectives that supports the microscope slide
for observation.

Revolving nosepiece: The objective lenses are attached to this part. It can be manually rotated
to select the objective lens that you wish to use.

Stage clips: They clamp over the edges of the microscope slide to secure it to the stage.

Diaphragm (or condenser): Located just below the stage, it can be hand adjusted to regulate
the amount of light entering the microscope. An image viewed through the microscope should
not be dark but should have plenty of light.

Mirror: This is adjusted to reflect light from the microscope lamp up into the microscope.
Although the mirror is sometimes used to regulate the amount of light entering the microscope,
this is not good technique.

Coarse adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is always used first, and it is used
only with the low-power objective.

Fine adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is used with the high-power objective
to “fine tune” the focus.

Arm: This is the back of the microscope and it is used along with the base to transport the
microscope.

Base: This is the bottom of the microscope and it is used along with the arm to transport the
microscope.

Note: Both eyes should be open when viewing through the microscope. This prevents eye
fatigue, which occurs when the non-viewing eye is kept closed. Keeping both eyes open does
take some practice, but it is highly recommended.

The history of microscopy

Ever since humans have studied the world around them, people have wanted to see things with greater detail
than the naked eye permitted. An important event that advanced the development of cell theory was the
invention of the microscope. There is some debate about specific dates and relative importance of contributions,
but the following all played a part.

In Holland, near the end of the sixteenth century, both Hans Lippershey and the father and son team of

Hans and Zacharias Janssen were credited with the invention of microscopes. Dutch clockmaker Anton van
Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723) was also recognised with inventing the first practical microscope-like instrument.
Leeuwenhoek’s device was just two lenses which, he discovered by accident, dramatically increased magnification
when placed one over the other, Robert Hooke (1635-1703) built another important microscope, Hooke’s
reflecting microscope was described in his 1665 book Micrographia, along with his illustrations of many of

the objects he examined using it.

A microscope with two or more lenses in it is a compound microscope (compound to combine or put together).
The word fens comes from the Latin word for lentil, which is the shape of a convex lens.

Marcello Malpighi (1628-1694) was an Italian physiologist who, in 1661, used a microscope to study blood
circulation. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, studied plant parts under a microscope and
discovered that plant parts are made of cells. A year later, Theodor Schwann, a German zoologist, examined
animal parts under a microscope and revealed that animal parts are also made of cells.

Around 1880 to 1890 Pasteur and Koch made many discoveries using microscopes. Louis Pasteur (1822-1896)
used the microscope for his work on yeast and bacteria while, in 1876, Robert Koch discovered the microbes
Bacillus anthracis - responsible for anthrax. For this Koch was awarded th

using two eyes; a type of microscope 
compound light microscope
a microscope with two or more lenses 
electron microscope
a microscope that uses electrons (tiny negatively charged particles) to create images 
eyepiece
where the eyes are placed when using a microscope
microscope
an instrument with lenses that is used for viewing very small objects
microscopy
the study of living things that can only be seen with the use of a microscope
monocular
using one eye; a type of microscope 
objective lens
lens in the column of a compound light microscope 
stain
substance, such as iodine, used to make cells more visible under a microscope 
stereomicroscope
a microscope with two eyepieces that uses low magnification

Modelling the circulatory system

Starter

The PowerPoint or interactive could be used as a quick labelling activity to introduce
the modelling activity.


Modelling the circulatory system

Depending on the group the students could be asked to design their own simulation
using the following resources.

Resources
    –    2 large hoops
    –    100 red and blue cards
    –    2 boxes/bucket
    –    labels for heart, lungs and cells


Task

Assign students to a role: Lungs (1 person), cells (1 person), heart (2 people to hold
hoops), blood (rest of class or a smaller group).

Arrange students around the room (refer to animation on slide 4).
Students move around to represent blood flow – picking up red cards at the lungs;
going through the hoop (heart); dropping off the red cards at the cells and picking up
blue cards; returning back through the heart (hoop) to lungs and dropping of blue
cards.
The circulation will stop when all the blue cards are at the lungs and the red cards are
at the cells.


Discussion

There are many difficulties with this model. Get the students to recognise some of
them and suggest how the model could be improved. The following questions could
be asked to stimulate discussion.

Did the model show how oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood? – oxygen
in red blood cells, carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma.

In the model circulation stopped, why does this not happen in reality? – discuss that
concentration gradients are maintained in lungs due to gas exchange and blood flow
and in cells due to respiration.

Was the movement of the blood realistic in the model? – discuss network of blood
vessels.

Ask students to draw the model and evaluate it.

Neurones and nerves
18
IntroductIon
Neurones (neurons) are nerve cells and transmit signals by electrochemical changes in their membranes. They cannot be 
seen without specialised techniques and equipment, e.g. staining and using electron microscopes. Nerves are bundles 
of neurones.
Aim
To improve knowledge of how neurones work.
Information
A neurone consists of dendrites, a cell body, an axon and the synapse. Nerve cells usually have several dendrites 
(branches) which increase in thickness as they get nearer to the cell body. Nerve signals travel from the dendrites to the 
cell body and then to axons. Axons are long and thin and often coated with an insulating layer of myelin. Nerve signals 
travel away from the cell body. A synapse is the junction between the axon of one neurone and the dendrite of the next. 
When an electrical signal reaches the end of the axon, a chemical (neurotransmitter) is released and travels across the 
junction. The dendrite that receives the neurotransmitter then sends an impulse to the cell body and the axon. Axonal 
nerve signals are called action potentials.
Nerve cells have to be stimulated before they can send off an impulse. Neurones have an ‘all or nothing’ response. Not all 
stimuli cause a response, i.e. an action potential; stimuli have to reach a ‘threshold’ or minimum value before an action 
potential is generated.

searchText:
© Learning Essentials Pty Ltd, 2004
Aim
– To stain and make wet mounts of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and note the effects of staining.
– To observe the similarities and differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Equipment
10
O B S E R V I N G
C E L L S
According to cell theory, cells are the smallest functional units of life. All living organisms are composed of cells
and cell products. Two basic types of cells are prokaryotic cells and eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic cells have a
more primitive (pro) nucleus (karyo) without a membrane. Bacteria and blue-green algae are prokaryotic cells.
Eukaryotic cells have true (eu) nuclei (karyo) enclosed by a nuclear membrane. Plant and animal cells are
eukaryotic cells.
Plant cells have cell walls and large vacuoles. Only photosynthetic cells have chloroplasts. Potato and
banana cells store starch in leucoplasts. Coloured plant cells have chromoplasts. The movement of cytoplasm
around the vacuole of a plant cell is known as cytoplasmic streaming. This enables cell products to be carried
to different parts of the cell.
Animal cells do not have any chloroplasts or cell walls. Some animal cells do not have vacuoles; if vacuoles are
present they are smaller in size. Human red blood cells do not have nuclei. This means that they have more
surface area for carrying oxygen and they bend easily when passing through fine capillaries. The red blood cells
of a frog have nuclei when they mature and divide. The white blood cells of frogs are similar to human in both
form and function.
Staining cells enables us to view cell organelles more clearly. However, the cells are killed during this process
because stains are toxic to cells.

searchText:
Understanding Biology – biotechnology and disease
©  Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
20
In 1998, the world’s first successful hand transplant was performed (using the hand of a man who died in a 
motorcycle accident). An Australian microsurgeon was one of the team of specialists involved in this ground-
breaking operation. 
The transplant required the usual treatments of immuno-suppressing drugs and other therapies. Immuno-
suppressing drugs restrain (suppress) the immune system so that it doesn’t recognise the ‘non-self’ tissue that is 
transplanted and so doesn’t attack it. This way, the body (often) accepts the ‘foreign’ tissue. However, despite the 
procedure being a technical success, no one foresaw the recipient’s emotional reaction to the surgery. This led to the 
receiver failing to take his medicine and his body completely rejected the transplanted hand. 
1 
The immediate reaction of many people upon hearing this story is surprise that someone who had lost a 
hand wouldn’t be thrilled to have a functional ‘living’ replacement. What sort of emotional problems do you 
think the recipient experienced? 
 
 
2 
For many years, science fiction stories have discussed the use of cryogenics to ‘deep freeze’ bodies of people 
who are suffering from incurable illness, planning to revive them once a cure is found. List arguments for 
and against the use of this technology. 
 
The artificial heart – A brief history
As early as the 1950s, researchers have worked on developing prototypes to replace a diseased heart. This device 
would have to be comfortable, not too large and constructed of materials unlikely to cause blood clotting. Since it is 
preferable that a patient does not undergo multiple operations, the device should also require little maintenance. The 
heart must also be able to respond to the requirements of the recipient, speeding up and slowing down as needed 
and be fully contained (sealed inside) to reduce the risk of infection.

Muscle tissue 3819525 -4281170 0 0 (which makes up muscles) can shorten to make your body move. Nervous tissue carries electrical signals between the brain and the body to control the body. searchText:
QS ts Science >:
Our Skeleton

Humans are vertebrates. This means that we have a backbone. All vertebrates have
a skeleton. A skeleton is made up of bones or cartilage (gristle) connected together
to form a semi-rigid structure. Sharks and rays have skeletons made of cartilage.
The skeleton provides support, allows movement and protects vital organs.

1 Give an example of a ‘vital organ’.

Without a skeleton we would not be able to stand upright. It allows the body to
move because many of our limbs (such as legs and arms) have joints. The main
parts of a human skeleton are the skull, ribs, vertebral column (backbone),
humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia, fibula, pelvis and scapula. There are 206
bones in the human skeleton.

The human skeleton has components other than bones, such as cartilage.
Cartilage is very tough — the end of the nose and the outer parts of the ears are
made of cartilage. Joints are where bones or cartilages join together. Ligaments
connect the joints of bones together. Tendons (sinews) join muscles to bones.

There are many types of joints. They include fixed joints which allow no
movement, such as in the skull. The bones of joints which move are covered in
cartilage (which is smooth) and have a lubricant called synovial fluid.

2 What does a ‘lubricant’ do?

Ball-and-socket joints (for instance the hip joint) are the most flexible joints. The movable bone can swivel
in many directions. Hinge joints (such as the knee) only allow the bone to move in one of two opposing
directions. Pivot joints only allow rotation. These are found in the elbow (between the bottom of the
humerus and the radius). Sliding (gliding) joints, are found in the wrist and ankle. In these joints the
surfaces of the bones slip a short distance over each ather.

Sometimes joints suffer ‘wear and tear’ and need to be dealt with by surgery. Silicones are useful materials
for some body-replacement parts. They resist acids, are flexible and are impervious to water.

Plant cells
Like animal cells, most plant cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane. Plant cells
also have a hard cell wall made of cellulose. Also like animal cells, plant cells contain tiny,
living machines called organelles. Golgi bodies and ribosomes are two organelles found in
plant cells. They have special jobs to do in the cell to help the plant grow and to keep it
healthy. Plant cells also contain large water-filled containers called vacuoles.
   Green plants contain important organelles called chloroplasts. These parts have a
chemical called chlorophyll in them. It is green. Green plants get their green colour from
the chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are involved in the way that green plants use sunlight to

Cell division
Cells do not last forever. They grow old and eventually die, so they need to be replaced.
For example, skin cells in humans get worn out and are replaced continually. The flaky bits
of dry skin that you scrub away are made of dead skin cells. Underneath this skin, healthy
new skin cells are ready to replace the lost cells.
   Cells also make living things grow bigger or stronger, by producing more of themselves.
For example, a plant grows taller and gets more leaves as new cells are made.
    To make more of themselves, cells separate into two parts that are the same. This is
called cell division. Its scientific name is mitosis.

the heart rate affects the flow of oxygen to the 
body and we could lose breath, become tired or 
show symptoms of lack of oxygen by parts of

Photosynthesis
Photosynthesis is the name we give to a special process that green plants use to make 
food using sunlight, or light energy. They use light energy to change carbon dioxide and 
water into a special sugar called glucose. Plants get their energy from glucose, and this 
energy allows them to grow and carry out all sorts of functions. 
Green plant cells contain a green chemical called chlorophyll, which traps light energy 
from the sun. During photosynthesis, water molecules are split apart using this light 
energy. The hydrogen parts of each water molecule join with carbon dioxide to make 
glucose, the special sugar that plants have as their food. The leftover oxygen part of each 
water molecule is released by the plant through its leaves.
The word photosynthesis is made up of two parts – photo means ‘light’ and synthesis 
means ‘to make something’.

IntroductIon
The chemical reaction known as photosynthesis is 
perhaps the most important reaction that occurs on Earth. 
Without it life as we know it would not exist. The reaction 
is carried out by green plants and involves the conversion 
of carbon dioxide and water into simple sugars such as 
glucose. Oxygen is also a product of the reaction, which 
needs to absorb the Sun’s energy to proceed. Chlorophyll 
is a chemical in the leaves of plants, which absorbs the 
Sun’s energy and allows this complex process to occur.

photosynthetic process.

carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

searchText: ﻿Photosynthesis: Making Energy Chloroplasts Photosynthesis is a process in which sunlight energy is used to make glucose. The site of photosynthesis is in the chloroplast (Fig 1.1) – an organelle found in the leaves of green plants. The main functions of chloroplasts are to produce food (glucose) during photosynthesis, and to store food energy. Chloroplasts contain the pigment, chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs most of the colors in the color spectrum, and reflects only green and yellow wavelengths of light. This is why we see leaves as green or yellow – because these colors are reflected into our eyes. 1. What is the primary pigment found in the chloroplast? ________________________________ Photosynthesis Glucose is another name for sugar. The molecular formula for glucose is C6H12O6. Plants make sugar by using the energy from sunlight to transform CO2 from the air with water from the ground into glucose. This process, called photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplast of the plant cell. During this process, oxygen (O2) is created as a waste product and is released into the air for us to breath. The formula for photosynthesis is: (reactants) (products) CO2 + H2O + sunlight ----> C6H12O6 + O2 This formula says that carbon dioxide + water molecules are combined with the energy from sunlight to produce sugar and oxygen. The reactants in photosynthesis (what is used) are CO2, water and sun. The plant gets water from the ground through its roots. The plant collects carbon dioxide from the air. Much of the carbon dioxide comes from living organisms that exhale (breath it out) it, but some also comes from factory smokestacks and car fumes. 7. We also use this glucose by eating plants. The oxygen produced is released into the air for us to breath. Photosynthesis is essential for all life on earth, because it provides food and oxygen. Plants are considered autotrophs because unlike us humans, they can make their own food using this process. 13. What is produced in photosynthesis? _____________________________________________ 14. searchText:
Photosynthesis word challenge
Teaching notes
The aim of this challenge is to make links between a word, image or sound
prompt and the topic of photosynthesis.
The activity helps students explore and extend their understanding of
photosynthesis. It is also useful to highlight misconceptions.
The activity is described here with some examples.
Prior learning: Leaf structure, testing for starch, process and word equation
for photosynthesis.


Running the activity
Students work in groups of two or three.
To keep things moving, have a time limit on responses. Use Teachit Timer (free
to all) to structure the session.
At its simplest:
Students are shown a word prompt and each group has to make a connection
between it and the topic of photosynthesis.
To add more challenge:
      Generate a random number, between one and twelve.
      Select a structure card from a set of three, 'Words', 'Connections’ or
       'Steps'.
The structure cards give the following instructions:
      Words - make a link to photosynthesis using the specified number of
       words.
      Connections - make the specified number of links between the word
       prompt and photosynthesis.
      Steps - using the specified number of short sentences or phrases (joined
       by words such as 'because') get from the word prompt to photosynthesis.


For example:

Word prompt                       Animal
Random number                       2
Structure card                    Steps

In this round, students must link the word 'animal' to the topic of
photosynthesis in two steps.
E.g 'a rabbit' (one step) 'because it eats plants which carry out photosynthesis'
(second step)

two dice.

searchText: Comparing Plant And Animal Cells http://khanacademy.org/video?v=Hmwvj9X4GNY Plant Cells shape - most plant cells are squarish or rectangular in shape. amyloplast (starch storage organelle)- an organelle in some plant cells that stores starch. Amyloplasts are found in starchy plants like tubers and fruits. cell membrane - the thin layer of protein and fat that surrounds the cell, but is inside the cell wall. The cell membrane is semipermeable, allowing some substances to pass into the cell and blocking others. cell wall - a thick, rigid membrane that surrounds a plant cell. This layer of cellulose fiber gives the cell most of its support and structure. The cell wall also bonds with other cell walls to form the structure of the plant. chloroplast - an elongated or disc-shaped organelle containing chlorophyll. Photosynthesis (in which energy from sunlight is converted into chemical energy - food) takes place in the chloroplasts. chlorophyll - chlorophyll is a molecule that can use light energy from sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide gas into glucose and oxygen (i.e. photosynthesis). Chlorophyll is green. cytoplasm - the jellylike material outside the cell nucleus in which the organelles are located. Golgi body - (or the golgi apparatus or golgi complex) a flattened, layered, sac-like organelle that looks like a stack of pancakes and is located near the nucleus. The golgi body modifies, processes and packages proteins, lipids and carbohydrates into membrane-bound vesicles for "export" from the cell. lysosome - vesicles containing digestive enzymes. Where the digestion of cell nutrients takes place. mitochondrion - spherical to rod-shaped organelles with a double membrane. The inner membrane is infolded many times, forming a series of projections (called cristae). The mitochondrion converts the energy stored in glucose into ATP (adenosine triphosphate), a high energy molecule, for use by cell. nuclear membrane - the membrane that surrounds the nucleus. nucleolus - an organelle within the nucleus. Ribosomal RNA is produced here, then exported into the cytoplasm where it forms the ribosomes. nucleus - The nucleus is a spherical body surrounded by the nuclear membrane. It contains mostly DNA in chromosomes. The nucleus controls many of the functions of the cell (by controlling protein synthesis). The nucleolus is found within the nucleus. ribosome - small organelles composed of RNA. Are sites of protein synthesis. rough endoplasmic reticulum - (rough ER) a vast system of interconnected, membranous, infolded and convoluted sacks that are located in the cell's cytoplasm (the ER is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane). Rough ER is covered with ribosomes that give it a rough appearance. Rough ER transport materials and produces proteins (which are sent to the Golgi body, or inserted into the cell membrane). smooth endoplasmic reticulum - (smooth ER) a vast system of interconnected, membranous, infolded and convoluted tubes that are located in the cell's cytoplasm (the ER is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane). It produces lipids (fats) and membrane proteins; smooth ER buds off from rough ER, moving the newly-made proteins and lipids to the Golgi body for further processing and to the membranes. vacuole - a large, membrane-bound space within a plant cell that is filled with fluid, mostly water. Most plant cells have a single vacuole that takes up much of the cell. It helps maintain water balance and the shape of the cell. vesicle - a small, membrane-bound space that helps to transport material in/out or within the cell. Some are storage vessels. eg. proteins produced in the rough endoplasmic reticulum are transported by vesicles produced at the tips of the rough ER, to the golgi body, for processing. Animal Cell shape - most animals cells are roundish or irregular in shape. cell membrane - the thin layer of protein and fat that surrounds the cell. The cell membrane is semipermeable, allowing some substances to pass into the cell and blocking others. centriole - during cell division in animal cells, two pairs of centrioles form from microtubules at each end of the cell. The two centrioles are arranged perpendicular to each other. Microtubules formed in the centriole grow into spindle fibers which then attach to replicated chromosomes and assist in separating them during mitosis. cytoplasm - the jellylike material outside the cell nucleus in which the organelles are located. Golgi body - (also called the golgi apparatus or golgi complex) a flattened, layered, sac-like organelle that looks like a stack of pancakes and is located near the nucleus. The golgi body modifies, processes and packages proteins, lipids and carbohydrates into membrane-bound vesicles for "export" from the cell. lysosome - vesicles containing digestive enzymes. Where the digestion of cell nutrients takes place. mitochondrion - spherical to rod-shaped organelles with a double membrane. The inner membrane is infolded many times, forming a series of projections (called cristae). The mitochondrion converts the energy stored in glucose into ATP (adenosine triphosphate), a high energy molecule, for use by the cell. nuclear membrane - the membrane that surrounds the nucleus. nucleolus - an organelle within the nucleus. Ribosomal RNA is produced here, then exported into the cytoplasm where it forms the ribosomes. nucleus - The nucleus is a spherical body surrounded by the nuclear membrane. It contains mostly DNA in chromosomes. The nucleus controls many of the functions of the cell (by controlling protein synthesis). The nucleolus is found within the nucleus. ribosome - small organelles composed of RNA. Are sites of protein synthesis. rough endoplasmic reticulum - (rough ER) a vast system of interconnected, membranous, infolded and convoluted sacks that are located in the cell's cytoplasm (the ER is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane). Rough ER is covered with ribosomes that give it a rough appearance. Rough ER transport materials and produces proteins (which are sent to the Golgi body, or inserted into the cell membrane). smooth endoplasmic reticulum - (smooth ER) a vast system of interconnected, membranous, infolded and convoluted tubes that are located in the cell's cytoplasm (the ER is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane). It produces lipids (fats) and membrane proteins; smooth ER buds off from rough ER, moving the newly-made proteins and lipids to the Golgi body for further processing and to the membranes. vacuole - fluid-filled, membrane-surrounded cavities inside a cell. The vacuole fills with food being digested and waste material that is on its way out of the cell. Smaller than plant cell vacuole. vesicle - a small, membrane-bound space that helps to transport material in/out or within the cell. Some are storage vessels. eg. proteins produced in the rough endoplasmic reticulum are transported by vesicles produced at the tips of the rough ER, to the golgi body, for processing. Plant cells
Like animal cells, most plant cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane. Plant cells 
also have a hard cell wall made of cellulose. Also like animal cells, plant cells contain tiny, 
living machines called organelles. Golgi bodies and ribosomes are two organelles found 
in plant cells. They have special jobs to do in the cell to help the plant grow and to keep it 
healthy. Plant cells also contain large water-filled containers called vacuoles.
Green plants contain important organelles called chloroplasts. These parts have a 
chemical called chlorophyll in them. It is green. Green plants get their green colour from 
the chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are involved in the way that green plants use sunlight to 
produce food, through photosynthesis.

Plant Growth and van Helmont’s
Experiment

People wondered for a long period in history how a tiny seed could grow into a large plant. They were
curious as to where all of the extra mass came from. Greek philosophers such as Aristotle (384-322 ac),
believed that plants gained their nourishment from the soil.

1 How long did Aristotle live?

It wasn’t until the seventeenth century that experiments were carried out to test the validity of this theory.
A Belgian physician, Jean-Baptiste van Helmont (1580-1644), demonstrated that soil contributes very litle
to the mass gained by plants as they grow. He placed a willow seedling of known mass into a pot which
contained a known mass of soil. He watered the plant regularly and reweighed the plant and soil after five
years, Here is a simplified version of the results of his experiment:

* mass of soil 90.9 kg
* mass of soil plus seedling 91.0 kg
* mass of soil plus plant after five years 167.6 kg
© mass of plant 76.8 kg

3 What was the change in mass of the soil?

4 Give a conclusion that could be drawn from these results.
Plants extract vital minerals from the soil, but these make up only a very small part of the mass of a plant.
Only a small amount of the water taken up by a plant is kept by the plant. Typically, over 90% of water is
lost in transpiration. This is the process by which water evaporates from plant leaves. A considerable
amount of the mass of a plant is gained from carbon dioxide absorbed from the air,

manganese, zinc, molybdenum, boron and nickel. These are called micronutrients or trace elements.

searchText:
Plant pops
Teaching notes

This activity is designed to give students a sense of the challenges facing ecologists when
assessing the population of different plants.

This activity, with elements of a competitive game, is a useful alternative when a field trip
or access to the school field is not possible.

The aim is to assess the accuracy of using quadrats as a technique for estimating the
population of a plant species. The activity helps students understand the significance of
positioning quadrats randomly and that populations can only be estimated as it is not
possible in practice, to count all the individuals in an area.

However, this activity is not designed to be an accurate representation of how quadrats
are used in the field. It is a fun activity to do on a wet day which will get students thinking.

The activity is based on the game ‘Battleships’.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013              20087                                   Page 1 of 6
                                                                            Plant pops
Preparation

Equipment per pair of students:

     X2 sheets of blank grids
     stopwatch
     pencil

Each student should have a sheet of blank grids. The first blank grid on the sheet is to
record the distribution of the plants in their survey area. The second blank grid is their
record of the ‘throws’ they have made onto their partner’s sample area.

The grids represent plots of land. You could assign a specific habitat to the plots e.g.
saltmarsh, woodland, chalk downland, water meadow, heathland, sand dune.

A home learning task could be given as preparation for this activity. Students could find
images of a plant species linked to one or more of the habitats listed above. They could
write a description of the plant and it’s habitat in their own words, using more than one
source of information. They should write a list of references at the end.

Some suggestions of plants:

        Sea lavender Limonium vulgare – saltmarsh
        wood sorrel Oxalis acetosella – woodland
        wild thyme Thymus praecox – chalk downland
        creeping buttercup Ranunculus repens – water meadow
        tormentil Potentilla erecta – heathland
        eyebright Euphrasia sp – sand dune.

A follow-on home learning task could involve students finding out how ecologists working
in the field, ensure that they have placed their quadrats randomly; or they could research
other methods of surveying plants.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013            20087                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                                 Plant pops
The activity

 Explain to students that their grids represent areas of land and that they are going to
investigate the most effective way of estimating the population of a certain species of
plant, using a quadrat. For convenience, the ‘quadrat’ is the same size as one square on
the grid.

 From the beginning they will know the actual population size of the plant species. Explain
that there are constraints on ecologists working in the field and that they do not have the
resources to count all the individual plants in the area. How many random throws of the
quadrat will give the best estimate?

Play

  I.   Decide for the class what percentage of the grid is to be occupied by the plant
       species. Each square is 4% of the whole, so choose multiples of 4, e.g. 32% = 8
       squares.

 II.   Without showing others, students shade in the required number of squares on their
       first grid. The plants may be regularly spaced, clustered or concentrated in one
       small region.

III.   Player 1 gives coordinates for a square, player 2 puts a cross through the square on
       their coloured grid and says if a ‘hit’ has been made. Player 1 marks the square on
       their empty grid to show if it was a hit or a miss.

       Each turn represents one throw of the quadrat.

       Play continues as Player 2 now gives the coordinates for a square.

       In this initial game, play continues until all the plants have been found on one of the
       grids. Students need to time how long this takes.

IV.    Class discussion

       How long did it take them to find all the plants on one grid? How many ‘throws’ of
       the quadrat do they feel would have given a reliable estimate of the population?

       What do they feel is a reliable figure? +/– 5% or 10%? What might it depend on?

       Plants may not be evenly spread over the area of the grid. Will the reliability of their
       estimate compromised by the positioning of the plants?

V.     Now they are ready to investigate further. Students can decide to limit the number
       of ‘throws’ to what they feel is a reasonable number. Alternatively, they may decide
       to give themselves a time limit for the game. These conditions represent the
       constraints of time and money on ecologists working in the field.

VI.    Keeping the number of plants constant in each game, students play 3 games using
       the limited number of throws or time limit that they have decided upon.


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013             20087                                    Page 3 of 6
                                                                         Plant pops
       What percentage population estimate did each game produce? What is the range
       of their results?




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013         20087                               Page 4 of 6
                                                                               Plant pops
Further points for discussion

  a) Point 2, ‘without showing others, students colour the required number of squares of
     their first grid’ enables students to ‘throw’ their quadrats randomly.

       What would happen if they had seen their opponent’s grid with the plants drawn in?

       What did happen when they scored a ‘hit’? Did they concentrate their throws in that
       area?

       How could they ensure that all their throws throughout the game, were random?
       Why is this important?

       How could they investigate the effect of bias?

  b) The 5 x 5 grid is small to allow more than one game to be carried out in a lesson. It
     represents a sample area of the larger habitat.

       How would students use their results to provide an estimate of the whole habitat
       area? What would they need to know?
       How accurate would this estimate be?
       How could they test their ideas?

       If time allows, pairs of students could come together into groups to carry out
       investigations to test some of these ideas.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Living things
46
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Plant structures
Most green plants have some common structures. These structures play different parts in 
the process of making food (photosynthesis) and distributing this food around the plant.
In most flowering plants, there are roots below the ground. They keep the plant in place 
by holding on to the soil. Roots absorb water for the plant to use in photosynthesis. 
Cells in the plant’s leaves carry out the work of photosynthesis, creating food (glucose) 
by absorbing sunlight and using water and carbon dioxide.
Many flowering plants have a system of tubes inside their stems. Two of these tubes are 
called the xylem and the phloem. 
 
●The xylem carries water from the plant’s roots around to all the plant’s cells. 
 
●The phloem carries food (glucose) from the leaves to the rest of the plant. This gives 
each cell the energy it needs to survive and grow.

© Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
32
An organ system is a collection of tissues or organs that work together, each with a specific task (or tasks) related 
to the healthy functioning of an organism. Plants and animals both have organ systems (Latin organum, meaning 
‘tool, instrument’). Plants have two main organ systems – one works below the ground, the other above ground.  
1 
Name the organ system that works below ground. 
2 
Name the organ system that works above ground. 
Roots, tubers and rhizomes form the plant’s underground organ system. 
Roots are usually (but not always) found underground. Their function is to 
absorb water and nutrients for the plant’s growth and development. Roots 
also store excess sugars and act as anchors, holding the plant in place and 
giving it stability as it grows. Tiny root hairs grow off roots to increase the 
roots’ surface area.
Tubers act like a pantry. They store food for the plant. Buds are often 
present on tubers (tuber comes from a Latin word meaning ‘swelling’ or 
‘knob’). 
Rhizomes are underground stems that grow horizontally (creep along) 
underground. Rhizomes grow roots and also store food, allowing a plant to 
spread across an area. Shoots, leaves, flowers and fruits are examples of a 
plant’s above-ground organs.
3

Preparing Unstained Red Onion Cells for a
Microscope Slide

Method
1.   Cut off a small piece of red onion
2.   Use forceps or your fingernail to peel away a very thin layer of skin from the inside
3.   Spread and smooth the onion skin flat on the middle of the microscope slide
4.   Add 2 - 3 drops of distilled water
5.   Carefully place a cover slip over the skin
6.   Gently dab the edges with a paper towel to absorb any excess solution
7.   Place the microscope slide onto the stage and secure with the stage clips
8.   Ensure the magnification is at the lowest setting to begin with (usually 4x or 10x)

9.   Use the adjustment knobs to focus on and observe the cell at a higher magnification

Method

searchText: Preparin g Wet Mount Microscope Slides Preparing a specimen Light microscopes function by allowing light to pass through the specimen to our eye. If the specimen is too thick, the object cannot be seen as clearly or may not be seen at all. Peeling, scraping, slicing and squashing are all techniques used to obtain thin specimens. Staining Specimens When looking at plant and animal cells under microscopes, we often need to stain the tissue we are looking at in order to see the different parts of the cell. There are many types of stains which biologists use and each stain reacts with different substances in the specimen. For example, iodine reacts with starch and turns it a blue-black colour. Take care when using stains because they can stain you as well. Activity 1: Looking at Euglena Euglena are unicellular organisms. They have chloroplasts and can make their own food, but they are also able to absorb food from their environment. They usually live in quiet ponds or puddles. Euglena move by a long whip-like structure, called a flagellum, which acts like a little motor and pulls the organism through the water. Equipment needed : Microscope slide, cotton wool, Euglena specimens Method : 1. Tease out the cotton wool and place one or two strands on your slide. 2. Put a drop of water containing the Euglena on the cotton wool. 3. Examine the slide under your microscope (under low power first) and draw what you see. Activity 2: Looking at Onion Cells An onion is made of layers, each separated by a thin skin or membrane. This membrane can be looked at by carefully peeling it off the onion and staining it. The membrane is on the rough surface of the onion layer. Equipment needed : Microscope slide, coverslip , onion membrane, staining solution, toothpick, tweezers Method : 1. Take a small piece of onion and using the tweezers, carefully remove the membrane on the rough surface. 2. Place a small sample on the slide and add a drop of staining solution. 3. Take care when using stains because they can stain you as well. Using Cover Slips A cover slip is a very thin piece of glass that is placed over a specimen. It is used to protect both the specimen and the objective lenses of the microscope. Cover slips are very fragile and can break easily. When you put a cover slip over a specimen, you need to lower it slowly to prevent air bubbles being trapped under the cover slip. On a slide air bubbles look like dark rings. Lowering a cover slip To prevent air bubbles forming under a cover slip, it is important to lower it slowly and carefully. The diagram below shows how to lower a cover slip. With one edge of the cover slip resting on the slide, support the opposite edge with a toothpick. Slowly lower the cover slip with the toothpick until it is just above the slide. Quickly remove the toothpick, allowing the cover slip to drop onto the slide. Remove any excess staining solution with a piece of paper towel. searchText: Name ______________________________ Period ___________________Date __________________ Prokaryote vs Eukaryote Worksheet Read the passage below. Then answer the questions that follow. The first cells to appear on Earth were prokaryotic cells. A prokaryote is an organism made of a single prokaryotic cell. The earliest prokaryotes may have arisen more than 2.5 billion years ago. Bacteria are prokaryotes. They are very small cells with a simple structure. Prokaryotes do not have a nucleus. This means that their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane inside the cell. Instead, prokaryotes have a single loop of DNA that floats in the cell’s cytoplasm. Protein-making bodies called ribosomes also form part of the cytoplasm. Like all cells, prokaryotes have a cell membrane. All prokaryotes also have a cell wall surrounding the cell membrane. The cell wall helps provide support and protection for the cell. Some prokaryotes are enclosed by an additional layer. This layer is called the capsule. The capsule has a sticky surface area, so it allows prokaryotes to cling to surfaces, such as your skin and your teeth. Eukaryotic cells are more complex than prokaryotic cells. They all have a cell membrane, ribosomes, and DNA as prokaryotic cells do. However, the DNA of eukaryotic cells does not float freely in the cytoplasm. Instead, it is found in the nucleus, an internal compartment bound by a cell membrane. The nucleus is one kind of organelle found in eukaryotic cells. Organelles are structures that perform specific functions. Most organelles are surrounded by a membrane. Some organelles have membranes that form channels which help transport substances from one part of the cell to another part of the cell. Eukaryotes are organisms made of one or more eukaryotic cells. The earliest eukaryotes, like the first prokaryotes, were single-celled organisms. They arose about 1 billion years later than the earliest prokaryotes. Later, multicellular eukaryotes arose. searchText: ﻿Increased surface area / absorption due to villi in the small intestine. A practical demonstration of the increased absorption thanks to the finger-like projections called villi in the small intestine is shown below. 1. Take two pieces of the chenille bath mat material from the villi model (10cm x 10cm each). 2. Cut the finger-like projections off one, but leave the other intact. 3. Place both into a beaker of coloured water (so that the demo is easier for students to observe) and allow them to soak for one minute. 4. Remove them both from the water. Squeeze the water from each into two separate beakers. 5. Measure the contents of each beaker using a measuring cylinder for each. You should notice that the one with the finger-like projections on absorbed approximately 3 times more water than the one without. This demonstrates that absorption is increased by the increased surface area due to the villi in the small intestine. This is a simple but effective way to demonstrate this point, as students often find the concept of surface area very difficult to understand. This will be particularly useful for those students in your class who may struggle mathematically, as the idea of increased absorption has been placed within a concept that they can understand. For those football fans amongst you, I also get students to remember the word villi by thinking of Aston Villa and saying: ‘The Villi !!!!!! The greatest team in the small intestine’ This sounds best if done in a Brummie accent......... if you’re brave enough to give it a go!!!

Activity sheet – Body systems and cells
Reproduction
All types of living things are able to produce ‘offspring’ (descendants) that are almost 
copies of themselves. This process is called reproduction. Reproductive systems enable 
living things to make seeds, lay eggs, have babies or produce offspring in other ways.
+ 1 Read the following passage and then write short answers to the following 
questions.
 
In humans, there are two sexes: males and females. Both carry genetic material called 
DNA in their cells. When one cell from each partner combine, the DNA of the two 
parents mixes together. The male provides the sperm cell and the female provides 
the egg cell. The sperm fertilises the egg, entering through the cell membrane and 
releasing its contents. In this way, the two cells combine. The new cell begins to divide. 
It grows and develops into a new human.

Key terms
binary fission
a form of asexual reproduction used by bacteria; the splitting of a parent cell into two equal daughter cells
fragmentation
asexual reproduction that occurs when a new organism grows from a fragment of the parent

a sex cell; in humans, the sperm and egg cells

an organism that has both male and female reproductive systems
offspring
an organism’s young, or child
parthenogenesis
asexual reproduction where a female fertilises her own eggs

a type of asexual reproduction where part of a plant breaks off, forming a new organism with no need for seeds or spores; similar to fragmentation

Reproduction in organisms

All living things are made up of cells. Cells are the building blocks of life. The simplest forms of life are
‘organisms made up of only one cell. All organisms must reproduce in order to make up for losses due to death.
If more organisms are being created than are dying at any one time there is pressure for the organism to spread
and colonise new habitats.

Asexual reproduction

Asexual (meaning ‘without sex’) is the simplest form of reproduction. There are a number of different types but

Respiration

Plants and animals use sugars and oxygen in a process called
respiration to provide energy for living.

oxygen + sugars — carbon dioxide + water + energy

Respiration occurs continuously in living things, during both day and
night. For respiration to occur in cells, the sugars and oxygen must
reach the cells. Very simple animals, such as amoebas, engulf their
food by a process called phagocytosis and absorb oxygen from the
surrounding water.

More complex animals cannot simply surround their food or absorb oxygen. These animals usually have
separate systems working together to make sure that both the oxygen and the food reach the cells. Oxygen
must be obtained from the air and transported around the body, Foods need to be broken down so that the
cells can absorb the necessary nutrients.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 3 Living systems extra worksheet 1: Respiratory diseases Science understanding, Science as a human endeavour Getting oxygen into your body is vital for our survival. Many different diseases of the lungs and respiratory system prevent you from being able to breathe as deeply as normal and breathing may cause you to cough or wheeze. Common diseases of the lungs include asthma, emphysema, bronchitis and pneumonia. These diseases may be chronic, which means they are long lasting or occur over and over again. Other diseases are acute, which means they come on rapidly and last a short time. Asthma Asthma is a chronic disease in which the bronchi in the lungs are swollen and tender. In this condition the bronchi react to factors in the environment, known as triggers. Triggers such as tobacco smoke, dust and pollens cause muscles in the walls of the bronchi to contract, making the airways narrow, as shown in Figure 3.1.1. The cell lining of the bronchi produces extra mucus. The mucus reduces the space inside the bronchi even more and the person has difficulty breathing. When people with asthma feel an attack coming on, they use puffers. The puffer contains chemicals that relax the muscles of the bronchi. This allows the bronchi to open up and the person is able to breathe freely again. Figure 3.1.1 The passage through which air can pass is very narrow during an asthma attack. Emphysema Emphysema is a chronic lung disease in which the bronchi, alveoli and blood capillaries are damaged. Emphysema is usually caused by smoking or long-term exposure to air pollutants (chemicals) and dust. The tissues of healthy bronchi and alveoli are elastic, which means that they are able to stretch and then return to their original shape. When bronchi and alveoli are exposed to pollutants and dust over long periods of time, they lose their ability to stretch. The bronchi become narrow and the alveoli break. Damage to the alveoli creates larger spaces within the lungs. Having large spaces reduces the surface area for gas exchange. The blood capillaries surrounding the alveoli are also damaged and less carbon dioxide and oxygen can be carried to the alveoli and away from them. Compare the photograph of the alveoli of a person with emphysema with the alveoli of a healthy person shown below. Figure 3.1.2 Figure 3.1.3 Alveoli of someone suffering from emphysema Alveoli of a healthy person. People with emphysema become breathless during physical activity and frequently have chest infections. They often have a bluish colour to their skin, especially around their lips. This bluish colour is known as cyanosis and is caused by a lack of oxygen in their blood. Emphysema develops slowly. Damaged alveoli and tissues of the bronchi do not repair themselves so the damage is permanent. A person with advanced emphysema has to breathe hard in an attempt to exhale fully and to get enough air into their lungs. Open your mouth as wide as it can go and then try blowing out a candle or match without making an ‘O’ shape with your lips. It is difficult. This is what breathing is like for people with emphysema, all the time. Questions 1 a Explain the difference between a chronic and an acute disease. b State whether asthma is an acute or chronic disease. Explain your choice 2 Refer to Figure 3.1.2. Propose the effect these holes in the alveoli would have on the person’s breathing. 3 Construct a flow diagram of events from the trigger to an asthma attack. 4 Explain why people with advanced emphysema often have a bluish tinge to their lips. 5 Explain why smoking is not good for the health of your lungs. 6 In many parts of Australia there is a distinct dry season. Explain why the dry season would be a difficult time for people who suffer from asthma. 7 Many coal miners used to suffer from emphysema. searchText: ﻿Chapter 3 Living systems extra worksheet 1: Respiratory diseases Science understanding, Science as a human endeavour Getting oxygen into your body is vital for our survival. Many different diseases of the lungs and respiratory system prevent you from being able to breathe as deeply as normal and breathing may cause you to cough or wheeze. Common diseases of the lungs include asthma, emphysema, bronchitis and pneumonia. These diseases may be chronic, which means they are long lasting or occur over and over again. Other diseases are acute, which means they come on rapidly and last a short time. Asthma Asthma is a chronic disease in which the bronchi in the lungs are swollen and tender. In this condition the bronchi react to factors in the environment, known as triggers. Triggers such as tobacco smoke, dust and pollens cause muscles in the walls of the bronchi to contract, making the airways narrow, as shown in Figure 3.1.1. The cell lining of the bronchi produces extra mucus. The mucus reduces the space inside the bronchi even more and the person has difficulty breathing. When people with asthma feel an attack coming on, they use puffers. The puffer contains chemicals that relax the muscles of the bronchi. This allows the bronchi to open up and the person is able to breathe freely again. Figure 3.1.1 The passage through which air can pass is very narrow during an asthma attack. Emphysema Emphysema is a chronic lung disease in which the bronchi, alveoli and blood capillaries are damaged. Emphysema is usually caused by smoking or long-term exposure to air pollutants (chemicals) and dust. The tissues of healthy bronchi and alveoli are elastic, which means that they are able to stretch and then return to their original shape. When bronchi and alveoli are exposed to pollutants and dust over long periods of time, they lose their ability to stretch. The bronchi become narrow and the alveoli break. Damage to the alveoli creates larger spaces within the lungs. Having large spaces reduces the surface area for gas exchange. The blood capillaries surrounding the alveoli are also damaged and less carbon dioxide and oxygen can be carried to the alveoli and away from them. Compare the photograph of the alveoli of a person with emphysema with the alveoli of a healthy person shown below. Figure 3.1.2 Figure 3.1.3 Alveoli of someone suffering from emphysema Alveoli of a healthy person. People with emphysema become breathless during physical activity and frequently have chest infections. They often have a bluish colour to their skin, especially around their lips. This bluish colour is known as cyanosis and is caused by a lack of oxygen in their blood. Emphysema develops slowly. Damaged alveoli and tissues of the bronchi do not repair themselves so the damage is permanent. A person with advanced emphysema has to breathe hard in an attempt to exhale fully and to get enough air into their lungs. Open your mouth as wide as it can go and then try blowing out a candle or match without making an ‘O’ shape with your lips. It is difficult. This is what breathing is like for people with emphysema, all the time. Questions 1 a Explain the difference between a chronic and an acute disease. b State whether asthma is an acute or chronic disease. Explain your choice 2 Refer to Figure 3.1.2. Propose the effect these holes in the alveoli would have on the person’s breathing. 3 Construct a flow diagram of events from the trigger to an asthma attack. 4 Explain why people with advanced emphysema often have a bluish tinge to their lips. 5 Explain why smoking is not good for the health of your lungs. 6 In many parts of Australia there is a distinct dry season. Explain why the dry season would be a difficult time for people who suffer from asthma. 7 Many coal miners used to suffer from emphysema. Propose why they suffered from it. 8 Compare asthma and emphysema using the table below. Asthma Emphysema Cause Chronic or acute Part of respiratory system affected Treatment

Plenary activities

1. Microscopy – taboo (pages 12-13)

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
at the top of your card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any
of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card. Before the lesson, copy
and cut up the taboo cards; each group of students will need a set.

 1. Students work in groups of at least four. Give each group a set of cards. Each
    group then splits into two teams.

 2. The cards need to be shuffled and placed face down.

 3. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile and
    describes the word at the top of the card without using the ‘taboo’ words. A
    member of the opposing team could sit by the clue-giver so that they can
    challenge if a taboo word is used. The rest of the clue–givers team must guess
    the word being described. Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or
    ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

 4. Should the clue-giver be correctly challenged or if their team correctly guesses
    the word then they must move on to the next card.

 5. Each clue-giver is allowed one or two minutes to describe as many words as
    possible to the players in their team before play passes to the next team. There
    are no penalties for a wrong guess.

 6. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other
ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to
reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

Investigating Seed Dispersal by Wind
Aim: To investigate how effective the drop and roll seed dispersal is.

Equipment:
• Some fruit with seeds, e.g. sycamore fruit

• Metre ruler

• Masking tape

• Electric fan



Method:
Step 1: Decide on a fixed height to drop the fruit from (ensure you are standing on a flat and
stable surface)

Step 2: Make a small cross on the floor below your dropping point, with the masking tape

Step 3: Drop your fruit above the cross, at your fixed
height, one at a time

searchText:
Seed: the fertilised ovule of a flowering plant which is
able to germinate and produce a new plant.

Many plants begin their lives as seeds. A seed contains a store of food, an
embryo and a seed coat (testa), The embryo has the material needed to
form the shoot and root, The seed coat protects the seed. When conditions
are right, the seed grows — a process called germination — and a seedling
is formed. Water, oxygen and warmth are needed before germination can
take place.

A root comes from the embryo and grows downwards to anchor the young
plant in the soil. At the same time, a shoot grows upwards into the air.

Leaves grow on the shoot and the seedling is able to support itself.

Until this stage is reached, the seedling depends entirely on its own food
store, The stored food is used up as the seedling grows.

Seeds contain very little water and can absorb more than their own weight in water. Sometimes the seed
coat must be cracked to facilitate the absorption of water. Some seeds need to be soaked in water. Others,
such as the carob (locust bean), need to have been eaten and passed through an animal’s digestive system.
‘The seed must also have a supply of oxygen. Many seeds will fail to germinate if they are lying very deep
in the soil. This is because oxygen from the air only reaches them very slowly. All plants have a fairly
narrow range of temperatures within which they will germinate. For wheat seeds, the best temperature for
germination is between 25°C and 30°C and for maize (corn) seeds it is between 37°C and 44°C.

Some seeds are said to be dormant. The seeds are alive but waiting for the best conditions to germinate.
Dormant seeds are able to stay alive even under severe weather conditions which would kill the seedling
if germination had taken place.

Most seeds can remain viable (capable of growing) for very long periods. Most seeds used by farmers and
gardeners, if stored correctly, can be kept for a year without losing their ability to germinate. The

searchText:
Skeletal system – comprehension
Task

Read the text in the box and then answer the questions.
 The skeletal system is a body system made up of bones along with cartilage,
 ligaments and tendons. There are 206 bones in the adult human body, which
 make up a skeleton. Bones are living tissue that can grow and repair itself.
 The skeleton has four main functions: support, protection, movement and the
 production of red blood cells.

 Without the support of the skeleton, the body would be completely floppy
 and limp. Having a skeleton gives the body support and holds the organs in
 place.

 The skeleton protects the organs because the bones are strong and hard.
 The rib cage protects the lungs and heart. The vertebrae of the spine protect
 the nerves of the spinal column.

 Muscles attach to the bones by tendons and this allows the bones to move
 when the muscles contract. Where two bones meet there is a joint.

Questions

1. Along with bones, what makes up the skeletal system?

   ..........................................................................................................................

2. How many bones are there in an adult human skeleton?

   ..........................................................................................................................

3. Is bone a living tissue?

   ..........................................................................................................................

4. What are the four main functions of the skeleton?

   ..........................................................................................................................

5. What would the body be like without a skeleton?

   ..........................................................................................................................

6. Which bones protect the lungs and heart?

   ..........................................................................................................................

7. What is the job of a tendon?

   ..........................................................................................................................

8. What is the term to describe where two bones meet?

                                               Skeletal system – comprehension
Answers

1. Along with bones, what makes up the skeletal system?

   Cartilage, ligaments, and tendons

2. How many bones are there in an adult human skeleton?

   206

3. Is bone a living tissue?

   Yes

4. What are the four main functions of the skeleton?

   Support, protection, movement, and the production of red blood
   cells

5. What would the body be like without a skeleton?

   Floppy and limp

6. Which bones protect the lungs and heart?

   The rib cage

7. What is the job of a tendon?

   To attach muscles to the bones

8. What is the term to describe where two bones meet?

   A joint

Find a Friend: Specialised Cells Activity

Teacher Instructions

This activity is good for consolidating or checking learning in a plenary or for revision.
Cards can be printed out A4 or A5 and laminated for repeated use.

How to use:
There are 3 types of card:

orange - diagram (with a part labelled as X);
blue - name of a part;
green - description or function of a part.

Give each student in the class one of the cards. This can be random or differentiated by giving easier
cards to weaker students and more tricky cards to higher ability students. Unused cards can be put onto
a table for students to go to if they can't find their ‘friends’. Where there are more students than cards,
give one card to a pair of students.

Students should then move around the room and find their two ‘friends’ with the matching diagram,
name and function. This encourages discussion and students that are unsure can get help from their
peers.

Once the students have found their friends, the cards can be stuck onto a board, wall or window to form
a display that students can refer to if necessary.

Introduction

afterwards. Today the prevailing belief is that all living things are made of cells and all cells come from pre-

13.10) Spray on skin

Science as a human endeavour

Professor Fiona Wood came into the public spotlight after the Bali
bombings in 2002. 202 people were killed, including 88 Australians,
and more than 200 were injured when suicide bombers attacked

two nightclubs. Professor Wood was a plastic surgeon working at the
Royal Perth Hospital at that time. She led a team of specialist health
professionals to save 28 survivors, some of whom had up to 92 percent

of their body burnt. These patients were susceptible to deadly infections
and shock.

Professor Wood’s early career in medicine was in plastic surgery and
research. In the 1990s she developed an interest in burns medicine,
especially in reducing the amount of scarring suffered by burns victims.
Professor Wood worked with another scientist, Marie Stoner, to

develop the technique of cultured sheets of skin which was an emerging
technology being investigated in the United States. The two scientists
moved from growing skin sheets to spraying on skin cells. As part of
their work they were involved in conducting clinical trials to make sure
procedures were safe and effective.

ADVANCED

Professor Fiona Wood.
Professor Wood was
awarded the Order of
Australia in 2003 and
was Australian of the
Year in 2005.

Professor Wood, through her work with burns patients and plastic surgery, has become
internationally recognised for her patented invention of spray on skin. Before this invention, it
took up to 21 days to culture enough cells to treat burns patients. Spray on skin has reduced
this culture time to five days and this has in turn reduced the level of scarring. The faster a
burn heals the less scarring there is. The technique is being continually developed and the goal

is to eventually produce wound healing that leaves no scars.

Focus 4.4: Reproduction

Stages of pregnancy—page 1

Skill: interpreting
Reproduction begins when sperm are ejaculated into the vagina. Once inside the vagina, the sperm move
towards the fallopian tube in search of an egg. If an egg is encountered, the sperm will surround it, but only
one will fuse with the egg and fertilise it. Fewer than one hundred sperm make it as far as the ovum or egg.
Once the egg is fertilised, the surface of the egg changes to stop any more sperm getting in. The fertilised
egg forms a zygote in the fallopian tube and begins its five-day journey to the uterus. Along the way, the
zygote divides several times to form new cells.
By the time it reaches the uterus, it has become a clump of up to 80 cells, called the morula. In
the uterus the cells continue to divide, forming a fluid-filled ball called a blastocyst. As the cells in the
blastocyst multiply, they start to move around and become different from each other. For the first eight
weeks, the developing individual is known as
an embryo.
After eight weeks the embryo becomes a foetus. The foetus is protected by a pool of amniotic fluid,
surrounded by the amniotic membrane. Oxygen and nutrients come from the placenta via the umbilical

cord.

It is designed to be delivered by two scientists or science communicators visiting a school, but a teacher could use the materials themselves too. The lesson is intended to be flexible and is made up of a set of short modules, mixing group activities with presentation and facilitator-led discussion. This guide outlines how we have found the lesson to work best, but we hope you will adapt the details to suit your own needs. Please share your suggestions and experiences by posting your comments at www.eurostemcell.org/resources. You can also email us at www.eurostemcell.org/contact. The lesson does not assume any prior knowledge of stem cells, or any detailed knowledge of cell structure or function. Materials and preparation Tip: You will need to print, cut-out and fold The lesson outline on page 3 provides a handy some of these materials in advance – look overview of the lesson.
