Structure of Plants

When scientists talk about the structure of plants, they are usually referring to the plant's roots, stem,
leaves and flowers, Not every plant has all of these parts. We are going to look at flowering plants.

The roots anchor the plant to the earth. They help the plant extract water and minerals from the soil. Water
flows up from the roots to the leaves (where some evaporates) by a process called transpiration. The stem
helps support the plant and keep it upright. Liquids travel up and down the stem. In the stem are special
tubes called xylem which carry water and dissolved salts from the roots to the leaves in the process of
transpiration. Phloem are tubes which carry sugars (made in photosynthesis) from the leaves to other parts
of the plant. Cellulose is a complex carbohydrate and makes up the majority of the cell wall of plant cells.

The leaves are where photosynthesis takes place. There is a green pigment (colouring) in leaves called
chlorophyll, which is essential for photosynthesis. A plant is a producer organism. This means that it
manufactures its own food, During the day it respires (uses up food and generates carbon dioxide) and
photosynthesises (absorbs carbon dioxide) at the same time. During the night it just respires, Animals
cannot make food. Animals simply use food made by plants or eat other animals and, in the process, give
out carbon dioxide, Carbon dioxide (CO,) is a colourless, odourless gas which makes up less than 1% of
air. Plants help to regulate the amount of carbon dioxide in the air and, hence, affect the greenhouse effect
and the world’s climate, To enter the plant, carbon dioxide must pass through tiny holes called stomates
which are found in the largest number on the underside of leaves. They allow oxygen and carbon dioxide
to move in and out of the plant. Water vapour can also move out of the plant through stomates.

7.5 | Sweating

Science understanding [ rounparion | stanparD | AbvaNceD

Your skin and sweat glands are part of the excretory

system. Sweat glands are located just under the skin and are found

all over your body. Each person has 2 million to 4 million sweat glands.
Sweat is essential for survival. Sweating is like a coolant that stops the
body from overheating. Excess sweating means your body has lost large
amounts of water and salts, resulting in dehydration. The body needs
salts to regulate the water content in the blood. It is therefore important
to drink water after exercise or when temperatures are very high.

The sweat gland is composed of two parts (Figure 7.5.1). The coiled
part is where sweat is produced. The duct leading to a pore on the skin
surface is the tube through which sweat is excreted from the body. The
fluid that produces sweat comes from the spaces between body cells.
This fluid, which is mainly water, has high concentrations of sodium
and chloride and low concentrations of potassium and urea. As fluid
travels up the sweat duct it changes, depending on conditions such as
temperature. The diagram demonstrates these changes when conditions

3)    Complete table:

4)    Veins take blood towards the heart. Arteries take blood away from the
      heart.

      * This can be remembered because ‘arteries’ begins with an ‘a’, and so
      does ‘away’, whereas ‘vein’ ends in ‘in’ and they take blood ‘in’ to the
      heart.

      Note: pupils may try to compare the structure of the vessels here. If so,
      this is an opportunity to remind them of the meaning of the word
      ‘function’.

5)    Choosing the correct words.
             oxygenated
             deoxygenated
             deoxygenated

       * The (pulmonary) artery which takes blood away from the heart to the
       lungs carries deoxygenated blood. It takes this blood to the lungs so that
       it can be oxygenated. As this blood vessel is taking blood away from the
       heart, it is called an artery.

       The (pulmonary) vein which takes blood into the heart from the lungs
       carries oxygenated blood. It takes this blood to the heart so that it can be
       pumped around the body. As this blood vessel it taking blood into the
       heart, it is called a vein.

6)   They have a very thin wall (just one cell thick) and so materials such as
     oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide can easily diffuse in and out of them.

     Note: It is also worth noting that capillaries are tiny compared to other
     blood vessels and so they can easily access cells.

7    As blood is passing through lung capillaries, it becomes oxygenated.

     Note: this is a basic answer. Pupils should be able to pick from the
     diagram that that this is a gradual process. They are likely to have already
     studied the blood, and so will be able to describe this in more detail i.e.
     each red blood cell contains haemoglobin. As the blood cell passes
     through the capillaries, more and more haemoglobin combines with
     oxygen to become oxyhaemoglobin.

8) * The haemoglobin in the red blood cells is likely to have given up most of
     its oxygen when it passed through the leg capillaries.

              The blood is deoxygenated.
              The blood now travels back towards the heart in veins.
              The valves in the veins help to stop the backflow of blood.
              The blood will enter the heart via the vena cava.
              Blood will pass through the right atrium into the right ventricle.
              It will leave and go to the lungs in the pulmonary artery.
              In the lung capillaries, the haemoglobin in the red blood cells
               becomes oxygenated again.
              The oxygenated blood enters the other side (left-side) of the
               heart through a vein (the pulmonary vein) and leaves in an
               artery (the aorta).
              The blood travels in this artery at high pressure to all areas of the
               body (including the leg muscle capillaries)
              The oxyhaemoglobin in the red blood cells will lose oxygen so
               that the cells in the tissues can respire.

9)    * A suggested full description in 100 words.

              The circulatory system transports blood around the body.
              The heart is the muscular organ that pumps the blood.
              Three types of blood vessels carry the blood.
              Arteries take blood at high pressure away from the heart and so
               have thick walls, but small lumens.
              Veins take blood at lower pressure towards the heart.
              They have larger lumens, but thinner walls.
              Veins have valves to stop blood flowing in the wrong direction.
              Capillaries are the smallest.
              They have walls that are only one cell thick.
              These features allow capillaries to easily exchange materials
               such as oxygen with nearby cells.

searchText: ﻿The Function of Villi in the Small Intestine Target Subject: Life science/biology Click and Print: Download a Word Document version of this activity to bring to your classroom. Author Sarah Hughes, Head of Science, New College Worcester, United Kingdom Purpose To examine a model of the inside of the small intestine to support understanding of the function of villi in digestion Background information The structure of the small intestine is designed for absorption of nutrients. The inside of the small intestine is lined with villi that absorb nutrients from the liquid mixture called chyme produced in the stomach from the food we eat. Biology books usually have a detailed picture of the villi. Some plastic science models also show villi. However, this easy to create model more accurately presents the concept of villi in a way that can be accessed tactually and visually. Blood vessels on the outside of the intestinal wall absorb nutrients so that they can travel around the body in the blood. Preparation Use a bath mat made of chenille or other material with loops, cover the outside of the rug (non-looped side) with mesh (preferably red) left over from a bag of onions from the grocery store or other source. The mesh will replicate the blood vessels. Roll the rug into a tube with the loops on the inside. Fasten the rug with Velcro or hook and eye closures. Materials Small bath mat, approximately 2ft by 3ft. Mesh or netting from an empty bag of onions, or other mesh or netlike material Velcro or hook and eye closures Tactile drawing of villi and small intestine Procedure 1. After reading about the digestive system and the structure and function of the small intestine, students examine tactile pictures and models of the small intestine and the villi. 2. Place hand or arm and hand inside the tube shaped intestine model. Notice the villi touching your arm and hand. 3. Examine the mesh netting simulating the small blood vessels on the outside of the intestine. Remember from your reading that the blood vessels in the wall of the intestine absorb the nutrients from food as it passes through the small intestine. 4. Open the "intestine" to more closely examine the villi. Notice how the villi create an increased surface area to maximize the absorption of nutrients. Resources Hughes, Sarah, Head of Science. Making Models: New College Worcester, United Kingdom, 2009. Miller, Kenneth R. PhD. And Joseph s. Levine, Biology: Foundation Edition: Pearson Education, Inc., 2010. About Sarah Hughes As the Head of Science at New College Worcester (NCW), Sarah Hughes is a Qualified Teacher of Visually Impaired learners. NCW is a Specialist School for Visually Impaired young people (aged 11 to 19 years) in Worcester, England. Sarah joined the school from a large mainstream High School in September 2007. When offering advice to teachers and support staff of visually impaired students she is always conscious of the fact that things are very different for a teacher in a specialist setting compared to one in a mainstream classroom with 30 students (and only one visually impaired student). In mainstream schools many teachers are regularly using technology to show animations and interactive whiteboard presentations. Since learning to teach visually impaired students, Sarah has introduced and developed the use of models in teaching and learning. These successfully complement the use of ICT in her classroom.

-—— EES ire Science
The Heart

The celis in your body need food, water and oxygen and must get
rid of waste products. A transport system is needed to move these
materials through the body. Your blood system does this.

The blood system consists of blood vessels (tubes) of different sizes
and a muscular heart which contracts rhythmically to pump blood
through the blood vessels. The blood system is often called the
circulatory system.

The blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called
arteries, Arteries have thick, muscular walls which contract in
rhythm with the heart and help force blood along. The regular
muscular contractions are your pulse, and you can feel your pulse
in your wrist and neck,

The blood vessels that carry the blood back to the heart are called veins. Veins have narrower, less muscular
walls than arteries and the pressure of the blood is lower. They are found closer to the surface of your skin,
and rely on the movement of other muscles in your body to help push blood back to the heart.

The large arteries and veins connected to the heart form numerous branches and become narrower, The
narrowest arteries and veins are connected by microscopic vessels called capillaries. Capillaries are very,
very thin (only a few cells thick) and allow substances to pass easily through their walls, This is how food,
water and dissolved oxygen pass from the blood to the cells, and how waste products from the cells pass
into the blood to be carried away,

The human heart weighs about 300 g on average, and is a pump with walls made of muscle. There are
specialised tissues in the heart that produce an electrical signal at regular intervals. This signal stimulates
rhythmic contractions of the cardiac muscle. When this muscle contracts, it squeezes blood out of the heart
and around the body. When the muscle relaxes, the heart fills with blood returning from its journey around
the body. One complete contraction and relaxation of the heart makes up a heart b

    used a microscope to examine a thin slice of cork. Hooke described it as
    consisting of “a great many little boxes.” These “little boxes” reminded him
    of the cubicles or “cells” in which monks lived, so he called them cells.

       What Hooke had observed were actually the remains of dead plant cells.
    The first person to observe living cells was a Dutch trader, Anton van
    Leeuwenhoek. Although van Leeuwenhoek’s microscope was rather simple,
    in 1673 it was powerful enough to enable him to view the world of
    microscopic organisms which had never before been seen.

       About 150 years passed before scientists began to organize the observations
    begun by Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek into a unified theory known as the cell
    theory. This theory has three parts:

       (1)    All living things are composed of one or more cells.
       (2)    Cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism.
       (3)    Cells come only from the reproduction of existing cells.

The liver is the largest of the major internal organs. It is located (roughly) under the bottom of the right side of your 
ribcage. The average human liver weighs just over 1.5 kg and is a dark brownish-red colour. It consists of a large 
right lobe and a smaller left lobe. The liver is involved in digestion, metabolism and detoxifying the body (removal of 
toxins).

Define toxin. 
The liver produces a substance called bile. Bile is used to break down fats

a cell and there are many of these cells suspended in a pool of blood.

The malleefowl
The malleefowl is an Australian ground-dwelling bird. 
They are shy, solitary birds who only come together to 
mate. The male malleefowl digs a big hole in the ground 
and fills it with organic material such as sticks, bark and 
leaves. He then waits for rain. Once the organic matter is 
damp, he covers it with a thick layer of sand. The organic 
matter begins to decompose and generates heat. Every 
day the male checks the mound’s temperature by poking 
his bill into it. When it is warm enough, the female lays her eggs inside the mound. Then 
she leaves the site and the male bird tends the mound daily, maintaining the internal 
temperature at 33°C. He does this by scraping away or adding the insulating sand. 
The eggs take 7–9 weeks to incubate. By this time the male bird has stopped 
maintaining the mound and has left the hatchlings to fend for themselves. The chicks hatch 
inside the mound and struggle their way out of the sand. They never know their parents.

searchText: The Microscope ­ Parts and Use Name:_______________________ Period:______ Historians credit the invention of the compound microscope to the Dutch spectacle maker, Zacharias Janssen, around the year 1590. The compound microscope uses lenses and light to enlarge the image and is also called an optical or light microscope (vs./ an electron microscope). The simplest optical microscope is the magnifying glass and is good to about ten times (10X) magnification. The compound microscope has two systems of lenses for greater magnification, 1) the ocular, or eyepiece lens that one looks into and 2) the objective lens, or the lens closest to the object. Before purchasing or using a microscope, it is important to know the functions of each part. Eyepiece Lens: the lens at the top that you look through. They are usually 10X or 15X power. Tube: Connects the eyepiece to the objective lenses Arm: Supports the tube and connects it to the base. It is used along with the base to carry the microscope Base: The bottom of the microscope, used for support Illuminator: A steady light source (110 volts) used in place of a mirror. Stage: The flat platform where you place your slides. Stage clips hold the slides in place. Revolving Nosepiece or Turret: This is the part that holds two or more objective lenses and can be rotated to easily change power. Objective Lenses: Usually you will find 3 or 4 objective lenses on a microscope. They almost always consist of 4X, 10X, 40X and 100X powers. When coupled with a 10X (most common) eyepiece lens, we get total magnifications of 40X (4X times 10X), 100X , 400X and 1000X. The shortest lens is the lowest power, the longest one is the lens with the greatest power. The high power objective lenses are retractable (i.e. 40XR). This means that if they hit a slide, the end of the lens will push in (spring loaded) thereby protecting the lens and the slide. Rack Stop: This is an adjustment that determines how close the objective lens can get to the slide. It is set at the factory and keeps students from cranking the high power objective lens down into the slide and breaking things. Diaphragm or Iris: Many microscopes have a rotating disk under the stage. This diaphragm has different sized holes and is used to vary the intensity and size of the cone of light that is projected upward into the slide. There is no set rule regarding which setting to use for a particular power. Rather, the setting is a function of the transparency of the specimen, the degree of contrast you desire and the particular objective lens in use. Coarse adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is always used first, and it is used only with the low power objective. Fine adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is used with the high­ power objective to bring the specimen into better focus. How to Focus Your Microscope: The proper way to focus a microscope is to start with the lowest power objective lens first and while looking from the side, crank the lens down as close to the specimen as possible without touching it. Now, look through the eyepiece lens and focus upward only until the image is sharp. If you can’t get it in focus, repeat the process again. Once the image is sharp with the low power lens, you should be able to simply click in the next power lens and do minor adjustments with the fine adjustment knob. If your microscope has a fine focus adjustment, turning it a bit should be all that’s necessary. Continue with subsequent objective lenses and fine focus each time. Note: Both eyes should be open when viewing through the microscope. This prevents eye fatigue, which occurs when the non­viewing eye is kept closed. Keeping both eyes open does take some practice, but it is highly recommended. Also, you should never let your eye touch the ocular lens. If your eyelashes touch the lens you are to close. Always remove eyeglasses when viewing through a microscope. If your eyeglass lens touches the microscope it may get scratched. Making a wet­mount slide Procedure: 1.­Place a clean slide on a paper towel on the lab table. Handle slides at the ends, not the center, to avoid getting fingerprints in the viewing area of the slide. 2.­Place a drop of water on the center of a clean dry slide 3.­Using the tweezers, place the specimen in the middle of the drop. 4.­While holding the cover slip upright, carefully place one edge of the cover slip next to the water. Hold the coverslip by the edges to avoid fingerprints. Set one edge against the slide and lower it until it contacts the liquid. The liquid should spread across the whole area of the coverslip. Slowly lower the upper edge of the cover slip onto the water. The objective is to minimize or eliminate air bubbles under the cover slip. You might find it helpful to use one toothpick to hold the lower edge in place, while using another to carefully lower the slip into place. 5.­An absorbent towel can be placed at the edge of the cover slip to draw out some of the water, further flattening the wet mount slide. 6.­Never view a slide without a coverslip. The coverslip protects the objective lens from the liquid on the slide. How To Stain a Slide: 7. Place one drop of Methylene Blue stain on one edge of the coverslip, and the flat edge of a piece of paper towel on the other edge of the coverslip. The paper towel will draw the water out from under the coverslip, and the cohesion of the water will draw the stain under the coverslip. 2. As soon as the stain has covered the area containing the specimen you are finished. The stain does not need to be under the entire coverslip. If the stain does not cover the area needed, get a new piece of paper towel and add more stain until it does. 3. Be sure to wipe off the excess stain with a paper towel, so you don’t end up staining the objective lenses. 4. You are now ready to place the slide on the microscope stage. Be sure to follow all the instructions on the previous pages as to how to use the microscope. 5. When you have completed your drawings, be sure to wash and dry both the slide and the coverslip and return them to the correct places! 6. All slides must be put away in the proper trays! Students will not leave until all materials have been put way properly. You are a team! 7. Remember – You break it you buy it!!! The microscopes you are using have a replacement cost of about $500. (CASH ONLY – NO CHECKS) Be very careful. Keep the power cords and microscopes at least 6 inches away from the edge of the counter. Microscope Parts and Use Worksheet Name:______________ 14 Period:_______ Microscope Part 1 2 13 3 4 12 5 11 6 9 10 7 8 8 7 9 6 10 5 11 3 4 12 2 13 14 1 1.­ Explain an important thing to remember as you turn the high­ power objective into place. 2.­ What should you always remember when you use the coarse adjustment? 3.­ Under what conditions would you adjust the diaphragm? 4.­ What should you always remember when handling microscope slides? 5.­ What is the purpose of the stage clips? 6.­ In terms of your eyes, what should you try to learn as you use the microscope? 7.­ What are the two parts used to carry the microscope? 8.­ What is the purpose of the coverslip? 9.­ What is the objective lens used to locate the specimen and first focus? 10.­ What are the chemicals called that are sometimes used to make the specimens visible? 11.­ What should you do if the high power objective lens touches or breaks the coverslip?

searchText: The Nucleus of a Cell The nucleus can be thought of as the control centre of a cell. It contains information about how the cell functions, as well as information about the organism as a whole. Inside the nucleus of a cell are structures called chromosomes . Chromosomes are only visible when the cell is undergoing cell division. On the chromosomes are genes which carry all the genetic information of the organism. A gene is responsible for passing on inheritable characteristics. All the cells in the body (except for the reproductive cells) contain the same number of chromosomes. The number of chromosomes contained in a body cell is called the diploid number . The gametes, or sex cells, of an organism contain half the number of chromosomes in a body cell. This is called the haploid number . Chromosomes occur in pairs. One chromosome from each pair has come from the mother and the other from the father. Each chromosome has the same set of genes controlling the same set of characteristics. E ach species of animal and plant has a specific number of chromosomes . Some of them are shown below. Plant Number of Chromosomes Animal Number of Chromosomes Fern 1262 Housefly 12 Watermelon 22 Crayfish 200 Wild oat 14 Orang-utan 48 Corn 20 Cat 38 Tomato 24 Cattle 60 Rice 24 Fowl 78 Fruitfly 8 Human 46 How many chromosomes exist in a Rice leaf cell? Crayfish antenna cell? Cat sperm? Tomato ova? Cow hair cells? Rice seed cell? Human heart cell? Human egg? Corn pollen? Chicken lung cell? DNA and the Genetic Code -114300 38100 Chromosomes contain a substance called d eoxyribo n ucleic a cid, or DNA for short. It is the DNA in the chromosomes that makes up your genes and determines your characteristics. The Structure of DNA In the 1950’s, it was proposed that the DNA molecule is shaped like a double helix , like the lo o kout tower in King’ s Park . The double helix is like a ladder that has been twisted into a spiral . 2752725 894715 The ladder’s uprights are made of a chain of alternating sugar and phosphate units. The rungs of the ladder are made of pairs of special molecules called nitrogen bases which attach to the sugars . These bases are different to the acids and bases you learnt about in Chemistry. The Nitrogen Bases There are four different nitrogen bases. They are Adenine, Cytosine, Guanine and Thymine. The four bases are represented by the first letter of its name, for example Adenine is represented by a capital A. The chemical structure of each base means that it can only pair with one other base. These are called complementary base pairs . A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The Genetic Code Organisms are different because the proteins in their cells are different. Proteins are made up of many smaller units called amino acids joined together in long chains. The DNA provides a code for the cells to make proteins. Each set of three bases as you move down one side of the DNA molecule, codes for a specific amino acid. Thes e sets of three bases are called codons . searchText: ﻿The Parts of a Typical Microscope Click on the parts for more info! Microscope Parts Magnification General Procedures Drawing Tips Making a Wet Mount Staining a Slide Final Note Top How to figure out the Magnification: Eyepiece Objective Lens Magnification Low Power 10 x 10 x 100 x Green = GO! Green = GO! Green = GO! Green = GO! High Power 10 x 43 x 430 x Yellow = Caution Yellow = Caution Yellow = Caution Yellow = Caution Oil Lens 10 x 97 x 970 x Red = STOP! Never Use This Lens! or 100 x or 1000 x GENERAL PROCEDURES: Microscope Parts Magnification General Procedures Drawing Tips Making a Wet Mount Staining a Slide Final Note Top 1. Make sure all backpacks are out of the aisles before you get a microscope! Always carry the microscope with one hand on the Arm and one hand on the Base. Carry it close to your body. 2. Remove the cover, plug the microscope in, and place the excess cord on the table! If you let the excess cord dangle over the edge, your knee could get caught on it, and the next sound you hear will be a very expensive crash. I will bill you later! 3. Always start and end with Low Power! The Green means GO! -- “Go ahead and put the slide on the stage.” “Go ahead and use the Coarse focus knob.” “Go ahead and remove the slide from the stage.” “Go ahead and put the microscope away.” 4. Place the slide on the microscope stage, with the specimen directly over the center of the glass circle on the stage (directly over the light). Then you have a 9 out of 10 chance of finding the specimen as soon as you look through the eyepiece! NOTE: If you wear glasses, take them off; if you see only your eyelashes, move closer. Be sure to close, or cover your other eye!! NOTE: If you see a dark line that goes part way accross the field of view, try turning the eyepiece. That dark line is a pointer that will be very valuable when you want to point out something to your lab partner, or your teacher! 5. If, and ONLY if, you are on LOW POWER, lower the objective lens to the lowest point, then focus using first the coarse knob, then the fine focus knob. The specimen will be in focus when the LOW POWER objective is close to the lowest point, so start there and focus by slowly raising the lens. If you can’t get it at all into focus using the coarse knob, then switch to the fine focus knob. 6. Adjust the Diaphragm as you look through the Eyepiece, and you will see that MORE detail is visible when you allow in LESS light! Too much light will give the specimen a washed-out appearance. TRY IT OUT!! 7. Once you have found the specimen on Low Power (100x), unless specifically asked to draw it on low power, center the specimen in your field of view, then, without changing the focus knobs, switch it to High Power. If you don’t center the specimen you will lose it when you switch to High Power (Yellow). [See Above] 8. Once you have it on High Power remember that you only use the fine focus knob! The Yellow means CAUTION! -- “Caution, use only the fine focus knob.” “Caution, do not remove the slide when it is on High Power.” -- The High Power Objective (430x) is very close to the slide. Use of the coarse focus knob will scratch the lens, and crack the slide. More expensive sounds . . . 9. NEVER USE THE RED LENS. The Red Means STOP!! -- “Stop! Don’t use that lens!” -- It is an oil immersion lens. Without the oil to lubricate the lens, you will destroy it! More expensive sounds . . . Also, the oil is needed to help gather enough light to actually see through the lens! 10. Tips On Making Good Drawings: Microscope Parts Magnification General Procedures Drawing Tips Making a Wet Mount Staining a Slide Final Note Top 1. Don’t even think of starting your drawing unless you have a PENCIL! Drawings in PEN are UNACCEPTABLE! This is for two reasons: (a) You can erase pencil! (b) You can shade in areas more easily in pencil. 2. Each Drawing must be 1/2 page in size, and must include clear, proper labels! In the upper left hand corner of each circle include the specimen name as written on the slide label. In the upper right hand corner, include the magnification (100x or 430x). 3. Labels should start on the outside of the circle. The circle indicates the field of view as seen through the eyepiece. All arrows should end with the point touching the object to be labeled! 4. Animal cells should always include at least the following five labels: Cell membrane, Nuclear membrane, Nucleus, Chromatin, Cytoplasm. 5. Plant Cells should always include at least the following seven labels: Cell membrane, Cell wall, Nuclear membrane, Nucleus, Chromatin, Cytoplasm, Chloroplast (this last does not exist in certain plant cells). 6. Remember: This class is about Connections! I don’t want you to Look at the cells; I want you to SEE them! In order to do that, you MUST: Apply your knowledge of cell structure to your drawings! An unlabeled drawing is nothing more than scratches on a piece of paper! Check out the Tutorial on LOOKING VS SEEING! How To Make A Wet Mount: Microscope Parts Magnification General Procedures Drawing Tips Making a Wet Mount Staining a Slide Final Note Top 1. Gather a thin slice/piece of whatever your specimen is. If your specimen is too thick, then the coverslip will wobble on top of the sample like a see-saw: 2. Place ONE drop of water directly over the specimen. If you put too much water over the specimen, then the coverslip will float on top of the water, making it harder to draw the specimens as they float past the field of view! 3. Place the coverslip at a 45 degree angle (approximately), with one edge touching the water drop, and let go. How To Stain a Slide: Microscope Parts Magnification General Procedures Drawing Tips Making a Wet Mount Staining a Slide Final Note Top 1. Place one drop of Methylene Blue stain on one edge of the coverslip, and the flat edge of a piece of paper towel on the other edge of the coverslip. The paper towel will draw the water out from under the coverslip, and the cohesion of the water (due to those perennial favorites - Hydrogen Bonds) will draw the stain under the coverslip. 2. As soon as the stain has covered the area containing the specimen you are finished. The stain does not need to be under the entire coverslip. If the stain does not cover the area needed, get a new piece of paper towel and add more stain until it does. 3. Be sure to wipe off the excess stain with a paper towel, so you don’t end up staining the objective lenses. 4. You are now ready to place the slide on the microscope stage. Be sure to follow all the instructions on the previous pages as to how to use the microscope. 5. When you have completed your drawings, be sure to wash and dry both the slide and the coverslip and return them to the correct places! 6. All slides must be put away in the proper trays! Students will not leave until all materials have been put way properly. You are a team! Final Note: NOTE: These procedures will remain the same, regardless of the type of stain, or the addition of a hypertonic/hypotonic solution to your specimen. REMEMBER: Be careful with the equipment, and be sure to leave the lab in the same condition it was in when you arrived.

There are certain diseases that prevent the lungs from 
operating correctly. Polio is an example of such a disease. 
It causes paralysis of muscles including the intercostal 
muscles, vital for breathing. In the 1950s, children with

of the child then the pressure inside decreased and increased 
to allow for normal breathing to occur. When the polio 
epidemic was at its highest it was not uncommon to see 
whole wards of patients in iron lungs.
Nowadays, with an increase in knowledge, iron lungs are 
no longer used. Instead positive pressure respirators or 
ventilators are used. These are a lot more compact and work 
differently to the negative pressure ventilator of the iron 
lung.

Activity sheet – Body systems and cells
Tissues, organs and body systems
Similar types of cells group together in an animal’s body to form a tissue, such as a muscle, 
which carries out a particular job. Different tissues group together to form an organ. 
An organ is a complete unit of the body that has a particular role or job to do. For example, 
the human heart is a fist-sized organ made up of cardiac muscle and connective tissues. 
Its function is to pump blood around the body.
Two or more organs work together in groups called body systems.
There are body systems for all sorts of things – including for breathing, for moving 
blood around the body and for digesting food. All the cells in a system need to do their 
jobs to make the whole system work.

Understanding Biology – human and plant life
35
The word transpiration comes from the Latin trans meaning ‘across’ or ‘through’ and spirare which means ‘to 
breathe or pass something through pores or tissue’. Transpiration is the word used to describe the loss of water 
from a plant, in the form of water vapour. The water is lost through tiny pores in the leaves. These pores are called 
stomata. The singular form of stomata is stoma, meaning ‘mouth’. Under the microscope, a stoma looks a bit like 
a little mouth, with lips that open and shut. Usually stomata open at sunrise and close at night. (Although some 
desert plants have stomata that open at night.) Therefore stomata, like the chloroplasts described below, are also 
activated to a large degree by sunlight.
1 
Write another word for vapour.                                            
Throughout the day, stomata open and close as the plant requires. When the plant is low on water, they close to 
prevent further water loss, although a certain amount is still transpired. When water is readily available, stomata 
open. In average conditions, over 90% of the water a plant takes up through its roots is transpired. 
All vascular plants transpire. Vascular means ‘vessel’. Vascular plants carry water and nutrients (dissolved minerals) 
through a system of vessels or ‘tubes’. The vascular system is easily observed by cutting a stick of celery crossways. 
To see transpired water vapour, tie a clear plastic bag over the cut section and leave it for several hours to become 
visible. You should see the colour drawing up the celery. If left for long enough, the leaves will also start taking in 
the colour. 
Plants actively photosynthesise during periods of light. This is when transpiration action is at its greatest. It is 
important not to confuse transpiration with evaporation – they are two different processes.

searchText: ﻿Life and Living Year 8 Using a Monocular Microscope 1. Ocular lens or eyepiece - most microscopes have a range of ocular lenses: X5, X10 or X12.5. 2. Body tube or barrel - holds the ocular and objective lenses at a proper working distance. 3. Coarse adjustment (or coarse focus knob) - moves the body tube up or down to the correct distance for viewing a specimen in focus. 4. Fine adjustment (or fine focus knob) - controls the body tube and permits exact focusing. 5. Arm - supports the body tube. 6. Revolving nosepiece - contains the objective lenses and can be rotated to change the objective lens. 7. Objective lens - changes the magnification of the microscope. A low power objective lens of X10 magnification and a high power objective lens of X40 magnification are often provided. Some microscopes also have a X5 objective lens. 8. Stage - a platform that holds the slides. 9. Stage clips - hold microscope slides in place. 10. Diaphragm - controls the amount of light reflected through the hole in the stage. 11. Mirror - collects and directs light through the hole in the stage and through the object being viewed.0 12. Base - supports the weight of the microscope. 13. Inclination joint - permits tilting to adjust to eye level. Setting up the microscope The following steps should become routine and be followed every time the microscope is set up for use. 1. Place the microscope squarely in front of you with the base positioned a safe distance from the edge of the bench. 2. Place the microscope lamp about 15 cm from the mirror. 3. Using the coarse adjustment, raise the body tube so that the objective lenses do not hit the stage when the nosepiece is rotated. 4. Using one hand to hold the microscope, turn the revolving nosepiece so that the low power objective (X10) is pointing downwards towards the stage. You will feel it click into position. 5. Remove the eyepiece lens. Adjust the mirror so that a strong beam of light comes up the barrel. 6. Replace the eyepiece lens and do not move the microscope because this will alter the amount of light entering the barrel. 7. Place the slide to be examined on the stage so that the specimen is over the hole in the centre. 8. Focus the microscope under Low power by completing the following steps a) Looking from the side with your eyes level with the microscope stage, wind the body tube down with the coarse adjustment until the low power objective is within 1 cm of the slide. b) Looking through the ocular lens, slowly turn the coarse adjustment knob so that the microscope tube moves upwards until the object is in focus. c) If you are unable to find the focus, repeat steps a) and b). NEVER lower the body tube with the coarse adjustment while you are looking into the ocular lens. 10. To focus the microscope under High power, the following steps should now be undertaken a) Once you have focussed the object under low power, looking from the side carefully rotate the nosepiece so that the High Power objective clicks into place. Take care to ensure that the objective misses the slide. b) Sharpen the focus under High Power with the fine adjustment knob. NEVER touch the coarse adjustment knob when using the high power objective lens. Preparation of a Wet Mount Slide A wet mount of a specimen can be prepared using the following procedure: 1. Clean your microscope slide by wetting it with water and wiping it dry on both sides with a paper towel. 2. Using a pipette, place a drop of water near the centre of the microscope slide. 3. Place the specimen to be observed in the drop of water using forceps, dissecting needles or toothpicks. 4. Touch one edge of the coverslip to the water. Allow the water to spread evenly along this edge, then slowly lower the coverslip over the drop. Support the upper edge of the coverslip with a toothpick while lowering it into place as this will prevent the trapping of air bubbles. If air bubbles are trapped they will interfere with your viewing, appearing as circular objects with thick black outlines. 5. At the end of the lesson remove the coverslip from the slide and dispose of it in the glass bin. Rinse your microscope slide under the tap, wipe dry with a paper towel and return it to the equipment trolley. Staining The reasons for staining specimens are to make certain structures more visible or to identify specific chemicals within the specimen. Many different stains can be used, such as - methylene blue stains the nucleus and the cell membrane. - iodine stains starch in granules in a cell. To prepare a stained wet mount, place a small drop of the stain on the slide with the drop of water. Magnification of a Microscope The overall magnification of a microscope can be calculated by multiplying together the magnifications of the ocular lens and objective lens being used. For example if the ocular magnification = X10 and objective magnification = X40 the overall magnification = 10 x 40 = X400 Measuring with a Microscope Objects examined under a microscope are usually so small that they cannot be measured with the smallest unit of a ruler i.e. mm or millimetres. A much smaller unit, the micrometer (m) is often used. 1m = 0.000001 m = 0.001mm or 1000m = 1mm An estimate of the size of microscopic objects can be made by comparing them with the size (diameter) of the field of view (the field of view is the circle of light you can see when looking through the microscope). The field of view for a particular magnification can be determined using the following procedure. 1. Prepare a wet mount of a piece of millimetre graph paper, or use a minigrid slide. 2. Focus this slide using the required magnification. 3. Carefully move the slide so that one grid line touches one side of the field, and another grid line passes through the diameter of the field of view. 4. Knowing that it is 1 mm between each of the grid lines, estimate the diameter of the field of view. For example if the following was obtained when the graph paper was seen through the microscope, the diameter of the field of view would be approximately 1.2 mm or 1200 m Estimating the Size of an Object under Low Power To determine the length or width of an object, you need to estimate how many would fit, end to end across the diameter of the field of view at low power. Then, if the diameter of the low power field of view is known: the length/width of one object = For example, the following cell was seen using a microscope with a field of view of 1200 m: It was estimated that about three cells will fit, lengthwise, across the field diameter i.e. the length of one cell = = = 400 m (or 0.4 mm) Biological Diagrams Drawing plant and animal specimens is one way of accurately recording observations you make in class, at home or in the field. Biological drawing should show clearly: 1. the external appearance of the whole specimen, or part of the specimen if that is what you have observed 2. any internal features that you see, sometimes revealed by dissecting it eg the internal parts of a flower 3. the positions of structures and how they relate to one another They should also include: 1. a scale or some other indication of how many times smaller or larger your drawing is compared with the real organism you observed 2. clear labels outside the diagram, with a line connecting each label to the appropriate structure. Avoid crossing lines from different labels. Try not to use arrowheads because these may be used within diagrams for other purposes, such as showing the direction of blood flow etc. You might sometimes need to annotate a drawing. This allows you to record extra information about the organism that you might not have been able to record in the drawing General tips for making good biological drawings 1. Use a sharp pencil, a soft rubber and a ruler. 2. Draw a soft outline of your specimen first. You will probably rub these out later. 3. Use a ruler to check proportions, for example, how many times does a leaf’s width measurement fit into its length and make sure your drawing reflects these proportions as accurately as possible. 4. Use common sense when deciding how large or small to draw your specimen. Just because cells are microscopic does not mean your drawing has to be so small that nobody can see any useful detail. It is better to make a drawing slightly too large rather than too small. 5. Include a scale line such as or write down the magnification (x10) or reduction (x ¼) of your drawing. This will enable others to work out its true size. 6. When you are satisfied that you have recorded your specimen’s structure accurately, draw in the final lines with an HB pencil. Do not shade the drawing, 7. If the specimen has an overall detailed pattern on some part eg scales on a snake, you only have to indicate the detail in a small section of your drawing and annotate the diagram to indicate that this is a sample of the all over pattern for a particular part. 8. You should find that you mainly use your ruler for labelling lines and checking size/proportions. There are no living organisms whose structure has perfectly straight lines! Some additional tips for biological drawing Do Avoid use smooth, continuous lines if many cells of the same type are visible in the field of view if a structure is missing/lost/damaged

Activity sheet – Cells
What are cells? 
All living things are made up of tiny parcels of matter called cells. Cells are the  
smallest units of living things. This is why they are sometimes called the building  
blocks of life. 
Living things may be made up of just one cell or many billions of cells. Anything that is 
made up of one or more cells is considered a form of life or lifeform.
The bodies of all types of animals, including humans, are made up of cells. Different 
types of cells have different functions or jobs. Human bodies are made up of hundreds of 
different types of cells, including types of blood cells, nerve cells and skin cells. 
All types of plants are made up of cells, too. Plant cells and animal cells have some 
similar parts and some different parts.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Living things
61
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
What else are bodies made of? 
Animals and humans are made of cells, which make up tissues, which make up organs, 
which work together in groups to make up body systems. The bodies of humans and 
some other animals are built around a structure called a skeleton. We call all the bones 
and joints in the body the skeletal system. The bones of our bodies help us stay upright 
and give us proper shape and strength. Plants do not need skeletons because they have 
hard cell walls, which give their tissues a solid frame. 
Attached to the human skeleton are muscles. Muscles allow us to move. Muscles are 
attached to bones by tissues called tendons. Muscles work together to push and pull on 
our bones, giving us the ability to move. When a muscle pulls, we say it contracts. When 
the muscle stops pulling, we say it is relaxed. Bones are joined together at places in the 
body called joints. Knees and elbows are examples of joints. Inside our joints, strings called 
ligaments tie the bones together.
+ 1 Read the text below. Circle any words that you think are spelled incorrectly.
 
We call all the bones and joynts in the body the sceletal system. Mussels are attached 
to bones by tendins. Muscles work together, often in pears – for example, the biceps 
and triceps in the arm. When the biceps muscle contracts, the triceps muscle relaxes 
and the elbow bends. When the triceps contracts, the biceps relaxes and the arm 
stratens.

Lysosomes

The lysosome is the waste disposal or digestive system in the
cell. It breaks down molecules using special digestive enzymes.
Like waste disposal in a city, lysosomes help keep excessive or
bulky macromolecules from building up in the cell.

This demonstrates why it is important for all parts of a cell to be
compartmentalised. In this case the cell couldn’t use the
destructive enzymes if they were not sealed oﬀ from the rest of
the cell.

Preparing a wet mount

To view many specimens under a light microscope it is first
necessary to prepare a microscope slide for viewing. This is
called preparing a wet mount.

To make a wet mount:

1. Place your sample on the slide. Note it should be extremely
  thin to be viewed under a light microscope.

2. Using an eyedropper or pipette, put a drop of water on the           Th coverslip should be gently lowered onto the sample
  sample. If you are dying your sample you can place a drop of          at an angle to reduce the chance of bubbles forming.
  the dye on top of it.

3. Place one end of the cover slip on the slide and gently drop the     Image 1.23 Air bubbles under the microscope
  coverslip onto the sample. You can also lower the coverslip
  onto the sample using the end of a toothpick. This will help to
  prevent air bubbles from getting trapped under the cover slip.

4. The water (or dye) should just fill the space between the cover
  slip and the slide. If there is too much liquid and the cover slip
  is floating around, remove some water by holding the edge of a
  paper towel next to the edge of the cover slip. If there is too
  little liquid and some of the space under the cover slip is still
  dry, add more liquid by placing a drop right next to the cover
  slip. A little practice will help you learn how much liquid to add.

The heart is a muscle in your chest made up of four chambers:

Your heart is protected by your ribs and pumps blood around your

2.2 Different types of work quiz
There are many types of work arrangements and it is important to understand the 
differences between them. 
Circle a, b or c to answer these questions.
1 
Fixed-term contract work is work that people do
a on a contract with a starting date but no finishing date.
b for one school term or semester while at school.
c on a contract that specifies the dates the work will start and finish.
2 
Voluntary work
a does not help you because you don’t get paid for your work.
b is for anyone who wants to help their community; it can teach you valuable skills 
and provide experience which can help with getting a paid job.
c is usually just for older people who have retired.
3 
When working for ‘commission only’, you
a get a regular wage plus a percentage of your sales.
b always make heaps of money because you get a percentage of what you sell.
c can work hard but may not earn anything if you don’t make any sales.
4 
Casual work is
a when you can always choose the hours or days you want to work.
b temporary, paid hourly and you can be offered irregular shifts.
c flexible, fairly laid-back and relaxed.
5 
A traineeship is work that 
a is on a train or a cruise ship.
b provides training, qualifications and wages.
c provides training and qualifications but no wages.

2.2 Where’s the best place to shop?
Read the information about places to shop. Then answer the following questions.
There are many different options and locations to buy 
from when shopping. The best place for a customer to 
shop depends on what they want to buy. Some customers 
want to spend time looking for the perfect option. In 
this case, a shopping centre where lots of different 
stores are grouped together would be the best place to 
shop. Customers who want to find the perfect item can 
look online where stores from Australia and around the 
world all sell their items, often at a cheaper price.
Customers who value convenience could choose to buy all their items from one store. 
Department stores and supermarkets sell many different kinds of items including food, 
clothing, technology, furniture, stationery and much more.
Customers looking for something unique or second-hand can also find the perfect place 
to shop. Opportunity shops, commonly known as ‘op shops’, offer second-hand items at a 
good price. Many markets also offer previously owned or cheap items for sale. However, 
customers at these locations may have to spend more time looking and sorting through 
items to find the perfect product.

Marcus buys a new set of golf clubs. The original price of the golf clubs was $1,500 but 
when Marcus went to the register to pay, the retail assistant reduced the price  
to $1,400. What percentage discount did Marcus receive?
 
original price – amount paid = $ discount
 
$1,500 – $1,400 = $100 discount
 
$ discount ÷ original price = decimal discount
 
$100 ÷ $1,500 = 0.067
 
decimal discount × 100 = % discount
 
0.067 × 100 = 6.7% discount
 rounded up to the next whole number = 7% discount
2.3 How much is the discount?
Read the information about calculating discounts. Then answer the following 
questions. You will need a calculator or working paper.
People often purchase things because they get discounts. A discount is when an amount of 
money is taken off the price you pay. The larger the discount you get, the cheaper the price! 
A discount is often shown as a percentage of the total price, such as 10% or 25%.
It’s hard to judge the best value if you’re not sure how much you save with a discount. The 
examples below show you how to figure it out. 
Tip: If your answer ends in 
a decimal, round it to the 
nearest whole number. 
•  If your answer ends in .5 or 
above, such as 4.6, 5.8 or 
10.9, round up to the next 
whole number. 
•  If your answer ends in .4 
or below, such as 7.2, 3.4 
or 1.1, round down to the 
whole number.
Annie purchases a new television for $1,500. 
Because she pays cash, the store manager gives 
her a 10% discount. Calculate the amount 
Annie pays for her new television.
 original price × % discount = $ discount
 
$1,500 × 10% = $150 discount
 
or $1,500 × 0.10 = $150 discount
 
original price – discount = amount paid
 
$1,500 – $150 = $1,350 cash paid

only work part-time, meaning they don’t work full-time each week. When you get a job it is

2.5 Casual work
Read the information about casual work then answer the questions on the next page.
Most students are employed on a casual basis and, like most things in life,  
there are advantages and disadvantages.
Let’s start with the not-so-good news about  
casual work. 
•  There are no fixed hours or days of work, so your income is not regular.
•  The number of shifts you are rostered on for can vary from week to week. 
•  It can be difficult to plan your social life until you have your roster.
•  Your employment can be terminated 
without notice.
• There is no paid sick leave or holiday pay.
Now some good news about casual work.
•  Casual workers get paid an extra 
percentage per hour because they don’t 
get sick leave or holiday pay. This is 
called casual loading.
•  If you work in hospitality – for example, 
in a café or hotel – you might get tips as 
well as your wage.
•  After school hours, weekends, public 
holidays and school holidays are often 
the busiest times for retail, fast food 
outlets and cafés. These are all times 
during which students are often available 
for casual work. 
•  Students can usually negotiate with their 
employers to take time off during exams.
•  Casuals are often paid an extra amount 
per hour for working at different times 
such as late evenings, weekends or public 
holidays. These are called penalty rates. 
The extra amount you receive depends  
on the award or agreement you are  
covered by.
•  Casual workers learn new skills and gain 
life experience and work experience. 
Be aware!
•   You should be paid for all the hours 
you work. If you are asked to do a one-
week trial or given a probation period, 
you should be paid for this time. Casual 
workers are paid by the hour which 
means that if you are asked to come in 
before your shift to ‘open’ or ‘close’ the 
business, you should be paid for this 
time.
•   A young worker at, for example, a 
fast food outlet, can be employed on 
a casual basis or on a traineeship. 
Sometimes young workers sign a 
traineeship agreement without clearly 
understanding what they are signing up 
for. There is a big difference between 
casuals and trainees in terms of wages, 
training and conditions of employment.

2.7 Other types of work and wages
Read the information about fixed-term contract work, temporary work and labour 
hire, working for commission and piecework. Then answer the following questions.
Piecework employees are paid a fixed 
amount for each unit they produce. The unit 
could be a piece of clothing or furniture you 
make, or a bucket of fruit you pick. So the 
faster you work, the more money you make. 
Working for commission means you 
get a percentage of each sale you 
make. Working for ‘commission only’ 
is illegal unless you are self-employed 
or working in real estate or in car 
sales. You should always receive the 
minimum wage for work that you do 
so make sure you understand what is 
involved before you accept a job that 
involves commission. 
Temporary work and labour hire is short-
term work. Employers often hire full-time 
or part-time temporary staff in busy times 
or when a full-time staff member is on 
leave. The job can be for days, weeks or 
months. Many employers find it easier 
to pay an agency to supply experienced 
workers. In these situations, the agency 
pays the workers an hourly casual rate. 
This is often called labour hire when the 
job involves manual work; for example, in 
manufacturing, trades or construction. 
Fixed-term contract work is usually 
done by workers with particular skills 
and experience who are needed for 
a specific job or project. Generally 
these workers are needed for a 
certain time, such as two weeks or 
during the snow season.

temporary or full-time temporary?

As you read the information below, underline the key points and highlight anything

Apprenticeships and traineeships in Australia
•  These systems combine paid work with 
training in a wide range of industries.
• They can be full-time or part-time.
•  You may be able to start one while you are 
still at school.
•  Training is on-the-job and/or off-the-job at 
college, TAFE or online.
•  Apprenticeships or traineeships are offered 
in approximately 500 different occupations.
•  The qualifications earned can be used to  
get a full-time job, continue studying or start 
a business.
•  Training is competency-based, which means 
you are assessed on your knowledge and the 
skills you can perform.
•  Rates of pay depend on the type of apprenticeship or traineeship you are doing,  
your age and sometimes your level of education.
•  Because you are being trained as you work, the pay rate is usually less than for casual, 
part-time or full-time jobs.

agreement.

3.2 Paying with cash versus credit
Read the information about cash, credit and debit cards. Then answer the question. 
 
1 
Are these statements true or false? If you answer false, edit the statement to make it true.
Statement
True or 
false?
a You must be 16 years old to get a credit card in Australia.
b Cash is not always accepted as a method of payment.
c A major disadvantage of credit is that it is more expensive to 
use than cash.
d Storing funds electronically is often safer than cash.
e Using cash can sometimes attract surcharges.
f Credit cards and debit cards allow people to spend more 
money than they actually have.
Why should I pay cash?
For many years, cash has been the preferred way of paying for the things we want to 
buy. It is something everyone recognises and when we see a note or coin we all know 
the value it holds. Cash has many other benefits over credit or debit cards.
First of all, anyone can use cash, no matter what their age. This is not the case for 
credit cards or debit cards. In Australia, you must be 18 years old to apply for a credit 
card. While there is no age restriction for debit cards, teenagers usually need their 
parent’s approval to get one. The main difference between a debit card and credit card 
is that a debit card uses your own money whereas a credit card is a form of borrowing 
money to pay for items. Neither credit cards nor debit cards are as simple to use  
as cash.
Secondly, cash is simple. If you only pay in cash, there is less chance of spending 
more than you can afford. This can easily happen with credit cards which often have 
a large limit on the amount you can spend, as well as high interest rates.
Cash is also always accepted. Some places may not accept credit or debit cards or 
require you to spend a certain amount of money before you can use them. This often 
means that people spend more just so they can pay using their cards.
Credit and debit cards also attract extra fees. This means that sometimes a product 
is more expensive because a charge or surcharge is added to the cost of the purchase.
Sometimes you get a discount for paying with cash. This is because businesses 
don’t have to pay the credit/debit card surcharge. That makes the product cheaper  
for you.
Cash does have disadvantages. One major problem with cash is that it can be lost 
or stolen. If you use a credit card or debit card, even if the card is lost the funds stored 
electronically are still safe.

3.6 Card fraud
Vanessa recently received a letter about debit and credit card fraud.  
She has some questions about the information.  
Read the letter and answer Vanessa’s questions on the next page.
16 November 2014
Dear Vanessa,
As Christmas approaches, we understand that many of our customers start 
using their debit and credit cards more frequently. This includes shopping 
in-store, but also Internet shopping. You may have recently made purchases 
over the Internet, whether it be buying presents for friends overseas or 
concert tickets for that next big event. But there are some important facts for 
you to know about fraud and how it could affect you.
What is fraud?
Fraud is defined as a form of deception used in order to gain financially or 
personally. In most cases, it involves criminals stealing information like card 
details and using them to pay for items with your money.
There are many different kinds of fraud. The two most common examples in 
Australia are:
•  card not present fraud: card details are used to complete transactions via 
phone, fax, mail or the Internet
•  counterfeit card fraud: a fake card is used to make purchases.
Card fraud is affecting a growing number of people due to increased online 
shopping and purchasing from overseas, where laws are not as strict as in 
Australia. An increase in hacking (using a computer to access and steal 
personal data) around the world may also contribute to increasing fraud 
rates.
How can you tell if you are a victim of fraud?
These signs may indicate the occurrence of fraud:
• unknown transactions appearing on your bank statement
• recently providing your credit card details to someone untrustworthy
•  amounts that differ from the actual amounts spent on purchases appearing 
from retailers on your bank statement. (Note that items purchased 
overseas may appear at different values in the bank statement due to the 
conversion of currency.)

Read the information about awards then answer the following questions. 
It’s a great feeling when you get your first pay – whether its cash, cheque or an amount 
credited to your bank account. Your employer must also give you a payslip which shows 
how your wages have been calculated. This is where you need to understand awards and 
how they affect your pay. 
An award is a legal document that sets out the minimum pay and conditions for employees 
working in a particular industry or type of occupation. For example, casual staff working in 
fast food outlets or take-away businesses could be covered by the Fast Food Industry award, 
while a casual sales assistant could be covered by the General Retail Industry award. 
Your employer should provide details of your employment status (casual, part-time or  
full-time) and the award you are covered by. The state or territory you live in, your age  
(until you are 21), the tasks or duties you perform and your job title (occupation) also  
affect the amount you are paid. 
Pay rates for trainees are usually based on the level of schooling 
completed, the type of traineeship and how long you have been 
out of school. Apprenticeship pay rates generally depend on the 
type of apprenticeship and whether you are in the first, second, 
third or fourth year of your apprenticeship. 
As there are so many different conditions of employment and 
different pay rates, understanding your wages and checking your 
pay can be confusing. Luckily, there is a great deal of information, 
advice and assistance available for young people starting work. 
The government website www.fairwork.gov.au has an online pay 
calculator you can use to check your pay and tells you how to get 
help via phone, fax, email or live chat. 
1

cosmetics and clothes. She wants to use the internet to find information about the 
award she could be covered by and what the minimum pay will be if she gets the job.

General Retail Industry           Hospitality Industry           Hair and Beauty Industry
2

3

should be paid for her meal breaks. How could she get this information?

4.2 Who is buying apps?
‘Appy customers spend big
The little programs that we download 
frequently are now big business for 
technology companies around the world.
Applications, commonly known as ‘apps’, are 
small pieces of software downloaded onto 
devices such as mobile phones and tablets 
that enable users to access additional features. 
These features could be in the form of games, 
news sites, weather reports or even programs 
enabling cheap international phone calls.
The year 2012 saw a huge rise in the creation 
and purchase of apps. There are now hundreds 
of thousands of apps available for purchase 
by customers. With so much choice, it makes 
the world of apps a confusing, and sometimes 
expensive place. While most apps are free 
and those that are not cost only a few dollars, 
the purchase of multiple apps in a week can 
still hurt the wallets of customers. The 
downloading of large file sizes of apps can 
cost customers even more – particularly if they 
go over their Internet download limits set by 
Internet providers.
The majority of smart phone users also use apps 
in today’s technology-obsessed world. But with 
the increase in apps, there has also been an 
increase in costs. These days, it is estimated 
the average smart phone user spends less than 
$20 a month on applications. 
So what are customers spending their money 
on? The most common apps downloaded are 
games. Many people believe this is because 
most users of apps are young people who use 
them for entertainment. This doesn’t mean 
that apps are just for kids though. There are 
also apps designed to help customers learn or 
provide them with valuable information.
App-user Jordan Coleman, a 42-year-old 
physiotherapist, says that the apps he uses 
‘help him to do almost everything in life.’ The 
apps he listed as being useful included a 
restaurant guide, language lessons, an alarm 
clock and sleep monitor and a train schedule 
which is ‘more useful and gives more accurate 
information than the employees at the train 
station’. When asked how much he would pay 
for an app, he responded, ‘If I used it every 
day? I would pay at least $20.’
Goes to show that apps aren’t just for the kids.

4.3 Understanding base rates and extras
Read the information about base rates and extra amounts then answer the  
following questions. 
Penalty rates, loadings and allowances are all extra amounts that can be added to your 
base hourly rate. The extra amounts you should receive are set out in the award you are 
covered by. Base hourly rates are calculated by dividing the minimum weekly wage by 
the normal number of hours worked per week by a full-time worker. For example, if the 
minimum weekly wage for a full-time worker is $400.00 per week, divide this by 38 (the 
number of normal hours worked each week) to find the base hourly rate of $10.52: 
$400.00 (weekly wage) ÷ 38 (hours worked) = $10.52 (base hourly rate)
1 
What is the base hourly rate if the weekly wage is $494.00 and the  
number of hours worked is 38?
2 
What is the weekly wage if the hourly rate is $20.00 and the number  
of hours worked is 38?
Casual loadings are extra percentage amounts added to the base rate of casual workers 
because they don’t receive paid annual leave or paid personal leave. The actual percentage 
depends on the award you are covered by, but is usually 15–30%. Under his award, John’s 
base hourly rate is $11.00. However, John is a casual employee so he is entitled to an extra 
15% of this amount per hour. 
To work this out on a calculator, press these keys: 1  1  .  0  0  ×  1  5  %  
The answer is 1.65, which means that $1.65 is added to John’s base hourly rate to make 
$12.65 per hour: $11.00 (base rate) + $1.65 (15% casual loading) = $12.65 (hourly rate)
3 
If Alyson is a casual worker with a base hourly rate of $12.00 and a casual loading  
of 20%, what is her hourly rate? Circle the correct answer.
$15.00          $14.40          $13.50
4 
On her 17th birthday Alyson’s base hourly rate goes up to $14.00. She  
also gets a casual loading of $20%. What will her new hourly rate be?
Penalty rates are higher rates of pay for work done outside normal working hours, such 
as late at night, on weekends and on public holidays. Penalty rates are sometimes called 
‘getting time and a half’ for 150% or ‘double time’ for 200%. The rate is calculated  
as a percentage of your base hourly rate and depends on your 
award. For example, some awards state that you must be paid 
200% of your hourly rate for working on a public holiday. 
Let’s look at John whose casual hourly rate is $12.65. If he works  
on Australia Day and his award states that he should receive 200%  
of his usual rate for working on a public holiday, his hourly rate for 
that day would be: 
$12.65 (hourly rate) × 200% (penalty rate)  
= $25.30 (public holiday hourly rate)
5 
Ben receives a penalty rate of 150% for working on a Sunday.  
If his usual hourly rate is $12.00, what is his Sunday hourly rate?

32 
Money Management – Work, wages and tracking expenses 
© Alison Lee and Blake Education 2013
6 
Using Ben’s Sunday hourly rate, calculate how much he will be paid  
if he works for 8 hours on a Sunday.
Allowances are extra amounts paid to employees for expenses such as cleaning your 
uniform, using your own car or tools, or for working in certain areas or in dirty or 
dangerous conditions. For example, when John has to work in a refrigerated coldroom, he 
receives an extra cold work allowance. He is also required to wear a uniform and receives 
an extra amount each shift for laundering (cleaning) it. 
7 
Justin receives a $1.25 uniform allowance for each shift he works.  
If he works 10 shifts each week, what is his total uniform allowance?

Statement

a Casual workers receive an extra loading because they 
don’t get paid annual leave or personal (sick) leave.
b Loadings are extra amounts you receive on top of your 
usual hourly rate.
c Amounts deducted from your wages are called loadings.
d Loadings are usually calculated by adding a percentage 
of the hourly rate.
e A penalty rate is money deducted because you did 
something wrong.
f Penalty rates are extra amounts paid for working outside 
normal hours, like Saturdays, Sundays or public holidays.
g You could be paid a penalty rate of 200% of your usual 
hourly rate for working on Christmas Day.
h An allowance is an amount you allow your employer to 
subtract from your wages.
i Apprentices using their own tools for work could be paid 
a tool allowance.
j You could be paid an allowance for working in cold 
conditions or for doing dirty or dangerous work.
k If you have to clean your own work uniform you could 
be paid a uniform allowance.
l If you have to use your own car while working you could 
be paid a car allowance.

by a full-time worker.

4.4 Superannuation
Read the information about base rates and extra  
amounts then answer the following questions.  
You may need a calculator or working paper.
Superannuation (super) is an extra amount an employer 
must pay to help fund their employees’ retirement. This 
means that when people retire from work and are not 
earning any wages, they can use their superannuation 
funds to pay for their living expenses. The rules about 
superannuation change from time to time. Currently, an 
employer pays 9.25% of their employees’ gross weekly 
wage for all employees:
•  aged 18 years or over and earning $450 or more 
each month
•  under 18 years, working more than 30 hours per 
week and earning $450 or more each month.
This amount must be paid directly into 
a superannuation fund. You can choose 
your own superannuation fund or your 
employer must pay into the MySuper fund. 
It makes sense to keep the same super fund 
throughout your working life – that way, you 
pay less in fees and it is easier to keep track 
of your superannuation savings. 
The percentage rate that employers 
have to contribute to their employees’ 
superannuation fund can change.  
In July 2013 the government proposed 
these rate changes in the future:
• 2012–13: 9% 
• 2013–14: 9.25% 
• 2014–15: 9.50% • 2015–16: 10%.

monthly earnings are $440.00. Does his employer have to pay Anthony superannuation?

4.5 Deductions and income tax
Read the information below about deductions and tax then answer the following 
questions.
Deductions are amounts that are taken out (deducted) from your wages. Your employer can 
deduct income tax from your wages but cannot deduct anything else that is not required by 
law without your written permission. If you are under 18, the employer must get permission 
from your parent or guardian. For example, if you work in a restaurant and you break 
something or a customer doesn’t pay their bill, this cannot be taken out of your wages. 
Employers use a ‘tax table’ from the Australian Tax Office (ATO) to work out how much tax 
to take out of their employees’ wages, and pays this money to the ATO. The ATO then has 
a record of how much tax you have paid and how much money you have earned. This tax 
is called PAYG, which stands for Pay As You Go. All employers must provide a payment 
summary at the end of each financial year (1 July to 30 June) which lists your earnings and 
tax paid for that financial year. You need this summary to fill out your tax return. 
If you filled out a tax file number declaration when you started your job and you earn 
under a certain amount, you may not have to pay any income tax at all. For example, in the 
2012–13 financial year, an Australian resident with an income of up to $18,200 each year 
($350.00 each week) usually did not have to pay income tax.

The illegal downloading of music, games and films is known as ‘piracy’ and it is an 
increasing problem in Australia. Read the article below and answer the questions on

4.5 Why is piracy illegal?
Not even three weeks into the New 
Year and already one of Australia’s 
largest retailers is feeling the sting 
of online downloads on their sales 
and profits. 
Australian Sales Manager of General 
Mart, Peter Gibson, said figures over 
the Christmas holiday season, were 
‘slow, especially in CD and DVD 
sales’. He blames poor sales figures 
on the rise in customers downloading 
content both legally and illegally.
‘We did see a huge increase in 
the sales of prepaid cards which 
customers 
can 
use 
to 
legally 
download music, films, books and 
other content,’ Peter Gibson said.
It is the illegal download industry 
that is causing retailers to panic. 
Worldwide, illegal downloads of 
music alone costs billions of dollars 
each year, let alone downloads 
of all the other kinds of content. 
When asked in a recent survey, 
most people said the reason they 
download content illegally is because 
they think one download won’t have 
much impact. Another reason often 
given is that music and films are 
too expensive to buy, especially for 
young people, so illegal downloading 
is the only option.
An important fact many pirates 
(people who choose to download 
content illegally) don’t consider is 
the way in which their piracy affects 
others. For example, if one person 
downloads a music album illegally, it 
means that music artists are not paid 
the money their artistic skill entitles 
them to. Many others lose money 
that is rightfully theirs, including 
songwriters, 
lawyers, 
marketers, 
sound engineers, musicians and 
even retailers like General Mart.
Governments around the world are 
trying new measures to prevent 
illegal 
downloads 
from 
ruining 
jobs 
and 
businesses. 
Penalties 
for downloading illegally can now 
include fines and, for some of the 
biggest offenders, jail sentences. 
These penalties are yet to be tested 
in Australia and no pirates have 
been jailed over this crime to date. 
However, in the United States, some 
pirates have been fined hundreds 
of thousands of dollars for illegally 
downloading just one or two albums 
from the Internet. Many people 
argue this harsh punishment does 
not fit the small crime committed.
As sales of CDs and DVDs decrease, 
retailers like General Mart are now 
faced with a tough decision: do they 
continue to stock CDs and DVDs in 
their stores or is it not worth it?
Peter Gibson admits, ‘We will be 
reducing the number of CDs and 
DVDs we offer to customers in our 
stores and hope customers come in 
and continue to purchase prepaid 
cards from us to download items 
legally.’
Another store bites the dust
Graeme Williams

5.1 What are shopping scams?
Read the information about shopping scams below then complete the following 
crossword and questions.
Common shopping scams
Every time we shop, we trust that the people we buy products from are telling us the truth. 
In some cases, the people we buy from may be untrustworthy scammers. They may sell us 
products of a lesser quality than we expect, or try to charge a higher price. 
One common scam is ‘double ticketing’. This is where a product has two price tags on it. 
When a customer takes the item to the register, the store charges the more expensive price 
even though they know it should be sold for the cheaper price.
Another common scam is ‘bait and switch’. This is where stores advertise a product for a 
very attractive price. When the customer comes into the store to buy the product they are 
told it is ‘sold out’ and offered a similar, more expensive product instead. What makes this 
dishonest is the fact that they might never have stocked the original product, or stocked 
only a few items so it sold out faster than customers would expect it to.
As more people start shopping online, the number of scams is increasing. Online 
anonymous sellers can use false or insecure websites to steal credit card information and 
money. Once scammers have your money, they could send you faulty products, products 
different to what you ordered or sometimes no product at all! 
In the case of online auction shopping, scammers can put fake bids on products to drive  
the prices up and make genuine customers pay more. These fake bids might be done by  
the seller themselves or by other people involved in the scam who are known as  
‘dummy bidders’.
