5.2 Asking questions to prevent getting scammed
Read the information about scams then complete the following question.
One of the top tips to prevent being scammed is to make further enquiries about products 
if you have doubts about it. An enquiry can be in the form of a letter, email, online form 
or phone call – the main aim is to ask questions to find out more information. If the seller 
cannot answer your questions, it could well be a scam!
1 
Shelley wants to purchase a new car. She found a 2008 hatchback on the website  
‘Car Yard Marketplace’ but needs to know the colour of the car, how many kilometres 
the car has travelled, whether it has a roadworthy certificate (a certificate that states 
the car is safe to be on the road) and when she can view the car. She wants a reply 
from the seller to ensure the sale is genuine before she goes to view the car. Her 
preferred contact is via email at shelley.wilson@email.com. Write the email for Shelley.

 Subject: 
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
 
 
                                                                                                                                         
Tips for structuring your enquiry
•  Format your enquiry like a standard letter. 
A professional enquiry is more likely to 
receive a professional reply.
•  Use clear and concise language. Don’t ask 
long questions. If necessary, break complex 
questions into parts or dot points.
•  Introduce your enquiry by listing the item 
you wish to discuss. Some sellers may have

•  Always be specific when asking questions. 
For example, if you want to know what 
colour the product is, ask for specific shades.
•  Always include your email, phone number 
or other contact information so the seller

An expense is something you spend money on. Expenses are sometimes called 
outgoings because your money is ‘going out’. If your income is more than your 
expenses, you can save money. But if your expenses are more than your income you 
will owe money. 
An expense can be for goods or services. Goods are solid things you can touch, such 
as food, books, cars or clothing. A service is something a person or company does for 
you, usually for payment. Examples of services include hairdressing, medical advice 
and treatment, accountancy, banking and phone and internet provision. 
1

or services. Circle the goods and underline the services, including references to people

Oh no! The Year 10 formal is on next Saturday night 
and there is so much I still need to organise. I have to 
go shopping for a new dress and shoes. Oh yes, and I’ll 
need some jewellery too. Of course I’ll need to get an 
appointment with my hairdresser and, if I can afford it, I’ll 
book the manicurist for my nails too. Dean is my date for

the formal. I should also pay for my mobile phone service 
before Saturday night. Alice said she would get some 
flowers for Ali’s mother too because we’re all going to her 
place for the after-party. Can’t wait, should be so much fun!
Fixed or variable? 
Expenses that don’t vary much and have to be paid regularly each week or month are 
called fixed expenses. These include rent, car payments and loan repayments. Variable 
expenses are those that vary or change according to how much you choose to spend. For 
example, food, clothing and entertainment expenses can vary from week to week.

5.4 Different types of expenses (cont’d)
Tax-deductible or non-tax-deductible?
Expenses that are necessary for you to earn an income or run your business are usually  
tax-deductible expenses. This means that these expenses are deducted from your gross 
income so you pay less tax. For example, if you own a business, the wages you pay to your 
staff and the rent you pay for your shop are tax-deductible expenses. If you are an employee 
and your job requires you to wear protective clothing, that clothing is a tax-deductible 
expense. Anything that is not related to earning your income is a personal expense and is 
not tax-deductible.

Providing a safe shopping experience is not only about protecting the rights of 
customers, but also protecting the rights of sellers. This includes laws designed to 
prevent thieves stealing items from stores which is known as shoplifting. Shoplifting

hidden in bags. The laws in Australia vary slightly from state to state, but the most

Read the information below about needs and wants and answer the following 
questions.
Basic needs are the things we require to survive. They include water, food, clothing and 
shelter. We also have other needs that significantly improve our quality of life, such as 
transport, education and health care. 
Personal circumstances, such as the place you live and your age, can determine whether 
something is really a need. For example, for someone living in a rural area or a place with 
no public transport, a car could be a need. It may not be for a person living close to school 
or work in an area with good public transport.
Wants are things we would like to have but these things are not absolutely necessary for 
survival. We should pay for our needs first and then decide which wants we can afford. Let’s 
face it – life would be pretty boring if we have none of our wants! However, advertising, 
marketing and peer pressure can persuade us to buy things we don’t need and cannot 
afford. When you are trying to stick to a budget or to save money, always think twice before 
spending. Ask yourself: Do I really need this? Can I live without it? What will happen if I 
don’t have it? How much can I save if I don’t buy it? Is there a cheaper alternative? 
It is important to understand your own 
needs and wants so you can make wise 
spending choices and learn how to budget 
and save. When you earn your own money 
you are able to see how much you have to 
work to earn the money you spend. This 
is called learning the value of money 
and it is an important lesson. Perhaps 
you will be less likely to splurge 
on expensive items you don’t 
really need when you 
consider how hard you 
have to work to earn  
that money.

3

4

7.2 Financial goals – save now, spend later 
When you plan to save for something over a certain time, you are setting a financial 
goal. Achieving that goal can feel great because you get to buy that special thing you 
wanted. You have also shown that you can be smart with money – a very important life 
skill! Financial goals can be short term, medium term or long term and involve small or 
large amounts of money. 
Answer the following questions about financial goals. You may need a calculator or 
working paper.

brother’s birthday.

The goods we buy at stores do not always last the way we expect them to. Sometimes, 
we purchase goods that don’t work as they should or are faulty. According to Australian 
law, there are two major kinds of faults that can occur in goods: major faults and  
minor faults.
Read the information below about faulty goods then answer the following 
questions.
7.2 When is a good faulty?
Major faults versus minor faults
A major fault is a problem with a good that means you wouldn’t have 
bought it if you had known about the problem. Imagine you purchased 
a new mountain bike and when you rode it for the first time you found 
out that the gears didn’t change! This is an example of a major fault.
A fault can be considered major if any one of the following occurs:
• The goods are different from the description given.
•  The goods are not fit for their usual purpose; that is, the goods 
don’t do what they are meant to do.
• The goods are unfit for a purpose that you told the seller about.
• The goods are unsafe for use.
All other faults with products are classified as minor faults. Examples of 
minor faults include a car that runs well but has some scratches on the 
paint, or clothing with stitching that is not quite straight.
Remedies for faults
Remedy is a legal term used for an action 
that corrects a wrong. In the case of major 
and minor faults, remedies ensure that the 
customer does not lose money or use an 
unsafe product.
The three most common remedies for faults 
are refunds, repairs and exchanges. A 
refund is when the customer returns an 
item to the seller and receives the money 
they originally paid for the item. A repair 
to the product may include new parts or 
components to return it to working order. 
An exchange may be for a newer, working 
version of the original product, or for credit 
that can be used to buy other goods.
In the case of a major fault, the customer 
chooses which remedy they want. For minor 
faults, the business chooses the remedy.

7.3 Steps to tracking expenses
Read the information below about tracking expenses and answer the following 
question.
Have you ever checked your wallet or your bank balance and found you had way less 
money than you thought you did? Did you wonder where it all went because you can’t 
remember spending that much? Even worse, have you found that you didn’t have enough 
money to go out, pay a bill or couldn’t afford to buy something you really wanted? 
To achieve financial goals, you need to make a written plan that shows how much money 
is coming in and how you plan to spend this money. This is called budgeting. When your 
income is more than your expenses, you can save money. 
The first step to budgeting is tracking expenses. This allows you to 
see what you usually spend your money on. To track your expenses, 
keep a record of everything you pay for or buy for a month or two. 
Then sort your spending into different categories or groups, 
such as food, transport, entertainment and clothing. 
You can track expenses by using an application on your 
mobile phone, writing in a notebook, keeping receipts or 
using a spreadsheet on your computer. Tracking expenses 
is easier if you use only one or two methods of payment, 
such as cash and debit card only, and avoid credit cards. 
Once you can see where all your money is going, you can make 
budgeting decisions about how much to spend on each category 
and how much you can save. Governments, businesses, families 
and individuals all track expenses so they can take control of 
their money, build budgets and achieve financial goals.

7.5 What remedies are available?
Read the information about remedies and answer the following questions.
The three major remedies available to customers are refunds,  
repairs and exchanges. Each remedy offers its own advantages  
and disadvantages.
In the case of refunds, the customer returns the faulty item and 
receives the money they originally paid for it. Refunds can be 
in cash, credit (refunded onto debit or credit cards) or in the form of store credit which 
allows the customer to return to the store later to purchase another item. A major advantage 
of cash or credit refunds is that the customer receives the remedy more quickly. This can 
benefit both the customer and the store as the customer often feels they have received 
better service and may be more likely to return to the store to make future purchases. 
Offering store credit is even better for the store as it ensures the customer will return and 
spend their money there, rather than at a different store. In the case of a major fault, the 
customer can choose the remedy they want, including the type of refund.
Repairs can be both simple and complex. Some repairs can be done in-store and may be 
as simple as using a special tool to change batteries in a product. Other repairs can take 
longer. In some cases, the good may have to be sent to another store, another state, or even 
another country! People are more likely to choose repair when the item is rare, they want to 
keep that particular item or the item has personal significance.
An exchange is probably the simplest form of remedy. It is most commonly done when the 
customer still wants to own the item and another one is available in the store. The store 
simply swaps the faulty item for a working version.

Read the information about making a complaint and answer the following question.
8.1 Tips for making a complaint
1 
Use the information above to make a list of the right and wrong ways to complain.
The right way to complain
The wrong way to complain
When you find that goods are faulty, it is common sense to return them to the store or 
manufacturer. If you are not satisfied with the quality of an item, you have the right to 
complain. This can be done in many ways. Usually, people visit the store they bought the 
item from. You can also complain by phone, email or letter. Whichever way you choose, 
it is important to know the right way to complain.
When returning a faulty item it is important to remain calm. Becoming aggressive 
when complaining about items only makes it more difficult to communicate with the 
salesperson. Stay composed and be patient with the salesperson you are complaining to.
It also helps to write down information if you are dealing with a large complaint. This 
is especially important when dealing with complaints in-store or over the phone. Keep 
records of who you speak to and when, and what was agreed. This helps avoid any 
confusion later.
If you are not happy with the solution first offered, it is perfectly fine to ask to speak to 
someone else. If you want to, ask to speak to a manager. If the manager is not in the store 
or is otherwise unavailable, ask for them to contact you when they can. 
If the response you receive in-store or over the phone is  
unsatisfactory, it may help to write a letter. This also  
means that all the important information is written  
down in one place for future reference. Make sure  
any letters you send are factual and reasonable.  
Don’t make false accusations or threats. 
In your letter, explain your rights under law.  
Also make sure you offer a way for the store  
or manufacturer to contact you. If you don’t  
provide contact information, you can’t expect  
the complaint to be addressed!
Finally, only as a last resort, seek legal advice regarding the complaint.  
Never threaten to sue or take a store to court straight away!

you have a better chance of getting the 
resolution you want. If a product has 
a major fault, explain your rights to 
refund, repair or exchange.
B: Explain the problem.
Clearly describe the problem with the 
product in as much detail as you can.
C: Include contact information.
Be sure to tell the person how and 
when is best to contact you in order to 
solve the problem you are complaining 
about.
D:  Name, title and address of 
person receiving the complaint
If possible, use the full name and 
job title of the person receiving the 
complaint to make sure it reaches the 
right person at the organisation.
E: Greeting and introduction
Use the name of the person you are 
addressing the complaint to. Introduce 
the product you wish to complain 
about, list when and where it was 
purchased and make reference to any 
proof of purchase you may have to 
support your claim.
F: Offer a solution
Outline the remedy or solution you 
want – it may be a refund, repair or 
exchange of the faulty good.
G: Sign off the letter
Include a formal farewell and your 
full name at the bottom of the letter.
H:   Provide information about 
previous interactions
In most cases, letters are written as 
a second step after visiting the store 
and trying to resolve the complaint 
in person. If a previous attempt to 
solve the problem has occurred, 
explain it to the person now 
handling the complaint.

Living and Work Literacy 4
Daniel Lyons and Lucy Tan have just completed Year 12 at Orangeville High School. This is a record 
of their conversation. 
	 Daniel:	 Since we’re leaving school next week I 
think I’ll apply for a job.
	
Lucy:	 Yes, me too. What are you going to do?
	 Daniel:	 I thought I’d just front up to a few places 
and see what they’ve got.
	
Lucy:	 I don’t think it’s that easy Daniel. We 
need to do some preparation. Are you 
after a part-time job or holiday job? Or 
do you want this to be the start of your 
chosen career?
	 Daniel:	 I hadn’t really thought about it.
	
Lucy:	 Do you have an up-to-date résumé?
	 Daniel:	 Not really. I have a few bits of paper 
and certificates in a folder somewhere at 
home.
	
Lucy:	 I’ve organised a job file. It contains my 
birth certificate, school reports, including 
the most recent ones, personal references 
from family friends and a school 
reference. I also have work experience 
reports as well as certificates and awards 
from my cricket and basketball teams. I 
used all that to prepare my résumé.
	 Daniel:	 That’s a good idea. I should do that too.
	
Lucy:	 Make copies of your original documents 
to send to employers so that you keep the 
originals.
	 Daniel:	 All right. Now, how are you going to go 
about getting a job?
	
Lucy:	 I'm going to write a letter applying for that 
job at the Ace Sports Store advertised in 
last Saturday’s Bigtown Gazette. But there 
are lots of other ways of looking for a 
job. Apart from the newspapers, we can 
check on the Internet, we can make direct 
approaches to employers – they call that 
‘cold calling’ – or we could contact an 
employment agency.
	 Daniel:	 What about going to Centrelink? Will they 
help?
	
Lucy:	 Yes, we can register our names there as 
looking for work. 
	 Daniel:	 I might try the Internet first as they have 
some good jobsearch sites.
	
Lucy:	 I think we need to be pretty active. We could write letters, knock on doors, fill out 
application forms, leave our telephone number, show we’re interested and keen. All that 
is supposed to help.
	 Daniel:	 OK. Thanks for your advice Lucy. Good luck! I’d better get cracking.

Dear Personnel Manager

2 Australian currency
Currency is the system of money that is used in a
particular country. Coins and bank notes make up
the Australian currency.
Australian coins are made at the Royal Australian
Mint in Canberra and consist of ‘silver’ coins
(5, 10, 20 and 50 cents) and ‘gold’ coins ($1 and
$2). Bank notes are printed by the Note Processing
Centre of the Reserve Bank of Australia at
Craigieburn, near Melbourne. All of Australia’s
currency is issued by the Reserve Bank and
distributed through banks. 
Prior to 1988, Australia’s bank notes were printed
on paper. Since then they are printed on plastic
(polymer), which is more durable and lasts about
four times as long. Furthermore, the polymer notes
are recyclable. They are also more difficult to
reproduce (by counterfeiters).
© Blake Education, 2006
6
Living and Work Literacy 1
Legal tender
Legal tender is currency that cannot be legally refused in payment of a debt. However, someone
who offers to pay a debt of $10 000 in 5 cent coins would not be popular. This is why the Reserve
Bank sets limits in relation to what people are obliged to accept when someone tenders (or offers
to pay) for an item. These limits are:
• $5 limit on 5, 10, 20 and 50 cent coins
• $10 limit on $1 and $2 coins.
There is no limit for bank notes – so you can pay a $10 000 debt in $5 notes and the person is
legally obliged to accept it.
Counterfeit money
Counterfeiting is copying money to make your own coins or bank notes. It is illegal and there are
heavy penalties for counterfeiters who are caught.
To guard against counterfeiting, the Reserve Bank publishes a detection guide to highlight the
differences between a counterfeit note and a genuine note. There are hidden patterns and specific
symbols in the clear window of legal notes. You can find out more about counterfeit money on the
Reserve Bank’s website.
 Australia was the first country in the
world to print all of its banknotes on
polymer rather than traditional paper.
 Australia’s first polymer bank note was
the commemorative Bicentennial $10
note, issued in January 1988.

Unfit and mutilated notes are those that are no

Introduced in Australia in 1981, automatic teller machines [ATMs] are a very common sight these days: outside banks, in nearly

ATMs are a modern convenience for busy people, who can now access their money electronically outside the traditional banking

An ATM allows consumers to undertake many operations including withdrawing money,

in time or on a particular date. Balance sheets are used for this purpose. They weigh up the assets, 
the liabilities and the owner’s equity in the business. The owner, or owners, have put money into

losses have been made.

7 GST 2)

what is tax?

Taxation, or tax as it is commonly known, is a voluntary contribution by income earners to the government, People paying tax to
the government allow for the upkeep of infrastructure for the general population. Examples of infrastructure include public roads,
hospitals, schools and the police. The three overriding principles of a tax system should be that it Is simple, fair and neutral.

History behind the GST

The letters GST stand for ‘goods and services tax’. The GST is 3 new tax that was introduced in Australia by the Liberal Government,
under the leadership of Prime Minister John Howard, in 2000, The Liberal-National Party Coalition won the 1999 federal election
with an election platform that featured the GST. Since the majority of the Australian population voted for the Coalition, they also
voted for the GST,

Before the GST became law, there was a lot of debate in parliament and in the media over the finer details of the new tax,
particularly over the issue of whether to tax fresh food. The Liberal Party negotiated with the Democrats, led by Senator Meg Lees,
in order to gain enough votes to ensure the Bill passed through the Senate.

What is the GST?

The GST is a broad-based tax of 10 per cent on most goods and services. It was introduced in Australia on 1 July 2000. Everyone
is subject to the GST, because it is included in the prices of most goods and services. The GST replaced the Wholesale Sales Tax
{sales tax) as the major indirect tax. Sales tax is a tax on the wholesale price of an item. Sales tax was imposed only on the sale of
goods whereas the GST applies to both goods and services. The Federal Government implemented the new tax in order to increase
the ‘base’ upon which revenue could be raised and to reduce the opportunities for people to avoid paying the correct amount of
income tax. The Federal Government made a concession for the GST by reducing personal income tax. At the same time, family
assistance, pensions and allowances were increased.

What items are GST-free?

The following items do not have GST included in their price: basic food, eligible childcare, water and sewerage rates, education,
most health services and products, hospital and nursing home services, and local government rates.

Food and the GST

GST does not increase the price of basic food, the general rule being that fresh or unprocessed food is exempt from the GST.
Replacing sales tax with a 10 per cent GST has meant that the prices of some food items have decreased. Some prices have risen—
for example, takeaway meals and restaurant meals.

1 Business goals 2

A goal is something that a person, group or business hopes to achieve in the future. Within a business there are three
types of goals: the personal goals of the owner, financial goals and social goals.

Owner’s personal goals

A person who owns a business is called an owner. On a personal level, owners operate a business for two main reasons. First,
independence atlows them to make their own decisions rather than follow or carry out the decisions of another person. Second,
a5 long as the decisions they make are wise, their job will be secure,

Financial goals

Financial goals relate directly to money. One financial goal is profit [Income ~ expenses = profit]. The main financial goal of
businesses, other than non-profit organisations, is to make a profit. For a business to make a profit, generally it must increase
sales and reduce expenses [sales earn a business income].

Another financial goal is business growth. If a business expands—for example, if a second or third store is opened—then more
income will usually be earned.

A third financial goal is that of an increase in market share. Market share refers to the total sales [expressed as a percentage] a
business has experienced in a given market. Most businesses will have an increase in market share as a financial goal because it
directly relates to an increase in sales of a particular product. The final financial goal is return on investment. Return on
investment refers to the expected percentage return that an investment will earn for the business. The larger the percentage, the
more profitable the business.

Social goals

Social goals relate to the community, One such goal, sustainable ecological development, refers to the use of resources by
businesses. This particular goal aims for the sensible use of resources by businesses so that there are enough resources for future
generations of people to use. Another social goal is community service. For example, businesses have a role to play in sponsoring
community events.

organisations and the laws which affect them. Most people going into a business for the first time

Geeta Pivari owns her own business as a 
hairdresser.
Her business is small in size.
She is responsible for the success or

She has unlimited liability. (If the 
business fails, Geeta as the owner

Geeta’s type of business is the most

It has perpetual succession and is known as

The owners of Goodfellas are the 
shareholders, who have put varying sums of 
money into the company.
The liability of these shareholders is limited, 
meaning that shareholders can only lose the

The shareholders are entitled to a share

Last year the profit of Goodfellas was $200

16 Buying and selling real estate
Whether you are buying a house, an apartment or a block of land, there are procedures that must
be followed, including research. This involves looking at advertisements for houses for sale or auction,
which can be found in newspapers, on the Internet and at the offices of real estate agents.
It is also important to calculate how much money you have for a deposit, how much you may need
to borrow and what would be the likely repayments.
When you have found the property you want, it is advisable to contact a solicitor. The purchase of
a house or unit involves:
• paying a holding deposit (this is not legally binding, but it gets things moving) 
• exchanging contracts (a legal document that binds the sale and involves the payment of an
agreed sum, usually 10% of the purchase price)
• arranging settlement (paying the balance of the money owing to the vendor or seller) – when
this happens, the property is legally owned by the purchaser.
Below is a typical newspaper advertisement for a unit.

with fabulous views. Stroll shops & transport
LMN Property. 8740 5555
Conveyancing
Conveyancing is the term given to the legal procedures required to arrange the purchase of a property.
These procedures are usually carried out by a solicitor, but they can also be done by a conveyancing
company with expertise in the process.
Conveyancing usually involves:
• a search on the title of the property to see that the current owner is legally entitled to sell it
• a survey check to see that the land or property described is in accordance with official maps of
the area (from the land titles office)
• obtaining council certificates of compliance that indicate that the plans comply with all council
regulations and that all rates and charges have been paid
• obtaining permission from other government departments in case the land is subject to future
development or resumption plans (such as a new freeway)
• obtaining a building certificate that describes
the condition of the building in case there are
faults (this is not compulsory but advisable) 
• arranging finance – a solicitor will usually help
with the document used as security for a loan,
called a mortgage (most buyers don’t have
enough money to buy a property outright and
have to borrow)
• checking the  contract for the sale of the
property – the contract can sometimes be a
complex legal document with many provisions
and clauses. It must be signed by both buyer
and seller when agreement is reached.

13 Buying second-hand goods 
  
‘Someone’s trash is another one’s treasure’.
Buying second-hand, rather than new, goods is a great way to save money. Some people love buying 
second-hand goods, while others will only buy new. There are advantages and disadvantages for each, 
as this scenario illustrates.
 A lunchtime discussion
Jessica: 
 Hey, I went down to the Sunday markets yesterday and bought  
a whole lot of clothes, really cheap.
Sophie: 
 I bet you bought rubbish. Yuck – imagine wearing clothes that 
someone else has worn.
Jessica: 
They’re all right when they’re washed.
Sophie: 
 I never buy second-hand stuff. If I want clothes, I go out and  
buy new stuff.
Jessica: 
Yeah, and you pay a fortune for them.
Noah: 
 What’s wrong with second-hand stuff? My brother rides a motor 
bike and he is always off to swap meets, where other riders swap 
bike parts. It’s a good way of getting stuff for your bike without 
spending too much.
Sophie: 
 But how do you know that what  
you buy is going to work? What if  
the parts break down? 
Noah: 
 Well, for starters, you can usually  
tell if what you are buying is OK.  
And anyway, you know the regulars at 
the meets. They won’t try to dud you.
Sophie: 
 But you get a warranty with stuff you buy new – you don’t get 
that if you buy second-hand.
Jessica: 
 But what about the environment? If we all bought new stuff 
and threw it away when we got sick of it imagine the waste. 
Buying second-hand is a type of recycling, really.
Sophie: 
Well, I guess it depends on the individual.
Where do you buy second-hand goods? 
There are many different places you can go to buy second-hand goods. They include:
•  local markets – there are many local markets operating throughout the country, often on a regular 
day of the week (Sunday is a very common day for local markets). 
•  garage sales – often someone within your neighbourhood will hold a garage sale. This is a way of 
getting rid of books, clothes and household goods quickly and cheaply. Garage sales can be a great 
place to pick up bargains. Sometimes keen buyers queue up in the early hours of the morning just 
to get the best things. 
•  charity stores – charity stores, or op shops, take goods donated by people and then sell them to 
raise money for the charity. ‘Vinnies’ (the St Vincent de Paul Society) and the Smith Family are just 
two examples of charities that run stores.

20 Career planning
The most logical way to approach a career choice is to analyse yourself in relation to your interests 
and your abilities. In today’s job market, it is important to look at your interests in a broad and 
open way. For example, ‘I like helping people’, ‘I like working with mechanical things’, ‘I like being 
outside and working with animals’, rather than ‘I want to be a vet, or a car mechanic’ as this 
narrows the job opportunities. 
Look at your skills in a broad sense, at what are called ‘transferable skills’, such as being good with 
numbers, computer keyboard skills, knowledge of mechanics of cars. In this way, these skills can be 
used for a wide range of jobs.
If you have special skills your school record (reports, references and other documents) should 
provide you with a useful guide.
Vocational pathways
In the past, young people were 
advised that after they left 
school they should train for 
a life-long career. Today, you 
can expect to spend some of 
your working life as a casual or 
part-time worker, you may be 
unemployed for some periods 
of time and you are likely 
to be involved in retraining 
or professional development 
programs. It is highly likely that 
your career path will change 
several times during your 
working life. 
There is much more flexibility 
today in the vocational 
pathways available to young 
people. Universities, for 
example, are now taking more 
mature-age students than ever 
before.
Workplace Training 
Unskilled people find it more 
difficult to find a job than 
those who are skilled in some 
way. This may involve formal 
education, e.g. at a university 
or TAFE, but it is also important 
to get ‘on-the-job’ training. 
Training, and therefore skills 
acquisitions, should be seen as 
a lifelong process. All workers 
can improve their skills, no 
matter how experienced they 
are.

4 Casual employment pitfalls 
Permanent or casual?
Permanent work usually involves regular, continuing employment. Casual work is more irregular and 
uncertain. Casual work is usually, though not always, part-time rather than full-time. Employers have 
no obligation to offer continuing work to a casual employee. However, this does not mean that casual 
workers are not protected in the workplace.
Sometimes an employer will hire contract workers to do a particular job. Contractors are different from 
casual employees in that they submit a quote for a job detailing the specifications and complete the job 
for a specific fee which is paid when the job is finished. For example, a builder may hire an electrician or 
a plumber to do specific tasks for an agreed price.
Typical casual work
Casual work is common among many groups of people, including those juggling work with study or 
childcare, those who can’t find suitable full-time jobs and work two or even three casual jobs to make 
ends meet, and those who choose to avoid the strict routine of full-time work as a lifestyle choice. There 
has been an increase in the ‘casualisation of the workforce’ as casual work opportunities expand.
Advantages
Some of the benefits of casual work are listed below.
It provides you with valuable work experience and helps you 
s�to develop transferable skills valued by employers.
Part-time jobs provide you with some income and 
s�independence.
It is a way to make new friends and develop networks.
s�It offers flexibility and the possibility to work as much or as 
s�little as you want, when you want. 
For students from overseas countries it is a way to make 
s�new friends, become familiar with Australian work culture 
and improve English language skills.
The pitfalls
Maintaining a balance between work, study and leisure is very important. 
Working too many hours may have a negative effect on your education 
and neglecting leisure time can even affect your health. For most 
young people, priority needs to be given to education as it equips you 
for the future. Another issue is the income you earn. Casual work can 
be unreliable and it may not provide you with a regular income. This 
can become a problem if it is your only source of income, especially if 
you are supporting others financially. Casual and part-time workers are 
sometimes mistreated regarding the allocation of shifts, payment and

Employers who do not stick to required minimum standards in

rights and entitlements
Just because you are a casual worker does not mean 
you are not protected under government legislation. 
You should be aware of your rights and also your

12 Changing prices
Have you ever noticed that the prices of goods and services often go up and down? For example,
prices can be reduced in the short-term when stores have a sale, a special promotion or offer a discount.
As a consumer, you should know whether these reductions are genuine. For example, when you see
a sale sign with ‘50% OFF’, you should be asking: ‘50% off what?’ What was the price before the
offer? Is the discount genuine? Wise consumers need to be well educated and aware of the marketplace
before buying.
Long-term changes in prices are also worth studying. A loaf of bread was much cheaper 30 years ago
than 10 years ago and cheaper than the price today. This is an indication that the general level of prices
is gradually rising. But are we necessarily worse off? To work this out it is important to look at what is
happening to average wages and general income levels. History has shown that they too are rising.
To measure price levels in relation to wage levels you can use a statistical tool called the Consumer
Price Index or CPI. This helps you to see if goods at ‘real’ or ‘constant’ prices have actually risen or
fallen relative to wage levels. For example, some goods have increased, such as petrol and some
food items, while others have actually fallen in price in real terms. For example, cars, airfares and
stationery items such as pens and paper have been consistently falling in price in real terms.
You can also measure whether real prices are rising or falling by calculating how many days the
average worker must work before he or she can buy a new car. That figure has dropped significantly
over the past 10 or 20 years.
What is the CPI?
The Consumer Price Index or CPI is an official measure of the change in the level of prices. It measures
the change in prices of a variety of goods and services over a three-month period. These items
include the goods and services typically bought by Australian households, including food, clothing,
household furniture and appliances as well as education, transport and health.
The index is calculated by assigning a value of 100 as a base, so that an index of 105 would indicate
that prices rose by 5%. The CPI is published every quarter, in March, June, September and December.
The CPI is also used as a measure of inflation (see below).

What is inflation?
Inflation is a rapid rise in the level of prices over a period of time. The rate of inflation is normally

offset by rises in the other three quarters.

Case study:  Sonia Orchard
When Sonia Orchard graduated from high school, her main interests were world peace and feeding 
Africa. ’At the same time I was well aware they were kind of difficult things to study for,’ says Orchard, 
now 35. ’There was no diploma in world peace at the time.’
Instead, she enrolled in law. Then switched to arts (majoring in literature and classical studies). Then 
did a short course in food preparation at Melbourne hospitality TAFE, William Angliss. In the next five 
years, she travelled through Europe, Africa, the US and the Caribbean, working as everything from 
an au pair to a dive instructor. She came back to Australia and worked as an environmental scientist 
in the Northern Territory (having also completed a science degree). Then she returned to Melbourne, 
enrolled in yet another course, a TAFE professional writing and editing diploma at RMIT University 
and wrote a non fiction novel, Something More Wonderful, about the death of her best friend from 
cancer. These days, she is working on her second novel and supports herself teaching writing and 
piano. (She also managed an Associate Music Australia diploma at the Victorian College of the Arts 
along the way.)
’Theres that thing: I don’t know how I found myself here,’ she laughs. ’But I think you’re constantly 
making small choices, based on what you believe in and what’s important at the time, that lead you 
in a certain direction.’
Extract from article:  
The Itch to Switch By Melinda Houston. Sunday Life Magazine, Sun Herald 16 April 2006
Many changes have taken place in the workplace and in workplace arrangements in the past twenty 
years. The most common of these changes include:
a greater variety of jobs available
greater use of technology, especially computers and telecommunications equipment
gradual reduction in unskilled work
changing gender roles as more women become involved in professional occupations such as 
doctors, lawyers, company directors
more flexible work arrangements such as flexi-time, rostered days off, and people choosing to 
work at home or to work part-time
an increase in casual and contract work
a greater number of job changes in a person’s working life
In the past, people tended to have a job for life. In today’s workplace this is less common and 
people can be expected to have quite a number of job changes throughout their working life. One 
case in point is Sonia Orchard.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
Of course, not everyone will have the same dramatic changes as Sonia Orchard. However, in today’s 
workplace employees change jobs, companies and careers sometimes every few years. Now there 
is rarely such a thing as a job for life. Our parents and grandparents were often happy to stay put 
in one job until retirement. It was seen as secure and a way to pay off a mortgage. Employees 
today do not want a job for life and employers rarely offer it. Sometimes employers will put workers 
off and then re-employ them on a casual basis or on contract. Some companies encourage their 
workers to move from job to job within the company structure or even to leave the company, work 
for someone else and then return. 
Workers may decide to take time off and travel extensively overseas. Some take parental leave to 
help raise children. Whatever the reason or the motivation, the important thing is to return to the 
workplace refreshed and with a broader range of experiences.

3 Durable: Australian money [notes] is made from polymer [plastic]. Prior to 1792, when the first polymer note was released,

supply because the Royat Australian Mint controls the money supply, The problem of inflation arises when too much money is
available. Inflation is an increase in the overall level of prices. With inflation a fixed amount of money buys fewer goods and
services than it did previously.

5 Acceptable: Money must be accepted by everyone. People must be confident that when they pay for a good or a service, their

10 Connecting services 
When moving into a new home you will need to have services such as gas, electricity, water and 
telephone connected. These services are known as ‘utilities’. Having these services connected involves 
setting up an account with one of the providers of these services.
If you are renting, some of these services, such as water, may be included in the rent, and others, such 
as gas, may not be available in the property you are renting.
Energy costs 
Gas and electricity are both forms of energy. There are various energy providers and it can be worth 
shopping around for the best deals. Some energy providers offer green energy. This is usually more 
expensive, but it means that some or all of your electricity usage is matched with energy from 
renewable sources, such as wind or solar power. This offsets the environmental impacts of using 
electricity that is produced from burning fossil fuels, such as coal. 
Many homes are also connected to a gas supply. Gas is mainly used for heating, and sometimes also for 
cooking. Check whether gas is available in the property, and whether there are any appliances in the 
home that run on gas. 
Choosing a provider
You may be able to choose which energy provider you want to open an account with. When making 
this decision, it can be helpful to compare energy costs, off-peak rates, connection and disconnection 
fees and green energy options. There are several energy providers to choose from, including: 
Energy bills
Energy bills usually contain a lot of information. They can sometimes be difficult to read, but they can 
tell you a lot about your energy use. Your energy bill will list your electricity use, which is calculated in 
kilowatt hours (kWh) as well as showing the pattern of your energy consumption, usually on a graph

fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas. These 
resources are limited and will one day run 
out. Burning fossil fuels to produce energy 
also harms the environment. Renewable 
energy is energy that is produced from 
sustainable sources – sources that will 
not run out. Forms of renewable energy 
include solar power, wind power, 
geothermal power, hydro-electric power 
and tidal power. At this point, renewable 
energy is more expensive to produce 
in Australia than coal-based energy. 
However this may change over time as 
new technology could develop, if a carbon 
tax or an emissions trading scheme is 
introduced or if more people switch to 
renewable energy.
Telephone costs
Telephone costs include both landlines and mobile 
phones. Telephone costs are rarely included in the rent. 
If you need a landline, you will need to open an account 
and get the phone connected. This usually involves  
a connection fee and then ongoing monthly fees and  
call charges. 
Paying bills
There are several ways you can pay your bills.  
These include:
•  by phone (Bpay, debit or credit card) 
•  in person at Australia Post (cash, cheque, debit or 
credit card)
•  by mail (cheque).
Overdue accounts often result in late payment fees being 
charged, so it is a good idea to note the due date on all 
bills received.

19  Consumers and the environment 
As consumers we can help to preserve the environment. Everything we buy can affect the environment 
in many ways, from how it was made to how it was packaged and what happens when we dispose of it. 
Manufacturing and use
The way a product is manufactured can affect the environment in a number of ways. The manufacturing 
process can result in chemical by-products or pollution and can sometimes use large amounts of water, 
which is a limited resource. Some companies are taking steps to reduce or offset the environmental 
impact of manufacturing their products. Although we can’t always avoid buying certain products,  
we can become aware of how the item was produced and try to choose the option that has the least 
environmental impact. 
Using some products can also harm the environment. Some appliances, for example, use a lot of 
electricity. Most electricity is generated by burning fossil fuels, which is unsustainable and harms the 
environment. By choosing energy-efficient products, we can minimise our energy use, reducing our 
impact on the environment.
Packaging
In recent years there has been a dramatic increase in the packaging of goods. Even some fruits and 
vegetables are packed in plastic these days. Packaging is often designed to make a product more 
attractive to consumers. It is also used to communicate information to the consumer. Some packaging  
is necessary in order to keep the item in good condition. However, a lot of products come with a lot 
more packaging than necessary. 
After an item is purchased, the packaging is almost always thrown away, creating a huge amount of 
waste that needs to be disposed of. Not all of this waste is recyclable, and a lot of it goes to landfill, 
where it can take hundreds of years to break down.
Some companies ensure that their packaging is made from recyclable material. Others try to minimise 
the amount of packaging they use. Purchasing products that use environmentally friendly packaging  
can help to minimise the amount of waste your purchase creates. 
Disposal and waste
As well as the packaging, it is also important to consider how the product itself can be disposed of at 
the end of its life. Some kinds of glass and plastic can take thousands of years to break down – and 
others may never fully break down. When purchasing a product, it’s important to be aware of whether  
it is recyclable or biodegradable, which means that it will be able to be re-used or will break down 
quickly when it is disposed of.
Electronic items, such as computers and mobile phones, can release toxic chemicals when they are 
thrown into landfill. The increase in the use of electronic goods, combined with the fact that they are 
usually replaced fairly regularly, means that electronic waste is a big issue today. Some companies have 
found ways to recycle electronic goods, often by taking them apart and re-using the components.  
This is known as ‘e-cycling’.
Being ethical consumers
Being an ethical consumer means making informed choices. As consumers become more aware 
of environmental issues, many manufacturers try to capitalise on this issue by claiming that their 
products are ‘green’, or environmentally friendly. The term ‘greenwashing’ describes the deceptive 
use of advertising or marketing in order to falsely claim that a company’s policies or products are 
environmentally friendly. Companies use tricks such as packaging their products in a green colour,  
to suggest that they are environmentally friendly. Recently, the Australian Competition and Consumer 
Commission (ACCC) has reported an alarming rise in complaints about misleading ‘green’ advertising, 
particularly by energy retailers.  The ACCC has made it very clear they won’t tolerate excessive claims 
being made in an attempt to fool consumers and are taking steps to stamp this out.

 19 Consumers and the environment
Fairtrade
It is also important to consider the conditions of the workers who produced the product. Not all 
workplaces provide safe working conditions, and some countries use child and slave labour to produce 
high volume at low cost. The Fairtrade movement aims to help producers in developing countries obtain 
better trading conditions and promote sustainability. 
Fairtrade ensures that products from developing countries are purchased at a fair price from individual 
producers and sold with a ‘fairtrade’ label to tell consumers in developed countries that the item was 
produced under fair conditions. 
What can we do?
There are many things we can do to ensure that as consumers we are environmentally aware. A green 
consumer will:
• buy goods that are environmentally friendly, such as recycled paper 
•  take cloth bags to the supermarket rather than accept plastic bags, which can contribute to landfill
•  refuse to buy any goods which have excessive packaging
•  buy energy-efficient light globes
•  buy appliances that have a high energy-efficiency rating
•  buy products that can be refilled (such as cleaning products), to minimise packaging
•  pressure the government to regulate packaging and greenwashing
•  recycle and reduce your waste.

12 Credit card fraud and  
identity theft 
What is identity theft?
Identity theft is accessing someone else’s personal details and pretending to be that person. This is 
usually done for some kind of financial gain. The most common forms of identity theft are:
•  someone buys items using your credit card or credit card details 
•  someone assumes your identity and: 
 –  withdraws money from your accounts 
 –  borrows money in your name  
 
 
 
 –  sets up a business under your name
 –  conducts illegal activities in your name.
Identity theft is a serious crime and it can have devastating effects.
How is it done?
Stealing 
The most obvious and direct method of identity theft is to steal your credit card or your wallet or 
purse, which may contain vital personal information.  
Card skimming 
Card skimming uses a device inserted into an ATM that records information from the magnetic strip 
of the credit card or ATM card. The PIN number is also recorded using cameras or other methods. 
The scammer can then use the information to create a fake card with your details on it. 
Searching 
Scammers can also gain access to your personal records by rummaging through your garbage or 
through council rubbish tips looking for personal information. Scammers can also get information about 
you from social networking sites such as Facebook and Twitter, so it is important to be careful about 
the information you post on those sites. 
Phishing 
Many scammers send emails pretending they are from a bank and are checking their records or security 
systems. They then ask you for your account number. This process is known as phishing. Some of these 
emails can look quite authentic and often contain the bank’s logo. 
Another method used is to send you money and then ask you to transfer that money to someone you 
don’t know. This is known as ‘money laundering’, and is a way of transferring funds earned illegally in 
order to hide their origin.
It is important to remember that banks will never send you an email asking you for your account 
number or other personal details. If you are in doubt, contact the bank and talk with them directly.
ISBN 978 1 76020 206 4

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 8 
27
Spyware
Spyware is software that spies on what you do on your computer. It may be sent to you in an email 
attachment which then sits in your computer somewhere and collects your personal information 
(especially banking and credit card details) without your knowledge. 
Key logging is a variation of this, whereby someone at another computer is able to record and copy the 
key strokes you make, especially when entering personal information such as your bank account details. 
How to protect yourself
•  Protect your computer by installing reputable antivirus and/or anti spyware software programs  
and keep them up to date.
•  Never send money or give your bank account details to anyone you don’t know.
•  Remember that a proper bank or financial institution will never email you asking for your  
personal details. 
• Contact your bank immediately if you notice any suspicious or unexplained transactions from any  
of your accounts.

5 Credit cards and debit cards
People often get confused with credit cards and debit cards, especially as they are both made of
plastic and appear about the same size.
The term ’credit’ involves purchasing goods or services and paying for them later or over time. In
other words, you can purchase something without having the actual money in your bank account.
You are then given time to pay this amount to a credit card company. When you purchase something
using a credit card you will sign a sales docket.
At the end of each month, the credit card company sends you a statement, which lists all the credit
purchases that you made in that month, the minimum amount that must be paid and the total
amount owing (this could include credit purchases from previous months). This statement also requests
payment by a certain date. If you only pay the minimum amount and not the full credit amount
you will be charged interest.
Credit cards are not necessarily linked to bank accounts. Examples of credit cards are Bankcard,
Mastercard, Visa, American Express and Diners Club.
A debit card, on the other hand, is linked to a bank account. When you use a debit card, the funds
are immediately deducted from (debited to) your bank account. You may use a debit card at an ATM
(Automatic Teller Machine) or at a retail outlet that has an EFTPOS facility (Electronic Funds Transfer
at Point of Sale). In this case, money is immediately transferred from your bank account to the store’s
bank account. You can pay for goods using a debit card and also draw out additional cash. Either
way, the funds come out of (are debited to) your bank account.

3 Dealing with difficult workmates 
Difficult and awkward situations always arise in the workplace. Some common ones are described below. 
The important thing is that you are aware when difficult situations crop up and know how to deal 
effectively with them. 
The boss from hell 
People in leadership positions often display vastly differing 
leadership styles. Some bosses lead by consensus and mutual 
cooperation and respect, while others have an autocratic 
leadership style, consulting nobody else, which can be 
intimidating. Yet others may be indecisive and muddled in 
their thinking, so that no real leadership takes place. You need 
to be aware of the many leadership styles and try to work 
harmoniously as part of the team. Leaders often project their 
own personality into the workplace and you may have no choice 
but to accept the type of boss you have. The term ‘mutual 
respect’ applies, no matter what style of leadership your  
boss uses.
It is important not to be too emotional 
or argumentative, but to try to manage 
situations sensibly. This could involve 
thinking before speaking, being 
diplomatic, or just trying to understand 
the situation. Of course, if the situation 
becomes intolerable and the boss begins 
personal abuse against you, then you 
may need to take the matter further.
The blocker
No matter what suggestions or innovations are made, the 
blocker is someone who will always find fault with an idea. They 
will say things like ‘that’s not how we do things here’ or ‘we 
have been doing it this way for the last 20 years’.
The best response to a blocker is to point out examples of 
technological progress which have occurred in recent years and 
how they have made a difference to efficiency and productivity 
in the workplace. It might also help to point out to a blocker 
what the price of bread was 20 years ago – in other words, we 
have moved on.
The office relationship
It is inevitable that personal relationships will 
develop in workplaces. It is human nature for 
people to be physically and emotionally attracted 
to each other when working side by side.
Dealing with an ‘office romance’ can be tricky. 
You should treat your ‘partner’ in the same way 
you would if you were not romantically involved 
– in other words, just like other work colleagues. 
Giving special favours is never a good idea as it 
will be seen by others to be unfair.
Raphael and Jessica were working together on an 
important project for a large IT company. Before 
long they had fallen in love. Their supervisor, 
Joe Brash, was horriﬁed and demanded that they 
immediately cease their relationship. Raphael 
and Jessica pleaded for leniency, saying that they 
tried not to let their feelings for each other affect 
their work output or their working relationship. 
Joe admitted that their work was ﬁne but insisted 
that they should not be romantically linked.
What do you think?
Tony had a reputation for being a 
tough boss. He constantly abused 
his staff for their work output and 
their attitude. He would boast to 
his friends that the only way to 
get work out of people was to ‘get 
stuck into them all the time’ and 
to ‘show that he was boss’.
What do you think?
Ron had been with the company 
for 25 years. He was loyal and hard 
working, but always critical of new 
ideas. He would always say things 
were better before and there was 
no need for all this new-fangled 
technology stuff. Despite his 
loyalty he was becoming a problem 
for the company’s future prospects.
What do you think?
ISBN 978 1 76020 204 0

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2009
Living and Work Literacy 6 
9
The drama queen
Sometimes people – both females and males – bring all their 
personal problems to work and this can have a negative effect on 
the whole workplace, as listening to personal problems can distract 
people from their work tasks.
While it is probably all right to sympathise at first, it is probably 
best to stay out of the person’s personal dramas, especially if they 
become stressful and affect the whole working environment. A 
better approach is to communicate with the drama queen only on 
work-related matters. 
The workmate who gets promoted
Sometimes the transition from work colleague to 
supervisor can be difficult. The person who once mixed 
with office mates now finds that he or she has been 
promoted and the relationship changes. However, 
this need not be a problem if both sides understand 
the situation. Again, mutual respect for each worker’s 
position should be mixed with mutual respect and 
friendship.

11	Designing	your	own	office
Regardless of what business you are in, you need a space to work. For many it might be an office. 
Whether you are a café owner, an electrician or a solicitor you will need some office space to keep 
basic records ( such as appointments or bookings) and financial records (such as cash and credit 
transactions, profit statements, balance sheets, money owed by customers and money owing to 
suppliers). An office may be small or large, depending on need, and it may have various items of 
furniture and equipment (such as those listed below). Office furniture and equipment today tends 
to be ergonomic in design (to prevent back, leg or arm and wrist injuries ).
Furniture	
Equipment
Desk and chair 
• Telephone
Filing cabinet(s) 
• FAX machine
Workspace (bench) 
• Computer and/or laptop
Shelves 
• Photocopier
Comfortable chairs 
Where a business employs several people in an office, the design of the office is important. Today’s 
modern offices tend to be more open plan, ideally with the supervisor or manager in the centre 
where they have the greatest access to employees.
Office desks are now called workstations, set up with computer terminal, telephone and other 
electronic equipment. Some businesses use ‘hot desks’ for people who work part-time or who work 
in the field. These people are then able to ‘book a desk’ for a specific time.

4 Different types of accommodation  
There are many different types of accommodation available. It is important to be aware of all the 
options available to you. The main differences between the options are cost, location and level of 
independence. Do you want to share with others, or would you prefer to live alone? Will you cook your 
own meals, or would you prefer somebody did that for you? Different kinds of accommodation suit a 
range of needs. These options are explained below.
Boarding
Full board means that you will live, or ‘board’, in a family home and all or most meals are supplied. 
These arrangements can vary widely. You can generally be guaranteed your own room, but would 
normally share bathroom/toilet facilities and eat in the family dining room. 
Some properties are classified as ‘boarding houses’. These places have a landlord or caretaker who runs 
the premises, either living in the property or controlling things from another location. 
Meals may be provided (in which case you are a ‘boarder’) but if you only receive cleaning services, 
linen or other household items you are a ‘lodger’. There will be a shared kitchen and bathroom, but 
there may be no communal, or shared, living space. Tenants have no say in who shares the boarding 
house with them. The owner chooses the tenants. 
You should be aware that living in boarding houses means you don’t have the protections available to 
renters (who are protected by the Residential Tenancies Act). This means you could be asked to leave 
without notice. 
Rental accommodation
Rental accommodation means paying a set amount of money each week or month to rent a property. 
This property can either be shared (in which case, all the costs are shared among the tenants) or 
individual. Types of rented accommodation include:
Studios
Studios are very small apartments made up of one main room without a separate bedroom. The main 
room might include a bed, lounge and a small kitchen (kitchenette). The bathroom is usually separate, 
although in some cases it may be shared. A studio has the advantage of allowing you to live alone 
relatively cheaply. 
Flats, units and apartments
Places with one or more separate bedrooms are usually flats,  
units or apartments. They vary in the number of bedrooms  
(usually between 1 and 3). As well as bedrooms, they usually  
have a separate living area, kitchen, bathroom and sometimes 
laundry. Some apartment buildings have a communal laundry  
area which may be located on the ground floor or basement  
and shared with other units. 
Houses, townhouses, semi-detached houses and 
terrace houses
Houses are identified as freestanding properties. Townhouses, 
semi-detached houses and terrace houses will share one or more 
common walls with a neighbour. Most houses have 2, 3 or 4 
bedrooms, a kitchen, bathroom, living area and laundry. Many 
houses will also have a garden and/or courtyard area.

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
11
Share accommodation 
Share accommodation is often preferred by students looking to save money. The cost of rent and bills is 
split between the occupants, and usually everyone provides some of the furniture. Rental properties can 
be shared by several tenants. Other kinds of shared accommodation include:
• hostels, which usually have secure private rooms with shared cooking and washing facilities
• student residences, which are often based on campus and usually include a furnished room with 
meals provided for an extra charge. 
• accommodation in exchange for work, which requires you to do work around the house in 
exchange for free or cheap accommodation.

16	Doing	business	on	the	Internet
The growth of the Internet has been spectacular over the last ten years and has changed our lives 
in more ways than we imagine. It has changed the way businesses operate and the way consumers 
behave. Buying and selling online, for example, has grown remarkably in recent times. Many business-
to-business transactions are also done via the Internet.
Buying	online
The Internet has created a huge 
marketplace for goods and services. 
Buying goods online has become very 
popular, as more companies offer online 
buying services. You can even sell goods 
online through websites like eBay, via a 
bidding system which puts buyers and 
sellers in touch with each other.
Nudie	juice:	A	case	study
Naked ambition
Sydney Morning Herald, Enterprise  
17 August 2004
The founder of nudie is ready to squeeze 
all he can out of his cute and catchy 
brand name.
Tim Pethick, former accountant, 
management consultant, restaurant owner, 
advertising director and chief executive, is 
now the man behind nudie.
Nudie fruit juices have been on the shelves 
for just over 18 months and even Pethick 
is amazed by how quickly his branding 
experiment has caught on.
Citing reasons for nudie’s success, Pethick 
says: ‘It’s the name, which is different 
and not one you’d normally expect to be 
associated with a juice; it’s the colour, it’s 
the characters, it’s the cheeky tone of voice we have on the labels and in our copy. All the elements 
come together to make the whole. And I think we’re very lucky to have all the right elements.’
But having all the right elements requires much more than luck. There has been some very careful 
planning behind nudie.
‘Primarily, what nudie is about is a different approach to building a brand. I don’t think brands are 
built very well in this country,’ says Pethick, who has worked for a number of years in the United 
States and the United Kingdom.
Building a dialogue with consumers is central to the nudie brand proposition, and the Internet has 
played an instrumental role in this. ‘We put our web address on everything so people always have a 
place to go if they want to know more. Because we don’t advertise, people first discover nudie on a 
fridge shelf or someone tells them about it. When you hear about it, you want to know more and the 
web is the first place people go to learn more. So they start this process of becoming involved with 
the brand.
For the 10 years before starting nudie, Pethick was employed in corporate roles investigating how to 
use technology to change the underlying structure of a business. ‘The Internet has become incredibly 
important. For many businesses – including ours – the Internet is now like a front door to the 
business,’ says Tall Tim, as he is known on the website. ‘And more importantly, given that the nudie

11 Employment relations
A work buddy or a mentor
Every worker needs a buddy to lean on; someone to go to for advice; a shoulder to cry on; perhaps 
a role model; someone to be a supportive friend. Sometimes a more senior colleague can act as a 
mentor, and take a new employee under their wing, encouraging, advising and maybe helping train 
a worker for future promotion. 
Employer–employee relations
A good relationship with the boss is an 
important part of maintaining a happy 
work environment. An understanding of the 
different roles and duties of people in the 
workplace is essential for a good working 
environment. Adopting an ‘us and them’ 
mentality to employers or supervisors is 
unproductive and fruitless.
Office gossip
It can be easy to get caught up in office 
gossip or politics. Criticising work colleagues 
behind their backs is in poor taste and 
regarded as unprofessional. Relaxing after 
work, having a drink with workmates and 
having fun is OK but you need to be careful 
that you do not lose the respect of your 
work colleagues through irresponsible or 
inappropriate behaviour.
 
From: 
Sabina Bartoli, Branch Supervisor 
 
To: 
Adam Roberts
 
Sent: 
Monday 7th August 2006 2.40 pm
 
Subject: 
Professional behaviour  
I have noticed that you have been rather rude to your work colleagues 
lately. Swearing at them, abusing them and blaming them for your errors is 
unprofessional conduct. I would like you to think about this and then we can 
arrange to have a talk about it. I would like to help but I cannot allow this sort of 
behaviour to continue as it affects the harmony in the office.
Office emails
	
Anna:	
Hi, my name is Anna and I am going to be helping you in your new job.
	 Karina:	
Thanks Anna, are you going to be like my buddy?
	
Anna:	
Yes, you could put it that way. I want you to feel happy at work. I want you to understand 
that you will be relating to your work colleagues as well as your supervisor. Your own 
personality and personal skills will be visible to others and you will be judged on them. 
	 Karina:	
I hope I don’t disappoint everyone.
 
Anna:	
Don’t worry about it. You are bound to make some mistakes but that is a normal part of 
learning your job. If you approach your job with a positive attitude you will be fine. It is 
only when people whinge and complain or criticise others that problems can arise.

7 Equal opportunity
Discrimination is defined as: Unfair treatment of a person or group on the basis of prejudice.
Society has come to realise that some groups of workers in the past have been treated unfairly. 
Equal opportunity is an important principle which operates in workplaces today and is now 
supported by legislation. In workplaces throughout Australia, it is against the law for any employee 
to be discriminated against by being refused employment or promotion, given less favourable 
conditions of employment or being dismissed because of their:
sex
pregnancy
race (colour, nationality, ethnic background)
marital status
sexual orientation
disability (physical or intellectual)
age
religion.
This law applies to all employees, including those on probation, apprentices, trainees, whether they 
are casual, permanent, part-time or full-time. 
The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission is a national independent statutory 
organisation established to promote and protect human rights in Australia. One of its main 
functions is to investigate and conciliate complaints of discrimination lodged under these laws: 
The Racial Discrimination Act 
The Sex Discrimination Act 
The Disability Discrimination Act 
The Age Discrimination Act.
The Commission also investigates and conciliates complaints of discrimination lodged under the 
Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission Act. Under this law you can make a complaint 
if you think you have been discriminated against in your employment on any grounds. The 
complaints process is private, confidential and free. 
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
Sex discrimination means 
being treated less favourably 
than someone else because 
of your sex or marital status 
or because you are pregnant.
Sexual harassment is a 
type of sex discrimination.
It is unlawful to dismiss 
a person from employment 
on the ground of family 
responsibilities such as 
care of children.
It is against the law for 
an employer to discriminate 
against any employees on 
the basis of race, colour, 
national or ethnic origin.
The Human Rights 
and Equal Opportunity 
Commission inquires into 
complaints of racial hatred. 
Racial hatred is defined as a 
public act which is likely to 
offend, insult, humiliate or 
intimidate a person or group 
and is based on race, colour, 
national or ethnic origin.
Employers are obliged 
to make reasonable 
arrangements to assist a 
person with a disability to 
carry out the required tasks 
of his or her job.
Age discrimination 
is not unlawful if a 
person is unable to 
carry out the required 
tasks because of his or 
her age. 
The law provides for positive age discrimination. 
This means helping people who experience a 
disadvantage because of their particular age.

18 Foreign currency

Each country has its own currency which is legal tender within the borders of that country. Normally it cannot be used for cash
transactions in another country. Foreign currency refers to currency [money] of another country, other than the place in which the
person is located. For example, if you lived in Australia and you were to travel to Japan you would need to purchase Japanese yen,
In this example, Japanese yen is the foreign currency.

Being able to change one country’s money for another country’s money allows people to travel and trade [exchange goods and
services}. Exchanging one currency for another can usually be done in both countries, Imagine if you couldn't exchange money at
all. Going te anather country but not being able to purchase products [a drink, food and a night's accommodation] would make your
holiday a disaster! Fortunately, this is not the case.

The value of a country’s currency fluctuates according to its supply and demand on the world markets, Supply refers to the amount
of the currency that is available for sale. Demand refers to how sought after the currency is on the world markets. For example,
the value of the Australian dollar fluctuates on wortd markets according to the demand for it. In May 2000, the Australian dollar
was worth 58 US cents, but in June 2000, it was worth 54 US cents. Australian currency is measured against all currencies but due
to the strength of the USA's economy, the US dollar is used as a benchmark, A benchmark is a standard which all countries aim

to achieve.

3 Foreign currency
When you travel to foreign countries you will find that they have different money systems or
currencies. For example, in the United Kingdom they use pounds, in Thailand they have Baht, while
in China the yuan is the currency used.
Exchange rates
Many countries use dollars, such as the United States, New Zealand, Singapore and Canada, however
they are still considered foreign currencies in Australia. If you are in Canada and want to buy a
hamburger you will need Canadian dollars. So you have to convert your Australian dollars into the
local currency. You can do this at a bank, financial institution or foreign exchange dealer. The conversion
is done by means of the exchange rate. This is simply the rate at which one currency exchanges for
another. For example, on 15 March 2005, the official exchange rate for Australian to Canadian dollars
was: A$1 = C$0.85. Below is a list in Australian dollars of the exchange rates on 11 March 2005. 
© Blake Education, 2006
8
Living and Work Literacy 1
Exchange rates fluctuate on a daily basis according to forces acting in the market place. Australia’s
exchange rate tells us how much other countries are prepared to pay for our goods and services.
For example, an increase in the demand for Australian coal would be likely to lead to an increase in
the demand for Australian dollars to pay for it. This puts upward pressure on the price of Australian
dollars (in relation to other currencies). Similarly, an increase in the demand for Japanese cars will
mean an increase in the demand for Japanese yen to pay for them. The value of the yen would then
be likely to increase. A fall in the exchange rate for Australian dollars will make it more expensive
for us to buy overseas goods and services.

Living and Work Literacy 3
1	Going	into	business
About two-thirds of businesses are still 
operating after five years. The majority of 
businesses that cease operations are not 
failures, but end because the owner retires 
or seeks a different lifestyle.

The story above illustrates how a 
sole trader might operate. Other 
forms of business are partnerships

Why	do	some	people	go	into	business?	
Case	study:	Angelina	Drano
Angelina Drano left school and worked for 
a plumber for wages. She went to a TAFE 
college to do her apprenticeship and gained a 
plumbing certificate. She was a fully qualified 
plumber, and decided she would rather have a 
plumbing business of her own. She no longer 
wanted to work for someone else, she wanted 
to work for herself. 
She had saved up some money but this 
was not enough to begin a business, so she 
approached her bank to apply for a loan. 
With the money she now had she purchased 
a truck and some tools and equipment. She 
advertised in the local newspaper to let people 
know she was available to do plumbing jobs 
in the area. She found it was important to 
quote competitively for jobs. If she charged 
too much, nobody would hire her – but if she 
charged too little, she couldn't cover her costs.
As a one-person business, Angelina was 
responsible for all the tasks that running 
a business required. This included making 
phone calls, ordering supplies, quoting on jobs 
and keeping business records. 
She found that if the income she received 
from her customers was greater than her 
expenses, such as repayments on the loan, 
purchase of supplies and renewing tools and 
equipment, she had made a profit. This profit, 
she felt, was the reward for taking the risk 
of possibly losing money. However, if her 
expenses exceeded her income, this would 
amount to a loss. 
Fortunately for Angelina she was successful 
and made enough profit for her to continue
