12 Industrial disputes
Industrial disputes occur when differences between employees and the employer arise. Some 
industrial disputes can be quickly and easily solved. A complaint about the state of the staff toilets 
or lunchroom can be brought to the attention of the employers. They examine the situation 
and agree to fix the problem. Most of the minor disputes can be solved in this way, by mutual 
agreement and a ‘give and take’ attitude by both parties. Reductions in pay rates, especially penalty 
rates, or cuts in leave entitlements however, are generally more controversial.
A typical dispute might take the following course:
Phase 1  The RU E-Tin Restaurant employs 20 people, most of whom work on weekends. The 
restaurant owners have decided to refuse to pay penalty rates for weekend work. All 
employees will be forced to take a cut in pay.
Phase 2  The employees call a stopwork meeting to discuss the situation. For this meeting they 
decide to call in a trade union organiser to discuss their options.
Phase 3  The trade union organiser addresses the meeting of employees and suggests they take 
their complaints, as a group, to their employer. If this proves unsuccessful they could 
decide to go on strike. She explains the types of strikes they have at their disposal, 
such as a lightning strike which is called quickly, often without trade union approval, 
a wildcat strike which is not organised by a trade union, a sit-down strike where 
employees go to work but do nothing, or a rolling strike where there is a succession of 
strikes at short intervals.
Phase 4  Negotiations with the employer fail and so a strike is called. Most employees withdraw 
their labour. Some however, are not trade union members and do not agree with the 
strike, and so they decide to return to work. Union members who are on strike then 
form a picket line at the entrance to the restaurant.
Phase 5  Meanwhile, the restaurant owners hear of this proposed strike and decide to lock out 
the workers and employ members of their own family to run the restaurant.
Phase 6  The restaurant owners and the employees meet again to try to resolve the dispute. No 
agreement is reached.
Phase 7  Since this is an industrial dispute, both parties are summoned to appear before an 
industrial court. The court calls for a compulsory conference between the two parties to 
try to resolve the dispute. This fails and so the matter is subjected to arbitration. 
Phase 8  The industrial court orders the employees back to work. Some of them go back to work 
and accept the reduced pay, while others resign on principle.

15 Bankruptcy 2

Bankruptcy is regularly reported in newspapers and on the nightly TV news. But what does bankruptcy mean? The word
‘bankruptcy’ refers to a financial situation where there is legal recognition that a person or a business is no longer able to pay their
debts [money owing]. A person or business must owe at least $1500 to be declared bankrupt, The person/business that owes the
money is called the debtor, The person/business to whom/which the money is owed is called the creditor.

For example, Caitlin [the debtor] is unable to pay Enrico [the creditor] the sum of $53000, Caitlin can either declare herself
bankrupt or it can be done by a creditor. In both cases, bankruptcy must be proven six months before filing for bankruptcy.

In the case of Caitlin, if she is unable to meet her debts, then her financial position should be legally recognised and her assets
controtled by an official. An asset is a valuable that can be sold in order to meet outstanding debts. The assets are handed over to
an official. The role of the official is to divide the assets [converted into cash) equally among creditors. It must be remembered that
although the assets have been converted into cash, not all creditors will be paid in full. Once Caitlin has been declared bankrupt,
her financial status is that of ‘bankrupt’.

Caitlin must remember that this financial state will remain for three years and in that time she cannot obtain credit of more than
$500 and she cannot change her name in order to operate a business. Enrico too must keep in mind that once Caitlin has been
declared bankrupt he cannot try to regain his debt [if not already recovered).

As mentioned above, in order for Caitlin’s debt to be paid, her assets were placed under the direct control of an official. The
Bankruptcy Act 1966 does not allow certain debtor's assets to be sold to pay creditors. Caitlin’s essential clothing, household
property, life assurance policies, income and means of transport (up to $2500 worth] will not be taken away from her.

6 Interview skills in the workplace 
You have completed an interview for a job and been successful in gaining that job.  
Do you think there will be no more interviews? Then think again! 
Interviews are now an integral part of the continuous  
assessment of a worker’s progress in an organisation.  
In other words, there are many other types of  
interviews apart from the initial job interview.  
They include:
annual reviews
s�internal reviews
s�disciplinary interviews
s�internal promotion interviews.
s�Annual reviews are often used by companies or organisations to assess the performance of their 
employees each year. Employees are expected to participate openly and honestly in the process, and in 
return receive feedback from their manager or supervisor. This process is sometimes referred to as an 
Annual Performance Review. It is sometimes assessed against agreed goals or performance indicators. For 
example, a salesperson could need to demonstrate a specific sales target for the year. 
Internal reviews are similar to annual reviews, except that they may occur more or less often and may 
be held for a specific purpose. For example: 
a new owner may wish to hold an internal review soon after taking over a business
s�there may be a problem in the company or organisation, such as falling profits or evidence of 
s�fraud, which requires an internal review of performance.
Disciplinary interviews are held when an employee has done something which is either impolite, illegal 
or against the company or organisation’s policies. They may involve a penalty, a demotion or a warning 
that future indiscretions will lead to instant dismissal.
Internal promotion interviews are a typical way of promoting employees to a higher position within 
the organisation. They may be one-on-one informal interviews or more formal, where the interview 
panel consists of three or more people.

Sarah had worked at the XL Furniture Company for a year.

positive and that you have a good work ethic. Your personal  
dealings with customers have been excellent and your sales

Sarah:  Thank you Emily for your advice and feedback.

17	Keeping	records
It is very important for businesses to keep accurate records of all financial transactions. A business 
needs to know the following.
Is the price right for the products they sell?
What is the business’s financial situation in relation to assets and liabilities?
Is the business making money?
How much does the business owe to others?
How much is owed to the business by others?
How much available cash does the business have to pay immediate bills?
How much tax does the business owe?
Many businesses fail as a result of poor financial planning and recording. A good accountant can 
supervise the financial transactions and make suggestions, and a business can also request an 
auditor (someone outside the business) to examine accounts on an official basis.
Financial transactions involve forms or documents, such as tax invoices, statements, cheques and 
receipts. In the past, book-keeping involved journals which recorded daily transactions, and ledgers 
which grouped transactions into specific accounts. Businesses today increasingly use computer 
technology to manage and analyse their accounts, and make particular use of spreadsheets which 
can do a great variety of calculations automatically.
Calculating	your	true	financial	situation

future. Part of this involves the communication between a business and its bank, and reconciling 
the bank balances. This is done via a Bank Reconciliation Statement (see example below).

5 Keeping the CV up to date 
It is important to keep your CV up to date, even if you currently hold a job. You may need it to apply 
for a promotion or a job opportunity that can further your career may suddenly come along. You may 
not realise it, but you do develop skills in the course of your work. You need to identify these skills and 
include them in your CV.
Who will read your CV?
You might assume that your CV is read by a person such as an employer 
or someone in the human resources department of an organisation. 
Increasingly, computers with special software are used to ‘read’ CVs to 
help sort through the huge numbers of applications that are submitted. 
These programs look for key words and phrases commonly used by the 
type of person that the employer wants. Once the computer does an initial 
sorting, the best CVs are read by people and analysed more closely.
What is a competency statement?
A competency statement can address an applicant’s knowledge, skills, abilities and  
even attitudes. In a few short sentences, the applicant identifies a specific situation,  
explains what action was taken and the results of that action. Competency statements 
are extremely important in a CV as they tend to impress the reader. 
Matching your skills to the job ad
When reading a job ad, you need to analyse what skills the employer is  
likely to want. If the job is in finance and accounting, the skills required will  
obviously be a high degree of numerical reasoning ability, as well as attention to detail and diligence. 
These particular skills may not be so important if you applied for a job as an actor or circus performer – 
other skills would then come into play.
Once you have identified the skills required for the job you are applying for, then  
you need to organise your own particular skills in your CV to match. It has been  
found that applicants who can do this successfully have a 30% better chance 
of being shortlisted for a job.
What are employers really looking for?
Recent research has highlighted the eight most common qualities 
employers ask for in job ads:

Living and Work Literacy 6
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2009
20 Life-long learning and pathways
The old traditional pathway was once: leave school  ➨ go to university or TAFE college ➨ get a job.  
Today there are many pathways available to people which don’t follow the traditional sequence. For 
example, a more common sequence today might be: school  ➨ job ➨ TAFE course ➨ different job ➨ 
university ➨ different job again. Another pathway could involve overseas travel or what some people 
refer to as a gap year.
Gap year
Many people are not sure what they want to do in their working life after they leave school. Taking 
a gap year and travelling or working can be a good option. If you have gained a place at university 
or TAFE, you can defer your studies for at least a year, perhaps more. Taking a gap year gives you a 
breathing space and time to contemplate your future. You will also gain maturity, confidence and 
independence through a year off formal study. You can even work while overseas if you get a work 
visa or work at home before travelling overseas or in Australia. Most people who take gap years do not 
regret it.
Gillian
Gillian worked hard at high school 
and gained entry to university to study 
for Arts/Law. Gillian thought about 
deferring her degree and having a gap 
year. She had worked at a jewellery store 
on Thursday evenings and Saturday 
mornings for the past three years and 
had some savings and a burning desire 
to travel.
She decided to go ahead and defer her 
studies for a year and work full time 
in the jewellery store for a couple of 
months before going on a trip to the 
United Kingdom. Once she reached 
London, she gained some temp work 
in an ofﬁce and travelled around 
on weekends. Then when she had 
accumulated more savings, she left her 
temp job and went to Europe where 
she backpacked for six months with a 
few English friends she had met. When 
she returned at the beginning of the 
following year, she realised that she had 
made the right choice. She had learned 
a lot about life in her time away and she 
felt she was now ready to settle down to 
her university degree.
University options
1. Mid-year enrolments
Universities today are far more flexible than in the past. 
You don’t have to enrol or start at the beginning of the 
year, as there is the option of mid-year enrolment. You 
may have missed out on the course of your choice or 
failed to apply in time. You may even have wanted a 
short break before resuming your studies. The Universities 
Admission Centre (UAC) will have information available for 
you. However, there are usually less places available than 
at the beginning of the academic year.
2. Changing universities
If you find that the course you have started is not for you, 
or if your personal circumstances have changed, there are 
ways of completing your studies by changing universities. 
You can receive credits for courses completed at one 
university and finish a course at another, although there 
are obviously some rules which you would need to find 
out about.
3. Success doesn’t require a uni degree
Many people think, quite wrongly, that a university 
degree is essential for success in the workplace. Many 
people achieve much with no formal qualifications. This 
doesn’t mean that everyone should abandon the idea of 
a university degree, but it is not the only option. Today 
there are many TAFE college courses which today are 
designed specifically to suit particular careers – without 
the large course fees. Furthermore, university degrees are 
no guarantee of success in the world of work.
There is plenty of advice you can get from your Careers 
Advisor at school, from parents and friends, or from the 
many websites which specialise in this field. Start with 
Career Guide Australia at www.yourcareerguide.com.au.

7

education? How?
8

Under what circumstances might this be necessary?  
Do universities place limitations on these changes? Give

9

10 Read Maya’s story. Was Maya disadvantaged by not doing a

11 Brad left school after year 12 and decided to work as a shop 
assistant. If you were Brad’s friend, what options would you 
suggest to him in seeking a future career?
Keith
Keith was a talented actor and writer who found that work opportunities were limited, 
so he decided to start a law degree at the University of Melbourne. He had completed 
three units of the course when his wife accepted a job as an arts director for a company 
in Darwin. He decided to approach the University of the Northern Territory to see if he 
could continue his law degree and gain credit for courses completed. This was granted 
and he did three more units of study. Three years later, his wife accepted an arts director 
job in Perth. He wanted to continue his legal studies and asked if he could complete his 
degree at the University of Western Australia. They accepted two of his three units from 
the Northern Territory, but this was acceptable to him. Keith went on to complete his law 
degree at the University of Western Australia.
Maya
Maya did not have a university degree but she was successful in the ﬁeld of real estate. 
When she left school, Maya got a job with the local branch of a large real estate 
company and began selling houses. Her personality, charm and eagerness to learn 
on the job made her an instant success. She enrolled in a TAFE college course in real 
estate and gained the necessary qualiﬁcation. After a few years she was promoted 
to manager of the local branch. Five years later, Maya decided to establish her own 
real estate ofﬁce. Working with a small number of staff she continued to build on 
her success. Selling real estate is not easy. Although Maya could have enrolled in a 
university course, she created a successful business with minimum qualiﬁcations, but 
she did require enormous energy and skill.

Living and Work Literacy 4
21 Promotion
Some useful tips
Work out what you want to achieve, and draw up a plan of how you will do it. Acquiring new 
skills may be necessary.
Look for opportunities. You may be able to come up with a more efficient process for something 
you are working on, or you may look for ways to gain new experiences.
Do some networking. Remember, ‘It is not what you know but who you know’. The more you 
know about the organisation you work for, the better. Usually the best way to learn about an 
organisation is to talk to people who already work there.
•
•
•
Your 
qualifications:
 This includes your formal 
education as well as informal 
qualifications like courses 
and workshops.
Your knowledge:
This may include 
content-specific knowledge 
about an area of work or 
a specific issue you have 
been working on, as well as 
knowledge about people, 
networks, and procedures 
and processes.
 
Your skills: 
This may include writing, 
negotiating, organisational 
and problem-solving 
skills.
 
Your experience: 
Experience gained at work, 
such as positions held and 
duties associated with 
them
Your values: 
Consider what you value and look 
for in a job and company, such as a good 
work ethic, self-management as well as the 
geographic location of a job.
 
Your personal 
attributes:
This would include 
reliability, a sense of 
humour, honesty, integrity 
and adaptability.
Self-assessment
Case study
Nathan said that he was not aware of all the options available to him after finishing Year 12. ‘I 
planned to go on to do a law degree after Year 12 although I wasn’t really looking forward to all the 
study involved. I thought twice about it, however, when I was offered training in the hospitality 
industry’. During Year 12, Nathan was employed as a part-time dishwasher at a local hotel. On 
completion of his final year, Nathan’s employer encouraged him to commence a traineeship. With 
further information about the hospitality traineeship and the enthusiasm of his employer, Nathan 
decided that this just might turn out to be his preferred vocation. He always enjoyed working with 
people and he felt that the industry offered good career prospects.
Nathan learned a broad range of skills during his traineeship and was soon involved in organising 
functions, weddings and other important events. He said, ‘I am ready for more responsibility and have 
my sights set on a management or supervisory position’.
Nathan says he learnt quickly during his traineeship due mainly to being able to put his newly 
acquired skills into practice.
Nathan was one of a class of 10 hospitality trainees. He said, ‘I made some very good friends during 
my training. We compared our different work environments and learnt from each other. We still see 
each other regularly, and who knows, given the nature of the hospitality industry, some of us might 
become very successful indeed’.
Although Nathan did well, promotion is not always an automatic process. If you want to progress in 
your career you should take active steps rather than waiting to be tapped on the shoulder. 

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2006
Living and Work Literacy 4	
43
Keep abreast of issues and new trends in your line of work by reading journals, surfing the 
Internet and attending relevant conferences.
Take stock of your achievements. Compile a record of all work-related achievements, samples of 
great work, letters of recognition and other materials that demonstrate good job performance.
Consider a horizontal move. It may be better to make a sideways move to a job at your current 
level in the short term so you can learn new skills that will help you move upwards in the future.
Be pro-active. Let your supervisor know that you are interested in progressing and learning more. 
Approach someone to act as your mentor. This is usually a more experienced person who can 
take you ‘under their wing’ and help develop your skills. 
Improve your skills. This is particularly important if you 
see a skills gap between the job you have now and the 
one you want.
Dangers
Seeking and gaining rapid promotion may be great, but 
you need to consider other factors, such as your health and 
your personal relationships. Is promotion worth it if you 
have a breakdown, or if you lose valuable friends? Working 
extremely long hours with not enough time for rest and 
leisure activities can cause problems. Taking annual leave is also an important part of this. Many 
Australians now are not taking their annual leave because they fear that their job may not be there 
when they return, or the employer may discover that they can get along well without them. Some 
are just too absorbed in their job to take leave. Taking holidays is an important part of the balance 
between work and leisure.

Living and Work Literacy 4
1 The workplace
In small groups, discuss experiences people you know have had when they began a 
new job. Make a list of the most common experiences or situations. 
T
R
Y
 
T
H
I
S
!
What is a workplace?
A workplace was once seen as an office, a factory, shop, building site or outdoor location where 
work was carried out. It was also regarded as a place where workers or employees worked for an 
employer and provided their labour in return for 
an income. While this is still true, the workplaces 
of today are much more varied. For many people, 
their workplace is not necessarily a fixed location. 
For example, truck drivers or delivery-van drivers, 
and some salespeople who have use of a company 
car to make contact with customers. 
Working from home is also a choice that some 
people have today. Some may use sewing 
machines while others use laptops, mobile phones 
and various other communication devices. Giving 
work to people who work at home under contract 
is called outsourcing. 
Their first job
Matt and Ilsa were young and keen, fresh out of school and they had just been offered their first 
real job. A year later they both felt they had done well and they wanted to share their knowledge. 
Therefore they decided to write down some suggestions for others starting a new job. They pointed 
out that starting a new job can be quite stressful or overwhelming at first, so it is important to 
consider how to ease the transition from school to work. Here are some of the things they suggested.
•	 Check out the best way to get to work to make sure you arrive on time.
•	 Become familiar with the workplace environment, e.g. where are toilets, kitchen or staffrooms? You 
need to know your way around the building or work site to avoid becoming lost and embarrassed. 
•	 Learn your job responsibilities. This may take some time, so be patient.
•	 Ask questions. This has the double effect of providing information and showing how keen you are 
to succeed. Do not be afraid to admit mistakes and to seek help from your supervisor or employer.
•	 Become involved in the social life of the workplace. There are usually many opportunities to meet 
co-workers socially and you can learn a lot over lunch or drinks after work. Be careful however, of 
becoming involved in gossip or office politics and make sure your behaviour is professional at all 
times. 
•	 Be aware of issues such as sexual harassment and discrimination in the workplace. You do not have 
to tolerate this but should report such instances to your supervisor.
•	 Take the initiative. Do not always wait to be asked to do a task. Comments like ‘That’s not my job’ 
or ‘Why should I?’ indicate a poor attitude to work.
•	 Show some interest in advancement. Look for opportunities to do more difficult tasks once you 
have mastered your own, or to take on more responsibilities.
•	 Give yourself time. Do not make any hasty decisions to quit until you have given your new job a 
fair trial.
•	 You need to have balance in your social life and work life. Eating well and getting plenty of regular 
exercise will help you to remain fit and healthy and ready for work.

Living and Work Literacy 4
13 Trade unions
What is a trade union?
It is an organisation which represents a group of workers who unite to maintain and improve pay 
rates and working conditions.
Falling membership
At the beginning of the 20th century, Australia had the most unionised workforce in the world. 
Although membership rose and fell at different times, over 50% of employees belonged to a union. 
Today, union membership is less than 25%. There are many reasons for the change, one being the 
increase in self-employed Australians.
The trade unions have embarked on membership drives aimed at signing up new members as well 
as retaining existing membership. Over the years, workers have become more critical of unions 
and want to see some benefit in being a member. The trade unions in turn have begun offering 
incentives such as discount housing loans, free legal services, travel services, credit cards and health 
benefits. The main focus of the trade union movement however, is to protect workers’ rights.
The trade union movement is also trying to address the falling membership by arranging 
amalgamations, so that small trade unions join together to form a large super union with more 
power. 
Changes to the Workplace Relations Act in 2006 resulted in increased interest by employees in 
joining a trade union. This was indicated by a 4% increase in membership from August 2004 to 
August 2005 from 1 838 365 to 1 911 900. 
The main union body is the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU). It plays a key role in wage 
fixing in Australia through submissions in National Wage Cases which set minimum rates of pay for 
award-covered employees.
Do I have to join a union?
You do not have to join a union. Federal laws 
make it illegal to either compel anyone to join a 
union or to prevent them from doing so. It is also 
illegal to discriminate against a person for either 
joining or choosing not to join a union.
What benefits are there in joining 
a union?
Unions can represent their members in the 
following areas:
Negotiate the terms and conditions of awards 
and enterprise agreements or Australian 
Workplace Agreements (AWAs) with employers. 
Investigate suspected breaches of award or 
underpayment of wages. 
Resolve industrial disputes.
Advise on health and safety and workers’ 
compensation issues. 
Investigate unfair dismissals and redundancies. 
Investigate sexual harassment and 
discrimination claims. 
Discuss superannuation issues.

13 Trade unions
Which union to join?
Each trade union has rules which allow it to cover certain types of work or certain trades. Advice on 
which union to join may come from your employer or the ACTU, which has offices (called Trades and 
Labour Councils) in all capital cities and regional areas throughout Australia. Most major unions are 
affiliated with the ACTU. 
Once you become a member of a union you 
are bound by its rules and are obliged to pay 
membership fees. You must give notice if you 
intend to resign from the union for any reason, e.g. 
if you are no longer going to work in the industry. 
Some of the larger unions in Australia are:
Australian Services Union
Community and Public Sector Union 
Australian Manufacturing Workers Union
Shop, Distributive & Allied Employees Union 
Liquor, Hospitality & Miscellaneous Workers Union 
Association of Professional Engineers, Scientists & 
Managers, Australia

There has been a determined struggle by 
workers to cooperate together for better 
working conditions since Australia was 
settled in 1788. In 1822, James Straighter, 
who was a convict shepherd, was 
sentenced to 500 lashes, one month solitary 
confinement and five years penal servitude 
for... ‘inciting his Masters’ servants to 
combine for the purposes of obliging him to 
raise the wages and increase their rations’.

9 Unemployment
Definitions   
A person is considered to be 
unemployed if they are:
not working
available for work
taking active steps to find work.
A person is considered to be employed 
if they work for one hour or more for 
pay, profit, commission or other form 
of payment.
The labour force includes all persons 
who are employed and unemployed.
The participation rate is the percentage 
of the population over 15 years who are 
in the labour force. 
Why are people unemployed?
Some may be in the process of 
changing jobs.
They may be unsuccessful in finding a 
job.
Some may have jobs which are seasonal 
with no work available in the off season.
In an economic downturn, 
unemployment levels may be high.
People with low skills or no job training find it more difficult to find a job.
Some people may need to consider retraining.
Young people may have difficulty finding a job because of their lack of experience.
Some people are fussy about the jobs they are prepared to do.
Youth unemployment
Many young people cannot find jobs because they have no experience. Yet how can they gain 
experience if no one will employ them? This is the dilemma faced by many young people and is a 
major reason why youth unemployment rates are higher than unemployment rates in the general 
community.

Useful terms
Broadband
A range of high-speed internet services, including ADSL, cable and satellite.
Dial-up
 A basic internet connection that runs through the telephone line. When connected  
to the Internet the telephone cannot be used
ADSL
 Stands for Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line. ADSL is an internet connection that  
runs through the telephone line but allows use of the telephone and internet at the 
same time. 
Upload
 If you send any material via the internet you are said to be uploading it. For 
example, sending emails or entering a web address into your browser.
Download
 When you receive material from the internet you are downloading it. This includes 
any web pages that you view as well as emails you receive and file attachments that 
you open.
File sharing
 This happens when you allow other users to upload a file, such as music or videos, 
from your computer. 
Megabytes  
and 
gigabytes
 How units of information on computers are measured. A megabyte is equal to 1000 
kilobytes or 1 000 000 bytes. A gigabyte is 1000 megabytes. A typical three-minute

audio files.

 Stands for Internet Service Provider – a company that provides an Internet

11 Communication 
Communication is an essential part of day-to-day life. It takes many forms. There are two major forms 
of communication technology which have become a significant part of how we communicate every day. 
They are the telephone and the computer. 
The telephone
If you are sharing a house that has a landline it may be necessary to work out a 
system for paying the bills. This can be either an even split of each bill, including 
line rental and all call charges, or each person can be responsible for their calls 
and the line rental is shared equally. This can be time-consuming to calculate,  
but most phone companies itemise each phone call made, especially long 
distance calls or calls to premium-rate numbers.
The computer
Most people own either a desktop computer or a laptop. When moving into a 
new house you may also want to arrange to have internet access. If two or more 
people in a household are sharing a computer there needs to be an agreement 
about what kind of plan is needed and who pays the monthly charges to the ISP 
(Internet Service Provider).

19  Health issues 
Moving out isn’t just about finding a new place to live. There will be other issues that you may not have 
had to consider until now. Taking care of your health is a big part of life.
Finding a GP
When you move into a new neighbourhood it may be necessary to register as a patient with a local 
doctor or GP (General Practitioner). Some medical practices have several doctors based in one medical 
centre. This means that you will generally have access to one of the doctors at all times, which can 
make it easier to get an appointment when you need one. If changing doctors, you may need to 
arrange to have your medical records transferred from your previous doctor. Some doctors will charge a 
small administration fee for doing this. 
Medicare
Medicare is Australia’s universal health care system. It provides all Australians with access to free or 
low-cost medical and hospital care. All Australian citizens can register with Medicare by filling in 
an enrolment form and being issued with a Medicare card. This card can then be presented at any 
Medicare branch to receive a refund on medical expenses. All you need is the doctor’s bill and your 
Medicare card. Alternatively, you can also claim your refund electronically, so the money is paid directly 
into your bank account. If your doctor bulk-bills, then you can simply sign a form acknowledging 
treatment and no payment is required. 
Health insurance
There are some medical services that Medicare does 
not cover. These include things like dental treatment, 
optical services and private hospital visits. Many people 
choose to take out private health insurance to help cover 
additional medical costs. There are several companies 
which offer private health cover (which gives you your 
own choice of doctor and access to a private hospital). 
Examples include Medibank Private, HCF and NIB. Some 
companies also offer extra levels of cover, for things like 
dental and optical care, for an additional fee. 
Ambulance
You may also choose to join an ambulance fund. 
This means that if you ever need an ambulance in an 
emergency, you don’t have to pay. Ambulance rides 
can cost hundreds of dollars, whereas the yearly fee to 
join an ambulance fund is usually only around $70 per 
year. Ambulance costs are not covered by Medicare.
Dental services
Regular dental check-ups can help prevent major 
dental issues from occurring. It’s a good idea to find a 
dentist in your area. Dental services are not covered by 
Medicare, but if you have a health care or concession 
card you may be eligible for public dental treatment, 
which is a lot more affordable. Some private health 
insurance funds also offer coverage for dental care.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
41
Mental health
If you are struggling to cope and need some support, there are many options available. Your GP will be 
able to refer you to a counsellor. Alternatively, organisations such as Beyond Blue, headspace and Lifeline 
can provide help. 
Sexual health
As well as your GP, there are several other places you can go for sexual health services. Your local Family 
Planning Centre or Sexual Health Centre will offer confidential advice and treatment, and many places 
will allow you to remain anonymous.
University health services
Most universities will offer information and treatment to students, including general health services, 
counselling, sexual health advice, travel advice and vaccinations. Most of these services are bulk billed.
Health and fitness
Although it is important to be covered for any medical problems that might occur, it is also important 
to look after your health, as this can prevent problems from occurring in the first place. Exercising 
regularly and eating a balanced diet will help you to stay fit and healthy. People who don’t exercise 
and who don’t eat a healthy diet run the risk of becoming unwell, overweight or even obese. Obesity 
is most commonly measured using the Body Mass Index (BMI), which measures a person’s weight-to-
height ratio.

Research two different private health insurance providers and the 
costs of basic hospital cover. Compare the cost of basic cover with 
the cost of extras cover. Are the extras that are covered the same in 
each case? Which do you think is better value?

20 Voting 
The right to vote is an important aspect of living in a 
democracy. In Australia, voting is compulsory and all people 
over the age of 18 are required to vote in all elections, 
whether for federal, state or local government. Failure to vote 
may result in a fine.
In order to take part in elections, you must be enrolled in 
your current electorate. This is determined by where you 
live. To enrol to vote, you must complete an enrolment 
application form, which you can obtain from any post office 
or from the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) website 
at www.aec.gov.au. 
To be eligible to be listed on the electoral roll, you must: 
•  be 18 years of age or older
•  have lived at your current address for  
at least a month
•  be an Australian citizen (either born in Australia or granted Australian citizenship).
After you have been placed on the electoral roll you will receive a card indicating which electorate you 
are enrolled in. If you move after you have enrolled, you must notify the AEC of your change of address.
Getting involved in politics
While elections are held only every three or four 
years, there are other ways of participating in a 
democracy. They can include:
•  forming pressure groups to lobby the 
government about a particular issue
•  attending public meetings, demonstrations  
or protests
•  joining a club
•  writing letters to the editors of newspapers
•  writing letters to local members of 
parliament
•  making an appointment for a personal 
interview with a member of parliament
•  approaching radio or television journalists  
or ringing a radio station on talkback radio
•  expressing our opinions in public places
•  joining a political party.
Political parties
Australia’s main political parties are:
Australian Greens Party   
www.greens.org.au 
Australian Labor Party    
www.alp.org.au 
Liberal Party of Australia 
www.liberal.org.au 
National Party 
 
www.nationals.org.au
You can find out more about their policies 
and goals from their websites, which are 
constantly being updated. Information about 
the political parties is also regularly broadcast 
on radio and television and reported in 
national newspapers.

5 Buying goods 
What are goods?  
Goods are things that have been produced for us to buy that we can see or touch. Goods include 
things like a loaf of bread, a pair of jeans, a DVD or a car. Services are different from goods – they are 
tasks that are performed for us, such as a haircut, a holiday booking or a bus trip (see unit 6 for more 
information on services). The diagram below shows how producers provide both goods and services for 
us to buy.
How can we buy goods? 
Goods are produced in places such as in a factory  
or on a farm. They then need to be transported  
to a place where consumers can buy them.  
There are several different ways that 
consumers can buy goods.
Retail stores
Retail stores, or shops, vary in size  
and location, from small corner 
stores to large department stores in 
shopping centres. Retail stores try 
to create a pleasant environment to 
encourage the shopper to buy. This 
might involve colourful displays, car 
parking facilities, background music 
and friendly service.  
Factory outlets
Some stores advertise themselves as 
‘factory outlets’. Factory outlets often 
sell end-of-season products, samples 
and seconds at a reduced price.  
Factory outlets are often located in 
industrial areas or on the outskirts of a city or suburb because the cost of renting the space is cheaper. 
They may not have the comforts and extra facilities of a retail shopping centre but this can mean that 
the prices are often cheaper.
Local markets
Local markets are held regularly in many communities. They may be held on a specific day, such as 
the first Sunday in the month, or on a weekly basis. Shoppers can often pick up bargains at markets 
because the traders do not have the same overhead costs that a retail store has. 
Direct selling
Not everyone has the time to visit shops, and others may live in remote locations where there are fewer 
shops to visit. Direct selling is a way of shopping without having to visit the shops. It can take several forms:
•  door-to door selling, where a representative of a company knocks on doors and tries to sell their goods
•  ‘party‘ selling, where a host throws a party and invites a company representative to show 
their products. This is common with cosmetics, women’s clothing and kitchen goods (such as 
Tupperware). The host often receives a free gifts if a certain sales target is reached.
•  mail order selling, where goods are advertised in a catalogue that is sent to potential customers. 
Shoppers are not able to see the goods they are buying, but most mail order companies will allow 
the products to be returned if the purchaser is unhappy with them.

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
18 Gambling 
Gambling can take many forms, but it is generally accepted to mean placing a bet or wager on an 
event or playing a game of chance for money. It may be putting a bet on a horse race or playing a 
poker machine – there are lots of examples.  
Why do people take the risk?
Many people find gambling fun. Some people only gamble occasionally (such as a once a year bet on 
the Melbourne Cup) while others gamble more regularly. Some people never gamble at all. Although 
gambling can be fun, there is a lot of risk involved, and some people take big risks that don’t always 
pay off. In Australia, people under the age of 18 are not allowed to take part in any form of gambling. 
This includes buying lottery tickets or scratchies, which are also kinds of gambling.
What are your chances?
Gambling is all about taking a risk in the hope that you will win some money. Generally, the greater the 
risk, the more money you could win. You may be familiar with the laws of probability – this means that 
there is a formula for predicting the likely outcome in each case. Many people keep gambling because 
they ‘feel lucky’ or think their number is bound to come up soon, but the laws of probability often show 
that the chances of this happening are actually very small.
For example, take the discussion between Daniel and Ellie.
Daniel: When I toss this coin Ellie, what are the chances of tossing a head?
Ellie: 
Well, I would say 50/50.
Daniel:  Correct, as there are two possibilities. But what if I told you that I have just tossed ten heads in  
a row? What are the chances of a head on this next toss?
Ellie: 
Oh, that would be a lot less than 50/50.
Daniel:  Wrong. Each individual toss still has a 50/50 chance of coming up heads. But if I asked what are 
the chances of tossing 11 consecutive heads, that is different. Do you follow?
Ellie:  
 I think so. You really need to understand the laws of probability if you are going to gamble,  
don’t you?  
Commercial gambling such as poker machines and horse racing is usually organised to make money  
for the organisation running it. This means that the more a person gambles, the more likely he or she  
is to return a certain percentage of their winnings to the organisation. Winning can be exciting, but  
the temptation to keep gambling in the hope of winning more can be a trap. In the long term, you  
are most likely to lose. The only way to avoid getting into trouble is to only gamble what you can  
afford to lose.
Compulsive gambling
Some people find that gambling becomes a habit that they are unable to control. This is known as 
compulsive gambling. Compulsive gamblers are characterised by:
•  a continual need to gamble, whether they are winning or losing
•  an inability to stop gambling
•  a tendency to gamble much more than they can afford.
Many compulsive gamblers don’t believe they have a problem. Compulsive gamblers may avoid telling 
people how much they gamble and how much they lost, or they may gamble until they run out of 
money. Some will sell or steal things to raise more money to gamble.
Compulsive gambling can lead to family relationship breakdown, an inability to work efficiently, financial 
problems and even criminal activity. Problem gambling is recognised as a mental health issue.

Many people struggle with gambling problems and there is help available. Gambling Help Line 
(1800 858 858) is on call 24 hours a day. Each state in Australia also has gambling help lines, such as 
Gamblers Anonymous.

 18 Gambling
Case study: Lee
Lee started gambling when he was 14, playing card games at home on the internet. ‘Internet poker is 
great, because you don’t have to be over 18 to play’, he boasted to his mates. By 19, Lee was a regular 
casino visitor, where he played blackjack and roulette.
‘It’s an adrenalin rush’, he would say. ‘You are pitting your skills and abilities against the system.’ By 25 
Lee was married with two young children, but he still gambled whenever he got the chance. He would bet 
on sporting matches, visit the casino and he still used online gambling sites. Before long Lee had gambled 
away his savings, lost his job and his marriage began to break down. Lee had become a compulsive 
gambler, and he needed help.

Living and Work Literacy 8
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
 20 Tax returns 
Almost everyone who earns money has to pay tax on the money they earn. If you have been in paid 
employment, at the end of the financial year you will need to fill in a tax return. If you earn more than 
$6000 in a financial year (1 July to 30 June) you must pay income tax.  The first $6000 you earn is 
called the ‘tax-free threshhold’. The amount of tax you will pay on the rest of the money you earn will 
be calculated according to your income. 
Tax file number
When you start work for the first time you will need a tax file number. This is a nine digit number 
that identifies you to the Australian Tax Office. To change jobs, apply for government benefits from 
Centrelink or to file a tax return, you will need this number. There are two ways of applying for a tax  
file number (TFN).
1.  If you are a secondary school student, the quickest and easiest way for you to get your tax file 
number is via the secondary schools TFN program. Applying this way is easy because your school 
verifies your identity, so you don’t need to provide any documents proving your identity.  You will 
still need to provide some information from your Australian birth certificate, Australian citizenship 
certificate or overseas passport.
2.  If you have left school you will need to complete a Tax File Number application. You can get an 
application form online from the Australian Tax Office at www.ato.gov.au or by phoning the tax 
office. You will need original documents to prove your identity.  
How income tax works
You pay income tax during the year as you earn it. If you are an employee, your employer will take it 
from your wages. The amount of tax you pay depends on how much you earn and whether you can 
claim any deductions, such as work-related expenses. When you start a new job, you have 28 days to 
give your tax file number to your employer before they must start deducting tax from your pay.  
Completing a tax return
At the end of the financial year, you need to work out whether you have paid too much tax or not 
enough. To do this you complete a tax return.  
A simple calculation: 
Gross income – work-related expenses (or deductions) = taxable income
Tax already paid – tax payable on your taxable income = tax refund.
Note that if you owe more tax than you have paid you will owe the tax office the difference.
Some people do their own tax return, either using e-Tax online or using the Australian Tax Office 
booklet (TaxPack) as a guide. Tax laws can be very complex so many people use the services of a tax 
agent or qualified tax accountant.    
To complete your return you will need your tax file number and a yearly payment summary, or group 
certificate, from your employer, as well as any other financial documents or records you’ve received 
during the income year. The income year ends on 30 June each year. You have until 31 October to 
lodge your tax return. If you use a registered tax agent you can lodge later than 31 October, but you 
need to see your agent before 31 October to qualify for their lodgement dates.
The tax office will process your return and issue you with a Notice of Assessment and refund, usually 
within a few weeks. If you owe tax, the earliest you will have to pay it is 21 November, regardless of 
when you lodge your return. If you have any problems or queries you can contact the tax office or your 
tax agent.

What can you claim?
Work related expenses – You can claim many expenses that relate to your work. To claim an expense,

17 Warranties 
A warranty is a written promise, given by the seller or the manufacturer, that the product they are 
selling is free from faults. A warranty also means that if a fault is found, the seller or manufacturer  
agrees to repair or replace the faulty product. As well as the warranty offered by the seller or 
manufacturer, almost all goods that you purchase are covered by an implied warranty. This means  
that the manufacturer is required by law to ensure that their product meets certain standards.
Manufacturer’s warranties
The manufacturer’s warranty guarantees that the goods will work for a certain period of time (this is 
known as the warranty period). If any faults occur within the warranty period, the manufacturer agrees 
to replace or repair the product. 
Express warranties
Express warranties are the normal warranties given by the manufacturer or retailer, including the details 
of what is covered and what is not. The express warranty may state that some parts are excluded, or 
whether both parts and labour are included. An express warranty may also state that a product will not 
be covered by faults caused by misuse, accident or carelessness.
Extended warranties
Some manufacturers or retailers offer what is called an 
extended warranty, at an additional cost. This is designed 
to cover you if the product stops working outside of the 
manufacturer’s warranty period. Extended warranties 
often offer cover for an extra 1, 3 or 5 years. Some 
extended warranties actually offer protection that you  
are already entitled to under the consumer guarantee,  
so it is important to find out what the extended warranty 
provides before purchasing one.
Implied warranties
When it comes to warranties, many people are unaware 
of their rights. If a product comes with a 12-month 
warranty, many people assume that after 12 months 
they have no more protection. However, there is also 
an implied warranty on all goods. This means that any 
product you buy must do what it says it will do for 
a reasonable period of time. For example, if you buy 
a lawnmower, you would expect it to be able to cut 
grass. This expectation should continue well beyond the 
12-month warranty that the manufacturer may provide. 
Implied warranties are also called statutory warranties. 
Knowing your rights
It is important to know your rights when it comes to warranties. If you have a problem with a product 
you have purchased, you should stop using it immediately and contact the seller or service provider. 
You might be able to negotiate whether the product should be repaired or replaced, or your money 
refunded, depending on the nature of the problem.

11 Budgeting
Budgeting is an important aspect of your life. A budget is simply a plan of your regular income and
expenses over a period of time. You may have a weekly budget, a monthly budget or a yearly one.
Businesses and governments also prepare budgets as they need to plan their financial dealings ahead
of time. Budgets help people and organisations to achieve goals, especially long-term goals.
Preparing a budget
To prepare a budget you need to follow a few simple steps:
• Define your goals: for example, you may want to buy a new bicycle or a second-hand car, go
on an overseas holiday, or you may want to buy some new clothes or a new stereo. 
• List all your regular sources of income: these might include pocket money or your weekly wages
if you have a job. You may also expect to receive occasional gifts, perhaps from relatives on
your birthday. You may also earn money doing odd jobs.
• List all your expenses: for a personal budget, these can be ordered into categories, such as
food, clothing, fares, entertainment, sports expenses and credit card repayments. If you are
preparing a household budget you would need to add things like electricity and telephone
charges, car expenses, rent or house repayments, rates and insurance.
• Set aside an amount of money for unexpected expenses or emergencies.
A budget will help you work out how much you are likely to save over a certain period of time. This
may involve making adjustments to how much you spend. You can also build the amount you want
to save into your budget.
When you analyse your income and regular expenses over time, you will start to see if you are over-
committed or if you are able to save some of your income to achieve your goal.
Spreadsheets
Spreadsheets are a useful way of recording financial transactions and making useful calculations,
especially for a budget. A spreadsheet is computer software that allows you to enter information in
columns and then make calculations using a formula.
A spreadsheet looks like an alphanumeric grid, with letters of the alphabet across the top and numbers
in sequence down the left-hand side, creating a series of cells that can be identified as A1, H4 or M25.
At the top of the spreadsheet is a space for entering a formula so that you can make calculations.
For example: M25 = M24+M23+M22 or M25 = J25+K25+L25
In the example below the formula is A5=SUM(A1:A4) There are more complex formulas than simple
additions, such as calculating interest rates and loan repayments.
There are also many more functions to a spreadsheet, including sorting words alphabetically in
ascending or descending order. The help menu of the software will help you learn more about using
spreadsheets.

14 Buying a car
Imagine that you have decided to buy a car. It would be very unwise to go out and buy the first car
you see without doing some important research. New cars are naturally likely to be more reliable
than used cars, but they are also very expensive. Here are some generally agreed tips on buying a
second-hand car. 
• Decide how much money you want to spend.
• Research car insurance: there are two types of car insurance. The first is comprehensive
insurance. This insures your car against damage. This means that if you smash your car and it is
insured for $10 000, the insurance company will assess the damage and pay some or the entire
amount depending on the damage. The second is called third party property insurance. This
covers you for any damage you do to another person’s car. It is cheaper than comprehensive
insurance as your own car is not covered. This should not be confused with compulsory third
party insurance (sometimes known as a ‘Green Slip’). This insurance is paid for as part of your
car registration and is designed to compensate people injured in car accidents, regardless of
fault.
• Research finance if you need to borrow money to buy the car you want. This involves checking
interest rates and general borrowing terms. It is also important to budget for the loan
repayments.
• Be aware of additional costs of motoring. These include costs of petrol, registration and
insurance, servicing and repairs, spare parts and the depreciation of your car’s value. When you
want to sell the car you will find its value has dropped and you need to factor this into your
calculations. 
• Check the details of the car, such as the year and make. This can be found on the compliance
plate, a small metal plate inside the car bonnet. It records the make and model of car and the
month and year the car was manufactured. 
• Check if a warranty is being offered and what the details are.
• Remember that there are other costs. For example, a new car will have a delivery fee, and a
used car will have to be transferred into your name, which involves a transfer fee and a 3%
stamp duty fee.
• If you are buying a second-hand car a vehicle check is a good idea. The NRMA, the RACV and
other motoring organisations conduct inspections for a fee. Licensed dealers must guarantee
that the cars they sell are roadworthy, registered and that no money is owed on them.
© Blake Education, 2006
30
Living and Work Literacy 1
Where to buy? 
The options available include:
• A licensed dealer: this method may be more reliable,
especially if a warranty is offered, but the
disadvantage is that prices are generally higher.
• Private sale via newspaper advertisements: you may
get a bargain in a private sale, especially if the seller
is in a hurry to sell and you can negotiate a price,
however you take a risk on the quality of the car. 
• Sale via the Internet: there are numerous websites
that list cars for sale. This method is increasing in
popularity as more people use the Internet for many
different types of transactions. Some of the websites
will have useful hints to assist you, however the same
risks apply as with a private sale.
• A car buying service: some companies and credit
unions offer a service (sometimes free) to search for a
car for you. This is especially useful if you are busy
and don’t have time to look.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 199 9	
Living & Work Literacy Book  1

14 Buying a car
Selling your car
If you want to sell your car the first thing you need to do is find out how much it is worth. You can
research this by checking the cars for sale advertisements in the newspapers and/or the Internet.
You can choose to sell your car privately and hope you get someone to buy or you can approach a
dealer. A third option is to trade-in your car on a newer model. If you are selling privately you need
to make sure you are paid in cash or with a bank cheque in case the buyer’s cheque is dishonoured
(bounces). 
Whichever method you decide it is always useful to wash and clean your car to make it presentable.

8 Buying wisely
Have you ever bought something and later regretted it? Did you forget to check out the alternatives?
Did you spend too much money? Did you later find out that you could have bought it at a much
cheaper price? Everyone has probably done one or more of these, so it is important to analyse just
what is involved in buying wisely. 
Consumers operate in a commercial economy by earning (or receiving) a money income and using
it to satisfy needs and wants. With a limited amount of money and unlimited needs and wants,
consumers must therefore choose wisely in order to gain the maximum satisfaction for their money.
So what is involved in buying wisely? Here are some useful tips:
• Clarify the purpose of your intended purchase. Ask yourself: Why do I want it? 
• Are you buying on impulse, or have you really thought about the purchase? If it is a hamburger
you want because you are hungry, this may not require much thought, but if you want to buy
a car or some expensive clothes you may need to think about it more. 
• Check the price. Does it truly reflect the likely level of satisfaction you will derive from the
purchase?
• Check the quality. Is it better to purchase a more expensive brand or is a cheaper brand better
value for money?
• Check other brands and visit other stores. This is called comparison shopping. Obviously this is
more important for relatively expensive items than it is for buying, for example, a milkshake.
There are many places where you can purchase goods, such as discount stores, factory outlets
and local markets. You can also check newspapers, magazines and the Internet. 
• Can you afford to buy this item? Is it within your budget? The consequences of poor budgeting
can be quite dramatic.
• Should you consider what alternative uses you could put your money towards? This is a good
check to see if you really do want something.
There are several key factors that affect what we buy. Price is an obvious one and so too is the state
of our finances – how much money we have and how much we are going to allocate to spending.
Other factors that influence what we buy include:
• Our age: older people usually have different wants and needs from younger people.
• Our gender: women and girls sometimes want to buy items that are different from men and
boys, however many of the same items are bought regardless of gender.
• Advertising and marketing: we are all influenced in some ways by advertisements and by
marketing schemes such as sales and special offers.
© Blake Education, 2006
18
Living and Work Literacy 1
• Convenience: we may decide to buy
something at a local shop because it is
closer, even though the item may be
more expensive than in a supermarket
located farther away.
• Service: because some items that we buy
may be faulty or may break down, we
may choose to buy from a retailer that
provides after-sales service. We may also
want to know whether an item has a
guarantee or a warranty. 
• The environment: more people today are
becoming conscious of the environment
and are purchasing goods that are
environmentally friendly. Some of these
products have ‘green labels’, which
indicate that a product has not and will
not harm the environment.

Cheque forgery and fraud
take a variety of forms,
from counterfeiting
cheques to faking
signatures. Theft of unused
cheque books through the
post also occurs. In the
United States, the American
Bankers Association
reported in 2000 that there
was an actual loss of
US$679 million in that year
due to cheque fraud.
4 Cheques
A cheque is simply an instruction from a person to his or her bank to pay a certain amount of money
to a person or organisation. The person writing the cheque is called the drawer, as they are drawing
on their bank account. The person or organisation who is to receive the cheque is the payee.
Below is an example of a typical cheque.
© Blake Education, 2006
10
Living and Work Literacy 1
Advantages of cheques include:
• they are easy to use
• they are relatively safe
• they can be sent through the mail
• they are easy to keep track of
• they have a record (the cheque book butt and bank
statement).
Disadvantages of cheques include:
• they use paper (in an age of electronic communication)
• signatures can be forged
• they are time-consuming to process
• some organisations or people may not accept cheques
without some form of identification
• they can go astray in the mail.
How cheques work

17 Insurance
How it works
Insurance is all about spreading risk. For example, if a group of 20 softball players all decide to put
$50 into a fund to cover any medical costs in case one of them is injured, then they have $1000 in
the fund. So if a player is injured, then there is $1000 to spend on medical treatment for that person.
The fund means that all the players are covered in case of injury and everyone agrees it is worth
$50 to ensure that there is money to go towards any possible costs. Insurance companies operate
in much the same way.
There are three main principles upon which insurance is based:
• Utmost good faith: this means that the person taking out an insurance policy must answer the
questions asked by the insurance company truthfully and disclose all relevant information. This
relates to both application forms and when making an insurance claim.
• Insurable interest: this means that the person who takes out an insurance policy must have an
interest in the property being insured. For example, you must own the car, boat, house or
whatever item that you are insuring.
• Indemnity: this means that when a person makes an insurance claim, he or she should be
compensated for the loss and no more. In other words, you are not meant to make a profit out
of insurance.
When you make an insurance claim, a person from the insurance company calculates the risk and
determines the premium for a policy (the actuary), while another person calculates the value of the
loss sustained (the assessor).

Types of insurance
• Life insurance (assurance): protection against loss of income.
• Property insurance: insurance for damage or loss of items such as a house, boat or caravan.
• Accident insurance: workers’ compensation and public risk policies.
• Motor vehicle insurance: a type of property insurance.
• Health insurance: protection against the high costs of health care.
• Travel insurance: insuring yourself against loss of luggage, cancellation of travel or accidents
overseas.

1 What is money?
© Blake Education, 2006
4
Living and Work Literacy 1
Money is very useful to us as it is a means by which we can buy things. It also enables us to compare
values and to measure our relative wealth. Money acts as a:
• medium of exchange
• measure of value
• measure of stored wealth
• means of recording and paying debts.
All modern forms of money should be:
• acceptable – everyone must be able to recognise it and accept it for payment
• divisible – it is needed to make both small and large purchases 
• portable – it must be easy to carry
• durable – it must last for a long time without being easily damaged or wearing out
• scarce – it must be limited in supply so its value is retained.
 Stones are used as money on the Pacific
island of Yap.
 Cowrie shells were accepted as money on
the west coast of Africa. They were used in
some parts of Africa until the middle of
the 20th century.
 Cigarettes were used as a medium of
exchange in prisoner-of-war camps during
the Second World War.
 Gold and silver have been used as money
throughout history.
 Precious stones such as diamonds have
been used as money.
 Rum was used as a currency in the early
colonial period of New South Wales.
 The first coins were struck in Lydia in
Turkey in the 7th century BC. They were
made from gold and silver.
 The original gold and silver coins were
known as standard coins.
 Early coins were not perfectly round. This
meant that people could clip or shave off
some of the precious metal before passing
them on again as coins. Coins were then
made with a milled edge to prevent this
practice.
 Coins today are made of a combination of
copper and nickel. They are worth more
than the value of the metal in them and
are therefore known as token coins.
 Most gold today is held as bullion (gold
bars) by the world’s largest banks.
 Paper money was first issued by the
Chinese in about 650 AD. Bank notes
became more widely accepted in Europe 
in the 17th century AD when ‘goldsmiths
notes’ were issued as receipts for the gold
they held for safekeeping.
 Cheques were first introduced in about
1650. Bank messengers were used to 
collect and distribute the cheques from
bank to bank.

5
Forms of money
We think of money in general terms as consisting of coins and bank notes (or paper money). Coins
and notes collectively make up what is termed currency, but there are other forms of money.
Cheques, for example, can be viewed as money in that they are used as a medium of exchange. 
A cheque is really a request from a person to his or her bank for the bank to pay a sum of money
to a person or organisation. Cheques are not as easily used or universally accepted as currency because
they are subject to certain rules and regulations. Sellers do not have to accept cheques as payment,
but they are legally obliged to accept currency. 
Debit cards and credit cards can also be classed as money in that they too are used in the commercial
exchange of goods and services, but they are also subject to rules and regulations.
Value of money
Goods and services have a money value that is measured by their price. Also, the money income we
receive is a reflection of the value of our labour.
We like to know what our money is really worth in terms of what we can buy with it. This is a measure
of its purchasing power. If prices increase, we can buy less with the money we have, while if our
income increases, we can buy more goods and services (assuming prices remain unchanged).
In fact, both income levels and prices change constantly. When prices and income levels rise rapidly
together there is inflation. This can be unfair to people on fixed incomes. In Australia, both the
government and the Reserve Bank of Australia attempt to control the rate of inflation.

18 Looking after the environment
As consumers, we are confronted with a wide variety
of products and it is important that we ask questions
such as: Are the manufacture, distribution and
consumption of these products harming the
environment? Are there alternatives to plastic bags?
Can more materials be recycled? Are there products
that are made in an environmentally friendly way? 
Green labels
You will notice that there are products marketed
as ‘environmentally friendly’, often with their labels
coloured green. This could mean that they have
received a ‘Good Environmental Choice’ label from
the Australian Environmental Labelling Association,
or it could be simply a marketing ploy by the company.
The issue of labelling also applies to food that has
been genetically modified (GM). GM foods are
those that have been engineered by genetics to
make them grow faster or become more disease
resistant. Genetic modification is a controversial new
technology and therefore there is a demand for
modified products to be labelled accordingly.
Another trend is the increasing popularity of organic
food. These foods are produced without the use of
fertilisers, pesticides or other chemical additives.
© Blake Education, 2006
38
Living and Work Literacy 1
The Australian Environmental
Labelling Association 
The Australian Environmental Labelling
Association was created to provide consumers
with a clear guide to the environmental
factors involved when they purchase a
product.
It encourages consumers to purchase products
with less environmental impact so that the
quality of the environment is improved in
the long term. It also encourages producers to
consider the effects on the environment in
the manufacture of their products. This is
part of the move towards sustainable
management of resources. 
There are now a growing number of
‘ecolabelled’ products, from laundry
detergents and cosmetics to timber products
and organic foods. Energy rating labels on
electrical appliances are another example. 
To find out more about The Australian
Environmental Labelling Association you can
look at their website.
Recycling 
In order to keep up with the demand for paper, forests of trees are being cut down in Australia and
in the rest of the world. However, paper can be recycled and many local councils in Australia now
have recycling policies to assist with this process. 
Plastic bags
Non-biodegradable plastic bags are very harmful to the environment; they don’t break down over
time, they clog the waterways and are a danger to fish and bird life. Currently there is a big push to
ban, or at least limit, the number of plastic bags.
In some countries, for example Ireland, consumers pay for plastic bags. This has dramatically reduced
the number of bags being used.
Saving energy
As a society we have become reliant on
fossil fuels to generate energy. Each year
a typical house pumps approximately 11
tonnes of carbon dioxide into the
atmosphere.
The benefits of reducing energy
consumption are immediate. Not only
does it save money, it will result in a
healthier world for future generations.

12	Marketing	and	promoting
Marketing is simply a set of strategies to promote, advertise and sell goods and services to 
consumers. It lets them know what is available. Marketing can involve a whole range of strategies, 
such as discounts, special offers, promotions, prizes, competitions and free gifts.
Important	terms
Target market: a specific group of customers a business is trying to sell to
Market segmentation: dividing up the market into specific sections (such as teenagers, retirees, 
females aged between 18 and 25)
Niche market: a small selective market (such as organically grown vegetables), for a limited number 
of customers 
The	four	Ps	of	marketing:
Product – what are you selling?
Price – what price will you sell it for?
Promotion – how will you let people know about it? 
Place – how will you distribute it?
These four Ps can be identified in the story of Amy and Malik below.
•
•
•
•
Amy and Malik decided to go into business selling snack foods and drinks from a mobile van at a 
beach suburb. In their marketing plan they first identified the products they were going to sell. This 
included soft drinks such as Coca Cola and Fanta, tea and coffee, and food items such as donuts, 
cakes, biscuits, packets of potato chips and peanuts.
The pricing of their products was based on the cost of the goods bought from suppliers, adding 
a margin for profit and establishing a selling price. They would also have to cover costs such as 
advertising, electricity, repayments on their van and other costs. The selling price had to be calculated 
carefully. If it was too high, nobody would buy 
their food and drinks, especially if there were 
competitors selling the same or similar food 
at cheaper prices. If, on the other hand they 
priced their products too low, they would be 
in danger of running their business at a loss.
They needed to promote their products so 
they printed letter-box flyers and distributed 
them in the area near the beach. They also 
advertised in the local newspaper and had 
large signs made for their mobile van. One 
of these advertised: ‘SPECIAL OF THE DAY’, 
which might be ‘DONUT AND COFFEE – $5’. 
They thought that this might appeal to a 
particular market segment (such as coffee 
lovers). They had identified their target market 
as the people walking to or from the beach.
They realised that the place where they 
were going to sell their products was very 
important, so they set up their mobile van 
where they could intercept the greatest 
number of potential customers. This was along 
the boardwalk right beside the beach. They 
needed local council permission to do this, 
which they applied for and received.

8 Mobile phone plans 
When shopping for a new mobile phone plan, there are a lot of things to consider. The key things to be 
aware of are:
•  what kind of phone you want  
•  the mobile phone plan options available
•  how (and how much) you use your phone (see diagram below).  
Selecting a mobile phone plan – the three stages
1 Select a phone
2 Mobile phone plan
3 Mobile phone usage
Facts about phone plans
•  Monthly plans or contracts can be economical, particularly if you use your phone a lot. Some 
contracts actually give you a new phone up front, and lock you in for a fixed period of time. Your 
monthly fees over that time period will cover the cost of the phone, as well as your usage. There 
are many plans available and you need to look carefully at the details.
•  Prepaid phones are handy if you don’t want to be locked into a long-term contract. You buy a 
certain amount of credit up front and when your prepaid credit runs out you can easily buy more. 
Although the price per call may be more expensive than in a monthly plan, prepaid plans mean 
you can control what you spend and don’t get any nasty surprises when the bill comes. You can 
also change service providers more easily.
•  Coverage – mobile phone coverage varies greatly in some parts of Australia, and some providers 
provide better coverage than others. Some handsets are also better at picking up mobile phone 
signals than others.

 8 Mobile phone plans 
•  Cap plans – these are contracts where you pay a minimum amount each month which covers 
you for a set value of calls, downloads and SMS messages. For instance, a $49 cap plan may give 
you $300 of ‘included value’. Cap plans do not limit your actual phone bill. When you use up 
your allowance you will be charged additional costs, and these are charged at varying rates. For 
example, call charges vary according to time of call, so calls after 8 pm may be cheaper than calls 
during the day.
•  Included value – every plan offers a different amount of included value, which is calculated at 
different rates and includes different types of calls and services. This means that ‘included value’ 
amounts cannot always be easily compared.
•  Bundling – many service providers offer special deals or discounts if you ‘bundle’ your landline, 
mobile phone and internet connection with the one company. It’s important to check whether you 
are actually saving money by doing this, as packages can be difficult to compare. 
Responsibilities
It is important to remember that a phone plan is a contract (see previous unit). When you sign up you 
are entering into a legal agreement to pay a certain amount of money for a set period of time, such as 
24 months. Even if you don’t make any calls, or if you lose your phone, you will still have to pay up each 
month. Be aware of any penalties for breaking a contract before it has expired. Owning a phone outright 
can be expensive initially, but protects you from having to enter into a contract with the provider.

3.2 Tax forms
Read the information about tax file numbers then answer the following questions. 
Tax file number (TFN) 
The Australian Taxation Office issues tax file numbers 
to people who work in Australia. This allows the 
government to manage and keep track of tax records. 
If you don’t have a tax file number, your employer will 
have to take more tax from your wages. You only get 
one TFN in your lifetime, so keep it safe and private. 
Don’t share it with your friends, put it on the Internet 
or store it in your phone.
If your school is part of the Secondary Schools TFN 
Program, you could get a tax file number through 
school. If not, visit the website www.ato.gov.au for 
information about getting a tax file number. It is a 
good idea to organise this before you start looking for 
jobs as it can take 28 days to process your application. 
If you are under 16 years you will need a parent or 
guardian to sign the application. You will also need 
to provide proof of identify documents such as your 
birth certificate, passport or Medicare card.
Tax file number declaration
When you start a job you will be asked to fill out a tax file number declaration. 
This is a form on which you declare or state your tax file number, which allows 
your employer to take the correct amount of tax from your wages. Your gross 
wage is the total amount you earn before tax is taken out. Your net wage is the 
amount you have left after tax has been taken out. 
1 
Penny has filled out a tax file number declaration for her 
employer. Her gross wage is $400 per week. Her employer will 
deduct $9.00 each week from her wages. What will be Penny’s 
net wage (amount she gets after tax is taken out)?
2 
Sam doesn’t have a TFN so cannot fill out a tax file number 
declaration. His wages are $400 per week but his employer 
must deduct $92.00 from his wages each week. What will Sam’s 
net wage be?
3 
Sam gets a TFN and fills out a tax file number declaration for his 
employer. How much more will his net wage be?

A budget is simply a written plan for how you intend to spend your money over a 
certain time. Preparing a budget allows you to balance your income and expenses by 
setting a limit on your spending in different categories. A good budget also allows for 
savings. This money is put aside for special purchases and emergency situations, such 
as being sick and unable to work or having large unexpected bills.
Look at Karl’s budget plan below. He is in Year 10, receives an allowance and has 
a casual job washing cars. Note Karl’s expenses and the limits he has set for his 
spending in each category. He also has a savings category.
