How does it work? 
Karl gets paid in cash, so each week he puts the 
planned amounts of money into separate labelled 
envelopes. When he needs to spend money at 
the school canteen, he takes it out of the food 
and drink envelope. He is careful to spread his 
spending over the week as he knows that when 
that money in the envelope is spent, he will have 
to wait until his next pay to fill it up again. He also 
uses the envelopes for keeping receipts and records 
his purchases on the front of each envelope. 
At the end of the week, Karl transfers any money 
left over to the following week. For example, if 
he doesn’t spend money on clothes in week 1, he 
has an extra $10 to spend on clothes in week 2. 
He can also transfer unspent money into different 
categories if necessary. So, if he doesn’t spend any 
money on transport, the next week he can use that 
money for extra entertainment. 
Another great thing about this budget system is that 
it allows for savings. Karl puts $35 into his savings 
envelope each week. Then he deposits this money 
into his bank account so it earns interest. This 
will help him to achieve his financial goal to save 
$3000 by the time he leaves school in 2015.

14 Needs and wants vs goods and
services

Needs and wants

There are particular items that are required by all people. They are called ‘needs’. A need, also referred to as an essential, is an
item that is necessary for survival, People require needs in order to survive. Water, food, clothing and shelter are essential for a
person's survival.

All other items, besides those categorised as needs, are referred to as wants. A want is not essential for survival. Examples of
wants include CD players, cars, microwaves, computers and tennis rackets. Wants are also called luxury items.

Do you see a change in people's needs with the advancement of modern society? As societies become more technologically
advanced, what was once considered a ‘want’ is mow for some people a ‘need’, Although not essential for basic survival, in
particular occupations a car is considered to be a need. For couriers and taxi drivers, whose job involves driving a motor vehicle
of some type, a car is a modern need.

Goods and services

A good is an item that can be purchased by a consumer. A good is tangible (you can touch it). Examples of a good include a
computer, a car, an iter of clothing and a pen.

When you purchase a good, you often need to purchase an additional good so the original good can function properly. The purchasing
of an additional good is called a complementary good. For example, if you purchase a CD player you also need to purchase a CD.

Goods can also be divided into individual and collective goods. An individual good is an item that is solely for personal use. For
example, Sarah's rollerblades are an individual good. On the other hand, goods that are used by the community are called

collective goods. For example, the local swimming pool is a collective good.

A service is an act performed for a consumer, Unlike a good, a service is intangible lyou cannot touch it, but you can see it being
done}. Examples of a service include work performed by a dentist, hairdresser, teacher and a mechanic.

15 Occupational health & safety 
Accidents can always occur in the workplace, just as they can in the home. Although some workplaces 
are potentially more dangerous than others, it is important that all workplaces are safe and safe practices 
are adopted. Each state in Australia has Occupational Health and Safety (OH & S) laws which set out the 
obligations of the employer in providing a safe working environment. Employees also have an obligation 
to work in a safe way so that they do not endanger themselves or others. In fact, each workplace is 
required to have an OH & S committee with representatives of employees and the employer to discuss 
current safety issues.
Positive action can save lives. Many workplaces have signs  
erected to warn workers and members of the public of  
possible dangers, as you can see from the signs on  
this page. Not all workplaces require the same degree  
of signage. For example, a chemical factory would be  
governed by strict rules with signs indicating danger  
areas and hazardous chemicals.  
Even an office can have dangers  
such as faulty power points,  
exposed extension cords, furniture  
and office equipment that is not  
properly installed and may be likely to  
fall on someone. Therefore, all workplaces  
must be aware of the OH & S requirements.
Workers compensation
If a worker is injured at work there is provision for them 
to be compensated and, if necessary, rehabilitated so 
that they can resume working when they have recovered. 
Compensation can pay for such things as medical and 
hospital costs, loss of earnings and permanent damage, 
disfigurement or loss of bodily functions such as sight 
and hearing. All employers are required to take out a 
special insurance policy to cover their employees for 
workers compensation.
Work Cover
Each state in Australia has a government authority to 
administer workers compensation claims. Two examples 
are Work Cover NSW and the Victorian WorkCover 
Authority. Their job is to assess claims and to make 
decisions on the amount and type of compensation 
required. Heavy penalties apply to people who make  
false claims. Where employers have been found to be 
grossly negligent in making the workplace safe, they  
may be prosecuted in a court of law and may have  
to pay damages.
There are work cover offices 
spread throughout each state, so 
that people have access to local 
services, where possible.

Living and Work Literacy 4
14 Paying income tax
Income tax is a percentage of each individual’s income that is paid to the government. The money 
raised is used to pay for government services and other expenditures. There are several types of 
taxes, such as income tax, company tax and the Goods and Services Tax (GST).
As an employee you are required to pay personal income tax. Under the Pay As You Go (PAYG) 
system, employers are required to withhold tax from the payments they make to you and send it 
to the Tax Office regularly. When you lodge your income tax return at the end of the financial year, 
you are entitled to a credit for the amount of tax which has been withheld from your pay. From the 
information you provide on your tax return, the Tax Office works out how much tax is payable on 
your income and whether you have paid more or less tax than required. If you have paid too much 
tax, you are entitled to a refund, but if you have not paid enough tax, you will have to pay the 
difference.
The financial year is from 1 July to 30 June the next year. You have from 1 July to 31 October to 
lodge your tax return unless it is prepared by a registered tax agent. Using a tax agent is becoming 
increasingly popular with taxpayers because of the complexity of the tax system and the tax return. 
When you lodge your tax return you need to quote your tax file number (TFN). This is a unique 
number issued by the Tax Office. Only one TFN is issued to you for your lifetime. Information on 
tax returns is available on the Australian Tax Office’s website (www.ato.gov.au). 
Lodging your tax return
A tax return is a document in which you declare your annual income so it can be assessed for tax. 
The Tax Office provides the form for you to complete your tax return.
You can lodge a tax return in paper form using TaxPack, or to do it more quickly, you can lodge 
online using e-tax. It is done over the Internet using a special software package which can be 
downloaded from the ATO website. It helps you prepare your tax return by doing many of the 
calculations for you, based on figures you provide. It also gives you an estimate of your tax liability 
for the year and whether you will have a refund or tax debt.
Calculating your tax refund or tax payable
You do not have to pay tax on your total income. The Tax Office will allow you certain deductions 
for work-related expenses, e.g. the purchase of tools is an allowable deduction for a carpenter, 
electrician or plumber. You can claim work-related travel expenses but not the cost of travelling 
from home to work.  Other allowable deductions include self-education expenses if the course 
is directly related to your job, and gifts and donations to registered charities. After you subtract 
these deductions from your total income, you arrive at your taxable income which is the amount 
you have to pay tax on. Under the PAYG system, you have already paid some tax so whether you 
receive a tax refund or have to pay tax depends on whether you have paid more or less tax than 
you should have.
Emma works in an office and bought a computer for $3000 in July 2006. She uses her computer for 
work 60% of the time. As a result she can claim 60% of the decline in value of the computer over a 
period, e.g. 4 years. This is a work-related expense.
Chanda also works in an office but has enrolled in a TAFE cooking course. This course has nothing to 
do with his work so he cannot claim self-education expenses. 
Emma’s tax return
Emma works as a computer operator and received a total income for the year of $45 000. She had 
work-related deductions of $5000. Her taxable income was therefore $40 000.
Emma had paid $8200 in tax instalments under the PAYG system. The tax payable on her taxable 
income (under the tax scales) was $7800. Therefore Emma received a tax refund of $400.

9 Paying your mobile phone bill 
Mobile phone technology has come a long way in a very short space of time. The first generation mobile 
phones were analogue but digital technology quickly paved the way for a new generation of phones that 
could send data at high speeds and provided extra features such as text messaging, or SMS.
New phone technology
Third generation technology, known as 3G, allows phones to send and receive information up to ten 
times faster than second generation phones. Handsets come with built-in cameras and microphones. 
Colour screens mean that messages can now include pictures, video and music, not just text. Mobile 
phone technology now allows people with 3G mobile phones to take photos, send and receive emails, 
watch movies, access public transport timetables and restaurant menus, open garage doors, activate 
security systems and turn on home heating or air conditioning. 
Mobile phone bills
The new range of features available on 3G mobiles mean that mobile phone bills have become 
much more complicated. Instead of just including call charges, they now include data charges, SMS, 
multimedia messages and voice and video calls. All of these things are charged at different rates, which 
can make it hard to keep track of the costs. 
Hannah 
Hannah was so excited when she got her 
first mobile phone. It was a present from her 
parents, who wanted her to be able to contact 
them in case of emergencies. Unfortunately, 
Hannah’s parents didn’t explain the different 
costs associated with using her new phone. 
The first thing Hannah did was to organise her 
contacts, entering the names and numbers of 
all her friends. She made a few calls while she 
was doing so, and ended up chatting to some 
friends for over an hour. Hannah didn’t realise 
how much the calls would cost.
She was also thrilled by how easy it was to 
send text messages (SMS), and she messaged 
all of her friends. She was sure they didn’t cost 
very much. Hannah’s friend showed her how 
to download ring tones for her phone, and she 
changed them regularly. She found that she 
could download video clips of her favourite 
songs. Unfortunately, she didn’t realise that 
these were ‘premium services’ that are charged 
at a higher rate.  
When Hannah received her first bill, she was 
horrified to find that it came to $1200. There 
was no way she could afford to pay the bill. 
Hannah’s parents helped her out this time, but 
they explained that she would not be bailed 
out again.

2 Payment for work
There are many forms of payment made to people who work. Some people work for an employer 
and receive wages or salaries, while others are self-employed.
Wages and salaries
Wages are calculated on an hourly basis. A wage earner may be offered overtime, which is more 
hours than the normal working day, and for these hours receives higher hourly rates called penalty 
rates.
Salaries are calculated on an annual basis even though the payment may be made in fortnightly or 
monthly instalments. A salaried worker has a job description and is expected to complete certain 
tasks during the day but is not entitled to overtime or penalty rates. Sometimes salaried workers 
may be expected to work extra hours to complete a particular task. The annual salary takes all this 
into account. 
Other incomes
People can also earn an income, not through any direct work but by using their money or their 
property. Their income may consist of interest, dividends or rent.
There are also people who receive an income, usually from the government, to assist them with 
their living expenses. This form of income is called an allowance.

4 Permanent or casual/full or part-time
There are many different working arrangements and entitlements for employees in the work force. 
However, all workers whether they are permanent or casual, work full-time or part-time, have 
certain rights. These include the right to be paid at least a minimum wage, the right to work in a 
safe and healthy workplace and the right to compensation if they are injured at work. 
What is the difference?
Permanent employees can expect regular, 
continuing employment, while casual work 
is more irregular and uncertain. Employers 
have no obligation to offer continuing 
work to a casual employee.
Full-time work is regarded as working 35 
hours per week or more on average, while 
part-time work is less than 35 hours per 
week, according to the Australian Bureau 
of Statistics.
Note that not all part-time workers are 
casual and not all full-time workers are 
permanent. There are many employees 
who have permanent part-time working 
arrangements. Equally, many casual 
employees work 35 hours or more in a 
working week.
Why do some people work 
part-time?
They may be caring for young children at 
home.
They may have other jobs, hobbies or 
interests.
They may have a personal preference to work 
part-time.
They may be financially secure and do not 
need the money.
They may have a job-sharing arrangement 
with another worker.
There may be no full-time work available 
for them.
•
•
•
•
•
•
Why do some people prefer 
casual work?
They may prefer the flexibility of working on a 
casual basis.
They may not wish to commit to a permanent 
position.
They may have other commitments.
•
•
•
Some employers may prefer to hire casual rather than permanent workers, as it may reduce their 
costs. For example, casual workers do not get all the entitlements (such as paid sick leave and 
annual leave) that permanent workers do. There is also an increasing trend for employers to prefer 
to hire workers under a contract rather than as permanent employees. There are many cases of 
employees who retire from their permanent positions only to be re-employed in the same or a 
similar role under contract. In these cases, the contract generally specifies a set of tasks to be 
completed for a set fee.

4 Personal budgets  
A budget is a plan of anticipated income, expenditure and savings over a period of time. Governments 
produce budgets, as do businesses, as they need to plan for the future. Individual people also need a 
budget. Whether it is for the short term or long term, a budget can help you to plan your spending and 
ensure that you will have enough money to cover your expenses. 
A budget can also help you to plan ways to achieve personal spending goals. You could have a weekly 
budget, a monthly budget or a yearly budget.  
All personal budgets are different depending on individual circumstances. Here are some examples:
Susan Baker
Susan Baker is a millionaire.  
She has made her money 
investing in real estate. Susan 
owns the apartment she lives  
in on the Gold Coast. Her goal  
is to save as much money as 
possible in a short time so that 
she can retire early. 
John Duncan
John Duncan is a single 
parent. He works part-time at 
a supermarket. John has three 
young children and his goal  
is to save a little each week  
for emergency expenses, such  
as possible medical bills for  
any of his children should  
they become ill. 
James Wilson
James is a student in his first year 
at university. He lives at home 
with his parents. James’ long 
term goal is to establish a career 
in law and start his own legal 
practice. 
How do you prepare a personal budget?
To prepare a personal budget, you need to estimate normal income and expense items and subtract  
the total expenses from total income. The difference between the two is the expected savings (or debt, 
if the figure is negative).
Programs such as Microsoft Excel, Moneydance and Quicken can do all the calculations for you.  
They can also analyse trends and patterns in income and expenses and help you to calculate expected 
savings.

19 Planning an overseas holiday
Congratulations! You have saved enough money for an overseas holiday. How do you plan for it?
Where do you begin?
Documents
The most important document you will need is a passport. This shows proof of your identity and
your country of citizenship. You cannot travel overseas without it. In fact, you would not be allowed
out of Australia, let alone allowed into another country. A passport is checked when you leave a
country and when you enter another country. You can obtain an application form for a passport
from any post office. You will need your birth certificate and two recent photographs to complete
the application.
Other documents you may need, depending on the destination, are:
• A visa: some countries require you to obtain ‘permission’ to enter. This is in the form of a stamp
in your passport that allows you to enter the country. Visas are obtained from the country’s
consulate in Australia and usually involve a fee.
• A health certificate: indicates required vaccinations that may be necessary to enter some
countries. 
• A work permit: may be needed if you want to work overseas. If you don’t have one and the
immigration officer at the point of entry suspects you are going to work in the country, you
may be refused entry. 
It may also be advisable to buy some foreign currency as Australian dollars are not generally accepted
for payment. You can buy foreign currency in cash at a bank or at the airport before you leave, or
you can purchase travellers’ cheques, which you can cash when you are overseas.  Most major travel
destinations today have ATMs and your debit or credit cards can generally be used to withdraw cash.
Your PIN is the same wherever you are in the world.
Organising the trip
Some of the decisions you will need to make before you go on your trip include:
• Destination: where do you want to go? Often people try to fit too many places on their
itinerary and end up with a rushed trip. Making a priority list of your most favoured
destinations is a good way to start.
• Method of travel: will you fly, go by ship, overland or a combination?
• Type of travel: you could choose a package tour, where everything is organised and you pay
upfront, or you can travel independently and do your own thing.  You can book
accommodation in advance or find it when you get there (or a combination of both).
• Costings: you need to research how much it is all going to cost and decide if you can afford it.
It is important to work out a budget. 
• Booking method: you can use a travel agent or book over the Internet. The advantage of using
a travel agent is that they have expert knowledge about airfare structures as well as special
deals, shortcuts for planning and other advice. Booking via the Internet is becoming very
popular and it may save you money, but you may not have the same safeguards that a
reputable travel agent can provide. Also, not all Internet fares and accommodation listings are
necessarily cheaper than booking through a travel agent.  
• Travel itinerary: it is a good idea to prepare an itinerary even if you don’t follow it exactly when
you are away. You can build in some flexibility in an itinerary.
• Travel insurance: for an overseas holiday this is a very good idea and in some countries it is
compulsory. Insurance will cover you not only for lost luggage, but also for medical expenses if
you get sick overseas. 
• Research: the more information you have the better prepared you will be for your trip. It is
important to get travel brochures, read travel books, check travel websites and talk to friends
who have travelled. This will ensure a more enjoyable trip.

9 Protection for consumers
Consumer shopping rights
Refunds: consumers are entitled to cash refunds or an
exchange if the goods they buy are defective or faulty. If you
change your mind about a product and want your money
back, the store is not legally obliged to give you a refund.
However, many stores do give refunds as an act of goodwill
(in the hope you will visit their store again).
Cooling-off period: consumers are protected against door-
to-door salespeople who visit uninvited. If you buy a product
and later change your mind, you are entitled to cancel the
deal. The cooling off period varies from state to state, but is
generally between five and ten days. The cooling-off period
only applies to contracts of $50 or more in all states (except
New South Wales where there is no minimum). It also does
not operate if you invite a salesperson to visit your home.
Guarantees: all goods for sale must meet a basic level of
quality and must ‘do what they are supposed to do’. For
example, if you bought a watch you would expect it to tell
the time, regardless of how nice it looks on your wrist.
Guarantees also contain specific conditions, for example, a
12-month guarantee to repair the product if a fault develops
during that period. Whatever the specific guarantees, there
is still the implied guarantee of basic quality (as mentioned
above). A warranty is basically the same as a guarantee.
Buying goods online: the rights of the consumer shopping
online are also protected. There are, however, additional risks.
For example, you may be dealing with an overseas company
whose reputation and honesty you cannot check. Therefore,
it is important to check an online seller’s contact details and
terms and conditions of sale. Security and privacy are also
important to avoid your personal details being made available
to others. Details about refunds, returns and guarantees
should also be checked. Dealing with an overseas company
has additional risks as some goods, for example, electrical
goods, have different systems that may not work in Australia.

How to complain
If you are unhappy with a product you have purchased, here are some steps that you can take:
• Go to the store where you purchased the product. Explain your case clearly and politely and ask
for a replacement or repair. If you are unsuccessful, you can ask to speak to the manager or
person in charge.
• Write a letter to the store outlining your complaint.
• Lodge an official complaint to the consumer affairs or fair trading organisation in your state. 
• Take your complaint to the Small Claims Tribunal. Your case may be heard with a representative
of the store and a referee who acts as a judge. The aim of the hearing is for the two parties to
reach a mutual agreement.
• Contact the ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission), a federal government
body, or the ombudsman in your state.
• Approach the media (radio, television or newspapers).

17 Repairs and  
maintenance issues   
There can sometimes be conflict between tenants and their landlords or agents over repairs and 
maintenance. The following conversations demonstrate the kinds of conflict that can take place 
regarding this issue.
Melissa  
Mr Johnson, I’m not happy. 
(tenant): 
 Those repairs I requested three

Melissa:  
 I disagree. The leaking tap in the

of water, and the broken light

inconvenient,  
not to mention dangerous. 
Mr Johnson:   I think you are being a bit fussy, 
Melissa. 
Melissa:  
 As a tenant I have

includes the right 
to have repairs

I want these

immediately 
or I will

Mr Johnson:   Making threats 
won’t help the situation, Melissa.
Melissa decides to ring her state consumer affairs 
department to seek some clarification. She talks 
to Jo, a consumer affairs public relations officer.
Melissa:  
 Hi Jo, my name is Melissa. I’ve just 
had an argument with my agent 
about some repairs to my apartment. 
I believe the repairs are urgent but 
my landlord doesn’t agree, and won’t 
fix them. 
Jo:  
 Okay Melissa, what kind of repairs 
are we talking about?
Melissa:  
 There are broken light fittings in the 
lounge room, and a leaking tap in the 
kitchen. Surely these things qualify as 
urgent repairs? 
Jo:  
 Urgent repairs usually involve safety 
issues, things like dangerous electrical 
faults, gas leaks, and blocked or 
broken toilets. Appliances or fittings 
that are not working properly would 
definitely be classed as urgent. 
Leaking taps where a substantial 
amount of water is being wasted can 
also be classed as urgent.
 Melissa:   Thanks for that. I will contact the 
agent again to tell them what you 
have said. If that doesn’t work, what 
should I do?
 Jo:  
 If they still won’t agree to the repairs 
there is an administrative tribunal 
you can apply to. See how you go.
Urgent repairs
It is important to distinguish between urgent and non-urgent repairs. Repairs are generally the landlord’s 
responsibility. If the tenant or resident caused the damage, however, the landlord can ask them to 
arrange or pay for repairs. Landlords or their agents also have a responsibility to respond to repair 
requests promptly. Tenants must continue paying rent when they are waiting for repairs to be done. 
Requests for urgent repairs
As a tenant there are a number of steps you should take if you need an urgent repair:
•  Contact the landlord or agent about the problem, and clearly state that the repair is urgent. It’s 
best to keep all your communication in writing, so you have a record of the discussions that have 
taken place. In most states, if the landlord or agent doesn’t arrange for the repair to be done, 
you can arrange this yourself, so long as it doesn’t cost more than $1000.

•  You would then need to contact the landlord asking to be 
reimbursed for the repair. The landlord usually has to pay  
you within 14 days. 
•  If the landlord refuses to pay you, or if the repairs will  
cost more than $1000, you can apply to the administrative 
tribunal in your state, which will grant you a hearing.  
The tribunal can order the landlord to arrange the repairs. 
Non-urgent repairs 
If the repairs are not urgent, you still need to contact the landlord 
or agent in writing to request the repair. If the repairs aren’t 
carried out within a reasonable time (this depends on the nature 
of the repairs), you can contact the administrative tribunal in your 
state. In most cases you have 60 days to make your application. In 
the meantime, you must continue paying rent until the matter is 
sorted out. 
Tribunals
There are various state tribunals whose task is to resolve disputes 
between tenants and landlords, each with different names.

19  Resignation strategies:  
knowing when to leave 
Knowing when the time is right to leave a job can be just as 
important as choosing the right job in the first place. Many 
people find that the job they are in is not really suitable for them, 
and they don’t need to stay and suffer. Workers really should be 
happy in their jobs, and many are. 
There are some resignation strategies you should know about. 
Thinking clearly about the decision
First, you should weigh up the pros and cons of resigning.  
What benefits would you lose? Would you be happier working 
elsewhere in a similar position? Or would you prefer an entirely 
different field?
Giving notice
When you decide that you want to resign, you are expected to 
give notice. This is usually done 30 days before your last day on 
the job. Giving notice allows the employer to make arrangements 
to replace you. Some organisations have a special resignation form 
while for others a letter of resignation is enough, as long as the 
exact date of leaving is included.
Some people don’t give notice. This could be due to a bitter argument in the workplace, with the result 
that they can’t stand to remain in the job a moment longer. By leaving before giving notice, a worker 
can lose some entitlements such as sick leave and holiday leave. 
Also, some employers are not interested in being given notice. If an employee decides to leave, they 
may want that employee to leave their establishment immediately. There have been some cases of 
employees being escorted by security guards out the door. For the employer, there is the risk that a 
disgruntled employee may harbour a grudge against their employer and during the 30 days’ notice may 
cause damage or access and steal company secrets. Policies on giving notice are therefore not always 
strictly enforced. Often the date of leaving is negotiated by mutual consent.
Burning bridges
Be careful in your behaviour when leaving a job, as you may find that in the future you are working for 
that same organisation again. In any case, it does not reflect well on any person to behave with bad 
grace. Also, a future employer may want a work reference from your previous employer and sometimes 
high value is placed on previous work references.
Tying up loose ends
If you want to leave in a positive way, it is 
important to tie up loose ends. Where possible, 
finish tasks that you have started and present 
the work you have done to your boss. You 
should also brief your boss on the progress 
of projects still unfinished. It will be much 
appreciated by your work colleagues and your 
employer.
Allie was not happy in her 
job. She found she was always 
ﬁghting with work colleagues 
and always seemed to be in 
trouble with her boss over her 
work output. Allie decided to 
leave. She didn’t conﬁde in her 
supervisor or anyone else, for 
that matter. She simply didn’t 
come into work any more.
ISBN 978 1 76020 204 0

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2009
Living and Work Literacy 6 
41
Personal considerations
You may have talked to your work mates about the 
possibility of leaving. However, telling everyone that 
you will be leaving before letting your employer know 
shows a lack of courtesy. After your employer knows, 
then it is okay to tell other people.
Try to show your appreciation for the job, and for 
the help you have received in your work. While you 
may have mixed feelings about leaving, maybe some 
sadness, you should also be thinking positively. This is 
an opportunity for you to get on with your working 
life and accept new challenges.

15 Responsible consumer behaviour
‘The customer is always right.’
This is a phrase often used to train sales staff in good customer relations. But is it true? Is the customer 
always right? Or are some customer behaviours unethical or even illegal? Being a consumer comes with 
both rights and responsibilities.
Returning goods
As a consumer you have the right to return goods if they are faulty or damaged. You may have your 
money refunded or you may be provided with a replacement item that is not faulty or damaged. 
However, you cannot return goods simply because you have changed your mind. Some stores may 
allow you to do this in order to maintain a good relationship with you, but it may not always be fair  
on the retailer. Consider the two scenarios below:
Ryan buys some new CDs from a music 
store. He takes them home and copies 
them onto his computer. He then takes 
the CDs back to the store and says he has 
decided he doesn’t want them anymore 
and wants his money back.
Samantha loves shopping for dresses. She often buys 
a few dresses, takes them home and wears them for 
several weeks, then takes them back to the stores, 
claiming that they don’t suit her and asking her 
money back. She loves telling her friends about how 
she always has a new outfit, and never has to pay.
Paying bills on time
Paying your bills on time is fair to the retailer or 
service provider, who might need money coming 
in to keep the business running. Although it is 
not illegal to pay bills late, it can result in late 
charges. If you find that you regularly have 
trouble paying your bills you may need to look 
at ways to reduce your spending. If you are not 
careful, bills and late charges can escalate very 
quickly. Consider the case below:
Sally had three credit cards. She boasted to her 
friends that she could use one credit card to  
pay off the others, so she could keep shopping 
as much as she wanted. The bills kept adding  
up until they were more than Sally could pay. 
Sally realised that the interest charges on her 
unpaid bills had accumulated. Sally was being 
charged interest on the total amount owed, 
including the interest she had already been 
charged, so the debt just kept on growing. 
Bag checks
In large, busy department stores and supermarkets, it is possible for people to walk out with goods that 
they have not paid for. To keep this from happening, many stores have a sales assistant at the front 
door to inspect people’s bags as they leave. Most people accept this procedure without any objections. 
All bag checks are voluntary, and a store cannot detain you, or touch you or your bag without your 
consent. However, a store has the right to set conditions of entry and can ask you to leave if you refuse 
to comply. If they suspect shoplifting they can call the police to deal with the matter. Consider the two 
scenarios on the next page.

 15 Responsible consumer behaviour
Lindsay goes into a large department store but decides not to buy anything. As she walks out of the 
store she is asked to display the contents of the bag she is carrying. Lindsay strongly objects to this 
and angrily shouts that this is an infringement of her rights. She refuses to open her bag.
Ethan also strongly objects to bag searches. Ethan, however, objects to bag searches because he often 
shoplifts and doesn’t want to get caught. Although he has been caught numerous times shoplifting 
from stores, he has also got away with it on some occasions.
Abusive behaviour
As a consumer you do have rights, but this doesn’t mean that you should be aggressive or abusive 
when trying to resolve a dispute with a company or store. Even if you are angry about the situation, 
being aggressive towards the salesperson makes them less likely to see your point of view. You can 
still be assertive in maintaining your rights, but there are other ways of doing this. Some consumer 
advocates recommend the ‘broken record technique’ in which you quietly and reasonably explain your 
concern and what you want done about it. Keep stating this until you feel you have been heard. Most 
stores want to maintain good customer relations and will respond to your request if it is reasonable. If 
you are not satisfied with the store’s response, you have the right to contact the office of fair trading in 
your state and take the matter further.

15	Risk	management
Managing a business is always a risk. Some 
businesses start well and then go through 
difficult times. Others start slowly and then 
experience success. Many fail after less than 
one year, while some last longer. Some 
people actually go out of business only to 
start up again and perhaps succeed. There is 
plenty of evidence of people who have gone 
into business and the venture has not been 
successful. Success and failure are part of the 
scene.
John	Symond	and	Aussie	Home	Loans:	A	case	study
John Symond started out as a solicitor. He spent 15 years doing conveyancing (property) work and 
became very successful. In 1984 he branched into lending to property developers, but by 1991 
his business had collapsed because of falling property prices during the recession. In 1992, John 
Symond launched a new business based around buying homes.
As the founder of Aussie Home Loans, John Symond is now worth over $470 million and has 1000 
staff working for him. Aussie Home Loans has $17 billion in home loans and is the leading non-bank 
lender in Australia.
The case study of John Symond is an example of a businessperson who experienced success, then 
failure and success again. One reason for his success is that he was prepared to take risks, though 
this is no guarantee that a business will succeed. 
Business	risks
There are many reasons for a business to fail. The sample case studies described below provide 
a cross section of the types of risks that a business can face. They show theft or fraud, natural 
disasters, changes in regulations, luck, economic downturn or just plain bad management.

11 Scams: A case study 
A scam is a trick aimed at gaining a person’s trust in order to defraud them. Many scammers use email 
and SMS to contact people in the hope that someone will read their message and believe it to be true.
The following is the type of email that is often circulated by scammers trying to defraud innocent 
people. The email tries to gain people’s confidence by offering them money. The extract below is 
based on real emails, but names and some of the wording have been slightly altered. The spelling and 
grammatical errors contained within are typical.
From: BARRISTER RICHARD JONES
Subject: HELLO SIR/MADAM
Dear Sir
With all due respect,
My name is Richard Jones an attorney by profession. In my quest to find a reliable trustee to  
manage the assets/estate of my late client valued at only $15,000,000.00 (fifteen million US dollars) 
this is the reason why you are receiving this email from me. She was a great woman doing good 
especially in the area of charity, in the last five years of her life.
I shall be willing to supply you with more detailed information concerning this business project upon 
hearing from you. I have no intention whatsoever to delve into your private life considering the fact 
you have never had any communication with me in the past, but due to the nature of this business 
project based on the fact that I lack the power to assume the role of a trustee or appoint any of my 
relation to become the trustee. By virtue of the facts and circumstances surrounding this project,  
I am left with no other choice but to carry out a discreet search for a reputable person outside the 
shores of my country in the United Kingdom and consequently seek your stewardship to stand as  
the Deceased’s Next of Kin.
You will be entitle to 40% of the total sum as your share, 10% will be mapped out to offset any 
expenses both parties might make during the course of this transaction while 50% will be for me.
If you wish to render your selfless service, but very rewarding, do provide me with the following 
information.
1. Your full names
2. Tel and fax numbers
3. Complete address
4. Your occupation and your age
I shall provide you with more detailed information upon hearing from you. If this transaction interests 
you kindly send your reply on this my personal email address.
Kind regards 
Richard Jones, Esq.
Why people get tricked by scams
Most scams work by convincing people to give out either money or their personal details to a complete 
stranger. There are many ways they can go about this. It is easy to be tricked by something that seems 
legitimate because it has a website, or a legitimate-sounding business name. But anyone can set up a 
website, and there is no way of being sure that it really is ‘official’. 
A lot of scams are ‘get rich quick’ schemes, which work by convincing people to part with large 
amounts of money by promising a much bigger return down the track. However, scams can also involve 
very small amounts of money – scammers can make just as much money convincing a large number of 
people to part with a small amount of money as they can by getting one person to put up a large sum.
Kinds of scams
There are many different kinds of scams. They may include:
•  Job opportunities, which target people looking for a new job. Promises of big incomes for little 
work are often part of the scam. They tend to be ‘work from home’ schemes. You may be tricked 
into signing a contract and/or paying an up-front fee.

 11 Scams: A case study
•  Business opportunity schemes such as pyramid schemes. These can be dangerous because, 
although you are promised big earnings, the scheme requires you to buy up supplies of a product 
up front before trying to sell it.    
•  Lottery scams, in which you are notified that you have a won a big prize in a lottery and you need 
to send some money to cover expenses so that the prize money can be sent to you. Remember 
that you cannot win money in a lottery unless you have entered it yourself or someone else has 
entered on your behalf.
•  Gambling software packages which promise to accurately predict the results of sporting events, 
such as horse races and major sporting contests.
How to avoid being scammed
•  Do not agree to an offer or deal without spending some time considering it or getting 
independent advice.
•  Do not hand over money or sign anything until you have thoroughly checked out the company, 
organisation or person you are dealing with.
•  Never give out your personal information or bank account details to anyone you do not trust.
•  Don’t believe everything you read. Do some research to verify the information that has been sent to 
you. If you suspect an email is a scam, it is best not to even open it, and definitely don’t reply to it. 
SCAMwatch is a website designed to help people become aware of scams and how they work. 
SCAMwatch is run by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. The site is at  
www.scamwatch.gov.au.

6 Sexual harassment
Sexual harassment in the workplace is any behaviour of a sexual nature which is unwelcome to 
the person concerned. Although sexual harassment is unlawful under the Sex discrimination Act of 
1984, it is still a common occurrence in Australian workplaces.
Some facts:
28% of women and 7% of men in Australia have experienced sexual harassment in some form in 
the workplace. 
Sexual harassment does not have to be physical in nature. It can include suggestive comments or 
jokes, intrusive questions about a person’s private life or repeated, unwanted invitations to go out 
on dates.
Physical sexual harassment occurred in 62% of cases while non-physical sexual harassment 
accounted for 38%.
•
•
•
Scott worked as a receptionist for a law firm. 
Morag, one of the lawyers, would often send SMS 
text messages and pictures of a sexual nature to his 
mobile phone. She would also tell him dirty jokes. 
Scott was unsure how to react to these jokes as he 
did not want to appear too narrow-minded, but he 
sometimes felt uncomfortable about them. Morag 
also showed Scott some pictures of pin-up men 
hanging on her office wall. At no time did Morag 
touch Scott inappropriately, nor did she ever ask 
him out on a date. 
Georgia worked on the cosmetics counter of a large 
department store. Her boss, Alex was constantly 
staring at her and making comments about her body. 
He also asked her to put on some perfume so he 
could check it out by kissing her neck. Georgia did 
not like this sort of behaviour and she told him so. 
He ignored her objections and then began touching 
her inappropriately and brushing up against her. 
When she objected again he called her into his office 
and told her she was being transferred to the dispatch 
office at the back of the store.
Emily and Ming started work 
together in a large insurance office. 
Ming found Emily to be an attractive 
and interesting person and he 
told her so. He would often make 
complimentary remarks about her 
appearance. Emily did not mind 
this and in fact, felt rather flattered. 
After a while Ming asked Emily out 
to dinner. She accepted and so began 
an office romance.

9 Skills required for specific jobs 
Nobody is completely unskilled. Everyone has skills of some sort or another, but perhaps they are not 
aware of them. In fact, people have skills which can be related to one or more occupations. Many skills 
are transferable, which means they can be used in a variety of occupations. Interpersonal skills such as 
being able to relate to other people and to communicate effectively are very important in almost any job. 
It is useful to complete a systematic analysis of your skills, and the skills you already have should be 
listed in your resume or CV. And you need to update them as you accumulate more skills.
Job-specific skills
There are some skills which are specific to particular jobs. For the 
position of typist, an applicant is expected to be able to type. Not 
only that, but to have reached a certain standard such as 50 words 
per minute. The skills required of a doctor are very different from 
those required of a carpenter or a computer operator.
While there are some skills that are relevant to all jobs,  
when you are choosing a career path, you need to assess  
your own particular skills and abilities as well as your  
academic performance. For example, a doctor not  
only needs very specialised skills but also a very high  
academic performance.
When choosing a career, assess three basic things:

2  your academic performance
 
3  your interests.
Being interested is very important as you 
will always learn more effectively if you are 
interested in something. Many people get 
persuaded into careers that they are not 
interested in, even though they may have the 
academic qualifications and the skills required.

began Australia’s first superannuation

to reach $2.3 trillion in ten years.

What is superannuation all about?
Superannuation is really a way 
of saving for your retirement. 
As employers, we must pay 
superannuation contributions on behalf 
of all our employees. This compulsory 
contribution is called the superannuation 
guarantee. For all employees between the 
ages of 18 and 70 who are paid $450 or more 
in a calendar month, their employer makes 
superannuation guarantee contributions to a 
super fund which complies with government 
guidelines. It does not matter if you are a full-
time, part-time or casual employee. 
How much do they contribute?
 
Employers must contribute a minimum 
of 9% (the charge percentage) 
of employees’ earnings base to a 
complying superannuation fund or 
a retirement savings account. This 
is normally done every three months. It is 
important to know that the superannuation 
guarantee is the responsibility of employers. 
Employees are not obliged to pay or do 
anything. However, as employees you can 
contribute your own money towards your 
retirement, as a sort of investment in the future.
What is a superannuation fund?
Superannuation funds are financial 
organisations which are run by 
trustees. Their responsibility is to 
ensure your money is invested with 
care. Each has its own rules but must 
also follow government rules that are designed 
to ensure all superannuation is properly 
managed.
I suppose superannuation will give 
you more money to live on when 
you retire than the age pension 
would provide.
The aim of the superannuation 
guarantee is to ensure as many 
Australians as possible enjoy the 
benefits of an income in their 
retirement. Superannuation does 
not replace the age pension. It remains 
for those who need it but for most people 
superannuation savings will replace or 
supplement the age pension to provide a 
greater level of retirement income.
What happens if you change jobs?
No problem. Your benefits 
accumulate no matter how many 
employers you have over your 
working life.
OK, when I retire, how do I get the 
money that is owed to me? 
Ella and Louis had just left school and 
were successful in gaining employment 
in an insurance office. They knew a 
fair bit about their rates of pay and 
general working conditions such as leave 
entitlements, but they confessed they 
knew nothing about superannuation. 
After all, it would be a long time before 
they retired. They felt however, that they 
should at least find out a bit about it so 
they asked their supervisor at work. Here is 
a record of their interview.

When you leave us, you will receive

these payments are known as eligible 
termination payments (ETPs). You 
may be terminating employment

Yes, but how do we actually get the

You have three payment choices. First,

What if I find I am broke. Can I get my

Not really. Superannuation is money

19 Tax File Number

All three levels of Australian government—local, state and federal—collect taxes. Individuals and businesses make these
compulsory payments to the government. The governments use the money to provide infrastructure (schools, roads, hospitals etc.)
for people within the community. The Commonwealth government collects taxes from income lincome taxes].

The Australian Taxation Office [ATO] works on behalf of the government to process the collection of income tax. A tax return is a
declaration of income earned by a person or business, The ATO then calculates whether or not that person or business has paid
the correct amount of tax, The ATO may require the additional payment of tax or, alternatively, issue a tax refund, To make the
process of collection of taxes more efficient, the ATO introduced the tax file number [TFN] in 1989.

ATEN is a number issued by the ATO, It is issued to the following: an individual person, a company, a trust, a partnership or a
‘Superannuation fund.

Just as people and businesses have their own personal identification numbers for bank accounts, the ATO assigns a particular TFN
to each individual taxpayer who applies for one. The taxpayer keeps the allocated TFN throughout their life. Although it is not
compulsory to have a TFN, it is recommended that one be obtained,

People without a TFN may experience delays with the ATO processing financial information. Having a TFN allows 2 person's tax to
be calculated correctly, for without a TFN a person may pay more tax than is required.

To receive a TFN, a Tax File Number Application or Enquiry form must be lodged. During this process certain documents must be

21	Taxes	and	the	GST
There are different types of taxes which affect individuals and also businesses. Individuals pay 
income tax based on the income they earn (using the PAYG or Pay As You Go system). A sole trader 
is an individual taxpayer and is subject to the same income tax rates that would apply to a wage or 
salary earner. Partnerships are treated in the same way.

The	GST	
The goods and services tax, or GST, is a broad-based tax of 10% on the value of most goods and 
services consumed in Australia. Some items, such as fresh food, are exempt. The GST is therefore 
included in the price of most goods and services.

6 Telephone and online payments
There are now many ways available to consumers to pay for
goods and services. The most common one, especially for
purchases of small value, is to pay cash in person. If you buy
an ice-cream, for example, it is appropriate to pay for it in cash. 
When you pay for something, you can:
• pay in cash
• write a cheque and deliver it in person or send it via the post
• pay in cash or with a cheque at a bank or post office
• use a debit card
• use a credit card
• use telephone banking
• use Internet banking
• use a direct debit order.

Telephone banking
By using the keypad on your telephone you can not only make payments, but also do most of your
banking. Using telephone banking, you can:
• check your account balances, including loan accounts
• check your transaction history
• stop payment on a cheque
• transfer funds from one account to another
• pay bills with BPay
• order a bank statement
• check interest earned on your investment accounts.
Telephone banking allows you to get information or carry out a transaction by ringing your bank
and following the prompts to press particular numbers on your telephone keypad. For example, if
you want account information you may be prompted to press 1, or to transfer funds to press 2.
Internet banking 
Internet banking is now very popular. The great advantage with this method is that you don’t have
to leave your home to do most of your banking.
Once you have organised to have access to Internet banking (this normally involves the bank issuing
you an account number and you choosing a password, see the Internet banking diagram on the
next page), you can do everything that you do using telephone banking, plus more, including ordering
a new cheque book; transferring money from your bank account to another person’s bank account;
and analysing your financial transactions on a monthly basis. 
Banks use special coding devices or encryption technology to ensure that no one else has access to
your banking details.
BPay
BPay is another way of paying bills or accounts using the Internet or telephone. You need to have
an organisation’s biller code (four or five numbers) and your customer reference number (usually
eight or more numbers). These are found on the bill or account that you are paying. You then use
your bank’s website or telephone service, entering both of these numbers with your computer keyboard
or telephone keypad, together with the amount you wish to pay (see the BPay system diagram on
the next page).
If you make regular BPay payments to an organisation you can save the details for future transactions
(such as Fern Hill City Council in the diagram on the next page).

8 The bond and the rent 
After signing a lease you will need to pay both bond and rent. It is important to note that these are 
separate payments.
The bond
As the owners of property, landlords need to have some way of protecting their assets. The bond is an 
up-front payment made by the tenant before they move into the property. If they cause any damage to 
the property while they are living there, the cost of the repair is taken out of the bond and the tenant 
may only get part of their bond money back. If a tenant has not caused any damage to the property, 
he or she is entitled to have their bond money returned at the end of the tenancy. 
The bond money is held by the Rental Bond Board (NSW) or the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority 
(Victoria), or similar organisations in other states and territories. At the end of the tenancy, the tenant 
can apply to get their bond money back, but the agreement of the landlord is required before the 
money is released. 
The rent
Tenants are expected to pay rent in full and on time. The rent is usually paid in advance. The landlord 
or agent is entitled to take action if rent is not paid in full on the due date.
Paying the rent
There are several methods of payment available to tenants (see box at right) and 
the method agreed upon may be included in the residential lease. Some payment 
methods may incur extra costs, such as credit card charges or fees.
When the rent is paid the landlord (or agent) must issue a receipt. If the rent is 
paid in person the tenant must be given a receipt on the spot. For other payments 
a receipt must be sent or available for pick-up within five days. A tenant should 
always keep a record of the rent paid as proof in case there are any disputes.
A receipt should contain the following information:
•  the tenant’s name
•  the address of the property
•  the date
•  the total amount paid
•  the period that the payment covers.
Problems with paying rent
Tenants sometimes have trouble meeting their regular rental payments, for a variety of reasons.  
If you run into trouble with your rent, consumer affairs advice is available from state government 
agencies (such as the NSW Office of Fair Trading or Consumer Affairs Victoria). There are similar 
agencies in the other states. When experiencing problems with rental payments, bear in mind the 
following do’s and don’ts:
Do
• contact your landlord or agent as soon as possible to explain any problems and try to work  
out a solution
• seek assistance from state or local consumer affairs organisations.
Don’t
•  withhold payment of rent because you are not satisfied with lack of action on repairs
•  fail to pay the final weeks’ rent at the end of the lease – this can be deducted from any bond 
money owing to you.

If your rent is more than 14 days overdue the landlord can give you notice to vacate and apply to the 
courts for an order to evict you. This is not automatic, however – tenants do have rights and a landlord 
cannot simply lock a tenant out for not paying their rent. A legal procedure must be followed and the 
matter resolved in court.
Increasing the rent
Landlords cannot increase rent at will. There are various state laws which govern rent increases.  
The rules surrounding rent increases state that:
•  The landlord must first give notice (generally 60 days written notice) of a rent increase.
•  The tenant may appeal against any rent increase which they believe to be excessive.
•  If the tenant cannot successfully negotiate the changes with the landlord, he or she may approach 
the Residential Tenancies Tribunal (NSW) or the Victorian Civil and Administration Tribunal (Victoria) 
to have the dispute settled. Other states have similar bodies. 
Disputes
Disputes between landlords and tenants can occur for various reasons. Problems often arise when the 
tenant requests that certain repairs are carried out and the landlord or agent either does not act or 
disputes the need for the repairs. These disputes can escalate and sometimes need to be resolved by the 
relevant Tribunal for that state.

3 The burden of personal debt 
The following two stories are fictitious, but they 
illustrate how easily personal debt can get out  
of control, and the burdens it creates. 
  
Dylan’s story
At 19 years of age Dylan had left school and was 
working in an office as a junior clerk. He was 
excited about earning money and decided to enjoy 
it. He applied for a credit card and was amazed 
at how easy it was to buy whatever he wanted by 
charging it to the card. When the account came, 
Dylan found that it was much higher than he 
had expected. As well as buying up big on clothes 
and DVDs, he had also been using his card to 
withdraw cash advances. He had been enjoying 
life without realising how much he was spending. 
Dylan couldn’t afford to pay off his account, so he 
just paid the minimum amount due. At the end 
of the following month Dylan was astonished to 
see the interest charges that had accumulated on 
the unpaid portion of his previous account. The 
interest was calculated from the original date of 
purchase. Dylan realised that every time he was 
unable to pay the full amount owing, he would 
have to pay interest, which would add up very 
quickly. He needed help.
Muna’s story
Muna was a single parent bringing 
up two children. Since moving to 
Australia she had supported her family 
with her savings and from casual work 
as a waitress at a city restaurant. The 
family had shifted between friends’

falling behind in the rent. Muna found

9 The condition report 
A condition report is a document that describes the general condition of the premises being let, 
including fittings and fixtures. It is necessary in situations where a bond has been paid. It is the duty 
of the landlord or his or her agent to prepare a condition report on the premises. They must give two 
copies of the signed condition report to the tenant before the tenant can occupy the premises. A fine 
can be imposed if this is not done. The tenant must fill out and promptly return the condition report 
to the landlord or agent. 
The condition report is an extremely important document. It may be used as evidence if there is a future 
dispute about who is responsible for any cleaning, damage, or missing items. It is important that tenants 
keep their copy of the condition report until the end of the tenancy. 
The landlord or agent has the right to claim some, or all of the bond money if there has been damage, 
if items are missing or if the premises are left dirty and untidy at the end of the tenancy. The condition 
report is therefore crucial as it is an agreement of the state of the premises prior to the tenancy. This 
protects the tenant from having to pay for any damage that they are not responsible for.

14 The influence of marketing 
Marketing is more than just selling. It includes the strategies used to promote, advertise and sell goods 
and services to consumers, including packaging, market research and sales promotion.  
The four Ps of marketing
Product 
Place
Price
Promotion
Product refers to the actual goods and/or 
services you are buying. This can include the 
item itself, the packaging, and also other aspects 
such as warranties, customer support etc.
Place is where you actually buy the product and 
how it gets there from the manufacturer
Price is the agreed financial value of the goods 
and/or services being purchased
Promotion is the way the product is advertised 
to bring it to the buyer’s attention.
Promotion and advertising
Advertising and promotion are the ways a company tries to get the attention of buyers and convince 
them to buy the product. Advertising takes many forms, from catalogues in your letterbox to 
major television and newspaper ads. The kind of advertisement used, and even the style of the 
advertisement, the newspaper it is placed in or the time it is shown on television are all carefully 
chosen depending on who the advertisement is aimed at.
Advertising is a highly specialised business and many companies hire an advertising agency to 
produce an ad or sometimes even a complete advertising and marketing strategy. Advertising costs  
a lot of money, and the cost of this is usually built into the price of the product.
Brand loyalty
Advertising may be informative, persuasive, or both. Informing potential customers of a new product 
and its features is only part of the purpose of an ad. Advertisements also try to ensure a product is 
recognisable, and to differentiate that product from its competitors. This is part of a strategy called 
‘brand loyalty’. Companies want customers to be familiar with, and drawn to, their brand. Apple, 
Nike and Coke are examples of companies that have established a strong brand.
Market research
Before a manufacturer spends money creating a product, they will conduct extensive research into 
their target market. This is so they can be sure that people will buy what they produce. Companies 
go to a lot of trouble to find out what you like. 
Market research is carried out in order to answer the following questions:
•  do customers like the product?
•  how much should we sell the product for?
•  what is the likely size of the market?
•  are there similar products already on the market?

31
Market research is carried out by a variety of methods, such as surveys, shopping centre interviews  
or taste tests.
There are different types of markets that products might be aimed at:
•  Target market – the customers you are targeting, or aiming to attract. 
•  Niche market – a small select market for a limited number of customers.
•  Mass market – a large number of potential customers.

Living and Work Literacy 4
Types of interviews
Simple one-on-one interview
Simple interview before a panel
Complex series of interview sessions (which may involve psychometric testing) 
Types of questions
Open questions, e.g. ‘Tell us a little about …‘
Hypothetical questions, e.g. ‘What would you do if …‘
Double-barrelled questions – two or more questions linked to the same topic
Behavioural questions, e.g. ‘What is your view of …‘
Multiple choice questions – used in aptitude tests
What is psychometric testing?
Psychometric tests aim to measure attributes such as intelligence, aptitude and personality. This 
provides an employer with an insight into how you might cope with stress, how well you work with 
other people, and how ambitious or motivated you are. 
Types of tests
Aptitude tests: these are used to assess your numerical and verbal abilities, your spatial reasoning 
skills and comprehension. They tend to use multiple-choice type questions. 
Example: Which of the following is the odd one out?
	
A car
	
B train
	
C bus
	
D bank
Obviously answer D is correct as the others are all forms of transport. Of course, there are more 
difficult questions than this. Some tests may also involve computer skills which test knowledge and 
application of computer programs.
Personality tests: these are not a mystery. You can find examples in magazines, books and on 
the Internet. Many are of dubious quality, but a good test is one which is proven to be reliable 
by extensive research and developed over time. Often there are no right or wrong answers, but 
responses can indicate how people think, how they view particular issues and what their interests 
and motivations are. From personality tests, psychologists develop a profile indicating which type of 
person you are.
	
Example: Which of the following statements best sums you up as a person? 
	
A I enjoy organising other people.
	
B I have a wide circle of friends.
	
C I look for variety in tasks.
	
D I always feel calm and relaxed.
Group tests: for some jobs, group tests may 
be used. You may be put with a group of other 
people and asked to build something with 
blocks, or with string, glue and newspaper. 
In these situations, employers are looking for 
people who are innovative and have lots of 
ideas, as well as people who can work co-operatively in a group situation.
Psychometric testing does not provide all the answers. However, it does provide an indicator of a 
person‘s character, aptitudes and preferences, to assist both employers and employees to find the 
best match of individual to occupation and working environment. It is not supposed to replace 
interviews or reference checking. Some companies may rely too heavily on these tests and as a 
result fail to employ some excellent people. Other experts believe they are very accurate in that 
they assess personal traits that may affect job performance and work behaviour.

18 The neighbourhood 
Every neighbourhood is different. Whenever you move into a new area, there will be things you need to 
know and things you need to consider in order to ensure you get along with your neighbours and are a 
respectful member of the community. 
Know your neighbourhood
The following information can help you to settle into your new neighbourhood. Find out about:
•  rubbish collection – which day of the week the rubbish is collected, whether there are special bins for 
recycling and garden waste 
•  public transport – where is the nearest bus stop and train station? When do the buses and trains arrive?
•  shops and facilities – where is the nearest supermarket, petrol station, shopping centre, post office, 
bank, park, library, swimming pool, gym, etc. 
•  neighbours – get to know the people living nearby. Be considerate of any needs or concerns they may have. 
Being a considerate neighbour
There are many things you can do to ensure that you are a good neighbour. It is important to treat your 
neighbours with respect and consider their needs as well as your own when going about your day-to-day lives.
Privacy 
Many homes are built very close together, and in these circumstances it is particularly important to 
remember that you are entitled to privacy in your home, and so are your neighbours. It is not considerate 
to look over fences or in windows, or to eavesdrop on your neighbours’ conversations. Also consider your 
own conversations – it is best to discuss private matters indoors, where the neighbours can’t hear you. 
Noise
There is a federal government organisation which aims to control unwanted noise and the impact it has 
on the community. The website is at www.noisewatch.org.au. You may wish to make a complaint about 
unnecessary noise in your neighbourhood, or you could be the subject of a complaint about noise. Many 
people can be affected by noise in a neighbourhood. It is important to be considerate of your neighbours, 
particularly if making a lot of noise late at night. It is considerate to warn your neighbours if you are 
planning a loud party or event. 
Pets
It is important to be aware of any council laws regarding keeping pets in your area. Some councils have 
restrictions such as which breeds of animals can be kept as pets, and curfews for cats. It is also important 
to be aware of how your pet affects your neighbours – issues such as noise, smell and damage to 
property can all be concerns. 
Garden maintenance
As a member of the community, it can be considerate to ensure that your property is maintained to a 
certain standard. Keeping gardens tidy, trees trimmed and lawns mown are all ways of ensuring that your 
property looks good and is making a positive contribution to the neighbourhood.
Resolving disputes
If you have an issue with your neighbour, the best place to start is to talk to them about it. Find a time 
to discuss the matter with them calmly. Clearly outline the reasons for your concern, and try to sound 
objective, rather than critical. If each person considers the other person’s viewpoint calmly, it will usually 
be possible to reach an understanding. If you are unable to resolve your dispute in this way, most states 
have a dispute resolution service, such as the Dispute Settlement Centre of Victoria, or the Dispute 
Resolution Centre in Queensland.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
39
Getting involved in the community 
Getting involved in your local community has many benefits. It can be healthy and enjoyable to interact 
with other people in your local area, and the sense of satisfaction of contributing to your community 
should not be underestimated. By participating in community activities you also learn skills which you 
can apply in later years. 
Two common ways that people engage with their local community are:
•  doing volunteer work, such as working with a local charity or council organisation 
•  joining a club, such as a sporting club, music or craft club.
Community support
Local councils provide various forms of support for members of the community. This support can include:
•  help for disabled or elderly residents  
• neighbourhood watch
•  childcare 
 
 
 
 
• clubs and sporting groups
•  housing and emergency accommodation.
If you are in need of any help, whether it is emotional, physical or financial, your local council could be 
a good place to start. Similarly, if you would like to offer help to others in your community, volunteering 
for one of these organisations could be a great way to make a contribution.

their lawns mown and gardens tidy at all 
times. Chris and Maya are both very busy,

neighbours feel about this? What could Chris

regarding rubbish collection, public

your local council and make a list of 
the services available in your area.

10 The online shopping experience 
Online shopping has become extremely popular in recent years.  
There are many advantages to online shopping, such as:
•  it is convenient
•  it saves time
•  it is often cheaper than buying from retail stores
•  you can shop interstate or even overseas
•  more and more companies are offering online shopping facilities.
Tips for smart online shopping
•  Find out as much as you can about the product that you want to buy. Ask the seller questions, 
and see if you can find photos of the same item on other sites, so you know exactly what you’re 
getting.
•  Make sure you know all the details of the sale, including shipping costs, delivery times, and 
whether you can return the product if it’s faulty or not as described.
•  Take steps to ensure that the seller is trustworthy. Do they have a registered business? Can you 
check customer feedback to show that they have a good record?
•  Check the payment options and make sure they are secure. Look for a padlock symbol at the top  
or bottom of the screen – this usually means that your information is safe.
•  Know what to do if something goes wrong. Do you have contact details for the seller? Does the 
website offer a mediation service to resolve disputes?
•  Check online auction sites. Learn how they work, what your rights are and what you can do if 
anything goes wrong.
•  Keep records. You should keep copies of any documents such as forms, emails or web pages as 
they are a record of the sale. Terms and conditions, warranties, receipts and payment forms and 
even advertising brochures could all provide proof of the sale that took place.
Problems may arise
• If something goes wrong with an online purchase there are some things you can do:
•  Start by contacting the seller. There might have been a simple misunderstanding that could easily 
be resolved.
•  If that doesn’t work, contact the people who run the website to see if they can help. Keep copies  
of all your correspondence.
•  Contact your bank to see if you’re able to stop the payment from going through.
•  Contact your local office of fair trading, or the ACCC. They may be able to help, or at least  
offer advice.
Problems with an overseas seller
If things go wrong when buying goods online from an overseas seller, you may have more difficulty 
in resolving the dispute. Start by trying the steps outlined above. If that doesn’t work, contact ICPEN 
(the International Consumer Protection and Enforcement Network. This worldwide organisation aims 
to protect consumers around the world by sharing information and encouraging global cooperation 
among law enforcement agencies.

2 Top tips for saving money 
There are two things you can do with your income – spend it or save it. Although it can be tempting to 
spend all your money, it’s a good idea to try and save some money whenever you can. 
Why save?
There are several reasons why it is a good idea to save some of your income, including: 
• saving for a rainy day – this means saving money in case you need a little extra in the future
•  saving for a major purchase
•  saving to guard against loss of job
•  saving money so you can invest it and make more money.
There are lots of tips for saving money. Different tips work for different people depending on their 
lifestyle, income and personal preference. Here are some suggestions for you to consider.
Saving tips
•  Be aware of when you make extra purchases – such as when you are tired, stressed or hungry – 
and try to avoid shopping at those times.
•  Leave your credit card at home if you are going somewhere where you think you will be tempted 
to spend.
•  Make your lunch every day instead of buying it.
•  Buy fresh foods to cook, rather than takeaway or pre-packaged foods.
•  Make a shopping list each week and stick to it. 
•  Try to buy clothes that are second-hand or on sale, rather than buying new or expensive clothes.
•  Don’t buy every gadget that comes onto the market.
•  Watch television or DVDs rather than go to movies.
•  Try to cut back on alcohol and cigarettes – the costs add up very quickly! 
•  Think about selling some of the things in your house that you don’t need.
•  Take cheap locally based holidays, and try to stay in places where you can cook your own meals 
rather than eating out all the time.
The story of Charles 
Charles had a good job and earned a good income. His only problem was that 
he couldn’t stop himself from spending it. As soon as he got paid he went 
shopping and spent all his money. One day Charles’ best friend Jake asked him 
if he would like to go on a holiday to Europe. Charles would have loved to go 
but had no money saved, so couldn’t afford it. 
Tina’s story 
Tina also had a job that paid well. She was careful with her spending patterns  
and only bought what she felt was necessary. She saved a percentage of her 
income every week. When her best friend, Leah, suggested that they should both 
go to Europe at the end of the year, Tina jumped at the chance. She had already 
saved enough for the airfare and by the end of the year would have enough 
money for a really good holiday.

2 Trade unions today 
What are they and how did they begin?
A trade union is a group of workers who unite to promote and defend wage rates and working 
conditions through common ideals and actions. The principle of unionism is that a group acting 
collectively can exert more power than an individual can in negotiating for better wages and working 
conditions. 
Trade unions have always generated considerable debate within the community, with many people 
fiercely opposed to them and many people strongly supportive of them. Australia’s history is littered 
with struggles between employers and trade unions, such as the Great Shearers’ Strike of 1891 – one of 
the first big industrial disputes in Australia. A more recent example is the 1998 Maritime Unions dispute.
The Australian Council of Trade Unions or ACTU was formed in 1927. It is the national organisation 
authorised to speak on behalf of the unions. At the state level there are Trades and Labour Councils 
(TLCs) which represent unions in issues affecting individual states. The ACTU and the TLCs have 
common aims. The most important ones are:

The ACTU states that all Australian workers have the right to join a union: ‘Whether you work in a small 
or large business, in an office or on a construction site – there is a union to represent you.’
Trade union issues today
Trade union activity today is highly dependent on the current state of industrial relations in the country 
and on the legislation that reflects it. Industrial relations laws are very complex and often the subject of 
much argument. They are constantly changing, especially when there is a change of government.
One of the most significant issues relating to trade unions today is the fall in membership. There are 
several reasons for this, but the most important one relates to the casualisation of the workforce.

16 Understanding credit cards 
What is a credit card?
There are lots of plastic cards you can acquire, such as loyalty cards, club membership cards and ATM 
cards (debit cards). A credit card, on the other hand, is a card that you can use instead of cash or debit 
to purchase goods and services. When your credit card is swiped you can either sign a sales docket or 
enter your PIN (Personal Identification Number) and you can take the goods home. This means you 
don’t have to pay for them immediately. When you receive your statement you need to pay for the 
goods you have purchased over the past month. Your statement will list a minimum amount that needs 
to be paid. However, if you only pay the minimum amount due, you will still be charged interest on 
the outstanding amount. When taking out a credit card, check the terms and conditions of the contract 
and, in particular, the interest charged on overdue accounts. Some people have several credit cards – 
this can be dangerous, as it makes it hard to keep track of all your purchases.
