14 Unfair and fair dismissal 
People leave jobs for different reasons. For example, you may leave of your own free will, or you may be 
asked or told to leave. There are different terms used for each situation.
Resigned – gave notice that you wished to leave your place of work
s�Retired – decided to finish your working life
s�Dismissed – forced to leave by the employer
s�Terminated – another term for ‘dismissed’
s�Sacked – a colloquial or slang word for ‘dismissed’
s�Redundant – being dismissed because there is no work for you to do
s�Retrenched – being dismissed to save the employer money
s�Fair or unfair?
As an employee, you are entitled to notice of termination, usually four weeks. You may be made 
redundant by an employer or you may be retrenched. If an employer gives adequate notice and 
provides a dismissed worker with full entitlements, the employee is considered to be dismissed fairly, no 
matter how he or she may personally feel about it.
So what is unfair dismissal? Sometimes personality clashes arise between an employee and the boss, 
and the boss may dismiss that employee – a personality clash is not a valid reason for dismissal. Some 
workers may not be as efficient or as fast as others and be targeted for dismissal. Dismissal of women 
who get married or who are expecting a child and workers because they belong to a trade union are 
examples of unfair dismissal. 
If a worker is dismissed for discriminatory reasons, that is considered unlawful and the worker has 
the right to appeal against the dismissal. Unfair dismissal laws have been written into the Workplace 
Relations Act which was revised in 2001 and again in 2008. Workers who believe that they have been 
dismissed on discriminatory grounds can lodge an application with the Australian Industrial Relations 
Commission. They must lodge an application with the Commission within 21 days of being dismissed.  
The Commission then considers things such as:
whether there was a fair and valid reason for the dismissal
s�whether the employee was notified of that reason and given 
s�the opportunity to respond
whether the employee has been notified of any 
s�unsatisfactory performance.
Laws about unfair dismissal do not apply to workers who are 
employed by a company with less than 100 workers. This issue 
has been debated at length by politicians and employers in

6 What are services? 
What are services?
Unlike goods, services are those things you want to buy that you can’t see or touch directly. There are 
many different types of services.  
Where do services fit in the economy?
Economic activity refers to all the goods and services that are being bought and sold in the country. We 
often classify economic activity into three broad groups: primary, secondary and tertiary (see diagram below).
Type of industry
Characteristics
Examples 
Primary
Obtaining raw 
materials from  
the Earth
    coal mining            wheat farming          fishing
Secondary
Manufacturing  
or processing raw 
materials into 
finished products
  steel making    car manufacturing     soft drink bottling
Tertiary
Providing services 
for people
  banking              retailing              medical services
  
 
Banking and financial services
Banks and other financial institutions provide a variety of financial services. They store money, invest 
money over long periods of time and lend money to people who need it. For example: 
Claire earns a good income and finds that she has saved quite a lot of money over the past year. She 
decides to open an investment account with a bank. The bank will pay her interest on the money she 
has invested. The rate of interest varies depending on the health of the economy at the time.
Claire’s friend Mia just got married. Mia and her husband want to buy a house. They apply to the bank 
for a loan. The bank is able to take the money that people like Claire have invested, and lend it to Mia 
and her husband. Mia and her husband will have to repay the money they have borrowed plus interest, 
which is what the bank charges for the use of their money.
Medical services 
Doctors and other medical staff, such as dentists, nurses and hospital workers, provide a variety of 
medical services.
Mia’s husband Tony has an accident at work and needs to see his local doctor or GP (general 
practitioner). The GP examines Tony’s injured leg and recommends that he go to hospital for an X-ray. 
The leg is broken, so Tony is referred to a surgeon to set his leg in a cast so that it will heal. For this 
accident, Tony required the services of a GP, a radiologist (for the X-ray), a surgeon to set his leg as well 
as a number of nurses and hospital staff.

Retail services cover a wide variety of services performed by people such as store managers, shop 
assistants, delivery workers, advertising executives, door-to door salespeople and warehouse staff.

The tourism industry is one of the largest industries in Australia. Tourism encompasses a wide variety of

1 What are your spending habits? 
Needs and wants
Managing your money is a juggle between spending and saving. When it comes to spending, we  
all have needs and wants. Needs are basic to our survival. They are the things we can’t do without.  
For example, we need food to survive, and we need basic clothing and shelter for protection against  
the cold. Wants, on the other hand, are the things that we would like to have but that are not basic  
to our survival.  
Some items can fit into either category. For example, a loaf of bread may qualify as a need, while a 
meal at an expensive restaurant could be seen as a want. They are both kinds of food, but the fancy 
restaurant meal is not essential to survival. Many items of clothing could also fall into both categories 
– some are necessary for survival, but others are luxury items. 
Your spending habits
It is good idea to analyse your spending habits. Remember that although we all have a limited income, 
there is no limit to the things we want. We need to decide which wants we satisfy and which ones we 
do without. This is not always easy – sometimes other factors are involved, such as emotion, and we can 
find ways to justify purchases that we may not really need to make. Consider the following comments:
Needs
•  food
•  clothing
•  shelter
Wants
•  television
•  movie ticket
•  mobile phone

13 What do I need to buy? 
  
Some premises come fully furnished but if you don’t have any furniture and you are moving into an 
unfurnished place, there will be some items you need. If you haven’t lived out of home before there 
may also be other basics that you will need. What do you need immediately? What can wait? How do 
you proceed from here? You can divide your requirements into two categories:
•  essentials – things you need to have as soon as possible
•  options – things you can live without for a while. 
Essentials
Basic furniture
You will need some items of furniture for your new home. A bed is important, to ensure you have 
somewhere to sleep. A table and chairs will provide you with somewhere to eat, and could also serve as 
a desk if you are studying. You may also need a couch to provide a place to relax or to entertain friends. 
Basic appliances
Essential kitchen appliances are likely to include a refrigerator, a stove and an oven. Most properties will 
have a stove and an oven installed. Other appliances that you may consider to be essential include a 
washing machine and a vacuum cleaner. 
Other basics
Other items that you will need include cutlery and crockery, such as plates, bowls, cups, pots and pans. 
You may also need to buy sheets, towels and pillows.
Options
Expensive furniture is not necessary. Some people make do with milk crates to put things on, such 
as the television or stereo, until they can afford something else. Small kitchen appliances, such as 
rice cookers and sandwich toasters can be handy but are options, rather than essentials. Although a 
television, computer and mobile phone may be seen as essential by many people, others may be able  
to live without them. 
Making some choices
Here are some of the choices you may need to make:
•  Do you want a landline or a mobile phone – or both?
•  Will you use a laundromat or buy a washing machine?
•  Do you need to buy more furniture, or get rid of some,  
if you are moving into a smaller place?
•  Should you consider contents insurance, if you don’t 
already have a policy?
•  Would you prefer to buy new or second hand? Websites 
such as eBay and the Trading Post can be a good source 
of second-hand goods. Will you buy furniture and 
appliances or hire them? Hiring appliances means you 
need less money up-front, but this can work out to be 
more expensive in the long run.
•  When buying new items for a shared house, will you 
have joint ownership or make individual purchases? Joint 
ownership costs each person less money, but problems 
could arise if you later move to different places.

7 What is a contract? 
A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more people or organisations. It has two  
basic elements:
•  offer and acceptance
•  consideration
To explain these two elements using a simple example, imagine that you go into a shop to buy a 
television. You check out all the options and finally, after discussions with the salesperson, you decide 
which one you want to buy. The marked price is $850 and you offer $800. The salesperson checks  
with the manager and tells you that your offer has been accepted. You have made the offer and the 
shop has accepted it, so an agreement has been reached.  
Consideration means that something of value must be exchanged. In this case the $800 is the 
consideration that you have both agreed to. This is a very simple contract which has two basic  
elements that lead to an agreement. Contracts don’t always have to be in writing, although some are 
required to be by law. Examples include loan contracts and contracts for the sale of a house or land. 
Entering a contract
A contract is a legal document that is enforceable in law,  
so it is important that you understand what you are 
agreeing to. Never rush into an agreement that you are 
unsure about. The law provides some protection against 
being forced into a contract unfairly. In some contracts 
where a purchase is made, a cooling-off period applies, 
which means you have time to reconsider in case you 
rushed into a purchase. 
•  Entering into a contract doesn’t just mean signing  
a legal document. You can also enter into a contract 
by agreeing to a purchase and paying for it, or when 
you click on the ‘submit’ button on a website. 
Terms and conditions
Contracts often contain many terms and conditions.  
They outline the rights and responsibilities covered by the contract. Sometimes the terms and conditions 
are written in very small print but they are still legally binding, so it is important that you read and 
understand them. If you have any concerns about the terms and conditions, seek advice before signing.  
By signing a contract you are agreeing to the terms and conditions. Ticking the ‘I Agree’ box  
on certain websites also means you have entered into a contract. 
Note: If you have been forced into a contract by unfair or unreasonable behaviour, you 
have the right to seek help. Contact your state consumer affairs organisation, such as 
your state Department of Fair Trading. The ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer 
Commission) is a federal government department that also regulates unfair behaviour with 
regard to contracts.

7 What is a lease? 
Read the definitions below to help you understand the terminology used when agreeing to rent a property.
landlord 
the person who owns a property and is prepared to let it
tenant 
the person who has permission to rent the landlord’s property to live in
lease 
 the rental contract stating the amount of rent to be paid, the method of payment, length  
of time and other conditions (see below). It is sometimes known as a tenancy agreement. 
rent 
the amount of money, per week that the tenant must pay to the landlord (or agent)
bond 
the money paid up-front as security in case of damage to the property
Tenancy agreements can be either verbal or written. It is better to have a written agreement because  
a written agreement: 
• gives you more security provided you follow the terms of the lease 
• means you cannot be asked to leave before the lease expires 
• means the amount of rent you have to pay is fixed for the term of the lease
• gives you the right to have repairs done provided they are reasonable.
There are two types of tenancy agreements – fixed-term and periodic. A fixed-term agreement is for 
a set period of time, often 6 months. A periodic agreement is an arrangement which runs from week 
to week or month to month. Written agreements must follow the wording of an official ‘Residential 
Tenancy Agreement’ form. A simplified version is illustrated below:

Conditions
In a lease agreement there will generally be a number of conditions that the landlord and the tenant 
agree upon. These may include things like:
• who is responsible for keeping the place clean, and the standards of cleanliness
• who is responsible for repairs, and how these should be done 
• who is responsible for mowing the lawn or maintaining the garden (if there is one).

Tips for tenants
Before moving in
•  Always read the lease (or Residential Tenancy Agreement) carefully before signing it. Never sign  
a blank sheet of paper.
•  If you are unsure about anything in the lease, get some professional advice.
•  The Office of Fair Trading in your state will probably have a guide for tenants that you should be 
able to access free of charge. Familiarise yourself with your rights and responsibilities as a tenant.
•  Check that the premises are clean and safe. You will probably have to pay a Bond, in which case 
you should carefully check the Condition Report (see unit 9).
•  Ensure you get receipts for any rent paid up front.
Before moving out 
•  Make sure you pay the final rent owing.
•  Arrange for the electricity, gas, water and telephone to be disconnected, and pay the final bills.
•  Check that the premises are in good order and condition.
•  Make sure that you have packed all your belongings. 
•  Organise for the landlord or agent to return any bond money paid.
•  Leave a forwarding address with the landlord or agent so you can receive any mail delivered to the 
premises after you leave.
•  Check the terms of your agreement to ensure you have met all conditions for leaving (such as  
cleaning or any repairs).

3 What is homelessness? 
The two stories above are fictitious, but they are based on things that happen in the community.  
These are the kinds of things that can lead to homelessness. 
Levels of homelessness
The Australian Bureau of Statistics divides the homeless into the following categories:
1 Absolute homeless (primary homeless): People without conventional accommodation (living on the 
streets, in deserted buildings, improvised dwellings, in parks, etc.) – sometimes called ‘sleeping rough’.
2 Relative homeless (secondary and tertiary homeless): People staying in boarding houses, 
people using Supported Accommodation Assistance Program (SAAP) and other similar emergency 
accommodation services, or people with no secure accommodation staying temporarily with friends 
or relatives in private dwellings.
On Census night in 2006, the homeless population in Australia was 105 000, according to the Australian 
Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Causes of homelessness
Some of the main causes of homelessness are:
• family members fighting amongst themselves can lead to one or more members leaving home 
• a family member physically assaulting other family members (this is known as domestic violence)
• mental or emotional abuse
• sexual assault
• financial problems within the household, such as unemployment or gambling problems
• physical or mental illness or intellectual disability within the family
• drug and/or alcohol abuse
• family bereavement, which can strain family relationships
• accommodation problems, such as overcrowding in the home. 
Sometimes more than one of these problems can occur within the one household.
Emma’s story
When I was 13, my father left home. My mum found a new partner who soon 
moved in. He abused my sisters and me on a regular basis. He also used to beat 
my mum but he always said he was sorry, and she forgave him.
I put up with this for about a year, then, when I turned 15, I decided I couldn’t 
take it anymore. I said to mum, ‘Either he goes or I go.’ Mum chose him, so I 
left home. I had nowhere to go, and ended up on the streets. I sometimes stayed 
with friends, but never for long. I moved closer to the city and started sleeping 
with guys I picked up on the street to get enough money to live on. I slept in 
abandoned houses and buildings with other young people who were just like me.
Luke’s story
I was 14 when I got kicked out of home. I always seemed to be fighting with my 
parents. They wanted to control me and I was a bit of a rebel at the time. At first 
I just stayed anywhere – camped, slept in cars – wherever I could find a place to 
be. I didn’t own anything except my clothes so it was easy to just keep moving.
One day a mate told me about a place that offered refuge accommodation. I 
went there to see if they could help me. The staff at the refuge organised for me 
to move into emergency accommodation. While I was there, my support worker 
helped me find a job as a labourer. I also got some information on going back to finish school. I enrolled 
in a TAFE course to become a plumber. Now I rent my own apartment, I’ve nearly finished my plumber’s 
apprenticeship and work full time for a large construction company.

Living and Work Literacy 7

Fact or fiction
*  All homeless people are older men.   FALSE 
Homeless people are all ages, and the breakdown between males and females is roughly 50/50.
*  You’re not homeless if you’re staying with friends.   FALSE 
Many homeless people stay with friends or relatives, but without a permanent home, they are still homeless.
*  Most homeless people sleep out on the streets or in an improvised shelter.   FALSE 
Very few homeless people sleep out – many stay in temporary accommodation.

Getting help
As a basic human right, all people are entitled to a safe and affordable place to live. If you find yourself 
without a home you can seek help either through government agencies or privately run services, such as: 
• State government agencies such as the Department of Community Services in NSW or the 
Department of Human Services in Victoria. There are similar agencies in all Australian states and 
territories. If you are under 18 years of age, you will be given special assistance.
• Centrelink, the federal government agency, can help with financial matters.
• Emergency organisations such as Kids Helpline (phone 1800 55 1800) or Lifeline (phone 131 114) 
can help if you are in urgent need of immediate housing and/or food.
Other sources of help can include organisations such as Alcoholics Anonymous, Alateen (for children  
who have an alcoholic in the family) and the National Children’s and Youth Law Centre (called Lawstuff), 
as well as family members, friends, school counsellors and other personal contacts.

11 Work environments: cultural issues
Multicultural issues 
When you begin a new job you’ll probably find yourself 
working with people of different racial backgrounds and 
religions. Their cultures may seem foreign to you, and your 
culture may be equally foreign to them. Recognition and 
respect for other people’s cultural beliefs is an important 
part of working harmoniously in a workplace.
Here are some comments you may well hear in a workplace. 
What do you think?
‘I don’t like working with Asians.’
s�‘Yes, but he’s a Christian.’
s�‘Ahmed is from Iraq you know. What can you expect from 
s�a fellow with that background?’
‘I don’t want to be supervised by a Serbian.’
s�Gender issues
Women and men should be treated equally in the workplace. It has now been decades since it was 
socially acceptable to treat women as being inferior to men. Women were once paid less, discriminated 
against and often passed over for promotion. Even today, women talk of the ‘glass ceiling’ when it 
comes to promotion prospects.
Despite the equal treatment you may hear these comments in the workplace.
‘That’s a woman’s job.’
s�‘You get the women to make the morning tea so the men can do the important work.’
s�‘Oh, don’t promote her. Now that she’s married she’ll only get pregnant and leave – and you’ll have to 
s�pay her maternity leave, you know.’
Disabled workers
In the past, people who suffered a disability, no matter how severe, were not welcome in the workplace. 
During the 1950s, parents of people with disabilities set up sheltered workshops to provide employment 
for their children. Some voluntary organisations also opened workshops. Today that situation is no 
longer acceptable. People with mild disabilities are accepted and encouraged to join the workforce 
and employers are obliged to provide them with opportunities and facilities to assist them as needed. 
Expectations of work output are often adjusted to allow for disabilities, but rather than have sheltered 
workshops, integration in the workforce is the goal.
All governments at every level in Australia as well as private organisations work together to ensure equal 
employment opportunities for people with disabilities. Some people with disabilities may require support 
or assistance to find an appropriate form of employment.
Assistance is available to:
help determine job interests and suitable types of employment
s�search for relevant jobs
s�prepare for job interviews
s�help with understanding employment conditions
s�provide ongoing support.
s�People with more severe disabilities may require more intensive support and some organisations 
provide this. Whatever the disability, making sure that wherever possible the workplace is accessible for 
employees with disabilities is a responsibility of all employers. Attitudes to working with people with 
disabilities are unfortunately still varied. You may hear comments like the following.
 
Jonah: 
I can’t work with him, he’s so slow.
 
Miriam:  But do you realise he has a disability? Give him a chance. How would you like to be 
discriminated against and have nobody prepared to employ you?

Anti-discrimination laws
Discrimination means treating people unfairly on the basis of some prejudice. Therefore, workers should 
not be discriminated against on the basis of their age, sex, race, religion or disability. In fact, it is now 
against the law to discriminate against any worker by:
refusing to employ them
s�preventing them from being promoted
s�giving them less favourable conditions of employment
s�dismissing them.

7 Work in the future 
Have you ever wondered what work will be like in the future?  
There will probably be many jobs available which haven’t been  
invented yet, and many jobs once popular are likely to  
disappear. This makes it hard to predict what will happen,  
but it is wise to be aware of the rate of change in  
our society in general – much of this change is  
driven by new technology. You only have to  
look at car manufacturing in today’s world  
to see how automated some industries  
have become. Modern communication  
technologies, especially the Internet, have  
also revolutionised the nature of work.
Workplaces are likely to be different too. Working from 9 am  
to 5 pm in an office or factory may not be the norm any more.  
For example, to borrow money from a bank you once went into the bank  
branch near you and made an appointment with the manager. Today it is common for bank employees 
to come to your house with a laptop computer loaded with financial software and talk about your loan 
application, which you could have submitted online. 
Some of the many changes that have occurred in the workplace in recent years are listed below.
Workplace changes 
R  Greater use of technology, such as computers and telecommunications equipment
R  Gradual elimination of unskilled work, which is increasingly done by machines
R  Increase in the importance of on-the-job training and higher qualifications
R  Skilled tradespeople in danger of losing their jobs due to complex computerised machinery 
replacing them, leading to de-skilling
R  A greater variety of jobs available, especially in the service sector
R  Greater job mobility with increased chances of working overseas
R  The concept of a ‘job for life’ which was once the norm,  
is becoming less common

5 Working conditions
Working conditions today:
1. Hours of work
A 35-hour working week is regarded as full-time work.
There has been a steady growth in casual and part-time work.
There has been a marked increase in the number of hours being worked by full-time workers.
2. Benefits and entitlements
Leave generally consists of: annual (or holiday) leave, sick leave, family leave (maternity and 
paternity leave), long service leave, special leave (for example, to attend funerals), leave without 
pay.
In August 2005, 76% of employees were provided with one or more types of paid leave.
Full-time employees were more likely than part-time employees to have leave entitlements (87% 
compared with 41%).
Entitlements include fringe benefits (rewards for employees, income in kind), holiday leave 
loading, termination payouts and rights relating to unfair dismissal.
Fringe benefits typically include a company car, children’s education expenses, entertainment 
allowances and assistance with paying housing loans. These are often associated with a ‘salary 
package’.
Employers are required to provide superannuation benefits of 9% of wages for their employees’ 
retirement. Employees can also contribute money from their pay towards their own retirement.

Living and Work Literacy 4
8 Workplace agreements
Workers are generally employed on the basis 
of an employment contract. This sets out the 
pay and working conditions agreed to between 
employers and employees. Employment contracts 
may be either awards or workplace agreements.
What is an award?
An award is the minimum rate of pay and 
working conditions for a particular job. It is set 
by an industrial court such as the Australian 
Industrial Relations Commission. Awards are 
generally negotiated by trade unions for 
relatively large numbers of workers on an 
industry basis, e.g. the mining industry or the 
hospitality industry. 
What is a workplace agreement?
A workplace agreement is an agreement between an individual employee and an employer in 
their specific workplace situation. It aims to provide more consultation and greater flexibility in the 
workplace.
History of employment contracts
Employment contracts are governed by Australian Government legislation which sets out how 
agreements can be made. To understand the current situation with regard to workplace relations, 
it is important to consider the most significant developments in recent history. Some of these 
developments were:
The Conciliation & Arbitration Act of 1904 established the Award System. It had extensive powers to 
prevent and settle industrial disputes by conciliation and arbitration. In 1907 the concept of a basic 
wage was adopted. Some workers were covered by state awards and some by federal awards. 
The Industrial Relations Act of 1988 established the Australian Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC). 
Its aim was to conciliate (resolving disputes by consultations and compulsory conferences), and 
to compulsorily arbitrate (settle disputes) where necessary. Each state also had its own industrial 
commission to cover workers under state awards. 
Equal Pay Case. In 1993, the AIRC was given the power to make orders to ensure equal pay for work 
of equal value for both men and women. Female workers once received little more than half the 
pay that male workers received.
Major changes often come with a change of government. The 1996 Workplace Relations Act 
introduced Australian Workplace Agreements (AWAs). The AIRC lost its authority when a new body 
called the Employment Advocate was established. Awards could still be negotiated with the trade 
unions but the intention was to simplify them and reduce them in number.
Useful definitions
Basic wage:  pay which was considered enough for a family to live in reasonable comfort. The 
principle of the basic wage was adopted for all future wage fixing cases.
Consultation: process of two parties talking together about issues.
Conciliation: a process which attempts to resolve disputes by compromise or voluntary agreement.
Arbitration: making a decision or a judgement on an industrial dispute.
Compulsory conference: an industrial court orders a meeting between two parties in dispute.

Bullying is often seen as something that happens in the 
schoolyard rather than the workplace. Yet it has been 
found that over one million Australians are bullied at work 
every year. A significant number of people are subjected to 
long-term bullying.
What is bullying behaviour?
There are several aspects of behaviour that can be

bullying can include the following behaviours.
It is important to understand the difference between bullying and a personality clash. With a personality 
clash, both people involved may develop a dislike for each other and engage in some form of mutual 
verbal abuse. A personality clash may only flare up once and then the people may agree to disagree or 
simply try to avoid each other. 
On the other hand, bullying tends to be one-sided, in a situation where there is a power or status

long period of time. It may be a series of incidents, each of which seems minor at the time, but when

The importance of communication
Communication is basic to all aspects of modern life and 
therefore important in every job. The quality or level of 
communication required depends on the nature of the job, 
and how much interaction with the public and other work

Writing notes or emails
These forms of written communication are in some circumstances just as important as reports and 
articles. However, informal language is generally acceptable in emails and notes.
Notes from a meeting can contain abbreviations to save time and to make sure everything is taken 
down, especially if you are making notes from a lecture or speech. Similarly, emails have developed a 
language of their own, without formal salutations and with the widespread use of abbreviations. Some 
people even ignore capital letters and punctuation in emails, and include emoticons. There may be an 
email policy in a particular workplace. Emails are still a written form of communication and can be used 
by others as proof that communication did take place. Some workplaces require emails to be written in 
more formal language.
Sharing your opinions
There may be situations in your work where you are required to give your opinions. This requires some 
thought because you may also have to give reasons and explanations for your opinions. There is no 
need to be nervous about giving your opinion, but it is important to be prepared. Remember that 
confidence and preparation are the keys to successful verbal communication. There is no point getting 
aggravated or aggressive if your opinions are questioned. Using logical reasons communicated clearly is 
generally the most effective way of convincing others.

Workers who are injured in the course

Evelyn worked at a car parts factory which 
made gear boxes. Her job was on a metal 
press where she had to press a button to 
operate the press. One day she accidentally 
caught her hand in the press, suffering 
serious injuries. She needed immediate 
medical treatment and was off work for 
ten weeks. She reported the incident and

medical bills and arranged a rehabilitation 
program which involved exercising her 
hand. She was able to continue working at 
the factory but was assigned different duties 
which did not affect her injured hand. Six 
months later, her hand was fully recovered 
and she was able to resume her normal 
work.
If you suffer an injury or illness at

Here are the steps you should follow:
1  Report the incident immediately to

Your employer then completes the

Naming Simple Compounds

Molecule or molecular compound is an assembly of two or more non-metal atoms
tightly bonded together.

A diatomic molecule is a molecule made from two atoms of the same element. The
following seven elements form diatomic molecules in their natural state:

       H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2

An allotrope is one of two or more distinct forms of an element, such as: graphite and
diamond (for carbon) and dioxygen (O2 - usually referred to simply as oxygen) and ozone (O3).

Molecular compounds (also known as covalent compounds) are composed of
nonmetal elements that bond together into larger particles using covalent bonds (bonds
created by the sharing of their valence electrons.

       Molecular formulas show the exact number of atoms of each element in the
       molecule.

       Empirical formulas are the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms in a molecular
       compound or an ionic compound...

Ionic compounds are composed of ions and usually contain both metals and non-metals.
The ions in an ionic compound form when the metal atoms give one or more electrons to the
nonmetal atoms. Consequently, the metal ion is positively charged (called an cation) and the
nonmetal ions are negatively charged (called the anions). Ionic compounds must be electrically
neutral, so the sum of the charges of the anions and cations must equal zero. Because the
formulas of ionic compounds must be empirical formulas, make sure the subscripts are reduced
to their simplest ratio.

Atom

Molecule

      2 or more chemically bonded atoms.
      Small, found everywhere.

Element

      Listed on the periodic table.
      Can be solid, liquid and gas.
      Contain protons, neutrons and electrons.
      Have atomic mass which is the sum of protons and neutrons.
      Contain all the same kinds of atoms.
      Can’t be chemically broken down.

Compound

      Group of molecules.
      Can form chemicals such as carbon dioxide, water, nitrous

Mixture

      When 2 or more substances are not chemically combined but
       are found together.
      Go through different processes.
      Different from a compound.
      For example air, soil, cake mixture.

Atoms and Ions (p13-14)
Atoms are electrically neutral (have no charge) because they contain an
equal number of ____________ ____________ and ____________ ____________ .
If an electron is removed or added, the atom becomes _____________ and
is now called an _____ .

When an electron is removed from an atom, the atom becomes a
____________ ____________ _____ . A positive ion is known as a _________ .
When an electron is added to an atom, the atom becomes a ____________
____________ _____ . A negative ion is known as an _________ .

The charge of an ion is written after the symbol of the element and in
superscript for example Na+ and O-2.

Cations
A cation is formed when an atom loses electrons. An atom will form a
positive ion if its outermost electron shell is almost empty. It will lose all
the electrons in the outermost shell so that only filled shells remain.

Draw a lithium atom and a lithium cation in the space below.




Almost all cations come from ________ atoms because they have _____
electrons in the outermost shell.

Anions
An anion is formed when an atom gains electrons. This will happen when
the outermost electron shell is almost full. The atom will gain electrons
until the outermost shell is full.

Draw a chlorine atom and a chloride ion in the space below.




All anions come from ____ - __________ elements because they have almost
_______ outermost electron shells.
 Naming Ions
The name of a cation (positive ion) is the same as the name of the atom.
For example a sodium atom loses one electron to become a sodium ion.

Sometimes atoms can form more than one type of cation. Iron can lose
two or three electrons to become Fe2+ or Fe3+. To distinguish between the
two ions, scientists add a roman numeral to the ion name to indicate the
number of electrons lost, for example Fe(II) and Fe(III).

Anions (negative ions) are named differently. The name of an anion is the
same as the name for the atom but ends in –ide. For example, a chlorine
atom becomes a chloride ion.

Questions
1. What are the three parts of an atom and what is the charge on each?




2. Which part of an atom can be lost or gained to form an ion? Why do
   you think this part of the atom can be lost or gained?

4. What is the difference between a cation and an anion?




5. If a neutral atom lost two electrons, what would be the charge of the
   ion?

   have?

                               Polyatomic Ions
All the ions looked at so far have been made of one atom with a charge.
These ions are called monatomic ions. Some ions are made from
molecules (two or more atoms chemically combined) which have a charge.
These are called polyatomic ions.

searchText:
Atoms and elements
Elements
An element is a simple substance that cannot be split into anything simpler by chemical reactions.
Atoms are the smallest particles of an element that can exist. Atoms of one element are all the
same, and are different from atoms of all the other elements.
There are over 100 different elements. All the elements are shown in the Periodic Table. Each
element has a chemical symbol, which is usually one or two letters. A symbol is written with the
first letter as a capital, and the second letter is small.

                   carbon       C            oxygen         O
                   nitrogen     N            hydrogen       H
                   gold         Au           silver         Ag
                   copper       Cu           aluminium      Al


Compounds
Elements can join together to make compounds. The name of the compound tells you the
elements that are in it. Compounds made from two elements always have a name which ends in ‘-
ide’.

These elements join together …                    … to make these compounds

carbon, oxygen                                    carbon dioxide

sodium, chlorine                                  sodium chloride

magnesium, oxygen                                 magnesium oxide


A chemical formula tells you the name and number of atoms in a compound. The smallest particle
of many compounds is called a molecule. Molecules are made up of atoms. Some elements are
also made of molecules. For example, a molecule of oxygen contains two oxygen atoms joined
together. The formula is O2.

          Elements                       Compounds                             Mixtures
Atoms of helium (He)             Molecules of carbon dioxide        A mixture of helium and
                                 (CO2)                              oxygen




Molecules of oxygen (O2)         Molecules of water (H2O)           A mixture of carbon dioxide
                                                                    and oxygen




A lump of carbon                 A lump of sodium chloride          A lump of bronze(an alloy of
                                 (NaCl)                             copper and tin)
                             ATOMS AND ELEMENTS QUIZ
1. Which of these things is an element?
A salt
B water
C oxygen
D air

2. The number of chemical elements in the world is:
A 4.
B about 100.
C about 1000.
D over a million.

3. The element that makes up most of the mass of your body is:
A oxygen.
B carbon.
C calcium.
D hydrogen.

4. Chemical elements:
A are always solids.
B are either solids or liquids.
C are always gases.
D can be solids, liquids or gases.

5. Which of these metals is not a pure element?
A gold
B copper
C silver
D bronze

6. The smallest part of an element is called:
A an atom.
B a molecule.
C a compound.
D an ion.

7. An element is something that:
A can be split up by a chemical reaction.
B cannot be split up by a chemical reaction.
C is made up of different kinds of atom.
D is a mixture of atoms and molecules.

8. The correct way to write the chemical symbol for calcium is
A CA
B Ca
C ca
D Ca
                                Compounds and mixtures
Elements are simple substances which cannot be split up in chemical reactions. Atoms are the
smallest particles of an element that can exist. Atoms of an element are all the same.
Each element has its own chemical symbol. For example, the chemical symbol for oxygen is O.
Some elements have their atoms joined to each other in small groups called molecules. Oxygen
is an example.




Compounds
Elements can join together to make compounds. A compound contains two or more elements
joined together. The name of the compound tells you the elements that are in it. Compounds made
from two elements always have a name which ends in ‘-ide’.
Many compounds exist as atoms attached to each other in small groups – molecules.




The chemical formula tells you the number of atoms of each element in a compound. Each
element in the formula is shown by its chemical symbol. For example:




A compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio.

The properties of a compound are different from the elements that make it up. For example,
hydrogen is an explosive gas and oxygen will relight a glowing splint but water is a liquid which will
put fires out.
 Chemical reactions
Compounds can react chemically by mixing them with other chemicals, or by using heat or
electricity. You can tell that a chemical reaction has occurred if there is a colour change or when a
gas is given off.
Most chemical reactions also involve an energy change. This is usually in the form of heat, but can
also involve light being given off, for example, in burning (combustion).
In a chemical reaction a new substance is always formed. Most chemical reactions are not easily
reversed (they are irreversible).
Some chemical reactions take place just by mixing. When you make a solid by mixing two liquids,
the solid is called a precipitate.
We can write word equations to show a chemical reaction. The chemicals that you start with are
called the reactants. The chemicals at the end are called the products. For example:

Magnesium + Oxygen                   Magnesium oxide
     Reactants                          Products




Physical changes
In a physical change no new substance is
formed. Melting, evaporating, condensing and
freezing are all examples of physical changes.
For example:




Mixtures
Elements and compounds can also be mixed together. A mixture is easier to separate than the
elements in a compound. Soil, river water and sea water are examples of mixtures that occur
naturally.
Elements and compounds melt and boil at a fixed temperature. Mixtures do not have definite
melting points and boiling points.
Air is a mixture of gases most of which is nitrogen and oxygen. The gases in the air can be
separated by fractional distillation.
                             Compounds and mixtures quiz
1 An atom is:
A the smallest particle that can exist.
B a group of particles that are all the same.
C the smallest particle of a compound that exists under normal conditions.
D the smallest particle of an element that exists under normal conditions.

2 A molecule is:
A the smallest particle that can exist.
B the smallest particle of an element that can exist.
C two or more atoms chemically joined together.
D the same as an atom.

3 The number of types of atom in a compound is:
A only one.
B one or two.
C two or more.
D three or more.

4 How many different elements are there in the compound with the formula NH3?
A one
B two
C three
D four

5 Which of these things does not show that a reaction has occurred?
A The mixture gets hotter.
B The substance changes from a liquid to a solid.
C The mixture changes colour.
D Bubbles of gas form in the mixture.

6 The substances that you get at the end of a chemical reaction are called:
A reactants.
B chemicals.
C products.
D gases.

7 Which of these changes is a chemical reaction?
A Melting some margarine in a pan.
B Boiling a kettle of water.
C Frying an egg.
D Cooling a drink by putting an ice cube in it.

8 Complete this word equation:
sodium carbonate + copper sulphate ® sodium sulphate + ____________
A copper sulphate
B copper oxide
C sodium carbonate
D copper carbonate

Microchip is a very familiar word used in bionics. Originally designed for computers, these tiny devices are now 
also used in home appliances, video cameras and televisions, and many other items. Even the family pet can have a 
microchip implanted (at the back of the neck) to provide ownership details in case they are lost. Microchips are also 
used in the operation of biomedical devices.
1 
List advantages and disadvantages of using a microchip implant in a pet rather than a standard tag on a 
collar.
 
2 
List two other examples of how microchips are used. 
Another familiar word used in bionics is laser. We’ve all heard of laser printers, laser copiers, laser surgery and, for 
the science fiction fans, laser beams! The word laser is an acronym (a word formed by the first letter of a number 
of words) for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Lasers can direct extremely fine beams of 
electromagnetic radiation of a specific frequency, with great precision and intensity. Laser technology is commonly 
used in minimally invasive surgery. A laser beam can concentrate a lot of energy onto a very small area.
3 
Laser beams are also used in CD and DVD players, and in very cheap devices such as laser pointers.

a Light that only goes on once.

Extending science worksheet
Build a material for a mission
As a scientist, your job goes far beyond just learning facts – your knowledge helps solve real-world problems. Imagine you’ve been hired by a team of engineers to design a new underwater exploration robot. This robot will need to withstand harsh ocean conditions: high pressure, corrosive salt water, freezing temperatures and deep darkness. To build it, you’ll need to carefully choose materials based on the atomic structure of their elements. This means thinking about where the elements are positioned on the periodic table and their properties – such as conductivity, strength and reactivity – as well as how different elements combine to form compounds or alloys. In this activity, you’ll apply everything you’ve learned about atoms, elements and the periodic table to design the perfect material for a robot capable of exploring the deepest parts of the ocean!

Key terms
catalyst
a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without undergoing any permanent chemical change
collision theory
a theory stating that the particles involved in a chemical reaction must collide in order to react
concentration
the number of active molecules in a set volume of solution
enzyme
a chemical that helps make chemical reactions happen; a type of catalyst
List the four factors that affect the speed of a reaction




Imagine you are playing a game.

You are on the red team and need to partner with someone on the green team to be able to progress to the next level in the game. 

Assess Scenarios A and B to determine which would allow you to move up to the next level more quickly.


From the list in question 1, select the factor that most closely resembles this scenario. 


Congratulations, you reached the next level! You are assigned to one of two fields. The goal of this level is to get to the other end of the field before the opposition players in the other field. One field is grass and the other is thick, deep mud. 
Identify the field you would prefer to be on so that you could achieve your goal faster than the opposition players.


The grass allows you to move quickly but the mud means you are a bit sluggish and slower. This is an analogy, a story used to explain. Identify the factor from question 1 that this story represents. HINT: Think about what can make a reaction faster and what can make it slower.

Paragraph organiser

The surface area of reactant pieces affects the rate of a reaction. When a solid reactant is cut into smaller pieces, it will react faster. This is because the smaller reactant pieces have a larger total surface area. This means that the reactant particles have a greater chance of interacting with each other.

Chemical and Physical Changes
 Aim: To distinguish between chemical and physical change.

This investigation is split into four activities. Your teacher will instruct you of the order of the activities
and let you know when to swap.
                                            Safety Information
Activity 1 – Burning magnesium              Bunsen burner – risk of burns/scalds.
Equipment:                                  Handle with extra care. Rinse any burns under
                                            cold running water for 10 minutes and inform
• Bunsen burner
                                            the teacher immediately.
• heatproof mat
                                            Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• tongs                                     Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher immediately.
• magnesium (2cm strip)                     Magnesium – risk of eye damage.
                                            Do not look directly at the light created by the magnesium.
Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 3: Holding the magnesium with the tongs, carefully hold the magnesium in the flame until it ignites.


Activity 2 – Cooking a pancake
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner                • mini frying pan                 • small cooking spatula

• heatproof mat                • pancake shaker (made up         • cooking oil
                                 to a batter with water)
• gauze

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the frying pan onto the gauze.

Step 3: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 4: Add a small amount of cooking oil to the pan and heat gently.

Step 5: Reduce the heat from the Bunsen burner and add a small amount of pancake batter to the frying pan.

Step 6: As the edges of the pancake batter begin to solidify, gently loosen with the spatula until you can
loosen the whole pancake from the base of the pan.

Step 7: Flip the pancake and finish cooking on the other side.

     Check with your teacher before consuming anything in a lab – it may not be safe to do so.

                                                                              Chemical and Physical Changes

Activity 3 – Boiling water
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner

• heatproof mat

• gauze

• beaker

• thermometer

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the beaker onto the gauze.

Step 3: Add 150ml of water to the beaker and place the thermometer into the water.

Step 4: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 5: Heat the water gently until you see bubbles begin to form and the water starts to boil.

Step 6: Switch off the Bunsen burner and leave the equipment to cool.


Activity 4 – Melting chocolate
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner

• heatproof mat

• gauze

• beaker

• square of chocolate

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the beaker onto the gauze.

Step 3: Add the piece of chocolate to the beaker.

Step 4: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 5: Heat the chocolate gently until you see that it is beginning to melt and become liquid.

Step 6: Switch off the Bunsen burner and leave the equipment to cool.

Chemical misconceptions                                                                                     21




                        Changes in chemistry
Target level
                        This probe is intended for use with 11–14 year old students who have been taught the
                        distinction between chemical and physical change. It may also be used with 14–16
                        year old students to check their knowledge.

Topics
                        Chemical and physical change.

Rationale
                        The distinction between chemical and physical change is not absolute, and there are
                        examples of changes which teachers find difficult to classify (see Chapter 2 of the
                        Teachers’ notes). Students are often expected to distinguish between chemical and
                        physical changes early in their study of chemistry, but some find this quite difficult.
                        The probe provided here asks students to explain what they mean by chemical and
                        physical change, to classify three examples and explain their reasons. Particle
                        diagrams for ‘before’ and ‘afterwards’ are provided to help the students.
                        These ideas are discussed in Chapter 6 of the Teachers’ notes.
                        During piloting, teachers suggested that this ‘could be a useful teaching tool’ that
                        helped ‘to clarify the idea in some pupils’ minds’. It was felt that the use of particle
                        diagrams was helpful. Students were reported to enjoy the activity, and found it easy to
                        understand what to do.
                        One teacher commented that the activity ‘helped [students] to grasp the differences but
                        they found it hard to define the changes’. It might be appropriate to suggest to students
                        who are not sure what to put for the definitions (at the start of the probe) to move on to
                        the examples, and return to the definitions later.

Resources
                        ■ Student worksheet
                          – Changes in chemistry

Feedback for students
                        A suggested answer sheet for teachers is provided. When providing feedback on this
                        probe teachers should bear in mind the difficulties of defining the physical/chemical
                        change distinction, as discussed in Chapter 2 of the Teachers’ notes.
 22                                                                     Changes in chemistry




Changes in chemistry – answers
Alternative reasons that may be accepted are given in parentheses

1. A physical change is a change where no new substance is produced.
(….a change that does not involve the breaking/forming of strong chemical bonds.)
(…..a change where molecules/ions etc are rearranged, but not changed.)

2. A chemical change is a change where a new substance is produced.
(…..a change that involves the breaking/forming of strong chemical bonds.)
(…..a change where new molecules/ions etc are formed.)

3. Physical change:
No new substance is produced
(the same molecules are present before and after the change)
(the change may readily be reversed)
(the energy change involved is modest)

4. Chemical change:
A new substance is formed
(strong chemical bonds are broken – eg in the oxygen molecules - and new chemical bonds are formed in the metal
oxide)
(different particles are present after the change - oxide ions rather than oxygen molecules)
(this change is not easily reversed)
(a great deal of energy is often given out in this change)

5. Physical change:
No new substance is formed (NB the solution is not a pure substance, but a mixture)
(the same particles are present after the change as before)
(this reaction is readily reversed – by evaporation)
(the energy change for dissolving is minimal)
Note, however, that the ionic bonds in the lattice have been disrupted, which may suggest dissolving could be
considered as a chemical change.


Note: Energy changes are not the best way to characterize these changes.

Chemical changes
Iron is typically found in the form of iron (III) oxide (Fe2O3), red hematite, which is smelted to form pure iron (Fe). Pure iron can then corrode to form rust, typically iron (III) oxide (Fe2O3). Discuss the statement “Chemical changes are irreversible”.






Reusable heat packs are activated when an aluminium disc creates friction, and a solution crystallises and releases heat. Placing the pack in boiling water primes (prepares) it for another use. Compare (the similarities and differences between) the two types of heat packs in terms of physical and chemical changes.








Discuss why baking cookies is a chemical change.




During World War II, submarines used diesel as a fuel. To burn diesel you need oxygen, so when the diesel engines were running, they needed air and had to operate near the surface. The submarines would dive when they needed to evade detection and then they would run on electric batteries which could be used for a fixed period of time. 
Today, submarines can operate at depths for months at a time. They get the oxygen from sea water. First, the salt is removed from the sea water. Research and describe the process that scientists use to separate water.





When an ionic substance dissolves in water, it dissociates (breaks up) into individual ions. For example, potassium chloride (KCl) splits into sodium ions (K+) and chloride ions (Cl–). A solution of potassium chloride has different properties to potassium chloride solid. Assess whether dissolving is a chemical change and justify your response. 
An ionic substance is made of positive and negative ions that are attracted to each other because opposite charges attract.

Chemical and Physical Change

Chemical and Physical change
Physical changes do not produce a new substance. Changes in
state (melting, freezing, vaporization, condensation, sublimation)
are physical changes. Examples of physical changes also include
bending a piece of wire, melting icebergs, and breaking a bottle



A chemical change occurs when a new substance is formed and
is not easily reversible. Observations to show a chemical change
could be a colour change, a new smell, the chemicals get hotter
or colder or a gas is produced.




Evidence for Chemical and Physical change

Examples of Physical Changes                       Evidence of Chemical Changes

    crumpling a sheet of paper                        Burning wood – temperature change
    melting an ice cube                               Mixing acid with universal indicator – colour change
    breaking a bottle                                 Seeing bubbles when vinegar and baking soda are
No change in temperature, colour,                         mixed – a gas is formed
                                                   Burning sulphur – creates a new smell
gas or smell




Observing reactions
To observe means to record or make note of something we have experienced. We also think of observations as
watching something, but in Science, observations may be made with any of our senses (by seeing, feeling,
hearing, tasting, or smelling) or even using tools to make observations that are then changed into something
our senses detect.

Observation tools include thermometers, microscopes, telescopes, radars, computer sensors and spaces probes.
Sometimes these tools can observe and collect data that humans cannot directly sense. By using these tools
scientists can often make many more observations and much more precisely than our senses are able to.




74 | P a g e    GZ Science Resources
 Chemical and Physical change in everyday situations




Reactants and products in a chemical change
A chemical change is a process that produces a chemical change to one or more substances. A chemical change
will produce a new substance. Other observations may include a temperature change, a colour change or
production of gas. Chemicals that are used, and you start with, in a chemical change are known as reactants.
Those that are formed are known as products.




Chemical equations
We show chemical changes as equations. All reactants must go to the left of the arrow and all products go to
the right of the arrow. An arrow must be used and not an equal sign. The arrow shows a chemical reaction,
where the reactants change into products.

Activity sheet – Chemical reactions
Chemical reactions in nature
Two chemical reactions that occur in nature are photosynthesis and respiration. 
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use carbon dioxide and water to 
produce food (glucose) and oxygen. Respiration is the process by which living things 
use food (glucose) and oxygen to produce energy. Carbon dioxide and water are also 
produced. All living things respire. The word equations for these reactions are:
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water 
 glucose + oxygen
Respiration:  glucose + oxygen 
 carbon dioxide + water + energy

Comparing elements, compounds and mixtures
Activity

Complete the beginning of each statement using the keywords. Use each keyword at least once.

    pure
                           atoms            molecules            elements     compounds         mixtures
 substances

Statements

   1                                                                    be broken down into something simpler.


   2                                  two or more elements or compounds mixed, but not combined, together.


   3                                                                 made when atoms join together in a group.


   4                                                        made when two or more elements have combined.


   5                                                                         made from only one type of atom.


   6                                                                        be separated into pure substances.


   7                                                       made from atoms or molecules all of the same type.


   8                              the smallest amounts of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.

                                                                                                       Comparing elements, compounds and mixtures

           Teaching notes
           Students could complete the statements on the sheet or they could be asked to write out the whole
           sentences.
           To extend the activity students could then be asked to use a different keyword to complete each of the
           statements.

           Suggested answers


                 1                Molecules can be broken down into something simpler.


                 2                Mixtures comprise two or more elements or compounds mixed, but not combined, together.


                 3                Molecules are made when atoms join together in a group.


                 4                Compounds are made when two or more elements have combined.


                 5                Elements are made from only one type of atom.


                 6                Mixtures can be separated into pure substances.


                 7                Pure substances are made from atoms or molecules all of the same type.


                 8                Atoms are the smallest amounts of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.

DESIGNING A COLD PACK



Background

Cold packs are applied to sporting and other injuries to decrease
the blood supply to an area. This will reduce bruising and swelling
that may result from an injury. Many ready made, instant cold
packs consist of a sealed plastic bag of crystals with a small bag
of water inside. When the water bag bursts the crystals dissolve
and this causes the temperature to drop to about 1 0 C for about
20 minutes.

Part A

The purpose of this investigation is to decide which chemical
works best as the “crytsals” at reducing temperature when mixed
with water

Equipment

4 test tubes and test tube rack

spatula

ammonium nitrate [NH4NO3] (5 g)
sodium ethanoate [NaCH3COO] (5 g)
sodium chloride [NaCl] (5 g)
calcium chloride [CaCl2] (5 g)


Test to find out which powder would be best suited to making a cold pack.

Part B (for the experts)

Extra Equipment

optimum mass to use with 30 mls of water. How many moles is this and
 what concentration will it give? Once again explain how you tested this

The concept of the ‘ionic product’ for water is a way of

substances can be measured in a similar manner,

occurs when the binary compound is put into water

called the ‘solubility product’ as its value is an indication  
of how soluble the compound is. The value is achieved

s     Why do rocks expand when                                                                                      G3
      heated?
?       The Kinetic Theory
        The movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases is described by the Kinetic Theory.
s




        Particles in a solid are fixed in position and cannot move from place to place. They are, however,
        able to vibrate.
s




        The particles in a solid lump of rock move from side to side, but around a fixed position. This
        vibration needs energy. In theory, if a particle has no energy it will no longer vibrate. This will
        happen at the temperature called absolute zero, which is ⫺273 ⬚C. No one has managed to get
T       anything this cold yet!
        As the temperature of the rock rises, the particles gain more energy. This means that they vibrate
        more. The higher the temperature, the more the particles vibrate. Eventually a temperature is
        reached where the particles vibrate so much that they break apart from each other, and can move
        around. This temperature is the melting point of the rock.
        When solid rock is heated up from one temperature to another, but not as high as its melting
        point, the rock expands. This means that its volume increases, but its mass stays the same. The
        rock has exactly the same number of particles at the higher temperature, but they are spread out
        more. Why does this happen?
        As the particles gain energy and vibrate more, they need more room for this movement. The
        particles move a little further apart. The higher the temperature the further they move apart.
        This is the reason why the rock expands.

                                                         rock particles




                                                     increase in temperature

        Note that the particles themselves do not get any bigger, they simply take up more space. It is like
        a group of people standing very close together watching a football match. As long as they do not
        move much they can stand very close. If they start to jump around they need more space. This
        happens when a goal is scored, and can cause a surge in the crowd. People standing at the front
        who have nowhere to move to can get squashed. Modern football stadiums have spectators
        sitting down to prevent this.


      Question
      A pen friend gets poor marks in a test about the expansion of rocks. He writes to say
      that his marks were low because he cannot understand how a solid lump of rock can
      get bigger when it gets hotter if the particles of the rock do not get bigger.
      Write a letter to help improve the pen friend’s marks when he re-takes the test.




444
      C D Lees, 2002, The Heinemann Science Scheme

searchText:
Elements and Compounds
Elements are said to be ______ substances and are made up of only one kind of atom. Elements
cannot be broken down into simpler substances.

There are ___ naturally occurring elements and many man-made elements. Each element has its
own unique _____________.

Elements can combine together chemically to form _______________.


Compound Formulae
Elements combine in predictable ways to make compounds. For example, a water molecule is
always formed when one oxygen atom combines with two hydrogen atoms. The chemical formula
for water is _________.

For each of the compounds below, state what elements the compound contains and how many of
each.
                                    Types of Elements it        Number of Atoms of Each
    Formula of Compound
                                          Contains                       Element
        Carbon Dioxide
               CO2
            Methane
             CH4
       Calcium Chloride
             CaCl2

        Copper Sulphate
            CuSO4


Naming Compounds
There are some rules for naming chemical compounds.

If the compound contains a metal atom and a non-metal atom,
      Write the name of the metal first
      Write the name of the non-metal second and change the ending to –ide

For example, table salt contains one sodium atom and one chlorine atom, NaCl. The name of this
compound is ______________ _________________.

Try writing the names for these compounds.

KCl    _____________________________              Fe2O3    _____________________________
NaI    _____________________________              Na2O     _____________________________
CaO    _____________________________              AgI      _____________________________
MgS _____________________________                 NiCl2 _____________________________
If the compound contains only non-metal atoms, you need to use prefixes to describe how many
atoms of each element are in the compound.
                    mono – one        di – two        tri – three      tetra – four

           The elements are named in the order they appear in the formula.
           The prefix is put in front of each element name to show how many are in the compound.
           The ending of the last element is changed to –ide.
           If there is only one atom of the first element, no prefix is needed.

For example, the formula for water is H2O. It contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Its scientific name is ___________________ ____________________.

Try writing the names for these compounds.

Year 9 Science
        ELEMENTS, COMPOUNDS AND THEIR SYMBOLS

Elements are substances made up of all the same kinds of atoms.
When different kinds of atoms join together, they form a molecule.
Compounds are substances made up of the same kinds of
molecules.




  Hydrogen atoms      Oxygen atoms form           Two atoms of hydrogen combine with
  form the element,   the element, oxygen.        one atom of oxygen to form a water
  hydrogen.                                       molecule. These water molecules form
                                                  the compound, water.

The periodic table shows all the elements known to man. Each
element is represented by a symbol. This symbol comes from the
first one or two letters of the element’s name. For example, carbon
is C and helium is He. Sometimes the symbol is taken from the Latin
or Arabic name of the element. For example, copper is Cu from its
Latin name of cuprum.

If an element has a single-letter symbol, it is always written as a
capital. Where the element has a two-letter symbol, only the first
letter is written as a capital and the second letter is written in lower
case.

searchText:
Teacher Demonstration 26
Elephant’s Toothpaste
This classic chemistry demonstration is a huge hit with kids of all ages. The title
becomes obvious as the reaction converts 125ml of 6% hydrogen peroxide to several
litres of harmless, frothy foam which can be safely washed down the sink. It looks just
like a giant tube of toothpaste being squished. Please be prepared for very excited
students who will want to see the demonstration more than once!

Materials:
• 125ml 6% Hydrogen Peroxide (also labelled 20Vol)
• 1 Sachet Dry Yeast (powder) + 4 tablespoons of warm water
• Detergent
• Food colours – optional (not cochineal)
• Empty bottle
• Funnel
• Plastic tray or tub
• Dishwashing gloves
• Safety goggles
* 6% Hydrogen peroxide (20Vol) is available in 400ml bottles from most retail chemists and cosmetics
suppliers and some supermarkets.


Instructions
                                   1 Gather all the materials and set them up on a desk
                                     with the students gathered around.




                                   2 Empty a full sachet of dry yeast into a cup.




                                   3. Add four table spoons of warm water and stir until
                                      well mixed.




                                                    Teacher Demo 26 – Elephant’s Toothpaste | Page 1
                                                                    © 2009 Ruben Meerman | ABC Science Online
 4. The foam produced is safe to touch and can be
   poured down the sink but you (and student helpers)
   should wear dishwashing gloves and safety goggles
   as a precaution and as standard practice when
   handling chemicals. Use a funnel to pour 125 ml
   (roughly half a cup) of 6% hydrogen peroxide into
   the empty soft drink bottle.

5. Add a large squirt of dishwashing liquid. Swirl the
   bottle to mix the detergent into the hydrogen
   peroxide.




6. Optional – add ten or fifteen drops of food colouring
   Swirl the bottle to mix the food colouring into the
   solution. If you are planning to repeat the
   demonstration, add food colouring the second time.

   Note: don’t use cochineal as it won’t colour the foam
   effectively


7. All the ingredients are now ready. Use the funnel to
   pour all of the yeast solution into the bottle.




8. The solution will begin to rapidly produce foam with
   a much greater volume than the original ingredients.
   The tiny bubbles are filled with oxygen gas (not air –
   see teacher notes).




9. As the foam expands, the bottle quickly fills to the
   brim. When the bottle is full, the excess foam begins
   to pour out of the bottle. The result resembles a tube
   of toothpaste being squeezed far too much.




10. 125ml of hydrogen peroxide produces
   approximately two litres of foam. The foam will be
   warm to touch because the underlying chemical
   reaction is exothermic (releases heat). Rinse all the
   materials and the plastic tray after the demonstration.



              Teacher Demo 26 – Elephant’s Toothpaste | Page 2
                            © 2009 Ruben Meerman | ABC Science Online
 Teacher notes
What is hydrogen peroxide?
Hydrogen peroxide (in a much stronger 30% concentration) is a chemical well known
to hairdressers as a bleaching agent. It is also used to bleach paper and many other
industrial chemical processes. In hair dressing bleach, the liquid is incorporated into a
thick gel which clings to hair preventing contact with the scalp.
The chemical symbol H2O2 for hydrogen peroxide is very similar to water’s H2O. The
H2 represents two hydrogen atoms while the O2 represents two oxygen atoms (water
molecules contain only one oxygen atom).
Hydrogen peroxide molecules are very unstable and naturally decompose into water
and oxygen gas. The chemical equation for this decomposition is:
                                  2 H2O2 Æ 2 H2O + 02
The equation above represents two hydrogen peroxide molecules decomposing into
two water molecules and one oxygen molecule (note that all oxygen gas molecules
are comprised of two oxygen atoms – ozone, by contrast, is comprised of three
oxygen molecules and has the chemical symbol O3). The decomposition of hydrogen
peroxide also releases a small amount of heat so the reaction is exothermic.
Hydrogen peroxide is stored in opaque plastic or brown glass bottles to minimise
exposure to light which accelerates the natural decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

Why does yeast accelerate hydrogen peroxide decomposition?
Hydrogen peroxide is a natural by-product of metabolism. All known animals which
metabolise oxygen produce a natural enzyme called catalase which catalyses the
decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into harmless water and oxygen gas. Catalase is
found in every organ in the body and in particularly high concentrations in the liver.
Hydrogen peroxide is harmful to living things because it is a strong oxidiser which can
cause damage to living cells at the molecular level.

Investigation: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions


Summary

Carry out three experiments to see if the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
Carry out a fourth experiment to determine if the reaction is endothermic or exothermic, record the
temperature change over time and graph the results.

Background

Some reactions between substances absorb heat energy and some give off heat
energy. Exothermic reactions release lots of energy in the form of heat when they react whereas
endothermic reactions absorb heat energy and therefore drop in temperature when reacting.

This practical contains four separate reactions, you are to predict and then record whether the
reactions are exothermic or endothermic by using a thermometer to record the temperature of the
mixtures.

For the last reaction (dilute sulfuric acid + magnesium ribbon), you are to record the temperature
change every 30 seconds until the reaction finishes. Record your data in a table and then graph the
change in temperature over time.
