Rocks and Minerals

All of the rocks in the Earth’s crust are composed of minerals. A mineral is a chemical compound which
occurs naturally in the Earth's crust. There are about 3000 different minerals in the Earth’s crust. Minerals
can be classified depending on their chemical makeup, crystal structure or physical properties.

Minerals can also be classified into the following four groups.

* Silicate minerals, all of which contain the elements silicon (Si) and oxygen (O), and include quartz,
feldspar, mica, garnet and tale. About 40% of the known minerals are silicates.

* Non-metallic minerals. These might contain a metal but don’t look like metals and aren’t used as
sources of metals. This group includes calcite, sulfur (S), rock salt, gypsum, fluorite and graphite (a
form of the element carbon, C) .

* Metal ore minerals are so named because they are economic sources of metals. The group includes
galena (contains lead, Pb), dolomite (contains magnesium, Mg), sphalerite (contains zinc, Zn),
bauxite (contains aluminium, Al) and haematite (contains iron, Fe).

* Gem minerals which are the precious and semi-precious stones such as opal, jade, garnet, topaz,
emerald, ruby, sapphire and diamond (the hardest naturally occurring substance),

Most rocks are made up of more than one mineral. For example, if you have two different samples of
granite, they will both contain quartz, feldspar and mica, but the proportions of each mineral will be
different. There are so many different minerals that identifying and classifying them is often difficult. Using
only one property is not of very much use because, for example, many minerals have the same shape or
colour. Several properties are, therefore, used to identify and group minerals. These properties include the
colour and the shape of crystals, cleavage (how something splits), lustre (how shiny something is), streak
test (what happens when it is rubbed on a hard surface) and hardness.

searchText: Rocks Rocks and Minerals All the rocks in the world are made up of chemicals called minerals . Minerals are solid, inorganic (not living) substances found in and on the earth . Minerals are the building blocks of rocks. Rocks can be a combination of as many as six types of min erals. Three types of rocks make up the Earth’s crust. Rocks are formed in three different ways to produce igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks. Igneous rocks form when molten magma cools and solidifies. Metamorphic rocks form when a rock is chemically changed by heat or pressure to form a new rock type. Sedimentary rocks form when fragments of rocks and other debris are cemented together. Igneous Rocks The rocks solidify from a mass of molten rock when a lava flow cools and hardens. There are two main types of igneous rock: extrusive and intrusive. Extrusive types form when molten rock comes to the surface and cools quickly, as with lava. This produces a very fine-grained rock. Intrusive rocks are those that solidified underground, cooling slowly to produce coarse-grained rocks. Examples: Granite, basalt, obsidian. Sedimentary Rocks Sedimentary rocks are formed when sediment (bits of rock plus materials such as shells and sand) get packed together . They can take millions of years to form . Sed i mentary rock is made up of lots of other rocks, or even animal remains( Fossils), all stuck together. Sedimentary rocks are built up of particles laid down as layers or beds of sediment and are later buried , compressed, a nd cemented into a solid mass . Examples: Sandstone, shale, limestone. Sedimentary rocks often have a layered appearance. Metamorphic Rocks Metamorphic rocks are igneous or sedimentary rocks that have been changed by heat, pressure, or both. Metamorphic rocks are usually formed deep within the Earth, during a process such as mountain building. Examples: Schist, slate, marble. The R ock Cycle O ver many years rock change from one type to another. This is called the rock cycle. Rocks can be changed by the weathering, erosion, heating, cooling and pressure. Weathering is the breaking down or dissolving of rocks and minerals on Earth ’ s surface. Water, ice, acids, salt, plants, animals, and changes in temperature are all cause s of weathering. Once the rock has been broken down, a process called erosion transports the bits of rock and minerals away. No rock on Earth’s surface is hard enough to resist weathering. Together, the processes of weathering and erosion carved the Grand Canyon, in the U.S. state of Arizona. What is the difference between rocks and minerals? 2 . People mined minerals from the ground to use as they were found, particularly gemstones, and later mined ores to extract metals such as Gold, Copper or Iron. In fact ages of human civilisation have been named after the mineral ores used — the Bronze Age and the Iron Age for example. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid that has a regular crystal structure and chemical make-up. Some minerals are made up of only one kind of atom. These minerals are called ‘native’ minerals and include gold and silver. Other minerals are made up of several or many different types of atoms. The mineral quartz (SiO,) is made up of molecules consisting of one atom of silicon (Si) and two atoms of oxygen (O). Quartz forms regular 18-sided crystals. Quartz is the most common mineral in the Earth’s crust. Gypsum Calcite Quartz There are over 3000 different minerals and many of these are common in rocks, however there are only about eight very common rock-forming minerals. Examples of common rock forming minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica, olivine and calcite. Some rocks are made up of several minerals (e.g. Granite) and some rocks are made of only one mineral (e.g. limestone). The appearance of rocks depends mainly on the type of minerals that make it up and the way the rock has been formed. Some rocks are made up of other broken down rocks that have been ‘cemented’ together and some are formed from interlocking crystals. The size of the mineral crystals or grains in rocks varies from very large (crystals about 5mm in granite) to microscopic (as in shale) making them very hard to see and identify. Mineral crystals are easiest to identify in rocks formed from slowly cooling molten rock deep under ground. Here is a list of common rocks found in the Earth's crust and the main minerals that make them up: e Sandstone — quartz and feldspar e Limestone — calcite ¢ Granite — feldspar, quartz and mica ¢ Basalt — feldspar, pyroxene and olivine e Rhyolite — quartz and feldspar 36 Junior Science - Astronomy & Geology

searchText: ﻿ The formation of sedimentary rocks varies so there are a variety of sedimentary rocks. All of these rocks require a very long time for the processes of weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction and cementation to occur. These processes can take millions of years. Three types of sedimentary rocks are formed when weathered rock particles, organisms die or precipitated particles are compacted and cemented together. These three types of rocks are referred to as clastic sedimentary rock, organic sedimentary rock and chemical sedimentary rock, respectively. Clastic sedimentary rocks consist of smaller rocks cemented together. Examples include conglomerate and brecchia. Organic sedimentary rock is formed when organisms die and layers form that are eventually covered by clastic sedimentary rock and compressed. Examples include coal and limestone. Chemical sedimentary rocks form as a result of a chemical reaction that produces a precipitation. Banded iron formations (BIF) are chemical sedimentary rocks that contain iron oxide layers and are usually composed of the minerals magnetite and hematite. searchText:
Oxford Sciences 8 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Shake, rattle and record
When the pressure that has built up between tectonic plates is suddenly released, it can cause an earthquake. Scientists use a special machine called a seismograph to measure the magnitude of movement in the Earth (the seismic waves) that an earthquake causes. 
Some of the earliest seismographs were created more than 2000 years ago in China using small bronze balls that would simply drop on to a surface to make a noise when the Earth shook. Today, seismographs are finely tuned machines that can tell scientists about the magnitude of seismic waves in great detail. 
In this task, you will create your own simple seismograph and explore how it works. This activity is best carried out in a group. 

Build your seismograph 
You will need the following materials to build your seismograph:
Free-standing table
Retort stand and clamp
Two retort stand clamps
Metal spring
Horseshoe magnet
Plastic cup
String
Marbles or stones
Pencil (or pen)
Long thin strips of butcher’s paper
The following steps will guide you through the construction of your seismograph.
Firmly clamp the base of your retort stand to your table.
Using one of the retort stand clamps, attach the spring to the top of the retort stand. 
Using the other retort stand clamp, attach the horseshoe magnet so that it straddles the spring.
Make a small hole in the bottom of your cup and push the pencil through it, then fill up the cup with marbles or other heavy material to secure your pencil in place. 
Attach a string handle to your cup either with strong tape or by punching a small hole in opposite sides of the cup and tying the string through these holes. 
Hang the cup onto the bottom of the spring. 
Adjust the heights of your clamps so that the tip of your pencil is just touching the base of the retort stand. If required, tape your pencil in place at the bottom of the cup to keep it secure. 
Test your seismograph 
Now test your seismograph. First, place one end of a strip of butcher’s paper under the pencil and slowly drag it across the retort stand so that a line appears on the paper. Once you have a good straight line appearing, try this again with a fresh piece of paper, but this time, get one member of your group to gently wobble the table as you pull to create a ‘table earthquake’. 
Experiment with different magnitudes of ‘table earthquakes’ to see how your seismograph responds. 
Investigate and improve your seismograph
There are lots of different parts required for this seismograph and it is quite likely that some of these things are not working perfectly. You will now analyse your seismograph, identify the problems and consider ways to improve the design. 
Analyse the seismograph
Before you can improve on the design, you must be sure you understand everything about it. Discuss the questions below with your group to make sure you understand each component in the seismograph. 
You might like to try some tests with your seismograph. Use the internet, your teacher or other resources to confirm your understanding. Write notes to record your thinking.
The spring
Describe the purpose of the spring. 


Suggest why it must be a metal spring.


Describe what might happen if a metal wire be used instead. (You might like to try this out to find out.)





The horseshoe magnet
Describe the purpose of the horseshoe magnet. 


Describe what would happen if you removed the magnet. (You might like to try this to find out.)



The cup
Describe the purpose of the marbles in the cup. 


Describe what would happen if you removed the marbles. (You might like to try this to find out.)



Identify problems
Now you understand how each component of the seismograph works, think about the problems you have encountered in its use. Is the paper wide enough? Is the paper hard to guide? Does the cup swing too much? Does the spring bounce too much? Is the pencil too loose in the cup?
Note down any problems you found with your seismograph that impacts on how well it measures ‘table earthquakes’.






Improve the design
For each of the problems you have identified, brainstorm possible ways to improve the seismograph with your group. Write down all your ideas, no matter how silly or unlikely. 









Now choose your best improvement idea for each problem and circle it. Implement these ideas into the seismograph design and then test your improved design with different magnitude table earthquakes.
Discussion and reflection
Compare how the machine worked before and after your improvements.






Identify which improvement made the most difference. Identify which improvement made the least difference. 









Describe the next improvement that you would like to try next (if you had time).







Your seismograph does not have a scale. Describe how you would describe the magnitude of your table earthquakes without a scale. 








Describe the Richter scale.








To detect the origin of an earthquake (i.e. the location where it occurred), you need the data from three seismographs in different locations. Discuss why this would be needed with your group and record your ideas below.

subject: Science
searchText: ﻿GEOLOGY The Structure of the Earth a) Inside the Earth Scientists think that the Earth is composed of layers. The outermost layer is like a thin skin and it is called the crust. The crust is solid and it is composed of rocks and minerals. The crust is not an even layer; it is thickest where there are mountains ranges (and in general under the continents) and thinnest beneath the deep oceans. The average thickness of the crust is about 30 km; the distance to the centre of the Earth is about 6500 km. That is, the crust is very thin compared to the distance to the centre of the Earth. The temperature in the crust ranges from about 200C (at the surface) to about 5000C (at the bottom of the crust). That is, the deeper you go into the crust (and the Earth) the hotter is becomes. Beneath the crust is a much thicker layer called the mantle. The mantle is about 2900 km thick and the temperatures range from about 5000C to 20000C. These high temperatures are enough to melt rock, and so the mantle is made up of partially solid, partially liquid (molten) rock. Sometimes molten rock spills out onto the crust as lava. At the centre is the core which contains two main layers. The outer core is believe to be made of molten iron and nickel. It has a thickness of about 2270 km and a temperature of about 30000C. The inner core is thought to be made of solid iron and nickel. It has a radius of about 1300 km and a temperature of about 4000oC. b) Plate tectonics The theory of plate tectonics proposes that the outermost part of the earth, the crust, is divided into a number of rigid plates which move in relation to each other. There are six or seven major plates and a number of smaller ones. Both continents and ocean floors form the upper part of these plates. The Australian continent is on the Indian-Australian plate. The tectonic plates are thought to be floating on the upper potion of the mantle and their movement is thought to be due to convection currents (movement of the hot mantle material) caused by the tremendous heat within the earth. The boundaries of these plates were determined by mapping the positions of earthquake epicentres because earthquakes tend to occur where plates meet or move apart. Since the plates are moving with respect to each other, the edges or margins of the plates will be geologically unstable: i) where two plates are forced together i.e. they are colliding, one plate is often forced under the other. The plate that is forced underneath moves back into the mantle. Collision zones of plates, called subduction zones, are often associated with earthquakes, volcanoes, ocean trenches and fold mountains. This type of plate movement i.e. plate collision, is thought to have caused the formation of the Himalayas, in Asia, and the Andes mountains in South America. The ring of volcanoes around the Pacific ocean also is thought to be due to the Pacific plate is being pushed under other plates. ii) where plates are moving apart, new material from the mantle rises up to form new crust. Mid-ocean ridges (mountains), volcanoes and earthquakes are often associated with these areas. Two plates moving apart are thought to have caused the formation of the mid-Atlantic ridge, a mountain range under the Atlantic ocean. iii) where plates move past one another, faults, or breaks, occur in the rocks. This is called lateral movement of plates. Active volcanoes are absent in these areas, but severe earthquakes can occur as the two plates move in "jerky" movements past one another. This type of plate movement occurs along the western coast of North America, and it forms the San Andreas fault. As the plates move over the surface of the Earth, they carry the continents with them. It is thought that the continents were originally one land mass and over the billions of years they have slowly moved apart (and they are still moving!). c) Volcanoes Sometimes, due to pressure in the mantle layer, magma (molten rock) is forced through a weak part in the Earth's crust. When this happens, a volcano forms. The fluid magma which flows out of a volcano, over the surface, is called lava. "New" rock is formed when molten lava cools. Smoke, steam, ash and other gases also pour out of a volcano during an eruption. d) Mountain building The layers of rocks that make up the Earth’s crust are being continually pushed, twisted, split and folded by Earth movements. Mountains are often formed because of these tremendous forces exerted within and on the Earth’s crust: Folding of the crust can occur because of these forces. For example when two plates collide, fold mountains often form at the edge (or edges) of the plate. Most of the Earth’s mountain ranges have been formed this way. Another way in which rock layers may react to huge forces is by splitting or faulting. When a crack or a break forms in a layer of rocks, the rock on one side of the crack can move up, down or sideways, relative to the rock on the other side of the crack. This may result in one part of the Earth’s crust being higher compared to an adjacent part. Igneous Rocks Rocks which at one time were molten i.e. magma, are called igneous rocks. These rocks are composed of interlocking crystals. (Crystals are solids with a definite shape and straight, sharp edges) Igneous rocks can form from magma in two ways: i) when magma reaches the earth's surface, it becomes lava. Lava cools relatively quickly and produces igneous rock made up of small crystals. An example of rock formed this way is basalt. Basalt is normally a dark-coloured, hard rock. ii) at times, magma cools and solidifies below the Earth's surface . When this occurs, cooling is very slow, and the rock formed is composed of large crystals. An example of rock formed this way is granite. The magma which forms granite is too thick to be forced through weaknesses in the earth's crust, and it forms great domes underneath the surface. In time, the surrounding softer rocks are eroded, leaving the rounded domes of granite. Granite is a multicoloured rock composed of quite large interlocking crystals. Sedimentary Rocks a) Weathering Weathering is the process by which rocks are broken down into smaller pieces or changed to other substances when exposed to the atmosphere. This process is caused by contact of the exposed outermost parts of the rock with water, air and living things. Two types of weathering occur: i) Physical Weathering - this results in rock being broken down into smaller pieces (the composition of the rock is not changed). - physical weathering can be due to - temperature changes - action of frost or ice - abrasion by moving particles - action of plants and animals ii) Chemical Weathering - this results in the rocks being changed into different substances. - chemical weathering occurs when air and water come in contact with rock and a chemical reaction with the rock occurs - some of the chemicals in the environment that cause chemical weathering are: - carbonic acid, which is formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water - humic acid, which is a weak acid formed from decaying plants in the soil. - oxygen and water b) Erosion Erosion is the process of removal of the weathered rock particles from the bedrock locality i.e. from the place where they were formed from the parent rock. The main agents of erosion are: i) water - moving water in the rivers, steams and in the ocean can transport rock particles from one place to another. The faster the movement of water, the larger the rock particles that can be moved. - water running over and through soil and rocks also causes erosion of small rock particles and soluble substances. ii) ice - a glacier is a very large river of ice and as it flows downhill it carves out a large valley by breaking off pieces of rock and carry them with it. iii) wind - the ability of wind to carry particles is less than that of water. However, wind can move much faster that water , and so can still carry quite large sand/rock particles. c) The formation of sedimentary rocks. The weathered materials carried by water, ice or wind in the process of erosion, will finally be "dropped" or deposited somewhere. This process is called deposition or sedimentation. The weathered material which is deposited during erosion is called sediment. Over time, different layers of sediment often form on top of one another. Layers of sediment can also be formed when a mixture of rocks and sand are deposited at the one time from the flowing water. The heaviest material will settle quickest i.e. it will form the bottom layer, then the next heaviest will settle etc. Thus layers, with the heaviest material at the bottom to the lightest as the top layer, will be formed. As sediment builds up, layer upon layer, it can be very slowly converted into rock, called a sedimentary rock. The process of forming many sedimentary rocks involves first compaction (pushing the particles in the sediment close together), and then secondly, the cementing of the particles together by chemicals. That is, in a sediment, the particles are just mixed together, but in a sedimentary rock, the particles are "cemented" together to form a solid piece of material. Some sedimentary rocks are formed from solids which have precipitated out of solution (salt), and other from remains of plants and animals that have been cemented together (limestone). Sometimes plants or animals e.g. shells, form part of a sediment. These dead plants and animals then become part of the sedimentary rock which forms. The remains or imprints of these plants and animals in the rock are referred to as fossils. d) Characteristics of sedimentary rocks i) Most sedimentary rocks have a layered structure. In a series of layered rock, normally the oldest (first deposited) rock is at the bottom, and the youngest (last to be deposited) is at the top. ii) Some sedimentary rocks show the remains of animals and plants trapped in the rock i.e. they contain fossils. iii) Many sedimentary rocks contain grains cemented together. iv) Sedimentary rocks are often much softer than igneous or metamorphic rocks. e) Some common sedimentary rocks Conglomerate - composed of large rounded pebbles (> 2mm in diameter) cemented together. Sandstone - composed of medium sized sand grains (< 2mm and visible to naked eye) Mudstone - composed of a mixture of silt and clay sized particles , cemented together Limestone - composed of calcium carbonate and is normally pale in colour - can be made of shell, coral or bone fragments cemented together - can be formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate from aqueous solution Coal - black or brown solid composed mainly of carbon - formed from plant material that has been compressed under layers of sediment. Metamorphic Rocks When solid rock is subjected to heat and pressure in the earth's crust, it can change into a different rock. This new rock is called a metamorphic rock. Metamorphic rocks are often formed from rock which is formed or buried deep in the Earth's crust where there would be high temperatures and pressures. They are also formed in the crust in volcanic areas because the magma heats the surrounding rocks to sufficiently high temperatures to change them into metamorphic rocks. Metamorphic rocks are normally much harder than sedimentary rocks and they sometimes have visible grains. Examples of metamorphic rocks include: - marble - often white, has visible grains and is formed from limestone. - quartzite - very hard, has visible grains and is formed from sandstone. - gneiss - has visible grains and normally contains dark bands. It is formed from shale, which must first be changed into other metamorphic rocks before gneiss is finally formed. Marble and quartzite are normally formed in areas where the heat is supplied by volcanoes. However, gneiss is formed deep in the crust where high pressure and temperature conditions exist. title: Teacher Sheet Lesson One
subject: Science
searchText: Teacher sheet lesson one Introduction This unit will be organised around an edStudio presentation that will contain the majority of the student resources. All of the investigations will be listed in the find and prepare sections of the lesson plans. Each page of the edStudio will be a new lesson and the students can individually work through the activities and submit their produced work electronically back onto the pages via the digital drop boxes. The edStudio presented in this unit will need to be personalised for each individual class. You will need to make a copy of the edStudio and then alter the permissions and/or modify the content to suit specific classes. It is possible to teach the lessons without the edStudio. If you do not wish to use it, a full list of the resources used has been included in the lesson plans. Student instructions for activities, that appear as pop-up boxes in the studio, are included on each teacher sheet as student information. Introduction — The structure of the Earth (website) Student information: Welcome to the unit. Today we will be looking at a slideshow that revises what you learned about rocks in Year 8 and introduces the structure of the Earth. You will then be working in groups to build up a model of the Earth. Please follow the instructions on this page to work your way through lesson one. First watch the slideshow Structure of the Earth (http://media2. teachertube.com/files/articles/3933.ppt#256,1,Unit 17 STRUCTURE OF THE EARTH) Afterwards, your teacher will lead a discussion on what you have viewed. Task 1 — Introductory reading Student information: Open the website Structure of the Earth (http://scign.jpl.nasa.gov/learn/plate1.htm) and read the information about the layers of the Earth. Do not navigate away from this page. When you have finished reading, create a page of notes of the relevant summary points, then create a labelled scale drawing of the four layers of the Earth. You may complete this task in your science journal or you may create an electronic document and save it in a new folder for this unit. Teacher information: The Structure of the Earth website contains a few interconnecting pages. Ensure the students only summarise the information on the page that opens from the link. 1 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 Task 2 — Make a model of the Earth Student information: Now you have read about the structure of the Earth you will construct a model. Collect your materials then follow the supplied instructions. Make a recording of your group building the model and submit it to your teacher. If you are unsure of how to record, read through the section ‘How to prepare a presentation’ below. Once you have finished, view another group’s recordings and models. Teacher information: Student instructions are provided at the end of this document. For this activity the students will need the handouts ‘Make a model of the Earth’ and ‘How to prepare a presentation’. Task 3 — From clay balls to the centre of the Earth Student information: In task two you constructed a model of the Earth from a description based on accepted scientific theory. How do we know what the Earth is composed of if we can never see all the layers? Use the activity From clay balls to the structure of the Earth to gain some ideas about how scientists are using experiments to discover what the inside of the Earth is made of. Teacher information: Refer to the website From clay balls to the structure of the Earth (http://geophysics.esci. keele.ac.uk/earthlearningidea/PDF/74_Clay_balls.pdf). A student activity sheet of the same title is included at the end of this document. You will need to personalise this activity to suit your class. Culminating activity — Discussion questions Student information: Think about the two activities that you have completed and then read through the discussion questions below and write your answers in your science journal. Consider other students’ answers and reflect on whether you agree or disagree. Discussion questions: 1. What did you predict the centre of the two plasticine balls was composed of? 2. Do you need to cut open the balls to make this prediction? 3. Would you need to open the balls in order to draw a definitive conclusion? 4. What is the difference between a prediction and a conclusion? 5. Have scientists made predictions about the Earth’s composition or drawn conclusions? 6. Will scientists ever be able to draw conclusions about the composition of the Earth? It is important for this resource that misconceptions are not created by the students engaging with the activity. Explain to the students that the activities they complete on the clay balls are not mini-experiments that mirror current scientific investigation. They are, however, investigating that it is possible to form hypotheses based on experimental evidence, which is how scientists are currently developing a concept of the structure of the Earth. 2 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 Make a model of the Earth Materials: • Four colours of modelling clay • Plastic knife • Piece of paper for labels • Metric ruler • Four toothpicks Method: 1. You first need to be in groups of two or three and then collect your materials from the front of the room. Remember to organise the recording of your activity now. 2. Each group will be making one labelled model of a slice of the Earth. Use toothpicks and paper to make the labels. Below is an image of a finished product. Schoch, Catherine © The State of Queensland 3. This will be a scale model so the group will need to work out how thick each layer should be. You will be making a 1 cm:1000 km model. Look up the thickness of each layer in your notes from task one. You will need to include the inner core, outer core, mantle and continental crust as four separate layers (the oceanic crust will be impossibly thin on this model so use the continental crust thickness). Remember to record yourselves working out this information. 4. Once you have worked out the measurements for your model you may commence building it. Use a different colour of plasticine for each layer. You need to be careful that each layer is the correct thickness. One member of your team needs to narrate your procedure while you record building your model. 5. Once the model is completed you may make some little flags from toothpicks and paper. Label each layer with its name, size and composition. Don’t forget to keep recording. 6. Now hold up your model for the camera and give a short presentation on your finished model, including how and why you made construction decisions. 7. Your group is now finished this activity. Upload your recording to a computer and make some final editing adjustments before you submit the final presentation. 3 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 How to prepare a presentation You will be completing several experiments during the course of your study this year. As part of these lessons you will be required to record your participation in and reflection on each one. We will be recording in an electronic format and keeping digital copies of these records. So, how do I do that? Good question. You will be provided with some form of recording equipment at the beginning of the lesson. This may consist of a camera, a video recorder or a digital voice recorder. You will use these items to make a recording of the experiment as your group is completing the activity. Remember, you cannot go back and record an experiment once your group has completed it. Things to consider Your presentation on your experiment will still need to have the elements of a normal experiment ‘write up’. So you will need to state in your presentation the following elements: • The aim of the experiment — what is your group trying to discover? • Your group’s initial hypothesis — what does your group think you are going to observe? • How your group is intending to investigate this hypothesis — this is an initial discussion of your method. • Images of your equipment during and after set up — name the equipment and say why it is the most suited to the task (e.g. because we are only using small measures of materials we will use test tubes instead of beakers). • A commentary of your experiment method including any safety considerations your group has recognised. • A commentary and any images of your observations — what did your group see during the experiment? • Your concluding statements, and a discussion of these questions: –– Why did you see your observations? –– Are they what you expected to see? –– Did you have observations that may have been caused by errors in your method? • Your group’s reflection on the experiment and an analysis of your level of success or failure: –– How did your group manage the experiment? –– How many errors did you think you made? –– How did your results compare with your hypothesis? In a written presentation you would normally write out descriptions of these points, but for an electronic presentation your group will need to speak about these aloud as the group is working through the experiment. It may be a good idea to nominate someone to act as the ‘presenter’ for the recording. They will be responsible for the main commentary and for asking questions of the other group members. Once the experiment is finished and cleaned away you can download your presentation and give it some finishing touches. If you are taking photos and recording your voices, then a slideshow may be the best option for your format. If you have a video recording, then some general editing and additional audio via a voice recorder may be a good idea. 4 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 From clay balls to the structure of the Earth You made a scale model of the Earth for task two. How do we know that these predictions about the Earth’s composition are true? The Earth is very large and no one has been able to drill all the way to the core. This is impossible. For task three you will be looking at how scientists have come to formulate predictions on the composition of the Earth’s layers. Follow the steps below and conduct some tests on two objects to see if you can predict what the objects are composed of. Step one: Form into groups of two or three. Collect your materials from the front of the room. What are the two objects? Do they look the same? Do you think they are the same? Explain your answer. What do you think the inside of the objects look like? Note: You are not to cut the objects open during this activity. Make a list of the tests you could carry out on the two balls and then wait for the teacher to lead you in a discussion of your classmates’ ideas. Now take your two balls and complete some of the tests on them. Make a record of your observations for each investigation. 5 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1

searchText: Teacher sheet lesson seven Introduction In the previous lesson you learned about formation of new crust at diverging plate boundaries. In this lesson you will examine destruction of old crust at converging plates. Task 1 — Convergent plate boundaries Student information: Go to the website Subduction zones (http://www.platetectonics.com/book/page_12.asp) and read about convergent plate boundaries. Open a new Word document, create a labelled diagram of a subduction zone and include events and landforms that occur in this zone. Save this in the folder for this unit. a) Why do volcanoes form at convergent plate boundaries? b) Why do some places seem to have lots of earthquakes? Task 2 — Subducting plate Student information: How do we know that one plate is sliding under another? Construct a model using the information provided in ‘Model instructions’. The model is based on data from earthquakes. Record your group’s activity and submit to your teacher. View another group’s recording. Teacher information: For more information about the subducting plate model, follow this link. http://www.geosociety.org/educate/LessonPlans/RealEvidence-SubductingPlate.pdf Reflection questions and instructions for this activity are included below. 1 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7 Model instructions The model you will be making today draws on actual earthquake data to provide evidence for the existence of a subducting plate. Earthquakes occur deep inside the Earth and the depth and size of all earthquakes is continuously being recorded. Research the answers to the following questions to review your understanding of earthquakes. 1. What is an earthquake? 2. Where do earthquakes usually occur? 3. What is the difference between the epicentre and the focus of an earthquake? Form into groups of four. Follow the instructions below to construct a model that shows the shape of the Nazca plate subducting under the South American plate. Remember you will need to make a recording of the activity and save it in the folder for this unit. First you need to collect the following materials from the front of the room. • Box • Scissors • 22 balls (or beads) of three colours • Copy of the map (whichever your teacher has provided) • Copy of the earthquake data table • Glue • 22 paper clips • Masking tape • String • 2 rulers 1. Use the information in the table to plot the earthquakes on the map provided. 2. Lay the box on the side and glue the map onto the top-facing side of the box. The bottom of the map should face the open end of the box. 3. At each epicentre on the map punch a small hole. It only needs to be big enough for the string to fit through. 4. Each of the balls (beads) will represent the focus of the earthquake. Each focus was recorded at its particular depth and these depths are contained within the table. For each epicentre of the map, find its focus. You will then need to attach a ball to a length of string that matches the depth of the focus. Make sure that you use an appropriate scale or you will not see the pattern in your finished model. Start with the deepest earthquake so you know they will all fit. 5. Work through all 22 epicentres on the map and hang each ball at the depth of each focus. 6. When you are finished with your model, answer the following questions either in a Word document or verbally as part of your recorded presentation. 2 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7 Questions 1. What information does an epicentre provide about an earthquake? 2. What is the difference between the focus and the epicentre of an earthquake? 3. What is happening to the rocks at the focus of an earthquake, and what do we call this? 4. What do you notice about the depth of the focus of the earthquakes as you go further inland from the coast of South America? 5. According to your model, what appears to be happening to the two plates that meet along the west coast of South America? 6. Draw and label a diagram of the model showing what is happening to the plates along the west coast of South America as described in question 5. 7. Describe the type of plate boundary that is present along the west coast of South America. 8. Explain how your data supports your conclusions in question 5. 9. How can your model explain the deep trench that lies off the coast of South America? 10. Use a map of the world that shows the plate boundaries to find some other areas where this same type of plate boundary is occurring. 11. How is volcanism related to this type of boundary? 3 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7

searchText: Teacher sheet lesson two Introduction Student information: In this lesson you will be looking at the changes to the Australian continent. Our landscape has been formed through several geological occurrences. You will be working through two learning objects and collecting information from them in order to construct a timeline. This will need to be recorded in your science journal. Task 1 — The timeline task The timeline task is detailed in the document Snapshots in time which your teacher will give to you. You need to find photographs from the internet as learning object images cannot be copied. Work through the two activities on this page and gather evidence to include in your timeline. Use appropriate copyright and referencing practices. Teacher information: The activity Snapshots in time is found in the Queensland Studies Authority Assessment Bank. You will need to access this site and download a copy of this resource for students. In order to access the site you will need to register and receive a password. More information about this can be found on the teacher sheet QSA Assessment Bank. The activity includes a student booklet and teacher guidelines. The student booklet needs to be provided to students. A link has been provided in the lesson overview and lesson plan for the QSA Assessment Bank homepage. Task 2 — Learning object: Palaeotraveller Student information: Learning object one is called Palaeotraveller (https://learningplace.eq.edu.au/cx/resources/ items/2b7ec0d6-14e4-bb27-3fc0-30c4953efb14/3/viewIMS.jsp). It provides information relevant to various locations at different points in time. It also contains an animated world map so you can see Australia’s changing position during these time periods. Refer to the supplied instructions to guide you through this activity. Please do not spend more than 10 minutes on this activity. When working through this activity you need to think about: a) what changes have occurred to the Australian continent? b) what features of the present landscape give us clues? Teacher information: The learning object can be downloaded and saved into a common folder for the students to access. This may help with navigation speeds. A copy of the student instructions has been included with this document if you wish to use it as a handout. 1 of 4 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson2 Task 3 — Learning object: Travel back in time Student information: Use the learning object Travel back in time (https://learningplace.eq.edu.au/cx/resources/ items/5a902fa5-4e1c-13f1-e92a-60c19ffbf3be/7/viewIMS.jsp?.hb=true) and the supplied instructions to make notes about evidence being used to support geological predictions. Select some of these pieces of evidence to incorporate into your timeline. Remember you may need to find other images from the internet. Please do not spend more then 10 minutes on this activity. In your science journal, write a sentence on how you think scientists have used evidence to support geological predications. Teacher information: The learning object can be downloaded and saved into a common folder for the students to access. This may help with navigation speeds. searchText: The plate tectonic story: a scientific jigsaw The idea of plate tectonics to explain that Africa was once joined to South America may seem obvious now but when Alfred Wegener published a scientific paper about 100 years ago suggesting that the continents had drifted apart everyone thought he was mad. He wasn’t the first person to notice that the coastlines looked similar. Even Francis Bacon in 16th Century had written about it. But Alfred was the first person to put forward a lot of scientific evidence that they had been joined. It was the fossils that did it. Alfred pointed out that the fossils in Africa and South America were remarkably similar – up to a point. It was obvious to him that the two landmasses had been joined and so the same animals had lived in both. Slowly the continents had drifted apart and the animal populations had evolved after that in different ways. He also spotted that the rock types in the two continents were similar too. ‘Perhaps’, he suggested, ‘there was once only one land mass and one huge sea’. He named his giant continent Pangea and the giant sea Panthalassa Other scientists were not convinced. They claimed that there had been land bridges between all the continents to allow the animals to walk across from one continent to the other. These bridges had long ago sunk into the sea, they argued. They certainly couldn’t believe that whole continents were on the move! It took 50 years – during which time the continents had moved another 1.75 m on average – before people finally realised that Alfred had been right all along. By the 1950s scientists were making measurements of the ocean floor – and they began to find some very strange things. They discovered long ridges of mountains with magma rising to the ocean floor in the middle of them. They also found that the rock closer to the ridge was much younger than the rock further away. The only explanation was that the two halves of the ocean floor were moving apart and new rock was forming in the gap. And when the scientists looked at the magnetic rocks on the ocean floor they found they were magnetised in opposite directions. Each time the Earth’s magnetic field had reversed direction, the new rock appearing at the surface was magnetised in the same direction as the Earth’s field at that time. From this it was a short leap to the idea of plate tectonics. Alfred would have been delighted to know he had been on the right lines all along. We now believe that the Earth is covered by plates that move slowly (eg around 35 mm per year – or the same rate as your finger nails grow) carried by the mantle. As the plates move together the rocks between are crushed and form mountain belts, other rock is forced down into the mantle. When plates move apart new rock rises up and solidifies to fill the gap. All the time geophysicists are working to understand better how the Earth works. They are now working on new ideas about how the mantle moves called ‘mantle dynamics’. It is possible that the new ideas will help us to predict when earthquakes will occur and when volcanoes will erupt, but we’re not there yet! However, we may soon be able to map the stress on the Earth’s surface, which should give us more of the information needed to warn people of an imminent earthquake. Questions Q 1. Why did Alfred find his theory was not accepted by other scientists? Q 2. What evidence resulted in his basic idea being accepted after all? Q 3. Explain the theory of plate tectonics Q 4. How do we believe that landmasses move about? Q 5. Scientists publish their findings in journals for other scientists to read. Why is it important for scientists to read what their colleagues around the world are doing? Q 6. Before a scientific paper can be published it has to be ‘refereed’ by other experts in the field. If Alfred had written a scientific paper, do you think the referees would have accepted it for publication? Explain your answer.

searchText: ﻿The Ring of Fire Overview In this activity, students investigate volcanoes and the theory of plate tectonics. They will use Encarta Encyclopedia 2000 and Encarta® Interactive World Atlas to locate cities and nations along the Ring of Fire as they design guided tours of some of the volcanic regions of earth. For a related lesson on plate tectonics and earthquakes, see the lesson This Dynamic Planet. Objectives In completing this activity, students will: • Locate the Ring of Fire on a world map • Explain the origins of the region's name • Identify nations and cities that lay along the Ring of Fire • Link plate tectonics to the location of earth's volcanoes Materials Materials for making a tour booklet Sample tour booklets (You might want to visit a travel agency for some booklets or brochures that students can use as models) Encarta Encyclopedia 2000 Encarta Interactive World Atlas Background Information/Fast Facts In introducing the activity, you might want to share some of the following facts with students. (All information comes from Encarta Encyclopedia.) • According to the Smithsonian Institution, 1,511 above-the-sea volcanoes have been active during the past 10,000 years, 539 of them erupting one or more times during written history. • On average, 50 to 60 above-the-sea volcanoes are active in any given year. About half of these are continuations of eruptions from the previous year, and the rest are new. • About 60 percent of the active above-the-sea volcanoes lie along the Pacific Rim. • The United States ranks third, behind Japan and Indonesia, in the number of historically active volcanoes. When measured from its submerged base, Mauna Kea, the highest summit in Hawaii, stands 32,000 feet, or 9,700 meters tall—higher than Mt. Everest. • As magma enters a volcanic reservoir, it may be anywhere from 1000oC (1832oF) to 2000oC (3632oF). • Not all eruptions consist of magma or molten rock. Some eruptions consist of gases, dust, rocks, or a mixture of all three. • When a volcano erupts, it may spew blocks of rock ("bombs") as big as a car. • Since the beginning of recorded history, an estimated 50 volcanoes have erupted in the area that makes up the present-day United States. Activities and Procedures 1. You might begin the lesson by sharing the Fast Facts with students. After presenting the last fact, ask students to speculate on the area of the United States with the greatest number of active volcanoes. (The nation's northwestern coast, especially the Cascades and Alaska.) 2. Have a student locate this region on a wall map of the world or in Encarta (either in the World Maps that accompany Encarta Encyclopedia or in Encarta Interactive World Atlas). Point out the region's location along the Pacific Rim. Call on students to suggest reasons for the high level of volcanic activity in this area. 3. If students are unfamiliar with the theory of plate tectonics, you might have them read about this topic in the Encarta Encyclopedia or assign "The Changing Earth," a 1973 National Geographic article found in the Article Archives. (This article presents the groundbreaking work of the 1960s that revolutionized the geophysical sciences.) 4. Refer students to the map in the encyclopedia article on volcanoes. Using this map, have them explain why the Pacific Rim is sometimes called the "Ring of Fire." If you are using Encarta Interactive World Atlas, assign students to use the Map Customizer to add cities and country borders to a tectonic map showing the plates and volcanoes of earth. 5. Divide the class into groups. Direct the students to "tour" a nation or city known for its volcano or volcanoes, using their customized maps. Make sure that each group picks a different area to tour. 6. Explain that the purpose of the tour is to design a trip guide for travelers who wish to visit volcanic sites. Students will find many useful features in both the Encarta Encyclopedia and the Encarta Interactive World Atlas. The trip guides can include pictures, site locations, and more. Make sure students take advantage of the Map Treks listed in the Follow Up section of this lesson. 7. When students are done, have them exchange trip guides. Students might evaluate each other's guides, noting positive features and suggesting improvements. Additional Activities Tracing Volcanic Growth Assign students to design storyboards showing the various steps in the creation of an active volcano. Explain that storyboards are like the frames in a comic strip or celluloid film. In fact, video and filmmakers often use storyboards to present a concept or story line as part of their development process. As a reference, tell students to look at the animated clip Formation and Eruption of a Volcano in Encarta Encyclopedia. When students are finished, have them present their storyboards to the class. Ask other students to watch the animated clip to see how closely students captured the sequence of events. Distinguishing Types of Volcanoes Request volunteers to use Encarta to research the various types of volcanoes (strato- or composite volcanoes, cinder cones, shield volcanoes, and perhaps calderas). Direct them to download pictures of each type of volcano. Have students turn these pictures into flashcards. When they are done, ask these volunteers to deliver a short oral report on volcanoes to the rest of the class. At the end of the report, have them challenge the class to a game of "Name that Volcano." Every time they hold up a flashcard, classmates should identify it by type. (Tell the volunteers that they should be ready to provide the name and location of each volcano.) Identifying Volcanic Rocks The lesson on volcanoes provides a good opportunity to develop, or build upon, prior knowledge of the rocks that form Earth's crust. You might point out that rocks are composed of minerals: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid elements or compounds with a fixed atomic pattern. Name the three types of rocks--igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. Then focus student attention on igneous rocks, the type of rock associated with volcanoes. Direct students to use Encarta to prepare a photo display of igneous rocks, such as pumice, granite, basalt, and obsidian. If possible, have them bring in examples of these rocks for the rest of the class to examine. You can expand upon this lesson, by having other groups of students prepare similar displays of the two other types of rocks. Use the displays as an opportunity to talk about the geology of your area. Visiting Extraterrestrial Hot Spots Encarta Encyclopedia 2000 includes a sidebar article on the 1998 discovery of the hottest spot in the solar system: Io's Pele Volcano. You might use this story as a chance to lead students into a virtual tour of extraterrestrial volcanoes. They can read the Planetary Science article and the articles about individual planets—especially Jupiter, the planet that holds Io in its gravitational force. With this background in mind, they can head into outer space via the Internet. Suggested sites appear at the end of this lesson. Use student tours of outer space to discuss what the presence of volcanoes tells scientists about other planets and moons in our solar system. Reporting on Volcanic Eruptions The Encyclopedia article Volcanoes has a number of sidebar articles on specific volcanic eruptions. Assign each of these sidebars to a group of students. Direct students to imagine they are on-the-spot TV reporters at each eruption. Based on the sidebars, have them develop spot news reports to the rest of the class. For articles, maps, or other media pertaining to this topic, look up the following in Encarta® Encyclopedia: Geology Pacific Ocean Plate Tectonics Plume (volcano) Volcano Refer to the following items in Encarta® Interactive World Atlas for relevant information: Volcanoes, Global Theme Searching on Volcano will turn up many articles and media items The following items in the Encarta® World English Dictionary® contain information about this topic: Caldera Cone Crater Dormant (volcano) Extinct (volcano) Fissure Igneous Lava Lithosphere Magma Pumice Pyroclastics Rift Subduction Vulcanologist Vulcanology For additional online information and media, view the following Encarta articles: Plate Tectonics Volcano For additional relevant information, visit the following Web sites: Continental Drift [Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology] http://tyrrell.magtech.ab.ca/tour/contdrft.html The Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology presents information on the movement of the continents in the earth's history. Volcano World http://volcano.und.edu/ Volcano World presents basic information about volcanoes as well as news on recent eruptions; funded by NASA and hosted by the University of North Dakota. Global Volcanism Program http://www.volcano.si.edu/gvp/ The Global Volcanism Program at the Smithsonian Institution offers an electronic version of the monthly Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network, with reports on current volcanic eruptions; a complete database of volcanoes; and other resources.

deep inside the Earth (plutonic rock). Basalt and granite are two types of igneous rock. The process by
which rocks are formed, broken down, moved and reformed over and over again is called the rock cycle.

Every day various physical and chemical processes are at work changing the appearance of the Earth’s
surface. Rocks that cover the Earth’s surface are being broken down into smaller pieces by wind, rain, ice,
plants and temperature changes. For example, rain can be slightly acidic and can dissolve some kinds of
rock. This slow breakdown is called weathering.

Weathering: the breakdown of rock into smaller fragments.
Erosion: the removal or transportation of rock fragments.

Once a surface has been weakened, it can be worn away. The removal or transportation of soil or pieces
of rock is called erosion, Erosion results mainly from wind, running water or rain, Humans can cause
erosion, for example, gully erosion, banks of rivers, clearing of land, soil tillage and so on. If too many
animals are kept on an area of land, then overgrazing can occur. The grass and roots are eaten and the
topsoil is not held together. This can then be blown away by strong winds or washed away by heavy rain.

title: This Dynamic Planet
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿This Dynamic Planet Plate Tectonics and Earthquakes Overview This is a two-part lesson. The first part simplifies the idea of plate tectonics and might be best used with elementary or middle school students. The activity uses familiar objects to teach unfamiliar concepts: the cross section of an apple to illustrate the earth's structure and a soccer ball to demonstrate earth's interlocking plates. With this background in mind, students use Encarta Encyclopedia to apply the idea of plate tectonics to the movement of continents, particularly the breakup of Pangaea. The second part of the lesson links plate tectonics to earthquakes through use of maps found on Encarta® Interactive World Atlas. In the World Atlas, students use the Map Customizer to locate earthquake belts and sites of major earthquakes in the past. They then make predictions about the location of future earthquakes. This lesson can be used with a related lesson on plate tectonics and volcanoes, The Ring of Fire. Objectives In completing this lesson, students: 1. Describe the theory of plate tectonics 2. Use plate tectonics to explain continental drift 3. Discuss the link between plate tectonics and earthquakes 4. Predict the regions most likely to experience earthquakes in the future Materials Part One: Globe, soccer ball, apple, knife (to cut the apple) Part Two: Tectonic map showing plates and earthquakes (can use Encarta Interactive World Atlas) Parts One and Two: Encarta Encyclopedia 2000 Background Information/Fast Facts In introducing the activity, you might want to share some of the following facts with students. (All information comes from Encarta Encyclopedia.) • Earthquakes, or seismic tremors, occur at a rate of several hundred per day around the world. • Approximately one million small earthquakes shake the world each year. • Nearly 80 percent of seismic energy results from tremors along the Pacific Rim. • Japan is shaken by more than 1,000 tremors each year. • The largest earthquakes in the United States have taken place in the Alaskan islands. • Scientists have discovered extraterrestrial quakes on other planets and their satellites. • Seismic events on the moon are known as moonquakes. Activities and Procedures PART ONE 1. Place a globe, a soccer ball, and an apple in front of the classroom. Ask students if they can guess what all three of these items have in common. (Students will probably focus on the shape of the objects.) After a few minutes, explain that each object represents a different model of earth. 2. Cut the apple in half lengthwise and hold the cross section up to the class. Tell students that the cross section represents the basic structure of earth: a thin outer crust (the apple's skin), a small inner core, and a vast molten interior. 3. Now hold up the soccer ball. Point out that the covering appears to be made of many pieces. Explain that scientists believe that in some ways this is how the earth's crust looks—a collection of pieces that fit together in different ways. Unlike a soccer ball, however, the pieces of crust that cover the earth move. In fact, they move all the time. Tell students that scientists call these chunks of crust "plates" and refer to their movements as "plate tectonics." 4. Next, focus student attention on the globe. Mention that scientists think that millions of years ago there was only one huge continent on earth. Challenge students to use what they know about the earth's structure and crust to speculate on why there are so many continents today. Students will most likely say "the pieces of crust moved around." Use this or similar responses to raise the central issue of how and why the plates move. 5. To explore this issue, write the following question on the chalkboard: "How and why do continents shift and rift and drift apart?" Assign students to use Encarta to answer this question. You might want to assign students particular tasks. For example, one group might check Encarta Encyclopedia articles; another group might investigate articles included in Geography in Depth in Encarta Interactive World Atlas; yet another group might focus on the World Atlas Map Treks. 6. When students have finished their research, organize discussion in the form of a geological conference set in the late 1960s or early 1970s. You, or a student volunteer, can set the mood of the conference by using "This Changing Earth," a 1973 National Geographic story found in the Encarta Encyclopedia Article Archives. PART TWO 1. Request a volunteer to use the Encarta Interactive World Atlas to locate and print a map showing tectonic plates and earthquake belts around the world. Make enough copies for all the students in your class. 2. Introduce the subject of earthquakes by sharing the Fast Facts. Ask students what they can infer about earthquakes based on these facts. (That earthquakes occur frequently throughout the world, particularly along the Pacific Rim, and in other parts of the solar system.) 3. Next, distribute copies of the tectonic map. Ask students to discuss reasons earthquakes might occur along the tectonic plates. Have students check their answers by reading articles on earthquakes found in the encyclopedia and the Geography in Depth feature. 4. Review the connection between tectonic activity and earthquakes, focusing on subduction zones and the elastic rebound theory. Ask students to indicate other causes of earthquakes (e.g., volcanic eruptions, human activities). 5. Remind students that one of the ways seismologists predict future earthquakes is by studying the location and severity of past earthquakes. Tell students to use Encarta's reference tools and multimedia to find tables listing the major earthquakes of the past, particularly those occurring during the 20th century. 6. After students have located this information, direct them to locate these sites, along with dates and magnitude, on a tectonic map of earthquake belts. Looking at the completed maps, ask students to indicate future danger zones. Elicit evidence in support of their predictions. 7. In a follow-up discussion, encourage students to discuss emergency preparedness plans. Do not neglect related dangers such as tsunamis. At this point, you might also want to incorporate one or more of the Alternate Activities into the lesson. Alternate Activities Designing an Earthquake-Resistant Home The articles in Encarta Encyclopedia include a number of film clips and photographs showing earthquake destruction, particularly in Mexico City and Kobe, Japan. Tell students to imagine they are part of a team of architects and engineers hired to design earthquake-resistant homes for the people of Mexico City or Kobe. Students should begin their study by viewing the film clips and photos. They should also read the suggestions in the encyclopedia article Earthquake and the Geography in Depth article in Encarta Interactive World Atlas. (Remind students to follow the link to the related topic Civil Engineering in the Encarta Encyclopedia Earthquake article.) When students are done, have them create an architectural plan in the form of a drawing or a blueprint. If possible, you might invite a local architect or civil engineer to review the plan for structural soundness. Encourage students to make the necessary modifications in their drafts. Creating an Earthquake Survival Guide Assign interested students to search the Web for pamphlets and booklets on earthquake preparation. (Some possible sites are suggested at the end of this lesson.) Based on these materials and information in Encarta, have students create an earthquake survival guide for people their own age. You might arrange for students to share their guides with schools in earthquake-prone areas. If students live in an area that has experienced earthquakes in the past, you might arrange for the guides—along with pertinent reference materials—to be placed on reserve in the school or community library. Linking Earth Science and Life Science Can animals predict earthquakes? Some people think so. Before the 1974 Haicheng and 1975 Tangshan quakes, pandas reportedly held their heads and screamed, horses stampeded and neighed, and snakes emerged from their underground dens in the dead of winter. Recount this information to students and have them research evidence of animal seismologists. In addition to libraries and Web sites, students might talk with experts in animal behavior and, if possible, interview people who have lived through earthquakes. The key question is: Did you observe any unusual animal behavior in the hours, days, or weeks before the quake? Writing an Earthquake FAQ Sheet Call on volunteers to explain the meaning of the acronym FAQ. (If your students don't know the answer to this question, refer them to Encarta's Computer and Internet Dictionary or remind them that the purpose of a FAQ Sheet is to answer the most common questions about a subject, hence the name "Frequently Asked Questions.") Now assign students, individually or in groups, to draw up a FAQ Sheet about earthquakes. Consider the possibility of submitting their finished FAQ Sheet to one of the educational Web sites for kids. For articles, maps, or other media pertaining to this topic, look up the following in Encarta® Encyclopedia: Continent Earthquake Geology Mountain Pangaea Plate Tectonics Seismology Tsunami Volcano Continental Drift Animation Refer to the following items in Encarta® Interactive World Atlas for relevant information: Continental Drift, Glossary Plate Tectonics, Global Theme For additional online information and media, view the following Encarta articles: Earthquake Plate Tectonics For additional relevant information, visit the following Web sites: Plate Tectonics, the Cause of Earthquakes http://www.seismo.unr.edu/ftp/pub/louie/class/100/plate-tecton ics.html The Nevada Seismological Laboratory uses aerial pictures and diagrams to show how the movement of the earth's crust can cause deformations and earthquakes. The University of Nevada, Reno Seismological Laboratory http://www.seismo.unr.edu/index.html The Nevada Seismological Laboratory offers a wide variety of earthquake-related information and links to related sites.

title: Time Line of the Development of the Theory of Plate Tectonics
subject: Science

searchText: ﻿Time line of the development of the theory of plate tectonics Table Of Contents Significant events in the development of the theory of plate tectonics are summarized in the table. Time line of the development of the theory of plate tectonics year event 1596 Flemish mapmaker Abraham Ortelius noted that the coastlines of the continents appear to fit together. He suggested that the continents were once joined and that the Americas were "torn away" from Europe and Africa. 1912 German meteorologist and geophysicist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in a supercontinent called Pangea. Wegener believed that Pangea’s constituent portions moved thousands of miles apart over long periods of geologic time, a phenomenon he called "continental displacement" (now known as continental drift). Until the 1950s and ’60s, however, his idea was rejected by most geologists because he could not describe the driving forces behind continental drift. 1929 British geologist Arthur Holmes proposed that convection in the mantle is the force driving continental drift. Although his ideas were not taken seriously at the time, Holmes’s mantle convection hypothesis later gained support. 1950s Oceanographic vessels mapping the ocean floor provided data on the topographic features of the ocean basin, leading to the discovery of mid-ocean ridges. These underwater mountain ranges encircling the planet form as Earth’s plates separate. 1960 American geophysicist Harry H. Hess developed the idea that oceanic crust forms along mid-ocean ridges and spreads out laterally away from the ridges. The following year, geophysicist Robert S. Dietz named the phenomenon seafloor spreading. Hess and Dietz’s work played a pivotal role in the development of the modern theory of plate tectonics. 1963 British geologists Frederick J. Vine and Drummond H. Matthews—as well as Canadian geophysicist Laurence W. Morley, who worked independently of the others—postulated that new crust would have a magnetization aligned with Earth’s geomagnetic field. They noted that this would appear over geologic time as bands of crust that exhibit alternating patterns of magnetic polarity. The later identification of such patterns of magnetic striping provided additional evidence that Earth’s plates separate at mid-ocean ridges. mid-1960s A global network of sensors designed to detect hydroacoustic signals was installed to monitor compliance with the Nuclear Test-Ban Treaty of 1963. The sensors also recorded earthquake activity. Scientists later found that earthquakes and volcanic activity occur almost exclusively at the edges of tectonic plates. 1968 The vessel Glomar Challenger set sail on an exploration of the mid-ocean ridge between South America and Africa. Core samples obtained from drilling revealed that rocks close to mid-ocean ridges are younger than rocks that are farther away from the ridges. mid-1970s Scientists created three-dimensional images of Earth’s interior by combining information from many earthquakes using an approach similar to computed tomography (CT) scanning. This technique, now known as seismic tomography, enables scientists to investigate the dynamic processes in the deep interior of Earth. Plate tectonics and the geologic past The extent to which plate tectonics has influenced Earth’s evolution through geologic time depends on when the process started. This is a matter of ongoing debate among geologists. The principal problem is that almost all oceanic crust older than about 200 million years has been obliterated by subduction. Although thick sequences of marine sedimentary rocks up to 3.5 billion years old imply that oceanic environments did exist early in Earth’s history, virtually none of the oceanic crust that underlay these sediments has been preserved. Despite these disadvantages, there is enough fragmentary evidence to suggest that plate tectonic processes similar to those of today extend back in time at least as far as the Early Proterozoic Era, some 2.5 billion to 1.6 billion years ago. plate tectonics. (2012). In Encyclopædia Britannica. Retrieved from http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/463912/plate-tectonics/261582/Unanswered-questions

Tsunamis
‘Tsunami’ is a Japanese word meaning harbour wave. Now tsunami refers to a large water mass that has a very 
high energy level, and causes devastation in low-lying areas. The waves are in series, much like the ripples sent 
out by a pebble dropped into a pond. Earthquakes on the seafloor cause tsunamis. These earthquakes result 
from plate movement. The sudden slippage causes the water to travel away from the seismic event. Underwater 
landslides, land slumping into the ocean, volcanic eruptions, nuclear testing underwater and meteorite impacts 
can also generate tsunamis. The depth of the water controls the speed of a tsunami. As the wave approaches the 
land, the depth of the water becomes shallower and slows the wave – the rear of the wave is still in deeper water. 
This causes the water to build up height as well as ‘sucking’ the water from the shoreline.

searchText:
W.S.50. Types of rock.

Name .....

Rocks can be divided into three main types depending on how they were formed. Read
the information below about the three types of rock.

Igneous rocks.

These are formed when molten magma
cools down and becomes solid. They are
made of tiny crystals, If the magma cools
quickly on the surface of the Earth then
the crystals are small. If the magma cools
slowly, deeper in the Earth's crust, then
the crystals are larger. Igneous rocks are
very hard.

Sedimentary rocks.

These are made from layers of SEDIMENT
(small particles) on the bottom of rivers or
seas. The sediments are compressed as
more layers build up on top of them. The
particles then become cemented together
to form solid rocks, The layers of rock are
called STRATA. Sedimentary rocks have a
grainy structure and they easily crumble.

Metamorphic (changed) rocks.
These are formed from igneous or
sedimentary rocks which are changed
by heat or pressure deep underground.
They are usually harder than the rocks
that formed them.
