searchText: Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 1 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com VOLCANO! TEACHER’S GUIDE Volcano is a planetarium program designed to teach your students about some of the basic large-scale geologic history and workings of our planet Earth. The students will learn about different types of volcanoes, how they work, and their association with earthquakes and continental drift. Then we will venture beyond Earth into the Solar System, investigating volcanism on the Moon, Venus, Mars, Io and Triton. This Teacher’s Guide is designed to help you, the teacher, better prepare your students for their upcoming presentation of Volcano when the Northern Stars Planetarium visits your school. This guide contains background information for you and a few worksheets for you to copy and distribute to your students. PROGRAM OUTLINE I. Our Changing Planet: Continental Drift A. How the world used to look B. How the continents moved to where they are today. C. All Dome World Map showing all plates & faults & volcano sites II. Problems with continental drifting A. Earthquakes B. Friction – causing heat build-up – volcanoes III. The different types of Volcanoes A. Composite type (explosive). Example – Mount St. Helens B. Shield type (quiet). Example – Hawaiian volcanoes C. Why? Pent-up gases! IV. Lava A. Pahoehoe type flows B. Aa type flows C. The ash, bombs, cinders, and types of rocks V. Volcanoes on the Moon? VI. Volcanoes on Venus? VII. Olympus Mons – a Giant Volcano on Mars VIII. Io – the first actively erupting volcanoes found beyond Earth IX. Triton – an ice volcano? Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 2 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com VOCABULARY Ash Fine particles blown from volcanoes by explosive gas expansions that pulverize the frothing lava and solid rock into a fine dust. Basalt The type of rock that comprises nearly all lava. Caldera What we call volcanic craters over two kilometers in diameter. Composite Volcano An explosive type of volcano. These volcanoes characteristically have thick lava with a large amount of dissolved gases. The release of these gases creates great explosions. The primary gases are carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen, hydrogen sulfide and steam. Most volcanoes in the world are composite. Mount St. Helens is a good example. They typically have a cone shape. Core The center region of the Earth. It is composed primarily of very hot and heavy metals, mostly iron and nickel. It is twice as dense as the mantle. It is the main source of heat that causes the convection currents in the mantle. The outer core is molten and the inner core is solid. From the mantle to the center of the core is 2,100 miles. Earthquake The shaking, rumbling, and physical breaking and displacing of rock and soil due to the release of pressures within the crust. Fault line The line between two tectonic plates. These often mark areas of earthquakes and volcanoes. For example: The San Andreas Fault in California marks the boundary between the “Pacific Plate” and the “North American Plate.” Sometimes plates are separating, sometimes colliding, and sometimes they are sliding beside each other. Volcanoes tend to be explosive “Composite” volcanoes where plates collide and quieter “Shield” volcanoes where plates separate. Geyser Geysers are formed when groundwater is heated by an underlying body of hot magma. As the temperature increases in the water, pressure builds until the geyser blows. Geysers can be found near “hot spots” like Yellowstone or along “fault lines” like in Iceland. Hot Spot A place where a narrow plume of hot magma rises up through the mantle and the extra heat often creates a volcano or at least hot geo-thermal activities such as hot springs and geysers. Examples are Hawaii and Yellowstone Park. Volcanoes found here tend to be quiet “Shield” volcanoes. Igneous Rocks All volcanic rocks are igneous, but not all igneous rocks are volcanic. Igneous simply means that the rock formed from a liquid magma. Granite is igneous but not volcanic because it formed underground. Basalt, obsidian and pumice are igneous and volcanic – they all formed above ground after emerging from a volcano. Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 3 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com Lava The liquid or molten rock that comes from a volcano. When it flows, it takes one of two different forms of texture, though the composition remains the same. The two types are: Aa A course, rough, crumbly type of lava. It usually flows from a central river of molten rock, 25 to 40 feet wide, and travels anywhere from 3 to 35 miles per hour, depending on the inclination of the volcano’s slope. The aa oozes out of the flow on all sides, hardening to a very coarse basalt rock. The term “aa” is derived from the Hawaiians and is the accepted scientific term for this type of lava flow today. Pahoehoe A smooth, billowy, wrinkled type of solidified lava. When it flows, it is the most fluid form of lava. When a river of pahoehoe flows, it quickly hardens on top but continues to flow underneath; when the lava drains out from beneath the crust, it leaves a tunnel or “lava tube” behind. The term “pahoehoe” is derived from the Hawaiians and is the accepted scientific term for this type of lava flow today. Lava Tube A tunnel that is left behind from a lava flow. They form from pahoehoe flows where the lava solidified on top but keeps flowing underneath. When the flow runs out, the lava tube is left empty. Mantle A thicker and denser part of Earth below the crust. The mantle slowly moves due to convection currents of heat working up from the core below. This convection is what makes the crustal plates slowly move about. The mantle is about 1800 miles thick. Obsidian A glassy rock formed from rapidly cooled, thick lava. Pele The Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes and fire. Plate Tectonics The idea that Earth’s crust is made of large continent-sized plates that float about on convection currents in the mantle. Therefore, our planet did not always look the way it does today, nor will it in the future because the continents are moving. Pumice A glassy, volcanic rock, similar to obsidian, but so full of gas bubbles that it will float on water. It forms from the rapid cooling of frothing, thick lava. Ring of Fire The series of faults that surround the Pacific Plate. It is collectively so named because of the large number of volcanoes found along it. Shield Volcano A less-explosive type of volcano. These volcanoes characteristically have a lower gas content and more liquid lava. The volcanoes of Hawaii are typical. The name is derived from their resemblance to a large shield laying on the ground. Tsunami A tidal wave caused by volcanic eruption or earthquake. Volcanology The scientific study of volcanoes and the reasons they erupt. Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 4 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com STUDY QUESTIONS 1. Explain the difference between “Composite” and “Shield” types of volcanoes. (Composites are explosive, Shields are quiet.) 2. What’s the difference between an active volcano and an extinct volcano? (Any volcano that has erupted within historic times – the last 5-10 thousand years – is considered active. This may be a long time in human terms, but not in geologic terms.) 3. The largest volcano on Earth, Mauna Kea in Hawaii, from base to summit is over 33,000 feet tall, while Mt. Everest from base to summit is only 29,000 feet tall. Why then do we say Mt. Everest is the world’s tallest mountain when Mauna Kea is over 4,000 feet higher? (Because the base of the two mountains are located at different levels. Mauna Kea’s base is on the ocean floor, while Mt. Everest’s base is measured from sea level. If we measure Mauna Kea’s height from sea level, it is only 14,000 feet tall. ) 4. Are there any remains of volcanoes in the State of Maine? (Yes) Where? (Traveller Mountain in Baxter State Park, Quoggy Joe Mountain in Presque Isle, and Haystack Mountain in Mapleton. Mt. Kineo in Moosehead Lake. Mt. Katahdin is not volcanic.) TRUE OR FALSE 1. The Earth is the only planet in our Solar System to have volcanoes. (F) 2. The Hawaiian volcano of Kilauea has thrown lava nearly 2,000 feet into the air. (T) 3. There are over one thousand active volcanoes on Earth. (F – only 600) 4. There are between ten and thirty volcanic eruptions each year. (T) 5. When Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, it was the largest volcanic eruption in the last two hundred years. (F) 6. Mount St. Helens exploded with such force that it threw ash over twelve miles high into the air. (T) 7. When the volcano named Krakatoa erupted in 1883 in the South Pacific, it was so loud it could be heard 3,000 miles away. (T) 8. Tsunamis can travel faster than the average jet plane. (T – over 600 m.p.h.) 9. Molten lava has a temperature of 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit. (F – the hottest measure temperature was 2,200 degrees F, which is 12 times hotter than boiling water.) 10. Pumice is a type of volcanic rock that can float on water. (T – as a matter of fact, large rafts of pumice floating in the ocean were once reported as “floating islands.”) Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 5 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com FAULT LINES AND HOT SPOTS Sliding Plates Sometimes two plates will slide past each other horizontally. This is a powerful source for earthquakes. An example would be the San Andreas Fault in California. Colliding Plates Sometimes two plates will collide head-on, crumbling the front edges and creating large mountains. An example would be the Himalayas, which formed when India collided with Asia. Separating Plates When two plates move apart, it allows hot magma to ooze up from the crack. It then hardens and makes new crust. Shield volcanoes usually form here. An example is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is separating, slowing making the Atlantic Ocean wider, as well as forming some islands, such as Iceland. Subducting Plates Sometimes when one plate collides with another, one will “subduct” or go under the other. When it goes underneath, the heat and friction melt the crust that is going underneath. This usually creates composite volcanoes. Mount St. Helens is a good example. Hot Spot Sometimes a narrow plume of magma rises up through the mantle, making a “hot spot” underneath a plate. It if is close enough to the crust, it can create shield volcanoes, like in Hawaii. If it is deeper, it can make geysers and geo-thermal heat, as we find in Yellowstone Park. Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 6 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com THE EARTH’S INTERIOR (not drawn to scale) Crust (22 miles thick) Mantle (1,800 miles thick) Core (2,100 miles thick) UNDERSTANDING TECTONIC PROJECT 1. Plate Tectonics: After your students have gained a basic understanding of how Earth’s crust is divided into plates roughly equivalent to the continents, give your students a copy of the world map below. Explain to them that at one time, all the continents were crammed together into one giant continent that scientists call Pangea. Have they cut the continents out and try to imagine how they might have once fitted together. (For a correct view of Pangea, see next page.) Then, using the map on the next page showing the directions the continents are moving, have your students predict how the world will one day look in the future. Volcano! Teacher’s Guide Northern Stars Planetarium Page 7 P.O. Box 302, Fairfield, ME 04937 207-453-7668 www.northern-stars.com info@northern-stars.com THE ANCIENT CONTINENT OF PANGEA Earth: 2

searchText: ﻿VOLCANOES Complete the following activities neatly using full sentence answers. 1) Using a dictionary define volcano. 2) Is this event natural or artificial? 3) Describe what causes a volcano. You may use Science Quest 9, page 293 to assist you with your answer. 4) What effect does a volcano have on the living and non-living environment? 5) Define disaster using a dictionary. Is a volcanic eruption only a disaster if it effects people in a significant way? This is your own opinion. 6) Are there any good effects of a volcanic eruption? 7) Now read the extract below and re-visit Question 6. Friends or Foes Millions of people all around the world live with volcanoes and most of these people benefit from having these restless neighbours. In Hawaii, hundreds of people visit the steaming volcanoes every day. In tropical areas such as Indonesia, the hardened volcanic rock quickly weathers into a rich soil. Rice plantations on volcanic soil can often yield two or three crops of rice a year. Building and road-making materials are often made from volcanic rock.

searchText: What Are Minerals – Teacher Notes Minerals are natural materials which are: (1) inorganic (not created by living things); (2) have a consistent chemical composition; and (3) when solid have constant crystal structures. Inorganic Minerals are inorganic. What is the definition of inorganic? (hint: it doesn’t have anything to do with the ‘organic’ vegetables you can buy at the grocery.) Inorganic broadly means not created by or consisting of living matter. In chemistry, it also means something doesn’t contain the element carbon. Gallstones form in your gallbladder, which is part of your digestive system. Digestive fluid from the liver containing varying amounts of salt, cholesterol, calcium or bilirubin crystallises and makes rocks! These rocks can be as small as a grain of sand, or as large as a plum. They can block the bile outlet and cause pain. Most people do not know they have them until they start to feel pain. Are gallstones minerals? Explain your answer. No. The come from a living thing, and they have varying chemical composition Consistent Chemical Composition A mineral is made of the same combination of elements no matter when or where in the world it was formed. This combination of elements (or composition) is like the ingredients in a cake; every chocolate cake needs flour, water, eggs, and –of course – chocolate. The ratio (the amount of one thing compared to the amount of another thing) of ingredients is also very important; if you had 2kg of chocolate compared to 1 gram of flour, you wouldn’t have a cake! Similarly, every piece of quartz in the world contains silicon and oxygen in specific ratios. We write down the chemical composition in what are called mineral formula. In the table are some common minerals and their formulae. With the help of a periodic table, list the elements present in each mineral. Minerals Mineral Formula List of Elements Quartz SiO2 Silicon and oxygen Potassium Feldspar KAlSi3O8 Potassium, aluminium, silicon and oxygen Calcite CaCO3 Calcium, carbon and oxygen Gypsum CaSO Calcium, sulphur and oxygen Diamond C Carbon Kaolinite (a type of clay) Al2Si2O5(OH)4 Aluminium, silicon, oxygen and hydrogen Biotite (a type of mica) KMg2AlSi2O10(OH)2 Potassium, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, oxygen and hydrogen An initiative supported by Woodside and ESWA What Are Minerals – Teacher Notes Constant Crystalline Structures Minerals form crystals. These crystals are the same shape no matter what size the mineral is – a piece of halite has the same structure no matter the size. In the pictures of halite crystals to the right, notice the similarities between the microscopic crystals and the huge crystals. A mineral’s crystalline structure depends on the atoms it contains. Atoms form bonds that link them together, but in specific arrangements due to the Halite (NaCl) crystals under a microscope different sizes of different atoms. As you move from left to right on the periodic table, the radius of atoms shrink. Halite crystals in a cave in Germany. Notice the man wearing a white hardhat in the bottom left corner for scale. Above is a model of the atomic crystal structure of calcite (CaCO3) which uses white, black, and red balls to represent the atoms of different elements, and silver bars to represent the bonds between atoms. Which colour balls represent which atoms? Coloured balls in the model Elements in calcite white Calcium (largest element in calcite) black Carbon red Oxygen (smallest element in calcite) An initiative supported by Woodside and ESWA What Are Minerals – Teacher Notes Same composition, different crystal structure Diamond is a mineral made of pure carbon, and is one of the hardest, most durable minerals on the planet. Graphite – often used as pencil lead – is one of the softest minerals; it is easily rubbed off onto paper, which is why we use it in pencils. Graphite is also made of pure carbon. The only difference between diamond and graphite is their crystal structures. Which crystal structure belongs to which mineral? Why might that crystal structure make the mineral hard or soft? Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
31
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resources and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Contact with Indigenous 
Australians’, with the students. Explain to the students 
that there were also other visitors who are not listed in 
the table. Discuss the reasons why European nations 
wanted to expand their territory by colonising other 
places. Then have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Exploring Australia’. They will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Discovering Australia’, to complete this 
activity. To extend the activity, you could have students 
list further factors that would be important to the first 
British settlers in sourcing food, water and shelter.
Have students read the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous 
contact with Europeans (1)’. Discuss the concept 
of terra nullius and what happened to Australia’s 
original inhabitants as a result. Explain that this was the 
beginning of a radical change in lifestyle for Indigenous 
people. Then have students complete the Activity 
sheet, ‘Indigenous contact with Europeans (2)’. 
extension activity
l  Read about Governor Bourke’s 1835 Proclamation of 
Terra Nullius with the class at: 
http://www.migrationheritage.nsw.gov.au, then use 
the website’s search option with the key term: terra 
nullius. 
 
 The web page provides information about the 
social and political context in both Britain and 
Australia around the time of European occupation. 
It also discusses the fact that not all British people 
supported the way Australia was colonised. 
l  Lead a class discussion about the meaning of and 
connotations of the terms ‘invaded’ and ‘colonised’. 
Discuss whether the Europeans invaded or colonised 
Australia, and encourage students to give reasons for 
their opinions.
Teacher’s notes – European contact with  
Indigenous Australians
Objectives
l To understand that Europeans colonised other 
places because they wanted resources
l To appreciate the impact of colonisation on the 
Indigenous inhabitants of Australia
l To undertake mapping and interpretative tasks
Prior knowledge
Students should have some knowledge of 
migration to Australia from 1788 to the present, 
including the varying attitudes towards new arrivals.
Background
The first visitors to Northern Australia were the 
Macassans from modern-day Indonesia. They were 
searching for trepang (sea cucumbers) and traded 
with the Indigenous people. Signs of their presence 
remain in the Macassan words still present in 
Indigenous languages in the north. 
 
During the 16th to 18th centuries, Europeans 
explored the world in search of resources. Explorers 
who encountered the west coast of Australia found it 
inhospitable. 
 
Australia was the only British colony that was 
subject to the ruling of terra nullius (land belonging 
to no one), which contributed to the extreme 
disadvantage experienced by Indigenous Australians.
Starter activity
Discuss what students know about the first explorers 
to Australia, where they came from and why. Then 
develop a class list of different reasons why people 
want to come to Australia to live. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

How were landforms created? 
Indigenous explanation
Geological explanation
Uluru, Northern Territory
The south side resulted from a battle between 
the Liru, the poisonous snakes, and the Kunia, 
the carpet snakes. 
Hard sandstone rock was laid down under 
the sea millions of years ago. The surrounding 
softer material has been worn away over time, 
leaving the monolith, Uluru.
Kandimal (Wolfe Creek Crater), Western Australia
Two Rainbow Snakes moved across the 
country, carving the paths of Stuart Creek 
and Wolfe Creek. The crater formed where the 
snakes came out of the earth.
Wolfe Creek Crater is the second biggest 
meteorite crater in the world. The meteorite 
hit the earth 2 million years ago.
Lake Eyre, South Australia 
Wikuda, a young boy, chased a white kangaroo 
and speared it. Wikuda put the skin down east 
of Anna Creek. The skin became Lake Eyre.
Once covered by the sea, Lake Eyre is now 15 
metres below sea level and salty. The wind has 
removed the sand. Now water flows in from 
the Diamantina River and Cooper Creek. 
Buda-dji (Barron Gorge), Queensland
Buda-dji, shaped like a carpet snake, carved 
out the famous gorge. 
Formed by the River Barron cutting down 
through the escarpment on its path to 
the sea.
Murray River, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia
Pondi the Murray cod was chased by the 
Ngurenderi the hunter from New South Wales 
to Lake Alexandrina, making the bends and 
banks of the river as he dodged and weaved 
his way.
The source of the river is a spring near  
Mt Kosciuszko. The river collects water from 
the tributaries as it flow to the sea through 
the mouth of the river, in South Australia.
The Three Sisters, New South Wales
Three sisters, Meenhi, Wimlah and Gunnedoo, 
were turned to stone as punishment for 
meeting three men they were not supposed 
to see. 
Sand was deposited in the sea where it 
hardened into sandstone. The land was 
uplifted and the sandstone was worn away by 
rain and wind, leaving the three rocks.

Understanding our origins
 
●It is believed that Australia’s Indigenous people came to Australia 
through South-East Asia. The first human migration was probably 
when Australia was part of the Sahul land mass. However, there 
were still large areas of water, so people needed boats or rafts to 
get from Sunda to Sahul. These people may have come via  
modern-day Malaysia.
 
●Indigenous Australians are the original inhabitants of Australia 
and its nearby islands. Indigenous people who live on the 
Australian mainland, Tasmania and islands such as Flinders Island 
and King Island are often called ‘Aboriginal’. The Indigenous 
people who inhabit islands near Cape York are called Torres  
Strait Islanders.
 
●The oldest Aboriginal remains were those of Mungo Man, found 
near Lake Mungo in New South Wales. Mungo Man is believed to 
be about 50 000 years old.
 
●Humans reached Tasmania about 40 000 years ago by travelling 
across a land bridge from the mainland. About 12 000 years ago, 
the glacial ice melted and the sea level rose to present-day levels, 
creating Bass Strait. The people in Tasmania were isolated from the 
mainland until European settlers arrived.

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
42
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Children
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution. An understanding of the factory 
system may be useful for understanding child labour.
Background
The position of children in Victorian society changed 
over time. At first, they were often seen as additional 
labour within the family. Most people lived on farms 
and having many children who could all work was 
valuable. However, there was less need for large 
families as people moved away from farms or became 
tenant farmers. At the time, people could not plan or 
restrict pregnancies so the population continued to 
grow. From a young age, children were often employed 
in factories or mines to supplement their parents’ 
wages. Sometimes it was easier for children to get jobs 
because they were cheaper to hire. 
When parents were employed and children weren’t, 
there were concerns about who would look after 
the children. Some families could rely on relatives or 
friends. However, many children were left to fend for 
themselves during the day, or at night if their parents 
worked night shifts. 
Governments in Britain and Australia decided that 
education might prevent these independent and 
unmonitored children from joining criminal gangs. 
They began developing education departments and 
systems to meet this need. 
Starter activity
Watch the documentary The Children who built 
Victorian Britain, BBC, 2007. It has good descriptions 
of the experiences of children during the Industrial 
Revolution. It’s great to watch by itself or you could 
pause it at regular intervals for students to take notes.  
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Education’, looks at the introduction 
of the education system in Australia and Britain. 
Students complete the information by crossing out the 
incorrect word in each set of brackets. Then students 
use that information to complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Education for all?’. Here, they consider the perspectives 
of different groups on aspects of education. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Child labourers’, provides students 
with an understanding of life as a child labourer in the 
industrial period. They use this information to complete 
the Activity sheet, ‘Plan a story’, where they plan a story 
about children during the industrial period.  
Extension activities
• 
 Work with the students to compile a table 
comparing children’s lives in modern times to 
children’s lives in the industrial period. You could 
include aspects such as education, housing, work, 
family life and ages for specific activities such as 
marriage and voting. 
• 
 Have students write a paragraph outlining what 
they appreciate most about today’s lifestyle.
• 
 As a class, read a passage from Oliver Twist by 
Charles Dickens (1812–1870). It is about a poor boy 
who lives in a workhouse and is then sold into a 
parish apprenticeship. Students may find Dickens’ 
language inaccessible; there are many movie 
adaptations available.
Objectives
• Understand the unique perspective of children 
during the Industrial Revolution
• Consider different perspectives on the same 
situation
• Use empathy to help create a narrative that 
demonstrates historical knowledge

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
45
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Resource sheet – Children
Child labourers
Factory lives
In the industrial period, many people moved to the cities to work in factories. Factory wages 
were low. This meant that everyone in the family, including young children, often had to work 
to help the family survive. The conditions in factories were harsh. 
• Children could start working at the age of five years.
• The work was boring and repetitive.
• They worked long hours, sometimes 14 or 16 hours a day.
• Overseers beat children who did not work fast enough.
•  Children lost arms and legs or died if they got trapped in 
the machinery. 
Workhouses
Some orphans and poor people were kept in places called 
workhouses. The people there were often separated from 
their family members. They were given very little food 
and worked very hard. Friedrich Engels called workhouses 
‘Poor Law Bastilles’. This meant he thought they were prisons 
for the poor.
Parish apprentices
Church parishes were made up of people who lived in the 
same area, and were led by a priest. The parish had to look 
after the poor in their community. This included children 
who were orphans or half-orphans, which meant they had 
only one parent. The parish helped the children find jobs 
by sending them out as apprentices to be taught useful 
skills. The children were fed and clothed for their work, but 
rarely paid. The masters took them as a charitable act. If the 
masters refused to take the children, they had to pay the 
parish a fine. 
Elizabeth Bentley began 
work at a flax mill when she 
was 6 years old. On busy 
days, she worked from 5 am 
to 9 pm. That’s 16 hours, 
with only a 40 minute break 
for lunch.
One boy, George Orange from Leeds, was taken and returned almost weekly. 
This made his parish a good amount of money through fines.
Friedrich Engels was a rich 
German. His father owned 
factories in England, but he 
didn’t want to be a factory 
owner. Instead, he wrote 
about the experiences of 
the working class.

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
46
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017

Plan a story

for a story about children during the industrial period. 
Structure of a story
• Introduction: introduce the people, location and time; hint at a problem to come.
• Complication: expand on the problem that needs to be solved.
• Resolution: have your characters solve the problem.

Education
+  Cross out the incorrect word in each set of brackets.
Before the Industrial Revolution, only upper and middle class (children / child) went to 
school or were tutored. (Pour / Poor) children learned how to work from (there / their) 
parents or became apprentices to a master to learn a trade. Masters did not pay wages to 
apprentices because they were learning, but usually provided food and (housing / house).
In the 1830s, governments in Britain and Australia became concerned that children 
(were / where) becoming criminals because they were not (been / being) educated. 
They were also left unsupervised all day while their parents worked.
In Australia, governments established schools (too / to) educate children. Some religious 
groups like the Catholics and Anglicans also established schools. School wasn’t compulsory, 
so some parents kept (their / they’re) children at home when they needed them to work.
Students usually learned English, Arithmetic, Geography and 
History. Boys (were / we’re) sometimes taught Latin, while 
girls were usually taught sewing and knitting. Students often 
learned by repetition, to teach them obedience.
Children who did well at school could apply to be pupil teachers 
when they finished their schooling. They assisted for (two / to) 
years and (by / buy) the age of 15 they could be teachers.
In 1872, Victoria became the first Australian colony 
to make education free, secular and compulsory. This 
meant that children did not have to pay, no religion 
controlled what (were / was) studied, and all children 
had to attend. Society now (thought / taught) that it 
was more important for children to study than work.
Schooling became compulsory in Scotland in 
1872 and in Britain in 1880. Compulsory education 
reduced the number of child workers. Most children 
(know / now) began work when they were 12.
Every morning we repeat our 
times tables as a class. T he 
teacher says it helps us to learn 
the numbers. T hen we write 
the alphabet on our boards. 
It has to look exactly like the 
way the teacher writes it. 
If we forget our numbers or if 
our writing is not neat, we get 
hit to make us remember.

ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
47
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Different groups in society
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
Racism was a significant element of society in the 
1800s. These xenophobic attitudes were connected to a 
newly developed sense of nationalism. This meant that 
a country was becoming more than the place you lived 
– it was an emblematic symbol of your identity. This led 
to an easy acceptance of imperialist attitudes in which 
the country controlling an Empire, such as Britain, 
valued themselves and their abilities over those of the 
people in the colonies they invaded and controlled. 
Imperial European countries and their cultures were 
more valuable than those of other countries.
In colonies such as Australia, these racist attitudes 
were expressed through the treatment of Indigenous 
Australian peoples as lesser beings, and their land 
being classifed as terra nullius or ‘empty land’. This 
devaluing and dehumanising treatment of Indigenous 
Australian peoples led to the discriminatory 
experiences of reservations, loss of citizenship, stolen 
generations and numerous other indignities both small 
and large.
Groups such as the Jews and the Irish were also 
discriminated against, even when they lived in 
European countries or in Britain. Negative stereotypes 
were applied to the ‘national’ or ‘racial’ identities of 
these groups, regardless of how little these stereotypes 
actually resembled the individuals and their 
communities. This view of ‘them’ and ‘us’ helped to form 
national connections but it also led to racist actions 
which negatively impacted on the persecuted groups.
Another significant development of the industrial 
period was the emergence of the middle class as a 
significant and powerful group. Previously, there was 
an upper class and a lower class. The technological 
changes of the industrial period resulted in a 
professional class of people such as teachers, lawyers 
and doctors. This middle class became significant, 
dominating understandings of culture, national 
identity and literature.
Starter activity
Ask the students to consider how our society treats 
different groups; for example, children, teenagers, 
migrants, disabled people and older people. How are 
these groups seen and how are they treated?
Discuss the power of stereotypes and the impact they 
can have on the way people are treated.
Resource and Activity sheets
On the Activity sheet, ‘Social hierarchies’, students use 
a Venn diagram to identify similarities and differences 
between the social hierarchies of the Middle Ages and 
the industrial period. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous Australian people’, 
shows a primary source illustration of an Indigenous 
Australian family in the first years of European 
settlement. Students use the Activity sheet, ‘Source 
analysis’, to guide them through the process of 
analysing the illustration. They are encouraged to 
consider different features of the image and how they 
help with understanding the values of the person 
who drew the source, as well as providing a stronger 
understanding of the socio-historical context. Make 
sure the students understand that bias means that a 
persons shows a prejudice towards (likes or dislikes) a 
group of people.
The Activity sheet, ‘The Irish’, informs students about 
how the English viewed Irish people during this time. 
Students add the missing vowels to complete the 
information, then consider three primary sources. On 
the Activity sheet, ‘Stereotypes and beliefs’, students are 
guided through the process of analysing these three 
primary sources. 
Extension activities
Have students work in small groups to research another 
group persecuted during this time period; for example, 
Africans, Jews, women in Australia and/or Britain, or the 
Chinese in Australia.
Ask students to find quotes and images that show 
how society viewed these different groups. Discuss the 
values these attitudes show.
Objectives
• Gain an understanding of how different groups 
in society were seen and treated
• Consider the impact that certain differences 
could have on the experiences of people who 
lived at that time 
• Consider how the industrial period may have 
changed different groups

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
12
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Factories
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
The Industrial Revolution can be considered to have 
begun with inventors who wanted to make products 
faster and easier. Technological developments were 
often resisted by the local skilled workers. The workers 
tried to sabotage the new machines and attack the 
inventors because skilled labour would no longer be 
needed to make quality products. These workers were 
trying to protect their livelihoods. 
Wealthy people often valued these new inventions 
because they made it possible to start factories. With 
these new machines and cheap unskilled labour, many 
products could be made at a discounted price, and 
then sold for a good profit. Many middle class and 
upper class people could now afford to buy these 
new factory products. But the lives of the lower class 
became far more difficult and precarious. Working 
in factories and coal mines was dangerous, dirty and 
unhealthy work. Many laboured for long hours for six 
or seven days each week. If they had a day off, it was 
usually on Sunday and they were expected to attend 
church. Family life became more complicated as 
children often had to work in the factories from a very 
young age to help support the family. 
In response, many men banded together to protect 
their working rights in the new trade unions. These 
trade unions took longer to become successful in 
places like England where the class system was 
entrenched. However, Australia was often described 
as a ‘working man’s paradise’ and moved quickly to 
adopt trade unions. They became a usual part of the 
Australian working experience and, later, political 
experience.
Starter activity
Show students images of inventions from the Industrial 
Revolution, such as the spinning jenny, cotton gin, 
sewing machine, telegraph and steam engine. 
Ask questions about the images and have students 
give reasons for their answers. 
• What do they look like?
• What might they do? How do you know?
• Why might they be important in that time? 
Repeat the activity with images of factory and coal 
workers from the same period. 
• How do you think they live?
• What were their living conditions probably like?
Discuss as a group what these images tell us about the 
Industrial Revolution.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Textiles workers’, provides an 
overview of the impacts of inventions in the textiles 
industry. All people with a first and last name are real 
people, with text referring to their lives. Those people 
with initials as surnames are fictionalised characters 
whose dialogue is based on historical facts. Students 
will use this information to complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Continuity and change’, where they consider the 
positive and negative aspects of inventions.
The Activity sheet, ‘Coal mining’, explores mining 
developments. From this information and a primary 
source – the testimony of Betty Harris – students learn 
about the effects of these developments.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Factories’, students consider how 
factories affected cottage industries. They also explore 
the new working environments of factory workers. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Australian and British trade unions’, 
looks at the different experiences of workers fighting 
for their rights in Australia and Britain.
Extension ideas
Have students explore primary sources relating to the 
lives of workers. They should choose one source and 
analyse it in terms of what it tells them about everyday 
life in that time. Here are two useful websites:
•  http://www.victorianweb.org/history/workers1.html
•  http://www.historyteacher.net/APEuroCourse/
WebLinks/WebLinks-IndustrialRevolution.htm
Objectives
• Learn about key inventions in the industrial 
period
• Consider the impacts of these inventions on 
the development of factories and the lives of 
the workers
• Explore the rise of the trade union movement 
in response to the expansion of factories
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.

Activity sheet – Factories
Coal mining
+  Read the information and answer the questions below.
Coal mining became more important during the Industrial Revolution, because coal was 
a more efficient fuel than wood. Steam engines used coal for fuel. These engines powered 
machines in factories, trains and steamships.
Families often worked together in a colliery (coal mine). Fathers and sons cut or ‘hewed’ the 
coal from the stone. Mothers and daughters carried or ‘hurried’ the coal through the pit.
A load of coal weighed up to 150 kg. Sometimes it was so hot and dirty in the pits that miners 
worked naked. In 1842, the British government passed the Mines Act which banned boys under 
the age of ten and women and girls from working underground.
1 What is Betty’s job called? What did her job involve?
 
 
2  What does Betty mean by ‘the family way’? How would this affect her ability to work?
 
 
 
 
3  How do you think Betty’s story contributed to the introduction of the Mines Act in 1842?
 
 
 
 
Betty Harris, age 37 years, to the 1840 Royal Commission into mines
I was married at 23, and went into a colliery when I was married … I 
am a drawer, and work from 6 in the morning to 6 at night. Stop about an 
hour at noon to eat my dinner; have bread and butter for dinner; I get 
no drink … I worked at drawing when I was in the family way. I have a 
belt round my waist, and a chain passing between my legs, and I go on my 
hands and feet. T he road is very steep, and we have to hold by a rope; and 
when there is no rope, by anything we can catch hold of … My clothes are 
wet through almost all day long … the belt and chain is worse when we are 
in the family way. My feller (husband) has beaten me many a time for not 
being ready. I were not used to it at first, and he had little patience.
Great Britain, Parliamentary Papers, 1842, Vol. XV, p.84

24
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Land
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution. 
Background
Before the Industrial Revolution, land was used the 
same way for centuries. During the Medieval period, 
farming land was organised by the village. They 
distributed land to the farmers and rotated it regularly 
so that people were not stuck with poor farm land all 
the time. In order to keep the land fertile, medieval 
farmers used the three-field system. This involved 
ploughing two fields and leaving one field fallow 
(unused) and then rotating fields each year for three 
years. 
During the Industrial Revolution, farming changed 
dramatically. New machinery meant less human 
labour was needed. The land was also fenced in due to 
‘enclosure laws’. This meant that the village no longer 
shared and rotated the land used by the farmers in the 
area. Instead, fields were owned by individuals. The 
owners of the rich, fertile fields grew richer and could 
buy more land. The owners of arid or infertile land 
became poorer. Many had to leave when they could no 
longer afford to own land.
Some people chose to move to Australia as settlers. 
Others were transported to Australia for committing 
crimes. Some of these crimes, such as ‘being homeless’ 
and ‘associating with bad people’, are not what we 
consider to be crimes today. 
Australia was a land rapidly changing from the natural 
to the developed as settlers took land from the 
Indigenous Australian peoples. They built cities and 
towns on the sites of regular Indigenous Australian 
camping locations. The names of the colonies of 
Australia changed regularly, reflecting these changing 
stages: 
• Indigenous Australian peoples and their culture 
• penal colonies
•  a nation of bush people with the first European 
settlers
• a place of impossible riches with the gold rush
• a working man’s paradise for the new working class
• a federated country
all within the industrial period.
Starter activity
Discuss how we use land today; for example, 
‘McMansions’, living in capital cities, multistorey 
apartment buildings. Then consider how land was used 
100 or 200 years ago; for example, smaller houses for 
larger families with gardens to grow food, more people 
living in rural areas. As a class, make a Venn diagram to 
show the similarities and differences.
Resource and Activity sheets
On the Activity sheet, ‘Advances in agriculture’, students 
complete a cloze activity to find out how the Industrial 
Revolution impacted on agricultural life. 
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Country or city’, 
students consider why people moved between 
the city and the country, and the advantages and 
disadvantages of each lifestyle.  
The Resource sheet, ‘The Pioneer’, has an image of 
Frederick McCubbin’s famous painting. Students use 
this image to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Landscapes 
of Australia’. Through analysing this painting they 
explore the changing view of Victoria from first 
settlement to a generation later.
The Activity sheet, ‘Changing Australia’, uses maps of 
Australia and its various colonies, states and territories 
to look at how European settlement of Australia 
changed over time. 
Extension activities
Provide maps, posters, paintings or photographs 
of your town or city from different time periods; 
for example, now, 50 years ago, 100 years ago and 
150 years ago. Websites such as http://trove.nla.gov.au, 
state libraries and local history groups may be useful in 
sourcing these images.  
Discuss with the class the changes over time shown by 
the images. 
Objectives
• Understand how the use of geographical 
regions changed over time
• Consider how land was used by different 
people and how that use affected population 
movements
• Analyse images to improve understanding of 
the historical time period 
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.

36
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Men
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution. They will benefit from knowing 
what suffrage is and who suffragettes were.
Background
The position of men in society underwent significant 
changes during the Industrial Revolution. Previously, 
a man was unquestionably the head of his household. 
Often all members of a family worked, but it was the 
man’s skilled labour that brought in the most money. 
With the move from skilled labour to mechanisation 
brought by the Industrial Revolution, skilled males 
became less valuable. Factory owners wanted cheap 
labourers to work with the machines in their factories. 
Women and children were cheaper than men, so were 
hired more often. An increasing number of fit and 
able men became subject to the Poor Law restrictions 
because they were could not find jobs to support their 
families. 
The Chartist movements in Britain (1838–1858) 
brought about discussions of universal male suffrage. 
People no longer believed that only rich men who 
owned property deserved the right to vote and be 
represented in parliament. In the late 19th century, 
there was also the suffragette movement pushing 
for women to have the vote. This also challenged 
the male social identity as the dominant, intelligent, 
knowledgeable gender. The conflict between the 
traditional idea of the strong man and the actual social 
reality was problematic for many men.
Starter activity
Present the following wage information to the class. 
• 
 Men usually earned 10–15 shillings a week
• 
Women usually earned 5 shillings a week
• 
Children usually earned 1 shilling a week 
Have the students consider which worker would be 
seen as more valuable in these situations:
• 
 A factory owner who is keen to spend no more than 
100 shillings a week staffing his factory. 
• 
 A family (mother, father and three children) who 
need to pay rent at approximately 5 shillings a 
month. 
Discuss the conflict between the needs of families and 
the needs of factory owners.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘The Poor Laws’, explores changes in 
the way that poor people were provided for. Students 
copy and complete comprehension questions for each 
section.
The Resource sheet, ‘Society’s expectations’, identifies  
differences between social expectations of men 
and the reality of men’s experiences. Students use 
this information to complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Expectations versus reality’, by writing third person and 
first person perspectives on how men lived. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Chartists’, discusses the movement 
that pushed for all men, including those who were 
poor, to have a say in how the country was governed. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Questioning voting’, students 
are guided through the process of writing complex 
questions about the Chartist movement. Then they 
choose one of these questions to answer. 
Extension activities
Have students research a famous Australian man 
who lived in the 1800s. Suggestions: Henry Lawson, 
Barcroft Henry Boake, Ned Kelly, Frederick McCubbin, 
Banjo Patterson, Edmund Barton, Alfred Deakin. 
Ask students to identify the ways this man fits what 
society expected of men at the time; for example, 
being the breadwinner, heterosexual, head of the 
house, married, strong and emotionless. Also identify 
the ways in which he did not fit this expected role; 
for example, being homosexual, intellectual, a carer, 
emotional or supported financially by a partner. 
Objectives
• Understand the social concept of masculinity
• Identify how the position of men changed 
during the Industrial Revolution
• Consider the importance of all men having the 
right to vote

Resource sheet – Men
Society’s expectations
The Industrial Revolution was a time of significant change for men. Some men became 
powerful with the development of factories. But in many ways, the traditional ideas about men 
and masculinity were challenged by the new ideas and practices of the Industrial Revolution. 
Society’s expectations of men
Reality for men
• Be the breadwinner
•  Be the only worker outside the 
house 
• Support his family
Many lower class men were unemployed because 
their wages were too expensive, compared to 
women’s and children’s wages. 
Women and children often became family 
breadwinners.
•  Head of the household
•  In charge of everything that 
happens
• Make all the decisions
Many women were the family breadwinners. This 
gave them more decision-making power. 
The suffragette movement pushing for women to 
have the vote threatened the position of men as 
head of the household.
•  Handle all situations with strength, 
showing no emotion
Men were expected to show no emotion, even 
though they had feelings like everyone else. This 
made them feel distant from their families because 
they couldn’t be honest with them about the 
problems they had.
• Heterosexual
•  All serious and responsible men 
are married
There had always been homosexuals in society. 
But in the 1800s, social change led to a growing 
awareness of homosexuality which only increased 
as more men and women expressed their true 
preferences. Homosexuality was against the law in 
many countries at the time.
•  Physically strong
•  Always stronger then women 
and children
Many physically strong, lower class men were 
unemployed. Therefore, their physical strength was 
not so valuable. Many middle class men worked in 
businesses where they did little physical labour. This 
did not fit with society’s expectation that they be 
physically strong.

40
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Chartists
The Chartist movement was a group of men, 
mostly working class, who wanted to change 
how the British government worked. But since 
they could not vote in elections, how could they 
change the government? Rich men who owned 
property could vote. They were usually from 
noble families. Poor men, women and children 
could not vote.
In 1838, the Chartists created a ‘People’s Charter’ 
to identify the rights they wanted. 
Rights from the People’s Charter
•  Full male suffrage – all males vote, 
whether they own property or not.
•  Secret ballot – people vote secretly so 
government ministers can’t mistreat 
people who didn’t vote for them.
•  Pay for parliamentarians, so poor people 
can afford to be parliamentarians too.
•  Equal-size electorates – one small district 
should not have more power than a 
large district.
•  Annual elections – people can change

59
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – New ideas
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
The 1700s and 1800s were a highly significant 
period when many new ideas emerged, including 
republicanism, liberalism and secularism. Sometimes 
this period is described as the Enlightenment. 
Emerging ideas challenged the status quo and 
allowed for the development of even more new ideas. 
The scientific approach of Enlightenment thinkers 
introduced a new focus on empirical learning and 
thinking. This paved the way for Darwin’s theory of the 
evolution of the species and later, and less admirably, 
social Darwinism.
This period was also significant for its development 
of national and imperial identities. Many European 
countries valued themselves and their successes based 
on their racial or national qualities. The governments of 
these countries saw value in extending their empires 
by invading other countries, particularly in Asia, Africa 
and the Americas, and turning them into colonies. The 
colonies and their people were seen as lesser in value 
and treated accordingly.
As the industrial period continued, the plight of the 
poor working class became more apparent. Social 
philosophers such as Friedrich Engels and Karl Marx 
began challenging society by outlining the idea of a 
new ‘communist’ society that could arise in the future 
after the Industrial classes rebelled and overthrew the 
class-based ruling system. 
Starter activity
Compile a class mind map summarising the social 
situation during the Industrial Revolution: poor 
working conditions, long hours, mistreatment of 
children, beatings and disregard for the poor. 
Ask the students to imagine that they lived during that 
time. 
• 
 What ideas do they have about changing their 
world?
• 
 What would be a perfect world for poor people? 
• 
 What would be a perfect world for rich people?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘New ideas and movements,’ asks 
students to match names with definitions for the key 
ideas and movements emerging during the 1700s 
and 1800s. Students then consider these ideas and 
movements and choose one historical person to 
research. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Communism’, informs students 
about the philosophers who developed the idea of 
communism and the key features of their ideology. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Darwinism and social Darwinism’, 
students discover the positives and negatives that 
resulted from Charles Darwin’s theory about the 
evolution of the species. 
The Activity sheets, ‘Imperialism’ and ‘Colonialism’, 
explore the situation in colonised countries ruled by 
empires. ‘Imperialism’ defines the term and focuses on 
the British colonisation of China. ‘Colonialism’ considers 
the individual impacts of imperialism on the people of 
colonial India. 
Extension activities
Have students choose one key idea or movement from 
this unit and construct a poster about it, using either 
ICT or poster paper. They should:
• 
 outline the features of the movement or idea
• 
 identify when it was important, and consider the 
time period and what else was happening in the 
world at this time
• 
 identify where it happened and why
• 
 identify key figures connected to it 
• 
 discuss why it was important.
Ideas and movements: Chartism, communism, 
Darwinism, social Darwinism, imperialism, nationalism, 
egalitarianism, suffragette movement
Objectives
• Understand the key ideas and movements 
during the industrial period
• Consider how issues like Imperialism can have 
positive effects for one country and negative 
effects for another country
• Identify individuals related to some key ideas 
and movements of the industrial period

Imperialism
+  1 Write each underlined word beside the correct definition below.
European countries often had great military strength. They had new weapons, such as guns 
and cannons, which they used to overpower other countries. Britain became one of the biggest 
empires in the world in the 1800s. They controlled large parts of Asia, Africa, Canada, Australia 
and many other key regions. The countries ruled by the British were called colonies. These 
colonies had little say in how they were ruled. They did not have the weapons of the British and 
so they had no hope of successfully fighting back. 
Britain won two wars in China in the 1800s: the First Opium War in 1842 and the Second Opium 
War in 1858. In both wars they gained more control over China. This was valuable because they 
wanted tea, silk, spices and other luxury products that only came from China. 
In many of the British colonies, particularly in Asia and Africa, local people were encouraged 
to learn English. Often, English became the official language of the colony. Local people who 
became Anglophiles and adopted British practices were often treated better than those who 
did not. But they were still not treated as well as British people.

My name is Rhett. I am an Anglo-Indian. My father, Geof frey,

53
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Social problems
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
In the industrial period, many people faced difficult 
decisions about how to survive. Working in the 
factories was not always possible, and some people 
were moved regularly between working and 
unemployment, depending on their employers. This 
left them in the difficult situation of needing other 
ways to pay their bills and feed their families. The 
poorest of the poor turned to the workhouses, which 
were the government-sanctioned form of poverty 
relief. People in the workhouses were treated badly: 
forced to work long hours on pointless tasks that 
taught them no skills, separated from their family 
members and given very little food. To avoid the 
workhouses, people turned to shady activities such 
as prostitution, baby farming (poor women were paid 
to look after other people’s children), renting out 
rooms and begging. Activities such as prostitution 
endangered their lives as they were often mistreated 
by men and even murdered like Jack the Ripper’s 
victims. 
Other people’s activities gradually became more 
criminal. For example, some people forced family 
members into prostitution and some baby farmers 
killed the babies in their care. Others turned to murder, 
theft and burglary. The consequences for these 
actions were extreme. Many people were executed 
or transported to Australia for their crimes. But not 
engaging in these activities could be almost as dire. 
They often faced the prospect of death every day. 
In the late 1800s, some people began questioning the 
way that poor people and criminals were treated and 
this led to more enlightened attitudes. Social reformers 
created groups for the protection of children (National 
Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, 
NSPCC) and the protection of animals (Royal Society for 
the Prevention of Cruelty to animals, RSPCA). They also 
began helping poor people by providing soup kitchens 
and working to get prostitutes off the streets.
Starter activity
What are the social problems in our society? Identify at 
least two contemporary social problems. 
Discuss the complexity of these problems and possible 
solutions for them. Make sure these solutions would 
improve our society.
Resource and Activity sheets
On the Resource sheet, ‘Baby farming’, students read 
two primary sources and one secondary source that 
provide information about the 19th century practice of 
baby farming. Students analyse these sources on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Primary and secondary sources’. They 
are encouraged to identify the differences between the 
types of sources and explain their value. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Social reformers’, looks at the lives of 
two key social reformers: Henry Mayhew and Josephine 
Butler. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Age of sexual consent’, outlines 
the way that social reformers brought about positive 
change for the protection of children. The Activity 
sheet, ‘Protecting girls’, consolidates the information on 
the Resource sheet.
Extension activities
With the class, brainstorm alternative solutions to baby 
farming for the mothers of illegitimate children during 
the Industrial Revolution. Solutions could include:
• 
 providing state-run or factory-run day care
• 
 fining fathers who did not contribute to their 
children’s upkeep
• 
 state-run orphanages
• 
 official adoption with government monitoring
• 
 group homes.
Have students choose one idea and compose a speech 
that supports their idea with clear explanations and the 
use of convincing evidence. 
Objectives
• Identify key social problems during the 
Industrial Revolution
• Understand the significance of these problems
• Learn about the methods people used in 
attempting to address these problems

Baby farming
Source 1
Baby farming became more frequent during the Industrial Revolution. 
When single women or widows became pregnant, they often struggled 
to both look after a child and keep a job to support them. Many women 
turned to ‘baby farmers’ to care for their children. Baby farmers were often 
married women or widows who took in and looked after babies for money. 
The problems began when mothers stopped paying for their children’s 
support or when the baby farmers became greedy. Many children in the 
care of baby farmers died of malnutrition or neglect. Some were murdered.
Baby farmers accused of murdering babies include Amelia Sach and 
Annie Walters in England, Minnie Dean in New Zealand, and Frances Knorr 
and John and Sarah Jane Makin in Australia.
Rachel Towns, Achieve! History – The Industrial Revolution, Clayton, 
Blake Education, 2017, Australia.

Criminal Amendment Act of 1885
The age of consent is when someone can legally engage in sexual activity. 
In Britain, the age of consent had been 12 years since the 
Westminster statutes of 1275. Twelve years was also the age you 
could get married. In the Middle Ages, people married young 
as they also often died young. However, as people began 
to live longer they began to see 12 year olds as children 
rather than potential marriage partners.
Social reformers including William Stead (editor of 
the Pall Mall Gazette), Bramwell Booth (Salvation 
Army) and Josephine Butler (a protector of 
women) became concerned about what they 
called the ‘white slave trade’. This referred to 
the practice of selling young girls to brothels 
as prostitutes. 
In 1883, William Stead wrote a series of 
articles called The Maiden Tribute of Modern 
Babylon. He described the terrible situations 
experienced by young women living in poverty, especially in London. Finally, he drew attention 
to the white slave trade by describing how easy it was for him to purchase a girl aged 13 years. 
He pretended that he worked for a French brothel, and approached a woman named Rebecca 
Jarrett who specialised in finding girls for brothels. Rebecca arranged for William to purchase 
Eliza Armstrong from her mother for five pounds. After demonstrating how easy it was to buy 
young girls for brothels, Bramwell Booth arranged for Eliza to move in with a Salvationist family.
William’s articles about purchasing Eliza resulted in a court case where he faced changes for 
buying a girl. He was imprisoned for three months. The publicity surrounding the articles, 
court case and prison sentence encouraged the government to change the age of consent 
from 12 years to 16 years with the Criminal Amendment Act of 1885.

5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – The Industrial Revolution in Britain
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Background
Many of the key features of the Middle Ages continued 
past the period of the Medieval era (approximately 
700 CE to 1400 CE). Most people lived on farms or 
worked on large estates for the wealthy elite. Moving 
between social classes was almost impossible, as those 
from the lower classes generally had little access to 
education or money and could not interact or compete 
successfully with those who inherited their wealth and 
power. 
Over time, social changes began to challenge these 
expected ways of living. There was a rapid population 
growth in the 1800s: from 8 million people in 1801 to 
26 million people in 1881. This was because people 
continued to have large families while improvements 
in medicines, sanitation and drinking water (later half 
of 19th century), and the quality of food reduced the 
mortality rate. 
Increasing numbers of people could not remain on 
the farms where they had traditionally lived because 
agricultural inventions meant their labour was 
unnecessary. They were forced to move to cities to look 
for jobs. Factory owners could then hire large numbers 
of people as unskilled labourers and so increase their 
production to meet the increasing need for material 
goods demanded by the newly established middle 
class. This led to a demand for improved transport to 
source raw materials from other countries (usually 
colonies) and send the finished products from factories 
in Britain to other parts of the country and overseas.
Starter activity
Show a video or series of images to introduce life in the 
industrial period. 
Useful documentaries include:
• Tony Robinson’s Worst Jobs in History, 
Episode: Industrial Jobs
• The Supersizers Go ..., Episode: Victorian, BBC
Brainstorm with the students what you found out 
about life in the industrial period.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Map of the British Empire’, asks 
students to use a map to identify the locations of key 
industrial countries and British colonies. Students will 
use a colour key to identify the trade sources of raw 
products.
The Activity sheet, ‘Technology and transport’, lists 
some key technological events for students to show on 
a timeline. As an additional activity, students are asked 
to research three more key events and add them to the 
timeline.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Causes of the Industrial 
Revolution’, students highlight key terms in a list of 
causes of the Industrial Revolution, organised into 
themes of agriculture, factories, people and transport. 
Students then compile a glossary of unfamiliar terms. 
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Essay plan’, students are 
guided through the process of creating an essay 
plan using the information from the Resource sheet, 
‘Causes of the Industrial Revolution’. Discuss the TEEEM 
structure with the class, especially if students have not 
used it before. As an extension activity, students are 
asked to use their plan to write an essay.
TEEEM Paragraph Plan 
Always start with a topic sentence and always end with 
a mini-conclusion. Put the evidence, explanation and 
essay keywords in the middle in whatever order you 
like. 
•  T – Topic sentence: introduce your specific topic
•  E – Evidence: to support your ideas
•  E – Explain: your ideas in your own words
•   E – Essay keywords: use keywords from the essay 
question and the topic sentence to show you are 
answering the question
•   Mini-conclusion: sum up what you said in that 
paragraph.
Extension ideas
Students could work individually or in small groups to 
research a different cause of the Industrial Revolution. 
Have them use what they find out to create an 
extended response, poster, video or ICT presentation.
Objectives
• Learn about the nature of the Industrial 
Revolution
• Identify key events that led to the Industrial 
Revolution
• Explore the trading relationships of countries

Britain had a large empire in the 1800s. It had conquered many countries including Canada, 
Australia, China, India, Cuba, Egypt and British Somaliland. These countries became colonies of

8
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Activity sheet – The Industrial Revolution in Britain
Causes of the Industrial Revolution
The Industrial Revolution started in the 1700s (18th century). It began in Britain and then in 
America, France, Germany and Japan. Many machines were invented and used in factories. 
New transport like trains and steamships made it easier for people and products to travel. 
+  1 Highlight the keywords (important words) in the table.
 2  In your workbook, compile a glossary of unfamiliar words and write definitions for them.
Theme
Cause: Explanation
Agriculture
•  Enclosure laws: The government forced people to fence in fields. Land 
was now owned by individuals, not villages.
•  Stock breeding: Farmers began to mate animals selectively to increase 
their quality.
•  Farm machinery: Jethro Tull’s seed drill made planting faster and easier.
Factories
•  Textile machines: People used new machines to make cloth more quickly.
•  Bank loans: After banks were invented, people could get loans to invest in 
factories, machines and land.
•  Government support: The government encouraged businesses to build 
more factories.
•  Unskilled labour in factories: Factory owners hired women and children 
as unskilled workers. It was cheaper than hiring men.
People 
•  People movement: There were not enough jobs in the country. People 
moved to the cities to find jobs in the factories.
•  Medicine: Improvements in medicine meant fewer people got sick or 
died. The population grew from 8 million in 1801 to 26 million in 1881.
Transport
•  Turnpike tolls: People paid tolls to use the roads. The toll money was used 
to improve the roads, which made travel easier.
•  Trains: Steam trains were invented in 1825. People and products could 
move around more easily.
•  Canals for transport: Canals were built in the 1760s so that boats could 
be used to move coal and steel. This was faster than using roads.

© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Transport
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
In 1710, Thomas Newcomen constructed a steam 
engine that generated vertical energy (up and down 
movement). Newcomen used this engine to make 
pumps for deep pit mining to prevent flooding. In 
1764, James Watt realised that he could use Thomas 
Newcomen’s ideas to construct a steam engine that 
used rotary motion (circular motion). This meant that 
different types of machines and transport could be 
invented. George Stephenson used James Watt’s rotary 
steam engine as a source of energy for the first steam 
train. This steam engine was also used in other forms of 
transport such as steamships. 
In 1770, James Cook went looking for the mysterious 
southern land. He confirmed sightings of Australia 
and New Zealand. Britain used Australia in particular 
as a convict settlement from 1788. Australia gradually 
shifted from a country of punishment to a country of 
opportunity as settlers arrived and took up pastoral 
land. These new settlers objected to the convicts and 
in 1840, New South Wales banned transportation. 
However, transportation to Australia only ended in 
1868 when Western Australia received a final ship of 
convicts. Western Australia continued to be a penal 
settlement for some time after 1868, but received no 
further transports.
Starter activity
Discuss the modes of transport that students use. How 
does transport technology influence their everyday 
interactions with people and the places they go? How 
would their lives be affected if walking was their only 
mode of transport?
Interesting fact: Improvements in transportation in the 
Victorian period (1800s) moved the average distance 
of spouses from about 5 km away to 30 km away, as 
people no longer had to rely on walking to meet and 
woo someone.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Transportation’, identifies the 
improvements in transport in the 1800s with an 
emphasis on the railway system. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Railways in England and Australia’, 
compares the development of railway systems in these 
countries. Students copy and complete comprehension 
questions for each section.
Through the Activity sheet, ‘Clippers and steamships’, 
students explore the realities of ship travel. They also 
consider how they would feel, experiencing that 
journey.
The Activity sheet, ‘Convicts and crime’, explores 
the reasons for transportation to Australia, and the 
perspectives of different groups of people. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Settlers in Australia’, students 
consider different reasons for moving to Australia. 
Guide the class through analysing the primary source 
emigration poster through CHIPS: 
•  caption (What words are there on the poster? Why are 
they used?) 
• history (What events were happening then?) 
•  interrogate source (What do you find interesting or 
unusual about the poster?) 
•  people (What people and animals are included? How 
are they represented?)  
•  symbols (What signs or symbols are used? How do 
these persuade and encourage people?).
Extension ideas
•   Students could visit the website ‘Convict Records’ 
to explore the different reasons people were 
transported to Australia and the lengths of their 
sentences. Have them compare and contrast three 
different convicts.
    http://www.convictrecords.com.au/crimes
•   Students could also use the Victorian Railway website 
to chart the development of steam trains in Victoria 
from the 1850s to the 1900s.
     https://museumvictoria.com.au/railways/theme.
aspx?theme=448&lvl=1
Objectives
• Learn about new developments in transport
• Explore how new transportation affected the 
movement of people
• Understand why people moved to Australia
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.

Transportation
Before the Industrial Revolution, most products were 
made and used locally. But after factories were built, 
business owners often got raw materials from the 
colonies because it was cheaper. They also sent their 
finished products further away to increase their profits. 
For transport, people could use either boats or horses 
and carts. This limited the distances they could travel 
and it was expensive. However, in the 1700s and 1800s 
transport changed.
Improvements in transport in the 1700s and 1800s
•  Road users paid turnpike tolls. The local authorities 
used this money to maintain and improve the roads so 
that people could travel faster.
•  From the mid-1700s, canals (inland waterways for 
boats) were built. This made it easier to get products 
onto boats and then around the country.
•  Railway tracks were laid, and horses were used to pull 
wagons along them. Now, heavy raw materials and products  
could be moved along regular routes; for example, from a coal mine to a port. 
+ 
1 How did people move products before trains were invented?
 
 
2 Why did people need better transport during the Industrial Revolution?
 
 
 
 
3 Who invented the steam train? 
 
 
 
 
 
4  Which event in the transport timeline do you think is the most important? Explain why.

This is a clipper, like the ones that brought many of the first 
Europeans to Australia. They were made of wood and the 
wind moved them swiftly across the water. They took 
two to four months to sail from Britain to Australia.
The poorest people travelled in steerage at the 
bottom of the ship. There was only one large 
room for all the steerage passengers. During 
storms, they had to stay in the dark because 
candles or lanterns might set the ship on 
fire. Water often leaked in through the sides of the ship 
so everything was wet. They slept in narrow wooden bunk beds  
and kept their possessions in large wooden trunks to keep them safe. 
Steamships like this were used in the 1890s and 1900s. 
They were powered by steam engines. At first, 
these ships weren’t much faster than clippers, 
but they were safer and more comfortable. 
Rich passengers travelled in cabins. There were 
restaurants and areas where passengers 
could read, play table tennis and 
hold concerts.
The poorest people travelled in 
steerage at the bottom of the ship. 
But steamships had more than one room in steerage. Each family had their own small cabin. 
Sometimes the cabins had a wash basin and a chest of drawers to help store their possessions. 
They could use lanterns or, later, electrical lights, even during storms.

Convicts and crime 
Crime rates increased during the industrial period because people moved from the country to 
the cities and could not find work. 
The prisons in Britain became overcrowded. They could no longer send convicts to America, 
so the government decided to transport them to Australia. From 1788 to1868, British criminals
