Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
30
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Women
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
Women had long been seen as inferior to men. This 
was reinforced by the Catholic and later Protestant 
churches who held to the idea of all women being 
tainted by the ‘sins of Eve’. Women were generally 
prejudiced against, treated almost as children and 
forced to work largely within the household. The few 
women who could express themselves through culture, 
literature or politics have often been misrepresented or 
ignored by history. It is important to remember that the 
absence of women’s writing or cultural activities does 
not mean that women were not engaging in these 
activities. Rather, women’s activities were devalued, 
there were more restrictions on their involvement in 
such activities, and little effort made to preserve them. 
Issues such as marriage and divorce were highly 
significant for women. Once married, many women’s 
rights to property and possessions passed to their 
husbands. Married women could engage in few 
activities without their husband’s support or presence. 
In the 19th century, divorce laws were finally 
introduced in Britain and its colonies, including 
Australia. However, women were still prejudiced 
against in the causes for divorce. In the late 
19th century, women challenged this inequality by 
seeking political representation through the vote 
(suffrage) and the right to be members of parliament. 
These women were called suffragettes or suffragists. 
Starter activity
Talk to students about voting. You may want to discuss 
a recent election. Discuss why we vote and what 
impact it could have if groups in society were not 
allowed to vote. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first two activity sheets look at suffragettes and 
their fight for the right of women to vote. The Activity 
sheet, ‘British suffragettes’, considers what women had 
to do to get the vote. The Activity sheet, ‘Australian 
suffragettes’, looks at when women obtained the right 
to vote in Australia. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Marriage and divorce laws’, explores 
the idea of allowed causes of divorces, and how this 
has changed over time. ‘Aggravated adultery’ meant 
that the husband had to be highly obvious about his 
adultery, or combine it with physical cruelty, two years’ 
desertion, bigamy, sodomy, bestiality, incest or rape in 
order to be divorced. Women could be divorced for a 
single act of adultery.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Writing women’, students learn 
about two significant female writers who championed 
equality in the 1800s.
The Activity sheet, ‘Caroline Chisholm’, provides 
in-depth information about Caroline Chisholm’s 
philanthropy in Australia.
Extension ideas
Watch one of the movie adaptations of Charlotte 
Bronte’s Jane Eyre to broaden the students’ 
understanding of women’s lives in the 1840s. The 
main character, Jane, was middle class. The way she 
was treated by servants and by the upper class (with 
the exception of how she is sometimes treated by 
Mr Rochester) fits with the experiences many middle 
class women would have at the time.
Objectives
• Gain a stronger understanding of the position 
of women during the Industrial Revolution
• Learn about female writers and how they 
influenced women’s rights
• Learn about a female inventor and consider her 
role in the Industrial Revolution

British suffragettes
+ 
 Read the information and answer the questions below.
Suffrage means the right to vote. In Britain in the 
1700s and 1800s, only rich men who owned property 
were allowed to vote. 
In the late 1800s, many women started to protest. 
They wanted to vote and they wanted more rights. 
These women were called suffragettes. 
Many men and some women thought that 
suffragettes should not have the vote. They mocked 
these women in the newspapers by describing them 
as silly or masculine. Suffragettes were sentenced to 
prison for protesting. Many went on hunger strikes; 
the jailers would tie them down and push tubes 
down their throats to force-feed them.
During World War I, a lot of British suffragettes 
stopped protesting to support the war effort. Many 
historians believe this patriotism is why women over 
30 years were given the right to vote in 1918. In 1928, the voting age for women  
was reduced to 21 years, as it was for men. Finally, women had equal suffrage.

library. Answer the question in your workbook.

protect themselves
• Breaking windows
•  Standing on street corners and 
preaching to the crowds
• Chaining themselves to railings
• Hunger strikes in prison
•  Emily Davison ran in front of 
King George V’s horse at a 
horse race in 1913 and was 
killed.

Women were expected to act in particular ways: be domestic, stay at home, let men make their

Caroline Chisholm
My name is Caroline Chisholm. I was born in 1808 in England. From a 
very early age I cared about being a philanthropist. A philanthropist is 
someone who helps people who are poor or uncared for. I only married 
my husband Captain Archibald Chisholm because he allowed me to be a 
philanthropist and help others.
In 1838, my husband and I moved to Sydney, Australia. T here were 
many people who travelled to Australia but then had nowhere to go. 
I focused on helping poor immigrant girls. Many arrived with little money 
and there were not many respectable or safe places for them to stay.

1 
Most Bills are introduced into the lower house by the relevant minister. This means that  
a Bill:
a is likely to pass there because the government has a majority.
b is likely to pass there because the opposition has a majority.
c is unlikely to pass there because the government has a majority.
d is unlikely to pass there because the opposition has a majority.
2 
How many times is a Bill read in the lower house before it can be approved?
a One

c Three
d As many times as necessary
3 
For a Bill to become law in a bicameral (two-house) parliamentary system:
a both houses need to approve the Bill.
b only the lower house needs to approve the Bill.
c only the upper house needs to approve the Bill.
d only the governor or governor-general’s consent is required.
4 
An Act commences formal operation:
a on the date it receives royal assent.
b on a day to be proclaimed in the Government Gazette (a government publication).
c retrospectively (before royal assent) if this is specified in the legislation.
d Any of the above may be correct.
REMEMBER 
Laws made by parliament are known as Acts, statutes or legislation. A proposed law is 
called a Bill. For a Bill to become law, it must be passed by parliament.
Case study: Forming a minority government
Usually there is a clear winner following an election. But in the 2010 federal election, 
neither of the major parties secured enough seats in parliament to govern in their  
own right. 
The House of Representatives is composed of 150 members. For a party to gain an 
outright majority they need to win at least 76 seats. This did not happen. The result is 
known as a hung parliament. A hung parliament means no party can pass laws without 
the support of other parties and/or the independents.
© Blake Education   978 1 92571 050 2	     Interactive Instant Lessons  The Australian legal system 

© Stella Tarakson and Blake Education 2012
17
Interactive Instant Lessons • Legal studies • The Australian legal system
Sources of law 
7 Parliament
This is not unprecedented in Australia. Hung state parliaments occur occasionally, but the 
only other time there was a hung federal parliament was in 1940, after the outbreak of 
World War II. 
The seats won in the 2010 federal election were: Labor Party 72, Liberal Party 44, Liberal 
National Party of Queensland 21, National Party 7, Independents 4, Country Liberal Party 1, 
Greens Party 1.
Both Labor and the Coalition (the Liberal Party, Liberal National Party of Queensland 
and the National Party) tried to gain the support of others in order to create a minority 
government. In the meantime, Julia Gillard, who was prime minister prior to the election, 
continued as caretaker prime minister until the issue could be resolved. If the issue had 
been unable to be resolved, another election may have been held. That was unnecessary, 
however, and Gillard’s Labor Party was able to form a minority government. 
5 
a  What is the term used to describe two or more parties who join together to form  
a government? 
 
b Which two Australian political parties typically do this when in power?

parties to side with. In your opinion, is this a threat to the concept of democracy or a 
necessary part of the democratic process? Outline your reasoning. 
 
 
 
7 
A ruling government can pass legislation because it can claim to have the mandate of  
the voters. Do you think this still applies in the case of a minority government? Explain  
your answer. 
 
 
 
 
8

a Bill
 
 
b delegated legislation

Case study: Franca
Franca was single and lived in a rental apartment with two friends. She had a casual office 
job and was studying part-time at university. She became friends with Alex, a young man 
who attended all the same lectures as her. Franca saw their relationship as platonic and 
believed Alex felt the same. One day he invited her over to his flat and Franca accepted.
Once there, however, she quickly regretted her decision. Alex made it clear he expected 
more, and became rough when Franca resisted. He told her he did not like women who 
played hard to get. Frightened and upset, Franca insisted she was not interested but he 
did not listen. Alex sexually assaulted Franca and her wrist was broken in the struggle.
Franca slid into a depression afterwards. Her broken wrist prevented her from working, 
and she was not entitled to sick leave. Her medical bills were costly and she was unable 
to pay her share of the rent. She dropped out of university because she could not bear to 
see Alex in the lectures. She felt her life was in a mess.
Franca was encouraged by her friends to make a report to the police. 
REMEMBER 
Legal wrongdoing is something that causes injury, damage or loss. Depending on 
the nature of the wrongdoing, it might be covered by criminal law or civil law. Some 
incidents can lead to action under both criminal and civil law.

reasons for your answer.

IntroductIon
The ever-increasing concerns about the rapidly rising 
levels of the greenhouse gas carbon dioxide has caused 
great interest in producing electrical energy by means

to create no such gas as there is no combustion involved. 
There are many forms of alternative energy in resources 
such as the wind, the Sun, the tides and the energy stored 
in ‘hot rocks’ under the Earth’s surface.
Aim
To investigate the implementation of a few of these 
alternative energy resources in some Australian situations.

a 
The basic unit of power is the watt, defined as

so the watt is a small unit of power.

household purposes is the kilowatt-hour, which  
is defined as the amount of energy produced (or 
consumed) when a device of power 1 kW operates  
for a time of 1 h. This is the commonly used unit for 
household consumption.

© __ When learning a new scientific concept, it can sometimes be difficult to understand what is going on —

especially when you cannot actually see it. To help you understand, a simple model can be invented to
explain what is happening. However, models do have their limitations and may need to be changed as your
understanding becomes better.

In a circuit the power supply—the battery or the powerpack—acts as an energy bank, supplying the
electrons with the same amount of energy as they travel. As the electrons move around the circuit, they use
some of this energy.

Some materials are more difficult for electrons to move through than other materials. Such materials
cause resistance in a circuit. Materials with low resistance allow the current to pass through easily; they are
good conductors. Materials with high resistance do not allow much current to flow through; they are
resistors. Sometimes the shape and length of the wire affects resistance, for example a thin piece of wire has
a higher resistance than a thicker piece of wire.

4.4 | Combating bacterial resistance

Science understanding FOUNDATION | STANDARD | ADVANCED

The development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria is getting worse

and poses a serious problem for human health. The first factor that is
contributing to this resistance is that antibiotics are widespread in the
environment. Antibiotics are commonly used to treat infectious diseases in
animals and so can sometimes be found in soil and water. Antibiotics are
also being found in human foods because some animals are fed antibiotics
to protect them from disease and help them grow faster. Antibotics are also
commonly used in hospitals. The widespread use of antibiotics increases the
exposure of bacteria to natural selection by antibiotics.

+ being able to destroy or inactivate the antibiotic molecules

searchText: ﻿Heat can be transferred from one place to another by three methods: conduction in solids, convection of fluids (liquids or gases), and radiation through anything that will allow radiation to pass. The method used to transfer heat is usually the one that is the most efficient. If there is a temperature difference in a system, heat will always move from higher to lower temperatures. A thermal infrared image of a coffee cup filled with a hot liquid. Notice the rings of color showing heat traveling from the hot liquid through the metal cup. You can see this in the metal spoon as well. This is a good example of conduction. CONDUCTION: Conduction occurs when two object at different temperatures are in contact with each other. Heat flows from the warmer to the cooler object until they are both at the same temperature. Conduction is the movement of heat through a substance by the collision of molecules. At the place where the two object touch, the faster-moving molecules of the warmer object collide with the slower moving molecules of the cooler object. As they collide, the faster molecules give up some of their energy to the slower molecules. The slower molecules gain more thermal energy and collide with other molecules in the cooler object. This process continues until heat energy from the warmer object spreads throughout the cooler object. Some substances conduct heat more easily than others. Solids are better conductor than liquids and liquids are better conductor than gases. Metals are very good conductors of heat, while air is very poor conductor of heat. You experience heat transfer by conduction whenever you touch something that is hotter or colder than your skin e.g. when you wash your hands in warm or cold water. CONVECTION: In liquids and gases, convection is usually the most efficient way to transfer heat. Convection occurs when warmer areas of a liquid or gas rise to cooler areas in the liquid or gas. As this happens, cooler liquid or gas takes the place of the warmer areas which have risen higher. This cycle results in a continous circulation pattern and heat is transfered to cooler areas. You see convection when you boil water in a pan. The bubbles of water that rise are the hotter parts of the water rising to the cooler area of water at the top of the pan. You have probably heard the expression "Hot air rises and cool air falls to take its place" - this is a description of convection in our atmosphere. Heat energy is transfered by the circulation of the air. This thermal infrared image shows hot oil boiling in a pan. The oil is transfering heat out of the pan by convection. Notice the hot (yellow) centers of rising hot oil and the cooler outlines of the sinking oil. Image courtesy of K.-P. Möllmann and M. Vollmer, University of Applied Sciences Brandenburg/Germany. A thermal infrared image of the center of our galaxy. This heat from numerous stars and interstellar clouds traveled about 24,000 light years (about 150,000,000,000,000,000 miles!) through space by radiation to reach our infrared telescopes. RADIATION: Both conduction and convection require matter to transfer heat. Radiation is a method of heat transfer that does not rely upon any contact between the heat source and the heated object. For example, we feel heat from the sun even though we are not touching it. Heat can be transmitted though empty space by thermal radiation. Thermal radiation (often called infrared radiation) is a type electromagnetic radiation (or light). Radiation is a form of energy transport consisting of electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. No mass is exchanged and no medium is required. Objects emit radiation when high energy electrons in a higher atomic level fall down to lower energy levels. The energy lost is emitted as light or electromagnetic radiation. Energy that is absorbed by an atom causes its electrons to "jump" up to higher energy levels. All objects absorb and emit radiation. ( Here is a java applet showing how an atom absorbs and emits radiation) When the absorption of energy balances the emission of energy, the temperature of an object stays constant. If the absorption of energy is greater than the emission of energy, the temperature of an object rises. If the absorption of energy is less than the emission of energy, the temperature of an object falls.

Extend your understanding 
Consider for a moment the Sun and our planet Earth. They do not touch each other, so thermal energy cannot be transferred from the Sun to Earth by conduction. Neither can heat be transferred to Earth from the Sun by convection as the space between them is essentially a vacuum. However, you can stand with your back to the Sun on a cold day and feel yourself begin to warm up. If it is not by conduction or convection, how does thermal energy from the Sun reach Earth? The answer is via radiation emitted by the Sun.
The Sun emits electromagnetic radiation that is absorbed when it reaches Earth. This absorption of electromagnetic radiation by particles on Earth causes them to move more rapidly, thus heating them.
All objects transfer some heat by emitting radiation. The hotter an object is, the more heat it radiates. Remember that the radiation itself is not hot – it is the absorption of the radiation by an object that causes it to heat up.

searchText: ﻿http://www.mansfieldct.org/schools/mms/staff/hand/convcondrad.htm Convection, Conduction and Radiation Back to Energy Heat Review Game Convection is the transfer of heat by the actual movement of the warmed matter. Heat leaves the coffee cup as the currents of steam and air rise. Convection is the transfer of heat energy in a gas or liquid by movement of currents. (It can also happen is some solids, like sand.) The heat moves with the fluid. Consider this: convection is responsible for making macaroni rise and fall in a pot of heated water. The warmer portions of the water are less dense and therefore, they rise. Meanwhile, the cooler portions of the water fall because they are denser. Conduction is the transfer of energy through matter from particle to particle. It is the transfer and distribution of heat energy from atom to atom within a substance. For example, a spoon in a cup of hot soup becomes warmer because the heat from the soup is conducted along the spoon. Conduction is most effective in solids-but it can happen in fluids. Fun fact: Have you ever noticed that metals tend to feel cold? Believe it or not, they are not colder! They only feel colder because they conduct heat away from your hand. You perceive the heat that is leaving your hand as cold. Radiation: Electromagnetic waves that directly transport ENERGY through space. Sunlight is a form of radiation that is radiated through space to our planet without the aid of fluids or solids. The energy travels through nothingness! Just think of it! The sun transfers heat through 93 million miles of space. Because there are no solids (like a huge spoon) touching the sun and our planet, conduction is not responsible for bringing heat to Earth. Since there are no fluids (like air and water) in space, convection is not responsible for transferring the heat. Thus, radiation brings heat to our planet. How a radiometer works: One must focus attention on the edges of the vanes to explain the behavior of the radiometer. Heat excites the black surface of the vanes more than it heats the white surface. Black is a good absorber and a good radiator. Think of black as a large doorway that allows heat to pass through easily. In contrast, white is a poor absorber and a poor radiator of energy. White is like a small doorway and will not allow heat to pass easily. The difference in temperature between the warm, black side and the cooler white side causes gasses to creep along the surface of the vanes. This effect is known as "thermal creep." The faster gasses from the black side strike the edges of the vane at an angle with more force than the molecules from the cold side. The equal and opposite forces cause the radiometer to spin. More details if you really, really want to know…. Why a radiometer runs backwards after the light is turned off. Heat escapes quickly from the black sides of the vanes. Thus, the black molecules cool off first. Meanwhile, the white molecules take longer to lose heat cool down. The result is that gasses from the white vane push off with more force (Newton's third law) and the vanes spin in the opposite direction.

searchText:
Electrical safety

Science understanding

STANDARD

Electricity is so common that we all take it for granted. However, it is also incredibly dangerous.
For example, a circuit can quickly overheat and catch fire if you piggyback double-adaptors or
powerboards. To avoid this, use separate plugs. Likewise, coiled or looped-up leads and extension
cords can rapidly heat up, possibly melting their insulation and exposing live wires. Straighten them
out first before using. Electricity is most dangerous if you accidentally become part of the circuit!

If that happens, current may flow through you to the ground. Serious burns or electrocution
can result.

Water can provide an easy route for electric current to flow through you to the ground. For this
reason, never use an appliance or turn a switch on or off if you are wet. Dry yourself first. Likewise,
never use electricity around swimming pools or filled basins or baths. For example, use your
hairdryer in your bedroom, not the bathroom.

Never touch someone who has collapsed from electric shock, because they may still be part of the
circuit! Turn off the power at the main switchboard and ring for an ambulance. Dial 000 from a
landline phone. From a mobile, dial 000 or 112 or 106.

Electricity |

Electricity is used to provide a versatile source of energy. It makes our lights work and, without it, we
wouldn't have radio, television, computers and CD players. We take electrical light globes (bulbs) for granted,
but they were only invented after a lot of hard work. Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor who
patented, in 1880, an electric light filament similar to those used in light globes today. Sir Joseph Swan (an
English scientist) came up with the idea for the incandescent electric lamp at the same time.

Electricity is the movement of electrons (negative particles) along a conductor. This flow of electrons is
called an electric current. For electricity to flow, it must have a complete pathway or circuit to follow. If
there is a gap, the circuit is broken and no current flows.

Energy can be stored in cells (sometimes called batteries) for conversion to

electrical energy when needed. Batteries are used when only low voltage (e.g. —j
3 volts to 12 volts) of electricity is used in calculators, watches and personal stereos

for example. Batteries are also used when things need to be portable. The first

battery was invented by the Italian Count Alessandro Volta in about 1800. The unit

of electrical measurement called the volt (V) was named after him.

Some electrical devices need large amounts of electricity to operate them. They are

powered by mains electricity (240 volts). Using batteries to supply large amounts

of electricity is not always practical — they would be too expensive and take up

too much space. Today people use a lot of electricity, at home and at work. This electricity is generated at
power stations. The first, very small, generator was made by the English scientist Michael Faraday in 1831,

searchText:
Magnetism and Electricity

63) ELECTRICITY FROM A KIWI FRUIT

You can make electricity with fruit.

HOW TO DOIT

THEME: ELECTRIC CELLS

1 Use wires to connect a copper plate to one terminal of a microammeter and a zinc plate to the other.

2 Cut twoslits, about 2cm apart, in a kiwi fruit.

3. Insert the two metal plates into the slits. (The microammeter will indicate a flow of current.)

copper,

EXPLANATION

The zinc attracts electrons from the citric acid in the kiwi fruit
so it becomes negatively charged. The copper donates
electrons to the solution and becomes positively charged. The
difference in charge causes electrons to flow through the wire
from the zinc to the copper.

TO INVESTIGATE

Do some fruits generate more current than others? To what
extent is the amount of current influenced by the depth of the
electrode in the fruit?

LINKED ACTIVITIES

1 Use a potato to test for a flat battery. Attach two wires to
the terminals of a 9V household battery. Insert the other
ends of the wires into a peeled potato so they are about
2-3mm apart. (If the battery is charged, bubbles of hydrogen
gas will appear around the wire connected to the negative
terminal; after a minute or so a blue colour will appear at
the wire connected to the positive terminal.)

2 Solve the following problem. Is it possible to recharge a flat
battery by leaving it in the sun for a while? Design an
experiment to test this question.

3 Solve the following problem. Battery manufacturers
sometimes claim that their products last longer than those
of other brands. Test their claims by inserting batteries into
electrical toys (or other devices with moving parts such as
battery shavers) and comparing the time taken to run down.
Calculate the brand that offers the best value for money.

Historica NOTE

One of the scientists who helped to
develop batteries was Robert Bunsen.
While doing research in chemistry, he
nearly died from arsenic poisoning
and lost the sight of one eye in a
laboratory explosion.

     What is Energy?                         Energy is what causes things to change.

There are many different types of energy. Here are just a few:

Type of Energy                            Changes Caused by this Energy
Heat                                      Change in temperature. e.g. a stove causes food to get hot.
Light                                     Nerve changes in your eye which allow you to see things,
                                                  or chemical changes in the film in a camera.
Sound                                     Vibrations in your ear which allow you to hear.
Electrical Energy                         Can cause a light bulb to glow and produce light,
                                                  or a stove element to get hot and produce heat.
Radio Waves                               Can cause electrical vibrations in an antenna.
                                          This allows reception of mobile phone, radio & TV programs.

     Two types of energy need special attention:                (learn these especially!)

 Kinetic Energy (KE)
 KE is the energy of a moving object. It causes the object to change its position by moving.
 If the moving object hits something, the KE can cause other changes, such as the damage
 done when moving cars collide.

 Potential Energy (PE)
 PE is energy stored in things, and not always obvious or apparent. There are 3 types:

           Gravitational PE is energy stored in an object in a high position. The energy is not
           apparent until the object falls down due to gravity. As it falls, it converts into KE.

           Chemical PE is energy stored in chemicals. The energy is not apparent until a
           chemical change occurs which releases the energy. Chemical PE is stored in
           chemicals like candle wax (can burn to release heat and light) or in a battery
           (can make electricity) or in petrol (can make a car move with KE).

           Elastic PE is energy stored in objects which have been stretched, compressed
           or twisted out of shape. When released, the elastic PE is released, often causing
           something to move with KE.
           e.g. When released, a stretched bow makes the arrow fly.

                                             Why Learn about Energy?
                                        Energy is the basic stuff of the universe.
                                      It powers all living things, all machines, the
                                            weather, the Sun... everything!


     Energy Transfers
 When energy causes a change, it always results in the energy transferring to a new

Energy and Energy Transformations

Energy makes things happen
Energy is not a substance or an object that you can touch or hold, but substances and objects can possess
energy. Energy is needed to make objects move or change their state. Energy is found in different forms such
as potential or kinetic energy, which can be transformed from one to another. An energy source is a system,
which generates energy by transforming one type to another more useful type, usually electricity.
Any change in speed, size, shape or temperature in an
object requires energy. Energy is the ability to do work.
Work is applying force to an object and making it move in
distance.
Energy is measured in a unit called a joule (j)


Energy can exist as Potential or Kinetic Energy
Energy can be classified into two types; kinetic energy (Ek)
and potential energy (Ep). Kinetic energy is seen when
particles, waves or objects move. All forms of stored energy
are called potential energy – this cannot be seen until it is
transformed (changed) into active energy.

Kinetic energy




85 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Potential energy




Energy is always conserved.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another.

The total amount of energy never changes. Energy can transform from one type to another. All types of potential
energy must be transformed into kinetic energy for work to be done.

Energy can be transformed from one type to another

                                                     Energy can be transferred from one object to another.
                                                     E.g. heat energy from the rocks cooking the food in a
                                                     hangi. The type of energy does not change.

                                                     Energy can also be transformed from one type into
                                                     another. E.g., electrical energy changed into heat and
                                                     sound energy when boiling a jug. One type of energy can
                                                     be transformed into many different types.

Kinetic Energy.

How sources of energy are transformed into useful energy and wasted energy
When energy is transformed, some of the energy turns into forms we don't want. This energy is called wasted
energy. Wasted energy takes the form of heat and sometimes sound or light.
During any energy transfer, some energy is changed into heat. The heat becomes spread out into the
environment. (dispersed). This dispersed energy becomes increasingly difficult to use in future energy transfers.
In the end, all energy is transformed into heat and eventually lost out into space.

Energy from Biomass

With fossil fuels running out, the world needs renewable energy sources — energy sources that can be
made again as fast as they are used up. Plant material is an example of biomass (biological mass) which
is a good renewable energy source. Biomass is material which is living or has been living.

Plants are able to trap the sun’s energy using the chlorophyll in their leaves. They use the energy to convert
carbon dioxide and water to carbohydrate and oxygen.

1 What is this process of energy conversion called?

Carbohydrates store energy. When they are burned in air, this energy is released. Wood has been a
traditional fuel for many cultures. It is renewable, and is easily stored and transported. It can be converted
to charcoal (carbon) by heating in the absence of air. Although burning wood releases carbon dioxide into
the air, this is absorbed by the next generation of trees. Trees take a long time to grow and forests take up
a considerable area of land which could otherwise be used for housing or farming.

Ethanol has the formula CH,CH,OH and is an alcohol (alkanol). In Brazil, many cars (approximately 20%)
run on ethanol rather than petrol, Sugar cane is a fast-growing tropical plant. The sugar (sucrose) it
provides can be fermented to make ethanol, The fermented mixture is distilled to give pure ethanol.
Ethanol is an excellent liquid fuel that can be used instead of petrol in cars (with slight modifications to
the engine) or can be mixed with petrol. When ethanol burns it produces carbon dioxide and water.
Ethanol itself is a clean, renewable fuel, but it needs a very large area to grow sugar cane, and the processes
of refining sugar and ethanol do cause pollution.

Many plants produce vegetable oils — sunflower oil and peanut oil are examples. These oils could be used
as fuels in the future. Scientists are trying to find ways of making diesel engines run efficiently using

vegetable oils.

Energy in Food Experiment
Apparatus and Chemicals

Boiling tube,
1Clamp stand,
Boss Head and clamp,
1Bunsen burner,
Heatproof mat,
1 Measuring cylinder, 10mL,
1 Mounted needle,
Tongs or forceps for food samples that cannot be impaled
Thermometer (–10 °C–110 °C)
Eye protection
Water
Balance, accurate to ± 0.1 g
Food sample

Procedure

      Use a range of foods – around 1 cm square or 0.5 cm cubed.

      Use the measuring cylinder to measure 10 mL of water into the boiling tube.

      Clamp the boiling tube to the retort stand.

      Measure the temperature of the water with the thermometer. Record the temperature in a
       suitable results table.

      Choose a piece of food and find its mass using the balance. Record the mass in the table.

      Impale the piece of food carefully on a mounted needle.

      Light the Bunsen burner and hold the food in the flame until it catches alight.

      As soon as the food is alight, put it under the boiling tube of water. Try to make sure that as
       much of the heat from the burning food as possible is transferred to the water. Do this by
       keeping the flame under the tube. (The food should be about 1cm from the boiling tube.)

      Hold the food in place until the food has burnt completely. If the flame goes out, but the
       food is not completely burnt, quickly light it again using the Bunsen burner and replace the
       food beneath the tube.

      As soon as the food has burned away completely and the flame has gone out, measure the
       temperature of the water again. Before measuring, stir the water carefully with the
       thermometer and note down the highest temperature reached in the results table.

      Calculate the rise in temperature.

      Calculate the energy released from each food by using this formula.



How Much Energy Is There In Food Equation
 We measure the energy in foods in either joules or calories and you can see this displayed on
food packets. A joule is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1g of water by 1°C, and a

What is Energy?

searchText:
Energy Transfer

Energy can be described as ‘the ability to do work’. It can take several forms, such as sound, light,
movement and heat. The unit of energy is the joule, which has the symbol J. The joule is very small so
we tend to use kJ (kilojoules) or MJ (megajoules). There are a thousand joules in a kilojoule and a million
joules in a megajoule. The average adult will need in the region of 5 MJ of energy a day to maintain health.
A typical power drill or hair drier may be rated at 500 watts. This means that it uses 500 joules per second.

Consider a wood barbecue. When wood bums it is reacting
with the oxygen in the air. This is an example of combustion.
Carbon dioxide (CO, ) is one of the products of this reaction.
The reaction heats up the surroundings, so heat is given out.
This is an exothermic reaction. ‘Exo’ comes from the Greek and
means ‘out’. Heat energy is given out by the reacting system.

‘Trees take in energy from the sun. They grow by a chemical
change called photosynthesis, Carbon dioxide from the air
combines with water to make new substances. This is an
endothermic reaction. ‘Endo’ also comes from the Greek and
means ‘in’. Energy is taken in by the system.

Carbon dioxide + Water —> Glucose + Oxygen

Green plants are producers — they make their own food. They contain chlorophyll and thus can
photosynthesise. This process produces a food called glucose (a type of sugar) and also oxygen.

This process uses the energy of the sun (solar energy) to drive the reaction. This solar energy is converted
to stored chemical energy in plants. This energy is used for growth by the plant and to provide energy for
the plant during darkness when photosynthesis cannot take place.

Without organisms which photosynthesise (such as green plants) and organisms which live in water (such
as phytoplankton), there would be no animal life. Animals would have no food to eat and no oxygen to
breathe. Animals are consumers. If they eat plants, they are first-order consumers

Energy

What is Energy?
 Energy is needed to make things move or change
 Some substances and objects may have many forms of energy at the same time
 Living things need energy
 Energy exists in many different forms
 Energy can change from one form to another
 Energy is not a substance. It cannot be weighed and doesn’t take up any space.

Active or Stored?
 Active energy occurs in action and is detected when particles, waves or objects move.
  For eg light, heat, electrical, sound, kinetic
 Potential energy cannot be detected until it changes into active energy. The energy is
  stored because of their position in space or their nature. For eg chemical, magnetic,
  gravitational, nuclear, elastic

Enzymes are a special class of proteins that act as very efficient biological catalysts. They have some differences from 
inorganic catalysts, in that enzymes:
• are often very specific in the reactions they catalyse
• only work over a narrow temperature range
• only work over a narrow pH range.
Individual enzymes are named by adding ‘-ase’ onto the name of the substrate with which they reac; e.g. urease 
controls the decomposition of urea. However some have trivial names, such as pepsin.

will ‘fit’. Intermolecular forces hold the substrate in a particular position. The substitute-enzyme complex can either 
decompose or react with another substance.

Oxford Sciences 8 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet

Grape catapult
Before humans used gunpowder and explosives to fire things through the air, they used catapults. The original concept of a catapult is attributed to the Greeks, who are said to have invented the idea as a modification of the crossbow. Like many technologies, the design and use of catapults flourished during times of war. They were still being used in combat during World War I, to fire grenades into enemy trenches. 
Catapults are an energy transformation machine. In essence, they transform the elastic potential energy in a springy material into kinetic energy in a flying object. 
In this task, you will design a way to harness the elastic potential energy of a rubber band to create a grape catapult that will be as accurate as possible.
The first step will be to create a grape target. On a large piece of butcher’s paper, create a target similar to the one shown and stick this up on a wall. 
You will also need the following materials to design and make your grape catapult:
Up to 15 ice-cream sticks 
1 or 2 rubber bands
1 plastic spoon
Hot-glue gun
To guide you in your design, you will use the steps of the engineering design process. The engineering design process has five major steps:
Discover. Consider the problem or objective from all angles, research it and brainstorm ideas. 
Ideate. Develop a possible solution and design a prototype.
Build. Build the prototype.
Test. Evaluate the prototype to see if it meets the objective.
Improve. From the test results, identify how to make your design better.
Discover
Your objective is to create a grape catapult from the materials provided that is as accurate as possible.
First, think about this objective and how you will tackle it. Follow the questions in the table below to help guide your thinking. Add any additional questions of your own at the end.
Question

What are some of the features that you have drawn?

Many ice-cream-stick catapult designs already exist. Research some existing designs and note down the features that you see. What do they have in common?

Most catapults include a lever of some type. What types of levers are possible? In particular, think about where the fulcrum (or pivot point) could be located along the lever.


Most catapults include a base of some type to support the lever. What designs are possible for the base of a catapult? Explore the options.

Other questions:

Ideate
Now that you have done some thinking, brainstorm ideas for a catapult design using only the materials you have been assigned. Think specifically about the base, the lever and how your catapult will transform the elastic potential energy into kinetic energy. 








Choose your best idea and develop it further. Write up a description of your catapult design including a labelled diagram of how it works. Use the following questions to help you.
What shape will your base be?
If you are using a lever, how will it be secured and where will the fulcrum be located?
What will be used to house the projectile grape before take-off?
How will you be able to vary your catapult launch characteristics (direction and force) to optimise the accuracy of the grape’s flight path?
What safety issues are involved in creating and testing your catapult?








Draw a diagram of your design here.





Build
Build a prototype of your catapult, being especially careful with the hot-glue gun. A prototype is a “first try” to test if your concept will work. Write down the steps you took to build your prototype below. 








Test
Once your catapult is created, check to see if it works by placing it 1 metre from your target on the wall. Fire a few grapes at the wall and write down your observations about where they hit the target, if at all. If there are problems, note these down. 




Improve
Based on your test observations, how could you improve your design? Note down any ideas you have that could make it better. 




Repeat steps 4 and 5 to implement as many of your improvement ideas as possible in the time you have.
Data and results
Gather data on the accuracy of your catapult by firing six grapes at the target (from 1 metre in front) and measuring the distance between the centre of the target and the point where each grape hits the target. After each trial, adjust the angle of the catapult and the power of the launch to optimise the results.

searchText: ﻿We have all noticed that when you heat something up, its temperature rises. Often we think that heat and temperature are the same thing. However, this is not the case. Heat and temperature are related to each other, but are different concepts. Heat is the total energy of molecular motion in a substance while temperature is a measure of the average energy of molecular motion in a substance. Heat energy depends on the speed of the particles, the number of particles (the size or mass), and the type of particles in an object. Temperature does not depend on the size or type of object. For example, the temperature of a small cup of water might be the same as the temperature of a large tub of water, but the tub of water has more heat because it has more water and thus more total thermal energy. ACTIVITY: Discuss what you think the answer is to the following question: Which object contains the most heat, a boiling pot of water or a gigantic iceberg? Click here for the answer. It is heat that will increase or decrease the temperature. If we add heat, the temperature will become higher. If we remove heat the temperature will become lower. Higher temperatures mean that the molecules are moving, vibrating and rotating with more energy. If we take two objects which have the same temperature and bring them into contact, there will be no overall transfer of energy between them because the average energies of the particles in each object are the same. But if the temperature of one object is higher than that of the other object, there will be a transfer of energy from the hotter to the colder object until both objects reach the same temperature. Temperature is not energy, but a measure of it. Heat is energy. Pose the following question to your students.Ask students to justify their answers. Which object contains the most heat, a boiling pot of water or a gigantic iceberg? NOTES FOR TEACHERS: This discussion is designed to help students differentiate between heat and temperature . This question can also be turned around by asking students to consider a pot filled with ice and the iceberg. Assume they are at the same temperature,say -10oC, and you wish to melt each of them. Which of these objects would absorb the most heat to get to a temperature of +10oC ? This should help them realize that the mass, not just temperature, is an important consideration in determining the heat (energy) content of an object. This might be good opportunity to ask students if they think they are other properties of an object which might affect its heat content (as lead up to the concept of specific heat ). Consider the following... SMALL HOT OBJECT The total heat content in 500mL (0.5kg) of boiling water in a tea pot can be approximated by determining how much energy would be removed in order to cool it to absolute zero ( about -273oC.) Although the boiling water has a relatively high temperature, it contains relatively little heat energy. LARGE COLD OBJECT Suppose a you were to cool a 1,000,000 tonne iceberg (109kg) to absolute zero. You could approximate the heat energy removed from the iceberg in order to do this. While the iceberg is relatively cold (low temperature) it contains an enormous amount of heat energy relative to the boiling water in the tea pot.

Energy is the ability to do work. Work is applying force to an object and making it move in distance. 1a Energy is measured in a unit called a joule (J). A joule, unit of work or energy, is equal to the work done by a force of one Newton acting through one metre. This unit is named in honour of the English physicist James Prescott Joule. W (work) = F (force) x d (distance) 4a/b Expansion and Contraction of matter Matter expands or gets bigger when it is heated up. It contracts or gets smaller when it is cooled down. Some types of matter, such as metals, conduct heat very well and therefore the effects of expansion and contraction are more obvious. Structures such as bridges and railway tracks that are made out of metal have to be built with gaps so they don’t warp out of shape when exposed to higher temperatures during summer. 4a/b Expansion and Contraction of matter When matter expands or contracts only the space between the particles changes: not the size of the particles. The particles in a solid vibrate more when it is heated, and take up more space. The particles in a liquid move around each other more when it is heated, and take up more space. The particles in a gas move more quickly in all directions when it is heated, and take up more space. 4a/b Expansion, Contraction and Density in Gases As matter expands the density (mass of matter in a given volume) will decrease making it “lighter”. In a gas the warmer particles that are moving faster due to their increased kinetic energy are colliding with each other more. You can use a magnifying lens to burn wood.
HOW TO DO IT
Safety warning: never look directly at the sun, as this may cause
permanent eye damage.
1  Hold a convex lens in direct sunlight, so the rays are
focused onto a dark piece of wood. 
2  Move the lens up and down until the spot of light is as
small as possible, then move the lens a few millimetres
further away from the wood. (The wood will turn black and
begin to smoke.)
EXPLANATION
Light rays and infra-red heat rays travel from the sun. As they enter the convex lens they become refracted
so they begin to converge. The focal point is where the rays meet. The focal point for heat is slightly
further from the lens than the focal point for light.
The heat and light in this activity were produced in the centre of the sun and took over 100,000 years
to travel to its surface, then about 8 minutes to travel the 150 million kilometres to earth.
The centre of the earth is hotter than the surface of the sun.
Just before the sun dies it will expand until its surface almost reaches the earth. This will destroy all
life on our planet. Don’t worry though, because it won’t happen for another 5 billion years.

HEAT
            Conduction, Convention & Radiation
Name:                                       Class:           Date:

                     INFORMATION - HEAT          TRANSFERS

Heat and temperature are important concepts in all areas of science and in
students’ day-to-day lives. People deal with heat and temperature in their
everyday experiences, yet many people hold serious misconceptions about them.
All matter is made up of particles. The particles of any particular object will be
moving because of the temperature of the object is. The hotter the object the
faster and more violently the particles in it are moving. Thermal energy (NOT heat
energy) is the energy possessed by an object because of it’s temperature. Heat is
thermal energy that is in transit. Heat moves (transfers) from warmer objects to
cooler objects.
Heat is the energy transferred from
one object to another because of a
difference in their temperatures
But how exactly is heat transferred from
warmer matter to cooler matter?
Heat is transferred in three distinct ways
which is by conduction, convection or
radiation; or all of which may be occurring at
any given time.


Conduction is the transfer of the heat through a solid object. In order for the heat
to be conducted, there should be physical contact between particles and some
temperature difference. When one part of an object is heated, the molecules within
it vibrate against one another; begin to move faster and more vigorously, when
these molecules hit other molecules within the object they cause heat to be
transferred through the entire object. Substances that conduct heat readily are
called conductors, while substances that don't conduct heat readily are called
insulators. Metal (e.g. copper, platinum, gold iron, etc) is a good conductor of
thermal energy, aluminum is a good
insulator. Wood falls somewhere in
between. Conduction is greater in solids,
where molecules are in close and constant
contact. As density decreases so does
conduction.     Therefore,    fluids   (and
especially gases) are less conductive due
to the large distance between particles in
a gas – there are fewer collisions between
 the particles means less conduction. Generally liquids and gases transfer heat
using convection not conduction.
Convection is the transfer of heat energy caused by the movement of a liquid or
gas (such as air). Heat is transferred when a heated liquid or gas moves from place
to another, carrying its heat with it. Unlike conduction where the particles remain
in place but pass on their vibrational energy as heat, in convection the particles
move from one place to another, carrying the
heat with them. The rate of heat flow will depend
on the temperature of the moving gas or liquid
and on its rate of flow.
Convection currents due to warmer air rising and
cooler air falling is a common mechanism by
which thermal energy is transferred. When air is
heated, it expands, and therefore becomes less
dense, so it rises. The rising warm air displaces
cooler air, which sinks. When the motion is
constant, it's called a convective loop or
convection    current.  Oil    heaters  and    air
conditioners cause convective loops by heating or cooling (respectively) the air
closest to them.
Radiation is a method of heat transfer which does not rely upon any contact
between the heat source and the heated object. For example, we feel heat from
the Sun or a fire even though we are not touching them. Radiation can travel
through empty space and transparent things such as air and glass, but it cannot
travel through opaque objects like surfaces and walls.
Radiation is the transfer of energy
by infrared waves (a type of
electromagnetic wave, like visible
light). All objects possess thermal
energy and therefore emit some
infrared waves. Hotter objects are
more thermal energy than cooler
ones and emit more radiant
energy as infrared waves. The
concept of heat transfer by
radiation can be understood using experiences familiar to us in everyday life: the
warmth of the Sun, a campfire, or an open oven door.
In most situations, more than one method of heat transfer takes place. For
example, in the boiling water and pasta convection example above, water
becomes warmer due to the transfer of heat from the stove burner to the pot and
then from the pot to the water (conduction). Developing the idea that heat
transfers occur in a variety of ways should be emphasized rather than defining the
differences between conduction, convection, and radiation.
It should be recognized that heat transfers can be used to explain everyday
 phenomenon. However this can be a very challenging and abstract idea for many
of us. Some people may continue to hold on to their belief that heat moves from a
colder object to a warmer object or that both “heat” and “cold” are transferred at
the same time. You feel colder not because you have gotten more cold, but
because you have lost some thermal energy by conduction, convection, or
radiation.

Aim
– To find out the effect of moderate exercise on body temperature, carbon dioxide output and pulse rate.
– To infer how negative feedback mechanisms control temperature.
Equipment
6
HOMEOSTATIC CONTROL OF TEMPERATURE AFTER EXERCISE
Thermoregulation is the ability of an organism to keep its body temperature within certain boundaries, even
when the temperature of the surroundings is very different. This process is known as homeostasis. Homeostasis
is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment irrespective of changes in either the
external or internal environment. In animals, homeostasis is controlled by hormonal and nervous systems.
Negative feedback mechanisms tend to produce stability. They act to restore the original state of the
organism. They are stimulus-response mechanisms, where the response produced affects the stimulus. Humans
are homeotherms and maintain body temperature in the range 36.1°C–37.8°C. During exercise, the body
produces more heat, carbon dioxide and wastes and the demand for oxygen and glucose increases. As the body
temperature increases, the temperature receptors in the skin and the hypothalamus detect the changes in
temperature. The thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus sends electrical impulses to the effectors via
motor nerves. The blood vessels near the skin dilate and heat is lost. The sweat glands produce more sweat and
heat is lost when the sweat evaporates from the skin. The response is a decrease in temperature until normal
body temperature is regained. This response affects the original stimulus by the negative feedback system. The
heart rate and breathing rate also increase to provide more oxygen and glucose to the exercising muscles. The
percentage increase in the heart rate is influenced by a person’s age, physical fitness, gender, size and emotions.

Up, up and away – a hot air story
The story of the invention of the hot air balloon begins in the small town of Alchemy in southern 
France. Two brothers, Joseph and Jacques Montgolfier, were in the paper manufacturing business. 
They noticed that whenever they burnt paper, the ashes floated up into air. They discovered that the 
smoke and heat from the burning paper had a lifting quality.
With this in mind, the brothers set out to design a craft that could capture the heat and smoke 
to allow the craft to lift off the ground. On 19th September 1783, the Montgolfier brothers were 
successful in creating and launching their invention: a hot air balloon.
Their hot air balloon was made from paper and cloth. They used a combination of chopped wool, 
straw and dried horse manure for burning in order to inflate the balloon. The straw provided the 
heat which heated the air inside the balloon. The wool and manure made lots of smoke and kept the 
flame low so the paper and cloth balloon did not catch fire.
The brothers were a little unsure how the balloon would fly or how safe it was, so they sent sheep, 
chicken and ducks up in their balloon. Their trials were a success – they managed to keep the 
animals floating for eight minutes and then land the balloon successfully.
On 21st November 1783, the Montgolfier brothers convinced the King of France to come and see 
their invention. This time, people would be on board instead of farm animals. Two of their best 
friends volunteered for the job. The balloon was successfully launched and rose about 150 m above 
the rooftops of Paris and successfully landed in a vineyard a few kilometres away.

Scientific explanation for the teacher
Solids are made of particles that vibrate about fixed positions. When they are heated the
particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate more quickly. As the vibrating particles bump
into each other, the energy is passed along the solid from the hot end to the cold end.
Metals are better conductors of heat than wood or plastic; this is why they heat up
quickly and cool down quickly. When the spoons are placed in the hot water the heat is
conducted up the handles of the spoons. As the heat is conducted more quickly by metal
than by wood or plastic, the metal spoon will have a hotter handle than the plastic and
wooden spoons.

temperature describes the range of ideas given by 4–13-year-olds.
In general, 8–9-year-olds describe heat as a ‘state of hotness’ along a continuum from
cold through warm to hot, while 8-12-year-olds tend to associate heat with living
objects, sources of heat, and the effect of heat on objects.


Conduction
Nearly all students are aware that one hot object is capable of ‘heating-up’ another
cooler object when they come into direct contact, e.g. a cool saucepan gets hot when
placed on a hot stove. Many students explain how metal gets hot faster than wood or
plastic by stating that a metal has an attraction for heat, and a tendency to hold heat.
Younger students (<13 years) tend to state that the strength of the object affects its
heating and so does the strength of the heat.

The types of questions that students were asked in regard to the conduction of heat
include:
1. Which materials are good for the thermal insulation of a house?
2. Which materials are good for the thermal insulation of a hot drink or of ice?
3. Why is the handle of a metal spoon hotter than the handle of a wooden or plastic
    spoon when they are placed in hot water?




Copyright DEST 2004
 Hot handle                                                                                 4EC127
Common explanations given by students are listed below.
 The material retains warmth or cold, better or less well.
 The material has the property to be cold or warm because of its nature.
 The material becomes hot or cold, more or less quickly.
 The material retains, lets in or lets out hot or cold air, better or less well.
 The material takes the temperature of its surroundings.
 The material is a conductor or an insulator.


Temperature
By 8 or 9 years of age, students think that temperature is related to levels of hotness.
Between ages 8 and 12 years, students are able to use and read a thermometer, but
may not apply this scientifically. Some pupils think that objects of different materials
in the same room are at different temperatures. They say that metal objects are colder
than wood–objects.

Temperature is also often related to size. More than 50% of 12-year-olds thought that
a larger ice cube would have a colder temperature than a smaller one, and hence the
large ice cube takes longer to melt.


Thermal equilibrium
Students also have difficulty with the fact that everyday objects heat up. Only 30% of
students, before instruction, think that the temperature of sand, sugar and water will
increase when they are heated. Students have difficulty with thermal equilibrium. If
several objects are in the same environment in prolonged contact, then they are at the
same temperature. Even though a metal plate and a plastic plate are on the same bench
most students consider that they are not at the same temperature. Similarly, different
materials (flour, nails, water) placed for several hours in an oven at 600C are said by
the majority of students to be at different temperatures. The reasons below are typical.
           Flour is at less than 600C because flour does not heat up very much.
           Nails are at more than 600C because the iron heats faster.
           Water is at 600C because it takes the temperature of the surroundings.
Of junior secondary students, 10% gave the correct answer before instruction and
30% gave the correct answer after instruction.


Teaching implications
Heat can be directly sensed by students, and comparisons between hot and cold can be
made by touching different objects. Objects that are sensed as hot are hotter than the
skin temperature, and substances sensed as cold are colder than skin temperature.
Touch gives a relative measure of hotness. If you place one hand on a metal plate at
room temperature and the other hand on a plastic plate at room temperature, even
though both plates are at the same temperature, the metal plate feels cooler because
the metal conducts heat away from the hand faster than the plastic plate. The use of
thermometers is essential to overcome errors of perception about the degree of
hotness. Many students will also consider heat and cold to be ‘substances’ that are in
various materials rather than the thermal energy of a material.




Copyright DEST 2004
 Hot handle                                                                                   4EC127
Misconceptions about metals being strong and attracting heat or holding heat can be
challenged by using lengths of wire with one end placed in hot water so that students
can feel the heat moving along the wire, i.e. conduction rather than attracting or
holding heat. Open discussions expose students to different explanations of these
phenomena so that alternative conceptions can be challenged, and help students
generalise their ideas to new examples and to appreciate their range of application.

References
Erickson, G., & Tiberghien, A. (1985). Heat and temperature. In R. Driver, E. Guesne & A. Tiberghien
       (Eds), Children's Ideas in Science (pp. 52–84). Buckingham: Open University Press.

Of course you know that the fridge is cold on the inside. But did you also know that a fridge is warm at the back on 
the outside?  How does the fridge get so cold inside? And why is it warm behind the fridge?
In most fridges, there is a system of pipes on the inside and the outside. The inside pipes are usually fused onto a 
silver coloured metal plate. Outside at the back, the pipes are connected to many small black metal plates. Where 
the pipes enter the interior, there is an expansion valve. There is also an electric motor, which is usually under the 
fridge at the back. This motor runs a compressor.
Inside the pipes is a refrigerant. In old fridges this is Freon, which boils at -30°C. But Freon is one of the gases that 
destroy the ozone layer in the atmosphere and so it is no longer used. Old fridges should have their Freon taken out 
professionally. Freon destroys ozone molecules in the atmosphere and so they cannot absorb the dangerous and 
skin-cancer causing ultraviolet rays from the Sun. These days, different refrigerants are used; for example, ammonia 
which boils at -32°C and HFC which has a boiling point of -27°C.

Hypotheses and variables
12
IntroductIon 
Information obtained from practical procedures can be first-hand or second-hand. 
First-hand investigations are those that you carry out yourself, e.g. practicals carried out at school or at home. Secondary 
sources refer to information you may have obtained from elsewhere, e.g. from text books, encyclopaedias or the internet. 
For each investigation it is important to state a hypothesis, identify the variables involved and state that the investigation 
is valid, i.e. if it tests what it says it is testing.
Aim 
To enable students to form hypotheses and identify the different types of variables.
Information
A hypothesis is a statement that can be tested by scientific method. It is often described as an educated guess based  
on observations. Factors that can be changed during an experiment are called variables. Usually only one variable is 
changed at a time. There are three major types of variables:
• 
independent
• 
dependent
• 
controlled.
The independent variable is the major part of the hypothesis (belief) that you are  
testing. It is the condition that you change to see what happens. The dependent 
variable is the thing that changes when the independent variable is changed.  
A controlled variable is one that is kept the same in each experiment.

Joules, watts, amps and volts
Joules are a measure of energy. You use energy every day and you need to maintain a level of energy to keep 
you functioning, even while you sleep. Every action you do expends energy. 
James Prescott Joule was an English physicist, born in 1818 in Salford, Lancashire. Joule studied the nature of 
heat, and discovered its relationship to mechanical work. He also stated that heat is a form of energy. This led to 
the theory of conservation of energy. The joule is the international scientific unit for measuring energy.
1 
What do you think the theory of conservation of energy is?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Think of a joule as the energy used when a 100 g mobile phone is lifted through a height of 1 metre and held 
against the force of gravity, which is almost 10 Newtons. One joule is defined as the amount of energy exerted 
when a force of one Newton is applied over a displacement of one metre. A joule is also the equivalent of one 
watt of power being radiated for one second. This means that the energy in food can be related to the amount 
of work that can be done from specific food items. Food energy is commonly measured in kilojoules (kJ).
2 
A chocolate biscuit has 300 kilojoules of energy. How many times must a 100 kg person walk up a 5 m high stair 
case to use up this energy? (Assume the force of gravity = 10 Newtons)
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Consider a 9 volt battery with a current of 1 amp. This means that 9 joules per second (or 9 watts) are being 
used. When one joule is used per second, the unit of power is called a watt, after James Watt. One watt of power 
is equivalent to the rate at which energy is produced by a candle. Think of a watt as a quantity of electrical 
energy flowing per second. The amount of power being used is the rate at which energy is expended, or  
Power = Volts x Amps, which can be written as P = VI.

searchText: ﻿Where Does the Energy Go? Aim: To find out where the heat energy from hot water goes to as the water cools down. Half fill your 250 mL beaker with cold water. 2. Place the beaker in your ice cream container and add cold water to the ice cream container until it covers the cold water in your beaker. 3. = c-Si ELECTRICITY AND MAGNETISM —

Resistance |

Electricity flows when electrons move through conductors.
1 What do we call a substance that doesn’t conduct electricity?

Good conductors include the elements copper (Cu), aluminium (Al), silver (Ag) and gold (Au).
2 What do these substances have in common?

Electrical resistance: the property of a substance to resist
(oppose) the flow of an electrical current

Electrons move easily through good conductors, such as copper which has little resistance to the flow of
electrons. They do not move as easily through other substances, which offer more resistance. Not all metals
are good conductors like copper. ‘Nichrome’ wire has a high resistance.

3 Nichrome is an alloy of iron (Fe) and two other metals. What are these two metals? (Hint: Ni and Cr.)
4 Which circuit will need more energy to push electrons around it, one having low resistance or one
having high resistance?

When electricity encounters resistance as it flows in a circuit, it gives off heat. The greater the resistance
the greater the heat given off.

5S Name three electrical appliances which use electricity to generate heat.
6 Why might Nichrome wire, rather than copper, be used in the element of an electrical kettle?

Light bulbs (globes) give out light as well as heat when a current flows through
them, The outside of the globe is made of glass containing an unreactive gas such
as argon (Ar) or nitrogen (N). Inside there is a coil of tungsten (W) wire called the
filament. The filament glows white hot when electricity flows. The unreactive gases
stop the wire from burning. If air gets in, the hot filament will react with oxygen in
the air and burn.

7 Copy the diagram of a light globe, and label the parts indicated by the arrows.
8 Does the element tungsten have a high resistance or a low resistance? Give a
reason for your answer.

Short circuits and fuses — Part 1

12a

}

NWN

In an electric circuit some electrical energy needs to be used up; that is, a resistance must slow the electric
current, otherwise the unusually large amount of current travelling through the circuit will cause some of
the circuit components to heat up, to melt or to spark. When components melt or get wet, electricity will
flow along the path of least resistance, possibly causing a short circuit which often leads to fire. Fuses are
designed to ‘blow’ before any item in a circuit causes a fire. When a fuse blows, the circuit is interrupted
and electricity no longer flows.

Ammeters measure the current. Since they have a very low resistance themselves and do not influence
the current, they are switched in series with the item to be measured. Voltmeters, on the other hand,
measure the potential difference and do not want any current to flow through them. Therefore, a voltmeter
has a very high resistance and is switched parallel with the item to be measured.

subject: Science
searchText:
Supercooling – the energetics of freezing


Class practical
Students melt sodium thiosulfate crystals, and these are then cooled to a state well below the melting point. The melt now
exists in a metastable supercooled state. The supercooled liquid will freeze rapidly on the addition of a crystal of sodium
thiosulfate or dust particles, or on stirring. Students add a crystal of the solid and this seeds the crystallisation process.
Temperature changes are observed throughout.



Lesson organisation
This is best carried out individually or in pairs. The experiment takes between 20 and 30 minutes.

Apparatus                      Chemicals
Each group will        Sodium thiosulfate-5-water, about 20 g
need:                  Refer to Health & Safety and Technical
Test-tube (Note 1)     notes section below for additional
Test-tube holder       information.
Stirring thermometer
(-10 – 110°C) (Note 2)
Beaker (100 cm3)
Bunsen burner
Tripod and gauze
Cotton wool, small
tuft to fit test-tube

Health & Safety and Technical notes
Read our standard health & safety guidance

Wear eye protection.

Sodium thiosulfate-5-water, Na2S2O3.5H2O(s) - see CLEAPSS Hazcard.

1 The test-tube must be very clean.

2 A temperature sensor attached to a computer can be used in place of a thermometer. Thus a continuous plot can be drawn as
the temperature changes occur.



Procedure
a Half fill a very clean test-tube with crystals of sodium thiosulfate-5-water.

b Put a tuft of cotton wool in the top of the test-tube to exclude dust.

c Warm the test-tube gently in a beaker of hot water (about 50 oC) to melt the crystals.

d When all the crystals have melted, remove the cotton wool, put a thermometer in the melt and record the temperature. If the
 liquid starts to crystallise on inserting the thermometer, re-heat in water to melt all the solid.

e Stand the test-tube in an empty beaker and leave to cool where it won't be disturbed.

f Observe the temperature at various intervals until the value is in the region of 30 – 40 °C. No crystallisation should have
occurred.

g Now add a fresh crystal of sodium thiosulfate, observe the rapid crystallisation which occurs, and once again continue to
monitor the temperature at regular intervals.

h Wait until the temperature has fallen to about 25 – 30 °C.




Teaching notes
Once the experiment is over the thermometer can easily be removed by flushing with water, since sodium thiosulfate is water-
soluble, or by re-melting the solid. Do not heat the test-tube directly over a Bunsen flame as at higher temperatures the
thiosulfate decomposes and may form toxic products.

The temperature changes occurring show a steady fall as the liquid cools. When a crystal is added to the supercooled liquid, the
temperature rapidly rises as solidification takes place, confirming this process is exothermic. The solid then cools to room
temperature.

All solids exhibit supercooling to a greater or lesser extent, but sodium thiosulfate is particularly prone to exhibiting this
metastable condition. With more time available, it is possible to cool down the melt to a value well below room temperature, but
to achieve this involves waiting for more time to elapse, thus lengthening the experiment considerably.

An impressive teacher demonstration can be carried out using cold running water to cool the melt down rapidly to about 5 – 10
°C before a crystal is added to seed the crystallisation process. The test tube warms up extremely rapidly and becomes quite hot
in the process.

Health & Safety checked, September 2014

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Temperature control and
water loss in humans

Introduction

Humans, like birds and other mammals, are endothermic. The human body is maintained at a relatively constant

temperature by a number of mechanisms:

+ Ifthe core temperature drops, the body can limit heat loss by constricting (narrowing) the peripheral blood
vessels (in the skin), raising body hair and generating extra heat by shivering.

* If the core temperature rises, the body can lose heat by sweating. As the sweat evaporates, it cools the skin
and the blood flowing through the skin. This process is made more efficient by dilating (widening) the
peripheral blood vessels so that more blood comes in contact with the cooled skin layer.

subject: Science
description: Science, Technology and Society. Teaching Guide, Demonstration.
searchText:
One hand feels warm and the other hand feels cold, but they are both in the same bowl of water.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Set up three empty ice cream containers in a row. Put hot
(but not scalding) water in the first, tepid water in the
second and cold water in the third.
2  Put your left hand in the hot water and your right hand in
the cold water for about 1 minute. Swirl the water a little
with your hands to keep the temperature even.
3  Quickly transfer both hands into the tepid water and
concentrate on what each hand is sensing. (The left hand
will sense cool water, and the right hand will sense warm
water.)
EXPLANATION
Your heat and cold receptors sense changes in temperature rather than absolute temperature. The tepid
water feels cold by comparison with hot water.
Most animals don’t perspire. In fact, humans and horses are among the very few mammals that do use
perspiration to cool themselves. Instead, dogs pant to evaporate water from their tongues (dogs pant
when they are hot rather than ‘puffed’), and kangaroos lick the underside of their wrists where the
blood vessels are near the surface.
Rattlesnakes can locate warm-blooded prey by sensing the heat they give off. Their heat sensors can
detect a temperature increase of 0.002oC.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Use body heat to expand air. Place an empty wine bottle in
the fridge until it is cold. Take it out and place a wet ping-
pong ball in the mouth of the bottle. Wrap both of your
hands  around the bottle. (The air inside the bottle will
expand as it is warmed by your body heat. Some of the air
will leave the bottle, causing the ball to plop up and down
in the opening.)
2  Feel heat conduction. Use your hand to compare the
temperature of a metal chair leg and a wooden table top.
(The metal will feel colder because the heat from your hand
is rapidly conducted away. The wood will feel warmer
because it is a poor conductor, so the heat from your hand is
not dissipated.)

title: Cotton Wool
subject: Science
description: Science, Technology and Society. Teaching Guide, Demonstration.
searchText:
You can squash a surprising amount of cotton wool into a beaker of water. 
HOW TO DO IT
1  Tightly pack cotton wool into a small beaker until it
reaches the 100mL mark. 
2  Remove the cotton wool from the beaker and replace it
with exactly 100mL of water. 
3  Slowly add all the cotton wool to the beaker, pushing it
down firmly with a pencil to remove all the air. Make sure
that none of the cotton wool is above the surface. (The
water level will only rise 3–4mL.)
EXPLANATION
Materials that contain a lot of air are usually good insulators.
Cotton wool consists mainly of air, and the amount of cotton
is relatively small. When cotton wool is submerged, the water
replaces the air, and the slight rise in the water level
represents the solid portion.
Emperor penguins have to stand on the bare ice throughout
the long Antarctic winter, yet they have absolutely no
insulation on their feet. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Insulate an ice block. Wrap an ice block in a large sheet of newspaper and secure it with a rubber
band. Place another ice block on a dish, uninsulated. Compare the rates of melting. (Air trapped in the
newspaper will insulate the first piece of ice from the heat in the room.)
2  Investigate insulation in cups. Obtain a polystyrene cup
and a tin cup of about the same size. Fill both with water
and put two ice cubes in each. Compare the rates of
melting of the ice. (The polystyrene contains air, which
insulates the contents, so the ice will melt more slowly.)
