title: Dry Ice
subject: Science
description: Science, Technology and Society. Teaching Guide, Demonstration.
searchText:
You can make fog come out of a beaker of water.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
1  Half fill a very large beaker with water.
2  Add about a dessertspoonful of dry ice. Safety warning: do
not touch the dry ice with your bare hands. (A dense white
fog will emerge from the beaker and spread across the floor.)
EXPLANATION
This activity involves three states of water and two states of carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide changes
from a solid to a gas and bubbles out of the water. As it is denser than air it accumulates near the floor of
the room. The carbon dioxide gas is very cold, so it cools the air around it, causing water vapour to
condense into droplets. Meanwhile, some of the liquid water in the beaker will have turned into ice as it
was frozen by the dry ice.
A whale’s spout is not a stream of water — it is just air
that has been blown out of its lungs. The air is warm and
moist from the lungs and when it hits the cooler, outer air
the water vapour in it condenses into fog.
Any known substance that can be heated to its boiling
point will evaporate. Iron evaporates at about 2900oC.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Does this can leak? Fill a tin can with icewater. Observe the
outside of the can. (The cold metal cools the air in contact
with it. As the air cools, the water vapour in it condenses
and will appear as drops on the outside of the can.)
2  Change the state of cola. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY — Safety glasses and laboratory coats
should be worn. Pour half a can of cola into a flask and attach it to a condenser. Predict what sort of
liquid will be collected from the condenser when the cola is boiled. (Cola is about 90% water by
volume, which will be collected by evaporation and condensation. A can of cola also contains, among
other things, about 6 teaspoons of sugar, kola nut extracts for flavour and carbon dioxide for
effervescence.)

title: Dyeing Daisies
subject: Science
description: Science, Technology and Society. Teaching Guide, Demonstration.
searchText:
You can make a daisy turn green.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain a yellow daisy and cut the stem so it is only 5–6cm
long.
2  Place the cut end of the stem in a small beaker containing
some undiluted blue food colouring.
3  Put the beaker and flower in a warm sunny part of the room. (After a few minutes the blue colour will
begin to appear in the petals. As more dye enters the petals they will eventually turn green.)
EXPLANATION
The food colouring travels up the xylem vessels in the stem of the plant and enters the petals. The green
colour results from the combination of the yellow petals and the blue dye.
TO INVESTIGATE
Does this phenomenon apply only to daisies? Also, is it possible to colour a flower with two different
colours?
Not all flowers are sweet smelling. The stinking corpse lily
(Rafflesia), of Malaysian jungles, is the world’s largest
flower, growing up to 1 m in diameter. It makes a smell like
rotting meat to attract flies to pollinate it.
Not all insect visitors at flowers are collecting nectar. 
Some orchids have their petals arranged in such a way as 
to resemble a female wasp. Male wasps are attracted to the
flowers and try to mate with them, but they only succeed 
in pollinating the flowers.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Dissect an orchid. Obtain a large orchid and identify the
features which make it different to other flowers. (Orchid
flowers are vertically symmetrical. The sepals are coloured,
the lower petal forms a lip that is a landing platform for
insects, and the male and female parts are combined into a
column inside the flower. Any insect that lands on the lip
and falls into the centre of the flower will brush against the
column, resulting in pollination.)
2  Have a scavenger hunt for plant reproductive structures
that don’t have petals. During spring, find the flowers of
grasses, eucalypts and bottle brushes plus the reproductive
structures of conifers, ferns and mosses.

title: Floating Apple
subject: Science
description: Science, Technology and Society. Teaching Guide, Demonstration.
searchText:
This apple will sink in hot water but float in cold water.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain a fresh apple and some large nails. Embed enough
nails in the underside of the apple so that it will only just
float in cold water. 
2  Place the apple in a large beaker of cold water. (The apple
will float.)
3  Place the apple in a large beaker of hot water. (The apple will sink.)
4  Add cold water to the beaker with the sunken apple. (The apple will rise to the surface.)
EXPLANATION
The hot water is less dense than the cold water (because water expands when it is heated), so the hot
water has less upthrust. (Upthrust is reduced in fluids of lower density.)
Heat causes the sea to expand. The El Niño effect is caused
by a large pool of relatively warm water (5–10oC higher
than normal) located in the eastern Pacific. Because this
water is warm, it has expanded, so sea levels along the
coast of South America can be up to 25 cm higher than
usual.
Some types of bacteria live in boiling water in hot springs. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make an underwater convection current. Take a small vial,
add a few drops of food colouring and fill it to the brim
with hot water. Place it in a large beaker of cold water. (The
coloured water is warmer and less dense, so it will move to
the top of the beaker.)
Underwater volcanoes make the continents move. Australia will have moved over 4 m northwards during
your lifetime.
2  Expand a bottle. Fill a plastic bottle with water and screw the lid on tightly. Place it in the freezer
overnight. (Water expands as it freezes, so the bottle will be swollen or cracked in the morning.)

A burning teabag will float into the air.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY Safety glasses and
laboratory coats should be worn.
1 Remove the string and the staple from a teabag, empty the 
tea from it and unfold it to form a cylinder about 10cm long. 
2 Stand the cylinder upright on a dish and use a match to light it all the way around the top rim, so it
burns evenly all the way down. If the teabag starts to topple over then use the spent match to lightly
support it at the side. (As the burning proceeds down towards the dish the teabag will suddenly lift 
1–2m into the air.)
EXPLANATION
The heat from the burning teabag causes the air above it to
rise. When most of the material of the teabag has burned away
it becomes light enough to be lifted into this convection
current that has formed above it.
It is difficult for aeroplanes to take off from high altitude airports on hot days. The reduction in air
pressure, caused by both the high altitude and the expansion of air due to heat from the runway,
means that some aeroplanes can only take off if they are half empty.
Dick Smith crossed Australia in a hot air balloon. He has been referred to as ‘Australia’s answer to
Leonardo da Vinci’ because he was also the first person to circumnavigate the world in a helicopter,
and to reach the North Pole by helicopter. He hasn’t owned Dick Smith Electronics since 1982.

1  Model a hot air balloon. Obtain a kitchen freezer bag and use a hairdryer to fill it with hot air. Turn the
hairdryer off then release the bag. (The bag will rise above your head because the  warm air inside is less
dense than the surrounding air.)
2  Make a twister. Cut a circle of paper about 15cm in
diameter, then cut into it turning it into a spiral. Tie a
length of cotton to the centre and let it hang a few
centimetres above a hot plate. (The convection currents will
start it spinning.)

You can make corn seeds explode.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY 
Safety glasses and laboratory coat should be worn.
1  Obtain a large beaker and clean it thoroughly.
2  Cover the bottom of the beaker with about 4 tablespoons
of cooking oil.
3  Place the beaker on a hotplate.
4  Add about 1/2 a cup of popping corn and 1/2 a teaspoon of salt, then cover the beaker.
5  Mix the contents regularly as it heats. (After a few minutes the corn will pop.)
EXPLANATION
Corn seeds contain a small amount of water that is mixed with the starch. When this water is heated it
eventually turns into steam, but the steam is trapped inside the seed by the hard outer coat. The steam
pressure builds up until the kernel explodes, exposing the starch in a frothy state.
TO INVESTIGATE
Do popping corn kernels germinate as readily as corn from seed packets? 
The kangaroo rat and the flour beetle obtain ALL their water from food such as seeds. They never drink.
Some seeds can remain alive for many hundreds of years. Even wheat seeds found inside the Egyptian
pyramids have sprouted when watered.
Peach pits contain cyanide.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Ecosystems
53
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Plant and animal biodiversity 
Adaptation
Adaptation is the name that scientists give to the way that living things change and 
become better suited to their habitats. 
Offspring are not identical to either of their parents. Each new generation of a species 
is a tiny bit different from the one before. The theory of evolution says that these tiny 
differences are not noticeable from generation to generation, but over thousands or 
millions of years these small differences can completely and obviously change the way a 
plant or animal looks or functions. Adaptation results in new species and new subspecies. 
In this way it contributes to the biodiversity, or biological diversity, of life on Earth.
+ 1 Explain why you think offspring are not identical to either of their parents.
 
 
 
 
The process of adaptation happens because of small variations within a species. 
Variations that give some individuals a better chance of survival than other individuals in 
their species lead to what we call ‘survival of the fittest’, or natural selection. An example 
of a variation that might give a better chance of survival is a different fur colour, which 
might make it easier for a small animal to hide from predators.
Because the changed individuals are more likely to survive, they are more likely to 
breed and produce offspring. Their offspring are more likely to have the changed feature, 
or trait. Over time, this can result in a complete change to all the individuals in a species. 
The new species trait is called the adaptive trait, or the adaptation.
BACKGROUND
habitat (say ‘hab-i-tat’) – the particular place where a group of living things live
marsupial (say ‘marr-soup-ee-al’) – a type of small furry mammal, with a pouch for its young
species (say ‘spee-seas’) – a group of living things that can breed together to produce fertile offspring

searchText:
ADAPTATION: DESIGN A SPECIES – Teachers’ Notes


Who is it for?           7-11 year olds

How long will it take? The activity is ideal as a 1 hour session. The ‘Design a Species’ activity
                         could be set as a homework project.

Learning outcomes: Students will learn about how animals are adapted to survive in different
                         habitats

What do you need?

       Interactive whiteboard or projector
       Computer to connect to whiteboard or projector
       ARKive’s Adaptation classroom presentation (PowerPoint)
       A3 paper
       Felt tip pens or colouring pencils
       Set of habitat cards
       Set of predator / prey cards


Summary:

This creative activity is designed to teach 7-11 year olds about the concept of adaptation – the
process whereby a species evolves characteristics that enable it to survive in a particular habitat.

Using the marine environment as an example, students learn about how different species are
adapted physically or behaviourally to survive in a particular type of habitat.

Working in groups, students are allocated a habitat (desert, polar or rainforest) and either a
predator or prey species. Groups then design and create their own new species of animal or plant
based on their allocated habitat. Students then present their new species to the rest of the class
for discussion.

Preparation guidelines:

    1. Read through the instructions to make sure you understand the activity.
    2. Print and cut out a set of habitat cards. For a class of 30 students you will need to print
       out 10 habitat cards.
    3. Print and cut out a set of predator / prey cards. For a class of 30 you will need to print out
       10 predator/prey cards.
    4. Download the Adaptation PowerPoint presentation.
 How to run the session:

   1. Begin by introducing the concept of adaptation by working through the Adaptation
      PowerPoint presentation. Using marine habitats as an example, discuss what physical
      and behavioural adaptations marine species have evolved to survive in the marine
      environment. See slide notes on the Powerpoint presentation for further guidance and
      information.

   2. Introduce the Design a Species activity explaining that in groups the students will be
      allocated a particular habitat (desert, polar, rainforest) and either a predator or prey and
      be asked to design a new species adapted to survive in that habitat.

   3. Use ‘spiny skipper’ a prey species adapted for the marine environment on the adaptation
      PowerPoint as an illustrative example.

   4. Suggest what things students will need to think about when designing their own species
      such as what the species will eat, how it move about etc.

   5. Divide students into small groups of 2-3.

   6. Provide each group with a habitat card (desert, polar or rainforest) and a predator or prey
      card.

   7. The groups should think about what species are found in their allocated habitat and the
      physical and behavioural adaptations they have which help them survive. Using this,
      groups should work together to design their own new animal or plant species adapted for
      their given habitat using the A3 paper and pens provided. Students can be as imaginative
      as they like! The different adaptations featured on their species should be labelled. Allow
      around 30 minutes for this.

   8. Students should then present their made-up species to the rest of the class, emphasising
      why particular adaptations were selected and what species inspired them.


Suggestions for extension activities:

      Introduce additional habitat cards such as the deep sea, rocky shore or mountains.

      If students have internet and computer access, groups could research species found in
       their allocated habitat using ARKive (www.arkive.org) for inspiration before designing
       their own species.

      Discuss the potential impacts of environmental factors such as climate change or human
       activities such as habitat destruction or pollution on particular habitats and the species
       that live there.

Ecology
Design an animal 19a

she The marsupial mole - a report

The Aboriginal name for the marsupial mole varies according to the locality in which it is found. In central
western Australia it is referred to as ‘the blind sand burrower’, Arra-jarra-ja, or Kakarratul for the northern
species and Itjaritjari for the southern species. Elsewhere in the southern Northern Territory, it is known as
Oorquamatia.

The marsupial mole looks like a mole or a small solid rat. It has a pouch like other marsupials, measures
about 10 - 20 cm and weighs 40 — 60 g. It has soft, fine fur of a cream-yellow colour. It has no external sign
of eyes, although there are eye spots hidden under the skin. There is also no sign of external ears, but there
are distinct ear openings beneath the fur. The nose is a small shield of horny skin used for pushing the sand
away to make a tunnel. The nostrils are small slits. The short tail, only about 2 cm long, is encircled with
rings and terminates in a tough lump. The limbs are short and powerful, each foot having five digits. The
third and fourth fingers are large and scoop-like, with sharp claws for digging. The pouch opens toward the
rear so that sand is not pushed into it.

The marsupial mole is believed not to drink, although it must eat food every day. It seems to reproduce
during early summer, but no details are known about its breeding.

Adapting creatures
Teaching notes
The idea behind this resource is to explore the concept of natural selection and
to explain in general why species evolve and why some become extinct. All the
information to run the activity is below. The additional PowerPoint structures
the activity for use on a whiteboard and includes images and links to clips.

Keywords
Adaptation, evolution, extinction, natural selection, offspring, reproduction,
species, survival of the fittest

Teaching sequence
Step 1
Begin with a few images of familiar species e.g. whale, camel, fish, frog, bird
   What are they?
   How do we know?

Step 2
Then show images of animals which have unusual adaptations (ones that might
be useful to the creatures described below) e.g. flying fish, giraffe, lungfish,
nocturnal aye-aye; video clip of darkling beetles in Namib desert or male
Namaqua sandgrouse collecting water in their feathers youtu.be/Of2Mu_D18I0 .
    Can students suggest how these adaptations arose?

Step 3
There are lots of crazy creatures in the world. Students are going to illustrate
their own species of animal, however it must have features which enable it to
live in the way described.
        A camel which lives in a very cold desert where all the trees are tall.
        A species of nocturnal frog which lives on a foggy beach.
        Fishes who live in ponds which dry up for 6 months of the year.
        A flightless, tree-climbing, fruit-eating bird.
Students work in pairs or small groups, each person in the group chooses a
different creature to illustrate. They draw their animal and add notes about its
adaptations (colour could be added later at home). Allow 10-15 minutes.
Show and discuss the finished creatures.

Step 4
Then throw a big problem into the mix…
E.g. imagine a whale which vacuums up swarms of flying insects. What would
happen if all the swarming insects suddenly vanished? If the change was too
quick for the species to adapt to then it may become extinct.
What change, linked to habitat or diet, would drive their species towards
extinction?
But, what if the problem was more minor?
    What if the swarming insects began to fly a little higher – out of the reach
       of many whales?
    How might this type of whale species alter over time?

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019        33937                              Page 1 of 2
                                                               Adapting creatures
Step 5
Students return to groups.
Possible changes are shown on the board.
Here are a few suggestions.
    For the camel the trees become taller
    For the frog the foggy spells reduce
    For the fish the ponds become drier for longer
    For the bird the fruit begins to develop at the very tips of the twigs
Students will mostly think about visible changes to their creatures’ body.
Encourage them to consider physiological as well as morphological changes
(depending on what they have covered so far in the syllabus).
E.g. the whale may require more energy to leap higher, may begin to have
more red blood cells to carry more oxygen.


Students alter their creatures and/or add annotations.

Then pose the questions:
   Why did the trees in the camel’s habitat become taller?
   Why did the fruit tree begin to produce fruit that was out of the tree-
     climbing birds reach?

Step 6
Show images of poison arrow frogs; poisonous mushrooms with names like
'destroying angel'; spines on an acacia; the trunk of a monkey puzzle (choose a
spikey one!). They all have defences against being eaten.

The swarming insects and the trees don't want to be attacked by the students'
creatures – it is not an advantage for them.
    Can they suggest adaptations which they might evolve to prevent them
      being eaten?
The problems which arose for the frog and the fish were not the result of a
feeding relationship but the result of a change in climate.
    What would students do to protect their creature and its food source from
      environmental change?

Step 7
Extension questions:

      What measurements could students take over time to show the
       evolutionary change that has occurred in their animal species? E.g. mass
       of muscles used by whale to rise above the water.

      What measurements could be taken to show the main factor which has
       driven this adaptation? E.g. average height the insect swarm flies at.

9.8 | Advantages of biological control

Science understanding jounsanion | stanovnn | apvancen |

Biological control is the use of a natural enemy (such as a predator) of a pest to control populations
of that pest. This method of control, when done correctly, has great advantages because it does

less damage to the environment than chemical pesticides. An example of insect populations being
controlled biologically is shown in Figure 9.8.1.

Figure 9.8.1 A parasitic wasp named
Trioxys lays an egg in an aphid. The
egg hatches into a larva that eats the
insides of the aphid before changing
into an adult wasp

Some pesticides can accumulate in food webs, leading to sickness and death in higher order
consumers. Biological control avoids this accumulation of poisons in food webs.

In addition, chemical pesticides will usually kill many other useful organisms, such as wasps and
praying mantises, that may be natural predators of the pests. So, pesticides may actually make a
problem worse. Pesticides also kill other useful organisms such as bees, which may be helping to
pollinate flowers. Biological control has a great advantage over pesticides because it targets only
the pest

Over time, pests can become resistant to the chemical pesticide. This means that some populations
of the pest are able to survive the poison. When this occurs, a stronger concentration of the
pesticide or a different pesticide needs to be used to control pest populations. In biological control
the pest never becomes resistant to the biological control agent.

Another advantage of biological control is that it can become permanently established. It does
not have to be regularly applied like pesticides. Once the control agent is released, it will keep
reproducing and so become a permanent part of the ecosystem. Therefore control over the pest
is ongoing.

There is more than one reflex arc. Figure 25-1 shows the patellar reflex that occurs when a
tendon in the knee is suddenly tapped. The action causes a muscle to tense and raise the
leg slightly. Simple reflexes such as the patellar are referred to as monosynaptic reflexes.
Figure 25-2 shows what happens when the tip of the finger accidentally comes in contact
with a flame. Just as the patellar reflex, the withdrawal reflex occurs immediately, without
first having to involve the brain. Yet it is more complex than the patellar reflex shown in
Figure 25-1, because it is a polysynaptic reflex.




1. Trace the paths of each reflex. How do the two reflex arcs differ in complexity?

response reflex. How do these interneurons function in secondary responses?

Electrical signals travel throughout your nervous system, carrying information from one
place to another. The nervous system is made up of the nerve cells, or neurons. The
neurons have gaps between them, called synaptic spaces, which an electrical signal has to
jump across in order to continue. In some electrical machinery, electrical signals jump
across a tiny gap as a spark. In your body, an electrical impulse is passed by a chemical
signal called a neurotransmitter.

suddenly blocked from passing into the synaptic spaces?

BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Behavioural adaptations to environment

The environment a species inhabits will affect how it adapts and evolves. Dispersion, or 'spreading-out’ activity,
plays an important role in many behavioural adaptations. Dispersion (disperse to part) can involve animals or
their food supply, For example, an animal that must travel long distances at regular intervals in order to eat will
need, among other characteristics, the strength and stamina to withstand the trips, Natural selection will favour
individuals who possess these features.

Other ecological adaptations are associated with daily life. Flexibility is important. Some important factors to
consider include:

Is it more advantageous for the species to live in groups or alone?

* If the species lives in groups, is it better to work together as a co-operating community (eg ants, bees), or
to just live as individuals who happen to share a habitat? This point applies to territory as well. Should the
animals defend their whole territory as a group or just defend their own small portion of it from others
(whether they are members of the community or not).

* Should parental care be long-term or non-existent? For long-term care, would it be more beneficial for one
or both parents to care for their own offspring or, as in the case of lionesses, the whole group protects
the young, with several females feeding cubs whenever possible.

The ability to adapt one’s behaviour helps to maximise an organism's fitness. Discuss this statement.
Describe the difference between adapted and inherited.

Biogeography involves the study of the geographical distribution of animals and plants. This branch of science is 
used to investigate why organisms (plant or animal) are found where they are, and how that affects the land and the

Biology – extended response question practice

Teaching notes

This resource is designed to help pupils learn to answer extended response
questions effectively.

Students have the word list in front of them plus various coloured pencils.

Use the PPT to reveal the clues one at a time. After each clue is revealed,
students decide which words to 'save or scrap', before showing the next clue.
Then show students the exam question.

They are then asked to underline certain words using different colours. At this
point go over some of their ideas to iron out any misconceptions such as
respiration makes energy.

When this is done students use prompts to help them plan an answer to the
question. A simple mark scheme is revealed and students write an answer to
the question.

As an alternative to using the PPT the clues, instructions and mark scheme
could be printed on paper and handed out to the students at the appropriate
time.

words.

BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Components of an environment — biotic and abiotic

The biotic components of an environment are the organisms present.
1 What are the abiotic components of an environment?

For scientific purposes, the living world has been divided into groups called biomes, meaning ‘zone of life’.
Biomes are large, naturally occurring communities of plants and animals forming recognisable groups occupying
a large territory, The two major world biomes are aquatic and terrestrial. They can be divided into more specific
Categories based on the species present.

Aquatic (aqua, water): These are the ‘wet’ biomes and consist of freshwater (eg ponds, rivers) and marine (eg
sea/ocean, estuary). The composition of the water, which differs between each, affects the kinds of species that
will be found.

2 What is the main difference between freshwater and marine conditions?

Desert (desertare, to forsake): Roughly 20% of the Earth is desert. A biome that commonly receives less than
50 cm of precipitation per year is classified as a desert. This lack of water means that many types of vegetation
cannot survive and deserts are recognisable by the vast stretches of sand on which little or no vegetation is
present. Any vegetation present has evolved to adapt to the arid conditions,

Forest (forestis, wood): Forests are biomes that are densely covered by various tree species (depending on their
geographical location), Smaller trees and shrubs are usually found beneath the tree canopy. Forests cover about
30% of the Earth and represent 70% of the carbon found in living organisms,

Tundra (tanturia, treeless plain): Commonly found in cold northern regions of North America, parts of Asia
and the Arctic districts of Europe, tundra are large, treeless areas. At ground level, the soil is cold and hard. As
expected, these are the most frigid of the biomes. Arctic tundra is found in the Northern Hemisphere (eg North

searchText:
Human senses 2.01


Experiment 2a. The blind spot (1)

(a) Close your left eye.
(b) Hold this page about 60 cm away from your face.

(c) Concentrate on the cross with the right eye and slowly bring the page closer to the face, still
concentrating on the cross.
(d) Repeat the experiment with the page held sideways so that the dot is above the cross; and
also with the page upside down with the dot on the left of the cross.
(e) Describe what you see in each case and explain it as far as possible.




Experiment 2b. The blind spot (2)

(a) Close the left eye and hold the page at arm's length.

(b) With the right eye, concentrate on the cross and bring the page slowly nearer your face. At
first, the short line on the right will disappear because its image falls on the blind spot.
(c) When the short line reappears, the image of the gap will be on the blind spot. Describe what
you see at this point.
                                                                                  Human senses 2.01


SOLUTIONS

Experiment 2a. The blind spot (1) - discussion - answers

The act of concentrating attention on the cross throws its image on to the fovea and the image of
the dot on to the periphery of the retina to the left of the fovea. As the book approaches the face,
the distance between the images of the cross and dot increases until that of the dot falls on the
blind spot, whereupon the dot disappears (Figs. 1a and b).
These results can be used to establish the relative positions of the blind spot and fovea since the
dot cannot be made to disappear when the experiment is repeated with the dot and cross in other
positions.
One is not usually aware of the blind spot because (a) both eyes are used, (b) the eyes make
constant scanning movements (c) the gap in the visual field never coincides with the image of
the object on which we are concentrating and (d) the brain 'fills in' the gap (see Experiment 2b).

Experiment 2b. The blind spot (2) - discussion - answers

When the image of the gap falls on the blind spot, the line appears to be continuous. It is as if the
brain does not normally recognize the absence of sensory information from the blind spot.

searchText:
Brain

How do you remember the way to your friend's house? Why do your eyes
blink without you ever thinking about it? Where do dreams come from? Your
brain is in charge of these things and a lot more.

In fact, your brain is the boss of your body. It runs the show and controls just
about everything you do, even when you're asleep. Not bad for something
that looks like a big, wrinkly, gray sponge.

Your brain has many different parts that work together. We're going to talk
about these five parts, which are key players on the brain team:

cerebrum (say: suh-ree-brum)

cerebellum (say: sair-uh-bell-um)

brain stem

pituitary gland (say: puh-too-uh-ter-ee gland)

hypothalamus (say: hy-po-thal-uh-mus)

The Biggest Part: the Cerebrum. Colour just the cerebrum in on the
diagram below.




The biggest part of the brain is the cerebrum. The cerebrum makes up 85%
of the brain's weight, and it's easy to see why. The cerebrum is the thinking
part of the brain and it controls your voluntary muscles — the ones that
 move when you want them to. So you can't dance — or kick a soccer ball —
without your cerebrum.

When you're thinking hard, you're using your cerebrum. You need it to solve
math problems, figure out a video game, and draw a picture. Your memory
lives in the cerebrum — both short-term memory (what you ate for dinner
last night) and long-term memory (the name of that roller-coaster you rode
on two summers ago). The cerebrum also helps you reason, like when you
figure out that you'd better do your homework now because your mom is
taking you to a movie later.

The cerebrum has two halves, with one on either side of the head. Some
scientists think that the right half helps you think about abstract things like
music, colors, and shapes. The left half is said to be more analytical, helping
you with math, logic, and speech. Scientists do know for sure that the right
half of the cerebrum controls the left side of your body, and the left half
controls the right side.

The Cerebellum's Balancing Act. Colour in the Cerebellum on the
diagram below.’




 Next up is the cerebellum. The cerebellum is at the back of the brain, below
the cerebrum. It's a lot smaller than the cerebrum at only 1/8 of its size. But
it's a very important part of the brain. It controls balance, movement, and
coordination (how your muscles work together). Because of your cerebellum,
you can stand upright, keep your balance, and move around. Think about a
surfer riding the waves on his board. What does he need most to stay balanced?
The best surfboard? The coolest wetsuit? Nope — he needs his cerebellum!
Brain Stem Keeps You Breathing — and More. Colour in the brain stem in the
diagram below.
 Another brain part that's small but mighty is the brain stem. The brain stem sits
beneath the cerebrum and in front of the cerebellum. It connects the rest of the
brain to the spinal cord, which runs down your neck and back. The brain stem is in
charge of all the functions your body needs to stay alive, like breathing air,
digesting food, and circulating blood.
Part of the brain stem's job is to control your involuntary muscles — the ones that
work automatically, without you even thinking about it. There are involuntary
muscles in the heart and stomach, and it's the brain stem that tells your heart to
pump more blood when you're biking or your stomach to start digesting your lunch.
The brain stem also sorts through the millions of messages that the brain and the
rest of the body send back and forth. Whew! It's a big job being the brain's
secretary!
Pituitary Gland Controls Growth and other things. Colour in the
pituitary in the diagram below.




The pituitary gland is very small — only about the size of a pea! Its job is to
produce and release hormones into your body. If your clothes from last year
are too small, it's because your pituitary gland released special hormones
that made you grow. This gland is a big player in puberty too. This is the
time when boys' and girls' bodies go through major changes as they slowly
become men and women, all thanks to hormones released by the pituitary
gland.
 This little gland also plays a role with lots of other hormones, like ones that
control the amount of sugars and water in your body. And it helps keep your
metabolism (say: muh-ta-buh-lih-zum) going. Your metabolism is everything
that goes on in your body to keep it alive and growing and supplied with
energy, like breathing, digesting food, and moving your blood around.

Hypothalamus Controls Temperature and other things. Colour in the
hypothalamus in the diagram below.




The hypothalamus is like your brain's inner thermostat (that little box on the
wall that controls the heat in your house). The hypothalamus knows what
temperature your body should be (about 98.6° Fahrenheit or 37° Celsius). If
your body is too hot, the hypothalamus tells it to sweat. If you're too cold,
the hypothalamus gets you shivering. Both shivering and swe

Burrowing bettong
The burrowing bettong (Bettongia lesueur) is a member of the Potoroidae family, which includes rat-kangaroos and potoroos. It has a similar shape to the kangaroo but is the only member of the Potoroidae family that lives in a single tunnel or warren burrow all year.

The Nervous System is the master control system of the body and consists of the CENTRAL

Competition in ecosystems
Ecosystems do not always operate in peace and harmony. The living things in an 
ecosystem have different needs, which cause them to compete in a number of ways. 
Animals compete for food, water and shelter in order to survive. They also compete 
amongst members of their own species for mating partners and they fight to protect  
their offspring. 
Even plants compete in order to survive. Plants produce their own food by using 
sunlight and other ingredients to make sugars. In an area crowded with plants, they must 
compete with the other plants for sunlight – for example, rainforest plants grow taller and 
taller so they can rise above the rainforest canopy (roof of leaves) and reach the sunlight. 
Plants must compete for growing space, water and nutrients in the soil. They also compete 
to attract insects that help them to reproduce.

Components of
Ecosystems

The environment is the conditions in which a plant or animal lives. An environment consists of living
(biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components. Abiotic components include things like air temperature, soil
pH, and so on.

1 Name two other possible abiotic components in an environment.

Ecology is the study of living things and their environment. The place where a plant or animal lives is its
habitat. There are many types of habitat in Australia, such as ocean and rainforests.

2 Name and describe two other types of habitat in Australia.

Population means all the members of a particular species (related organisms) found in an area. An
ecosystem is a group of living things together with their habitat or environment. You rarely find a single
type of organism living on its own. Populations of different species can be found sharing a habitat. There
is usually interaction with other species. When there is a collection of different species that exist with
others, this is a community, Koalas, for example, breed and live in the trees.

3 What do eucalypts provide for koalas?

The trees, in turn, need water, sunshine and nutrients from the soil. The soil is made up of the remains of
plants and animals that have rotted down, There are three categories of populations: producers, consumers
and decomposers.

Green plants are producers. They are the first link in all food chains. They contain chlorophyll and so can
photosynthesise, This process produces a food called glucose (a type of sugar) and also oxygen. It uses the
energy of the sun to drive the reaction. This solar energy is converted to stored chemical energy in plants.

4 What would happen to life on Earth if all the green plants suddenly died?

Animals are consumers. If they eat plants, they are first-order consumers or herbivores. The chemical
energy in the green plants is transferred to the animal when it eats the plant.

Crocodiles have been on Earth in their present form, or close to it, for millions of years. Although differences exist 
between species, crocodiles tend to have long jaws, a protective armour, a streamlined body and a long tail. They play an

crocodile, Crodylus johnstoni. They are often referred to respectively as ‘salties’ and ‘freshies’. Despite the names, saltwater 
crocodiles are also commonly found in fresh water and freshwater crocodiles, although they prefer fresh water, can 
sometimes be found in slightly saline water, if the more aggressive saltwater crocodiles are not present. Saltwater 
crocodiles grow to much larger sizes than freshwater crocodiles and have broader snouts. Both species are almost 
exclusively carnivorous, but only saltwater crocodiles can catch large prey such as cattle. Freshwater crocodiles breed in

Crown-of-thorns starfish
Crown-of-thorns starfish are large starfish that eat coral polyps. In some years large 
outbreaks of the starfish occur on Australia’s greatest tourist attraction, the Great Barrier 
Reef. The females produce approximately 60 million eggs a year. The eggs drift for months 
in the water as zooplankton, feeding on microscopic algae. In an outbreak year more of 
the eggs reach maturity because more nutrients have washed into the sea, creating more 
algae for the zooplankton to eat.  
Once they grow larger they settle on coral. Adult starfish can reach 30 cm in diameter. 
They are covered in sharp poisonous spines that can pierce clothing. A single starfish can 
move up to 20 m per hour, searching for food, and in a year they can eat around 6 m2 of 
living coral reef. As adults they have few predators.

The Ecology of Deserts
In desert ecology is the sum of the interactions between both biotic and abiotic factors in a
desert habitat, ecosystem, and community. Some of the abiotic factors also include latitude
and distance from the coast, soil, and climate.

Deserts are most notable for their dry climates resulting from rain-blocking mountain ranges
and/or remoteness from oceanic moisture. Deserts occupy one-fifth of the Earth's land surface
and occur in two belts: between 15° and 35° latitude in both the southern and northern
hemispheres. This can be seen in the diagram below. Deserts receive an extremely low
amount of precipitation, less than enough to support growth of most plants. Deserts are
defined as areas with an average annual precipitation of less than 250 ml per year, Perth has a
rainfall of approx 852ml per year. Hot deserts usually have a large diurnal (day) and seasonal
temperature range, with high daytime temperatures (45 °C), and low night time temperatures
(0 °C). During daylight most of the sun's heat reaches the ground (no clouds), and as soon as
the sun sets the desert cools quickly by radiating its heat into space.




Deserts support diverse communities of plant and animals that have evolved resistance
extreme temperatures and arid conditions. Desert ecology is characterized by dry, alkaline
soils, low net production and opportunistic feeding patterns by herbivores and carnivores.
Lichens and blue-green algae are significant primary producers in the desert.

Diseases of the nervous system

Science understanding [Founoarion | stanparD | ADVANCED

Diseases of the nervous system affect the ability of the body to control movement and other
functions. Parkinson’s disease and cerebral palsy are two diseases of the nervous system.

Parkinson's disease

‘The muscles of a person with Parkinson’s disease are often tight, causing their voluntary
movements to be slower than normal. The person may also experience uncontrollable tremors.
‘These changes are caused by a reduction in the number of neurons that make a chemical called
dopamine. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter, a chemical that carries messages from one cell to.
another. Dopamine enables human muscle movement to be smooth and coordinated. When
approximately 60% to 80% of the dopamine-producing neurons are damaged, too little dopamine
is produced and the symptoms of Parkinson’s disease appear.

Scans of the brains of people with Parkinson’s disease reveal the loss of dopamine-producing
neurons in part of the midbrain. They also show accumulations (build up) of a certain protein. This
protein is produced as the neurons degenerate. It is, in effect, waste that the body cannot get rid of
as quickly as it is produced.

The degeneration of the neurons and the evidence of accumulated proteins are both used in

the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease. However, they can only be detected once the disease has
progressed far enough to produce symptoms. The person may have had the disease for more than
20 years by that stage.

A current theory is that the early stages of Parkinson’s disease affect the olfactory bulb, the part
of the brain that controls your sense of smell. There is an increasing amount of evidence that loss
of a sense of smell and sleep disorders are present in people with Parkinson’s disease long before
their muscles are affected. Research is focusing on these early symptoms in the search for ways of
slowing or stopping the progress of the disease.

Drought and Australian ecosystems 
Drought describes a time of abnormally low rainfall in a certain area, when there is not 
enough water to meet normal needs. Australia is often affected by drought. Sometimes a 
drought can last for many years. 
If water supplies in an ecosystem are low for a long time, plants wither and die. This 
causes food shortages for all the living things that rely on those plants for food, and loss 
of shelter for some animals. Eventually, the animals that do not have enough food stop 
breeding and may die out. The food web of an ecosystem can be harmed in this way. In 
places where drought has gone on for a long time, some ecosystems never recover.

Echolocation
Ghost bats live in northern Australia and are Australia’s only carnivorous bat species. 
Ghost bats have long, large ears that are very sensitive to sound. They use echolocation 
to hunt at night for large insects, lizards, birds, frogs and small bats. Used by many bat 
species, echolocation involves using sound waves to locate food and find their way 
around in the dark.
The sound waves bounce back from animals and objects around the bats. They listen 
for the returning waves to work out the size, location and direction of movement of 
animals nearby. If the waves return quickly, they know the animal is close by. If the sound 
waves are intense, this tells them that the animal is large. If the waves return first to the 
bat’s left ear, then moments later to its right ear, this means the animal is on their left.

Understanding Biology  – Ecosystems and living things
33
An ecosystem consists of communities of organisms and the physical environment in which they live. (Remember, 
populations are groups of individuals belonging to the same species, and communities are the sum of the different 
populations living in a given area.) 
All life on Earth is dependent on energy from the Sun. Green plants produce energy by photosynthesis. They are 
autotrophs; that is, they produce their own food from non-living (inorganic) components.
1 
Write another name for autotrophs.                                                         
Animals, fungi and most micro-organisms are unable to use directly the molecules that are present in non-living 
substances. They rely on plants to make complex molecules. If these organisms feed directly on green plants (that is, 
are herbivores), we call them primary consumers.  
2 
What do we call an animal that eats a primary consumer? 
A food chain is the sequence of organisms through 
which energy (and materials) flow in a community. 
Figure 1 shows a simple food chain. The arrow means 
‘is eaten by’ or ‘energy is transferred to’.
3 
In this food chain what is the:
a producer?                                       
b tertiary consumer?                                         
Ecologists describe the successive levels of nourishment in 
a food chain as trophic levels. Producers make up the first 
trophic level; primary consumers are the second trophic 
level, and so on. As you progress up through trophic levels, 
generally the organisms become larger and less numerous. 
Food chains do not exist in isolation. They form complex 
linkages called food webs. Figure 2 shows a simple food web. 
4

producers and consumers involved with these 
organisms? Explain your answer.

BOOK 1: HOMEOSTASIS

Ectotherms and endotherms

Multicellutar animals can only survive within a relatively narrow band of temperatures. lan
There are exceptions but the lower limit is usually 0°C (freezing point of water) and 45°C
(when proteins are denatured, or ‘cooked'). The optimum temperatures for particular
organisms are even more restricted.

1 Explain what is meant by optimum temperature.

Cellular respiration releases energy when glucose is oxidised (combines with oxygen to
form carbon dioxide and water). Most of this energy is released as heat and will affect the
body temperature of the organism. We can divide animals into two groups, depending on
how their body temperature is requlated ~ ectotherms and endotherms.

Ectotherms

Many animals lose most of the heat energy generated from cellular respiration to their
environment. Their body temperature is variable and is determined by their surroundings.
These animals are ectotherms. You may also see such animals referred to as being
poikilothermic (having variable temperatures) or even (inaccurately) as being cold-
blooded. Usually their body temperature is only slightly higher than ambient temperature
but, depending on their activity level, can be much warmer than their surroundings.

2 Explain what is meant by ambient temperature.

Animals can absorb heat from the sun or hot surfaces (generally heated by the sun), They
lose heat by radiation from their bodies, evaporation (perspiration etc) and conduction to

Chapter 7 Body coordination
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1: Endocrine system


Hormones are chemical substances that act as messengers in the body. They
are produced in endocrine glands scattered throughout the body. Together, all
these glands form the endocrine system.

A part of the brain called the hypothalamus constantly checks the internal
environment of the body and, if these conditions change, the hypothalamus
sends signals to the nearby pituitary gland. The pituitary gland responds to
these signals by either secreting hormones or releasing less of a particular
hormone. The hormones from the pituitary gland control the activities of other
endocrine glands such as the thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal glands,
pancreas, ovaries and testes. The endocrine system controls important
aspects of the body such as body temperature, rate of metabolism and water
content.

Although hormones reach all your body cells they do not affect all the cells.
Hormones are specific and act only on their target cells.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Environmental effects on the abundance
of sand hoppers on sandy beaches

Introduction

There are several species of small amphipod crustaceans or ‘sand hoppers’ that live on sheltered, sandy beaches
around Sydney, They ‘surf’ up the beach on waves then burrow quickly into the sand, feeding on algae and the
remains of dead organisms. They themselves are food for juvenile fish and seabirds. Marine ecologists at the
Australian Museum have studied them intensively because amphipods are thought to be more sensitive to oil
pollution than other species. As a result, changes in their population may prove to be a useful indicator of the extent
of oil pollution and/or ecosystem damage. The data in this activity is a small section of the data from this study.

Aim

To find any links between the abundance of amphipods
and the environmental factors of water temperature and
wavepower (the force generated by waves on the beach).

Method

The amphipods were sampled by removing a core of sand 2. cm wide and 5.5 cm deep, dumping It into a fine mesh
sieve and counting the animals as they hopped around. Ninety cores were taken every month for two years from
one section of Silver Beach near Kurnell, south of Sydney. Environmental data were collected at the same location.

Gathering data on distribution and abundance of animals
17
IntroductIon
In order to manage and control native and feral animals, agencies have to know where a particular species tends to be 
located (distribution) and how many individuals there are in a particular area (abundance). Because these animals are 
often nocturnal, living in remote areas or wary of humans, a wide range of sampling techniques are used. These include 
collecting faecal samples (scats) and using sand plots.
Aim
To gain a greater understanding of the various techniques used to gather data on the abundance and distribution of 
particular fauna.
Information: Scats
The excreta (scats) of animals can give information on their diet and how it changes with locations and seasons. Predator 
scats consist mainly of the parts of their prey that can’t be digested. The collection of scats is relatively simple, the scats 
can be stored and analysed when it is convenient, and there is no effect on the wildlife being studied. The shape as well 
as the contents can help identify the animal being studied. Usually the samples are heated before analysis to remove 
water and kill any pathogens present. Identifying the contents usually involves microscopic analysis and comparison with 
known samples. The red fox, Vulpes vulpes, is an introduced predator that has contributed to the decline of some native 
species and has been declared a vermin species. Wild dogs, Canis lupus familiaris, pose similar dangers.

over the period of a year in an area of a national park in NSW. Note that the data are not independent, because a scat can

The average adult brain weighs about 1.4 kg and fills most of the space in the skull (cranial cavity). Of all the body’s 
organs, the brain is the most complex. We can explain how the heart, liver, kidneys and other major organs function, 
but there is still much about the brain and how it works that we don’t understand.  
1 
Brainstorming – We know less about how the brain works than any other organ. Suggest possible reasons 
for this. 
 
We rely on the brain to quickly process and/or recall information. If you walk into your house at dinner time and 
smell fried onions and meat, you know, without seeing it, what you will have for dinner.   
2 
List three other things that we take for granted, thanks to the brain. 
 
Alcohol and the developing brain
Alcohol and cigarettes are known for their damaging effects on the health of their users and on the health of 
developing embryos. We also know that abuse of these substances leads to the destruction of brain tissue (and the 
tissues of other major organs). However, evidence now suggests that these substances are damaging to the brains of 
adolescents and teenagers in a way previously unrealised. Until the age of eighteen years, the brain is still undergoing 
various stages of development with much of the ‘wiring’, in the form of neurones, yet to be completed – or indeed, 
many of the neurons are yet to be created. For this reason, the brain of an individual this age has often been referred 
to as ‘a work in progress’.  
3 
It is illegal to sell alcohol or cigarettes to individuals under the age of eighteen. Why? 
 
What is a neuron?
If you consider the brain as the supercomputer of the Central Nervous System (CNS), then neurons are its wiring.

© Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008

The nervous system uses electrical impulses to control the body. There is another important control system – the 
endocrine system. This system works (more slowly than the nervous system) by releasing chemicals called hormones. 
Hormones are special chemical ‘messengers’ which control various activities inside an organism. Human hormones 
are secreted by endocrine glands in response to their environment. Some hormones only act on specific body parts; 
others cause a more general response. Areas in which hormones exert their effects are reproduction, growth and 
development, control of the internal environment and regulation of energy production.
1 
What transports hormones from their point of manufacture to where they are used? 
 
The output of a hormone is usually regulated – the effects they produce often slow down or stop output of the 
hormone.  
2 
Write the name of a process by which output of hormones can be regulated. 
Many hormones are released in response to stress, while others show a daily (circadian) pattern, often peaking  
in the early morning, probably to prepare the body for the stress of getting up.  Aldosterone (a corticosteroid)  
has the formula C21H28O5. It helps in the regulation of the salt and water balance of the body by affecting  
proximal tubules.
3 
Name the main elements present in aldosterone.
 
4 
Which organ contains proximal tubules? 
Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal gland. There are two adrenal glands – one on each kidney.
The level of hormone changes in response to changes in blood pressure and the levels of electrolytes such as sodium 
(Na+) and potassium (K+) in plasma. If the kidneys excrete too much sodium, an excess of body fluid is also lost. 
Heart function can be affected if potassium levels go outside certain levels.

© Zenda Spry-Pohl, Raimund Pohl and Blake Education 2008
Hormones and nerves
Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands. These glands secrete hormones directly into 
the circulatory system. Each hormone has a specific chemical function and is received by specific target cells 
causing a specific bodily response. The pituitary gland is called the master gland. It is about the size of a pea, 
and found at the base of the brain. The pituitary secretes stimulating hormones such as luteinizing hormone 
(LH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and thyroid stimulating 
hormone (TSH). The pituitary produces growth hormone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
Luteinizing hormone triggers ovulation in females, and in males triggers the production of testosterone and 
the manufacture of sperm in the testes. Follicle stimulating hormone stimulates the early maturation of ovarian 
follicles, and in males the production of mature sperm. ACTH targets the adrenal glands that sit on top of the 
kidneys to produce steroids. ACTH is also necessary for the production of the sex hormones oestrogen and 
testosterone. Progesterone is essential for the maintenance of pregnancy and the proper functioning of the 
menstrual cycle. Progesterone is found in both males and females as it assists with raising body temperature.

All animals need to eat food. Plant-eaters may forage (search) for food among the plants,

searchText: ﻿How do Humans affect their Environment The human population has significantly changed our environment. Here are some examples. Land Degradation Land has been extensively cleared Deforestation has increased soil salinity, Erosion has muddied rivers and oceans, Removal of top soil has decreased soil fertility, Less plants means decreased biodiversity (less shelter and food for animals). Houses, roads and other buildings now cover much of the land. Some big cities have very few plants. Water The amount of drinkable fresh water has reduced due to pollution from sewerage, chemicals, salinity and sedimentation. High levels of nitrogen have caused algae and bacterial blooms in many rivers (Eutropication) making them toxic. Air Burning fuels such as fossil fuels and forests have increased the amount of waste gases (eg CO2) in the air. This combined with methane and CFC’s have resulted in more heat trapped in our atmosphere (Green House Effect) changing out temperature and weather. CFC’s have collected in the upper atmosphere and this has created a thinning (hole) in our ozone layer. This allows cancer causing radiation through. CO2 and SO2 are soluble gases and dissolve into the water in the clouds. This makes the water acidic and the rain becomes acidic (acid rain) Pollution Rubbish is released vast quantities. Plastic has entrapped animals (birds) and chocked then (whales). Heavy metals (lead, mercury and cadmium) have accumulated in animals, water and soils. Factory waste is commonly pumped into rivers and the oceans. Pesticides are being used in larger doses and more concentrated forms to control weeds and insects. Food The high demand for human food has meant bigger farms, over hunting, over fishing, altered ecosystems (snapper V blowfish) Foreign organisms Introduced plants (eg. Skeleton weed and Patterson’s curse) have become invasive weeds and many areas are choked in weed growth that has no natural enemy. Introduced animals (eg.rabbits, foxes) have exploded in numbers out competing local animals. Biotechnology have allowed for the production of new organisms that have become resistant to toxins (eg. cereal crops) and concentrated farming like fish farms.

Human senses

If a person is to survive and function properly, he or she must respond to changes in the environment.
Anything that causes a response from us is called a stimulus (plural stimuli). We detect stimuli from both inside
and outside our bodies and act upon them, The parts of the body that detect these stimuli are called receptors.

an effector at a specific location, there is a response. The effector, usually a muscle or a gland, does something.

Part A – Measuring the speed of a nerve impulse and the reaction time
Aim
To investigate how the speed of a nerve impulse varies according to the visual and auditory inputs

Equipment
This reaction time experiment requires visual information (the movement of the ruler) to travel to your brain. Then your

Questions:
 1. What is the function of a leaf?

 2. What is the difference between the length of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?

 5. Are your results reliable?

                                                                              Investigating Leaf Adaptations


Answers:
 1. What is the function of a leaf?
    The leaves contain a lot of chlorophyll, which is a green pigment that absorbs sunlight for the
    process of photosynthesis.

 2. What is the difference between the length of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?
    You would expect the leaves grown in shade to be longer.

 3. What is the difference between the width of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?
    You would expect the leaves grown in shade to be wider.

 4. What is the difference between the area of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?
    You would expect the leaves grown in shade to be larger.

 5. Are your results reliable?
    Answers may vary. This is a reasonable sample size as it provides a good range to take an
    average, without being so large a sample size that it takes too long to collect data.

 6. What type of data have you collected?
    Continuous data

Teaching notes

This learning grid could be used in a variety of ways.

 1. Students will need a die. They roll the die twice to obtain a pair of
     numbered coordinates. This will identify a cell on the learning grid. They
     need to write down the word or phrase from that cell. Repeat three or four
     times to provide the student with a collection of keywords. The student
     should then include all the keywords in a sentence or piece of extended
     writing.

 2. Ask students to write a piece of extended writing using a minimum of
     twelve keywords from the learning grid. The teacher or the students could
     choose the keywords.

 3. Use the grid as the basis for a bingo game in class. The student highlights
     six words and/or phrases and ‘crosses’ these off as the teacher gives the
     definition of the word and/or phrase. An alternative could be to ask
     students for the definitions.

 4. Students could play battleships in pairs against each other. Both students
     ‘hide’ five submarines – each occupies a single cell on the learning grid.
     The first student challenges the second student with a coordinate to
     identify a cell but must also give a definition of the word and/or phrase in
     the cell.

 5. Ask the class to provide a definition for each cell in the learning grid.
     Students add them to a blank version of the learning grid. Students could
     cut the definitions grid up and swap their pile of definitions with a
     neighbour who then places them onto the keyword grid.

  6. Provide each student with a copy of the revision checklist and ask them to
     tick the 36 cells based on their comprehension of the words and phrases.
     A ‘happy face’ would indicate full comprehension. The sad face would
     indicate a lack of knowledge and the neutral face of some understanding
     but requiring additional work.

CASE STUDY:

Introduction of the
cane toad to Australia

A historical case study of the events surrounding the
release of Australia’s most hated invasive animal and

the lessons learned

The introduction of cane toads (Bufo marinus)
to Australia in the 1930s is one of the foremost
examples of an exotic animal release gone
wrong. Originally imported from Hawaii and
released in Queensland as a biological control
for beetle pests of sugar cane, the cane toad
is nowa well-established pest itself. Cane
toads currently range across Queensland, the
Northern Territory and into New South Wales
and Western Australia. Despite being less
widespread than foxes or rabbits, community
surveys consistently rank the toad as our most
hated invasive animal’ and it is listed as a key
threatening species el me Ei €

Today, ‘most eeond ion the cane
toad was deliberately released as a biological
control, but may not be familiar with the
events that led to their release.

Background: Sugar cane had been
commercially grown in Queensland since the
1860s and losses caused by white grub attacks
began to be a serious problem in the 1880s.
The grubs — the larvae of up to 13 different
species of native beetles — eat the roots of the
cane, causing the plants to die. The problem
was significant enough for the Queensland
government to bow to pressure from
canegrowers and establish the Queensland
Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations (BSES)
in 1900. By 1935, entomologists employed
by BSES had been studying the biology of the
cane beetles and investigating solutions to
their impacts for around 25 years’.

Plenty of good science was produced during
this time — the life cycles of several beetle
species were described and an understanding
of their biology and ecology had been worked
out enabling more focused control measures.
Many field and lab trials were done in a bid to
develop effective controls including the use of
various chemical insecticides, soil-fumigation
methods, biocontrols such as parasitic fungi and

aa

Invasive Animals CRC

native insects, physical removal methods, and
agricultural and cultivation practices. Some of
these showed promise but were prohibitively
expensive or not readily available, and others
were simply not effective’.

How it happened: A government
entomologist working for BSES, Reginald
Mungomery, imported the toads, bred them
and released them‘. He was convinced
the cane toad was the answer toa major
agricultural crisis in the sugar industry, as they
had reportedly solved similar beetle problems
in Hawaii, the Philippines and Puerto Rico’.

In 1932, a paper was presented by a woman
named Raquel Dexter at the 4th Congress
of the International Society of Sugar Cane
Technologists in Peurto Rico onthe use of
Bufo marinus as a biological control for beetle
infestations in sugar crops there*. The toad
was subsequently taken from Peurto Rico
to Honolulu to control beetle infestations
in Hawaiian sugar cane fields. In June 1935,
Mungomery travelled to Hawaii where he
captured 102 toads and brought them back
to Australia. When he arrived at the Meringa
experimental farm near Gordonvale in far
north Queensland on 22 June 1935, all but one
toad had survived the journey. The toads were
housed in a purpose-built enclosure and left
to breed. On 19 August that year, 2400 toads
were released into sites around Gordonvale*.
In less than two months the number of toads
had increased at least 24-fold. Further releases
of toads in the Cairns and Innisfail areas soon
followed.

Opposition: AnotherAustralian entomologist,
Walter Froggatt, voiced concerns about the
release around this time, writing prophetically
‘this great toad, immune from enemies,
omnivorous in its habits, and breeding all
year round, may become as great a pest as
the rabbit or cactus’*®. He lobbied the federal
government to exercise caution and the

CASE STUDY: Introduction of the
cane toad to Australia

A historical case study of the events surrounding the release of Australia’s
most hated invasive animal and the lessons learned

Director-General of Health banned any further
release of toads in December 1935°. But this
ban was to be short lived. BSES and local cane
growers subsequently lobbied the Queensland
Premier and Minister for Agriculture, who in
turn pressured the Prime Minister Joseph
Lyons, who rescinded the ban in September
1936‘. Toads were then released throughout
the sugar cane regions of Queensland.

Shortfalls in risk assessment: As
reported by Griggs’, ‘all the cautious testing
characterizing the previous investigations into
cane grub control methods was completely
forgotten when it came to the cane toad.
There is no evidence of any pre-release testing
by the BSES entomologists to determine

if the toads evenate the cane beetles’.
The extremely short timeframe between
the toads arriving in Australia and the first
release supports this. The beetles that the
toads were supposed to cont rol were native
Australian species, different to those causing
problems in Hawaii and Peurto Rico, yet no
trials were carried out to see if this translated
to Australian conditions. Risk assessments of
potential harms from the introduced species
were not done.

It is not surprising that cane toads were
imported and released with apparently
little-to-no checks or control measures in
place. Colonial Australia had a rich history
of acclimatisation societies and settlers who
introduced foxes, rabbits, deer, blackberries
and other species in the 1800s, mainly for
food, hunting, or the purpose of making the
new country feel more like mother England’.
Acclimatisation societies were viewed as
scientific organisations and were the precursor
to many zoological societies that still exist
today. Quarantine was a state responsibility in
the early 1900s and mainly focused on human
health, with animal health only coming into
focus after the second World War*.

The cane toad was first recognised as a pest
in Western Australia where it was listed as
vermin under the state’s Vermin Act in 1950°.
No serious attempts were made to raise cane
toad control as a national issue until the early
1980s. The Commonwealth first took some
responsibility for the problem in 1986, with
federal funding and establishment of a cane
toad Research Management Committee".

www.feral.org.au/pe

Conclusion: There is little doubt that those
involved believed they were doing the right
thing by importing and releasing the cane
toad. Despite warnings from other scientists,
appropriate pre-release testing of potential
impacts was not done and initial control
measures were overturned in the face of
industry pressure. It is likely that the lessons
from the cane toad debacle have influenced
the strict quarantine laws and risk assessment
procedures Australia has in place today".

The adaptations of mangroves

Introduction

Mangroves are trees that form woody plant communities in shallow tidal water. They live on sheltered shores in
bays, estuaries and the sheltered side of offshore islands. They make an essential contribution to the ecology of
coastal and marine environments. Their roots provide habitats for many marine animals such as crabs, prawns,

‘Their canopy provides a habitat for about 35 species of insect and many birds that eat mangrove nectar and pollen.
Mangroves are specifically adapted to their tidal environment. This environment includes soil (mud) that is
always waterlogged with salty water and a varying water level caused by tides ebbing and flowing underneath
the mangroves. These conditions would kill other land plants. So how do mangroves survive?

You may need a text book to help with this section
The nervous system connects every part of the body to the brain by nerves. The brain controls the body – it sends 
(and receives) signals along these nerve fibres. The electrical impulses sent along the nervous system travel very 
quickly, e.g. from the big toe to the brain in a few thousandths of a second. Nerves can be very short or over a metre 
long. The nerves along which signals travel are made up of bundles (varying from a few hundred to a few thousand) 
of long, thin cells called neurones.  
Neurones are specialised nerve cells that transmit signals by electro-chemical changes in their membranes. They 
are ‘long distance’ nerves. There are three major types of neurones – sensory neurones, motor neurones and 
interneurones. Neurones are made up of a cell body, nucleus, axons, dendrites and protective and supportive 
structures. The gap between the axon of one neurone and the dendrite of the next is called a synapse. Electrical 
impulses ‘jump’ across each synapse.  
1 
Draw a diagram showing the cell body, nucleus, myelin sheath, axon and dendrite of one neurone and a 
synapse and the dendrite of the next neurone. 
2 
Write your own definition for nerve (in biology terms). 
 
Dendrites are short extensions of the cell body. They receive stimuli and carry them to the cell body. Axons are 
much longer and there is usually only one axon per neurone. The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell 
body to other cells. Axons are branched. When an impulse reaches the end of the axon branches, chemicals are 
released (neurotransmitters) to the dendrite of the next cell. When the neurotransmitter reaches this dendrite, a fresh 
electrical signal is generated and this travels through this next cell, and so on.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Nest predation in Australian
urban environments

Introduction

Many bird species live in urban environments where many people enjoy watching them. Birdwatchers in many
urban areas have reported that the number of small birds has been decreasing. They have also reported that the
number of currawongs (a predatory, native bird) have been increasing. Even though it seemed that currawongs
were causing the deciine in the number of small birds, there were other possible explanations such as other birds,
cats, kookaburras or possums.

In 1993, ecologists from the Australian Museum carried out an experiment to test whether currawongs were
eating the eggs of the smaller birds and causing their numbers to fall. They distributed 2000 artificial nests
containing soft plasticine eggs to volunteers across Australia, The volunteers put the nests into trees in their
backyards, and observed any animals visiting the nest for two weeks. At the end of the two week period they
took the nest down and sent it, with their observations, back to the Museum. At the Museum, the scientists
identified the nest predators from the beak, tooth and claw marks they had left in the plasticine eggs.

searchText:
BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Parasitism, mutualism and commensalism

Relationships between organisms take several forms. Symbiosis is the term used to describe how different
plant or animal species live together. The effects of the relationship are then classified as parasitism,
mutualism or commensalism.

Parasitism

The word parasite comes from an old word meaning ‘one who eats at another's table’. A parasite is an
organism that obtains its nutrients by living in or on another organism. The parasite obtains nutrients at the
expense of the host organism it associates with. Thus, parasitism involves one organism depriving another of its
nutrition, In this case, the parasite benefits and the host suffers. An example of a parasitic relationship is the
tapeworm. Tapeworms can infect humans and other animals, living in the alimentary canal of the host. The
tapeworm takes much of the nutrients its host ingests, leaving the host undernourished as a result (and in
extreme cases, dead),

Mutualism

As the name suggests, mutualism involves a relationship that is of mutual benefit to both organisms. A well-
known case of mutualism involves various species of birds living on or near larger animals, such as horses, cows,
thins and giraffes. The birds eat the tiny bugs that would otherwise irritate or damage the skin of the larger
animal. in exchange for providing this easy meal, the larger animal benefits by having its body kept free of
pests, Similar examples occur in the oceans with smaller fish performing the same task on larger species. For
example, a remora is a fish that has a disk on its head, which it uses like a sucker to cling onto other fishes,
especially sharks. Remoras feed on food scraps left over by their hosts or on parasites of the host. They can also
swim alone and have been seen clinging to the hulls of ships.

Plant responses to temperature 
+ 1 Read the information below, then underline any examples of how plants 
respond to temperature changes.
Oranges grown in cool regions have green skin while their fruit forms in the hot summer 
months. In autumn when the fruit ripens, the skin colour changes to orange. This colour 
change is due to the cooling air temperature. Ripe oranges grown in tropical climates 
normally stay green-skinned because there are no cooler months. 
Plants are very sensitive to temperature changes and day length. Deciduous trees 
lose their leaves in autumn when the temperature drops and days are shorter. The trees 
become dormant and their sap doesn’t flow. In countries where snowfall is frequent 
this leaf-fall and dormancy protects the trees from freezing. Bulbs such as tulips flower 
best when they have been through a period of chilling, as if packed under snow. In 
Australia these conditions are rare so commercial growers ‘force’ tulips into flowering by 
refrigerating them for several months.

Key terms
abiotic factors
non-living factors that influence an ecosystem, such as wind, water, salinity and temperature
biotic factors
living factors that influence an ecosystem, such as animals, plants and bacteria
capture–recapture
a method of estimating the number of organisms by capturing, marking and releasing a sample of the organisms
emigrate
when an animal leaves an ecosystem
immigrate
when an animal enters a new ecosystem
population dynamics
the study of changes in species population numbers and the factors that may contribute to these changes
quadrat
a randomly selected square plot used to estimate the number of organisms

Researchers discovered two species of insects 
inhabiting the same ecosystem, comprising mainly 
light coloured trees. The insects were very similar 
in all aspects apart from their colour. Species X was 
light coloured and species Y was dark in colour. 
The researchers suspected that the colour of the 
insects might influence their numbers. Their idea 
was that the darker coloured insects would stand 
out against the light background of trees and hence 
it would be easier for predators to see and eat them. 
To test this, they decided to use a ‘capture, release 
and recapture’ method. In this, the insects are 
captured, marked and then released. After an 
interval, the same area is used to trap more of the 
same type of insect. The researchers carried out this 
process and captured more light coloured insects 
than dark coloured insects.
1	
Both light coloured and dark coloured 
butterflies are found in the same 
ecosystem. This is a:
a	 conclusion.
b	 fact.
c	 hypothesis.
d	 forecast.
2	
The suspicion of the researchers that the 
colour of these insects influences the 
numbers present is a:
a	 conclusion.
b	 fact.
c	 theory.
d	 forecast.
3	
The process of ‘capture, release and 
recapture’ is:
a	 a theory.
b	 an experiment.
c	 data.
d	 an observation.
4	
The number of insects captured and 
counted is:
a	 irrelevant.
b	 data.
c	 an interpretation.
d	 proof.

The researchers decided that more work 
must be carried out in order to come to a 
justifiable conclusion. Which would be the 
most scientific thing to do next?

from the ecosystem.

predators.

the ecosystem.
