searchText: POPULATIONS http://www.ib.bioninja.com.au/standard-level/topic-5-ecology-and-evoluti/53-populations.html#previous-photo 5.3.1 Outline how population size is affected by natality , immigration, mortality and emigration The change in population size over a given period of time can be summarised by the following equation: Population Size = ( N + I ) - ( M + E ) N atality : Increases to population size through reproduction (i.e. births) I mmigration: Increases to population size from external populations M ortality: Decreases to population size as a result of death (e.g. predation, senescence) E migration: Decreases to population size as a result of loss to external populations 5.3.2 Draw and label a graph showing the sigmoid (S-shaped) population growth curve Population Growth Curve 5.3.3 Explain reasons for the exponential growth phase, the plateau phase and the transitional phase Initially, population growth may be slow, as there is a shortage of reproducing individuals which may be widely dispersed As numbers increase and reproduction gets underway, three stages of population growth are seen: Exponential Growth Phase There is a rapid increase in population size / growth as the natality rate exceeds the mortality rate This is because there is abundant resources (e.g. food, shelter and water) and limited environmental resistance (disease and predation uncommon) Transitional Phase As the population continues to grow, eventually competition increases as availability of resources are reduced Natality starts to fall and mortality starts to rise, leading to a slower rate of population increase Plateau Phase Eventually the increasing mortality rate equals the natality rate and population size becomes constant The population has reached the carrying capacity (K) of the environment Limited resources, predation and disease all contribute to keeping the population size balanced While the population size at this point may not be static, it will oscillate around the carrying capacity to remain relatively even (no net growth) 5.3.4 List three factors that sets limits to population increase Every species has limits to the environmental conditions it can endure and must remain within appropriate levels for population growth to occur Some of these factors are density-dependent, while others are unrelated to the density of the population Factors affecting population growth:

Teaching notes

The objectives are to know how to use a quadrat, how to estimate numbers of
organisms and to suggest why distribution of organisms may be uneven. It is suitable
for Key Stage 3 and GCSE students. The Word document and the PowerPoint should be
used together.
Slide 2 introduces the concepts of quadrats using paving slabs. There is a patio
worksheet (page 2) students can complete or the exercise can be completed as a
group using the PowerPoint.

Slide 3 and 4 introduce the idea of sampling a field. It would help if you have a real
quadrat to show to students. Students throw the cardboard quadrat onto the field and
count the number of daisies and dandelions. Before the lesson, print pages 4 and 5
and stick together to make the field. Alternatively print page 6 onto an A3 sheet.
Quadrats can be made of card with a 4cm square window. A quadrat template is
provided (page 3).
Slide 5 asks students to calculate the number of each plant in the whole of the field.
Ask each group to write their result on the board.

If you are not using the PowerPoint then the activity can still be carried out. Ask
students to randomly throw their quadrat 10 times onto the field. They should count
the number of dandelions and daisies inside it (if only part of the plant is inside the
quadrat, it still counts). They should record their results in a table. Ask students to
calculate the average number of each plant in a quadrat. If each quadrat is 1 m 2,
estimate the number of each type of plant in the whole field (70 m 2). Gather the class
results together on the board and ask questions such as; why are everyone’s results
different?, why are there areas where no plants are growing?, why should quadrats be
thrown randomly? Etc.

 Activity:                              Reaction Time
In this activity we will look at the effect of various conditions on reaction time. It is difficult to
calculate reaction time based on time (seconds) because the amount of time is so small – it is
difficult to measure. Instead, since we know acceleration due to gravity, we can measure how
far a meter stick falls before you catch it. From that distance, we can calculate reaction time.

          Meter Stick
          CD/MP3 Player, Radio, or Television

IMPORTANT: YOU MUST BE VERY QUIET DURING STEPS 1-3. THERE SHOULD BE
ABSOLUTELY NO TALKING.

          thumb and index finger of your dominant hand (the hand you write with). Your
          thumb and index finger should be held one inch apart. Without warning, your lab

          Write down how far the meter stick fell in the Data Collection and Calculations

7.4 | Reflexes

Science understanding FOUNDATION | STANDARD | ADVAN

Reflexes are messages that travel from where they are received, along a sensory neuron to the
spinal cord. Within the spinal cord, a relay neuron transmits the message straight back along motor
neurons to the first place they were received. This causes a response called a reflex action.

Because reflexes do not have to pass all the way up to the brain and back, they are very fast.
Reflexes help protect you from danger. Examples of reflexes are: pulling your hand away from a
hot object, blinking your eyes to stop something getting into them, and pulling your foot away after
standing on a sharp object. A message is sent to the brain shortly afterwards. Only then can the
brain register pain.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Ecosystems

Achieve!
Relationships
Living things in an ecosystem interact in different ways. Some living things have learned 
to depend on each other to survive. 
Collaboration
Animals of the same species may live in groups, rather than on their own. A group of 
animals from the same species is called a population. As a population, animals can share 
the jobs of finding food and water, protecting each other from predators, raising their 
young and finding shelter. This is called collaboration. It means ‘working together’. 
Symbiotic relationships
Certain species develop a relationship with a completely different species that benefits 
one or both animals. This is called a symbiotic relationship. When the symbiotic 
relationship benefits both species it is called mutualism. An example is the clownfish, 
which lives amongst the poisonous tentacles of a sea anemone. The clownfish protects 
the anemone from the bigger fish that eat anemones. In return, the clownfish is protected 
from predators by the anemone’s stinging tentacles. The clownfish is not hurt because it 
has a special mucus on its skin that protects it from the sting.

Relationships between organisms in ecosystems
Key terms
commensalism
a type of relationship between two organisms of different species in which one organism benefits and the other is not affected
community
different populations living in the same location at the same time
competition
contest between organisms that require or seek similar resources, such as shelter and food
ecosystem
a community of living organisms and their non-living surroundings
mutualism
a type of relationship between two organisms of different species in which both organisms benefit
parasitism
a relationship in which one organism (parasite) lives in or on the body of another organism (host) and benefits, while the host is harmed
population 
a group of individuals of the same species living in the same location at the same time
predator
an animal that hunts and feeds on another (prey) for food
prey
an animal that is hunted and killed by another (predator) for food
symbiosis
a close physical relationship between two organisms of different species

Ecology

Respiration 15a

SS

The respiration process ~ an explanation
Photosynthesis catches energy and respiration releases it.

You may have learnt that plants trap energy from the sun and use it to convert low-energy carbon dioxide
and water to high-energy glucose and low-energy oxygen. This process is called photosynthesis, Plants store
their glucose as starch, a complex carbohydrate molecule. Animals obtain their food by consuming plants
or other animals, so they are called consumers. Inside the digestive system of animals, the complex starch
is broken down again into a simpler form, glucose. The glucose travels to the cells and is further broken
down in the process of respiration. During respiration energy is released and made available to the cells. The
cells use the energy for many chemical reactions, as welll as for heat.

‘The sun's energy, which is trapped by the plants during photosynthesis, is released during respiration. In
other words, respiration is an energy-releasing process. It occurs in all living things, in their cells, During
respiration oxygen is used up as the glucose is broken down in many controlled reactions, Carbon dioxide
and water are produced as the waste products. These become the raw materials needed for photosynthesis.

There is a cycle involving photosynthesis and respiration. In this way we do not run out of food, oxygen
and carbon dioxide,

searchText:
Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Riderless bikes
In this module, you have been learning about how your body detects changes in its environment and uses a type of feedback signal to respond. Many engineering systems work in a similar way, detecting changes and responding to a feedback signal. 
Heater thermostats work on this principle. As they heat the air around them, they measure the air temperature, which becomes a feedback signal. When this signal indicates that the temperature is above or below a preset level, the heater responds by switching off or on. 
In this task, you will explore another common mechanical engineering system that you may be surprised to learn responds to its environment – a bicycle. 
When a human rides a bike, we use our biological control systems to help stay upright. When we sense we are falling to one side, our cerebellum is alerted, and we shift our body a little to the other side to rebalance. But how does a bike stay upright without a rider? 

Investigate centres of gravity
Aim
To investigate how changing the centre of gravity affects the stability of a riderless bicycle
Equipment:
An old bicycle (make sure the handlebar shaft slopes backwards  – most do)
A small hill with open space at the bottom
A 2–4 kg weight (e.g. a dumbbell)
Cloth bag
Duct tape
Measuring tape

Part A
Method
Setting the handlebars straight to begin with, push the bike down the hill as fast as you can. You may need to run with it for a short distance. The bike should stay upright for quite a while. Use a measuring tape to measure the distance the bike travels before it falls over. Repeat this “hill push” two more times. (Note: Try to ensure the bike is pushed with the same starting speed in each trial.)
Record your results in the table in the Data and results section. Calculate the average of your measurements. 
Lock the handlebars in place, so the wheel is in line with the bike frame but cannot turn. You can use duct tape or rope to do this. Push the bike down the hill with locked handlebars and measure the distance it travels. Repeat the “hill push” another two times. 
Record your results in the table in the Data and results section. Calculate the average of your measurements. 
Reflect
Did you notice the shorter distance before the bike fell over with the handlebars locked? Before reading on, discuss with a partner why you think this happens and write down your ideas.



Part B
The reason the bike stays upright for longer with free-moving handlebars is that handlebar movement is part of the feedback loop that controls this engineering system. When a moving bike starts to lean to one side, the handlebars flop to that side a little, which steers the front wheel towards the lean. When this happens, the direction of the bike changes and the front wheel comes back underneath the middle of the bike (in line with the centre of gravity) and it is balanced again. 
You may like to take a video from behind of your bike travelling down the hill and watch it in slow motion to help you understand this effect.
You are now going to explore how changing the centre of gravity of a bike affects this riderless bike control system.
Method
Examine your bike and identify three locations for your weight to be attached – one near the front, one near the middle and one near the rear of your bike. Make sure these locations are along the centreline of the bike (i.e. not at the ends of the handlebars or pedals). Adding weight towards the front of your bike will shift the centre of gravity forwards. Adding weight towards the rear will shift it backwards. 
Show the three locations you have chosen on the diagrams in the Data and results section. 
Attach your weight in the front location by wrapping it in the cloth bag and taping it onto the bike. Make sure the weight cannot swing and is as close to the centreline of the bike as possible. 
Setting the handlebars straight to begin with, push the bike down the hill as fast as you can. You may need to run with it for a short distance. 
Record the distance the bike travels before it falls over. 
Repeat this “hill run” another two times, recording the distance it stays upright each time in the table in the Data and results section. Calculate the average of your results. 
Move the weight to middle location and repeat steps 3 to 6. 
Move the weight to the rear location and repeat steps 3 to 6.

Sound and communication

Sound is a form of energy that requires a medium for propagation, ie it can travel through a gas, liquid or solid,
but not a vacuum. Vibrating objects produce sound. How quickly an object vibrates is called its frequency and is
measured in cycles per second or hertz (Hz).

High notes have high frequencies and are produced by rapidly vibrating objects. Low notes have low
frequencies and are produced by slowly vibrating objects. Pitch is the property of sound that we recognise
as lower and higher notes.

The wavelength of a sound wave is related to frequency (and pitch). The higher the frequency, the shorter

the wavelength. Wavelength is measured in metres.

in places. Air passing from the lungs can cause the vocal cords to vibrate. The frequency of the sound is

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian Curriculum  Name:
Extending science worksheet
Spoiled by oil
Oil has been one of the most useful products known to humans. Oil and its by-products are used in millions of products all around the world. However, only a few countries produce oil, which means that it must regularly be shipped across oceans.
Over the years, there have been a number of oil tanker accidents at sea, resulting in oil leaking into the environment and causing havoc to the ecosystems. When these accidents occur, environmental engineers are tasked with cleaning up.
In this task, you will investigate one method used in oil spill containment: floating boom design. This project is best done in a small group.
Floating boom design
When oil spills occur in the ocean, most of the oil floats on the surface. One strategy used to clean up oil spills is to create a floating boom that will stop the oil from spreading. The goal of a floating boom is to prevent oil from reaching delicate land-based ecosystems and to collect it in one place so it can be removed more efficiently by skimming or vacuuming.
In this task, you will design a floating boom and test it in a miniature oil spill.
Before you start, you need to create your oil spill test site from the following materials:
A plastic tub (A4 size or bigger)
Sand
Water
Place the sand in the tub and add water to make it sticky. Pile the sand up at one end of the tub to make a beach. Add more water to turn the sand into a shoreline as shown in the diagram.

Now it is time to design your floating boom.
Your design objective is to design a boom that satisfies the following specifications:
The boom must float in the water between your shoreline and the far end of the tub.
The boom must stop oil that is spilled at the far end of the tub from reaching the shoreline.
Due to cost restrictions, the boom must be made from a maximum of four items chosen from the following list:
4 straws
A polystyrene cup
A plastic cup
2 corks
Plastic wrap
A plastic plate
A plastic knife, fork or spoon
Duct tape
To guide you in your design, you will use the steps of the engineering design process. The engineering design process has five major steps:
Discover: Consider the problem or objective from all angles, research it and brainstorm ideas.
Ideate: Develop a possible solution and design a prototype.
Build: Build the prototype.
Test: Evaluate the prototype to see if it meets the objective.
Improve: From the test results, identify how to make your design better.
1. Discover
First, think about the three components of your design objective. How will you tackle this task? Answer the questions in the table below to help guide your thinking. Add other questions of your own at the end.
Question
Notes 
Think about the key features of a floating boom. Describe what your boom must be able to do.

Think about the materials available for your boom. Describe the features of each material that could be useful.

Think about the materials available for your boom. Describe how you could secure them together.

Other questions:

Now that you have done some thinking, brainstorm some different ways that the materials from the list could be combined to create a floating boom. Space has been left for you to draw some sketches if required.




2. Ideate
Choose your best ideas and develop them further. Decide which materials you will use (no more than four from the list are allowed) and write up a description of your floating boom design. Include a labelled diagram showing how it fits together.






Diagram:





3. Build
Build a prototype of your floating boom. A prototype is a “first try” to test if your concept will work. Write down the steps you took to build your prototype below.
Steps:









4. Test
Once you have constructed your floating boom, it is time to test how well it works. First, place the boom in your oil spill test tub, approximately halfway between the beach and the far end of the tub. Then, slowly add one-third of a cup of oil to the far end of the tub. Make sure your boom is located between the ‘oil spill’ and the beach. It is best to use a coloured oil, such as a dark vegetable oil, so that it can be easily seen.
Let the oil spill spread out for three minutes, gently rocking the test tub every 30 seconds to help it disperse.
After three minutes, you should get an idea of how effective your boom has been. Make some observations of the effectiveness of your boom. Describe what has worked and what has failed.




Extension activity
You could also measure the effectiveness of your boom. Two ways to measure its effectiveness are suggested below:
The feather test: Dip a craft feather into the water on each side of the boom and compare the effect of the oil on each one.
Surface area test: Take a photo of your oil spill from directly above the test tub. Print your photo and use it to estimate the percentage of the water’s surface area covered with oil on each side of the boom. To help you estimate, draw a square grid over your photo and count the squares that are covered by oil compared to those that are not.
5. Improve
Based on your test observations, describe how you could improve your design. Note down any ideas you have that could make it better.






If you have time, implement your improvement ideas and repeat steps 4 and 5. You will need to create a new oil spill by draining your tub and adding fresh water and oil.
Discussion and reflection
Compare all the class floating boom designs. Identify and describe the design that has worked best. Identify a common feature of really successful designs.





If you did the feather test, describe how the oil affected the feather. Describe how this would affect a bird and its surrounding ecosystem.





The best way to combat the effects of an oil spill is to prevent it from happening. Brainstorm some ways to reduce the incidence of oil spills in our oceans.

Get the Big Picture. Read the paragraphs in the below and look at the diagram. Then
answer the questions that follow.

The nervous system gives directions to all the other systems in your body. It also gets
information from your senses and keeps track of how well the different parts of your body are
working together. The nervous system is made up of two parts: the central nervous system
(CNS), and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Peripheral means “not central.” Your brain and
spinal cord make up your CNS and send and receive messages through your PNS.

Your senses allow you to perceive the world by seeing, hearing, feeling, tasting and smelling.
Your sense organs collect information about the world and send it to your brain. The brain
decodes the signals and makes them meaningful.

Many drugs act to disrupt the normal functioning of the nervous system. Drugs can change your
brain’s ability to think and to control the rest of your body.

Scientists use two methods to survey the plants in a community, the transect method and the quadrat method.
A quadrat consists of a square, rectangular or circular frame which is used to identify and calculate the
abundance of plant species within a given area. Rectangular quadrats with a width-to-length ratio of 1:2, 1:4 or

Transects are lines or belts that are set out in an area to study the type and abundance of a species. A line
transect is made by laying out a tape measure or a rope marked at regular intervals along the area to be
studied. The name and position of plant species are recorded and profile diagrams are drawn to scale. Belt

                             Symbiotic Interactions
Read each scenario below. First, indicate which kind of symbiotic interaction is being described.
Write P for parasitism, M for mutualism, or C for commensalism. Be prepared to explain your
reasoning for your choices.

_________ 1.	Some shrimp and crab live and capture food from within the tentacles of giant
              anemones.

_________ 2. A pearlfish spends the day inside the alimentary tract, or intestines, of a sea
             cucumber. The fish emerges from the sea cucumber at night to feed on small
             crustaceans. The pearlfish gets a safe place to live. The sea cucumber does not gain
             anything from the relationship, nor is it harmed.

_________ 3. A cymothoid isopod lives inside the mouth of a snapper fish. The isopod severs
             blood vessels in the fish’s tongue, causing the tongue to atrophy and degenerate.
             The isopod then hooks its pereopods, or legs, to the base of the fish’s tongue,
             essentially replacing the tongue. The isopod stays there for the rest of its life, feeding
             on blood, mucus, and stray pieces of food from the fish.

_________ 4.	A boxer crab carries a pair of small anemones in its chelipeds, or claws. When
              approached by a predator, the crab waves the stinging tentacles of the anemones to
              deter the predator. The anemones benefit from the small particles of food dropped
              by the crab during feeding.

_________ 5.	An alpheid shrimp digs and maintains a deep burrow. While underground, the shrimp
              is safe. Above ground, it is vulnerable to predators. A goby fish lives in the burrow
              with the shrimp. The goby fish sits at the entrance, keeping watch for predators, and
              signals the shrimp with a flick of its tail when it is safe to come out. Or, if a predator
              swims by, the goby darts into the burrow and the shrimp retreats further inside.
              These two animals are completely dependent on each other—the goby benefits by
              getting a burrow to live in and the shrimp knows when predators are near.

_________ 6.	Corals feed off the byproducts of a microscopic algae living within their own tissue,

              of the coral animals, which use the energy to extract calcium from the seawater and

              and obtain plant nutrients from the coral.

searchText:
INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Temperature regulation in
ectotherms and endotherms

Introduetion

The body temperature of ectothermic (‘warmed from the outside’) animals is determined by the temperature of
their environment. Ectotherms are unable to maintain the same level of activity when the environmental
temperature changes. In extreme cold, for example, ectotherms become too cold to move and, as the
‘environment warms their bodies, they become more active. In contrast, endothermic (‘warmed from the inside’)
‘organisms generally maintain a constant body temperature despite changes in environmental temperature.
Being endothermic enables animals to maintain activity in a wide range of environmental temperatures.

‘Animals that live in deserts experience extreme daily variations in temperature—from below zero in the early
morning up to more than 40°C in the afternoon. Animals that live high in alpine areas experience months of
extremely low temperatures followed by months of more moderate temperatures. Even in summer, temperatures
often drop below freezing at nights.

Animals usually have several adaptations to survive in the range of temperatures they experience in their habitats.
These adaptations may by structural (features of the structure of the body), behavioural (specific behaviours) or
physiological (features of the inner workings of the body). The adaptations for the regulation of body
temperature in endotherms differ greatly to those in ectotherms. In order to maintain a constant body
temperature, endothermic animals have a number of adaptations to help them retain heat when it is cold or lose
heat when it is hot. Ectotherms often have adaptations that help them to maximise the beneficial and minimise
the adverse effects of changes in environmental temperatures.

Aim
To use secondary data to identify adaptations that help regulate the body temperature of ectothermic and
endothermic animals from desert and alpine environments.

The brain

IntroductIon
The human brain is part of the central nervous system and controls and coordinates our conscious and unconscious actions.
Information
The three major regions of the brain are the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata. The cerebrum is 
largest part of the brain and also the newest, evolutionarily. It is the front and upper part of the brain and is divided into 
two hemispheres. Its surface is called the cerebral cortex. The cerebrum is made up of four lobes (subdivisions). These  
are the frontal lobe (speech), the parietal lobe (general sensory area), the occipital lobe (vision) and the temporal lobe 
(auditory). The medulla oblongata links the brain and the spinal cord and controls many autonomic functions such as 
heart beat and breathing. Figure 1 shows the left exterior of the human brain.
As we have evolved, the size of our brains has increased. A human brain is approximately three times the size of the brain 
of a mammal of equivalent mass, and has approximately 50 to 100 billion neurones.

Understanding Biology – human and plant life
© Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
14
The nervous system uses electrical impulses to control the body. The 
nervous system is necessary for instant communication and reaction. 
The communications are short, fast and tend to be limited to a small 
area. It is an important control system but not the only one. 
There is another important control structure – the endocrine system. 
This is a slower system, with longer term effects. The endocrine system 
is a network of glands (and cells) in animals that send hormones (Greek 
hormaein, meaning ‘to set in motion, to move’) throughout the body. 
Plants do not have an endocrine system. 
Hormones are ‘chemical messengers’ that cause or prevent specific 
reactions. Areas in which hormones exert their effects are reproduction, 
growth and development, control of the internal environment and 
regulation of energy production. Some hormones, such as those 
produced in the thyroid gland (and growth hormones), affect all the cells 
of the body, not just limited targets.    
1 
What do the nervous system and the endocrine system have in 
common?
 
2 
Name two differences between the nervous system and the 
endocrine system.
 
 
3 
Name three areas over which hormones exert an influence. 
 
Hormones are secreted (released) by glands into the bloodstream which then carries them to the target sites. Figure 
1 shows the location of the major glands (and some other organs). Hormones control and regulate the body’s 
activities by sending messages to tissues, cells or organs. Only small amounts of hormones are required to perform 
these functions. Hormones have specific protein receptors or sites to which they bond. The receptors can ‘recognise’ 
what they must bond to as they travel through the bloodstream. When bonding occurs, a reaction is triggered.
The pituitary gland is sometimes called the ‘master gland’ because the hormones it secretes affect so many other 
glands.

Understanding Biology  – Ecosystems and living things
35
An environment (surroundings) is a combination of the living things, physical 
features and geological features in a particular area. We tend to divide 
environmental factors into biotic and abiotic features. Living creatures are 
described as biotic (biotikos meaning ‘to do with life’). Things like sunlight 
and the amount of water present are abiotic factors – i.e. without life  
(a- meaning ‘not’). 
1 
Name other abiotic factors of an environment.
The area in which an organism lives is its habitat. Habitats can be aquatic, terrestrial or arboreal. 
2

a aquatic 
b terrestrial 
c arboreal

a aquatic 
b terrestrial 
c arboreal 
4

these words? Explain your answer.
Living creatures can be divided into two major groups, flora and fauna. Flora (floris meaning ‘flower’) refers to 
plants, and fauna refers to animals. 
5

There are different names used to describe groups of organisms. A species is a group of related organisms that are 
capable of breeding to give fertile offspring.

A population is the number of a particular species in a habitat at a given time. For example, if we count all the 
people living in Australia, that number is Australia’s population. However, if we only count the people living in 
NSW, that number is the population of NSW.

The nervous system allows living things to detect what is going on around them. ‘This is called sensitivity.
Any change which the nervous system detects is called a stimulus. The nervous system processes the
information and then a gland or a muscle reacts. This reaction is called a response.

‘The nervous system is made up of the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system. The
central nervous system includes the brain and the spinal cord for many involuntary and automatic
responses. The peripheral nervous system is a network of nerves that spread throughout the body. They
connect the nerve endings in muscles, glands and sense organs to the central nervous system.

Part B
Nerves are made up of special cells called neurones. The bundles of neurones look like the wires in a
telephone cable. These nerve cells carry electric impulses or messages at gfeat speed around the body. There
are three kinds of neurones: sensory neurones carry messages to the central nervous system; motor neurones
carry messages from the brain; and connector neurones carry messages in the brain and spinal cord.

BOOK 2: THE SENSES

Vision II

The retina is a thin sheet of cells lining the inside of the eyeball which contains photoreceptors. Photoreceptors
are cells that contain light-sensitive pigments, such as rhodopsin. (A pigment is a substance that absorbs visible
light of a specific frequency and reflects visible light at a different wavelength, ie has a definite colour.) These
cells convert light images into electrochemical signals that are sent to the brain via the optic nerve for the brain
to interpret. These photoreceptors are of two main types: rods and cones. In an average human eye there will
be around 125 million rods and 6 million cones,

Rods are sensitive to blue-green light and are responsible for vision in dim light. They are more sensitive to
light than cones, but cannot distinguish between colours. Rods are connected in groups and cannot distinguish
fine detail.

Cones are responsible for colour vision. Colour blindness in humans is a result of certain colour-sensitive
pigments being missing from cones. Colour blindness can be inherited and pedigrees can be used to describe
how the condition is passed on, Cones can be individually connected to nerve fibres and give better visual acuity.

Nocturnal and diurnal animals have a different distribution of rods and cones, hence the difference in their
night and day vision. The greatest concentration of cones (and no rods) is at the fovea (central area of retina).
Concentration of rods decreases and concentration of cones increases towards the outer edges of the retina.

Electromagnetic waves carry energy and travel in straight lines at 300 000 kilometres per second (km s) ina

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Water balance in
terrestrial environments

Introduction

Water balance occurs when the amount of water gained by the animal is balanced by the amount of water they
lose over a given period of time. Terrestrial animals gain water from their diet (including food and drink) and
from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins in their cells (such as by cellular respiration). They lose
water when it evaporates from their skin and respiratory system and in their faeces and urine.

The amount of available water in terrestrial environments varies greatly. In arid environments such as deserts, where
the amount of available water is usually extremely small, animals have a range of adaptations to maintain water
balance. Kangaroo rats generally live in arid environments whereas laboratory rats live in a controlled environment.

Activity sheet – Living things and ecosystems
What is an ecosystem?
An ecosystem is a complex system that includes all the plants, animals and non-living 
things found in a certain place, as well as all the different ways those things interact.  
We say that something interacts with something else when it acts in a way that affects  
the other thing. 
For example, a garden pond contains living things – also called organisms – such as 
frogs, snails, fish, water birds, water plants and algae, as well as non-living things such as 
fresh water, rocks, sand, air, sunlight and soil. The garden pond ecosystem is all of these 
living and non-living things as well as all of the ways these things interact and depend on 
each other – from a fish eating a snail to water lilies using sunlight to make food. All the 
living things in an ecosystem are known as a community. The variety of living things in 
the ecosystem is known as the ecosystem’s biodiversity.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Adaptation of the Wompoo Fruit
Dove to environmental conditions

Introduction

The Wompoo Fruit Dove (Ptilinopus magnificus) is a species of bird that lives in the rainforests of eastern Australia
and New Guinea. Scientists have named several subspecies (the name of a subspecies is the third word in its
scientific name) of Wompoo Fruit Dove from different locations. These subspecies vary only slightly from one
another in their markings but vary markedly in size. All subspecies of the Wompoo Fruit Dove are endangered,
largely due to the destruction of their rainforest habitat.

Rainforests exist only in warm places where rainfall and humidity are high all year round. Rainforests are very
diverse places that support a large number of species in their moist, humid environment. Wompoo Fruit Doves
eat the abundant fruit in the rainforest and rarely move more than a few kilometres away from their place of
birth in their lifetime.

searchText: ﻿People have long asked, "What is the world made of?" and "What holds it together?" What is the World Made of? Why do so many things in this world share the same characteristics? People have come to realize that the matter of the world is made from a few fundamental building blocks of nature. The word "fundamental" is key here. By fundamental building blocks we mean objects that are simple and structureless -- not made of anything smaller. Even in ancient times, people sought to organize the world around them into fundamental elements, such as earth, air, fire, and water. Today we know that there is something more fundamental than earth, water, air, and fire... By convention there is color, By convention sweetness, By convention bitterness, But in reality there are atoms and space. -Democritus (c. 400 BCE) Around 1900, people thought of atoms as permeable balls with bits of electric charge bouncing around inside. But is the atom fundamental? Is the Atom Fundamental? People soon realized that they could could categorize atoms into groups that shared similiar chemical properties (as in the Periodic Table of the Elements). This indicated that atoms were made up of simpler building blocks, and that it was these simpler building blocks in different combinations that determined which atoms had which chemical properties. Moreover, experiments which "looked" into an atom using particle probes indicated that atoms had structure and were not just squishy balls. These experiments helped scientists determine that atoms have a tiny but dense, positive nucleus and a cloud of negative electrons (e-). Trivia: The term "atom" is a misnomer. Why? [Answer] Is the Nucleus Fundamental? Because it appeared small, solid, and dense, scientists originally thought that the nucleus was fundamental. Later, they discovered that it was made of protons (p+), which are positively charged, and neutrons (n), which have no charge. So, then, are protons and neutrons fundamental? Physicists have discovered that protons and neutrons are composed of even smaller particles called quarks. As far as we know, quarks are like points in geometry. They're not made up of anything else. After extensively testing this theory, scientists now suspect that quarks and the electron (and a few other things we'll see in a minute) are fundamental. This is the modern atom model. Electrons are in constant motion around the nucleus, protons and neutrons jiggle within the nucleus, and quarks jiggle within the protons and neutrons. This picture is quite distorted. If we drew the atom to scale and made protons and neutrons a centimeter in diameter, then the electrons and quarks would be less than the diameter of a hair and the entire atom's diameter would be greater than the length of thirty football fields! 99.999999999999% of an atom's volume is just empty space! Scale of the atom. While an atom is tiny, the nucleus is ten thousand times smaller than the atom and the quarks and electrons are at least ten thousand times smaller than that. We don't know exactly how small quarks and electrons are; they are definitely smaller than 10-18 meters, and they might literally be points, but we do not know. It is also possible that quarks and electrons are not fundamental after all, and will turn out to be made up of other, more fundamental particles. (Oh, will this madness ever end?)

An introduction to atomic structure
All matter is built from particles called atoms. Atoms are the building blocks of  
all materials on earth. More than 100 types of atoms have been discovered. We call  
them elements.
The structure of an atom
For a long time people thought that atoms were the smallest particles in existence.  
We now know that atoms are made up of even smaller sub-atomic particles: electrons, 
protons and neutrons.
•	 Electrons are very tiny and light. They have a negative charge.
•	 Protons are much larger and heavier than electrons and have a positive charge.
•	  Neutrons are larger and heavier like protons, but have no electrical charge (they are 
neutral).
How are the particles arranged?
An atom has a nucleus in its centre. Protons and neutrons can be found inside the 
nucleus. Electrons are constantly spinning around the outside of the nucleus. Each atom 
has an equal number of protons and electrons. This means it has no overall charge. 
Scientists use simple diagrams to show the structure of an atom. This is a diagram of a 
helium atom. It contains:
•	 2 protons
•	 2 neutrons
•	 2 electrons.

What parts make up an atom?
An atom has three main parts: protons, neutrons and electrons.

Protons and neutrons make up the centre of an atom. The centre part of
an atom is called the nucleus.

The electrons are outside the nucleus. They orbit around the nucleus at
very fast speeds. Electrons are much smaller than protons or neutrons.

Protons and electrons have electrical charges.

     Each proton has a positive (+) charge
     Each electron has a negative (–) charge
     A neutron is neutral. It has no charge.

A neutral atom has the name number of protons as electrons.

                          PROTONS = ELECTRONS

This means that the number of positive charges equals the number of
negative charges. They balance each other so the entire atom has no
charge.

The atomic number is also the same as the number of protons.

Every atom has mass. The mass of an atom is called its atomic mass.

An atomic mass is not an exact scale reading of mass – like grams or
kilograms. It is a way of comparing the mass of one atom against the mass
of another atom.

The mass of an atom is the mass of its nucleus. A nucleus contains protons
and neutrons, so the number of protons plus the number of neutrons gives
us the mass of an atom.

Electrons are so light that they are not counted in the atomic mass.

Each proton is given a mass of one and each neutron is given a mass of one.

For example, a lithium atom has 3 protons and 4 neutrons. The atomic
mass of a lithium atom is 7 (3 + 4 = 7)

The atomic mass is sometimes called the atomic weight.

                                Introduction
Chemistry is the study of matter and energy and the interaction between
them. The elements are the building blocks of all types of matter
in the universe. Each element is made up of only one type of
atom, each with its specific number of protons known as its
atomic number.
 Understand that matter is made up of atoms



                 An atom is the smallest
                 neutral particle that makes
                 up matter.

                 The type of atom and the
                 way these atoms are
                 arranged and connected
                 to each other determines
                 the type of matter – and
                 therefore the physical and
                 chemical properties of the
                 matter.
 Matter is made up of atoms
                                        The Particle Theory of Matter

                       1. All matter is made up of very small particles
                       (atoms, ions or molecules)

                       2. Each substance has unique particles that are
                       different from particles of other substances

        3. There are spaces between the particles of matter that are
        very large compared to the particles themselves
4. There are forces holding particles together

5. The further apart the particles, the weaker
the forces holding them together

6. Particles are in constant motion

7. At higher temperatures particles on average
move faster than at lower temperatures.
        Elements are pure substances that combine
            to make mixtures & compounds
Matter can be divided into pure substances which
include elements (atoms of the same type) and
compounds (different atoms joined together) and
Mixtures which can either be homogeneous (evenly
mixed) or heterogeneous (unevenly mixed)
                        Elements are pure substances that
                    combine to make mixtures & compounds
           A molecule forms when atoms join together – either
           the same type of atom to form a molecule of an
           element (such as oxygen gas – O2) or different types of
           atom to form a molecule of a compound (such as
           water - H2O).




Oxygen Molecule – O2              Water Molecule – H2O
              Matter exists in different states – solid,
                        liquid and gases
All matter can be found as either solid, liquid or gas
depending upon the temperature. Each type of matter
has its own specific temperature ranges that it will exist
in each of these three states. Gases,          liquids
and solids can be made up of                   atoms,
molecules, and/or ions.
 Solutions are made from a solute
      dissolved in a solvent

    A solution is made up of a
    solvent and a solute. A solvent
    is a substance such as water
    that is able to dissolve a solute.
    The solvent ‘pulls apart’ the
    bonds that hold the solute
    together and the solute
    particles diffuse (spread
    randomly by hitting into each
    other) throughout the solvent
    to create a solution. The
    solution is a mixture with evenly
    spread solvent and solute
    particles. These particles can be
    physically separated by
    evaporation.

                                                                 ideas of what an atom looks like.

                                                                 changed.

searchText: Atomic Structure and Chemical Reactions Junior Science Understand that matter is made up of atoms An atom is the smallest neutral particle that makes up matter. The type of atom and the way these atoms are arranged and connected to each other determines the type of matter – and therefore the physical and chemical properties of the matter. Scientists use models to show the relationship of protons, electrons and neutrons within atoms and ions Scientists and philosophers have used models to represent their ideas of what an atom looks like. As more discoveries have been made, the model of the atom has changed. Atoms contain protons, electrons and neutrons Atoms contain smaller particles, the number of these determine the type of atom. Atoms have a central nucleus, which contains protons (p) and neutrons (n). Electrons (e) orbit outside the nucleus, arranged in energy levels. Atoms have equal number of protons and electrons Protons are positively charged; electrons are negatively charged; neutrons have zero electrical charge. Atoms have no overall charge because the number of protons = number of electrons. Summary  All matter is made up of atoms. Atoms consist of protons, neutrons and electrons.  The charges of protons and electrons are equal and opposite. Each different type of element has a different number of protons in its atoms Positive protons bond to each other with a special type of force in the centre of an atom, called the nucleus. Each type of atom has its specific number of protons. Neutral neutrons, in approximately the same number as protons, also join together with the protons to form the nucleus. The positive charge of the nucleus holds the same number of negative electrons in position around it. Atomic and Mass number The atomic number is unique for each element. An atom has the same number of electrons as protons. The atomic number of an atom is equal to the number of protons . The atomic mass (mass number) of an atom is equal to the number of protons and neutrons. Both numbers are normally found in the periodic table. Calculating protons, neutrons and electrons Number of protons: For an atom = atomic number Number of electrons: For an atom = atomic number Number of neutrons: For an atom = atomic mass - atomic number atom or ion number of protons Atomic number number of electrons number of neutrons Mass number carbon (C) 6 6 6 6 12 magnesium 12 12 12 12 24 (Mg) fluorine (F) 9 9 9 10 19 The electrons in an atom are arranged in a series of energy levels. Electrons move or ‘orbit’ around the nucleus in energy levels or shells. The energy levels further away from the nucleus are able to fit more electrons. The first energy level is filled first, followed by the second and so on until all the electrons (the same number of protons in an atom) have been used. Maximum numbers of electrons in each energy level are:  2 in the first EL (nearest the nucleus)  8 in the second EL  8 in the third EL (before the fourth shell starts to fill)  8+ in the fourth EL An atom’s electron arrangement is known as its Electron configuration A shorthand way of describing the way electrons are arranged in an atom is called the electron configuration. The information for the number of electrons is found by an elements Atomic Number (number of electrons = number of protons in a neutral atom). Each EL is filled to its maximum capacity, starting with the lowest EL first (EL number 1). The EL are separated by a comma. The EL are filled until all the electrons are placed. Elements are arranged on the periodic table according to their atomic number Each element has an atomic number, which tells us how many protons are contained inside each atoms nucleus. This number of protons is matched by an equal number of electrons, which move around the nucleus. The periodic table starts with Hydrogen (H) Atomic number 1 and ends with elements that have over 100 protons such as Copernicium (Cn) Atomic number 112. Elements can be classified as metals or non-metals. A few elements are called semi-metals or metaloids (e.g. boron and silicon), because they show some, but not all, of the properties of metals. Groups are numbered vertical columns and periods are horizontal rows The columns (downwards) of a periodic table are called groups. The rows (across) of a periodic table are called periods. There is a relationship between the period number and the number of electron energy levels an atom has. In the periodic table, elements have something in common if they are in the same row. All of the elements in a period have the same number of electron energy levels. Every element in the top row (the first period) has one energy level for its electrons) All of the elements in the second row (the second period) have two energy levels for their electrons. It goes down the periodic table like that. Using the Periodic table to write electron arrangements (Extension) Period number gives number of energy levels Last number of group gives electrons in outer energy level. i.e. group 17 - 7 electrons in outer energy level. Ions An ion is an atom or group of atoms, which has gained or lost electrons. Elements are most stable when the outer energy level (valence shell) is full. The first energy level needs 2 electrons to be stable. The other energy levels need 8 electrons to be stable. Elements can lose or gain electrons when they react with other chemicals to form ions and achieve stability. Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons. Ions are atoms or groups of atoms with electrical charges. Ions normally form in pairs of atoms when one or more electrons are passed between them. Depending on how many electrons are present in the outside energy level or how many are “missing” determines the total number of electrons transferred. Atoms that lose electrons form positively charged ions, or cations. Atoms that gain electrons form negatively charged ions, or anions. The number of protons compared to electrons determines the charge (Extension) If an atom has the same number of electrons as it does protons then it will be neutral. A negative ion will have more electrons than protons. A positive ion will have less electrons than protons. Atomic Number Number of protons Number of electrons Electron arrangement F- 9 9 10 2,8 Ne 10 10 10 2,8 Mg2+ 12 12 10 2,8 The (last) number of the group on a periodic table gives the number of electrons in the outside Energy Level. If there is 3 or less, in groups 1,2 or 13 then electrons will be lost to form positive ions. If there is 5, 6 or 7, in groups 15, 16 or 17 then electrons will be gained to form negative ions Compounds Compounds form from two or more different elements bonded together (in the form of atoms or ions) Ionic compounds are the product of chemical reactions between metal and non-metal ions. Ionic compounds are made up of a fixed ratio of cations and anions. They exist in huge structures in a lattice structure. We call these structures crystals. Compounds are neutral substances. For ionic compounds, the charges of the positive ions are balanced by the charges of the negative ions. Ionic Bonding (Extension) Ionic Bonding is where one atom completely takes valence (outside energy level) electrons from another to form ions and the resulting negative and positive ions hold together with electrostatic attraction. This type of bonding occurs when a metal and non-metal react and there is a transfer of electrons to form ions. The ions then combine in a set ratio to form a neutral compound with negative and positive charges balanced out. Ion table - Light shaded ions will be more commonly used in class Naming a compound (Extension) A compound is named after the atoms or ions that make it up. Many compounds are made up of ions, a positive and negative ion bonded together known as ionic compounds. Other compounds are made up of atoms bonded together. All compounds are neutral and have the same total number of protons as the total number of electrons. Some compounds have common names such as water. Ionic compounds (made of ions bonded) have names of two parts. The positive ion (Metal) is first then followed by the negative ion (non-metal). The compound sodium chloride is made of a sodium ion bonded to a chloride ion. Chemical compound formula (Extension) Elements in a compound combine in fixed amounts. It is possible to write a formula for a compound. Each compound has a chemical formula indicating the proportions of each combined element. This formula for water (H2O) tells us that there are 2 Hydrogen atoms and 1 Oxygen atom in a molecule of water Elements in a compound combine in fixed amounts. It is possible to write a formula for a compound. A formula tells you the type of atoms that are in a compound and the number of each atom. The visual method for balancing compounds (Extension) If we want to form a balanced ionic compound then each space in the positive ion must be filled by a tab from the negative ion. In this case 2 chloride ions are needed for each copper ion to form copper chloride. Product formula (Extension) When products are made in a reaction the name of it is often a combination of the names of the chemicals it is formed from. For example MgCl2 is called magnesium chloride Cross and Drop method for balancing ionic compounds Charged ions make neutral Ionic Compounds (Extension) The formula for magnesium oxide is MgO made of Magnesium ion has a charge of +2 and oxide ion has a charge of –2. A compound overall has to have no charge. Therefore, the +2 charge of magnesium ion cancels out the –2 charge of oxide ion and so the ratio of ions is one to one. The charge on the ions arises, as magnesium has to lose two electrons in order to have a full outer energy level and gets a charge of +2, and oxygen has to gain two electrons in order to have a full outer energy level and gets a charge of –2. The formula for aluminium oxide is Al2O3 but the Aluminium ion has a charge of +3, and oxide ion has a charge of -2. A compound overall has to have no charge. Two aluminium ions with a combined charge of +6 are required to cancel out the charge on three oxide ions with a combined charge of –6. The charge on the ions arises as aluminium has to lose three electrons in order to have a full outer energy level and gets a charge of +3, and oxygen has to gain two electrons in order to have a full outer energy level and gets a charge of –2 Testing for Oxygen gas How to test for Oxygen Gas 1. Put a small amount of Manganese dioxide into a boiling tube and add hydrogen peroxide. BE CAREFUL WITH THESE CHEMICALS and ALWAYS FOLLOW LAB SAFETY RULES 2. Put a bung with a delivery tube over the boiling tube and put the delivery tube into an upside down test tube to collect any gas. 3. Heat the tube gently with a Bunsen burner. 4. Remove delivery tube and place thumb over test tube. 5. Remove thumb quickly and place a glowing splint into the test tube. 6. If the splint re-ignites then it is likely the gas produced was oxygen. Testing for Hydrogen gas How to test for Hydrogen Gas 1. Put a small piece of magnesium metal into a test tube with a small amount of dilute hydrochloric acid. 2. Place another test tube upside down over top of the first test tube 3. Collect the gas in the upside down test-tube. 4. Place thumb over top of the test tube 5. Hold a lit match at the mouth of the test tube and remove thumb quickly 6. If the gas makes a loud ‘pop’ then it is likely that the gas produced is hydrogen. Testing for Carbon Dioxide gas How to test for Carbon Dioxide Gas 1. Put a small amount of calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid into a boiling tube. 2. Put a bung with a delivery tube over the boiling tube. 3. Place the delivery tube into a test-tube filled with clear limewater 4. Observe the gas bubbling into the limewater. 5. If the limewater turns cloudy then it is likely that the gas produced is carbon dioxide. Carbon Dioxide is a colourless gas and limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide

Atomic Structure                                                 Junior Science
Understand that matter is made up of atoms

An atom is the smallest neutral particle that makes up matter.

The type of atom and the way these atoms are arranged and connected to
each other determines the type of matter – and therefore the physical and
chemical properties of the matter.



Scientists use models to show the relationship of protons, electrons and neutrons within atoms and ions

Scientists and philosophers have used models to represent their ideas of what an atom looks like. As more
discoveries have been made, the model of the atom has changed.




Atoms contain protons, electrons and neutrons

Atoms contain smaller particles, the number of these determine the type of atom. Atoms have a central
nucleus, which contains protons (p) and neutrons (n). Electrons (e) orbit outside the nucleus, arranged in
energy levels.
 Atoms have equal number of protons and electrons

Protons are positively charged; electrons are negatively charged; neutrons have zero electrical charge.

Atoms have no overall charge because the number of protons = number of electrons.

Summary

   ❑ All matter is made up of atoms. Atoms consist of protons, neutrons and electrons.
   ❑ The charges of protons and electrons are equal and opposite.




Each different type of element has a different number of protons in its atoms

Positive protons bond to each other with a special type of force in the centre of an atom, called the nucleus.
Each type of atom has its specific number of protons. Neutral neutrons, in approximately the same number as
protons, also join together with the protons to form the nucleus. The positive charge of the nucleus holds the
same number of negative electrons in position around it.
 Atomic and Mass number

The atomic number is unique for each element. An atom has the same number of electrons as protons.
The atomic number of an atom is equal to the number of protons               .
The atomic mass (mass number) of an atom is equal to the number of protons and neutrons.
Both numbers are normally found in the periodic table.

Calculating protons, neutrons and electrons

Number of protons:
For an atom = atomic number
Number of electrons:
For an atom = atomic number
Number of neutrons:
For an atom = atomic mass - atomic number

  atom or ion number of protons Atomic number number of electrons number of neutrons Mass number
    carbon (C)       6                6               6                   6               12
   magnesium         12               12              12                 12               24
       (Mg)
    fluorine (F)     9                9               9                  10               19


The electrons in an atom are arranged in a series of energy levels.

Electrons move or ‘orbit’ around the nucleus in energy levels or
shells. The energy levels further away from the nucleus are able to fit
more electrons.
The first energy level is filled first, followed by the second and so on
until all the electrons (the same number of protons in an atom) have
been used.
Maximum numbers of electrons in each energy level are:
    ❑ 2 in the first EL (nearest the nucleus)
    ❑ 8 in the second EL
    ❑ 8 in the third EL (before the fourth shell starts to fill)
    ❑ 8+ in the fourth EL

An atom’s electron arrangement is known as its Electron configuration

A shorthand way of describing the way electrons are arranged in an atom is called the electron configuration.
The information for the number of electrons is found by an elements Atomic Number (number of electrons =
number of protons in a neutral atom). Each EL is filled to its maximum capacity, starting with the lowest EL first
(EL number 1). The EL are separated by a comma. The EL are filled until all the electrons are placed.
 Elements are arranged on the periodic table according to their atomic number

Each element has an atomic number, which tells us how many protons are contained inside each atoms
nucleus. This number of protons is matched by an equal number of electrons, which move around the nucleus.

The periodic table starts with Hydrogen (H) Atomic number 1 and ends with elements that have over 100
protons such as Copernicium (Cn) Atomic number 112.

Elements can be classified as metals or non-metals. A few elements are called semi-metals or metaloids (e.g.
boron and silicon), because they show some, but not all, of the properties of metals.

Groups are numbered vertical columns and periods are horizontal rows

The columns (downwards) of a periodic table are called groups.
The rows (across) of a periodic table are called periods.
 There is a relationship between the period number and the number of electron energy levels an atom has.

In the periodic table, elements have something in common if they are in the same row. All of the elements in a
period have the same number of electron energy levels. Every element in the top row (the first period) has one
energy level fo

searchText: ﻿<!--This file created 11/24/99 2:14 PM by Claris Home Page version 3.0--> Inside the Atom A WebQuest for High School Chemistry Designed by: Bob Bartelt Bobbo1137@aol.com Introduction | Task | Process | Evaluation | Conclusion | Credits | Teacher Info Introduction Since antiquity, man has wondered, “what is the universe made of?” Ancient philosophers were able to intuit the idea of the atom thousands of years before the enlightenment with virtually no assistance from what would today be considered “science”. Today our conception of the atom is limited more by the frailty of the human mind than by anything else. The quest for the atom is not a quest to discover atoms-atoms are everywhere. They quest for the atom is the quest to understand the atom, what its made of, how it’s held together. Your search will lead you into the depths of history, to the time when the very idea democracy was first introduced. The journey then stalls for nearly 2000 years where you will pick it up when the ages old ideas of magic and religious superstitions finally gave way to science and reason. From the brilliant minds of ancient Greek philosophers to the massive particle accelerator of today, you will be led on a journey to unearth a mystery, millennia old, and still alive and well today; and in the end you will discover the wonder and the beauty of… The Atom, the Building Block of the Universe The Task As a young college student, I found it impossible to decide between my two great intellectual passions: Chemistry and History. After majoring in both, I undertook the only career that would force me to continue to learn about both, teaching. Your assignment today is to blend my two great loves into one coherent and organized presentation that will demonstrate your mastery of both history and science. Your task is to explain the evolution of atomic theory and show both me and the rest of the class how we today have come to understand the fascinating world of the atom. Atoms are far too small to be seen by the naked eye, and as a result, scientist and philosophers have been forced to create theories and conduct experiments to attempt to “crack” into the mystery of the atom. There have been several major bench mark discoveries/theories in the development of modern atomic theory. It is your job to create a PowerPoint presentation that illuminates the shadowy and imperceptible world of the atom. Your PowerPoint presentation should provide information about all of the following models/theories of the atom: 1) Atomism and the earth, fire, wind, water model 2) The solid sphere model 3) The plum pudding model 4) The planetary or nuclear model 5) The orbital model 6) The electron cloud or quantum mechanical model Your PowerPoint presentation should have an attention grabbing introduction that convinces the audience that your presentation will be fun and exciting. For each of these models you need to provide the following information: 1) The person or people most responsible for the development of the model. 2) A description of the experiment that was conducted and a summary of the data that was produced that led to the development of the model. (you are exempt from doing this for the model #1) Be sure to include the date when the model was first presented. 3) A graphical representation of what that model of the atom would look like if we were able to actually see atoms. (this image may be created by you or taken from the internet, be sure to sight where the image came from if you use the internet) You are also expected to have a coherent conclusion that ties all of the different models together and leaves the audience with a feeling of closure and comprehension. Web Links General Information/Timelines • Wikipedia • Brief timeline (this should get you oriented to some of the major dates in the development of atomic theory and science in general) • Another Brief timeline • In depth timeline (Lots of information) • Visual timeline (LOTS of great picture, and a good-albeit brief-explanation of the history of the universe) In Depth Examination of Individual models • John Dalton • Plum Pudding • Planetary or Nuclear Model • The Orbital Model • If you read all of it, it will blow your mind • The math behind the planetary model • Excellent Graphic for the orbital model • Quantum Model • Find “Quantum Atom” on this page (If you read all of it, you should understand. This web page would have changed to world if it had been around two hundred years ago) Evaluation You will be assessed on four different criteria: Objectives Beginning 1 Developing 2 Accomplished 3 Exemplary 4 Score The presentation addressed all three requirements for every model set forth in “The Task” Glaring omissions and evidence of little to no effort. Information is present, but shows little understand and effort. Information is present but lacks coherence or evidence of genuine understanding. Information is present and shows a genuine understanding of the material, not just mindless memorization. __ The PowerPoint The presentation is simple and lacks graphics. Shows little effort to make the presentation enjoyable for the class Use of graphics and other effects is minimal. Uses graphics and other effects. These graphics are sometimes used inappropriately or unnecessarily. Uses graphics and other effects appropriately to enhance the presentation of the PowerPoint. __ The Presentation The presentation was poor and showed no evidence of previous rehearsal. The presenter is knowledgeable, but shows little familiarity with the PowerPoint. The presenter is knowledgeable and is familiar with the PowerPoint. The presentation fails to simulate and maintain interest. The presenter is knowledgeable and is familiar with the PowerPoint. The presentation is also interesting. __ Organisation The presentation and power point are out of sync and are difficult to follow. The presentation and power point often failed to coincide. The presentation and power point work well together, but the information is scattered and hard to follow The presentation and power point work together well and the information is logically presented and easy to understand __ Conclusion The quest for the atom had been a long and arduous one, and it still continues to this day. In your research you may have notices that the structure of the atom is more or less settled, but the structure of the nucleus is still uncertain. The massive particle accelerators of today are looking deeper into the atom than enlightenment scientist could have dreamed. We still need young scientists to continue searching the depths of the nucleus for particles still smaller than protons, neutrons, and electron. It’s possible that one of you could be the one who proves or disproves string theory. What’s string theory? Last updated in December 2006. Based on a template from The WebQuest Page

Atoms are made up of a positively charged nucleus surrounded by cloud of
negatively charged electrons (charge -1), as shown in Figure 7.3.1. The nucleus is
made up of two sub-atomic particles known as protons (charge +1) and neutrons
(charge neutral).




Figure 7.3.1
The number of protons in the nucleus determines what type of atom it is. For
example, all helium atoms have 2 protons; all carbon atoms have 6 protons and all
gold atoms have 79 protons. Therefore the number of protons in the nucleus is
referred to as the atomic number.




      Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 The number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus determines how heavy the atom
is. The electrons can be ignored because they are about 1800 times lighter than
protons and neutrons. For this reason, the number of protons and neutrons in the
atom is known as the atomic mass.

All of this information is summarised by the atomic symbol, which includes the
chemical symbol for the element. Below is the atomic symbol for an oxygen atom
with 8 protons and 8 neutrons.

                                 atomic mass 

                             atomic number 
All of the atoms in an element must have the same atomic number. However, the
atoms may have different atomic masses. In other words, all atoms in an element
have the same number of protons but may have different numbers of neutrons. For
example, all carbon atoms have 6 protons. Most carbon atoms have 6 neutrons so

have the atomic symbol               . However, a small percentage of carbon atoms have 7
neutrons so have the atomic symbol                     . Others may have 8 neutrons so have the

atomic symbol           . Atoms with the same atomic number but different atomic masses
are known as isotopes.

Atoms have no electric charge. In other words they are charge neutral. This is
because there is always an equal number of protons (charge +1) and electrons
(charge -1).

The electrons are confined to electron shells that surround the nucleus like the layers
of an onion. The first (inner-most) electron shell is the smallest and can only hold a
maximum of 2 electrons. The second electron shell is slightly bigger so can hold a
maximum of 8 electrons. The third electron shell is even bigger and can hold a total
of 18 electrons.

1    Chemistry


    Chemistry Worksheet, Atomic Number and Mass Number

    Goal: Atoms are composed of electrons, protons, and neutrons. It is the difference in the numbers of
    protons in the atoms that determine the different elements. You can determine the composition of an
    atom of any element from its atomic number and its mass number.

    Tips:

        -   You must be aware of what the numbers on the periodic table mean and become familiar with
            the shorthand notation of writing the mass number and atomic number next to the symbol of
            the element.




        -   Remember that the atomic number - is the number of PROTONS in the nucleus of the atom of
            that element.
        -   Remember that the mass number (a.k.a atomic mass)- is the number of PROTONS and
            NEUTRONS in the nucleus of the atoms of that element.
        -   The periodic table gives us the atomic number of each element. For example, Hydrogen has the
            atomic number of 1 and Oxygen has the atomic number of 8. Just look at the whole number on
            the periodic table!
        -   There is also a short hand notation where the mass number is written on the upper left hand
            corner next to the symbol of the element, and the atomic number is written on the bottom left
            hand corner.
        -   Since each of the atoms on the periodic table is electrically neutral, that means that the number
            of protons (positive charge particles) in the nucleus of an atom MUST EQUAL the number of
            electrons (negatively charged particles) around the nucleus.
        -   To determine the number of neutrons in the nucleus subtract the mass number and the atomic
            number:
                o Number of neutrons = mass number – atomic number
        -   Always have a periodic table in front of you!

Atoms
There are four distinct models for representing atoms: the billiard ball model, the plum pudding model, the 
planetary model and the shell model.
John Dalton in 1803 developed the concept that pure substances were made of indivisible solid particles called 
atoms. John Joseph Thomson in 1897 discovered negatively charged particles that he called electrons. His 
model was the plum pudding model. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford discovered the small positive nucleus, which 
was surrounded by electrons. Niels Bohr in 1913 proposed that the electrons were arranged in layers around 
the nucleus and that this arrangement accounted for the chemical and physical properties of the atom.
1

the nucleus in the atomic models.

All of the chemicals you use are formed when atoms react with each other. Knowing how atoms are organised 
is the basis of chemistry and enables you to make your own compounds.
The atomic number of an atom is found by counting the number of protons in the nucleus. Protons are 
electrically positive particles. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in an electrically balanced 
atom, so an element with an atomic number of 5 has 5 protons and 5 electrons. The neutral particles in the 
nucleus are called neutrons. The number of neutrons and protons makes up the mass number of the element. 
Electrons are arranged in shells. The first shell can have only two electrons. The second, third and fourth shells 
can have up to 8 electrons.

Balancing chemical equations
You do not need to draw molecular diagrams each time to balance chemical equations. 
Look at the example below.
sodium chloride + fluorine gas 
 sodium fluoride + chlorine gas
 
NaCl 
+ 
F2 
 
NaF 
+ 
Cl2
At the start there is
1 atom Na + 1 atom Cl + 2 atoms F = 4 atoms in total
At the end there is
1 atom Na + 2 atoms Cl + 1 atom F = 4 atoms in total
Even though the total number of atoms is the same, the equation is not balanced because 
we have more atoms of fluorine and less of chlorine at the start of the reaction. We use 
trial and error to see what numbers we need to add to the front of the compounds.
 
2NaCl 
+ 
F2 
 
2NaF 
+ 
Cl2
If we put a 2 in front of the NaCl we now have 2 atoms of chlorine each side but now we 
have 2 atoms of sodium at the start of the reaction, so we also have to put a two at the 
front of NaF. Now there are two fluorine atoms on each side, so the equation is balanced.
Remember: A large number at the front means you multiply the number of atoms in 
one molecule by that number.
