Balancing chemical equations

Reactants= the chemicals that your start with. These react together.

Products=the chemicals that are made as a result of the chemical reaction.


          C3H8 + O2 ----------> H2O + CO2
          Equation= a line which shows the reactants and products in a chemical
          reaction.

There needs to be the same number of each element on each side of the equation.

Some equations are already balanced.



C     +       O2        CO2

C=                            C=

O=                            O=



Some are not

H2        +        O2   H2O

H=                      H=

O=                      O=

If we write the equation as

2H2       +        O2   2H2O

H=                      H=

O=                      O=



It now has equal numbers of each type of element on each side of the equation.

We call the big number 2 written in front of the H2 and H2O the coefficient.
                   How to Balance Most Chemical reactions.

   1.   Write down your given equation.


        C3H8 + O2 --> H2O + CO2
2. Write down the number of atoms per each element that you have on
each side of the equation.


        C3H8 + O2 ------------------> H2O + CO2
        C=                                 C=

        H=                                 H=

        O=                                 O=


   3. Leave hydrogen and oxygen for last

4. If you have more than one element left to balance: select the element
that appears in only a single molecule of reactants and in only a single
molecule of products. This means that you will need to balance the carbon
atoms first.

5. Add a coefficient to the single carbon atom on the right of the equation
to balance it with the 3 carbon atoms on the left of the equation.


        C3H8 + O2 -----------> H2O + 3CO2
        C=                                 C=

        H=                                 H=

        O=                                 O=


       The coefficient 3 in front of carbon on the right side indicates 3
        carbon atoms just as the subscript 3 on the left side indicates 3
        carbon atoms.
       In a chemical equation, you can change coefficients, but you must
        never alter the subscripts.
 6. Balance the hydrogen atoms next. You have 8 on the left side. So you'll
need 8 on the right side.



  2.   C3H8 + O2 ------------------> 4H2O + 3CO2
       C=                                 C=

       H=                                 H=

       O=                                 O=

      On the right side, you now added a 4 as the coefficient because the
       subscript showed that you already had 2 hydrogen atoms.
      When you multiply the coefficient 4 times by the subscript 2, you
       end up with 8.
      The other 6 atoms of Oxygen come from 3CO2.(3x2=6 atoms of
       oxygen+ the other 4=10)

7. Balance the oxygen atoms.

      Because you've added coefficients to the molecules on the right side
       of the equation, the number of oxygen atoms has changed. You now
       have 4 oxygen atoms in the water molecule and 6 oxygen atoms in
       the carbon dioxide molecule. That makes a total of 10 oxygen
       atoms.
      Add a coefficient of 5 to the oxygen molecule on the left side of the
       equation. You now have 10 oxygen molecules on each side.


       C3H8 + 5O2 ------------------> 4H2O + 3CO2
       C=                                 C=
       H=                                 H=
       O=                                 O=

Balancing Chemical Equations

Remember that with a formula you are shown how many of each atom is
in one molecule of a compound

The subscript is the name given to the number directly to the right of the
element. It tells you how many atoms there are of that particular element.
If there isn't a subscript, that means there is only one atom. For example,
let's look at the water molecule.




Reactants=the chemicals at the start of a chemical reaction.

Products=the chemicals made in a chemical reaction.

The reactants are on one side of the arrow.

Products are on the other side of the arrow.

A balanced chemical equation has equal numbers of all elements on each
side of an equation.

Some equations are already balanced for example. Carbon burning in
oxygen.

           Reactants                           products

Carbon + oxygen gas------carbon
dioxide

 C + O2                   -----------              CO2
1 carbon                                                  1 carbon

2 oxygen                                                  2 oxygen

Some do not
 2 hydrogen                                    2 hydrogen

2 oxygen                                      1 oxygen
Notice there are more oxygens on the reactants side than on the products
side.

To balance this equation we will need the following




4 hydrogen                                    4 hydrogen

2 oxygen                                      2 oxygen
The coefficient is the number that goes in front of a chemical formula

a the mass of any gaseous product is too

b any heat energy involved must be

c the mass of a gaseous product is to be

important to remember that:
a the mass of hydrogen, the lightest gas 
known, can be ignored.
b each of these gases forms molecules 
which have 2 atoms in them.
c chlorine is not a very active gas.
d only the amount of chlorine, the 
heaviest of the three, needs to be 
considered.

searchText:
REACTIONS AND EQUATIONS

The Law of Conservation of Mass states that




Why is this important to remember when we are reacting two substances
together?




Balancing Equations

Because of the Law of Conservation of Mass, all of the atoms that appear
on the reactant side of the equation must also appear on the product side.

Let us see what balancing involves.

Consider the following equation:

NaOH          +    Pb(NO3)2             Pb(OH)2      +        NaNO3

In this example, the numbers on each side do not match.

Let’s try using a T diagram


                         Reactants                 Products
Na                       1                         1
OH                       1                         2
Pb                       1                         1
NO3                      2                         1

You will notice that we didn’t split the OH or the NO 3 into separate atoms.
This is because the OH stays as OH on both sides and NO 3 stays as NO3 on
both sides. It makes it simpler for us to balance to leave them as they
are.
 Balancing involves inserting numbers in front of formulae so that the
atoms can be equal on both side.

In this example, if we look at the T diagram, you will see that to start with,
the sodium is equal on both sides so we will leave this one for now.

Next you will see that the OH is different. We will have to make them the
same. So if we put a 2 in front of the NaOH, we can change the number of
OHs on the reactant side.

2NaOH         +     Pb(NO3)2              Pb(OH)2      +        NaNO3

This changes our T diagram

                          Reactants                  Products
Na                        1 2                        1
OH                        1 2                        2
Pb                        1                          1
NO3                       2                          1

You will notice that the sodium has also changed. This is because we
have 2 NaOH so now we have 2 Na and 2 OH.

If we keep working down the diagram, the next one that is out of balance
is the NO3. Let’s put a 2 in front of the NaNO3 to balance this one.

2NaOH         +     Pb(NO3)2              Pb(OH)2      +       2NaNO3

                          Reactants                  Products
Na                        1 2                        1 2
OH                        1 2                        2
Pb                        1                          1
NO3                       2                          1 2


If we look closely at our T diagram, you will see that the numbers in the
reactants column is the same as the products column. This means that
our equation is now balanced.
 Try this one as a class

NaHCO3           Na2CO3         +     CO2   +   H2O


REMEMBER
There must be the same number of atoms on each of the equation.
You cannot change a formula to help you balance.
You can only put numbers IN FRONT of a substance to change the number
of atoms.




Try to balance these equations.

   1) Mg    +     HCl               MgCl2   +   H2

   2) Mg    +     O2            MgO

   3) SO2     +       O2        SO3

   4) KClO3               KCl   +     O2




All we need now is plenty of practice.
 a) NO      +          O2             NO2

b) Fe      +       HCl               FeCl2      +       H2

c) Al     +        O2               Al2O3

d) FeS        +       HCl             FeCl2         +       H2S

e) C2H6        +        O2            CO2       +       H2O

f) Mg      +       CO2                MgO       +       C

g) Ca(OH)2            +      CH3COOH                    Ca(CH3COO)2            +    H2O

h) KOH         +        H2SO4               K2SO4       +         H2O

i) Pb(NO3)2             +    ZnCl2              Zn(NO3)2            +       PbCl2

j) AlCl3       +        NaOH                Al(OH)3          +     NaCl

k) Ca      +       H2O                Ca(OH)2           +     H2

l) Ca(NO3)2             +    (NH4)2CO3                   CaCO3          +     NH4NO3

m) K3PO4          +        Fe(NO3)2             Fe3(PO4)2           +       KNO3
 Here are some more challenging examples.


  1) C12H22O11          +       O2            CO2       +       H2O


  2) Mg(HCO3)2                     MgO       +      CO2         +     H2O

 Teacher Guide for the Balancing Equations Race:
The problem with balancing equations:
There’s a problem with education that never gets any press. No politician has
come out against it and no teacher union has ever made a stand to end it. We all
know it exists, but we brush it under the rug and pretend it isn’t there.

The problem: Chemistry worksheets are boring.

Your students say worksheets are boring and, quite frankly, they’re right. I didn’t
like answering the same questions over and over again when I was in school,
and neither do they. Unfortunately, there’s no way around it, because to get
good at doing chemistry problems you need to do hundreds upon hundreds of
them.

There’s a book out by a competitor of mine that has a bunch of worksheets in it.
To get around this problem, they add clip art that makes the worksheets a little
more visually stimulating. My students like to give the scientists and students in
these pictures little mustaches and horns. Although the clip art does succeed in
breaking up the boredom, I have a feeling that this isn’t what they had in mind.

The solution: Make the activities vastly different from one another! Instead of
having a big worksheet where your students answer the same boring questions,
have a race where each team competes against the rest of the class! Instead of
boring worksheets, this is competition – survival of the fittest – a bloodthirsty
quest for dominance in the classroom!

OK. It’s still just a worksheet. The difference here isn’t that the worksheets are
different, it’s that your students have a different perception of the activity. This
difference is what sells the worksheet and gives your kids a little more practice
balancing equations.

Doing the balancing equations race:
Divide the students into teams of two. (For honors classes, have each student
work on his or her own.) The kids should be sitting side-by-side so they can work
together more efficiently. Pass out one worksheet face down for every student.
At the count of three, have the students start working.

There are many different ways you can run this activity. The first way involves
having students come up to the front of the room with their answers when they’ve
finished the worksheet. If all of the answers are correct, they win. If they aren’t,
send the kids back to their seats without telling them which problem is wrong.
They’ll grumble a little bit, but ultimately this is practice for having them check
their work during a quiz. When they’ve made an adjustment to their answer,
recheck, and so on until a group wins the race.

This can be done as a word or formula equation.
When writing a formula equations from a word equations there are certain
formula that need to be remembered. Use the information from last lesson
to complete the following.
Diatomic gasses. These are gasses which have molecules made of two
atoms of the same elements.
 Gas name                          Formula

 Nitrogen
 Chlorine
 Hydrogen
There are common formula that need to be remembered.
 Compound name                      Formula
 Water
 Carbon dioxide
 Methane                            CH4
 Elemental carbon                   C
There are also common acids that have set formula
 Acid name                             Formula
 Nitric acid                           HNO3
 Sulphuric acid                        H2SO4
 Phosphoric acid                       H3PO4
 Carbonic acid                         H2CO3
For metals in a chemical reaction just the symbol of the metal is written.
For ionic compounds the formula is worked out using the “drop and swap”
method and the table of common ions. This table is given at the end of this
booklet.

Integrated Science                                             Name ___________________________
Unit 3: Matter, Energy & Atmosphere                            Date: _______________Per: ________

                                         Formula Worksheet
Learning goal: To understand the information a chemical formula provides.

In order to study the atmosphere in further depth, you must understand a little more chemistry. This
worksheet is designed to help you understand what is meant by a chemical formula.

One of the main components of ‘acid rain’ is nitric acid, 2 HNO3. Let’s examine this molecule a little
closer:

There are two molecules represented here. The coefficient, or the number in front of the molecule, is
two. If there is no coefficient, then it is assumed there is one of the molecule.

There are 3 different elements in this one molecule: Hydrogen, Nitrogen and Oxygen. Each new
element starts with a capital letter. If an element has two letters in its symbol, the second is lower cased;
for example, sodium, Na.

There is a total of 5 atoms in this molecule. This is determined by the subscripts to the lower right of each
element. There is one Hydrogen (it is assumed to be one if there is NO subscript), one Nitrogen and
three Oxygens. If there is a subscript outside a set of parenthesis, that subscript distributes (is multiplied
by) to each atom inside the parenthesis.

There are a total of ten atoms in these two molecules of HNO3. This can be determined by multiplying
the coefficient by each subscript. There are two hydrogen atoms, two nitrogen atoms and six oxygen
atoms. This adds up to ten total atoms.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS 14

Chemistry is a science that studies the composition and properties of substances and how those
substances interact and transform to create new substances. Physical changes involve the changing of a
substance from one state to another without altering the chemical nature of the substance. For example,
melting ice and boiling water are physical changes. The bonds between the water molecules are affected
but the molecules remain unchanged. In a physical change, no new substance is formed and it is
relatively easy to reverse the change.

1 What physical change is the ‘opposite’ of boiling?
2 Why is electricity passing through a light globe a physical change?

3 Give an example of a physical change not already mentioned.

Chemical reactions occur when atoms are rearranged to form new substances (compounds). In a
chemical change, new substances are formed when atoms form new bonds with each other. Chemical
changes are called chemical reactions, Chemical reactions happen when one or more of the following
take place:

* Achange in temperature
* Anew substance appears
© The original substance disappears
* Achange is difficult to reverse,
4 State whether the following are physical changes or chemical changes.
& Soup from a can is warmed in a saucepan.
Ice-cream melts.
A tomato ripens.
Sugar dissolves in a cup of coffee.
Milk turns sour.
Water is added to a glass of cordial, 2  
A mixture of flour, water and yeast is heated to make bread,
5 Name another chemical reaction not already mentioned.

erenoe

Energy is often needed to start a chemical reaction. A match must be struck against the side of a
matchbox to ignite it. A naked flame must be placed next to gas coming from a Bunsen burner to light
it, These are examples of activation energy. Not all chemical reactions occur at the same rate (speed).
Magnesium (Mg) and gold (Au) are both shiny metals. A piece of magnesium can burn in a few seconds

Chemical reactions – heating copper sulphate and heating cobalt chloride

Teaching notes
The resource is for use after the students have watched or carried out the two practicals -
heating copper sulphate and heating cobalt chloride.
The practical itself could be shown as a teacher demonstration or done as a class
practical. If it is not possible to carry out the practical, then there are several videos
available showing the reactions. The following videos are available at the time of writing:
      copper sulphate being heated and then rehydrated
       http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M6IIbZx7xvQ
      heating cobalt chloride
       http://www.youtube.com/watch?feature=endscreen&NR=1&v=oC3FtY29FUs
      rehydrating cobalt chloride
       http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1WCISnxqbas


Before carrying out the practical with students, an appropriate risk assessment
must be carried out. Please refer to CLEAPPS guidelines for full risk information.


Precautions
      Copper sulphate and cobalt chloride solids may irritate the eyes and skin.
      Water added to anhydrous solids produces heat.
      Substances should be heated in heatproof test tubes in the hottest part of a Bunsen
       burner flame.
      Eye protection should be worn and care taken in handling hot apparatus.
      Both chemicals can cause damage to the environment and should be disposed of in
       accordance with current CLEAPPS guidelines.

Answers

Heating copper sulphate

Before heating, the copper sulphate was blue in colour.

After heating, the copper sulphate was white in colour.

During heating it was observed that it changed from blue to white and a vapour was
given off.

The copper sulphate was left to cool and a few drops of water were then added. We
observed that it changed from white to blue and heat given off.

This is an example of a reversible chemical reaction.

Why do you think the arrow above points in both directions?

Because the reaction will go in both directions – it is reversible.

What does hydrated mean?

It contains water.

What does anhydrous mean?

It does not contain water.

Heating cobalt chloride

Before heating, the cobalt chloride it was dark pink in colour.

After heating, the cobalt chloride was light blue in colour.

During heating it was observed that it changed colour from dark pink to light blue and
a vapour was produced.

The cobalt chloride was left to cool and a few drops of water were then added. We
observed that it changed colour from light blue to pink and heat was given off.

This is an example of a reversible chemical reaction.

Both copper sulphate and cobalt chloride changed colour when water was added to them.

How could this be useful in the chemistry laboratory?

Since both change colour when water is added to the anhydrous chemical, they can
be used to test to see if a liquid is or contains water. Cobalt chloride is available as
papers which need to be heated to turn them blue and they will then turn pale pink if
the substance is water.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS SUMMARY WORKSHEET

   Atoms with partly filled electron shells tend to be unstable and reactive.
   Chemical reactions take place when atoms lose, gain or share electrons.
   Atoms bond together because of the attraction between opposite charges.

Common Chemical Reactions
1. The more reactive metals react with water.
   General reaction: metal + water       hydrogen gas + metal hydroxide
   Example:         Calcium + water      hydrogen gas + calcium hydroxide
                    Ca   + 2 H2O          H2    +       Ca(OH)2

             (a)    Sodium + water
             (b)     Na +   H2O

2. Many metals react with acids.
   General reaction:   metal + acid                hydrogen gas + metal salt
   Example: magnesium + hydrochloric acid           hydrogen gas +
   magnesium chloride

            (a)      zinc + hydrochloric acid
            (b)              +
            (c)     calcium + sulfuric acid
            (d)       Ca   +   H2SO4

3. Most metals react with oxygen. This can be a fast reaction (combustion) or a
   slow reaction (tarnishing).
   General reaction:    metal + oxygen               metal oxide
   Example:        magnesium + oxygen                  magnesium oxide
                      2 Mg     +  O2                  2 MgO

             (a)      copper       + oxygen
             (b)       Cu          +  O2

4. Acid and base reactions.
    Acids contain hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water.
    Bases neutralise acidic solutions by removing H + ions.
    Bases that are soluble in water are called alkalis. Alkaline solutions
      contain hydroxide ions (OH-).
   General reaction :       acid + base                     water + salt
   Example: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide              water + sodium
   chloride

The need to classify chemicals into 
different groups:
a is unnecessary if chemicals are simply 
listed in alphabetical order.
b comes about because there are so many

c reflects the history of their discovery.
d is based on the relative importance of

As chemicals are classified into different 
groups, the important principle is that the 
chemicals within a particular group:
a have similar physical properties, such 
as mass and colour.
b are usually in the same state, i.e. all 
liquids or all solids.
c have chemical formulae which start 
with the same element, e.g. HCl and 
H2O.
d have many chemical properties in 
common.

One broad classification of chemicals is to 
put them into two groups called ‘organic’ 
and ‘inorganic’. The original classification 
into these groups generally meant that:
a organic chemicals were those found in 
living things, while inorganic chemicals 
were nothing to do with living things 
and were found within the rocks and 
the atmosphere of the Earth.
b only food products were included in 
the group called ‘organic’.
c only minerals such as iron ore and 
aluminium ore were classified as 
inorganic chemicals.
d the points in B and C were the critical 
ones.

A simple classification of chemicals is to 
put them into two groups called ‘elements’ 
and ‘compounds’. When this system is 
used: 
a the ‘compounds’ group would have 
many more chemicals in it than the

c the group called ‘organic’ chemicals 
would be left out.
d most of the ‘inorganic’ chemicals would 
not be included.

The group of chemicals which we call 
‘compounds’ all consist of:
a two elements combined together.

Common ions and formulae of ionic compounds

Symbols of common ions

You are not expected to know all the names and symbols of common ions, but you should be able to
work out the formulae of ionic compounds. The names and symbols of some ions are shown below.

sodium Na* bromide Br

potassium Kt iodide i.
lithium Li* hydrogencarbonate HCO}

copper(II) cut sulphide s
magnesium M sulphate soy

Formulae of ionic compounds

Ionic compounds contain positive and negative ions. The number of positive charges must equal the
number of negative charges so that the compound has no charge overall. When the positive ion has the
same number of charges as the negative ion, it is easy to work out the formula of the compound formed.
Sodium chloride contains sodium ions, Na*, and chloride ions, CI". As both ions have single charges,
the formula is simply written as NaCl, i.c. the positive ion followed by the negative ion with no charges
written. Similarly, ammonium chloride is NH4Cl; magnesium oxide is MgO, and so on. The fun starts
when the number of charges is different, as in magnesium chloride. The “cross-over” method may help:

Step1 Write the ions side by side: Step 4 Write the formula as follows:
2+ -
Mg Cr a) write the positive ion without its charge:
Step 2 Draw arrows that cross each other: Mg
Mg?* cr b) write the number as a subscript unless it is 1:

Pe Mg

Step 3 Write the charges at the arrow ends: ©) write the negative ion without its charge:

Mg** cr MgCl
d) write the number as a subscript unless it is 1:
1 2 MgCl, «all done!

Watch out for compound ions, e.g. ammonium, hydrogencarbonate, hydroxide, nitrate, sulphate and
carbonate. If you need more than one of them to balance the charges, put brackets around their symbol
at step (a) or (c). For example, sodium hydroxide is NaOH, but magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)2;
copper(II) sulphate is CuSO,4, but ammonium sulphate is (NH4)2SO4.

60
© Janine Haeusler and Blake Education 2014
Resource sheet – Conservation of mass
Conserving mass (1)
When a chemical reaction occurs, the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form the 
products. No new atoms are created, and none are destroyed. Mass is conserved. This 
means that the mass of the products at the end of the reaction is equal to the mass of the 
reactants at the beginning. We use molecular drawings to show this.
carbon C 
+ 
oxygen gas O2 
 
carbon dioxide CO2
 
 
 
 
The number of atoms of each element at the start is the same as at the end, so we say that 
the equation is balanced. What if the equation is not balanced?
magnesium Mg + 
oxygen gas O2 
 
magnesium oxide MgO
 
 
 
 
Something is wrong. There are more oxygen atoms at the start of the reaction than at the 
end, but we know that atoms cannot be lost during a chemical reaction. If there were two 
molecules of magnesium oxide at the end we would have the correct number of oxygen 
atoms, but one too many magnesium atoms. There must have been 2 magnesium atoms 
at the start of the reaction. 
 
 
+ 
 
 
 
2Mg 
 
+ 
O2 
 
 
2MgO
We say that this equation is balanced. We place a large number at the front to show how 
many molecules of each reactant and product there are. Placing a large number at the 
front of a formula multiplies the whole of the formula by that number. For example, 2MgO 
means 2 atoms of magnesium and 2 atoms of oxygen.

     (NaOH) and hydrogen gas.
  3. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) combines with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to
     produce sodium chloride (NaCl) and water.
  4. Hydrogen gas combines with fluorine gas (F2) to form hydrogen
     fluoride (HF).
  5. The reaction of potassium chloride (KCl) and silver nitrate (AgNO 3)
     yields potassium nitrate (KNO3) and silver chloride (AgCl)
  6. The decomposition of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) produces
     sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), carbon dioxide, and water.
  7. The reaction of aluminium sulphate (Al2(SO4)3) and barium chloride
     (BaCl2) produces aluminium chloride (AlCl3) and barium sulphate
     (BaSO4).

     dioxide and water vapour.

Elements and atomic numbers
Student:................................................................................................................... Class:.................................................


Atomic numbers and mass numbers
1. Each element is characterised by its atomic number (Z). The atoms of an element may not be
   identical, however, because elements can exist as isotopes. Isotopes have different numbers of
   neutrons and are distinguished by their mass numbers (A).
   Elements can be represented by the following notation:
                                                                                 Z  atomic number  number of protons
                                                                                 A  mass number  number of protons plus neutrons
      For example, the common isotope of iron has 26 protons and a mass number of 56. The number of
      neutrons is therefore: 56 – 26 = 30 neutrons.

         Beryllium (Be)                                               4                      5

Atomic weight of an element
2. The atomic weight of an element is sometimes referred to as its relative atomic mass. The atomic
   weight is the average or weighted mean of the isotopes of that element, taking into account the
   relative amounts of each type of isotope. Thus, atomic weights are often not whole numbers.

 Naming ionic compounds
The name of an ionic compound is simply the name of the cation combined with the
name of the anion. For example, the name for the compound made from magnesium
cations (Mg2+) and oxide anions (O2-) is magnesium oxide.

However, some metallic atoms can produce several cations with different charges.
For example, copper atoms can form copper cations with charges of +1 or +2. To
distinguish between these ions, the charge of the ion is included in the ion name
using Roman numerals: the two types of copper ions are named copper (I) ion (Cu+)
and copper (II) ion (Cu2+). The Roman numerals are also included in the name of the
compound. When copper (I) ions form an ionic compound with chloride ions (Cl-), the
compound is named copper (I) chloride. Similarly, when copper (II) ions form an ionic
compound with chloride ions (Cl-) it is named copper (II) chloride.



Chemical formulas
The chemical formula for an ionic compound combines the chemical symbols for
each ion in the compound, but you don’t include the charges on the ions. Sodium
chloride, made from sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl-), has the chemical
formula NaCl.

However, you must ensure that the total charge of the cations and anions in the
crystal lattice adds to zero. For example, the chemical formula for magnesium
chloride is MgCl2. This is because the magnesium ion (Mg2+) has a charge of +2 and
the chloride ion (Cl-) has a charge of -1, so each magnesium ion needs two chloride
ions to balance the total charge.

Similarly, the formula for sodium nitride is Na3N. The sodium ion (Na+) has a charge
of +1 and the nitride ion (N3-) has a charge of -3, so there must be three sodium ions
to balance the charge of each nitride ion in the crystal lattice.

If the charge of one ion does not divide evenly into the charge of the other, then both
ions will need to be multiplied in the chemical formula. For example, the formula for

Resource sheet – The periodic table
Naming groups in the periodic table
Elements on the periodic table can be divided into metals and non-metals. They can be 
further broken down into different groups based on their properties.
The metals found in Group 1 are very reactive. This means they react violently with 
water. They are also soft and can be cut with a knife. Examples include lithium, sodium 
and potassium, which are also known as the alkali metals. Hydrogen is in Group 1 of the 
periodic table but it is not considered part of the alkali metals because it is a non-metal.
The metals found between Groups 2 and 3 are called transition metals. They have the 
typical properties of metals – they are hard, dense and have high melting and boiling 
points. The semi-metals or metalloids are located along the stepped line between metals 
and non-metals. Boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium and polonium 
are all semi-metals. They are called semi-metals because they have some characteristics 
of metals and some of non-metals. For example, silicon is shiny, but it is brittle, so it would 
break it you hit it with a hammer.
The non-metals in Group 7 are very reactive. They are called halogens. Halogens are 
poisonous non-metals. Examples include fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. 
Like most non-metals, they have low melting and boiling points. 
Group 8 – sometimes known as Group 0 – is found on the right-hand side of the periodic 
table. These elements are very special because they do not react to form compounds. They 
are found by themselves in nature. They are called noble gases.

Radioactivity had been discovered and alpha particles were identified as tiny positive protons. A

When the English scientist James Chadwick (1891 - 1974) discovered the existance of neutrons,
which were as heavy as protons but carried no charge, the atomic model changed to include neutrons

History of the atom
Identify the evidence supporting Democritus’ model of the atom. 


Identify the relationship between the complexity of atomic models and time. 


Identify something you interact with on a daily basis that is not made of atoms. 


Democritus’ model of the atom was a theoretical model. Thompson’s model was an evidence-based model. Compare these two types of models from the descriptions. Use the graphic organiser on the next page to list their similarities and differences.
Democritus was a natural philosopher. Natural philosophers believed that two things made up the natural world: atoms and the void. Atoms were completely solid, with no gaps; they came in a variety of sizes and shapes, were indivisible and infinite in number. Atoms moved about in the void, repelling each other when they collided or combining into clusters. The clusters formed by tiny hooks or barbs on the surface that held the cluster together. All changes in the visible world were a result of these interactions. Atoms could change places, but could not be changed, destroyed or created from nothing.
Berryman, S. (2016) “Democritus”, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, accessed at https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/democritus/
Before Thomson’s model, the accepted model of the atom did not have any charged particles, because the atom was considered to be indivisible. Thomson discovered the electron, a subatomic particle, when experimenting with a cathode-ray tube. To account for electrons, he devised a new model, with negatively charged particles spread throughout the solid positive mass of the atom, like raisins in a plum pudding.
American Board for Certification of Teacher Excellence (ABCTE) (2007) “Modern atomic theory: Models”, accessed at http://www.abcte.org/files/previews/chemistry/s1_p5.html
If you want to know more about Democritus’ idea of the atom or Thomson’s atomic model, do some research online.

searchText: ﻿History Of the Periodic Table Dmitri Mendeleev Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian scientist born in Siberia in 1834, is known as the father of the periodic table of the elements. The periodic table of the elements is an important tool used by students and chemists around the world to help them understand and simplify the often complex world of chemical reactions. Mendeleev was Professor of Chemistry at the University of St. Petersburg (now Leningrad) in Russia. Mendeleev's work as a whole amounted to more than 400 books and articles as well as a large number of manuscripts which are preserved at the University of Leningrad. Mendeleev dedicated his life to research and education. Mendeleev made it his special responsibility to educate people wherever he went. When he traveled, Mendeleev would ride in the third class section of the train just to share findings with peasants over a cup of tea. In 1869 Mendeleev arranged all the known elements (63 at that time) in order of increasing mass of the atoms. He found that the properties of elements repeated themselves at regular intervals. He arranged them in the form of a table so that athe elements with similar properties would fall into a vertical comumn. Because the properties of elements repeated themselves at regular intervals or periods the table is called the Periodic table of elements. Mendeleev left gaps in the table to make the elements fit into proper columns and announced that the gaps represented elements not yet discovered. Mendeleev predicted the properties of the undiscovered elements by judging the properties of the elements above and below the gap in the table. Mendeleev died on January 20, 1907 at the age of 73. A copy of the Periodic table was carried high over his funeral procession as a fitting emblem of Mendeleev's career. For more information on History of Periodic Table or on the discovery and naming of each element simply click on the hyperlink! The Periodic Table The Periodic table of the elements was devised by Dimitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic number and noticed that the properties of the elements repeat themselves at regular intervals. If you are not familliar with the Periodic Table take some time to examine the elements in the table below.If you click on an element the name and number will appear in the boxes below. Try to memorise the names and symbols of the first twenty elements. Teacher Area Student Area Periodic Table of the Elements Top of Form H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar K Ca Sc Ti V Cr Mn Fe Co Ni Cu Zn Ga Ge As Se Br Kr Rb Sr Y Zr Nb Mo Tc Ru Rh Pd Ag Cd In Sn Sb Te I Xe Cs Ba La Hf Ta W Re Os Ir Pt Au Hg Tl Pb Bi Po At Rn Fr Ra Ac Bottom of Form Top of Form Name Number Mass Bottom of Form Legend Metals A solid substance that is a good conductor of eat and electicity. Can be formed into many shapes. Metalloid "Middle elements" - conduct heat and electricity better than nonmetals, but not as well as metals. Easier to shape than nonmetals, but not as easy as metals. Solid at room temperature. Nonmetals A poor conductor of heat and electricity. Not easily formed into shapes. Note The Lanthanum and Actinium series have been omitted Information about Elements. Elements are represented in the Periodic Table by their chemical symbols. The chemical symbol may be one letter as in Carbon, or two letters as in Na (Sodium). If their are two letters in the symbol the second is always written in lowercase. Besides the chemical symbol the Periodic Table usually gives the Atomic Number (above the symbol) and the Mass Number (below the symbol). Often the Mass Number is replaced by the Relative Atomic Mass Structure of the Periodic Table The Periodic Table is structured so that elements underneath each other have similar chemical properties The vertical columns which make up the Periodic Table are called Groups. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties. Some groups have special names for example the elements from Group I are called the Alkali Metals The Horizontal rows of elements are called Periods.                        How to Balance Chemical Equations
The Law of Conservation of Mass states that matter is never created or destroyed.
When writing chemical equations, the Law of Conservation of Mass has to be satisfied.
The number and kind of atoms contained in the reactants must equal the number and
kind of atoms in the products. If the atoms are not equal, we have defied the Law of
Conservation of Mass. Therefore, we must balance the equation.

Balancing chemical equations is easy if you follow some rules.

       You can only add a coefficient in front of a chemical formula
       You cannot change any subscripts, nor add any subscripts
       You may not place a coefficient in the ‘middle’ of a chemical formula
       You must end up with the same number and kinds of atoms on both sides of the
       equation when you are finished. Count atoms on both sides upon completion to
       check yourself.

Practice with this example.          Reactants are on the left side of the arrow -
CO + H2          CH3OH               products are on the right.

Count the number of atoms on the left side of the arrow, and compare it with the
number of atoms on the right side.

If you draw a vertical line under the arrow, you can easily see the two sides of your
equation. List the atoms as shown.

CO + H2            CH3OH

C -1               C–1
O–1                O–1
H–2                H–4

If you list the atoms in the same order on both sides, you can easily see which atoms
are equal and which are not. Here, you see that we do not have the same number of
hydrogen atoms on both sides. We must follow the rules above to balance this
equation. Add a coefficient of 2 in front of the H2, but do not change any subscripts.

CO + 2H2            CH3OH             For every molecule of CO, we must use 2 molecules
                                      of H2 to produce 1 molecule of CH3OH.

The 2H2 means there are 2 molecules of H2 – therefore there are 4 atoms of hydrogen.
Recheck the number of atoms for accuracy. The number of atoms on both sides of the
equation is now equal. We have satisfied the Law of Conservation of Mass.
 Name:______________________________________ Class: ________________ Date: _____________


Here’s another example:

Al + O2           Al2O3                  Count the number of atoms and list them under
                                         the equation. Compare each side.
Al – 1            Al – 2
O–2               O–3

You might try adding a coefficient of 2 in front of the Al to balance the aluminum atoms.

2Al + O2            Al2O3
                                          It’s OK if the first coefficient you try does not
Al – 2              Al – 2                balance the equation.
O–2                 O-3


But: How should we fix the number of oxygen atoms? By looking at the subscripts for
oxygen, you see that we cannot get them to match without adding coefficients. If we
add a coefficient of 2 in front of the O2 on the left, we will then have 4 oxygen atoms.
We cannot achieve 4 oxygen atoms on the right using a coefficient. Let’s try the lowest
common multiple of 2 and 3. That number is 6. We will attempt to have 6 oxygen
atoms on both sides of the equation.

To do this, add a coefficient of 3 in front of the oxygen on the left, and a coefficient of 2
in front of the Al2O3 on the right. Remember, you cannot add a coefficient in between a
molecular formula.

2Al + 3O2                  2Al2O3          Now we have balanced the number of oxygen
                                           atoms in our equation, but have caused the
Al – 2                     Al – 4
                                           aluminum atoms to be unbalanced.
O–6                        O–6

         The coefficient is multiplied by each subscript to get the total number of atoms.

Replace the ‘2’ in front of the Al with a ‘4’ to balance the number of aluminum atoms.

4Al + 3O2                    2Al2O3         Now we have a balanced equation.



Difficulties encountered when balancing equations like the one above may be solved if
you are patient, follow the balancing rules, count numbers of atoms correctly, and give
the ‘trial and error’ method a try.

searchText: ﻿Important Definitions Nucleus: The core of an atom. Proton: Has a positive charge and is found in the nucleus of an atom. Neutron: Has no charge and is found in the nucleus of an atom. Electron: Has a negative charge and is found in a cloud around the nucleus. Atomic Number: The number of protons in an atom. Mass Number: The number of protons and neutrons in an atom.

searchText: Ionic Compounds Ionic compounds are formed from a positive ion and a negative ion combining together. The ions combine together so that the positive charges and the negative charges balance each other out to form a neutral compound . Table salt is a common ionic compound. It is formed when one sodium ion, Na + , combines with one chloride ion, Cl - . The positive charge on the sodium ion balances out the negative charge on the chloride ion to form sodium chloride, NaCl . Your Task: You will be given a set of wooden blocks representing different ions. The length of each block corresponds to the size of the charge on the ion. One colour will r epresent the positive ions and a second will represent the negative ions. Use the wooden blocks to construct models of the ionic compounds that can be formed . searchText:
CHAPTER 4: Compounds — Formulae and Naming

(a) COMPOUNDS CONTAINING ONLY NON-METALS

i) Most compounds containing only non-metals exist as molecules in which the
atoms are bound together by sharing electrons (covalent bonding).

Being molecular, the formula of each of these compounds indicates the composi-
tion of the molecules.

A few compounds containing onlv non-metals, such as silicon carbide and silicon
dioxide, exist as covalent network lattices. Thus the formula of each of these
compounds is just the simplest ratio of atoms in the lattice e.g. SiC and SiO,.

Naming compounds of two non-metals.

Unless common names are used, the name of a non-metal compound also tells us
he composition of the molecules, or the simplest ratio of atoms in the lattice; that is,
he formula is self evident from the name.

Rules for Naming

1. The name of the element closer to the bottom, left-hand corner of the periodic
table is given first.

searchText: ﻿Ions and Compound Formation Atoms consist of a central nucleus made up of positively charged protons and neutrons which have no charge. The nucleus is orbited at high speed by much smaller negatively charged electrons. Protons and neutrons have the same mass, while electrons have about 1/2000th the mass of protons and neutrons. An atom has an equal number of protons and electrons, so the positive and negative charges balance each other to produce a neutral atom (one with no overall charge). The simplest atom is hydrogen, whose nucleus contains only a single proton, orbited by a lone electron. All other atoms contain the three types of particles. Scientists use two special numbers to describe atoms. The atomic number of an atom is the number of protons it contains and the mass number is the number of particles in an atom’s nucleus (the number of protons + neutrons). The atomic numbers of hydrogen, helium, lithium and beryllium are 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. Scientists use the following notation to describe an atom’s structure: If we know the atomic and mass numbers of an atom, we can figure out how many protons, electrons and neutrons it contains. For example, potassium has an atomic number of 19 and a mass number of 39. This means there are twenty protons in the nucleus. Because the number of electrons is the same as the number of protons, there must be 19 electrons whizzing around the outside of the atom. The mass number of 29 tells us there are 29 particles in the nucleus, but since we know 19 of these are protons, the other ten must be neutrons. Electron Shells Electrons orbit the nucleus in special regions, or shells. Only 2 electrons may fit in the innermost shell of any atom, then up to 8 in each of the next 2 shells for elements up to atomic number 20. The inner most shells are ‘filled’ first. This may be compare to filling spaces on a bookshelf, where we fill the bottom shelf first, then only move up if each lower shelf is filled. Take sodium, for example, with 11 electrons. 2 electrons orbit in the inner shell, 8 in the next, leaving one to orbit in the third shell. Atoms can become charged if they gain or lose electrons. Charged atoms are called ions. For example, sodium has only one electron in its outermost shell. This means that sodium will readily give up this electron. When it loses this electron, sodium becomes positively charged. Conversely, the chlorine atom forms a negative ion when it gains an electron. When sodium and chloride are able to exchange an electron, an ionic bond forms between them and the compound, sodium chloride, is formed. The molecular formula for this is: NaCl. Magnesium readily gives up its 2 outermost electrons, forming Mg2+. So when magnesium combines with chloride the molecular formula is MgCl2, because 2 chloride ions are needed for each magnesium ion in order to balance the charge. Questions 1. searchText: ﻿CHEMICAL CHANGE ISOTOPES Isotopes: atoms of one element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The number of protons is fixed for any given element, however the number of neutrons can often vary. The Mass Number of an element is always a whole number but because there can be more than one type of the same element, the RAM of an element (this is the number underneath the symbols on the periodic table) is often not a whole number because it is an average of two or three isotopes of the same element. Example Chlorine has two isotopes and can have either 18 neutrons or 20 neutrons (the number of protons ‘Z’ is always 17). 3517­Cl or 3717Cl (Chlorine Isotopes) In nature any random sample will contain 3/4 (75%) of 3517Cl and 1/4 (25%) of 3717Cl. To calculate its Relative Atomic Mass (RAM) we do the following. 75% x 35 + 25% x 37 RAM = 35.5 On the periodic table you can see that the RAM is 35.5 Try this: Natural Silicon in silicon ore contains 92% 2814Si, 5% 2914Si and 3% 3014Si. Calculate its the RAM of silicon in nature.

searchText: Law of conservation of mass Purpose To attempt to verify & observe the Law of Conservation of Mass - In any chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the mass of the products. You will need Balance (accurate to 0.01 g), 100mL beaker, 50mL vinegar, 10g baking soda (sodium hydrogen carbonate), 100mL conical flask, balloon, weighing paper, graduated measuring cylinder, funnel. What to do Record the mass of the empty 100mL beaker. Pour about 15 mL of vinegar into the beaker. Record the mass of the beaker & vinegar. Weigh out ~5 g of baking soda onto a piece of weighing paper. Record the exact mass of baking soda used. Place the beaker/vinegar and the weighing paper/baking soda on the pan of the laboratory balance. Measure and record the mass of these reactants/containers. Carefully pour the baking soda into the beaker of vinegar and allow the reaction (fizzing and bubbling) to complete. Measure and record the mass of the remaining products. Record the mass of the empty conical flask. Pour about 15 mL of vinegar into the 100 mL flask using the funnel to make certain the neck of the flask does not get wet. Obtain the mass of the flask & vinegar. Prepare the sample of baking soda as before and now determine and record the mass of the reactants, the flask and the balloon (which will be the cover for this container) Add the baking soda to the flask and quickly cover the mouth of the flask with the balloon. Measure and record the mass of the products/container/balloon. Results: trial one Item Mass (grams) Beaker + Vinegar Baking soda Total (beaker and reactants) Final mass (after reaction) Difference Results: trial two Item Mass (grams) Conical flask + Vinegar Balloon Baking soda Total (flask, balloon and reactants) Final mass (after reaction) Difference Questions What evidence was there that a chemical reaction occurred? Account for the difference in mass for trial one. Account for the difference in mass for trial two. Did the experiment demonstrate the law of conservation of mass? Explain. Suggest two improvements that could be made to the method that would increase the accuracy of this demonstration .

searchText: 152 Classic chemistry experiments 61. Mass conservation Topic Mass conservation. Timing 20 min. Description Students react potassium iodide with lead nitrate. They weigh reactants and products to show there is no mass change. Apparatus and equipment (per group) 3 ▼ Two < 100 cm beakers 3 ▼ 10 cm Measuring cylinder ▼ Access to an accurate balance (0.01g). Chemicals (per group) –3 ▼ Potassium iodide solution 0.01 mol dm –3 ▼ Lead nitrate solution 0.009 mol dm (Harmful). Teaching tips Students get confused with errors in an experiment. This is a good opportunity to reinforce the idea of errors and that small differences do not necessarily indicate weight loss or gain. The teacher can state that if weight is gained or lost, the results would be repeatable, and therefore the same for all groups in the class. Emphasise the process of not trying to weigh exact amounts of reactants, you simply require an accurate mass. Background theory Accuracy in measurements, errors, and repeatability. Safety Wear eye protection. Ensure students wash their hands thoroughly after the experiment. Answers 1. Yes, this is confirmed by the colour change. 2. Potassium iodide + lead nitrate → potassium nitrate + lead iodide 3. Although at some degree of accuracy the experiment appears to show a mass change this is within the limits of experimental error and these results tend to indicate no mass change. Classic chemistry experiments 153 Mass conservation Introduction The aim of this experiment is to show that mass is not gained or lost in a chemical reaction. The term cyborg or cybernetic organism conjures up images of humanoid robots with super-human abilities, 
commonly found in science fiction. Cybernetics is the science of control and communications in animals and 
machines. A cyborg is a ‘blend’ of human and machine. The idea of attaching artificial parts to humans modernised 
the Frankenstein story.  
1 
What is meant by humanoid? 
2

‘ordinary’ humans.

4 
Draw and describe a cyborg in your workbook.
The field of Bionics is concerned with developing engineering solutions for impaired (damaged or destroyed) body 
parts. It specialises in creating electrically operated devices to replace or enhance the functions of body parts.  
5 
List six bionic devices and the body part(s) each one repairs or assists. 
 
 
6 
Name a high-profile person who uses (or used) a bionic device. 
Biomaterials and bionic devices
Advances in science and technology have increased our ability to improve, enhance and prolong life using bionic 
devices. By adopting a multidisciplinary approach, biomaterials (materials developed to replace living tissue) have 
been formed to create biomedical devices. A biomedical device is a piece of equipment used for a medical purpose, 
such as helping a person to walk or ensuring a heartbeat remains steady (pacemaker). When biomedical devices are 
implanted within the body, as a pacemaker is, they are called implants. These prosthetic devices have revolutionised 
our approach to illness, injury and disability by taking over, at least in part, the work performed by a damaged or 
destroyed body part.

METALS AND NON-METALS and the PERIODIC TABLE


Elements are arranged on the periodic table due to their properties. Two big groupings are the metals
and the non-metals. Metals all share certain properties.

                       PROPERTIES OF METALS AND NON-METALS
Metals

    • Capable of being highly polished (they have a lustre or are
      shiny when cut).
    • Good conductors of heat and electricity.
    • All are solid at room temperature (except for mercury).
    • Can be hammered into thin sheets (malleable) and
      stretched into wires (ductile).
Non-metals

      • Usually don't shine when polished.
      • Poor conductors of electricity (except carbon), and heat.
      • Exist as solids, liquids and gases at room temperature.
      • Those that are solid are brittle (they shatter).

Metalloids
This group have some metal properties and some non-metal properties.

searchText:
Chapter 5                                    Chemical
reactions
              More balancing
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1:

chemical equations
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                     LOGICAL/MATHEMATICAL


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________

Balanced chemical equations show the atoms and molecules that take part in
a chemical reaction. These equations take into account the Law of
Conservation of Mass by ensuring that there is the same number of each
atom in the products as there is in the reactants.

Equations are balanced by adding coefficients (numbers) to the chemical
formulas in the equation. The coefficient multiplies every atom in the
molecule. For example, putting a coefficient of three in front of the chemical
formula for water (3H2O) gives a total of 6 hydrogen atoms and 3 oxygen
atoms.


Method 1: Using integer coefficients
Many chemical equations can be balanced by simply balancing the number of
each type of atom in the reactants and products one by one. Take for
example the combustion of methane, which has the unbalanced chemical
equation:

   CH4         +              O2                             CO2                +               H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
 Step 1: Balance the carbon atoms (C). There is one carbon in the reactants
and one in the products, so no change is necessary.

   CH4         +              O2                             CO2                +               H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 2: Balance the hydrogen atoms (H). There are four hydrogen atoms in
the reactants and two in the products so the water molecule is multiplied by
two.

   CH4         +              O2                             CO2                +           2H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 3: Balance the oxygen atoms (O). There are two oxygen atoms in the
reactants and four oxygen atoms in the products (two from the carbon dioxide
and two more from the two water molecules). Therefore, the oxygen molecule
in the reactants is multiplied by two.

   CH4         +             2O2                             CO2                +           2H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 4: Check that the equation is balanced by looking at the number of each
atom on either side of the equation.

   Reactants: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O

   Products: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 2
 Method 2: Using half-integer coefficients
One of the challenges when balancing chemical equations is that not all
equations can be balanced using the same method. Therefore, scientists
develop different strategies for dealing with different equations.

One useful strategy is to first balance the equation using half-integer
coefficients such as 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and so on. However, it doesn’t make sense
to have half a molecule so the whole equation is then multiplied by a factor
of two.

This technique comes in handy when you find that there is an odd number of
an atom of one side of the equation and an even number on the other side of
the equation. Take for example, the combustion of ethane, which has the
unbalanced chemical equation:

   C2H6        +              O2                             CO2                +               H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 1: Balance the carbons (C) by multiplying the carbon dioxide by two.

   C2H6        +              O2                            2CO2                +               H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 2: Balance the hydrogens (H) by multiplying the water by three.

   C2H6        +              O2                            2CO2                +           3H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 3: Balance the oxygens (O). There are 2 oxygens in the reactants and
7 oxygens in the products. There is no way we can balance the oxygens by
multiplying any single molecule by an integer. Therefore we multiply the
oxygen molecule by 3.5 to give 7 oxygen atoms in the reactants and 7 in the
products.

   C2H6        +            3.5O2                           2CO2                +           3H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water

NAMING COMPOUNDS

If a compound contains only two elements its name usually ends in ‘-ide’. In a compound that contains
a metal and a non-metal, the metal comes first in the compound’s name. For example, iron (III) oxide,
Fe,O,, contains the metal iron, Fe, and the non-metal oxygen, O. Sodium chloride (NaCl) contains the
metal sodium, Na, and the non-metal chlorine, Cl.

These are some name changes for elements present in compounds:
F, fluorine — fluoride I, iodine — iodide Br, bromine — bromide
O, oxygen ~ oxide N, nitrogen — nitride S, sulfur — sulfide
1 Name two things that the elements above have in common.

potassium bromide

Often in chemistry atoms form groups that stay together during reactions, acting in a similar way to a
single atom. For example, when four oxygen atoms bond with a sulfur atom, a sulfate ion, SO,*, is
formed. Now consider magnesium sulfate (MgSO,) in a reaction, This compound can ‘break up’ to
form a magnesium ion (Mg”) and a sulfate ‘unit’ with the five atoms that form the sulfate unit
remaining intact. A group of atoms that stays together in chemical reactions is called a radical. If
more than two elements are present in a compound and one of these is oxygen, then the compound's
name usually ends in ‘-ate’. These radicals (groups of atoms) are common parts of compounds:

SO, = sulfate -CO, = carbonate -NO,= nitrate -PO, = phosphate

Naming compounds that contain radicals is not as confusing as it may first appear. The metals keep

most (or a recognisable part) of their names and the presence of oxygen in the radical group usually
denotes an ‘-ate’ ending to the name.

searchText: ﻿ Naming Compounds - (Chemical Formulae) Prefixes Mono _____________ Di _____________ Tri ___________ Tetra _____________ Pent _____________ Hex ___________ 7: _____________ 8: _____________ 9: ___________ 10: _____________ Naming covalent compounds of two non-metal elements 1. Covalent compounds are combinations of two or more non-metal elements. They are not ionic. 2. These compounds consist of molecules (eg, H2O, CO2, CO, SO3) in which atoms are sharing electrons so that each one has a full valence shell. 3. Some covalent compounds have “common names” that do not follow any particular set of rules. These must be learned - for example: Compound Common name Compound Common name H2O water CHCl3 chloroform CH4 methane HCl hydrogen chloride NH3 ammonia HBr hydrogen bromide H2O2 hydrogen peroxide HF hydrogen fluoride 4. For most other covalent compounds there are a number of rules to follow for naming them. 5. Naming rules (nomenclature) 1) The name of the first element in the formula is the same as the element itself. (eg; CO2 is carbon dioxide) 2) The name of the second element in the formula has its ending changed to IDE (eg; CO2 is carbon dioxide) 3) If there are more than one of the first element’s atoms, the prefixes di (2), tri (3), tetra (4), penta (5), hexa (6), hepta (7), octa (8), nona (9), deca (10) are used to show how many atoms there are. (eg; P4O10 is tetraphosphorus decoxide) 4) For the second element, the prefixes mono (1), di (2), tri (3), tetra (4), penta (5), hexa (6), hepta (7), octa (8), nona (9), deca (10) are used to show how many atoms there are. Ionic compounds are formed between metals (left on the periodic table) and non-metals (right on the periodic table). 2. These compounds consist of a lattice of positive and negative ions. (eg, NaCl, AgNO3, Fe2O3) is which the metal has “donated” one or more eletrons to become positive, whilst the non-metal has accepted electrons to become negative. 3. Some ionic compounds have “common names” that do not follow any particular set of rules. These must be learned - for example: Compound Common name Compound Common name Fe2O3 rust NaCl Salt or table salt 4. For most other covalent compounds there are a number of rules to follow for naming them. 5. Naming rules (nomenclature) i) The Metal is named first and does not have its name changed, so it is written as seen in the periodic table. ii) The charge on the metal is indicated by roman numerals in brackets after its’ name. This is not necessary for metals that only exist in one state. (eg. Sodium is written as Na, because it only comes as Na+, whilst iron would have to be written as Fe(II) or Fe(III), as it exists as Fe2+ and Fe3+. iii) The non-metal ion has a suffix added which indicates its’ charge or form. searchText: ﻿Naming Compounds & Writing Formula Metallic substances The name of the metallic substance is the same as the element. The formula is the element symbol. (sodium – Na, iron-Fe, copper-Cu etc) Ionic compounds Rules for naming: 1. The metal or positive ion is named first and keeps its normal name. 2. The non-metal or negative ion is named second and has the end of its name written as –ide, -ate or –ite. 3. If the metal ion has several valencies, indicate its valency using roman numerals. (sodium chloride, ammonium sulfate, iron sulfite etc) Writing formula: 1. The positive ion is written first. 2. The negative ion is written second. 3. The number of each ion is adjusted so that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge. Subscripts are used to indicate the number of each ion present. (sodium chloride-NaCl, ammonium phosphate- (NH4)3PO4, iron(II) hydroxide- Fe(OH)2) Covalent Compounds Rules for naming 1. The name of the element closer to the bottom left side of the periodic table is named first and keeps its normal name. 2. The name of the second element has its name changed to end in –ide e.g. sulphide, chloride, oxide, nitride etc 3. Prefixes are used to indicate the number of atoms of each element. 4. If there is only one atom of the first element then no prefix is used. For example, CO2 – carbon dioxide 5. Molecules composed of one element are given the name of that element. For example, H2-hydrogen, O2-oxygen, Cl2- chlorine Number of atoms Prefix Number of atoms Prefix 1 mono- 6 hexa- 2 di- 7 hepta- 3 tri- 8 octa- 4 tetra- 9 nona- 5 penta- 10 deca- Examples: 1. searchText: ﻿The alkali metals, found in group 1 of the periodic table (formerly known as group IA), are very reactive metals that do not occur freely in nature. These metals have only one electron in their outer shell. Therefore, they are ready to lose that one electron in ionic bonding with other elements. As with all metals, the alkali metals are malleable, ductile, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. The alkali metals are softer than most other metals. Cesium and francium are the most reactive elements in this group. Alkali metals can explode if they are exposed to water. The Alkali Metals are: Lithium Sodium Potassium Rubidium Cesium Francium The 38 elements in groups 3 through 12 of the periodic table are called "transition metals". As with all metals, the transition elements are both ductile and malleable, and conduct electricity and heat. The interesting thing about transition metals is that their valence electrons, or the electrons they use to combine with other elements, are present in more than one shell. This is the reason why they often exhibit several common oxidation states. There are three noteworthy elements in the transition metals family. These elements are iron, cobalt, and nickel, and they are the only elements known to produce a magnetic field. The Transition Metals are: Scandium Titanium Vanadium Chromium Manganese Iron Cobalt Nickel Copper Zinc Yttrium Zirconium Niobium Molybdenum Technetium Ruthenium Rhodium Palladium Silver Cadmium Hafnium Tantalum Tungsten Rhenium Osmium Iridium Platinum Gold Mercury Rutherfordium Dubnium Seaborgium Bohrium Hassium Meitnerium Ununnilium Unununium Ununbium The 7 elements classified as "other metals" are located in groups 13, 14, and 15. While these elements are ductile and malleable, they are not the same as the transition elements. These elements, unlike the transition elements, do not exhibit variable oxidation states, and their valence electrons are only present in their outer shell. All of these elements are solid, have a relatively high density, and are opaque. They have oxidation numbers of +3, ±4, and -3. The "Other Metals" are: Aluminum Gallium Indium Tin Thallium Lead Bismuth Non-metals are the elements in groups 14-16 of the periodic table. Non-metals are not able to conduct electricity or heat very well. As opposed to metals, non-metallic elements are very brittle, and cannot be rolled into wires or pounded into sheets. The non-metals exist in two of the three states of matter at room temperature: gases (such as oxygen) and solids (such as carbon). The non-metals have no metallic luster, and do not reflect light. They have oxidation numbers of ±4, -3, and -2. The Non-Metal elements are: Hydrogen Carbon Nitrogen Oxygen Phosphorus Sulfur Selenium The halogens are five non-metallic elements found in group 17 of the periodic table. The term "halogen" means "salt-former" and compounds containing halogens are called "salts". All halogens have 7 electrons in their outer shells, giving them an oxidation number of -1. The halogens exist, at room temperature, in all three states of matter: Solid- Iodine, Astatine Liquid- Bromine Gas- Fluorine, Chlorine The Halogens are: Fluorine Chlorine Bromine Iodine Astatine The six noble gases are found in group 18 of the periodic table. These elements were considered to be inert gases until the 1960's, because their oxidation number of 0 prevents the noble gases from forming compounds readily. All noble gases have the maximum number of electrons possible in their outer shell (2 for Helium, 8 for all others), making them stable. Helium Neon Argon Krypton Xenon Radon

Periodic Table
Dmitri Mendeleev devised the Periodic Table, and it was first published in 1869. The 
table is divided into eight columns called groups and rows called periods. The groups 
are numbered from 1 to 8, and these numbers refer to the number of electrons in the 
outermost shell of each element. Each outer electron shell can hold a fixed number of 
electrons. Group 1, which is very reactive, has 1 electron. Group 7 has seven electrons and 
is also very reactive. Group 8 has eight electrons and the elements do not react readily, if at 
all. Each period is also numbered and tells you how many electron shells there are in each 
row. 
The electronic configuration of an element is written by the number of electrons in 
each shell, e.g. 2.8.3. The configuration tells you that the element is in Group 3 from 
its outermost shell with 3 electrons and that it is in the third row of the Periodic Table 
because there are 3 shells of electrons. This identifies the element as aluminium.
The name and atomic number of an atom of the first 20 elements are listed at the right.
1 
complete the table by identifying the group, row and element for each electronic 
configuration.
In an electrically balanced atom, the number of electrons must equal the number of protons in the nucleus. The 
number of protons in the atom is equal to its atomic number. The higher the atomic number, the further it is 
down the Periodic Table.
2 
given the atomic number, write the electron configuration of each element; e.g. atomic number 16, electron 
configuration 2.8.6.
Protons are found in the nucleus and are electrically positive. Neutrons also are found in the nucleus but have 
no electrical charge. Protons and neutrons give the element its mass number. Electrons are found in ‘shells’ 
around the nucleus. The first shell can have only 2 electrons, while the second, third and fourth shells will fill up

Substances that are not mixtures are called pure substances. Pure substances are either elements

          Compounds are pure substances formed from two or more different elements

                                                   Periodic table - battleships

Teaching notes

This activity works just like the traditional game of battleships. It is played
in pairs and they need a copy of the periodic table.

Each student needs a grid to mark their own battleships on and one to
mark their turns on. They then add battleships to their grids (they should
all be simple rectangles and can be placed horizontally or vertically on the
grid).

They could add the symbols for the elements to each square that their
battleships cover.

They should take it in turns to choose a square by reading out the
coordinates and name of the element occupying that square in the
periodic table. If they get a hit they get another go. When one of their
battleships has been hit the student should tell their opponent what type
of vessel they have hit.

The first person to sink their opponents’ battleships wins, (or set a time
limit and the winner is the person with the most ‘hits’).

searchText: ﻿THE PERIODIC TABLE INTRODUCTION The periodic table was first published by Mendeleev in 1869. The modern form of the table is the one you are familiar with. The Periodic Table places the elements in order of Atomic Number, in Groups of similar chemical properties. You need to know the names and symbols of the first 20 elements and a few more. EXERCISES 1. Place the following elements on the periodic table: (Use a black pen) METALS : Li, Be, Na, Mg, Al, K, Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Ag, Sn, Ba, Au, NON METALS : C, N, O, F, H, He, P, S , Cl, Br, I, Ne, Ar, Kr, METALLOIDS : Si, B 2. On the chart, colour in the three areas of metals, nonmetals and metalloids in different colours. 3. Using a completed periodic table, place the atomic number (number of protons) for each element on your sheet. Put it at the bottom of your periodic table regardless of where it is on your completed table. 4. At the top of each box, write the name of your element in small writing. 5. Number the groups across from 1 to 18. Label Group 1 – Alkali metals, Group 2 – Alkaline Earth metals, Gp 17 – Halogens, Gp 18 – Noble gases, Gps 3-12 – Transition metals. QUESTIONS 1. Which elements have symbols that do not begin with the element’s name? Can you find the origin of these names? HINT: The symbols are derived from Latin. 2. Some groups have special names. From your table, list the elements from the following groups :- Noble gases, Halogens, Alkali Metals. 3. A dark staircase – shaped line separates the metals form the nonmetals. For the first 80 elements, find the number of metals and nonmetals. Calculate the percentage of metals in the first 80 elements. 4. How many symbols can you make using your full name? (Use the lab’s periodic table also). Try to name all the symbols you find.

THE ATMOSPHERE 2

The Noble gases In 1904 Sir William Ramsay was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discover-
ing a new Group of elements, the Noble gases. This Group is now known to consist of helium (He), neon
(Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe) and radon (Rn). Radon was discovered by Fredrich Ernst Dorn
in 1898. These gases are all colourless, tasteless and very unreactive. They are unreactive because they
have full outer (valence) electron shells. In total, the Noble gases make up around 1% of the earth’s

Resource sheet – Atoms and elements
The periodic table (1)
Elements such as carbon, gold and copper have been known since ancient times. 
Hydrogen was discovered in 1766. By 1800, scientists had started sorting the elements 
into groups. At that time many elements had not yet been discovered. In 1869, a Russian 
scientist named Dimitri Mendeleev ordered the elements according to how heavy they 
were. He displayed this information in a chart and called it the periodic table.
Look at the periodic table on the inside front cover of this book. The periodic table 
contains more than 100 elements, but only 92 of them are found naturally on earth. 
The rest are man-made. Elements that have similar properties are grouped together in 
columns in the table. For example, helium (He) has similar properties to neon (Ne) – both 
are gases that do not react – so they are grouped together.
The elements grouped on the left-hand side of the periodic table are metals.  
The non-metals are grouped on the right-hand side.
Each element has a chemical symbol. Some symbols have one letter, while others have 
two or three. For example, C is the symbol for carbon. Chlorine, which was discovered 
after carbon, has the symbol Cl. Some symbols come from the element’s Latin name. The 
symbol for iron is Fe, which comes from its Latin name, Ferrum.

THE PERIODIC TABLE

Lavoisier took the first step in classifying elements in 1789. He divided

the twenty-five or thirty elements known to him into metals and non pe genoale Gane cases
metals. In 1829 Johann Dobereiner noticed that where groups of three oF increasing atomic number,
similar elements (triads) occurred, the relative atomic mass of the .
middle element came approximately between those of the other two. However, for many elements the
idea did not work. In 1864 John Newlands found that if the elements known to science at the time were
arranged in order of increasing relative atomic masses, a pattern emerged. Starting at any element, every
eighth element was ‘a kind of repetition of the first’. Because of the similarity of this pattern to the
musical scale, he called it the law of octaves. This ‘law’ is not very reliable,

1 Explain the difference between atomic mass and atomic number.

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeléev (or Mendeléeff) made a breakthrough. He arranged the elements in order of
increasing relative atomic masses in a similar way to Newlands but, in order to obtain a better repetition,
he left gaps for elements which he assumed must exist but had not yet been discovered. He found that
many properties then followed a repeating pattern, or periodic variation.

Not only did Mendeléev have to leave gaps for undiscovered elements, he also had to correct some
relative atomic masses that had been determined erroneously to make the elements fit into the right
groups, Mendeléev predicted the existences of 21 missing elements including ‘eka-silicon’ which is now
named germanium. His predicted chemical and physical properties were very close to those actually
found when germanium was discovered.

The Periodic Table we now use lists the elements in order
of atomic number (not atomic mass). Figure 1 shows an
outline of the Periodic Table. There are just over 90
naturally occurring elements.

© A brief history
In 1829 scientists knew about 40 elements. German scientist Johann Dobereiner noticed that lithium,
sodium and potassium had very similar properties. Calcium, strontium and barium were also similar to
each other. Chlorine, bromine and iodine formed another triad. In 1864, English scientist John Newlands
replaced the triads with a law of octaves, which was based on the atomic weights of 60 known elements as
well as their properties. Dmitri Mendeleev, from Russia, refined the periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for
some elements which had not been discovered. Mendeleev predicted the properties of some of those
missing elements quite accurately. However, there were some inconsistencies; certain elements were too
heavy for their position in the periodic table. Henry Mosely (England, 1914) resolved these problems, when
he based the order of the elements on their atomic number rather than their weight. Today we know 103
elements and they are all organised into the periodic table of elements.
