The graphs show various patterns with a description of what is occurring and an example.
Graph
Description

Increasing at a constant rate
Example: Imagine a dripping tap. A water droplet falls into a bucket at the rate of 1 drop every 3 seconds. Therefore, as the time increases, the water level increases at a constant rate.

Decreasing at a constant rate
Example: If you eat one chocolate every 5 minutes, then the number left in the packet will decrease at a constant rate.

Decreasing at a decreasing rate
Example: When spectators leave a stadium, there is a sudden decrease in numbers, then the remainder slowly trickle out (i.e. the numbers are decreasing, at a decreasing rate).

Increasing at an increasing rate
Example: Think about the descriptions of the COVID-19 case numbers in 2020 and 2021. Atoms in chemical compounds have a characteristic combining power or valency. This involves the
number of electrons in an incomplete outer shell and can be defined in several ways:

* It represents the charge on an ion

* It is equal to the number of electron pairs shared in a molecule

* It is the number of electrons transferred when forming an ion.

searchText:
Writing Ionic Formulae
An ionic solid is formed when positive ion and negative ion react to form
a compound. The positive ion and negative ion are attracted to each
other because they have opposite charges.

                     Rules for Writing Ionic Formulae

  1. Only positive and negative ions will combine.
     A positive sodium ion, Na+ will combine with a negative chloride
     ion, Cl-.
     A positive sodium ion, Na+ will not combine with a positive calcium
     ion, Ca2+.

  2. The overall charge of the formula is neutral.
     The formula for sodium chloride is NaCl. The positive charge on the
     sodium ion is balanced by the negative charge on the chloride ion
     so the formula is neutral.

  3. The number of each ion is written on the lower right hand
     side of the ion.
     The formula for calcium chloride is CaCl2. This shows that for each
     calcium ion, there are two chloride ions.

  4. Where only one ion is needed, it is not necessary to write
     the number.
     When one sodium ion combines with one chloride ion, the formula
     can be written as NaCl, not Na1Cl1.

  5. If more than one polyatomic ion is needed, the ion needs to
     be written in brackets.
     When a hydroxide ion, OH-, combines with an aluminium ion, Al3+,
     the hydroxide ion needs to be written in brackets. The formula for
     aluminium hydroxide is Al(OH)3.

Example 1: Sodium chloride
Write the charge on the sodium and chloride ions.

     Na         Cl

For each sodium ion, how many chloride ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for sodium chloride below.


Example 2: Calcium chloride
Write the charge on the calcium and chloride ions.
      Ca         Cl

For each calcium ion, how many chloride ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for calcium chloride below.
Example 3: Sodium oxide
Write the charge on the sodium and oxide ions.

     Na         O

For each oxide ion, how many sodium ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for sodium oxide below.


Example 4: Magnesium oxide
Write the charge on the magnesium and oxide ions.

In modern agriculture, the use of pesticides is necessary. Aerial spraying (‘crop dusting’) is used to cover large or 
inaccessible areas. However, not all of the chemicals sprayed reach their intended sites. It has been estimated that 
about 85% of pesticides delivered in this way can drift tens of kilometres from the point of delivery. 
Many agricultural operations can generate particulate matter into the 
atmosphere during hot, dry weather. Methane (CH4) gas is produced by 
many agricultural activities – the two major sources are rice production and 
ruminant livestock. In one day, a sheep can produce approximately 30 litres 
of methane and a dairy cow up to 200 litres.
People who live in rural areas are not exposed to the same pollutants as those 
who live in cities, but they have to contend with nuisance odours and other 
more toxic airborne pollution.

presence of Greenhouse gases. Methane is a Greenhouse gas, 
which means it contributes to the Greenhouse Effect.

would be around 30°C less than it is, and the daily temperature 
would fluctuate much more than it currently does. However, 
many people think that continued emissions of Greenhouse gases

Australian megafauna

The word ‘megafauna’ literally means ‘large animals’, but it usually refers to extinct animals that were much larger than 
their counterparts of today. Australian megafauna existed in large numbers until about 50 000 years ago, though dates 
for their extinction vary considerably. Two major theories exist for their extinction: climatic change and human 
intervention.
Remember to distinguish between extinct species that no longer exist and extant species that are still in existence.

Australia split from Gondwanaland about 40 mya and

searchText: The Carbon Cycle – extracting information from a text Instructions  Read the short text below;  Complete the tasks underneath. “Living things are mostly made up from a handful of elements. Carbon is one of the most important of these. Carbon is found in the bodies of animals and in plants. Plants get the carbon from the atmosphere in the form of carbon dioxide. They take this in through their leaves. It is formed into sugars in the plant by the process of photosynthesis. Some of the sugars are used to provide the plant with energy in the process of respiration, which releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. They convert some of the sugars to other carbohydrates, which form the structure of the plant. When the plants die, the structural carbohydrates are broken down by decomposers in the process of decomposition. This releases the carbon in the form of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Some plants don’t decompose when they die. They get trapped in underground or underwater without the oxygen that decomposers need to break them down. This has caused some of the plants that did this hundreds of millions of years ago to form fossil fuels like coal. Fossil fuels are being dug up and are burnt in power stations as a fuel. This releases carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere in a process called combustion. The carbon may have been trapped underground for millions of years. This started on a large scale during the industrial revolution and continues to increase year after year. Some plants get eaten by animals. The carbon from the plant in the form of sugars and starches are mostly broken down inside the body of the animal. When the animal carries out respiration, some of the carbon is released back into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Some of the carbon is trapped in the body of the animal as part of its tissues. Some of the carbon passes straight through the animals because it isn’t digested. This is part of the animal’s dung. This is broken down by decomposers. When the animal dies, the carbon that is trapped in the body of the animal is released into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide when decomposers break the body of the animal down. This jigsaw helps students engage with the carbon cycle. Students

students.

gives them some familiarity with the key parts and processes
involved.

Students can then use the jigsaw they have created to do individual
research on the carbon cycle. There is a worksheet that follows on
from the jigsaw activity (resource 19849, ‘Carbon cycle questions’).

The diagram can either be printed on paper each time it is used, for

card for multiple uses.

discussion.

searchText:
The Carbon Cycle
All living things are made of carbon.
Carbon is also a part of the ocean, air, and even rocks.
The Earth is a dynamic place, carbon does not stay still.
In the atmosphere, carbon is attached to some oxygen in a gas called
carbon dioxide.
Plants use carbon dioxide and sunlight to make their own food and
grow.
The carbon becomes part of the plant.
Plants that die and are buried may turn into fossil fuels made of
carbon like coal and oil over millions of years.
When humans burn fossil fuels, most of the carbon quickly enters
the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and traps heat in the
atmosphere.
Without it and other greenhouse gases, Earth would be a frozen
world.
Humans have burned so much fuel that there is about 30% more
carbon dioxide in the air today than there was about 150 years ago,
and Earth is becoming a warmer place.
Ice cores show us that there is now more carbon dioxide in the
atmosphere than there has been in the last 420,000 years.

Chapter 6                                     Sustainability
EXTRA WORKSHEET 4: Changing climate of
Antarctica
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                      VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


In 2009 it was reported by the U.S. Geological Survey that the ice sheets in
the southern part of the Antarctic Peninsula (Figure 1) were disappearing and
that the change in the amount of ice was significant. Since 1998
approximately 4000 square kilometres of ice has been lost from one area.
This area of ice lost is about one and a half times the size of the Australian
Capital Territory (ACT). This loss of ice is regarded as very strong evidence of
the effects of global warming on the planet.




Figure 1
This map identifies the main areas of Antarctica.


However, in the same year it was reported by the Australian Antarctic Division
that the ice is expanding in eastern Antarctica (see Figure 1) and parts of
eastern Antarctica are becoming cooler. Ice core drilling in the ice off
Australia's Davis Station in East Antarctica revealed that in 2008 the ice had a
maximum thickness of 1.89 metres. The ice had not been this deep for 10




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 years. Since the 1950s, when continuous record began, the average
thickness of the ice at Davis has been 1.67 metres.

Data collected do not provide any evidence of large scale melting of ice over
most of Antarctica. The loss of ice in the west over the last 30 years has been
more than offset by increases in the Ross Sea Region which is just one part
of eastern Antarctica.

Over the past 30 years the area of sea ice around Antarctica has expanded.
The changes in Antarctic sea ice are thought to be an outcome of
modifications in the path followed by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (see
Figure 2). Warm moist air is directed towards Antarctic causing the ice to melt
in the west and increased snow fall in the east.




Figure 2
When the Antarctic Circumpolar Current moves closer to Antarctica it carries warm moist air
towards the continent.




Effect on plants and animals
Flowering plants


             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 2
 Antarctica is home to only two species of flowering plant and both these grow
on the Peninsula. The range (area over which they are found) and abundance
(number of plants in an area) have both increased in the last few decades.

Krill

Krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that are a very important food source for
animals in the Antarctic. Krill numbers in Antarctica have declined by as much
as 80% since the 1970s. Krill feed on algae that live just under the surface of
sea ice. Where the amount of sea ice is decreasing, so too does suitable
habitat for krill.

Krill feed the fish of Antarctica and are the main food source for baleen
whales. In the years 1925 to 1975 baleen whales were hunted and their
numbers decimated. Without krill it will be difficult for baleen whale numbers
to recover to pre-hunting levels.

Penguins

With the shrinking sea ice in western Antarctica, the Adélie penguins
(Pygoscelis adeliae) have declined in numbers over the last 20 to 25 years. In
other parts of Antarctica the colonies are stable or increasing in numbers.
Adélie penguins feed only on krill. The penguins nest on land and parent birds
go out to the sea ice to find food for their chicks. A reduction in the amount of
sea ice not only reduces the Adélie penguins’ food supply, it also increases
the distance the parent birds have to travel to find food.

Some penguins are benefiting from the changes taking place in Antarctica.
Gentoo penguins (Pygoscelis papua) (Figure 1a) are nesting on the Antarctic
Peninsula. Studies of the bones and other remains found in penguin colonies
indicate that Gentoo penguins did not nest in this area before 1950. These
penguins feed on fish and squid as well as krill.

Chinstrap penguins (Pygoscelis antarctica) (Figure 1b) are also benefiting
from the changes. Where Adélie penguins are abandoning their nesting sites
Chinstrap penguins are taking their place. There is no evidence of Chinstap
penguins on the Antarctic Peninsula until about 50 years ago when the
average temperatures started to rise. Chinstrap penguins eat a wider variety
of food than the Adélie penguins and they also prefer open water.

Different types of water
In many parts of Australia, water is often in short supply. There are different types, or 
grades, of water, and not all of them are safe to drink. Drinking water can be used for 
anything but should not be wasted. Storm water is the water that runs off after a heavy 
rainfall. It is safe to drink if carefully stored. Grey water is not safe for drinking and cannot 
be stored for long, but can be used to water gardens. Black water is dangerous and 
smelly until after it has been treated.

Global climate change
Key terms
climate
the weather conditions at a particular place, averaged over a long period of time, based on the collection and analysis of large amounts of data
climate change
periodic change in the Earth’s climate
Coriolis effect
the influence of the Earth’s rotation on the direction of movement of air or water
solar radiation
radiant electromagnetic energy from the Sun
weather
the temperature, humidity, rainfall and wind on particular days in a particular place
wind
the sideways movement of air as a result of lower-density warm air rising through the atmosphere
Recall the four spheres that contribute to the global climate.


Draw a flow diagram to show how solar radiation interacts with the global spheres identified in question 1.

This is a diagram of air movement.

searchText: Global Systems An ecosystem , short for 'ecological system', includes all the living organisms ex isting together in a particular area. These plants and animals within an area interact with each other and with the non-living elements of the area, such as climate, water, soil and so on. An ecosystem can be very small, such as a puddle or an area under a large rock, or it can be vast, such as an ocean. A sustainable ecosystem is one that is diverse and supports all of the living things in that ecosystem. Biosphere is all of the ecosystems in the world added together. In this part of the term we will look at some of the different systems that work together in world and see how some of them are changing. Key words Word Meaning Ecosystem Sustainable ecosystem Biosphere Producers Plants that make food for an ecosystem by photosynthesis. Primary consumers (herbivores) Animals that eat plants . Secondary consumers (carnivores) Animals that eat primary consumer animals. Tertiary consumers (carnivores) Animals that each primary and secondary consumer animals.

Greenhouse gas from farm animals
Animals that chew cud, such as cattle and sheep, are called ruminants. A part of their 
intestines called the rumen, which is one of four stomachs, contains billions of bacteria 
and protozoa that help to break up grass into useful nutrients. This produces methane 
gas, which is a greenhouse gas, as a by-product. Greenhouse gas from farm animals 
accounts for about 10 per cent of Australia’s greenhouse gas emissions. CSIRO scientists 
are trying to find ways to reduce emissions of methane gas from cattle and sheep. They 
have three projects underway:
 
l study of gut microbes in ruminants
 
l measuring methane emissions from cattle
 
l  investigating how anti-microbial properties contained in different foods affect the 
microbes in the rumen.

Irrigation – Benefits and challenges
Australia is a dry continent. However, some parts of Australia, such as far north 
Queensland, sometimes receive very high rainfall. When this happens, the water flowing 
along rivers is collected in reservoirs and directed to dry areas. This water is used for 
crops in a process called irrigation. Irrigation means that instead of only growing grass 
and tough shrubs, farmers have enough water to grow citrus and other fruit trees,  
grass for dairy cattle, grapes, rice and vegetables. Although irrigation helps farmers  
to grow crops, it also creates some problems.

Plants and the carbon cycle

Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis. Some carbon is
returned to the atmosphere almost immediately through respiration. The remainder is used to build
leaves, wood and roots, and may be stored for hundreds of years either as the tree itself or in wood
products made from it, such as the frames of houses or furniture.

Plant litter (fallen leaves and twigs) and roots become part of the soil when decomposer organisms
break them down. As the litter is broken down, carbon is released into the atmosphere.

Bushfires, controlled burns or using firewood to heat homes rapidly releases stored carbon into the
atmosphere. Most of the carbon will be in the form of carbon dioxide. There may also be carbon
monoxide and methane, depending on the conditions of burning. Following burning, carbon may
also be added to the soil in the form of charcoal, which remains stable for many years.

Scientists may not have discovered a time machine yet, but they do have

searchText: Nitrogen Cycle An important process in ecosystems is the recycling of nitrogen through its living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components. The living components, or biota, of the ecosystem participate in the nitrogen cycle in a number of ways. If you look closely at the diagram, you will notice that we show the various ways in which nitrogen cycles through nature. Colour the arrows red (except K ) (1 mark) Approximately 78% of the air is composed of diatomic nitrogen. Nitrogen is essential to life because it is a key component of amino acids and nucleic acids. Even ATP, the basic energy currency of living things, contains nitrogen. Colour the air blue . (1 mark) Neither plants nor animals can obtain nitrogen directly from the atmosphere (A). Instead, they must depend on a process called nitrogen fixation (B). Key players in nitrogen fixation are legumes (C) and the symbiotic bacteria that are associated with their root nodules. Legumes include clover, peas, alfalfa and soy-beans. The bacteria associated with their root nodules are nitrogen-fixing bacteria (D). These bacteria convert nitrogen in the soil to ammonia (NH 3 ), which can be taken up by some plants. The bacteria and the plants are in a symbiotic relationship. Cyanobacteria are also nitrogen-fixing bacteria: they are prominent in aquatic ecosystems. Colour parts C and D in green. (1 mark) Nitrogen is fix ed into the soil through the actions of bacteria and, as we mentioned above, through bacteria that’s associated with root nodules of legumes. Both of these methods of fixing nitrogen lead to its incorporation into ammonia (NH 3 ) in the process known as ammonification (E). The soil is a major reservoir for ammonia and other nitrogen-containing compounds. After nitrogen ha s been fixed, other bacteria convert it into nitrate, in a process called nitrification (F). In the first step of nitrification, Nitrosomonas (G) convert ammonia to nitrite (NO 2 ), and in the second step, nitrite is converted to nitrate (NO 3 ), by Nitrobacter (H). The nitrate (NO 3 ) is then consumed by plants (I) as the diagram shows. Colour the nitrogen- fixing bacteria and the nitrogen containing compounds orange. (1 mark) However, not all plants consume nitrate: as we mention ed before, some plants are able to use the ammonia from the soil. In both cases, nitrogen enters the primary producers in the biotic community. The plants may then be consumed by animals (J). Herbivores are the primary consumers, and the nitrogen of the plants is used for the synthesis of key organic compounds such as amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. Colour a herbivore purple. (1 mark) The final aspect of the nitrogen cycle is the process of denitrification (K). This process is performed by a variety of microscopic bacteria, fungi and other organisms. Nitrates in the soil are broken down by these organisms and nitrogen is released into the atmosphere (A). This completes the nitrogen cycle. Colour the K arrow black . (1 mark) Questions: 1. Oxygen gas and ozone have very different properties. Oxygen is colourless, odourless and

Most ozone is found in the stratosphere, about 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface in a

In the mid-1980s it was discovered that pollution was making the ozone layer very thin near
the North and South Poles resulting in an ozone hole. The Earth’s natural protection was
being destroyed, which could increase the likelihood of people developing skin cancer.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 6 Sustainability extra worksheet 3: Polar bears and global warming Science Understanding Science as a Human Endeavour, Verbal/Linguistic Logical/Mathematical Polar bears are found in Greenland, the former Soviet Union, Canada and Alaska. They inhabit the shorelines of the Arctic continents and islands where ice forms each winter. It is from these platforms of ice that polar bears hunt for the seals and young walruses that are their main source of food. Figure 1 The range of polar bears – shown in green. The polar bear is classified as a vulnerable species with 8 of the 19 polar bear subpopulations in decline. Vulnerable species are species that are experiencing a rapid population decline and are in danger of becoming extinct if the drop in numbers continues. Large scale hunting of polar bears by European, Russian and American hunters and trappers from the 1600s right through to the mid-1970s caused international concern about the future of the polar bear. The polar bear population was estimated at 5000 to 10 000 bears in the 1950s and 1960s. In 1973 an international agreement to strictly regulate commercial hunting came into effect. In 2007 the bear population was estimated at 20 000 to 25 000. Effects of global warming The International Union for Conservation of Nature now lists global warming as the most significant threat to polar bear populations. Malnutrition (inadequate diet) and starving to death are two possible effects of global warming on polar bears: • Sea ice is melting earlier in the year. Since polar bears hunt off the sea ice their feeding season is shorter. This means that the bears may not build up sufficient fat reserves to enable them to survive through summer and early autumn when food is in short supply. • With less sea ice the bears must swim further to capture their food. This increases the rate at which their fat reserves are used up. • Poor nutrition leads to fewer cubs being born, lower birth weight and an increased death rate for the cubs. Global warming may also affect the ability of pregnant female bears to build suitable dens in which to give birth to their cubs and tend their cubs for the first weeks of their lives. Matter of dispute Not all researchers have reached the same conclusions about the status of polar bear populations. In a report presented to the United States Senate in 2007, some scientists challenged the computer modelling of the effect of global warming on polar bear populations. Points raised include: 1 Of the 13 populations of polar bears in Canada, 11 are stable or increasing in numbers. 2 In the last 10 000 years, polar bears survived several periods where there was a much warmer climate than there is today. 3 There are a lot more polar bears now than there were 30 years ago. For example, in the Davis Strait area there is a population of 2100 now compared to 850 in the mid-1980s. Counter arguments put forward by other scientists who do believe that polar bear populations are under threat include: 1 The numbers of bears are increasing because of the controls on hunting both of the polar bear and controls on the hunting of the bears’ food supply – the harp seal. 2 In the area of Western Hudson Bay in north-eastern Canada the population of bears has shrunk by 22% over the last ten years – from 1194 animals in 1987 to 935 in 2004. 3 The population of bears may be increasing in two areas of Canada, but two others are definitely in decline. For the other 15 areas, proposals about the status of the populations cannot be made using the statistics available. Therefore the status for the polar bear population as a whole is unknown. Table 1 on the following page was presented to a meeting of the Polar Bear Specialist Group (PBSG) in Copenhagen (Norway) in 2009. It was updated in March 2010. East Greenland Unknown Insufficient data Foxe Basin 2197 (1994) 2300 (2004) Insufficient data New survey is ongoing. Australia is a land of weather extremes. The Southern Oscillation is one cause and it gives rise to
the El Nifio and La Niiia effects.

The Southern Oscillation is a sequence of changes to the way the atmosphere and water circulate
across the Pacific Ocean and Indonesian islands. In most years, a cold current flows northwards
along the coast of South America, then westwards along the equator, where it is warmed by the
Sun. This ‘normal’ situation is shown in Figure 7.4.1. The result is a difference of 3°C to 8°C
between the cooler eastern Pacific and the warmer western Pacific.

Figure 7.4.1 In normal conditions where there is no El Nifo or La Nifa, the trade winds
blow strongly from the eastern Pacific Ocean to the west. This brings average rainfall to
northern Australia.

EI Nifio is one extreme of the Southern Oscillation and is probably one of the most important
influences on the climate in Australia, particularly in Queensland and much of New South Wales.
In El Nifio years, there may be little or no difference in temperature between the western and
eastern Pacific. With little temperature difference, there is also little pressure difference. The trade
winds that normally blow strongly from South America weaken and the winds carrying a lot of
moisture do not reach Australia. Cool air descends over Australia bringing little rainfall. During an
EI Nifio event, large areas of Australia may experience drought.

The opposite of El Nifio is La Nifia. During a La Nifia, the central and eastern Pacific Ocean

becomes much cooler than normal. The trade winds blow more strongly than usual and Australia

experiences more cloud and wetter-than-normal conditions, especially in the north. When La Nifia
takes over, Australia often experiences floods.

Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Terrarium biosphere
The biosphere comprises all living things on Earth including animals, plants, fungi and microorganisms. 
The organisms of the biosphere would not be able survive without the interactions that are made between the biosphere, the lithosphere (the Earth’s mantle and crust), the hydrosphere (all water on Earth) and the atmosphere (layer of gases surrounding Earth). Through these interactions, matter that is critical to life such as carbon, water, nitrogen, and other nutrients can be exchanged, used and cycled by different organisms for survival.
Build a terrarium
Aim
To build your own terrarium to examine how matter (such as carbon) is cycled through the Earth’s spheres. You will also investigate what conditions can affect the cycling of nutrients. 
Materials
A clean, clear glass jar with a lid (e.g. a mason jar, 500 mL to 1 L in size)
Potting mix or soil
Pebbles 
Charcoal mix or fragments
A selection of small plants (e.g. fittonia, ferns, peperomia)
Long tweezers
Moss or algae 
100 mL of water from a nearby pond or outdoor water source 
Distilled water
Scissors
Label
Sticky tape
Method
Place the pebbles/gravel at the base of the jar. This bottom layer should be roughly 2–3 cm in height (this will vary depending on the size of the jar).
Add potting mix or soil to the jar until it is approximately one-third full of soil. 
Sprinkle some charcoal mix or fragments on top of the soil layer. 
Carefully place a selection of plants in the soil so their roots are submerged into the soil. You might like to do this with tweezers. Do not overcrowd the jar with plants. 
Cover the exposed soil surrounding the plants with a layer of moss or algae. 
Add 50 mL (100 mL if you have a larger jar) of the pond water to the jar. Then add distilled water so that the plants are given a good watering but are not completely submerged in water. (You might want to ask your teacher for guidance on this.)
Seal the jar with the lid, label it with your name and place the terrarium near a window in the classroom. Monitor the jar over the next few weeks. 
Monitoring your terrarium
The organisms in your terrarium will take some time to adapt to their new environment. If your plants are wilting, open the jar and spray the plants with water, and then reseal it.
Over the next two to three weeks, monitor your terrarium to observe any changes to the environment (e.g. condensation, size of the plants, growth of any new species). Fill in your observations in the table below. 

Observations

The lithosphere

The biosphere

The hydrosphere
Throughout the course of your observations, you might have noticed a build-up of water droplets along the sides and top of the terrarium. How does this occur and why is it important for the life that exists in your biosphere?


The atmosphere

Make predictions about your terrarium

Polluted water is water that is not fit for the purpose for which it is intended. Pollutants in water can include toxic 
chemicals and pathogens. When we refer to ‘water pollution’, we tend to concentrate on contamination that has been 
caused by human activity. 
The manufacturing industry is responsible for a major part of water 
pollution. Many factories discharge polluted water (effluent) into rivers, 
lakes or oceans. Although there are statutory limits on the amounts of 
pollutants that can be in this waste water, total volumes can be huge and 
can severely degrade water quality. Industrial pollutants that enter water 
supplies include heavy metals (e.g. mercury), organic solvents and oils. 
1

Describe the type of pollution it generates and the possible impact  
of this pollution.
2 The building industry contributes surface run-off, such as sediment from 
building sites. Name another aspect of the building industry that contributes 
to water pollution. Describe the possible impact of this pollution.
Generating large quantities of electricity always impacts on the environment. Power stations can burn fossil fuels 
(coal, oil or natural gas), use nuclear power or utilise moving water or wind. When coal is burned, it forms sulfur 
dioxide (SO2) which is a major contributor to acid rain. When acid rain falls it enters bodies of water, causing 
them to become too acidic for aquatic life. Both coal-fired power stations and nuclear power stations require large 
amounts of water for cooling. The hot water discharged into rivers or oceans can cause thermal pollution.
3 Discuss the possible consequences of thermal pollution in a body of water.

Location

50
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Coral reefs
Objectives 
● To recognise the significance of coral reefs
● To learn about the locations and types of coral 
reefs
● To understand the use and abuse of coral reefs
● To appreciate the need for coral reefs to be 
sustainable
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that the oceans contain 
a huge variety of life, which is important for human 
consumption, recreation and tourism, and essential 
to preserving ecosystems.
Background 
Coral reefs are very complex and fragile ecosystems 
that exist in the oceans. Their ecological significance 
is often compared with that of tropical rainforests 
on the land because of the diversity of species 
found within them. Coral reefs require warm, clear 
water less than 60 metres deep. Their future is 
threatened by fishing, tourism, oil spills, pollution, 
agricultural chemical run-off, silt and sewage. 
Climate change also poses a threat to the 
sustainability of coral reefs.
Starter activity
Ask students to list the kinds of creatures they 
associate with the ocean, and specifically with coral 
reefs. Encourage students to share any experiences 
they have with coral reefs. You could use a mapping 
application such as Google Earth to view coral reefs.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘What are coral reefs?’ introduces 
students to the structure of reefs and the kinds of 
animals that live there. Discuss the meaning of the 
terms in bold. Students could use the Internet to 
help them complete the last activity. To extend the 
activity, you could use the key terms on the sheet to 
start a class pictorial coral reef glossary.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Types of reefs’, students 
complete cloze exercises to explore the three main 
types of reefs, and the underlying structure and 
examples of each type. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Where are coral reefs?’ provides 
an opportunity for students to practise their mapping 
skills. Students will need an atlas or Internet access, 
and a blank world map, the completed Activity sheet, 
‘Types of reefs’, to complete this activity. A map is 
provided on the CD-ROM in the Artwork > Unit 9 
folder. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Life on a coral reef’, provides an 
opportunity for students to investigate the different 
kinds of marine creatures that live around coral reefs. 
Students will need to use the Internet to label marine 
creatures shown in the illustration, then draw and label 
a further list of marine creatures. You could challenge 
students to find the most unusual coral reef creature 
they can to add to the illustration.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Protecting reefs’, students 
explore threats to the reef, and efforts to protect and 
restore reefs. Explain that carbon dioxide from power 
stations and motor vehicles causes warming of the 
atmosphere, which in turn threatens coral reef habitats 
which take thousands of years to form. 
Emphasise sustainability when students complete 
the sentences on the Activity sheet, ‘What can be done 
to ensure that coral reefs are sustainable?’ Discuss the 
idea that all parts of the environment are connected, 
and that people can’t protect an area like a coral reef 
without considering what happens to the water they 
use and the rubbish they generate in their own homes. 
The Resource sheet, ‘How are coral reefs used?’,  
informs students about the ways coral reefs are used 
today, and the increasing number of visitors to coral 
reefs. Encourage them to think of other ways that 
people use coral reefs. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘How can 
people help to save the reefs?’ They may find it useful to 
refer to the Resource sheet, ‘How are coral reefs used?’ 
Encourage them to use the space at the bottom of the 
sheet to list other ways different people can help to 
save coral reefs.
extension activity
Have students work in small groups to create a pictorial 
glossary of marine life around coral reefs. They could 
focus on the creatures in a specific marine park, such as 
the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park or Ningaloo Marine 
Park. To extend the activity, have them identify food 
chains or webs within the marine parks.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
44
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Water
Objectives 
● To recognise that water is essential for survival
● To understand how people, plants and animals 
rely on water
● To learn about the need to conserve water 
to ensure sustainability of food supplies and 
communities
Prior knowledge
Students have knowledge of some of the uses of 
water and have some understanding of droughts 
and floods.
Background 
Water is essential for life. All the ecosystems on 
land and within oceans and seas rely on it. Access 
to water is also critical for the production of food 
and industrial products. This is why some rivers 
have been dammed to provide a continual supply. 
Due to people’s need for water, the welfare of the 
environment and habitats for wildlife have at times 
been overlooked.
In recent years, long-term droughts have 
been followed by major floods, such as those in 
Queensland and Victoria in 2011. These floods 
replenish rivers, dams and groundwater as well 
as adding fertile silt to flood plains. However, 
the human cost is enormous through loss of life, 
livelihood, homes and possessions, as well as the 
effect on the Australian economy.
The Murray-Darling Basin is important to the  
3 million people who live in and around the basin 
and depend on the water it provides. The Murray-
Darling Basin is also extremely important to the 
rest of Australia, as one-third of the food supply is 
produced in the region. This contributes $9 billion 
to Australia’s economy through food supply and 
exports such as cotton and rice. 
Starter activity
Brainstorm with the class a list of issues related to 
water; for example, effects of droughts and floods, 
pollution of waterways, global problems such as lack of 
drinking water, local water restrictions, water recycling. 
Guide students to realise that water management is an 
extremely important issue, both now and in terms of 
sustainability for the future.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Fact file – water’, with the 
students. Students will unjumble words to complete the 
water facts. Ask the students to identify any facts they 
found surprising, and discuss why. 
Provide the Resource sheet, ‘Case study – Murray-
Darling Basin’. Discuss what the map shows. You could 
have students identify the region on a complete map of 
Australia to assist their understanding of its size. Review 
the key features of maps with the class, and explain the 
meaning of tributary, source and mouth in the context of 
a river system.
Have the students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Using 
the Murray-Darling Basin map’. They will need to refer to 
the Resource sheet, ‘Case study – Murray-Darling Basin’. 
Provide the Resource sheet,  ‘What can be done to 
make the Murray-Darling Basin sustainable?’ and read 
it with the students. Discuss the role of government in 
water management, and the importance of community 
concerns. Introduce the concept of irrigation and give 
examples like Mildura which can exist in an extremely 
dry area and have a thriving agricultural industry 
because of water from the Murray River.
Ask students to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Water 
supply issues’. You could have them use the Internet 
to conduct further research into the issues raised. 
Encourage them to think about these issues and what 
they can do to help make water sustainable. 
extension activity 
●  Collate the water questions students composed on 
the Activity sheet, ‘Water supply issues’. Have them 
work in small groups to answer the questions. 
●  Students could use the Internet to investigate the 
use of water for growing crops like cotton and rice. 
Discuss whether this use of water can be justified. 
Students should identify which crops in Australia 
are sustainable and give reasons. Encourage them 
to consider the issue of cost in terms of equipment, 
infrastructure and time involved in changing 
agricultural products.

Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Geothermal energy
Objectives 
● To learn about geothermal energy
● To understand the difference between  
natural geothermal energy and  
engineered geothermal energy
● To appreciate the advantages and difficulties 
associated with geothermal energy
Prior knowledge
Students should understand that the earth has 
layers and the earth’s core is molten. They  
should be aware that erupting volcanoes spew  
out hot lava. 
Background
In the past, geothermal energy was only harnessed 
in volcanic regions where naturally occurring hot 
water and steam came to the surface. For centuries 
Japan and New Zealand have used this resource for 
cooking. More recently it has been used to  generate 
electricity and pipe steam to heat houses, and for 
tourism attractions.
Engineered thermal energy is a renewable 
resource capable of producing base load (24 hours 
per day) energy. It does not release carbon dioxide 
into the atmosphere. No waste is produced during 
the process. The environmental impact is minimal – 
drill holes, pipelines and power plants. 
Potentially, geothermal energy could produce 
enough energy to supply Australia for a very long 
time. However, the necessary infrastructure of 
powerlines is not currently in place and would be 
very expensive. Small earthquakes can occur as a 
result of the drilling – one plant in Switzerland had 
to be shut down after earthquakes caused damage 
to buildings. Obtaining the information needed to 
map suitable sites is also very expensive.
Starter activity
Before class, conduct an Internet image search or 
YouTube search for ‘geothermal mud pools’. Select 
images and /or movies to show the class. Display 
them, and ask students to explain what that think 
is happening. Some students may have visited the 
mud pools in Rotorua, New Zealand. 
Tell the students that this is an example of heat and 
steam coming from within the earth’s surface. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘What is geothermal power?’, 
with the students. Ensure the students are familiar with 
the meaning of each word shown in bold. Discuss the 
difference between natural geothermal energy and 
engineered geothermal energy. To extend the activity, 
you could watch the Internet video about Paralana 
geothermal plant (Internet search terms: ‘Paralana 
geothermal plant’).
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Hot rocks’. 
Review the concept of the layers of the earth. You could 
use the analogy of an egg: the earth’s crust is like the 
shell of the egg, the mantle is like the egg white and 
the core is like the egg yolk. Allow time for students to 
practise and revise their verbal explanations for how 
geothermal power is generated. This particular diagram 
shows a binary cycle geothermal power plant – further 
information about how it works is readily available on 
the Internet. 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages’, with the students. Discuss the items in 
the lists and ensure students understand why each one 
is either an advantage or a disadvantage. You could 
work with the class to compare these advantages and 
disadvantages to those of another type of energy 
source, such as coal, wave or solar. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Hot 
rock energy production’. They may need to refer to 
the Resource sheets, ‘What is geothermal power?’ 
and ‘Advantages and disadvantages’. After they have 
completed the activity, students could work in small 
groups to discuss their ideas for the second section. 
extension idea
●  Have the students cut out or draw the diagram 
from the Activity sheet, ‘Hot rocks’. Challenge them 
to label the diagram to explain what is happening 
and how it works. Students may like to work in 
pairs. The diagram shows a binary cycle geothermal 
power plant. Further information about the use and 
function of these power plants is readily available on 
the Internet.

global Patterns In fIshIng 3
Commercial whaling 
Commercial whaling – the harvesting of whales, mostly for meat – is carried out by a number of countries. 
Australia is one of many nations opposed to commercial whaling. Commercial whaling is regulated by the 
International Whaling Commission (IWC). The IWC is responsible for protecting whales around the world. 
Whaling has been practised for centuries in some parts of the world. It is considered an integral part of 
some traditional cultures in places such as Greenland and Alaska. Today, whaling is a highly controversial 
practice. Many countries are against it on environmental grounds – a number of whale species are 
threatened and their populations continue to decline. 
Conservation groups and other non-government organisations protest at many levels about commercial 
whaling – from political lobbying to physically preventing whaling activities at sea.
As the number of whales has decreased over the years, the whaling industry has changed to new locations, 
new target species and new harvesting techniques.
The move by many nations to protect the whales in their waters is relatively recent. The benefits of 
protection are both environmental and economic – many argue that whale-watching tourism is more 
profitable than commercial whaling. Even though the IWC exists to regulate whaling and protect whales, it 
is limited as a governing body. Nations do not have to belong to it, and therefore are not bound by its 
rulings on the industry – such as the introduction of quotas.
Commercial whaling – research

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
27
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Indigenous art 
Indigenous art styles
 
●Rock art varied throughout Australia as Dreaming stories and food supplies differed 
from place to place. Some sites displayed the lives of the people, with drawings 
showing fish, animals, weapons and animal tracks as well as mythical beings. The 
heritage-listed Dampier Archipelago in Western Australia has many collections of 
rock art, as does Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory.
 
●Rock engravings or petroglyphs (petro meaning ‘rock’ and glyph meaning ‘symbol’) 
were carved into large flat sandstones by rubbing designs into them with a hard 
stone. The Olary region of South Australia has excellent examples – designs there 
include fish and crocodile heads.
 
●Rock paintings were made in shelters like caves. People used ochre to make red, 
yellow kaolin to make white, and charcoal to make black. 
 
●Hand painting was very common, especially in the southern parts of Australia. 
Artists placed one hand on the surface of a cave or rock and blew ochre over 
it, leaving the outline. Examples of this can be seen in the Cave of Hands in the 
northern Grampians.
 
●In Arnhem Land, some paintings show the internal organs of humans and animals. 
This style is known as X-ray art.
 
●Dot painting began in the Central and Western desert. Artists used ochre, sand, 
blood, charcoal, small rocks, flowers, feathers and seeds to create the art on ground 
for ceremonial events. The paintings showed symbols of the landscape as well as 
Dreaming stories. The meanings of the symbols varied according to the tribe and the 
region where they were painted. In 1972, the community at Papunya, 240 kilometres 
north-west of Alice Springs, transferred the method to modern canvas using acrylic 
paints. Sacred objects were not allowed to be shown on modern paintings. 
 
●For ceremonial occasions, Indigenous people painted their faces, arms and upper 
bodies with symbols, often relating to totems.

The Australian climate
There are a variety of different climates within Australia. These different climates are due 
to factors such as latitude (how close you are to the equator), altitude (height above sea 
level) and distance from the coast. Indigenous Australians closely observe the weather as it 
is critical to their food supply, their shelter and their links to the land. Europeans introduced 
their ideas of four distinct seasons, but most parts of Australia do not fit this classification

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
55
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Indigenous tourism
Objectives
l To appreciate the importance of tourism for 
Indigenous people
l To understand the role of Indigenous people in 
Australian tourism
l To identify reasons that visitors take part in 
Indigenous tourism  
Prior knowledge
Students should understand that people  
visit places away from home for a variety  
of reasons.
Background
Indigenous tourists can be domestic – from 
Australia – or international. Indigenous tourists 
visit at least one Indigenous cultural site, art gallery,  
museum or Indigenous community.
The Australian Tourism Authority actively 
encourages and promotes Indigenous tourism, 
as do state government departments. Indigenous 
tourism allows overseas and Australian visitors to 
appreciate Australian Indigenous culture, past and 
present, as well as places of cultural significance. 
Indigenous tourism is run by Indigenous people 
or part-owned by Indigenous people. Alternatively, 
Indigenous people may be employed as guides and 
in other capacities. Indigenous tours have become 
more popular as people are becoming aware of the 
rich heritage and culture of Indigenous Australians. 
Their history of sustainable use of resources has also 
created interest. Indigenous tour operators provide 
a range of nature-based tourism events, cultural 
heritage and education programs on topics such 
as bush tucker, medicines, art and craft, as well as 
performances.
Starter activity
Create a class list of students’ tourism experiences. 
Classify them into categories, such as visiting family 
and friends, cultural, ecotourism, sport, relaxation  
and retail. Explain that Indigenous tourism is 
increasingly important in Australia, especially for 
Indigenous Australians employed in tourism who can 
showcase their culture and history. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism (1)’, with 
the class. This provides examples of the great variety of 
activities and cultural experiences available. Discuss the 
different types of attractions tourists want to visit, and 
which attractions the students would most like to visit. 
Then have students complete the writing frame on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism (2)’. 
 
To complete the mapping exercise on the Activity 
sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism – locations’, students will 
need the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism (1)’, and an 
atlas or mapping application. Some students may need 
assistance with developing a key for the different kinds 
of attractions.  
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous 
tourism visitors’. Discuss what the graph shows – 
numbers of International and domestic tourism 
visitors – and how to read the data presented. Explain 
that while these visitors do not exclusively look for 
Indigenous experiences, they include at least one 
in their plans. Note that the decreasing numbers of 
tourists largely reflects the effects of the global financial 
crisis and the increasing value of the Australian dollar. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Being a responsible 
tourist’, with the class, which provides tips about being 
respectful at Indigenous tourism attractions. Students 
will use this information to help them explain why it is 
important for tourists to respect Indigenous culture.  
extension ideas
Have students choose a region such as the Kimberley, 
Uluru or Kadadu, and research a journey through the 
region with an Indigenous guide. They could create an 
itinerary and a visual diary to record the things they 
would expect to see.

Being a responsible tourist
The Australian government actively promotes the involvement of Indigenous people in 
tourism as it is a way for them to display their heritage and earn an income. It is important 
that Indigenous culture, beliefs and sites are treated with respect. Here are some ways to be 
a responsible tourist.
You may need a permit to enter many 
Indigenous communities and lands.
Always respect people’s privacy.
Some places of cultural importance may not always 
be open to visitors – respect these closures.
Some places may only be 
visited by men or by women.
Be aware that English may be 
a second language for many 
Indigenous people.
Always ask permission to 
photograph Indigenous people, 
cultural activities and places.
Ensure you buy a souvenir from Indigenous 
people as this helps them to support their families.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
35
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
How did Indigenous people live? (1)
 
●Indigenous Australians were hunter-gatherers who moved according to the 
availability of food. This way, their food supply was sustainable. The types of food 
available depended on whether they lived inland, near rivers or on the coast. The 
men hunted kangaroos, wallabies, echidnas and possums as well as snakes, lizards 
and birds such as ducks, especially along the Murray River. Spears and boomerangs 
made from local trees were used to catch and kill. Fish and eels were caught in traps 
in some areas, such as south-west Victoria.
 
●Fire was used to drive animals out and to ‘clean up’ the land. Fire was also used to 
keep travel corridors open and to encourage the growth of food plants such as 
bracken, daisy yams and grasses so that these resources could be sustained from 
year to year.
 
●Women and young children collected berries, yams, 
seeds, eggs and insects. If they lived near the coast, they 
collected oysters and mussels too. Seeds were ground 
between stones and cooked as cakes.
 
●Indigenous people knew how to hunt and gather 
sustainably so their food supplies would last. For 
example, they did not hunt young kangaroos or take 
more berries than they needed. However, it is thought 
that their practice of using fire did change parts of the 
landscape.
 
●Indigenous people understood the seasons and how 
they affected the food that was available. Along the 
Murray River they caught wildfowl and freshwater 
crayfish in spring, or netted fish in summer. They knew 
how to get groundwater in the desert from springs, rock 
holes and soaks, and dug wells to find water. Water sources  
were regarded as sacred. It was essential for people to  
remember where they were.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
20
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Land management
Indigenous methods of finding food
Indigenous people traditionally led a nomadic life inland and a semi-nomadic life near 
the coast and rivers. They knew how to care for the land, and only took what they needed 
so that their land use was sustainable.
Men and women spent most of the day collecting food. Women dug up yams and 
other roots as well as collecting seeds. Women and children collected ants, honey ants and 
witchetty grubs and killed small animals with digging sticks. Men hunted in groups when 
catching kangaroos and emus, and hunted alone to catch small animals like possums, 
snakes and birds.
People along rivers and near the coast caught fish. There is a fish trap at Brewarrina in 
New South Wales that is 40 000 years old, and is still being used. Coastal tribes collected 
oysters, mussels and crabs, which are a good source of energy.
When hunting, people used fire to scare out animals so they could kill them. People 
also set fire to certain areas at particular times of year to encourage grass to grow. This 
helped to feed the animals and sustain their numbers, so that there were enough for 
people to hunt. Over time, fire has changed the environment by encouraging fire-resistant 
plants to grow.
If a person’s totem was a particular bird, animal or plant, they would not kill or eat that 
thing, as this was regarded as cannibalism.
Water was sourced from rivers and waterholes. When these dried up, tribes had to 
move in search of more water.
At times, tribes would meet to socialise through feasting, perform ceremonies and 
trade with each other. Often it was the harvesting of a particular food source that brought 
people together. For example, when Bogong moths migrated to the Snowy Mountains 
during summer, tribes from around the area would meet and feast on the roasted moths. 
The bunya nut festival in the Bunya Mountains, Queensland, is another example.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
38
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Sustainable fishing
Background
As the population of the world increases so does the 
demand for fish, especially in developing countries. 
Improved technology has made it easy to locate 
schools of fish, and led to improved fishing methods. 
Some of these methods, such as the use of cyanide, 
the blasting of reefs and bottom trawling cause 
great damage to the environment. Longline and 
purse-seine fishing result in large numbers of fish 
being caught, many as bycatch – fish that are not 
marketable. Many of the bycatch are dead when 
they are thrown back into the ocean. Overfishing 
has resulted in the significant reduction of many fish 
stocks, with some species such as southern bluefin 
tuna becoming critically endangered. Due to market 
demand, much illegal fishing occurs. 
Taking too many fish commercially means there 
is not enough food for marine animals such as 
seabirds, turtles and sharks. Marine parks have been 
established to help protect fish species and to allow 
stocks to replenish, but fisheries say this affects their 
income. Governments have introduced quotas to try 
to make fish stocks sustainable. 
Aquaculture has been used in many places 
around the world for prawns, oysters, mussels, 
barramundi and tuna to supplement the wild 
catch. However, aquaculture farms can cause other 
problems such as contamination from fish food and 
chemicals. 
Starter activity
Discuss the different reasons people have for fishing. 
Bring out the idea that some people fish for fun, some 
for money and other to get the food they need to 
survive. Work with the students to define key fishing 
terms such as wild catch, aquaculture, bycatch and 
overfishing. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Sustainable fishing’, with the 
students. Review the meaning of each term shown in 
bold. Ask students to share any experiences they have 
with fishing and discuss the types of fish they eat. 
 
Provide students with the Resource sheet, ‘Bluefin 
tuna – wild catch or farm?’ Students will need to refer 
to this Resource sheet to complete the questions on 
the Activity sheet, ‘Fishing for bluefin tuna’. Extend the 
activity by leading a discussion about the negative 
impacts of aquaculture, such as the reduction of wild 
stock and the large quantities of anchovies and sardines 
that must be sourced to feed the farmed fish. Ocean 
and coastal pollution also occurs from chemical use and 
dissolved and solid fish waste. 
Have the students read the Resource sheet, ‘Orange 
roughy – overfishing and conservation’. They will 
need to refer to this Resource sheet to complete the 
questions on the Activity sheet, ‘The orange roughy fish’. 
You could extend this activity by having students work 
in small groups to list arguments for and against the 
statement: Fishing for orange roughy should be banned. 
extension activity
●  Students could use the Internet to find more species 
of fish and other marine species that are threatened, 
and possible solutions to these problems. The 
websites of organisations such as the Australian 
Marine Conservation Society, World Wildlife Fund 
and Greenpeace will be useful. 
●  Students could investigate the number of marine 
parks in Australia, map their locations and annotate 
the map to show which marine creatures live there. 
Objectives 
● To learn about the increasing demand for 
fish that results from an increasing human 
population
● To understand the difference between wild 
fishing and aquaculture
● To learn that conservation is essential for the 
sustainability of fishing 
● To appreciate that while fishing is an important 
recreational activity for some people, other 
people rely on the food fishing provides in 
order to survive 
Prior knowledge
Students should know that many people enjoy 
fishing for recreation and that fish is eaten regularly.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
39
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Sustainable fishing
The health benefits of eating fish are well known and often promoted. People in many 
countries eat fish every day. Over 1 billion people throughout Asia depend on fish, 
including subsistence islanders in Papua New Guinea and people in the Philippines, who 
depend on fish for their animal protein. Many people are employed making and mending 
boats, nets and other equipment, as well as in fish processing.
In Australia, the fishing industry is number six on the 
list of the most valuable food-based primary industries. 
Almost 3.4 million Australians fish for recreation and 
contribute to the economy by buying fishing licences 
and fishing gear. Some Indigenous Australians fish for 
food, for cultural practices and to earn money. 
As the number of people in the world increases,  
so does the global demand for fish. This, combined  
with changes to methods of fishing, has resulted in 
overfishing. This means that more fish are being  
caught than the ocean can produce, so the  
overall number of fish is decreasing. 
Bycatch is also a significant problem 
– this is the term for the fish and other 
marine creatures that the fisheries catch 
in their nets, but do not want and cannot 
sell. Often these creatures die.
Bluefin tuna is highly valued for its 
flavour, especially when served raw. It 
is overfished in the Pacific Ocean, and 
in most other parts of the world. One 
bluefin tuna caught on a longline off the 
Japanese island of Hokkaido was sold for 
$396,000 in early 2011. That was a price  
of $12,000 per kilo! 
Resource sheet – Sustainable fishing
Purse-seining involves 
putting a long net around a 
group of fish, then closing 
the bottom of the net to 
capture them. 
Midwater trawling involves dragging a 
huge net behind a boat. It catches a large 
number of fish. The use of technology such as 
electronic fish-finders makes it easy to work 
out where the fish are. 
ISBN 978 1 92571 049 6

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
40
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Bluefin tuna – wild catch or farm?
Tuna is an extremely popular fish, particularly bluefin tuna, and stocks in the Pacific 
and Indian Oceans are decreasing due to overfishing. With wild catch fishing methods, 
fisheries can catch entire schools of tuna. 
 Southern bluefin tuna are prized as an eating fish, especially for the traditional Japanese 
food sashimi. These tuna live for up to 40 years, grow to two metres long and weighing 
up to 200 kilograms. Due to the high demand for tuna, there are strict quotas in place to 
protect the population. Any fisheries catching more than their quotas are breaking the 
law. Illegal tuna fishing still occurs because people are prepared to pay a great deal of 
money for them.  
Tuna farming at Port Lincoln in South Australia began in the early 1990s. By farming 
the tuna instead of catching them in the wild, the hope is that tuna populations can be 
sustained. However, farming can cause other problems such as contaminating the oceans 
with farm chemicals and the food fed to the fish. Controlling fish diseases is also more 
difficult.
The following information describes how southern bluefin tuna are farmed.
 
●The tuna are caught by purse seine net in the Great Australian Bight in January.
 
●They are transferred live to a towing cage.
 
●The cage is towed very slowly for about 20 days to near Port Lincoln.
 
●The tuna are swum into smaller cages and bred in captivity.
 
●They are fed six days per week, weather permitting.
 
●When there is a growth rate of 40%, usually in  late winter, they are harvested.
 
●They are processed and placed in boxes, frozen or with chill packs.
 
●The fish are then flown to Japan, South-East Asia and Europe.

Conserving the orange roughy
Orange roughy is a bright red fish with a large, bony head and big eyes. It lives in cold, 
deep waters in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, especially around seamounts 
which are volcanic mountains under the sea. 
This species may live beyond 150 years. It matures between 20 and 40 years of age and 
feeds on prawns, fish and squid. Very young fish are rarely caught by fisheries, but larger 
specimens can be caught well before they can reproduce at about 30 years of age. 
The New Zealand orange roughy fishery is the oldest and largest in the world. It was 
established in the late 1970s and production peaked at approximately 22 000 tonnes in the 
mid-1980s. That figure has now been reduced to about 8650 tonnes. 
In New Zealand, orange roughy fishing is managed under a quota system in a 
200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, in order to help keep stocks at a sustainable 
level. Measures are being taken to restrict where fish can be caught, and marine national 
parks established to provide a safe place for fish to grow and breed. Similar restrictions 
apply to orange roughy fishing in southern Australian waters.

Lesson V.
THE TASMANIAN BLACKS.
	
The Tasmanian blacks were not nearly so tall as the 
sailors of Tasman thought them to be. Indeed, they were 
shorter than the Australian blacks, and belonged to a 
different race, not unlike the negroes, having curly or 
frizzly hair, and a shiny, black skin.
	
Black people of the same kind are still to be found on 
islands of the Indian and Pacif ic Oceans, mostly hiding 
away in dark parts of the forests. The Tasmanian blacks 
were also very shy, and would not make friends with the 
whites.
	
After the white people went to settle in Tasmania they 
often tried to be friendly with the blacks. Governor Davey 
got a friend to draw a picture showing that the whites 
ought to be kind to the blacks, and the blacks ought not 
to kill the whites. This was printed, and copies of it were 
stuck on the trees for the blacks to see.
	
Yet still the f ighting went on. Tribes of blacks hiding 
in the bush would come out now and then, and kill some 
lonely settler; and then the whites would take their guns, 
and kill as many blacks as they could f ind. A long line 
of riflemen tried to drive all the blacks into a corner of 
the island, but only one was caught.
	
At last a settler named Robinson began to search for 
the blacks in a friendly way, and, after f ive years of 
very dangerous work in tracking them through the bush, 
he collected them together. Houses were built for them 
on South Bruni Island, and in other places, where they 
were kindly treated. Yet they all died off. The last black 
woman lived till 1876.

SANITARY CONDITION OF 
ADELAIDE.  
Prior to the introduction of 
a system of deep drainage, 
Adelaide was drained partly by 
an imperfect system of sewers 
laid down by the corporation, 
and discharging in the park 
lands, and partly by open 
street-channels, by which the 
drainage ultimately found its

sewers, but cesspits were 
chiefly used, and their 
contents buried in the park 
lands. With this condition 
of things, Adelaide has been 
described by one witness as 
having been a “city of stinks”, 
with its subsoil surcharged 
with sewage. In 1885 a system 
of deep drainage was completed. 
The city is now free from 
offensive odours, the subsoil 
is recovering, the street 
channels are used only for 
surface water, and the Torrens 
has been changed from a f ilthy 
sewer to a beautiful hike.

As early as 1854, underground 
sewers were laid down in 
the city of Sydney. These 
discharged directly into the 
harbour. Owing to complaints 
about the drainage and water 
supply and the pollution 
of the harbour, a board of 
inquiry was appointed in 
1875. As a result of their

commenced in 1880, and is now 
in course of construction. 
Main sewers have been laid

to the harbour, and to convey

portion of the city by a large

Bondi, where a strong current 
there prevailing carries away

Resource sheet – Symbols of Federation
A national flag competition
In January 1911, Prime Minister Edmund Barton held a competition to design a flag to represent 
the new Commonwealth of Australia. Five joint winners shared the prize, and the flag was flown 
for the first time on 3 September 1901 at the Exhibition Building in Melbourne. 
A National Flag
The national flag question is becoming a warm one … opinions 
rage through the press as to what the flag should contain to make it 
emblematic. 
Someone wants bars, out of compliments to the States, which shouldn’t 
be entertained … Someone wants a kangaroo, but though this is typical 
enough, it is hoped that the successful artist will not embrace it, as the 
’roo looks ratty … One thing that should go on the flag is the Southern 
cross, with six stars, and each star would stand for a State without further 
embellishment. The “Jack” in the corner would complete a true heraldic 
design — the flag of a nation in the Pacific, affiliated with one in the 
North Sea. For official purposes the field could be blue, not too light and 
not too dark …
Source: Clarence and Richmond Examiner (Grafton, NSW: 1889–1915) Sat 27 Apr 1901, Page 4
Source 2 (About the design that won the competition)
… a staled réchauffé of the British flag, with no artistic virtue, no 
national significance ... Minds move slowly: and Australia is still Britain’s 
little boy. What more natural than that he should accept his father’s  
cut-down garments, — lacking the power to protest, and only dimly 
realising his will. That bastard flag is a true symbol of the bastard state of 
Australian opinion.
Source: The Bulletin magazine, 28 September 1901
Source 1 (Before the competition winners were announced)
Definition
réchauffé: a dish of warmed-up food, left over from a previous meal

We’re all Australians Now
In 1915, Andrew Barton ‘Banjo’ Paterson wrote the fourteen verse poem, ‘We’re all Australians Now’, 
as an open letter to Australian troops. 
In this poem, ‘Sydney’ is the battleship HMAS Sydney. This ship was flying the Australian flag when 
it defeated the German warship SMS Emden. 
Here are Verses 6, 7 and 14. 
Our six-starred flag that used 
to fly
Half shyly to the breeze,
Unknown where older 
nations ply
Their trade on foreign seas.
Flies out to meet the 
morning blue
With Victory at the prow;
For that’s the flag the Sydney 
flew,
The wide seas know it now!
And with Australia’s flag 
shall fly
A spray of wattle bough,
To symbolise our unity,
We’re all Australians now.

Massacres 
Henry Mayrick and his brothers Alfred and Maurice were early settlers in the Western Port and 
Gippsland areas of Victoria. This source is part of a letter Henry wrote to his mother in April 1846. 
Definitions
wretches: victims, sufferers
unsparing perseverance:  
cruel persistence or determination
conceive: understand
penalty: price
familiarised: used to
participated: involved in 
remedy: change or fix
aloof: distant, detached
Source: H.H Mayrick, letters, 1840-1847, La Trobe Library,  
SLV H15789 – 15816
The blacks are very quiet here now, poor 
wretches, no wild beast of the forest was ever 
hunted down with such unsparing perseverance 
as they are; men, women and children are shot 
where ever they can be met with, some excuses 
might be found for shooting the men by those 
who are daily getting their cattle speared, but 
what they can urge in their excuse who shoot 
women and children I cannot conceive. I have 
protested against it at every station I have been 
in in Gipps [Gippsland] in the strongest language 
but these things are kept very secret as the 
penalty would be hanging … I remember the 
time when my blood would have run cold at 
the bare mention of these things but now I am 
become so familiarised with scenes of horror, 
from having murder made a topic of everyday 
conversation. I have heard tales told, and some 
things I have seen that would form as dark a page 
as ever you could read in the book of history  – 
but I thank God I have never participated in them 
– If I could remedy these things I would speak 
loudly though it cost me all I am worth in the 
world, but as I cannot I will keep aloof and know 
nothing and say nothing.

Resource sheet – The Stolen Generation
Walter’s story
February 1903
Dr Walter E Roth was the Northern Protector of Aborigines, based in Cardwell, north Queensland. 
He wrote to D Graham, a Protector in Townsville:
Source 1
Sir, I have the honour to inform you that my attention has been drawn 
to the following h-c children roaming about the blacks’ camps in the 
neighbourhood of Cardwell . . . it seems to me a great pity to see the 
lad “Walter Peter” loaf ing around the camp instead of learning a trade 
at the Industrial School. 
Source: Queensland State Archives Item ID336387, (A/58751) Correspondence, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
June 8, 1903 
Dr Roth writes to the Under Secretary, Department of Public Lands:
Source 2
I would accordingly suggest that (1) “Walter” be 
brought up under the Industrial Schools Act of 
1865 . . . being a “child born of an aboriginal or 
half-caste mother.
Source: Queensland State Archives Item ID336387, (A/58751) Correspondence, 
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
August 1903
Fourteen-year-old Walter was charged with the offence of being neglected 
because he was a “child born of an aboriginal or half-caste mother”.
While locked up and waiting to be sent to an industrial school for two years, 
Walter became very ill from distress. His mother Nellie Bliss came to the lock-up. 
She howled and screamed in grief because her child was being taken away. 
Walter was released, but later tricked by Dr Roth into boarding a boat that took 
him away to Cairns. 
ISBN 978-0-6481150-8-3

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   Analysing and Interpreting Primary Sources – Making a Nation – Australia 1750–1918
14
© Blake Education 2020
Resource sheet – The Stolen Generation
A letter to Dr Roth
Source 3
November 27, 1903
In November a (iv) M. Matthews, Cardwell to Dr. Roth, Northern 
Protector of Aborigines, November 27, 1903.
Sir,
I would like to draw your attention to the way which “Walter” was 
kidnapped from here last Monday night – and sent away to Cairns to 
the Missionary Station. I presume the parents were informed by the 
police that he was to be let go on Tuesday morning but by that time he 
was well on his way to Cairns. He was coaxed to the steamer by telling 
him that the Inspector was on board and wanted to see him and he 
could go to his parents again on Tuesday morning. As I have known 
him since he was born, I know he had never been neglected in any 
way, was always well clothed and always had plenty to eat and now 
that he is over fifteen years of age and can earn “his own living” he is 
disgracefully taken away from his parents by the police.
His mother is crying after him and partly blames me for taking him to 
the boat. 
If other police left the blacks alone and looked after some of the 
neglected “whites” it would be much more to their credit as you know 
yourself the “blacks” here are not neglected and I consider it is about 
time it was put a stop to; even if Walter is a halfcaste why should he be 
kidnapped away from his parents. 
I would kindly ask you to give me a reply to this so as to know if there is 
any chance of his coming back to his parents.
I think it is one of the most disgraceful things that I have ever seen that 
the boy should be decoyed away from his parents in such a manner.
Trusting for a favourable reply,
I remain, Yours faithfully
M Matthews
Source: Queensland State Archives Item ID336387, (A/58751) Correspondence, Aboriginal and 
Torres Strait Islander

The role of a Protector
The  role of a ‘Pr _ t _ ct _ r of Aborigines’ 
was held by men in most states of 
A _ str _ l _ _ from the middle 1800s 
through to the early 1900s. The Protector 
was the legal guardian of Indigenous 
children to the age of 16 years. The 
Protector had the power to remove 
Ind _ g _ n _ _ s children from their family 
and place them in homes or in work. They 
also had control over who Indigenous 
adults could marry, where they could 
l _ ve, their h _ _ lth and their money. 
Aboriginals Protection and 
Restriction of the Sale of Opium 
Act 1897
This Act was created to pr _ t _ ct 
Indigenous people from disease 
and m _ str _ _ tm _ nt by the 
white community. But in practice, 
it meant that Indigenous people 
could be removed from their homes 
and placed in reserves. 
Dr Walter E Roth
Dr Roth was the ‘Northern Pr _ t _ ct _ r 
of Aborigines’ in Queensland. His job was 
to enforce the laws of the ‘Aboriginals 
Protection and R _ str _ ct _ _ n of the 
Sale of Op _ _ m Act of 1897’. Roth was 
well known for strongly applying the laws 
of the Act. 
The Industrial and Reformatory 
Schools Act 1865 (1865–1911) 
Queensland
This set of laws helped to set 
up special schools to educate 
children under the age of 15 who 
had broken the law or who were 
described as ‘neglected’. 
One way the Act defined a 
n _ gl _ ct _ d child was: “Any child 
born of an aboriginal or half-caste 
mother.” (7.)
