Courtroom tips
Tip 1: Court etiquette
Court etiquette requires that everybody stands when the judge enters or leaves the room. People 
entering or leaving the courtroom should bow to the judge’s bench as a mark of respect. Judges 
are referred to as ‘Your Honour’ and lawyers should stand while addressing the judge. Barristers 
should not argue with the judge. They can say ‘With respect, I submit that …’, but when a judge 
passes a ruling it must be accepted. An appropriate phrase is ‘If your Honour pleases’. Unlike in 
US courtroom dramas, Australian lawyers remain behind the bar table. They do not stride around 
or approach the witness stand. Lawyers refer to other lawyers as ‘my learned friend’. 
Tip 2: The art of cross-examination
The purpose of cross-examination is to challenge a witness’s evidence with a view to discrediting 
them. Although leading questions (questions that suggest their own answer) are not permitted 
in examination-in-chief, they are often used in cross-examinations. It is a rule among barristers 
never to ask a question in cross-examination that they do not know the answer to, as they might 
not get the answer they want. Once they have the information desired, they should stop asking 
questions and not give the witness the opportunity to continue talking. Demanding ‘yes’ or ‘no’ 
answers is acceptable, although the judge may allow the witness to explain themselves more fully.
Tip 3: Hostile witnesses
Barristers cannot ordinarily cross-examine their own witnesses. But if a witness gives evidence 
that favours the other side or contradicts evidence in their previous written statements, the 
barrister can try to have them declared hostile and is then able to cross-examine the witness.
Steps to take
  1 
Divide into small groups and allocate roles.
  2 
Arrange the room so that it looks like a courtroom.
  3 
Ensure everyone knows their role or character story.
  4 
The barrister for the plaintiff opens their case, then calls their first witness.
  5 
The witness is questioned by the plaintiff’s barrister, then by the defendant’s barrister.
  6 
This is repeated for each of the plaintiff’s witnesses.
  7 
The barrister for the defence opens their case and calls their first witness.
  8 
Each witness is questioned by the defence barrister, then by the plaintiff’s barrister.
  9 
The judge sums up then reaches a conclusion with the help of the jury (if there is one).
10 
The judge makes their decision, passes an order and explains it to the class.
Dr Wong
I am Mabel’s GP. It is my opinion that Mabel will never be able to live independently again. 
She needs constant care and a nursing home is the best place for her. Her condition is 
such that she will suffer chronic pain for the rest of her life. I believe her lifespan will 
be much shorter than it would otherwise have been. Mabel is suffering from depression 
brought on by her accident and has expressed a wish to die.

Jason
Yvonne was not my type. I only went along with things as I could see Nikolas fancied the other one. 
Yvonne was quiet and grumpy. I bought her a few drinks but she didn’t lighten up. She got drunk 
easily, too. When she left I didn’t care. I went a bit later, thinking I should leave Nikolas to it. I wasn’t 
fussed – win some, lose some. After I left I went straight home. I live on my own. I watched TV for a 
few hours then went to bed.
Forensic evidence
Yvonne’s autopsy found she had died of suffocation. The findings were consistent with someone 
holding a pillow over her face. There were no signs of struggle. This was explained by high 
levels of Rohypnol found in her blood. Rohypnol is a prescription drug for insomnia that is also 
known as a ‘date rape’ drug. Its symptoms include nausea, dizziness, problems seeing and talking, 
sleepiness and passing out. There is no evidence as to who put the drug in Yvonne’s drink. The 
autopsy found she did not have sexual intercourse that night. [Hint: Whoever plays the pathologist 
should do some further research into the effects of Rohypnol, and perhaps suffocation.]
Courtroom tips
Tip 1: Court etiquette
Court etiquette requires that everybody stands when the judge enters or leaves the room. People 
entering or leaving the courtroom should bow to the judge’s bench as a mark of respect. Judges 
are referred to as ‘Your Honour’ and lawyers should stand while addressing the judge. Barristers 
should not argue with the judge. They can say ‘With respect, I submit that . . . etc.’, but when a 
judge passes a ruling it must be accepted. An appropriate phrase in those circumstances is ‘If 
your Honour pleases’. Unlike in American courtroom dramas, Australian lawyers remain behind 
the bar table. They do not stride around or approach the witness stand. Lawyers refer to other 
lawyers in court as ‘my learned friend’. 
Tip 2: The art of cross-examination
The purpose of cross-examination is to challenge a witness’s evidence with a view to discrediting 
them. Although leading questions are not permitted in examination-in-chief, they are often used in 
cross-examination. It is a rule among barristers never to ask a question in cross-examination that 
they do not know the answer to, as they might not get the answer they want. Once they have the 
information desired, they should stop asking questions and not give the witness the opportunity to 
continue talking. Demanding ‘yes’ or ‘no’ answers is acceptable, although the judge may allow the 
witness to explain themselves more fully.
Tip 3: Hostile witnesses
Barristers cannot ordinarily cross-examine their own witnesses. However, if a witness gives 
evidence that favours the other side or contradicts evidence they had given in previous written 
statements, the barrister can try to have the witness declared hostile. The barrister is then able 
to cross-examine the witness.
Tip 4: Have fun!
Few things match the drama of the criminal courtroom. Part of a barrister’s skill is to present 
their case in an engaging and entertaining manner, which helps get the jury on side. The best 
way to do this is to enjoy yourself and add a touch of theatre!

Case study: Equity and the law
The British adversarial system saw the development of the common law courts. 
Historically, these courts required a rigid adherence to the rules of evidence and 
procedure. This often led to injustices and harsh decisions. Medieval litigants (people 
involved in lawsuits) were able to petition the king to ‘do equity’ for them – that is, to 
ensure fairness and justice. Equity eventually evolved into a body of law that ran parallel 
to the common law and relieved some of its harshness. For example, it protects weak 
parties when they are taken advantage of by stronger parties.
The High Court case Blomley v Ryan (1956) 99 CLR 362 involved the sale of a farm 
for a very low price by an intoxicated elderly man. The buyer knew of the old man’s 
drinking spree and even brought a bottle of rum to the negotiations. The High Court 
held that because the buyer took advantage of the seller’s condition, equity would not 
allow specific performance. In other words, the party taking advantage of the weaker 
party cannot insist the contract be performed. The court described other factors and 
vulnerabilities that could lead to a similar result, including poverty, illness and illiteracy.

Justice is hard to define, but a just law or judgement should have the characteristics of

Case study: Equality of treatment
Four people are caught speeding along the same busy road at the same time. They are

the school zone is in operation and each is fined the same sum.
Rachel, 28, is a single mother. She has never been booked before. She is picking up her

She is frantic because her ex-husband made a few attempts in the past to pick up their 
child without authority. Rachel is worried her ex might try to abduct their son if she is  
not there in time. 
Jason, 44, has been booked for speeding on several occasions, and has had his licence 
suspended more than once. He is a busy executive whose motto is ‘Time is money’. He 
often risks speeding fines, seeing them merely as a cost of business. For him, it is cheaper 
to pay the occasional fine than to lose money by spending more time on the road.

2 
Outline the purpose of Fleming’s application.
 
 
REMEMBER 
When people break criminal laws, they are punished. Most punishments reflect elements 
of deterrance, rehabilitation, incapacitation or retribution.
Case study: R v Fleming [2006] QCA 26 
R v Fleming involved an application to appeal against the severity of a sentence. The 
Queensland Supreme Court, Court of Appeal division, commented on the purposes of 
criminal punishment in this case. 
Fleming, a 45-year-old unemployed man, wanted to appeal against his prison sentence.  
He had threatened to injure two public officers who were conducting an approved 
inspection on his property. The purpose of the visit was to inspect for the presence of 
unregistered dogs, and Fleming tried to stop them carrying out their duties. He was 
abusive, made obscene gestures and threatened violence.
Fleming had a long history of abusive and violent criminal offending, dating back to when 
he was a teenager. He had never been imprisoned, but always fined or given community 
service orders (orders to perform work to benefit the community). He regularly breached 
these orders.
This time, Fleming was imprisoned for four months, but allowed out early on condition 
he broke no further laws. The maximum penalty the judge could have given him for this 
offence was five years’ imprisonment. Fleming claimed he should not have been given 
a prison sentence. He noted he had pleaded guilty early on, and was suffering from 
depression. 
The Court of Appeal said the judge who passed the sentence was entitled to order 
imprisonment because:
• there was a need to protect public officers carrying out their lawful duties
• the applicant had a record of persistently offending.
The court noted: ‘The sentencing judge was perfectly entitled to identify this as a 
reasonable opportunity to impose a penalty which might at last work some actual 
personal deterrence.’
The application for leave to appeal was refused.

14 Trial procedures
Examining a witness
Examining a witness is a skill. It is important for the lawyer to listen to the answers and respond 
accordingly, rather than simply reading out a list of prepared questions. 
The aim of an examination-in-chief is to have the witness tell the story in their own words. 
Lawyers are not meant to ask leading questions of their own witnesses. A leading question is one 
that suggests its own answer. It directs the answer given by the witness and may sound more like 
a statement than a question. It could result in a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ answer rather than an explanation.
Leading questions are permitted in cross-examination, however. The purpose of a cross-
examination is to reveal the truth. Lawyers might try to show that a witness is lying, has a bad 
memory, or was unobservant or biased. The opposing side tries to cast doubt on the witness’s 
testimony; the other side might be able to clear this up in their re-examination. 
2

questions. Rephrase them so that the opposing side will not be able to object.
a Did you see Francis enter the bedroom?
 
b You were at your office at 5pm, weren’t you?
 
c The traffic lights turned green as you approached, didn’t they?
 
Leading questions are allowed on some preliminary matters during examination-in-chief; for example, 
‘You are Mabel Smith, aged 44 years, and working as a receptionist in the defendant’s clinic?’
3

REMEMBER 
In Australia, the statutory minimum age of criminal responsibility is 10 years old. There 
is a legal presumption that a child between the ages of 10 and 14 is not capable of 
committing a criminal act. Young people over 14 but not yet 18 are considered fully 
responsible for any offence they might commit, but they are not treated the same  
as adults.

Case study: Kelly and Tara
Kelly, aged 9, and her sister Tara, aged 11, went to their local shopping mall. They wanted 
to buy some costume jewellery with their pocket money. They entered a store and made 
their selection, then realised they didn’t have enough cash. Tara replaced a set of cheap 
bangles on the stand, but Kelly picked them up and slipped them into her pocket. Tara 
hesitated a moment before taking an extra set for herself and hiding them in her bag. 
Neither girl had broken the law before. They paid the shop assistant for all the goods 
except the bangles. As they tried to leave the store the assistant accused them of 
shoplifting and called the police.

Joshua’s parents went away for the weekend, leaving him alone in the house. Joshua,

cans in the fridge in preparation. His friends arrived, but then a large group of teenagers

Assignments in Junior Science – Waves
A history of the telescope
Waves
17a
When Phoenicians were cooking on
sand around 3 500 BC, they discovered glass. But
it took thousands of years before glass was shaped
into a lens for the first telescope. Lenses that could
change the magnification of objects were known
in Europe at the end of the thirteenth century. 
The spectacle maker Hans Lippershey
(1570–1619), born in Germany and working in
Holland, is often credited with the invention of
the first telescope in 1608. If one placed a
biconvex lens (a lens used to correct long-
sightedness) about 40 cm away from a biconcave
lens (a lens used to correct short-sightedness) and
then looked through them, distant objects
appeared closer. This spyglass was used for
spotting the army’s enemy.  
The telescope was introduced to astronomy
in 1609 by the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei
(1564–1642), who became the first man to see the
craters of the moon and went on to discover
sunspots, the four large moons of Jupiter and the
rings of Saturn. Galileo’s telescope was a simple
refractor telescope, using a plano-convex lens and
a plano-concave eye lens in a tube. This
arrangement magnified up to 30 times but
provided only a narrow field of view: Galileo
could see no more than a quarter of the moon’s
face. The German Johannes Kepler (1571–1630)
invented the form of the refracting telescope that
is the basis for modern refractors; it has a convex
eye lens. However, Kepler’s telescope produced
large inverted images with some chromatic
distortions (the lenses acted like a prism and split
the starlight into its constituent colours resulting
in coloured fuzzy edges of the images).    
In 1704, Sir Isaac Newton announced a
new concept in telescope design: instead of lenses,
a curved mirror was used to gather in light and
reflect it. This reflecting mirror acted like a light-
collecting bucket. Newton’s reflector telescope
could magnify o

can reveal that an artwork is fake.

Forgery check 2

Each artist has their own characteristic style, colours, pattern of brushstrokes and signature.
Sometimes, a check of these features is all that is needed to prove an artwork as fake.

Non-destructive investigation techniques

If more evidence is needed, then the next step for the forensic investigator is to use simple non-
destructive techniques that do not damage an artwork.

+ A stereomicroscope shows detailed brushstrokes and can indicate whether the varnish over the
paint has been artificially cracked to make the painting look older than it is.

+ X-rays show whether cracks are just on the surface paint layers (suggesting fake ageing) or pass
through all the paint layers to the canvas below (suggesting real ageing).

indicate that the painting has been changed, painted over or had bits glued on.

Examples of people’s attempts to produce replacement materials for impaired 
or lost body parts are scattered throughout history.  
1 
What is meant by impaired? 
Early Egyptians, Greeks and Romans all left evidence (artefacts) that illustrates 
their use of artificial limbs, including wooden noses! Silver and gold wires, 
bones, clay, skins and wood have all been used to repair injuries. Mummified 
remains dating back to 1100 bc (Egypt) have been identified as having stitches 
(sutures) in the body tissues, while plaster casts date back to at least 2000 bc. Many South American tribes took 
advantage of the large, sharp pincers found on soldier ants to ‘stitch’ surface wounds. The ants were placed on the 
open skin and became defensive, pinching the lips of the wound closed in an attempt to attack. Once the pincers 
were securely in place, the ant was pulled away and its pincers remained in the skin. 
Society’s reawakened interest in ‘natural remedies’ has recognised what American Indians, Australian Aborigines 
and ancient Egyptians have long known about the value of using honey to disinfect wounds. Evidence suggests that 
these people also used animal skins and/or clay mixtures to form casts. All of these things are early examples of 
biomaterials.
2 
Why might a cast be used? What is its purpose? 
3 
Find out three therapeutic devices or treatments used today that were invented more than 1000 years ago.
How biomedical devices help to improve quality of life
It is always better to posses a healthy organ or limb, than a prosthetic device, because the device is never as effective 
as the real thing. However, when we lose a functioning body part, prosthetic devices allow people to recover at least

LESSON 8 E&C                        FLASH LIGHTS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
       Apply their understanding of simple circuits, batteries, copper wire and globes to
        construct a torch.
       Use conductors and switches to construct a torch.


        EQUIPMENT


Per Class
       blu-tac
       masking tape


Per Group
       2 D batteries (1.5 volts)
       two lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation
        removed at each end
       one small globe (have some spares)
       cardboard cylinders (recycled such as from paper towel or rolled up card)
       aluminium pie dishes (small)
       alfoil
       paper clips or split pins


Preparation
       Collect a variety of light sources e.g. pen light, torch, candle, sparkler, bedside
        lamp, kerosene lantern, mosquito lantern, spotlight, flare or emergency beacon
        (preferably one powered by battery, one by mains power and one chemical).

Safety
    Care must be taken if using sparklers and other light sources.
        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


Light Sources
     Chemicals: candles, flares, sparklers, kerosene lamps, mosquito lanterns.
     Battery: torches, pen light, toys that light up, caving head lamps, spotlights.
     Mains Power: bedside lamps, house lights.


History of Flash lights
      Searching in a dark closet before 1896, one had to use a candle or kerosene
       lantern. Accidents occurred and fires followed. A safer alternative was needed.
      In 1896, the first flashlight was invented.
      Portable electric lights were called "flash lights" since they would not give a long
       steady stream of light. The bulbs were inefficient and the batteries were weak,
       allowing the user to flash the light on for only a few seconds.
      Very early lights did not have an on/off switch, just a ring that would push against
       a band of metal. When batteries and bulbs became more efficient, the switch
       was improved.


Example of a Torch

5.3 | Butterflies and mobiles

Science as a human endeavour [| fowsoiow | stanoano | Aovancen

A company called Qualcomm has copied how a butterfly wing produces
colour to develop a new type of display for mobile phones and other devices.
Rather than using a battery-powered light source for the phone display, it uses
light from the room or sunlight as its source. This means that the phone’s
battery lasts longer between charging. The phone contains tiny reflective units
that cause light waves entering it to overlap, or interfere with other light waves.
Some light waves cancel each other out and some add to each other. This
produces different colours in the same way that the wings of a Morpho

butterfly cause light to interfere and create colours.

The basic unit of the display that causes the interference of incoming light is a tiny square of glass
and metal (called an interferometric modulator display element or IMOD). This unit has two layers
of reflective surfaces with an air gap between them (Figure 5.3.1).The air gap can be closed or
opened by applying a small voltage across it. When it opens, light waves can reflect off the bottom-
reflecting membrane and the top-reflecting surface (the ‘thin film stack’). If the gap is the right size,
then the two reflected waves of light add to each other and appear a certain colour, such as blue.
When the air gap closes or is collapsed, no light reflects off the surfaces and they appear black.

CHARACTERISTICS OF EACH COMPONENT ON THE ELECTRICITY' D}DEMONSTRATION BOARD BOARD We recommend that you have a "play" with the demonstration board before you read all of this information, to give you some familiarity with how some of the components behave. Circuits you can try are on an attached sheet. Each component (buzzer, motor, etc.) on the board will work when DIRECT CURRENT (from a battery or D.C. power supply) is connected to them. They are not designed to work with alternating current (A.C.), which is the type of current we receive through the mains power supply. Each component has a certain amount of Resistance to electric current. It is helpful to be aware of the approximate resistance of each component, especially when you want to predict what will happen before you connect up a circuit. The resistances liven are the MEASURED RESISTANCES, when a 6 volt battery was connected to them. An explanation of resistance is given in the section on "Electricity - the main concepts" (a) Globes - There are two types, the only difference being their resistance. (i) one marked 6v 2w - resistance 27 ohms. (ii) the other marked 3.8 V 0.3 A - resistance 18 ohms. Globe (ii) glows more brightly than globe (i) when each is separately connected to a 6 volt supply. (Try it). The electric current flows into the base of the globe, through the filament and out of the metal side of the globe. The current can also flow in the reverse direction. The reason for the glass casing is to protect the filament from being knocked or touched when it gets white hot. and to keep oxygen away from the filament. If the filament was exposed to oxygen when it was hot it hot, it would instantly burn out. (b) continuity tester - This has many uses. When the two probes are connected together (that is, there is no resistance between them) the light emitting diode (L.E.D.) lights up. Therefore, if the L.E.D. lights up brightly when the probes are being used, the ~two points being touched by the probes are connected electrically. Other uses are listed in the ex]experiment section. The continuity tester works best when connected to a nine volt D.C. supply. (c) variable resistor - (Also known as a Potentiometer, or POT for short). The resistance between the centre socket and the ~o outer sockets can be changed from 10 ohms up to 10k ohms (10,000 ). The resistance between the two outer sockets is always 10k ohms. There is a protective 10 ohm resistor on the central socket of the pot on the demonstration board. If there was no resistor, the pot could BURN OUT Ok~ if a power supply is connected only across the pot. This is a danger with the students' pot, as there is no resistor attached to the central terminal. Students should always ensure that the pot is in series with another component such as a globe. (d) motor - The resistance of the motor is around 18 ohms when running with a 6 volt battery supply. The motor will change direction of spin if the leads in the two motor sockets are swapped. The optimum voltage supply to run the motor is only 3 volts, but it can run comfortably at 9 volts, provided it is not left running for a long period of time. It will spin at 6 900 revolutions per minute at these voltages, if not restricted. Provided in the kit is one means of restriction - an icypole stick, with a hole to fit onto the motor shaft. See later experiments with the motor for details. (e) buzzer - The resistance of the buzzer is around 600 ohms. There are two other sockets connected to the POSITIVE TERMINAL of the buzzer, each with an additional l50 ohm resistance. These resistors decrease the current going into the buzzer, and hence make in softer. If the students are using the demonstration board, you may PREFER to have them use only the "soft" volume socket. You can do the same with the students boards (as outlined in the later experiments). The buzzer needs at least S volts power supply with the positive of the supply connected to the positive of the buzzer. the following information provides suggestions for extended experimental options in the physics using the Electricity Demonstration Board. In other words. let them solve the problem. A.CHARACTERISTICS OF SOLAR PANELS. There are various aspects of the solar panels that can be investigated. (a) Plotting the light intensity on the panels against the current and voltage output. The output of the panels can be placed in series with a milliammeter and 100 ohm resistor, with a voltme[er in parallel ~ith the 100 ohm resistor. A light intensity meter used b>photographers can be used to measure the light intensity at the panel surface usin~ a 150 ~,~tt ii~ht globe as the source. (b) Using the set up as in (a), determine the percentage efficiency of the solar panels. For a particular distance of the panels from the ligh~ source (say x cm), the surface area of a sphere of radius x can be calculated (say area Y cmz). Assuming the light globe actually emits 150 joules per second as light, and that the light is evenly distributed over the imaginery surface of the sphere or radius x, it is easy to calculate the amount of light energy per second reaching the solar collectors. Using_' the P = IV for the output of the solar panels, you can determine the percentage efficiency of the panels. This efficiency can be determined for various distances from the globe. ~c) A variation on (b) could be to use colour filters to see if the panels are sensitive to particular colours. Ad.~ustment of distance may be necessary to keep the overall light intensity on the panels constant. There are a range of extensions to this topic, including visiting showroom of the latest solar technology, and writing up on their research. Students could also construct their o~ solar water heater, and determine the efficienc~~ of energ~ transfer. T]~_ ELEtmfRIC ~FoTOR The measureable parameters relevant to the motor are (a) its ms~ximum speed of rotation, (b) the best operating voltage, and the current dra~ by the motor at this voltage (the power consumed for various voltages can be determined); (c) the output power of the motor, and hence its relative efficiency' for a Oarticular load on the motor: (di the ms~ximum torque of the motor. Some of these parameters are more difficult to measure than the others, particularly (c) and (d). SUGGESTIONS (a) Use a stroboscope to determine the frequency of rotation for various inpu~ voltages immx. 9 volts, for short time only). Plot f vs input voltage. ib) From the graph of (a), determine the minimum voltage for ms~ximum f. (c) Put a piece of pencil with its lead removed on the end of the shaft so that it can act as a pulley. A long cotton thread with a light weight can be attached to the pulley. If the motor is then raised to a height of at least 2 metres, the students can then attempt to determine the power output (rate of change of potential energy of the weight) versus the input power to the motor. Because of the speed of the motor, students may wish to gear the speed of rotation do~, or file most of the pencil shaft down - the motor can make a light weight move ~.~]ERY rapidly. The challenge is to get the motor operating_ at its optimum efficiency! ld) By having a long ic.vpole stick firmly attached to the shaft lyou may want to file a The school will probably have other motors that students can compare. Students may not be aware of how many motors are in the average house. There maybe anything up to forty motors in one home, including in toys (trains and slot cars), appliances with moving parts - vacuum, dishwasher, washing machine, video, tape recorder and player, record player, exhaust fans, hair dryer, blow heaters, cooling fans, electronic type~Titers and printers, food processors. mix-masters, electric can openers, tumble driers, refrigerators and freezers (you hear the motor going on or off occasionally), electric tools in the workshop - drills, grinders, electric planes and touters, electric saws, etc. Try and estimate how many motors you have in your home. 7. ENERGY CHANGES - THE ~I4iN CONCEPTS There are a number of energy transformations that can be sho~m using the demonstration board. (a) If you have a circuit with a battery and a light globe {as with a torch), the energy changes that take place are - chemical energy (stored in the battery), electrical energy (transferred through the wires by means of electric current) and finally light and heat energy (given off by the light globe). (b) The motor produces mechanical energy (working energy) ~'hich can be used to produce kinetic energy ( energy,' of motion ). (c) The buzzer produces sound energy. LESSON 9 E&C                   SECRET CODES




         AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
      Design a circuit that enables communication without words.



         EQUIPMENT



Per Class
      one set of group equipment for demonstration model

Per Group
   2 D cell batteries (1.5 V)
      1 toothpick
      1 rubber band
      2 x 15 cm wires
      2 x 90cm wires
      1 light globe
      2 Pop sticks

Preparation
        Prepare a demonstration model.


Safety
        Care with rubber bands.
        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   A code is a system of symbols, letters, words, or signals that are used instead of
    ordinary words and numbers to send messages or store information. A code is
    used to keep the message short or to keep it secret.


   Secret writing has been employed about as long as writing has existed.
    Cryptology has long been employed by governments, military, businesses and
    organisations to protect their messages. Today, encryption is used to protect
    storage of data and transactions.


   Morse code is made up of dots and dashes that are translated into long and short
    taps, lights or noises of some sort. For example, during the day, tap on
    something or use a whistle; at night use a flashlight to send your signals.


   Morse Code
         When you leave your globe on for a long time, this is a dash
         When you quick flash your globe, this is a dot
         An extra long dash of light signals the end of your response
          LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Students to role play how they could communicate with a partner without using
       words.
                                                    Sign language, miming, codes,
  What are some ways you used to                    facial expression.

  What is Morse Code?                               or flashes of light to communicate
                                                    with others.

  with circuits to show Morse Code?                 that you can easily turn on and off
                                                    to create flashes.


2. Activities and Strategies
      Discuss aim and equipment.
      Demonstration by teacher : How to build a pop stick pressure switch.
              Take a wire and tightly wrap the bare wire around the end of a pop stick.
             Repeat with a second wire on a second pop stick.
             Place the two pop sticks and wire on top of each other with the wires
                touching.
             Wrap the rubber band around as tight as possible at the opposite end (to
                the wires) on the pop sticks.
             Place the toothpick in between the two pop sticks a couple of millimetres
                in front of the rubber band.




     Students to:
             Set up a circuit with two batteries and a globe and test the switch to make
               sure it works.
             NB: The wires should touch when you push down on the switch and make
               the globe light up. When you do not push, the wires separate and the
               globe does not light up.
             Using your international Morse Code chart send a message to another
               group. Write down the words and underneath the code sequence before
               you attempt to send the message.


Hints for the Circuit
             Each group of four makes a simple circuit with a globe that includes the
               pressure switch (this could be done in pairs if enough equipment is
               available).
             The globe will be placed behind a wall (a book, box, cardboard) for one
               pair to see without being able to see the switch.
             In pairs students will face each other across their desks separated by the
               wall.
             The pairs will communicate using Morse Code by switching their globe on
               and off using the code sheet to make words.
             Therefore, each paired group will build a circuit that extends under the wall
               so that partners can only see the globe and not the switch.

LESSON 5 E&C                        CONDUCTORS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
      Classify materials as conductors or insulators.
      Describe the role insulators and conductor in everyday appliances.


        EQUIPMENT


Per Class
      a selection of insulators and conductors:
            insulators (wooden pop sticks, plastic spoons, glass jars, paper, rubber,
              ceramic tiles, cotton, foam cups, kitchen sponge)
             conductors (alfoil, iron nails, steel wool, coins, copper, aluminium cans,
              drawing pins, paper clips)

Per Group
      2 D Batteries (1.5 volt)
      3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
       at each end
      2 globes
      cardboard (1 piece about 10x10cm)
      paper clips
      a few insulators and conductors as listed above
      masking tape


Preparation
     Collect a range of materials to test; students could bring one each from home.

Safety
    Mains electricity must not be used.

        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS
 Circuits
      A circuit is a path in which electricity flows.
      Electrons are tiny particles that are found in atoms.
      Electric current is the movement of electrons, which creates the flow of
       electricity.
      The power supply pushes electrons through a circuit. This power supply can
       come in many different forms (for example, a battery is a power supply).
      You can think of the power supply as a pump that creates pressure to force
       water to flow in a hose.
      In a series circuit the batteries and light bulbs are connected in a line. There is
       only one path for the electrons to flow along. Therefore, the current through each
       of the circuit elements is the same.
      This is why when one Christmas tree light blows, the rest do not light up.
      Electricity can be transferred to heat, light, sound and motion energy.


Conductors and Insulators
      A conductor allows electricity to flow through it. Examples include metals such as
       wire made of aluminium, steel or copper.
      An insulator does not allow electricity to flow through it. Examples include non
       metals such as plastic, wood and foam.


Additional Information
      A parallel circuit is one in which electric current travels along more than one path
       (as in the home), because there is more than one path for the electricity to
       follow. Some parts of the circuit can be on while others are off.
      Voltage can be thought of as electrical pressure, which pushes the electrons
       through the circuit. Electric pressure is measured in volts.
      The most basic electrical devices in the home e.g. a kettle, are made from
       simple pieces of wire which resists the flow of electricity. The wire will become
       warm, perhaps red hot when electricity flows through it.
      The household voltage in Australia is 240 Volts.
      Wiring in houses is designed to have very low resistance so they don’t become
       warm with electricity flowing through them.
           LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Direct students into groups.
      The students to design a simple circuit using two batteries, a globe and copper
       wire.
      The circuits should be built and taped onto a sheet of cardboard or their desk to
       hold the components in place.
      The group with their globe shining first is the winner.
      The teacher introduces the concept of materials that conduct electricity
       (conductor) and those that do not (insulators).

Cow’s Eye Dissection
Purpose: To identify and examine the various parts of a cow’s eye.

Materials: gloves     scissors   scalpel     forceps   cutting mat    newspaper
cow’s eye

Procedure:
Part A: External features of the eye
1. There is some fat around the eye. What colour it the fat?

2. What is the purpose of the fat around the eye?

3. What is the job of the muscles on the outside of the eye?

4. Cut the fat and muscles off the eyeball so that you can see the sclera.

5. What colour is the sclera? ________        iris? ________   pupil? ________

6. The cornea is the tough, clear covering over the iris and pupil. It is
   normally clear and colourless; however in your cow’s eye it may be cloudy.
   Why do you think it may have become cloudy?


7. The optic nerve carries information from the retina to the brain. Identify the
   optic nerve on the back of the eye. Describe what it looks like.


Part B: Internal features of the eye
1. Carefully use the scalpel to make a small cut near the centre of the eye.
   With the scissors, cut around the entire eye so that you have two equal
   hemispheres.

2. What colour is the sclera?

3. What did you notice about the texture of the sclera? Why is this important?


4. The jelly inside the eye is the vitreous humour. Gloop your vitreous
   humour onto the parts identification worksheet.

5. What is the job of the vitreous humour?


6. Pick up the back of the sclera, which contains the optic nerve. The retina is
   a thin layer on the inside of the sclera. Gently peel off the retina with the
   forceps and place it on the parts identification sheet.

7. What is the purpose of the retina?

8. You may have found it difficult to remove the retina because it was attached
   to the optic nerve. This area is called the __________ __________.
 9. They black, shiny layer under the retina is the choroid coat. It contains
   blood vessels that provide nutrients for the eye. Why is the choroid coat
   dark?


10. Use the forceps to carefully peel the choroid coat from the sclera and
   place it on the parts identification sheet.

11. You have now removed everything from the back half of the sclera.
   Place it on the parts identification sheet.

12. Pick up the front half of the sclera that contains the cornea, iris and lens.
   Remove the lens with the forceps.

13. When you remove the lens, you should notice a watery fluid between the
   lens and the cornea. This is the aqueous humour. What is its function?


14.   Look at the lens. Is it concave or convex?

15.   Gently squeeze the lens. Why is it important that the lens is flexible?

16.   Place the lens on the newspaper. What do you notice about the writing?

17.   Place the lens on the parts identification sheet.

18. Use your fingers to carefully remove the iris. When you look at the iris
   closely, you should be able to see thin lines. These are the muscles that
   cause the iris to contract or dilate. Draw the iris in the space below.




19.   What is the purpose of the iris?


20.   What is the hole in the iris called?

21.   Is the iris transparent, translucent or opaque?

22.   Place the iris on the parts identification sheet.

23.   Cut the cornea out of the sclera. What is the purpose of the cornea?

24. With your scalpel, cut through part of the cornea. You should feel and
   hear it crunch. The cornea is made of multiple layers to make it thick and
   strong. Why must the cornea be tough, especially in grazing animals such
   as the cow?


25.   Place the cornea on the parts identifications sheet.

searchText: ﻿Electric Current Electric current is a measure of the rate of flow of charge (electrons) The charge flows when the circuit is complete. Charge is measured in coulombs (C) The rate of flow is the number of coulombs flowing per unit of time. When 1 coulomb of charge flows in 1 second it is called an ampere (A) Current is measured using an ammeter. Ammeters are connected in series with the source of electricity An ammeter is connected from its positive terminal to the positive terminal of the source. The usual current flowing in our homes is about 8 A Voltage Voltage is a measure of the electrical pressure which causes the electrons to flow in the circuit. It is measured in volts (V) A volt meter is used to measure the voltage. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the appliance to be measured. A volt meter is connected from its positive terminal to the positive terminal of the source. Some typical voltages are : dry cell 1.5 V house voltage 240 V car battery 12 V smoke alarm 9 V Electricity is transmitted from the power stations at very high voltages ie. 66 000 V

Current – picture it!
Task

   1. Read carefully through the text.
   2. Put the images in the order that they appear in the text.
   3. Glue the images in the spaces provided on the worksheet and quote a small
       part of the text that you are linking the image to – this cannot be more than
       eight words! Next, say why you are matching the image to that piece of text.



        When you think about the word ‘current’ what is the first thing that
        comes to mind? Perhaps the current in a river or something present-
        day?

        The current of a river is the flow of water. As the current flows from high
        ground to low ground it can carry things with it, like leaves, twigs and
        even boats. Current can only flow from high ground to low ground.

        Current in an electrical circuit is very similar, it also flows and carries
        electrical charge. The electrical current that flows in one direction is
        called direct current. Just like a river, it cannot flow backwards and
        forwards, it can only flow from one side of the battery to the other.

        As long as the current flows through the wires and cell any components
        in the circuit, like lightbulbs or buzzers will work. However, it is very
        important that there are no breaks in the electrical circuit because if
        there were, the electrical charge would not be able to flow back to the
        cell.

        We can think of the cell as being responsible for ‘pushing’ the current
        around the circuit. A bigger push from the cell will mean that more
        current can flow.

        To measure the current we use a piece of equipment called an
        ammeter, and it is placed in the circuit so that it can measure the
        current that flows through it. An ammeter measures current in units
        called ‘amps’ or ‘amperes’. Amps are given the unit symbol, A, for
        example, 10 A is 10 amps. Remember that the ammeter must be part of
        the circuit and not on the outside of it.

                                                                        Current – picture it!

        The amount of current that leaves the cell must be the same as the
        amount of current that returns to the cell. No matter where we measure
        the current in a series circuit, it will always be the same.

searchText: ﻿Batteries and Cells A cell is a device which converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It is used in an electrical circuit to drive motors, lights etc. A battery is a combination of cells. The cells are connected in either series or parallel to provide higher voltage or longer life. When connecting cells in series, connect them positive to negative. Electrical circuits An electrical circuit allows electrons to flow from the source, through conductors and return to the source. When they flow through an appliance energy is transferred to the appliance and it works. ie a light glows or a motor runs. The electrons will not flow unless the circuit is complete. Circuits can be represented by circuit diagrams. Symbols represent the various parts of the circuit.

Electric Shock Comprehension
                                          Answers

1        The coma position involves the victim lying on their side with the leg closest to
         the ground fully extended and the other leg bent at the knee. The arms are
         stretched in front of the victim.

2        A current of 50 mA needs to flow for about 4 000 m s. This is about 4 seconds.

3        Th three factors are: voltage, the path taken and the skin resistance of the victim.

4        The first thing you should do is remove the source of the electricity from the
         victim. Use an insulator to separate the victim from the source.

5        The body of the car will probably be a conductor. If the wires are in contact with
         the car , the car will be “live” and will conduct a current to all of its surface.

6        You should reassure the victim, treat burns and send for medical assistance.

7        You should position the person in the coma position, open the mouth and clear
         any obstruction.

8        If the current flows across the chest it will effect the heart and may cause the heart
         to fibrillate.

searchText:
Safety With Electricity
Below are two press articles which refer to electrical safety. Read the articles and answer
the questions which follow. You may need to refer to other sources for some of the
answers.


Schoolgirl Dies
An 11-year-old Sydney schoolgirl has died from injuries received in a pool accident which also killed her
best friend. A spokesman for Westmead Hospital said she died early yesterday morning. She never
recovered from receiving electric shocks in a swimming pool on 19 December. Her friend, also 11, died
later that same day. A live wire came into contact with the water in which the two girls were swimming
after the pool filter's electrical cable was accidentally cut.

The Age, 27 December 1988


Electrical Shocks More Likely in Summer
By DAVID THOMSON

People are twice as likely to suffer electrical shocks in summer as in the rest of the year, the SEC
has warned.
  A survey of the number of shocks reported in the 10 years to 1986 found that 65 per cent of
them occurred between October and March, the SEC's acting Victorian Chief Electrical
Inspector, Mr Ian Graham, said.
   He said the risk increased in summer because portable appliances were used outdoors and in
tents and caravans, people were barefooted or near water, especially pools, and people tried to do
their own electrical repairs and installations.
   Mr Graham said 500 electrical shocks had been reported to the SEC last year. There had been
another 100 cases in council supplied areas. About one-tenth of all shocks were the result of
dampness.
    He said there had been 17 fatalities from electrical appliances in 1987. There have been two
deaths from electrical contact with swimming pools since wiring regulations were revised in
1976 to isolate electrical equipment, including earthing and lighting, from pools.
   Mr Graham said checking existing electrical fittings was much more difficult than issuing
guidelines for new works.
   "We cannot check every single pool in Melbourne; we do not have the right to interfere."
    Mr Graham said pool owners should check permanently wired electrical fittings such as
pumps and underwater lights. Variations in water levels and heat caused power lines to sag,
which was dangerous where they crossed water.
    He said there had been a number of fatalities caused by hair dryers falling into baths. Mr
Graham said people should remember that it was illegal and unsafe for unlicensed tradesmen to
work on fixed wiring of houses, and that caution was needed with extension cords to tents and
caravans.

Questions

         avoided ?

2        List the reasons why it is more likely that more electric shocks are experienced in
         summer.

3        How could a hair drier falling into a bath cause a fatality ?

4        Why would dampness contribute to a large number of electrical shocks ?

searchText:
Electrical Safety World
                                  Teacher’s Guide

Electrical Safety World uses information, experiments, games, and activities to teach
students the principles and practices of electrical safety. The site is geared for a range of
interests and reading levels and can be used by students in elementary and middle school.
(Non-readers will be able to play the games with adult assistance.)

This Teacher’s Guide contains three sections:

      Site overview.
      Questions and activities to review key safety principles.
      Experiments, guidance and set-up.

I. SITE OVERVIEW
 The informational areas of the site explain the basic science of electricity and electrical
safety principles with text, pictures, and experiments. The games simulate common
indoor and outdoor electrical safety situations, giving students a chance to put safety
principles into practice. The activities ask students to apply electrical safety know-how in
their own lives.

Here’s what each area contains:

      The Travels of Electricity (INFORMATIONAL)
       What electricity is, where it comes from, and how it travels. Covers the electric
       distribution system, conductors, and insulators. Contains experiments about
       circuits and conductors/insulators.

      How Electricity Can Hurt You (INFORMATIONAL)
       How electricity behaves and how it can hurt people. Covers grounding, electricity
       and water, appliance safety, and the effects of electric shock. Contains
       experiments about electricity and water, and short circuits.

      In Case of Emergency! (INFORMATIONAL)
       Teaches students how to respond to electrical fires, electric shock, downed power
       lines, power lines on a vehicle, and power outages.

      Tree and Power Line Safety (INFORMATIONAL)
       Explains the hazards of trees near power lines, and how students can climb, plant,
       and trim trees to avoid power line contact.

      Find the Hidden Dangers (GAME)
       A game to test students’ understanding of how to play it safe around electricity
       outdoors. Within busy street scenes, students must identify electrical hazards
       involving power lines and electrical equipment.

      Make the Safe Choice (GAME)
       A game to test students’ awareness about electrical safety inside the home. The
       game presents electrical hazards that are relevant to students’ lives and asks
       students to identify the safest response.

      Shock Blocker (GAME)
       Students play against the computer to prevent water from creating a path for
       electricity to flow from a power line, electrical outlet, or lightning bolt.

      Tell Me More About Electricity (INFORMATIONAL)
       This section is not safety-related but instead provides additional information for
       students interested in other aspects of electricity. Covers electricity basics,
       electricity generation, pioneers of electrical discovery, electric vehicles, and
       energy efficiency/conservation.
    Home Safety Audit (ACTIVITY)
    A checklist students can use with parents to inspect their home for electrical
    hazards.

   Tell Your Story (ACTIVITY)
    Profiles a real-life shock victim who is an Olympic kayaker. Asks students to
    interview someone who has had an electric shock, to tell their own electric shock
    story, or to report on one from a newspaper article. Focus is on sharing how the
    incident occurred and how it could have been prevented.

   Safety Certificate
    This is a checklist of site locations students can use to map their progress, plus an
    electrical safety pledge. We recommend students print the certificate before
    starting the site and have a parent or other adult sign it after they have visited the
    main areas.

   Glossary
    Definitions of electricity-related words found on the site. These definitions may
    be accessed by clicking on the words wherever they appear highlighted on the site
    (usually their first reference within a section.)

   Links to Related Sites
    Hot links to related sites about the science of electricity, electrical inventions, and
    electrical safety.
 II. QUESTIONS AND ACTIVITIES

These questions and activities review the key safety principles from Electrical Safety
World. Here are a few ideas for how to use them with your class:

      Use as discussion points for verbally reviewing basic electrical safety information
       with the whole group.
      Use as a pre- and post-test to assess student understanding of electrical safety
       principles before and after visiting Electrical Safety World. (To use as a written
       test for older students, cut and paste the questions into your word processing
       program, delete the answers, and print out one sheet for each student.)
      Put students into small groups and assign each group several questions; ask them
       to use the website to find the answers. (Answers to questions 1-12 can be found in
       The Travels of Electricity; questions 13-19 are based on How Electricity Can Hurt
       You.)
      After all students have completed all sections of the website, organize the class
       like a game show: “contestants” can continue to answer questions until they get
       one incorrect, at which point a new contestant takes their place.

Electrical Safety Questions

1. What is electricity a form of? (Energy.)

2. What does electricity travel on to get from the power plant to people’s houses?
(Overhead and underground power lines.)

3. What other equipment is involved in getting electricity to where it can be used by
people? (Some or all of the following are correct: substations, pole-mounted and pad-
mounted transformers, service drops, meter boxes, electrical wiring, appliance cords.)

4. How fast does electricity travel? (At the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second.)

5. Could you move faster than electricity? (No!)

6. List some good conductors of electricity. (Metal, water)

7. Is the human body a good conductor of electricity? Why/why not? (Yes, because it is
mostly water.)

8. What will happen if electricity travels through you? (You will be shocked and could be
badly hurt or even killed.)

9. List some good insulators. (Special rubber, glass.)

10. Why are insulators important? (They keep electricity from leaving wires.)
 11. What would happen if a power line were to fall from the power pole to the ground?
(It would energize the area around it with a lot of electricity and people touching the line
or coming near it would be hurt or killed.)

12. If you overload an outlet by plugging in too many things, what can happen? (Cord
insulation can overheat and melt, causing a shock and fire hazard.)

13. Why are people good conductors of electricity? (Our bodies are mostly water, and
water conducts electricity.)

14. Do you have to be touching the ground directly to conduct electricity? (No, you could
be touching something that is touching the ground, like a ladder.)

15. Why should you never touch anything electrical while you have wet hands or while
standing in water? (Water conducts electricity and you could be shocked.)

16. What is the purpose of rubber or plastic insulation around appliance cords? (It keeps
the electricity in the wires and prevents you from getting a shock.)

17. If a person is shocked, what can happen? (Muscle spasms, weakness, rapid pulse,
severe burns, unconsciousness, or death.)

18. Why can birds sit on power lines without being shocked? (The birds do not touch the
ground or anything in contact with the ground.)

19. Why could a kite caught in a power line be dangerous to try to retrieve? (If you touch
the kite while you are in contact with the ground or anything touching the ground, like a
ladder, electricity will travel from the power lines down the kite and into you, and you
will be shocked.)

Activities for Going Further

      Prepare a one-minute presentation or play for your class on the basics of how
       electricity travels from the power plant to appliances in people’s homes.

      Prepare a poster showing electricity going through a person on its way to the
       ground. The source of the electricity could be a power line or an appliance cord.

      Think of three ways you can convince your friends to be safe around electricity.
       Share them with the class.

      Create a radio commercial about outdoor or indoor electrical safety.

      Write an essay describing electrical hazards found in an imaginary house.
 III. EXPERIMENTS

Complete a Circuit

Materials:
Students will need the materials listed (1 D-cell battery, 1 1.2-volt lightbulb, 1 E-10
lightbulb base, two 12-inch pieces of insulated solid strand 18-22 gauge copper wire with
one inch of insulation removed at each end, masking tape). Bulbs, bases, and wire can be
purchased at stores like Radio Shack. Make sure the lightbulbs and bases match.


Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Explain to students that electricity can be dangerous if it is not handled correctly,
       and emphasize they should never experiment with the electricity that comes from
       a wall outlet. It’s much more powerful than the electricity made by small batteries
       and could seriously injure or even kill someone.

Objective:
Students will build a circuit and equate it to the path of electricity that comes from power
plants.

Getting It Across:
   1. Have students read the information and follow the steps on the page.
   2. Make sure they are able to identify the circuit electricity travels from the battery
       to the lightbulb and back, and the circuit electricity travels from power plants to
       homes and back. They should be able to equate the wires in the experiment with
       power lines and electrical wiring in the electric distribution system.

Questions and Answers:

      What part of the distribution system is like the wires in the experiment? (Power
       lines and electrical wiring.) What happens if you only tape one of the wires to the
       battery? Why? (The bulb does not light. The circuit is not complete unless both
       wires are taped to the battery, allowing electricity to flow in a circle.)
 Experiment with Conductors and Insulators

Materials:
Students will need 1 D-cell battery, 1 1.2-volt lightbulb, 1 matching lightbulb base, one
12-inch piece and two 4-inch pieces of insulated solid strand 18-22 gauge copper wire
with one inch of insulation removed at each end, and masking tape. Bulbs, bases, and
wire can be purchased at stores like Radio Shack. Make sure the lightbulbs and bases
match. Students will also need a variety of things they think might conduct electricity,
such as toothpicks, rubber bands, paper clips, plastic, fruit, etc.

Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Explain to students that electricity can be dangerous if it is not handled correctly,
       and emphasize they should never experiment with the electricity that comes from
       a wall outlet. It’s much more powerful than the electricity made by small batteries
       and could seriously injure or even kill someone.

Experiment Tips:
    Teachers should strip the wires ahead of time and make sure the batteries are
      fresh. Though the illustration does not show it, use tape to stick the wires to the
      ends of the battery.
    Students are likely to know that metals are good conductors, but they may be
      unaware that things with a lot of liquids in them also conduct well. Some things to
      have on hand include lemons, pickles, and potatoes. When testing these, make
      sure students stick wires into the wet part of the item.
    The key in the conduction of electricity is the movement of electrons. Metals are
      elements that freely share electrons. In liquids, dissolved ions can carry a charge
      as well. That is why water helps in the conduction of electricity. Salty water,
      loaded with sodium and chloride ions, helps even more.

Objective:
Students will learn the difference between conductors and insulators.

Getting it Across:
   1. Have students bring in things they think might conduct electricity.
   2. Have teams read the information and follow the steps on the page.
   3. Students should first test their circuit by connecting it without any trial material.

Questions and Answers:
    Ask teams to share their predictions and results. Were the results the same? If not,
       why not? (Answers will vary. Be sure the experimental setup was not at fault.)
    What conclusions can students draw about conductors and insulators? (Answers
       will vary. Students might generalize that metals are good conductors or plastic is a
       good insulator.)
 Electricity and Water

Materials:
Students will need the circuits they made for the “Conductors and Insulators” experiment,
plus a glass pint or quart jar, 2 nails, 2 alligator clips, salt, and water.

Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Explain to students that anything can conduct electricity when wet. Remind
       students that they can mix water and electricity safely in this experiment because
       the voltage is so minimal (1.5 V per D-cell battery).

Objective:
Students will demonstrate that water is a conductor of electricity.

Getting it Across:
Be sure students add plenty of salt to the water. Then have them predict, experiment, and
note their observations. Share results.

Questions and Answers:
   1. Ask students why they think the salt is needed. (Students will need to add a lot of
       salt to their water in order for electric current to flow. The voltage of the battery is
       so low that additional particles must be added to make the water MORE
       conductive. It is the impurities in water that make it a good conductor. Pure water
       will not conduct electricity. However, pure water is only found in the laboratory.
       That’s why there is so much emphasis on the conductivity of water as regards
       electrical safety.)
 Ben Franklin Was Lucky!

Materials:
Students will need the circuits they made for the “Complete a Circuit” experiment,
modified as shown in the illustration (strip a 1-inch section of insulation off the middle of
each wire). Students will also need a 6-inch piece of thicker wire with one inch of
insulation removed at each end.

Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Remind students that they are able to work with these batteries and wires because
       the voltage is minimal (1.5 V per D-cell battery). They should never experiment
       with the electricity that comes from a wall outlet. It’s much more powerful than
       the electricity made by small batteries and could seriously injure or even kill
       someone.

Objective:
Students will be able to describe a short circuit and compare it to the story about Ben
Franklin.

Getting it Across:
1. Have students read the information and follow the steps on the page.
2. Be sure students understand that they should immediately disconnect the thick wire
   and the battery after they observe what happens. The wires will get hot. This is a clue
   to why Franklin got shocked.

Questions and Answers:
 Students’ predictions and results will vary.
 Why is this called a “short circuit”? (Because the electricity travels a shorter route
   than the intended circuit. Electricity is not able to complete its intended path because
   the circuit is grounded somewhere.)
 Why did Ben Franklin get shocked? (His arms functioned like the thick wire in the
   experiment. Electricity traveled through his body instead of through the circuit, and
   he got shocked.)

What Makes the Electrons Flow? If you could see the atomic world inside a copper wire, you’d see that the atoms of copper can lose electrons so easily that there are billions of “loose electrons” hanging around between the atoms. These electrons are not going anywhere, but can easily jump from atom to atom. Copper atom Loose electron Every battery or other power source has an electric field. The field of a battery is produced by chemical reactions. The “mains” power is produced by magnetic effects in a generator at a power station. When the wire becomes part of a circuit, the electric field instantly reaches through the wire and exerts a force on every electric charge. The charged particles within the copper atoms cannot move, but the “loose” electrons immediately gain energy from the field and begin flowing in the wire. This flow of electrons is the electric current. The amount of “push” that the electric field can give the electrons is called “voltage”. searchText: Electricity and Safety Electricity can be dangerous for a number of reasons. It can cause fires. Remember , if current runs through a wire with high resistance it produces heat. This is good in a toaster, but not so good in some other situations. If resistance it too high in a wire it can over heat and cause a fire. This sometimes happens because too much current is put through a wire or a short circuit has occurred. What is a short circuit? Sometimes electricity takes a short cut through the wrong wire or through some other object that conducts electricity, such as a metal knife. We call this a short circuit. A short circuit is usually made accidentally. It bypasses part of a circuit. This can happen when two bare wires in a circuit touch each other. The part of the circuit bypassed by the short circuit stops working , and a large amount of current could start to flow through the short cut . This can generate a lot of heat in the wires and cause a fire Electricity can give you and electric shock . This is where current flows through a person. The heart and nerves of the bod y are controlled by electrochem ical impulses, so a large current can disrupt these and cause injury. An electric shock can also cause burns on the skin and internal tissues. Being Safe. Make sure wires are insulated. That is they have a plastic coating on them. If a wire has frayed insulation, have it repaired. Do not use electricity near water. Do not overload any one power outlet. Fuses and Circuit Breakers . Every electrical device in your home that is connected to a power supply is protected by a fuse somewhere along the circuit connecting it to electrical supply. The biggest fuses in your house are located in the fuse or circuit breaker panel . This is mounted on the wall where electrical power lines come inside your house and split into the c ircuits that run through your home . Without fuses, power surges from electric generators or short circuits within your house could burn out appliances, circuit boards and wiring. Any of these could lead to fires or further damage to the electrical systems within the building. Fuses all contain a filament or strip made of metals. This filament melts and break s when a certain current or "load" has been exceeded. It mel ts and breaks the circuit. This stops the current and prevents a fire. A new fuse must be used to re-establish the circuit. Depending on the circuit, different fuses will burn out(melt) at a specific current. Most household ci rcuits carry 10, 15 or 20-amp. Fuse wires are one-time use. Once they burn out, they have to be replaced. Circuit Breakers are like light switches. They do the same job as fuses but do not “burn out” when the current gets too high. When they overheat they switch off and lock. This "lock" (actually its more of a spring) causes the switch to shut off. You can flip the breaker to reset it, but generally if it’s too hot, it won’t stay on until it has cooled to a safe operating temperature. Make sure plugs and appliances have an earth wire. W hen a short circuit in the appliance occurs the earth wire allows the electricity to be safely conducted to the earth. This is better than the electric current running through you to the Earth. If in doubt use a qualified electrician .

LESSON 4 E&C                     SWITCHED ON




           AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
          Explore the concept of flow of electricity in simple circuit and how this can be
           controlled using switches.
          State that adding more batteries make globes shine brighter.


           EQUIPMENT


Per Class
          masking tape
          a bag of lollies e.g. M&Ms

Per Group
          2 D batteries (1.5 volts) per group
          3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
           at each end
          1 small globe (have spares)
          pop sticks for supporting batteries
          blu-tac
          alfoil
          4 drawing pins
          4 large paper clips
          2 split pins
          1 sponge cut in half (optional for extension)

Preparation
          Extension: cut sponges in half and cut a small square from the middle of each
           using a Stanley trimmer. The squares should be a uniform size i.e. 3cm x 3cm.
Safety
           Mains electricity must not be used.
     BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   Electrons flow from the negative end of the battery.
   As each electron move through a conductor, it pushes on the one ahead of it,
    such that all the electrons move together as a group.




   The tube is full of marbles, just as a conductor is full of electrons. If a single
    marble is inserted into this full tube on the left-hand side, another marble will
    immediately try to exit the tube on the right.
   Light globes consist of a glass bulb, which has a filament in between the two
    wires which go into and out of it. The filament is made from a very thin wire,
    which has a high resistance to electricity.
   This resistance causes the filament to heat up and glow when electricity
    passes through it.
   The electric current travels along the wire, enters the filament, heats up the
    filament, creates light and exits the globe through the other wire.
   The light that is seen from the light globe is the glow of the filament.
   Voltage e.g. 1.5 volts is a measure of how much energy each electron is given
    by the battery.
   A pressure switch is shown below that is suggested in the extension activity.
       LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
 Take students outside.
 Have all students stand in a circle arms distance apart. They are the carriers of
   electricity (electrons). They release their arms once in position.
 Nominate two students to be the battery, they form an arch with their arms held
   high for students to walk though.
 Nominate a student to stand next to the battery and hold a bowl of M&Ms or
   similar at the edge of the circle.
 Nominate two students to be the light, they form an arch with arms together out at
   waist height. Students need to bend down to pass through.
   The students are given an M&M as they pass the battery as energy. They then use
   some of this energy to get under the arch of the light and they must keep some of the
   M&M in their mouth to make it back to the battery to be given more energy. The
   students must walk around the circle and always stay an arms width apart.
  This represents the flow of electricity in a simple circuit.

Electricity In The Home

Read the following passage and answer the questions which follow.

Questions

1       Why do the wires in an electrical cord need to be thicker when connected to an
        electric room heater than when connected to a table lamp ?

2       How does the plug fuse reduce the risk of fire ?

3       What is the most common cause of a fuse “blowing’?

4       Why is the lowest value fuse wire chosen to protect a circuit carrying a normal
        current ?

5       Some electrical cords on appliances have two wires instead of three. Which wire
        would be missing on the “two wire” cord ?

6       In what circumstances is it safe to use a “two wire” cord instead of a “three wire”
        cord ?

7       What is the function of the earth wire ?

8       Why is the external casing of an electrical cord (flex) made of PVC, rubber or
        textile ?

9       A three wire cord has three wires capable of carrying an electric current. Name the
        three wires and describe the function of each wire.

10      From the table show, what plug fuse would you fit to appliances of power rating:

         (a)      400 W              (b)      2 kW         (c)   100 W ?

11      From the table show, what thickness of flex would you connect to:

        (a)       an iron            (b)      a vacuum cleaner   (c)   a toaster




                                     Electricity In The Home

Electricity in the Home / h drive / yr 9 disk / 1998 ed
                                                     Answers

1        An electric room heater draws more current than a table lamp so the wires may
        get hot if the current encounters resistance . Thicker wires offer less resistance and

searchText:
Electricity – pairs game

Introduction

A simple game designed to increase students’ confidence in the symbols of circuitry. Most
students have played ‘pairs’ at some time or other, so the rules are generally known to all.


Instructions

Divide the class into groups of between two and four players. Photocopy one set of the
sheets (as well as a sheet of answers) for each group. It is best to photocopy them onto
card or stiff paper that is thick enough so the typing cannot be seen through it!

Cut the sheets into individual cards. Remove any pairings not relevant to your group.

The aim of the game is to make pairs. A pair consists of symbol or graph with its
appropriate name. The answer sheet is given to each group to help them check the
pairings are correct.


Rules of the game

The cards are shuffled and spread out randomly face down on the bench.

The first player turns over two cards. If they are a pair, the player removes them and has
another go. If they are not a pair they are turned face down again. When the first player
has finished their go, play moves to the next player.

The winner is the one with the most pairs at the end.


Variations

One player can be nominated in each group whose sole responsibility is to check the
answers.

Groups of students can be formed according to their ability and different groupings of
cards given to them. The less able may find that sheets one and two are enough to start
with.

Also, with a bit of manipulation the names can be photocopied onto one colour of card and
the symbol or graph onto another. Therefore, when a student picks up a pair of cards they
are picking up two different colours. The game is faster this way.
