searchText: ﻿ Electricity is a form of energy where the energy supply comes from rapidly moving electrons. You may remember from year 8 that there are two main forms of electrical energy; • Static electricity • Current electricity Try this exercise to reacquaint you with static electricity 1. STATIC ELECTRICITY: SOURCES OF ELECTRICAL ENERGY A convenient source of electrical energy in the laboratory is the cell. The electrons the cell releases come from chemical reactions that occur within it. That is, cells are electron sources, and they can 'pump' electrons around an electrical circuit. A battery is made up of two or more cells linked together. 2. CIRCUITS a) Simple Circuits A circuit is a completed loop of conducting material joining the terminals of a cell or a battery. In the drawing of circuits, the following symbols are used: A circuit is drawn using straight ruled lines and in a rectangular shape even though in reality it may look quite different. Draw examples of circuits in the space below. i) a cell, a switch, a globe ,an ammeter, a resistor joined by conducting wires. ii) 2 cells, 2 globes, a bell and a resistor joined by conducting wires b) Electric Current An electric current is a flow of charged particles, pumped by a cell, around a circuit. In metals, the electric current is a flow of electrons. For a current to flow, the circuit must be complete. The size of current flowing around a circuit can be determined by examining the brightness of a globe in the circuit (the brighter the globe, the greater the current). A switch is a device for breaking a circuit. I can be drawn open or closed. Questions 1. In which of the following will an electric current flow? 2. Consider the following circuit: Which globes will glow when the following switches are on? i) Switch A ii) Switch A and Switch C iii) Switch B and Switch C iv) Switch A and Switch B 3. Now you draw a circuit in which there are 3 globes and 2 switches and 2 cells. When 1 switch is closed only 1 globe glows and when the other switch is closed the 2 other globes glow. ACTIVITY 1: Simple Circuits Materials: 1 electricity kit Examine all the components of the kit carefully and make sure you understand what each is. Method: 1. Build each of the following circuits and determine whether the globe is off, dim or bright. Draw each of the circuits and write your answer under each circuit diagram.. 2. Using 2 cells, 1 switch, 2 globes and conducting wires, build as many different circuits as you can, in which the light globes glows when the switch is on. Draw each of these circuits in the space below.. 3. Complete the tables by either connecting Put a  for lamp ON up each circuit, or by "tracing" the electron and a X for lamp OFF flow around the circuit. PROBLEM SHEET 1 – Simple Circuits 6. Complete the tables for the switches in the following circuits: 3. RESISTANCE Resistance in a circuit is any device that restricts or inhibits the current through it. 1. If a device e.g. a piece of wire, has a high resistance then the flow of electricity through it is greatly reduced. 2. If a device has a low resistance then the flow of electricity through it will be only slightly reduced. 3. The greater the resistance of a device, the smaller the current that will flow through the circuit. 4. When an electric current flows through resistance in a circuit, some of the electrical energy is transformed to heat energy i.e. heat is produced when electricity flows through resistance. 5. The greater the resistance, the greater the amount of heat produced. 6. Different conductors can have different resistance properties. For example, copper has a low resistance but nichrome and tungsten have high resistance. Light globes contain a piece of high resistance wire, which produces much heat (and thus light) when an electric current is passed through it. Thus, a light globe can be regarded as a device with high resistance. Example 1. Which of the following circuits has the greater resistance? 2. Which of the following circuits has the lower resistance? ACTIVITY 2: Resistance Method: 1. Set up the following circuit 1. How bright is the globe ? ______________________________________________________ 2. Replace the copper wire with a piece of nichrome wire (of the same length as the copper wire). How bright is the globe now ? ___________________________________________ 3. Compare the brightness of the globe with that obtained for the copper wire. _______________________________________________________________________________ 4. Which wire has the greater resistance, copper wire or nichrome wire? ______________________ 5. Now replace the nichrome wire with a small piece of 'steel wool' wire. Describe what happens to the globe now. ___________________________________________________________ 6. Explain what happened with the ‘steel wool wire’ . ____________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________ 7. Electrical energy is more easily transformed to heat energy using ______________ resistance wire. Application of Resistance 4. SHORT CIRCUITS A 'short circuit' is an alternative conducting pathway of lower resistance, which by-passes a particular resistance, globe or other appliance in a circuit. It is not necessarily the shortest path however. E.g. in the following circuit, the light globe will not light up because of the 'short circuit' between points A and B (i.e. it is 'easier' for the electrons to travel through wire AB rather than through the light globe.) ACTIVITY 3: Short Circuits Method: 1. Set up the following circuit 2. Sides A and B are made of two wires each, joined together by twisting the ends 3. Place another conducting wire between A and B. This is the short circuit. 4. Predict what you think will happen. ________________________________________________ Test your prediction. 5. What happens to the globe when the wire between A and B is connected ? ______________________________________________________________________________ 6. Explain what happened to the globe. ______________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________ 5. FUSES Fuse wire is a relatively high resistance conductor with a low melting point. A fuse wire will melt if too large a current is passed through it. When it melts the circuit is broken and current can no longer flow. A fuse is a protective or safety device, included in a circuit, which melts when a short-circuit or overload results in too high a current passing through the circuit. In circuit diagrams, a fuse has the symbol Example In which of the following circuits would you expect the fuse to blow if a wire was placed between A and B? ACTIVITY 4: Fuses Method: 1. Identify the following statements as true or false a) An electric current can flow more easily through a wire of high resistance than through a wire of low resistance. b) Wire with high resistance restricts the flow of electricity through it. c) If a wire has a low resistance, it will probably heat up considerably when a current is passed through it. d) A 'short circuit' is a circuit which is very small. e) A 'short circuit' can occur if in a particular circuit an alternative pathway of low resistance is produced. f) Fuse wire is made from wire which has low resistance and low melting point. g) Fuse wire is made from wire which has high resistance and high melting point. h) Nichrome wire has a higher resistance than copper wire. i) The wire used to make the filament in a light globe has high resistance and low melting point. 2. Making an Electromagnet
 Aim: To build an electromagnet

Equipment:
• Insulated copper wire                               Safety Information
                                                      Take care when handling and cutting
• Wire strippers
                                                      wire to avoid cuts.
• Battery (9V)

• Iron nail (approx. 50mm)

• Crocodile clips - optional

• Paperclips

Method:
Step 1: Wrap the copper wire around the iron nail, leaving
about 10cm lengths at each end. Try not to wrap it overly
tightly around the nail - you should be able to remove the
nail from the coil after wrapping.

Step 2: Carefully strip the insulation from the ends of the
wire to expose the copper inside and to make a connection.
(Or connect with crocodile clips, if available).

Step 3: Connect the exposed ends, one to each terminal of
the battery.

Step 4: Test your electromagnet by observing whether it
attracts the paperclips.



  Exploring further
  You could investigate how the number of coils in your wire affects the strength of the electromagnet.

  You could investigate how the number of batteries connected affects the strength of the electromagnet.

  You could investigate how the metal core inside the coil affects the strength of the electromagnet.

subject: Science
searchText: Gamma ray 1 Gamma ray Gamma rays (γ-rays) are electromagnetic waves with the smallest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum.[1] They were discovered in 1900 by Paul Villard, and named in 1903 by Ernest Rutherford. Gamma rays are like x-rays, but the waves are smaller. Both gamma rays and x-rays are photons with very high energies, and gamma have even more energy. They are also a type of ionizing radiation. Gamma rays can travel through thicker materials than x-rays can. Gamma rays are produced by some types of radioactive atoms. Cobalt-60 and potassium-40 are two isotopes that emit gamma rays. Cobalt-60 is created in accelerators and is used in hospitals. Potassium-40 occurs naturally. Small amounts of potassium-40 are in all plants and animals. Gamma rays from potassium-40 each have an energy of 1460 thousand electron volts (keV). Gamma rays and X-rays can also be distinguished by their origin: X-rays are emitted by electrons outside the nucleus, while gamma rays are emitted by the nucleus.[2] Gamma rays in medicine Gamma rays can also go through the skin to kill cells, such as cancerous cells. Doctors can use radiation therapy machines which produce gamma rays in hospitals to treat people with some types of cancer.[] Doctors also use gamma rays to find disease. In hospitals, doctors can give patients radioactive medicine which emits gamma rays. Doctors can find some types of disease by measuring gamma rays which come from a patient afterward. You can also use gamma rays to sterilise (clean) hospital material.[] References [1] The electromagnetic spectrum is made of many types of waves that are like light, but you can not see all of them. reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿Health Effects of Noise Noise Exposure Noise is perhaps the most common occupational and environmental hazard. As many as 30 million Australians are exposed to potentially harmful sound levels in their workplaces. Outside of work, many people pursue recreational activities that can produce harmful noise. Non-occupational sources of noise include chain saws and other power tools, amplified music, and recreational vehicles such as motorcycles. Some types of toys for children can produce sounds capable of causing permanent hearing damage. Common Sources of Noise Sound Loudness (dB) Gunshot (peak level) 140 to 170 Jet takeoff 140 Rock concert, chain saw 110 to 120 Diesel locomotive, stereo headphones 110 to 120 Motorcycle, lawnmower 90 Conversation 60 Quiet room 50 Whisper 30 to 40 Noise can be described in terms of intensity (perceived as loudness) and frequency (perceived as pitch). Both the intensity and the duration of noise exposure determine the potential for damage to the hair cells of the inner ear. Even sounds perceived as "comfortably" loud can be harmful. Sound intensity is measured as the sound pressure level in the decibel (dB) scale. Noise can cause permanent hearing loss at chronic exposures equal to an average of 85 dB or higher for an eight-hour period. The decibel scale is a logarithmic scale. A 3-dB increase represents a doubling of the sound intensity. Four hours of noise exposure at 88 dB(A) is considered to provide the same noise "dose" as eight hours at 85 dB and a single gunshot, which is approximately 140 to 170 dB, has the same sound energy as 40 hours of 90-dB noise. Health Effects When sounds are measured in decibels, the softest sounds we can hear are about 1 dB and extremely loud sounds are about 150 dB. Most people find sounds louder than 130 dB very painful. To reduce the risks of hearing damage, workers in noisy jobs are now required to wear protective ear muffs. The cabins of noisy machinery are insulated to reduce noise. Apart from deafness, another common hearing problem caused by too much noise exposure is tinnitus. This is when you hear a constant ringing sound in your ears.

title: How Sound Travels
subject: Science
searchText:
How Sound Travels


Objectives:

1. To demonstrate that sound moves through different states of matter.

2. To observe that sound moves better through a solid than it does through a
  liquid or a gas.

Materials needed:

Demo: bell, tuning fork, cork, balloon, two spoons, musical triangle, slide
   whistle, two wood blocks, windup clock, 12" ruler, large jar filled
   with water, paper bag, metal can and lid, plastic container with lid,
   metal bar, music box motor.

Each group needs: meter stick, windup clock, self-sealing plastic bag filled
    with water, a block of wood (the same thickness as the plastic bag of
    water), two plastic cups with one end of a string through the hole in
    the bottom of one cup and the other end of the string through the hole
    in the bottom of the other cup. Knot the ends of the string to stop it
    from pulling out of the holes (home-made telephone), a third plastic cup
    with a string attached to the bottom of the cup, a metal rod.

Strategy:

Have the children identify different sounds made behind a screen (or desk) by
using various materials: ringing a bell, hitting a tuning fork on a cork,
blowing up a balloon and releasing air by stretching the neck of the balloon as
the air escapes, tapping two spoons together, striking the musical triangle,
blowing a slide whistle, hitting two wooden blocks together and ringing an
alarm clock. Record the children's answers on the board. Show the materials
used and check against the predictions made.

Hold a ruler over the edge of a desk and vibrate it asking such questions as:
What is happening? What is your evidence? What is always happening to an
object when it is making a sound?

Strike a tuning fork on a cork and quickly lower it into a glass of water.
Ask the questions stated above. Does sound travel through other things?

Activities:

Demo: Does sound travel through paper? through plastic? through metal?
   1. Put a ringing alarm clock in a paper bag.
   2. Close the bag. Can you hear the clock ringing now?
   3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 using a plastic container and a metal can.

    Does sound travel through water?
    1. Fill a glass jar nearly full of water.
    2. Have one student cover one ear with her/his hand. Put the other
      ear against the glass jar.
    3. Ask another student to hit two spoons together under water.
      Do you hear a sound?

Sound travels through different kinds of matter. Sound travels through gases,
liquids and solids.

Group: What kind of matter does sound travel best in--air, water, wood or
    metal?
  A. 1. Hold a plastic bag of water against one of your ears. Cover
       your other ear with your hand. Have someone hold a ticking
       clock against the bag of water. Listen.
    2. Keep the clock in the same place. Remove the bag of water. Listen.
    3. Place a block of wood between your ear and the clock. Listen.
       Do you hear the clock best through the air, the water or the wood?
   B. 1. Place the clock 20 cm away from your ear and listen to the ticking.
    2. Have your partner hold the clock at the 20-cm mark on the meter
       stick. Place your ear at the end of the meter stick and listen.
    3. Have your partner hold a metal rod to your ear and place the clock
       against the rod 20 cm away from your ear. Listen. Does sound move
       differently through some solids than it does through others?

  C. 1. Take the plastic cups (telephone) and hold your cup to your ear
       while your friend talks slowly and clearly into the other cup. Keep
       the string tight. How does it work? What is vibrating? How do the
       vibrations of your friend's voice reach your ear?
    2. Can a third person talk and listen if another cup with a string is
       attached? Take the separate cup with the string and attach it to
       the first line. Keep all strings tight while one friend talks into
       one cup and the other two friends listen. Can you hear the message
       of the third party? How many lines could you attach? Does each
       addition weaken the vibrations?

Draw three squares on the board and in each square draw molecules spaced
accordingly to illustrate the three states of matter: gas (molecules far
apart), liquid (molecules closer together) and solid (molecules closest
together). Have students identify the different states of matter for each
square.

Finally, take the small music box motor, hold it in your hand and allow the
music to play. Ask the students if they hear the music. Now place the music
box motor on top of your desk or on a large surface area and listen to the
melody. Is there any difference? Can the students hear the music now? Why?

searchText:
It is possible to predict exactly where the image of an object will appear when that object is in front of a
curved mirror. If you select a point on an object (traditionally the tip of a vertical arrow), draw a couple
of light rays from that point and follow some rules about reflection, you can find the position of the
reflected arrow tip. The position where the two light rays from the object meet or appear to meet after
reflection fixes the image. 
Here are some things about light rays that you need to know to draw concave mirror diagrams:
•
A parallel ray is a ray that is parallel to the axis.
•
A focus ray is a ray that travels through the focus.
•
An incoming ray travels from the object to the mirror.
•
A reflected ray travels away from the mirror.
•
After an incoming parallel ray is reflected, it becomes a reflected focus ray.
•
After an incoming focus ray is reflected, it becomes a reflected parallel ray.
•
If an incoming ray does not hit the mirror, extend it backwards.
•
Reflected rays that don’t seem to meet might do so if they are extended backwards. 
•
If reflected rays do not meet, a clear image is not produced.
•
If the image is on the same side of the mirror as the object, it is a real image. 
•
If the image is on the opposite side of the mirror to the object, it is a virtual image.
Compared to its object, an image can be closer to the mirror, further away or the same distance from the
mirror. It can be smaller, larger or the same size. It can be upright or inverted, and real or virtual. 
The following diagram shows how drawing a parallel ray and a focus ray from the tip of an arrow can be
used to position the reflected tip of the arrow:

searchText: Infrared 1 Infrared Infrared (IR) radiation is a type of electromagnetic radiation (a wave with electricity) . The wave is longer than light which humans can see and shorter than microwaves. The word infrared means below red. It comes from the Latin word infra (meaning below) and the English word red. (Infrared light has a frequency below the frequency of red light.) Red light has the longest wavelength that human eyes can see. Picture of dog in mid-infrared Infrared waves cannot be seen by the eye. The infrared wave is between 750 nm and 1 mm. People sense infrared as heat. Most remote controls use infrared to send the control signals. Telecommunications Before Bluetooth was invented, some computers, personal digital assistants, and mobile phones were using the infrared technology to send files to other devices. Bluetooth replaced infrared in the early 2000's. Infrared is limited by the need to have both devices in a "line of sight" with each other.[1] Infrared lasers are used to provide the light for optical fiber communications systems. Infrared light with a wavelength around 1,330 nm (least dispersion) or 1,550 nm (best transmission) are the best choices for standard silica fibers. Spectroscopy Infrared vibrational spectroscopy (IR spectroscopy) can be used to identify molecules by listing their chemical bonds. An IR spectrometer is a machine that shines infrared light from a set range of frequencies on a sample. It measures which exact light frequencies are absorbed by the sample. Each chemical bond in a molecule vibrates at a frequency which is characteristic of that bond. A group of atoms in a molecule may have multiple modes of oscillation caused by the stretching and bending motions of the group as a whole. If an oscillation leads to a change in dipole in the molecule, then it will absorb a photon which has the same frequency. The vibrational frequencies of most molecules correspond to the frequencies of infrared light. Typically, the technique is used to study organic compounds using light radiation from 4000–400 cm−1, the mid-infrared. The spectrometer records all the frequencies of absorption in a sample. This can be used to gain information about the sample composition in terms of chemical groups present and also its purity (for example a wet sample will show a broad O-H absorption around 3200 cm−1). Invasive procedures 
In medicine, a procedure is a process carried out on a patient that is designed to lead to an improvement in the 
patient’s health. The procedure can be designed to either investigate or fix a problem. By their very nature, major 
operations are invasive procedures. Any surgical procedure that involves ‘invading’ the body in a way that can lead 
to severe trauma and shock is considered invasive. Examples include: traditional open-heart surgery, which requires 
a large incision to be made in the patient’s chest, followed by breaking open the breastbone; hysterectomies (the 
complete removal of a woman’s uterus); and hip replacements. 
1 
Define trauma and shock, as used above. 
 
2 
List a different example of an invasive procedure. 
Wherever possible, invasive surgery is avoided or modified in order to reduce stress and trauma. For example, 
women who require operations involving the uterus often choose laparoscopy (keyhole surgery) as an alternative 
to a full hysterectomy. Sometimes a full hysterectomy is necessary, for example, to treat cervical cancer and 
endometriosis. 
3 
Women who undergo full hysterectomies require hormone replacement therapy (HRT). What does this tell 
you about the uterus? 
 
Non-invasive and minimally invasive procedures
These either do not involve physically entering a patient’s body or minimise the entry as much as possible. The 
advantages of non-invasive and minimally invasive surgical procedures are great to the patients, the surgeon and the 
tax-paying public. Considerable amounts of money are spent annually on our health system, of which large amounts 
go toward post-operative care (post, meaning ‘after’). The longer a person remains in hospital, the greater the cost 
and the fewer the beds available for other patients.
4

Aim

To investigate a number of different ways in which sounds are produced.

_ clamp stand

What to do
Carry out the experiments below, and for each one answer these three questions.
1 What is producing the sound?
2 How can the sound be made louder or softer?
3 How can the sound be made higher pitched or lower pitched?

A The tuning fork

Hold the tuning fork by the stem and hit one prong firmly against the rubber bung. Look
closely at the fork. What is happening while it is making the sound?
Sound the tuning fork again and touch one prong against the hanging ping-pong ball.
What happens to the ball?
Hit the rubber bung softly with the fork, so it just makes a sound, and then touch the
ping-pong ball again. Is there any difference between hitting the tuning fork firmly and
softly?
Sound a different sized tuning fork. Is the note higher or lower than with the first tuning
fork?




B The rubber band
Wearing goggles, pluck one of the rubber bands sideways and look closely at the band
while it is making the sound. What does it do?
 Pluck the other rubber bands. What difference do you notice in the sound? Can you see
a pattern? (The longer the band, the . . . )
Try plucking the same rubber band softly and then firmly. Is there a difference in the
sound?

What to do

1 What is producing the sound?
2 How can the sound be made louder or softer?
3 How can the sound be made higher pitched or lower pitched?

C The ruler

Hold the ruler down on the bench so that your hand is about 3 cm in from the
edge of the bench and about 20 cm of ruler extends over the edge of the bench.
Push the end of the ruler down slightly and let go. Does the ruler make a sound?
How does it move to make the sound?
Try again, but push the ruler down a bit more this time. Does the sound get louder or
softer?
Try again, but move the ruler so the amount hanging over the end of the bench is
shorter. Does the sound get higher or lower?




D Drinking straw pipes

Flatten about 2 cm of the end of a drinking straw. Cut the tapered end so that it makes a
point, like this:




Put this cut end into your mouth and blow.

Does it make a sound? What do you feel?
Practise with the straw until you can remember the sound. Can you change the
loudness?
Cut off 2 cm of the rounded end of the straw to make it shorter. Blow into the pointed
end again. Has the sound changed? Is it higher or lower?

title: Joes Eye and Questions
subject: Science
searchText:
Eye
For concentrated complexities, no other organ in Joe's body can equal me. No larger than a Ping-Pong ball, I have tens of millions of
electrical connections and can handle 1.5 million simultaneous messages. I gather 80 percent of all the knowledge Joe absorbs. He
thinks of me as a miniature television camera. I consider the comparison insulting. I am much more sensitive than the biggest, costliest
TV camera ever made. I am responsible for one of the greatest of all miracles - sight.

Today's world is giving me a hard time. I was not built for it. For Joe's prehistoric ancestors, the eye's main job was to see things at a
distance danger to be avoided, game to be killed. Only lately have I been called on for continuous close-up work.

Look at my anatomy and you will understand why I am having difficulty adjusting to today's demands. First, my front window - my
clear, 20 cent size cornea. It starts the seeing process by bending light rays into orderly patterns. Next, my pupil - an adjustable gateway
for light. In bright sun it is nearly closed; on a dark night it is wide open. Up to this point there is nothing about seeing that a cheap
camera could not handle.

My wonders really begin with my lens-a little envelope of fluid the size and shape of an oval vitamin pill. My lens is surrounded by a
ring of tiny, superbly strong, unbelievably hard-working muscles. When they tense, my lens fattens for near vision; when they relax, it
flattens for distant vision. This was a fine arrangement for Joe's caveman ancestors. Since they were mainly interested in things six or
more meters away, the muscles were relaxed most of the time. But Joe now lives in a close-up world-lots of reading, deskwork and
such. This keeps my ciliary muscles tensed a lot of the time. They grow tired.
In front of and behind my lens I have two fluid-filled chambers In front the fluid is like water; in back it is about the consistency of
egg white. The watery fluid keeps me firmly inflated. Both fluids must be absolutely clear to permit passage of light. Those "specks"
Joe sees when he looks at a bright light are cellular remnants left over from his days in the womb when I was under construction.
They will float aimlessly in his eye fluid as long as he lives.

When Joe looks at some object, the light passes through my lens, which brings it into correct focus on my retina, a kind of onionskin
wallpaper, which covers the rear two thirds of my interior. Except in Joe's brain, I do not think that
anywhere else in his body is so much packed into so small a space. Covering less than three-square centimeters, my retina
contains 137 million light-sensitive receptor cells 130 million shaped like rods for black-and-white vision, seven million shaped like
cones for color vision.

The rods are scattered all over my retina. Let a firefly pass at night and a complex chemistry gets under way. The faint light bleaches
rhodopsin, a purplish-red pigment in my rods. The bleaching process generates a tiny wisp of electricity--a few millionths of a volt, far
 too little to tickle a mosquito. This feeds into my straw-size optic nerve and is transmitted to Joe's brain at about 450 km. per hour. The
brain interprets the signals flooding in and hands down its verdict: a firefly. All of this intricate electrochemical activity has been
completed in about .002 second!

If my rods seem complex, my cones are far more so. They are concentrated in the fovea, a pinhead size, and yellowish depression at
the rear of my chamber. This is the center for acute vision - reading, any close work--and for color. A leading theory is that these
cones, too, have bleachable pigments, one each for red, green and blue. Like an artist mixing paints on a palette, Joe's brain blends
these colors to make scores of other hues. If anything should go wrong with this intricate electrochemical process, Joe would be -
color-blind--as one in eight men is to some degree. In dim light, activity of my cones diminishes, color sense vanishes and every thing
becomes gray, as my rods take over.

While Joe sees with me, he sees in his brain. A crushing blow at the back of his head, severe enough to destroy the optical center of his
brain, would produce permanent blindness. A lesser blow and he sees “stars” - a chaotic electrical disturbance. Joe gets clinching
evidence of the brain's role when he dreams. He "sees" pictures, even with my lids closed in total darkness. Had he been born blind, he
would dream in terms of other sensory stimuli: touch, sound, even smell.

Joe was not born with the eyes he has today. At birth he could see only light and shadow. In the first few months he was farsighted,
like his caveman ancestors. To study his rattle, he held it as far as possible from his face. At first, Joe's eyes were poorly coordinated;
I would wander in one direction, my partner in another. Our wandering worried Joe's mother. It
should not have. A few months after birth we were moving in exact unison. By the time Joe was six, his vision was excellent.
But my peak sight did not come until age eight.

When he was young, Joe used to read in dim light. His mother warned that he was "ruining" his eyes. Nonsense. The young see
better in dim light than adults; and viewing under even the most adverse circumstances does no harm.

I have a number of other unusual attributes. Tiny though they are, my muscles, milligram for milligram, are among the body's
strongest. In an average day, I move about 100,000 times - to bring objects into sharp focus. Joe would have to walk 80km to give
his leg muscles similar exercise.

My cleaning equipment is similarly striking. My lacrimal glands produce a steady stream of moisture--tears to flush away dust and
other foreign material. My eyelids, of course, act as windshield wipers. Joe blinks three to six times a minute- more when I am tired.
This keeps my cornea moist and clean. The tears also contain a potent microbe-killer called lysozyme, which guards me from infective
bacteria.
 I try to ward off fatigue by resting as much as possible. I get time oh when Joe blinks. And my partner and I spell each other for a
while I may carry 90 percent of the work load, while Joe's other eye loafs; then it goes to work and I rest.

Nature gave me superb protection, placing me in a bony cavern with protruding cheekbones and forehead to act as shock absorbers
for direct blows. She also gave me supersensitive nerves to activate the alarm if there should be a potentially damaging intruder such
as cinder.

Still, I do have my troubles. My focusing apparatus often fails to work perfectly. Eyeglasses can correct 95 percent of this trouble.
Disease is a more serious problem. One potential disorder is really a plumbing problem either too much fluid entering me or too little
draining away. Pressure builds up, reducing the blood supply to my optic nerve. This is
glaucoma.

In severe instances, glaucoma can cause permanent blindness in a few days. More often it is a leisurely performer, producing
symptoms so mild they are apt to go unnoticed. These symptoms: colored halos around bright lights, loss of side vision, difficulty in
adjusting to the dark, a blurring of vision. At his age, Joe has one chance in 40 of glaucoma damaging his sight or blinding him
completely. His doctor can check for glaucoma simply by pressing a little gadget called a tonometer against my eyeball. Joe should
have this test every year. The treatment for glaucoma? Drugs in drop
form, or surgery.

Astigmatism is another of my common ailments. In this one, my cornea is not a spherical surface and distorts vision like a bubble flaw
in a piece of glass. Eyeglasses correct this condition A detached retina is more serious. It occurs when my retinal wallpaper blisters or
peels, and usually announces itself with flashing lights, image distortion blurring spots. A surgeon can "tack" my wallpaper back in
place with 80 percent chance of success.

Both my cornea and my lens-normally totally transparent tissue--can cloud and lead to blindness. If it is the cornea, Joe can re gain
sight with a corneal transplant. If it is the lens, he will need a cataract operation, and either thick eyeglasses or contact lenses
afterward.

Fortunately, Joe has so far escaped all these things. Just the same, I am growing old--like Joe's other organs. The transparency of my
lens is lower, accommodation muscles are weaker, hardened arteries are diminishing blood supply to my retina. These processes will
continue, but Joe should not worry unduly. The odds are heavily in favor of my providing him with serviceable vision as long as he
lives.
                                                       Questions
1. What is the role of the iris? (Use the term dilate and constrict in your answer)
                           2. What is the role of the lens?
                          3. What is the role of the retina?
                 4. What is the role of rods and cones in the eye?
                        5. Compare myopia with hyperopia.
                             6. What causes glaucoma?
                                 7. Why do we blink?

searchText: 2019 Version Light and Sound Junior Science What is light? Light is a form of energy that we can see and is given out by hot objects. It is made up of waves that travel outwards from a light source. Some of the waves reach our eyes, but most continue elsewhere. Waves can be transverse or longitudinal The two main types of wave form are transverse waves and longitudinal waves. All types of electromagnetic waves, including light, as well as water waves travel as transverse waves. Sound waves travel as longitudinal waves. Particle movement in transverse and longitudinal waves Longitudinal waves (sound) are a compressing and expanding wave that needs a medium to travel in. A medium could be gas, solid or liquid. Transverse waves (light) are a moving wave where each part of the wave travels up and down in repeating motion as the wave moves forward. These do not need a medium to travel through and can travel through empty space. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave Sound waves are mechanical waves requiring particles. (a medium to travel through) Air particles vibrate back and forward creating repeating patterns of high (compressed particles) and low (spaced apart particles) pressure. Sound travels in the form of longitudinal waves. One wave stretches from one compressed area of particles to the next. Waves of sound energy travel through air, water or solid. Waves generated from Earthquakes can be transverse or longitudinal The waves generated from an earthquake travel through the ground as both longitudinal and transverse waves. Primary (or P) waves are longitudinal waves and move the fastest. They are similar to sound waves and can travel at 5000 metres per second through solid rock. Longitudinal waves can also travel through liquid and gas, travelling at the speed of sound through air. Secondary (or S) waves are transverse waves and can only travel through solids. They travel at nearly half the speed of P waves. Waves transfer energy Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another without also transferring matter. Some waves need a medium (matter) to travel through in order to transport their energy from one location to another and are known as mechanical waves such as ocean waves, sound waves and earthquake waves. Other waves can travel through the vacuum of space where there is little or no atoms. These are know as electromagnetic waves. Examples of those waves include light waves, microwaves and radio waves. Electromagnetic radiation travels as waves Light and other types of electromagnetic radiation from the sun and even further away stars travel through space in a vacuum – Light does not need matter or a medium through which to travel. Each particular type of electromagnetic radiation, including each different colour of light, has a unique fixed length of wave, called the wavelength (λ), that it travels in. GZ Science Resources 8 Types of Electromagnetic radiation Some objects, such as the sun, release large amounts of energy. The energy can be emitted from the energy source in the form of electromagnetic radiation and travels in electromagnetic waves. Light, radio waves and x-rays are all forms of electromagnetic 9 radiation. GZ Science Resources Features of a wave Waves have troughs, the lowest point, and crests, the highest point. A wavelength is the distance between two closest crests. The amplitude of a wave is a measure of its height. The height is taken from a midpoint between a trough and a peak up to the top of a peak of a wave. A higher amplitude wave indicates a wave has more strength and that a light wave contains more photons, little packets of light energy. A nanometre is very small Small objects such as atoms, viruses and light waves need to be measured using very small units called a nanometre. A metre (m) can be divided into one thousand equal parts called millimetres (mm). If one millimetre is divided into a thousand equal parts then we have a micrometre (µm). If one micrometre is divided into a thousand parts then we have a nanometre (nm). A nanometre is one- billionth of a metre. Wavelengths can be measured in metres (m) or nanometres (nm). The type of electromagnetic radiation can be determined by its wavelength. 11 Frequency of a wave The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. The frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Because all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed then more waves of shorter wavelength will pass by a point over the same time as waves of longer wavelength . wave speed = wavelength x frequency Waves always travel at the same speed. A scientific value that always remains the same is called a constant. The constant for the speed of light is c = 3x108 m/sec or 300,000 kilometres per second. Because we know the speed of light, if we know either the wavelength (λ) in metres or the frequency ( f ) in hertz then we can calculate the other. Wavelength = speed of light / frequency c Frequency = speed of light / wavelength λ f 13 Light energy is carried by photons The amount of energy in a wave depends upon the frequency of the wave. The energy of a photon can be calculated by multiplying the frequency by another constant called Planck’s constant (h). This constant is named after a famous German scientist called Max Planck who made many discoveries about light and how it also travels as particles called photons. A photon does not have mass like matter does, it only contains energy. Planck’s constant is 6.626 x 10-34 joules per second. This value is so small because a photon is so tiny but there are so many of them within a light wave. Structure and Function of the human ear Sound waves travel through the ear canal and cause the eardrum to vibrate. The small bones of the inner ear transfer this vibration to the inner ear cochlea. The cochlea is fluid filled and lined with many hair-like nerve cells. Different length nerve cells detect different wave frequencies and transmit this information to the brain using electrical impulses that move along the nerves. Audible range of humans and other animals Humans can hear between 20 – 20,000 Hertz, a measure of frequency. The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. In comparison to many other animals, humans have a very limited audible range. Bats and dolphins can hear and produce sound at an exceedingly high frequency – and use it to bounce back off objects as sonar to “see” without light. Low rumbling noises of elephants and moles are below our auditory range but can travel long distances. Pitch and Loudness of sound Sound can be described by “characteristics” called pitch and loudness. Pitch is related to frequency – the higher the frequency then the higher the pitch of the note (a single sound at a particular level). Loudness is related to amplitude – the higher the amplitude the louder the sound. Reflecting sound waves Sonar (originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging) is simply making use of an echo. When an animal or machine makes a noise, it sends sound waves into the environment around it. Those waves bounce off nearby objects, and some of them reflect back to the object that made the noise. Whales and specialized machines can use reflected waves to locate distant objects and sense their shape and movement. Total internal reflection When waves are going from a dense medium to a less dense medium they speed up at the boundary. This causes light rays to bend when they pass from glass to air at an angle other than 90º. This is refraction. Beyond a certain angle, called the critical angle, all the waves reflect back into the glass. We say that they are totally internally reflected. All light waves, which hit the surface beyond this critical angle, are effectively trapped. The critical angle for most glass is about 42 °. Fibre optics makes use of this so light rays can travel down a glass fibre that has curves in it. Light energy can travel as rays Light travels fast and in straight lines. At the speed of light, which is 300,000 kilometers per second, light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to travel 149 million kilometers to earth. Light can go around the earth 7 times in one second. Light travels perfectly straight, until something bends it. The straight paths of light are called light rays.. Gaze Light energy can be reflected, refracted or dispersed Light travels in a straight line until it strikes an object or a force. Light can be: 1. Reflected by a mirror 2. Refracted by a lens 3. Absorbed by the object Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction) which is travelling through it, absorption where it enters but doesn’t leave again, or scattering (including reflection) where it bounces off. To see an object, light from that object— emitted by or scattered from it— must enter the eye. Transparent Translucent Opaque 22 Shadows are created when light rays are stopped A shadow is a dark area that is formed due to light travelling in straight lines which opaque objects block. An object that stops direct light rays creates a shadow. The shape of the shadow resembles the shape of the object. The shadow created when the Moon blocks the light from the Sun to the Earth is called a solar eclipse. The length of the shadow depends on the angle of the light source The length of the shadow formed on the ground depends on the angle that the light rays hit the object blocking the light.  Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                       4




When light energy hits an object, several different things can happen. What happens depends on the substance making up
the object. Some substances allow light energy to pass through them. Other substances will not allow light energy to
pass through and either reflect (bounce off) or absorb the energy.

                    ii)       Give three examples of such materials.


                    iii)      What name is given to materials which will not allow light to pass through?

                    iv)       Give two examples of such materials - one which reflects the light, and one which absorbs the
                              light.




Reflection of light energy


When light energy strikes an object, some of the energy is absorbed and some bounces off. The reflected waves which
bounce off the object enable us to see it.

6.         Draw a diagram showing the path of the light energy that enables us to see a book which is lit by a desk lamp.
           Show the direction of the light energy.

           The letters and word in the image are    the same as    or reversed compared to the word written on the
            paper.


8.         Write the word AMBULANCE as it would be painted on the front of an ambulance so a driver
           looking at it through a car mirror would read it correctly.
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                       5




Absorption and reflection of light

Although sunlight appears to be white, it is not actually a single pure white colour. It is made up of seven different
colours that you can see, called the visible spectrum. The colours of the visible spectrum are red, orange, yellow, green,
indigo and violet. Each of these colours correspond to light of different wavelengths with red light having the longest
wavelength and violet light having the shortest wavelength.

Different materials absorb some of the colours in sunlight (white light) and reflect others. The colour we see in an object
depends on the colours that are reflected back to our eyes. For example, a yellow object absorbs all colours except
yellow, and it reflects yellow.

White objects appear white because they reflect all the colours of sunlight, but black objects appear black because they
absorb all the colours and reflect none.

of        the bananas, and the different colours in the sunlight (white light) and in the reflected light.

Bending of light

10.       Place a coin in an empty cup and move your eyes until it is just out
          of view. Ask your partner to carefully fill the cup with water.
                   What happens to the coin?




11.       Put a pencil in a beaker of water. Look at the pencil from the side of the beaker. What do you see?




When light energy meets a new substance, the light changes direction or bends. When light bends going from one
substance to another, we say that the light is refracted. The light bends when going from one substance to another
because it moves at different speeds through different materials. It travels slower through water and glass than it does
through air.

title: Loud Music Causes Hearing Loss
subject: Science
searchText:
Loud Music Causes Hearing Loss
It is not uncommon among concertgoers to leave a concert unable to
hear. In most cases their hearing returns shortly. Unfortunately,
permanent hearing loss from loud concerts is becoming increasingly
common. The situation can be even more serious for musicians,
because they suffer more frequent and prolonged exposure to loud
music than most people. It can also be more devastating for a
musician to lose his hearing, because his livelihood and passion often
leave with his hearing.

Sound levels at concerts can be in the range of 120 to 140 db, well
beyond the 100 db normally recognized as the threshold at which
short-duration exposure can cause hearing loss. The loss is caused by
damage to fragile tissue strands within the cochlea. These strands are
called hair cells and resemble tiny hairs. They move with the fluid in
the cochlea to stimulate the electrical impulses in the auditory nerve.
The hair cells become damaged in the presence of loud noise.

The mechanism of damage is much like the mechanism by which
constant walking on grass can damage it. A person walking on a lawn
occasionally doesn't damage the lawn, because the grass has a
chance to recover between tramplings. But if the grass is subjected to
frequent traffic, it soon loses its ability to spring back and becomes
permanently damaged. Damage to the hair cells occurs the same way.
The louder and more frequent the exposure to loud noise, the more
damage the hair cells sustain.

Fortunately, our ears often warn us when we have subjected them to
potentially damaging sound levels. Temporary hearing loss is one
indication; ringing in the ears is another. If you experience either of
these symptoms after exposure to loud sounds, it's an almost sure
indication of temporary damage that could become permanent with
repeated exposure.

For people who are unable or unwilling to remove themselves from
noisy situations, earplugs can help preserve hearing. Earplugs are
especially effective at reducing the intensity of high frequency sound,
which is what does the most damage to the hair cells. A 15 or 20 db
reduction in the intensity of high frequency sound can delay or prevent
hair cell damage.

searchText:
Juliette M. Walker - Crown Community Academy



Now Hear This!

Juliette M. Walker        Crown Community Academy
751 E. 84st. Apt#2e         2128 S. St.Louis
CHICAGO IL 60619            CHICAGO IL 60623
(773) 488-3157            (773) 534-1680

Objective(s):

In this project, students will be able to describe how sounds are heard by the
human ear by creating a model of the human inner ear. This activity may be
utilized by grades 3 - 8.


Materials Needed:

Students may be placed into cooperative learning groups of 3.
 1long paper roll (used gift wrap rolls are perfect)
 plastic wrap        medium sized disc of foil rubber bands
 2cardboard paper discs doublestick tape             pink tissue paper
 flashlights        1 large box scissors       cardboard fork shape
(1 set of each item is needed for each group)

Strategy:

1. Students will create an eardrum by stretching a piece of plastic wrap across
  the end of the paper roll fixing it in place with a rubber band.
2. Students will create a set of ossicles with two cardboard discs and a fork
  shape of thin cardboard. This will be held together with doublesided tape.
3. Students will then attach a disk of shiny foil to one end of the roll, and
  will attach the other to the plastic wrap "ear drum" on the tube. This will
  complete the middle ear.
4. Students will then make an outer ear from a cone of cardboard with a hole
  at its end and will place it on the inside of the tube. Students may design
  their cone with pink tissue paper, for a more realistic look.
5. Students will then place the middle of the model of the ear on a box,
  leaving the ends of the rolls hanging off of the front and back.
6. Students will then shine a light onto the mirror and will ask a partner to
  to talk into the ear and watch for vibrations.
7. Have the students to watch the window of the ear. Have them describe how it
  responds to shouting, whispering, whistling etc.

Performance Assessment:

Students will be evaluated based upon their models, and oral explanations as
to how their ear works.

Conclusions:

This project works because the sound waves from the students voice makes the
plastic wrap vibrate. These vibrations are transmitted into the cardboard
"ossicles" and can be seen by watching the foil disc for movements. This is
a simple model of how the ear works.

References:

This project was adapted from the Encyclopedia of Science Projects written by
Pam Robeson, and Mick Seller (Shooting Star Press, 1994) (Aladdin Books, ltd,
1994)

searchText: Microwave 1 Microwave A microwave is a kind of high-frequency radio wave. It is often used to cook food in a microwave oven. We can see waves travelling through water. There are many sorts of these waves, such as ripples, swell, tsunami, and even sound waves that we do not see, but we hear if our ears are under the water. Likewise, many different types of waves can travel through the air. We detect one type with our eyes as colours; we detect another type when it lands on our skin, as warmth; another type is called X-rays. Other types of these invisible waves are called microwaves. We cannot see them. They can quickly penetrate quite deep into materials that contain water, for example most food. The energy in these waves makes the water molecules vibrate faster, which means the water gets hotter. Although they can also heat some metals, there are materials, including many plastics, which they pass right through, without heating at all. Mirrors and Lenses

Ray diagrams in a plane mirror
Ray diagrams are used to show an image of an object reflected in a mirror. Straight lines from the object are
drawn towards the mirror. Using the rule from the angle of incidence and reflection the lines are then reflected
back. Arrows are used on the lines to show the light rays’ direction.

The main rule for mirrors is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.




                                                                           This means that the angle of the light ray
                                                                           between where it arrives and the

                                                                           where it hits on the surface of the mirror
                                                                           is the same angle it leaves and the same
                                                                           perpendicular (normal) line.




Convex and concave mirrors
Mirrors work because light is reflected from them. The three types of mirrors are:




The images in the plane mirrors are the same size, the right way up but laterally inverted (changed right to left)
and is a flat reflecting surface.

The images in the concave mirror are
   a) magnified and the right way up when you are near to the mirror
   b) smaller and upside down when you are further away from the mirror
The images in the convex mirror are reduced and the right way up

The image formed in a convex mirror is always
upright and smaller in size. The light rays

the mirror where light rays do not actually pass

Refraction

A glass or plastic lens is transparent. This means that
light can be transmitted through the object without the
light being absorbed.

The medium of a plastic or glass lens has a different
optical density to air. Light rays entering the lens are
refracted to a different angle.

Refraction is when light travels between two optically

                                       The ray of light bends or refracts inwards when it moves into the
                                       glass. This makes the angle of refraction smaller than the angle of
                                       incidence.

                                       When the ray emerges from the glass back into the air then it
                                       continues on a parallel path to the original ray.


                                       A medium is any space or substance which will allow light to travel
                                       through it called transmission. Examples of different media include
                                       air, water and glass. Each medium has different optical density. The
                                       optical density of a medium affects the speed at which light rays
                                       travel through. When a light ray passes from one medium into
                                       another (e.g. from air into water) it will change direction where two
                                       media meet. This ‘bending’ of light is called refraction and it always

Assignments in Junior Science – Waves
If you want to see an object clearly when using a lens, you have to hold the lens a certain distance away
from the object and a certain distance from your eye. It is possible to predict where the focused image will
be, if the object is a known distance from the lens. Of course when using a lens, you just move your eye
to where the image is clearest and sharpest. To position images by drawing, a couple of rays from a point
on an object (e.g. the tip of an arrow) are selected, and drawn following some rules about refraction. The
refracted image position of the arrow tip will be given by where these rays meet.  
Here are some things about light rays that you need to know to draw images in a convex lens:
•
A parallel ray is a ray that is parallel to the axis.
•
A focus ray is a ray that travels through the focus.
•
A centre ray is a ray that passes through the centre of the lens.
•
An incoming ray travels from the object to the lens.
•
A refracted ray travels away from the lens.
•
Light rays should be drawn as though they refract (i.e. bend) at the middle of the lens.
•
After an incoming parallel ray (1 in the diagram below) is refracted, it becomes a refracted focus
ray (2).
•
An incoming centre ray (3) continues in a straight line through the lens.
•
After an incoming focus ray (4) is refracted, it becomes a refracted parallel ray (5).
•
If incoming rays do not reach the lens, extend them backwards.
•
If refracted rays do not seem to meet, extend them backwards. 
•
If refracted rays do not meet, a clear image is not produced.
•
If the image is on the other side of the lens to the object, it is a real image. 
•
If the image is on the same side of the lens as the object, it is a virtual image.

searchText: Radio wave 1 Radio wave Radio waves make up part of the electromagnetic spectrum. These waves are packets of energy with differing wavelengths, similar to visible light waves, X-rays or Gamma rays, except longer. A radio wave, like other electromagnetic waves, is similar to an ocean wave or any other type of wave. Both types of wave have a hill and valley shape, repeating over and over. A wavelength is measured as the distance from the top of one crest to the top of its neighboring crest. While the wavelength of visible light is very very small, less than one micrometer and much less than the thickness of a human hair, radio waves can have a wavelength from a couple centimeters to several meters. Antennas designed to detect radio waves are usually similar in size to the wavelength they wish to detect. This is why many radio antennas (like those on cars) must be very long. If the antennas are not close to the size of the wavelength they do not usually do a good job of detecting the waves. Manmade radio waves have been used for a long time to send information, receive information, and to 'see' objects. Radar uses radio waves to 'see' distant objects by bouncing waves off an object and seeing how long it takes for the waves to return. Radar can even be used to find oil or see what chemicals are in soil. Radios also use these waves to send and receive information. Natural radio waves were first discovered in the 1930s by Karl Guthe Jansky, working for Bell Laboratories. Before his discovery, everyone thought only people could generate radio waves. Bell was detecting static on his radio channels, and had Jansky try to figure out where this static, or interference was coming from. Surprisingly, the interference was coming from space! This discovery eventually led astronomers to look at radio waves along with optical waves to find things in the sky. These radio astronomers use giant Radio telescopes, shaped like satellite dishes, to gather and analyze the waves. Uses Radio waves are used for many things today. They broadcast radio and television, communicate with satellites, let mobile phones communicate with each other, make radar systems, and allow computers to share information without wires. Assignments in Junior Science – Waves
Reflection, refraction, diffraction, scattering
Waves
10a
Sound and light carry messages from one place to another. Light waves are transverse waves that do not
require a medium for transmission. Sound waves are longitudinal waves that do require a medium for
transmission. Sound and light waves seem to travel in straight lines ... or do they? 
Reflection
Like a bouncing ball, light can bounce off a
surface. The reflected light changes direction
when it bounces off a surface. Measurements
show that the angle of incidence equals the
angle of reflection (the law of reflection).
Smooth surfaces act as mirrors – light rays are
reflected uniformly and form images. Each bit of
a rough surface also obeys the law of reflection,
but the overall effect of the uneven surface is to
scatter the light everywhere. Clear images are
not formed. 
Optical fibres are tubes with an extremely thin
glass core. They are produced so that light will pass along the fibres bouncing off the walls (internal
reflection). As (ideally) no light leaves through the sides, a light ray is able to travel large distances in the
fibre.  
Sound is also reflected. We detect echoes when a reflected sound wave reaches our ears some time after
the original sound wave was heard. Reverberations are sounds that bounce off surfaces in all directions
and cause annoying background noise. 
Refraction
During refraction, light and sound waves change direction as if travelling
around a corner. When waves pass from one medium into another, the path of
the waves bends. There is also a corresponding change in the speed and the
wavelength of the waves. 
When light enters glass from the air, it bends one way; when it travels from glass
to air, light bends the other way. Objects appear to be bigger when seen through
a convex lens and smaller when seen through a concave lens.

Refraction
 Aim: To observe the relationship between angle of incidence and refraction


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Ray box
                                                         Filament bulb – risk of burns
• Single slit plate
                                                         Handle with extra care. Rinse any
• Lab pack (if needed)                                   burns under cold running water for
                                                         10 minutes and inform the teacher immediately.
• Protractor

• Pencil and ruler

• Paper




                Figure 1. Set-up



                                                                 Figure 2. Measurements


Method:
Step 1: Place the glass block flat in the middle of the paper and draw around it.

Step 2: Direct the light from the ray box onto one of the longer sides of the glass block, at a diagonal
angle.

Step 3: Trace over the ray as it leaves the ray box and enters the glass box (the incidence ray). You can
tidy up the line with the ruler afterwards.

Step 4: Trace over the ray as it leaves the glass block on the other side (the emergent ray). You can tidy
up the line with the ruler afterwards.


                                                 Page 1 of 2
                                                                                                 Refraction

Step 5: Remove the glass block and join the incidence and emergent rays with a straight line.

Step 6: Use the ruler and protractor to mark normal lines at the point where the incidence ray enters
the glass block, and the point where the emergent ray leaves the glass block.

Step 7: Measure the angle of incidence (A), angle of refraction (r) and angle of emergence (B). Record
these in the table.

Step 8: Repeat steps 1 to 7 for at least four different angles of incidence.


Results:


      Angle of Incidence                 Angle of Refraction                   Angle of Emergence




Questions:

1. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction.

2. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of emergence.

3. What is the name of the type of wave by which light is transmitted?

4. Explain refraction in terms of density and wave speed.



                                                 Page 2 of 2
 Answers:
1. The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of refraction; A > r.

2. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal.

3. Transverse wave (electromagnetic spectrum wave).

4. The velocity of the light wave is decreased as it enters a denser medium (the glass block). As
   it enters at an angle, the ray is ‘bent’ (refracted). When the light ray emerges into the original
   medium again (air) it resumes the same velocity and angle as before it entered the glass block.

Science in the news – living ear grown in lab

Teaching notes

This task can be used when covering cells, tissues and organs with GCSE students or high achieving
KS3 groups.
It is based on the article from The Week magazine called ‘Living ear grown in lab’. Further information
and web links can be found at http://www.nhs.uk/news/2013/08August/Pages/Artificial-ear-grown-in-
lab.aspx.
All links were available at the time of publishing.


Starter
As an interesting stimulus show the class the famous image of a human ear grown on a mouse's back
(http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/1949073.stm). You may also like to show them a video
(http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LHHe_q3DNas).
Ask the students to discuss in pairs why they think scientists have done this and feedback their ideas.
Explain that some people have lost ears through injury or because they were born without them (you
might like to show a suitable image at this point) and this kind of research is helping to work out ways
of building human tissue in the lab to help such people. It is called tissue engineering. The image
shown at the start shocked the world when it was released in 1997. Since then, tissue engineering is
making progress and the same team have recently announced improvements to the human ears they
are engineering.


Main
Students complete Task 1. If you have access to microscopes and slides with cartilage then students
could use them to take a look at some cartilage and draw what they observe.
Go through the answers with the students:


Answers

2. Cartilage is a tissue because it is made up of one type of cell (chondroblasts). The ear is an organ
   because it is made up of several different tissues all working together to perform a function.
3a. Cartilage in the outer ear contains mostly elastin in its extracellular matrix so it is flexible.
3b. The cartilage that makes up the rings around the trachea contain mostly collagen so it is strong
    enough to hold open the trachea so air can pass through.
4. Titanium was used because it is lightweight so the ear would be light enough to wear and also it is
   non-reactive. This is important so it does not react with the cells.
5a. The rat's immune system would have attacked the foreign cartilage cells and rejected the ear if it
    had a functioning immune system.
5b. If the ears are to be used in humans then the patient's immune system would have to be
     suppressed or the ear would be rejected. With a weak immune system the patient would be at
     risk from infections.
5c. To avoid this problem the replacement ear would have to be made using the patient's own
    cartilage cells.

Then ask students to work in small groups to complete Task 2. They should cut out the cards and use
the information to answer the question: 'How close are we to building replacement outer ears?'

Ask students from each group to read out their statement. Discuss with the class what steps the
researchers need to take next.



Plenary
Discuss with the students the need for scientists to develop techniques to build other replacement
body parts such as whole organs. Talk about why this is more complicated and why. For example,
organs are made up of many tissues working together, they require a blood supply and connection to
the nervous system.
Ask the students to consider the question: 'How close are we to building replacement organs?' Ask
them to stand in a line to form a continuum to show where they think we are in this endeavour.



Homework idea
Ask the students to do some research into other teams that are working in the field of tissue
engineering and summarise their work in their own words. For example, another recent news story
reported that a team have grown a miniature human brain (see http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-
23863544)

Assignments in Junior Science – Waves
Seeing is believing
Waves
13a
Our eyes are one of our sense organs. They detect light. 
On the outside, our eyes have protective eyelids. Closed, the eyelids protect eyes from smoke, onions, dust,
bright lights and physical intrusion. The eyelids are surrounded by hairs called eyelashes and by touch
receptors, that work together to protect our eyes. 
Eyes are cleaned and lubricated by tears that are produced in the tear gland. Positioned near the
eyebrows, the glands are not an external feature of the eye. Tears are released through tear ducts found
near the corners of the eyes. 
The coloured part of our eye is called the iris. It is a ring of muscle that changes the size of the pupil, the
dark central area. Light passes through the pupil. If the light is too bright, the iris decreases the size of the
pupil. If there is not much light, the iris increases the size of the pupil. 
A cross-section of the human eye reveals a thin, clear skin, the cornea, that covers the front of the eye. Its
properties allow light to pass through it. All the light that enters the eye is organised by the cornea and
lens. The lens is made from a clear translucent material and is surrounded by a lens muscle. When the
lens muscle relaxes, it becomes a large ring and the lens is made thin; when it contracts, it forms a small
ring and the lens becomes thick. The cornea and lens focus the light rays onto the retina, which is located
at the back of the eyeball. If a viewed object is close to the eye, the lens thickens so that the image of the
object is focused and clear on the retina. For a distant object the eye lens is flattened. The retina has light
receptors that are sensitive to the colours of light and to light brightness. The image of the object is upside
down on the retina. The receptors in the retina send electrical impulses to the brain via the optic nerve,
which is located outside the eyeball

 Answers
1. How was the current in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current remains the same / unchanged in a series circuit.

2. How was the current in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current is shared between the number of branches / bulbs in the parallel circuit.

3. How was the voltage in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage is shared between the bulbs in a series circuit.

4. How was the voltage in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage remains the same for all bulbs in a parallel circuit.

searchText: ﻿SERIES AND PARALLEL CIRCUITS There are two basic arrangements of components in a circuit. Series Circuits The resistors are added end-to-end so that the whole current flows through each resistor in turn. • There is only one path for the current through the circuit. • If one component stops working, they all stop working. • Resistance increases with more components added. Parallel Circuits The resistors are on separate branches, and the current splits up to flow through each branch, depending on its resistance. • Current splits up - there are multiple pathways. • If one component is turned off, the others keep working. • Resistance decreases for more and more resistors connected in parallel.
