searchText:
Sight, Sound and Colour

Structure and Function of the human ear



                                                               Sound waves travel through the ear canal and
                                                               cause the eardrum to vibrate. The small bones
                                                               of the inner ear transfer this vibration to the
                                                               inner ear cochlea.

                                                               The cochlea is fluid filled and lined with many
                                                               hair-like nerve cells. Different length nerve cells
                                                               detect different wave frequencies and transmit
                                                               this information to the brain using electrical
                                                               impulses that move along the nerves.

Audible range of humans and other animals

Humans can hear between 20 – 20,000 Hertz, a measure of frequency. The frequency of a wave is calculated by
the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time.

In comparison to many other animals, humans have a very limited audible range. Bats and dolphins can hear
and produce sound at an exceedingly high frequency – and use it to bounce back off objects as sonar to “see”
without light. Low rumbling noises of elephants and moles are below our auditory range but can travel long
distances.




Pitch and Loudness of sound

                                                           Sound can be described by “characteristics”
                                                           called pitch and loudness. Pitch is related to
                                                           frequency – the higher the frequency then
                                                           the higher the pitch of the note (a single
                                                           sound at a particular level). Loudness is
                                                           related to amplitude – the higher the
                                                           amplitude the louder the sound.



105 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Reflecting sound waves

Sonar (originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging) is simply making use of an echo. When an
animal or machine makes a noise, it sends sound waves into the environment around it. Those waves bounce
off nearby objects, and some of them reflect to the object that made the noise. Whales and specialised machines
can use reflected waves to locate distant objects and sense their shape and movement.




Structure of the Human eye
                                                         The human eye is a “collecting” organ that allows light
                                                         to reach sensory nerves which then transmit electrical
                                                         signals to the brain. The convex lens focuses the images
                                                         seen onto the retina of the eye. Various sensory cells in
                                                         the retina called rods and cones detect both amount of
                                                         light and colour of light. The iris opens to let more light
                                                         into the eye when it is dimmer. The muscles around the
                                                         lens change the shape of the lens. The blind spot is the
                                                         point of entry of the optic nerve on the retina and has
                                                         no light receptors. The cornea is the tough transparent
                                                         layer at the front of the eye.

                                                         Messages from the retina travel through the optic nerve
                                                         to the brain. The brain further processes the images in
                                                         various parts of the brain responsible for language,
                                                         speech and thinking.


White light is made from colours mixed together
                                                 White light is a combination of all the other colours of light mixed
                                                 together. The main colours that make up white light can be seen
                                                 in a rainbow. They are red, orange, red, green, blue, indigo (a dark
                                                 inky blue) and violet. They can be remembered by the acronym
                                                 ROY G BIV.

                                                 The sun releases visible light of all wavelengths, when combined
                                                 becomes white light. When this white light hits the surface of a
                                                 red apple all the other colours of light except red are absorbed.
                                                 The red light is instead reflected, and when hitting our eyes, we
                                                 see the apple as red because that is the only wavelength
                                                 detected.
106 | P a g e    GZ Science Resources
 We see colours because of what wavelengths are reflected
A colour is a property processed by an object as
a result of the way it reflects, absorbs or emits
light of a specific wave length.

We see a tree as green because the leaves absorb
the red and blue light waves, and only the green
light is reflected into our eyes.




Prisms work by diffracting colours of different wavelengths
                                                    A prism is a triangular block used to disperse
                                                    white light. This causes light of different colours to
                                                    be refracted differently and to leave the prism at
                                                    different angles, creating an effect like a rainbow.
                                                    The degree of bending of the light's path varies
                                                    with the wavelength or colour of the light used,
                                                    called dispersion. This can be used to separate a
                                                    beam of white light into its spectrum of colours.


Primary and Secondary colours

 Combining light colours is said to be
 additive. Each wavelength of light
 adds to another.

 The three main colours of light are
 called primary. Two primary colours
 together make a secondary colour
 and all three primary colours
 together make up white light.

 NOTE: Paint absorbs light waves. The
 paint is called subtractive because
 with each addition of colour more of
 the wave lengths are absorbed. The
 three primary colours of paint are
 cyan, yellow and magenta. When
 these three are added together the
 resulting colour is black: all the
 different wavelengths of coloured
 light are absorbed.

Lighthouse features

How does sound move?

If a tuning fork is struck, it vibrates. When the prongs of the fork move forward, energy is transferred from the prongs to
the air particles and the particles are pushed closer together to form a patch of compressed air. Once formed, this area of
compression moves through the air as the particles collide with other particles and pass their energy on. This causes a
travelling vibration which is called a sound wave.

When the vibrations reach the ear drum, it is made to vibrate in step with the tuning fork. The vibrating ear drum passes

The frequency of a sound wave determines the pitch of the sound. Low notes have a small

searchText:
Sound is Vibration


Objectives:

This lesson is designed for grade levels 1 - 3.
1. To understand that sound is caused by vibration.
2. To understand that sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.
3. To understand that high pitched sounds are caused by more vibrations and low
  pitched sounds are caused by fewer vibrations.

Materials Needed:

plastic ruler(s), tuning forks of 2 or 3 different pitches, ping-pong ball
attached to a string with tape, boom-box-type radio, balloon filled with air,
paper plate, tiny pieces of torn paper, baggie filled with water, scissors,
several glass bottles of the same size, large container for water, styrofoam
cups, wire coat hangers, string (different types), wire cutters, pencils (with
wooden ball attached to the eraser end if possible), stopwatch, flower pots of
varying sizes attached to rope, long tubes of PVC pipe cut to different lengths
for different tones, xylophone, plastic straws, tape.

Strategy:

1. Ask children if anyone knows what a vibration is. Ask children to vibrate
their bodies. Write vibrate on board. Put a plastic ruler overhanging the edge
of a table; hit the ruler and watch it vibrate. Ask: "Can we see the vibration?
Can we hear the vibration? Can we feel it?" Show tuning fork; hit; listen;
touch vibrating tuning fork to ping pong ball attached to a string. Observe the
effect; ask same questions. Pass tuning forks around so children can experience
the sound and feel the vibration; note differences in pitch. Hold inflated
balloon in front of boom-box speaker with volume turned up loud. "Can you feel
the vibration? Where is it coming from?" Place small paper plate with tiny
pieces of paper on it on top of speaker. (Boombox must be turned so that
speakers are facing up.) Observe what happens to the papers. Explain that all
sounds are caused by something vibrating; sound is vibration, etc.

2. How do vibrations from tuning fork and ruler reach us as sound? The
vibrations cause waves to carry sound through the air. (You will perhaps need
to discuss waves, depending on age and experience of children.) "We know
sound
travels through air. Does it travel through a solid? Put your ear on the desk.
Tap the desk. What do you hear?" Try several such examples. "Does sound
travel through a liquid?" Get children to talk about experiences they have had
such as talking underwater in the bathtub or swimming pool. Can they hear
sound
under water? "Try putting a plastic baggie filled with water next to your ear.
Have another child speak loudly directly into the other side of the baggie. Can
we hear the sound through the water? Does sound travel through a solid, a
liquid, and a gas (air)? When was it the loudest?" (through the solid) "Why
do you think this may be true?" (The molecules in a solid are more tightly
packed, so the vibration can travel without being dispersed as it does in air.)

3. Show a child's xylophone or an autoharp. Strike a short bar, then a long bar
and ask children what they heard. Do the same for the lengths of PVC pipe.
(Hit the end of the pipes with the palm of your hand.) Make a kazoo out of a
plastic straw by flattening one end and cutting it into a triangular shape;
blow. As one person blows through the kazoo, another takes a scissors and snips
an inch or so off the end. Keep doing this and ask the students to notice
 what's happening to the sound as the straw gets shorter. Help them relate the
shortness of length to high pitch through a variety of such experiences.

4. Now allow the children to experiment and "play" with all the materials so
that they develop strong physical understanding of vibrations in all the ways
that have been presented. Have a set of 8 identical bottles and a container of
water and have them fill the bottles with varying amounts of water. See if they
can match the scale of the bottles to that of the xylophone. Give children the
opportunity to make a string phone or wire-hanger chime. (Tie a length of
string to each end of a wire coat hanger. Put the other end of each string in
your ears, tap the hanger against something like a desk. Listen for the ringing
through the string.)

Performance Assessment:

1. Children must: Arrange bottles with varying amounts of water in row
according to pitch. Explain the relationship between the amount of water and
the pitch. Tell what is vibrating. Blow across or just into the top of each
bottle and explain how the relationship between pitch and the amount of water in
the bottle changes. Hypothesize as to why this might be.

2. Make a stereo coat hanger as explained above. Tell how you might make one
with a higher pitch (shorter wire). Cut hanger with wire cutter to get
different lengths and different pitches.

3. Make a straw kazoo. Listen to its pitch. Have your partner cut off an inch
or two with a scissors while you are blowing. What happens to the sound? Cut
off another inch. What do you notice now?

searchText: ﻿Sound Production in Musical Instruments [OCR from document pages] Sound Production in Musical Instruments What produces thi ind? rq How can th| chang Musical Instrument Families Musical instruments are classified by the way they make sounds. Sounds are the result of vibrations and in each type of instrument the vibrations come from a different source. String Instruments Vibrating strings provide the sound in stringed instruments. The player makes the strings vibrate in one of three ways: plucking, bowing or hitting. How the pitch is changed The length, thickness and tension of the string all affect its pitch. Longer, thicker or looser strings will vibrate more slowly than shorter, thinner or tighter strings. Faster vibrations will cause a note that is high in pitch and slow vibrations will cause notes that are low in pitch. The different pitches on stringed instruments are obtained by having many strings of different lengths or by changing the vibrating length of the string by stopping them at different points. Five examples of the type of instrument. String Instruments Wind Instruments Percussion Instruments Musical Instrument Families Musical instruments are classified by the way they make sounds. Sounds are the result of vibrations and in each type of instrument the vibrations come from a different source. Wind Instruments Sound produced by wind instruments comes from a vibrating column of air inside the instrument. There are two types of wind instruments, brass and woodwind. For brass instruments, the column of vibrating air is caused by the vibrating lips of the player. The vibrating column of air in woodwinds can be created in one of three ways: by blowing across an edge, like the flute, by blowing between a reed and a fixed surface, as in the clarinet or by blowing between two reeds, as in the oboe. How the pitch is changed Wind instrument pitch depends on the volume of air that is vibrating. A larger volume of air vibrates more slowly than a smaller volume causing a lower pitch. The player can change the pitch by opening and closing holes along the instruments length Musical Instrument Families Musical instruments are classified by the way they make sounds. Sounds are the result of vibrations and in each type of instrument the vibrations come from a different source. Percussion Instruments In percussion instruments the source of sound is a vibrating membrane or a vibrating piece of solid material. The percussionist normally causes the materials to vibrate by hitting them but many are played by shaking or rubbing. How the pitch is changed Due to the complex ways the sound source vibrates, most percussion instruments do not have a definite pitch. The pitch of these instruments depends on the amount of material that is vibrating. This means that the instruments must have a different vibrating body for each note. The pitch of percussion instruments with membranes also depends on the thickness and tension in the membrane.

searchText:
Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Soundproofing
Cities are noisy places. The constant assault of noise on the ears of city dwellers has been found to have had an impact on hearing abilities. There are estimates that as many as 1 in 6 adults who live in cities have some form of hearing loss. Engineers who specialise in sound are called acoustic engineers. One of their common tasks is to reduce the amount of noise that enters buildings and workplaces. 
When a sound wave travelling through the air hits a solid material, some of the sound energy is reflected back towards the source, some of it is transmitted through the material and some of it is absorbed by the material (and turned into heat energy). 

Different materials reflect, transmit and absorb sound to different extents. Acoustic engineers make use of these properties to minimise the transmission of sound. This is called soundproofing. 
Investigate soundproofing materials 
Aim
To investigate which materials have good soundproofing properties
Materials
Device that can emit sounds at specific frequencies (e.g. tone emitter or mobile phone app)
Decibel meter (e.g. handheld meter or mobile phone app)
Shoebox 
Range of soundproofing materials (e.g. polystyrene, cotton wool, rubber, cardboard, fabric, foil, bubble wrap)
Method
Find a quiet location to carry out your experiment.
Place the sound-emitting device inside the shoebox. Leave the lid off. 
Place the decibel meter about 1 metre away from the sound-emitting device.
Set the sound-emitting device to a frequency of 100 Hz and generate a loud tone. (Note: This volume level must be kept constant for the rest of the experiment.)
Measure the level of the sound generated by the sound-emitting device in decibels (dB) and record it in the table in the Data and results section. 
Adjust the sound-emitting device to 500 Hz, measure the sound in decibels and record it in the table. 
Adjust the sound-emitting device to 1000 Hz, measure the sound in decibels and record it in the table. 
Place the lid on the shoebox and repeat your measurements at the three different frequencies. Record your results in the table. 
Choose five different soundproofing materials and list them in the table. For each material, use it to cover the box and repeat the measurements at the three frequencies. Record your results in the table.

Discussion and reflection
Rank the soundproofing materials in order from least soundproof to most soundproof.




Using the words “reflection”, “absorption” and “transmission”, describe what is happening to the noise coming from the sound-emitting device as it travels through the shoebox and the soundproofing material and arrives at the decibel meter. 





Identify the characteristics of the materials that were best at soundproofing. Describe what they have in common. In particular, consider the density of the materials (how compact they are). 





Identify the characteristics of the materials that were worst at soundproofing. Describe what they have in common. Again, consider the density of the materials.





Analyse the effect of the soundproofing materials at different frequencies. Describe the effect, if any, the frequency of the sounds had on the amount of sound energy that was absorbed by the soundproofing materials. 





Imagine you are an acoustic engineer, and it is your job to soundproof a drum rehearsal room. The only materials you have to use are glass, wood and rubber. Identify which of these soundproofing materials you would use and why. Using what you have learnt about the characteristics of a good soundproofing material, explain why your chosen material is best. 





Extension activity: The Epidaurus Theatre – an acoustic masterpiece
As well as reducing sound, acoustic engineers must sometimes enhance sound, such as in concert halls and theatres. A lot of scientific planning goes into choosing the materials and shapes in modern theatres to optimise how sound waves travel from the stage to the audience in a systematic manner. 
In the 4th century BCE, long before the nature of sound waves was well understood, a theatre was built in Epidaurus in Greece that is generally accepted to be an acoustic masterpiece. In this large, open-air theatre, audiences of up to 14,000 people can easily hear actors and musicians from the back seats … without microphones!

Investigate and describe the secret behind the Epidaurus Theatre’s amazing sound properties.

searchText: Sources of Light We can see most objects because light bounces off of them into our eyes. However some objects are a source of light as they are luminous . This means they produce their own light eg the sun or a torch. Objects that do not produce their own light eg the moon or people, are non-luminous . They require light from another source to be seen. Non-luminous objects can be classified into 3 groups: Transparent – Light can trav el through it easily without any interference eg glass, air, water Translucent – Some light is transmitted but some is absorbed. Vision is interfered with eg frosted glass. Opaque – No light is transmitted eg people, wood and metal. When ever light is prevented from hitting a surface by an opaque object a shadow is formed.

searchText:
Early telephones contained a carbon microphone in a handheld mouthpiece along with a separate
earpiece, dialing mechanism and other parts. The microphone changed sound waves into varying electric
currents. The earpiece converted varying electric currents from another telephone back into sound waves. 
High pitch sounds have high frequencies and result in electric currents that change direction (alternate)
quickly (with high frequency). Deep or low pitch sounds with their lower frequencies end up as electric
currents with a lower frequency. Soft sounds have vibrations with small amplitudes, while loud sounds
have vibrations with large amplitudes.
A carbon microphone is a small box with two metal plates – one fixed and the other free to vibrate, each
connected by wire with other parts of an electrical circuit. Carbon powder fills the space between the two
plates. When the carbon powder is loosely packed, it conducts electricity poorly. When it is compressed, it
is a better conductor of electricity.
A soft, deep sound hits the free-moving plate (diaphragm) of a carbon microphone resulting in weak and
low frequency vibrations of the plate. These plate vibrations cause weak and low frequency electricity
pulses in the wires leading away from the carbon microphone. 
The diagram at right represents a medium pitched normal sound. The sound
wave has been represented like a transverse wave in the diagram, although it
is really a longitudinal wave. Transverse waves are easier to draw and
differences can be shown clearly, so particular sound waves are often sketched
like transverse waves.

searchText:
Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Spectrometer 
When the different wavelengths of light are separated out, we see the emission spectrum of the light. 
The instrument that is used to observe emission spectra is called a spectrometer. In its simplest form, a spectrometer consists of a box with two key elements: 
a slit to produce a thin parallel light beam
a diffraction grating that spreads out the different colours in the light beam by wavelength. 
Electrons move around the nucleus of an atom in spaces that are at set distances from the nucleus. These spaces are known as electron shells. Different elements absorb and emit different wavelengths of light depending on the number and location of electrons in their electron shells. Spectrometers can be used to identify elements based on their emission spectrum. 
Build a simple spectrometer
Aim
To build a simple spectrometer and use it to investigate the emission spectrum of sodium
Equipment
A thin box, such as a cereal box
A Stanley knife
A piece of diffraction grating
Sticky tape
Aluminium foil
Graph paper
Method
Use the Stanley knife to cut a small square hole in the top of the box. The square should be approximately 1 cm x 1 cm. This is the viewing hole.
Put the piece of diffraction grating inside the box so that it covers the viewing hole. Secure it with sticky tape.
On the bottom of the box, directly opposite the viewing hole, cut a vertical slit that is approximately 0.5 mm wide. This slit must have straight, sharp edges. If you are having trouble creating straight, sharp edges, take a piece of aluminium foil and fold it twice to create a sharp edge. Do this twice. Place the two pieces of folded foil at the location of the slit, making sure there is a 0.5 mm gap between them. Secure them with sticky tape.

Keep your graph paper handy. You will need it soon.
Pick up the box and point the slit at a light source (for example, a light globe). Look through the viewing hole, towards the slit. You should see an emission spectrum beside the slit. If you don’t, the diffraction grating may not be aligned correctly. Try rotating the diffraction grating by 90°.
Investigate how a spectrometer works
Explore the main components of your spectrometer to make sure you understand how it works. Use the questions below to guide you. You could discuss the questions with your group, research them online, ask your teacher or test modifications to your spectrometer to find the answers.
The slit
What is the purpose of the slit?



Why should the slit be as narrow as possible?


The diffraction grating
What is the purpose of the diffraction grating?


Predict what you think will happen if the diffraction grating is misaligned by 90°.




Calibrate your spectrometer
Your spectrometer is useful to allow you to see an emission spectrum of light. However, you currently have no way of measuring which wavelengths of light you are seeing. If you want a more precise instrument that can identify which wavelengths are present, you need to calibrate your spectrometer. 
Calibration is the process of configuring an instrument so that it can accurately measure something. 
Method
Cut out a strip of graph paper and tape it inside your spectrometer, next to the slit, as shown in the diagram. 
Point your spectrometer at a source of white light (for example, an incandescent lamp) and notice where the emission spectrum of this light is located on the graph paper. 
Mark on the graph paper the beginning and the end points of the emission spectrum that you see inside your spectrometer. 
The blue end of the spectrum will be approximately 400 nm and the red end will be approximately 700 nm. Label the end points of your emission spectrum on the graph paper with these wavelengths. 
Create a scale on your graph paper to indicate each 100 nm mark between 400 nm and 700 nm. 
Your spectrometer is now calibrated. 
Predict the sodium line
When you apply enough heat to salt, the electrons in the sodium atoms are temporarily excited and absorb energy. After a while, the electrons fall back into their original location and emit the extra energy as a bright yellow light. This yellow light has a wavelength of approximately 589 nm. 
On an emission spectrum, the location at 589 nm is called the ‘sodium line’. 
You will now predict the location of the sodium line and then check your prediction using your spectrometer to observe heated sodium.
Equipment
A small ceramic bowl
A heat mat
20 mL of ethanol
10 mL of saturated salt solution
Matches
An oven mitt
A white tile 
Note: Your teacher may prepare the heated sodium for you.
Method
Use the scale you created on your graph paper to predict where the sodium line is. Mark this location on your graph paper.
Place the ceramic bowl on the heat mat.
Add 20 mL of ethanol to the bowl.
Add 10 mL of saturated salt solution to the ethanol.
Being careful to ensure your ceramic bowl is well away from fire hazards, use a match to light up the ethanol/saturated salt solution. 
While the solution is burning, use your spectrometer to observe the flame. Look for a bright yellow line in the emission spectrum. This is the sodium line. 
Compare the location of sodium line of the solution with your prediction.
While wearing the oven mitt, extinguish the burning solution by carefully placing the white tile on top of the ceramic bowl to prevent oxygen fuelling the flame. 
Caution: The ceramic bowl and tile will be very hot. Leave your equipment in a safe place to cool before packing up. 
Discussion and reflection
Describe the accuracy of your prediction of the sodium line location. Explain what this tells you about how precisely your instrument is calibrated.




Describe any other colours that you saw in the emission spectrum of the solution. Explain why these other colours could be seen.




Extension activity
Predict what you think would happen to the emission spectrum in your spectrometer if you doubled the length of the box (and therefore doubled the distance between the slit and the diffraction grating). 




Construct a double-length spectrometer to test your prediction.

The speed of waves varies depending on the medium (i.e. substrate, substance) the wave is travelling
through. For light waves, denser mediums slow down the waves. For sound waves, denser mediums
increase the speed. Sound waves must travel through a medium. A vibrating particle in this medium
bumps into another particle, which then also starts to vibrate and so bumps into yet another particle. The
kinetic particle theory can be used to explain the speed of sound in different mediums. 
Explain how an iron bar conducts sound faster than air does. 
(Hint: Think of the proximity of particles.) 
Predict and explain whether cold air particles (molecules) will transmit sound at a higher speed
than hot air particles. (Hint: Think of the speed of particles.) 
Light waves are not dependent on the presence of a medium. Their electromagnetic vibrations can travel
through a vacuum as well as a medium. However, when light waves spread through a medium, their
energy is absorbed by the atoms of the medium and then given out again.
Explain why light travels more slowly in glass than it does in air. 
Explain why air allows light to travel through it at nearly the same speed as in a vacuum? 
Light travels at a speed of 300 000 000 m/s and sound at 333 m/s. 
a Convert these speeds into km/s. (Hint: 1 m equals 1/1000 km.) 
b Now convert these speeds into km/h. (Hint: 1 s equals 1/3600 h.)

than listen for the sound. Explain.

Six km away fireworks are shot into the air. Calculate how soon you 
are able to see and hear them. (Hint: Recall the formula for speed)

later you hear the thunder. How far away is the thunderstorm?

searchText: ﻿ Lesson 2 e&c DANCING WITH STATIC­­­­­­­­­­­­­­ AIM OF THE LESSON During this lesson students will: • Describe how a transfer of energy from one material to another can create static electricity. • Name some examples of static electricity. EQUIPMENT Per Class • 1 foam cup filled with water • 1 compass or sharp object • 5 tea bags • a variety of materials eg nylon; wool; fur; silk; paper; cotton; rubber; chux; stockings; polyester; plastic; sponge ( a few of each is best) Per Group • 2 balloons • 1 plastic comb or plastic pen cover • 1 ball of wool (not acrylic) or piece of wool cloth • 1 empty soft drink can • 5 or 6 styrofoam balls/ packing foam/ beans out of bean bag or puffed wheat Preparation • Collection of materials to test (Students could bring in one each and could be a piece of clothing as they do not need to be cut). Safety ▪ Nil Background Information for teachers Electricity ◦ The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber – electron. ◦ Electricity is a form of energy that is used in many ways in daily life. ◦ Electricity can be observed in the natural environment – eg lightning. ◦ All matter is made of small particles called atoms. ◦ Within atoms are tiny particles called electrons which are negatively charged. Static Electricity • When materials come in contact with each other electrons may be transferred from one material to the other. • This causes a build up of charge which is called static electricity. • If a substance picks up electrons it becomes negatively charged. • When materials have different charges they attract each other. When they have similar charges they repel. • When there is a very big difference between these charges, when the objects come in contact they produce a spark. • By rubbing certain objects together they become charged with electricity. • Wool cloth and human hair readily give up electrons. • Humid weather reduces the effectiveness of static electricity. • When students rub materials on their hair it is best if the hair is fine and dry with no gel or hair spray. Electric Shocks • If you rub your feet on a carpet, your entire body can become charged. • The excess electrons in your body need to go somewhere. Therefore, when you touch something that is not charged (like a large piece of metal) it absorbs the extra electrons suddenly. • The electrons flow quickly through the tip of your finger into the object you touch with a ZAP! • The flow of electrons might be great enough for you to see a tiny spark and hear a snapping sound. Balloons • A balloon rubbed with a wool cloth becomes negatively charged. • When this balloon is held above some foam balls, the neutrally charged balls become positively charged and leap upward to cling to the balloon. • After several minutes, some of the electrons may drain off the balloon onto the balls. This will cause the balls to become negatively charged and be repelled by the balloon. When this happens they may actually leap off the balloon and back to the table. • The repelled foam balls may then transfer their excess electrons to the table after a few minutes and once again leap toward the balloon. Activities • After the Styrofoam clings to the balloon, students who are patient and wait several minutes may see some of the Styrofoam leap forcibly away from the balloon back to the table. • Students who observe very closely will notice that the same grains of tea will alternately leap toward and away from the comb. Investigating Scientifically • Prediction: what you think may happen in an experiment based on your experiences. Lesson Outline 1. Introduction (Engaging Students) Demonstration • Fill a foam cup with water. • Ask a student to rub a plastic comb with a ball of wool or their hair for 10 secs but do not put the comb down. • Use a compass to put a tiny hole in the bottom of the foam cup to produce a very fine stream of water ( a tap is better if available). • As soon as the water starts to flow hold the charged comb next to the stream of water without touching it. The comb should cause the stream of water to bend towards it. The comb is attracting it like a magnet. Transfer of energy or electrons. Getting a shock when stepping out of a car. Combing hair causes unusual attractions. Turning the TV off sometimes causes a zap and shock. Lightning. Clothes out of the dryer cling together. 2. Activities and Strategies • Write down the aim, equipment and method for the activity as a class. • Discuss what is meant by a prediction. Students write a prediction for each activity. • Students conduct the activities on the handout. 3. Focus Questions (Explain and Elaborate) Opposite charges. Like charges. Electrons moving from one material to another. Static electricity is through the air. Other electricity travels in wires. 4. Reflection • In groups, students share one idea that summarises what they have learnt about static electricity. • These could then be shared with the class. • Students to write a conclusion. Extension Activities • Investigate a range of other materials found in the classroom to see if they attract or repel other materials e.g. plastic rulers, erasers, pencil cases. Record your results in a table. Links to other learning Areas • Write a poem about lightning. • Design a bookmark using lightning or static electricity as the focus. • Research about Benjamin Franklin who flew a kite in a lightning storm. • Write a story about a lightning storm. • Make up a crossword puzzle or word sleuth that includes the types of materials you have used in this lesson. • Find out if we see lightning or hear thunder first and why this is so. ACTIVITY 2 DANCING WITH STATIC Aim (What are we going to find out?) Equipment (What do I need to complete the task?) Method (How is the task to be done?) Results (What did I observe?) No Method Prediction (What I think will happen) Observations (What I saw) 1 Rub a balloon with a ball of wool and hold the balloon over a friend’s hair. 2 Rub two balloons with a ball of wool and then hold the balloons side by side. 3 Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near some small torn up pieces of paper. 4 Rub a balloon on a ball of wool, see if you can get it to stick to the wall. 5 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and bring the balloon close to the foam balls. Wait to see what happens. 6 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and hold it above ¼ teaspoon of tea leaves on your desk. Wait to see what happens. 7 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and hold it next to an empty soft drink can which is on its side on a flat surface. • Rub a plastic comb or a plastic pen cover with a selection of materials. • After rubbing each material hold the comb near some foam balls. • Record the material you used and your observations. searchText: ﻿STATIC ELECTRICITY Atomic Structure The structure of the atom has a cloud of electrons orbiting around a nucleus in energy shells. It is the outer electrons that are involved in the production of static electricity. Static Electricity Friction between two surfaces can rub electrons off one object and onto another. The object that gains electrons becomes negative - the other becomes positive. This produces static electricity. Static Electricity: stationary charges on an object. e.g. A plastic comb rubbed on a cotton cloth becomes positively charged by losing electrons. Interaction of Charges Charge Law: Similar charges repel each other while opposite charges attract each other. Examples of Static Electricity Lightning • Caused by the friction between the air and the clouds. • Convection currents within the cloud also cause ice particles to produce static charge. • Charge on the ground below the ground becomes oppositely charged. • Lightning is discharged to the ground or tallest structure with a large charge density. Pollution Control • Chimneys have special electrostatic traps to attract smoke particles. • This reduces the amount reaching the atmosphere. Getting "Zapped" • Moving cars build up a charge as they move through the air. • Passengers sometimes get "zapped" as they get out of the car and touch the metal part of the door. • The charged flows around the person to the Earth.

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the
keyword on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word
itself or any of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.

 1. Students work in teams

 2. Each team needs a set of cards.

 3. The cards need to be shuffled and placed face down.

 4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile,
    and then describes the symbol and keyword at the top of the card without
    using the words below. The rest of their team must guess which word is
    described. Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes
    with’ and no gestures or sounds. The rest of the team guess the keyword
    and/or draw the symbol.

 5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the
    opposing team may challenge and the individual must move on to the
    next word.

 6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words/symbols
    as possible to the players in their team before play passes to the next
    team.

 7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
    point.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding
other ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary
in addition to reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term and
symbol.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could
research the keywords and symbols.

Testing Electrical Conductivity of Materials
What you will need:
• 1 bulb/lamp in holder

Attach your equipment to the mat using masking tape. Follow the instructions and record your results
into the table provided.

You might find that your wires are longer than those shown on the mat – do not cut your wires to size,
just place them as close as possible to the guide lines.



What you need to do:
•   Test each of your materials in turn by placing them in the space shown on the mat and attaching

Making observations:
•   If the bulb lights up, then the material is a conductor. This means that the material is allowing the
    current to flow through it. Conductors have a low resistance.

    stopping the current from flowing through it. Insulators have a high resistance.

searchText:
The Speed of Sound:

 Sound travels at different speeds depending on what it is traveling through.
Of the three mediums (gas, liquid, and solid) sound waves travel the slowest
through gases, faster through liquids, and fastest through solids.
Temperature also affects the speed of sound.
Medium=

Molecules=

Properties=

Collide=

Magnitude=

Rapidly=

Obstacles=

Effectively=

Ocean dwelling=

Majority=

Gases:
The speed of sound depends upon the properties of the medium it is passing
through. When we look at the properties of a gas, we see that only when
molecules collide with each other can a sound wave move. So, it makes
sense that the speed of sound has the same order of magnitude as the
average molecular speed between collisions. In a gas, it is important to know
the temperature. This is because at lower temperatures, molecules collide
more often, giving the sound wave more chances to move around rapidly. At
freezing (0º Celcius), sound travels through air at 331 meters per second
(about 740 mph). But, at 20ºC, room temperature, sound travels at 343
meters per second (767 mph).
Liquids:
Sound travels faster in liquids than in gases because molecules are more
tightly packed. In fresh water, sound waves travel at 1,482 meters per
 second (about 3,315 mph). That's well over 4 times faster than in air! Many
ocean-dwelling animals rely upon sound waves to communicate with other
animals and to locate food and obstacles. The reason that they are able to
effectively use this method of communication over long distances is that
sound travels so much faster in water.
Solids:
Sound travels fastest through solids. This is because molecules in a solid
medium are much closer together than those in a liquid or gas, allowing
sound waves to travel more quickly through it. In fact, sound waves travel
over 17 times faster through steel than through air. The exact speed of
sound in steel is 5,960 meters per second (13,332 mph)! But, this is only for
the majority of solids. The speed of sound in all solids are not faster than in
all liquids.


Sound travels faster in a liquid than in a gas
because the particles are ____________ together in a
liquid.
Sound travels faster in a solid than a liquid because
the particles are _________ together in a solid.

Topical science - healing light
Task
Read the following article and answer the questions.

       Imagine a vivid red light.
       Now think of a time when you were younger and hurt yourself; perhaps you fell
       over and grazed your knee, or scalded yourself whilst helping in the kitchen.
       Imagine simply shining a red light on the injury and the wound healing more
       quickly than usual! This really does work. Not in seconds or hours, that still only
       occurs in science fiction, but shining a certain type of red light onto a wound
       does speed up healing time.
       The light in question is deep red (close to the infra-red part of the
       electromagnetic spectrum). It has a wavelength of 670 nanometres and it
       causes the mitochondria in cells to release more energy (ATP).
       How does it do this?
       At first, scientists speculated that the red light affected the enzymes found in
       mitochondria by speeding up their activity.
       However, the most recent research reveals that it is water which is affected by
       the red light. Water seems to become less viscous (sticky) under this
       wavelength of light.
       The light causes each water molecule to move slightly further away from its
       neighbour, making water 'runnier'. Cells are full of water and it seems enzymes
       in mitochondria work more easily when they are surrounded by water which is
       more fluid.
       Scientists are investigating how this effect could be used to help heal skin
       wounds and burns. It may also be used to help treat some cases of infertility in
       males.

  2. What is the role of mitochondria in cells?

     List them in order of viscosity.

     deep red light on water molecules.

4.9 | Treating preventable blindness

Science as a human endeavour | FouNoanion | stawoaro | apvanceD |

Four out of every five blind people living in developing countries would not be blind if they had
access to basic healthcare and treatment. This means that around 80% of the world’s blindness
could be prevented. Almost half of these cases of blindness are due to cataracts. Cataracts are

a clouding of the lens of the eye and can happen as a person ages. Trachoma can also cause
blindness. Trachoma is an infectious eye disease that spreads through contact with an infected
person’s hands or clothes, It can lead to a condition in which the eyelids turn inwards and scrape
on the cornea which can eventually lead to blindness. Diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma and age-
related macular degeneration are other leading causes of blindness that could be treated or
prevented through early diagnosis.

1| In pairs, research the leading causes of preventable blindness in the world today and outline
treatment options. Create six questions to guide your research using the questions starters
what, where, when, why, who and how. Record them on the chart on the following page.

Some key ideas that could be included into your questions and research include:
+ the causes of preventable blindness, such as cataract, trachoma, diabetic retinopathy
+ how these conditions could be diagnosed and treated

+ the prevalence of preventable blindness amongst Indigenous Australians

+ the work of the Fred Hollows Foundation

+ why two-thirds of the world’s blind are women.

searchText: Ultraviolet 1 Ultraviolet Ultraviolet is the part of the spectrum shown on the left side of the picture above as black—because humans cannot see light of such short wavelength (or high frequency). Many animals such as some insects, some reptiles, crocodiles, salamanders, and small birds can see things that reflect this light. The name 'ultraviolet' uses the ancient Latin prefix ultra-, which means 'behind', 'beyond', or 'far'. Ultraviolet is beyond the visible violet light in terms of frequency, wavelength, and energy. Its wavelengths are between about 10 nanometers (nm) about 400 nanometers. UV is a common abbreviation of ultraviolet, mainly used in technical contexts. Frequency and wavelength are closely related. The equation that shows this relationship is: ν = c/λ (nu, i.e. frequency = speed of light ÷ lamda, i.e., wavelength), so saying that something has a short wavelength is equivalent to saying that it has a high frequency. Ultraviolet radiation Ultraviolet light can damage or kill cells. Any electromagnetic radiation (light) that has a wavelength shorter than 450 nm may cause trouble. Therefore humans that live in places with more ultraviolet light have adapted by getting darker skins. Pigments absorb the ultraviolet radiation, so it does not get through the skin to kill or injure cells inside. Injury to the skin by ultraviolet is called "sunburn." The only difference between violet light and ultraviolet light is the wavelength (or the frequency). The only difference between ultraviolet light and x-rays is also the wavelength or frequency. Ultraviolet is beyond violet, x-rays are beyond ultraviolet, and cosmic rays are beyond x-rays. Cosmic radiation can also be called gamma rays, or gamma radiation. Technically, electromagnetic waves with a frequency of 789 terahertz or more are called ultraviolet. This corresponds with a wavelength from 380 nanometers down to approximately 5 nanometers. A single light quantum or photon of ultraviolet Indoor tanning device carries an energy around some 3.26 electron volt. The higher a photon's frequency, and so the shorter its wavelength, the more energy a photon carries. Ultraviolet 2 Although the air of the Earth is transparent to a broad range of ultraviolet, some ultraviolet sunlight is absorbed at a very high altitude by the ozone layer. Recent and ongoing destruction of ozone in high altitudes caused by human influence—mostly by industrial chemicals and air travel—has greatly increased the amount of ultraviolet light reaching the Earth's surface. This, in turn, has increased the risk of skin cancer to mankind, and this risk will only increase with time unless the ozone layer is better protected. Ultraviolet wavelengths less than 200 nanometers, X-rays, and gamma rays, are collectively called ionizing radiation since the energy in any such light quantum is high enough to 'kick' an electron out of an atom. This is why these kinds of radiation are dangerous to life. Ordinary glass does not let radiation through if its wavelength is less than 200 nanometers, so it acts as a shield against the more dangerous range of ultraviolet light, but some special sorts of glass do not shield as well, including many car windows. One use for ultraviolet radiation is tanning. Use of tanning devices can cause skin cancer because ultraviolet goes through the skin and causes destruction to cells causing sunburn. Because of the destructive power of ultraviolet light, it can be used to kill germs. Sunlight is a powerful disinfectant. Ultraviolet lamp An ultraviolet lamp is one that emits light mostly at a frequency higher than violet, called ultraviolet. These lamps are often used to kill microbes (germs). They can be very powerful, so the people who work around them when they are turned on may need to wear protective glasses and keep their skin covered to avoid injury. In the laboratory pictured, ultraviolet lights are turned on when the workers are gone so that anything on the table surface will be killed. Besides ultraviolet light, which makes up most of the light produced by these lamps, there is also a little violet and blue light. So people can easily tell when the ultraviolet lamps are turned on. searchText: ﻿VOLTAGE, CURRENT AND RESISTANCE Voltage / Potential Difference (V): provides the energy to drive electrons around a circuit. Measured in - volts (V) Current (I): a measure of the rate at which charge (electrons) flows in a circuit. Measured in - Amperes (A) Resistance (R): a measure of the difficulty electrons have in moving around a circuit. Measured in - Ohms () Voltage equals current times resistance V = IR The resistance of a wire is dependent on the following. • Type of material used. e.g. Copper has a lower resistance than nichrome wire. • Diameter of the wire. e.g. Thin wire has a greater resistance than thick wire. The filaments in globes are very thin to give them high resistance which makes the metal get very hot and glow. • Length of the wire. e.g. Long wire has more resistance. Rheostats (variable resistors) used to control fans and lights have the wire wound around a non-conductor to save space.

searchText: Waves and Rays What is light? Light is a form of energy that we can see and is given out by hot objects. It is made up of waves that travel outwards from a light source. Some of the waves reach our eyes, but most continue elsewhere. Waves can be transverse or longitudinal The two main types of waveform are transverse waves and longitudinal waves. All types of electromagnetic waves, including light, as well as water waves travel as transverse waves. Sound waves travel as longitudinal waves. Transverse waves (light) are a moving wave where each part of the wave travels up and down in repeating motion as the wave moves forward. These do not need a medium to travel through and can travel through empty space. Longitudinal waves (sound) are a compressing and expanding wave that needs a medium to travel in. A medium could be gas, solid or liquid. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave Sound waves are mechanical waves requiring particles. (a medium to travel through) Air particles vibrate back and forward creating repeating patterns of high (compressed particles) and low (spaced apart particles) pressure. One wave stretches from one compressed area of particles to the next. Waves of sound energy travel through air, water and solid substances. Waves transfer energy Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another without also transferring matter. Some waves need a medium (matter) to travel through in order to transport their energy from one location to another and are known as mechanical waves, such as ocean waves, sound waves and earthquake waves. Other waves can travel through the vacuum of space where there is little or no atoms. These are know as electromagnetic waves. Examples of those waves include light waves, microwaves and radio waves. 93 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Features of a wave Waves have troughs, the lowest point, and crests, the highest point. A wavelength is the distance between two closest crests. The amplitude of a wave is a measure of its height. The height is taken from a midpoint between a trough and a peak up to the top of a peak of a wave. Frequency of a wave The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. The frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Because all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed then more waves of shorter wavelength will pass by a point over the same time as waves of longer wavelength. wave speed = wavelength x frequency Waves always travel at the same speed. A scientific value that always remains the same is called a constant. The constant for the speed of light is c = 3x108 m/sec or 300,000 kilometres per second. Because we know the speed of light, if we know either the wavelength (λ) in metres or the frequency (f ) in hertz then we can calculate the other. Wavelength = speed of light / frequency Frequency = speed of light / wavelength Light energy can travel as rays Light travels fast and in straight lines. At the speed of light, which is 300,000 kilometers per second, light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to travel 149 million kilometers to earth. Light can go around the earth 7 times in one second. Light travels straight, until something bends it. The straight paths of light are called light rays. 94 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Light energy can be reflected, refracted or dispersed Light travels in a straight line until it strikes an object or a force. Light can be: 1. Reflected by a mirror 2. Refracted by a lens 3. Absorbed by the object Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction) which is travelling through it, absorption where it enters but doesn’t leave again, or scattering (including reflection) where it bounces off. To see an object, light from that object— emitted by or scattered from it—must enter the eye. Transparent, Translucent and Opaque Shadows are created when light rays are stopped A shadow is a dark area that is formed due to light travelling in straight lines which opaque objects block. An object that stops direct light rays creates a shadow. The shape of the shadow resembles the shape of the object. The shadow created when the Moon blocks the light from the Sun to the Earth is called a solar eclipse. 95 | P a g e GZ Science Resources The length of the shadow depends on the angle of the light source The length of the shadow formed on the ground depends on the angle that the light rays hit the object blocking the light. If the light rays hit the object straight on, then this will create the smallest possible shadow. The greater the angle the light rays hit the longer the resulting shadow. The changing of length of shadow can be seen as the Sun moves across the sky. In the morning and afternoon, the shadows created are the longest as the Sun is at the greatest angle. The shortest shadows are formed at midday when the sun is directly over-head (in Summer). Sources of light and reflectors of light Light is a form of energy. The Sun is our most important source of light, which is produced along with heat energy, that is transformed from matter during a nuclear reaction. Other sources of light energy such as electrical lighting, fire and the glow from bioluminescent animals are produced during energy transformations as well. Light sources need energy to be transformed to produce light. These are also called illuminators. Objects that appear to produce light such as the Moon or shiny objects but do not use energy are reflectors of light. Light rays must originally come from a light source, such as the Sun’s light reflecting off the moon. 96 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Waves and Rays Review Questions 1. Identify the diagrams as either transverse or longitudinal waves 2. Complete the table below showing a list of examples of transverse and longitudinal waves Ripples on water sound light ‘Mexican’ wave pressure waves (P) in an earthquake vibrations in a guitar string radio waves squashing and releasing slinky 3. identify parts of the wave trough crest amplitude wavelength 97 | P a g e GZ Science Resources 4. Identify the following cups below as either translucent, transparent or opaque, then list at least 3 examples for each 5. Identify as either a light source (S) or light reflector (R) 6. Draw the light rays from the light source, and show the shadow formed by the object on the floor and wall of the diagram 98 | P a g e GZ Science Resources

Wet cells, Dry cells and Batteries

The electrochemical cell.

A simple device that converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy.
A battery is one or more electrochemical cells together. Alessandro Volta
invented the first battery (or "voltaic pile") in 1800.

Wet Cell

A wet cell has a couple of parts




The electrodes. These are plates of _________ or ________. One plate breaks
down and gives away electrons. The other plate collects these __________.

The plate that gives away electrons us called the Anode.

The plate that collects electrons is called the Cathode

An Electrolyte. This is a __________that __________electricity. This
movement of electrons gives a current.

A wet cell is not very portable as the electrolyte can _________. Also as the
anode gives away its electrons it breaks down. Once the anode has
completely broken down the wet cell will stop working.

An example of a wet cell used today is :________________________________

_____________________________________________________________
 Label the electrodes and electrolyte in the diagram below.




What were the problems with a wet cell?



Dry Cell

A dry cell has the same basic parts as a wet cell, but has characteristics that
make it more useful. The electrolyte is a _________, not a liquid. As a result it
does not splash around and spill if the cell is moved. The zinc electrode has
been made into part of the outer casing of the battery. The other electrode
is often made of graphite.




Why is the dry cell so useful?
 Photovoltaic Cells

Another word for photovoltaic cell is ________ cell. These convert solar
energy directly into _________ energy. The solar energy knocks ______________
off of the silicon crystals inside. As the electrons move away they form an
electric current.

The current can be used straight away or it can be used to charge a battery
for later use.



Primary and Secondary Batteries

Primary batteries (disposable batteries). These are designed to be used only
once and then thrown away. This is a problem as the batteries must be
replaced regularly. Also the wastes in these batteries are toxic, so safe
disposal is not always easy.


Secondary batteries (rechargeable batteries or storage cells). These are
designed to be recharged and used many times.

Information sheet 1

White light

White light is a mixture of many different colours.

White light can be split into a spectrum using a prism, a triangular block of glass or
perspex. Light is refracted (changes direction) when it enters the prism, and each
colour is refracted by a different amount. Light leaving the prism is spread out into its
different colours, a process called dispersion.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017                                              26290                                                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                              White light
Information sheet 2

White light

White light can be generated by a variety of sources both in space and by artificial
sources on Earth. For example, the Sun is a source of white light. Artificial sources
include fluorescent light bulbs and white LEDs which produce white light. White light is
a mixture of many different colours, each with a different frequency (number of waves
that pass a point in space in a time interval, usually one second).

White light can be split up into a spectrum of these colours using a prism, a triangular
block of glass or Perspex plastic. Light is refracted when it enters the prism, and each
colour is refracted by a different amount. This means that the light leaving the prism is
spread out into its different colours, a process called dispersion.

When white light passes through a prism, it is dispersed and the different colours of
the spectrum separate. Dispersion causes rainbows and the colours of the spectrum
include: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet (lowest to highest
frequency).
Dispersion happens because the different colours of light travel at different speeds in a
medium such as glass. The amount of bending increases as the change in speed
increases, therefore blue light bends more than red light.




                   White light




                                          Prism




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017           26290                                Page 3 of 6
                                                                                White light
Information sheet 3

Splitting white light

White light can be split into a spectrum of many different colours using a prism. This is
a block of glass with a triangular cross-section. The light waves are refracted as they
enter and leave the prism. The shorter the wavelength of the light the more it is
refracted. As a result, red light is refracted the least and violet light is refracted the
most, causing the coloured light to spread out to form a spectrum.

When a ray of light goes from one material to another, it bends. The amount of
bending depends on the angle at which it strikes the surface, as well as on the
difference in the speed of light in the two materials. The bigger the speed difference,
the more it bends.

Prisms work because the speed of light changes as it moves from one medium to
another (air to glass). The speed at which it travels causes the light to be refracted
and bend. All light strikes the front of a prism at the same angle, but when it hits the
back of the prism, the different colours are travelling in different directions due to the
change in speed. The colours strike the back of the prism at different angles. They
come out of the prism at different angles which separates then into the colours of the
spectrum. This creates an effect similar to a rainbow.

searchText: X-ray 1 X-ray X-ray is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, with wavelength shorter and energy higher than ultraviolet radiation. The wavelength of X-ray covers a wide range. Radiation with shorter wavelength (higher energy) than X-ray is called Gamma ray. X-rays can go through many solid materials. They can be produced by hitting metal with fast-moving electrons. X-ray photography is used in medicine to see bones and cancer, and other things inside bodies. A Computed tomography scanner combines an X-ray machine and computer to construct a three dimensional (3D) picture. X-rays are photons, tiny packets of energy that interact with atoms in the body. The way they interact depends on the wavelength (energy level) of the x-rays. X-rays with low-level energies ("soft" x-rays) go An X-ray photograph of lungs. through the Photoelectric effect, mid-level energies go through Compton scattering, and high-level energies ("hard" X-rays) go through pair production. Medical x-rays can experience the Photoelectric effect and sometimes Compton scattering. Radiation therapy that treats cancer use Compton scattering and sometimes Pair production. There are small amounts of X-rays in the atmosphere. Like other ionizing radiation, X-rays can change living cells. This means that exposing the human body to high doses of x-rays for a long time should be avoided. Changing living cells can be dangerous. It can cause cancer and other diseases. It can also be good, as cancer cells can be killed that way. Like with any treatment, there are side-effects. X-rays cannot see soft tissue very well. To detect tumors, other imaging technologies are used; such as Magnetic resonance imaging. Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                      1




                                 Light Energy
If you can read this, you are relying on light energy. Light energy and our eyesight are the
two things we need to be able to see; without one or the other there would be no sight.
Can you imagine what life would be like without light energy? Quite simply, there would
not be any life at all. Plants need light to live and if there were no plants, there would be no
animals, including people.


Sources of Light

Light energy is one of the forms of radiant energy that comes to us from
the Sun. This light energy is formed in nuclear reactions that occur within the Sun.
Other objects and substances can also give off their own light energy. These objects
are said to be luminous. The light carries energy away from luminous objects as
electromagnetic waves.

1.        Give examples of objects or substances that are luminous.




Many light sources emit light energy because they are hot. However, there are light sources which give out light without
getting hot. These include fluorescent tubes, the paint on the hand and numerals of clocks, fireflies and some deep sea
fish.

2.        Which of your examples given in a) emit light energy because they are hot?



3.        Draw energy flow charts to show where the light energy comes from for the following objects:
          a)        a candle


          b)        a torch


          c)        an electric light bulb



4.        Most things that can be seen are not luminous. For example, you can see this page and the writing on it yet they do
          not produce their own light.




a) Explain why you can see this page even though it does not emit its own light energy.




                    b) Explain why the Moon shines brightly in the night sky.
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy   2
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                           3




How light travels

One scientific theory proposes that light energy travels in a wave motion. The light that we
can see has a wavelength of about th of a millimetre. Light energy travels at a speed of about
300 million metres per second.


                              1.        If the Sun is 150 million kilometres away from the
                                        Earth, how long does it take light energy from the Sun
                                        to reach Earth?




                    2.        Approximately how long would it take for light to travel across the M.L.C. oval?




Although light cannot normally be seen as it passes through air, conclusions can be made about how it travels. For
example, light will travel in a straight line unless some other substance is placed in its path.

3.        Can you see around a corner of a brick building? (without the aid of mirrors). Explain your answer.




4.      a)          Cut out a shape from a piece of cardboard.             b)       Hold your shape in front of a light
source.
                    Sketch your shape below.                                                 Sketch the shape of the shadow it
produces.




         c)        Explain the shape of the shadow. Include a diagram showing what has happened to the "rays" of light
         (a        ray diagram).
          (In diagrams, lines called rays are used to show the direction in which the light energy is traveling. A light
         ray can be thought of as a very narrow beam of light.)




          d)        Repeat the experiment described in a) and b), but this time cut the shape out of an overhead projection
                    sheet.
                    What happens?
                    Explain your observations. Again, use a ray diagram to show what is happening to the light energy.
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                       4




When light energy hits an object, several different things can happen. What happens depends on the substance making up
the object. Some substances allow light energy to pass through them. Other substances will not allow light energy to
pass through and either reflect (bounce off) or absorb the energy.

5.         a)       i)        What name is given to materials which allow light to pass through?

                    ii)       Give three examples of such materials.


                    iii)      What name is given to materials which will not allow light to pass through?

                    iv)       Give two examples of such materials - one which reflects the light, and one which absorbs the
                              light.




Reflection of light energy


When light energy strikes an object, some of the energy is absorbed and some bounces off. The reflected waves which
bounce off the object enable us to see it.

6.         Draw a diagram showing the path of the light energy that enables us to see a book which is lit by a desk lamp.
           Show the direction of the light energy.




7.         When you look at an object in a flat mirror, you see an image. A mirror
           reflects the light from an object and makes the image which we see.

           Write a short word on a piece of paper, then look at the word in a mirror.
           What does the image of your word look like?



           Select the correct words in the following sentences to summarise your
           observations:

           The image is     the same way up or upside down        compared to the word written on the paper.
           The image is     the same size as or smaller than or larger than        the word written on the paper.
           The letters and word in the image are    the same as    or reversed compared to the word written on the
            paper.


8.         Write the word AMBULANCE as it would be painted on the front of an ambulance so a driver
           looking at it through a car mirror would read it correctly.
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                       5




Absorption and reflection of light

Although sunlight appears to be white, it is not actually a single pure white colour. It is made up of seven different
colours that you can see, called the visible spectrum. The colours of the visible spectrum are red, orange, yellow, green,
indigo and violet. Each of these colours correspond to light of different wavelengths with red light having the longest
wavelength and violet light having the shortest wavelength.

Different materials absorb some of the colours in sunlight (white light) and reflect others. The colour we see in an object
depends on the colours that are reflected back to our eyes. For example, a yellow object absorbs all colours except
yellow, and it reflects yellow.

White objects appear white because they reflect all the colours of sunlight, but black objects appear black because they
absorb all the colours and reflect none.


9.        Using coloured pens or pencils, colour and complete the following diagrams, showing the colour of the leaf and
of        the bananas, and the different colours in the sunlight (white light) and in the reflected light.

                white light                                       white light




                                                                                                    yellow bananas
               green leaf




Bending of light

10.       Place a coin in an empty cup and move your eyes until it is just out
          of view. Ask your partner to carefully fill the cup with water.
                   What happens to the coin?




11.       Put a pencil in a beaker of water. Look at the pencil from the side of the beaker. What do you see?




When light energy meets a new substance, the light changes direction or bends. When light bends going from one
substance to another, we say that the light is refracted. The light bends when going from one substance to another
because it moves at different speeds through different materials. It travels slower through water and glass than it does
through air.

A sound wave can blow out a candle.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain an empty, plastic 2 L milk container and remove

The tap on the end of the container produces a compression

through the opening with enough force to blow out the
candle.

anyone’s ear. Blow up a balloon until it is half inflated, then
burst it with a pin.(The air is slightly compressed inside the
balloon, so there will be a bang when it expands rapidly.
This is similar to the way thunder is produced — a bolt of
lightning heats the air around it, which suddenly expands,
and we hear this compression wave as thunder.)
2  Calculate how far away a thunderstorm is. In a thunderstorm, lightning and thunder are produced at

The brain automatically makes corrections to the images it
receives from the eye and this helps us to interpret our
surroundings. (For example, as objects get further away they
look smaller, but we understand that they are still the same
size.) But when unusual images are presented to the brain, it
can give us the wrong information. 
A young baby’s head makes up about one-quarter of the
length of its body. In some parts of Africa, a child is
deemed to be old enough to begin school when he/she 
can put one arm over his/her head and touch the other
shoulder. Younger children’s heads are too big to allow
them to do this.

you will probably miss because we normally use both eyes to
estimate distance.)

with the circumference of your neck. (The length will be roughly twice as long.) Is there another body
part that is twice as long again?

You can make a musical note by rubbing a wineglass.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Put a crystal wineglass on the table and hold it by the neck
rather than the base.
2  Wet a finger and rub it smoothly in one direction around
the rim of the wineglass. (With a bit of practice a musical
note will be heard.)
EXPLANATION
The rubbing causes vibrations in the glass. When these
vibrations match the natural frequency of vibration of the
wineglass, the glass will vibrate at that frequency (that is,
resonate).
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum, so outer space is
always silent.
Some people believe that plants respond to music and there
have even been PhD theses written about it. The results of
one study showed that many flowers prefer classical music
and jazz, definitely do not like loud rock music and are
unaffected by country and western.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Rattle a needle. Obtain two wineglasses that both make exactly the same note. (You may need to add
water to one to change its note.) Stand a sewing needle in one of the glasses. Wet your finger and rub
the rim of the other glass, which should be very close to but not touching the first glass. (The first glass
will resonate and its vibrations will make the needle rattle against the glass.)
2  Use resonance to amplify sounds. Tie a length of string to
the base of a polystyrene cup. Pull the string taut to the
cup and stroke it with the skin of your fingertip. Then let
the string go slack and stroke it. (The sound will only be
audible when the vibrations are transferred to the cup by
taut string. The sound waves reflect and rejoin inside the
cup to become amplified.)

When we look at an object, each eye sees it from a slightly

neighbouring galaxy, which is visible on a clear night.
Blindness or partial blindness affects 28 million people worldwide.

The Galapagos Islands consist of 13 major islands. They are located in the Pacific Ocean, 1000 km from the coast
of Ecuador which is in South America. Charles Darwin's visit to the Galapagos Islands in 1835 was the Starting
point for his theory of natural selection. This theory describes a process by which organisms that have
favourable variations survive and reproduce at a higher rate than other organisms.

An inherited variation that increases an organism's chance of survival in a particular environment is called an
adaptation. The finches and the giant tortoises living on the Galapagos Islands are two examples of adaptive
radiation. This means that a single lineage has diversified into a variety of species that have different adaptive
features. Adaptive radiation is an example of divergent evolution,

Approximately 10 000 years ago, small finches (grass quits) travelled 1000 km across the Pacific Ocean from
South America to the Galapagos Islands. These islands were relatively free of competitors. The grass quits
underwent radiation, producing 13 species that occupy a variety of niches,

10 million years ago, the ancestors of the giant tortoises arrived in the Galapagos Islands by clinging to a piece
of wood that drifted from a river mouth on the Pacific coast of the South American mainland all the way to San
Cristobal Island. The tortoises then spread throughout the islands, When Darwin arrived, there were
approximately 300 000 giant tortoises on 11 of the islands, The tortoises on individual islands developed into
their own sub-species. This was due to the effect of the founder principle, genetic drift and natural
selection, These islands were isolated and the animals were subjected to different environmental conditions,
which resulted in their gradual evolution into different species.
