INTRODUCTION
Humans, along with familiar species such as orangutans, gorillas, lemurs, baboons, and chimpanzees, are
primates. Among living primates, modern humans are most closely related to chimpanzees. The two species
shared a common ancestor that lived about 6–7 million years ago. One of the traits that distinguish humans
from all other primates, including chimpanzees, is the way we walk. Chimpanzees are primarily quadrupedal,
which means that they walk on four limbs. Chimpanzees move with their hands turned under so that their
knuckles make contact with the ground, which is why they are also described as knuckle-walkers. Humans, on
the other hand, are bipedal, meaning that we walk on two legs.
We walk with our feet close together and directly underneath our hips, enabling us to balance on one leg
while the other leg swings forward. Chimpanzees can walk on two legs only for short distances. Because their
feet are not directly under their hips, they sway side to side to help maintain balance when walking on two
legs.
Because humans are the only primate to walk on two legs, bipedality most likely evolved in the lineage that
led to humans. When did this human trait first evolve? The “Human Feet Are Strange” activity will help answer
that question. Part 1 focuses on observing modern human footprints and what we can infer from them. In Part

                                             HUMAN FEET ARE STRANGE
OVERVIEW
The activity “Human Feet Are Strange” was developed to supplement the film Great Transitions: The Origin of
Humans (http://www.hhmi.org/biointeractive/great-transitions-origin-humans). In the film, starting at time
mark 9:40 minutes, paleoanthropologist Dr. Tim White describes the Laetoli trackway, a set of preserved
hominid footprints in Eastern Africa discovered in 1976. Fossils of the hominid species Australopithecus
afarensis have been found near the Laetoli footprints. Since A. afarensis was the only hominid species known
to be living in the area at the time, it is assumed that the footprints at Laetoli were made by A. afarensis.
Dr. White also says that, “human feet, we’re all used to them, but they’re really strange.” What does he mean
by that statement, and what is the significance of the Laetoli footprints? Students will explore these questions
in this activity.
Students first study footprints made by themselves or their classmates. The prints are made by covering the
soles of the feet with water-soluble paints and then walking on a 3 foot × 10 foot sheet of paper (“classroom
trackway”). They are then asked to analyze the shape of their feet and the position of their toes, arches, and
stride. Next, students make observations and draw inferences from an illustration of the 3.6-million-year-old
trail of Laetoli footprints (“Laetoli trackway”), compare their own footprints with those of the Laetoli trail, and
evaluate the evidence in support of the conclusion that the Laetoli footprints were made by a fully bipedal
human ancestor. This activity ends with a summary activity, which students can complete as homework.
KEY CONCEPTS AND LEARNING OBJECTIVES
•        The fossil record provides a history of life on Earth and includes not only the fossilized bones of dead
         organisms but also trace fossils, such as footprints.
•        Bipedalism, or walking primarily upright on two legs, is one of the traits that distinguish modern humans
         from all other modern primates.
• The observation of living organisms can provide insights into traits and behaviors of extinct species.
Students will be able to
•        learn the difference between observations and inferences and
•        draw inferences based on observations and other types of evidence.

Chapter 2                                     Geological time
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1: Carbon-14 dating


Carbon-14 dating is also known as radiocarbon dating. Carbon-14 dating is
really important for finding the age of organic materials from living things that
lived in the last 40 000 to 50 000 years. Organic materials are compounds
containing carbon that are produced by living organisms. These compounds
include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and vitamins.



Formation of carbon-14
Carbon-14 is formed high in the atmosphere by cosmic rays (radiation from
the Sun) changing nitrogen atoms in to carbon-14 atoms. The carbon-14
atoms combine with oxygen and form radioactive carbon dioxide. The
proportion of carbon dioxide molecules which are radioactive is tiny. There is
only 1 radioactive carbon atom in 1 000 000 000 000 carbon atoms
(1 million million).



Carbon-14 in plants and animals
The radioactive carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants in photosynthesis and
made into sugar. Some of the sugar is then converted into many different
organic compounds such as proteins, lipids and vitamins in the plant. When
the plant is eaten by animals, the radioactive carbon atoms become part of
the animal’s body tissues. When organisms die they stop absorbing
carbon-14.




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                  ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
 Radioactive decay of carbon-14
Carbon-14 atoms decay into nitrogen atoms. In comparison to other types of
radioactive decay, the decay of carbon-14 is very fast. The half-life of carbon-
14 is 5730 years. Only half of the original radioactive carbon will be left after
this time. The decay curve for carbon-14 is shown in Figure 1. The vertical
axis shows the percentage of carbon-14 remaining. Carbon-14 decays so fast
that radiocarbon dating is not accurate beyond about 50 000 years. Any older
than that and carbon-14 dating is not accurate because so little radioactivity is
left that is the amount is hard to measure.

Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Catching illegal wildlife traders
The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus) is a well-known Australian monotreme. It is featured on the 5-cent coin. Found across almost all Australian habitats, from snowy mountains to deserts, it can be recognised by the quills on its back. These quills are modified hairs that can be up to 5 centimetres long.
The echidna uses smell to detect ants, termites, and other invertebrates. It has sharp claws that it uses to pull apart logs and dig into ant and termite nests. It uses its long, sticky tongue to catch insects and grind them against the roof of its mouth.
When threatened by cats, foxes, dogs, dingoes, or goannas, the echidna rolls into a ball or digs into the ground, exposing only its quills. 
Breeding occurs once a year (from June to September). The female lays a single soft-shelled egg (about the size of a grape) that hatches after 10 days in her pouch. The baby, called a puggle, is blind and hairless, and feeds off milk that is secreted onto the fur in the mother’s pouch. When the baby develops its quills, the mother leaves it in a burrow. She returns every few days to feed it until the baby is about seven months old.
Short-beaked echidnas are a protected species in Australia. This makes it illegal to capture or trade them. Unfortunately, they are highly prized in many zoos around the world. This means many illegal wildlife traders sell wild echidnas as “captive-bred”.
To combat this, scientists use a range of testing techniques, including high-resolution X-ray fluorescence and stable isotope analysis, to examine the keratin that makes up the echidna quills. This keratin is similar to the molecules found in human hair and nails. As the quills grow, they carry a record of the diet of the animal over time. 
Explain why some researchers describe an echidna’s quill as a time capsule.




Using the drawing of a quill below, describe where you might find information about:
The diet of the echidna in the previous few weeks 
The diet of the echidna several months ago  

High-resolution X-ray fluorescence shines high-energy X-rays at the echidna quill. The energy of the X-ray causes the atoms within the hair to become excited and emit their own forms of energy. The amounts and intensity of these secondary levels of energy can be measured and used to detect how much of a particular element is present in the hair.
Compare the radiation levels of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.




Identify which type of radiation is most likely to be used for the high-resolution X-ray fluorescence process. Justify your answer.





The echidna’s quills were sampled at every 200 μm for 24 elements.
Explain why the quills had to be washed before they were tested.





The researchers found that there was a difference in the element levels between wild echidnas and captive echidnas. Captive echidnas had more variable element patterns than wild echidnas because the zoos provided many different types of foods that would not always be found in the wild. In contrast, wild echidnas were more likely to eat only the foods that were found in their local environment.

Cell division plays an essential role in the growth, repair and reproduction of

multicellular organisms. Cell division is the splitting of one (parent) cell = >
into two identical (daughter) cells. There are two main types of cell
division — mitosis and meiosis. Cells fall into two main classes somatic
cells and germ cells.
Somatic cells: cells making up the tissues, organs, and parts of the body 4

other than the germ (sex) cells.

Somatic cells (somatic, from the Greek, meaning ‘body’) are involved in growth and body maintenance.
Mitosis (binary fission) produces new cells for growing organisms and also replaces cells, which have
been damaged or have died. Many single-celled organisms reproduce asexually (without sex) using
mitosis. Before cells divide in mitosis they grow, otherwise they would be smaller after each cell division,

[ Diploid: double, refers to two of each chromosome, a complete set. (Remember Diploid: Double.)
Somatic cells are usually diploid (2n), meaning they have a full set of chromosomes, one from each parent.
| Germ cells: also called gametes, for example egg (ovum) cells or sperm cells.

Gametes (from the Greek, meaning ‘wife’) are set aside for reproductive purposes, but are not always
used. These cells undergo meiosis, a cell division that produces haploid (n) cells. These cells require
fusion (joining) with gametes from the opposite sex to restore the complement (full number).

| Haploid: half, refers to half of one full set of chromosomes. (Remember Haploid: Half.)

Human females are born with a lifetime’s supply of gametes. When they reach maturity, one gamete
(sometimes more) will be released monthly, Human males are not born with their gametes, Instead,
males begin to form gametes at maturity and they are then produced as required.

{\ Cell Division 11

When human sex cells (gametes) join at fertilisation they produce a single cell (a zygote). This cell starts
to divide and, after nine months (and billions of cell divisions), a baby is born,

There are thin, thread-like, microscopic structures called chromosomes present in the nucleus of a cell.
The chromosomes can only be seen when a cell is dividing. Chromosomes occur in cells in pairs (apart
from in sex cells), Humans have 23 pairs (2n) of chromosomes. Other species have different numbers
of chromosomes. Chromosomes are strands of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), and consist of sections
called genes. These contain the instructions for controlling cells, and need to be able to be copied
precisely, because a mistake made early in replication will be repeated in every cell.

There are two processes by which cells can divide: mitosis and meiosis. In mitosis the cell continues to
duplicate and divide, producing daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell. These are

needed for growth and to replace the millions of cells that die every day.

}i\ More About Mutations:

*

changing DNA (32)

Throughout evolution, random changes have occurred to DNA, These changes can be harmful or
beneficial, depending on how, and in what sort of environment, they are expressed. For example
consider the following scenario. A species of bird has toes. Among this population, through mutation,
some birds carry a gene producing webbed feet. Possession of webbed feet would improve swimming
ability and ability to walk through marshlands. This would enable these birds to be more successful
feeders in wet areas. The webbed-feet birds would breed successfully in wetlands and the trait would

increase through time.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY 12

Chemical evolution and
the origin of life

Introduction

Most biologists believe that the first life evolved on Earth more than 3 billion years ago, about 1 billion years after
the Earth was formed. Biologists have hypothesised that before life began, a process of chemical evolution
occurred in which the chemical building blocks of life were formed throughout the following series of events:

The inorganic (non-living) constituents of living things were present on the Earth when life began.

Environmental conditions that were favourable for chemical reactions existed. These chemical reactions formed
more complex chemicals from the inorganic constituents.

These complex chemicals became the building blocks of life and included amino acids (which form proteins),
sugars and nitrogen bases (which form nucleotides then combine to form nucleic acids), sugars (which combine
to form polysaccharides), glycerin and fatty acids (which combine to form fats and other lipids) and ATP
(Adenosine triphosphate — an energy transport molecule).

These building blocks became arranged into membrane systems which formed the first cells. These cells were
prokaryotic bacterial cells and they did not need oxygen. (There was no free oxygen in the atmosphere at this
time in Earth’s history). Cells that do not require oxygen are called anaerobic cells.

There is a large amount of evidence that has given scientists confidence that chemical evolution did happen and
that it made the evolution of the first living organisms and biological evolution possible,

Genetic material is found in the form of chromosomes, made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and
proteins. DNA has a backbone with a tightly-coiled, long double-helix structure (resembling a spiral
staircase). The material of chromosomes is called ‘chromatin’, which means ‘coloured threads’. This is
what genetic material resembles after it has been stained and viewed under a microscope.

| Chromatids: pairs of parallel strands of a duplicated chromosome joined by a single centromere.

When genetic material replicates, the two copies remain attached for a time, While in this state, each
thread-like structure is called a chromatid. The pair are referred to as sister chromatids. This difference
in naming tells us that the genetic material is still undergoing replication, The chromatids are attached
at one area called the centromere. A protein ‘belt’ (a kinetochore) forms around the centromere. Each
part of the sister chromatids is referred to as an arm. The short arms are called p-arms (from the French,
petit meaning ‘small’) and the long arms are q-arms.

down. The last thylacine died in captivity in 1936. Some scientists 
want to clone a thylacine and reintroduce it to Tasmania, but there are 
arguments against as well as in favour of this issue.
Thylacines were native animals of Tasmania. It was only because 
European settlers feared them that they were exterminated. Had

thylacine would still be living in Tasmania today. Reintroducing cloned 
Tasmanian tigers would only make right the wrong done by people of

Connect 4 – genetics and inheritance

Teaching notes
This could be a starter, plenary or revision activity.
It can be carried out using scraps of paper, exercise books, with laminated
cards, or on an interactive whiteboard. There is a Magnet interactive resource
that can be used with the activity.
Working in pairs, students look at the words and phrases, trying to choose four
which are connected in some way. They agree on one or two sentences which
include the four words and explain the connection between those words. They
can then put up their hands; the class is stopped and everyone listens to the
connection. If the explanation is agreed to be valid, those four words are
scrubbed from the list and everyone has to start again with the remaining
words and phrases.
It is up to you to decide whether to continue with the game if a combination of
words does not match one of the suggested answers. You could praise
students for their ingenuity but urge the class to continue to search for a group
of four which matches the suggested answers; this way you will not be left with
a group of mismatched words at the end. (However, your class might enjoy
rising to the challenge of linking, for example, recessive, meiosis, clone and
Franklin!)

Haemophilia, sickle cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis and colour blindness
are all examples of inherited diseases.
Vegetative reproduction is an example of asexual reproduction in which
the offspring are all clones and identical to the parent plant.
A,C,T and G are the four bases found in DNA. A always pairs with T and C with
G.
These people all worked on the structure of DNA. Levene and Chargaff
described the base pairs, whilst Franklin, Watson and Crick worked out that
the DNA molecule was a double helix.
Chromosomes contain DNA. Sequences of bases in DNA make up the code
for different genes.

Characteristics are controlled by pairs of alleles. If the alleles in the pair are
identical, the gene is homozygous; if they are not identical, it is known as
heterozygous. One of the alleles will be dominant and the other recessive.
Meiosis and mitosis are both types of cell division. Meiosis forms haploid
daughter cells whereas mitosis forms diploid daughter cells.

Developments in selective breeding
Success with wheat breeding
William Farrer was one of the first people to improve wheat crops so they could grow in 
Australian conditions. Farrer developed the basis for a good wheat crop, which has heads 
level for harvesting, high grain yield, makes excellent flour and resists disease – especially 
a mould called rust.
Problem with wheat breeding
The sets of genes that plants in a crop have are almost identical. This makes them 
susceptible to disease. The wild originals of the plant may have genes for disease 
resistance that are no longer present in the crop plants. 
During the mid-1900s, Russian scientist Nikolai Vavilov and others, 
such as CSIRO’s Sir Otto Frankel, suggested that wild seeds of crops 
be placed in freezer storage in case we ever need to reverse the 
specialisation of crops by back-breeding.

DinyYBRID INHERITANCE IN CORN

Background

In the mid-1800s, Gregor Mendel experimented with how traits are passed from parents to their offspring. He
discovered that hereditary determinants (genes) are discrete entities that do mot mix in offspring. He also
found that genes have different forms (e.g. dominant or recessive) and that they pass from parent to offspring
according to the laws of probability. He chose common garden pea plants to be the focus of his research
because they are easily grown in large numbers, their reproduction can be manipulated and they have obvious
traits such as flower colour, seed colour, seed shape, pod colour, pod shape, flower position and plant height,
Mendel selectively cross-pollinated purebred plants that had a particular trait, and observed the outcomes over
many generations. A cross between plants with one pair of contrasting traits is called a monohybrid cross.
When pure-breeding plants homozygous for dominant and recessive traits were crossed, the offspring of the
first generation (F1) always had yellow peas, However, the following generation (F2) consistently had a 3:1 ratio
of yellow peas to green peas. Mendel found similar results for other contrasting pairs of characteristics, When a
hybrid plant was test crossed, it produced 2 phenotypes in the ratio of 1:1.

searchText:
Name: _______________________________________________

DNA - The Double Helix

The nucleus is a small spherical, dense body in a cell. It is often called the
"control center" because it controls all the activities of the cell including cell
reproduction, and heredity. How does it do this? Chromosomes, found in the
nucleus, are microscopic, threadlike strands composed of the chemical DNA
(short for deoxyribonucleic acid). In simple terms, DNA controls the
production of proteins within the cell. These proteins in turn, form the
structural units of cells and control all chemical processes within the cell.

Chromosomes are composed of genes. A gene is a segment of DNA that
codes for a particular protein, which in turn codes for a trait. Hence you hear it
commonly referred to as the gene for baldness or the gene for blue eyes.
Meanwhile, DNA is the chemical that genes and chromosomes are made of. It stands for
deoxyribonucleic acid. DNA is called a nucleic acid because it was first found in the nucleus. We
now know that DNA is also found in organelles, the mitochondria and chloroplasts, though it is the
DNA in the nucleus that actually controls the cell's workings.

In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick established the structure of DNA. The structure is a
double helix, which is like a twisted ladder. The sides of the ladder are made of alternating sugar
and phosphate molecules. The sugar is deoxyribose.

Colour all the phosphates pink (one is labelled with a "p"). Colour all the deoxyriboses (D)
blue.

The rungs of the ladder are pairs of 4 types of nitrogen bases. Two of the bases are purines -
adenine and guanine. The pyrimidines are thymine and cytosine. The bases are known by their
coded letters A, G, T, C. These bases always bond in a certain way. Adenine will only bond to
thymine. Guanine will only bond with cytosine. This is known as the Base-Pair Rule. The bases
can occur in any order along a strand of DNA. The order of these bases is the code the contains
the instructions. For instance ATGCACATA would code for a different gene than AATTACGGA. A
strand of DNA contains millions of bases. (For simplicity, the image only contains a few.) Note that
the bases attach to the sides of the ladder at the sugars and not the phosphate.

Colour the bases on the DNA:

thymine = orange.           adenine = green.
guanine = purple.          cytosines =yellow.

The combination of a single base, a deoxyribose sugar, and a phosphate make up a nucleotide.
DNA is actually a molecule of repeating nucleotides. Examine the nucleotides closer. Two of the
bases are purines - adenine and guanine. The pyrimidines are thymine and cytosine. Note that the
pyrimidines are single ringed and the purines are double ringed. Colour the nucleotides using the
same colours as you coloured them in the double helix.

The two sides of the DNA ladder are held together loosely by hydrogen bonds. Colour the
hydrogen bonds grey.
 Messenger RNA

So, now, we know the nucleus controls the cell's activities through the chemical DNA, but how? It
is the sequence of bases that determine which protein is to be made. The sequence is like a code
that we can now interpret. The sequence determines which proteins are made and the proteins
determine which activities will be performed. And that is how the nucleus is the control center of
the cell. The only problem is that the DNA is too big to go through the nuclear pores. So a
chemical is used to to read the DNA in the nucleus. That chemical is messenger RNA. The
messenger RNA (mRNA) is small enough to go through the nuclear pores. It takes the
"message" of the DNA to the ribosomes and "tells them" what proteins are to be made. Recall
that proteins are the body's building blocks. Imagine that the code taken to the ribosomes is telling
the ribosome what is needed - like a recipe.

Messenger RNA is similar to DNA, except that it is a single strand, and it has no thymine. Instead
of thymine, mRNA contains the base Uracil. In addition to that difference, mRNA has the sugar
ribose instead of deoxyribose. RNA stands for Ribonucleic Acid.

Colour the mRNA as you did the DNA.
Colour the ribose a DARKER BLUE, and the uracil brown.

Achieve!
DNA discoveries
DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is found in the nuclei of cells and contains 
genetic material called genes. Since the 1940s scientists have known that DNA is the 
molecule of life, but they didn’t know what the molecule looked like. They knew DNA 
consisted of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). These 
bases joined together in pairs; A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. Scientists 
also knew that the structure had a phosphate backbone but they weren’t sure how the 
bases formed along it. In 1953 two scientists named Watson and Crick proposed that the 
bases are paired like rungs in a twisted ladder that attaches to the phosphate backbone. 
The formation is called a double helix.

First, you need to find something that contains DNA. Since DNA is the blueprint for life,
everything living contains DNA. For this experiment, we like to use green split peas. But there
are lots of other DNA sources too, such as:
• Spinach
• Chicken liver                                                  Start
• Strawberries
• Broccoli

Certain sources of DNA should not be used,
such as:
• Your family pet, Fido the dog
• Your little sister’s big toe
• Bugs you caught in the yard




 Step 1                                                       Blender Insanity!
                                                              Put in a blender:
                                                               • 1/2 cup of split peas (100ml)
                                                               • 1/8 teaspoon table salt (less than 1ml)
                                                               • 1 cup cold water (200ml)

                                                              Blend on high for 15 seconds.
                                                              The blender separates the pea cells from
                                                              each other, so you now have a really thin
                                                              pea-cell soup.

                                               How to Extract DNA from Anything Living


Soapy Peas                                                       Step 2
Pour your thin pea-cell soup through a
strainer into another container (like a
measuring cup).
Add 2 tablespoons liquid detergent (about
30ml) and swirl to mix.
Let the mixture sit for 5-10 minutes.
Pour the mixture into test tubes or other
small glass containers, each about 1/3 full.




 Step 3                                                       Enzyme Power
                                                              Add a pinch of enzymes to each test tube
                                                              and stir gently. Be careful! If you stir too
                                                              hard, you’ll break up the DNA, making it
                                                              harder to see.
                                                              Use meat tenderizer for enzymes. If you
                                                              can’t find tenderizer, try using pineapple
                                                              juice or contact lens cleaning solution.

Alcohol Separation                                              Step 4
Tilt your test tube and slowly pour
rubbing alcohol (70-95% isopropyl or
ethyl alcohol) into the tube down the side
so that it forms a layer on top of the pea
mixture. Pour until you have about the
same amount of alcohol in the tube as

searchText:
Activity 1 - DNA Extraction
DNA belongs to the group of acids originally found within the nucleus of the cells, hence the name nucleic acids.

We will extract DNA from fruit to investigate how it looks and feels. This procedure is similar to what scientists have to do
before they can use the information contained in this DNA. This information can be used to improve crops so that they are more
                     resistant to disease, insect invasion or changes in climate.




Objectives
       Extract DNA from plant cells
       Understand the general structure of cells

Materials
       1-small ziplock bag
        20 ml of extraction buffer
       Skinned kiwi fruit (each fruit cut into 8 pieces) or one large strawberry (each provides ~30 g per student pair)
       500 ml beaker (class)
       Cheese cloth
       ice water bath
       Ice cold 95% ethanol (2 ml)
       1 small test tube
       1 glass hook
       Transfer pipettes

Procedures

    1. Cut half of one kiwi fruit or the strawberry into pieces and place in the ziplock bag.

    2. Add 20mL extraction solution in the zipper bag. Close bag and CAREFULLY squeeze out air.

    3. Crush the kiwi/strawberry and extraction solution thoroughly for 5 minutes. CAREFUL don’t break
       the bag!

    4. Using the ice water bath, alternate cooling the mixture for one minute and continue to press the
       contents together for one minute. Repeat this three times

    5. Use the cheese cloth or gauze in a funnel to filter the mixture.

    6. Using the large transfer pipettes, aliquot approximately 2 ml of the kiwi/strawberry fruit solution
       into a test tube.

    7. Add approximately 2 ml of ice-cold ethanol to each tube by dropping it slowly down the side of the
       test tube, allowing it to rest on top of the kiwi/strawberry fruit mixture. Do not agitate the solution.

    8. Let the solution sit for two minutes without disturbing it. The DNA stands should form at the
       junction between the filtrate and the isopropanol and will appear as transparent, slimy, white mucus
       which can be carefully removed with the glass hook.

Activity 1 - DNA Extraction
DNA belongs to the group of acids originally found within the nucleus of the cells, hence the name nucleic acids.

We will extract DNA from fruit to investigate how it looks and feels. This procedure is similar to what scientists have to do
before they can use the information contained in this DNA. This information can be used to improve crops so that they are more
                     resistant to disease, insect invasion or changes in climate.




          The various chemicals used allow us to separate DNA from the cell. First of all, the cell wall needs to
          break open. The soap/detergent/extraction solution ruptures the outer part of the cell, while the salt helps
          separate DNA from other cellular chemicals, such as carbohydrates. The process of cooling helps
          protect the DNA from enzymes that normally do not bother the DNA because the DNA remains
          separated from the rest of the cell by the nuclear membrane. The cold temperature slows down these
          enzymes. Filtering removes most solid matter in the mixture. The last cooling helps the DNA solidify
          and precipitate.




Objectives
       Extract DNA from plant cells
       Understand the general structure of cells

Materials
       1-small ziplock bag
        20 ml of extraction buffer
       Skinned kiwi fruit (each fruit cut into 8 pieces) or one large strawberry (each provides ~30 g per student pair)
       500 ml beaker (class)
       Cheese cloth
       ice water bath
       Ice cold 95% ethanol (2 ml)
       1 small test tube
       1 glass hook
       Transfer pipettes

Procedures

    1. Cut half of one kiwi fruit or the strawberry into pieces and place in the ziplock bag.

    2. Add 20mL extraction solution in the zipper bag. Close bag and CAREFULLY squeeze out air.

    3. Crush the kiwi/strawberry and extraction solution thoroughly for 5 minutes. CAREFUL don’t break
       the bag!

    4. Using the ice water bath, alternate cooling the mixture for one minute and continue to press the
       contents together for one minute. Repeat this three times

    5. Use the cheese cloth or gauze in a funnel to filter the mixture.

    6. Using the large transfer pipettes, aliquot approximately 2 ml of the kiwi/strawberry fruit solution
       into a test tube.

    7. Add approximately 2 ml of ice-cold ethanol to each tube by dropping it slowly down the side of the
       test tube, allowing it to rest on top of the kiwi/strawberry fruit mixture. Do not agitate the solution.
    8. Let the solution sit for two minutes without disturbing it. The DNA stands should form at the
      junction between the filtrate and the isopropanol and will appear as transparent, slimy, white mucus
      which can be carefully removed with the glass hook.

Technician preparation for experiment

Time Required: ~ 20 minutes

*Night before put 95% ethanol in freezer*

   1.   Make extraction solution (see below).
   2.   Start water heating to 60°C.
   3.   Prepare ice-water bath.
   4.   Prepare fruit pieces.
   5.   Gather materials for each student group as listed below.



Extraction Solution
Materials (100 ml)

       10 ml of clear shampoo (Suave daily clarifying shampoo)
       1.5 g of table salt
       Distilled H2O

Procedure (modify amount depending on the size of a class)

   1. Mix 90 ml of distilled water and 1.5 g of salt.
   2. Add shampoo until solution volume is 100 ml. Stir slowly to avoid foaming of the shampoo.
   3. Measure 20 ml of solution into 1L zipper bags (1 per student pair).
 Procedure Questions
  1.   Why do we “crush” the kiwi/strawberry fruit?
  2.   Why do we use shampoo?
  3.   What does the salt do?
  4.   Why do we need to cool the mixture?
  5.   What does the cold ethanol do?
  6.   Why can’t we use room temperature ethanol?



Discussion Questions
  1. To extract DNA from cells, what must you isolate it from in the case of a plant such as strawberry?

  2. What steps did we use to extract the DNA?

  3. What is DNA used for when it is extracted?



Answers to Procedure Questions
  1. Why do we “crush” the kiwi/strawberry fruit? Crushing the kiwi/strawberry fruit physically
     breaks apart the cell walls.

  2. Why do we use shampoo? After the cell walls have been disrupted during mechanical mashing of
     the fruit, the detergent in the shampoo disrupts the cell and nuclear membranes of each cell to
     release the DNA. It does this by dissolving lipids and proteins that hold the membranes together.

  3. What does the salt do? The salt neutralizes the negative charges on the DNA and thus enables the
     DNA strands to stick together. It also causes proteins and carbohydrates to precipitate.

  4. Why do we need to cool the mixture? DNases or restriction enzymes that destroy DNA are
     present in the cell’s cytoplasm. They are there to protect the cell from invasion by viruses. Once the

searchText:
The Nucleus of a Cell
The nucleus can be thought of
as the control centre of a cell.
It contains information about
how the cell functions, as well
as information about the
organism as a whole.

Inside the nucleus of a cell are
structures called
chromosomes. Chromosomes
are only visible when the cell is
undergoing cell division.

Genes are sections of
chromosomes which determine
the characteristics of the
organism.

                   The Structure of DNA
Chromosomes are made of a substance called deoxyribonucleic acid,
or DNA for short. It is the sequence of the DNA in your chromosomes
that makes up your genes and determines your
characteristics.

DNA is a complex chemical compound. It is made
up of molecules called nucleotides. The basic
structure of a nucleotide is shown on the right.
Nucleotides have three main parts: a phosphate
group, a deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogen
base.

                      The nucleotides are arranged
                      in a way that makes a double
                      helix. A double helix is
                      shaped like a twisted ladder, like
                      the lookout tower in King’s Park.

                      The uprights of the ladder are
                      made of alternating phosphate
                      and sugar groups. The nitrogen
                      bases pair up to form the rungs
                      of the ladder.

The Nitrogen Bases
 There are four different nitrogen bases. They are Adenine, Cytosine,
Guanine and Thymine. The four bases are represented by the first
letter of its name, for example Adenine is represented by a capital A.

The chemical structure of each base means that it can only pair with one
other base. These are called complementary base pairs. A pairs with
T, and C pairs with G.

Questions
1. What does DNA stand for?

2. Nucleotides are the building blocks of DNA. What are the three parts
   of a nucleotide?

3. In a DNA molecule, what do the letters A, T, C and G represent?



4. DNA is often compared to a twisted ladder. Explain why this is a good
   comparison.




5. What are complementary base pairs?




6. Complete the strand of DNA below by writing in the complementary
   bases.


    A    C    T     A    G     C     A    T     C    G    T     G    A



The Genetic Code
Organisms are different because the proteins in their cells are different.
Proteins are made up of many smaller units called amino acids joined
together in long chains.

The DNA provides a code for the cells to make proteins. Each set of
three bases as you move down one side of the DNA molecule, codes for a
specific amino acid. These sets of three bases are called codons.
 The table below shows all the codons and the amino acids they code for.
There is more than one codon for almost all of the 20 amino acids. There

DNA, chromosomes and genes
A new life begins as just one cell. All the information for growing a living thing is found 
inside the nucleus of this cell. For most animals, this cell is a fertilised egg, containing 
genetic information from two parents. This genetic information is stored in DNA, in 
genes and chromosomes.
DNA
 
●The letters DNA stand for deoxyribonucleic acid (say de-ox-ee-rye-bo-new-clee-ick 
ass-id). When people talk about DNA, they usually mean the information that DNA 
contains, not the acid itself. 
 
●DNA is found inside the cells of nearly all living things. 
 
●DNA is like a set of instructions for building and operating a living thing. It provides 
the information to make the proteins that make up cells, as well as instructions as 
to how the cells form, what shape they will be, what things they can do and so on. 
Chromosomes and genes
 
●Chromosomes are tiny threads made of DNA. Genes are short pieces of these 
threads. 
 
●Each chromosome consists of thousands of different genes. 
 
●Every gene carries information about a specific characteristic. 
 
●Chromosomes are found inside the nucleus of cells. In each cell, the genetic 
information is exactly the same, containing the same instructions. 
 
●Chromosomes come in pairs. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. 
 
●One chromosome of every pair comes from the mother and one in every pair 
comes from the father.

searchText:
DNA extraction from strawberries
      This is a classroom friendly DNA extraction from strawberries. It is safe, cheap and fun.


Materials for one extraction:
    Zip lock plastic bag
    1 strawberry (fresh or defrosted)
    10mL DNA extraction buffer
    Gauze, cut into squares
    Funnel
    Ice cold ethanol
    Plastic transfer pipette
    Clear test tube, plastic/glass               http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Image:FraiseFruitPhoto.jpg
    Long wooden skewer



DNA extraction buffer:
Makes 50mL (enough for 5 extractions)
     5 mL liquid dish washing detergent or shampoo
     0.75g salt
     45mL water
To make: Measure detergent and water in a measuring cylinder, weigh
out the salt and combine ingredients into a labelled bottle or beaker.

                 http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Image:Measuring_cylinder_hg.jpg

What to do:
1. Make the DNA extraction buffer following the method above.

2. Wash the strawberry, remove the sepals (the green leaves) and put it into a zip lock plastic
   bag. Add 10mL of the extraction buffer and seal the bag tightly, making sure any air bubbles
   are pushed out and crush the strawberries with your fingers on the bench surface for 1 minute.
Note: Do not crush the strawberries too much as this will cause the DNA to shear/degrade.

                                          What is happening?

                                                 Crushing the strawberries breaks open many of the
                                                 strawberry cells, releasing the nuclei where the DNA
                                                 is.

                                                 The soap in the detergent or shampoo in the
                                                 extraction buffer breaks down the fatty membranes of
                                                 the cells, breaks open the nuclear membrane and
                                                 releases the DNA into solution.

                                                 The salt makes the DNA molecules stick together,
                                                 and separate from the proteins that are also released
                                                 from the cells.


3. Place the funnel lined with gauze into the test tube.

4. Pour the strawberry DNA extraction buffer mixture into the gauze and filter the mixture into the
   tube through the gauze.



                                                                        Document prepared by Carolyn Jones
 5. Keep the liquid filtered into the tube in the tube and discard the gauze and the strawberry pulp.

                                         What is happening?




                                                         The gauze retains strawberry cell debris.
                                                         The strawberry DNA is dissolved in the
                                                         DNA extraction buffer, which will pass
                                                         through the gauze into the test tube.




6. Layer an equal volume of ice-cold ethanol on top of the strawberry solution in the test tube
   using the plastic transfer pipette provided.

7. Observe what happens at the interface of the alcohol and strawberry solution when you twirl a
   long wooden skewer through the interface. Keep the tube still at eye level and do not shake it.

                                      What are you seeing?



                              The DNA collects between the layer of alcohol on top and strawberry
                              extract underneath!

                              DNA is insoluble in alcohol, so it precipitates. What you see is the
                              precipitation of strawberry DNA - long, thread-like DNA molecules at
                              the interface of the alcohol and DNA solution.




8. You can collect the DNA strands onto a wooden skewer. The whitish, gooey, stringy stuff is
   DNA containing strawberry genes! This contains the code for all of the proteins required by the
   strawberry throughout its life.




                                                           http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Image:DNA_ORF.gif



                                                                  Document prepared by Carolyn Jones

Genetics
8
© Suada Bilali, Chris Greef and Blake Education 2010
Assignments in Junior Science – Book 7 – Genetics
Chromosomes with their genes are made up of the chemical DNA or deoxyribonucleic 
acid. DNA is a long molecule that stores all genetic information. It looks like a double 
helix or a twisted ladder, as you can see in the diagram at the right. 
DNA has only four repeated subunits, the nucleotides. In humans, a DNA molecule 
is about 2 cm long. In a 1 mm section of a DNA molecule there can be 8 million 
nucleotides. Each nucleotide is made up of a sugar unit, a phosphate unit and a base unit. 
The phosphate links the sugars to make the long strand (i.e. sugar – phosphate – sugar 
– phosphate – sugar). The bases of one strand lock onto the bases of the other strand to 
form the double strand. 
Although the sugar and phosphate units are all the same, there are four kinds of bases: 
adenosine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The bases only join in certain 
pairs: A – T and C – G. In order to code for a particular gene such as tongue rolling, the 
DNA section of a particular chromosome is a certain length and the bases are in a particular order.
1 	Identify the chemicals sugar, phosphate and the four bases of the DNA section by: 
• shading sugar horizontally 
• shading phosphate vertically 
• labelling each base as A, C, G or T.  
One sugar and two bases have been identified for you. 
When a cell divides, it first has to make a copy of its DNA molecules. First, the double helix untwists. Then it splits 
open into two strands. The nucleotides which are floating around in the nucleus come into contact with the open 
strands and matching bases lock together. After a few minutes, two new double strands have been produced. It is 
important that the two new double strands are identical to the original.

levels nearer the surface. The sequence of fossils in layers is known as the fossil record.

Evolution and Mutation

Genes are the potential of an organism. The environment may or

may not allow the full development of this potential. Genes are Bole)
contained in chromosomes in the nucleus of cells. Genes are short iS) Py e-Q<

lengths of chromosomes and are the basic unit of inheritance. They © )
usually copy themselves exactly each time a cell divides (meiosis and mitosis) but,

occasionally, the unexpected happens — and the unexpected is usually (but not always) unpleasant.

Genes are made of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), which has a very complicated structure. If this
structure is altered in any way, a different gene may result. This is called mutation. Alleles are different
genes that influence one characteristic. Mutations can remove one allele and replace it with another.

Mutations very rarely occur spontaneously — perhaps one in a million may happen without apparent
cause. The rate is increased by substances called mutagens. Some of these are produced by the cell
themselves and others come from the environment. These include:

* some chemicals
= radiation
= increased temperature.

Chemicals that are suspected of being mutagens include nitrous acid (HNO,) and nitroso compounds
which are present in treated meats such as salami and bacon, mustard gas (used in warfare), tobacco
tars, and fungi that spoil foods. (Some of these substances may also cause cancer — they are
carcinogenic.)

Radiation includes gamma radiation (a form of nuclear radiation), X-rays, cosmic rays (from space) and
ultraviolet (UV) light. There are also natural radioactive sources from the Earth itself. The ozone layer
Protects us from much of the harmful radiation from space, but this has been damaged by such man-
made chemicals as CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons).

An increase in temperature can cause a five-fold increase in the rate of mutations. Violent temperature
changes can cause an even greater change in rate.

If mutations occur in gametes (germ or sex cells), they are inherited.

ER] Evolution of icefish

Science understanding FOUNDATION | STANDARD | ADVANCED

Fish of the Family Channichthyidae, found in the waters around Antarctica, are very unusual. They
have evolved in extremely cold water and are commonly called icefish (Figure 4.7.1). There are

25 species of icefish. Scientists have been interested in these fish since they were first discovered,
because of their amazing ability to avoid freezing to death in extremely cold waters.

Icefish ‘antifreeze’

Research has shown that an icefish’s body contains special ‘antifreeze’ chemicals called
glycoproteins, which seem to work by preventing ice crystals growing. The antifreeze chemical coats
ice crystals so water cannot come into contact with the surface of the crystal and add to the size of
the crystal. These chemicals are so effective that they are being researched for possible applications
where freezing needs to be prevented. Possible applications include increasing the ability of crop
plants to withstand frost, lengthening the shelf life of frozen foods, and potential applications in
surgery, storing organs for transplant and treating hypothermia.

Figure 4.7.1 Ocellated icefish, Chionodraco rastrospinosus

Icefish blood

Another amazing fact about the icefish family is that they have almost no red blood cells. Red blood
cells contain a chemical called haemoglobin, which bonds to oxygen. The haemoglobin transports
oxygen around the bodies of all the other vertebrates. But icefish contain no haemoglobin and

their blood is almost transparent. Oxygen is not very soluble so scientists wondered how oxygen
was carried in the blood of these fish, and how their blood can carry enough oxygen to the cells to
maintain respiration.

Research discovered that:

genetic mutations

Understanding Biology  – Ecosystems and living things
37
Exobiology (also called astrobiology) is the study of the origins, evolution and distribution of life within our universe, 
not just on the planet Earth (exo meaning ‘outside’). NASA’s exobiology program is an example of one of several 
organisations actively investigating this mystery. The interest taken by institutions like NASA has given the field a 
new respectability. It is believed the question of the origins of life can best be answered by dividing it into the study 
of the four main parts listed below:
• Prebiotic evolution (pre meaning ‘before’, biotic meaning ‘living/life’)
• The evolution of biogenic compounds (How did they originate?)
• Early evolution of living organisms (e.g. How did life arise and evolve?)
•  Evolution of more advanced organisms (e.g. Does life exist on other planets? If so, is it more/less advanced 
than life on Earth?)
Note that other groupings than the above have been made, but we will only consider the above.
The main elements of life are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorous and sulphur (commonly abbreviated 
as CHONPS). We usually think of these elements as making up Earth’s life forms, but they are also part of the make-
up of the planets, stars and other space matter. Because of this, there is every reason to believe that other life forms 
exist in our universe, since it is so large. 
Scientists have traced the origins of the elements as far back as coming from stars. From there, they went on to form 
planets and other space matter. What we don’t know is where the elements came from in the first place, in order 
for the stars to be formed. This is one of the many mysteries scientists are trying to solve. With so many different 
compounds in existence, there are many pathways to investigate.

EXTRA WORKSHEET 1: Carbon-14 dating
SCIENCE INQUIRY                            LOGICAL/MATHEMATICAL, VISUAL/SPATIAL


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________

Carbon-14 dating is also known as radiocarbon dating. Carbon-14 dating is
really important for finding the age of organic materials from living things that
lived in the last 40 000 to 50 000 years. Organic materials are compounds
containing carbon that are produced by living organisms. These compounds
include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and vitamins.



Formation of carbon-14
Carbon-14 is formed high in the atmosphere by cosmic rays (radiation from
the Sun) changing nitrogen atoms in to carbon-14 atoms. The carbon-14
atoms combine with oxygen and form radioactive carbon dioxide. The
proportion of carbon dioxide molecules which are radioactive is tiny. There is
only 1 radioactive carbon atom in 1 000 000 000 000 carbon atoms
(1 million million).



Carbon-14 in plants and animals
The radioactive carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants in photosynthesis and
made into sugar. Some of the sugar is then converted into many different
organic compounds such as proteins, lipids and vitamins in the plant. When
the plant is eaten by animals, the radioactive carbon atoms become part of
the animal’s body tissues. When organisms die they stop absorbing
carbon-14.




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                  ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
 Radioactive decay of carbon-14
Carbon-14 atoms decay into nitrogen atoms. In comparison to other types of
radioactive decay, the decay of carbon-14 is very fast. The half-life of carbon-
14 is 5730 years. Only half of the original radioactive carbon will be left after
this time. The decay curve for carbon-14 is shown in Figure 1. The vertical
axis shows the percentage of carbon-14 remaining. Carbon-14 decays so fast
that radiocarbon dating is not accurate beyond about 50 000 years. Any older
than that and carbon-14 dating is not accurate because so little radioactivity is
left that is the amount is hard to measure.




Figure 1
Carbon-14 decay curve.

EXTRA WORKSHEET 2: Dinosaurs and
extinction
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                    VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


Extinction
Extinction means the death of all organisms of a particular species. About
65.5 million years ago there was a ‘mass extinction event’, meaning many
species became extinct at the same time, and fairly quickly. In some groups
every species died, including all the dinosaurs. This extinction is called the
K–T extinction or the Cretaceous–Tertiary extinction. The causes of the
extinction are still being researched and several different theories have been
proposed, including climate change, asteroid impact, volcanic eruptions,
change in food supply or sex ratios.



Climate change
During the Mesozoic era the climate was much milder (warmer) than it is now.
There were no ice caps, sea levels were much higher, and there was less
difference in temperature between the poles and the equator. Carbon dioxide
levels were more than ten times higher and there was a lot more oxygen in
the atmosphere.

These conditions seem to have changed in the late Cretaceous. If oxygen
levels also fell at this time and dinosaurs breathed as birds do today, then the
dinosaurs may have had great difficulty getting enough oxygen into their
bodies. Another possible cause of the extinction is that dinosaurs would have
been unable to regulate their body temperatures in a colder world.




           Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
 Asteroid impact
In 1980, a scientist called Walter Alvarez and others scientists were studying
a rock layer from Italy which dated to the time of the K–T extinction. They
found that the rock layer had a very high level of a rare metal called iridium in
it. Iridium is more common in asteroids and comets than on Earth. Much of
the iridium on Earth falls as dust from the atmosphere due to meteorites
burning up. The only other source of iridium is volcanic activity. This led to the
hypothesis that a large object hit the Earth and deposited an unusually large
amount of iridium.

Some studies have concluded that an asteroid hit the Earth near the time of
the extinction and that this asteroid formed the Chicxulub Crater in Central
America (Figure 1). However, another study found that the Chicxulub asteroid
hit the Earth about 300 000 years before the extinction. That research also
suggested that the high iridium levels may be explained by volcanic activity.

If an impact did occur around the time of the extinction, then it could have
caused a rapid heating of the Earth, followed by a rapid cooling as the dust
thrown into the atmosphere reduced the amount of sunlight reaching the
ground. More research is needed to decide if the asteroid theory is correct.




Figure 1


           Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 2
 The site of a possible asteroid impact on the Yucatan Peninsula.



Volcanic eruption
Another theory for the cause of the extinction is that volcanoes erupted in
what is currently the Deccan region of India (Figure 2). These volcanoes
covered an enormous area, about half the size of India, and rock from them
has been dated to 65.5 million years ago. The eruptions would have released
dust and other material, including iridium, into the air. This material might
have blocked sunlight and so reduced photosynthesis in plants. There were
clearly changes in the Earth’s climate at least half a million years before the
extinction of dinosaurs, which corresponds with the date of eruption of the
Deccan volcanoes. However, much more data is needed to show the
significance of these eruptions.




Figure 2
The Deccan Traps, site of a massive series of volcanic eruptions that may have been
involved in the extinction of the dinosaurs.




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                  ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 3
 Change in food plants
There was a great change in the plant fossils during the middle to late
Cretaceous period. The gymnosperms which dinosaurs had been feeding on
largely disappeared and a new flowering type of plant appeared in the fossil
record. Fossilised dinosaur dung indicates that most dinosaurs kept eating the
gymnosperms. This could mean that the dinosaurs were unable to adapt to a
new diet of flowering plants when the gymnosperms disappeared. Much more
data is needed for this hypothesis.



Sex ratio changes
A new theory proposes that a brief period of rising temperatures changed the
proportions of males and females in the dinosaurs. Crocodiles are modern-
day relatives of the dinosaurs. If the temperature rises, then more male than

Chapter 1                                        DNA and
genetics
EXTRA WORKSHEET 3: Mutations

As DNA is copied, mistakes can occur causing changes in the order of the
bases along the DNA strand. This type of change is called a mutation. Some
mutations happen naturally. Some mutations are the result of damage caused
by chemicals, radiation or other factors. Factors that may cause mutations are
known as mutagens. Mutations can result in the disease known as cancer,
which is uncontrolled cell growth.

The effect of mutagens has been known for a very long time. Over 2500 years
ago, long before chromosomes or DNA were discovered, the Greek
philosopher Hippocrates identified tumours (cancerous growths) in patients.
He described these as ‘cancer’ because the tumour shape resembled a crab,
and the Greek words for crab were carcinos and karkinoma.

Ultraviolet (UV) light from the Sun is a natural mutagen, as are some viruses.
Tobacco smoke contains mutagens. Mutagens are also found in some food
and drink.


Point mutations
Mutagens affect DNA in different ways. Some mutagens change a single base
in the DNA code. These are point mutations. A point mutation is shown in
Figure 1. Changing only one base for another sometimes has little effect on
the functioning of the gene.




Figure 1


Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1   Page 1
 Example of a point mutation.


Frameshift mutations
Other mutagens delete or insert bases into the DNA molecule, causing a
change in the sequence of bases that follow. These are major changes to the
DNA and are known as frameshift mutations. A frameshift mutation is shown
in Figure 2.




Figure 2
Example of a frameshift mutation.


Mutations and DNA repair
Infrequent (irregular) small doses of mutagens have little effect. Many
potential mutations will be naturally repaired by your cells before the mutation
can cause permanent damage. Proteins within the cell nucleus ‘cut out’
damaged sections of DNA and fill the gap with the correct sequence of bases.

But when mutations occur faster than they can be repaired, some areas of
damage can go uncorrected. The genetic information can be permanently
mutated and may cause disease. Permanent mutations can occur if you are
exposed to a large amount of mutagen, or if small exposures are continued
over a long period of time. For example, nicotine in cigarette smoke can block
the process of repairing damaged DNA in lung cells. The result of long-term
cigarette smoking is lung damage and potentially lung cancer, which can be
fatal.


Mutated cells
Normal cells respond to changes in their environment in particular ways. Cells
with mutated DNA do not behave normally. Mutations can occur in ordinary
cells of the body (somatic cells) but they can also occur in the cells that
produce gametes (germline cells), such as in the ovary and testes.




Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1   Page 2
 Mutations in somatic cells can damage the cells and change the functioning of
organs; for example, mutated bone marrow cells can stop the bone marrow
from functioning properly. Somatic mutations do not affect any offspring.

However, if a mutated egg or sperm produces an embryo, the germline
mutations are passed on to the offspring. The mutation will be found in every
cell of the new individual, including any gametes they produce. Germline
mutations are passed from generation to generation.

           __________________________________________________________

Teacher/Technician Notes
• Use fresh fruit (strawberry or kiwi works well). You may want this to peeled and chopped
  into chunks before the lesson to avoid the need for peelers and knives in the lab.

• Check for any fruit allergies to ensure you order fruit which is safe for all of your class to use.

• Pineapple juice is used as it contains an enzyme which removes the proteins from the DNA.
  If this is unavailable, contact lens cleaning solution may be used as an alternative.

• You may choose to mush the fruit in polystyrene cups to prevent damage to the glassware
  (or just if you don’t like the noise created by metal forks scraping glass!).

• First, test the fruit you are using with the method. If you find that the pulp is too
  thick to be filtered in a filter funnel, then you may wish to use a sieve lined with
  kitchen roll and press the liquid out using the back of the fork instead.

• Ethanol (alcohol) should be stored in the freezer and then kept on ice in the lab – ideally
  this should be requested halfway into the practical to ensure it remains ice cold.




                                                     Page 1 of 1                                visit twinkl.com
 Extracting DNA from Fruit
  Aim: To extract DNA from cells.

Equipment:
• fruit - peeled and          • boiling tube                      • spatula
  chopped into chunks
                              • boiling tube rack                 • pipette
• pineapple juice
                              • measuring cylinder
• table salt
                              • funnel
                                                                  Safety Information
• washing-up liquid                                               Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
                              • filter paper
• ice-cold alcohol                                                Apply pressure to wounds and
                              • glass rod
• 2 beakers                                                       inform teacher immediately.
                              • fork

Method:
Step 1: Roughly measure 80ml water into a beaker. Add 1 spatula of table salt and stir
well with the glass rod, until all the salt has dissolved.

Step 2: Add 10ml of washing-up liquid to the same beaker and stir gently to mix
together. Put this beaker to one side.

Step 3: Into the second beaker, place the chopped fruit and mush it carefully with a fork.

Step 4: Pour the contents of the first beaker (from steps 1 and 2) into the second
beaker with the fruit pulp.

Step 5: Stir it a little to mix the contents then leave at room temperature for 20 minutes.

Step 6: Rinse and clean the empty beaker.

Step 7: Set up the filter funnel over the clean beaker.

Step 8: Filter the fruit pulp mix. The filtrate should be a slightly coloured liquid. (The
colour of the liquid will depend on the type of fruit you used).

Step 9: Discard the filter paper and pour the filtrate into a measuring cylinder.

Step 10: Add pineapple juice to the filtrate in a ratio of 1:5 pineapple juice to filtrate.

Step 11: Leave at room temperature for 5 minutes.

Step 12: Pour out the mixture from the measuring cylinder into a boiling
tube and stand in the boiling tube rack.

Step 13: Carefully pour or pipette ice-cold alcohol down the inside of the
boiling tube, in a ratio of 1:1.

Step 14: Leave to separate for 5 to 10 minutes before observing the DNA.

Genetic diseases – mutations
Sometimes the codes in genes are changed, and the developing cells receive a wrong message. A change in the codes 
could cause the cells to make a wrong protein, or no protein at all. As a result, the cells do not function normally. 
Changes in the genes are called mutations, derived from a Latin word meaning change. Mutations can be dominant 
or recessive. If dominant, they will be expressed and hide the normal form of the gene. If recessive, the normal gene 
will hide the mutation. To have the characteristic of the recessive mutation, a person must have both genes with that 
mutation.

Genetic Variation
Label the following diagram




Humans have __ pairs of chromosomes in every cell. They exist in pairs
because you get ____ of them from your mother and half from your _______.

Egg cells and sperm cells are called gametes. Each gamete contains half of the
parents 46 chromosomes, one of each pair.

A gene is a section of DNA which codes for a specific characteristic e.g. hair
colour. Since we have two of each chromosome, we have two copies of each
gene, these are called alleles. You get one from each parent.

You can be homozygous; both alleles are the same or heterozygous where each
allele is different.

Some genes are dominant and some are recessive. A dominant gene always
expressed if present and a recessive gene only shows if there are two copies.

Your phenotype is a description of the characteristics that are shown.

Your genotype is a description of the exact combination of genes you have.

Brown hair (B) is dominant over blonde (b). If my phenotype is brown, I have
brown hair, my genotype could be Bb (heterozygous) or BB (homozygous).

EXD) Genetically modified food

Science understanding [_Founp STANDARD

The Green Revolution of the 1950s increased food production by using new and improved
chemicals to control weeds, insect pests and diseases. New varieties of crops and fertilisers also
helped to increase food production.

The Gene Revolution of the 21st century uses genetic modification to grow crops that have the
potential to produce more food with a higher nutritional value than traditional crops. The Gene
Revolution also uses fewer chemicals. Scientists believe that by using gene technology they can
improve a variety of crops including corn, wheat, rice, canola, chicory, squash, potato, soybean,
alfalfa, cotton, banana and tomato.

() Compare the Green Revolution and the Gene Revolution.

Below are some of the arguments for and against the use of genetically modified (GM) food.

Arguments for the use of genetically modified crops

+ GM crops are potentially more resistant to disease, can grow in less space, can provide greater
yield and need less pesticide

+ Genetically modified, pest-resistant crops need less insecticide spray, which is better for the
environment and saves the farmer money.

+ Current agricultural methods will not be able to grow enough food to feed the 9 billion people
predicted to populate the world by 2050.

+ Genetic modification can improve crops more quickly than conventional selective breeding
processes.

+ Scientists can add genes that make plants tolerant to frost, drought and salinity (high salt levels).
‘They can also add genes to make crops resistant to insect pests. These genes can be turned ‘of?”
and ‘on’ in different parts of the plant. Genetic modification is one tool that farmers can use to
maintain or increase crop yields as the climate changes.

+ GM foods can improve a poor diet by providing nutritionally improved foods.

+ Improved nutrition should have health benefits in both developed and developing countries.

Patience Instructions
A 5 or 10 minute activity where the aim is to use your knowledge of the glossary key terms to make
one continuous link, matching key word with definition.

 1. Shuffle the cards.

What does genetics have do with me?
Has anyone ever told you that you have your father’s nose or your grandmother’s hair? Many of our features are 
inherited from our parents, and theirs from their parents. Inheritance or heredity is the passing of characteristics 
from parent to offspring – you. Characteristics include eye colour, hair colour, height, nose shape – and many more. 
We all inherit slightly different combinations of these features from our parents. Even brothers and sisters look 
different, because they inherit different characteristics from their parents.

searchText: ﻿DIAGNOSTIC TEST GENETICS Multiple Choice Questions 1. The number of chromosomes in a human body cell is: A. 23 B. 23 pairs C. 2 2. The sex chromosomes of a normal human male are: A. XX B. XY C. XXXX 3. The chromosomes that are not sex chromosomes are called: A. X and Y B. autosomes C. chromatin 4. In a pedigree, an affected male is shown by a: A. blank circle B. shaded circle C. shaded square 5. The inherited appearance is the: A. phenotype B. genotype C. co-dominance 6. Homozygous is known as: A. hybrid B. pure-breeding C. wild type 7. The less frequently inherited characteristic is called: A. recessive B. co-inherited C. dominant 8. Genes determining sex-linked conditions are found on the: A. autosomes B. Y chromosome C. X chromosome 9. A disease of blood clotting inability is: A. haemophilia B. haemochromatosis C. heparin 10. The ratio of phenotypes of offspring of a monohybrid cross is: A. 1:2:1 B. 3:1 C. 9:3:3:1 True-False Questions 11. Genes are made of DNA. 12. Somatic cells are body cells not gametes. 13. A variation of a gene is an allele. 14. Recessive characteristics are always indicated by capital letters. 15. If the genotype is brown eye colour, then the phenotype is BB. Short Answer Questions 16. How can one determine the genotype of an animal with a dominant characteristic (e.g. a rabbit with brown fur)? 17. Why does the father determine the sex of a child? 18. How can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child? 19. Why do more males than females have sex-linked diseases such as red-green colour blindness? 20. What are the possible children’s blood type if parents have A and AB blood types? DIAGNOSTIC TEST GENETICS ANSWERS 1.B 2.B 3.B 4.C 5.A 6.B 7.A 8.C 9.A 10.B 11.T 12.T 13.T 14.F 15.F 16. Breed the animal with one which has the homozygous recessive characteristic (e.g. an albino rabbit). If any offspring are albino, the parent was heterozygous/hybrid. If no offspring ar albino, the parent is homozygous/pure-bred. 17. The mother has only the sex chromosome, the X chromosome, in the egg. If the father’s sperm contains another X chromosome, the child will be a girl. If the sperm has a Y chromosome, the child will be a boy. 18. The allele for blue eye colour is recessive. Hence, two heterozygous/hybrid may carry the dominant brown allele as well as the recessive blue eye allele. If the two recessive alleles are in sperm and egg, the child will have blue eyes. 19. The sex-linked diseases are carried on the X chromosome. A male only has to have one X chromosome with the defective gene to inherit a sex-linked disease, but a female must have both chromosomes with defective genes to suffer from the disease. The latter is less likely. 20. If parents’ genotypes are AA and AB – Possible child’s genotypes are A and AB – Child could be A or AB type If parents’ genotypes are AO and AB – Possible child’s genotypes are AA, AB, AO, BO – Child could be A, B or AB types

\\\\ Genetics Review: terms to know

Reciprocal cross

Whenever we cross a male possessing a specific trait with a female possessing a different trait, the
procedure is called a reciprocal cross. Mendel created reciprocal crosses when he crossed female yellow
peas with male green peas.

[1] What would have been an alternative reciprocal cross using the same characteristics?

1 Filial: to do with a son, daughter, child or offspring.

F, and F, generations

This is a shorthand term for ‘first filial’ and ‘second filial’ generations. The first generation progeny
(offspring) of a reciprocal cross are called the F, generation. The abbreviation F, means, “The resulting
progeny of the reciprocal cross being studied’.

[2] Why do we usually say F, rather than use the complete definition given above?

The F, generation is the progeny of crossing the F, individuals. Members of the F, generation can be
allowed to self-fertilise (in plants) or cross-fertilise with other members of the F, generation. Either way,
the progeny is referred to as the F, generation.

Cell cycle: growth and reproduction
All cells grow and reproduce. They use either of the processes mitosis or meiosis.
Mitosis occurs in somatic cells. These are cells used for growth and development of an organism.

Meiosis is exclusively used by germ cells. Germ cells are involved in reproduction. Male and female
reproductive cells are referred to as gametes. When a female gamete (ovum) is fertilised by a male
gamete (sperm) a zygote is formed.

Bb ________________________ The Five (5) Steps Associated With Solving a Genetics Problem: If you take the time to follow the directions below, you will be able to solve most genetics problems. 1. Determine the genotypes of the parents or whatever is given in problem. 2. Set up your Punnett square as follows: *# sq. based on possible gametes that can be formed. possible parental Possible parentalgametes gametes otherOther possible possible parental gametes parental gametes 3. Fill in the squares. This represents the possible combinations that could occur during fertilization. 4. Write out the possible genotypic ratio of the offspring. 5. Using the genotypic ratio determine the phenotypic ratio for the offspring. . Part 2: Sample Problem (Just read this over, it is a practice problem) A heterozygous male, black eyed mouse is crossed with a red eyed, female mouse. Predict the possible offspring! Step 1: Determine the genotype of the parents. The male parent is heterozygous which means he has one allele for black eyes and one allele for red eyes. Since his eyes are black, this means that black allele must be dominant over the red allele. So the male parents genotype is “Bb” (B = allele for black eye, b = allele for red eye). The female parent has red eyes, there is only one way to have this recessive phenotype, so she must to be homozygous recessive. Homozygous recessive means that her genotype must be “bb”. Therefore, genotype of the parents is Bb x bb. Page #1 Step 2: During meiosis (the formation of sex cells) one member (allele) of each gene pair separate. The male mouse (Bb) produces some sperm containing “B” (the allele for black eye) and some sperm containing “b” (the allele for red eyes). On one axis of the Punnett square you put the two possible gametes for the male. Possible Sperm B b b Possible Eggs b Repeat this for the other axis for the possible female gametes. Since she is “bb” you must put “b” and “b”. Step 3: During fertilization sperm meets the egg. The Punnett square show us the various possibilities during fertilization. The offspring must be one of these genotypes listed in the squares. B b If the sperm contains a “B” allele If the sperm contains a “B” and it and fertilizes fertilizes an eggthe egg containing containing the b Bb the “b” allele, the resultant “b” allele, the resultant offspring offspring will will have the have the genotype genotype “Bb”. “Bb” b Repeating the process we can see all of the possible genotypes. B b b Bb bb b Bb bb Step 4: The genotypic ratio is determined by counting each possible genotype. You’ll note there are two “Bb” for every two “bb”. Therefore, we write the ratio as 2 : 2 Bb : bb Page #2 Normally we reduce to the lowest terms: 1 : 1 Bb : bb Step 5: The Bb will produce a black eyed mouse (phenotype) and the bb will produce a red eyed mouse (phenotype). The phenotypic ratio is written as 1 : 1 black eye : red eye Ratios tell you there is an even chance of having offspring with black eyes as there is for having offspring with red eyes. That would be the same as a 50% probability of having red eyes, or a 50% probability of having black eyes. . **On the following pages are several problems. dominant gene and the masked gene is the recessive gene. Dominant genes are represented by a capital
letter and recessive genes by the corresponding lower case letter e.g. in pea plants the gene for taliness
is dominant to the gene for dwarfness, therefore, “T”’ represents the gene for taliness and “'t” the gene

Hybrid organism: the offspring of a cross between two parents that differ in one or more characteristics
