    Aim: To observe the different reactivities of different metals and acids.

Equipment:
• 8 test tubes
                                                               Safety Information
                                                               Hydrochloric acid [1M] – possible
• Test tube rack                                               bacterial presence
• 2 corks or bungs to fit the test tubes loosely               Wear safety goggles. Rinse     skin and inform
• Bunsen burner                                                teacher immediately.

• Wood splint (1 per group)                                    Sulphuric acid [0.5M] – irritant to skin and eye

• 25cm³ dilute HCl (1M)                                        Wear safety goggles. Rinse     skin and inform
                                                               teacher immediately.
• 25cm³ dilute sulphuric acid (0.5M)
                                                               Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• Granules, filiings of foil pieces of copper, iron,
  magnesium and zinc                                           Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
                                                               immediately.




Method:
It might be useful to stand your test tube rack over plain white paper or a mini whiteboard to help you
with labelling and identifying the contents.

Step 1: Place six test tubes in the test-tube rack.

Step 2: Add a 2–3cm depth of dilute hydrochloric acid to the first three tubes.

Step 3: Add a 2–3cm depth of dilute sulphuric acid to the remaining three tubes.

Step 4: Add a small piece of a different metal to each of the tubes with
hydrochloric acid in them. Record which metal you add to each tube.

Step 5: Add a small piece of the same metals to each of the tubes with sulphuric
acid in them. Record which metal you add to each tube.

Step 6: Observe any reactions and make a note of your observations in your
table of results.

Step 7: From your observations, choose one of the metals that reacts rapidly
with the acids. Collect and test the gas produced. Your teacher will show you
how to test the gas being produced in these reactions.




                                                       Page 1 of 4
                                                                                  Metal and Acid Reactions

Choose another of the metals that reacts rapidly with the acids. In a clean test tube, add a piece of
this metal to a 2–3cm depth of one of the acids. This time, however, place a cork loosely in the top
of the test tube so that any gas produced escapes slowly. Light a wood splint, remove the cork and
immediately hold the flame to the mouth of the tube. If nothing happens, you may need to try again.

Questions
 1. Write down the metals you tested in order of the most reactive to the least reactive.

 2. What gas was produced by the reaction?

 3. When a metal and an acid react, they always produce the gas you found and a salt. Show this as a
    word equation.

 4. Describe how you tested for the gas, and the observations you made if the gas was present.

 5. Complete the following word equations:

    a. hydrochloric acid + magnesium 

    b. hydrochloric acid + copper 

    c. sulphuric acid + iron 

    d. sulphuric acid + zinc 

 6. Complete the symbol equation for the reaction between sulphuric acid and magnesium.

    a. H2SO4 + Mg




                                                Page 3 of 4
                                                                                    Metal and Acid Reactions

Answers
1. Write down the metals you tested in order of the most reactive to the least reactive.
   magnesium – zinc – iron - copper

2. What gas was produced by the reaction?
   hydrogen

3. When a metal and an acid react, they always produce the gas you found and a salt. Show this as a
   word equation.
   metal + acid   salt + hydrogen

4. Describe how you tested for the gas, and the observations you made if the gas was present.
   Capture the gas produced with a loosely fitting bung placed in the neck of the test tube, and test
   the gas using a lit splint held into it. If a squeaky pop is heard then hydrogen gas is present.

5. Complete the following word equations:

   a. hydrochloric acid + magnesium        magnesium chloride + hydrogen

   b. hydrochloric acid + copper      copper chloride + hydrogen

   c. sulphuric acid + iron     iron sulphate + hydrogen

   d. sulphuric acid + zinc     zinc sulphate + hydrogen

6. Complete the symbol equation for the reaction between sulphuric acid and magnesium.

    a. H2SO4 + Mg     MgSO4 + H2

Neutralisation
When an acid and a base are mixed, the chemical reaction that occurs is called 
neutralisation. The chemical reaction can be shown in the following word equation:
acid + base

6 Indicators
Acids and bases change the colour of certain dyes. These dyes are called indicators, Indicators tell us
whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral. Some indicators in the school laboratory are kept as liquids
in dropper bottles, while others are dried onto strips of paper. Litmus, phenolphthalein, methyl orange and

bromothymol are some common indicators. Indicators can also be made from plants, for example, the
liquid from boiled rhubarb stems turns red in acids and green in bases.

pH scale

Scientists have an accurate way of measuring acidity. They use a very sensitive indicator called pH paper.
The pH paper changes into one of several colours when dipped into a liquid substance, The colour is
matched to numbers on a pH scale, The pH scale gives very acidic solutions the number 1, very basic
solutions number 14, and neutral solutions number 7.

searchText: ﻿Precipitation Reactions Sometimes it is necessary for chemists to identify the presence of ions in solution for example testing water samples. When identifying unknown positive ions and negative ions we can use precipitation reactions in order to determine what ions are in solution. When an ionic solid dissolves in water we call this an aqueous solution. Some ions in aqueous solutions react to form insoluble precipitates. This is due to the chemical properties of the new ionic compound which affect its solubility in water. Some salts produced from these reactions give bright coloured precipitates that are characteristic of those ions. These solids form due to strong ionic bonds between positively and negatively charged ions that make the salt insoluble in water. A chemical reaction can be thought of in terms of reactants and products. We add reactants together to get products: REACTANTS ➔ PRODUCTS To understand what happens in a chemical reaction between two ionic solutions, all you need to recognise is that the ions simply swap partners. For example: a b c d a d c b Lead Nitrate + Potassium Iodide ➔ Lead Iodide (solid) + Potassium Nitrate This is true for all precipitation reactions. Materials Required Dropper bottles containing solutions of: Silver Nitrate, Barium Chloride, Sodium Hydroxide, Sodium Chloride, Potassium Bromide, Potassium Iodide, Copper Nitrate, Iron(II) Sulfide, Iron (III) Chloride, Lead Nitrate and Zinc Sulfate. 8 test tubes Test tube rack What to do? • Mix ten drops of each solution in separate test tubes. • What compound forms the solid precipitate (look at solubility rules)? • Record your observations for each reaction in the table provided. Results Table Reactants Name of Ionic Solid Formed Observations AgNO3 + NaCl Silver Chloride Eg A white precipitate forms when the two solutions are mixed. This indicates a chemical change has occurred. AgNO3 + KBr AgNO3 + KI NaOH + FeS NaOH + FeCl3 NaOH + CuNO3 Pb(NO3)2 + KI BaCl2 + ZnSO4 Solubility Rules We know which compound is the solid due to the ions solubility in water (this is due to the chemical properties of these ions). • All ionic compounds that contain lithium, sodium or potassium are soluble in water. • All ionic compounds that contain nitrate ions are soluble in water. • All metal hydroxides are insoluble in water (except LiOH, NaOH and KOH). • Chloride, fluoride and iodide form precipitates with silver and lead ions. • Barium ions form solids with sulfate ions. What to do? • Write word equations for each reaction. • Make sure you indicate which compound forms the solid. • Use the solubility rules to help you determine this. comes from the acid used. For example, if calcium reacts with hydrochloric acid, the salt 
that is produced is called calcium chloride.

searchText: ﻿Reaction of zinc with iodine This experiment involves the synthesis of a metal salt by direct reaction of a metal and a non-metal. Zinc powder is added to a solution of iodine in ethanol. An exothermic reaction occurs, forming zinc iodide, which can be obtained by evaporating the solvent. Zn + I2 → ZnI2 This experiment illustrates the difference between metallic and non-metallic elements and their reaction to form a compound with new properties. Materials Apparatus and chemicals Eye protection Each group (or demonstration) requires: 3 x Test-tubes and bungs Test-tube rack Measuring cylinder (10 mL) Electric kettle Small filter funnel Filter paper Pasteur pipette Thermometer (0–100 oC) Spatula Watchglass Weighing boat or suitable container for zinc powder Chemicals Solid iodine (Harmful, Dangerous for the Environment), about 0.5 g Zinc powder (Highly Flammable. Contact with water can also release a flammable gas, dangerous for the environment), about 0.5 g Ethanol (Highly Flammable) about 5 mL Procedure SAFETY: Wear eye protection a Measure out 5 mL of ethanol using a measuring cylinder. Place a thermometer in the ethanol and record the temperature. b Add the ethanol to 0.5 g of powdered iodine in a test-tube. Stir carefully, using the thermometer, to dissolve the iodine. The solution should be dark brown. Note the temperature. c When all the iodine has dissolved, slowly add the zinc powder using a spatula and stir the mixture with the thermometer. The temperature should rise, indicating an exothermic reaction. d When the reaction is finished, the color of the iodine should have faded and excess zinc will be left. If not, add further small amounts of zinc powder and stir until the brown color due to iodine has gone. e Filter the solution into another test-tube. f Using a pipette, transfer a few drops of the filtrate on to a watch glass and allow the solvent to evaporate. This can be sped up by placing the watch glass on a beaker containing some hot water. Zinc iodide will be left as a white solid. What’s going on? In this reaction a metal and non metal are being reacted together to form a new substance with different properties. The new substance that is formed is called an ionic substance. This is because in this reaction the two elements are going through a chemical change where they are being transformed from neutral atoms to form positive and negative ions. The zinc metal is losing two electrons to form Zn2+ and the iodine molecules are gaining electrons to form two I- ions. As you will see the physical appearance of the two reactants will change with the formation of the new products, along with their chemical properties. Observations • Note the physical appearance of each substance • Note what occurs during the reaction • Note the appearance of the new substance Questions 1. How do you know a reaction has occurred? 2. What do you think exothermic means? 3. How have the physical and chemical properties of each reactant changed? 4. What is an ion? * This experiment is an assessment item and is to be handed in as a written up lab report, containing an aim, method, procedure, observations, discussion and conclusion. It is due next Friday 16/5/2008.

searchText: Types of Reactions Chemical reactions can be categorized into a variety of types. Five common types that we will study are synthesis , decomposition , combustion , single replacement and double replacement . Be familiar enough with the description of each type so that you are able to classify a reaction if given a chemical equation or verbal description. 3980878 228479 Synthesis: Synthesis reactions involve the formation of more complex compounds (many atoms) from simpler compounds and/or elements. The most common synthesis reaction involves the formation of a compound from its elements. Examples: H 2 ( g) + O 2 (g) → 2 H 2 O (g) H 2 ( g) + N 2 (g) → 2 NH 3 (g) General: A + B → AB Synthesis reactions are also referred to as combination, for mation, and addition reactions. 3115945 204470 Decomposition: Decomposition reactions involve the breaking down of more complex compounds (larger, more atoms) into simpler compounds and/or elements. These reactions can often be thought of as being the opposite of synthesis reactions. Decomposition reactions often require heating in order to occur. Examples: 2 H 2 O (l) → 2 H 2 ( g) + O 2 (g) 2 KClO 3 ( s) → 2 KCl (s) + 3 O 2 (g) General: AB → A + B Combustion: Combustion reactions involve the reaction of a substance with oxygen gas (O 2 ). It is often referred to as burning. The products of the reaction are oxides of the elements in the reactants. Hydrocarbon combustion leads to the formation of carbon dioxide gas and water vapor . Examples: 2 Mg ( s) + O 2 (g) → 2 MgO (s) CH 4 ( g) + 2 O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) + 2 H 2 O (g) General: AB + O 2 (g) → A x O y + B w O z Some combustion reactions are also synthesis reactions. For instance, the combustion of magnesium leads to t he formation of magnesium oxide. Single Replacement: 3308350 6350 Single replacement reactions involve the reaction of an element with an ionic compound. The single element replaces one of the ions in the compound. If the lone element is a metal, then it will replace the positive ion in the compound. If the lone element is a nonmetal , then it will replace the negative ion. Examples: 2 Al ( s) + 3 CuCl 2 ( aq ) → 3 Cu (s) + 2 AlCl 3 ( aq ) 2 NaCl ( s) + F 2 (g) → Cl 2 (g) + 2 NaF (s) General: A + BC → AC + B ( if A is a metal) A + BC → BA + C (if A is a nonmetal ) Single replacement reactions are also referred to as single displacement reactions. 3175000 68580 0 0 Double Replacement: Double replacement reactions involve the reaction of two ionic compounds to form two different ionic compounds. The positive ion in one compound replaces the positive ion in the other compound. Examples: 2KI ( aq ) + Pb (NO 3 ) 2 ( aq ) → PbI 2 (s) + 2 KNO 3 ( aq ) HCl ( aq ) + NaOH ( aq ) → NaCl ( aq ) + H 2 O (l) General: AB + C D → AD + BC Double replacement reactions are also referred to as double displacement reactions, and less commonly as metathesis reactions. Many double replacement reactions involve the formation of a precipitate. The two reactants and one of the products are aqueous solutions of ionic salts and the other product is an ionic salt that is not soluble in water. It is seen as a precipitating solid. This is sometimes termed a precipitation reaction . Some double replacement reactions involve the reaction of an acid with a base; these are a special case of double replacement reactions known as acid-base neutralization reactions . searchText: Neutralisation Reactions: Reactions of acids and hydroxides Background A neutralisation reaction is when an acid reacts with a base, in this case a hydroxide. This reaction produces water and a salt. Neutralisation reactions are very common. Every time we brush our teeth, the toothpaste, which contains a base, neutralises the acids left on our teeth by bacteria. Indigestion, which is caused by too much acid in the stomach, can be relieved by taking an antacid, which are bases in liquid or tablet form. The general reaction equation for an acid combining with a hydroxide is: acid + hydroxide → water + salt When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, it produces water and sodium chloride. HCl + NaOH → H 2 O + NaCl Aim : To investigate the neutralisation of a hydroxide with an acid. Equipment : Test tubes x 7 Test tube rack Universal indicator Distilled water Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) Potassium hydroxide (KOH) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) Sulphuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ) Nitric acid (HNO 3 ) Safety glasses Lab coat Method : Put one cm of distilled water in a test tube and add one drop of universal indicator. What colour is the indicator in distilled water? This is the colour you are aiming for. Put approximately 12 drops of sodium hydroxide in a test tube. Add one drop of universal indicator. Record the colour in the results table. One drop at a time, add the hydrochloric acid until you notice a colour change. Record the colour in the results table. Record how many drops of acid you added in the results table. Repeat the process for all combinations of hydroxide and acid. Results : Results for Sodium hydroxide No. of Drops of NaOH Initial colour of indicator Final colour of indicator No. of drops of acid added HCl H 2 SO 4 HNO 3 Results for Potassium hydroxide No. of Drops of KOH Initial colour of indicator Final colour of indicator No. of drops of acid added HCl H 2 SO 4 HNO 3 Questions: At what point was the solution neutral? Explain why. Bees can give you a very nasty sting. The painful sting is caused by the methanoic (formic) acid they inject. What can be done to relieve the sting? Explain why vinegar would not relieve a bee sting. Write a word equation for each of the reactions you conducted in your experiment. Sodium hydroxide + Hydrochloric acid → Neutralisation Reactions: R eactions of acids and carbonates Background The reaction between an acid and a carbonate is a neutralisation reaction. These reactions produce water and a salt, as well as a third product, carbon dioxide. The general reaction equation fo r an acid combining with a carbonate is: acid + carbonat e → water + salt + carbon dioxide When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium carbonate, it produces water, sodium chloride and carbon dioxide. HCl + Na 2 CO 3 → H 2 O + NaCl + CO 2 You can test for carbon dioxide using limewater. The limewater goes from clear to milky if carbon dioxide is present, due to the formation of a calcium carbonate precipitate. Aim : To investigate the reaction of metal carbonates with an acid. Equipment : Test tubes Test tube rack Test tube stoppers 100 mL beaker Limewater Pipette 10 mL measuring cylinder Samples of various metal carbonates Acids (hydrochloric and nitric) Safety glasses Lab coat Method : Pour 25 mL of limewater into the beaker. Be careful not to shake the limewater bottle. Into a test tube, put a pea sized sample of sodium carbonate. Measure 3 mL of hydrochloric acid in the measuring cylinder. Pour the acid into the test tube and quickly stopper it. Once the reaction has finished, using the pipette, add a small amount of limewater to the test tube by dribbling it down the side of the test tube. Record your observations in the results table. Repeat the experiment with other combinations of acids and carbonates. Record all your tests and observations in the results table. Results : Carbonate Acid Observation of reaction Observation of limewater test Sodium carbonate (Na 2 CO 3 ) Hydrochloric (HCl) Questions: Write a word equation for each of the reactions you conducted in your experiment. The first one has been started for you. Sodium carbonate + Hydrochloric acid → For each of your word equations, write a formula equation underneath. Reaction of Metals with Acids Background The reaction between an acid and a metal is not a neutralisation reaction because metals are not bases and the reaction does not produce water. Instead, this type of reaction produces hydrogen gas and a salt. Some metals, like sodium, react violently while some are unreactive, or inert. The general reaction equation fo r an acid combining with a metal is: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas When hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium metal, it produces magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas. HCl + Mg → MgCl 2 + H 2 The test for hydrogen gas is the ‘pop’ test. The gas produced can be collected in an inverted test tube. When a lit match is held near the mouth of the test tube, a popping sound can be heard as the hydrogen reacts with oxygen in the air to form water. Aim : To investigate the reaction of metals with an acid. Equipment : Test tubes Test tube rack Samples of various metals Hydrochloric acid Sulphuric acid Acetic acid (vinegar) Matches Safety glasses Lab coat Method : Pour 2 cm of hydrochloric acid into a test tube. Add a small piece of magnesium to the acid. If there is a noticeable reaction, hold a second test tube inverted over the reaction tube. This will collect the gases produced in the reaction. Hold a lit match to the mouth of the test tube you collected the gas in. If hydrogen has been produced, you should hear a small popping sound. Record your observations in the table. Repeat the magnesium reaction with sulphuric and acetic acid. Try other combinations of acids and metals. Record all your tests and observations. Results : Acid Metal Observation of reaction Hydrogen test Hydrochloric (HCl) Magnesium Sulphuric (H 2 SO 4 ) Magnesium Acetic (Vinegar) Magnesium Questions: Which of the metals you tested was the most reactive? Which of the metals you tested was the least reactive? Write a word equation for six of the reactions you conducted in your experiment. The first one has been started for you. has a pH of 2. Sulfuric acid is an important chemical in industry because it is cheap and used in

searchText: ﻿THE REACTIVITY OF SOME METALS Activity Series Aim: To test the chemical properties of some metals and arrange them in order of their chemical activity. Materials: Aluminium, magnesium, copper, iron, lead, tin, silver and zinc Steel wool 6 test tubes and rack Zinc sulphate solution (saturated) Copper sulphate solution (saturated) Dilute hydrochloric acid Procedure: 1. Place 5ml of zinc sulfate solution in each test tube. 2. Add a metal sample to each and leave it for 3 to 5 minutes. 3. Record any reactions that occur. A reaction may be indicated simply by a dark deposit on the metal. If the metal remains shiny, you can infer there was no reaction. 4. Wash and clean the samples. Then repeat the steps 1 to 3 using copper sulfate and hydrochloric acid. Again recording your results. Results: Hydrochloric Acid Zinc Sulfate Solution Copper Sulfate Solution Aluminium Copper Iron Lead Magnesium Tin Silver Zinc Questions and Conclusions: Look carefully at your data table and answer these questions. 1. What usually happens when you add dilute hydrochloric acid to a metal? 2. Which metals reacted with: (a) All three test solutions (acid, zinc sulphate and copper sulphate)? (b) Two solutions only? (c) One solution only? (d) No none of the solutions? 3. Try to put the metals in order from most reactive to least reactive. 4. Suppose you want to make a metal tank to hold copper sulfate solution. Which would be the best metal to use and why?

       Rust is made when iron gets wet and oxygen gets to

4. Define the term ‘displacement’ by using an example
                                                            (3)
       Displacement is when a less reactive metal takes the
       place of a more reactive metal. For example,
       magnesium might take the place of a different metal

       reactive than the one being kicked out displaced.

could be obtained from magnesium carbonate.
                                                           (3)
       Magnesium carbonate could be put in a test tube and
       heated. It would then become magnesium oxide and
       carbon dioxide gas. You could use a Bunsen burner

Teaching notes
This ‘peer-assessment’ task is designed to be used by students after they have
studied types of chemical reactions. It should be used to consolidate learning.

Students of secondary age are notoriously critical. They take delight in noticing
Donald’s errors, misconceptions and lack of exam technique. Sometimes
however, Donald surprises the students with a great answer!

To stimulate discussion, Donald’s work has been most successfully used in pair
or small group work, followed by targeted whole class questioning.




The following marks and comments are expected from students:

     1.       Donald would score 1 mark.

     Donald has correctly recalled that oxidation involves oxygen (being added
     to a substance).



     2.       Donald would likely score 0 marks.

     To gain the mark, Donald needs to use the term ‘combustion’ which is the
     type of reaction where oxygen combines with another substance (fuel) to
     produce heat and light.



     3.       Donald would likely score 1 mark.

     Donald has recognised the need for oxygen and linked this to the idea of

     would best be represented by an equation (iron + oxygen → iron oxide)
     iron becoming iron oxide. However, the actual formation of the iron oxide

     and this would get Donald the second mark – simply saying ‘oxygen has
     got to it’ isn’t quite enough.



     4.       Donald is confused and would score 0 marks.

     Donald should have said that a more reactive metal takes the place of a
     less reactive metal (he said the opposite) for the first mark. Magnesium is
     a good example to use, but he needs to say that it would ‘kick out /
     displace’ a less reactive metal and give an example (he said more or less).

                                   Types of chemical reaction assessment activity
     The third mark could be obtained by illustrating the idea of displacement
     fully by using an equation.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014        23322                           Page 5 of 8
                                   Types of chemical reaction assessment activity
     5.       Donald would likely score just 1 mark.

     Unfortunately, Donald has made the common error of using an ‘equal’ sign
     instead of an arrow in the middle of the equation. The reactants do not
     equal the products, they simply react together to make them.




     6.       Donald would likely score 2 marks (at most).

     One mark will be scored for the word ‘heat’ or ‘heating’ and he may be
     lucky to get another mark for a procedural comment such as using a test
     tube or a Bunsen burner. However, Donald should have stated that the

     illustrate the process using an equation (magnesium carbonate →
     type of reaction that needs to occur is thermal decomposition or he could

     magnesium oxide + carbon dioxide).




     7.       Donald has done quite well and would score 3 marks.

     Donald’s first three equations are perfect.

     He has got confused in the last equation – potassium as a more reactive
     metal displaces silver, leaving potassium chloride, not potassium silver
     (which could not be a compound – it is two metals).



     8.    Donald seems much less confident writing whole word equations.
     He would probably score just 3 marks out of a possible 8.

     The first equation asked for the thermal decomposition of lithium
     carbonate, not copper carbonate so it should be:

                    lithium carbonate  lithium oxide + carbon dioxide

     The second equation gets 1 mark for the reactants, but Donald has not
     given the product. It should be:

                          magnesium + oxygen  magnesium oxide

     Donald gets 1 mark for the products. However, he has forgotten that
     combustion involves oxygen combining with the fuel and so it should be:

     Donald has correctly written the reactants, so he can have 1 mark for this.
     However, he has forgotten that displacement will only occur if the metal is
     more reactive than the one in the compound. In this case, copper is less
     reactive than iron and so there is no reaction. It could be written in one of
     these ways:

                       copper + iron chloride  copper + iron chloride

                             copper + iron chloride  no reaction




     9.       Donald would likely score 2 marks.

     In 6-mark questions at GCSE, responses are marked in bands of 1-2, 3-4,
     5-6. In each band, literacy is also considered. The same idea can be used
     at KS3 to develop understanding of this way of marking.

     Donald does make a fairly good explanation of what thermal
     decomposition means (breaking down using heat) although breaking down
     would be preferable to chopping up.

     However, to get 3-4 marks, he would need to give a correct example,
     which he has not done. Sodium carbonate can indeed undergo thermal
     decomposition, but it would become sodium oxide and carbon dioxide.

     To get 5-6 marks, the example should be given clearly as a word equation
     (or even a symbol equation) and it should perhaps be noted that there is
     one reactant, yet two products.

     Students should also note his incorrect spelling of the word
     ‘decomposition’. This is particularly silly because the word is in the
     question. He would still get 2 marks though as this band does not require
     accurate spelling.

     Overall, Donald would score about thirteen marks. He needs to improve
     his ability to write word equations and his understanding of scientific
     terminology (e.g. combustion, thermal decomposition) in order to improve.
     He needs to review the definition of displacement and use a reactivity
     series to work out whether elements will displace each other.

Multiple choice test topics – Chemistry 27
© Grahame Dobinson and Blake Education 2008
Topic 5 
1 
Perhaps the simplest type of chemical reaction is a combination reaction. It usually involves 
elements, or even compounds, bonding together to make a new compound. Three chemical 
reactions are listed below.
 
 (i)  magnesium(s) + oxygen(g) → magnesium oxide(s)
 
(ii)  sodium(s) + chlorine(g) → sodium chloride(s)
 
(iii)  calcium carbonate(s) + heat energy → calcium oxide(s) + carbon dioxide(g)
 
Of the three reactions, the ones which are combination reactions are:
a (i), (ii) and (iii). 
b   (i) and (ii). 
c   (i) and (iii). 
d   (ii) and (iii).
2 
If a combination reaction does not occur between two chemicals, it could mean that:
a both of the chemicals are inactive.
b only one of the chemicals is inactive.
c one chemical could have a protective coating, e.g. an oxide, which prevents it from reacting.
d any of the above options might be true.
3 
When the element helium is mixed with the element argon and the mixture is heated strongly, 
there is no evidence of a combination reaction occurring. This is due to the fact that:
a the mixture has not been heated strongly enough to cause a reaction.
b the proportions of helium and argon are incorrect and so no reaction occurs.
c both elements are always extremely unreactive.
d while helium is quite an active element, argon is not.
4 
Four combination reactions between metals and non-metals which occur quite readily are:
 
(i)  potassium(s) + fluorine(g) → potassium fluoride(s)
 
(ii)  sodium(s) + chlorine(g) → sodium chloride(s)
 
(iii)  magnesium(s) + oxygen(g) → magnesium oxide(s)
 
(iv)  sodium(s) + iodine(s) → sodium iodide(s)
 
This is because in every case:
a there is an active metal and an active non-metal.
b the metal is an active one, even though the non-metal is inactive.
c the non-metal is an active one, even though the metal is inactive.
d the metals are in the solid state, otherwise there would be no reaction.

searchText:
Writing Equations

Chemists write equations to represent what is happening in a chemical reaction. Equations are
useful because they provide an easy way to show complex reactions.

Word Equations

    The simplest form of chemical equation is a word equation.
    The most general word equation is:
       Reactants → products
    This general equation can then be expanded to:
       Substance A + Substance B → Substance C + Substance D
    For example, consider the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid. This reaction
     produces magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas. It can be written as a word equation.
       Reactants → products
       Magnesium + Hydrochloric acid → Magnesium chloride + Hydrogen gas

Example 1: Lead reacts with oxygen gas to produce lead (IV) oxide. Write a word equation to
describe the reaction.




Using Formulae

    A chemical equation tells you even more information if it includes the element symbols and
     chemical formulae of all the substances involved.
    In the example above, the reactants and products can be written using symbols for the
     elements and compounds.
    The reaction can be written as:
       Mg + HCl →MgCl2 + H2

Rules for Formula Equations
    Metals are written as single atoms: copper is written as Cu and iron is written as Fe
    Non-metal gases are written as diatomic molecules: oxygen is written as O 2, hydrogen is
     written as H2, chlorine is written as Cl2 etc.

Example 2: For the reaction in example 1, write a formula equation.




Example 3: Write the formula equation for the following word equation:
              Carbon + Oxygen gas → Carbon dioxide


Questions
 1. Write word equations for the following reactions.
   a. When sulphuric acid is added to iron metal, hydrogen gas and iron (II) sulphate are formed.




    b. If sulphuric acid is poured onto solid sodium carbonate, bubbles of carbon dioxide are
       produced, as well as water and sodium sulphate.




    c. Magnesium burns easily in oxygen, producing magnesium oxide.




    d. An iron nail exposed to the oxygen in air will rust, forming iron oxide.




    e. When solutions of lead nitrate and sodium iodide are mixed, a yellow precipitate of lead
       iodide is formed, as well as sodium nitrate in solution.




2. For each of the word equations, rewrite it using the chemical formulae.

Case study: Discrimination in the workplace
Ms Evans was an intelligence analyst with the National Crime Authority. She was a single 
mother and had to take a considerable amount of carer’s leave to look after her sick child. 
She was reprimanded even though she did not exceed her entitlements. Allegedly her 
manager said, ‘You hold a key position and someone like you has to be there 100 per cent’ 
and ‘If I had known of your situation I would never have hired you’. Evans was put under 
pressure to not take carer’s leave, was moved to a different team, and her contract was 
not renewed.
Section 14(2) of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) states that:
It is unlawful for an employer to discriminate against an employee on the ground of 
the employee’s sex, marital status, pregnancy or potential pregnancy: 
(a) in the terms or conditions of employment that the employer affords the

Case study: Human rights in the Constitution
High Court judges are sometimes prepared to find that human rights are implied in the 
Australian Constitution. An example is the landmark case of Australian Capital Television v 
Commonwealth (1992) 177 CLR 106.
The case arose due to a challenge to the Political Broadcasts and Political Disclosures Act 
1991 (Cth). The Act banned the broadcast of political material leading up to an election.  
A majority of the High Court held that the Act infringed an implied right in the 
Constitution. Sections 7 and 24 of the Constitution provide for the election of 
senators and members of the House of Representatives. This, as well as the system 
of representative government created by the Constitution, was held to mean that 
Australians should be able to freely discuss political matters. In other words, there is 
an implied freedom of political discussion and communication in Australia. The Act in 
question infringed this right, and so the ban was declared to be invalid. 
Later High Court cases widened and extended the scope of this implied right. However, 
more recent High Court cases restricted it again. The implied right still exists, but its 
scope keeps changing.

International crimes include transnational crimes (which affect more than one

reprehensible they are seen as being against the whole of the international community.
Case study: Gaddafi
The year 2011 saw the end of the 42-year Gaddafi regime in Libya. Gaddafi’s early actions 
included shutting down American and British military bases, expelling Italian settlers and 
banning the non-Arab Berber language from schools. The regime became increasingly 
fundamentalist Islamic and sponsored anti-Western terrorist attacks. Dissent within the 
country was brutally stamped out. People trying to form a political party were executed, 
and it was illegal to talk to foreigners about politics. Gaddafi threatened to kill dissidents 
who escaped the country.
Political protests grew and intensified in 2011, sparking off a civil war between Gaddafi 
loyalists and rebel forces. Demonstrators and unarmed civilians were massacred. In June 
2011, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for Gaddafi’s arrest for crimes 
against humanity; however, Libya refused to acknowledge the authority of the ICC. 
The end of the regime came on 20 October 2011. Gaddafi was captured and killed by 
rebel Libyan forces. Some reports stated he was killed in crossfire; others claimed he was 
deliberately executed.

International law develops through international treaties, conventions and other types

Case study: Northern Territory Emergency Response (NTER)
Australia ratified the International Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial 
Discrimination and then passed the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth).
When a nation ratifies the convention, it agrees to various undertakings, including:
• not to engage in actions of racial discrimination
• not to sponsor or support racial discrimination by any person or body
• to review government policies that are discriminatory and to amend the law
• to prohibit racial discrimination, hatred and violence
• to ensure remedies for victims of racial discrimination
• to combat prejudices through education.
Has Australia fulfilled its obligations? A report on child abuse in Indigenous Australian 
communities in 2007 led to an intervention by the Howard government. Called the 
Northern Territory Emergency Response (NTER), the action sparked indignation throughout 
the international community.

15 Focus 1.4: Future shocks

- Black holes—page 1

Name:

Skills: interpreting, applying, analysing, evaluating

Black holes are incredibly dense, far denser than the closely packed neutrons that make up neutron stars.
Whatever form the matter inside a black hole takes, there cannot be atoms as we understand them. The
mass of a black hole is thus very large for its size. For example, a black hole with the same mass as the Earth
would be less than two centimetres across! All that mass creates a fiercely strong gravitational field in the
space around a black hole.

The strength of any gravitational field decreases in what is known as an “inverse square’ relationship.
Thus, ifyou double your distance ftom the centre of a black hole, the gravitational field strength decreases
to a quarter. This means that the gravitational field near a small black hole weakens very rapidly with
distance. This is different from our experience in Earth’s gravitational field. For us, a change of several
metres, or even several kilometres, does not create a noticeable change in the gravitational field. That is
because our distance from the centre of the Earth is over 6000 kilometres.

Only the mass of a body, and the distance from its centre, affect the strength of its gravitational field. The
radius of the Earth is about 6370 km, and its mass is about 6 x 10” tonnes. The table below shows how the
gravitational field strength changes with distance near the Earth’s surface, and near a black hole having the
same mass as the Earth.

Apparent brightness is a measure of the brightness of stars as they appear to us on Barth. Just because

searchText: Doppler effect The Doppler effect , named after physicist Christian Doppler who proposed it in 1842, is the change in frequency of a wave for an observer moving relative to the source of the wave. It is commonly heard when a vehicle sounding a siren or horn approaches, passes, and recedes from an observer. The received frequency is higher (compared to the emitted frequency) during the approach, it is identical at the instant of passing by, and it is lower during the recession (as it moves away) Light and the Doppler effect The Doppler effect for electromagnetic waves su ch as light is of great use in A stronomy and results in either a so-called “ redshift ” , as things move a way from the observer or a blue shift as they move towards the observer. This colour change is used to help investigate the movement of galaxies and their stars. Since most galaxies are moving away from each other this is supporting evidence for the Big Bang theory.

Exogenesis and the origin of life on Earth

IntroductIon
Exogenesis (literally ‘outside origin’) is a theory that life began elsewhere in the universe and travelled to Earth. 
Geogenesis proposes that life arose independently on Earth.
Panspermia, from the Greek pan, ‘all’, and sperma, ‘seed’, is a theory that states that the universe is full of spores/seeds that 
germinate when they find a favourable environment. The theory is not new, but has been revived at intervals since the 
18th century. Many reputable scientists including Jöns Jacob Berzelius (1779–1848), Lord Kelvin (1824–1907), Hermann 
von Helmholtz (1879–1927) and Svante Arrhenius (1859–1927) have proposed versions of panspermia. Many in the 
scientific community believe that it is highly probable that life exists elsewhere in the universe because of the immense 
numbers of potential sites. Until we can survey our galaxy in detail for signs of life, the panspermia hypothesis will remain 
difficult to support or disprove.
Aim 
To analyse evidence in support of the theory that life on Earth occurred as a result of extraterrestrial life forms landing 
on Earth.
Information

Sir Fred Hoyle (1915–2001) and Chandra Wickramasinghe (1939–) argued that life forms have continued to enter the  
Earth’s atmosphere, and that these are responsible for outbreaks of new diseases and the genetic novelty necessary for 
macroevolution. Using spectroscopic analysis of light from distant stars, they claim to have found evidence that traces of life 
exist in the dust between Earth and these stars.
Box 2
Arrhenius proposed that radiation pressure from sunlight (electromagnetic radiation) could propel spores through space. 
Kelvin thought that micro-organisms could travel in rocks (lithopanspermia), which would provide protection from radiation.

searchText: 21/09/2017 CERES: Hubble's Classification System Hubble’s Classification Scheme Go back to Lesson. Edwin Hubble developed a galaxy classification scheme consisting of four types: elliptical, spiral, barred spiral, and irregular. Three of these types are represented in the "tuning fork" diagram below. Elliptical Galaxies An elliptical galaxy shows no spiral structure and can vary from almost round (what Hubble called E0) to almost cigar shaped (called E7). This classification is based on our perspective from Earth and not on the actual shape. Spiral Galaxies As their name implies, spiral galaxies have outstretched, curving arms suggestive of a whirlpool or pinwheel. Hubble distinguished different sub- classes according to the tightness of the arms and the size of the nucleus. He called these Sa, Sb, and Sc. In terms of the arms, Sa is the tightest wound while Sc is the most open. In terms of the nucleus, Sa has the largest while Sc has the smallest. The galaxies that appear to have a spiral disc but no visible arms are called S0. Barred Spirals Barred spirals show the same spiral structure as normal spirals, and also a prominent bar through the nucleus. The spiral arms emerge from the end of the bar. The sub-classifications are the same as for normal spirals. Irregulars Certain galaxies lack either an obvious spiral structure or nuclear bulge, appearing instead as a random collection of stars with no obvious order. They are distinguished from ellipticals by their lack of symmetry. http://btc.montana.edu/ceres/html/Galaxy/galhubble.html 1/1

searchText: Stars initially form from clouds of dust and gas……………… The force of gravity makes the dust particles come spiraling in together. As they do, gravitational energy is converted into heat energy and the temperature rises……………… When the temperature gets high enough, hydrogen nuclei undergo nuclear fusion to form helium nuclei and give out massive amoun ts of heat and light. A star is born…………… The star immediately enters a long stable period where the heat created by the nuclear fusion provides an outward pressure to balance the force of gravity pulling everything inwards. In this stable period it ’ s called a MAIN SEQUENCE STAR…….. Eventually the hydrogen begins to run out and the star then swells into a RED GIANT. It becomes red because the surface cools………… A small star like our Sun will then begin to cool and contract into a WHITE DWARF and then finally as the light fades completely it becomes a BLACK DWARF……………………….. Big stars start to glow brightly again as they undergo more fusion and expand and contract several times forming heavier elements in various nuclear reactions. Eventually they explode in a SUPERNOVA…………… The exploding supernova throws the outer layers of dust and gas into space leaving a very dense core called a NEUTRON STAR. If the star is big enough this will become a BLACK HOLE…………... The dust and gas thrown off by the supernova will form into SECOND GENERATION STARS like our Sun……………….

Luminosity of stars and the HR diagram
32
IntroductIon
The luminosity of a star is a measure of the total output of 
energy per second from the star. The energy radiates in all 
directions from the star and so only a tiny fraction of the 
energy reaches the Earth. A formula that has been derived 
by scientists to calculate luminosity is given below. It can 
be used for any star.
Aim
To use some basic data and formulae about stars to gain 
more information about them.
data: Luminosity
The formula for luminosity (L) is L ∝ R2T 4, where R is the 
radius of the star and T is its surface temperature (K).  
The units for L are watts (W) and normal SI units apply 
elsewhere. The luminosity of the Sun is approximately 
3.8 × 1026 W. It is used as a reference and assigned the 
symbol L0.
Interpreting the data
The following questions should help in understanding 
the formula. 
1 
If R is doubled, by what factor does L increase? 
 
 
2 
If T is doubled, by what factor does L increase? 
 
 
3 
If both R and T are doubled, by what factor does L 
increase now? 
 
 
4 
If the star α-Centauri has L = 8.0 × 1026 W, it means 
that its luminosity is about twice that of the Sun. 
Does this mean that α-Centauri has both a larger 
radius and a higher temperature than the Sun?  
(Yes/No)  
 
Explain your answer.  
 
 
data: Hr diagram
A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram is one in which the 
luminosity (or a closely related quantity called ‘absolute 
magnitude’) is plotted against the temperature (or 
‘spectral class’) of stars. It forms a sort of graph with  
many stars represented.

What do you think a star is made of? _________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Stars are gaseous objects in space that give off light and heat. They are made mainly of hydrogen and helium, with traces of heavier elements such as boron, carbon and nitrogen. For example, our sun contains about 80% hydrogen and 19% helium, while the remaining 1% is made up of the heavier elements. Compared with the size of the Earth, the sizes of stars are enormous. The sun is over one million times the size of the Earth, while one of the largest stars, Canopus, is 80 000 times the size of our sun. 2. In the core of the sun, hydrogen nuclei join together (fuse) and release energy. This type of reaction is called nuclear fusion. What does fuse mean in the above paragraph? _____________________________________________________ _ 7. What is released when hydrogen nuclei fuse together? _____________________________________________ The reaction that occurs in stars involves the fusion of hydrogen nuclei to produce helium. In the fusion reactions that occur in the sun, about 655 million tonnes of hydrogen are converted to 650 million tonnes of helium every second. Bursts of glowing gases shoot up from the surface. The upper part of the sun’s atmosphere is called the corona. Although the corona is outside the chromosphere and photosphere it is about 1 000 000 o C hotter than them. The core is where the fusion of hydrogen occurs, releasing the energy. 10.2 Time of death

Science inquiry skills

STANDARD | ADVANCED

‘The human body starts cooling immediately after death. This is accompanied

by other changes that can help forensic scientists tell how long a person has
been dead.

Blood starts to settle or ‘pool’ in the lowest parts of the corpse because the
heart is no longer pumping. Blood pooling usually takes around 6 hours. The
location of pooling can also indicate whether the body was moved after death.

Rigor mortis is the stiffening of muscles because of a build-up of lactic acid
after death. Rigor mortis moves through three phases, each lasting 6 to 12
hours. Stiffening starts in the eyelids and jaw and spreads until the whole body
is stiff. The muscles then release and once again become flexible.

bloating (n) expanding
with gas

decomposition (nr)
breaking down, rotting

g00 (7) sticky
substance

inflate (v) fill with gas

moult (v) to lose its
skin or covering

Skin colour changes, first turning pale and then blue then green. The green colouring happens
within 2 days and is caused by bacteria decomposing the internal tissues. Four to seven days after

death, veins become more obvious, giving the skin a marble-like appearance.

Decomposition of the body proceeds in clear steps. Bloating occurs 4 to 7 days after death as
decomposition gases inflate the corpse. The soft tissue of the body decays extensively in the second
week, leaving little except sticky goo by the end of a month. After that, only the skeleton, nails, hair

and perhaps some dried, leathery skin will be left.

Different species of insects are attracted to different stages of body decomposition and will
consume flesh or lay eggs in or on the body. The eggs hatch, releasing larvae such as maggots or
caterpillars. These moult and grow, each new growth stage being known as an instar. Later on,
a pupa or cocoon is spun in which the larvae undergo metamorphosis, changing into their adult

form. A typical life cycle is shown below in Figure 10.2.

searchText: Types of Nebulae Nebula are clouds of gas and dust in space. There are five main types of nebulae: * Reflection Nebulae * Emission Nebulae * Dark Nebulae * Planetary Nebulae * Supernova remnant Type of Nebulae Description of Nebulae Example Reflection Nebulae The dust and gas of this type of nebula does not emit its own light. Instead, it reflects light from nearby stars and/or galaxies The Iris nebulae Emission Nebulae These nebula make their own light. Energy from a nearby star heats up the gas and dust in the nebul a. The gas and dust gets energized and start s to release light. The Eagle nebula Dark Nebulae These nebula are dense and block out the light from stars and other nebula behind them. The Hors e head nebula Planetary Nebulae These are made when a star is dying. They have a dense central core and huge outer shell of energized gas which gives o f f light . The Cats eye N ebula Supernova remnant When a large dying star explodes it pushes a large shock wave of energy into space. This pushes and energizes gas and dust in front of it. This gas and dust give off light. The Crab Nebula Question . Which two types of nebula are caused by dying stars? Which type of nebula has its particles energized by nearby stars? Universe formation - theories
There are several different theories about how the universe began. The Big Bang theory is currently the most 
accepted theory. It suggests that the Universe was originally concentrated into a single, very small ball. The 
early universe was so highly unstable that an enormous explosion occurred. This formed the galaxies and stars. 
Evidence to support this theory is based on the expansion of space, as shown by the redshifts of distant galaxies 
and cosmic background radiation.
Redshift is the increase in wavelength of electromagnetic radiation. It is an example of the Doppler effect, 
which shifts the wavelength of emitted light of celestial objects towards the red (longer) wavelengths indicating 
that the objects are moving away from the Earth due to the continuing expansion of the universe. Redshift 
is based on the visible electromagnetic spectrum as well as other parts of the spectrum such as gamma rays, 
x-rays and ultraviolet waves. In 1965, the astronomers Robert Wilson and Arno Penzias discovered cosmic 
background radiation and showed that this radiation was from the Big Bang.

state described in the Steady State theory, matter must be continually being created. Einstein’s theory says that 
mass can be created from energy, as shown in the equation E = mc2. (Energy equals mass multiplied by the

searchText: Where Does a Star get its Energy From? The sun is a star. The stars you see in the night sky are suns. Our sun is just one of innumerable other suns. In a star 2 hydrogen atoms are joined together to make one helium atom. This happens over and over again, with many hydrogen atoms. When two atoms are fused together to make another element it is called nuclear fusion. When this fusion occurs a lot of energy is released. This is how a star gets its energy. The reason this can happen is because the sun is huge and has a lot of gravity. Gravity is the force of attraction between all matter. It is the gravity that causes enough pressure to “ squash ” (fuses) the hydrogen atoms together. In space we find Nebula. Nebulae are clouds of dust and gas. Slowly the dust and gas comes tog ether due to gravity. Eventually the cloud becomes very dense with a lot of gravity. This gravity gives enough pressure to cause the fusion. Indigenous Australians
Indigenous contact with Europeans (1)
The arrival of Captain Arthur Phillip from England with the First 
Fleet in 1788 changed the lives of Indigenous people forever. It took 
about 100 years for the impact of European occupation to reach the 
centre of Australia. 
It is thought that there were about 750 000 Indigenous 
Australians when European settlers arrived. At first, the Indigenous 
Australians and the Europeans were curious about each other and 
treated each other with respect. However, this soon changed as the 
two groups could not understanding each other’s culture.
Soon after the arrival of the colonists, diseases such as smallpox, 
influenza and measles spread throughout the Indigenous people, 
who had no immunity to them. This resulted in many deaths.
The land was not developed in a way the Europeans understood 
– there were no houses, fences or farmed animals. They took over the 
land, especially around waterholes and areas with fertile soil. They 
built towns and tried to farm the land the way people did in England.
The Europeans did not understand the Indigenous relationship 
with the land or their sustainable use of resources. Many conflicts 
occurred when Indigenous Australians resisted being pushed off 
their land. 
The colonisation of Australia was based on the legal concept 
of terra nullius, which means ‘land of no one’. In 1835, the British 
government officially declared Australia to be terra nullius.

Resource sheet – The Dreaming
Dreamtime, landscape and lifestyle 
 
●For thousands of years, Indigenous Australians have told stories to pass 
their culture from generation to generation. Dreaming stories told 
Indigenous Australians about how to live their lives.
 
●In the Dreaming stories, there are close links between the physical, 
human and spiritual worlds. The stories are told through song, dance and 
painting, as well as speaking.
 
●The Dreaming relates to the time of creation, when the Spirit Ancestors 
came out of the earth. They moved across the land and created sacred 
places. They made important features of the landscape like mountains, 
rivers, lakes and waterholes. They made flora and fauna, and the laws of 
the landscape too. Their movements are recorded in Dreaming Tracks, 
which join the sites the Ancestral Beings passed. 
 
●Dreaming stories tell about the Indigenous culture and customs, and the 
laws of the community. They also explain how people should behave and 
the consequences of disobedience, including punishments.
 
●In the stories, living sustainably and caring for the land and its features, 
plants and animals, are an important part of the traditions and culture.
 
●Dreaming stories also contain practical information such as where food 
grows and in which season it ripens. Indigenous people believe that each 
type of food was created by the Spirit Ancestors.
 
●Totems are objects of nature which become family emblems. They are 
given to people in certain areas. Some people are given personal totems 
at birth. Totems are important in song and dance.

Where are coral reefs?
You need a world map, an atlas or Internet map search, and the completed Activity sheet, 
‘Types of reefs’.
Coral reefs need special conditions to exist. Coral lives in both temperate and tropical 
waters. Shallow reefs form between the latitudes 308N and 308S. The maximum depth for 
tropical corals to grow is about 60 metres, because the special algae corals contain need 
sunlight. The algae use sunlight and the polyps’ waste products to make oxygen and food 
for the corals to grow. The water must be clean and clear so light can reach the coral. 
The best seawater temperatures for growth are 24–31°C. This is why there are no reefs 
near the mouths of major rivers like the River Ganges and the Indus River, which carry very 
dirty water. Coral reefs don’t grow in places where rivers meet the ocean. This is because 
the rivers put nutrients, pollution and fresh, colder water into the ocean.

59

Teacher’s notes – Forests
Objectives
● To understand the importance of forests for the 
production of oxygen
● To appreciate the significance of forests 
providing a sustainable habitat for animals, 
food and medicinal plants
● To learn that demand for timber and other 
products creates problems for the environment
● To learn that the forest products people choose 
to buy can contribute to the conservation and 
sustainability of forests
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that people use forest 
products every day.
Background
Forests in all regions of the earth are extremely 
important as trees take in carbon dioxide and 
produce oxygen. With the climate changing and the 
need to reduce carbon emissions, the conservation 
of forests is crucial to sustainability. The health of 
the planet is not the only factor – we also need 
to manage the ever-growing demand placed on 
forest products by our increasing population. 
This increasing demand has led to the need for 
plantation timber and the preservation of old 
growth timber. Rainforests have been particularly 
vulnerable to wealthy nations using the land for 
oil palms and rubber plantations. Illegal logging 
relies on corruption in countries like Indonesia and 
is aided by the demands for forest products from 
other countries. Environmental organisations like the 
World Wildlife Fund (WWF) are trying to promote 
sustainable forestry in many countries.
Starter activity
Work as a class to make a list of the ways people use 
forests, and the ways people use products made 
from forest resources. Then discuss the sustainability 
of the products made from forest resources, and 
any alternative products people can use that have a 
lower environmental impact.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Forestry (1)’ with the 
students. Discuss the role of forests in sustaining 
biodiversity and providing employment for rangers 
and workers in the timber and tourism industries. 
Ensure students understand the words in bold, 
especially the difference between native and 
plantation forests.
 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ’Forestry 
(2)’, which provides an opportunity for students to 
review and summarise the information from the 
Resource sheet, ‘Forestry (1)’. Students will need this 
Resource sheet to complete the activity. 
 
On the Activity sheet, ’Protecting East Gippsland’s 
old forests’, students investigate an Australian example 
that highlights the importance of conserving and 
using old-growth forests. The students will use a word 
bank to complete the information.
Provide students with the Resource sheet, 
’Rainforests in Kalimantan, Indonesia’, which shows the 
differences between original rainforest and logged 
rainforest. Encourage students to suggest reasons why 
people log rainforests.
Students could work in pairs or small groups to 
discuss and complete the Activity sheet, ‘Logging 
the forests’. Students will find it useful to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Rainforests in Kalimantan, Indonesia’. 
extension activity
●  As a class, investigate how people can find out 
whether the forest products they use come from 
sustainable sources. 
●  Discuss the environmental problems and social 
issues associated with illegal logging and what can 
be done to prevent it.

60

Forestry (1)
Resource sheet – Forests
Forests are extremely important to the health of the earth. They absorb carbon, 
which is emitted when fossil fuels are burned. Forests produce oxygen, which 
people and animals need to live. They also provide wood, which people use to 
construct houses and other buildings, and to manufacture products such as furniture 
and paper. 
Forests provide a habitat for animals, birds and a great variety  
of plants that provide fruit and medicines.
About 19% of Australia is covered with forest. Native forests cover approximately 
147 million hectares, and plantation forests cover approximately 2 million hectares. 
Plantation forests contain trees such as pines and blue gums, for commercial use.
Forests must have water, soil and nutrients to survive.  
Many forest catchments provide an important source of  
drinking water for towns and cities.
Some people in Tasmania and Victoria do not want old-growth forests logged 
because biodiversity is lost, as are the habitats of birds, animals and plants.
Many old-growth forests are in national parks and state parks. Picnic areas, camping 
grounds, bushwalking tracks and nature walks are available in many parks.

Teacher’s notes – Solar energy
Objectives 
● To learn about solar energy
● To recognise the advantages and 
disadvantages of solar energy
● To understand the need to have a suitable 
home design to make the best use of 
solar energy
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware of solar energy 
through observation of panels on roofs, solar 
garden lights and roadside signs. They should 
understand that they experience the energy of the 
sun when they are outdoors, especially in summer. 
Background
Solar power has become a much talked about and 
promoted form of energy. The first major use of solar 
cells was as a backup power supply to the Vanguard 
1 satellite in 1958. Solar power is still used for 
telecommunication satellites and remote stations. 
 
Today, Solar power is used to power offshore 
oil rigs, navigational buoys and railway crossings. It 
is also used for to provide electricity, heating and 
decorative light in domestic homes. 
 
In the past, governments have promoted the 
use of solar energy through rebates and an ability 
to return excess power to the grid. However, it 
takes a number of years to make up the expense of 
installing solar panels. 
 
Like other forms of renewable energy, interest 
and investment in solar energy has been increasing 
globally. Large solar plants are being constructed 
in the United States, Canada, Spain, Mongolia and 
China. 
Starter activity
Lead a class discussion about what solar power is and 
how it is used. Some students might have solar power 
at home – ask them to share their knowledge about 
it. Encourage students to identify advantages and 
disadvantages associated with solar power. Record their 
ideas in a chart or mind map, and put it aside to revisit 
at the end of the unit. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet ‘What is solar power?’, with the 
students. This sheet explores key features of solar power, 
such as where to place solar panels and the need to 
insulate and use energy-efficient appliances. 
 
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Solar 
power’. They will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘What is solar power?’, to complete the questions. This 
activity will reinforce their understanding of the uses 
of solar power both domestically and in larger-scale 
applications. Discuss the use of solar power compared 
with diesel-powered generators or coal-fired power 
stations in terms of emissions of greenhouse gases. 
 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages (1)’, with the class. Encourage the 
students to think of any other advantages or 
disadvantages they could add to the lists. 
 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Advantages and disadvantages (2)’. They will need 
to refer to the Resource sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages (1)’. 
extension activity
Revisit the chart or mind map you made with the 
students for the Starter activity. Work with the class to 
add to the chart, and correct the previous information 
as needed. Ask students to consider the future of 
solar power in Australia, and to give reasons for their 
predictions. Add this information to the chart and 
display it in the classroom.

What is solar power?
Solar power is renewable energy from the sun which can be converted to electricity. 
Most of Australia has a great deal of sunlight, but there is less in the southern and 
south-eastern areas. To make the most of solar power in homes, it is necessary to have 
energy-efficient heaters, insulation in the walls and ceilings, and solar hot water. Solar 
panels should be placed on north-facing roofs or in open spaces in order to generate the 
most power. 
Case studies
 
●Solar power is extremely effective in small communities like Windorah in 
Queensland, which has a population of 100. Windorah has a group of five solar 
dishes which began generating electricity in 2008. Using them saves 100 000 litres of 
diesel each year, reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 300 tonnes per year.
 
●A Solar Concentrator Power Station is being built near Mildura in Victoria and is 
expected to be fully operational in 2013. The sunlight will be captured by curved 
reflective mirrors which track the sun throughout the day. The project will produce 
enough electricity to power more than 45 000 homes and reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions by about 400 000 tonnes per year.
 
●On average, Mildura receives 2938 hours of sunlight each year. There are 10.7 hours 
of sunlight per day in January and five hours per day in June.
 
●Melbourne receives 2200 hours of sunlight in an average year, with eight hours per 
day in January and four hours per day in June.

11
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Wave power
Objectives 
● To learn about wave power
● To consider the advantages and disadvantages 
of using wave power, now and in the future
● To consider the effects of technological 
development on power generation
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of the  
need to use clean, renewable energy, now and in 
the future.
Background
The idea of using wave power has been around for 
at least 200 years. The technology is now available 
and has been proven to be a viable source of power, 
although there is concern about the longevity of 
the equipment. As with all new technology, the 
cost of research and development and the initial 
infrastructure costs are significant factors. However, 
as fossil-fuel-generated power becomes more 
expensive and society focuses on reducing carbon 
emissions, this method of power generation will 
become more affordable. 
 
Australia is well placed to utilise wave power 
with its vast coastline and huge oceans washing the 
shores. Wave power sites include Geraldton in the 
west, along the south coast, in Tasmania and on the 
northern coast of New South Wales. 
 
In the Asia Pacific, Japan is seeking safer 
alternatives to nuclear power and the government 
is investigating ways to use their 4.47 million square 
kilometres of territorial waters for power generation. 
Starter activity
Have students share their experiences of the ocean. 
Guide the discussion to bring out the ideas that waves 
are continuous, and they are powerful. 
Raise the idea of using the power of the ocean to 
generate electricity. Encourage students to suggest how 
they think this could work.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘What is wave power?’, with the 
students. You could provide images of coastal features 
such as the 12 Apostles on the Victorian south coast 
to extend the idea of waves shaping coastlines over 
time. Tell the students that wave energy has also been 
responsible for many shipwrecks, both near coasts 
and out at sea. Look carefully at the diagram showing 
how wave power is harnessed. Point out that as well as 
harnessing energy, this technology can supply another 
scarce resource – fresh water. 
 
Have students complete the cloze exercise on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Generating power’.  Encourage them to 
consider the role of technology in providing renewable 
energy. 
 
Provide students with the Resource sheet, ‘Opinions 
about wave power’. Take the opportunity to discuss 
the difference between an opinion and a fact. Students 
could decide what their own opinions are about wave 
power. 
 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages’, students summarise what they have 
learned about wave power, and categorise their 
knowledge into advantages and disadvantages. 
Students may find it useful to refer to the Resource 
sheets, ‘What is wave power?’ and ‘Opinions about wave 
power’. Then students will write a persuasive letter to an 
electricity supply company.  
extension idea
● Students could design a survey to find out what 
people know about wave power. They could also find 
out whether people think it is a good idea or not, and 
the reasons for their opinions.

12
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
What is wave power?
Every day a huge amount of energy is created by waves pounding the Australian coasts. 
This energy is largely responsible for shaping our coastlines. As renewable energy 
becomes more important, experiments are being conducted to see if electricity can 
be produced economically from this source. Wave power is continuous and does not 
produce greenhouse gas emissions. 
Wave power captures energy from the surface waves, unlike tidal power which uses the 
ebb and flow of the tides. The first wave power farm was built in Portugal in 2006. It can 
produce electricity continuously.
The CETO wave power farm is based in Perth, Western Australia. The diagram below 
shows how it works. 
Resource sheet – Wave power
The CETO wave power converter
These buoys are 
powered by the waves 
to drive pumps that are 
anchored to the sea floor.
The pumps pressurise 
the water, which 
then passes through 
a pipeline to the shore. 
The high-pressure seawater 
then drives turbines, which 
generate electricity without 
producing emissions.
As well as generating electricity, the wave power 
converter can remove the salt from seawater so it can be 
used for drinking or irrigation like any other fresh water. 
Reproduced with permission

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
21
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Wind power
Objectives 
● To learn about wind power and its advantages 
and disadvantages
● To learn how and where wind power can  
be generated
● To understand different opinions about  
wind farms
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that wind is an integral 
part of weather and climate, and be able to give 
examples of the use of wind in daily life.
Background
As the demand for energy increases with a growing 
global population, fossil fuel resources are dwindling. 
Increased energy consumption means carbon 
dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions are 
contributing to climate change. In an effort to reduce 
greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy sources 
such as wind are being explored. Governments 
are setting targets to encourage the use of clean, 
renewable energy such as wind power, although it 
cannot generate a base load (24-hour) supply.
Starter activity
Introduce the concept of the wind. Discuss with 
the students what it is, and how people harness 
the power of the wind. As well as its potential to 
generate energy, encourage students to consider its 
role in sailing, in sports such as hang gliding and kite 
surfing, and its effect of different kinds of aircraft. 
Point out that people cannot control the wind, and 
discuss its potential to cause damage; for example, 
storms and cyclones and spreading bushfires.
Activity sheets
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Wind power’. 
Students will need an atlas, a blank map of Australia 
and Internet access to complete this activity. A map 
is provided on the CD-ROM in the Artwork > Unit 4 
folder. Before students begin the activity, make sure 
they understand the meaning of each term in bold. 
When they have finished, discuss the distribution of 
the wind farms and any patterns in the kinds of places 
they are located. To extend the activity, students could 
research global use of wind power. Countries such as 
New Zealand and China use wind-generated power. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Wind power and sustainability’, 
students will extend their knowledge about wind 
power, and the importance of using renewable energy.
The Activity sheet, ‘Carbon dioxide emissions’, 
provides a graph of carbon dioxide emissions per 
person in Australia. Students are guided through the 
process of analysing the graph, then explaining what 
this means in terms of future energy use. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘How wind turbines work’, 
students will gain an understanding of how wind 
power is generated by completing the description of 
how each part works.
The Activity sheet, ‘Current use of wind power’, 
provides information about wind power, and presents 
a pie graph showing the capacity for wind power 
electricity generation in Australia, for each state and 
territory. Have the students consider the proportions 
in terms of physical size and population of each state, 
and other natural resources it may be more efficient 
to harness. Students will answer questions about the 
graph, and list advantages and disadvantages of wind 
power. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Opinions about wind farms’, 
with the class, and ensure they understand the meaning 
of each term in bold. Then students write their own 
opinions about wind farms. Encourage them to provide 
reasons for their opinions. 
extension idea 
●  Ask students to design a survey to find out what 
people know about wind farms, and their opinions 
on whether wind farms are a good idea or not.

Wind power
Wind is a renewable energy resource – this means that it does not produce carbon 
dioxide or any chemicals that affect public health or the environment. The use of 
renewable energy is an important factor in reducing the impact of climate change and in 
making sure we can continue to produce energy in the future.

Opinions about wind farms
Not everyone agrees that wind farms are a good idea. Some people do not like the look 
of wind farms as they are often located in places that are considered areas of beauty, such 
as near the coast or on hills. But are they worse than large power lines?
The wind farm Waubra, 35 km north-west of Ballarat in Victoria, consists of 128 turbines. 
There have been claims of illness caused by the low-level noise of the blades turning. 
Some residents have reported suffering headaches, high blood pressure, rapid heartbeats 
and nausea. One person moved to Ballarat to get away from the noise. His son operates 
the farm but will not live there.
Some people are concerned about the fate of birds and bats that fly into the blades of 
turbines. In northern Tasmania a number of wedge-tailed eagles have been killed as they 
glide on the wind currents (thermals) created by the wind turbines when looking for their prey.
Wind turbines are built-in factories that use a lot of energy, creating pollution. However, 
this occurs only for a short time, unlike the pollution continually created when electricity is 
generated by coal.

Achieve!
What is geothermal power?
Geothermal power is a form of renewable energy that comes from heat in the earth’s 
crust. Geo means ‘earth’ and thermal means ‘heat’. For every 100 metres down into the 
earth you go, the temperature increases by about 38C.
Natural geothermal energy
 
●Natural geothermal energy is produced when water seeps into the earth’s crust, 
where it is heated by hot volcanic rocks and then rises to the surface as steam.
 
●In North America, hot springs have been used for cooking for thousands of years. 
 
●In countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines, China, Japan and New Zealand this 
resource has been used for heating, power generation and cooking. 
 
●Five geothermal energy plants are planned for Fergusson Island, which is part of the 
Papua New Guinea archipelago. 
 
●In the Philippines, geothermal power provides 27% of the country’s total electricity 
production. 
Engineered geothermal energy
 
●Australia has a vast amount of hot granite within the earth directly beneath it. This 
could be used to produce power by injecting water into breaks in the rocks, which 
is then returned to the surface as steam. This is called engineered geothermal 
energy because it involves using technology to produce energy from heat deep 
inside the earth. 
 
●South Australia, in particular, has great potential for this form of renewable energy. 
A small geothermal plant capable of generating 520 mega-watts of energy has 
been built at Paralana next to the Beverley Uranium Mine. A plant at the Cooper 
Basin also shows a promising future in hot rock geothermal energy. There are 
thought to be enough hot rocks in South Australia to provide power for all of 
Australia for a very long time. However, the set-up costs for geothermal plants, such 
as the costs of drilling, are high.

Hot rocks
Millions of years ago, the granite rocks in the Cooper Basin in South Australia were on the 
surface of the earth. Over time, they were covered by a layer of sedimentary rocks that is 
now four kilometres thick. This layer insulates the granite, which absorbs heat from deep 
within the earth. The granite four kilometres below the surface has a temperature of more 
than 250°C.
