43
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Health and opportunities
Objectives 
l To understand the need for good health, 
education, employment and income 
opportunities
l To recognise differences between Indigenous 
and non-Indigenous health and opportunities
l To appreciate ways to overcome this disparity, 
and to be aware of the variations between 
urban and remote Indigenous people 
l To improve mapping and graphing skills
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required.
Background
Indigenous people had no resistance to diseases 
such as measles, smallpox and influenza, which were 
brought to Australia by European settlers. Traditional 
diets were well-balanced and contained little fat. 
Modern urban diets can be high in fat and sugar 
and low in fibre, which has been linked to obesity, 
diabetes and heart disease. These influences, plus 
other lifestyle factors acquired from Europeans 
such as smoking and alcohol consumption, have 
contributed to the high incidence of kidney and 
other diseases in Indigenous Australians. As a result, 
Indigenous life expectancy is not as high as it is for 
non-Indigenous people. 
 
In remote centres, lack of education reduces 
employment opportunities and contributes to social 
problems. 
 
Indigenous people in other countries such as 
New Zealand and the United States also experience 
disadvantages.
Starter activity
This is a sensitive topic that relates to low socio-economic 
areas as well as to Indigenous people. Ask students to 
think about the things they need to lead a healthy life 
and to have a successful future. Point out that not all the 
people who are disadvantaged are Indigenous, that not 
all Indigenous people are disadvantaged and that many 
Indigenous people have been successful in fields such as 
law, medicine, music and sport.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘What happened after European 
settlers arrived?’, with the students. Make sure students 
understand the meaning of the terms shown in bold. 
Students could work in pairs to answer the questions. 
 
Examine the graph on the Activity sheet, ‘Australian 
populations’, with the students. Make sure they 
understand how to read and interpret the graph. Discuss 
why these statistics are a valuable measure of Australian 
society.
 
Have students complete the mapping activity on the 
Activity sheet, ’Distance from major cities’. They will need 
an atlas or access to a mapping application, and a blank 
map of Australia. A map is provided on the CD-ROM in 
the Artwork > Unit 7 folder.   
 
Read and discuss the Resource sheet, ‘Opportunities in 
Australia (1)’, with the class. Then have them complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘Opportunities in Australia (2)’. You could 
extend this activity by exploring the website:  
http://www.indigenous.gov.au with the students, which 
provides further information about the government’s 
Closing the Gap policy. Students could list current 
government projects that are aimed at each category 
listed on the Activity sheet.
extension ideas
l  Students could research Indigenous people from 
another country and compare their treatment and 
outcomes with Australia’s Indigenous people; for 
example, the Maori people in New Zealand, the Inuit 
people in Canada or the Native Americans in the 
United States. 
l  Have students research the history of the White 
Australia Policy in Australia. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
49
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Indigenous climate
Objectives
l To understand the difference between weather 
and climate
l To appreciate the importance of weather 
observations in Indigenous life
l To compare Indigenous and European 
interpretations of climatic events
l To learn how to graph and analyse data
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of  
the impact of weather on the clothes they wear, 
their sporting activities and decisions about  
holiday destinations.
Background
Weather and climate play a very important part in 
our decision making and daily lives. Early Indigenous 
Australians made detailed observations of weather, 
as their survival depended on knowledge of plant 
germination and growth, and the cycles of animals. 
This knowledge is linked to their sustainable use of 
the land and to the Dreaming. Indigenous Australians 
in different areas had many different experiences, 
as the size of the Australian continent and its 
topography created diverse conditions. Information 
was passed orally from generation to generation. 
Detailed accounts of the climate of northern 
Australia still exist, as well as for south-western 
Australia, the Grampians and the Sydney region. 
However, Indigenous climate information for the 
south-east of Australia has largely been lost due to 
European occupation.
The concept of four seasons, which the Europeans 
brought from the Northern Hemisphere, does not 
really fit with the Indigenous seasons. Up to six 
seasons have been identified in south-west Australia 
and the Northern Territory, and three in the centre  
of Australia.
Indigenous knowledge of weather and climate is 
now being recognised by the scientific community as a 
valuable contribution to the climate change discussion. 
Climate change is expected to contribute further to 
erosion of coastlines and rising sea levels. This may force 
some Torres Strait Island communities to move, causing 
physical and social disruption. 
Starter activity
Ask students to brainstorm why we need to know 
about the weather and climate. Discuss which 
occupations depend on this information. Explore the 
idea that today, a change in the weather doesn’t much 
affect whether people go to work or school not, where 
people live or what people eat. Why do the students 
think Indigenous Australians need to know about the 
weather? 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘The Australian Climate’, with 
the class. Students will rearrange sentence fragments 
and rewrite complete sentences about seasons from a 
European and Indigenous perspective. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Climate 
statistics for Maningrida, NT’. Maningrida is a town in the 
Northern Territory on the north coast of Arnhem Land. 
Students will complete a climate graph by continuing to 
plot the data from a table. 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Yolgnu seasons’, with 
the class. Students will learn about the features of the 
different Yolgnu seasons, and how this affects where the 
Yolgnu live and what they do. 
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Yolgnu and 
Maningrida seasons’, students will need the completed 
Activity sheet, ‘Climate statistics for Maningrida, NT’, 
and the Resource sheet, ‘Yolgnu seasons’. Students will 
answer questions to help them analyse and interpret 
the information provided.
extension ideas
Students could research climate data for their local area, 
or an area they would like to visit, and graph the data 
using the climate graph on the Activity sheet, ‘Climate 
statistics for Maningrida, NT’ as a model.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
33
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Indigenous use of the land
Objectives
● To understand what hunting and gathering 
means for a traditional society
● To recognise the sustainable use of the land by 
Indigenous people
● To become familiar with key terms such as: 
Indigenous, inhabitants, remains, archeology, 
tradition, spirituality, prehistoric
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that there were Indigenous 
inhabitants in Australia before British settlement, and 
that there are still Indigenous people today. Some 
Indigenous people live traditional lifestyles today, or 
integrate traditional aspects into their lives. 
Background 
Early Indigenous Australians could only use the 
resources available in their local area. They spent a 
large portion of their daily lives acquiring enough 
food sources. Food also dictated the movement of 
the tribes. 
 
Through their Dreamtime stories, Indigenous 
Australians understood sustainable use of the land, 
and practised this for thousands of years. Tribal 
cultural practices and their food sources differed 
according to their location. There was no cropping, 
although women in some areas replanted some 
roots. Kangaroos and other animals were not tamed 
or used as beasts of burden. Fish traps were built in 
coastal areas like Albany in Western Australian and 
along some inland rivers, but the catch was always 
sustainable.
Starter activity 
Ask students about their understanding of the hunting 
and gathering lifestyle. Discuss how this compares 
with their own lifestyles. You could work with the class 
to research the food sources that were available to 
Indigenous Australians in your local area. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous 
Australians and sustainability’. Point out the timescale 
referred to – Mungo Man’s age of about 60 000 years, 
compared to European occupancy of Australia a little 
more than 200 years ago.  Discuss the differences 
between the methods of transferring knowledge and 
cultural practices compared with what happens today.

Indigenous Australians and 
sustainability
Indigenous Australians are the original inhabitants of Australia and its nearby islands. 
The earliest human remains, dated at about 60 000 years old, are those of Mungo Man.  
He was found in Lake Mungo in New South Wales in 1974.
There is no written record of life in prehistoric Australia. Knowledge about this time 
is found in archeological evidence and in Indigenous oral traditions. Before European 
settlement, all Indigenous Australians based their lifestyles on their Dreaming beliefs. 
The Dreaming (also called the Dreamtime) stories connected humans, animals, fish, birds 
and the land. These connection brought a sense of caring about and spirituality towards 
the land and all the life it supported. The stories explained how to live sustainably so that 
the earth could support all kinds of life, both now and in the future.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
18
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Land management
Objectives
l To understand the meaning of the term 
‘hunters and gatherers’
l To appreciate the need to look after the land
l To identify differences between Indigenous  
and European use of the land
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that there are different 
ways of using and caring for the land.
Background 
Early Indigenous Australians gained all the 
nourishment they needed while living sustainably 
on the land. The kinds of foods eaten by different 
tribes varied according to their location and the 
season. Dreamtime stories told them how to 
care for the land and its resources. Water became 
sacred, and in some areas wells were dug to tap 
underground supplies. Fire played an important 
part in warmth, cooking and hunting. Tribes would 
burn off areas at particular times of the year to 
encourage grass to grow. This provided a food 
source for the animals they hunted. The use of fire 
changed the vegetation, with fire-resistant species 
such as eucalypts and acacias becoming dominant.
Starter activity
Work with the class to define these key terms  
which are used throughout the unit: nomadic,  
semi-nomadic, cannibalism, sustainable, 
aromatic, legalised, hunters and gatherers.
Resource and Activity sheets
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Hunting 
and gathering’. Then discuss how this way of finding 
food compares with the way people obtain food 
today. Introduce the idea of a global food chain, and 
compare it with the local supply of food Indigenous 
people relied on. 
 
Have students read the Resource sheet, 
‘Indigenous methods of finding food’. Discuss 
the importance of sustainable use of resources to 
Indigenous Australians, and how sustainability relates 
to food supply today. For example, more people are 
growing their own vegetables and fruit, eat foods that 
are in season and are concerned about food miles 
and other environmental factors associated with food 
production. 
 
To complete the Activity sheets, ‘Finding food’ and 
‘Sustainable land use’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous methods of finding food’. 
 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Food preparation’, with the 
students. Through this activity, students will gain an 
understanding of how Indigenous Australians ensured 
a constant food supply despite limited options for 
storing food. They will also learn about the availability 
today of some traditional foods.
 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Use of resources’, students 
complete a cloze exercise exploring the kinds of tools 
and equipment Indigenous Australians made, and how 
they were used. Students may need assistance with 
finding illustrations of the tools from online or library 
sources for the second part of the activity.  
extension ideas
l  Have students work in small groups to research 
the availability of bush tucker – in their local area, 
Australia-wide and internationally. Students could 
also compile a collection of recipes that use these 
ingredients.
l  Visit the Indigenous plant section of the local 
Botanical Gardens, and look for plants that can 
be used as food sources. Make sure the students 
understand that it is not safe to eat these plants unless 
they are taught how to prepare them correctly.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
5
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Sustainable energy
Objectives
● To understand the concept of sustainability
● To recognise the need for sustainability
● To identify renewable and non-renewable 
resources
● To learn how sustainable energy can assist 
with climate change and the health of the 
environment
Prior knowledge
● Students should have some understanding of 
resources and the fact that they can be used up, 
especially as the population grows. They should 
also know that the use of fossil fuels has an 
impact on climate change, air quality and health, 
and that is is possible to generate power from 
renewable energy sources. 
Background
There has been much discussion regarding the 
need to use renewable energy as our understanding 
of  the effects of burning fossil fuels increases, 
and our fossil fuel supplies decrease. However, all 
forms of renewable energy have advantages and 
disadvantages. Wind power, solar power, tidal power, 
geothermal energy and biomass are regarded as 
green energy sources. Hydro-electric power and 
nuclear power are considered sustainable energy 
sources by some people. 
Starter activity 
Compile a class list of all the ways students use 
power. Then introduce the idea that power is also 
used to produce and distribute everything they buy. 
Add to the list the things the students buy regularly. 
Resource and activity sheets 
Provide students with the Activity sheet, 
Sustainability’. Read the introduction and speech 
bubbles with the students. Encourage them to 
suggest further examples of sustainability, then 
discuss what sustainability is. Students will work in 
pairs to write their own definitions for sustainability. 
 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Why do we need 
sustainable energy?’, with the students. For each fossil 
fuel, point out the number of years it is expected 
to last at current rates of consumption. Encourage 
students to suggest reasons why countries still use 
fossil fuels. Introduce the idea that it is cheaper in 
terms of money for countries to continue using fossil 
fuels than to invest in the research, technology and 
infrastructure need to use renewable energy sources.  
 
Ask students to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Global 
supplies of fossil fuels’. They will need a copy of the 
Resource sheet, ‘Why do we need sustainable energy?’, 
an atlas or access to an Internet map search, and a blank 
world map. A map is provided on the CD-ROM in the 
Artwork > Unit 1 folder. Some students may need 
assistance with developing an appropriate key. When 
they have completed the mapping activity, students 
answer questions about the regions that have large 
and small fossil fuel reserves. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Renewable and non-
renewable resources’ with the students. Ensure students 
understand the meaning of ‘resource’ and that resources 
can be renewable or non-renewable. Introduce the idea 
that while some resources are renewable, they can also 
be scarce, like bananas after a cyclone in Queensland. 
Also, some resources require sound environmental 
management to be used sustainably; for example, fish 
supplies can be unsustainable due to human activities 
such as ocean pollution and overfishing. Students 
could use the Internet to check their answers to the last 
question.
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Reducing 
energy use’. Some students might prefer to work in pairs. 
You could compile a class list of their ideas for reducing 
energy use. .
extension idea
●  Take a tour of the school, and have the students note 
ideas for reducing energy use. If possible, choose 
several ideas and develop a plan to implement them.

ACHIEVE!   History: Rights and freedoms
17
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – 1900–1965
Prior knowledge
Students may benefit from a knowledge of interactions 
between British colonists and Indigenous Australian 
peoples prior to 1901.
Background
As part of the Federation of Australia, legislation that 
reinforced the secondary position of Indigenous 
Australian peoples was introduced. These changes 
were embedded within the Constitution, which is 
the central document that shaped the formation of 
Australia as a nation. Relevant changes include the 
decision not to count Indigenous Australians in the 
census (the document that records the population of 
Australia) and the Commonwealth Franchise Act of 1902 
which prohibited Indigenous Australians from voting 
in Federal elections. This meant they had no legal 
opportunities for resistance and representation. At the 
same time, women were given the right to vote. This 
clearly demonstrates the attitudes of the time. 
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, there was 
a theory that Indigenous Australian peoples were 
a ‘doomed race’. Authorities of the time may have 
believed it was unnecessary to include in the census a 
race that would soon be extinct.  
These changes served to remove Indigenous Australian 
peoples from the political and legal sphere. They were 
treated as children; unable to make political, economic 
or social decisions for themselves or for the nation. 
In the late 1800s, Aboriginal Boards were established in 
most states. These boards attempted to act as ‘parents’ 
to the Indigenous Australian peoples. Someone under 
their authority often had to apply to the board to 
obtain wages, ask for permission to marry or to visit 
friends and relatives in different reserves. 
The restrictions on the lives of the Indigenous 
Australian peoples varied from state to state. But one 
thing remained the same – their lives were limited 
simply because of their race.
Starter activity
Consider what it is like to have someone else make all 
the important decisions for you: where you must live, 
where you can go, how much money you have and 
what kind of work you can do. Is it fair? What would it 
be like if this control continued for your entire life?
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Aboriginal Boards’, provides 
information about the restrictions on the lives of 
Indigenous Australian peoples in Australia. Students 
will refer to this information in as they complete the  
Activity sheet, ‘Restricted lives’. Here, students interpret 
the information from the table and make general 
statements based on the data. Then they write a 
creative response about life for Indigenous Australian 
people in 1960.  
On the Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous Australian Anzacs’, 
students explore the treatment of Indigenous 
Australian soldiers and nurses in different wars. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Soldiers and nurses’, follows on 
from the previous Activity sheet. Here, students use 
primary source images to identify key features about 
the wars and how Indigenous Australian people were 
represented and treated during these wars. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Source: Half-blood to octaroon’, 
uses a specific photograph to explore views of 
interracial relationships. Students will use the 
information on this Resource sheet to complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘CHIPS analysis’. Here, they analyse the 
source photograph and consider the context of the 
time in which it was published, 1947.
Extension ideas
Ask students to research life on a reserve in the 1940s 
to 1960s. Website suggestions:
•    Lake Tyers, Victoria 
indigenousrights.net.au/land_rights/lake_
tyers,_1962-70/early_history_of_lake_tyers
•    Moore River Settlement, Western Australia 
www.noongarculture.org.au/moora
•    Bamaga, Queensland 
https://www.qld.gov.au/atsi/cultural-awareness-
heritage-arts/community-histories-bamaga
Have students write a report about their findings. 
Objectives
• Consider the treatment of Indigenous Australian 
peoples prior to the 1967 Referendum
• Consider how the institutionalisation of racism 
that occurred with Federation impacted on the 
lives of Indigenous Australian peoples 
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

Auber Octavius Neville (1875–1954) was Chief Protector of 
Aborigines in Western Australia from 1915 to 1936. From 1936 
until his retirement in 1940, he was Commissioner for Native 
Affairs.
In 1947, Neville wrote a book called Australia’s Coloured 
Minority: Its Place in the Community. In this book, Neville 
expresses his opinion that the only way of absorbing 
Indigenous Australian people fully into the white Australian 
culture was ‘breeding out the colour’.

different racial groups should not

60
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Closing the gap
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge about the treatment 
of Indigenous Australian peoples in Australia may be 
useful.
Background
The Indigenous Australian civil rights movement in the 
1960s led to the right to vote and a Referendum that 
changed the legal exclusion of Indigenous Australian 
people from society. Later, the lands rights and ‘sorry’ 
movements of the 1980s and 1990s led to changes 
in the rights of Indigenous Australian people and the 
expectations of how they should be treated. 
Although there have been many battles for civil rights 
and a change in views about historical wrongs, there 
are still many difficulties for Indigenous Australian 
peoples today. 
The restrictions of the past continue to affect the 
present – racism and prejudice prevent many 
Indigenous Australian people from successfully 
accessing education, improving health outcomes 
and choosing occupations. A disproportionately 
large number of Indigenous Australians experience 
physical and mental illnesses and often they don’t 
have the support networks that are in place for other 
groups in society. This cycle of problems was reflected 
in the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in 
Custody. Indigenous Australian people make up a 
disproportionately large number of those sentenced 
and imprisoned. 
There are some positive stories. Many Indigenous 
Australians are achieving positions that are perceived 
by society to be of high status and influence: 
academics, politicians, lawyers and doctors. There are 
more opportunities for Indigenous Australian people to 
gain scholarships, enter targeted occupations, access 
new networks and build supportive communities. 
However the gap is still very much in place and more 
must be done to address the problems that Indigenous 
Australian people continue to face due to the injustices 
of the past. 
Starter activity
Brainstorm representations of Indigenous Australian 
people in the media in Australia today. 
• Television: 
 –  Cleverman (2016), dystopian Indigenous Australian 
series
 –  Marngrook (since 2007), series about Indigenous 
Australian football
 –  NITV (National Indigenous Television Channel)
• Films: The Sapphires (2012), Rabbit-Proof Fence (2002) 
• Media personalities: Adam Goodes, Jessica Mauboy
• Book: Gracey by James Moloney
Discuss what this says about the position of Indigenous 
Australian people in today’s society. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Celebrating Indigenous Autralian 
culture’, look at expressions of Indigenous Australian 
culture, both traditional and modern. Students will 
answer questions to check their understanding.
The Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous Australian deaths 
in custody’, discusses the Royal Commission into 
Aboriginal Deaths in Custody. Students match terms to 
definitions and analyse key recommendations. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Football’, explores some positive 
and negative events in AFL football that relate to 
Indigenous Australian culture.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Where are we now?’, students 
read a variety of different views relating to Indigenous 
Australian people in society.
Extension ideas
Have students research one of the programs that aims 
to improve the wellbeing of Indigenous Australian 
people. For example, Close the Gap: Indigenous Health 
Campaign. 
Students should find out:
• the purpose of the project
• why it is needed
• how it works
• how successful it is. 
Objectives
• Consider the modern situation for Indigenous 
Australian people
• Learn about the significance of racism in 
Australia

Celebrating Indigenous Australian culture
Activity sheet – Closing the gap
+  Answer the questions in your workbook.
1  What do Indigenous Australian musicians often write songs about?
2  What is one difference between the music of Archie Roach and the music of 
Jessica Mauboy? 
3  Why are both kinds of music important? 
4  Why is Indigenous Australian art so significant?
5  What is the significance of traditional Indigenous Australian dances?
6  Listen to a song by Jessica Mauboy, Isaiah Firebrace or Kaylah Truth. Compare and 
contrast the style and lyrics of the song with one by Archie Roach, Ruby Hunter or 
Yothu Yindi.
Indigenous Australian dances are 
taught by one generation to the 
next generation. Dances are not 
simply movements to music – they 
tell stories. Many dances tell stories 
from The Dreaming. Children 
learn dances as a way of finding 
out more about their culture and 
connecting to their community.
Indigenous art has been made continuously in 
Australia for over 50,000 years. There are many 
different styles of Indigenous Australian art 
and each area in Australia has its own styles 
and forms. The use of the dots technique is 
perhaps the most familiar to non-Indigenous 
Australian audiences.
There are a number of Indigenous 
Australian instruments and the 
didgeridoo is probably the most 
well-known one. Some people 
believe that it is the oldest 
instrument in the world. 
Modern music is very important within the 
Indigenous Australian culture. Songs tend 
to focus on issues that are significant to their 
community, such as land, family, history and 
protest. Some musicians challenge people’s 
thinking, like Archie Roach. Others like Jessica 
Mauboy and Isaiah Firebrace don’t always 
follow this tradition, but they certainly make 
Indigenous Australian artists more visible in the 
wider community.

Indigenous Australian deaths in custody
+ 1  Read the information below. 
In the late 1980s, Prime Minister Bob Hawke became concerned about the regular deaths 
of Indigenous Australian people that were occurring while they were in custody. In 
1987 a Royal Commission was formed. Their task was to research the deaths and make 
recommendations so that future deaths could be prevented.
The Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths 
in Custody seemed to suggest that there were 
issues both in the sentencing and imprisoning of 
Indigenous Australian people.
Indigenous Australians make up around 2% of the 
total population but they were 17% more likely to 
be arrested. 
The Commission suggested that racism had an 
impact on how many Indigenous Australian 
people were jailed. They also thought it affected 
the treatment that Indigenous Australians 
received while they were in prison. This could 
have led to the deaths in custody.
2  Write each underlined word in 
the information above beside the 
correct definition.
a ___________________: treating someone differently because of their skin colour or race
b __________________________: educated suggestions for improving a situation
c __________________________: official inquiry into an area of concern
d ________________________: when a judge tells someone what their punishment is 
e _____________________: prison or detention
3  The Royal Commission made this recommendation: Recognise the difficulties faced by 
Indigenous Australian youth and provide support before they reach custody. 
 
In your workbook, explain what you think this means, and how it could be carried out. 
Some Royal Commission 
recommendations
•  Give staff cultural training
•  Identify punishments that could be 
more successful than imprisonment
•  Keep statistics about deaths to help 
find ways to reduce their number
•  Recognise the difficulties faced by 
Indigenous Australian youth and 
provide support before they reach 
custody
•  Police should not act violently 
towards Indigenous Australian 
people or threaten them

Students may benefit from an understanding of the 
American Civil Rights movement in the 1950s and 
1960s (See previous unit: Civil Rights movement, USA).
Background
After World War II, people became more concerned 
about the treatment of different races and religious 
groups. This new awareness was matched in a number 
of countries by increasing civil rights actions.
In the United States, there had long been groups like 
the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement 
of Colored People). But it was only in the 1950s and 
1960s that their actions began having a wider impact. 
Their attempts to fight for political rights through 
court cases, petitions, boycotts, Freedom Rides and 
sit-ins had an enormous impact. There is still racial 
discrimination and inequality there today, although the 
situation has greatly improved.
In Australia in the 1950s and 1960s, there was also 
an increasing concern about racial discrimination. A 
number of groups began protesting about the unequal 
treatment of Indigenous Australian peoples: the use 
and abuse of reserves, restrictions on who they could 
marry and what they could drink, minimal access to 
education and limited political representation. 
 Many Indigenous Australian peoples looked to the 
large and powerful civil rights groups in America for 
ideas on how to protest. They also used Freedom 
Rides, protest marches and court cases to fight 
for the same rights as other Australians. In 1949 
Indigenous Australians were officially made citizens 
but the changes to their rights were limited. In 1962, 
Indigenous Australians were finally allowed to vote 
in Federal elections. There was a Referendum in 
1967 where everyone voted on whether Indigenous 
Australian people should be included in the census 
and whether special laws just for Indigenous Australian 
people should be abolished. Ninety percent of 
Australians voted for these changes. 
Starter activity
You could watch ‘Eyes On The Prize (Part 3):  
Ain’t Scared of Your Jails, 1960–1961’ (55 mins),  
www.youtube.com/watch?v=neDpuJVc4Ko with the 
students. This documentary shows what the US Civil 
rights experience was like, with an emphasis on sit-ins 
and Freedom Rides. Make sure you review the movie 
first as there is violence and students may find some 
scenes disturbing. 
Alternatively, choose stills from this documentary or 
other relevant images of sit-ins or Freedom Rides. Lead 
a class discussion about how effective these ways of 
protesting were.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Looking to America for ideas’, 
discusses Australia’s links to the United States and asks 
students to match protest terms and definitions.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Freedom Rides’, students are 
given information about the Freedom Rides in Australia 
and map the journey taken by one group. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Charles Perkins and Ann Curthoys’, 
provides information about two Freedom Riders and 
primary sources about their experiences. 
Note: Perkins’ source uses the term ‘nigger’. Make 
sure that students understand that this is a historical 
term and very much outdated in usage. It was highly 
offensive at the time and still is today. 
Students use the Activity sheet, ‘Free riders – source 
analysis’, to guide them through the process of 
analysing the sources on the previous Resource sheet. 
Make sure the students understand that bias means 
that a persons shows a prejudice towards (likes or 
dislikes) a group of people.
The Activity sheet, ‘Aims, tactics and outcomes’, looks 
at other protest actions of Indigenous Australian civil 
rights groups.
Extension ideas
Go onto trove.nla.gov.au and research references 
to the Australian Freedom Rides in the 1960s in the 
newspapers. Use terms like ‘Freedom Rides’ or ‘Freedom 
Riders’ to help you find information. 
• What is happening in the article?
• How is the situation represented?
• Include a quote and explain what it means.
Objectives
• Identify the actions of the Indigenous 
Australian Indigenous Civil Rights movement 
during their protests 
• Consider how the Indigenous Australian Civil 
Rights movement was influenced by the US 
African-American Civil Rights movement
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

Charles Perkins and Ann Curthoys
Charles Perkins and Ann Curthoys were Arts students at the University of Sydney when they

5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Human rights
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Background
Racism has long been a key element of our world. 
European countries like England and Spain invaded 
numerous countries in Africa, Asia and America in the 
15th and 16th centuries. They used their perception 
of racial superiority to justify their mistreatment 
of native people. In the 18th and 19th centuries in 
Australia, Indigenous peoples were forced off their 
land because they did not use the land as Europeans 
did. In other countries such as India, white people were 
automatically given the best jobs and opportunities, 
Anglo-Indians, (half-British, half-Indian) were given 
middle-ranking positions, while the lowest positions 
were reserved for Indians. This racism was also 
entrenched in America where legislation allowed 
for ‘separate but equal’ toilets, water taps and other 
facilities for white and black people. 
As part of the Paris Peace Conference (1919–20), the 
question of a Racial Equality clause was introduced 
by Japan. The Japanese saw themselves as a superior 
race that had quickly modernised in the 20th century 
to keep up with Europe and America. Japan had also 
supported the Allies (England, France and America) 
in World War I because Germany tried to take land 
claimed by Japan. However, Australian Prime Minister 
Billy Hughes wanted to maintain the racial exclusivity 
of the White Australia Policy (Immigration Restriction Act 
1901) and blocked a racial equality clause that might 
challenge the ‘whiteness’ of Australia. 
After World War II, the situation on the world stage 
was different. Racial issues that were easily dismissed 
after World War I were now centre stage. No-one could 
deny that the German’s genocidal treatment of Jews, 
Gypsies, Slavs and other groups deemed ‘subhuman’ 
(Untermenschen) by the Nazis had a racial factor. The 
introduction of the Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights on 10 December 1948 was a move towards 
improved human rights.
Starter activity
Have the students work in small groups, and provide 
each group with poster paper. Ask each group to 
identify the rights that they think everyone in a society 
should have. The students should also explain the 
reasons for their choices.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘League of Nations’, looks at Japan’s  
attempt to introduce a racial equality clause into the 
key legal documents of the Treaty of Versailles at the 
1919 Paris Peace Conference. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Racial Equality Proposal’, follows 
on from the previous Activity sheet by exploring the 
different attitudes of Japan and Australia towards this 
proposal. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Eleanor Roosevelt and Herbert 
Evatt’, students are introduced to two key people who 
contributed to the Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights’, identifies key features of this document. On the 
Activity sheet, ‘My rights’, students use the Resource 
sheet to help them develop their own Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights.
Extension ideas
Imagine that you are creating your own society.
• What laws would you make?
• What would you do with people who broke the 
rules?
• What rights do you think everyone should have?
• In what situations would you treat people 
differently? Why?
Objectives
• Consider the role of the League of Nations 
and the United Nations in the development of 
human rights
• Learn about changes in perspectives about 
race over the 20th century
• Develop an understanding of key legal 
documents

Universal Declaration of Human Rights
In World War II, the Nazis persecuted and killed:
• Jews 
• Gypsies
• Slavs
After World War II, images and stories of these horrors shocked many people and helped to 
make racism less acceptable. The League of Nations had rejected racial equality in 1919.  
In the 1940s, the United Nations could no longer ignore the need for racial equality.  
In 1948, the United Nations created the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 
Articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
There are 30 articles in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 
Each article explains a right or responsibility that every person in 
the world should have. It is an important document that helps 
people to think about the rights that people currently have, and 
compare them to the rights that people should have.  Many 
countries still do not treat all people according  
to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.   
Summary of the first five articles
1 Every person is born equal.
2  No-one should be treated differently because of their race, colour, sex,  
language, political views or religious beliefs.
3 Everyone has the right to life, freedom and safety.
4 No-one should be a slave.
5 No-one should be tortured or treated in a way that is cruel, inhuman or degrading.
• mentally disabled people
• physically disabled people
• homosexuals.
… recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and 
inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the 
foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world …
Preamble 
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948
Definitions
inherent: a part of a 
person or thing that 
cannot be taken away
dignity: the quality of 
being worthy of respect
inalienable: cannot be 
given nor taken away
foundation: the idea 
or structure on which 
something is based

Teacher’s notes – Native title
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge about the treatment 
of Indigenous Australian peoples in Australia may be 
useful.
Background
In the 1960s Indigenous Australian people were 
granted the right to citizenship and inclusion in 
Australian society. In 1962, Indigenous Australians were 
given the right to vote in Federal elections which finally 
allowed for the possibility of Indigenous Australian 
representation. This was followed in 1967 by the 
overwhelmingly successful Referendum in which 90% 
of Australians voted ‘yes’. This Referendum changed 
the Constitution so that Indigenous Australians would 
be included in the census (the collection of data 
about the population of Australia). It also removed the 
rights of states to enforce special laws for Indigenous 
Australians. These laws had meant that Indigenous 
people could have different rights, depending on the 
specific laws of the state they lived in.
This did not mean that racial equality had been 
established. Although institutional racism had been 
challenged, it was just the beginning of a much larger 
battle against racism which continues to this day.
The British designated Australia as terra nullius (empty 
land) to justify their colonisation and settlement of 
a land that belonged to other people. This decision 
meant that successive governments had no problem 
with removing Indigenous Australian peoples 
from their land. Indeed, they saw themselves as 
compassionate for placing Indigenous Australians 
in reserves and ‘caring’ for them. The reserves were 
generally on poor quality land that was not suitable for 
European use. 
This view of Australia as empty land was challenged 
through legal cases like that of Eddie Mabo. His case 
ran from 1982 to 1992 and became known as the Mabo 
case. The High Court recognised that native title existed 
and that Indigenous Australian peoples had rights to 
their land. 
Similarly, the 1990s brought a rising concern about the 
need for reconciliation and a national apology. Steps in 
this process include the introduction of National Sorry 
Day in 1998. This is now a day of commemoration held 
on 26 May each year. 
Starter activity
Lead a class discussion about the historical problems 
that Indigenous Australian people faced (e.g. rape, 
murder, attacks, prejudice, sent to reserves, rights taken 
away).
Discuss how this past treatment of Indigenous 
Australian peoples affects all Australians today. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Eddie Mabo’, introduces important 
elements of his life and his fight for Indigenous 
Australian rights. 
Students use this Resource sheet to complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘The Mabo case’. Here, students learn 
more about the political and social background to 
the Mabo case and write a paragraph about the 
implications of Eddie Mabo’s victory.  
On the Activity sheet, ‘Native Title Act 1993’, students 
compare and contrast two key native title cases: the 
Mabo case and the Wik decision. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Reconciliation’, leads students 
through the process of making a timeline of key events 
relating to reconciliation. 
Tthe Activity sheet, ‘National Sorry Day’, focuses on 
Kevin Rudd’s apology speech in 2008. Students then 
write their own apology speech to the Indigenous 
Australian people.
Extension ideas
Have students work in pairs or small groups. Ask them 
to use http://trove.nla.gov.au to find newspaper articles 
about Eddie Mabo or National Sorry Day.
Students should:
•  choose one newspaper article
•  identify the views reflected in the article 
•   discuss the bias (prejudice for or against) of the writer, 
using supporting evidence from the article
•  suggest reasons for the writer’s bias.
Objectives
• Consider key events in modern history that 
have contributed to the fight for the rights of 
Indigenous Australian peoples 
• Learn about the significance of National Sorry 
Day and the Mabo case

inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.

My name is Eddie Koiki Mabo. I am an Indigenous Australian man from 
Mer Island in the Torres Strait Islands. My mother died when I was born, 
29 June 1936, and my uncle Benny Mabo adopted me, changing my 
surname from Sambo to Mabo. I spent my childhood learning about the 
land that we lived on and developing the skills of my ancestors. I grew up 
believing that the island we lived on was our land.
When I was in my early twenties, I moved to Townsville and married Bonita 
Neehow. We had ten children together, seven of our own and three adopted. 
I often worked as a labourer, working on pearl boats, cane fields and the 
railways to support my family. Leading up to the Referendum in 1967, 
I became a member of the civil rights movement. I thought that we deserved 
to be treated the same as everyone else. 
In 1972, I wanted to travel back to Mer Island to visit 
my adoptive father Benny. He was dying 
from tuberculosis, but the authorities 
would not let us come over and see him 
before he died. It made me very angry.
Later in the 1980s, I started to give talks 
about how the Torres Strait Islanders 
on Mer Island cared for the land and 
had a connection to it. It seemed wrong 
to think that this land belonged to the 
government and not to the people 
who lived on it. Some lawyers and 
I decided to fight for my right to 
this land as a test case for more 
Indigenous Australian peoples to 
claim land.

Teacher’s notes – Restrictions and rights
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge about the position of 
Indigenous Australian peoples before Federation and 
the social changes in the 1960s may be useful.
Background
In the 1960s, a number of social issues began to 
rise in prominence. Racism, sexism, militarism and 
homophobia became issues that were challenged 
by different groups in society. The horrors of World 
War II had awakened the world to the potential 
consequences of viewing groups of people as ‘lesser’. 
This led to the creation of the United Nations Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. This document 
identified the rights that all humans deserved, 
regardless of their background or beliefs. 
The idea that all people should have certain rights 
was revolutionary. Even in the 1940s and 1950s, black 
and white people were still segregated in America, 
coloured people (African and Indian) were living under 
Apartheid in South Africa and Indigenous Australian 
peoples were kept in reserves and controlled with 
special laws in Australia. 
During this time, women were also dealing with sexist 
attitudes that limited their opportunities for education 
and employment. Homosexuals were treated with 
prejudice and faced dangerous consequences if their 
sexuality was revealed. This was also the time of the 
Cold War, which was a battle of communism (led by the 
Soviet Union) and capitalism (led by the United States).
In response to these challenges, society began moving 
away from its rigid traditional social behaviour and 
more people began questioning the status quo. One 
aspect of this was the hippy movement of the 1960s 
which focused on a lifestyle outside of the norm. But 
there were many others. Peace groups protested about 
wars in Korea and Vietnam, the women’s liberation 
movements fought against sexism, the civil rights 
movements challenged the racist ideas that skin colour 
shaped ability, personality or intelligence, and, later on 
in the 1970s, people fought for gay rights. All of these 
groups and movements challenged the traditional 
structure of society. In many ways, the fight for the 
rights of one group contributed to the fights for the 
rights of other groups.
Starter activity
Watch a documentary about the 1967 Referendum. 
Suggestions:
•   1967 Aboriginal Timeline – Introductory cultural 
competency module 
www.youtube.com/watch?v=gXVVDG_NFaQ (3 mins)
•   We Made History in the 1967 Referendum  
www.youtube.com/watch?v=qasH5oJiSaU (4 mins)
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Changing rights’, provides a useful 
overview of the restrictions placed on Indigenous 
Australian peoples in the key areas of the census, 
voting and special laws. Students research quotes to 
support the facts provided in the voting and special 
laws sections. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Essay plan’, students are guided 
through the process of creating an essay plan using the 
information from the Activity sheet, ‘Changing rights’. 
Discuss the TEEEM structure with the class, especially 
if students have not used it before. As an extension 
activity, students can use their plan to write an essay.
TEEEM Paragraph Plan
Always start with a topic sentence and always end with 
a mini-conclusion. Put the evidence, explanation and 
essay keywords in the middle.
• T – Topic sentence: introduce your specific topic
• E – Evidence: to support your ideas
• E – Explain: your ideas in your own words
•  E – Essay keywords: use keywords from the essay 
question and the topic sentence to show you are 
answering the question
•  Mini-conclusion: sum up what you said in that 
paragraph.
Extension ideas
Have students write their own essay question, based on 
their knowledge of the rights of Indigenous Australian 
people. Make sure they use task words such as: discuss, 
justify, identify, explain, compare or contrast. Students 
could then prepare an essay plan for the question.
Objectives
• Consider how Indigenous Australian peoples 
were restricted around Federation
• Identify how Indigenous Australian peoples 
gradually regained rights in the 1960s
• Plan and write an essay on a historical issue

Activity sheet – Restrictions and rights
Body paragraph 1: Census
Topic sentence (introduces your body paragraph) – When Australia became a Federation in 
1901, the role of Indigenous Australian people in society was limited by their exclusion from 
the Census.
How were Indigenous Australian people restricted?
Evidence – Indigenous Australian people were excluded from the census.  
‘aboriginal natives shall not be counted’ – Constitution in 1901
Explain – A census counts the entire population so that the government can see where 
services are needed. Excluding Indigenous Australians meant their place in Australian 
society was restricted. Their voices were not heard and their needs were not considered.
How did the situation change? 
Evidence – ‘a moral victory’, Sherlyne Ngalmi
In 1967, a referendum was held about changing some laws and the Constitution. Over 90% 
of Australians voted yes.
Explain – The government and the community began to see that the rights of Indigenous 
Australian people were not being considered and voted to change this.
How were the rights of Indigenous Australian people restored?
Evidence – ‘It allowed people to be counted in the census’, Sherlyne Ngalmi
Explain – Indigenous Australian people had the right to be counted in the census. This 
showed that Australians wanted to include Indigenous Australian people in their society.
Mini-conclusion (sums up your body paragraph) – Excluding Indigenous Australian people 
from the census meant that they were not seen as part of the Australian population. This 
situation only changed in 1967 after a successful Referendum.

49
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – The Stolen Generations
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of the European 
treatment of Indigenous Australian peoples may be 
useful.
Background
Indigenous Australian peoples often experienced 
prejudice and discrimination from the first days of 
the arrival of Europeans in Australia. This prejudice 
included removal from their land, beatings, being sent 
to reserves, rape and massacres. Many Europeans felt 
justified in their treatment of Indigenous Australian 
peoples because they believed that the colour of their 
skin showed that Indigenous Australians were lesser 
people in terms of ability, intelligence and character. 
Under the protectionist policies of the colony 
governments, most Indigenous Australians were 
removed to reserves. On the reserves, they were taught 
English, European farming methods and enough 
skills to serve white people as labourers and domestic 
servants. The view of the colony governments was that 
Indigenous Australians were like children who needed 
to be protected by white people.
In the 1930s, many governments moved towards a 
policy of assimilation. They still believed that people 
with darker skin were lesser beings and needed to be 
protected like children, but they began to treat children 
with both Indigenous Australian and European parents 
as different to those of ‘pure’ Indigenous Australian 
ancestry. These children were often taken from their 
homes and immersed in white Australian culture. 
The children affected by this policy later became 
known as ‘the Stolen Generations’. This was the 
dominant policy from the 1930s to the 1970s, although 
children may have been taken before and after this 
period. 
Starter activity
Have the class watch Philip Noyce’s film, Rabbit-proof 
fence (2002). It is based on the true story of three 
Indigenous Australian girls who are taken from their 
families, escape, and then make the long journey back 
home. The film is adapted from the book written by 
Doris Pilkington Garimara, the daughter of one of the 
girls in the story. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Children of our blood’, explores the 
situation for people with both Indigenous Australian 
and European parents. Make sure the students 
understand that bias means that a person shows a 
prejudice towards (likes or dislikes) a group of people.
The Resource sheet, ‘Stolen children’, provides four 
primary sources that relate to the Stolen Generations in 
Australia. 
Students use the Resource sheet with the Activity 
sheet, ‘Plan a story’, to help them plan a story about the 
Stolen Generations.
The Activity sheet, ‘Bringing Them Home report’, 
provides information about the inquiry into the Stolen 
Generations that was completed in 1997. Students will 
answer questions about the inquiry and some of the 
recommendations made in the report. 
Extension ideas
Use the library or internet to find further primary 
sources about the Stolen Generations. Students could 
also look for primary sources that relate to reuniting 
the families who were separated in this time.
Students could present their findings as a poster or a 
multimedia presentation.
Objectives
• Consider how Indigenous Australian peoples 
were treated in Australia
• Explore the treatment of Indigenous Australian 
children
• Plan and write a historical story
The terms ‘half-caste’ and ‘full-blooded’ were once commonly used. Today, they are highly offensive, especially to 
Indigenous Australian peoples. These terms are linked to the historical belief that people of different racial groups 
should not marry nor have children – a racist idea that is considered completely unacceptable in today’s society.

24
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Working for change
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of the European 
treatment of Indigenous Australian peoples may be 
useful.
Background
Many Indigenous Australian people were unhappy with 
their situation after European settlement. They had 
been moved away from their land – their food places, 
sacred spots and familiar locations. The European 
colonists fenced off the best land for their farms. 
Indigenous Australian peoples were moved to less 
desirable land and often to reserves and missions. 
Federation brought with it legislation that reinforced 
the secondary position of Indigenous Australians. 
They were excluded from the census and banned from 
voting.
Many Indigenous Australians began fighting for their 
rights. They formed groups, identified significant days, 
compiled petitions, established a ‘tent embassy’ and 
organised strikes. 
One significant figure in this early resistance period is 
William Cooper. He began a protest group and made 
many deputations. He also organised the first Day of 
Mourning on 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary of 
colonisation.
Cooper was unusual because he was one of the few 
Australians to protest at the German Consulate in 
Melbourne about the treatment of Jewish people 
before World War II. At this time, many nations would 
not even accept Jewish refugees, let alone condemn 
Germany’s actions.  
Starter activity
Paul Kelly’s song ‘From little things, big things grow’ 
tells the story of Vincent Lingiari and the strikes at Wave 
Hill Station. Play the song for the class. Then lead a 
group discussion about the story told in the song and 
why it is important.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource Sheet, ‘Protection, assimilation, 
integration and self-determination’, identifies different 
ways in which Indigenous Australian peoples were 
viewed and treated in Australian society. 
Students use the information from the Resource 
sheet to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Where do 
we fit?’. Here, students create a cartoon to explain 
each term: protection, assimilation, integration and 
self-determination. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Profile: William Cooper’, looks at one 
of the most significant pre-1945 Indigenous Australian 
civil rights figures. As an extension activity, students 
could research how William Cooper’s actions led to 
today’s NAIDOC week.
The Activity sheet, ‘Civil rights actions’, highlights some 
of the actions of Indigenous Australian civil rights 
groups. Students will use complete a timeline showing 
key events. 
Students will use the previous Activity sheet to help 
them complete the Activity sheet, ‘Petition for change’. 
Here, students identify a significant modern issue and 
write a petition to fight for change. You could have 
students work in pairs or small groups to complete this 
activity.
Extension ideas
Have students choose a key Indigenous Australian 
figure, group or protest to research. 
Ideas:
• Fred Maynard
• William Ferguson
• Australian Aborigine’s League
• Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association
• Tent Embassy
• Day of Mourning
The students should identify and briefly describe their 
topic, then explain why the topic is significant to the 
Indigenous Australian Civil Rights movement.
Objectives
• Consider the policies of assimilation and 
integration
• Identify some of the early Indigenous 
Australian protest groups and explore the ways 
they fought for change

Resource sheet – Working for change
Protection, assimilation, integration  
and self-determination
Social attitudes and government policies have influenced the way that Indigenous Australian  
peoples are treated and governed.
Self-determination, 2000s
•  In 2007, Australia endorsed the UN 
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous 
Peoples.
•  There was a new focus on Indigenous 
Australian people having choices. They 
could retain their Indigenous Australian 
culture or adopt European-Australian 
culture or any combination of the 
cultures they wished.
•  There was an attempt to include 
Indigenous Australian people in 
community and government decisions.
Integration, 1960s–1970s
•  As part of the civil rights movement, the 
need for Indigenous Australian people 
to live like white people was questioned. 
•  The movement included activists like 
Faith Bandler and Charles Perkins and 
groups like the Federal Council for the 
Advancement of Aborigines and Torres 
Strait Islanders (FCAATSI).
•  There was an attempt to recognise some 
Indigenous Australian culture.
•  People began to think that Indigenous 
Australian people should be able to 
access their own culture.
Assimilation, 1930s–1950s
•  People began to criticising the treatment 
of Indigenous Australian people. These 
included Xavier Herbert, who was a 
Protector of Aborigines in Darwin and 
later wrote the novel Capricornia.
•  The government began an official policy 
of absorbing Indigenous Australians of 
mixed descent into the white population.
•  Indigenous Australians were forced to 
live like white people. They had to speak 
English and could not visit their relatives. 
Protection, 1890s–1920s
•  A massive number of Indigenous 
Australian people had died.
•  The British decided to protect 
Indigenous Australian people as if they 
were an endangered species.
•  The Aborigines Protection Act 1886 (VIC): 
People of mixed descent were removed 
from reserves. This was to separate 
‘half-castes*’ who might survive in 
Australian society from ‘full-bloods’ who 
they believed would soon be extinct.
* The terms ‘half-caste’ and ‘full-blooded’ were once commonly used. Today, they are highly offensive, especially to 
Indigenous Australian peoples. These terms are linked to the historical belief that people of different racial groups 
should not marry nor have children – a racist idea that is considered completely unacceptable in today’s society.

59
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Australian women in the war
Background
During WWII, Australian women played a major 
role both on the home front and abroad. There was 
resistance to women taking on traditional male roles. 
However, necessity overcame this resistance. Women 
joined a number of organisations closely affiliated with 
the armed services.
Starter activity
Brainstorm what jobs the class thinks women and men 
should have in a war. Write the students’ ideas on the 
board and encourage them to give reasons for their 
views. Explain to the students that the roles of women 
and men in society were very different in that time, 
compared to today. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Women on the home front’, 
outlines some of the jobs women did during WWII. 
It also introduces the idea that the role of women 
in society changed dramatically at this time. Read 
the sheet with the students and make sure they 
understand the meaning of the terms shown in 
bold. Ask students if they think the poster would be 
effective for recruiting women, and to give reasons for 
their opinions.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Jobs done by Australian 
women’, asks students to compose a list of jobs 
performed by women during WWII. It also defines 
acronym and provides a table of related acronyms. To 
extend the activity, students could research one of the 
organisations listed in the table.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Looking at a poster and a 
photo’, asks students to respond to the recruitment 
poster on the Resource sheet, ‘Women on the home 
front’. It also provides a photo of women repairing a 
plane for students to respond to. 
	
In the Activity sheet ‘Australian women serving 
abroad’, students are provided with information about 
nurses serving abroad and the Australian Women’s 
Army Service. Students will answer questions about 
this information. Question 2 answers: a Australian,  
b drove, c service, d worked, e necessary, f people.
	
In the Activity sheet, ‘Letter to a husband’, students 
will read and respond to a wartime letter.
Extension ideas
• 
Have the students imagine that they are involved 
in WWII. Ask them to write a letter to a close friend 
or relative who is posted overseas for the war.
• 
Word building – write the words information, 
communication and organisation on the board. 
Explain to the students that these words are the 
noun forms of verbs. Work as a class to construct a 
verb/noun table like the one below. 
Verb
Noun
inform
information
communicate
communication
organise
organisation
regulate
regulation
negotiate
negotiation
navigate
navigation
Objectives
• To recognise the role of Australian women on 
the home front in WWII
• To recognise the role of Australian women 
abroad in WWII
• To develop skills in responding to primary 
documents
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.

60
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Women were usually paid 
less than men. During the war, 
many women had to make all 
the family decisions and deal 
with finances for the first time. 
They also had to cope with not 
knowing if family members who 
were at war were safe.
This poster is called ‘Join us in 
a victory job.’ It was made in 
1943. Its purpose is to persuade 
women to join organisations 
during WWII. It shows women in 
the WRANS, AWAS, WAAAF, AWLA and AAMWS,  
and a munitions worker. It is a recruitment poster. 
Voluntary work
Women did a lot of voluntary work, raising money for the war effort and sending clothes 
and food to soldiers overseas. One of the biggest voluntary organisations was the 
Australian Women’s Land Army (AWLA), established in 1942. Women aged between 18 and 
50 could join. The AWLA was a voluntary organisation because its members were civilians, 
not formally enlisted in the army. Women working in the AWLA were paid a small amount 
of money by farmers for jobs like planting crops, driving tractors and milking cows. Their 
efforts helped maintain Australia’s food supply.
Resource sheet – Australian women in the war
Women on the home front 
Before WWII, most Australian women worked at home, raising children and doing 
domestic chores. This work was unpaid. During the war (1939–45), many men left their 
jobs to fight in the war. These vacant jobs were filled by women.  
They included:
• working in factories, especially 
munitions factories
• working on farms
• driving army vehicles and ambulances
• working in telecommunications
• working as mechanics
• collecting intelligence information. 
Join us in a victory job – poster 
created for the Department of 
National Service, 1943
Courtesy, Australian War 
Memorial ARTV00332

Activity sheet – Australian women in the war
Australian women serving abroad
During WWII, many Australian women served abroad (overseas). Nursing services were 
closely linked to the Australian navy, army and air force. Women served as nurses in the 
Middle East, Greece and Singapore. They worked under extremely difficult conditions and 
often put up with the same conditions as soldiers. When hospitals weren’t available, they 
worked in temporary medical wards. At times nurses went to the battlefields to care for 
wounded soldiers.
Many nurses were sent to Singapore because Singapore was an Allied base. When Japan 
invaded Singapore in 1942, sixty-five nurses were evacuated on the ship the Vyner Brooke. 
The Japanese bombed the ship and twelve nurses drowned. Other nurses were captured 
by the Japanese and shot. One nurse, Vivian Bullwinkel, pretended she was dead and 
survived. She lived to tell how brave here colleagues had been.
+

Letter to a husband 
+ 
Read this letter from a woman to her husband who was fighting overseas in WWII.
Dear Joe,
I miss you so much and hope you are safe. The children miss you too. We were all 
so happy when we got your letter. I’ve started working in a munitions factory. A 
lot of women are now working outside of home because there just aren’t enough 
men left here to do all the jobs that need to be done. When I’m not at the factory, 
I’m trying to keep up with the housework. The children are doing more chores now, 
and they’re getting used to me being the boss of the house. You’d be so proud of 
them. Sally’s been knitting scarves to put in comfort parcels to send to soldiers who 
are far away from home. She’s hoping you get one of her scarves. Robbie’s joined a 
salvage corps. You should see some of the things he collects!
My darling, we only hear bits of news about Singapore and I can’t imagine what 
you’re going through. I want you to know that everything is fine here. I’m learning 
how to do new things every day.
Love always, 
Rosie xxx
PS – We’re growing our own vegies.

Teacher’s notes – Concentration camps
Background
Much of the information on concentration camps and 
what happened to the people who were sent to such 
camps is too horrific to present to students. Therefore 
some details and images have been deliberately 
excluded from this unit. Between 1939 and 1945, Nazi 
concentration camps were established to imprison 
people the Third Reich considered to be ‘undesirables’. 
These camps were used as slave labour units. Millions 
died from starvation and diseases. Many were 
murdered.
Starter activity
As a class, write sentences about how the students 
would feel if they were sent away from their families 
to a concentration camp. Tell students that when they 
were first sent to such a camp, they probably would 
not have known what was going to happen to them. 
List these words on the board to help with composing 
the sentences: confused, angry, scared, worried, lonely.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
	
The Resource sheet, ‘What were Nazi concentration 
camps?’ defines concentration camps and provides 
information about Auschwitz, the largest Nazi 
concentration camp. Read the sheet with the students 
and make sure they understand the meaning of each 
term shown in bold. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘About 
concentration camps’, students will need to refer to 
the Resource sheet, ‘What were Nazi concentration 
camps?’. Students will answer comprehension 
questions and multiple choice questions to complete 
sentences.
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘Writing sentences’, students 
will identify subjects and verbs in given sentences, 
then write their own sentences about concentration 
camps.  
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Children in concentration 
camps’ asks students to complete a cloze activity 
which provides information on children in 
concentration camps, and introduces David Kaplan 
and Anne Frank. 
	
The Activity Sheet ‘A primary source – Ebensee 
photo’, provides a primary source photo of boys freed 
from a concentration camp in 1945. Students will 
complete questions to guide their response to this 
photo.  
Extension ideas
• 
Students could work in pairs or individually to 
write five questions they would like to ask the 
boys in the photo on the Activity sheet, ‘A primary 
source – Ebensee photo’.
• 
Students could write a letter to Anne Frank or 
David Kaplan.
Objectives
• To learn about concentration camps
• To respond to a primary document
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.

36
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Concentration camps
What were Nazi concentration camps?
Between 1939 and 1945, Nazi Germany established many concentration camps. 
Concentration camps were prisons where people were made to work extremely hard. 
This is called forced labour. The camps were called concentration camps because the 
prisoners were concentrated in one place – that is, held together in one location. 
At first, concentration camps were used to imprison people who disagreed with Hitler 
and the Nazi Party. Jehovah’s Witnesses, disabled people and homosexuals were also 
imprisoned. However, throughout WWII, most of the prisoners were Jewish – millions were 
imprisoned and killed. This genocide of Jews is known as the Holocaust.
Many people in these camps died 
from starvation and exhaustion. 
Conditions were extremely harsh 
and only a few people survived. 
Nazi doctors carried out medical 
experiments in concentration 
camps. Prisoners were forced to let 
these doctors experiment on them.
Who guarded these camps?
These camps were run and guarded 
by Hitler’s SS. The SS stands for  
the German word ‘Schutztaffel’.  
It means a protective squadron.
Auschwitz concentration camp
Auschwitz, in Poland, was the largest concentration camp. Over a million people were 
killed there. Some were shot but most were killed with toxic gases. Auschwitz was used as 
a slave labour centre and an extermination centre. Bergen–Belsen and Buchenwald were 
the names of two smaller German concentration camps.
On 27th January, 1945, Soviet troops freed prisoners from the Auschwitz concentration 
camp. There is now a museum at Auschwitz in honour of the people who were 
imprisoned, tortured and killed there.

Look carefully at the photo of the Ebensee concentration camp, in Austria. It was taken by

conditions. This photo is a primary source because it was taken at the actual time.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
5
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Background
At the start of World War I (WWI) in 1914, Britain, 
France and Russia were allies. These nations formed 
the Triple Entente (Allied powers). Australia fought 
with them. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy formed 
the Triple Alliance (Axis powers). Italy changed sides 
during the war. The USA entered WWI in 1917 and 
fought with Britain, France and Russia. WWI was won 
by the Allied powers and Germany was defeated.
	
The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919. 
The newly formed Weimar Republic (government 
established in Germany after WWI) became 
increasingly unpopular with Germans because it had 
signed the treaty which demanded they pay Allied 
nations, especially France and Belgium, millions of 
dollars in war reparations. This discontent was seized 
upon by the newly formed Nazi Party. 
	
The Great Depression created international 
financial and social insecurity. Resultant 
unemployment helped Hitler and Mussolini rise to 
power. Japan, Germany and Italy increased territorial 
acquisitions to secure raw materials. Other nations 
could not afford to successfully implement sanctions 
to prevent this empire building.
Starter activity
Write these country names on the board: Austria-
Hungary, Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Italy. Work 
with the students to identify which nations belonged 
to the Triple Entente (Allied powers) and which 
belonged to the Triple Alliance (Axis powers). Remind 
students that each group was trying to prevent the 
other from building up military powers and annexing 
land, and that other nations fought with these groups.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘The Treaty of Versailles’, provides 
background information on the Treaty of Versailles, the 
treaty’s demands on Germany and Germany’s reaction. 
Read the sheet with the students and make sure they 
understand the meaning of each term shown in bold.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Understanding the 
Treaty of Versailles’, students will need the Resource 
sheet, ‘The Treaty of Versailles’, and a dictionary. 
Students will write definitions and complete a 
cloze activity to check their comprehension of the 
information on the Resource sheet.  
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Newspaper 
headlines’, students need to refer to a newspaper or 
online news site. Students choose the three most 
interesting headlines from the newspaper. Then they 
write three headlines of their own about the Treaty 
of Versailles from the perspectives of journalists from 
different nations. You could extend the activity by 
asking students to write the first few paragraphs in the 
news articles for the German and French journalists, or 
a journalist from another nation of their own choosing.
	
The Resource sheet, ‘The Great Depression 
and insecurity’, outlines how high unemployment, 
territorial expansion and a policy of appeasement 
contributed to WWII. Read the sheet with the students, 
and discuss the meaning of each term in bold. You 
could locate the countries mentioned on a world map. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Understanding the Great 
Depression’, asks students to recall basic information 
from the Resource sheet, ‘The Great Depression and 
insecurity’, and to fill in a timeline.
Extension idea
• Divide students into small groups and ask them 
to imagine they are at the Versailles Peace 
Conference. Have them present arguments about 
whether or not Germany should have to pay war 
reparations, and if so, how much they should pay.
Teacher’s notes – Contributing causes
Objectives
• To recognise German discontent with the 
Treaty of Versailles
• To develop an awareness of how the Great 
Depression contributed to WWII
• To understand the meanings of key words.
Prior knowledge
Students need to have an understanding of World 
War I, and the nations that fought on the different 
sides.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012

Resource sheet – Contributing causes
The Treaty of Versailles
Soon after World War I (WWI) ended, a number of world 
leaders met to officially end the war. This meeting was called 
the Paris Peace Conference. It was held at Versailles Palace, 
near Paris. One purpose of the conference was to make 
Germany pay war damages. The most powerful nations 
represented at this conference were Britain, France, the 
United States of America, Italy and Japan. William Hughes, 
the Australian Prime Minister, also attended. Germany was 
not invited. 
Germany believed the peace treaty would be based on 
a fourteen-point plan developed by Woodrow Wilson 
(President of the USA) aimed at keeping world peace. France 
thought this plan was not severe enough – they wanted 
Germany to accept blame for starting WWI. 
After much debate, the Treaty of 
Versailles was signed on the 28th of 
June, 1919. This treaty included a war 
guilt clause and Germany had to accept 
blame for starting WWI. Germany also 
had to pay millions of pounds to some 
Allied nations, especially France. 
The Treaty of Versailles demanded that:
•   Germany pay huge war reparations.
•   Germany restrict the growth of its 
military forces. 
•   Germany decrease its territory. 
How did Germany react to  
The Treaty of Versailles?
Many Germans felt that the Treaty of 
Versailles was too severe. The huge war 
reparations Germany had to pay meant 
Germany’s economy suffered. Extreme 
groups in Germany promised they 
could make Germany a better nation. 
The Nazi Party was formed in 1919 and 
Adolf Hitler became the party’s leader 
in 1921. He promised to overturn the 
losses Germany experienced as a result 
of the Treaty of Versailles. 
Allied nations at  
the end of WWI
• Australia 
• Britain 
• Canada
• France
• Italy
• Japan
• Russia
• United States of 
America

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
9
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The Great Depression and insecurity
A depression is a severe slump in an economy. Businesses find it hard to make any profit 
and people lose their jobs. On 24th October, 1929, the New York stock market crashed.  
This marked the beginning of the Great Depression and it continued into the 1930s. 
The Great Depression spread to other countries. Some countries decided they needed more 
land to supply raw materials to help their industries survive. Japan invaded Manchuria in 
1931. Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935. Germany invaded parts of Eastern Europe. 
During the Great Depression there was very 
high unemployment, which created a feeling 
of insecurity (not being safe). Many people 
were poor. 
In some countries, people turned to leaders 
who promised to make their nations strong. 
These leaders built up their supplies of 
arms (weapons) and tried to take land that 
belonged to other nations. Adolf Hitler from 
Germany and Benito Mussolini from Italy  
were two such leaders. 
Resource sheet – Contributing causes
Policy of appeasement
In the1930s, France and Britain 
decided the Treaty of Versailles was 
too harsh on Germany. They followed a 
policy of appeasement (compromise 
in the hope of avoiding another war). 
In 1938, Germany, France, Britain and 
Italy signed the Munich Agreement, 
which agreed to Hitler’s claim that 
part of Czechoslovakia belonged to 
Germany. Neville Chamberlain, the 
British Prime Minister, believed Hitler 
would not claim any more territory 
but in March 1939 Hitler invaded all of 
Czechoslovakia. 
Some historians argue that the 
Great Depression contributed to 
the policy of appeasement because 
Allied nations were not in a financial 
position to stop Hitler’s imperialism. 
The financial losses caused by the 
Great Depression also meant that 
France and Britain did not put as 
much money into building up their 
supplies of weapons.
