18
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Survival on the battlefield
Food
The food Australian soldiers ate during WWII depended on where they were located and 
the climate they were in. However, there were some basic foods that were issued to all 
soldiers. These foods needed to last a long time and be easy to transport.     
Hi, I’m Tony. It’s 1942. I’m an Australian soldier based in El Alamein, Egypt. It’s really 
hard to get fresh food here and the food we do get is rationed. I’m eating my dinner 
– bully beef, again. It’s canned corn beef and I’m sick of it. Then I’ll have a biscuit 
and cup of billy tea with some sweetened condensed milk. Luckily, I still have my 
enamel mug. 
Sometimes we get to eat stew. It’s made in an army cookhouse and put in this 
metal pot called a Dixie, and brought to us in a jeep. Problem is we only get food 
from the cookhouse when things are quiet. My mate Max tried turning some bully 
beef into rissoles. They tasted disgusting. 
I really miss my wife’s cooking. She makes the best Sunday roast. Can’t wait to get 
back to Australia. Too many flies here. This morning I swallowed a fly and I hate 
it when they get up my nostrils. The sand – so much sand. It gets into everything. 
Sometimes I get Weet-Bix for breakfast but sand gets into that too. Sometimes we 
get canned cheese and the sand even gets into that. 
The other day a group of us found a fig tree. I didn’t like figs back in Australia but 
now I love them. It’s so hard to get fresh fruit here. We have to be really careful with 
water. It’s rationed to two pints a day. Can’t use it to wash clothes, only to drink and 
believe me – you get really thirsty here.

Comfort parcels
The Red Cross and Australian Comforts Fund sent parcels to many soldiers. These parcels

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Survival on the battlefield
Intelligence
Intelligence and secret communication helped soldiers survive in the war. 
In WWII, technology wasn’t as advanced as it is today. Methods of intelligence included 
aerial reconnaissance (using aircraft to collect information about enemy forces), espionage 
(using spies), the use of radar, and the use of radio operators and decoding machines. 
Intelligence officers collected information about enemy forces. There were two main ways 
this was done.
• Radio (wireless) operators would record what they heard on paper. Each country used 
their own codes and intelligence officers would try to crack these codes. US intelligence 
broke Japanese naval codes and found out a lot of information about Japanese 
movements in the Coral Sea. This information helped the Allies win the Battle of the 
Coral Sea in May 1942. If the Japanese had won this battle, they could have captured 
New Guinea. Australia would have been open to a Japanese attack.
• In WWII there were many spies. A spy secretly collects information about an enemy. 
Donald and Peter Field were two Australian spies sent to New Guinea to gather 
information about Japanese forces. They worked as signalman and intercepted enemy 
messages from Japan. They were sworn to secrecy about their work for 60 years. 
+ 1	 List three methods of communication used in WWII, and three used today.
Used in WWII
Used today
2	 Describe one modern way a country could find out about an enemy’s next move.

59
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Anzac spirit
Background
Anzac Day originally commemorated the Australian 
and New Zealand army corps’ battle at Gallipoli in 
WWI. Now Anzac Day is a time to pay respect to all 
Australian servicemen and servicewomen involved 
in wars. The spirit of Anzac Day is a concept that 
encompasses courage, determination and mateship.
Starter activity
Ask students if they know what a commemoration 
is. It may be helpful to point out the similarity to the 
word memory. Provide students with the following 
definition: 
A commemoration is a public ceremony which 
remembers and celebrates what people have done. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘About Anzac Day’, provides 
background information on what Anzac stands for, 
why we remember Anzac Day and the spirit of Anzac 
Day. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Remembering 
the history of ANZACs’, students will need to refer to 
the Resource sheet, ‘About Anzac Day’. Students will 
complete a definition exercise, answer comprehension 
questions and construct a sentence about Anzac Day. 
Answers to question 2: a) remember, b) bravery,  
c) spirit, d) marches, e) people, f) served.
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Glorification or 
commemoration?’, provides two different teenagers’ 
perspectives on Anzac Day. Note that definitions of 
commemoration and glorification are provided on 
the following Activity sheet. You could share these 
definitions with the students before they read the 
Resource sheet.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Different opinions’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘Glorification or commemoration?’. Students will 
answer questions about the teenagers’ perspectives, 
and then give their own opinion. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Anzac Day symbols’, defines the 
word symbol. Students will complete a cloze exercise 
about symbols relevant to Anzac Day. 
Extension ideas
• Ask students to write five questions they can use to 
interview people about what they do on Anzac Day. 
Students could conduct the interviews with people 
of varying ages, and prepare a report outlining what 
they found out. 
Objectives
• To learn what Anzac stands for
• To understand the concept of commemoration
• To discover how the Anzac spirit lives on
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.

60
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – The Anzac spirit
About Anzac Day
What does Anzac stand for?
ANZAC stands for the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. During WWI, on 25th April, 
1915, Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli, in Turkey. The Anzacs dug 
trenches and fought Turkish troops for months. Many of the Anzacs were very young. Even 
though the Anzacs were defeated by Turkish forces, they will always be remembered. 
Who do we remember on Anzac Day?
Even though the original Anzacs fought in WWI, on Anzac Day we remember all the brave 
men and women who have served in wars and peacekeeping operations for Australia. We 
remember people who fought in WWI, WWII, The Korean War, the Vietnam War, the War in 
Iraq and the war in Afghanistan.
Anzac Day is held each year on the 25th April.
How do we remember Anzac Day?
The main way people remember Anzac Day is by going to, or watching an Anzac Day 
march. Major Australian cities and many towns hold these marches. Anzac Day is a public 
holiday. This reminds people that it is a very special day.
People lay flowers and wreaths at the base of war memorials to show that they respect 
and remember the men and women who served in the armed forces.
What is the Anzac spirit?
The Anzac spirit is the idea that the bravery and determination of the Australian and New 
Zealand soldiers lives on. The courage of the Anzacs will not be forgotten and people can 
try to be like them. The Anzac spirit is remembered in the Anzac Day motto: Lest we forget. 
The word lest in this motto means so we won’t.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
62
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – The Anzac spirit
Glorification or commemoration?
Hi, I’m Mitch. I don’t get this whole Anzac Day thing. 
Sure I like the public holiday but why are we glorifying 
war? We watch all these soldiers and their relatives 
march. If you ask me, we shouldn’t be remembering 
any wars. Think of all the innocent people who lost 
their lives. Think of all those young guys who were 
wounded for life. Think of all the places that were 
bombed. I reckon people are way too happy on Anzac 
Day. Heaps of them get drunk and some of them play 
that stupid two-up game. On the one hand, kids are 
told gambling is wrong, but it seems no one cares 
about it on Anzac Day. I think the whole Anzac Day 
thing is a myth.
Hi, I’m Libby. I attended the Dawn Service with my family this morning. Usually I hate 
getting up really early but for one special day of the year – Anzac Day – I don’t mind. 
After all, it’s a national day of commemoration when all Australians can remember 
the people who’ve fought for our country. Some of my friends think Anzac Day is a 
waste of time but they’ve forgotten that the courage of the Anzacs lives on today. 
It’s true that some veterans get drunk on Anzac Day but that’s probably because 
they’re trying to forget some of the horrors of war.  I know some of the veterans play 
that game, two-up, where they toss coins into the air. I don’t like gambling but I think 
that since soldiers played two-up in WWII, it’s ok for them to play it on Anzac Day. 
Even though I hate wars, Anzac Day is very special for me. I think everyone should 
respect those who’ve sacrificed so much for their country. The Anzac spirit should 
never be forgotten.

11
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Kokoda Trail
 
Background
Australian forces were sent to Kokoda to prevent 
Japanese forces from invading from the north coast to 
the south coast and capturing Port Moresby. Australia’s 
aim was to push the Japanese back and the only way 
this could be done was by defending the Kokoda Trail. 
The term ‘Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels’ refers to the indigenous 
Papua New Guineans who greatly assisted Australian 
soldiers on the Kokoda Trail.
Starter activity
Using a map of Papua and New Guinea, work with the 
students to locate Gona, Buna, Kokoda, Port Moresby, 
the Kokoda Trail and the Owen Stanley Range. Discuss 
what the map tells you about the terrain. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Stopping further Japanese 
invasion’, describes the location of the Kokoda Trail 
and outlines why Australian forces were sent there. 
Students will learn about the role of these forces and 
the conditions they endured. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Thinking about 
the Kokoda Trail’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Stopping further Japanese invasion’. 
Students will complete a missing letter exercise and 
a cloze exercise, and write their own sentences about 
the Kokoda Trail. 
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘A letter from a soldier’, 
students will complete a cloze exercise that provides 
a young soldier’s perspective on fighting along the 
Kokoda Trail. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels’, outlines 
who these ‘angels’ were and their role on the Kokoda 
Trail. Students will answer related comprehension 
questions. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Studying a photo from the 
Kokoda Trail’, asks students to examine a primary 
source photo. Students will use a word bank to help 
them construct a paragraph based on this photo.
Extension ideas
• Remind students that the Kokoda Trail is also known 
as the Kokoda Track. Have students visit the website:
	
http://kokoda.commemoration.gov.au 
	
Students could watch the short video about the 
Kokoda Trail, and then write down the names of two 
of the battles fought here. Possible answers: The 
Battle of Isurava, The Battle of Mission Ridge, The 
Battle of the Beachheads.
• Students could explore other aspects of the same 
website, such as the Veteran’s Accounts.  
Objectives
• To learn about the location of the Kokoda Trail
• To identify the role of Australian soldiers in 
Kokoda 
• To learn about the conditions endured on the 
Kokoda Trail
• To learn about Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels
• To examine a primary source photo
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – The Kokoda Trail
Stopping further Japanese invasion
Australian troops were sent to Papua New Guinea to prevent Japanese forces advancing 
towards Australia. Japan began occupying areas of Papua New Guinea from January 1942.  
In late July 1942, they landed forces in the north at Gona and Buna. They were preparing 
for an overland attack on the south coast 
city of Port Moresby. If Japan got control 
of Port Moresby and used it as a military 
base, attacking Australia would be easier. 
The Japanese would become more 
powerful in the Pacific.
The Kokoda Trail (or Kokoda Track) 
was the main route connecting Gona 
and Buna on the north coast with Port 
Moresby on the south coast. It went 
through steep mountains called the 
Owen Stanley Range. This mountain 
range made it difficult for Japanese 
forces to reach Port Moresby. 
What did Australian forces do?
Australian forces fought to protect Kokoda, a village 
on the Kokoda Trail. The Japanese wanted this 
village because it had an airfield. The Australians 
fought to prevent Japanese forces from getting any 
further along the trail but they nearly reached Port 
Moresby. Australian soldiers struggled until more 
soldiers were sent to help them. By early 1943, after 
close battles, the Japanese were defeated in New 
Guinea and were forced to withdraw. 
Conditions on the  
Kokoda Trail
The trail was often very 
narrow and soldiers had to 
battle their way through 
thick jungles and dangerous 
mountains. A number of 
Australian soldiers sent there 
were only 19 years old and 
had little military training. 
These soldiers navigated 
rivers and coped with 
swamps, mud and diseases.

I miss you so much. Things are really hard here. We’re working our way along

Activity sheet – The Kokoda Trail
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels is the name given to indigenous Papua and New Guineans who 
greatly assisted Australian forces on the Kokoda Trail. They were called Fuzzy Wuzzy 
Angels because of their frizzy hair and because they helped Australian soldiers. 
What did Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels do?
• Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels carried ammunition and 
supplies to Australian military forces.  Their 
loads were about 40 kilograms. Fuzzy Wuzzy 
Angels also often helped Australian soldiers 
carry their heavy packs.
• Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels carried wounded 
Australian soldiers on stretchers along the 
Kokoda Trail over very rough ground to try to 
get medical help. 
• Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels knew a lot about the 
local landscape and gave Australians valuable 
information. They also worked as scouts 
because they knew the Papua New Guinea 
landscape so well.
1	 Who are the Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels?
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
2	 What were three things the Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels did?
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
3	 What does the word volunteered mean?
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
4	 Was the treatment of Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels always fair? Explain your answer.
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
Treatment of  
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels
Many more Australians would 
have died without the help of 
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels but they 
were not always treated well. At 
first they had volunteered but 
authorities made it very difficult 
for them to leave the Australian 
army. They were not paid equal 
rates and there were times when 
they were not given enough food.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
29
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Thai–Burma railway
Background
The Thai–Burma railway was built because the 
Japanese wanted to move their troops and supplies 
to Burma (now Myanmar) without the threat of 
Allied submarine attacks. Asian workers and POWs 
were forced to work on this railway. The conditions 
they worked under were shocking. International 
conventions governing the treatment of prisoners 
were ignored. Starvation, beatings and diseases led 
to the deaths of thousands of people. The railway 
became known as ‘the railway of death.’
Starter activity
Brainstorm why transport is important, especially 
during wartime. Ask students why, during war years, 
railways could be considered a safer method of 
transport than shipping. Record students’ ideas. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Railway of death’, explains 
why the Japanese wanted the railway built. It also 
describes who worked on it and the brutal conditions 
workers endured. Note that students will use the 
terms in bold to complete a definition exercise on the 
following Activity sheet. You could also discuss the 
meanings of these terms as you read the information 
with the students. Afterwards, you could revisit the 
discussion from the Starter activity and talk about how 
the information on this Resource sheet affects the 
students’ ideas.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Learning about 
words’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘Railway of death’. Students will locate the words 
in bold on the Resource sheet and match them to their 
definitions. Students will also read about adjectives 
and complete a simple adjective exercise. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘A primary source – Australian 
POWs’, asks students to respond to a photo of 
prisoners laying track on the Thai–Burma railway. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Time capsule’, explains what a 
time capsule is and provides examples of items that 
could be placed in a time capsule. Students are asked 
to imagine being a POW working on the railway, and 
choose items that could be put inside a time capsule. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘A letter from a prisoner’, asks 
students to complete a letter from a POW who was 
working on the Thai–Burma railway, to his wife at 
home.
Extension ideas
• Many Australian POWs working on the Thai–Burma 
railway were captured after the fall of Singapore. 
	
Challenge students to use the Internet to find out:
	
– the date of the fall of Singapore
	
– what damage this event caused to Allied forces
	
– two other interesting facts about this event.
	
These websites will be useful:
	
www.ww2australia.gov.au/japadvance/ 
singapore.html 
	
www.historylearningsite.co.uk/ 
fall_of_singapore.htm

• To learn about the construction of the  
Thai–Burma railway

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
30
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – The Thai–Burma railway
Railway of death
The Japanese invaded Burma (now 
Myanmar) in 1942. They decided to  
build a railway between Thailand 
and Burma to make it easier to move 
troops and supplies. Using a railway 
was safer than shipping by sea, due 
to the possibility of attack from Allied 
submarines.  
The Thai–Burma railway was built 
between 1942 and 1945. It was 
approximately 415 kilometres long.
The people who constructed 
the railway worked under terrible 
conditions. It became known as ‘the 
railway of death’.
Diseases
Workers suffered from  many 
severe diseases, including beriberi, 
dysentery, cholera and malaria. 
They also suffered from ulcers and 
dehydration.
Working conditions
Workers were treated as slaves. POWs were 
forced to walk over 300 kilometres just to 
reach the railway site. POWs who couldn’t 
walk that distance were shot or left to die in 
the jungle. Food was inadequate and often 
rotten. Clothing was scarce. Men usually 
had no shoes and worked with no shirts. The 
weather was humid and workers had to cope 
with monsoonal rains.
Workers had to carry heavy loads and were 
given little time to rest. They were often 
beaten. Even sick people were forced to work.
Who worked on it? 
Thousands of Asian labourers and 
Allied prisoners of war (POWs) 
were forced to work on this 
railway. Many of the POWs had 
been captured in Singapore. Over 
2 600 Australian POWs died there.
Thailand
Burma
Bangkok
kilometres
0     20     40     60     80    100

Learning about words
+ Read the Resource sheet, ‘Railway of death’. 
1	 The words in the left column are shown in bold on the Resource sheet.  
Find each one on the Resource sheet.  
Then draw lines to match each word to its meaning in the right column. 
• approximately
• constructed
• captured 
• forced
• inadequate
• rotten
• scarce
• humid
• cope
• monsoonal
An adjective is a describing word. Adjectives describe nouns.  
Here are some examples: blue, big, horrible, lovely, kind.
2	 In each sentence below there are two adjectives (in italics) that describe a noun 
(underlined). Remember, a noun is a naming word.  
Circle the correct adjective in each sentence.
a)	 Even sick / happy people were forced to work on the Thai–Burma railway.
b)	Workers were made to carry light /heavy loads.
c)	 Sunny / humid weather didn’t help the POWs.
d)	Workers had enough / inadequate food.
e)	 Beriberi, cholera and malaria are mild / severe diseases.
f)	 The Thai–Burma railway was tall / long. 
Hint: When we read, 
we come across new 
words. Sometimes 
you can work out the 
meaning from reading 
the whole sentence. 
Other times you 
might need to use a 
dictionary.

A letter from a prisoner
+ Imagine you are a prisoner of war, 
working on the Thai–Burma railway. 
Complete this letter to your wife. You 
could tell her about conditions there, 
and about the things in Australia you 
really miss.
Dear Emily,
I hope this letter gets to you safely. I know that our letters are censored and that 
a lot of them aren’t even sent. Still, I think it’s worth a try. Darling, I miss you so 
much and want you to know that I’m still alive.  I was so happy to receive your 
letter. Some of the guys here are angry that the Japanese won’t let their families 
write more than 25 words but I don’t care. Just hearing from you was great.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
35
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Three significant Australians
Background
Nancy Wake, Charles Mene and Sir Edward ‘Weary’ 
Dunlop were three Australians who made significant 
contributions to the war effort. 
	
The rebellious Nancy Wake was a key operator 
in the French Resistance movement. Wake inspired 
thousands and often risked her own life to help POWs 
and wounded Allied air personnel escape from the 
Nazis. 
	
Mene, an Indigenous soldier from the Torres Strait, 
served all the way through WWII, and on into the 
Korean War. 
	
Dunlop, an officer and a surgeon, protected and 
provided medical assistance to Australian POWs on 
a daily basis. This assistance was given despite the 
extremely harsh conditions he, and others, endured.
Starter activity
Brainstorm what it would be like being a doctor in a 
POW camp. Write students’ ideas on the board and 
ask them to identify the most significant difficulties 
they think a doctor would encounter. For example, a 
doctor might have had to amputate a leg and do his 
or her best to clean wounds with very limited medical 
supplies.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Nancy Wake’, provides information 
on Wake’s life and her role in the French Resistance. It 
also defines the French Resistance. A primary source in 
the form of a photo is also provided.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Recalling 
information’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Nancy Wake’. Students will answer 
questions about Wake and construct a sentence about 
to explain what courageous means. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Charles Mene’, provides 
background information on Mene’s role in WWII and 
raises the issue of differences in pay for Indigenous 
and non-Indigenous soldiers. You could work with 
students to locate the places mentioned on a world 
map. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop’, 
provides background information on Dunlop’s role 
as a POW surgeon, first in Changi and then on the 
Thai–Burma railway. You could show the students the 
photo of Australian POWs working on the Thai–Burma 
railway on the Activity sheet on page 32, and have 
them discuss what it tells them about the health of the 
POWs and their work conditions. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Thinking about 
Charles Mene and Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop’, students 
will need to refer to the two previous Resource sheets. 
Students will complete a definition exercise and 
comprehension questions. 
Extension ideas
• Students could imagine they are interviewing 
Nancy Wake, Charles Mene or Sir Edward ‘Weary’ 
Dunlop. Have them write five interview questions. 
Students could then use the Internet to try to find 
the answers to their questions. 
• Students could write a short report about Australia’s 
role in the Middle East Campaign in WWII. The 
following website would be useful.
	
www.anzacday.org.au/history/ww2/overview/ 
ww2-03.html
 
Objectives
• To learn about Charles Mene
• To learn about Sir Edward Weary Dunlop
• To learn about Nancy Wake
• To study a primary source document
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of conditions on 
the construction of the Thai–Burma railway would 
be useful.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Nancy Wake 
Nancy Wake moved from New Zealand to 
Australia when she was a toddler. She grew up in 
Sydney and left home at 16. When she was in her 
early twenties, Nancy left Australia for Paris where 
she worked as a journalist. 
In 1933, Nancy visited Vienna and saw how 
the Nazi Party treated Jews. Disgusted by this 
treatment, she decided to do anything she could 
to help those persecuted by Nazis. In 1939, Nancy 
married Henri Fiocca, a wealthy French man.  
In that same year, Germany invaded Poland.  
Nancy joined the French Resistance.  
Resource sheet – Three significant Australians
What was the French Resistance?
The French Resistance was an underground 
organisation that worked against the Germans 
after they occupied parts of France. The main 
aim of the Resistance was to weaken the 
German army so that Allied forces could win. 
The Resistance provided intelligence reports 
to Allied forces and killed German soldiers. 
They also helped many wounded soldiers and 
prisoners of war escape. 
Why is Nancy Wake 
remembered?
Nancy Wake was a courageous 
woman who helped save over 
a thousand lives. She delivered 
weapons and supplies to 
resistance workers. Once she rode 
a bicycle hundreds of kilometres 
in three days to find a radio 
operator. In 2004, Nancy received 
Australia’s highest civilian honour 
– the Companion of the Order of 
Australia. She died in 2011.
1945 studio portrait of Nancy Wake. 
Courtesy, Australian War Memorial 
P00885.001
The Germans tried to catch Nancy. Once she 
was caught but released before the Gestapo 
discovered her true identity. Nancy fled to 
England and convinced the British government 
to train her as a spy. She was dropped back into 
France and worked with the Resistance in the 
French mountains. The Gestapo called Nancy ‘the 
white mouse’ because they couldn’t catch her.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012

verb (a doing word).

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Charles Mene
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders participated in WWII. Charles Mene was from a  
pearling family on Mabuiag Island.  
Although there was opposition to Indigenous 
Australians joining the Australian militia 
(Australian Army Forces), Mene managed to 
enlist on 4th September 1939, just one day 
after Prime Minister Menzies announced that 
Australia was at war with Germany. 
Mene originally served with the Wireless 
Guard on Thursday Island. Thursday Island 
became a military headquarters in WWII and 
served as a base for Australian and American 
military forces. Mene completed further 
military training in Ingleburn, near Sydney. 
In 1940 Mene was sent to the Middle East and joined 
the Syrian campaign. 
Mene survived fierce fighting as the Allies tried to 
prevent German forces from gaining control of eastern 
Mediterranean areas. Mene also fought with Allied 
forces in Tripoli, where they tried to prevent an Axis 
invasion of Egypt.
Mene then served in Papua New Guinea. He fought 
Japanese forces on the Kokoda Trail and survived 
horrific conditions – 111 men from Mene’s unit lost 
their lives. 
After Japan surrendered, Mene joined the Australian 
contingent of the British Occupation Force of Japan. 
He later served in the Korean War. 
Mene was awarded a military medal for the bravery 
and leadership he displayed.
Resource sheet – Three significant Australians
Paying Indigenous 
soldiers
When Charles Mene joined 
the militia, Indigenous 
soldiers were not paid the 
same amount of money as 
non-Indigenous soldiers. 
Mene and other Indigenous 
soldiers still chose to fight for 
their country. They showed 
other Australians that their 
contribution to defending 
Australia was just as valuable 
as the contribution of other 
soldiers. 
Queensland
Mabuiag Island
Papua New Guinea
Torres Strait
Thursday Island
0             50          100 
kilometres
Cape York 
Peninsula

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
39
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Three significant Australians
Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop
Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop was an Australian surgeon. In 1939 he joined the Australian 
Army Medical Corps. Dunlop was sent to Israel, Egypt and Greece.  He also worked at 
Tobruk and was then sent to Java, in Indonesia.
In March 1942, the hospital in Indonesia where Dunlop worked was captured by the 
Japanese. Dunlop was made a prisoner of war (POW). At first he was sent to Changi.  
Later he was sent to a prison camp in Thailand.
Conditions in the Thai camp were very harsh. The Japanese forced the POWs to work  
on the Thai–Burma railway. The prisoners were weak and didn’t have the right tools to 
build a railway.
What did Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop do?
• Dunlop constantly protected other prisoners. 
• Prisoners often suffered from diseases such as malaria and beriberi. Dunlop did his best 
to keep sick prisoners alive, but he had limited medical supplies. 
• Dunlop operated on wounded prisoners. Often, the only light he had was from  
kerosene lamps.
• As an army medical officer, Dunlop decided which prisoners were fit enough to work. 
Why is Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop remembered?
Dunlop is remembered because he was a 
respected officer, and a talented surgeon 
who showed great courage. An example 
of Dunlop’s courage was his saving of the 
life of another POW called Bill Griffiths. 
The Japanese were going to kill Griffiths 
but Dunlop stood in front of the Japanese 
bayonets and refused to move until the 
Japanese promised not to kill him.
Dunlop was knighted in 1969. Over ten 
thousand people attended his state funeral 
in 1993. 
Weary?
Sir Edward always worked extremely 
hard. The nickname ‘Weary’ comes from 
a play on words. ‘Dunlop’, Sir Edward’s 
surname, is also a brand of car tyres.
‘Tyre’ sounds like ‘tire’, meaning 
‘needing to rest’. Weary also means 
tired, or needing to rest. 
This is an example of traditional 
Australian humour.

40

   1. Wile E. Coyote sets up a pulley to lift a gigantic boulder over a valley highway in an attempt to squish the
      Roadrunner. Wile E. Coyote puts 3402 J of energy into the pulley while the pulley does 2938 J of work. Calculate
      the efficiency of the pulley.




   2. Wile E. Coyote’s previous attempt of killing the Roadrunner failed so he decided to use an inclined plane to push
      a boulder down onto the Roadrunner. The output work done by the inclined plane is 875 J and the input work is
      1285 J. Calculate the efficiency of the inclined plane.




   3. After another failed attempt, Wile E. Coyote grabs a stick to create first class lever. He inputs 445 J of work and
      the output work of the lever is 430 J. Calculate the efficiency.




   4. Wile E. Coyote tries chasing after the Roadrunner with his Acme 200 Cyclone bicycle. The output of bike is 2890 J
      of work while the input was 4122 J. Calculate the efficiency of the Acme 200 Cyclone.




   5. Wile E. Coyote wants to poison the Roadrunner by putting arsenic in some bird feed. The arsenic comes in a can
      so he must use a can opener. If Wile E. Coyote applies 34 J of work and the can opener does 27 J work then what
      is the efficiency of the can opener?




   6. In his last attempt Wile E. Coyote creates a catapult to launch a boulder. After construction, Wile E. Coyote sets
      up the catapult and waits for the Roadrunner. When the Roadrunner appears he puts 793 J of work into the
      catapult while it does 720 J of work. What is the efficiency this catapult?

searchText:
Energy Efficiency
When energy is changed some of it is always wasted.

We can measure the amount of useful energy we get by the
efficiency.

           Efficiency = useful energy output x
                            100
                      total energy input
The                                                     examples
below all show energy changes in engines. The work that they do is
their ‘useful energy out’.

Calculate their efficiencies.

1. A petrol engine takes 1000J of chemical energy and does 250J of
   work.

2. A diesel engine uses 6000J of chemical energy and does 2100J of
   work.

3. An electric motor uses 50J of electrical energy and does 40J of
   work.

4. A cyclist (a human engine) has 200J of energy and does 30J of
   work.

The following questions are harder, you will need to decide what
form the useful energy is in.

5. A rocket engine takes in 800J of chemical energy and changes
   this into 480J of kinetic energy and 320J of heat energy.

6. A jet engine gas turbine takes in 1200J of chemical energy and
   gives out 960J of kinetic, 180J of heat and 60J of sound energy.

7. A TV takes in 600J of electrical energy and gives out 300J of light,
   240J of sound and 60J of heat energy (be careful here!).

searchText:
Energy Problems
An object positioned above the ground has gravitational potential
energy, Ep. It can be calculated using the equation:
     EP = mgh
Where m is the mass of the object (kg), g is the acceleration due to
gravity (9.8m/s2 for objects near Earth) and h is the height (m).

An object that is moving has the ability to do work. The energy of
moving objects is called kinetic energy, Ek. It is calculated using
the following equation:
     EK = ½mv2                                                 Ep
Where m is the mass of the object (kg) and v is its speed (m/s).

                                                            wheng
1. Find the potential energy of a ball with a mass of 0.5kg m           h
             held at the top of a 6 metre ladder.

2. Calculate the gravitational potential energy of an 8kg rock placed
   8m above the ground.

3. A crane lifts a 10kg crate off the ground to a height of 2 m. How
   much potential energy does the crate have?

4. Tony stands o a diving board 11 metres above the surface of the
   water. If he has 6468 J of energy, what is his mass?

5. A 2.5 kg textbook is on a desk that is 70cm high. How much
   potential energy does the book have? (hint: remember to change
   cm into m)

6. Matthew has a mass of 65kg and he is standing on an observation
   deck looking over the city. If he has 159.25 kJ of energy, how
   high is the observation deck? (hint: remember to change kJ into
   J)

7. Maggie is flying a plane at a height of 9500m. Her mass is 55 kg.
     a. How much potential energy does she have in joules?
     b. How much potential energy does she have in kilojoules?

8. Tanya has potential energy of 4900J standing on a diving board.
   If her mass is 50 kg, how high is the diving board?
 9. Find the kinetic energy of a family car that has a mass of 980kg
   when travelling at a speed of 20m/s.

10. What is the kinetic energy of a 2 tonne truck travelling at a
  speed of 90km/h? (Hint: remember to change mass into kg and
  speed into m/s)

11. Calculate the kinetic energy of a 50g tennis ball travelling at
  5m/s.

12. Calculate the kinetic energy of a 156g cricket ball travelling at
  72km/h.

13. Calculate the mass of a bird flying at 10m/s with a kinetic
  energy of 50J.

14. A skateboarder has 2025J of kinetic energy. If his mass if
  50kg, at what speed is he travelling?

15. A person on a bridge drops a 3kg stone into the water 5m
  below. If the surface of the water is taken as the baseline,
  calculate:
     a. The initial gravitational potential energy of the rock. Ek
     b. Its kinetic energy just prior to striking the water.
     c. Its speed just prior to striking the water.          ½  m        v2
16.   A 2kg bag of rice sits on a shelf 2m above the floor.
      a. What is its potential energy?
      b. If the bag of rice fell, how much kinetic energy would the
         bag of rice have gained by the time it reaches the ground?
      c. What would be the velocity of the bag of rice when it hits
         the ground?

17. A helicopter is hovering 200m off the ground when a loose
  object from inside the cabin falls out. Assuming the initial
  velocity of the object while in the cabin is 0m/s and ignoring air
  resistance, calculate the velocity of the object just before it hits
  the ground.

18. In archery, the bow can store 50J of elastic potential energy. If
  all of this is converted to the kinetic energy of the 0.25kg arrow,

searchText:
A cup with a hole in it will lose water, but not if it is in free fall.
HOW TO DO IT
This activity should be done outside.
1  Fill a polystyrene cup with water. Use a pen to put a hole
near the bottom of the cup. (The water will drain out.)
2  Place your finger over the hole and fill the cup again.
3  Hold the cup up high and let it drop to the ground. (The
water will not come out of the hole while the cup is falling.)
EXPLANATION
The force of gravity makes the water drain from the cup when it is held in the air. When the cup is falling,
both the water and the cup are accelerating at the same rate so the water is apparently weightless in
comparison to the cup.
Astronauts train for weightlessness in space by moving
around and ‘floating’ inside a diving aeroplane
(affectionately referred to as the ‘vomit comet’). The
apparent weightlessness that space shuttle astronauts
experience in space is actually caused by the same
phenomenon — the craft is continuously falling in a curved
path around the earth.
In 1944, an airman fell out of a Lancaster bomber at an
altitude of 5 km and lived.
If a bullet is fired from a gun that is horizontal, it will hit
the ground at the same time as another bullet which is
simply dropped from that height. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Does the path of an object influence the time it
takes to fall to the ground? Place two 5c coins,
touching each other, near the edge of a table in the
positions shown in the diagram. Flick coin ‘A’ with a
ruler, so it is propelled across the room, and coin ‘B’
will fall more directly to the floor (you will hear the
sound better on a wooden floor). (They will both hit
the ground at the same time because gravity acts
equally on both coins.)

When you let the key go, the padlock will fall towards the floor
but will not hit it.

4 Obtain a length of string about 1m long.

title: First Law-questions
subject: Science
searchText:
Unit: Force & Motion
Topic: Newton’s First Law - Questions
Answer all questions on a separate sheet of paper.

1.        Does the law of inertia pertain to moving objects, objects at rest or both?

                                                               both

2.        If you were in a spaceship and fired a cannonball into frictionless space, how much force would have to be exerted
          on the ball to keep it moving once it has left the spaceship?

                                                               None

3.        An elephant and a mouse both have the same weight - zero - in “gravitation-free” space. If they were moving toward
          you with the same speed, would they bump into you with the same effect? EXPLAIN!

 NO! The larger mass of the elephant means it has a larger inertia. This means it will be more difficult to change its
                                    state of motion and will therefore “run” you over.

4.        In the cabin of a jetliner that cruises at 600 km/h, a pillow drops from an overhead rack. Does a passenger walking
          up the aisle have to worry about the pillow slamming into her and knocking her over? Explain.

                NO. Since both are in the “same” relative motion, the pillow will simply fall to the floor.

5.        Many automobile passengers have suffered neck injuries when struck by cars from behind. How does Newton's law
          of inertia apply here? How do headrests help to guard against this type of injury?

When hit from behind, the car accelerates forward as does the body since it is pushed by the seat. The head however,
             unless there is a headrest, tries to “stay put.” This results in the head “snapping back”.

6.        Suppose you place a ball in the middle of a wagon, and then accelerate the wagon forward. Describe the motion of
          the ball relative to the ground?

                                                 The ball maintains its position.
          - Describe its motion relative to the wagon?

                            The ball rolls to the back of the wagon.

7.        If an elephant were chasing you, its enormous mass would be most threatening. But if
          you zigzagged, its mass would be to your advantage. Why?

 Its large mass means it has large inertia resulting in the elephant having a difficult time
                                  changing its direction.

8.        Two closed containers look the same, but one is packed with lead and the other with a few feathers. How could you
          determine which has more mass if you and the containers were orbiting in a weightless condition in outer space?

                                                           Shake them.

9.        If suddenly the force of gravity of the sun stopped acting on the planets, in what kind of path would the planets
          move?

                                                          Straight lines.

10.       A helium balloon is held by its string in a car with the windows rolled up. The car, initially at rest, accelerates
          forward. Which direction does the balloon move? Explain.

     Forward. A helium balloon floats to the top of the atmosphere. As the car accelerates forward, the air in the car
              “hangs back” due to its inertia, causing the balloon to “rise” to the “top” of the atmosphere.

   Forces are pushes or pulls.
   A force has a size and a direction, shown by an arrow.
   Symbol F
   Unit newton (N)
   Net Force is the combined effect of all forces on an object.
   Forces in the same direction add together.
   Forces in opposite directions subtract.
   Weight force is force due to gravity.    F=mxg          g = 10 m.s-2    m = mass
   Friction force opposes motion of object. Often causes heat.

     The 50 kg box needs a force of 500N to lift it against gravity (F = m x g     F = 50 x 10)

    Symbol P
    Unit watt (W)
    1 watt means 1 joule of energy transferred (work done) each second.

P is power of machine in watts

t is time taken to transfer energy, in seconds

Examples:
1.   Calculate the power output of the weightlifter above if box is lifted in 2 seconds.
     P = W/t             P = 1000 / 2 = 500 W

     F=mxg               F = 800 x 10 = 8000N
     W=Fxd               W = 8000N x 10 = 80000J
     P = W/t             P = 80000 / 20 = 4000W


Momentum
 Momentum is the tendency of objects to keep moving once they are in motion.
 Units kg.m.s-1
  momentum = m x v       m is mass, in kg         v is objects speed, in m/s (ms-1)

searchText:
Forces

Force can cause an object to change its velocity or shape.
Forces push, pull, tug, heave, squeeze, stretch, twist or press.
Forces can change:
             The shape of an object
             The movement of an object
             The speed of an object
             The direction of an object
Not all forces can be seen but the effects can be measured. Forces can
either be contact forces, where the force needs to be in contact with the object                      experiencing
the force OR non-contact forces that will act on an object from a distance without touching it.

Units of Force, Motion and Energy in Science

 Quantity                                      What is it measured in?        Symbol       Equipment used


 Force (including weight)                      Newton                         N            Spring balance

 Mass                                          kilograms                      kg           scales



 Velocity / speed                              metres per second              ms-1         Ticker timer

 Acceleration                                  metres per second per second   ms-2         Ticker timer
 (including gravitational acceleration)

 Energy (including Work)                       Joules                         J




Contact and non-contact forces




Pushes, pulls, friction and tension are contact forces. The object that causes the force touches the object it acts
upon. Non-contact forces such as electrostatic forces, magnetic forces and gravitational forces act without
contact between the object.
113 | P a g e       GZ Science Resources
 Gravity is a force, which acts between bodies even though they are not in contact

Objects create a gravitational field around them. Gravity gives objects of mass in the field a weight force.
    the bigger the object; the stronger the field
    the further away from the object, the less gravitational pull
Any other object within the field is pulled to the center of the mass:
       >accelerating
       >feeling weight
When gravitational force is acting on an object then we can say the object has weight force




Thrust force

Thrust (or applied force) requires some parts of an object (whether gas, liquid or solid) being pushed forcefully
from itself (rocket fuel from a rocket, for example). Once the rocket has left, the "thrust" is no longer present. It
also requires reaction (actual touching) of the thrust medium against the object.

Acceleration is the state of an object, due to a force applied. It is dependent on the force, and on the mass of
an object, but is not a force itself. Friction force opposes an object that is experiencing thrust force. Thrust and
friction are “paired forces” that act in opposite directions on an object.



Friction often provides opposing force acting on moving bodies


                                                   Friction is a force that opposes motion. If an object has
                                                   no motion, then there is no friction.

                                                   When friction occurs, and one surface moves against
                                                   another, the movement causes Kinetic energy to be
                                                   changed into heat energy.

                                                   Smooth surfaces create less friction than rough surfaces.
                                                   Friction that occurs between air or water and a solid body
                                                   is called resistance.

                                                   If friction and thrust forces are equal and opposite, then
                                                   they are said to be balanced.



114 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Support forces

Support forces are equal and opposite to an object experiencing weight
if the forces are balanced. Support force in air is called lift and in water is
called buoyancy.

Buoyancy is an upward support force caused by a fluid that opposes the
weight (gravitational force) of an object in the fluid, usually water. Once
the object remains at a set depth then the support force and weight force
are balanced.




Balanced and unbalanced forces




                                                                           If pairs of forces acting on an
                                                                           object are equal and opposite,
                                                                           they are said to be balanced.

Isaac Newton – Founder of classical physics
Motion

Isaac Newton was born into a farming family in
Woolsthorpe, England, in 1643. He went to the
Free Grammar School in nearby Grantham. His
school reports described him as idle and
inattentive. Isaac mostly kept his own company
and was known as a sober, silent, thinking lad.
When he did associate with others, it was nearly
always with girls. Isaac is remembered for his
strange inventions and extraordinary inclination
for mechanical works. Among these was a
windmill powered by a treadmill run by a
mouse.
Later, his mother made Isaac leave school in
order to help run the family farm. But with
support from his uncle, Isaac continued his
studies at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1661.
Newton’s aim at Cambridge was a law degree,
but soon he became involved with other topics
like algebra, optics and astronomy. Newton did
a lot of studying of other scientists and ancient
philosophers. 
To test a question about colours, he stared at the
sun with one eye until all the colours changed.
As a result, he had to shut himself up in a dark
room for several days before he could get rid of
the spots floating before his eyes.
Despite some evidence that his progress had not
been particularly good, Newton received his
bachelor’s degree in 1665. His scientific genius
suddenly emerged when the plague closed the
university in the summer of 1665 and he had to
return home to Woolsthorpe. There, in a period
of less than two years, he began revolutionary
advances in mathematics, optics, physics and
astronomy. In 1666 Newton had early versions
of his three laws of motion. Newton had also
reached the conclusion that white light is not a
single entity, as most scientists since Aristotle
had believed. When Newton passed a thin beam
of sunlight through a triangular glass prism, the
spectrum of the rainbow colours formed.
However, Newton did not publish any of his
work then.

searchText: ﻿Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy Kinetic Energy Kinetic Energy is associated with the motion of an object. It depends on the mass and velocity of the object. A bullet travelling towards a target, a javelin moving through the air and a person running all have kinetic energy. An object’s Kinetic Energy (KE) can be calculated using the formula Kinetic Energy(J) = ½ mass( kg) x velocity 2(m/s) KE = ½ mv2 Example Calculate the KE of a football which has a mass of 0.4 kg travelling at 5m/s Formula Working Answer/ Units Potential Energy Energy can be stored in a variety of ways such as in food, as stored energy for our body, in petrol as stored energy for a car, in water turning the turbines to create electrical energy or a skier at the top of a mountain has stored energy which becomes kinetic energy (for movement) An object’s Potential Energy (PE) can be calculated using the formula Potential Energy(J) = mass (kg) x gravity(9.8m/s/s) x height(m) PE = mgh Example Calculate the PE of a tennis ball which has a mass of 0.05 kg hit to a height of 8m Formula Working Answer/ Units Kinetic energy and potential energy are related. Imagine a high board diver plunging straight down into the water. At the moment immediately before she leaves the board, her potential energy will be at a maximum. At this stage the diver is stationary and has zero kinetic energy but her position, high above the pool means her potential energy is high. When the diver leaves the board her KE increases until the instant prior to entry to the water when KE is at a maximum. At this point, PE is at a minimum since her height is now reduced to zero. searchText:
Mass and weight – what is which?
Motion
15
36
© Chris Greef, Suada Bilali and Blake Education 2006
Assignments in Junior Science – Motion
Mass is defined as the amount of substance in an object. Its base unit is the kilogram (kg).
Weight is a force. It is a force that arises because of gravity. The larger an object, the stronger the gravity
force; so huge objects like stars have strong gravity, which causes things to weigh more there than on
smaller objects. Weight is measured in newtons (N). 
It is common to say ‘My weight is 50 kg’, but this is scientifically incorrect and probably arises from the
confusion between mass and weight that many people have. (A person of mass 50 kg actually has a
weight of 500 N.) We should actually say ‘My mass is 50 kg’.
We are going on an imaginary journey through the solar system. As well as food and radiation suits, we
are taking a giant triple beam balance for measuring our mass and a bathroom scale for our weight. On
earth, the giant triple beam balance shows your mass as 60 kg and the bathroom scale gives your weight
as 60 kg (although this is really 600 N!). 
Let’s fly towards the moon. At a certain point between the earth and the moon, the gravitational
forces of the earth and moon cancel each other. At that point:
a How strong is the gravitational force on us? 
(newtons) 
b What is your mass? 
(kilograms) 
c
What does the bathroom scale show your weight to be? 
(kilograms) 
d What is your weight in scientific measure? 
(newtons) 
Now let’s land on the moon and take our measuring devices with us onto the moon’s surface. The
moon’s mass is about six times smaller than the earth’s mass. This means that the moon’s gravity
is one-sixth that of the earth’s gravity, i.e. the moon’s gravity is six times smaller than the earth’s. 
a What is your mass on the moon, as measured by the giant triple beam balance? 
b What does the bathroom scale show your weight to be? 
c
What is your scientific weight? 
d If you can jump 1 metre high on e

Motion
Speed is the word we use to describe how fast an object is moving. Speed is calculated by the distance travelled 
divided by time. In science, it is measured in metres per second. The equation for speed is:
Velocity is not the same as speed. Velocity does describe how fast an object is moving, but it also describes the 
direction in which the object is moving. Therefore a change in the direction of an object is a change in velocity, 
but not necessarily a change in speed. Velocity is calculated the same way speed is, but the units are usually in 
metres per second plus direction, e.g. 30 ms–1 east.
Acceleration is the change in the velocity of a moving object, and can refer to an increase in velocity or a 
decrease (negative acceleration). The equation for acceleration is:
The units are expressed in metres per second per second or ms–2. 
Acceleration is directly related to Newton’s Law: Force = mass × acceleration.

Year 10 Energy and Change 2009



                            YEAR 10 ENERGY AND CHANGE 2009


MOTION

Everything in the universe is in a state of motion. The earth itself is filled with moving things. The earth
spins on its axis. The planets of our solar system orbit the sun. Our solar system moves through space as
part of the Milky Way Galaxy. The stars and galaxies move away from each other. It might seem
impossible to find a simple way to describe and understand the motions of all these objects. However, this
is just what physicists have done.


WHAT CAUSES MOTION ? (photos from Nardelli et al, 2004)
You are already familiar with the idea that forces are a push, pull, twist or stretch which can produce a
change in the shape, speed or direction of an object. Objects move because they have unbalanced forces on
them. Usually there is more than one force acting on an object, so the movement is a result of the combined
effect of those forces.

Arrows are often used to represent forces with the direction of the arrow showing which way the forces are
operating. The length of the arrow is used to show the size of the force i.e. the longer the arrow the bigger
the force.




                                    ▼
The arrows describing these forces on the kayaker are even in length which means that the forces are the
same size. These forces are acting in opposite directions, which means the force of the kayakers mass
(called his weight) is pushing against the force of the water which is pushing up. These forces are balanced
so he doesn’t move up or down.




  1
 Year 10 Energy and Change 2009



The lateral arrows are uneven in length which means the forces are uneven. The forward force is produced
by the kayaker pushing his paddle in the water and this is greater than the force of drag (or friction) in the
water so the kayaker moves forward in the water.
Everyday you experience forces on your body which push and pull you in a range of directions. These
forces include that of the air pushing on you; which is surprisingly high; some 100 000 N for every square
metre of body size (the average human body is approx. 0.8 m2). We call this air pressure and it is a
measure of the force exerted per square metre of body area. As the force of gravity is pulling the air
particles towards the earth’s surface then the air pressure is greatest closest to the surface and decreases as
you rise through the atmosphere. Air pressure at the surface varies depending upon the air temperature and
movements.




Similarly water particles push against your body exerting a considerable force when you are immersed
underwater. The deeper you go the more water particles pushing down on your body so the greater the
force. In fact for even 10 m of depth there is another 100 000 N pushing in on your body.

There are other forces acting on your body under the water too including the force of the diver’s mass
(weight) and the force of the water pushing up on the diver (buoyancy). The following diagram shows some
of these forces. When a diver has these forces all perfectly balanced it is called neutral buoyancy.

  2
 Year 10 Energy and Change 2009




ANOTHER APPLICATION OF FORCES IN SPORT : SURFING
Read the following passage which describes how Layne Beachley uses forces to her advantage when surfing.




  3
 Year 10 Energy and Change 2009



                                                              Surfing is like skating downhill while being
                                                              pulled uphill. The force of gravity pulls the
                                                              surfer down the wave while the drag pulls the
                                                              surfer back up the wave. Surfing is a fine
                                                              balance between the forces of gravity, buoyancy
                                                              and drag. The force of friction prevents the
                                                              surfer from slipping off the surf board. Rubbing
                                                              wax on to the deck of the board gives it a rough
                                                              surface which in turn increases the force of
                                                              friction. Friction is a force acting in the opposite
                                                              direction to that in which the object is moving.

                                                              QUESTIONS:
                                                              1.Think about another sporting example where
                                                              friction is useful. Describe the situation and
                                                              explain how friction plays a role.

Measuring Forces • Meters that measure forces usually have springs in them. The bigger the force the more the spring is squashed or stretched. • Spring balance or forcemeter or newtonmeter are often used in schools. • A spring is stretched by the pulling force and squashed by the pushing force. • The amount of force has a unit called a newton (N) • Notice that 1kg = 10N. What would 2kg be? 0.5kg? 100kg? Balanced and Unbalanced Forces • The forces acting on an object determine how that object will move. If we push on some object and the object doesn’t move, then the force we exert must be balanced by another force. • An unbalanced force will produce acceleration Newton’s First Law of Motion If the forces acting on an object are balanced, then the object will either stay still or keep moving at the same speed in the same direction. Thus a force is needed to make something speed up or slow down or change direction. Eg. In a car crash, a large force acts on the car and quickly stops the car. However, the driver will keep on moving with the same speed in the same direction until a force slows him or her down. The force is hopefully provided by a seatbelt or airbag. Without either, the driver may continue moving right through the windscreen and out of the car. Newton’s Second Law of Motion If there are unbalanced forces acting upon an object, then the object will accelerate in the direction that the net force acts. The size of the acceleration depends upon the mass of the object and size of the force. This is illustrated by the relationship F=m.a In sport, acceleration can be improved by better force from muscular contraction or reducing the weight of the object to be moved. Eg for javelin, shotput etc you can improve strength and for running you can reduce weight. Laboratory: Tug of War Acceleration due to Gravity • A free falling object has an acceleration of 9.8ms-2 (more commonly rounded to 10ms-2). If a body has an acceleration of 9.8ms­­-2, this means that after one second, the body has a velocity of 9.8ms-1‑, after 2 seconds, a velocity of 19.6ms-1 and so on. • Gravity is a force that causes the pendulum to accelerate and swing back and forth. We will use a pendulum to find the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity because the pendulum executes simple harmonic motion. The mass of an objects is the same regardless of where it is located in the universe. • The weight of an object is the force of gravity that acts on the object. The weight of an object depends on where it is located in the universe. • Weight is measured in newtons (N) because it is a force. • Weight can be calculated from Fw = m.g where g is the acceleration due to gravity and on earth, is accepted as 10Nkg-1. • The weight of an object on the moon is 1/6 that on Earth because the gravitational field strength is less. Worksheets • Some ‘quick’ problems • ESA book (y11) • 12 physics pathfinder exercises. Equilibrium • When the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. • In this case, the object is either not moving (static equilibrium) or it is moving in a straight line at constant speed (dynamic equilibrium). searchText: ﻿ Motion energy is correctly termed kinetic energy (you may remember this from last year). It is the energy something posesses if it has movement, for example a bullet has a lot of kinetic energy because it is moving very fast. This kind of energy is of great interest to athletes as it is how they will win their race! Stability is also an important aspect of sport, whether you are a javelin thrower, a gymnast or a sprinter you will want to maximise stability in a variety of positions. 1. CENTRE OF MASS The centre of mass of a sportsperson is the single point through which the whole mass of the body can be seen to act. The postion of the centre of mass can affect the balance of an athlete. Examples of the effect of the centre of mass include; gymnasts whose centre of mass is off centre at inappropriate times can lose their balance; divers with the same problem will have trouble executing a high scoring dive. Weightlifters stand with their feet apart to lower their centre of mass and give them greater stability (ASTA, 2000). ACTIVITY 1: Determining the Centre of Mass Materials: 1 Plumb-bob 1 sheet of shapes to cut out scissors, glue, poster paper The centre of mass can be determined using a plumb-bob, which consists of a piece of thread with a mass on one end. Method: 1. Cut out the model. 2. Push a pin into any point on the model and tie the plumb-bob to the pin. 3. Trace the vertical line on the model formed by the hanging thread. 4. Push the pin into another point on the model and again trace the vertical line formed by the hanging thread. 5. The point where these two lines intersect is the centre of mass. Mark it with a big X 6. Now cut out the remainder of the figures, find their centre of mass. 7. Place them in correct order to show the changes in the centre of mass of an athlete performing the long jump. 8. Glue to the paper provided and write an appropriate heading to explain your series of figures. 2. FORCES Forces are a very important part of our every day life. While we may not want to execute a triple cartwheel with a round off on our way to school we want to be able to get off the bus safely and manage walking up and down stairs and getting around in general. We experience many different forces nearly all of the time. A force is a push or a pull which one object applies to another object. The unit of force is the Newton (N). In each of these situations give an everyday example of a; force that get objects moving. Example…………………………. force that stops moving objects . Example…………………………. force that changes the direction in which an object is moving. Example…………………………. force that stretches an object. Example…………………………. force that might squash, bend, twist or turn objects. Example…………………………. force that prevents movement of objects by balancing other forces acting on the same object. Example…………………………. Some forces act at a distance e.g. gravity (weight), electric forces, magnetic forces. Some forces act on contact e.g. impact (collision) forces, elastic forces, friction, muscular forces.  Some important forces that we will look at are WEIGHT and FRICTION. Mass is the amount of matter in an object (and has the unit of kg). Weight is a measure of the force of gravity on an object (and has the unit of N). Thus, mass of an object remains constant no matter where the object is. However, the weight of an object varies, depending on the force of gravity being exerted on the object. Weight and mass are related according to the equation weight = mass x "g" where "g" is the force of gravity. If weight has the unit of N and mass the unit of kg then "g" will have the unit of N/kg (Newtons per kilogram). On earth "g" has the value of approximately 9.8 Nkg. Examples 1. a) What is the weight of an apple which has a mass of 0.25 kg? b) What is the weight of a 500 g object? 2. Gravity is 2 N/kg on the moon. a) What would be the weight of a 6 kg object on the moon? If an object is resting ("sitting") on a table, the object exerts a force on the table. This force Fw is equal to the weight of the object. Examples 1. A book of weight 10 N is resting on a table. What force does the book exert on the table? 2. A box of mass 40 kg is placed on the floor. What force does the box exert on the floor? ACTIVITY 2: Mass and Weight. Friction is a force which arises whenever one object moves, or tries to move, over another. Friction always acts in the direction opposite to the direction of the motion. Factors that affect friction are - the nature of the two surfaces in contact - lubrication between the two surfaces - the size of the force pushing the two surfaces together. searchText: ﻿NEWTON’S SECOND LAW OF MOTION What does this mean? What variables govern the acceleration of the following bodies? NEWTON’S SECOND LAW can be stated as: a = _F_ m where a = acceleration in msֿ² F = total force on the object (Newtons) m= mass of the object (kg) Can also be stated as F = m a Example: A space shuttle has a mass of 2.2 million kilograms, of which 86% is the mass of fuel, most of which is burnt during the launch. There are two forces acting on the space shuttle; downward pull of gravity, at 22 million Newtons, and the upward thrust resulting from the burning of fuel which is about 29 million Newtons. The forces acting on the space shuttle are not balanced. The total force acting on the space shuttle is 7 million Newtons upwards. Newton’s second law of motion can be used to estimate the acceleration of the space shuttle at blast off: a = _F_ m = 7 000 000 N upwards 2 200 000 kg = 3.2 msֿ² The space shuttle is gaining speed at the rate of only 3.2 msֿ² or 11.5 km/h each second. Small acceleration at blast off is not a problem because as the fuel is burnt, the mass of the space shuttle gets smaller. As this happens the acceleration gradually increases, and the space shuttle gains more speed quickly. Practice Exercises 1. What force will accelerate an 18 kg object at 3 msֿ²? 2. Find the mass of a block if a 65 Newton force accelerates it at 2.5 msֿ². 3. An 8000 N force acts on a 125 kg vehicle. What acceleration is produced? 4. A 150 kg motorcycle is retarded at 2.5 msֿ². Find the force that is required. 5. What acceleration would be given to a 950 kg car by a 222.6 N retarding force. 6. A 10 kg sled is pulled across the snow so that the total force acting on it is 12 N. What is the size of the average acceleration of the sled? 7. What total force would cause a 1.5 kg glass salad bowl to accelerate across a table at 0.30 msֿ²? 8. Two identical toy carts, A and B, each with a mass of 1.0 kg, are pushed across a smooth, level table top with same force. One of them contains a heavy brick. Cart A accelerates more rapidly than Cart B. a. Which toy cart contains the brick? How do you know? b. If the acceleration of the cart A is 2.0 msֿ², what is the total force acting on each cart? c. If the acceleration of cart B is 0.5 msֿ², what is the mass of the brick?

searchText: Newton ’s Laws of Motion Activities 1 st Law of Motion What is Newton ’s first law of motion? Activity 1: Lazy Coins You will need: A piece of A4 paper, five 2 0c coins What to do: Place the paper on a desk so that about 5cm of the short side hangs over the edge. Place a 2 0c coin on the opposit e end of the paper. Hold the end of the paper hanging over the edge of the desk and pull it v ery quickly. If you do this fa st enough, the coin should remain unmoved. Repeat the steps above, but with two coins stacked on top of each other. Keep going to see how many coins you can do this with. Repeat this activity, but pulling t h e paper slowly rather than quickly. Questions: What force acted between the paper and the coins as the paper slid beneath the coins? Why can you leave the coins unmoved when you pull the paper out quickly? Why could you not leave the coins unmoved when the pap e r was pulled out slowly? Activity 2 : Tricky Tricks You will need: A clothes peg, a small square of cardboard, a 10c coin. What to do: Stand the peg on one end. Place the cardboard on top of the peg. Place the coin on top of the cardboard. Holding the peg at the base, try to flick the cardboard out from under the coin, keeping the coin balanced on top of the peg. For a challenge, try to do this without holding the peg still. Questions: Explain why the coin can remain on top of the peg using Newton’s first law. Activity 3 : Crazy Coins You will need: Five coins , all the same size What to do: Place one coin on the desk. Put another coin about 10 cm in front of the first coin . Flick the second coin into the first. Describe w hat happens . Stack two coins on top of each other. Place another coin 10 cm in front of the stack. Flick the coin into the stack. Describe w hat happens . Repeat with a stack of three coins and four coins . Questions: What did you observe about the coins moved by the flicked coin ? Explain your observations in terms of Newton ’s 1 st Law. As a challenge, try flicking a stack of two coins into a stack of three or four. Activity 4 : Crash Test Dummies You will need: A toy car, plasticine, two books (like a dictionary), a piece of cardboard, baby powder What to do: Use the cardboard and a book to make a slope. Make a small person from the plasticine. Dust your person with baby powder so it loses some of its stickiness. Sit your person on top of the car. Gently push the car down the slope. Note where the car comes to a stop. Put the other book between the bottom of the ramp and where the car stops. Roll the car down the slope again. Questions: What happened to the plasticine person when the car hit the book? Explain your observations in terms of Newton’s 1 st Law. 2 nd Law of Motion What is Newton ’s second law of motion? Activity 1: Creating Craters You will need: Sand, large flat container, two rocks of different sizes What to do: Fill the container with sand and smooth the surface. Drop the two rocks from the same height into the sand. Carefully remove the rocks and c ompare the diameter of the crater s created. Questions: Which rock made the bigger crater? Explain your observations in terms of Newton ’s second law. Activity 2: Newton ’s Race You will need: Toy cars, plastic cup, sticky tape , wooden board, piece of cardboard, six 50g masses, masking tape, two bricks, coloured dots, a metre ruler What to do: Stick the plastic cup to the roof of the toy car with sticky tape . Stack the bric ks on the end of a row of desks and make a slope with the wooden board . Put the cardboard on top of the wooden board and tape the end to the desk. Run your car down the slope three times, placing a sticky dot where it stops each time. Measure the distances from the base of the slope to each of the dots. Record your measurements in the table below. Add two masses to your cup, and then run the car dow n the slope three more times . Measure and record. Repeat the process with 4 and 6 masses. Mass Added Distance 1 Distance 2 Distance 3 Average 0 g 100 g 200 g 300 g Results: Questions : How does increasing the mass affect the force (in this case the distance the car rolls) of objects in motion? Explain your answer using the data you have collected. What would happen i f you added 8 masses to the car? Predict how far it would roll. Explain the results of your experiment in terms of Newton ’s second law. Activity 3: Mass vs Acceleration You will need: Motion trolley, set of 10 slotted masses, pulley and clamp, string, 3 bricks, stopwatch, ruler What to do: Clamp the pulley onto the edge of a desk. Tie one end of the string onto the trolley. Tie the other end of the string onto the slotted masses. Thread the string over the pulley. Pull the trolley back and release it to check it runs freely. Mark a spot on the desk where you will release the trolley from each time. Measure the distance from this spot to the pulley. Pull the trolley back to the marked spot. Release the trolley and measure the time it takes to reach the pulley. Record the time below. Repeat twice more and calculate an average. Add one brick to the trolley and repeat the process. Continue until you have results for two and three bricks. Results: Distance: _______________ Number of Bricks Time of Trial 1 Time of Trial 2 Time of Trial 3 Average Time Acceleration 0 1 2 3 Questions: Calculate the acceleration of the trolley for each mass using the formula a = 2d where d = the distance travelled t 2 t = the average time What happened to the acceleration of the trolley as you increased the mass? Explain your observation in terms of Newton ’s second law. 3 rd Law of Motion What is Newton ’s third law of motion? Activity 1: Fun with Balloons You will need: Balloon, flexible straw, sticky tape, pencil with an eraser on the end , pin What to do: Attach the balloon to the end of the straw which is furthest away from the bend. Push the pin straight through the straw about ha lf way between the ball o on and the bend in the straw. Push the end of the pin into the eraser on the pencil. Blow up the balloon, but le ave the straw straight. Releas e the air in the balloon. What happens? Blow up the balloon and bend the straw to a 90 ⁰ an gle before allowing the air to e s cape. What happens? Blow up the balloon again and bend the straw to a 45 ⁰ angle before allowing the air to escape. What happens? Remove the pin from th e straw and blow up the balloon. Release the straw. What happens? Questions: What did you notice about the direction of the air flow and the direction of the balloon? Explain your observation in terms of Newton ’s third law. Activity 2: Film Canister Rocket You will need: Film canister, water, alka -seltzer tablet What to do: Half fill the film canister with water. Break an alka -seltzer tablet in half. Drop half of the alka -seltzer tablet into the water in the film canister. Place the lid firmly on the film canister. Turn it upside down so that it is sitting on the lid of the film canister and place in an open area. Questions Describe what happens to the film canister. Draw an action-reaction diagram to describe what is happening in your canister. Explain what is happening using Newton’s third law. Describe a real life example where you have seen Newton’s third law in action.

yA-m Reaction time

Science understanding Founparion | STANDARD | ADVANCED

Reflex actions happen very fast, compared with other actions by the body in response to danger.

You are travelling very quickly on your skateboard or bike and suddenly see someone walk in front
of you. You have to make judgements about how far away the person is, what actions you can take

to avoid them, which action is the best in the situation, and whether you have the time and skills to
carry it out. You then have to follow through on your decision.

The time it takes for you to do all these things is your reaction time.

Experiments show that when you are attentive you have a reaction time of between 0.2 and
1.5 seconds. However, police estimates show that the average driver takes up to one second to
react in an emergency.

Once you have reacted, you have to bring your skateboard or bike to a stop. The distance you

travel before stopping is the reaction distance. This distance depends on the speed at which you are
travelling and your reaction time.

To calculate reaction distance:
