searchText: Speed and Acceleration using a Ticker Timer coil magnet ticker tape power input ( a.c .) vibrating bar carbon paper disc A ticker timer is a piece of equipment which can be used to measure speed and acceleration. The ticker timer has a bar which vibrates at a known frequency of 50 times per second. A piece of ticker tape is passed under the bar and a carbon paper disc is threaded between the bar and the ticker tape. There is a small nodule at the end of the bar which produces a dot each time it hits the tape. The time between each dot is 1/50 th of a second, or 0.02 seconds. By measuring the distance between 6 dots (5 spaces) and dividing by the time taken (0.02 x 5 = 0.1 sec) the average speed can be calculated. Look at the ticker tape below. Use the following method to calculate the speed the tape was moving. Draw a line through a dot near the left. Draw a second line through the fifth dot after that. Measure the distance between the dots in cm. Calculate the speed in cm per second by dividing by 0.1 seconds (the time it takes to make 5 dots) Try the two examples below To calculate acceleration using a ticker timer, you must calculate the average speed of multiple intervals on your ticker tape. Look at the ticker tape below. Speed = Change in speed = Calculate the acceleration of this ticker tape by Putting a line through the first dot. Put a line through every fifth dot after that. Use the method on the previous page to find the average speed between the first two lines. Repeat the process for the other 3 intervals to get the average speed for each interval. Find the change in speed between each interval. The acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time between the intervals, in this case 0.1 seconds. A similar distinction (exist / exists) between distance and displacement. Distance (are / is) about

searchText: 1586865 4348480 Name: Class: Mark: /10 % 40000 20000 Name: Class: Mark: /10 % 3714750 371475 0 0 YEAR 10 SCIENCE ARC TRANSITION ASSESSMENT SIX THE SCIENCE OF AIRBAGS -2771775 2382520 0 0 PART ONE: Air Bag Study Guide Research airbags and complete the following questions. 1. What is the intended purpose of an air bag? 2. W hat is a major concern with air bags? 3. What is being done to make air bags safer? 4. W hat are three rules for drivers of cars with passenger-side air bags? 1. 2. 3. 5. What gas fills up the air bag? 6. Explain how an air bag works. 7. How long does it take for the air bag to inflate? PART TWO: It's a Crash Test, Dummy The engineers who design air bags are able to determine the exact quantity of chemicals needed to inflate the air bag to the proper volume, and in the correct amount of time. If the air bag is under inflated or inflates too quickly, the passenger will still be injured by the steering wheel. If the air bag over inflates or inflates too slowly, the passenger will hit the inflating airbag and be injured. It is critical to get just the right amount of gas in the air bag. During th is exploration, you will attempt to find the amount of sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) required to react with 25 ml of acetic acid (vinegar) so that the bag is inflated, with no appreciable quantity of either reactant left. This will allow you to develop some idea of a limiting reactant. (Depending on the atmospheric pressure, the amount of baking soda required to fully inflate the bag should be between 1.5 and 3.0 grams.) In this reaction, acetic acid combines with sodium bicarbonate to form water, carbon dioxide, and sodium acetate. The chemical equation for this reaction is: HC 2 H 3 O 2 + NaHCO 3 ---> H 2 O + CO 2 + NaC 2 H 3 O 2 The carbon dioxide is the gas that fills the bag, and the sodium acetate will be dissolved in the water. It is important to realize that this is not exactly how an air bag works, but is a good analogy that allows you to simulate the inflation of a protective device in the classroom. Be prepared for some messes with the egg drop test. It is recommended that a plastic sheet be placed under the "drop zone" to assist in cleaning up. It is important to find a container for the egg drop that is the right size; three-pound butter tubs or small shoe boxes work well. Also be sure to wash your hands well after handling raw eggs. It’s a Crash Test, Dummy Introduction In a real automobile safety restraint system, the air bag is a large plastic bag of about 65.0 L which fills with nitrogen as soon as a sensor tells it that the car’s forward momentum has been drastically lowered. The nitrogen is produced by the rapid decomposition of sodium azide (NaN3), which produces nitrogen gas (N2). In this lab, we will create our own air bag technology utilizing sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and acetic acid (vinegar). Your task is to find the correct amounts of sodium bicarbonate and acetic acid to use to create the right amount of gas (carbon dioxide) to fill the bag. If done correctly, your bag should fill up, but not pop open. There also should not be any sodium bicarbonate or acetic acid left in the bag. Part 1 Procedure : Before starting, look at the data table in which you will record the amount of acid, the amount of sodium bicarbonate, a description of how the bag inflated, and whether there was acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left over. 1. To keep it simple, you are always going to have the same amount of acetic acid in the bag: 25 ml. Add 25 ml of acid to the bag. 2. Then measure 0.5 grams of sodium bicarbonate and record it in the data table. Place the sodium bicarbonate in a small piece of tissue. 3. Drop the sodium bicarbonate wrapped in tissue into the bag. Flatten the bag to remove the air and seal the bag as quickly as possible. As soon as the acetic acid soaks through the tissue, the chemicals will begin to react and bubble; the gas that is produced is carbon dioxide (CO 2 ). The bag should begin to inflate. 4. When the bubbling stops, mix the ingredients around to be sure that the reaction is complete. 5. Then test how inflated the bag is by pinching it. Write a description in the data table. 6. If all of the sodium bicarbonate seems to be gone, open the bag and add a small amount of sodium bicarbonate to see if more bubbles form. If they do, then there was still some acetic acid left in the bag. If not, then all of the acetic acid reacted. Make a note in the data table if there was acetic acid left in the bag. 7. Repeat this process by increasing the amount of sodium bicarbonate by 0.5 grams until all of the acetic acid is used up, indicated by the presence of sodium bicarbonate in the bag (because there was no acetic acid left to react with it). DATA TABLE Part 2 Now you will put this knowledge to the test: a crash test. You will design and build a “vehicle” for your crash test dummy, a raw egg. The goal here is to build your vehicle so that it will protect the egg from breaking, even when dropped from a height of 2 meters. The only materials you can use are: a container for the egg (e.g., a small cardboard box or large butter tub) two plastic bags acetic acid sodium bicarbonate tape a graduated cylinder a balance a meter stick Procedure : Follow the steps below using the ratio of sodium bicarbonate to acetic acid that inflated the bag, with no acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left over. (You wouldn’t want acid in your air bag, would you?) 1. Inflate one or both bags, whichever you think would work best. 2. Place the inflated bag(s) and the egg in the container. 3. Drop from 2 meters. 4. Check your passenger. Did it survive the crash? Analysis and Conclusions : 1. How much sodium bicarbonate had been added when there appeared to be no acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left after the reaction? 2. Did this amount of sodium bicarbonate (when there was no acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left) inflate the bag fully? title: Velocity
subject: Science
searchText: Velocity Speed is the distance and object travels in a set amount of time. Velocity and speed are very similar ideas, but velocity is a vector , and speed is not. Suppose we knew that someone was driving at thirty-five kilometres an hour (35 km/hr), but the direction wasn't given. How would you draw an arrow to represent a vector? You can't know how to draw the vector if you only have one value (either amount or direction). In this example, you were never told about the direction. Physicists would say that the speed is thirty-five kilometres an hour (35 km/hr), but the velocity is unknown. On the other hand, if you're moving at 35 km/hr in a northern direction, then you would have an arrow pointing north with a length of 35. Physicists would say that the velocity is 35 km/hr north. Velocity is the rate of motion in a specific direction . I'm going that-a-way at 30 kilometers per hour. My velocity is 30 kilometers per hour that-a-way. Average speed is described as a measure of distance divided by time. Velocity can be constant, or it can change (acceleration). Speed with a direction is velocity . Remember vectors? You will use a lot of vectors when you work with velocity. Our real world example of navigation on the ocean used velocity for every vector. Velocity is a vector measurement because it has an amount and a direction. Speed is only an amount (a scalar). Speed doesn't tell the whole story to a physicist. Think of it another way. If I tell you I'm driving north and ask you how long until we get to the city. You can't know the answer since you don't know my speed. You need both values. Acceleration is the rate at which an objec t changes its speed or velocity . Suppose you are riding your bike. You start out going very slowly, hardly pedalling at all. Now you begin to pedal as hard as you can, to speed up - you are accelerating. Now that you are going at a normal speed, you stop pedalling so hard, and just pedal normally. You're still going, but you're not getting any faster, just going along at your normal speed. You're not accelerating anymore. If you stop pedalling now, friction will work on your bike tires (and you'll have friction from the air , too), and you'll soon start to go slower. That's negative acceleration, or deceleration. You're still going, but you are slowing down. One important cause of acceleration is gravity . Suppose you dive off a cliff or a high diving board. You will start off falling slowly, but as gravity pulls on you, you will speed up (accelerate) until you are going very fast. The acceleration of Earth's gravity will speed you up at about 9.8 meters per second per second (9.8 m/s 2 , or 9.8 meters per second squared ). That means that for every second you fall, you'll be going 9.8 meters/second faster. Standing on the cliff before you jump, you're going zero meters/second. One second after you jump, you'll be going 9.8 meters/second. Two seconds after you jump, you'll be going 19.6 meters/second. Three seconds after you jump, you'll be going 29.4 meters/second. Key words Word Meaning Average speed The distance an object travels in a set amount of ___________. Velocity Acceleration What causes acceleration on a bicycle? What causes deceleration (negative acceleration) on a slowing bicycle? What causes the acceleration of a falling ball? What causes deceleration (negative acceleration) on a slowing ball ? A typical traffic accident
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-12
It was a Friday evening when the fatal accident
occurred. Andy Allen was an Agricultural
Chemicals salesman who spent a lot of his
work
time
travelling
throughout
the
countryside visiting farmers with samples of his
firm’s product. His job was to persuade farmers
to
buy
his
company’s
drenches,
feed
supplements and other products. His car was a
recent model and he appreciated its comfort as
he spent a lot of his day sitting in it as he
travelled from farm to farm.
Andy had been away from home the whole week. He was tired and looking forward to getting home
to spend the weekend with his wife and young daughter. It had not been a good week. The farmers
were not keen to spend money trying new products and, on top of that, he never slept well in strange
motels. As he was driving towards home, he was thinking about what he could do next week to try
to improve his sales figures because his boss had been hassling him about it.
The road he was travelling on was a major one between two large towns. The road surface was quite
new and Andy was making good time. He had only about another 100 kilometres to go, so estimated
that he would be home in about another hour. He decided to ring his wife on his mobile phone to
let her know the time he expected to be home. With annoyance and impatience he found that he was
catching up to a large slow truck on the hills. As well as that, it had just started to drizzle, so he had
to put his windscreen wipers on.
Belinda Brown was on her way home on the same road, but travelling in the opposite direction. She
was thankful that it was Friday. She worked in the local solicitor’s office in the large town that she
had just left behind. She lived with her husband and four-year-old son on a small property about
20 kilometres out of town. It was 6.30 pm, and just starting to get dark. Jason, having been picked up
from childcare, was whining from the back seat, as he was tired and hungry.

While compulsory seat belts have had a big effect on reducing the road toll, it was felt that even more
could be done. Over recent years two new technologies have been developed to give additional
protection to people who find themselves involved in a road accident. What was needed was for the
body to be cushioned so that it could come to rest a little more slowly.
An air bag inflates in only a fraction of a second so that a person moving forward into their seat belt
is cushioned before their head can reach the hard obstructions in front of them.
The other new feature that most new cars now have is what is called a ‘crumple
zone’. This means that during a collision, the front part of the car is designed so
it will slowly crumple up, taking much of the force of the collision.
The passengers are held safely in a stronger compartment
that stays intact but will come to rest more slowly as the
front of the car takes much of the force.

A basketball can be used to propel a tennis ball.

searchText:
Braking distances
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-11
Friction
When brakes are applied, they rely on the grip of the
tyres on the road and the grip of the brake pads on the
tyres to bring the vehicle to a stop. Another word for
grip is friction, which is a force that resists movement.
Friction depends on the roughness of the two surfaces
that are in contact. The rougher the surfaces, the greater
the friction or grip.
Besides friction, two other factors that affect a car’s
ability to brake are its mass and speed. Generally, the
heavier a vehicle is, the more force that is needed to
bring it to a stop, and usually the longer it will take for
this to occur.
This can easily be understood if you
imagine a large truck, a medium car, a
small car and a motorcycle all travelling at
exactly the same speed. If they all have to
stop suddenly, it will take a much greater
force to stop the large truck than the
smaller vehicles. Now if the same force is
used, then it will take a much longer
distance to stop the truck than a car or
motorcycle.
Similarly, if two identical vehicles are travelling at different speeds, one at 20 km/h, the other at
60 km/h, then it is easy to understand that the faster car will take longer, or need a greater braking
force, to bring it to a stop.
This property, combining speed and mass, is called momentum.
Momentum = mass × speed
In most cases the exact mass of a car is not known. It has been found by testing, that an average
family sized car with good brakes, travelling on a dry road, will be able to reduce its speed by 7 m/s
to 8 m/s every second. This means that a car travelling at 60 km/h will take just over two seconds
to stop, after the brakes are applied.
Calculating braking distance
To calculate the braking distance, remember that:
distance = average speed × time
To calculate the average speed, find the mean of the initial speed and the final speed (zero).
average speed =
initial speed + final speed

searchText:
DNA profiling
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-9
This is probably the most important discovery for use in forensic science since the development of
fingerprinting over a hundred years ago. While blood grouping can positively exclude a suspect, it
can only give a probability as to guilt. DNA profiling can actually prove a
person’s identity, except in the case of identical twins. No wonder it has been
said to have revolutionised crime solving.
It was in September 1984 at Leicester University, England, that Professor Alec
Jeffreys stumbled across his exciting discovery. He was working on parts of DNA
where there was a sequence of bases that varied greatly in unrelated individuals.
He and his team found a way in which these sequences could be made visible
as X-ray lines that looked a little like a bar code. These ‘bar codes’ give a unique
pattern for every person, hence the original term of ‘genetic fingerprinting’.
How a DNA profile was produced

The reason why a person keeps moving forward in a collision is the property of inertia. It means that
a body will continue moving in the direction it was going, or will remain at rest, unless it is acted on
by a force. This is also called Newton’s First Law of Motion.
This property is clearly seen if you are standing up
in a stationary bus. If the bus takes off suddenly,
your feet, which are attached to the bus floor, will
move forward with the bus because this force is
acting on your feet. However, the rest of your
body will try to remain behind where you were
and you feel as if you are falling backwards.
Now if the bus stops suddenly, again your feet,
which are in contact with the bus floor will stop,
but the rest of your body will attempt to continue
moving forward at the same speed, until your
legs, which are attached to your feet, pull your
body back. This means that you feel as if you are
falling forwards.

2
S P E E D
A N D

2-9
Factors affecting reaction time
In unexpected situations, such as the car in
front braking suddenly or a child or animal
running out onto the road, it takes some time
for the driver to react to the danger. The
situation must first be observed, then it takes a
certain amount of time for the message to reach
the brain, where it is processed, and then
another message is sent to the muscles of the
leg to contract and push on the brake.
The time from when the situation first occurred, up to the time the brakes were applied, is called the
reaction time. This time can be affected by a number of things, including tiredness and hence the
alertness of the driver, being under the influence of alcohol or other drugs, or being distracted by
things either inside the vehicle or outside it.
Calculating reaction distance
By rearranging the formula for calculating speed (v = ), the distance travelled can be calculated if
the speed is known.
ie
reaction distance = time taken to react × average speed
It has been measured under test conditions, that the average reaction time for an alert driver is about
0.75 seconds. However, in normal situations on the road, a driver will not be as alert as when he or
she knows he or she is being tested. Hence it is more realistic to assume a reaction time of about two
or three seconds.
Now using the formula above for calculating distance, we can easily work out how far the car will
travel in the time it takes the driver to react. For example:
What is the distance a car will move, while travelling at 60 km/h, when an alert driver takes
one second to react to a child who has run out onto the road?
Note: It is best to convert km/h to m/s (divide it by 3.6) so that calculations are easier and the
final distance will be in metres.
distance = time × speed
= 1 second × 60 ÷ 3.6 m/s
= 16.7 metres
Summary
Reaction distance depends on the alertness of the
driver and the speed at which the car is travelling.

Why should there

2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-4
Forces during a collision
During a collision, a person sitting in the vehicle comes under a tremendous force
that is very hard to imagine. The person’s body must slow from a driving speed of
possibly 60 km/h or more to zero in only a few seconds when the vehicle hits a
stationary body such as a tree or barrier.
This force is better understood when we use the analogy of a
car falling from the top of a tall building. The greater
the speed at which the collision occurs,
the greater the force needed to
stop the car, and the greater the
force on the person’s body. Hence
the higher the building we imagine
the car falling from.
The effect of speed on stopping distance
It takes only a few experiments in a car to see that the greater the speed of a vehicle, the longer the
stopping distance, and hence the greater the chance of an accident occurring.
When a moving vehicle needs to stop suddenly, the time it takes for it to actually stop depends on
two main things:
1. The reaction time, which is the time it takes a driver to observe a situation and react to it.
2. The braking time, which is the time it takes for the vehicle to actually stop once the brake has
been applied. So,
Stopping Time = Reaction Time + Braking Time

excellent brakes on a good road at a range of different speeds.

DNA is a gigantic molecule found in the
nucleus of every cell and in every living
organism. It looks something like a ladder

chemical that chromosomes are made of.
These are large entwined strands of DNA.
They can be divided into smaller sections

parent to child. So the DNA from related
people is always more similar than DNA from
unrelated people. In the same way, the DNA of closely related animals and plants is also more alike
than the DNA of organisms that are only distantly related. It has been found that the DNA of the
primates has about 90% in common with the DNA of humans.
The only people who share exactly the same DNA are identical twins, because they started out as a
single fertilised egg, that in its early stages split apart, and then grew into two separate babies who
are genetically identical.
The legs of the ‘ladder’ consist of alternating molecules called sugars and phosphates (marked as ‘s’
and ‘p’ in the diagram above). The ladder twists itself into a ‘double helix’ to save room as it fits into

only four different bases, and they always pair up in exactly the same way:
adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) always attaches to guanine (G).

characteristics (see below).
This DNA, or genetic code, is unique
to every person and is a combination
of which 50% is inherited from the

Speed or velocity is a measure of how far an object moves in a certain time

at which a vehicle would take one hour to cover 35 kilometres.
A speed of 10 m/s is the speed at which 10 metres is covered in
every second.
A speed given in m/sec can be converted to km/h by multiplying by

hour, you divide the distance (40 km) by the time (0.5 hours).
40 ÷ 0.5 = 80 km/h

Circles

A circle is formed by the set of points in a plane that are all the

A chord is an interval (or line segment) joining two points on

A membrane is the essential protective covering of a cell. Membranes separate one cell from another. All living
organisms are made up of cells; so membranes are essential to all life. The cell membrane is made up of a
phospholipid bilayer in which protein molecules float. The membrane also contains cholesterol molecules,
which give the membranes some rigidity and water resistance. Any factors that distort or alter proteins and lipid
molecules affect the permeability of the membrane.
Beetroot cells contain a pigment called betacyanin in their vacuoles. A special membrane called the tonoplast
surrounds the vacuoles. When beetroot cells are subjected to variation in pH, detergent, alcohol and high
temperatures, the pigment will leak out because these factors alter the tonoplast and cell membrane structures.

A C T I V I T Y
Enzymes are globular proteins. They act as catalysts that speed up chemical reactions without being
destroyed or altered during the process. Enzymes are extremely efficient and may be reused. Enzymes are specific
and react with a particular substrate. A substrate is a molecule with which the enzyme reacts and produces
products. The active site is the only part of the enzyme that reacts with the substrate. However, its unique
protein structure under certain circumstances can easily be denatured.
Some of the factors that affect enzyme reactions are enzyme concentration, pH, temperature, substrate and
product concentration, activators and inhibitors. Enzymes react best at optimum temperature and optimum pH. If
the environment of the enzyme is too acidic or too basic, the enzyme may irreversibly denature until it no longer
has the necessary shape for proper functioning. The enzyme tested in this experiment is catalase, an
intracellular enzyme. It is produced by cells to prevent the accumulation of toxic hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen
peroxide is decomposed by catalase to water and oxygen. This reaction occurs spontaneously without catalase,
but the enzyme speeds the reaction considerably.

Human reproduction II: Birth

‘An embryo obtains food and oxygen from the mother's blood via the placenta, which also removes waste.
The placenta forms on the wall of the uterus as the embryo develops. The placenta and embryo are joined
by the umbilical cord. The blood of the mother and baby do not meet or mix. The two blood supplies

are separate.
1 Will a baby necessarily have the same blood group as the mother?
Explain your answer.

The baby floats in a bag of liquid called the amniotic fluid. The
fluid acts as a shock absorber and protects the baby. It cushions the
baby from minor physical knocks the mother may receive. Samples
of the amniotic fluid containing cells of the unborn baby can be
used to check the sex of the child or for early detection of certain
disorders.

After about nine months the baby is usually fully developed and in
the correct position to be born. Hormones within the mother's
body signal the uterus to begin contractions, or /abour. These
contractions start to push the baby out.

The baby passes head-first, usually facedown, through the cervix

and down the vaginal canal. After the baby is born, the umbilical

cord is tied and cut. The navel, or belly button, is where the cord was attached. There are no nerves in the cord,
So it does not hurt the baby when the cord is severed. The placenta (or afterbirth) comes away from the mother
soon after the baby is born. It is checked for abnormalities and weighed (it should weigh about the same as the
baby, otherwise it may not have been fully expelled). It is then discarded, unless permission has been given to use
it for medical purposes, such as the extraction of stem cells.

Some babies are not in the upside-down position when they are ready to be born, These babies are either
born bottom first in a breech birth, which can cause injury to both mother and baby, or by caesarean section.

BOOK 2: MEDICAL ETHICS

In vitro fertilisation

Not all couples that wish to have a baby are able to do so. About 15% of couples will experience difficulty in
trying to achieve a pregnancy. There are many reasons why a couple can be considered ‘infertile’, and
sometimes no cause for the infertility can be found.

1. Give two reasons why a male might be infertile.
2. Give two reasons why a female might be infertile.

The infertile couple has options. One of these is in vitro fertilisation, or IVF, a medical procedure to help
fertilisation. in vitro fertilisation — literally, ‘in-glass’ fertilisation ~ involves fertilisation of ova outside of the
body. Techniques vary, but the following shows a common sequence:

* Fertility drugs are given to the female to stimulate ova production.

* Ova are removed from the ovary by laparoscopic surgery, a minimally invasive technique that only involves
making a smail incision,

* The ova are placed in a glass container, sperm is added and they are incubated for about 24 hours for
fertilisation to take place.

* The fertilised eggs (zygotes) are transferred to a growth medium to ensure they can divide and grow
into embryos.

+ Embryos that develop normally are identified. A small number (two to four) are placed in the woman's
fallopian tube or can be implanted into the womb.

+ Embryos not used immediately may be frozen (in liquid nitrogen) for later use.
3 Give two non-medical options for an infertile couple.

Discuss why scarce medical resources are used on these procedures when some people have to wait a long
time for treatment for life-threatening conditions.

P L A S M O LY S I S
If a plant cell is immersed in a hypertonic solution, water will leave the cell. This process is called
plasmolysis. The loss of water causes the cell to lose the pressure exerted by the fluid in the plant cell’s vacuole
(called turgor pressure) and the plant cell becomes flaccid. During plasmolysis, the cellular membrane pulls away
from the cell wall and shrinks.
When plant cells are placed in hypotonic solution, water enters the cell and the cells become turgid. They do
not burst because of the rigid cell wall. If a plasmolysed plant cell is again placed in hypotonic solution, water
will enter the cell. This process is called deplasmolysis. When plant cells are placed in isotonic solution, no
change will occur because the amount of water entering and leaving the cell is at equilibrium.

Aim
To use a model to investigate:
• The effect of size and shape on SA:V ratio.
• The effect of SA:V ratio on the rate of diffusion into a cell.
Hypothesis
Write a hypothesis to explain how surface area to volume ratio affects cell size, cell shape and a cell’s
ability to obtain nutrients.
Equipment (per group)
20
EFFECT OF SURFACE AREA TO VOLUME RATIO ON CELL SIZE
Most cells are microscopic in size because as a cell gets larger, it needs more food and produces more waste.
Therefore, more materials must be able to move into and out of the cell through the cell membrane. To keep
up with these demands, a growing cell needs a larger surface area through which to exchange materials. As
the cell’s volume increases, its outer surface grows too. However, the volume of a cell increases at a faster rate
than the area of its outer surface. As the size of the cell increases the surface area to volume ratio
decreases. Materials must be able to reach all parts of a cell quickly. When volume is too large relative to surface
area, diffusion cannot occur at sufficiently high rates.
The shapes of cells can also affect the amount of surface area of a cell. Cells that are spherical in shape have a
large surface area to volume ratio and are more efficient in obtaining nutrients, gases and getting rid of wastes.
However, cells come in a great variety of shapes. Rod-shaped cells have more surface area compared to their
volume than spherical cells.
In this experiment, the cell models are made of agar which has an acid-sensitive dye, phenolphthalein,
incorporated into it. The dye changes from pink to clear in the presence of acid. The uptake of acid and hence
colourless areas of the cell models represents the uptake of nutrients by the cell.

Organic chemistry

Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. At one time, the term ‘organic compound’ meant
a compound that was found in plant or animal materials, such as sugars, fats and proteins. All of these
compounds contain carbon. Now the term organic compounds is used for almost all carbon compounds,
whether they come from plants and animals or are made in a laboratory. However, compounds such as
carbonates (-CO,*) and carbon dioxide are not usually described as organic compounds.

compounds. However, the Earth contains less than 0.01 % by mass of carbon. This huge discrepancy
between the proportion of compounds that contain carbon and the proportion of carbon in the Earth
indicates that carbon atoms have some very unusual bonding properties. The bonding in most organic
substances is covalent.

DISSOLVING AND DISSOCIATING

A general (but not infallible) rule says like dissolves like. This means that polar solvents tend to dissolve
polar/ionic substances and non-polar solvents tend to dissolve non-polar substances.
Remember, in a solution:

* the solvent and solute particles are evenly distributed (homogenous) throughout the solution

* the solute particles are too small to be seen

* there are forces of attraction between solvent and solute particles.
Before a substance can dissolve in water the forces between its particles and between water molecules
must be broken, This results in new bonds being formed between the water and the solute. Breaking
bonds requires energy to be put in (endothermic; endo: within); making bonds gives energy out
(exothermic; exo: outside). If a covalent molecule is very large (it can consist of tens of thousands of
atoms, e.g. cellulose and polythene) or is non-polar, it will not dissolve in water. The bonding in
covalent network structures (e.g. diamond and silicon dioxide) is too strong to be overcome by any
possible bonds between particles in the structure and water molecules.

•  Gases consist of minute, discrete particles (usually molecules) in continuous,  
chaotic motion and with high speeds.
•  The average speed of motion increases with the absolute temperature, which  
is thus some measure of the average energy of motion, i.e. kinetic energy.

•  Collisions between molecules and bombardment of the walls of the containing 
vessel occur, the latter is the cause of gaseous pressure, which is force per unit area.

molecules. At low pressures, molecules may even be considered as point masses,  
i.e. have negligible volume.
•  At low pressures, the forces of attraction between molecules

HARD WATER 18]

When soap solution is added to soft water and shaken, a lather (foam) readily forms. If soap solution is
added to hard water, lather does not form immediately, More soap has to be added until it removes all of
the hardness. Hardness in water wastes soap. Other indications of hard water include hard deposits in
hot water systems and kettles. Synthetic (‘soapless') detergents are not affected by hard water.
There are two sorts of hardness: temporary and permanent. Temporary hardness is caused by carbonates
and can be removed by boiling. Permanent hardness is not removed by boiling. Chemicals called water
softeners can be used to remove hardness so that less soap is needed. Dissolved calcium (Ca) and
magnesium (Mg™) tons are a major source of hardness, Water can also be ‘softened’ by passing it through
an ion exchange medium, where calcium and magnesium ions are replaced by sodium ions. The
medium is usually made up of organic resins and can be regenerated by passing brine (salt solution)
through it. Chemical water softeners work in a different way; they react with these ions and remove
them from solution by precipitating them out.

decahydrate, NayCOs.10H,0) and a commercial brand, Softa. Below is an extract from her practical

METALS 13

Metals are found on the left-hand side and centre of the Periodic Table. Most metals are lustrous (shiny)
and they are often silver in colour. Metals are good thermal and electrical conductors, whereas most
non-metals are poor conductors.

1 What is meant by @ good thermal conductor?

Metals are malleable; they can be beaten into shape. They are also ductile; they can be drawn into wires.
Non-metals are brittle; they snap instead of bend. Metals are usually denser than non-metals. Metals are
solids at room temperature (with the exception of mercury, Hg). They usually have high melting points.
Very few metals occur native (uncombined) in the natural state. They are usually found combined with
other elements. The earliest metals to be used by humans were copper (Cu), tin (Sn), silver (Ag) and gold
(Au) - all of these metals can be found native.

2 Explain why copper, tin, silver and gold can be found native.
Very few metals occur uncombined in the natural state. They are usually found chemically joined with
other elements in minerals. A mineral is a naturally-occurring pure substance. An ore is a material from
the Earth’s crust that contains enough of a substance to make it worth mining. Iron (Fe) exists in the
forms of haematite and magnetite, which are both forms of iron oxide (i.e, iron combined with oxygen
in a compound). Iron ore is very similar in chemical composition to iron rust.
Aluminium (Al) is found as bauxite (aluminium oxide) and lead (Pb) as galena (lead sulfide, lead
combined with sulfur). Copper occurs in the ores malachite and azurite, which are both forms of copper
carbonate. Another important ore of copper is chalcopyrite, a yellow mineral consisting of sulfides of
copper and iron.

RELATIVE ATOMIC MASS 22

Because individual atoms are so small, units such as the gram are too large for describing low numbers of
atoms. Atomic mass units (amu) are the basic units of mass for atoms. One amu is equal to 1.66 x 10” kg.

Chemists need a standard against which they can compare atoms. The first standard was hydrogen (the
simplest atom) which gave a hydrogen atom a mass of 1.0000 amu. Later, naturally-occurring oxygen
was used instead of hydrogen and assigned a mass of 16.0000 amu. However, oxygen exists as Isotopes,
where some atoms have a different number of neutrons and hence different masses. In 1961 the isotope
carbon-12 ("C) was adopted as the standard measure and one atom of carbon-12 is defined as having a
mass of 12 amu, In other words, the mass of 1 amu is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom,

Because the masses of all atoms are compared to this standard, they are often called relative atomic
masses (relative meaning compared to each other). Some older textbooks refer to atomic mass units as
daltons, named after John Dalton (1766-1844).

Most Periodic Tables give relative atomic masses as well as atomic numbers, Remember:
* Atomic number is the number of protons (and is also equal to the number of electrons)
* Atomic mass (mass number) is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons

* Relative atomic masses of elements are often not whole numbers because in nature they are
mixtures of isotopes

The mass spectrometer was invented around 100 years ago. It is a very useful tool for identifying the presence of 
isotopes of metals and non-metals. It can also be to identify molecular compounds. A mass spectrometer acts as 
a very accurate balance for finding masses. When molecules are put into a mass spectrometer, they can be broken 
down into fragments.
Positive ions (cations) travel through a vacuum and are deflected by electric charge 
and magnetic fields. The degree of deflection can be used to identify the species. 
The amount of deflection depends on the mass of the particle and its charge. 
Here is a sequence followed in a typical mass spectrometer.
Step 1: The (very small) sample is vapourised by heating.
Step 2: The sample is introduced into the ionising chamber.
Step 3: High energy electrons bombard the sample and cause it to form positive ions.
Step 4: The positive ions are accelerated out of the ionising chamber by applying a high voltage.
Step 5: The beam of ions is focused and collimated (turned into a narrow beam).
Step 6: An ‘electrostatic analyser’ deflects cations of a narrow mass range into the magnetic analyser.
Step 7: The electromagnet is adjusted to select cations of a specific mass to hit the detector.
Step 8: The detector produces a small electric current which is amplified and then recorded.
Step 9: The strength of the electromagnet is adjusted to allow more massive cations to be detected.

THE MOLE

Many everyday names represent a fixed number of objects. For example:

* a soccer team: 11 * adozen eggs: 12

* anetball team: 7 a gross of woodscrews: 144

1 Give another name that stands for a fixed quantity.

Chemistry is all about objects like atoms, molecules and ions, These objects are all so small that there
must be many billions of them before they can be seen. A special number used in chemistry is 6.02 x 10",
called the mole. It is also called Avogadro’s number, in honour of Amedeo Avogadro (1776-1856). The
mole is simply a convenient unit of measurement that chemists use because it fits in with ‘natural’
numbers. It is like saying there are 365 days in a year, the diameter of the Earth is 12 800 km, light
travels at 300 000 kilometres per second (approximately), and so on.

Units of measurement are often used in mathematics questions:

Divide the total number by the number in one dozen: 36 + 12 = 3 dozen.

0.5 x 6.02 x 10" = 3.01 x 10”

iv How many moles of water molecules are in 57 x 10” particles of water?
Divide the total number of particles by the number of particles that makes up a mole:
57 x 10” + 6.02 x 10" = 9.5 x 10"

Transition metals occupy the middle of the Periodic Table, between Groups II and III. They are sometimes known 
as the ‘d-block’ elements. Most definitions classify transition metals as those with incomplete inner d-subshells. 
They don’t follow the normal way of electrons filling shells in sequence. Copper, cadmium and zinc have complete 
d-subshells and so don’t meet this criterion. Copper and cadmium are often included despite this, because they have 
physical and chemical properties in common with the main body of transition metals.

WATER QUALITY AND OXYGEN

The quality of water is determined by many factors. Two important considerations are the amount of
oxygen dissolved in the water sample and the biological oxygen demand (BOD) of that sample. BOD is
an indication of how much oxygen is needed by organisms in a sample of water.

Oxygen becomes dissolved in water in many ways; including by diffusing from the atmosphere, by
aeration (rapid movement) and by underwater green plants.

Aerobic life forms are those that require oxygen for life. The amount of oxygen dissolved in water can be

indicator of the health of a water-based ecosystem, it is important to measure the level of dissolved

searchText:

1
The diagonal of a rectangle forms an angle of 26∞with the longer side. The longer side is 
15 cm. Determine the length of the shorter side to the nearest centimetre.
2
The shorter side of a rectangle is 15 cm and the diagonal is 24.9 cm. Determine to the nearest
degree the angle between the shorter side and the diagonal.
3
A 15-metre rope attached to the top of a yacht’s mast makes an angle of 77∞with the deck.
Calculate the height of the mast to one decimal place.
4
A wire supporting a radio mast is 27 m long. It makes an angle of 67∞with the ground.
Determine, to one decimal place, the distance along the ground from the base of the mast to
the point the wire is anchored.
5
The side of a pyramid makes an angle of 68∞with its base, and the perpendicular height of the
pyramid is 23.2 m. Determine the slant height to the nearest metre.
6
A 15-metre ladder is leaning against a wall. The base of the ladder is 3 m from the wall. Find to
the nearest degree the angle the ladder makes with the ground.
7
The slant height of a cone is 15 cm and its perpendicular height 11 cm. Calculate to the nearest
minute the angle between the side of the cone and its base.
8
Lucy wants to clean out the gutter on her house. The gutter is 9.3 m above the ground. Lucy
knows that a ladder must extend at least 80 cm beyond a gutter to be safe. If the ladder makes
an angle of 70∞with the ground, determine the shortest ladder (to the nearest cm) that is safe
for Lucy to use.
9
The perpendicular height of a cone is 14 cm and the radius of its base is 6 cm. Determine the
angle between the side of the cone and its base to the nearest minute.
10 An isosceles triangle ABC has sides AB and BC that are both 12 cm in length. The
perpendicular from B to the midpoint of AC is 9 cm. Determine the size of the angle ABC to
the nearest degree.
11 In the rectangle ABCD, AD = 30 cm and –ADB = 27∞. Determine the length of AC to the
nearest centimetre.
12 A rectangle has a diagonal length of 14.5 cm. The diagonal makes an angle of 56∞45’ with the
shorter side. Find the perimeter of the rectangle to the nearest centimetre. 
13 Drew has a ladder that can extend to 9.5 m. An angle of 12∞between the ladder and the wall 
is considered safe. Can Drew safely use this ladder to access a roof that is 8.5 m above the
ground, given that the ladder must also extend 80 cm beyond the roof?
14 A surveyor is determining the distance across a canyon. She marks Point A on one side of the
canyon and Point B directly opposite it on the other side of the canyon. Then she walks 20 m
from Point B to Point C along a line that is perpendicular to the line AB. She measures the
angle BCA as 27∞30’. How wide is the canyon?

quadrant 1 all ratios are positive; in quadrant 2 only sine is positive, cos
and tan are negative; in quadrant 3 only tan is positive; and in quadrant

Maximising Exam Marks in Senior Chemistry – Book 1
Nuclear chemistry deals with the nuclei of atoms. The nucleus 
contains most of the mass of an atom (protons and neutrons) but 
occupies very little space. Ernest Rutherford first proposed the 
existence of the nucleus in 1911. James Chadwick discovered the 
neutron in 1932. Table 1 shows the properties of the nucleons.
1 
What does amu represent? 
The number of protons present in a nucleus of an atom gives the atomic number of that element. 
2 Suggest why protons and neutrons are referred to as nucleons.
Why does the nucleus hold together? You would expect the positive protons to repel each other. Part of the answer 
involves ‘binding energy’. If you look at the numbers of protons and neutrons in a particular atom and calculate the 
mass the nucleus should be, you will find that the actual mass of the nucleus is less than the theoretical value. The 
‘missing’ mass (mass deficit) has been transformed into ‘binding energy’ which holds the nucleons together. 
Some elements have isotopes, i.e. their atoms will have the same number of electrons and protons, but different 
numbers of neutrons. In 1919, Francis Aston used a mass spectrometer to measure mass and percentages of isotopes 
accurately. Isotopes can be identified by writing the mass number after the name of the element e.g. carbon-14 or 
uranium-235. The mass quoted in data tables is usually the weighted average of the naturally occurring element.
3 Nucleus A has 15 protons and 16 neutrons, whereas nucleus B has  
16 protons and 16 neutrons. Are they isotopes? Explain your answer.
4 Uranium has three naturally occurring isotopes, uranium-234,  
uranium-235 and uranium-238. A Periodic Table gives the  
relative atomic mass of uranium as 238.02. What does this tell  
you about the relative proportions of the isotopes in nature?

Many people, when they hear the word ‘radiation’, think of nuclear reactions and radioactivity, but the
word means much more than that. Three main classes of radiation include electromagnetic radiation
(EMR), nuclear radiation, and cosmic radiation. All three types of radiation can travel in a vacuum,

Infra red (IR), ultra-violet (UV), visible (white) light and radio waves are examples of electromagnetic
radiation, Radioactivity is a type of nuclear radiation and cosmic radiation (or cosmic rays) come from
the sun and other objects in outer space. The sun releases cosmic rays during spectacular eruptions
called solar flares,

If you have ever lain on a beach and got a suntan, then the change in skin colour was caused by UV rays
from the sun. If you switch on an electric iron, after a while, without touching it, you can feel heat being
given off. Heat is a form of IR, which we cannot see. Radio signals are not just transmitted on Earth but occur
naturally from outer space, for example from stars, and can be detected on Earth by large radio telescopes.

EMR is always around us and is a form of energy associated
with electric and magnetic fields. It behaves like a wave and
travels through space at the speed of light, 300 000 kilometres
per second. There are different types of electromagnetic
radiation. Each type has a different wavelength and frequency,
but the same speed, Wavelength is measured in metres. The
frequency of a wave is the number of cycles per second
passing a certain point. The unit of frequency is Hertz or Hz.
One cycle per second is 1 Hz. Different wavelengths of EMR
carry different amounts of energy. Short-wavelength radiation
carries more energy than long-wavelength radiation.

Large, unstable atoms (radioisotopes) can break up and give off energy (gamma rays and X-rays) and
particles, Gamma rays and X-rays pass through solid objects and can be used to take pictures

The work of James Prescott Joule
16
IntroductIon
Until about 1880 ‘heat’ was considered to be a weightless 
material fluid that flowed from one body to another.  
This fluid was called ‘caloric’. The theory was useful in 
developing ideas about quantities such as heat and 
specific heat capacities. For example, the unit of heat was 
called the ‘calorie’, and was defined as that amount of heat 
that would raise the temperature of 1.0 g of water by 
1.0 Celsius degree. However, evidence from further 
investigations suggested that this theory was not valid 
and that heat, like kinetic and potential energy, was a 
form of energy. James Joule reasoned that if heat was a 
form of energy, then it could be transformed into other 
forms and that there would be a definite ‘conversion 
factor’ according to the Law of Conservation of Energy. 
Joule set out to determine this conversion factor by 
changing mechanical energy into heat energy.
Aim
To collect some data from an experiment similar to Joule’s 
experiment and so calculate the ‘conversion factor’.
data
Joule’s apparatus is shown in Figures 1 and 2. A 
calorimeter was divided into compartments using baffle 
plates, and filled with a known mass of water. The solid 
masses M1 and M2 were wound up to the levels A and C 
respectively and then allowed to drop back through 
height h, to B and D. This caused the paddles in the 
calorimeter to spin and thus transformed the potential 
energy of the masses into heat energy of the water, so 
raising its temperature. This was repeated a number of 
times by winding the masses back up and repeating the 
drop. Any rise in the temperature of the water was 
recorded. Some data derived from such an experiment is 
given below. 
•

• 
Mass of M1 = Mass of M2 = 70.0 kg
• 
Number of times masses were dropped = 20
• 
Distance of drop = 3.0 m
• 
Temperature rise in water = 5.

Wave transmission I
23
IntroductIon
Two basic types of mechanical wave transmission that 
commonly occur are (a) transverse and (b) longitudinal. 
Both types are transmitted in elastic media. The 
longitudinal mechanical waves are transmitted because 
the medium shows some resistance to compression forces 
and so ‘rebounds’ in an elastic manner. The speed of the 
rebound is reflected in the ‘compression modulus’ for the 
medium. The bigger the value of this modulus, the more 
elastic the medium is to compression waves and the 
greater the speed of the waves in it. A similar logic applies 
to mechanical transverse waves in media that are subject 
to shear forces by the waves and so each medium is 
assigned a ‘shear modulus’.

waves and their transmission through various media.

searchText:
Glossary
Contribution margin – the amount that each item
sold contributes towards the expenses of the
business. Selling price less variable costs (cost of
purchasing the items).
Cost of goods sold – the total costs related to the
goods that have been sold. Sales revenue less cost
of goods sold equals gross profit.
Credit transactions – sale or purchase of goods or
services where no cash changes hands at the point
of sale.
Creditor – supplier of the goods or services that
have been purchased on credit.
Creditors schedule – list of amounts owing to
creditors for the credit purchase of goods or
services
Current assets – items of value owned or
controlled by the business that are cash or will be
turned into cash within a period of 12 months
Current liabilities – amounts owed by the
business that must be paid within a period of 12
months
Debtor – customer who has purchased goods or
services on credit
Debtors schedule – list of amounts owed by the
debtors (accounts receivable)
Deposits not credited – amounts which have been
received by the business but have not yet been
banked (are not recorded on the bank statement)
Depreciation – the allocation of the cost of a non
current asset over its effective working life
Desired profit – the amount that the business
hopes to earn after all costs have been met.
Direct deposits – amounts that are deposited
directly into the bank account.
Discount allowed – an inducement to a debtor to
get them to pay their account quickly.
Discount received – offered by the creditor as an
inducement to pay the account quickly
Drawings – amounts of cash or other assets
withdrawn from the business by the owner
Fixed cost – a cost that will not vary with the
number of items sold eg wages, electricity
Entity assumption – the affairs of the business
and the affairs of the owner must be kept separate
Expenses – costs incurred in the process of
earning revenue
FIFO – First In, First Out – a stock management
system where the oldest stock is the first to be sold
Goods and services tax (GST) – a value added
tax which must be added to the selling price to get
the price which must be paid by the customer.
Currently GST is 10%

Accounting equation – expresses the relationship
between the amounts owned by the business and
the amounts owed by the business. Usually
expressed as A = L + P or A = L + OE (owner’s
equity).
Accounting period (reporting period) – the period
for which accounting reports are prepared. This
cannot be longer than 12 months.
Accounts payable – amounts owing by credit
customers
Accounts receivable – amounts owing to credit
suppliers
Accrual basis of reporting – profit or loss is
calculated taking into account all revenues earned
and expenses incurred for the accounting period,
whether or not they have been received or paid
Accrued expenses – expenses that are incurred
before they are paid (these are liabilities)
Accrued revenues – revenues that are earned but
not yet received (these are assets)
Accumulated depreciation – total of depreciation
that has been written off so far
Allocated cost – the amount of the original cost
that is written off over the useful life of the asset
(depreciation)
Assets – item of financial value owned or
controlled by the business, it has future benefits for
the business.
Bad debts – an amount that will not be received
from a credit customer
Balance sheet – Statement of financial position – a
statement reporting all of the assets and liabilities
of an entity and showing the owner’s equity
(proprietorship)
Bank reconciliation – the process of checking the
bank balance in the records of the business against
the bank balance as shown by the bank
Breakeven – the point at which all of the costs of
the business are covered by the revenue of the
business (the business makes no profit or loss).
Carrying value – the cost of an asset less the
accumulated depreciation (written-down value)
Cash flow statement – a statement showing all
cash inflows less all cash outflows
Cash payments – cash outflows of the business
Cash payments journal – book used to record the
cash outflows of the business
Cash receipts – cash inflows of the business
Cash receipts journal – book used to record the
cash inflows of the business
Continuous recording – ongoing recording of the
stock or inventory (manually using stock cards or
using technology)
© Blake Education   ISBN  978 1 92561 072 7	
    Accounting Fundamentals Book 1

Gross profit – the difference between the sales
revenue and the cost of goods sold. It is available
to cover the cost of other expenses and for net
profit.
Identified cost – a stock management system
where all items of stock carry a tag showing the
cost price of the item.
Imprest system – system for recording of petty
cash
Income – revenue derived from the trading
operations of a business
Inventory – stock held by the business for resale
Lead time – the time it takes for stock which has
been ordered to arrive at the business
Liabilities – amounts owed by a business
Mark up on cost – a calculation of the selling price
of an item, based on the cost price plus a
percentage to cover other costs.
Net profit – sales revenue less all expenses
incurred in earning that revenue. Net profit
increases owner’s equity.
Non cash expenses – expenses such as
depreciation or bad debts for which no cash is paid
out.
Non current assets – items of value owned or
controlled by the business which will be of benefit
to the business for a period longer than 12 months
Non current liabilities – amounts owed by the
business which will not need to be paid within the
next 12 months
Payments – outflows of cash from the business
Payments by authority – payments made by the
bank on the authority from the account holder
Perpetual recording – continuous recording of
stock or inventory – each purchase or sale (and
returns) is recorded at cost price at the time of
transaction.
Petty cash – small amounts of cash used to pay
for expenses that cannot be paid by cheque.
Petty cash advance (float) – the amount that is
kept in the petty cash fund.
Prepaid expenses – expenses that are paid before
they are incurred (these are assets)
Prepaid revenues – revenues that are received
before they are earned (these are liabilities)
Profit and loss statement – Statement of financial
performance – a statement reporting all of the
revenues and expenses of an entity in an
accounting period
Purchases journal – book used to record the
credit purchase of goods or services
Purchases returns – stock returned to the supplier
Receipts – inflows of cash to the business
Reducing-balance method – a method of
calculating the depreciation of an asset based on
the carrying value (written-down value) at the end
of the previous period.
Reimbursement – the cheque drawn to bring the
petty cash balance back up to the imprest amount
Reporting period – accounting period – the period
for which accounting reports are prepared. This
cannot be longer than 12 months.
Returns in – stock returned to the business by a
customer
Returns out – stock returned to the supplier
Revenue – income earned from the operations of
the business
Sales journal – book used to record the credit sale
of goods or services
Sales returns – stock returned to the business by
customers
Single entry recording – a recording system
which has one entry for a transaction, usually in a
cash book. Subsidiary records may also be
maintained.
Statement of cash flows – a statement reporting
on all of the inflows and outflows of cash for an
entity, classified as operating, investing and
financing operations
Statement of financial performance – Profit and
loss statement – a statement reporting on all of the
revenues and expenses incurred by an entity in an
accounting period. It is a summary statement.
Statement of financial position – Balance sheet –
a statement reporting all of the assets and liabilities
of an entity and showing the owner’s equity
(proprietorship) It is a position statement.
Statement of receipts and payments – a
statement reporting all of the inflows and outflows
of cash in an accounting period. It is a summary
statement.
Stock card – a manual record of all movements of
stock into or out of the business
Stock loss – recorded stock is greater than the
stock on hand as per the stock take.
Stock take – counting of stock on hand in a
business for the purpose of calculating and
accurate gross profit
Straight-line method – a method of calculating the
depreciation of a non current asset by allocating the
cost evenly over the useful working life
Trading statement – a statement showing details
of the sale of goods and the cost of goods sold,
used to calculate the gross profit.
Unpresented cheques – cheques that have been
written out but have not yet been presented to the
bank for payment.
Variable cost – the cost of buying in item for sale.
Total variable costs will vary with the level of
activity of the business
Working capital – difference between current
assets and current liabilities. Amounts available for
payment of short term liabilities.

Terms you should know

Accrual accounting — a method of recording and reporting where all revenue is included in the period in which
it is earned and all expenses are included in the period where they are incurred
Accrued expenses — expenses that are incurred before they are paid (these are liabil
Accrued revenues - revenue that are earned but not yet received (these are assets)
Prepaid expenses — expenses that are paid before they are incurred (these are assets)
Prepaid revenues — revenues that are received before they are earned (these are liabilities)

14 LIQUIDITY MEASURES

Terms you should know

Cash cycle — the time taken for cash outlaid by the business to return as cash to the business

Creditors turnover — the length of time the business is taking to pay creditors. Measured by dividing the total
credit purchases by the average creditors.

Debtors turnover — the length of time that the debtors are taking to pay. Measured by dividing total credit sales

3 QUALITATIVE CHARACTERISTICS/PRINCIPLES

Terms you should know

QUALITATIVE CHARACTERISTICS

Comparability — ability to compare accounting information from one accounting period to another

Materiality — accounting information includes all information whose omission or misstatement would affect the
decisions of users

Relevance — inclusion of information that will influence the decisions of the users

Reliability ~ accounting information must represent the affairs of the business without bias or misstatement
Timeliness — reports must be prepared in sufficient time to form the basis of effective decisions
Understandability — the qualitative characteristic of reports that are easily understood by the users
PRINCIPLES

Accounting period (reporting period) — the period for which accounting reports are prepared, This cannot be
longer than 12 months.

Conservatism — income should not be included until earned but expenses should be included as soon as they
become liable. Profits should not be overstated.

Entity assumption — the affairs of the business and the affairs of the owner must be kept separate

Going concern — the business has a future life and will not cease in the foreseeable future

Historical cost — recording of assets at the price paid for them

Monetary - the principle of measuring all items in records and reports in a common monetary unit — eg Australian
dollars

GLOSSARY

Accounting equation — expresses the relationship
between the amounts owned by the business and the
amounts owed by the business. Usually expressed as
A= L + OE (owner's equity) or A = L + P (proprietorship)

Accounting period — principle — the length of time for
which accounting reports are prepared. This cannot be

longer than one year.

Accrual accounting — an accounting method where
revenue is recorded and reported when earned (not
necessarily received) and expenses are recorded and
reported when incurred (not necessarily paid)

Accrued expenses — expenses that have been incurred
but are not yet paid. Classified as a current liability

Accrued revenue — revenues that have been earned, but
not yet received. Classified as a current asset.

Asset turnover — the relationship between the sales of
the business and the assets that were used while the
sales were made. Measures the sales per $ of assets
employed

Assets — items of financial value owned or controlled by
the business, which will assist it in earning revenue in the
future.

Bad debt — an amount that will not be received from a
credit customer.

Balance sheet — Statement of financial position — a
statement showing the assets, liabilities and owner's
equity of a business on a particular date.

Bank deposit form — document used to record deposits
at the bank

Bank overdraft — the withdrawals from the bank account
greater than the deposits into the account

Budgeting — planning. The preparation of forecast
statements for the business

Capital — the initial investment by the owner into the
business

Cash cycle — the time taken for cash outlaid by the
business to return as cash to the business

Cash flow — cash coming into the business less the cash
going out of the business

Cash register roll — the record of all cash received and
placed in the till

Cheque — an order from the owner of the account (the
payer) to the bank (drawer) to pay to the entity named
(the payee) the amount specified. Used to make most
cash payments for a business.

Comparability — qualitative characteristic — ability to
compare accounting information from one accounting
period to another

Concepts — see qualitative characteristics.

Conservatism — accounting principle — income should

© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 92253 854 3

not be included until earned but expenses should be
included as soon as they become liable. Profits should
not be overstated.

Credit checks — checking of the financial viability of a
prospective customer before extending credit to them

Credit note — document used to record the return of
goods

Creditors turnover — the length of time the business is
taking to pay creditors, Measured by dividing the total
credit purchases by the average creditors.

Current assets — assets that are expected to be of
benefit to the business in the short term (less than
12 months)

Current liabilities — liabilities that must be paid within
12 months

Debt ratio — measures the relationship between the
assets of the business and the finance provided by
external parties.

Debtors collections — the total of the amount collected
(received) from debtors in the period.

Debtors turnover — the length of time that the debtors
are taking to pay. Measured by dividing total credit sales
by the average debtors.

Discount allowed/expense — an inducement to a debtor
to get them to pay their account quickly. It is a reduction
in the total owing.

Documents — evidence of transactions

Entity assumption — the affairs of the business and the
affairs of the owner must be kept separate

Equity ratio — measures the relationship between the
assets of the business and the amount contributed by the
owner.

Expense — cost incurred while earning revenue

Factoring — selling of debts (amounts owed by
customers) to a finance company to obtain cash from the
debts immediately

Gearing — the proportion of assets that have been
financed by external entities.

Going concern — accounting principle — the business
has a future life and will not cease in the foreseeable
future.

Gross profit ratio — the relationship between the sales
and the gross profit. Measure the amount of each $ of
sales that is retained as gross profit.

Historical cost — accounting principle — recording of
assets at the price paid for them

Income — revenue earned from the business activities of
the business

Interest cover — the number of times that the profit can
be divided by the interest expense.

Concepts and Management Book 3

>>P

Invoice — document used to record credit purchases or
sales.

Key performance indicators — KPIs — indicators used by
the management of the business to assess the success
of the trading operations. Non-ratio indicators.

Liabilities — amounts owed to an external entity

Liquidity — the ability of the business to pay its
short-term debts from its short-term resources

Loss — excess of expenses over revenues. Decreases
owner's equity.

Materiality — qualitative characteristic — accounting
information includes all information whose omission or
misstatement would affect the decisions of users.

Mortgage — a loan secured on property (usually having
been bought with the funds from the mortgage)

Net profit ratio — relationship between the sales and the
net profit. Measures the amount of each $ of sales that is
retained as net profit.

Net worth — assets minus liabilities

Non current assets — assets that will be of benefit to the
business in the long term

Non current liabilities — amounts that will have to be
paid in a period longer than 12 months

Opportunity cost — the cost of being involved in the
business opportunity. The benefit foregone by choosing a
particular alternative.

Owner's equity — the amount the business owes to the
‘owner, and is equal to assets minus liabilities. Also known
as Proprietorship or Net Worth.

Prepaid expenses — expenses that have been paid, but
not yet incurred. Classified as a current asset.

Prepaid revenue — revenue that has been received, but
not yet earned. Classified as a current liability.

Principles — guidelines, which assist in the accounting
system and reports to ensure that they are consistent
across time and consistent with other businesses.

Profit — excess of revenue over expenses.

Profit and loss statement — statement of financial
performance — a statement that lists all revenues and
expenses and shows the result of the trading activities of
a business for an accounting period. It is a summary
statement.

Profitability - measurement of the adequacy of the profit
received. It measures the effectiveness of the business in
using the resources available to it.

Proprietor — owner of the business

Proprietorship — Owner's equity, the amount that is
owed to the owner by the business. It is a residual of
assets minus liabilities.

Proprietary ratio — the relationship between the total

© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 92253 854 3

Glossary (cont)

assets of the business and the amount contributed by the
owner.

Qualitative characteristics — guidelines for the
preparation of accounting records and reports so that
they represent the affairs of the business in a true and
fair manner.

Quick asset ratio — measures the relationship -between
the quick assets (those than can be turned into cash
quickly) of a business and those current liabilities that
must be paid in the very short term.

Receipt — document used to record the cash received
into a business.

Relevance — qualitative characteristic — inclusion of
information that will influence the decisions of the users.

Reliability — qualitative characteristic — accounting
information must represent the affairs of the business
without bias or misstatement.

Return on assets — measures the relationship between
net profit and the assets that were used to earn it.
Measures the amount of net profit per $ of assets
employed.

Return on owner's investment — measures the
relationship between the net profit and the amount of
owner's equity in the business.

Stability — the ability of the business to pay its debts in
the long term.

Statement of financial performance — profit and loss
statement ~ a statement that includes alll of the revenues
and expenses of the business in the accounting period
and is used to report on the profit or loss.

‘Statement of financial position — balance sheet — a
statement that includes all assets and liabilities of the
business and shows the owner's equity.

Stock loss — the stock in the warehouse is less than the
stock shown in the records.

Stock turnover — measures the length of time, on
average, that the stock stays in the warehouse.

Terms of trade — the terms on which the credit customer
has purchased the goods — for example, 2% discount if
paid in 10 days, net amount due in 30 days.

Timeliness — qualitative characteristic — reports must be
prepared in sufficient time to form the basis of effective
decisions.

Transaction — economic or financial event in the life of a
business

Two-fold effect of transactions — every transaction has
two effects on the affairs of a business.

Variance — difference between the actual amounts and
the budgeted amounts on the accounting reports.

Working capital ratio - measures the relationship
between the current assets and current liabilities of the
business,

‘The main feature of the sub-tribe of animals to which modern humans belong is that they walk
upright on two legs. This feature is called bipedalism. A summary of the adaptations that humans
have for upright walking are:

+ an S-shaped spine with lumbar curve and wedge-shaped vertebrae—this bends the vertebral
column into an upright position instead of sloping forward as in chimps and gorillas (see
diagrams 1 and 2 below)

+ awide, short pelvis—this allows attachment of muscles between the legs and pelvis, which
support the upper body as we walk (see Diagram 1 below, and Diagram 5 on Page 66)

+ large hip sockets and long legs—this enables large legs that support weight (see Diagram 3)

+ carrying angle of femur—knees bent inwards for more stable standing and walking (see
diagrams 3 and 7)

+ a femur with enlarged outer condyle—this bears much of the weight in the knee (see Diagram 7)
+ arches in the foot—this allows for energy absorption and storage while walking

+ an enlarged first metatarsal and big toe—this allows for weight support while walking
(see Diagram 4)

+ acentral foramen magnum (the place where the spinal cord exits the skull)—this allows the skull
to balance on top of the vertebral column without large muscle support (see diagrams 1 and 6).

DNA: the molecular basis of heredity, found in cell nuclei, consisting of a double helix held

substances: four nitrogen ‘bases’, a sugar and phosphates. The four bases are adenine (A), thymine (T),

‘The sugar involved is deoxyribose, hence the name deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA,

Base-pairing

In the same way that jigsaw puzzles fit together, nucleotides have specific
pairing rules. Adenine on one strand will pair with thymine on the other, and
guanine on one strand will pair with cytosine, producing a ladder-like structure,

K\ DNA: the raw material of genetics

Genetics is the study of inheritance — how characteristics are passed from one generation to the next.
Genetic material is stored in the nucleus of each cell. The major bodies involved in this process are
called chromosomes, Each chromosome is made up of genes. Genes are the instructions that are
responsible for the components and appearance of an organism. They are found in the nucleus of a cell.

A gene: ihe part of a chromosome that determines the inheritance of a characteristic or of a group of
characteristics.

Each chromosome is made of a single molecule of DNA. The DNA molecule is a chain of many genes
connected together. DNA is a nucleic acid and is a very large molecule. If the DNA in a single cell was
uncoiled and put in a straight line, it would be a metre long. The backbone of the DNA molecule is two
chains wound around each other, forming a shape rather like a twisted ladder, called a double helix.
There are a large number of smaller molecules (amino acids) attached. The order in which these side
groups are attached determines the code of a particular nucleic acid. The code tells the cell how to
reproduce itself. Cells divide in an organism for growth, repair and reproduction.

Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize for their contributions to the understanding of
the genetic code. Watson and Crick came up with our current double helix (spiral) model of DNA. In
humans each DNA molecule is thought to contain from a few to many thousand genes. Each gene can
be thought of as a series of ‘rungs’ on the DNA ‘ladder’.

\\\ Gene Expression: a look at cats

Genetics and environment
The environment in which an organism lives can affect how its genetic information is
expressed. The Siamese cat has a pale coat arising from a mutation in the pigmentation
gene. Pigmentation produces an organism's colour. The Siamese mutation
(selected for by breeders because of the distinct appearance it produces) results
in the chocolate colour only being expressed at the coolest parts of the body. On
cats, these areas are the face, ears, paws and tail.

[1] Give another example of how an organism's environment can affect its phenotype.

[2] Some animats (including humans) have defective pigmentation genes, producing white hair, pale skin and red eyes with a
blue or pink iris, Name this condition,

Random X-inactivation

Another easily recognisable cat is the Calico cat, which has a ‘patchwork’ coat of yellow, black and
white. With the exception of identical twins, no two Calicos will be alike because their colouration is
randomly decided during early development. Fur colour on cats is determined by genes on the X
chromosome and the patchwork results from a process called random X-inactivation. As the name
suggests, certain instructions on the X chromosome are inactivated at random.

Female cats receive two X chromosomes (males receive one). In Calico cats, one chromosome will
contain the black gene (X”) and the other contains the (alternative) yellow gene (X’). As cells divide
during development, one X chromosome in each cell will be inactivated at random. Daughter cells
arising from the original parent cell will possess instructions to grow fur of the remaining colour.
Sometimes the genes are instructed not to produce any colour and this is where the white fur appears.
(Note: linkages to other genes are involved in this.)

Genetic issues in the 21st century

Many of you will be familiar with the term genethics, or the ethics (morals) behind genetic research, Since 2001,

complex ways, revealed the importance of re-thinking current methods of pharmaceutical development.

A species is made up of related organisms capable of interbreeding. They have a two-part name: the genus
(first letter capitalised), then a Latin species name (no capitals). Scientists classify all humans currently living on
Earth as members of a single species, Homo sapiens. The list below shows how we can classify Homo sapiens

The primates that most closely resemble humans are chimpanzees, gorillas and orang-utans. Skeletons of Homo
sapiens differ from these because of a very early adaptation to standing upright (erect posture) and walking on
two feet (bipedalism). Humans have an S-shaped spinal column, putting the centre of gravity of the human
body directly above the feet. This, and the modified pelvic region, makes walking upright easier.

Other anthropoids can walk upright to a limited extent, however, they all have spines which are straight or
arched. They also have prehensile (grasping) feet and use their front limbs (hands) to lean on when walking.

is fully opposable to the other fingers. Thus hands are able to make and manipulate tools. Tools were first

The mutagenic nature
of Agent Orange

Introduction
Mutagens are substances that can cause permanent mutations. Mutations are changes to DNA: the genetic
material responsible for controlling reproduction and the development of life. Once a mutation has occurred in
a strand of DNA, the mutation will be replicated every time the cell divides. Mutations may be beneficial, harmful
‘or may have no obvious effect. One of the harmful effects of mutations is the formation of some cancer cells.
Mutations do occur naturally, but mutagenic substances make them occur more frequently.

During the Vietnam War in the late 1960s, the US military sprayed an estimated 95 milion litres of Agent Orange (a
herbicide mix) on about 10 percent of the area of southern Vietnam. Agent Orange has since been found to contain
significant amounts of the chemical dioxin: a known mutagen. Many Vietnam War veterans have subsequently
suffered from a range of medical problems that have been attributed to their exposure to Agent Orange.

Aim
To investigate the mutagenic nature of Agent Orange.
