Agent Orange is the code name for a herbicide developed for the United States military which was primarily used in tropical

climates. Although the genesis of the product goes back to the 1940s, serious testing for military applications did not begin
until the early 1960s. Agent Orange is a 50:50 mix of two chemicals:

The combined product was mixed with kerosene or diesel fuel and sprayed from aircraft, vehicles and by hand,

Agent Orange was effective in defoliating (killing the leaves) and ultimately killing broad-teaf trees and shrubs in the dense
jungles in Southeast Asia. The goal of the largest military defoliation campaign in history was to deny the enemy food or cover

The body's defence system

Damaged cells (and white blood cells) secrete increased quantities of histamine, a hormone found in minute
quantities throughout the body. Histamine causes blood vessels to dilate, lowers blood pressure and makes

damaged tissue.

increase in body temperature and pulse rate if a large area is affected. The increased temperature of the body is
a defence mechanism to make it harder for pathogens to survive. The swelling may also be painful and throb
due to the pulse from connected arteries, Pain is also caused by the release of certain chemicals by the body.

ensure that blood clots in order to stop pathogens from circulating to the rest of the body. Macrophages
(histiocytes) are specialised types of white blood cells that are attracted to the damaged tissues. They are

BOOK 2: REPRODUCTION

The endocrine system

The endocrine system helps control our bodies by secreting (releasing) hormones from glands. Some hormones
only act on specific body parts, others cause a more general response. The principal controller of hormone
production is the hypothalamus (a part of the brain). The main glands concerned in reproduction are the
pituitary, testes and ovaries,

The pituitary is located at the base of the brain and is less than 1 cm in diameter and 0.5 g in mass. As welll as
releasing hormones that control growth and reproduction it manufactures others, which, in turn, control many
other glands.

The gonads are where gametes are produced. The male gonads are the testes and the female gonads are the
ovaries. Hormones from the pituitary gland and the steroid hormones from ovary or testis control reproductive
function in both sexes. In women, fluctuations of these hormones govern each menstrual cycle, stimulating
ovulation and preparing the uterus for pregnancy. The hypothalamus causes the pituitary gland to produce
gonadotropins — hormones that stimulate gonads.

The sex steroids also bring about the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In males, androgens
cause beard growth, deepening of the voice and increase in muscle size. Oestrogen and progesterone cause
breast development and the menstrual cycle in females. The male steroids are anabolic (building up) and
are among the banned substances that some athletes have used to encourage muscle development and
‘enhance performance.

When puberty is reached, humans produce follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH).
FSH causes the formation of sperm in males and stimulates the development of ova in females. LH causes the
production of androgens in mates and for females stimulates ovulation. FSH starts off the menstrual cycle.

The role of white blood cells

There are five main types of white blood cells or leukocytes (leuko white/colourless, cyte cell). Ail leukocytes are
formed from stem cells present in bone marrow. Depending on the cell type, the leukocyte will either mature
while still in the bone marrow or, as in the case of the T-cells, they are formed in the bone marrow then travel
to the thymus to mature. (The thymus is situated near the breastbone/tracheal region.)

There are fewer white blood cells in the blood than red blood cells. It is estimated that they are outnumbered
by at least 700 to one. However, this does not mean they are found in small numbers! In fact, a conservative
estimate would number hundreds of millions (probably more) though many die within 24 hours. Once formed,
white blood cells begin circulating throughout blood, the lymph system and tissues.

When body tissue is damaged, chemicals are released that attract white blood cells to the site of the damage.
Invading bacteria also cause the release of chemicals that attract white blood cells. The primary role of all
leukocytes is to protect the body from invasion by disease-causing viruses and bacteria. White blood cells also
perform general housekeeping duties by digesting dead and dying cells and other unwanted matter found
within the body. The three main types of white blood cells are: granulocytes, monocytes and lymphocytes.

What is life?

Characteristics of living things

Most of us can recognise the difference between living and non-living things. Living organisms are identified

* take up nutrients (organic compounds) from the environment
* reproduce (‘life arises from life’)

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY 12

Using amino acid sequences to
define evolutionary relationships

Introduction
Classification in biology is largely based on the structural characteristics of organisms. Organisms with similar
structures are placed in the same group as it is assumed that they are closely related to each other and share a
relatively recent common ancestor. However, it is often unclear which structural characteristics are more
important from an evolutionary point of view. Also, comparing structural characteristics is not generally helpful
when species are very different. The study of the biochemical similarities between organisms has recently
become possible and has provided new evidence about evolutionary relationships.

Biochemical studies have made it possible to compare the biochemicals (such as proteins and nucleic acids) in
various species. The degree of difference between the same protein or nucleic acid in different species provides
‘a measure of the length of time since the two species shared a common ancestor. This is because mutations occur
relatively regularly. So, the longer it is since a common ancestor, the greater the difference between molecules.
It is this information that can be used in conjunction with fossils and other evidence to piece together
evolutionary relationships.

Cytochrome € is a protein that first appeared in ancient bacteria about two billion years ago. It is an essential

Generally changes of state are reversible; for example, liquid water can be changed to solid ice and vice
versa. Most chemical reactions are theoretically reversible. This means that not only do reactants form
products; but (depending on conditions) products can be changed back to the original reactants.
Equilibrium reactions are special types of reversible reactions,

Alexander William Williamson (1824-1904) was the first person to systematically study reversible
reactions, He was also the first person to come up with the concept of dynamic equilibrium, Dynamic
equilibrium describes the equilibrium, or balance, of forward and reverse reactions happening simultane-
ously, Therefore an equilibrium reaction involves two reactions that are occurring at the same time but
in opposite directions, In other words, reactants are being changed to products at the same time that
products are being changed to reactants. At equilibrium, the rates of the forward reactions and reverse
reactions are the same. This is shown by using the equilibrium symbol (=).

EXTRACTION AND REFINING OF METALS

In order to extract metals from their ores, energy is needed. The more reactive the metal, the more
difficult it is to decompose (break down) its ore.

Copper The most important ores, the sulfides, contain between 1 and 12 percent of copper. Ores are
mined and then crushed and concentrated by flotation. This technique allows comparatively heavy
substances to float on water. Finely-ground copper ore is mixed with water and flotation reagents are
added, Air is blown through this mixture to form a froth. The froth mixes with the sulfide but not with
the other substances. The ore floats to the top, leaving other substances behind. Oxides and carbonates
of copper are reduced (oxygen, etc. removed) with carbon. Sulfides are smelted in a furnace, resulting in
copper that is approximately 98 percent pure, This can be further purified to 99.9 percent through
electrolysis. Electrolysis uses large amounts of electricity to attract pure copper to an electrode,

1 Define each term,

a energy b sulfide ¢ flotation d reagent e reactive
2 Draw a flow chart to show the production of copper metal from its ore.

Iron is extracted from iron ore (haematite) in a blast furnace, Coke (a form of carbon) and limestone
(calcium carbonate) are added with iron ore to a blast furnace where the raw materials are strongly
heated. The coke provides the heat to produce carbon monoxide (CO) which takes the oxygen from the
iron oxide. The limestone removes impurities, which melt in the furnace and are removed as slag. Hot
air is blown in near the bottom of the furnace. The molten iron produced is then cast into ingots. This
cast iron usually requires further treatment before it can be used.

3 Suggest why it is important to remove impurities from substances being mined.
4 Draw a flow chart to show the production of iron metal from its ore.
More active metals such as aluminium (Al) need to be extracted from their ores by electrolysis. Sodium is
extracted from sodium

Plastics and heat

Plastics are divided into two major groups according to their behaviour when exposed to heat.
Thermoplastic plastics soften when heated and harden on cooling. This means that they can be melted
down and reformed many times. Thermosetting plastics can be moulded when they are initially liquid
but once set, do not soften when heated. Bakelite was the first thermosetting plastic.

1 Give an example of when a thermosetting plastic is more useful than a thermoplastic plastic.
2. Give an example of when a thermoplastic plastic is more useful than a thermosetting plastic.

Polyethylene There are two forms of polyethylene (polythene): low-density
polyethylene (LDPE) and high-density polyethylene (HDPE). Both polymers
have ethylene (ethene) as the monomer, Figure 1 shows the structures of
ethylene and polyethylene. The polyethylene molecule consists of thousands
of repeating units; the diagram only shows a small part of the chain.

3 Give the molecular formula of ethylene.

4 The molecular formula of polyethylene is often written as (C,H,),-.
Explain what is meant by this formula.

Polyethylene is an addition polymer. It is formed by many ethylene
molecules joining together when the carbon-carbon double bond breaks, and igure 1

forms bonds with adjacent molecules. Polyethylene is very cheap, strong, flexible and chemically
unreactive, LDPE is used to make packaging materials (especially supermarket shopping bags) and HDPE

IntroductIon
The term ‘torque’ is one that is often used in relation to 
forces and their effects. Another term that means the 
same is ‘moment’. The torque or moment of a force is a 
measure of its turning effect about a point. The simple 
actions of turning a key in a lock, opening a door and 
turning a tap on or off all involve torque.
Aim
To understand the meaning of torque and look at some of 
its various applications. 
data: Force at an angle
The torque of a force depends upon (a) the size of the 
force and (b) the perpendicular distance from the line of 
action of the force to its fulcrum or turning point. Hence 
the formula for torque is: 
Torque = Force × Distance (perpendicular)
The symbol for torque is τ, and the SI units are newton 
metres (Nm). Three diagrams are supplied and you are 
asked to determine the torque in each case.

Factorising is writing an expression as a product of its factors. It is one way of simplifying an expression 
and is a necessary skill in the solution of many mathematical problems. Factorising over Q gives factors

Maximising exam marks in senior maths – advanced book 1 43
© Barbara Lynch and Blake Education 2008
22 – Checklist for success 
Revision time
Done 
✓
I have tried all my homework and asked the 
teacher about any problem areas.
I have made a revision plan by dividing the 
course into blocks of time and have worked 
hard to stick to it.
My revision plan includes recreation and 
relaxation.
My revision plan includes a couple of free 
times in case I need to catch up because of 
sickness, etc.
I have altered my revision plan if I need to 
(sickness, etc.) immediately I needed to and 
not waited until the end.
I have helped myself learn by making my own 
notes of important points with examples, and 
organising a summary of the work in my own 
words.
I have thought about key ideas and methods, 
learned formulae, made summary tables and/
or mind maps.
I have ticked off my list of things as I have 
revised and always look at how much I’ve 
done rather than how much I have left to do.
I have rewarded myself each time I reach a 
target by going to the refrigerator or watching 
TV or calling a friend.
I have moved to the next topic knowing that 
I can talk to myself about the definitions of 
terms, the key points, real examples, formulae 
and graphs.
I know what sorts of questions I am likely to 
be asked: short answer/multichoice/…
I have practised each type of exam question 
(theory, skills, interpret, analyse)
I know what to do with questions with several 
parts.
I have worked through at least the last 2 year’s 
exams against the clock in the required time 
using only the tools I am allowed to use in the 
real exam.
I have had practice working for 2–3 hours 
without a break like I will need to do in the 
exam.
I have worked out how long each type of 
question should take by dividing the total 
exam time for each type by the number of 
questions.
I have checked that I have an approved calcu-
lator and spare batteries.
I know what will be on the formula sheet 
provided.
I have checked that I have pencils, pens,  
highlighters, ruler, eraser and other math-
ematical equipment.
I know what written notes (if allowed) and 
other things I can take into the exam.
I have a watch or clock I can use.
I have checked when the exam is on and 
where.
I have worked out how long it takes to travel 
to the exam and how I will travel.
The night before the exam
Done 
✓
I have put together what I need for the exams: 
calculator, spare batteries, pencils, pens, 
highlighters, written notes (if allowed), ruler, 
eraser and other mathematical equipment, 
and a watch or clock.
I have put out the clothes I need.
I have not done any more questions or tried to 
'cram', but have just read through my notes to 
refresh my memory and looked at questions I 
have already done correctly.
I have checked the length of the paper and 
worked out how long I should spend on each 
question.
I keep telling myself how much I know and 
understand.
I have double-checked when the exam is and 
where.
Everyone works differently so you should change this checklist to suit yourself and add some other things 
if you like. The important thing is to have a plan. That way you are less likely to put off the things you find 
hard. Finally, don’t stress about a problem, do something about it: spend more time on it or see the teacher.
ISBN 978 1 92561 002 4

44
© Barbara Lynch and Blake Education 2008
 
22 – Checklist for success (cont’d)
I have double-checked my alarm clock 
(mechanical and human) to give myself plenty 
of time.
I have had a shower or a bath to relax and 
gone to bed at a reasonable time.
Exam morning
I will 
✓
Have a good breakfast or lunch before I leave 
home.
Collect all my exam equipment.
Leave home in plenty of time to get there.
Check that I am at the right room and the 
starting time for the exam.
During the exam – good habits
I will 
✓
Use my reading time to read the paper 
carefully, set times for different questions/
sections and to work out which questions I 
will do first and which ones I think are harder 
and need to be done later in the exam.
Spend the correct amount of time on each 
question and go on to the next one even if I 
haven’t quite finished because I know I will 
have most of the marks for the answer by then 
anyway.
Return to unfinished questions after I have  
attempted all the questions I need to.
Try to write something down if I have a men-
tal block because I know that writing down 
a few relevant facts, equations or formulae, 
will probably jog my memory enough to get 
started (and I won’t get any marks for a blank 
sheet of paper).
Never leave out answers to multiple choice or 
short answer questions. I will have a go since 
there are no marks lost for wrong answers and 
I won’t get marks for gaps!
Always try to ask myself 'What does the 
examiner want?'
Answer the question asked, not the one I 
think was asked.
Use the method the examiner has said to use 
(if specified).
Give the answer in the form the examiner has 
asked for (if specified).
Reread the question when I have finished to 
make sure I have answered the question
Be extra careful with questions that I find easy 
because I may not think carefully enough.
Watch out for key words like 'hence' (use 
something done or given in an earlier part) 
and 'show' (prove or demonstrate).
Not use the calculator when the question asks 
for exact answers.
Use estimation to check my answer is sensible.
Use my calculator wisely, making sure that I 
put in brackets where I need them, that I am 
in the right mode (radian/degree).
If I have a graphing calculator, always adjust 
the window so I can see the key features of 
any graph. 
If I have a graphing calculator, use the CALC 
and not the TRACE button.
Take care to not make arithmetic and 
algebraic mistakes.
Round my numerical answer at the end rather 
than during the working.
Show all my working.
Make sure my answers are written legibly and 
logically.
Make sure I have put units on the answers if 
necessary.
Above all, take the chance I have been given 
to show the examiner what I know and 
understand and will feel confident that I have 
done my best, whatever my mark.

12 – Discrete probability questions 
Some students will call these questions ‘Binomial Probability’ questions and will use a formula.  
Some will work them out by first principles or with a tree diagram. You should try these questions  
using the method that your teacher suggests. 
1 
The amount of mineral water in a bottle is advertised to be 600 mL. The probability that there is less 
water than the labelled amount is 0.12. For 5 randomly selected bottles of water, find the probability, 
correct to three decimal places that: 
a 2 contain less than the labelled amount.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b at least 2 contain less than the labelled amount.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
If the probability of selecting a boy over 2 metres tall in a town is 20 
81, 
a what is the probability, correct to three decimal places, that a 
sample of 8 has exactly 2 boys over 2 metres tall?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b what is the smallest sample size that should be taken so that the  
probability of selecting no boys over 2 metres tall is at most 0.09?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3

Each ball is replaced before the next is taken. 
a If the mean number of black ball selected is 1.6 with a variance  
of
 
24

 ii the number of balls selected. 
 
 
 
 
 
b If the box is known to contain 15 balls, how many black balls and white balls were there in the box?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4 a A machine making car parts is checked every hour. A random sample of 10 is taken as they leave the machine 
and if fewer than 2 defective parts are found in the sample then the machine is allowed to keep going. But if there 
are 2 or more defective parts then the machine is stopped and adjusted. What is the probability, correct to three 
decimal places, that the machine is allowed to keep going even though 8% of the parts being produced by the 
machine are defective?
trap

1 – probability of ‘at most 2’.

Factorising is writing an expression as a product of its factors. It is one way of simplifying an expression 
and is a necessary skill in the solution of many mathematical problems. Factorising over Q gives factors 
containing only rational numbers, while factorising over R gives factors containing irrational numbers as  
well. Expanding usually means multiplying out brackets. If you know about the Binomial Theorem, you  
can use that instead of multiplying. Some calculators can be used to factorise and expand expressions.

the question carefully or not giving the answer in the form specified. Fractions with real denominators are 
generally considered to be in simplest form. Remember, sometimes complex numbers are written as  
a + bi and sometime as a + ib. The complex plane (Argand diagram) is essential in solving many problems,

A particle P moves in a straight line such that its

Rsin(3t – α).

motion of P.

e Find the time after t = 0 when P first reaches its maximum speed.
2

is 5 units and P returns to its initial position every  
2 seconds. If the particle is initially at its extreme  
positive position:
a write down the equation for the position of the  
particle at time t seconds
b find the time the particle will take to move from its rest 
position to the point halfway between the rest position  
and its equilibrium position.
3

waves with simple harmonic motion of period 7 sec, the 
height of the waves from crest to trough being 8 m.  
a Explain why the height of the target above the trough is 
given by y = 4 + 8sin
2π 
7 t.

c A gun on the ship is aimed so that the centre of the target would be hit  
if the target stayed stationary in its topmost position. The bullet travels 
with a horizontal velocity of 2500 ms–1. By how much will the bullet miss 
the target? Assume that the ship is not rising and falling with the waves.
hint

expression first. Be careful to choose the

things to know
For simple harmonic motion (SHM) with displacement x(t) after time t, amplitude a and frequency f, x(t) = asin(2πft + α).  
If there is no displacement at time t = 0 then the phase α is zero. The period T of the motion is given by T = 1 
f .
Alternatively, the equation for simple harmonic motion can be written as x(t) = asin(nt + α) where the angular frequency 
n =2πf. Using differentiation it can be shown that v (t) = an cos(nt + α) and a(t) = -an2sin(nt + α) = -n2x(t), the condition 
for SHM. It is recommended that you use the correct terminology for centre, amplitude and period rather than personal 
notation that may be hard for the examiner to interpret.

to find α. The centre of motion is not the time.

maximum speed. Remember to solve the equations 
completely before you discard values.
things to know

you know the theory and understand the 
terminology. You have learned the formula

hint

diagram or graph to show 
the situation. Period and 
frequency should not be 
confused and be careful of 
your Algebra. Your calculator 
should be set to radians.

As well as Venn diagrams and tree diagrams, you can use other ways of counting possibilities.

Of course you don’t have to use either unless the examiner tells you to!

Earth’s atmosphere

When we think about what surrounds us, we usually say ‘the air’, Sometimes we describe the air as
‘fresh’, at other times it might be ‘polluted’. The air, in fact, is part of Earth’s atmosphere. Without the
atmosphere there would be no life on Earth as we know it. The troposphere is 78% nitrogen and 21%
oxygen, with tiny amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases. The five layers of the
atmosphere in order are named and described in the table below.

(5) CLIMATE AND WEATH

To complete this topic, students will need:
* to write answers on 8 separate sheet or in a workbook
* Internet access

*7 climate graph templates per small group for Question 4 - see inside back cover.

‘Weather is what you get and climate is what you
expect,’ This is a common description of how to
remember the difference. Two of the most common
conditions that are graphed are mean temperature
and precipitation, which are displayed either in a
tabular form or as a climatic graph (also referred
to as a climograph). The combined line and bar
graph allows for a quick, generalised assessment
of the average climate for a specific place.

DEFINITIONS
weather is the combination of atmospheric
elements such as temperature, precipitation and
humidity that occur at a specific time and place
climate describes the same atmospheric
conditions that have been averaged over a long
period - often 30 years or more

mean = the average of a set of measurements

precipitation is any water that falls to Earth in the
form of rain, hail, sleet or snow

Students will need graph paper (see inside front cover) to complete this topic.

Many scientists, geographers and environ-
mentalists believe that global warming is Earth's
greatest environmental threat. The global trend
shows increasing temperatures, which could be
caused by the enhanced greenhouse effect
trapping more heat in the lower layer of the
atmosphere. Greenhouse gases include water
vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide
and several others. Increasing amounts of
emissions add to CO, in the atmosphere. A
range of human activities contribute to these.

DEFINITIONS
environmentalists are people who show concern
for the world’s natural environment

global warming is the increase in average
temperatures over the globe

the greenhouse effect is the natural warming
caused when heat that is reflected back from
Earth is trapped by gases in the lower layers of
the atmosphere

emissions are gases and particles that are
discharged into the atmosphere

The third Australian culture - from the bush to the burbs to the beach

by Bernard Salt

The first 200 years of white settlement yielded two distinctive
Australian cultures: the bush and the city. A third culture
‘emerged in the latter decades of the 20th century and remains
ascendant ~ the culture of the beach. At the turn of the 20th
century there were 3.8 million people of various backgrounds
on the Australian continent, About 2.3 million of these lived in
inland and rural areas.

The capital cities then contained barely 1.2 million
collectively. The balance lived on the coast in port-based cities.
By the turn of the 2ist century, the number in the bush had
increased to 3.3 million, while the number in the capital cities
had skyrocketed to 12.5 million. The balance of 3.6 million
lived in coastal towns and cities. This collection of around 3
million people linked by a common geography is more than
sufficient to exert an influence over the culture of a nation
with fewer than 20 million.

At the time of Federation, the bush ruled: the swagman, the
squatter, corked hats and windmills defined the Australian
nation. But during the 20th century, things changed. The total
number living in the bush did not dectine; rather the number
living elsewhere increased at a faster rate.

This led to the rise of a distinctive second Australian culture
— the culture of the city, or more precisely, the culture of
suburbia.

But in the latter part of the 20th century, Australians forged
a new ternitory within their island continent ~ the beach
Facilitated by new values and concepts such as leisure,
entertainment, lifestyle and retirement and aided by new
social and financial arrangements such as superannuation,
Australians began clustering in large numbers along the coast
and in most parts of the well-watered edges of the continent:
along the eastern seaboard, across the Fleurieu Peninsula of
South Australia, and along the length of the south-west cape
of Western Australia,

This third Australian culture is now a critical mass. This
non-metropolitan piece of Australian geography contained 3.6
million people out of a total of 19.4 million at June 2001, up
from less than 300 000 one century before. This third
Australian culture will remain a powerful force for decades to
come, especially during the early years of the 21st century as
baby boomers greet retirement from 2006 and seek their own
version of ‘suburbia by the sea’,

ESERT LANDFORMS

Across the globe there are many dry areas that
receive 250 millimetres or less total annual
precipitation. Deserts can be hot or cold. In hot
deserts the wind and rain form the land into
different shapes. Although there is not much
water, when it falls it is usually in heavy storms.
Rain strikes the hard ground. It does not have
time to soak in so runs off in wild torrents
causing a lot of erosion. The wind in deserts is
usually strong and contains millions of sand or

a torrent is a large volume of fast-moving water

precipitation is all types of water that reach
Earth’s surface either as a liquid (rain, dew) or

erosion occurs when the land is worn away by
running water and blowing wind

deposition occurs when eroded material is carried
away and then settles in a new place

rock particles, which also cause erosion. Eroded
material is then deposited. Desert landforms are
the result of this erosion and deposition.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
37
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Customary law  
and Australian law
Objectives
l To understand that we need to have laws in 
order for society to function
l To appreciate Indigenous law
l To gain an understanding of the conflict 
between Indigenous law and Australian law 
Prior knowledge
Students should recognise right and wrong within 
a family, a community and a society and understand 
that there are consequences when the law is broken. 
Background 
Indigenous customary law came into being through 
the Dreaming, which determined the relationships 
between people and the land and became the basis 
of Indigenous culture. Laws were passed on through 
stories, song and dance. Different tribes had different 
specific laws. 
 
When laws relating to social interaction were 
broken, the elders and community members met 
with victims and offenders. They resolved the issues 
with mediation and determined the punishments, 
which were dealt out quickly – sometimes these 
punishments seem harsh and violent to Europeans. 
When laws relating to sacred matters were broken, 
the elders generally determined the punishment.
 
After European occupation, Australian law was 
written down and was the province of the judicial 
system, with resolution of crimes taking a long time 
and involving jail for some matters. This led to some 
Indigenous Australians being placed in custody and 
resulted in conflict between the cultures. 
 
Customary law is still practised today In some 
Indigenous communities. 
Starter activity
Lead a discussion about the reasons we have laws, 
how they are made and who administers them. 
Introduce the idea of more than one system of law 
operating within a region.
Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Customary law (1)’, with the 
students. Discuss the fact that different tribes had 
slightly different laws, and how this could affect people 
travelling across tribal boundaries. Students will 
complete sentence starters to summarise what they 
have read. You could tell students that current Australian 
state and territory boundaries were not finalised until 
after 1901 when they were created at the time of 
Federation. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Customary law (2)’, students 
will explore further the traditions of Indigenous law. 
Students will need a dictionary to complete the first 
question. Point out that, unlike the Australian legal 
system, customary law did not separate religion, 
traditions and social rules. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Comparing customary law and Australian law’. Students 
will learn about some traditional punishments in 
customary law, and compare the dispute resolution 
process with the Australian legal system. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Circle sentencing’, with 
the students. Sensitively discuss factors that could 
contribute to the higher percentage of Indigenous 
people in custody, such as cultural differences, lack of 
access to legal advice, and health and social issues such 
as remote locations and high unemployment rates. 
To complete the activity sheet, ‘Circle courts’, students 
will need an atlas or access to a mapping application, 
and a blank map of Australia. A map is provided on 
the CD-ROM in the Artwork > Unit 6 folder. Discuss the 
distribution of courts in relation to population centres.  
extension ideas 
Have students visit the website below to read more 
about circle sentencing and evaluate the importance 
and success of this process:
www.creativespirits.info/aboriginalculture/law/ 
circle-sentencing
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

before Europeans came to Australia. Customary Indigenous law is based on beliefs, 
culture and the land, which all came from the Dreaming. Laws were passed down 
through generations using stories, song and dance. 
Each tribe has their own system of law, so while there are many similarities between 
tribes, there are also many variations. Tribal areas were largely defined by language 
groups, although rivers and other natural features may have formed boundaries. In 
1788, there were at least 250 tribal areas. Many tribes shared common areas which 
were used for ceremonies. People asked permission of neighbouring tribes if they 
wanted to travel through their lands.

Customary law (2)
The Dreaming provides Indigenous Australians with much more than a set of rules or 
laws to follow. The Dreaming is the basis for Indigenous lore – a body of knowledge, 
beliefs, customs and traditions. Rules for how to behave (customary law), are a part of 
Indigenous lore. Indigenous lore sets out clear rules for the way society should function, 
including how everyone should behave, ceremonial relationships and who can marry.

colonists. This legal system was originally the same as the one in England. 
In remote parts of Australia, customary law is still practised and this can come into

In Australia there is a higher percentage of Indigenous Australians in jail than  
non-Indigenous Australians. In 2011, Indigenous people made up 26% of Australia’s 
prison population but only 2.5% of the total population. In the Northern Territory,  
83% of the prison population is Indigenous. 
One strategy being used in New South Wales to try and reduce the number of 
Indigenous people in jail is circle sentencing. The ‘circle’ consists of four Indigenous 
elders, the offender, the victim, a defence lawyer and a magistrate. They try to work 
out a fair sentence for the offender that does not include going to jail. They talk about 
the background of the offender and the situation, and how the crime has affected the 
victim and the community. Often the sentence involves community work. People can 
only use circle sentencing if they plead guilty. 
There are similar courts with different names in other states and territories. The 
sentences given are strict, but the process helps to reduce the number of people who  
re-offend.

Teacher’s notes – Native title
Objectives 
l To understand the reasons for native title and 
Indigenous land use agreements 
l To create and analyse a graph
l To learn about and empathise with the 
traditional values of Indigenous Australians
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of what 
belonging to a family or community means. 
They should also be aware that traditions can be 
expressed in many ways.
Background
When Australia was occupied by the Europeans, 
Indigenous people were subjected to dispossession 
of their lands and a lack of understanding of their 
culture. The Indigenous population was severely 
diminished by introduced diseases. There were 
many instances of conflict between Indigenous 
people and European settlers. In the late 19th and 
early 20th centuries, many Indigenous people 
were forced to live on missions and reserves. The 
European approach to assimilation resulted in 
the stolen generations. It was not until 1967 that 
Indigenous people were counted in the national 
census. 
 
In 1992, after ten years of hard work by Eddie 
Mabo and his friends, native title was recognised.  
However, it can be difficult to prove in the courts. 
 
Indigenous land use agreements are a voluntary 
agreement between traditional owners and people 
who want to use the land. These agreements don’t 
require native title, but can help to support a native 
title claim. They are a way for people to work out 
a mutually beneficial way of managing and/or 
developing an area. Common land uses include 
pastoral grazing and mining. 
Starter activity
Discuss native title with the students, and find out what 
they know or think they know about it. In particular, 
explore which categories of land the students think can 
be subject to native title – such as houses, farms, and 
national parks. (Many people are unaware that native 
title can only apply to government-owned land, national 
parks, public land and pastoral leases.) Record their ideas 
in a chart or mind map for later review.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘History of native title’, with the 
students. Make sure students understand that Mabo’s 
victory was important to more people than those in the 
Murray Islands – it meant that other Indigenous people 
could also apply for native title for their own land. On the 
Activity sheet, ‘About native title’, students will answer 
questions relating to the information of the Resource 
sheet.
Have students complete the cloze activity on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous land use agreements’. Tell the 
students that the areas covered by ILUAs are private and 
must be respected, which is why people need permits 
to enter places such as Uluru. It may be useful to discuss 
the similarities and differences between ILUAs and 
native title before students answer the second question. 
extension ideas
l  Review the chart from the discussion in the starter 
activity. Work with the students to correct and add to 
it as needed. 
l  Students could research the life and work of Eddie 
Mabo, and prepare a report outlining why the Mabo 
case is so important. 
l  The Indigenous Land Corporation is an independent 
statutory authority of the federal government which 
helps Indigenous people to buy and manage land. 
Students could explore their website and prepare a 
report outlining what they do, and what has been 
achieved: http://www.ilc.gov.au
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

62
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Native title
History of native title
The occupation of Australia in 1788 by the British was based on the principle 
of terra nullius, which means ‘land belonging to no one’. At the time, British law 
allowed the settlement of ‘uninhabited or barbarous country’. They did not 
understand the Indigenous way of occupying, using and connecting to the 
land. The British took over the land, especially around waterholes and areas 
with fertile soil. They built towns and tried to farm the land the way people did 
in Britain.
 
In 1982, Eddie Mabo argued that the Queensland government should 
recognise that Indigenous people on the Murray Islands, his original home in 
the Torres Strait, already had a system of law and customary use of the land 
at the time of British occupation. In June 1992, five months after Mabo’s death, 
the High Court of Australia decided that Mabo was right. Native title was 
recognised and this overturned the idea of terra nullius.
Native title means that Australian law recognises some Aboriginal and 
Torres Strait Islanders’ rights to their land and waters, based on their laws 
and customs. In order to gain native title, Indigenous people have to prove an 
unbroken connection to their land and waters.
Native title can only be gained on Crown land (government-owned land), 
national parks, public land and pastoral leases, and it cannot be sold. Native 
title allows Indigenous people to live in the area, camp, carry out traditional 
ceremonies, hunt, fish and gather food, as well as visit and protect important 
sites. Native title can only be gained through the courts.

Teacher’s notes – The Dreaming
Objectives 
l To understand the importance of mythology in 
prehistory
l To appreciate the significance of the Dreaming 
to the lives of Indigenous Australians
l To understand the relationship between the 
Dreaming stories and the Australian landscape
Prior knowledge
Students should have some experience of using 
storytelling to pass on information and ideas. 
Background
Stories played an important role in prehistoric times. 
Prehistory means ‘before written records’, and during 
this time people told stories to explain creation, 
the formation of physical features and natural 
phenomena like thunder, rainbows and stars. These 
stories taught people about traditions, culture and 
how they should live. They were told from generation 
to generation, and represented through dance, song 
and painting.  
Starter activity 
Ask students to imagine what life was like before 
people used written language. Ask questions such as: 
How do you think people communicated with each 
other? Could they communicate with people who 
lived far away? How could they remember or record 
important events? Tell students that we use the term 
‘prehistory’ to describe the time before people used 
written language. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Dreamtime, landscape 
and lifestyle’, with the students. Discuss the idea that 
the significance of the Dreaming forms the basis of 
Indigenous life, past and present, and is acknowledged 
in ‘Welcome to Country’ greetings at public ceremonies 
today. 
 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Understanding the Dreamtime’, where they summarise 
what they have learned from the Resource sheet, 
‘Dreamtime, landscape and lifestyle’. Discuss their 
answers as a class, and have students revise or add to 
their own answers to incorporate class ideas.  
 
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Creation 
story – the Rainbow Serpent’. Point out that many 
different tribes have their own versions of creation 
stories. Explain that this type of story tells of the creation 
of the landforms, vegetation and animals, as well as 
human society. Students will use vowels to complete the 
verbs in a version of the Rainbow Serpent story. 
 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘How were landforms 
created?’, with the students. Make sure students 
understand the meaning of the geological terms shown 
in bold. Explain that the Indigenous explanations are 
examples, and have been summarised. Students may 
wish to use the library or Internet to find out more 
about these explanations.  
 
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Finding landforms’, 
students will need an atlas and the Resource sheet, 
‘How were landforms created?’ They will complete a 
mapping task and comprehension questions about the 
information on the Resource sheet.
extension ideas
Research a detailed Indigenous explanation of the 
geographic features of Uluru at:
www.austhrutime.com/mythology_uluru.htm 
Other landforms such as Wave Rock, the Darling Scarp, 
Wilpena Pound, Arkaroola and the Grampians also have 
interesting stories to explain their existence. You can find 
information about these stories by selecting ‘Aboriginal 
Australia’ on the left menu of the www.austhrutime.com 
website, and scrolling down the list of articles.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
When Europeans settled Australia in 1788, life for Indigenous people was changed 
forever. Indigenous people were driven inland as the new settlers took over coastal 
land for farming. Indigenous Australians did not have any resistance to European 
diseases like influenza and smallpox, so many died – causing the population to drop, 
especially near the coast. Over time, the Indigenous people’s way of life was changed 
and their diet altered, especially with the introduction of sugar and flour. This led to an 
increase in the rate of medical problems like diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease, 
and eye and ear problems. It took much longer for Indigenous people in inland 
regions to be affected by new settlers looking for land. 
 
From the end of the 19th century until the 1970s, many children were taken from 
their families by government officials and placed in institutions. It was believed that 
this would help them to fit into European society. This caused significant and lasting 
damage to the children, their families and their tribes. 
Overall, Australia has a very high standard of living. But there are distinct 
differences in standard of living between some Indigenous and non-Indigenous 
people.

Teacher’s notes – Indigenous art
Objectives
l To understand the significance of Indigenous 
art as a way to record thoughts, beliefs and 
early ways of life
l To appreciate the Indigenous connection to the 
Dreaming
l To realise that Indigenous art is found in other 
continents
l To understand that Indigenous Australian 
painting is considered the oldest continuous  
art form known today
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of the 
Dreaming and its importance to Indigenous life.
Background
Art using a variety of mediums has been a means 
of expression for people for thousands of years. 
Petroglyphs and rock art in caves, overhangs 
and on boulders have contributed to our current 
understanding of pre-history. Humans have always 
used art in its many forms to record information 
and ideas about spirituality, lifestyle and food 
sources. Some Indigenous paintings of sailing ships 
and buffalo hunting depict contact with European 
people. As Indigenous Australian art is so significant, 
both for its spirituality and the history it records, it 
is essential that it be respected and preserved for 
all Australians. Many modern Indigenous Australian 
artists continue to pass on stories of spirituality and 
country using traditional symbols and colour. 
Starter activity
Discuss why people create art, both today and in 
the past. Ensure students understand the distinction 
between pre-history (before use of a formal writing 
system) and history (when written records were 
kept). Explore what can be learned from early art and 
why it is important to our understanding of the past.
Resource and Activity sheets
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Rock art’. 
As they complete the cloze exercises they will gain an 
overview of Indigenous art in Australia. 
Read and discuss the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous art 
styles’, with the class. Make sure students understand 
the meaning of each term shown in bold.  Then have 
students complete the questions on the Activity sheet, 
‘Different kinds of rock art’. To extend the activity, you 
could help students use the library or Internet to find 
examples of each type of art. 
Have students read the Resource sheet, ‘Threats 
to rock art’. Discuss the ways some is threatened, both 
intentionally and unintentionally. Then have studetns

Threats to rock art
Rock art is important to Indigenous Australians as it records their history and culture. 
It must be preserved so that future generations of Australians can understand it and learn 
from it. In the past, Indigenous Australians regrooved and repainted rock art to preserve it. 
Cave art at Yuendumu in the Northern Territory cave art has recently been restored.

and dust can  
cause damage

in the Northern

against paintings

Activity sheet – Land management 
Food preparation
+ 1 Cross out the incorrect word inside each set of brackets.
A lot of food was eaten (raw / rawe) by Indigenous Australians. Meat was cooked 
quickly on hot (coals / koles), mostly to remove feathers and fur, but it was not cooked 
all the way through. Some (cedes / seeds) were ground between stones to make flour, 
which could be made into cakes to be cooked on the fire or in stone ovens. Food 
could not be (storred / stored), but it was preserved in a few places. For example, 
(fish / fisch) were smoked in hollow gum trees along the lower River Murray and strips of 
(kangeroo / kangaroo) were sun-dried in some central (desert / dessert) areas.
In the 1970s, non-Indigenous Australians began to understand the use of native foods. 
Gradually kangaroo meat was legalised for sale, and then emu and crocodile (meet / meat). 
Aromatic plants like lemon myrtle and fruits and nuts such as quandong, Paterson’s plum 
and macadamia nuts, have become available. Some restaurants specialise in ‘bush tucker’ 
while others offer (native / natif) foods on their menus.

searchText:
Map symbols and key

A map uses symbols to represent features or objects on the
ground. A map is not a drawing of how things really look.
Most maps use many symbols. So we can easily understand
the map, all the symbols used are grouped together in one
place. This is called the key. Another word used instead of
key is legend. A key on one map could be called a legend on
another map.

Max Quickdrawer and Paula Mapmaker help us learn
about maps. Last week Max and Paula went on a hot-air
balloon flight. The flight left from the park near their school.
They floated over their school and landed about five
kilometres away at Cape Beauty.

Paula drew the map of Cape Beauty (on a
separate sheet) as they floated by. Paula used
symbols on her map to show clearly some of
the features that she saw. The symbols help us

MIND MAPS SHOW LINKS

This topic is suited to small group or class brainstorming activities.

A mind map is not a typical map found in an atlas or a street directory. It is a diagram that shows the
links between a main idea or theme and its subsets. A mind map provides an overview or summary
that is easy to interpret because it is in graphic form. A typical mind map can look like a tree or river
with lots of branches and sub-branches. To create a mind map, start with a main theme or idea and
group subsets around it, creating branches for each new subset or sub-subset. Some mind maps use

colour, small pictures or photos to add interest.

Mind maps provide a good opportunity for a group to brainstorm the ideas. Detailed mind maps are

Step Process
1 Schedule Once you know how much total time you have, allocate a time span to each of the steps below. Write

the minutes next to the step.

2 Brainstorm From memory write down on small pieces of paper or sticky tags as many words or short phrases your
group can associate with the topic. They should be ideas not actions. Don’t discuss the importance of
anything at this stage.

3 Organise Spread out all the pieces of paper from step 2 so that the whole group can see them. Try to find some
common threads for several bits of paper and bunch these together. Identify terms that each bunch
could be grouped under. Write these on a different-coloured piece of paper and add to the top.

4 Layout On your poster paper draw a box around the central theme. Then try to visualise the best layout for the
groups you have categorised in step 3 by placing the bits of paper onto the poster. Rearrange them if
necessary.

5 Link Think about lines and arrows that could be drawn to show some action or relationship between items.

Then create a word or short phrase as a link.

6 Complete Once the group has agreed on the arrangement of all the items, convert the map into a permanent form
by drawing and labelling the concepts and links. Use colour, different label fonts/strengths and even
small graphics to better communicate your group's understanding of the central theme.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Origins of the  
Australian continent
Objectives
l To understand the concept of supercontinents
l To understand the concept of plate tectonics 
l To learn that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander 
peoples are the original inhabitants of Australia
Prior knowledge
l Students should have some familiarity with a 
map of the world and should be able to identify 
the continents.
Background
Pangea is the name given to the supercontinent 
that once contained all the continents of the earth. 
It began to break into Laurasia in the Northern 
Hemisphere and Gondwana in the Southern 
Hemisphere about 200 million years ago. Eventually, 
Laurasia and Gondwana broke up and the continents 
drifted apart very slowly to their present locations. 
 
In 1912 Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, 
presented his theory of continental drift and 
suggested that the continents had once fitted 
together. However, the idea was not supported 
by the scientists of the time. When evidence of 
plate tectonics was discovered, scientists revisited 
Wegener’s ideas. The theories of continental drift 
and plate tectonics were accepted about 50 years 
ago. These theories helped people understand the 
dynamism of the earth and why earthquakes and 
volcanic eruptions occur in specific areas.
The concept of geological time compared to 
human time needs to be explored in order to put the 
movement of the continents, and particularly the origin 
of Australia and its first inhabitants, into perspective. 
The melting of ice caps raised the sea level and 
formed Tasmania. It also changed what we now know 
as Central Australia and demonstrates that climate 
change has always occurred.
Starter activity
Brainstorm what the students know about how 
earth’s continents came to be arranged as they are. 
Students could visit: 
http://austhrutime.com/venerable.htm  
to research the origins of Indigenous Australia.
Discuss the difference between geological 
time – millions of years – compared with the first 
settlement of Australia about 60 000 years ago.  
Ask students for their ideas about how Indigenous 
people came to Australia, and where they came from.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Origins of the Australian 
continent’, with the students. Given the continents 
that made up Gondwana, have students list the 
continents that must have made up Laurasia. Students 
could create a glossary in their workbooks, including 
supercontinent, Gondwana, Pangea and two more words 
of their own choice.
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘The 
continents’. They will need an atlas and the Resource 
sheet, ‘Origins of the Australian continent’.
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Sunda and 
Sahul’. Discuss the technique of using shading to show 
the amount of land there was during the Pleistocene 
era. You could explain that the sea level was lower due 
to lower temperatures which meant more water was 
stored in ice at the north and south of the earth. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Origins’. 
Discuss the diagrams with the students, and point out 
the vast amounts of time between the eras shown. 
Students will complete a cloze activity about the 
theories of continental drift and plate tectonics. 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Understanding our 
origins’, with the students. If they are keeping a glossary, 
students could add the terms Indigenous, archeologist 
and Sahul. To extend the activity, you could do a class 
Internet search for maps of early human migration and 
discuss what you find out. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Origin 
match-up’, in which they will match definitions to key 
terms. Students may need to refer to the Resource and 
Activity sheets in the unit. 
extension activity
l  Use the Internet to find out where recent earthquakes 
have occurred and what has happened to the land 
and people.
l  Research the movement of Indigenous people from 
the north of Australia to the rest of the continent. 
Students will find that the coastal and tropical areas 
were colonised first, but eventually desert areas and 
the Tasmanian highlands were also colonised.

Australian continent
Origins of the Australian continent
It is hard to imagine now, but Australia was once part of a huge supercontinent named 
Gondwana which existed mostly in the southern hemisphere. Before that, Gondwana 
was part of Pangea (Greek for ‘all lands’), a massive supercontinent made up of all the 
continents we know now. 
Pangea began splitting into Gondwana and Laurasia – another supercontinent – about 
200 million years ago.  Gondwana was enormous, made up of present-day Africa, South 
America, India, Australia and Antarctica.
How do we know? Some of the same kinds of rocks and fossils are found across the 
modern land masses that made up Gondwana, but not anywhere else. 
In 1861, an Austrian geologist named Eduard Suess first suggested the theory that 
Gondwana had existed. Suess realised that the fossil plant Glossopteris (a fern-like tree) 
could be found in all the land masses of the former Gondwana, and decided that this 
meant these lands were once joined together. Suess named Gondwana after a district in 
India where the fossil plant was found.

5  Read the information below and write definitions for the terms in bold, using your existing knowledge and the 
context to infer meaning.
Colossal squid have an average length of 12–14 metres, making them the world’s biggest invertebrates. They have the 
largest eyes of any species in the animal kingdom. They hunt prey using bioluminescence – emitting light to dazzle and 
confuse the intended victim. Two of their common targets are the Patagonian toothfish and the Antarctic toothfish.
Patagonian toothfish are predatory fish, closely related to Antarctic toothfish. They are found in the cold waters of many 
oceans, including the Southern Ocean of the Antarctic region. Their average weight is 9 to 10 kilograms and some are as 
long as 2.3 metres. They have extraordinary longevity; some toothfish have been known to live for up to 50 years. They 
feed on squid, smaller fish and prawns.
Sperm whales prey on various types of squid. Adult sperm whale bulls grow to around 15 metres long. Many sperm 
whales have scars on their backs, apparently caused by the barbed tentacles of the colossal squid.
Albatrosses are large seabirds that live in the Southern Ocean region. The Great Albatross has the largest wingspan of 
any bird species alive today, and can fly vast distances. Albatrosses are colonial birds who choose a mate for life, and 
nest in communities. They feed on squid, including the colossal squid, and fish and krill. Nineteen of the twenty-one 
species of albatross are currently considered to be endangered.

Because the Equator is a circle of 360 d — — — — — —, angles of latitude are measured in degrees of arc, minutes

Lines of longitude
1 Complete the passage below using words from the box.
longitude               half               London               single               imaginary               curved 
meridian                 reference                 west                 measured                 circumference                 coordinates
Angles of longitude are determined by the use of i— — — — — — — — lines (or meridians) running from the North 
Pole to the South Pole. They start at a single point (the North Pole), bulge out around the Earth’s c— — — — — 
surface, then return to reach a s— — — — — point at the South Pole. A longitude number shows the point where a 
certain m — — — — — — — meets the Equator. Every meridian crosses the Equator, so the Equator is the point of 
r— — — — — — — — for all longitude measurements. Zero degrees north / south and 90 degrees east / west 
are the c— — — — — — — — — — of the North and South Poles. These lines of longitude are m — — — — — — — 
from the central line, which is located at Greenwich in L — — — — —, England. The global standard of time 
measurement also has Greenwich as its base reference. The Greenwich Meridian is considered to represent zero  
degrees l— — — — — — — —. These angles are measured from zero to 180 degrees east or w— — — of the 
Greenwich Meridian. The location 180 degrees east of the Greenwich Meridian is the same as the location 180 degrees 
west, because 180 degrees is h— — — of the Equator’s total c— — — — — — — — — — — — (360 degrees).
Drawing lines of longitude

HINT:  Lines of longitude look like the segments of a 
peeled orange, starting at a Pole at a single point 
then curving out over the Earth’s surface and 
meeting at a single point at the opposite Pole.
At the 180 degree line of longitude in the Pacific Ocean is a 
theoretical line, known as the International Date Line, that 
separates the two hemispheres. In order to accommodate the 
locations of various island countries, this imaginary line is not 
perfectly straight. Travelling east across the line requires you to 
subtract 24 hours from today’s date. To the left of the line, the 
date is always one full day ahead of the date for the locations 
to the right.
GMT (Greenwich Mean Time) is now known 
as Coordinated Universal Time (abbreviated 
to UTC). Sometimes, it is written as GMT/
UTC. UTC is the standard time zone from 
which we measure all the other time zones 
across the world.

A battle that shaped a nation?
Prime Minister John Howard (1996–2007) believed that the battle at Gallipoli was the place  
where Australia ‘became a nation’ and that this battle shaped the Australian identity. 
Source 1: An excerpt from John Howard’s Anzac Day Parade speech given in Canberra,  
25 April 2001. 
Resource sheet – Anzac traditions
And also today we think of those still abroad in our name in places such 
as East Timor and Bougainville.
But as importantly, we gather in ever-increasing numbers to each 
pledge anew our determination, not merely to dwell upon the legacy 
of the past, but also to build upon it. To extend a culture of proud 
self reliance and personal initiative. To create a just society where 
an individual’s rights are respected but their responsibilities are also 
recognised. To offer our children, and their children, all the possibilities 
of the world should they only have the heart and the will to grasp them. 
To build strong communities where men and women strive together for 
the common good and none need live in fear or isolation.
Source: Licensed from the Commonwealth of Australia under a Creative Commons Attribution 
4.0 International Licence.  The Commonwealth of Australia does not necessarily endorse the 
content of this publication. http://pmtranscripts.pmc.gov.au/copyright
Source 2: An excerpt of an ABC interview with John Howard recorded in 2009 
where he discusses the impact of the Gallipoli battle on the Australian identity. 
It’s the undisputed iconic moment in Australian history. No matter 
how hard some people may try to say, ‘Oh, it shouldn’t be like that,’ or, 
‘It wasn’t like that,’ the fact is, it’s got this place in our hearts and our 
history that will never be removed. People rightly see it as a time and 
a place and an event, a tragic one, that put some wonderful Australian 
characteristics on display – mateship, courage ... endurance, resilience, 
ingenuity.

31
© Blake Education 2020
Irregularly enlisted 
Resource sheet – Indigenous Australians at war
EMPTY SADDLES FILLED.
UNIQUE SCENE AT RECRUITING RALLY.
	 There was a unique scene during the progress 
of the Empire Day recruiting rally at the Post 
Off ice yesterday. Until a week or two ago the 
Federal authorities had set their face against 
the enlistment of half-caste aboriginals, but now 
this condition has been waived. Following on this 
decision Chaplain Lieut.-Colonel Garland visited 
the aboriginal settlement at Barambah, where a 
number of half-castes promptly answered the call of 
the Empire. Yesterday a batch of 17 attended at the 
recruiting rally, without uniform. Shortly after 
1 o’clock the members of this newest acquisition 
to the Australian Imperial Force marched down 
Queen-street and drew up at the Post Off ice steps. 
Here Chaplain Lieut Colonel Garland delivered 
a stirring address to the thousands who had 
assembled, and during his address a long line of 
Light Horsemen, each soldier leading a horse with 
an empty saddle, trotted down Queen-street past 
the recruiting base. Chaplain Garland referred to 
his visit to Barambah, and expressed the opinion 
that very soon there would not be half a dozen 
eligible half-caste aboriginals left at Barambah. 
(Applause.) He felt sure that they would be welcomed 
as brothers and quickly made the pets of the unit 
to which they were attached. A lot was said about 
a white Australia, yet here we had the spectacle 
of half-caste aboriginals going to reinforce our 
soldiers simply because those “things” who held up 
veranda posts would not do their duty. He believed 
that Australia was worth f ighting for, but he was 
beginning to believe that there were people in 
Australia who were not worth f ighting for. It made 
his heart bleed to see the married men, the men 
over 45 years of age, the men growing old and the 
men with three, f ive, and seven children having to 
come forward simply because the young, un-married 
men would not do their duty.
	 Amid a scene of great enthusiasm, Chaplain 
Lieutenant-Colonel Garland gave the oath to a half-
caste from Barambah, bringing the total recruits 
secured from that centre to 17. The Light Horsemen 
then rode up, and amid considerable cheering the 
new recruits each mounted a riderless horse and 
proceeded up Queen-street, riding with the ease so 
characteristic of the Australian aboriginal.
ABORIGINAL RECRUITS.
	 We have received from Barambah 
Settlement a letter written on behalf of 
16 discharged coloured soldiers who want 
to know why they were discharged from the 
A.I.F. on June 13. They resent being made 
to appear as “slackers,” through no fault 
of their own. And they allege that when 
they were discharged from the military 
camp they were told that they would be 
met at the Central Railway Station by the 
Chief Protector of Aborigines, who would 
hand over to them their pay and discharge 
papers. Instead they were at the station 
handed over to a police escort, and were 
brought back to their settlement “like a 
lot of prisoners.“ The letter concludes: 
“We will ask the public of Brisbane 
and Murgon if us coloured members of 
the Empire who risked our lives and 
volunteered for the freedom and liberty 
of the British Empire got a fair do or not. 
Also we never got our pay or discharge 
papers.”
	 The military authorities explain that 
headquarters at Melbourne only gave 
approval for coloured men to be enlisted 
on condition that one of the parents was 
of European origin. That condition was 
later on qualif ied to the effect that a 
coloured man must have been associated 
with white people for some time prior to 
enlistment. The men rejected were stated 
by the military authorities to be full- 
blooded aboriginals. When they arrived at 
the camp they were specially examined by 
a medical off icer, and were subsequently 
removed from the camp as unf it for 
military duties. They were not half-
castes, and the military authorities state 
that full-blooded aboriginals are not 
wanted, as they will not make soldiers. 
The instructions issued to headquarters 
at Brisbane state that half-castes can 
be enlisted at the discretion of the 
commandant. It was pointed out that white 
men have an objection to a “blackfellow” 
being associated with them at the camp.

Excerpts from the newspaper column written by W.F. Cordett. 
The well-known N.S.W. western district heavyweight Tiny Ryan 
is lying wounded at Heliopolis, Cairo. His letter to me, dated 
June 26, supplies the following address, which I give in the 
hope that some of his friends may write to him: No. 1802, 2nd

Since my last letter to you from on board the transport I have

. . . These bombs make a very powerful explosion. We have Indian

Things are fairly quiet in the Australian trenches at the time

there is always something doing.
... I saw the Triumph sink just below our trenches. It was

Good enough to fight, but not good enough 
to vote
During World War 1, Indigenous Australians were unable to vote. Laws controlled where they lived 
and worked and who they married. Indigenous Australians fought for their country, but as a group 
they did not gain full voting rights until the 1960s and were not counted in the Census until 1967.

© Blake Education 2020
Fighting for  
the Empire
During World War 1, Australians saw 
England as the ‘mother country’. Many 
Australians wanted to fight with the British 
Empire because of this special relationship. 
+ 1	 Read Effie Kiel’s essay. Underline 
the words that show the writer 
feels she is a part of the British 
Empire. One example has been 
underlined already. 
2	 Describe how this source supports the 
point of view that many Australians felt 
they had a special relationship with the 
British Empire.
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
THE BRITISH EMPIRE.
A CHILD’S ESSAY.
At the Buln Buln East State school in connection 
with the celebration of Empire Day, a prize was 
given for the best essay on “The British Empire” 
and the prize was awarded to Miss Eff ie Kiel, 
whose essay was as follows:—
THE BRITISH EMPIRE.
The British Empire is the largest and greatest 
Empire in the World. An Empire can be great 
without being large, but the British Empire is both 
great and large. Our King rules over 400,000,000 
subjects or 24% of the earth’s population. If we 
look at the map of the world we will see that 
many places are colored red, this means that 
these places belong to the British Empire. If 
they were put together they would form a tract of 
land 12,000,000 square miles in area.
	 We can all help to make the Empire great. One man 
could not make an Empire; statesmen, explorers, 
scientists, soldiers, sailors, and many others 
are needed to make one. The British Empire was 
not formed in one year, neither was it formed 
in one hundred years. Men have been building 
it up for hundreds of years, men such as Drake, 
Raleigh, Hawkins, Blake, Nelson, Clive, Pitt, 
Wolfe and Cook. 
	 What is the reason of our Empire being so 
great? There are many reasons. Great Britain 
is surrounded by water, and thus while the 
neighboring countries were f ighting she had time 
to colonize other places. The British people are 
fond of the sea and so they are able to effectively 
protect her colonies. We should be careful not 
to become lazy or proud as our Empire will then 
decay as the Roman and Spanish Empires did. 
	 The British people have always been fond of 
liberty, but sometimes they have denied this to 
others. They taxed the Americans unjustly and 
the opium trade is a blot on their fame; but they 
treat their colonies fairly. We have one flag the 
Union Jack (red, white and blue,) the colors of 
the Empire stand for courage, purity and loyalty. 
The Union Jack floats in almost every part of the 
world and wherever we see it, it reminds us of 
the great British Empire and our responsibility 
as citizens of it. EFFIE KIEL, 12 yrs, 9 mos.

Matron Mary Anne (Bessie) Pocock (1863-1946) was an Australian nurse who served in the Boar 
War and World War 1. She received medals for her service and was described as a kind and highly 
organised nurse. These quotes are from her diary, written in 1916 when Pocock served in France.

July 6th 
Nothing in the tent to work with DREADFUL! Sister came to help 
about 9/30am. Such bad cases, poor boys, so dirty and tired. Some 
had laid out for several days, they told me. Jaw cases very bad, 
chest also. 5 operations – excise eyes, 20 operations on eyes today 
and 5 of those, both eyes gone. Poor chaps. Terrible – Terrible!
Got straight this afternoon. M.O.’s coming in all day – seeing 
eyes. Seem to forget that you are alone, trying to do all the 
smashed up and wash some dirt of(f) your men. 
. . . No time off for anyone hardly today.

If rations are good enough for men working in trenches etc. it

July 22nd
Very cold again. Did not sleep so well today . . . We do not get 
enough to eat – 2 sardines and one boiled egg alternatively. 
Awfully bad food and not enough of it.

Some buttercups blooming at my bedside in the tent. Grass a

Guns very noisy and frequent – hardly ever stop. Not many

night – still today, abdominal wounds – leg – head cases – another 
appendicitis.

24 Hour Clock #11 
24 hour clock, filling in charts, addition and subtraction 
 
The 24-hour clock is a way of keeping time where the day runs from midnight to 
midnight and is divided into 24 hours, numbered from 0 to 23.  The 12-hour clock 
requires the use of am and pm to clearly identify the time of day. Since the 24-hour 
clock uses a unique two-digit number to identify each of the 24 hours in a day, am and 
pm are unnecessary.  
 
The 24-hour clock begins at midnight (which is 0000 hours). So, 1:00 a.m. is 0100 hours, 
2:00 AM is 0200 hours, and so-on up until 11:00 am which is 2300 hours.  When 
converting from the 12-hour clock to the 24-hour clock and vice versa, the minutes and 
seconds do not change.  
 
The 24-hour clock is the most commonly used time notation in the world today. The 12-
hour clock is, however, still used in a few countries, particularly the United States, 
Canada (except Quebec) and Australia. 24-hour notation is also popularly referred to as 
military time or astronomical time in the US and Canada 
 
The military does not use a colon between the numbers. For example:  1300 hrs. 
However you will find that airlines use a colon.  For example:  13:00 hrs.  You can 
choose to use colons or not.

Area: Home Decorating #1 
Addition, multiplication, using formulas, percents 
 
What does math have to do with home decorating? Most home decorators need to 
work within a budget. But in order to figure out what you'll spend, you first have to 
know what you need. Understanding some basic geometry can help you stick to your 
budget.  In this section we will learn how to calculate the area of a square and 
rectangle.  We have used inches and feet in this section as most carpenters and building 
stores still use the imperial system. 
 
Area of a square or rectangle = Length x Width  
A = L x W 
 
 
Example: 
Imagine you're planning to buy new  
carpet for your home. You're going to  
put down carpet in the living room,  
bedroom, and hallway, but not in the  
bathroom. The diagram beside shows  
you the dimensions of each room.  
 
Problem: 
Calculate the square footage of all the space except the bathroom.  Most 
contractors work with the imperial system when calculating area.  Most 
materials come in square feet. 
 
Solution: 
Step 1: 
Start by figuring the total area of the floor plan.  
 
 
A = L x W 
 
 
L = 7 feet + 5 feet + 10 feet = 22 feet 
 
 
W = 7 feet + 5 feet = 12 feet 
 
 
A = 22 feet x 12 feet = 264 square feet  
 
Step 2 
Calculate the area of the bathroom. 
 
 
A = 7 feet x 5 feet = 35 square feet 
 
Step 3: 
Subtract the total area from the area of the bathroom. 
 
 
264 square feet – 35 square feet = 229 square feet 
The square footage of all the space except the bathroom is 229.

Area: More on Home Decorating #2 
Multiplication, exponents, addition, using formulas, percents, rounding decimals 
 
Calculating how much carpet you'll need is a fairly simple task if your home has only 
square or rectangular rooms. But what if you have a circular alcove at the end of one 
room? How do you figure the area of a circle? Geometry comes to the rescue again with 
a handy formula: 
Area = Pi x radius2 
 
 
 A =  x r2 
 
A circle's radius is one half of its diameter, or one half of what you get if you measure 
all the way across its widest part. "Squaring" something means you multiply it by itself. 
Pi is a number that roughly equals 3.14159; we usually round it off to 3.14. 
 
 
Example: 
If your living room has a semi-circular  
alcove as in this floor plan you'll  
need to use this additional equation to  
figure out its area.   
 
Problem:   What is the square footage of the  
living room? 
 
Solution: 
Step 1: 
To figure the radius of your alcove (the number you'll  
need to plug into the equation) you'll divide its diameter in 
half. Its diameter is the same as the width of the living room: 
12 feet. Half of that is its radius: 6 feet. 
 
Step 2: 
A = 3.14 x (6 feet x 6 feet)  
A = 113 square feet (rounded to the closest square foot)  
 
Step 3: 
If your alcove were a complete circle, it would have an area of 
113 square feet. Because it's a half circle, the area is half of 113 
 
113 ÷ 2 = 56.5 square feet.

Area: Painting Your Home #3 
Addition, multiplication, division, estimation 
 
To calculate how much paint you will need for one room you will need to find the area 
of all the walls in the room.  We already know that A = L x W.  Paint comes in 1 gallon 
cans.  1 gallon of paint will cover 350 square feet. 
 
 
Example: 
The Triggs family want to paint their living room walls a pale yellow. 
They will need to do two coats.  How much paint will they need?  The 
dimensions of the living room are below.   
a. Wall one: 16 feet by 10 feet 
b. Wall two: 16 feet by 10 feet with a window that is 3 feet by 5 
feet 
c. Wall three: 12 feet by 10 feet  
d. Wall four: 12 feet by 10 feet with a doorway that is 3 feet by 8 
feet. 
 
Problem: 
Calculate the area of all the walls.  Make sure you subtract the area of the 
window and door. 
 
Solution: 
Step 1:   
Calculate the area of all the walls 
a. Wall one: A = 16 x 10 = 160 square feet 
b. Wall two: A = 16 x 10 = 160 square feet (subtract square 
footage of window) 
Window: A = 3 x 5 = 15 square feet 
Wall two: 160 – 15 = 145 square feet 
c. Wall three: A = 12 x 10 = 120 square feet 
d. Wall four:  A = 12 x 10 = 120 square feet (subtract square 
footage of door) 
Door: A = 3 – 8 = 24 square feet 
Home Math Workbook
14
Measurement in Your Home

Wall four: 120 – 24 = 96 square feet 
Total area = 160 + 145 + 120 + 96 = 521 square feet 
Total Area = 521 square feet x 2 coats = 1042 square feet 
Step 2: 
Calculate the amount of paint when 1 gallon covers 350 
square feet.  
1042 square feet ÷ 350 square feet = 2.98  
The Triggs family will need 3 cans of paint.

square feet.

Australia has three time zones (ignoring daylight saving in summer):

Eastern Standard Time is 30 minutes ahead of Central Standard Time.
