Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Conversions – length, time 
1
When you measure quantities such as distance, speed and mass, you need to use different units 
of measurement – depending on which quantity is being measured, and in which country the 
measurements are being made.
In Australia, metric units of measurement are used such as centimetres, metres, kilometres, 
kilometres per hour, grams and kilograms. In the USA, Imperial units of measurement such 
as feet, inches, miles, miles per hour, pounds and ounces are used. In Britain, metric units 
are often used for mass and some lengths, but road distance and road speeds are commonly 
measured in miles and miles per hour.
The size of the quantity you are measuring often  
determines the units to use. For example, the speed of  
a marble rolling along the floor would normally be  
measured in metres per second. Land speed records  
in a car would be measured in kilometres per hour.
So if the speed of a skater is measured in kilometres  
per hour in one place, and in miles per hour in  
another place, how do you compare them?  
The secret is in converting units of measurement,  
so you can make meaningful comparisons.
Converting units of length or distance
The metric system of measurement makes it easy to convert units. It involves either 
multiplying or dividing numbers by tens, hundreds, thousands and so on. For quantities such 
as length and mass, conversions can be made by simply moving the position of the decimal 
point in numbers an appropriate number of places in the correct direction. 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
Sprint your way through the following metric conversions.  
Remember:
•  when you are converting from a smaller unit to a bigger unit, the appropriate 
number or factor should be divided 
•  when you are converting from a bigger unit to a smaller unit, the appropriate 
number or factor should be multiplied.
a  1.6 kilometres (km) =                    metres (m)
b 256 millimetres (mm) =                    centimetres (cm) [to 1 decimal place]
c  14 m =                     cm
d 765 m =                    km (to 3 decimal places)
Imperial units of length include inches, feet, yards and miles. 
Conversion between units does not involve multiplying or dividing 
numbers by tens, hundreds or thousands. Some examples are 
shown in the box at the right.
When converting from Imperial units of measurement to  
metric units and vice versa, it is helpful to know the 
conversion factors – that is, the numbers by which you 
multiply or divide to correctly convert the units.  
Some examples are shown in the box at the right.

12 inches (in) = 1 foot (ft)
3 feet (ft) = 1 yard (yd)
5280 ft = 1 mile (mi)
1760 yd = 1 mi

Converting units of time
Time is measured by the same units everywhere, and these 
units include seconds, minutes and hours. When comparing 
or converting time units from one to another, it is helpful to

When converting time, it is important to understand when and how to convert

First convert 0.89 hours to minutes:

Some foods cannot be cooked all at once.  You must cook them in several

Susie’s Crazy Day
 
Susie got up late this morning. She was in a rush to get the kids dressed, fed and out 
the door.  She made oatmeal for the kids but didn’t have a chance to eat any herself.  
She grabbed a bagel as she ran out the door. 
 
At school, Susie was really busy finishing off a project about her community.  She had 
to go to different businesses and community organizations to find out more 
information.  She was really hungry at break time and ate an apple, a yogurt and she 
had a glass of juice and coffee with sugar.   
 
At lunch she rushed home to greet her children and make lunch for them.  Every day 
the children come home for a hot lunch.  She had some left over caribou stew from last 
night.  They each had one bowl of stew and some bannock.  After walking the children 
back to school, Susie headed over to the learning centre.   
 
When she arrived at the learning centre, class was already underway.  She slipped into 
her desk after getting herself some coffee and started working on her math.  She was 
hoping to complete her 130 level this term and start the 140 level in February, although 
she struggled with algebra sometimes.  Finally, it was break time, and someone had 
brought in dried fish.  She devoured two pieces and went back to work on her math.  
 
When school was done, she headed home to get supper ready so she could get her two 
boys to the hockey rink by 6:00 pm.  They were in a tournament this weekend.  She was 
rushed so she made macaroni and cheese with some frozen vegetables on the side.  She 
also enjoyed a can of diet coke at the rink. 
 
After a long day of school, hockey and homework, Susie finally put the boys to bed and 
then enjoyed a big helping of ice cream!

More on Calories #25
Order of operations, multiplication, addition, rounding to the hundredths place 
 
Use the information below to figure out how many calories you should be eating each 
day.  You will need to know how much you weigh in kilograms and how tall you are in 
centimetres.  Round your answers off to the nearest one hundredth (two decimal 
places). 
 
Note:  
1 foot = 12 inches  
1 inch = 2.54 cm. 
 
1 kilogram = 2.2 lbs. 
 
The Harris-Benedict formula 
The Harris-Benedict equation is a calorie formula using the factors of height, weight, 
age, and sex to determine basal metabolic rate (BMR). This makes it more accurate than 
determining calorie needs based on total bodyweight alone or just age. Follow the 
formulas below. 
Men: BMR =  
66 + (13.7 X wt in kg) + (5 X ht in cm) - (6.8 X age in years) 
Women: BMR =  655+ (9.6 X wt in kg) + (1.8 X ht in cm) - (4.7 X age in years) 
 
 
Example:  
You are a 30 year old female.  You are 5' 8 " tall and you weigh 150 lbs. 
Problem: 
How many calories should this person eat each day? In other words what 
is the BMR for this person? 
Solution: 
First you must figure out the weight in kilograms and then the height in 
centimetres.  Round your answer off the nearest calorie. 
 
 
150 lbs ÷ 2.2 = 68.18 kilograms 
 
 
5’ 8”= 68 inches (5 feet = 60 inches plus 8 inches) 
 
 
68 inches x 2.54 = 172.72 cm 
BMR = 655 + (9.6 x 68.18 kg) + (1.8 x 172.72) – (4.7 x 30) 
 
 
 
  655 + (654.53) + (310.896) – (141) = 1479.426 
 
 
 
  This person should eat 1479 calories per day

Nutrition Math Projects
 
Nutrition is an important part of our everyday life.  Here are some projects on nutrition 
that you might think about doing on your own or with your class. 
 
1. Develop a week-long meal plan that is nutritionally balanced for you or for your 
family.  Use the NWT Food Guide as a guide for planning your meals.  You can 
download a copy of the NWT Food Guide from 
http://www.hlthss.gov.nt.ca/pdf/brochures_and_fact_sheets/healthy_eating_and_act
ive_living/2005/english/nwt_food_guide.pdf  
2. Team up with the Community Health Representative in your community and 
develop a workshop on calorie intake and BMI.  Offer the workshop to children and 
teens at the local school.  You can ask them to figure out how many calories they 
should be eating and hand out the BMI chart.   
3. Make a poster for the community on calorie intake and BMI.  Put it up around town 
for people to read. 
4. Keep a food diary of all the food you eat in one week including quantity.  Research 
on the Internet how many calories are in each food that you ate.  Calculate how 
many calories you ate in one week and compare it to how many calories you should 
be eating.   
5. Compare nutrition food labels and make a list of what foods are better to eat. For 
example you could compare two different kinds of pizzas from the local store.  
Compare the calories, fat and fiber.  Give a presentation to your class on which 
foods are better than others.

Perimeter #4 
Addition, multiplication, estimation 
 
Perimeter is the distance around a 2-dimensional object.  We use perimeter to measure 
the distance around the yard so we can order the correct amount of fencing.  We can 
also use perimeter to measure the distance around a room to plan for installing base 
boards.   
 
For perimeter of a square, triangle or rectangle you simple add each side up or 
multiply the length by 2 and the width by 2. 
 
 
Example: 
Lisa and Mike would like to install a new fence around their property.  
They would like to put in a wood fence that is 6’ tall so their dogs can’t get 
out.  The width of their yard is 50 feet and the length is 40 feet.  They will 
also need to put in a post every six feet to secure the fencing.  The posts 
cost $13.50 each.  Fencing costs $8.50 per foot.   
 
Problem 1: Calculate the perimeter of their yard. 
 
Solution 1: P = 2W + 2L  
P = 2 x 50 feet + 2 x 40 feet 
 
P = 180 feet 
 
Problem 2: How many posts do they need? 
 
Solution 2: 180 feet ÷ 6 feet = 30 posts 
 
Problem 3: How much will it cost in materials for the fence? 
 
Solution 3: Posts  
 
30 posts x $ 13.50 = $405 
 
 
Fencing 
 
180 feet x $8.50 = $1530 
 
 
Total   
 
$405 + $1530 = $1960 
 
 
The total cost for the materials for the fence is $1960.

Multiplication and division 
 
The class wants to have a cookout with their families.  The students are planning the 
menu now.  They need to know how much food to buy for everyone.

cookies.  One package of cookies has 12 cookies.

They will need 66 cookies for everyone.

Round to the nearest whole number  6

Saving on Electricity #20 
Order of operations, subtraction, multiplication, division, percents 
 
Before we see how much electricity costs, we have to understand how it's measured. 
When you buy gas they charge you by the litre. When you buy electricity they charge 
you by the kilowatt-hour (kWh). When you use 1000 watts for 1 hour, that's a kilowatt-
hour.  For example:

Watts and watt-hours 
Watts is the measure of the rate of electrical use at any moment. For example, a laptop 
computer uses about 50 watts.  If your device lists amps instead of watts, then just 
multiply the amps times the voltage to get the watts. For example: 
2.5 amps   x   120 volts   =   300 watts 
 
What is the difference between watts and watt-hours: 
• 
Watts is the rate of use at this instant.  
• 
Watt-hours is the total energy used over time.  
 
How much does electricity cost? 
The cost of electricity depends on where you live, how much you use, and possibly 
when you use it. There are also fixed charges that you pay every month no matter how 
much electricity you use. Check your utility bill for the rates in your area. If it's not on 
your bill then look it up on the utility's website.

Short Cut to Converting Temperatures #6 
Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, positive and negative numbers (addition and 
subtraction) 
 
Short-cut Method #1 
To convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit try this short cut method: 
 
Step 1:   
Double the temperature:   
17°C + 17 °C = 34 
Step 2: 
34 is in the 30s, so subtract 3 (if the number is in the 40s, subtract 4): 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
34 - 3 = 31 
Step 3: 
Add 32: 
 
 
 
31 + 32 = 63°F 
 
If the number in Step 2 is going to be a negative number then you must add in the 
second step. 
Step 1: 
Double the temperature  
-10 °C + (-10 °C) = - 20 
Step 2: 
-20 is in the 20’s, so add 2 
 
-20 + 2 = -18 
Step 3: 
Add 32 
 
 
 
-18 + 32 = 14 °F 
 
To convert form Fahrenheit to Celsius try this short cut method: 
 
Step 1:   
Subtract 32:  
 
 
50°F - 32 = 18 
Step 2: 
18 is in the 10s, so add 1:  
18 + 1 = 19 
Step 3: 
Cut in half:   
 
 
19 ÷ 2 = 9.5°C 
 
If the number is going to be negative in Step 2 you must subtract in the second step. 
 
Step 1: 
Subtract 32  
 
 
10°F - 32 = - 22 
Step 2: 
-22 is in the 20’s so subtract 2 -22 - 2 = -24 
Step 3: 
Cut in half  
 
 
-24 ÷ 2 = -12°C

Should You Replace Your Refrigerator? #21 
Reading charts, multiplication, division, comparison 
 
In most homes the refrigerator is the second-largest user of electricity (13.7%), right 
after heating costs. With most appliances you save energy by using them less, but you 
can't very well do that with your fridge. The main way to save money with your fridge 
is to use an efficient model. New fridges aren't just a little more efficient, they're 
incredibly more efficient. A 1986-era fridge uses 1400 kWh a year, while a post-2001 
fridge uses only 500 kWh - a 64% savings. And the most efficient fridges use as little as 
200 kWh. 
 
Here are some sample yearly costs to run various fridges, based on an average NWT 
rate of electricity (24 cents per kWh) 
• 
$336 - Old 1976-86 fridge (1400 kWh/yr.)  
• 
$120 - Post-2001 fridge (500 kWh/yr.)  
• 
$102 - Post-2001 Energy Star fridge (425 kWh/yr.)  
  
Should you get a new fridge? 
Should you replace your current fridge with a newer, more efficient model? If your 
fridge was made before 2001, then yes, you should probably trade it in. If it's 2001 or 
later, it's probably better to hold onto it until it needs replacing.  
 
Let's take a look at the typical electrical savings by upgrading to a new, efficient fridge 
based on what year your existing fridge was made.

Assumes electricity rate of $0.24 per kWh 
 
So now we're ready to figure out whether it makes sense to replace our current fridge. 
  
1. Find the annual cost of your current fridge. 
If you no longer have the paperwork that came with your fridge you can most likely 
look up the brand name and find the rating on the Internet. Figure your annual cost. 
For example, if your fridge uses 800 kWh/yr. and you're paying 24¢/kWh, then 
you're paying $192/yr. to run it.  
 
2. Find the annual costs of the fridge you'd like to buy. 
The annual kWh usage of the new fridge is printed on the yellow label on the fridge. 
Even if you shop online you'll still see the kWh per year listed. Once you know the 
annual kWh, multiply it by the amount you pay for electricity. For example, if the 
fridge you'd like to buy uses 425 kWh a year and you pay 24¢ kWh, then it'll cost 
you 425 x $0.24 = $102/yr. to run this fridge. 
 
3. Figure the annual savings. 
Take the old fridge's cost minus the new fridge's cost to find the savings. 
 
4. Figure out how many years it will cost to pay off the fridge using your electricity 
savings. 
Take the cost of your fridge – say $895 and divide it into the savings per year in 
electricity – say $233 per year.  It will take you 3.8 years to pay off your fridge with 
your savings.

Temperature #5 
Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, positive and negative numbers 
 
Temperature is a form of measurement.  Temperature is a degree of hotness or coldness 
that can be measured using a thermometer. It's also a measure of how fast the atoms 
and molecules of a substance are moving. Temperature is measured in degrees on the 
Fahrenheit, Celsius, and Kelvin scales. 
 
In the 1700s, G. Daniel Fahrenheit developed a scale used by meteorologists for 
measuring surface temperature. The scale was named for the developer, and the unit of 
measure has become known as degree Fahrenheit (°F).  
 
Also in the eighteenth century, a second scale was developed for measuring surface 
temperature; it became known as the Celsius scale. The unit of measure in the Celsius 
scale is the degree Celsius (°C).  
 
A third scale later developed for use by scientists became known as the Kelvin scale. 
This scale begins at absolute zero and is sometimes more convenient to use because it 
does not involve negative temperatures. (The word degree is not used in Kelvin 
measure.)  
 
The United States primarily use the Fahrenheit scale, the rest of the world uses the 
Celsius scale, and scientists use either the Celsius or Kelvin scale. Since we can use 
three different scales to measure temperature, it seems reasonable to have formulas for 
changing or converting from one scale to the other. Here are some useful conversion 
formulas.  
C° = (F° - 32°) ÷ 1.8 
F° = 1.8 x C° + 32 
K = C°+273

Time #10 
Addition, subtraction, problem solving 
 
Time is a funny thing.  Often we run out of time during the day or find 
ourselves rushing to get to places on time.  For many cultures time is 
attached to the seasons: time for fishing, time for hunting or time for 
resting.  In this day and age, we are ruled by the clock.   
 
Don't forget there are: 
1. 15 minutes in quarter of an hour.  
2. 30 minutes in half an hour.  
3. 60 minutes in an hour.  
4. 12 hours in half a day.  
5. 24 hours in a whole day.  
 
Directions:  Read the following word problems and solve. 
 
1. Lisa has to be at work for 7:00 pm – she will work a 10 hour shift.  When does she 
get off? _____________________ 
2. You get home at 5:15pm and you have a friend coming to pick you up to go to a 
party at 8:30. You have to do the following: 
• switch the laundry (5 min) 
• walk the dog (30 min) 
• gather and take out the trash (10 min) 
• cook and eat dinner (60 min) 
• do the dishes (20 min).  
• shower (10 min) 
• do your hair (15 min) 
• iron clothes (10min) 
• get dressed (10 min) 
a. Do you have enough time before your friend comes? _________________ 
Home Math Workbook
39
Measurement in Your Home

 
b. How much time do you have left or how much time do you need? 
_________________ 
3. Jill works from 7:00 am to noon and then from 4:00 pm to 11:00 pm.  How many 
hours does she work? _____________________ 
4. You have to be at work for 8:30 am.  These are the things you must do: 
a. Walk the dog (15 min) 
b. Have breakfast (10 min) 
c. Feed your children breakfast (15 min) 
d. Have a shower (15 min) 
e. Get dressed (5 min) 
f. Get your children dressed (10 min) 
g. Walk your children to daycare (15 min) 
h. Walk to work (10 min) 
i. Pick up a coffee (10 min) 
a. When should you wake up if you want to make it to work on time? _________ 
b. Where do you think you can cut down on time? ________________________ 
5. The movie starts at 7:30 pm.  You get off work at 5:00 pm.  You have to do the 
following before you go to the movie and you would like to get there 15 minutes 
ahead of time. 
• Pick up your daughter from after school care (15 min) 
• Make supper (40 min) 
• Eat supper (20 min) 
• Clean-up (10 min) 
• Walk the dog (20 min) 
• Make lunches for the next day (20 min) 
• Bike to the theatre (10 min) 
a. Will you make it on time? __________________________ 
b. How much time do you have to spare or need? _______________________

Weight and Height #9 
Converting metric to imperial and vice versa, multiplication, division 
 
What do you weigh yourself in - kilograms or pounds?  How do you 
measure your height - in feet and inches or centimetres?  Most people 
use the imperial measurement system (pounds and inches) to weigh 
and measure themselves, even though Canada switched over to the 
metric system almost 40 years ago.  Sometimes on forms we are asked 
for our weight and height in metric terms, so it is good to know how to convert pounds 
to kilograms and vice versa and inches to centimetres and vice versa.  
 
2.2 pounds = 1 kilogram. 
1 inch = 2.54 centimetre 
1 meter = 3.2808399 feet 
1 foot = 12 inches 
 
 
Example: 
Lisa goes to the doctor’s office and she is asked to write down how 
much she weighs in kilograms and what her height is in 
centimetres.  She only knows how much she weighs in pounds 
and how tall she is in feet and inches.  She weighs 140 lbs and is 5’ 6” 
tall. 
 
Problem: 
Convert Lisa’s weight to kilograms and her height to centimetres.

Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Australia has three time zones (ignoring daylight saving in summer):
• 
 Eastern Standard Time is used in Queensland, New South Wales (excluding Broken Hill), 
Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT.
• 
 Central Standard Time is used in South Australia, the Northern Territory and Broken Hill.
• 
 Western Standard Time is used in Western Australia.
Eastern Standard Time is 30 minutes ahead of Central Standard Time.  
It is 30 minutes earlier in Adelaide than Brisbane. 
Eastern Standard Time is 2 hours ahead of Western Standard Time.  
It is 2 hours earlier in Perth than Brisbane.
Papua New Guinea is also in this time zone. 
1 
When it is 8:00 am in Sydney, what is the time in 
a Brisbane? 
b Adelaide? 
c Perth? 
d  Port Moresby (Papua New Guinea)?

a Sydney? 
b Darwin?
 
Central Standard Time is 30 minutes behind Eastern Standard Time.  
It is 30 minutes later in Melbourne than Adelaide.  
Central Standard Time is 1 hour and 30 minutes ahead of Western Standard Time.  
It is 1 hour and 30 minutes earlier in Perth than Adelaide.
Japan, Korea and the eastern part of Indonesia are also in this time zone.
3 
When it is 12 noon in Adelaide, what is the time in 
a Melbourne? 
b Perth? 
c Tokyo (Japan)? 
d Seoul (South Korea)?

a Adelaide? 
b Hobart? 
Western Standard Time is 2 hours behind Eastern Standard Time.  
It is 2 hours later in Sydney than Perth.

It is 1 hour and 30 minutes later in Adelaide than Perth.
China, Malaysia and the Philippines are also is this time zone.

searchText:
8 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Elephants in Thailand 
3
The Asian elephant is a smaller cousin of the  
African elephant, with relatively smaller ears.  
It is the largest terrestrial mammal in Asia. 
The elephant’s massive size and strength  
made it a reliable beast of burden. It is  
a national symbol of Thailand and has  
served many roles in that country’s  
long history. It has been used in timber  
logging, as a war machine and in  
processions and ceremonies. 
In 2010, it was estimated that only  
about 2 000 wild elephants remained in  
the forests of Thailand. It was estimated  
there were approximately 3 000  
domesticated elephants. 
Today, domesticated elephants are  
more likely to be seen carrying tourists  
or performing in some form of  
entertainment than working in  
the jungle or on farms.
1 
Around 1900 it was estimated that there were at least 100 000 domesticated elephants 
working in Thailand. By 1952, that number had dropped to around 13 400. 
 
In 2010, it was estimated that there were only 3 000 domesticated elephants and  
2 000 wild elephants in Thailand.
 
Express the number of domesticated elephants in Thailand in 2010 as a percentage of 
a the number of domesticated elephants in 1900. 
b the number of domesticated elephants in 1952.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
c the total number of elephants in 2010.
d the number of wild elephants in 2010.
2 
Tan is a mahout (an elephant handler). He is 1.68 m tall and has a mass of 68 kg. 
 
His elephant is 2.8 m tall and has a mass of 4.76 tonnes (4 760 kg).
a Express Tan’s height as a percentage of the height of his elephant. 
b Express Tan’s mass as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
3 
Tan’s elephant eats around 135 kg of plant matter each day. 
 
Express this as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
9
Once they are born, baby elephants enjoy a 3 to 5 year childhood before their training begins. 
They learn to push, carry and stack logs as well as how to walk in a procession.  
Working elephants have a career of about 50 years. 
4 
Tan began training his elephant when it was 4 years old.  
The training took 5 years.  
Tan and the elephant then began work.  
His elephant is now 25 years old.
a How many years has the elephant been working? 
b What percentage of its life did the elephant spend in training? 
c What percentage of the elephant’s life has it been working? 
5 
The law in Thailand requires working elephants to be retired at age 61 after working  
for 50 years. They are usually released into the wild. 
 
An elephant at a sanctuary is 72 years old. 
 
What percentage of its life did the elephant spend working?  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
Each year, the town of Surin in north-eastern Thailand hosts an Elephant Round-up Festival. 
More than 300 domesticated elephants are brought to the town by their mahouts.  
The festival lasts 10 days. The elephants demonstrate their skills and participate in parades 
and battle re-enactments. 
6 
The average elephant drinks 160 litres of water each day. 
a How many kilolitres of water are needed for each elephant for 10 days? 
b How many kilolitres of water are needed for 300 elephants for 10 days? 
7 
The average elephant has a mass of 4 800 kg.  
It eats 130 kg of plants and vegetables each day. 
a What is the total mass of plants and vegetables the average elephant will eat  
during the 10 days of the festival?  
b Express this as a percentage of the mass of the elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
8 
A female elephant stands 2.3 metres in height and has a normal mass of 3.2 tonnes  
(3 200 kg). She gave birth to a baby. Shortly after birth, the baby stood 90 centimetres 
high and had a mass of 90 kg.
a Express the baby’s height as a percentage of its mother’s height.  
Answer correct to the nearest whole number.
b Express the baby’s mass as a percentage of its mother’s mass.  
Answer correct to one decimal place.
9 
A male elephant has a mass of 3.4 tonnes.  
Its brain has a mass of 5 kg. Express this as a percentage of the elephant’s mass.  
Answer correct to two decimal places.

The Islamic architecture of the Moghul period in India  
is a fusion of Arab, Central Asian, Persian and Hindu  
elements. The best known example is the Taj Mahal  
which was completed in 1648.
1 
Kathryn and Adam were visiting the Taj Mahal.  
They were amazed at the symmetry and beauty  
of this building. Adam noticed this tessellation  
in a section of paving. The pattern is formed by

on the tessellation.

b How many axes of symmetry are there  
in the unit square?   
 An axis of symmetry is a line where the figure  
can be folded or reflected so that the two halves  
match exactly.
 Draw the axes of symmetry on the diagram. 
c What is the order of rotational symmetry  
of the unit square? 
A figure has rotational symmetry if it exactly  
matches its original position more than once  
when it is turned through one revolution.

It is also formed by repeatedly translating a square unit.

Knots and naughty miles 
16
World War 1 was largely fought and won on land but this could not have taken place without the 
movement of ships. Ships were used to transport supplies and manpower needed on the battlefields 
from overseas countries. Command of the seas and supply lines was essential to the armed forces 
on land.
The nautical mile is based on the circumference of the planet Earth. If you divide the circle 
made by the equator into 360 degrees and then divide a degree into 60 minutes, a single 
minute of arc on the planet Earth is 1 nautical mile. The nautical mile NM is a non-SI unit 
used mainly by navigators in the shipping and aviation industries.

The device that sailors used to make their measurement of speed was a rope with knots tied 
at equal distances along it, tied to a chip of wood. The sailor would throw the chip of wood 
over the side and when the chip was in the water they would start to count the number of 
knots that passed over the back of the ship in thirty seconds. This was the speed the ship was 
travelling. The knot is defined as one nautical mile per hour.

a  10 knots pass in 30 seconds? 
b 15 knots pass in one minute?

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
We use electrical energy to power our homes, 
schools and places of work. Generating 
electricity by burning coal or gas in a power 
station is not sustainable, and produces carbon 
dioxide. Using sunlight to make electricity 
is sustainable. A solar panel is a grid of 
photovoltaic cells that convert sunlight  
into electric power. 
Power is measured in watts.  
One kilowatt (kW) = 1000 watts (W). 
A single solar panel produces between  
100 and 200 watts, depending on the brand  
and size. A system of several panels can be 
installed on a house roof to generate some  
or all of the energy used by the household.
1 
How many 100 W panels are needed to produce each amount of electrical power? 
a 1 kW 
b 3 kW

What is the total power generated? Answer in kilowatts.

a What is the area of the panel in square millimetres? 
b Converting to metres, the panel measures               m long by               m wide. 
c What is the panel’s area in square metres?
d How many square millimetres are there in one square metre? 
4

each 1.8 m long and 1.1 m wide. The roof is a rectangle 30 m long and 8 m wide.
a What is the area of one solar panel in square metres?

c What is the area of the roof?
d What percentage of the roof area is covered with solar panels?
e How many whole panels will fit across 30 metres of roof if each panel is 1.1 m wide  
and they are laid side-by-side?

How many panels will that be?

© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
Anyone who has a garden and a water 
supply can grow food. People without 
gardens can join a community garden, 
or share a friend’s garden. 
Food grown at home doesn’t need 
transporting which reduces greenhouse 
gases. Home gardeners can control how 
much pesticide and artificial fertiliser 
they use, and home-grown vegetables

those bought in shops.

Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The city of Angkor was the capital of the Khmer 
Empire. Its ruins are located near the modern 
city of Siem Reap in Cambodia.
The temples of Angkor were built during the 
period 802 to 1432. During this time, the 
Khmer Empire was one of the great powers 
of South East Asia. At the height of its power, 
the Khmer Empire ruled over a vast territory 
covering large parts of modern-day Cambodia, 
Laos, Thailand, Myanmar (Burma) and 
southern Vietnam.
Angkor Wat (meaning City Temple) is the 
best known of the temples in this area. It was 
built as a Hindu temple during the reign of 
Suryavarman II (1112 to 1152). It was later 
restored for use as a Buddhist shrine in the  
16th century.
Angkor Wat is surrounded by a moat, 190 metres wide, that forms  
a giant rectangle measuring 1.5 km by 1.3 km. The rectangular wall  
around the enclosure measures 1025 m by 800 m, and has a gate in each side. 
1 
Calculate the perimeter of the moat. 
2 
Calculate the perimeter of the walled enclosure inside the moat. 
3 
What is the area of the enclosure? 
4 
a Calculate the area of the large rectangle, including the moat, in square kilometres.
b Convert your answer to square metres.

9.5 m wide leads from the main entrance to the central temple. The central temple complex 
consists of three storeys. The corners of the second and third storeys are marked by towers.  
The central tower rises 31 m above the third storey and 55 m above the ground.

There are more than 100 temples in the area around Angkor. Many of the temples were left to 
the jungle for centuries and today are found in various stages of decay.

concentric walls. The outer wall measures 700 metres × 500 metres.
a What is the perimeter of the outer wall?

10 Near Banteay Kdai is a large pool, the Pool of Ablutions (Sras Srang). This rectangular 
pool is 400 metres wide. It covers an area of 320 000 square metres.

11 Another temple is Preah Khan (Sacred Sword). The temple is surrounded by a wall.

searchText:
24 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The Great Wall in northern China is one of the 
great human-made wonders of the world. Like 
a gigantic dragon, the Great Wall winds up and 
down across deserts, grasslands and mountains. 
The first sections were constructed more than 
2 000 years ago by independent kingdoms to 
keep out marauding nomads. These sections 
were later rebuilt and joined together. 
The wall as it is known today dates from the 
Ming Dynasty (1368–1644) when a determined 
effort was made to revitalise the whole project. 
This time, the wall was faced with some 60 
million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs. 
The Great Wall stretched approximately 
8 850 kilometres from east to west. 
Unfortunately, some of the sections are  
now in ruins or have disappeared.
A comprehensive archaeological survey has concluded that the wall of the Ming era  
measured 8 850 km. This is made up of 6 259 km of actual wall, 359 km of trenches  
and 2 232 km of natural defensive barriers such as hills and rivers.
1 
What percentage, correct to 1 decimal place, of the Ming-era wall was
a actual wall?
b trenches?
c natural defensive barriers?
2 
The average height of the Ming-era Great Wall measured  
10.1 metres and the average width was about 4.6 metres.  
Assume the wall was a rectangular prism.  
Use these dimensions to calculate
a the area of a one face of the wall 1 000 metres long.
b the volume of a 1 kilometre section of the wall.  
Answer in cubic metres.
3 
In the Ming era, the wall was faced with approximately  
60 million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs.  
The length of actual wall was 6 259 kilometres. 
 
What was the average volume of bricks and stone slabs  
used for each kilometre of the wall?  
Answer to the nearest cubic metre.
The Great Wall of China 
11
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
25
One of the best-preserved sections of the Great Wall is situated at Badaling, about  
70 kilometres north of Beijing. Most tourists visit this section of the wall.
Made of stone and bricks from the hills, this portion of the Great Wall is 7.8 metres high and  
5 metres wide. The inside has been formed by tamping earth and small stones, which makes 
the wall very firm and strong. 
4 
Use these dimensions to calculate
a the area of a one face of the wall 500 metres long. 
 
b the volume of a 1 kilometre section of the wall (assuming it is a rectangular prism). 
Give your answer in cubic metres.

One of the most striking sections of the Ming Great 
Wall is where it climbs extremely steep slopes.  
In one section, the cross-section is a trapezium.  
The wall has an average height of 6.5 metres.  
It is 6 metres across the bottom, narrowing to  
5 metres across the top.
5 
a Calculate the area of a trapezium 6.5 m high with parallel sides measuring  
5 m and 6 m.
b Calculate the volume of a trapezoidal prism 10 m long, 6.5 m high  
with parallel sides measuring 5 m and 6 m.
c Calculate the volume of a 5 kilometre section of this part of the Great Wall. 
Give your answer in cubic metres. 
Over time, the Great Wall has slowly decayed due to the forces 
of nature. People have removed some of the stone to use in other 
structures. Today, less than 30% of the Great Wall still stands in 
good condition.
6

The common yabby, Cherax Destructor, is an Australian freshwater crustacean. In the wild, yabby 
populations remain strong. They have moved into new habitats created by reservoirs and farm 
dams. Their colour depends on the water clarity and habitat they live in – yabbies can range from 
black, blue-black or dark brown in clear waters to light brown or green-brown in ‘dirty’ waters.
Yabbies occasionally reach up to 30 cm in 
length and up to 310 g in weight, but are more 
commonly 10 to 20 cm long. Like all crustaceans, 
yabbies have to moult as they grow. As they grow 
older, they moult less. After each moulting, their 
weight can increase by up to 50%.

size of around 310 grams for adult yabbies is reached in 2 to 3 years. The minimum

14 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
Advertising 
6
Proudly brought to you by a range of calculations involving advertising times, rates, revenue and 
marketing methods.
Billions of dollars are spent every year on television advertising. This money allows 
commercial free-to-air television stations to exist. Many viewers find advertisements irritating, 
but television advertising is a highly effective way for companies, corporations, governments 
and non-profit organisations to get their messages across to the public.
Unless otherwise indicated, express answers correct to 2 decimal places.
1	
When television advertising is purchased, it is sold in packages, not as single 
advertisements. Different advertising rates are charged according to the city or region in 
which they screen, and the time of day they are shown.
a	 Why do you think advertising rates vary according to the city or region in which they 
are shown?
b	 Why do you think advertising rates vary according to the time of day they are shown?
2	
The basic time unit for advertisements is 30 seconds. Channel 4 charges the following 
rates for advertisements shown between 7 am and 9 am:
•	 In Melbourne – $19 000 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Sydney – $21 500 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Brisbane – $14 200 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Adelaide – $5 200 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Perth – $6 700 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
	
Use these rates to calculate how much advertisers pay per advertisement on Channel 4 in 
each city.
3	
An advertiser purchases 30 × 30-second advertising spots to run between 7 am and 9 am 
over the course of two weeks (i.e. Monday to Friday). On average, how many times per 
day would the advertisement be shown?

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
15
5	
Prime weekday viewing times are from 6 pm to 9.30 pm. During these times, a 50% 
loading is added to the 7 am to 9 am costs. Between midnight and 7 am, the advertising 
costs are 45% of the 7 am to 9 am costs. 
	
An advertiser wants to run this advertising schedule on Channel 4 in Perth: 
	
J 30 × 30-second advertisements between 7 am and 9 am
	
J 30 × 15-second advertisements between 6 pm and 9.30 pm
	
J 30 × 45-second advertisements between midnight and 7 am
	
What would be the total cost of the campaign?
6	
An advertiser ran 30 × 30-second advertisements on Channel 4 in Adelaide between 7 am 
and 9 am across two weeks. The advertisements offered a special deal on a product, which 
lasted for the length of the advertising campaign. 
	
The deal let viewers purchase the product at 50% of its regular price. The regular price 
was $59. The advertising campaign resulted in 216 sales of the product.
a	 Was the revenue gained from product sales during the advertising campaign more or 
less than the cost of the campaign?
b	 By how much did the revenue gained from the product sales exceed, or fall short of, the 
cost of the campaign?
7	
A movie is scheduled to screen between 8.30 pm and 10.30 pm on a commercial TV 
station. The actual running time of the movie is 108 minutes. However, the station has 
to include 35 × 30-second advertisements and 8 × 15-second station promotions during 
the movie. The movie cannot run past 10.30 pm as the station then crosses live to an 
international tennis tournament.
a	 What length of movie time will need to be cut out to accommodate all the advertising 
and TV station promotions?
b	 What percentage of the total movie time is this?
Advertising (cont’d)

Cost of 30 ads
Cost of 1 ad
15 seconds
45 seconds
60 seconds

15-, 45- and 60-second spots too.

•	 45-second advertising spots are charged at 140% of the 30-second rate
•	 60-second advertising spots are charged at 160% of the 30-second rate

between 7 am and 9 am.

34 
Maths in Technology 
© Barbara Lynch and Blake Education 2007
Bar codes 
16
Bar codes were originally devised to help supermarkets speed up their checkouts. Later it was found 
that they could be linked to inventory and price-control computers. There is some variation in how 
the barcodes are arrived at, depending on the country. These exercises show examples.
1	
The barcode shown is from a box of tissues and is made up of two parts: human-readable 
numbers and a machine-readable barcode.
a	 For the numbers, the 9 at the beginning is a code for the country, the next 6 digits are 
the company that made the tissues, the next five digits indicate what the product is and 
the last digit is called the ‘check digit’. For this box of tissues:
 i the company number is …………..
 ii the product number is ……………
 iii the check digit is …………….
b	 The bars themselves are rather difficult to decode without a special reader. (They are 
not the numbers underneath!) There are four different widths for the gaps between the 
black bars and there are four different widths for the black bars themselves.
	 There are also double-bar dividers at the beginning, middle and end. List the next 
four black bars in the barcode for the tissue box by checking their width and then 
completing the following:
	 (11), 4, 1, 2, 2, …………
2	
Barcodes can be a problem when they need to be placed on a very small package. In 
these cases, bar codes are shortened by leaving out a set of four digits, all zeros. What 
does the barcode 0 57000 01235 become when it is shortened?
9 310088 001914
1
2
3
4

© Barbara Lynch and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Technology 
35
3	
The check digit lets the scanner work out if the number has been scanned correctly. Ignore 
the country code at the beginning and the check digit at the end when you complete the 
following check on the barcode in question 1.
a	 Find the sum of all the even-positioned digits: 
	 1 + 0 + 8 + …. + …. = …….
b	 Find the sum of all the odd-positioned digits: 
	 3 + 0 + 8 + …. + …. + … = …….
c	 Multiply the number obtained in Part b by 3: 
	 ……… × 3 = ………
d	 Add the numbers obtained in Parts a and c: 
	 …… + ……... = …….…
e	 Find the number that needs to be added to the number obtained in Part d to bring it up 
to the nearest multiple of 10:
	 ……………… 
	 This should be the same as the check digit on the end of the barcode.
f	 The barcode looks genuine, but is it?
4	
Another box of tissues has the following barcode:
 9 310004 14197 6
a	 What is the country code?
b	 What is the check digit?
c	 What is the company number?
d	 What is the product number?
e	 Find the sum of the even-positioned digits. 
Add this to three times the sum of the odd-
positioned digits. What is the number that 
needs to be added to this result to get a 
multiple of 10?
f	 Is the check digit correct?
5	
For the barcode 0 57000 01235 x, find x.

The Cane Toad (Bufo marinus) is also known as the Giant Neotropical Toad or Marine Toad. It is 
a large, terrestrial true toad native to Central and South America. Cane Toads were introduced 
to Australia to eat cane beetles. The ‘whitegrub’ larvae of these beetles eat the roots of sugar 
cane and kill or stunt the plants. About 100 toads were imported from Hawaii to the Meringa 
Experimental Station near Cairns. The toads bred quickly and more than 3 000 were released in  
the sugar cane plantations of north Queensland in July 1935. 
1

b arthritis
By 2002, Cane Toads had spread throughout the eastern and northern half of Queensland. 
They have now extended their range to the river catchments surrounding Kakadu National 
Park, near Katherine, in the Northern Territory. In New South Wales they occur on the coast as 
far south as Yamba and there is an isolated colony near Port Macquarie.

Papua New Guinea is home to a large number  
of species of birds. 
The bird-of-paradise is universally identified with the  
island of New Guinea. An adult bird-of-paradise is  
depicted on the national flag of Papua New Guinea.
There are 44 species of birds-of-paradise worldwide  
and 35 species are found in Papua New Guinea.  
A few species are also found in surrounding islands  
and north-eastern Australia.
The smallest bird-of-paradise in size is the

34 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Mosquitoes are insects that make up the family Culicidae. They have a pair of scaled wings, a pair of 
halteres, a slender body and long legs. The females of most mosquito species suck blood from other 
animals. This has made them the most deadly disease carriers we know. They have killed millions of 
people over thousands of years and continue to kill millions per year by spreading diseases.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a halteres  
b pupae
2 
Mosquitoes can grow to 16 mm in length and 2.5 mg in weight. 
a How long can mosquitoes grow, in centimetres?
b How many mozzies are needed to make up 1 gram of mozzie flesh?
3 
A mosquito can fly continuously for 1 to 4 hours at speeds of 2 km/h. They are capable of 
travelling more than 110 km from their breeding sites.
a How far could a mosquito travel in 4 hours?
b How far could a mosquito travel in one night, without resting? (Allow 6 hours of 
darkness.)
c How long would it take a mosquito to travel 110 km, without resting?
d How long would it take a mosquito to travel 110 km if it had a 5 km/h assisting breeze 
and no rests?
4 
Most species of mosquito feed at night or at dusk or dawn. During the heat of the day, 
most mosquitoes rest in a cool place but might still bite if disturbed. After drinking blood, 
adult females lay a raft of up to 400 (depending on the species) tiny, white eggs in still or 
very slow-moving water. How many eggs could these numbers of mosquitoes lay?
a 5 
b 6 
c 18 
d 23
Most eggs hatch into larvae in about 48 hours. As they grow, they shed or moult their skin 
about four times, growing larger after each moulting. The larvae eat micro-organisms and 
organic matter in the water. Mosquito larvae, commonly called ‘wrigglers’, must live in water 
for about 10 days, depending on the water’s temperature. The pupae are lighter than water, 
and float on the surface while changing into adult mosquitoes over about two days. The 
newly emerged adult rests on the surface of the water for a short time to allow itself to dry and 
all its parts to harden before it can fly. A mosquito’s adult life is about ten weeks.  
5 
Use the information above to  
label the diagram of the mosquito 
life cycle. 
6 
What is the total time, in hours, 
for a mosquito to complete its  
life cycle?
Over the past 20 million years or so, 
mosquitoes have been honing their 
hunting skills. They are now experts at 
finding people to bite. Mosquitoes have 
a battery of sensors designed to track 
prey. They can sense carbon dioxide 
and lactic acid from up to 40 metres 
away. 
Blood suckers - mosquitoes 
16
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
35
Certain chemicals in sweat also seem to attract mosquitoes.  
If you are wearing clothing that contrasts with the 
background, especially if you move while wearing that 
clothing, mosquitoes can see you and zero in on you. 
Mosquitoes detect heat, so they can find warm-blooded 
mammals and birds easily once they get close enough.
7 
Mosquitoes were observed at these distances from 
a mammal. For each distance, decide whether the 
mosquito is likely to smell the mammal. 
a 30 m 
b 45 m 
c 5 000 cm
d 30 000 mm 
e 0.05 km 
f 0.02 km
Repellents like DEET work by disorienting the mosquito as it gets close to its potential next 
meal, but do not kill mosquitoes. Surprisingly, this works about 95% of the time. 
8 
How many successes is a mosquito likely to have if it makes these numbers of attacks on a 
person wearing DEET?
a 50                 b  36 
c 120              d  59 
e 12               f  250
9 
The concentrated mosquito repellent DEET is mixed in with water. Low concentrations of 
DEET are sufficient for most outdoor protection. A 15% concentration is recommended for 
most purposes. Which of these repellent mixtures would be satisfactory for most purposes?
a 50 mL water, 10 mL DEET 
b 110 mL water, 20 mL DEET
c 120 mL water, 17 mL DEET
In Australia, diseases transmitted by mosquitoes include Dengue fever, Australian 
encephalitis, Ross River fever and Barmah Forest virus disease. Ross River fever and Barmah 
Forest virus disease have a wide variety of symptoms, from rashes with fevers to arthritis that 
can last from months to years. Ross River fever is the most commonly reported mosquito-
transmitted disease in all states of Australia. Malaria is rare in Australia.

c Which year had the least infections?
d Suggest an explanation for the nature of the graph

infected with Ross River fever in South Australia. 
a What is the simplest ratio 
of infected males to infected 
females?
b Are males more likely to be 
infected than females?

Japan’s high speed trains are called 
Shinkansen (bullet trains). The first 
bullet train was operated between 
Tokyo and Osaka in 1964, the year the 
Olympic Games were held in Tokyo. 
Today bullet trains run between many 
cities in Japan. On some lines, trains 
run every 5 to 10 minutes.
The fastest trains are called ‘Nozomi’. 
They connect major cities like Tokyo, 
Nagoya, Osaka and Hiroshima, 
making few stops in between. 
1 
A Nozomi train leaves Tokyo at 7:50 am and arrives at Shin-Osaka at 10:29 am.  
It makes only 4 stops in the 552 kilometre journey. 
 
How long does the journey take?  
Answer in hours and minutes.
2 
A slower Hikari train leaves Tokyo at 9:33 am and arrives at Shin-Osaka at 12:30 pm.  
It makes 6 stops between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka.
a How long does the journey take? Answer in hours and minutes.
b Convert your answer to hours, correct to 2 decimal places.
3 
A Nozomi train leaves Kyoto at 3:45 pm. The 380 kilometre journey to Hiroshima takes 
1 hour and 36 minutes. At what time does this train arrive in Hiroshima? 
4 
A train takes 2 hours 18 minutes to travel from Tokyo to Kyoto,  
a distance of 513 kilometres.
a Convert the time to hours. Give your answer as a decimal. 
b Use the rule: Speed = Distance 
Time
 to calculate the average speed of the train, correct to  
1 decimal place.
5 
A train takes 1 hour 25 minutes to travel from Tokyo to Nagano,  
a distance of 222 kilometres.
a Convert the time to hours, correct to 2 decimal places. 
b Calculate the average speed of the train, correct to 1 decimal place. 
Bullet trains in Japan

Buying Fresh Produce #9
Division of decimals, multiplication of decimals, rounding off decimals to the nearest cent and 
metric conversion  
 
In the produce section of your store, fruits and vegetables are often priced both in 
kilograms and pounds.  You will need to convert kilograms to pounds and pounds to 
kilograms in this exercise.   
 
Remember:  1 kilogram (kg) = 2.2 pounds (lb) 
 
 
Example 1:    
Bananas cost $.89/lb. 
Problem 1:   
How much would it cost for 5 lbs of bananas?   
Solution 1:   
5 x $.89 = $4.45 per 5 lbs of bananas 
Problem 2:  
And how much would it cost for 5 kg?   
Solution 2:  
We first must convert the cost of the bananas to kilograms. 
$.89 x 2.2 = $1.96 (rounded off to nearest cent)  
$1.96 x 5 = $9.80  
It will cost $9.80 for 5 kilograms of bananas.  
 
Example 2:  
Oranges cost $3.89/kg. 
Problem 1:  
How much would it cost for 3 kg of oranges? 
Solution 1:  
3 x $3.89 kg = $11.67 for 3 kg of oranges. 
Problem 2:  
And how much would it cost for 3 lbs of oranges? 
Solution 2:  
We first must convert the cost of the oranges to pounds. 
$3.89 ÷ 2.2 = $1.77(rounded off to nearest cent) 
 
 
 
$1.77 x 3 = $5.31  It will cost $5.31 for 3 lbs of oranges.

Shopping for the Kitchen
 
Buying Large Quantities #11
Division, multiplication of decimals, subtraction of decimals 
 
One way to save money is to buy food in large amounts.  But you should be able to use 
the food you buy.  And you must know how to compare quantities and costs.   
 
 
Example 1: 
The Coop Warehouse sells macaroni in 1.5 kg (or 1500 g) boxes for 
$5.89.  Another store sells smaller 500 g boxes for $3.19.   
Problem: 
 
How much can you save if you buy the 1.5 kg box? 
Solution: 
 
Step 1:  Divide to compare quantities.  
 
1500 ÷ 500 = 3 
   3 - 500 gram boxes makes a 1.5 kg box.   
Step 2:  Multiply to find the cost of 3 - 500 grams boxes of macaroni 
 
 
   $3.19 x 3 = $9.57 
 
 
   Three 500 g boxes cost $9.57 
Step 3:  Subtract to find the savings  
   $9.57 - $5.89 = $3.68 
 
 
You can save $3.68 if you buy the 1.5 kilogram box of macaroni. 
 
Example 2: 
The local grocery store sells small and large cans of tomatoes: 1kg 
(1000 grams) for $3.89 or 500 grams for $2.89. 
Problem: 
 
How much can you save if you buy the 1kg can of tomatoes? 
Solution: 
 
Step 1:  Divide to compare quantities. 
1000 ÷ 500 = 2 
 
 
 
Step 2:  Multiply to find the cost of 2 smaller cans of tomatoes 
   2 x $2.89 = $5.78 
 
 
 
Step 3:   Subtract to find the savings 
 
 
 
 
   $5.78 - $3.89 = $1.89 
 
 
 
You can save $1.89 if you buy the 1 kg can of tomatoes.

searchText:
6 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
When you measure quantities such as distance, speed and mass, you need to use different units 
of measurement – depending on which quantity is being measured, and in which country the 
measurements are being made.
In Australia, metric units of measurement are used such as centimetres, metres, kilometres, 
kilometres per hour, grams and kilograms. In the USA, Imperial units of measurement such 
as feet, inches, miles, miles per hour, pounds and ounces are used. In Britain, metric units 
are often used for mass and some lengths, but road distance and road speeds are commonly 
measured in miles and miles per hour.
Converting units of speed
A unit of speed is always shown as a unit of length or distance  
divided by (or ‘per’) a unit of time. Metric units of length or  
distance include centimetres, metres and kilometres; and  
Imperial units include feet, yards and miles. 
It’s time to look at converting units of speed. Let’s  
start with converting kilometres per hour (km/h)  
to miles per hour (mph or mi/h).
For example, the maximum speed limit in  
Australia is 130 km/h on the open highway in  
the Northern Territory. What is this speed in mph?
Converting km to mi: 130 km = 130 ÷ 1.61 = 80.75 mi
In both units of speed, the time unit is the same:  
h (hours).
So 130 km/h = 80.75 mph
1 
Complete the sentences:
a To convert km/h to mph, we                              the km/h figure by 1.61.
b To convert mph to km/h, we                              the mph figure by 1.61.
2 
a 150 km/h =                          mph
b 32 mph =                          km/h
What happens when both the units of distance and the units of time need to be converted?  
Two examples are shown below.
How do we convert 18.6 km/h to m/s?
First convert the unit of length or distance: 
18.6 km = 18 600 m
Then convert the unit of time: 
 
 
1 h = 3 600 s
We now have an equation to solve: 
 
 18 600 m ÷ 3 600 s = 5.17 m/s  
(Rounded to 2 decimal places)
How do we convert 50 mph to m/s?
First convert the unit of length or distance: 
50 mi × 1 609.34 = 80 647
Then convert the unit of time: 
 
 
1 h = 3 600 s 
The equation: 
 
 
 
 
80 647 ÷ 3 600 = 22.40 m/s
Conversions – speed, mass, volume  
2
© Blake Education   978 1 92571 014 4	     Maths in Extreme Sport

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
7
3 
Try these speed conversions!
a Convert 8.5 mph to m/s. 
b Convert 1.53 m/s to km/h. 
c Convert 419.23 m/s to mph. 
d Convert 390 km/h to m/s.
Converting units of mass 
4 
Answer these questions about metric units of mass. 
a How many grams (g) are there in 1 kilogram (kg)?
b How many kilograms (kg) are there in 1 tonne or 
metric ton (t)?
c How many grams (g) are there in 1 tonne (t)?
Two Imperial units of mass are ounces (oz) and  
pounds (lb):
5 
Convert the following Imperial measurements to  
metric measurements.
a 18.76 oz =                g  
b 0.92 lb =                g 
c 388 lb =                kg   
d 14 lb 6 oz =                  kg
6 
Convert the following metric measurements to Imperial measurements.
a 199.9 g =                oz 
b 8 459 g =                lb 
c 68.3 kg =                lb
d 19 kg =                  lb                  oz  (Round your answer to the nearest full ounce.)
Converting units of liquid volume
Units of measurement of liquid volume also vary between metric and Imperial systems.  
Here we will look at just two units – metric litres (L) and Imperial gallons (gal).
 
3.79 L = 1 gal
7 
If a fuel tank holds 90 L, how many gallons is this?
8 
It takes 659 630.6 gal of water to fill an Olympic-sized swimming pool.  
How many litres is this? (Round your answer to the nearest litre.)
9 
A container with a volume of 1 000 cm3 will hold  
exactly 1 L of water. If a cube has equal sides of  
0.46 m, how many litres of water would it hold?
10 A fire-fighting helicopter can drop 4 000 L of water  
in one dump.  
a What is the volume of the water reservoir on  
the helicopter, in cm3?
b How many gallons of water does it hold?
Conversions – speed, mass, volume (cont’d) 
2
Did you know?
People often confuse mass and 
weight, thinking they are the same 
thing. In fact, they are different.
Mass refers to how much matter 
is contained in something. It is 
measured in metric units such as 
grams, kilograms and tons, and 
Imperial units such as ounces and 
pounds.
Weight refers to the force with 
which gravity pulls downwards 
on an object or living thing. It is 
measured in newtons (N), which is 
the unit of measurement for force.
1 lb = 16 oz
1 oz = 28.35 g
1 lb = 453.59 g
1 lb = 0.45 kg

‘Cops on the Beat’

Forget watching people acting as cops – this is the real stuff! TV crews are dispatched with teams of 
police as they crunch the numbers on crime with percentages, money, length and graphing.
This action is definitely not acted. ‘Cops on the Beat’ takes you out on the streets, into homes, 
shops, offices – even down to the waterfront – where every day and night our police are 
confronted with a side of life that most of us only ever imagine.
1	
‘Cops on the Beat’ went with a police team to investigate a suspected stolen car operation 
in the inner city. On arriving at a warehouse, they arrested four men and two women and 
impounded 14 vehicles that had been reported stolen.
a	 The police said the vehicles had an estimated total street value of $290 000. Included 
in the haul was a Porsche worth $105 000. What was the average value of each of the 
other vehicles found in the warehouse (to the nearest whole dollar)?
b	 One of the vehicles had some damage to its right-hand side, which had been caused 
during the theft. The vehicle had an estimated street value of between $16 500 and  
$17 000 but the police said that if it had been sold illegally with the damage, the asking 
price would drop by 30–40%. Using these estimations given by the police, calculate the 
minimum and maximum value of the vehicle had the thieves been able to sell it in its 
damaged state.
c	 This operation was the third of its type that this police investigation unit had uncovered 
in 12 months. The combined total value of all stolen vehicles recovered in the three 
investigations was $1 389 543, but the total value of all vehicles stolen during those 12 
months was estimated at $12 500 000. What percentage of the estimated stolen vehicle 
market has this investigation unit been able to recover over the past year (to 1 decimal 
place)?
2	
Another investigation followed by ‘Cops on the Beat’ was into a fraud carried out by the 
manager of a company. Over the course of two years, she had siphoned off a total of  
$567 000 from customers’ accounts into her own bank accounts for her personal use.
a	 In one account she had operated for nine months, she was collecting 7.2% interest per 
annum. She opened this account with $245 000 and did not add to it. How much was

total stolen funds is this (to 1 decimal place)?
d	 The police, however, stated that in all 38% of the 
total amount stolen was unaccounted for. How 
much money is this?
e	 Given the woman’s confession about the gambling 
money, how much more money over and above 
this figure could not be traced?
3	
Down to the waterfront – and ‘Cops on the Beat’ are stopping recreational fishing boats to 
check the size of the catch. Large quantities of undersized fish are finding their way onto 
the black market – in particular, King George whiting. Where the police are swooping, the 
legal maximum limit of King George whiting for recreational fishers is 75, and each fish 
must be 30 cm or more in length. During the operation police inspected 68 fishing boats. 
These boats contained a total of 2940 fish of which 1371 were King George whiting. In all, 
160 whiting were found to be undersized. Seven of the boats had more than 75 whiting on 
board.
a	 What was the minimum number of whiting in total that these seven boats could have 
contained?
b	 The seven boats actually contained 1098 whiting between them. What was the average 
number of whiting on board each of those seven boats (to the nearest whole fish)?
c	 The seven boats also accounted for 85% of all the undersized whiting seized. How many 
fish is this?
d	 Do you think there is evidence here that the owners of these seven boats could be 
involved in the illegal sale of whiting? Explain.
4	
One man was caught with 16 King George whiting in all, including two that were 29.7 cm 
and 29.85 cm respectively. The man showed police an old battered steel ruler and claimed 
he used it to measure every fish he caught. The police let him off with a caution.
a	 By what percentage was each of the undersized fish below the legal limit?
b	 Do you think the police treated the man fairly? Why or why not?
c	 What advice might the police have given the man when they cautioned him?
5	
The break down of fish inspected during the operation is below. Construct either a column 
graph or a pie chart to provide a graphic representation of the break down of this data.

Ease is the space between the body measurement and the finished garment. A designer adds volume 
to certain types of garments to create the ‘look’ they seek, like in a bridal gown’s full skirt. Ease is 
an important calculation in the making of fashion garments. It’s all a matter of Maths!
body measurements + ease + designer’s ease = actual garment measurments
Tegan and Josh are off to Japan for the holiday season and will go shopping in Tokyo to see the 
famous fashion designs of JOJI-SUN. Walking past the windows of the chic department store PAKU 
in Tokyo Central, they see JOJI-SUN’s awesome clothes. ‘Okay let’s try them on! You first!’
1 
A JOJI-SUN dress is sized S, which is equivalent to an 
Australian size 8, with bust 75 cm and waist 55 cm. It is form 
fitted with an average ease measurement of 7 cm.  
a What is the circumference of the dress at the waist including 
ease? Answer in whole centimetres. 
b Hence use the formula C = 2π r where C is the circumference 
and r is the radius to find the radius of the waist of the dress, 
correct to 2 decimal places.

ease.
d Hence find the radius of the dress at the bust in centimetres, 
correct to 2 decimal places.

the picture. It is marked size M, which is equivalent to a man’s 
32 inch waist. The sarong is worn tight with an ease of ½ inch 
and designer’s ease of 1 inch.

b Find the measurement of the actual waist of the sarong, 
including eases, correct to 1 decimal place.
c Hence find the radius of the actual waist of the sarong,  
including eases, correct to 1 decimal place.

at the bottom is 52 inches. Find the radius of the circle

at the waist. Calculate the measurement of the  
actual waist of the sarong, including eases and the 
additional wrap panel, correct to 1 decimal place.

than the size of the garment. Designers describe the space between your actual body measurements 
and a finished garment as ease. Ease is important in the design process as it results in the 
dimensions we see and how a garment behaves on the body. Ease is also essential for good body 
movement and comfort.

Maths in Technology 
© Barbara Lynch and Blake Education 2007
Doing work 
19
Work has different meanings depending on the context. It can be a place of employment, a piece of 
fine art or handwork like knitting. Work is done on an object by a force to produce energy, to change 
its position, to lift it up, to change its velocity, and heat it up and so on. Power is how quickly that 
work is done. Engines do work for us and so does gravity.
1	
The students in 9Z have decided to knit a blanket and 
send it to their favourite charity. The blanket will be made 
up of knitted squares 10 cm by 10 cm. The whole blanket 
will be 1.8 m wide and 2.4 m long.
a	 How many squares does the class need to knit?
	 The class is capable of producing 25 squares each 
week in term time unless they have exams when their 
production falls by 2 squares per week.
b	 In a 12-week term of which two weeks are for exams, 
how many squares can they knit in total?
	 During the following two week of holidays, the class 
knitted a total of 60 squares.
c	 How many squares will they need to knit to finish the blanket?
d	 At that time, approximately how many weeks should they expect to take to finish the 
blanket if sewing the squares together will take a week?
2	
A block of wood placed at the top of a ramp of height h m starts sliding down. When it 
reaches the bottom of the ramp it is going at a speed of v metres per second. The slope is 
perfectly slippery. The speed at the bottom depends only on the height of the slope and 
can be calculated using the formula: 
v =

36 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
A bird of prey, or raptor, is a bird that hunts for food primarily on the wing, using its amazing sense 
of vision. The talons and beaks of raptors tend to be relatively large and powerful, and adapted for 
tearing or piercing the flesh of their victims.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a altitude 
b juveniles
The Wedge-tailed Eagle is Australia’s largest living bird of prey and one of the largest eagles 
in the world. It reaches about 1.0 m in length and has a wingspan of 2.3 m. Females are 
larger than males – they average 4.2 kg in weight with males at about 3.2 kg. This eagle has 
a characteristic long, wedge-shaped tail, and legs that are feathered all the way to the base of 
the toes.
2 
Change these eagle measurements to the units shown.
a 2 m =            cm 
b 1.0 m =            cm 
c 2.3 m =            cm 
d 430 cm =            m 
e 450 cm =            m
Australia’s second largest eagle, the White-bellied Sea Eagle, has shorter, more rounded wings 
than the Wedge-tailed Eagle and no feathers on its lower legs. The White-bellied Sea Eagle is 
about 0.8 m long with a wingspan of roughly 2.2 m. Males weigh close to 3.1 kg and females 
3.5 kg.
3 
Change these eagle weights to the units shown.
a 3 kg =            g 
b 2 kg =            g 
c 2.3 kg =            g  
d 4000 g =            kg 
e 5200 g =            kg
Eagles can be seen perched on trees or poles or soaring overhead at altitudes up to 2000 m.  
An eagle’s nest is a large structure of dead sticks, usually reused for years and often reaching 
considerable sizes. Over many years, a nest can be built up to 1.8 m across, 3 m deep and 
about 400 kg in weight. 
4 
Change these measurements to the units shown.
a 2000 m =            km 
b 2300 m =            km 
c 600 m =            km 
d 3 km =            m

The diet of the Wedge-tailed Eagle reflects the available prey, but the most important live 
items are rabbits and hares. Rabbits usually comprise 55% of the diet, but might comprise up 
to 90%. Other food items include lizards, birds, foxes, feral cats and other mammals. Lambs 
comprise less than 10% of an eagle’s total diet, with most of the sheep meat consumed sourced 
from carcasses, dying sheep or road fatalities. Less than 2% of all lambs killed are the result of 
an eagle’s attack; foxes and crows account for the remainder. 
5 
The average daily requirement of food for a captive adult eagle is about 600 g.
a If rabbit makes up 55% of the eagle’s diet, what is the weight of rabbit needed per day?
b If rabbit makes up 90% of the eagle’s diet, what is the weight of rabbit needed per day?
c If 200 lambs are lost to predators, how many are likely to be lost to eagles?
d If 500 lambs are lost to predators, how many are likely to be lost to foxes and crows?

44 
Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
The planet we live on has taken 
a very long time to become a 
place where humans can live. 
We take for granted the fact 
that life forms such as air-
breathing, complex organisms 
like humans can exist on Earth. 
It has not always been so. 
For most of the life of our 
planet, conditions have not 
been suitable for any life forms, 
except in the oceans. 
By looking at the immense time scales involved in the evolution of life on Earth, we can see 
how important it is to live sustainably on the planet to keep conditions right for human 
existence. It’s a long way to the next human-habitable planet.
1 
This work sheet is about working with large numbers written in scientific notation.  
A number written in scientific notation has two parts: a number that is one or more,  
but less than ten, multiplied by a power of ten. 
 
For example, we can write ninety six million as a  
basic numeral 96 000 000, or in scientific notation as 9.6 × 107.  
Four thousand can be written as 4000 (basic numeral) or  
4 × 103 (scientific notation).
a Write forty two million as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
b One billion is one thousand million. Write one billion as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
c Which of these numbers are correctly written in scientific notation? 
i 2.5 × 104 
 
 
ii     13.6 × 106 
iii 8 × 105  
 
 
iv     0.753 × 108 
2 
Scientists estimate Earth to be four billion, six hundred million years old.
a Write this number as a basic numeral.
b Fill in the gaps to write the age of Earth as a number in scientific notation:   
 4.     × 10     
c Complete the sentence: Earth is four point          billion years old.
d Scientists believe that a collision between Earth and  
a second planet named Theia led to the moon being formed.  
This happened four point five billion, or 4.     × 10    years ago.
e How long after Earth formed did the collision happen? Write the answer   
i in words  
ii     as a basic numeral  
iii     as a number in scientific notation.
Earth – the only home we have 
21
ISBN   978 1 92571 066 3

© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in sustainability 
45
3 
Life began to evolve on Earth during the Proterozoic era,  
which lasted from 2420 million years ago to 541 million years ago.
a Write these two numbers in scientific notation.
b How long did the Proterozoic era last? Write your answer 
i as a basic numeral  
ii     in scientific notation.
c Single-cell life forms have been found in rocks that are 1800 million years old.  
How long after the start of the Proterozoic era is this? Answer in scientific notation.
d The first multi-cell life forms appeared one billion years ago.  
How many years is this before the end of the Proterozoic era?  
Answer in scientific notation.
4 
An event called ‘The Great Dying’ occurred at the end of the Permian period (252 million 
years ago). Almost all life on Earth became extinct due to a large rise in CO2 in the 
atmosphere. Massive eruptions of lava in Siberia are thought to have been responsible.
a The eruptions produced 1.5 million cubic kilometres of lava.  
Write this in scientific notation.
b One kilometre = 1000 metres. Volume = length × width × height.  
How many cubic metres are there in one cubic kilometre?  
Answer in scientific notation.
c Write the volume of lava from part a in cubic metres, in scientific notation.
5 
Butterflies first appeared on Earth 40 million years ago.  
Modern humans evolved 2 hundred thousand years ago.  
How many years before humans did the first butterflies appear? Write your answer 
a as a basic numeral  
b in scientific notation.
6 
There are probably many human-habitable planets like Earth in our galaxy, but a long 
way off. One possibility is a planet that orbits the star Gliese 667C. It might have air and 
water. It is 22 light years from Earth. One light year is the distance travelled by light in 
one year.
a Calculate the number of seconds in one year.  
(3600 seconds = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 365 days = 1 year).  
Answer in scientific notation.
b Light travels at 3 × 105 km per second.  
Use your answer from part a to find how many kilometres there are in a light year.  
Answer in scientific notation.
c Write the distance from Earth to Gliese 667C in kilometres, in scientific notation. 
d Mars is the next planet from the Sun after Earth. When Earth and Mars are closest  
to each other, the distance between them is about 54.6 million kilometres.  
Which option correctly completes the statement?
 The distance from Earth to Gliese 667C is about                times as far as Mars. 
i 38 thousand  
ii     38 million  
iii     38 billion
e If it takes 6 months to get to Mars, how long would it take  
to travel to Gliese 677C at the same average speed?
f Name at least two important differences between Mars and Earth.

8 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Elephants in Thailand 
3
The Asian elephant is a smaller cousin of the  
African elephant, with relatively smaller ears.  
It is the largest terrestrial mammal in Asia. 
The elephant’s massive size and strength  
made it a reliable beast of burden. It is  
a national symbol of Thailand and has  
served many roles in that country’s  
long history. It has been used in timber  
logging, as a war machine and in  
processions and ceremonies. 
In 2010, it was estimated that only  
about 2 000 wild elephants remained in  
the forests of Thailand. It was estimated  
there were approximately 3 000  
domesticated elephants. 
Today, domesticated elephants are  
more likely to be seen carrying tourists  
or performing in some form of  
entertainment than working in  
the jungle or on farms.
1 
Around 1900 it was estimated that there were at least 100 000 domesticated elephants 
working in Thailand. By 1952, that number had dropped to around 13 400. 
 
In 2010, it was estimated that there were only 3 000 domesticated elephants and  
2 000 wild elephants in Thailand.
 
Express the number of domesticated elephants in Thailand in 2010 as a percentage of 
a the number of domesticated elephants in 1900. 
b the number of domesticated elephants in 1952.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
c the total number of elephants in 2010.
d the number of wild elephants in 2010.
2 
Tan is a mahout (an elephant handler). He is 1.68 m tall and has a mass of 68 kg. 
 
His elephant is 2.8 m tall and has a mass of 4.76 tonnes (4 760 kg).
a Express Tan’s height as a percentage of the height of his elephant. 
b Express Tan’s mass as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
3 
Tan’s elephant eats around 135 kg of plant matter each day. 
 
Express this as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
9
Once they are born, baby elephants enjoy a 3 to 5 year childhood before their training begins. 
They learn to push, carry and stack logs as well as how to walk in a procession.  
Working elephants have a career of about 50 years. 
4 
Tan began training his elephant when it was 4 years old.  
The training took 5 years.  
Tan and the elephant then began work.  
His elephant is now 25 years old.
a How many years has the elephant been working? 
b What percentage of its life did the elephant spend in training? 
c What percentage of the elephant’s life has it been working? 
5 
The law in Thailand requires working elephants to be retired at age 61 after working  
for 50 years. They are usually released into the wild. 
 
An elephant at a sanctuary is 72 years old. 
 
What percentage of its life did the elephant spend working?  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
Each year, the town of Surin in north-eastern Thailand hosts an Elephant Round-up Festival. 
More than 300 domesticated elephants are brought to the town by their mahouts.  
The festival lasts 10 days. The elephants demonstrate their skills and participate in parades 
and battle re-enactments. 
6 
The average elephant drinks 160 litres of water each day. 
a How many kilolitres of water are needed for each elephant for 10 days? 
b How many kilolitres of water are needed for 300 elephants for 10 days? 
7 
The average elephant has a mass of 4 800 kg.  
It eats 130 kg of plants and vegetables each day. 
a What is the total mass of plants and vegetables the average elephant will eat  
during the 10 days of the festival?  
b Express this as a percentage of the mass of the elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
8 
A female elephant stands 2.3 metres in height and has a normal mass of 3.2 tonnes  
(3 200 kg). She gave birth to a baby. Shortly after birth, the baby stood 90 centimetres 
high and had a mass of 90 kg.
a Express the baby’s height as a percentage of its mother’s height.  
Answer correct to the nearest whole number.
b Express the baby’s mass as a percentage of its mother’s mass.  
Answer correct to one decimal place.
9 
A male elephant has a mass of 3.4 tonnes.  
Its brain has a mass of 5 kg. Express this as a percentage of the elephant’s mass.  
Answer correct to two decimal places.
