Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
The tiger is a mammal of the Felidae family and is native to much of eastern and southern Asia. It 
can grow up to 4 metres long and weigh up to 300 kilograms. Aside from great bulk and power, the 
tiger’s most recognisable feature is the pattern of dark vertical stripes overlaying near-white to 
reddish-orange fur. 
Whenever you see a colour code letter, find your answer in the shape at the end of the 
worksheet and colour that section. Colour code: R = red, B = blue, G = green, Y = yellow. 
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a deciduous 
b mangrove  
c mutation
2 
In the 1920s, about 100 000 tigers existed in the wild. In the 1990s, five different scientists 
made these estimates of the wild tiger population: 4840, 7040, 6270, 5010 and 6540. 
Calculate the average estimate of wild tiger numbers.
3 
Of the tigers surveyed, it was estimated that 3100 of these were Bengal Tigers, 400 were 
Siberian, 500 were Sumatrans, 1200 were Indo-Chinese, 40 were South Chinas and  
700 were Malay Tigers. Calculate the average percentage of these tiger species making up 
the existing numbers.
a Bengal 
b Siberians 
c Sumatrans 
d Indo-Chinese 
e South Chinas 
f Malay
4 
a Calculate the average percentage reduction in tiger numbers from 1920 to 1990.
b Suggest why there has been such a decrease in tiger populations.
5 
The Bengal Tiger is found in parts of India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Burma. It 
lives in varied habitats: grasslands, subtropical and tropical rainforests, scrub forests, wet 
and dry deciduous forests and mangroves. Males in the wild usually weigh about 210 kg  
while the average female weighs about 140 kg. Conservationists have estimated the 
current number of Bengal Tigers to be 1400 – 40% of their population 10 years ago. 
a How many Bengal Tigers were there 10 years ago?
b How much heavier is the male than the female, as a percentage? (R)
6 
The Indo-Chinese Tiger is found in Cambodia, China, Laos, Burma, Thailand and 
Vietnam. These tigers are smaller and darker than Bengal Tigers. Males weigh about  
170 kg while females are smaller at 125 kg. Estimates of the total Indo-Chinese Tiger 
population are 1 500, with about three hundred left in the wild.
a What percentage of Indo-Chinese Tigers lives in the wild? (B)
b What percentage of Indo-Chinese Tigers lives in captivity? (Y)
c How much lighter is the female than the male, as a percentage? (Y)
7 
Sumatran Tigers are found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra. They are close 
to extinction. Sumatran Tigers are the smallest of all living tiger subspecies, with adult 
males weighing about 110 kg and females about 80 kg. The wild population is estimated 
to be 450. Habitat destruction is the main threat to the existing tiger population – 
however, about 60 tigers were recorded as being shot and killed between 1998 and 2000.
a What percentage of the wild population of tigers was shot and killed between 1998 and 
2000? (G)
b How much heavier is the male tiger than the female tiger, as a percentage? (R)

searchText:
Environmental Math Projects 
 
 
1. According to World Health Organization estimates in 2006, 1.1 billion people do not 
have access to improved sources of drinking water, negatively impacting almost 
every aspect of daily life.  Nearly everywhere around the globe, collecting water 
falls to the task of women and children, who often have to carry water for several 
miles a day. In addition to the time and energy spent on water collection, there are 
many consequences resulting from unsafe and unsanitary conditions. Although 
most citizens in Canada generally have reliable access to clean water, conditions 
such as drought, pollution, increased population and unequal distribution of 
natural resources threaten our water supply. This makes it necessary for each of us 
to conserve water and find ways to reduce our daily water usage.   
a. Research ways to reduce your water use.  
b. Present your finding to your class and to others in the community. 
c. Implement your research in your home. 
 
2. Develop some posters for your community about reducing water use.  On the poster 
give 5 tips for reducing water and show people how they can save money too! 
3. Start a recycling program at your learning centre or school.   
4. Write a letter to your local grocery store and ask them to give out free cloth bags for 
one week.  Then encourage people in your community to use them! 
5. Look at your electricity bill.  Try to reduce your kWh in the next month.  Calculate 
how much money you save.

8
Starfish or sea stars are any echinoderms belonging to the class Asteroidea. They typically have five 
or more ‘arms’ which radiate from a central disk in a symmetrical way. Most starfish have 5 arms, 
but some have more or fewer.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a radiate 
b regenerate 
c spawning 
d buoyant
While starfish are commonly represented as having only 5 legs, there are some that exhibit 
many more, as you can see below. 
Nine Armed Starfish       Sunflower Starfish 
   Cushion Starfish     Spiny Beaded Starfish

walking around, for attaching tightly to rocks and for holding on to prey. With so many

a How many centimetres per hour is this?
b How many metres per hour is this?
c How many kilometres per hour is this?

The Crown of Thorns Starfish can move up to 600 m in a week. How fast on average is 
this, in metres per hour? 
Some species of starfish have the ability to regenerate lost arms and, over time, can grow 
an entire new arm. Most species must have the central part of the body intact in order to 
regenerate, but a few can grow an entire starfish from a single ray.

6 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Fish ‘n’ chips – sharks 
2
Sharks are a type of fish with a full cartilaginous skeleton and a streamlined body. They breathe 
with the use of five to seven gill slits. Sharks have a covering of dermal denticles (the skin feels like 
sandpaper) to protect their skin from damage and from parasites and to improve fluid dynamics. 
They also have replaceable teeth.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a cartilaginous 
b dermal 
c denticle 
d embryos  
e predatory
Sharks range in size from the small Spined Pygmy Shark, a deep sea species of only  
22 centimetres in length, to the Whale Shark, the largest fish, which grows to a length of 
approximately 12 metres and 25 tonnes. The White Pointer grows to 7 m and 2 tonnes,  
Tiger Sharks to 5 m and 900 kg, Thresher Sharks to 5 m and 0.4 tonnes and Basking Sharks  
to 12.3 m and 19 tonnes. Humans can be up to 272 cm tall and 310 kg in weight.
2 
Draw column graphs to compare the height and weight of a human with those of the 
given sharks.
 
Height  
 
 
 
 
 
       Weight
The teeth of carnivorous sharks are not attached to the jaw, but embedded in the flesh. In 
many species, the teeth are constantly replaced throughout the shark’s life. Sharks have about 
3 000 teeth spread over 5 rows. The front set is the largest and does most of the work. In some 
sharks, a row of teeth is replaced every two weeks. Sharks live for approximately 25 years.
3 
a Approximately how many teeth does a shark have in a single row?
b How many teeth are replaced every four weeks?
4 
Calculate the approximate number of teeth each 
shark may have in its lifetime, if it lives for:
a 5 years. 
b 12 years.
c 2 years. 
d 15 years.
e 25 years.
Sharks rarely attack humans unless provoked. In 
2006, there were approximately 98 shark attacks on 
humans. Of these attacks, 64 were unprovoked and 
18 were provoked, with the remainder uncertain. 
5 
Calculate the approximate percentage of  
attacks that were:
a provoked. 
b unprovoked.

Great Whites account for about five-twelfths of all annual reported shark attacks. Of these 
Great White attacks, about one-third of the people die.
a If 100 shark attacks were reported in one year, how many would be Great White attacks?
b How many people would die from this number of Great White attacks? 
Great White Sharks are ovoviviparous – that is, the eggs are kept inside the female body until 
they hatch. About 40 eggs develop in the female’s uterus, hatching there and continuing to 
develop until they are born. The Great White has an 11 month gestation (pregnancy) period. 
There is not much room for the embryos to grow and they must eat each other to make more 
room – these sharks develop their predatory skills well before they enter the wild. On average, 
8 Great White Sharks are born from an original litter of 40. Great White Sharks reach sexual 
maturity at about 12 years and live for 40 to 100 years.

What is the probability of a Great White being born?
10 Assuming the shark can get pregnant again straight after she gives birth, how many 
sharks could be born to a Great White female that died at the age of:
a 50 years? 
b 100 years?

of shark is landed from the Southern Shark Fishery each year. This makes the annual 
wholesale value of the fishery AU$13.831 million. Each shark caught weighs about 15 kg.

Flowers of the sea - anemones and jellyfish 
5
Sea anemones are a group of water-dwelling, predatory animals. They are named after the 
anemone, a flower found in many gardens. Sea anemones are closely related to coral and jellyfish. 
A jellyfish has no head, brain, heart, eyes or ears. It has no bones, either. To capture prey for food, 
jellyfish have a net of tentacles that contains poisonous, stinging cells. When the tentacles brush 
against prey – or a person’s leg – thousands of tiny stinging cells explode, launching barbed stingers 
and poison into the victim.

44 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Faster, higher, pushing boundaries further … These extreme sports freaks are addicted to travelling 
fast – hitting breakneck speeds on road, rail and in the air. Exercise your extreme calculation skills 
by crunching the numbers involved in these speed records. 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
The land speed record in a vehicle is held by Andy Green, who went an amazing  
1 228 km/h in 1997 in his ‘ThrustSSC’ vehicle powered by two massive jet engines.  
This is just 7 km/h less than the speed of sound.
a Convert 1 228 km/h to miles per hour (mph).
b Convert this speed to metres per second (m/s).
c What is the speed of sound in m/s?
2 
The motorcycle land speed record is currently held by Chris Carr, who clocked an 
awesome speed equivalent to 158.11 m/s.
a Convert this speed to km/h.
b Convert this speed to mph.
The land speed record – maintained for at least 1 km – was first measured in 1898 at a 
frightening 63.15 km/h. This record was broken many times during the 1900s. Here’s a 
snapshot of some of the landmark records:
• In 1899, the record stood at a hair-raising 105.88 km/h.
• By 1906, this had increased by nearly 100 km/h to an astonishing 205.44 km/h.
• The 400 km/h mark was exceeded for the first time in 1932, when the somewhat more 
serious speed of 404.49 km/h was achieved.
• Just 15 years later, the record had cracked the 600 km/h mark – 633.79 km/h in 1947.
• In 1970, the 1 000 km/h barrier was broken, with the record set at 1 014.52 km/h. The 
record of 1 228 km/h set in 1997 has stood for 11 years, and was the current record at 
the time of printing this book.
3 
a By what factor did the land speed record increase from the previous record in each of 
the years 1906, 1932, 1947, 1970 and 1997?

most? 
c Between which years did the speed increase the most in km/h?

graph to represent 
the land speed record 
information. Put each 
year along the x-axis 
(horizontal axis) and 
speed along the y-axis 
(vertical axis).

1 mile = 1 609.34 metres

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
45
5 
Not quite sport, but a sporting connection … In the build-up to the Beijing Olympics in 
2008, China set a new world record – it put into service the Beijing-Tianjin Intercity Rail. 
This high speed train became the fastest commercially operating rail service in the world. 
At the maximum operating speed on this train, it would be possible to travel 87.5 km in 
just 15 minutes.
a What is the train’s maximum speed in km/h?
b How far would the train travel in 10 minutes at maximum speed?
c In travelling time, how long would it take to journey 500 km at this speed?
6 
On the subject of fast trains, a number of non-commercially operating trains on rails 
have achieved speeds faster than the Chinese Intercity train. In fact, the highest speed 
ever recorded by a ‘train’ – in this case a railed vehicle associated with the testing of US 
army rocket-propelled missiles – is 10 400 km/h.
a Convert this speed to m/s.
b How many km/s is this?
c If a track for a railed vehicle capable of travelling at this speed was built from the east 
coast across Australia to the west coast – approximately 4 000 km – how long would it 
take the rocket-propelled vehicle to travel from one side of the country to another if it 
could maintain this speed?
d If the vehicle kept travelling at this speed from one side of the country to the other for  
2 h 17 min – how many kilometres would it have travelled?
Slowing down a pace now, but still at the extreme end of sports action – hot air ballooning!
•   American adventurer and businessman, Steve Fossett,  
was well known for pushing the boundaries. In 2002,  
he became the first person to circumnavigate the  
world non-stop in a hot air balloon. His balloon was  
10 storeys high and was named ‘The Spirit of Freedom’.  
He made the trip solo. 
•   He took off from Northam in Western Australia on  
19 June 2002 and returned to land in Queensland on  
3 July 2002. The flight took him 13 days, 8 hours and  
33 minutes. He covered a distance of 20 626.48 miles.
•   Fossett’s top speed during the flight was 186 mph over  
the Indian Ocean, and he set a new record for the  
longest distance flown in a balloon over 24 hours –  
3 186.8 miles on 1 July 2002.
•   Steve Fossett went missing in October 2007 after failing to return from flying his plane 
over the Nevada Desert in the USA. A year later, the wreckage of his plane was found.
7 
a For how many hours in total was Fossett flying on his circumnavigation of the Earth?
b What was Steve Fossett’s average speed in mph during the circumnavigation?
c Convert the total distance flown to km and the average speed to km/h.
d Convert the maximum speed during the circumnavigation to km/h.
e If Steve Fossett had flown at his average speed constantly for the entire flight, how far 
(in km and in miles) would he have flown after:
 – reaching the halfway point? 
 
– one week?

Timber frame houses used to be built of hardwood from wild 
forests. These days, governments restrict the harvesting of trees 
from public land, to protect what is left. Most building timber 
comes from plantations of fast-growing pine trees. Mature trees 
are felled, the trunks cut into logs between 4 and 6 metres long, 
loaded onto a truck and taken to a mill for cutting into lengths  
of timber.

In what century was it considered fashionable to wear eyebrows that were made from a

Since 1915, one day in the year has involved the whole of Australia in solemn ceremonies of 
remembrance, gratitude and national pride. That day is Anzac Day – 25 April.

to Egypt for combat training. It was here that the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps

something went wrong. The landings were over 2 km north of the intended area – a 6 km

Tag and Release Programmes
Game fishing might bring on an adrenalin rush, but 
there’s a serious side too.
The protection of marine resources is important. 
For many species of fish caught in Australian 
waters, there are regulations about how many fish 
can be taken in one catch, and the minimum mass 
and/or length of fish that can be legally caught and 
kept. With some species, it is illegal to keep any 
fish caught. These regulations aim to ensure that 
different species do not become scarce. 
 
In Australia, tag and release programmes are 
encouraged by fishing associations, government 
departments and environmental groups. They 
involve the insertion of a tag into a caught fish, and 
the release of the fish back into the water. If tagged 
fish are re-caught, details such as location caught 
and length and mass of the fish are recorded.
This data is sent to the agencies that run tag and 
release programmes, and is vitally important in the 
management of marine resources.

Game fishing is fishing at the serious end! This sport involves fishing for large ocean fish with a mass 
of 400 kg or more. It is popular in many parts of Australia, including along the north coast of 
Queensland. Species of game fish found in that region include Black marlin, Sailfish, Yellow fin tuna, 
Mackerel and Wahoo. Many companies offer fishing charters where groups of people can hire out a 
boat and crew and try their hand at this extreme sport.

Two couples – Anastasia and Brad, and Omar and Sally – go on a game fishing charter trip 
for a day aboard the vessel The Monster. It leaves Port Douglas in North Queensland at 9 am 
on a Saturday morning.
The Monster is powered by two 440 horsepower (hp) diesel engines. Horsepower is a unit of 
measurement of power used in relation to engines. Its use is not as common now as it once 
was. Today, the most common unit of measurement of power is Watts (W). When measuring 
engine power, 1 hp is approximately equal to 746W. 
1 
What is the maximum power output of The Monster’s two engines in watts?
At sea, distances can be measured in nautical miles (n miles). This unit is different from miles, 
the Imperial unit of measurement for road distances. The speed at which a boat travels across 
the surface of the sea is often measured in knots (kn).  
 
• 1 kn is equal to 1 n mile per hour or 1 n mile/h 
 
• Speed can also be measured in the metric units of kilometres per hour (km/h) 
 
• 1 kn is equivalent to 1.88 km/h
2

b If a boat is travelling at 64.5 km/h, what is this speed in kn?
Back on our charter, plenty of fishing action went on while the boat was in motion, but The 
Monster also stopped at two different spots during the day where the engines were turned off.

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
There are three primary colours: red, yellow and blue. These colours can be mixed together to give 
secondary colours: red and yellow make orange, red and blue make purple, and blue and yellow make 
green. Artists use colours in this way. Computers use a system based on red, green and blue. Printing 
uses cyan, magenta, yellow and black.  
It was difficult to describe the approximately 1900 colours available to designers and so the 
Pantone® Matching System was created in 1963. Each of the standard colours is given a number 
such as PMS 194. This number can be used for the fabric, the computer screen or the printed 
brochure without any confusion.
1 
Mauve was the first colour that was not made from insects or plants, and could be  
mass-produced in a factory. In what year did William Perkin accidentally make mauve 
while he was looking for a treatment for malaria? How old was he then? 
 
Hint:  year 
age  = 103 1 
9 and year + age = 1874
2 
So that the designer can see all the colours easily, 
Pantone guides often consist of a number of cardboard 
strips, each printed with related colours. In one 
particular colour guide there are 7 shades per blade. 
How many blades are there in this guide if there are  
1 925 textile colours?
3 
De Milo Designs need 60 different colours for the 
autumn season. To make sure that everyone is working

Whales are mammals and are more closely related to humans than to the many fish and creatures 
they share the oceans with. Like us, they are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and suckle 
their young. Baleen Whales are characterised by having baleen plates for filtering food from water, 
rather than teeth. This distinguishes them from the other group of whales, the toothed whales or 
Odontoceti.

Commercial whaling in Australia started in about 1820.  
By 1845, twenty-six thousand Southern Right Whales  
had been killed. Almost 100 years later, they were a 
protected species. Between 1936 and 1938, approximately 
twelve thousand Humpback Whales were killed. A 10 year 
moratorium on Humpback whaling was declared in 1939. 
After killing commenced again in 1949, almost sixteen 
thousand Humpbacks were killed in Australia by 1963. 
Australia ceased whaling in 1978.

remained on the east coast of Australia. In 2005, approximately two thousand whales 
were observed in the same oceans. Humpbacks, along with the Bowhead, Blue and Right

another saw 500. What was the average number of whales observed? (Y)

figure of 2000. (Y)

A pelican is any one of several large water birds with a distinctive pouch under the beak. Pelicans 
belong to the bird family Pelecanidae. Darters, cormorants, gannets, bobbies, frigatebirds and 
tropicbirds also belong to the pelican family. Pelicans are found on all continents except Antarctica.
Swans are large water birds of the family Anatidae, which also includes geese and ducks. Swans are 
closely related to geese, and scientists group the two in the tribe Cygnini.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a monogamous 
b gliding 
c soaring
Pelicans are large birds with enormous, pouched bills. The smallest is the Brown Pelican, 
which can weigh as little as 2.5 kg and have a wingspan of as little as 1.8 m. The largest is 
believed to be the Dalmatian Pelican, at up to 15 kg with a maximum wingspan of nearly  
3.5 m. The Australian Pelican weighs about 5.5 kg and has a wing span of approximately  
2.4 m – its 45 cm bill is the longest of any bird. 
2

b Identify and label each pelican.

shores. Breeding may occur at any time of year, depending on environmental conditions, 
particularly rainfall. All pelican species lay at least two eggs. Hatching success for undisturbed 
pairs can be as high as 95 percent, but because of competition between siblings, usually all 
nestlings but one die

Pelicans are highly mobile, searching out suitable areas of water and an adequate supply  
of food. A layer of special fibres deep in the breast muscles holds the wings rigidly horizontal 
for gliding and soaring. Pelicans are not capable of sustained flapping flight, but can remain 
in the air for 24 hours at a time. Flight at a height of 1 000 m is common, and heights of

Besides the constant fear of death on the hills and dunes of Gallipoli, some logistical challenges 
included feeding the soldiers. Food supplies came from as far away as Greece and Egypt and 
perishables just wouldn’t survive. The soldiers’ food came in tins with the staples being corned beef 
(Bully Beef), rice, tea, cocoa, jam and ‘hard tack’. Hard tack is basically a very hard biscuit made 
of flour, water, salt and sugar. It lasts longer than bread, although it was so hard soldiers would 
sometimes break their teeth trying to eat it.
Unlike bread, hard tack biscuits are very, very hard. Some soldiers preferred to grind them up 
with old ammunition shells, mix them with water and eat it as porridge.

Crime, wars, natural disasters, politics, sport,

How significant? 
6
Numbers can be expressed correct to a particular number of decimal places or a particular number 
of significant figures. The number of digits we use to describe a measurement is the number of 
significant figures. Numbers with too many decimal places or too many significant figures are  
rounded off.
1	
Count the number of significant figures in each of the following:
a	 23
b	 203
c	 230
d	 23.00
e	 2003.0
2	
Write the following correct to  
3 significant figures:
a	 4852
b	 72.76
3	
Write 5.048 correct to 2 significant figures.
4	
Write the number 2.477 correct to:
a	 2 decimal places
b	 2 significant figures
5	
Write the number 0.0275 correct to:
a	 2 decimal places
b	 2 significant figures
6 
a	 Write correct to 2 significant figures:
 i 2.52
 ii 109
b	 Hence find an approximate value 
of 2.52 × 109.
7 
a	 Write correct to 2 significant figures:
 i 0.3267
 ii 0.0599
b	 Hence find an approximate value 
of 0.3267 ÷ 0.0599.
Rules for counting significant figures
• Count all zeros within a number as significant 
(2305 and 2.005 have 4 sig figs).
• Count all zeros to the right of the decimal point as 
significant (56.00 and 5.050 have 4 sig figs).
• Don’t count zeros that keep the decimal point in 
place as significant (3200 has only 2 sig figs).  
Rules for Rounding:
Numbers with too many decimal places or 
too many significant figures are rounded off.  
Remember, all digits after the rounding digit 
are dropped. If the digit to the right of the 
rounding digit is equal to or more than 5,  
add 1 to the rounding digit.

© Barbara Lynch and Blake Education 2007

Australian fashion companies bring textiles, clothing and footwear into Australia from overseas.

Gas Mark 5? How is that going to cook my cheese cake? Is it 350º Fahrenheit (F) or is it 180º 
Celsius (C)? In this episode, TV celebrity chefs Lorenzo and Ada are going to bake an authentic Italian 
cheese cake originating from Lorenzo’s home town of Pescara, on the Adriatic coast.
oven and out!
Around the world, ovens vary in the way they cook. Wood-fired ovens are complicated to use 
and require a lot of experience. Folklore has it that once the oven seemed hot to touch, a small 
fistful of flour would be thrown into the oven to see how long it took to brown, as a guide to 
temperature! Today’s ovens are generally heated by electricity or gas, and have been built to 
accurately control temperature.

a fan-forced oven?

Gas Mark is the old term for 
the temperature setting on 
an oven.
160°C = 300°F = Gas Mark 3
170°C = 325°F = Gas Mark 4
180°C = 350°F = Gas Mark 5
Fan-forced ovens circulate 
the hot air in the oven and 
so the food cooks 10% faster 
at a 20°C cooler temperature 
than a conventional (not 
fan-forced) oven.
Recipe – Lorenzo’s Cheese Cake – Crostata di Ricotta
Ingredients (serves 12)

cheese

Method
Collecting all the ingredients takes about 15 minutes. 
I 
 Process the flour, almond meal, icing sugar and butter in 
the bowl of a food processor for 2 minutes. Add the egg 
and process for another 1 minute. Knead until smooth on a 
floured board (5 minutes). Shape into a disc and cover with a 
tea towel. Place in the refrigerator for 30 minutes.
II 
 Preheat oven to 350ºF for 20 minutes. Roll out the pastry to 
a 3 mm thick disc. Line a tin with pastry. The tin should be 
round with a removable base and base radius measurement of 
20 cm. Be tidy. 
III  Cover the pastry base with baking paper and fill with pastry 
weights, rice or dried beans, to stop it rising. Place on a baking 
tray and bake in the oven for 10 minutes. Remove the paper 
and weights and bake for a further 10 minutes or until golden. 
IV  Separate eggs. Beat the yolks, ½ of the caster sugar, ricotta 
cheese and Sambuca. Add the cream and set aside.
V 
 Whip eggs whites until stiff, for about 4 minutes, and then 
add the other half of the caster sugar. Combine with the 
cheese mixture and place it into the tin that has the pastry 
and bake for 45 minutes at 350ºF. Cool for 1 hour then dust 
with the 10 g of icing sugar. Serve.

Knots and naughty miles 
16
World War 1 was largely fought and won on land but this could not have taken place without the 
movement of ships. Ships were used to transport supplies and manpower needed on the battlefields 
from overseas countries. Command of the seas and supply lines was essential to the armed forces 
on land.
The nautical mile is based on the circumference of the planet Earth. If you divide the circle 
made by the equator into 360 degrees and then divide a degree into 60 minutes, a single 
minute of arc on the planet Earth is 1 nautical mile. The nautical mile NM is a non-SI unit 
used mainly by navigators in the shipping and aviation industries.
1

around the equator of the Earth?

Islands

to Nauru

The device that sailors used to make their measurement of speed was a rope with knots tied 
at equal distances along it, tied to a chip of wood. The sailor would throw the chip of wood 
over the side and when the chip was in the water they would start to count the number of 
knots that passed over the back of the ship in thirty seconds. This was the speed the ship was 
travelling. The knot is defined as one nautical mile per hour.

a  10 knots pass in 30 seconds? 
b 15 knots pass in one minute?
8

 Compost made only of paper and straw will not

Maths in War & Conflict

Little Boy and Fat Man 
9
During the final stages of World War 2, the United States dropped two atomic bombs over the 
Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in a successful attempt to hasten the end of the war. The 
nuclear weapon known as ‘Little Boy’ was dropped over Hiroshima on August 6 1945. ‘Fat Man’ was 
released over Nagasaki on August 9 of the same year.
The capture of Tinian, one of the Marianas Islands, provided American forces with a valuable 
airstrip from which to mount raids on Japan. The islands served as the base from which the 
atomic bomb attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were staged.
1 
Colour the seas, nations and islands different colours.
2

a Tinian 
b Nagasaki 
c Sapporo.
3 
Name the features at:
a 26°N, 141°E 
b 16°N, 146°E 
c 45°N, 129°E
Hiroshima was the primary target of the first nuclear 
bombing mission on August 6. A B-29 bomber was 
launched from Tinian in the west Pacific, about six 
hours flight time from Japan. Two other B-29s were also 
launched. After leaving Tinian the aircraft made their 
way separately to Iwo Jima where they met at an altitude 
of 2440 metres and set course for Japan. The aircraft 
arrived over the target in clear visibility at 9855 metres. 
4

Japan.

return trip.

a   Iwo Jima? 
b  Hiroshima?
8

9

The gravity bomb known as ‘Little Boy’ was released at 8.15 am from a height of  
 
9855 metres.  ‘Little Boy’ contained 60 kilograms of uranium-235 and took 57 seconds to 
fall from the aircraft to the predetermined detonation height about 600 m above the city. 
It created a blast equivalent to about 13 kilotons of TNT. The uranium-235 weapon was 
considered very inefficient, with only 1.38% of its material exploding.

The radius of total destruction was about 1.6 km, with

15 What was the total area of destruction?

contained the fires (assume a circular shape).
At the time of the attack the population of Hiroshima was approximately 345 000. 
Approximately 80 000 people were killed immediately and another 70 000 were injured. It has 
been estimated that, of the people who died on the day of the explosion, 60% died from burns, 
30% from falling bricks, timber and other materials and 10% from other causes. 
18 Find the total number of people who were killed or injured by the blast.
19 Of the number of people who were killed or injured, what percentage was killed 
immediately by the blast? 
20 Of the people who were killed in the blast, how many died from:
a  flash or flame burns? 
b falling debris? 
c other causes?
On the morning of August 9 1945, the nuclear bomb code-named Fat Man was detonated. 
The bomb contained 6.4 kg of plutonium-239, and was dropped on Nagasaki’s industrial 
valley at 11.01 am. The estimated population of Nagasaki at the time of the bombing was 270 
000. Fat Man exploded 43 seconds later at 469 m above the ground. 
21 What was the time when Fat Man exploded?

On August 15, six days after the detonation over Nagasaki, Japan announced its surrender to 
the Allied Powers. They signed the Instrument of Surrender on September 2, officially ending 
the Pacific War and therefore World War 2.
25 After the bombing of Nagasaki, how many hours did it take for the Japanese to

38 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
You shoot two hours of tape and end up using 25 seconds of it. Welcome to a behind-the-scenes look 
at how all that stuff ends up on the cutting room floor, from the hours and minutes down to the 
hundredths of seconds.
Behind the scenes in any commercial or public television studio are many people who work 
on editing and preparing finished programs for broadcast. They use a range of technology to 
process footage shot on film by camera operators. Timing has to be highly accurate, so when 
camera operators shoot film, in or out of the studio, a time code appears on the tape accurate 
to hundredths of a second. Editors can then take the material shot by the camera operators 
and select the bits they want to go into a finished program with a high degree of precision.
To read a time code
Time codes are shown as numbers with colons or points separating them into pairs that show

Luge is a winter sport where competitors lie on their backs on an amazingly fast, sled-like vehicle 
and fly down a twisting ice-covered course – typically between 1 000 and 1 500 km in length. 
They can reach speeds in excess of 130 km/h. Competitors are timed over a number of runs, and the 
person with the fastest combined times wins the competition. Luge competition is held in women’s 
and men’s singles and doubles and mixed doubles.
‘Luge’ is the French word for ‘sled’. The luges used in elite  
competition, including the Winter Olympics, consist of a  
fibreglass shell with steel runners that slide over the surface of  
the ice. A luge can be steered, but it has no brakes. Once the luge  
is in motion, the competitor lies down and completes the course.  
To stop it, they sit up and pull the front of the luge upwards.

is put on one end of the bar and you apply your effort at the other end. This allows you to

where E is the effort, D1 the length of the bar from the effort to the fulcrum, L the load and

Marinara on the menu  – oysters and scallops 
6
Bivalves are molluscs. They have two-part shells. This group of animals includes scallops, clams, 
oysters and mussels. Bivalves are exclusively aquatic and are found in marine and fresh water. 
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a salinity 
b hessian
The oyster becomes sexually mature at about 1 year of age, and then always as a male. After 
about 3 years, it can change sex and reproduce as a female. From then on it can change sex 
back and forth throughout its life. When reproduction takes place, the male releases its sperm 
into the water and the female sucks it in to her shell and fertilises the eggs. A female can 
contain as many as 1.1 million eggs. Fertilised eggs develop within the female in the first  
10 days. The larvae swim freely in the water for a couple of weeks and so spread to other 
areas. Afterwards, the larvae fall to the bottom and land on rocks, shells or stakes. Then the 
oyster is known as a brood and it is about 0.3 mm in size. The oyster lives for about 8 years.
2

workbook draw and annotate a diagram of the life cycle.
3

of these survival rates?
a 1% 
b 2% 
c 0.002% 
d 0.003% 
e 0.0001% 
4

40 parts water. Simplify the salinity of these batches of water, and decide if reproduction 
can take place. 
a 2:20 
b 2:100 
c 5:400 
d 4:120 
e 2:90
Oysters are filter feeders – that is, they consume a variety of species of phytoplankton, bacteria 
and viruses from the surrounding water. Adult oysters can filter 10 L of water per hour as they 
search for food. 
5

a 2 hr? 
b 3 hr?  
c 6.5 hr? 
d 5 hr 30 min? 
e 6 hr 25 min?
6

a 50 L? 
b 70 L? 
c 65 L? 
d 125 L?  
e 241 L?
The harvesting of oysters in oyster farms for market occurs prior to spawning, when the oysters 
are in peak condition. Oysters are brought in from the farm and graded into various shell 
sizes, such as bistro 50–60 mm, plate 60–70 mm and standard 70–85 mm. The oysters are then 
packed into hessian bags. For bistro oysters, 45 dozen oysters are packaged in each bag. Then 
the oysters are transported in refrigerated trucks directly to the wholesaler or retailer. Oysters 
stored at 5°C have a shelf-life of less than 10 days.
7

a 90 dozen 
b 225 dozen 
c 440 dozen 
d 4 860 oysters

Scallops are edible bivalves, similar to oysters and clams. They are found on the bottom of 
bay waters and in the sea. They do not attach themselves to a permanent anchorage. Instead, 
they move themselves through the water by opening and closing their shells. As a result, the 
muscle that controls the ‘hinge’ of the shell is much larger than that of oysters or clams. 
Scallops in Bass Strait are collected in dredges which are towed along the seabed by vessels 
travelling at four to six knots. The dredges are made from strong, wire-mesh boxes that are 
four metres long, with a mouth about three metres wide and 30 cm high. 2.5 scallops per

10 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Octopus, squid and cuttlefish live in the oceans and do not have backbones. They are Cephalopoda, 
which means ‘head foot’. Members of this group have feet or tentacles connected to the head, 
not the body. They can change the colour of their skin to mimic their environment and hide from 
predators. They also eject a thick blackish ink in a large cloud to help them escape from predators. 
They can move quickly by sucking water into their mantle cavity and quickly squirting it out of 
their siphon in a fast, strong jet.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a lair 
b larval 
c respiratory 
d  chameleon.
Octopuses have 8 arms which create an umbrella  
shape around their central rounded head. Each  
arm has two rows of suckers and is 3 to 4 times longer  
than the body. The head has two large eyes. Octopuses  
can be many different colours, from red to a pale grey, with or  
without mottling and with or without protrusions on their skin.
2 
How many arms altogether on these numbers of octopuses?
a 5                 b  7                  c  25               d  53                  e  49
3 
How many octopuses are there for these numbers of arms?
a 16               b  24                 c  104             d  216                e  560
In some species of octopus, the female lays 200 000 eggs. She hangs these  
eggs in strings from the ceiling of her lair. At around the time the eggs hatch,  
the mother dies and the young larval octopuses spend a period of time drifting in  
clouds of plankton where they feed.
4

a 5 
b 7 
c 9 
d 15 
e 24
5

a 400 000 
b 600 000 
c 100 000

6

How many human adults could these numbers of Blue Ringed Octopuses kill?
a 6 
b 8 
c 15 
d 21 
e 34
7

a 26 
b 52 
c 78 
d 104 
e 69
When Blue Ringed Octopus mate in early autumn, the male dies. The female lays 
approximately 50 eggs in late autumn. Once the eggs are hatched 6 months later, the female 
dies. The young octopuses develop quickly, and mature and mate the following autumn.
8 
Draw a timeline to show the life cycle of the Blue Ringed Octopus.
Mighty molluscs - octopus, squid & cuttlefish

When bitten by a Blue Ringed Octopus, a feeling of sickness is felt within a few seconds. 
Within 10 seconds, the victim is blind. Within one minute, there is a loss of sense of touch, 
speech and the ability to swallow. Paralysis sets in and the body goes into respiratory 
arrest within a further 3 minutes. Draw a timeline to show the effects of the octopus bite.
10 When referring to octopus flesh, fishers use terms such as ‘U/25’. This is pronounced 
‘under twenty-five’ and refers to the number of octopuses per kilogram – in this case, 
fewer than twenty-five octopuses per kilogram. 26!!40 is pronounced ‘twenty-six forty’ and 
means that there are twenty-six to forty octopuses per kilogram. For each weight listed,

(largest eyes in the animal kingdom) is 20 m, a Calamari Squid is 60 cm, and an Arrow 
Squid is 75 cm. In your workbook, draw a horizontal bar graph to compare these lengths.

grams of flesh for eating that could be recovered from squid with the weights listed below.

original weight of each squid, to the nearest gram.

e 1.1 kg

ability to rapidly alter their skin colour. Their skin changes very quickly to camouflage 
them from predators. The colour change is produced by groups of red, yellow, brown 
and black pigmented cells. If there are 200 of these specialised pigment cells per square

Maths in War & Conflict 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011
Missile mayhem 
18
A guided missile is a self-propelled rocket used as a weapon. Missiles are propelled by a jet engine 
and generally have one or more explosive warheads. In military terms, the word missile describes a 
powered, guided munition, whilst the word rocket describes a powered, unguided munition. 
A cruise missile is basically a small, pilotless airplane. Cruise missiles have a 2.6-metre 
wingspan, are powered by turbofan engines and can fly 800 to 1600 kilometres, depending on 
their design. 
1 
How many centimetres in: 
a   2.61 m? 
b 2.34 m? 
c 2.5 m? 
d 5.03 m?

a  2.612 m? 
b 2.34 m? 
c 2.3 m? 
d 2.13 m?
3 
How many metres in:
a 800 km? 
b 1200 km? 
c 1500 km? 
d 1340.6 km?
The job of a cruise missile is to deliver a 450 kilogram high-explosive bomb to a precise 
location – the target. The missile is destroyed when the bomb explodes. Since cruise missiles 
cost between $500 000 and $1 000 000 each, it’s a fairly expensive way to deliver a   
 
450 kilogram package. 
4 
Calculate the median cost of one missile.

a 3 missiles 
  
b 6 missiles
c 12 missiles 
  
d 23 missiles.

c $5 200 000?

a 900 kg 
b 450 kg 
c 2700 kg

rocket booster and weigh approximately 1500 kg.

b weight

Mobile phones

Mobile telephones have now become part of everyday life for many people. This means individuals 
can be contacted 24 hours per day.

a	 make calls while driving?
b	 use their phones at some time during a trip?

The risk of a learner driver being involved in a fatal car crash is 10 times as much as for 
an experienced driver. This risk is increased by a factor of 4 when the driver is using a 
mobile phone while driving. By what factor is the risk of a learner driver being involved 
in a fatal car crash increased if they are using a mobile phone?
5	
‘Optical zoom’ is like magnifying a picture. So if a picture is magnified six times it is 
usually described as having 6× zoom; the size of the image is six times larger when 
zoomed than when it was not zoomed. The word ‘optical’ just means that it uses the 
camera lens, not a digital system. The camera in Elly’s mobile phone has 12× optical 
zoom but her sister Bea’s has only 8× optical zoom.
a	 What would be the dimensions of the zoomed image of a tree if the unzoomed

to the unzoomed image?

Staging an art exhibition is often a major event for an artist, a gallery and a community. Art 
galleries are generally located in major cities and key regional centres. Important shows are often 
exhibited internationally as a way of exchanging ideas between countries.
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, complete the calculations in it to find the answer.

modern artist Ivana Paintalot to exhibit at their gallery 
for their June show.

produced, including an essay about her work by 
a specialist writer. The cost price to the gallery for

$14.95. What would the profit be if 500 were sold? 
b There are 16 two-metre square oil paintings and 
12 one-metre square charcoal drawings. The retail 
price for the two different forms are $8250 each 
and $3450 each respectively. 
 i Calculate the possible revenue to the gallery if 
 
all the paintings and works on paper are sold.

    frame each of the works. How much does the gallery receive for the framing?

gallery’s profit on framing.

4  of Ivana’s paintings and 2 
3  of the works on paper were sold, how much would 
    the gallery receive for the sales?

rodney mcClick
For the July show, Gallery Praxis is exhibiting Rodney McClick, a young modern photographer.

Gallery Praxis has approximately 800 people on its mailing list, of which 20% are 
overseas clients. The artist’s list is 30% of the size of the gallery’s list and everyone is local. 
a How many invitations could be sent if the gallery combines its list with that of the artist?
b How many invitations are being sent to overseas patrons? 
c Rodney McClick has produced 40 photographs of the Australian outback. The works are 
priced at $1750 each. Rodney sells 70% of his images off the wall. 
 i How much was received from sales?
 ii If the gallery pays him 60% of that value, how much money did Rodney earn?

Native fish - Golden Perch & Murray Cod 
9
The Golden Perch, commonly called a yellow belly, is a medium-to-large fish with a deep, laterally 
compressed body. It is considered rare in much of its original range, although it is still present in 
large numbers in many locations. Its maximum weight is 23 kg and maximum length is 760 mm, but 
it is usually less than 400 mm and 4 kg. The body colour is generally olive-green with a yellow or 
cream belly. The mouth is large, with the lower jaw protruding slightly. The tail is rounded.
Murray Cod are an Australian native fish. They were once widespread throughout the  
Murray-Darling system, and found in some surprisingly small streams. This species was the most 
common of the larger native fish in the Murray-Darling system at the time of European settlement. 
Wild stocks are now estimated to be less than ten percent of the population present at that time.
Whenever you see a colour code letter, find your answer in the shape at the end of the 
worksheet and colour that section. Colour code: R = red, B = blue, G = green, Y = yellow.

Golden Perch are predominantly found in warm, turbid, slow-flowing rivers. The species is 
long-lived, with a maximum age of about 25 years, although most live less than 11 years. 
Males are reproductively mature at 2 years and females at 4 years.

Adult and immature fish are migratory. Extensive upstream movements of more than  
1 000 kilometres have been recorded for some adult fish. Outside the breeding season, 
individuals occupy home ranges of about 100 m2 for weeks or months before relocating to 
another site where a new home range is established.

Hatching occurs after 1 to 2 days and newly

Murray Cod reach at least 60 cm and 3 to 4 kilograms in smaller streams. In larger rivers they 
grow to about 90 cm and weigh 20 kg. The largest Murray Cod ever officially recorded was 
183 cm and 113 kg. Unfortunately, excessive fishing has led to a serious lack of large, mature 
breeding cod in wild populations. There are now very few cod above the minimum legal 
angling size of 50 cm. Egg counts range from less than 10 000 eggs for a barely mature female 
to approximately 90 000 for older females, which weigh around 22 kg.

The eggs of cod are large, about 3.5 mm in diameter, and sticky. They are usually deposited 
onto hard surfaces such as logs, rocks or clay banks. 
The male guards the eggs during incubation and they hatch after 5 to 13 days. The larvae are 
about 6 mm long at hatching and have a large yolk sac. Larvae drift downstream for 5 to 7 
days, particularly by night in spring and summer.

Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
‘Out in the Wild’ 
8
The documentary crews are roaming Africa to find out what some of the biggest, cutest and most 
striking animals on the planet are up to. They’ve found some amazing statistics about weights, 
heights and more.
You can travel to the ends of the Earth … and you don’t have to leave home to do it.  
‘Out in the Wild’ brings the world of wildlife to your TV …
1	
The ‘Out in the Wild’ crew visits a region in Tanzania to observe the behaviour of some 
zebra families. Each zebra family has one male (stallion) and 2–6 females (mares), 
together with any young foals. There are also bachelor groups of males that do not have 
families. In the region visited by the crew, the total number of zebras was 216.
a	 151 of the zebras lived in families. What was the total number of male ‘bachelors’?
b	 There were 32 stallions in families. How many families were in the group?
c	 There were a total of 18 foals in the group of zebras. How many adult females were in 
the group?
d	 What was the average number of females per family in the group of zebras? (Answer to 
1 decimal place.)
2	
Further south in Africa, in Botswana, another ‘Out in the Wild’ crew visits a meerkat 
colony with 24 meerkats living together. The total length of an adult meerkat is  
25–31 cm, and their tail length is typically 19–24 cm. They weigh 620–940 g.
a	 In this meerkat colony there are 14 males and 10 females. What is the ratio of males to 
females?
b	 The heaviest male meerkat in the colony is 830 g and the heaviest female is 770 g. 
What proportion of the male’s weight is the female’s weight? (Answer to 2 decimal 
places.)
c	 Four of the juvenile meerkats have a combined tail length of 52 cm. What is their 
average tail length?
d	 One juvenile has a tail 12.4 cm long. When fully grown, her tail will measure 21.2 cm. 
What percentage of the fully-grown tail length is her tail now? (Answer to 1 decimal 
place.)

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
19
3	
One of the most popular segments on ‘Out in the Wild’ was the filming of the birth of a 
baby giraffe in the wild, six years ago.
a	 Female giraffes gestate or carry their young for 457 days. How many months is this? 
(Answer to the nearest whole month.)
b	 When it was born, the young male calf weighed 61 kg and stood 2.01 m high. Six years 
later, the crew revisits the area just south of the Sahara Desert and catches up with the 
same giraffe. Now he is an adult bull weighing 1345 kg and standing 5.67 m high. 
When the calf was born, what percentage of its adult weight and height were its birth 
weight and height? (Answer to 1 decimal place.)
4	
A recent 2-hour special of ‘Out in the Wild’ was filmed at Kruger National 
Park in South Africa. Part of it covered the habits of a population of Southern 
White Rhinoceros. These animals generally move in small groups and are 
quite sociable, although males are very territorial.
a	 Southern White Rhinos behave routinely and have 
favourite places to walk, feed and wallow. Daily 
movements of up to 15 km are not uncommon for 
females. The crew tracked one group of females and 
found that the 4 adults and 1 calf each walked an 
average of 7.8 km per day over the course of a week. 
What was the total distance covered by  
one rhino in a week?
b	 If this rate of movement was 
maintained for a year, what is  
the total distance each rhino  
will have covered?
c	 One bull rhino spent the entire seven days in his home territory, an area of savannah 
totalling 2.37 km2, in the shape shown below. Calculate the value of x, to 2 decimal 
places).

Paying Bills Math Projects 
 
1. Do some comparison shopping for credit cards.  Find the best interest rate. 
 
2. Simulate a house buying scenario in your community. Use actual advertisements for 
houses and for housing loans. Get students to find the best loan deals. Which is best 
- fixed or variable interest? What will they pay in total for the house? What will it be 
worth at the end of the loan period? How much will they have paid after 10 years 
and how much will they own by then?  
 
3. Paying extra on your mortgage is a good idea.  It can shave years off your loan and 
save tens of thousands of dollars in interest charges. For example:  If you increased 
your mortgage payments by just $170 from $830 to $1,000, you could:  
• Save almost $48,000 in interest over the entire amortization period of your 
mortgage  
• Own your home about 8 years sooner  
Find out some other ways you can pay down your loan more quickly without being 
penalized.    
4. Do you have a cell phone?  Take a look at your bill.  What are you actually paying 
for?  Can you cut down on your costs?  Is there a better plan for you?

Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
On Christmas Day in 1859, the Victorian Acclimatisation Society released 24 rabbits to hunt for 
sport, to help settlers feel more ‘at home’.  By 1886, rabbits had spread as far as the Queensland-
NSW border and by 1900 they reached Western Australia and the Northern Territory. In the next 
60 years, rabbits invaded 4 million square kilometres of Australia, making it one of the fastest 
colonising mammals anywhere in the world. Rabbits are small mammals in the family Leporidae.
The European Red Fox was introduced to Victoria by fox hunters in 1871 and declared a pest in that 
state by 1901. Foxes crossed the border into NSW around 1893 and were declared a pest there soon 
after. They had spread through most of Australia by 1930.
1

a colonising 
b myxomatosis  
c warren
2

largest rabbits grow to 50 cm and more than 10 kg. Calculate the total weight of: 
a 6 Pygmy Rabbits and 6 of the largest rabbits. 
b 5 Pygmy Rabbits and 7 of the largest rabbits.
3 
Many people use the expression ‘breed like rabbits’. Rabbits have an extremely high 
reproductive potential. They are able to have their first litter at 3 months of age and then 
give birth to litters of 6 young every six weeks. Calculate the number of rabbits that can 
be reproduced during one year by:
a a single adult pair.  
b a single adult pair and their offspring.

700 sheep. The number of rabbits per warren varies from 10 to 50, depending on the 
amount of green feed available. Ten rabbits eat as much as one sheep.

a the average number of rabbits on Jacko’s paddock, if there are 30 rabbits per warren.
b the number of sheep that could have eaten the amount of food the rabbits ate.

the paddocks in question 5, calculate the value of lost production to each farmer.
Commercial harvesting, including hunting, has not been effective in reducing wild rabbit 
numbers to protect natural resources. Shooting may remove a portion of the population but 
these are quickly replaced by reproduction. Rabbit shooters harvest only 1.5% of the rabbit 
population. Even after a 70% reduction in population size, rabbits can regain their former

30 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
The lion is a member of the family Felidae, and one of four big cats in the genus Panthera. With 
exceptionally large males exceeding 250 kg in weight, it is the second-largest living cat after the 
tiger. Wild lions currently exist in Africa and Asia, with a critically endangered population in north-
west India. They have disappeared from North Africa, the Middle East and Western Asia.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a defecating 
b synchronise 
c scavenging
Weights for adult lions generally lie between 150 and 250 kg for males, and 120 and 180 kg 
for females. Head and body length is 170 to 250 cm for males and 140 to 170 cm for females. 
Shoulder height is about 125 cm in males and 100 cm in females. 
2 
For these adult lions, calculate the midpoint of the given ranges for the:
a weight of a male. 
b weight of a female. 
c length of a male. 
d length of a female.
3 
Use the midpoints you calculated in the previous question to draw rectangles to represent 
a male and female lion. Use a scale of 1:100.
Lions spend much of their time resting, and are inactive for about 20 hours per day. Although 
lions can be active at any time, their activity generally peaks after dusk with a period of 
socialising, grooming and defecating. Hunting most often takes place at dawn. Each day, lions 
spend an average of two hours walking and 50 minutes eating.
4 
On average: 
a how many minutes per day are spent resting?
b how many minutes per day are spent walking?
c how many hours per day are spent eating?
d how many seconds per day are spent eating?
5 
On average, what percentage of a lion’s day is spent:
a resting? 
b walking? 
c eating?
Lions can reach speeds of 60 km/h for short bursts. They sneak up to within 30 m of their prey 
before launching an attack. Lions generally prey on medium size animals such as zebras, 
gazelle and wildebeest. On average, they are only successful in five out of twenty attempts. A 
lioness uses her weight and paws to knock her quarry down. She then secures the meal with a 
bite to the throat or neck, generally suffocating the victim. If a lioness cannot catch her prey 
in the first few hundred metres, she gives up and chooses another victim.
6 
Change these lion speeds to m/s.
a 120 km/h 
b 90 km/h 
c 40 km/h 
d 60 km/h 
e 100 km/h
7 
At 60 km/h, how long would it take a lion to run these distances to catch its prey?
a 20 m 
b 30 m 
c 35 m 
d 40 m 
e 60 m 
8 
How many times is a lion likely to be successful at catching prey in these numbers of 
attempts?
a 20 
b 60 
c 120 
d 16 
e 24
Queens and kings of the jungle - lions 
14
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
31
A lion can gorge itself, eating up to 30 kg in one sitting. If it is unable to eat the entire kill, 
it will rest for a few hours before eating more. On a hot day, the pride may retreat to shade, 
leaving a male or two to stand guard. An adult lioness requires an average of 5 kg of meat per 
day, a male 7 kg.
9 
On average, how much meat will these lions need to eat over the time shown?
a A male, 12 days 
b A male, 3 weeks 
c A female, 23 days 
d A female, 2 months
10 On average, how many equivalent ‘days of meat’ are these amounts for a lioness? 
a 30 kg 
b 25 kg 
c 10 kg 
d 12 000 g
11 Scavenging makes up about 12% of a lion’s food source. Lions listen for vultures and 
hyenas, which are scavengers, and go to the scene to take what they can for themselves. 
How much food is likely to be scavenged by these lions during the given time?
a 1 male, 12 wks 
b 2 males, 10 wks 
c 1 female, 16 wks 
d 3 females, 1 yr
12 Most lions now live in eastern and southern Africa. Their numbers have rapidly decreased 
over the last two decades. One current estimate of the African lion population is 31 000, 
living in the wild. This has decreased from 100 000 in 1990 and 400 000 in 1950.
a Draw a line graph to show the changes in the wild African lion population since 1950. 
b Calculate the percentage decrease in the lion population since 1950. 
c Suggest why the number of lions has been decreasing.
d From your graph, what was the lion population in 1970?   
 
e From your graph, when was the lion population 150 000?
Like lion numbers, habitat for lions has declined over the past two decades. Since the 1960s, 
the human population, land cultivation and number of livestock have steadily increased. In 
2001, scientists estimated the habitat for lions was about 5 200 000 km2, and suggested that 
this is half of that available in the 1950s. More detailed estimates suggest that the lion habitat 
is approximately three million km2, with about half of this area protected by a national park 
or reserve. Much of the lion’s habitat is fragmented and unprotected.
13 a What area of land was available for lion habitat in the 1950s?
b Find the length ‘x ’ of the rectangle below  
given that its area is 10 400 000 km2.
c Draw this rectangle to scale on  
the map of Australia.
d Shade a square of area  
3 000 000 km2 on the map.
e From detailed estimates, what  
percentage of the lion’s habitat  
is protected by national parks and reserves?
14 Explain the significance of the lion’s habitat  
being fragmented and unprotected.
500 km

3000 km

Australian Red Cross was formed on 13 August 1914 exactly nine days after the outbreak of World 
War I. Lady Munro-Ferguson, who had worked for British Red Cross in Scotland and was the wife of 
the Governor-General, called on the wives of each State Governor to form a local committee in each 
capital. The women readily agreed and so Australian Red Cross was born.
During World War 2, Red Cross transported 40 000 pairs of socks, 25 000 shirts, 20 000 
underpants, 10 000 pairs of shoes and boots, 10 000 pairs of pyjamas, 5000 overcoats and 
many other items people thought would be useful to soldiers on the front in Europe. The effort 
from many small communities ‘beggared the imagination’. By the end of the war Red Cross 
unit of Rutherglen had forwarded, among many other items, more than 1200 shirts, 8500 
pairs of underpants, 1200 pairs of pyjamas, 2400 pairs of socks, 75 sheets, 770 pillow-cases, 
450 bed sheets and 390 handkerchiefs.

There are risks in managing an event: risks to human life, the environment, the organisation 
hosting the event, the operation or project, and to the reputations of the organisation and other 
people. It is important to insure against some eventualities and to prepare for others.
Be insured!
1

should be allowed for unforeseen happenings. If

much should be allowed for emergencies?

searchText:
Saving Water Saves Money! #19 
Multiplication, division, rounding decimals 
 
Saving water is not only good for the environment but it is also good for your pocket 
book.  When we save water we don’t have to pay for it.  It costs about $2.86 per cubic 
metre for water use.  There are 1000 litres of water per cubic metre. 
 
A household with two adults and two children can easily save about 55,000 litres of 
water in the bathroom alone, which is $157.30 a year. 
 
 
Example:  
You replace your regular shower head that uses 20 litres per minute with a 
new low-flow shower head that only uses half as much water (10 litres per 
minute).   
 
Problem: 
How much water and how much money will you save each year if the 
shower is used 15 times each week (52 weeks per year) and each shower 
lasts 10 minutes and the price of water is $2.86 per cubic metre? 
 
Solution: 
Water Savings  
15 showers per week X 52 weeks per year X (20 litres per minute – 10 litres 
per minute) X 10 minutes per shower = 78,000 litres 
Convert litres to cubic metres   
78,000 ÷ 1000 = 78 cubic metres (m3) 
Cost Savings  
78 m3 per year X $2.86 per m3 = $223.08 per year 
You would save $223.08 per year in water costs.  You will actually save more than 
this because you will also save on the cost to heat the water! 
 
 
 
 
Home Math Workbook
59
Environmental Math

 
Directions:  Answer the problems below.  Round to the nearest cent where necessary. 
 
1. You replace your regular toilet that uses 16 litres per flush with a new 
low-volume toilet that only uses 6 litres per flush.   
a. How much water will you save each year if the toilet is 
flushed 6 times each day, 365 days each year? 
_______________________ 
b. How much money will you save each year if the price of water is $2.86 per 
cubic metre? When converting to cubic metres - keep the two decimal points 
and then multiply.  ___________________________ 
 
2. You replace your regular top-loading washing machine that uses 150 litres of water 
per load with a new Energy Star front-loading washer that uses only 50 litres per 
load.   
a. How much water will you save in each year if you do 5 loads of laundry each 
week of the year (52 weeks per year) _______________________ 
b. How much money will you save each year if the price of water is $2.86 per 
cubic metre? ________________________ 
 
3. Your faucet in your bathroom has been dripping for some time now.  It drips at a 
rate of 10 drips per minute which equals about 8 litres per day.   
a. How much water will you save in one year if you fix the leaky faucet?  
__________________ 
b. How much money will you save in one year if water is $2.86 per cubic metre? 
__________________ 
 
 
 
Home Math Workbook
60
Environmental Math

 
4. Leaving the tap running while you clean your teeth can waste 7 litres of water 
assuming you brush your teeth twice a day.   
a. How much water will you save in one year if you turn off the tap while you 
brush your teeth? ___________________ 
b. How much money will you save in one year if water is $2.86 per cubic metre? 
5. You decide that you are no longer going to have baths.  You usually take 2 baths per 
week.  Each bath is about 430 litres of water. 
a. How much water will you save in one year if you cut out your baths? 
___________________ 
b. How much money will you save in one year if water is $2.86 per 
cubic metre? _____________________________ 
6. You usually give your child a bath every night.  You decide that to 
save on water you will only bath her 3 times per week.  You usually 
only fill the bath up half way which is about 215 litres of water. 
a. How much water will you save in one year if you reduce your child’s bathing 
to 3 times per week? ___________________ 
b. How much money will you save in one year if water is $2.86 per cubic metre? 
_____________________

Silent and deadly – snakes and scorpions 
12
A snake is a long reptile, covered in scales. All snakes are carnivores. Snakes do not have eyelids, 
limbs, external ears or legs. While venomous snakes comprise a minority of the species, some 
possess potent venom that is capable of causing painful injury or death to humans. However, venom 
in snakes is primarily used for killing or subduing prey, rather than for self defence.
Scorpions are eight-legged carnivorous arthropods and there are about 2000 species of scorpions. 
Most scorpions are relatively harmless to humans, with their stings only resulting in pain, 
numbness or swelling. However, a few scorpion species, mostly in the family Buthidae, can be 
dangerous to humans.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a venom 
b toxic  
c neurotoxin
Snake venoms are like soups. Most of them contain many 
different components and some of these are toxic to people. 
For example, in the venom of the Common Tiger Snake, 
there are at least 6 neurotoxins which affect the human 
nervous system.

worn skin and to help get rid of parasites such as mites and ticks. Moulting is repeated 
periodically throughout a snake’s life. An older snake might shed its skin twice a year. A 
younger, still-growing snake might shed four times a year. If a snake reaches maturity in

32 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Whether it’s at elite level or street level, skateboards take a fair bit of punishment. It’s critical for 
a skater’s equipment to be built to take what’s dished out to it. Let’s look at the bits and pieces that 
make up a skateboard, and some of the specifications that go along with them.
There are four main components to a skateboard:
• the deck
•  the trucks (the axle that connects  
to the underneath of the deck)
• the wheels
• the bearings (inside the wheels).
So whether you’re putting together your own skateboard from the components, or purchasing 
one complete – how do you decide what’s right for you? 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
The Deck
A US skateboarding authority recommends the guidelines in the table below for skateboard 
decks. Measurements in the table on the right have been converted to centimetres.

(feet, inches)

a Use the figures in the tables above to write a formula for converting feet to centimetres.
b Now write a formula for converting inches to centimetres.
2 
Samantha is 121.92 cm tall and uses a skateboard deck that is 73.66 cm long. Her friend 
Adrian is 185.42 cm in height and uses a skateboard deck that is 82.55 cm long. 
a Calculate the ratio of height to deck length for both Samantha and Adrian.
b Whose height : length ratio is higher – Samantha’s or Adrian’s?
3 
What is the height : length ratio for a skateboarder who is 172.72 cm tall with a 
skateboard deck length of 81.28 cm?
4 
What statement can you make about the recommended ratio of a person’s height to deck 
length, as the person’s height increases?
5 
Suggest why the recommended ratio of height to deck length changes as it does.
6 
Would skateboard wheels with a larger diameter roll faster or slower than wheels with a 
smaller diameter?

7 
Skateboarders who spend a lot of time 
riding ramps typically choose wheels of 
diameter 55–65 mm. Why do you think this 
is so?
8 
A skateboard has wheels of diameter 56 mm. 
a What is the circumference of the wheels? (Use the π value given by your calculator). 
b What is the circumference of the wheel in cm? Answer to 2 decimal places.
9 
By how much is the circumference of a skateboard wheel with a diameter of 65 mm 
longer than the circumference of a skateboard wheel with a diameter of 56 mm?  
Answer in cm.
10 The skateboard wheels in the illustration on the previous page are cylindrical in shape.  
Wider wheels have more surface in contact with the ground.
a What could be one advantage of having more wheel surface in contact  
with the ground?
b What could be one disadvantage of having more wheel surface in contact  
with the ground?
11 The surface area of an open-ended cylinder is calculated  
using the formula:
 
SA = 2 π r × height (h)
 
In the case of a cylindrical skateboard wheel, height can be taken  
as the width of the wheel. A wheel has a diameter of 5.4 cm and a  
height of 4 cm, as shown in the diagram. Using the formula above,  
calculate the surface area of the wheel. Your answer should be in cm2. 
 
The width of skateboard decks does not vary a 
great deal. Most are 7.5–8 inches wide (19.05–
20.32 cm). The size of the skateboarder’s feet 
is also a consideration – people with larger feet 
should use wider skateboard decks.
The Trucks
There are a range of different trucks available 
of varying quality, width and design. 
Essentially, trucks need to match the width of 
a skateboard deck, and be strong and flexible 
enough to do what a skateboarder wants his or 
her board to do.
The Wheels
There are many different types of wheels.  
They are constructed differently – using 
different materials – and come in a range of 
diameters. The two main measurements to 
consider for skateboard wheels are wheel 
diameter and hardness.
The hardness of wheels varies according to the 
types of surfaces they will be ridden on, and 
is given by a number. The higher the number, 
the harder the wheel. Typically, skateboard 
wheels have a diameter of 52–54 mm, with a 
hardness of 95–100a. Cruising skateboarders 
often prefer softer wheels, as they traverse 
rough terrain more often. Typical hardness of 
these wheels might be 75–85a.

30 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Skateboarding – pastime, means of transportation, and extreme sport! Today, mind-blowing speeds 
and tricks on skateboards have reached levels that were not even dreamed of just a couple of 
decades ago. As with any extreme sport, there are always those who want to push the boundaries 
that little bit further …
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
Danny Way from California, a renowned extreme skater, 
holds a number of records. In 2004, he set the world record 
for the longest jump and the highest air off a ‘Mega Ramp’ he 
designed. The jump measured an impressive 79 feet in length, 
and 23.5 feet in height. The same style of ‘Mega Ramp’ was 
used in Way’s successful jump over the Great Wall of China 
in 2005, where he became the first human to jump the wall 
without the aid of a motor.
a How long and high were Danny Way’s jump records, in metres?
b Danny reached an amazing speed of 55 mph before leaving the 
ramp. Read ‘Did you know?’ box about Joel King’s record on a  
jet-powered skateboard. 
 What percentage of Joel King’s speed did 
Danny Way achieve without a motor?
c If speed on leaving the ramp is the 
only factor in determining the height 
and length of a skateboard jump, what 
height and length of jump would be 
achieved by exiting the ramp at the 
same speed Joel King travelled on his  
jet-powered board? Answer in feet, and 
then convert your answer to metres.
d Speed on exiting the ramp is clearly not 
the only factor that determines how long 
and high a jump is. What other factors 
do you think might influence the jump?
2 
Chad Fernandez, an American 
professional skateboarder, performed the 
longest skateboard rail grind – 10.31 m  
(36 ft 9 in or 36.75 ft). If the rail length was 15.00 m in total,  
what proportion of the rail was covered by Fernandez’s grind?
3

a what is this figure as a fraction in its simplest form?
b what is this figure as a percentage?
4

How far short of Fernandez’s record was this grind?
5

shorter than those set on snowboards and skis. Identify one main difference  
between grinding on skateboards and skis/snowboards that accounts for this.
Skateboarding – jump, grind & slalom  
14
Did you know? 
On 29 August 2007, Englishman Joel King 
clocked up an astounding 110 mph  
(177.1 km/h) on a jet-powered skateboard 
… Now that’s extreme! He laid down on his 
back on the 1.5 m long board, which had a 
kerosene engine strapped to the back. It took 
him just over 2 seconds to reach the record 
speed. The board, which was constructed 
without any steering mechanism or brakes and 
cost King £7 000 (about $16 000) to build.
American Gary Hardwick clocked 63 miles 
per hour – about 101 km/h – on a skateboard 
without any help from engines.
Biker Sherlock holds the record for the fastest 
speed while being towed by a motorcycle –  
90 mph, or 145 km/h …Insane!

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports

6 
Slalom competition in skateboarding involves placing a course of cones along a road, and 
the skaters weave between them. Slalom courses vary in length, but typically consist of 40, 
60 or even 100 cones – placed 2 m (about 6 ft) apart. Competitors are judged by the time 
they clock for the course, and how many cones are touched or knocked over on the way. 
 
The record for slalom skateboarding around 100 cones placed 6 ft apart was set by  
Martin Sweeney of the UK in 1991. Sweeney did the course in an incredible 21.7 s – 
without knocking over a single cone. The previous world record for the same slalom 
course was 25.27 s. 
a How much time did Martin Sweeney shave off the world record?
b What percentage did he take off the previous record?
c On average, how often did Martin Sweeney skate past a cone on his record-breaking 
slalom run?
7 
The table below shows the results of a  
women’s slalom skateboarding competition.
a The women’s scores are averaged to find the overall winner of  
the slalom event. Calculate each woman’s average (mean)  
time for the three slalom courses.
b Rank the competitors in order from 1 to 4, according to their  
average times across the three slalom courses.
c Construct a column graph to show the results of this competition. Put the four 
competitors on the x-axis (horizontal axis). Put the times on the y-axis (vertical axis). 
Use colour coding to show the times for all three slalom courses (40, 60 and 100 cones) 
in a single column for each competitor. Make sure you include the key for the colour 
coding on your graph.
The Ollie
The ollie is a skateboarding trick invented by Alan ‘Ollie’ Gelfand in 1976, and this trick 
transformed the sport. It is an aerial manoeuvre which forms the basis of many other 
skateboarding tricks, such as the kick-flip, the heel-flip and the pop-shoveit. The ollie involves 
becoming airborne on a skateboard without holding the board. Danny Wainwright from 
England holds the official record for the highest ollie at 44.5 inches (113 cm). 
8 
A skateboarder sets up a jump by building a temporary brick wall which is the equivalent 
of 10 house bricks high. She intends to practise her ollie technique by jumping over the 
bricks. The bricks have the dimensions 230 mm long × 110 mm wide × 76 mm high. 
a Sketch a house brick in a 3D drawing, showing the dimensions given.
b What is the total height of the jump in mm? Now convert this figure to cm.
c If the skateboarder successfully performs an ollie to jump the bricks, how far short of 
Danny Wainwright’s world record is this jump? Answer in cm.
