16 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
So what does it feel like to fly? Skydivers know – jumping out of an aeroplane with a parachute is  
an incredible experience. Imagine the feeling of total freedom as gravity pulls you towards the 
Earth, which – for a short while anyway – seems like a long way down as you plummet towards it 
at 200 km/h! That’s called free-falling. When the parachute opens, the ride downwards becomes a 
lot more controlled and you get to take in views like you’ll see nowhere else – from 1 000 metres or 
more above the Earth.
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
Use the diagram to help you answer the following questions.
1 
If the skydiver fell at an  
average speed of 200 km/h  
between Point A and Point B,  
how far had she fallen after  
30 seconds? 
 
Answer in kilometres. Then 
convert your answer to metres.
 
Hint: you need to convert 
30 seconds to hours. When 
calculating the conversion, 
answer to 4 decimal places.
2 
How much further is there to dive 
between Point B and the ground?
 
Answer in metres. Then convert 
your answer to kilometres.
3 
For this skydive, calculate  
the percentage of the total 
distance covered:
a between Point A and Point B.
b between Point B and the 
ground.
4 
What is the total time the 
skydiver spent in the air?
5 
For this skydive, calculate the 
percentage of the total time  
spent in the air:
a between Point A and Point B.
b between Point B and the ground.
6 
Complete the sentence:
 In this dive, the skydiver spent just 8.57% of the time in the air covering  
              % of the total distance. The remaining               % of the time  
in the air was spent covering                % of the distance.
Skydiving – falling fast 
7
Altitude 2 700 m 
Point A, Time = 0
Point B 
Parachute opens  
Time = 30 s from  
Point A
Ground 
Time = 5 min 20 s  
from Point B
© Blake Education   978 1 92571 014 4	     Maths in Extreme Sport

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
17
7 
a What is the skydiver’s average speed in m/s between Point B and the ground?
b What is this figure in km/h?  
Hint: use 4 decimal places when converting seconds to hours.
8 
How much slower in km/h is the skydiver’s average  
speed between Point B and the ground, compared with  
the average speed between Point A and Point B?
9 
Construct two line graphs. 
• In the first graph, show the relationship between the distance  
fallen by this skydiver and the time spent in the air. 
• In the second graph, show the relationship between the skydiver’s  
average speed and the time spent in the air.
• In both graphs, time should go on the x-axis (horizontal axis). 
• In the first graph, distance fallen should go on the y-axis (vertical axis).  
In the second graph, average speed should go on the y-axis.
• Remember, you will need to work out a suitable scale for your graphs.
• On both graphs, form the line by joining the three points that can be plotted from 
the information given. Before constructing the graphs, draw up two tables of x and y 
values, showing in each one the three sets of co-ordinates that can be plotted.
10 In skydiving competitions involving the accuracy with which divers can  
land on or close to a target, teams of five people compete over eight rounds,  
accumulating points as they go. 
 
The winning team is the one with the least points on the day. Typically,  
the height from which they jump is 2 700 m. The ‘dead centre’ of the  
target is a disc 2 cm in diameter, and measurements are made in 1 cm  
intervals for the distance away from dead centre each skydiver lands,  
up to 16 cm away. 
 
If you hit dead centre, the score is 0.00. If you land 16 cm away, the  
score is 0.16 (that is, 0.16 of a metre away). Scores are added and  
count both for individuals and for teams.
a A skydiver scores 0.09 for one jump.  
How far away from dead centre did she land?
b The same skydiver has a total score  
of 0.33 after three jumps. What is  
her average score for each jump?
c Was the score for the first jump  
above or below her average score?  
By how much?
d If the score for her third jump was  
equal to the average score for the  
three jumps, was the second jump  
scored higher or lower than the  
average score? By how much?
e What score did she receive for her second jump?

Skydiving – formations & handicaps 
8
What’s more extreme than going skydiving yourself, or with friends? Doing it while in the thick  
of fierce competition with other skydivers, that’s what! It all unfolds thousands of metres up in  
the air …
In competitive skydiving, points are awarded to individuals or teams for performance. In 
formation skydiving, teams gain points for performing patterned routines while free falling 
(dropping through the air without their parachutes open). 
The two types of formations are known as randoms and blocks. Randoms involve the team 
making a single formation. Blocks are double formations, with a specific movement pattern 
between them. 
For example, a block formation 
could involve four team members 
linked together in a circle, then 
each team member separates, does 
a 360° turn, and links up in the 
circle again. 
Blocks are worth 1 point for

The handicap system in competitive skydiving works on a formula which compares the

between the top team in any one season with the other teams competing against it.
The top team prior to this competition was Dragonz, and so this team has no handicap.

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
We use electrical energy to power our homes, 
schools and places of work. Generating 
electricity by burning coal or gas in a power 
station is not sustainable, and produces carbon 
dioxide. Using sunlight to make electricity 
is sustainable. A solar panel is a grid of 
photovoltaic cells that convert sunlight  
into electric power. 
Power is measured in watts.  
One kilowatt (kW) = 1000 watts (W). 
A single solar panel produces between  
100 and 200 watts, depending on the brand  
and size. A system of several panels can be 
installed on a house roof to generate some  
or all of the energy used by the household.
1

a 1 kW 
b 3 kW
2

What is the total power generated? Answer in kilowatts.

There are 1000 millimetres (mm) in one metre (m).
a What is the area of the panel in square millimetres? 
b Converting to metres, the panel measures               m long by               m wide. 
c What is the panel’s area in square metres?
d How many square millimetres are there in one square metre?

each 1.8 m long and 1.1 m wide. The roof is a rectangle 30 m long and 8 m wide.

and they are laid side-by-side?

28 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
And now for something completely different! Sphereing or Zorbing (also sometimes called  
Globe-riding) involves participants travelling inside a sphere which is usually constructed of 
transparent, flexible plastic. 
There is one sphere inside another sphere, with an  
air layer in between to act as a shock absorber.  
The inner and outer spheres are often joined by  
dozens of ropes. A person enters the inner  
sphere through a porthole.
The name ‘zorbing’ originates with three New  
Zealand business partners. They conceived  
the idea for a sphere, called it the ‘zorb’, and  
patented it and trademarked the name in  
1994. They created the company Zorb Ltd,  
and set about franchising the business model.
Sphereing is generally done just for fun,  
not competition. The sphere usually moves  
down a gentle slope so the rider rolls downhill,  
but it is also possible to travel on a level  
surface or on water. 
Most spheres are constructed for a single rider, but some hold two or three. The length of 
sphereing runs can be up to 0.81 km (0.5 mi), and they typically reach speeds of 32–48 km/h 
(20–30 mph).
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
In 2006, the Guinness Book of Records officially recognised two world sphereing records – 
the longest continuous distance travelled, and the fastest speed.
 
Both records were made at the Matarua Farm near Rotorua in New Zealand. Steve Camp 
rolled the longest continuous distance of 570 m, and Keith Kolvers set a world zorb speed 
record of 52 km/h (32 mph).
a In the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Jamaican sprint champion Usain Bolt set a new world 
record for the 100 m sprint. He ran it in 9.69 seconds. Which speed was faster – Bolt’s 
run at Beijing, or Kolvers’ speed inside the sphere?
b The longest recorded golf drive in the world was hit in 1974 by Mike Austin at the 
National Seniors Open in 1974. Assisted by a 30 mph wind, Austin drove the tee shot a 
massive 1 545 feet. Was this a longer or shorter distance than Steve Camp’s continuous 
roll in a sphere? By how much?
2 
Some spheres contain a harness, which holds the participant in a relatively fixed position 
inside. Others allow participants to move freely within the sphere. If a person was 
strapped into a harness inside a sphere which rolled 100 m, and the sphere completed 
one complete rotation every 12.98 m, through how many degrees would the person rotate 
in that 100 m roll?
3 
Spheres typically have a diameter of around 3 m.
a Define diameter.
b If a sphere has a diameter of 3 m, what is its radius?
Sphereing or zorbing? 
13
© Blake Education   978 1 92571 014 4	     Maths in Extreme Sport

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
29
A number of different quantities of circles and spheres can be calculated using formulae. 
These include the following.
•  The circumference of a circle = 2 π r. Assume π = 3.14.
•  The surface area of a sphere = 4 π r 2  
Area is measured in units of length squared; e.g. m2 or cm2.
•  The volume of a sphere = 4 
3π r 3  
   Volume is measured in units of length cubed;  
   e.g. m3 or cm3.
4 
a Define circumference.
b Define surface area of a sphere.
c Define volume of a sphere.
5 
On a sphereing run in Queensland, the spheres in use have an outer diameter of 2.91 m.
a What is the radius of the outer spheres?
b What is the circumference of the outer spheres?
c If the circumference of the inner sphere is 6.15 m, what is the diameter of the  
inner sphere?
d If a person of height 173 cm was standing inside the inner sphere, how much space 
would there be between the top of the person’s head and the surface of the sphere?
6 
Calculate the surface area: 
a for the outer sphere described in question 5.
b for the inner sphere described in question 5. 
 
Remember, the units are squared!
7 
Using the dimensions given for the spheres in question 5, calculate the volume of air  
held between the outer sphere and the inner sphere. Remember, the units are cubed!
a To do this, you will need to complete a three-stage calculation. First list the three stages.
b Now, perform those calculations!
8 
In question 5, you calculated the radius of the outer sphere  
and the diameter of the inner sphere.
a What is the radius of the inner sphere?
b Calculate the total volume of the outer sphere. 
c Calculate the volume of the inner sphere.
d Calculate the volume of air held between the outer and inner spheres.
9 
A standard men’s basketball has a diameter of 23.8 cm.  
a Calculate the volume of this basketball.
b Using your answer to question 8b, how many basketballs would fit inside  
a sphere with the dimensions given in question 5?

32 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
The smallest bee is the dwarf bee, Trigona Minima, which is about 2.1 mm long. The largest bee in 
the world is Megachile Pluto, which can grow to about 40 mm in length. 
In Australia, the first European Wasps were found in Tasmania in 1959. By 1978 they had also been 
found in Victoria, South Australia, New South Wales and Western Australia. European Wasps are 
more aggressive than bees and will attack when their nests are disturbed.  
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a forage 
b pollen 
c pollination 
d nectar  
e wax
2 
Draw pictures of the Trigona Minima bee and the  
Megachile Pluto bee, using a scale of 2:1.
Honeybees live in hives or colonies. A small hive contains about 
20 000 bees, while larger hives can have 120 000 bees. Hives 
include one queen, hundreds of drones and thousands of worker 
bees. The worker bees are female and do not breed. The queen 
bee is female and creates all the babies for the hive. The drone 
bees are male and do not have stingers. 
3 
How many honeybees live in these small hives?
a 3 
b 5 
c 12 
d 23 
e 65
4 
How many large hives are needed to support these numbers of bees?
a 240 000 
b 600 000 
c 200 000 
d 900 000 
e 2 million
The worker bees collect pollen and nectar from flowers. The pollen is used as a protein source 
and the nectar is an energy source. Bees turn the nectar into honey. Workers visit about four 
thousand flowers to make one tablespoon of honey. Beekeepers are very careful when they 
remove honey from the hive. They try not to hurt the bees and leave sugar syrup to replace 
the honey they take.
5 
Calculate the quantity of honey, in tablespoons, produced from bees visiting these 
numbers of flowers.
a 8 000 
b 12 000 
c 40 000 
d 15 000 
e 26 000
6 
If a tablespoon of honey weighs 30 g, how many tablespoons make up one kilogram?
7 
Calculate the number of flowers visited to make these quantities of honey.
a 30 g 
b one kilogram 
c 3 kg 
d 20 kg 
e 170 g
There are about 80 000 commercial bee hives in Queensland. Each hive produces about 70 
kilograms of honey. The Queensland bee industry supplies honey, beeswax, honeycomb, 
queen bee exports and pollination services. 
8 
Assume that 133 320 flowers produce 1 kg of honey. For a hive to produce 70 kg of honey, 
how many flowers does a single bee have to visit if, in its hive, there are:
a 20 thousand workers? 
b 50 thousand workers?
9 
Calculate the annual production of honey in Queensland, in:
a kilograms. 
b tonnes.

production at $4.50 per kilogram.

European Wasps to survive the winter. This means that if a

Stunt flying – dives and speed 
18
Stunt flying is where pilots in a huge range of different planes – from 70 year-old  
biplanes to modern supersonic jets – perform many different acrobatics in the air. 
It is one of the most dangerous and spectacular extreme sports. Pilots must be highly skilled,  
steady and sure enough to fly at high speeds performing acrobatics and formation flying with 
absolute precision. They must also enjoy showing off their awesome skills in front of big crowds.  
Air shows around the world attract millions of people each year, and stunt flying teams are often  
a part of major sporting and cultural events.

The city of Angkor was the capital of the Khmer 
Empire. Its ruins are located near the modern 
city of Siem Reap in Cambodia.
The temples of Angkor were built during the 
period 802 to 1432. During this time, the 
Khmer Empire was one of the great powers 
of South East Asia. At the height of its power, 
the Khmer Empire ruled over a vast territory 
covering large parts of modern-day Cambodia, 
Laos, Thailand, Myanmar (Burma) and 
southern Vietnam.
Angkor Wat (meaning City Temple) is the 
best known of the temples in this area. It was 
built as a Hindu temple during the reign of 
Suryavarman II (1112 to 1152). It was later 
restored for use as a Buddhist shrine in the  
16th century.
Angkor Wat is surrounded by a moat, 190 metres wide, that forms  
a giant rectangle measuring 1.5 km by 1.3 km. The rectangular wall  
around the enclosure measures 1025 m by 800 m, and has a gate in each side.

24 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
There are two main types of camels – the Dromedary which 
is one-humped and the Bactrian Camel which has two humps. 
The term ‘camel’ is also used to describe any of the six  
camel-like creatures in the family camelidae. These are the 
two true camels and the four South American camelids:  
the Llama, Alpaca, Guanaco and Vicuña.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a feral 
b dehydrated 
c hydrated 
d ingest
A fully-grown adult camel stands 1.85 m at the shoulder and 2.15 m at the hump. The hump 
rises about 60 cm from its body. 
2 
Change these camel measurements to the units shown.
a 2 m =         mm 
b 3 m =         mm 
c 1.85 m =         mm
d 2.15 m =         mm 
e 4 m =         cm 
f 3 m =         cm
g 1.85 m =         cm 
h 2.15 m =         cm
3 
Currently there is a large feral population of Dromedary Camels. This population is 
estimated at 700 000 in central Australia. These feral camels are descended from the 
camels that were introduced as a means of transport in the 19th century. The feral 
population is growing at approximately 11% per year. If growth rates remain constant, 
how many camels will exist in Australia:
a after 1 year? 
b after 2 years? 
c after 4 years?
4 
Camels are scattered throughout the arid interior of Australia, with an estimated 50% in 
Western Australia, 24% in the Northern Territory and 25% in western Queensland and 
northern South Australia. If there are 700 000 camels in total, how many are located in:
a Western Australia? 
b the Northern Territory? 
c all other parts of Australia?
Camels can withstand changes in body temperature and water content that would kill most 
other animals. Their body temperature can range from 34°C at night to 41°C during the day. 
Only above this threshold will they begin to sweat. The safe body temperature range for a 
human is 35.6°C to 37.2°C. 
5 
Write a temperature scale on the arrow below. Then shade the temperature ranges for a 
human and a camel. 
Camels can withstand a weight loss due to sweating of approximately 25%. Most mammals 
can only withstand 3.5% dehydration before heart failure results from the thickened blood.  
A camel’s blood remains hydrated, even though the body fluids are lost, until this 25% limit  
is reached.
The Camelidae family - camels 
11
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
25
The Camelidae family - camels (cont’d) 
11
6 
Calculate the maximum safe weight loss for a camel of each weight listed. 
a 300 kg 
b 550 kg 
c 220 kg 
d 350 kg 
e 490 kg
7 
Calculate the maximum safe weight loss in these other mammals if they weigh:
a 85 kg 
b 90 kg 
c 210 kg 
d 350 kg 
e 490 kg
Camels eating green herbage can ingest sufficient moisture in milder conditions to maintain 
their body’s hydrated state without needing to drink. In extremely dry areas, they need access 
to water holes. A thirsty camel can drink 200 litres in three minutes. It can drink water that is 
too salty or brackish for other animals to drink.
8 
How much water can a camel drink in:
a 6 min? 
b 9 min? 
c 1 min? 
d 5 min? 
e 2 min 30 s?
9 
How long would it take a camel to drink:
a 400 L? 
b 800 L? 
c 100 L? 
d 120 L? 
e 250 L?
A camel carcass can provide a substantial amount of meat. The male Dromedary carcass 
can weigh 400 kg or more, while the carcass of a male Bactrian can weigh up to 650 kg. The 
carcass of a female camel weighs less than the male, at about 330 kg. The hump is considered 
to be a delicacy.  
10 How much meat could be obtained from these numbers of male camels, in tonnes?
a 5 Dromedary Camels 
b 7 Bactrian Camels 
c 12 Bactrian Camels 
d 9 Dromedary Camels 
11 How many female camels are needed to supply these quantities of meat?
a 660 kg 
b 990 kg 
c 1200 kg 
d 3 tonne
Feral camels wander widely according to the conditions. Sometimes they cover 70 kilometres 
in a single day. They would only travel half this distance if they were working in a camel 
train, carrying large loads.
12 How long would it take a feral camel to travel:
a 140 km? 
b 350 km? 
c 700 km? 
d 820 km? 
e 1500 km?
13 How far could a working camel walk in: 
a 4 days? 
b 5 days? 
c 12 days? 
d 3 weeks? 
e 5 weeks?
14 Large camel trains consist of about 65 camels and 5 camel handlers. A large bull camel is 
expected to carry up to 600 kg and small camels to carry about 350 kg. How much weight 
could these camels carry, in tonnes?
a 4 bulls 
b 7 bulls 
c 6 small camels 
d 4 bulls and 3 small camels  
e 3 bulls and 5 small camels
15 All camels moult in spring and grow a new coat by autumn. Camel hair is used for high-
quality coats, garments and artist’s brushes. A camel can shed 2.25 kilograms of hair at 
each moult.
a How much hair is lost by 60 camels at a single moult? 
b How many camels are needed to produce 40 kg of camel hair after one moulting?

Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The Great Wall in northern China is one of the 
great human-made wonders of the world. Like 
a gigantic dragon, the Great Wall winds up and 
down across deserts, grasslands and mountains. 
The first sections were constructed more than 
2 000 years ago by independent kingdoms to 
keep out marauding nomads. These sections 
were later rebuilt and joined together. 
The wall as it is known today dates from the 
Ming Dynasty (1368–1644) when a determined 
effort was made to revitalise the whole project. 
This time, the wall was faced with some 60 
million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs. 
The Great Wall stretched approximately 
8 850 kilometres from east to west. 
Unfortunately, some of the sections are  
now in ruins or have disappeared.
A comprehensive archaeological survey has concluded that the wall of the Ming era  
measured 8 850 km. This is made up of 6 259 km of actual wall, 359 km of trenches  
and 2 232 km of natural defensive barriers such as hills and rivers.
1

a actual wall?
b trenches?
c natural defensive barriers?
2

10.1 metres and the average width was about 4.6 metres.  
Assume the wall was a rectangular prism.

a the area of a one face of the wall 1 000 metres long.
b the volume of a 1 kilometre section of the wall.  
Answer in cubic metres.
3 
In the Ming era, the wall was faced with approximately  
60 million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs.  
The length of actual wall was 6 259 kilometres. 
 
What was the average volume of bricks and stone slabs  
used for each kilometre of the wall?  
Answer to the nearest cubic metre.

11

5 metres wide. The inside has been formed by tamping earth and small stones, which makes 
the wall very firm and strong.

6.5 m

Wall is where it climbs extremely steep slopes.

It is 6 metres across the bottom, narrowing to  
5 metres across the top.

a Calculate the area of a trapezium 6.5 m high with parallel sides measuring  
5 m and 6 m.
b Calculate the volume of a trapezoidal prism 10 m long, 6.5 m high  
with parallel sides measuring 5 m and 6 m.
c Calculate the volume of a 5 kilometre section of this part of the Great Wall. 
Give your answer in cubic metres. 
Over time, the Great Wall has slowly decayed due to the forces 
of nature. People have removed some of the stone to use in other 
structures. Today, less than 30% of the Great Wall still stands in

tallest building in the world, a record it held for

The patterns and shapes in textile designs vary between cultures. For example, there are the Maori

Understanding How Mortgages Work #32 
Using formulas, positive and negative numbers, exponents, multiplication, division 
 
Tom wants to buy a house sometime soon. He knows that real estate is a reasonably 
safe way to build wealth. It is slow, but generally low risk. He will come across many 
choices of mortgages. A mortgage is just a fancy word for the process of borrowing 
money to buy a house.  
 
The bank actually buys the house and keeps the title deed. You agree to pay off the 
borrowed amount each month, usually over a period of 20 to 30 years. When you have 
finally paid it off, you get the title deed, meaning you now fully own the house. 
If you stop paying for any reason, the bank has the right to sell the house. After all, 
they own most of it. 
 
 
Example:  
 
Tom's house will cost $300,000. He needs to pay a deposit of 10% and will pay the 
remaining 90% over 30 years at 8% per annum. So he will need to pay a deposit of 10% 
of $300,000 = $30,000. The remaining amount he owes is $270,000. 
 
Monthly Payments 
 
The formula for the amount Tom has to pay each month is 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A = amount to pay each month 
L = loan amount (or principal) 
r = interest rate (per year as a decimal - or divide by 12 to get the rate per month) 
n = number of payments (years x 12)

Visa Bill #31 
Analysing data, division 
 
Credit cards are plastic cards issued by a bank or other business allowing the holder of 
the card to purchase goods and services without using cash, also called “buying on 
credit.”  They allow you to purchase things that you may not currently have the money 
to buy.  
 
When you use a credit card, the credit company that issued the credit card pays the 
store.  Later, you will get a bill in the mail from your credit card company for the 
amount you purchased.  At that time, you can either pay the bill in full, or only pay a 
minimum amount, and wait till later to finish paying.  If you wait till later, you will 
owe the credit card company interest on the amount that you do not pay. They often 
charge very high rates of interest for money that is not paid.   
 
Credit card issuers usually waive interest charges if the balance is paid in full each 
month, but typically will charge full interest on the entire outstanding balance from the 
date of each purchase if the total balance is not paid. 
 
For example, if a user had a $1,000 transaction and repaid it in full within this grace 
period, there would be no interest charged. If, however, even $1.00 of the total amount 
remained unpaid, interest would be charged on the $1,000 from the date of purchase 
until the payment is received.

Waste or waist? 
11
Celebrity chefs Ada and Lorenzo are shooting the next episode of their TV cooking show at Lorenzo’s 
house. Picture Lorenzo’s refrigerator: a carrot, some cauliflower, 6 beans, some garlic, the last of the 
sliced ham, one egg, half a tin of pineapple and some pretty hard cheese. Using his leftovers will save 
his wasted food from the rubbish tip where it would cause nasty methane gas. 
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, complete the calculations in it to find the answer.
1 
Using leftovers for one meal allowed Lorenzo to have one 
‘free’ meal every week. If, on average, a meal at home 
costs $8.52, how much does Lorenzo save every year of  
52 weeks by using his leftovers this way?
2 
A worldwide chain of coffee houses has a policy of 
keeping a tap running continuously to keep their utensils 
clean. As a result, they waste 23 million litres of water per 
day. How many billions (thousand millions) of litres of 
water do they waste in a year of 365 days?
3 
5 percent of a particular country’s leftovers would feed the 
4 million people of Costa Rica for a whole day. Botswana 
has a population of 1.6 million. What percentage of 
leftovers from this particular country would feed the 
people of Botswana for a day?
4 
In 2004, the approximately 20 400 000 Australians put three million tonnes or  
$5 billion worth of food in the rubbish bin. A billion is a thousand million.
a What mass in whole number kilograms per year is that per person? 
b What value of food in dollars and cents per year is that per person? 
c Correct to 1 decimal place, what mass in kilograms is that per person?
d Correct to 1 decimal place, what value of food in dollars and cents per week is that per 
person?
e Each week in Australia, the equivalent of one in five supermarket bags full of food goes 
in the rubbish and hence into landfill. If each full supermarket bag weighs 3 kg, find for 
each Australian, each year, the number of supermarket bags full of food: 
 i trashed 
       ii purchased. 
5 
It has been noted that nearly half of all food 
bought by American households is wasted. 
a If the average American household wastes  
$US 500 per year in uneaten food, how much 
does that household spend on food each year?
b If there are 115 million households in the  
United States, find the total amount spent on:
 i uneaten food     
 ii food altogether.

unless you need two.

them.
   Only buy frozen food in 
bulk.
   Organise your fridge.

twice by cooking double, 
but remember to reheat at a 
high enough temperature.

that is edible. If these households waste between £UK250 and £UK400 of edible food each 
year, how much do households spend on food each year?
7

If this amounts to 408.7 million tonnes being dumped by the 61 million people in Britain, 
find:
a what weight of food in kilograms is dumped by each person in Britain
b the amount of money wasted in dumped food in Britain.
dumped food waste produces methane gas!

methane emissions are produced each year by

Idea: between a and b, where a is the even

9 
According to statistics taken in Japan, companies who manufacture and sell food, 
together with the restaurants that prepare food, produce 11 million tonnes of food waste 
each year. Also, 70% of food leftovers are recycled, half being turned into animal feed. 
a How much food waste in whole number tonnes is recycled:
 i altogether?  
 ii into animal feed?
b This means that less than 5% of the food waste is turned into the greenhouse gas, 
methane. How much methane in tonnes is produced?
10 Methane gas can be used to produce clean electricity.  
One million tonnes of waste dumped as landfill at 
Cranville produced 4 million cubic metres (m3) of landfill 
gas within a year of the tip being closed. Half of the gas

a What volume of methane was produced by a  
million tonnes of waste?
b 1 Watt hour (Wh) is the power of 1 Watt used for  
1 hour. An electric stove uses 8 thousand Watts  
(8 kilowatts or 8 kW) hours. How many kilowatts  
will the stove use if it is on for 3 hours?
c Power is sold by the kilowatt hour. If a megawatt hour 
(MWh) is a million Watt hours, how many kWh are 
there in a MWh?
d The methane gas from Cranville tip can produce  
5000 MWh of electricity and this can be sold at 7 cents 
per kWh. How much can be earned from selling the  
gas from Cranville as electricity?

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Weedy dragons and wet horses - seahorses 
7
Seahorses belong to the family of fish which also includes pipefish and leafy sea dragons. There are 
over 32 species of seahorse. They are mainly found in tropical and subtropical coastal and reef 
waters all over the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans. All seahorses have bodies that are protected 
by strong external plates, arranged into a series of ‘rings’. These rings help to protect the body of 
the fish, but also result in the fish having only limited flexibility of the body. 
Seahorses stay in small areas. On average, males stay in one square metre of habitat and 
females in one hundred times that area. They bob around in sea grass meadows, mangrove 
stands and coral reefs where they are camouflaged by their murky brown and grey patterns 
which blend into the sea grass backgrounds.
1

a  
               b 
 
                    c

Draw a scale on the line below and mark in the range of seahorse lengths.
Seahorses and pipefishes are notable for being the only species in which males become 
‘pregnant’. The male seahorse can give birth to 2 000 babies at a time. Pregnancies last 
anywhere from 10 to 25 days.
5

a 5 
b 6 
c 12 
d 15 
e 23
6

b 26 000 
c 28 000 
d 13 000 
e 9 000
Out of every 1000 infants born, fewer than five survive to adulthood, which helps to explain 
why litters are so large. The survival rates of these infants is actually fairly high compared to 
most fish. This is because they are sheltered in their father’s pouch during the earliest stages of 
development. The eggs of most other fish are abandoned immediately after fertilisation.

Seahorse populations have been endangered in recent years by overfishing. In Australia, 
seahorse fishing is strictly illegal. The seahorse is used in traditional Chinese herbology, 
and as many as 20 million seahorses might be caught each year and sold for this purpose. 
Unfortunately, seahorses around the world are rapidly moving towards becoming an 
endangered species. There is a huge trade in seahorses and their underwater habitats are 
threatened by pollution.

Seahorses lack a tail fin. Since this fin provides most fish with their main swimming power, 
seahorses don’t swim very fast. However, they are extremely maneuverable, and can hover 
precisely. Seahorses can swim forwards or backwards by moving their dorsal and pectoral fins. 
The main thrust comes from their dorsal fin, which beats 70 times a minute. Pectoral fins on 
each side of the face are used to steer.

searchText:
What's in a Bag? #24 
Multiplication, addition 
 
Did you know that plastic bags are generally not degradable? If we throw 
them in a landfill and wait 200 years, or even 2000 years from now, and 
dig them up, most plastic bags would still be there as plastic bags.  
 
Paper sacks are reusable and recyclable, but they cost more than plastic. 
It takes a 15-20 year old tree to create 700 grocery sacks! Even better is to 
use cloth bags for your groceries.   
 
1. Say you used cloth bags each week at the grocery store.  On average you save 14 
bags per week.  
a. How many bags do you save in one year? __________________ 
b. How many trees would you save in one year if you don’t use paper bags? 
______________________ 
c. How many trees would be saved if 30 people used cloth bags instead of paper 
bags in one year (at 14 bags per week)? ________________________ 
 
2. Some stores are charging for plastic bags.  They charge 5 cents per bag.   
a. How much money would I save in one month (4 weeks) if I used cloth bags 
instead of plastic?  On average I would need about 10 plastic bags per week. 
______________________ 
b. How much would you save in one year (52 week)? 
_________________________ 
c. How much would you save in 2 years? _____________________________ 
d. How much would you save in 10 years? ____________________________ 
e. How long would it take you to recover your costs if you bought 5 cloths bags 
for $1.50 each? __________________________ 
 
 
Home Math Workbook
74
Environmental Math

 
3. Some stores are thinking of increasing the price per bag to 50 cents to encourage 
people to bring cloth bags.   
a. How much money would you save in one month (4 weeks) if you used cloth 
bags instead of plastic?  On average you would need about 12 plastic bags per 
week. ______________________ 
b. How much would you save in one year? ____________________________ 
c. How much would you save in 2 years? _____________________________ 
d. How much would you save in 10 years? ____________________________ 
e. How long would it take you to recover your costs if you bought 10 cloths bags 
for $2.50 each? _________________________ 
4. Your community decides to promote using cloth bags.  They give each family 3 
cloth bags to use at the grocery store.  There are 40 families in your community.  On 
average each family uses about 9 plastic bags per week. 
a. How many plastic bags are saved in one week if all the families use their cloth 
bags instead? _________________ 
b. How many plastic bags are saved in 1 month? _____________________ 
c. How many plastic bags are saved in 1 year? ______________________ 
d. Let’s assume your grocery store uses paper bags.  How many trees are saved 
in one month if each family uses their cloth bags instead of paper bags (9 per 
week)? ______________________ 
e. How many trees are saved in one year? _________________ 
f. How many trees are saved in 10 years? _________________ 
 
 
Home Math Workbook
75
Environmental Math

24 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
‘What’s it Worth?’ 
11
The team casts its expert eye over various valuables, and tells us exactly what they think they’re 
worth. It’s all about buying price and selling price, and how they change over the years.
Based on a British show, ‘What’s it Worth’ features a team of antique and collectables experts 
who visit shows and exhibitions around the country. The experts look at various objects owned 
by different people and value these objects. Sometimes the owners get a very nice surprise … 
other times, not so nice!
1	
A pair of vases from the 1920s is valued at $950 for the two. The owners had purchased 
them in England five years ago for £120 each. If the exchange rate is one English 
pound for $2.40 Australian, how much more is the pair of vases worth now than when 
purchased? (Answer in $ Australian.)
2	
The ‘What’s it Worth’ experts value a 200-year-old Chinese statue at $28 750. It is made 
of solid gold and weighs 835 g. If gold is worth $790 Australian per ounce, and there 
are 28 grams to an ounce, calculate the value of the gold in the statue (to the nearest 
whole dollar).
3	
An unusual and rare set of rice bowls featuring handpainted Japanese artwork dating 
back to 1907 was presented for valuation.
a	 The original owner of the bowls bought them new, 11 years before they were painted. In 
what year were the bowls made?
b	 If they were sold as individual bowls, the experts estimated they would be worth up to 
$95 each. But sold as a complete set, they are worth up to 55% more than the combined 
cost of the individual pieces. Up to what price could the current owner expect to receive 
for them if they chose to sell them as a set of six bowls?
c	 Suggest why the bowls might be worth more as  
a set.
4	
A fanatical collector of soft drink containers started 
collecting on his 19th birthday. He has just turned 
62.
a	 Over the first 5 years he was collecting, his 
collection grew from zero to 2360 cans and 
bottles. What was the average number of 
containers he collected per year during this time?

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
25
‘What’s it Worth?’ (cont’d) 
11
b	 Over the next 22 years, this average figure decreased to 227 containers collected every 
year. Over the 3 years after that, he did not add to his collection. Then he collected 
avidly for the following 4 years, adding another 1929 containers to the collection. 
	 Since then, he has averaged 97 containers per year. If he has never sold or given away 
any containers, what is the total number of containers in his collection now?
5	
An 80-year-old solid blackwood dresser cabinet is auctioned. Its reserve price is set 
at $1800.
a	 What is meant by the reserve price?
b	 Bidding started slowly but became keenly contested by two bidders. The auctioneer 
started taking bids at $1200. There were two $100 bids, followed by seven $50 bids. 
The bidding then increased by $20, and there was a total of six such bids. These were 
followed by three $10 bids, and finally five $5 bids. 
	 What was the final price bid for the dresser?
c	 Did the dresser sell at auction? (That is, was it above or below the reserve price?)
d	 By how much did the dresser exceed or fall short of its reserve price?
e	 What percentage above or below the reserve price was the final bid?
6	
An antique extendable table was valued by the 
experts at $6500. It was a round table with an 
insert that slotted in to increase the size of the 
tabletop. The dimensions of the tabletop and 
insert are shown. 
	
Give answers to 2 decimal places.
a	 What is the area of the round tabletop?
b	 The insert increases the area of the tabletop by 
1.84 m2. What is the total area of the extended 
tabletop with the insert in place?
c	 Calculate x.

Kitchen Math Workbook
23
Shopping for the Kitchen
 
Which is the Better Deal? #10
Metric conversion, division of decimals 
 
Often grocery stores have several brands of food items and often they come in different 
sizes.  It is important that you can compare different food items to make sure you are 
getting the best deal.  To find out which size is cheaper you must find the unit price for 
the product. 
 
You will need to know the following for this worksheet. 
1 L = 1000 mL 
 
1 kg = 1000 grams  
 
 
Example 1:   
4 kg of chicken cost $9.80 or 5 kg of chicken costs $11.15. 
Problem:   
Which is cheaper? 
Solution: 
Find the unit price for each package.   
 
$9.80 ÷ 4 kg = $2.45/kg 
 
$11.15 ÷ 5 kg = $2.23/kg 
The 5 kg package of chicken is cheaper.   
 
Example 2: 
750 mL of pop for $2.29 or 550 mL for $1.89 
Problem: 
Which is cheaper? 
Solution: 
Find the unit price for each one.   
 
Step 1:  First you must convert the mL into L and then compare. 
 
 
 
750 mL = .75 L 
550mL = .55 L 
 
Step 2: 
$2.29 ÷ .750 = $3.05 per L 
 
 
 
$1.89 ÷ .55 = $3.44 per L 
 
The 750 mL bottle of pop is cheaper.

White-water rafting – the costs 
12
As with any extreme sport, appropriate equipment is essential for white-water rafting. Fans of the 
sport usually need to travel some distance to reach the waterways to pursue their sport. One of the 
realities of pursuing most sports or hobbies is their cost. Just as Roula found …
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where

Roula decided to take up white-water rafting.  
She visited a supplier and priced the basic  
equipment she’d need: 
• Life jacket – $230 
• Paddle – $140 
• Helmet – $90 
• Raft – $1 820 
• Rope – $40 
1

cost Roula?
2

a the raft? 
b the life jacket? 
c the helmet?
3

a How much would she save off the total price by purchasing online?
b If she purchased online, how much in total would she spend?
4

equipment she needs could be hired for a further $80 per weekend. She planned to go 
rafting on 12 weekends in a year.

than purchase it?

condition after one year, they would buy it back from her for 45 per cent of the purchase

a If Roula did this, how much would the supplier pay her for the raft after 12 months?
b How much would the raft have cost her for the 12 months if she sold it back to the 
supplier?
c How many times would the supplier have to hire the raft out before they had recovered 
the money paid to Roula for the used raft?

varied. One raft she saw measured 4.2 m long and 2.1 m wide. Another one was 5.5 m

The retail selling price of a piece of clothing in a shop is the price you see printed on the swing tag or 
label. This price reflects the cost of designing, making, selling and distributing the item. Of course, 
the shop owner adds a retail margin to cover costs such as rent and wages, as well as their profit.  
In this topic, you will see who makes the money and how much and how a shop adjusts its margins 
across a range of clothes to make the most amount of money! The fashion buyer needs to make 
many of these calculations as a part of the job. They are particularly interested in the return on the 
money invested in designing and making the goods. This is called ROI (return on investment).

contribution. How much money will come from the traders?

Papua New Guinea is home to a large number  
of species of birds. 
The bird-of-paradise is universally identified with the  
island of New Guinea. An adult bird-of-paradise is  
depicted on the national flag of Papua New Guinea.
There are 44 species of birds-of-paradise worldwide  
and 35 species are found in Papua New Guinea.  
A few species are also found in surrounding islands  
and north-eastern Australia.
The smallest bird-of-paradise in size is the  
King Bird-of-paradise which on average has  
a mass of 50 g and is 15 cm long. 
The Curl-crested Manucode is 44 cm long  
and has a mass of 430 g.
The male Black Sicklebill, with its long tail,  
is the longest bird-of-paradise species at 110 cm.

Simplify your answer.

a male Black Sicklebill. Simplify your answer.

of a male Black Sicklebill. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
There are many other types of birds found in New Guinea.
The Papuan Eagle (also known as the Kapul Eagle) has an average length of 83 cm.  
Its wingspan measures 157 cm and its average mass is 2 000 g.

42 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Through the centuries the Chinese used characters for writing numbers.  
They were very advanced in their mathematics and it is believed that they had a  
highly developed number system as early as 1 500 bc.
There are characters representing the numbers 1 to 10.  
Other characters are used for larger numbers like 100 and 1 000.
The basic symbols are:
Writing numbers using the Chinese characters is similar to writing out numbers in  
English (e.g. ‘one thousand, nine hundred, forty-five’). Since it reflects spoken language,  
the Chinese system does not use the positional system we use with Hindu-Arabic numerals.
Multiples of 10, 100 and 1 000 are constructed using a multiplication principle.  
For example, 30 is written vertically, using the symbols for 3 and 10 as 3 times 10:

Water is the most precious commodity  
on the planet. Sustainable water use  
often means using as little as possible,  
especially in dry countries like Australia.

V represents volume in litres;  
t represents time in minutes.

t > 4, V > 500, V  500, t  4.

b She wasted over 500 litres

a 20  V  200

44 
Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
The planet we live on has taken 
a very long time to become a 
place where humans can live. 
We take for granted the fact 
that life forms such as air-
breathing, complex organisms 
like humans can exist on Earth. 
It has not always been so. 
For most of the life of our 
planet, conditions have not 
been suitable for any life forms, 
except in the oceans. 
By looking at the immense time scales involved in the evolution of life on Earth, we can see 
how important it is to live sustainably on the planet to keep conditions right for human 
existence. It’s a long way to the next human-habitable planet.
1 
This work sheet is about working with large numbers written in scientific notation.  
A number written in scientific notation has two parts: a number that is one or more,  
but less than ten, multiplied by a power of ten. 
 
For example, we can write ninety six million as a  
basic numeral 96 000 000, or in scientific notation as 9.6 × 107.  
Four thousand can be written as 4000 (basic numeral) or  
4 × 103 (scientific notation).
a Write forty two million as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
b One billion is one thousand million. Write one billion as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
c Which of these numbers are correctly written in scientific notation? 
i 2.5 × 104 
 
 
ii     13.6 × 106 
iii 8 × 105  
 
 
iv     0.753 × 108 
2 
Scientists estimate Earth to be four billion, six hundred million years old.
a Write this number as a basic numeral.
b Fill in the gaps to write the age of Earth as a number in scientific notation:   
 4.     × 10     
c Complete the sentence: Earth is four point          billion years old.
d Scientists believe that a collision between Earth and  
a second planet named Theia led to the moon being formed.  
This happened four point five billion, or 4.     × 10    years ago.
e How long after Earth formed did the collision happen? Write the answer   
i in words  
ii     as a basic numeral  
iii     as a number in scientific notation.
Earth – the only home we have 
21

Life began to evolve on Earth during the Proterozoic era,  
which lasted from 2420 million years ago to 541 million years ago.
a Write these two numbers in scientific notation.
b How long did the Proterozoic era last? Write your answer 
i as a basic numeral  
ii     in scientific notation.
c Single-cell life forms have been found in rocks that are 1800 million years old.  
How long after the start of the Proterozoic era is this? Answer in scientific notation.
d The first multi-cell life forms appeared one billion years ago.  
How many years is this before the end of the Proterozoic era?  
Answer in scientific notation.
4 
An event called ‘The Great Dying’ occurred at the end of the Permian period (252 million 
years ago). Almost all life on Earth became extinct due to a large rise in CO2 in the 
atmosphere. Massive eruptions of lava in Siberia are thought to have been responsible.
a The eruptions produced 1.5 million cubic kilometres of lava.  
Write this in scientific notation.
b One kilometre = 1000 metres. Volume = length × width × height.  
How many cubic metres are there in one cubic kilometre?  
Answer in scientific notation.
c Write the volume of lava from part a in cubic metres, in scientific notation.
5 
Butterflies first appeared on Earth 40 million years ago.  
Modern humans evolved 2 hundred thousand years ago.  
How many years before humans did the first butterflies appear? Write your answer 
a as a basic numeral  
b in scientific notation.
6 
There are probably many human-habitable planets like Earth in our galaxy, but a long 
way off. One possibility is a planet that orbits the star Gliese 667C. It might have air and 
water. It is 22 light years from Earth. One light year is the distance travelled by light in 
one year.
a Calculate the number of seconds in one year.  
(3600 seconds = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 365 days = 1 year).  
Answer in scientific notation.
b Light travels at 3 × 105 km per second.  
Use your answer from part a to find how many kilometres there are in a light year.  
Answer in scientific notation.
c Write the distance from Earth to Gliese 667C in kilometres, in scientific notation. 
d Mars is the next planet from the Sun after Earth. When Earth and Mars are closest  
to each other, the distance between them is about 54.6 million kilometres.  
Which option correctly completes the statement?
 The distance from Earth to Gliese 667C is about                times as far as Mars. 
i 38 thousand  
ii     38 million  
iii     38 billion

to travel to Gliese 677C at the same average speed?

Frances is the principal of Fairview High School. She has been at the school for a very long time

Frances leaves on the afternoon of 21 December. It is already 1 October, so the parents

Travelling by air is the quickest way, and sometimes the only way, 
to reach a destination. Sydney to Melbourne is a one-hour air trip. 
Flights to holiday destinations such as Vietnam or Europe take 
many hours, but the same trip over land and sea takes weeks or 
months. The downside to such quick journeys is the large amount 
of greenhouse gases produced by aeroplanes. Travellers wanting 
to live sustainably can pay a ‘carbon offset’, which helps to fund 
projects that reduce carbon dioxide, such as tree planting.
1 
Trees take carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere and 
store it while they are alive.  
A carbon offset company charges three dollars

Timber frame houses used to be built of hardwood from wild 
forests. These days, governments restrict the harvesting of trees 
from public land, to protect what is left. Most building timber 
comes from plantations of fast-growing pine trees. Mature trees 
are felled, the trunks cut into logs between 4 and 6 metres long, 
loaded onto a truck and taken to a mill for cutting into lengths  
of timber. 
The diagram shows the end of a log and the cross sections  
of timber pieces to be cut from the log. 51 × 100 mm  
cross section timber is used as wall framing timber.  
The 25 × 100 mm can be used for decking.  
All measurements are in millimetres.

It has a diameter of 300 mm and is 5 m long.

i the radius of its base?

which is stripped off the logs and sold as mulch.

which is a standard size used for roof beams.  
38 × 100 mm is machined to 35 × 90 mm and used as framing timber.

Since 1915, one day in the year has involved the whole of Australia in solemn ceremonies of 
remembrance, gratitude and national pride. That day is Anzac Day – 25 April.

to Egypt for combat training. It was here that the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps

6 
Maths in War & Conflict 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011
Hard tack and the Anzacs 
2
Besides the constant fear of death on the hills and dunes of Gallipoli, some logistical challenges 
included feeding the soldiers. Food supplies came from as far away as Greece and Egypt and 
perishables just wouldn’t survive. The soldiers’ food came in tins with the staples being corned beef 
(Bully Beef), rice, tea, cocoa, jam and ‘hard tack’. Hard tack is basically a very hard biscuit made 
of flour, water, salt and sugar. It lasts longer than bread, although it was so hard soldiers would 
sometimes break their teeth trying to eat it.
Unlike bread, hard tack biscuits are very, very hard. Some soldiers preferred to grind them up 
with old ammunition shells, mix them with water and eat it as porridge. 
The recipe below has been based on a recipe used during World War 1.
Ingredients (makes six biscuits)
• 190 g white flour 
• 375 g wholemeal flour 
• 40 g sugar 
• 21 g milk powder 
• good pinch salt 
• 220 ml water 
1  During World War 1 the metric unit of measurement was not in use. The British system of 
measurement was used. Rewrite the list of ingredients above, as it would have appeared 
in 1914, if 1 cup flour is 125 g, 1 tbsp sugar is 8 g, 1 tbsp milk powder is 7g and 1 cup 
water is 220 ml.
2  How many grams of milk powder in: 
a  3 tablespoons? 
b 6 tablespoons? 
c 8 tablespoons? 
d 13 tablespoons?

Alex and Ellie have written books on the importance of Mathematics in a number of occupations. 
Their latest  book is about event management and they decide that they should manage an event 
to launch the book. They have a small budget so they need to keep costs to a minimum. They have

manuscript is delivered to the publisher.

excluding the holiday break?

Little Boy and Fat Man 
9
During the final stages of World War 2, the United States dropped two atomic bombs over the 
Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in a successful attempt to hasten the end of the war. The 
nuclear weapon known as ‘Little Boy’ was dropped over Hiroshima on August 6 1945. ‘Fat Man’ was 
released over Nagasaki on August 9 of the same year.
The capture of Tinian, one of the Marianas Islands, provided American forces with a valuable 
airstrip from which to mount raids on Japan. The islands served as the base from which the 
atomic bomb attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were staged.
1

2

a Tinian 
b Nagasaki 
c Sapporo.

c 45°N, 129°E
Hiroshima was the primary target of the first nuclear 
bombing mission on August 6. A B-29 bomber was 
launched from Tinian in the west Pacific, about six 
hours flight time from Japan. Two other B-29s were also 
launched. After leaving Tinian the aircraft made their 
way separately to Iwo Jima where they met at an altitude 
of 2440 metres and set course for Japan. The aircraft 
arrived over the target in clear visibility at 9855 metres. 
4

a   Iwo Jima? 
b  Hiroshima?

The gravity bomb known as ‘Little Boy’ was released at 8.15 am from a height of  
 
9855 metres.  ‘Little Boy’ contained 60 kilograms of uranium-235 and took 57 seconds to 
fall from the aircraft to the predetermined detonation height about 600 m above the city. 
It created a blast equivalent to about 13 kilotons of TNT. The uranium-235 weapon was 
considered very inefficient, with only 1.38% of its material exploding. 
10  Using the 24-hour clock, what time was the bomb dropped?

The radius of total destruction was about 1.6 km, with

16 How many square metres is this?

contained the fires (assume a circular shape).
At the time of the attack the population of Hiroshima was approximately 345 000. 
Approximately 80 000 people were killed immediately and another 70 000 were injured. It has 
been estimated that, of the people who died on the day of the explosion, 60% died from burns, 
30% from falling bricks, timber and other materials and 10% from other causes. 
18 Find the total number of people who were killed or injured by the blast.
19 Of the number of people who were killed or injured, what percentage was killed 
immediately by the blast? 
20 Of the people who were killed in the blast, how many died from:
a  flash or flame burns? 
b falling debris? 
c other causes?
On the morning of August 9 1945, the nuclear bomb code-named Fat Man was detonated. 
The bomb contained 6.4 kg of plutonium-239, and was dropped on Nagasaki’s industrial 
valley at 11.01 am. The estimated population of Nagasaki at the time of the bombing was 270 
000. Fat Man exploded 43 seconds later at 469 m above the ground. 
21 What was the time when Fat Man exploded?

powered, guided munition, whilst the word rocket describes a powered, unguided munition.

wingspan, are powered by turbofan engines and can fly 800 to 1600 kilometres, depending on

In World War 2, the Japanese army had advanced through Asia en route to Australia. Port Moresby, 
the capital of Papua New Guinea, was a significant base for both armies. Had the Japanese set up 
base in Port Moresby the Australian mainland would have been under severe threat of invasion. 
The Kokoda track was a seldom-used trail from the small coastal village of Buna on the north coast 
of Papua over the Owen Stanley Ranges to Port Moresby, passing through the village of Kokoda. In 
1942 the Japanese tried to capture Port Moresby by sea attack and then overland through Kokoda. 
The seven-month resistance of this ultimately unsuccessful campaign is regarded by some as one of

that starts at 7 pm and finishes at

will it take up in the tent?

cocktail party is 1 for every 20 guests. 
How many wait staff will be needed for 
a party of 95 guests?

a How many wait staff will be needed 
for a party of 95 guests?

altogether if a butler is needed to 
supervise the wait staff?

in a 750 mL bottle if a glass contains 
120 mL? What about if it contains  
180 mL, the standard pour at the bar?

be filled to the brim with champagne 
from a 750 mL bottle? Give your 
answer in fraction form.

should only fill a flute to ⅔. How 
much champagne should you put in 
a 225 mL flute?

glasses can you really pour from one 
standard bottle of champagne?

A wedding reception usually runs for the

forget where they left their glass, 
therefore you will need twice as many 
clean glasses as guests. How many 
glasses will be needed for a party of  
95 guests?

Red Cross 
5
Australian Red Cross was formed on 13 August 1914 exactly nine days after the outbreak of World 
War I. Lady Munro-Ferguson, who had worked for British Red Cross in Scotland and was the wife of 
the Governor-General, called on the wives of each State Governor to form a local committee in each 
capital. The women readily agreed and so Australian Red Cross was born.
During World War 2, Red Cross transported 40 000 pairs of socks, 25 000 shirts, 20 000 
underpants, 10 000 pairs of shoes and boots, 10 000 pairs of pyjamas, 5000 overcoats and 
many other items people thought would be useful to soldiers on the front in Europe. The effort 
from many small communities ‘beggared the imagination’. By the end of the war Red Cross 
unit of Rutherglen had forwarded, among many other items, more than 1200 shirts, 8500 
pairs of underpants, 1200 pairs of pyjamas, 2400 pairs of socks, 75 sheets, 770 pillow-cases, 
450 bed sheets and 390 handkerchiefs.

                                 Ball Bounce Activity
Your activity is to compare how high 4 different balls bounce when dropped from
1 metre in height. You will compare golf balls, tennis balls, squash balls and
table tennis balls.
Aim: to find which ball bounces highest when dropped from one Metre.
Hypothesis: The tennis ball will bounce the highest when dropped from one
metre.
Independent variable (The thing that is changed): The type of Ball.
Dependent variable (the thing that happens as a result of the independent
variable that we measure): Bounce height.
Controlled variables. Things we need to keep the same. All balls dropped
from one metre. All balls land on the same surface. Method of measuring
bounce height. Temperature of the balls. Temperature of the day.
Equipment (what you will need): a tennis ball, a golf ball, a table tennis ball, a
squash ball and a metre ruler.

Stand a one metre ruler up so that the zero end is on the floor.

               In science, graphs are used to visually display data gained through experimentation. There are a number of
               different types of graphs, and it is important that you choose the right one to display your data.
               Although software is available for creating graphs, drawing your own graphs is a useful skill to develop.

               Line graph
               A line graph is used to display data that is continuous. That is, each point is related to the one before and the
               one after. Examples of continuous data are length, weight and temperature. For example, suppose that you
               measured the temperature in a beaker of water while it is being heated over a Bunsen burner for a period of
               10 minutes. The data you collected is shown in the following table.


                 Time (min)               Temperature (˚C)

                          3                              59

                          5                              72

                          6                              86

                          8                              98

                          9                              99

                        10                             100


               When drawing a line graph, you need to use the following steps.

                1 Draw two axes at right angles to each other.

                2 Make sure the axes are long enough to show all of the information, with an arrow on the end of each.

                3 Mark each axis with a suitable scale; for example, 1 cm ¼ 10˚C.

                4 Name each axis to show what it represents.

Identify the Controls and Variables

 Smithers thinks that a special juice will increase the productivity of workers. He
creates two groups of 50 workers each and assigns each group the same task (in
this case, they're supposed to staple a set of papers). Group A is given the
special juice to drink while they work. Group B is not given the special juice. After
an hour, Smithers counts how many stacks of papers each group has made.
Group A made 1,587 stacks, Group B made 2,113 stacks.

Identify the: 1. Control Group

2. Independent Variable

3. Dependent Variable

4. What should Smithers' conclusion be?

5. How could this experiment be improved?



Homer notices that his shower is covered in a strange green slime. His friend

Name_________________________________________

Observation – Inference – Prediction

Purpose: To practice distinguishing between observations, inferences and predictions.

Scientists spend a great deal of time observing the natural and built world. When a scientists observes he or
she takes in information using the five senses. Often tools such as microscopes are used to extend the senses
and make the observations more precise and accurate.

Observations may be qualitative or quantitative. Qualitative observations are those that describe qualities,
properties or characteristics of objects or phenomena. Color, texture, smells, sounds are all examples of
qualitative observations. Quantitative observations are those that can be measured in numbers. Mass,
volume, speed, temperature are a few examples. Tools are often used to make quantitative observations.

Observations in science should always be facts (a statement that can be proven true or false), not opinions (an
expression of a person’s feelings that cannot be proven).

Observations lead to inferences. An inference is an educated guess or reasonable conclusion drawn from the
observation. It is a possible explanation for the observation.

Predictions can be made from inferences. A scientific prediction is an educated guess about a future event. It
can be made without knowing whether it is correct; it may be an incorrect guess. That’s ok. Scientists learn
from incorrect guesses as much as correct ones.

For example, a student wakes up to thunder one morning.
He may observe the thunder – using his sense of hearing, he made a factual, qualitative observation.
The sound of the thunder led to the inference that it was raining – it might not have been raining.
The student then predicted that they would not go outside during school that day because of the rain.

Book 2: Safety & equipment
    in the laboratory

Name:            Block:
                          1
    1.   Students are not to enter the lab (ie: be at lab benches with lab materials) unless a teacher is present.
       Students are NEVER to enter the lab prep room.

  2. Never run or ‘muck around’ in the laboratory. During a lab, you MUST remain at your own bench.

  3. There is no food or drink permitted in the laboratory. At desks is OK.

  4. Water bottles & bags/backpacks are to be left at your desk during labs.

  5. NEVER taste or smell any substance in the lab, unless instructed to do so safely by your teacher.

  6. Always listen carefully and follow instructions specifically. If there is anything you don’t understand, ask
       your teacher. It is very important for your safety that you understand all instructions.

  7. Always clean up and return equipment to the correct place when finished an experiment.

  8. Keep benches and floor areas tidy. This means all chairs must be pushed in when working at the lab
       benches, and extra books/equipment is never to be placed on the floor.

  9. Breaks and accidents (even minor) must always be reported to your teacher immediately.

  10. NEVER attempt to pick up broken glass. Inform your teacher, and keep others clear of the area.

  11. Laboratory equipment and chemicals are ONLY to be used as directed by your teachers’ instructions.

  12. Waste products/remains from experiments are to be disposed of as instructed by your teacher. Remember,
       not everything is safe to rinse down the sink, or throw away in the bin.

  13. Be sure any burning material (eg. Match) is put out completely before throwing away.

  14. All hot equipment is to be placed to a heatproof mat, NOT directly on the benchtop.

  15. ALWAYS wear safety glasses during experiments with hazardous materials or when heating.

  16. Long hair and loose clothing must be tied back during experiments.

  17. Long pants & closed toed shoes must be worn during experiments

  18. ALWAYS wash your hands after any experiments in the laboratory.

  19. Use gas taps & water for EXPERIMENTS only.

  20. Bench tops are to be cleaned and disinfected following EVERY practical experiment.

  21. When heating or mixing substances, NEVER point towards yourself or others.

  22. Never mix chemicals or do your own experiments unless you have permission from your teacher. This is
       wasteful, and could be very dangerous.

  23. Always rinse/clean glassware following an experiment.

  24. Always use tongs to pick up equipment/objects that have been heated

  25. If you need to leave a Bunsen Burner, ALWAYS turn it to the visible orange/yellow safety flame

Misbehaviour & breach of safety rules in the laboratory will result in immediate consequences, including

The Scientific Method Homework and Study Guide	
  
                                        Teacher Answer Key

Define the following terms:

1. data: The information gathered from making observations.

2. independent variable: The variable that is deliberately changed by the scientist.

3. dependent variable: The variable observed during the experiment. It is the data collected as a result of
   changing the independent variable.

4. scientific method: A series of steps used by scientists to solve a problem or answer a question.

Short Answer:
1. List the steps to the scientific method.

           1) Observe / Ask a question.
           2) Form a hypothesis.
           3) Design a controlled experiment.
           4) Record and analyze the results.
           5) Draw a conclusion.

2. How is a theory different from a hypothesis?

       A hypothesis is an “educated guess” that is testable through observations and experimentation. A theory is a
       broad statement of what is believed to be true based on many experiments and considerable amounts of data.

3. Give two examples of quantitative data.

       There are many possible answers. Any type of answer that is “numerical” should be accepted. Possibilities
       might include: Number of students who failed a particular test. The amount of weight gain by mice when
       fed a particular diet.

4. Give two examples of qualitative data.

       There are many possible answers. Any type of answer that is “descriptive” should be accepted.
       Possibilities might include: Starch turns purple in the presence of iodine. During mating season, male bird
       plumage becomes bright and colorful.

5. How many variables should an experiment test at a time? Explain your answer.

       Only one variable can be tested at a time. If several variables were changed at the same time, the scientist
       would not know which variable was responsible for the observed results.

6. Why is it important that scientists communicate and report their findings?

       In order for the findings to be considered “valid”, the experiment must be repeated by other scientists so that
       the results may be verified and corroborated.                                             Copyright

       b) Describe the control group: The control group will consist of a set number of rats that will not receive
                                      the new blood pressure medicine.


       c) What is the independent variable? The administering or not administering of the blood pressure
                                            medicine.


       d) What is the dependent variable? The observed changes in blood pressure of the test subjects.

          All rats should be fed the same diet and in the same quantity.
          All rats should be kept at the same stress level.
          All rats should be housed in the same type of cages.
          All rats should be kept at the same temperature.
          The rats should be all of one species.


       f) What is the ONE factor that will be different between the experimental group and the control group?
          Whether or not the rats receive the new blood pressure medicine.


8. What is meant by the term “controlled experiment”?
   In a “controlled experiment” only one variable is changed at a time. All other variables should be
   unchanged or “controlled.”



9. Why must experiments be repeated many times?
   Experiments are repeated in order to see that the same results are obtained each time. Results cannot be
   considered “valid” until it is determined that the experiment will always yield the same conclusion.

   damage to the membrane can be measured by the amount of red dye released into the solution.

       Independent variable: The different alcohols being tested.

Introduction to the Scientific Method Worksheet
Long ago, many people believed that living things could come from nonliving things.
They thought that worms came from wood and that maggots came from decaying
meat. This idea was called
spontaneous generation. In 1668,
an Italian biologist, Francesco Redi,
did experiments to prove that
maggots did not come from meat.
One of his experiments is shown
below.


Redi placed pieces of meat in
several jars. He divided the jars into
two groups. He covered the first
group of jars with fine cloth. He left the second group of jars uncovered. Redi
observed the jars for several days. He saw flies on the cloth of the covered jars, and
he saw flies laying eggs on the meat in the uncovered jars. Maggots appeared only
on the meat in the group of jars left uncovered.

Questions
1. Which is not a step in the scientific method?
      a. Problem or question.                    c. Ask other people for their opinion.
      b. Research.                               d. Arrive at a conclusion.

2. What was the problem in Redi’s experiment?
      a. How do maggots appear in meats?
      b. How do worms appear in wood?
      c. Is spontaneous generation a valid explanation for maggots in meats?
      d. All of the above are examples of problems.

3. What do you think his hypothesis was?
      a. Maggots grow through spontaneous generation.
      b. Maggots come from eggs laid by flies.
      c. Maggots find their way into woods and meats.
      d. The problem cannot be solved.

4. How did he test his hypothesis?
      a. He placed food in two jars, covering one jar and leaving the other
uncovered.
      b. He placed food in two jars and left both jars uncovered.
      c. He placed food in two jars and covered both jars.
      d. He put food in one jar and no food in a second jar.

5. What was the variable in his experiment?
      a. Covering both jars.
      b. Covering one jar and leaving the other uncovered.
      c. Leaving both jars uncovered.
      d. There was no variable in this experiment.

6. What do you think Redi’s conclusion was?
      a. Living things come from other living things.
      b. Living things are created through spontaneous generation.
      c. He did not have enough data to arrive at a conclusion.

Introducing variables

Variables are things in an experiment that can change or be controlled, There are three types of variables:

(@) an independent variable what you change; that is, the variable you are testing, which should be
the only thing you change in an experiment

(b) a dependent variable ~ what you measure; that is, the variable that changes depending on the
value of the independent variable

(©) a controlled variable ~ what you keep the same so that you can be sure any change to the
dependent variable is caused by changes to the independent variable. If you do not keep these
other variables the same, you won’t know which variable has affected your results

Writing up a Practical Report


Scientists write up the results of their experiments and observations in
a practical report. The following headings are often used in a practical
report:

Aim - states the problem or purpose of the experiment. Often the hypothesis is stated as the aim.

Equipment - a list of the apparatus used in the experiment

Method - a step-by-step list of what was done in the experiment. This is written in the past tense and in
sufficient detail so that someone else could repeat the experiment.

Diagrams - showing how the apparatus was set up are often used. Completed in pencil and it is labelled with
arrows.

Results/Observations - shows your observations and measurements, often presented in a table or as a graph.

Conclusion - this is the answer to the aim or problem being investigated. States what happened, supports it
with evidence and explains why: scientific understandings

DNA or deoxyribonucleic acid is found in the centre of almost all living cells. DNA is an incredibly 
long, thin strand of material about two metres in length, coiled inside each cell. Forensic scientists 
use DNA, such as in a strand of hair found at a crime scene, to identify matching DNA of another 
individual, such as the suspect. This process is called genetic fingerprinting.

200 000 profiles of DNA crime scenes. The population of the US is about 308 367 000.

Environmental crime

 The world is now facing numerous environmental challenges and threats. Environmental crime, 
including illegal trading of natural resources and dumping of hazardous waste, is a serious and 
growing international problem. As the world’s natural resources rapidly diminish, environmental 
crimes such as illegal logging and fishing are increasing and are billion dollar activities.
In 1989 the oil tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef, spewing vast amounts of oil 
into the ocean.
1

the ocean.

Experts have come to believe that each person’s fingerprints are unique, even those of identical

Ned Kelly

Time has clouded the legend of Edward ‘Ned’ Kelly, an Irish–Australian bushranger of the late 19th 
century. Ned, along with a band of accomplices known as The Kelly Gang, became symbolic for his 
daring defiance of authority. The debate about Ned’s status as ruthless criminal or victimised folk 
hero will most likely continue throughout history.
Edward (Ned) Kelly was born in Beveridge, just north of Melbourne, between June 1854 and 
June 1855. In 1869, he was arrested for assaulting a Chinese pig farmer. A year later Ned 
was arrested for assaulting Jeremiah McCormack and late that same year was sentenced to 
three years’ imprisonment for receiving a stolen horse. In September 1877 Ned was arrested 
for drunkenness and in October of the following year the infamous exchange at Stringybark 
Creek saw Ned shooting Sergeant Kennedy dead. Later that same year the Kelly Gang robbed 
the National Bank at Euroa of £2260. The following year the Kelly Gang robbed the local 
bank in Jerilderie of £2414. In June 1880 the Kelly Gang took about 70 hostages at the 
Glenrowan Inn, before being captured. In November of that same year Ned Kelly was hanged

          Page 1
       Renewable & Non-renewable Resources - Teacher Background




Our Earth processes cycle materials between reservoirs in the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere
(water), biosphere (living things) and lithosphere (rocks). Matter is neither created nor destroyed
but may be reassembled in different forms. The hydrogen which was once part of a water molecule
may be used by a plant to make starch which is eaten by an animal to create its fat supplies and on
the death of the animal be buried deep in sediment to become part of an oil molecule, only to be
burned and become part of a water molecule again. We tend to use the term “renewable” if the
resource is replenished on a human time scale. Modern humans have only been around for less than
200,000 years.
The Sun, which is the source of all energy used on earth, either directly as sunlight, wind and heat or
trapped in fossil fuels, is consuming its own hydrogen and will eventually swell and engulf the Earth
in about 5 billion years. However, since that is a long time in human terms, it is considered a
renewable resource. Our planet’s ability to re-create complex materials and the speed of their
replenishment varies. The environmental conditions necessary for deposition of our vast reserves of
iron ore in Western Australia no longer exist since plants released oxygen into our atmosphere over
a million years ago. Iron ore and most other minerals are considered a finite resource and non-
renewable. Fossil fuels are being used at a rate that far exceeds their rate of replenishment (a rate of
many millions of years) and are also considered non-renewable. Resources that are continuous such
as sunshine, wind and waves are considered renewable. Resources such as biomass, soil, water and
forests are considered sustainable as long as the rate of use does not exceed the rate of
replenishment.

  The major resources on Earth are water, air, living things, rocks (including minerals and
                        fossil fuels), soil and energy from the Sun.

Australia is rich in both living and non-living resources.

Resource          Something that is useful to living things.
                  Renewable resources can be replenished within a human time scale.
                  Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced once they have been used or require
                  very long (geologic) periods of time to replenish.

Reserve           A known quantity of a resource.
