ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
29
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – A seafaring people 
Objectives
l	 Recognise that the dominance exerted by 
the Vikings was due largely to their skills as 
boatbuilders and sailors
l	 Identify the main features of Viking boats 
(e.g. shallow hull, symmetrical design, single 
large sail) 
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of where 
Scandinavia is located and of the extensive bodies 
of water the Vikings had to navigate. 
Background
Much of the widespread influence and dominance 
of the Vikings can be attributed to their prowess as 
boatbuilders, sailors and navigators. They had the 
most extensive fleets of their time, and their ability 
to swiftly sneak up on unsuspecting villages and 
cities by way of sea routes was second to none. 
Starter activity
As a class, brainstorm all the current modes of 
transport used by human beings. If one country 
was to try to dominate as many other countries 
as possible and they could only use one mode of 
transport to do it, which mode of transport would 
they would pick? Why? 
Explain to students that during the Viking Age 
the most advanced and swiftest mode of transport 
was the boat. The society that built the largest 
and fastest boats would be able to dominate 
through war and trade. The Vikings were the best 
boatbuilders and sailors of their time.
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can complete the Activity sheet ‘The Vikings 
and their boats’ with a partner. This sheet introduces 
students to the three main types of Viking sea craft. 
Students could then read the Resource sheet 
‘Viking longships 1’ before attempting the Activity 
sheet ‘Viking longships 2’. These sheets focus on the 
structure of the longship and why it was such an 
impressive vessel. 
The Activity sheet ‘Building a longship’ is a good 
activity for kinaesthetic learners and encourages 
students to imagine a Viking journey by longship.
Finally, the Activity sheet ‘Viking ships versus 
modern technology’ emphasises the differences 
between Viking and modern sea craft.
Extension activity
Vikings ships were made of wood. Ask students to 
consider why this might have been the case. For 
example, wood was easy to harvest and work with, 
and it was also a renewable resource (that is, if 
harvested carefully it would not run out). What would 
have been the advantages of using wood? What 
would have been the disadvantages?

The Vikings and their boats 
The Vikings were excellent boatbuilders and sailors. They built three main types of boats:
●
●longships (also known as dragon-ships)
●
●merchant ships 
●
●small boats.
The most famous Viking sea craft was the longship. Longships were narrow and about as 
long as a basketball court. This made it easy for them to move quickly over the water. The hull 
(main body of the ship) was also very shallow, so it could sail in water only one metre deep 
or right up onto a beach. Another great thing about longships was that the bow (front of 
the ship) and stern (back of the ship) were identical. This meant that longships could change 
direction very quickly. Longships were used mainly to transport troops during times of war. 
The Vikings also built merchant ships to transport goods between cities and countries. 
There were large and small merchant ships. Large merchant ships were used to carry heavy  
loads. They weren’t as long as longships, but they were very wide. The hulls of the large mer­chant 
ships were deep so that they could carry a lot of goods, and these ships sailed the open 
seas. Smaller merchant ships were used to sail short distances and down rivers. 
The most common type of Viking watercraft were small boats. These boats were used for 
fishing and to carry people and goods between villages.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
31
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Viking longships 1
The Vikings worked hard to make their longships the fastest and most agile ships of their 
day. They did this in three ways:
●
●They built their boats using wood. Wood is a light material that floats well, is easy 
to work with and moves quickly over water. It is also a material that was easy to 
find in Scandinavia. 
●
●They attached a large square sail to a central mast. The sail was enormous, so it was 
good at catching a lot of wind. It was made of linen or wool and then covered in 
animal fat to make it waterproof. Ropes made of hemp or horsehair held the sail in 
place. The sail was designed so that it could be turned easily to catch the wind from 
any direction. 
●
●They made the longships large enough so that they could fit several oarsmen 
along each side. That way, when the wind died down and they couldn’t use the sail, 
they would still have enough manpower to row the ship.
The Vikings tried to make their longships look as scary as possible. They often dyed 
their large sails red, like blood, to frighten their enemies. They carved large dragon-like 
heads and added these to the prows of their longships.  The Vikings believed that these 
would scare the spirits that lived in the towns and villages they raided. They removed 
the prow heads when they were sailing home, so that their families would not be 
frightened.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
41
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Crafty Vikings 
Objectives
l	 Recognise the inventiveness and creativity of 
the Vikings  
l	 Identify the influence of Viking inventions on 
future generations 
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required. 
Background
Despite their limited resources, the Vikings were 
very crafty people. Not only were they exceptional 
boatbuilders, they also invented lots of things we 
still use today, such as the magnetic compass. The 
Vikings had their own alphabet, called the futhark, 
and their weapons were more advanced than others 
of their time. The harsh conditions experienced by 
the Vikings may well have inspired them to think up 
ways to make their lives just that little bit easier. 
Starter activity
What does the phrase ‘necessity is the mother of 
invention’ mean? Provide some examples of things 
that have been invented in response to specific 
needs. 
Resource and Activity sheets
This unit contains five Activity sheets, the first four of 
which explore different aspects of Viking inventiveness. 
The Activity sheet ‘Ready for battle’ introduces students 
to weapons used by the Vikings. The Activity sheet 
‘Clothing and armour’ describes the clothing and 
armour worn by Viking men and women. The Activity 
sheet ‘Clever Vikings’ introduces students to four Viking 
inventions. The Activity sheet ‘The futhark’ describes 
the Viking alphabet and invites students to create 
messages using the alphabet. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Viking accomplishments’, 
contains a crossword that includes various aspects 
of Viking inventiveness and culture that have been 
covered in the unit. The answers to the crossword clues 
are: ACROSS: 2 leather; 4 chainmail; 7 comb; 9 futhark; 
10 spear; 12 axes; 13 sword. DOWN: 1 cloth; 3 metal;  
4 compass; 5 loom; 6 cloak; 8 saex; 10 shield; 11 iron;  
14 skis; 15 warp.
Extension activity
As a class, brainstorm a list of recent inventions that we 
live with or use during this modern age. Of these, which 
inventions are likely to stand the test of time and still 
be around in 500 years? Why will they still be relevant 
then? What ensures that an item will not date and will 
continue to be needed over time?

Clothing and armour 
The Vikings wore simple, warm clothes that they made from wool, flax and linen. Men 
wore plain pants with a tunic over the top. Women wore long dresses. Both wore long 
thick cloaks made of felted wool to protect them during cold days. 
+	 1   What sort of clothes do people wear now? What are they made of?
_________________________________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________
Vikings wore shoes made from leather, and their belts were made of leather or rope. They 
liked to decorate their clothes and made intricate (complicated and detailed) braid trims 
for important pieces of clothing. Pins were used to fasten clothes and cloaks. The pins 
were made of bone or metal and sometimes even gold.
2   What are your shoes made of? Did you make them yourself? 
_________________________________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________
In battle, men wore chainmail over their tunics to protect them from sword blows. 
The chainmail was made of small metal rings bound together. It covered a man’s torso 
as well as his upper arms and legs. Chainmail was expensive and heavy to wear, so not 
everyone wore it. Many men chose instead to wear body armour made of leather and 
quilted cloth. Helmets were made of iron, with a nose plate to 
protect the nose and a guard to protect the eyes.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
59
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Did the Vikings  
discover North America? 
Objectives
l	 Understand what is meant by an artefact, a 
fossil and a primary source
l	 Learn about the location and historical 
relevance of L’anse aux Meadows 
l	 Recognise how far from Scandinavia the 
Vikings travelled
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading 
skills and be able to identify Scandinavia, Europe 
and North America. 
Background
Christopher Columbus is credited with being the 
first European explorer to discover North America. 
However, as recently as the 1960s a small group of 
archaeologists found proof of Viking settlement in a 
small coastal village in North America. The discovery 
of Viking artefacts at L’anse aux Meadows confirmed 
that the Vikings had discovered at least this small 
part of the North American coastline, many centuries 
ahead of Christopher Columbus. 
Starter activity
How does the stuff that we leave behind give others 
clues as to how we lived? Divide the class into small 
groups. Give each group a sheet of paper with a list 
of items on it. One list may have, for example, a teddy 
bear, a dummy, a bag of nappies, a bag of wool with 
knitting needles, a rocking chair, a pair of spectacles, 
a range of cake tins, a rolling pin, one bed and one 
cot, and a closet full of women’s clothing. Tell each 
group that they have to hypothesise, based on the 
evidence left behind, who lived in the house where 
the items were found, how old they may have been 
and what sex they were. Invite each group to also 
make up a theory as to why the inhabitants of the 
house disappeared. Each group can present their 
findings to the rest of the class. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Artefacts, fossils 
and primary sources’ before completing the Activity 
sheet ‘Unearthing the past’. These sheets help students 
learn how to distinguish between artefacts and fossils, 
and how to identify primary sources. Students may 
require additional support and explanation in order 
to understand what a fossil is. A good website to visit 
is www.oum.ox.ac.uk/thezone/fossils/intro/form.htm, 
which is hosted by the Oxford University Museum of 
Natural History.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The artefacts 
of L’anse aux Meadow’ before completing the Activity 
sheet ‘Artefact detective work’. These sheets encourage 
students to deduce behaviours by using primary 
evidence.
Finally, students can work with a partner to complete 
the Activity sheet ‘The Vikings and North America’. 
Extension activity
What is the Arctic Circle? Working in pairs, students can 
research online (using internet search engines such as 
Firefox or Google) what the Arctic Circle is, where it is 
located, how cold the region is and how icy conditions 
hamper sea travel. Students can then produce an 
information booklet on the Arctic Circle region. The 
information booklet should be produced with a Viking 
reader in mind and should contain basic details as well 
as possible tips on how to survive in this region. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
60
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Artefacts, fossils and  
primary sources
An artefact is an object that was made by people long ago. Artefacts could be something 
natural that humans reshaped (such as a flint knife) or they could be items that involved 
a lot of work (such as a decorated bowl). Artefacts usually lie forgotten and buried for 
years – sometimes hundreds or thousands of years – before being rediscovered by 
archaeologists. 
Archaeologists study the past. They visit areas where people lived and excavate these 
sites looking for artefacts. They use special tools to scrape and brush away soil. They work 
very slowly and carefully to uncover artefacts without breaking them. 
Artefacts are called primary sources because they come from the actual historical 
period that is being studied. Historians can use primary sources to work out what life was 
like during a specific time in history. 
Not all artefacts survive. Some artefacts – such as clothes made of wool – decay 
over time or decay underground. Others might be washed away in storms or taken by 
explorers. 
A fossil is a very different thing from an artefact. An artefact is something that was 
made by people. A fossil, on the other hand, is the remains or the impression of something 
that was once alive long ago. There are two main types of fossils – animal fossils and plant 
fossils.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
62
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The artefacts of L’anse aux Meadow
The Vikings told long elaborate tales, called sagas. These sagas were passed on orally 
from one generation to the next. Then, between the 12th and 14th centuries, the 
sagas were written down. The sagas told of Viking kings, battles and great journeys. For  
a long time, historians didn’t know whether any part of the sagas was real or if it was  
all make-believe. 
One of the sagas told the story of Leif Eriksson and his discovery of a place called 
Vinland. Some historians thought that Vinland may be in North America – but they had 
no proof. Then in the 1960s, a group of archaeologists discovered the remains of a Viking 
village in a place called L’anse aux Meadows, on the island of Newfoundland, off the 
eastern coast of Canada. 
Archaeologists uncovered many things at L’anse aux Meadows. Among them were:
●
●the foundations of eight Viking buildings
●
●the remains of a fireplace
●
●a bronze pin
●
●a stone oil lamp
●
●a spindle whorl (for spinning wool) made of stone
●
●some needles made of bone
●
●a small pair of scissors.

discover North America?

searchText:
ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
17
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Farming and raiding 
Objectives
l	 Understand that Vikings were first and 
foremost farmers 
l	 Recognise the role of dwindling resources on 
the Vikings’ decision to move further out of 
Scandinavia 
l	 Consider the importance of raiding to the 
dominance of the Vikings
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of where 
Scandinavia is and the difficulties inherent in living 
there. They should also have some concept of how 
far the Vikings managed to travel from Scandinavia. 
Background
Most Vikings were farmers. Even those Vikings 
who left Scandinavia in search of better resources 
ended up living simple, farm-based lives in their 
new lands. 
The raids for which the Vikings became 
legendary were well planned, swift and fierce. The 
dominance of Vikings throughout Europe during 
the Viking Age is due in no small part to their 
effectiveness as warriors, the speed and scope of 
their exploits and the fact that they were feared by 
many people. 
Starter activity
As a class, discuss the assumptions we make about 
people depending on how they live. For example, 
how would we tend to describe the people who 
live in peasant, farming societies? List on the board 
the sorts of words we might use to describe their 
characters. How would we describe the people who 
live in warrior societies, where fighting is considered 
important? List these words on the board too. 
The Vikings were both farmers and warriors. Are 
our assumptions sometimes too simplistic? How 
important is it to have an open mind when studying 
history and other cultures?
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Viking farmers’ 
and then complete the Activity sheet ‘Then and now’. 
Encourage students to imagine the life of a Viking 
farmer and to consider how much easier our lives are 
today because of modern technology.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Away on 
a Viking raid’ as a class. They can then complete 
the Activity sheet ‘To raid or not to raid?’. After this, 
everyone’s results can be shared with the rest of the 
class to prompt discussion about the complexities 
of raiding.
Finally, students can complete the Activity sheet 
‘Help plan a raid’. Some students may require assistance 
with sequencing. You might choose to do the 
sequencing as a class and then let students draw their 
own pictures in their workbooks individually.  
Extension activity
Divide the class into three groups. One group will argue 
that raiding is important and necessary. Another will 
argue that raiding is barbaric and unnecessary. The 
third group will adjudicate and determine which side 
has the most convincing case. Give the first two groups 
five minutes to prepare their arguments, and then four 
minutes each to present their case. While the arguing 
sides compose their arguments, the adjudicating group 
can develop a marking scheme to help them decide 
which side wins the debate.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1

© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Farming and raiding
Viking farmers 
My name is Magnus. I am a Viking farmer.
Most Vikings are farmers. People think of us only as fearsome pirates, but 
there is more to us than that. When we aren’t sailing to new lands, we are 
tending our small farms and looking after our families.
I grow crops such as onions, leeks, peas, beans and cabbages. My friend, 
Ivar, grows cereals such as barley, oats and rye.
Farming is difficult work. The soil is hard and poor. It takes a lot of effort 
to break it up, so we use oxen to help us plough the fields. We cannot sow 
crops through the winter because of the snow, so we only have a few 
seasons a year in which to grow food.
Viking farms have animals, but the animals must be tough to withstand 
the cold. We have some cattle and sheep. The manure from the animals 
is good for the soil. The sheep survive the cold well, and they give us milk 
as well as meat. Ivar also has pigs. Sometimes the cold is so harsh that the 
animals get sick. We do not have the time or food to care for sick animals, 
so if an animal is injured or starving we kill it and eat it straightaway. 
My son’s favourite food is fish. He is a great fisherman. 
He has had lots of practice because we live so close 
to the sea. He also gathers seaweed for his mother, 
although he hates eating it. My son is a good boy. 
He will grow up to be an honourable man.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
20
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Away on a Viking raid
Resource sheet – Farming and raiding
My name is Ingrid. My husband Rolf and I have five children. Rolf is often away 
for months at a time on raids. A raid is a very fast, surprise attack. While he 
is gone, I take care of all the household chores, as well as looking after the 
animals on the farm.
Our Viking men are famous for their raids. People fear being attacked by them 
because the attacks usually come as a surprise, and are swift and brutal.
Rolf is a strong man. He is one of the oarsmen in the longship the men take on 
their raids. He is a fearsome warrior. I find it hard to imagine him terrorising 
people; at home he is so gentle.
When we were first married, I asked Rolf not to leave me to go on raids. He 
explained that the raids are important. We do not have much land suitable for 
growing crops or grazing. As our villages grow, we need to find other places 
to farm and raise our families. The raids also help improve our trading options. 
By taking over key cities, we are able to use new trade routes.
Rolf told me that the longships they sail are fast and agile (able to move 
quickly and easily). They can be sailed up rivers and brought in 
close to towns and villages. He said the raids are carefully 
planned and the weapons he uses are stronger than those 
used by his enemies.
My husband is very proud of his skill as a sailor and 
warrior. Our eldest son sees the glory that his father 
receives and wants to follow in his father’s footsteps.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
21
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
To raid or not to raid?
Read the Resource sheet ‘Away on a Viking raid’. It explains what a raid is, and it also 
explains why Vikings went on raids. The Vikings were feared people, but the raids they 
went on were still dangerous missions. 
+	 1	 Together with a partner, pretend you are Vikings and come up with three 
arguments for and against raiding. Add the arguments to the table, giving the 
case for and the case against. An example argument has been done for you. 
The case for raiding
The case against raiding
We need to raid other villages and 
monasteries to get the food we need 
in order to survive the long, cold winter 
months.
Raiding is dangerous and what little food 
we steal from the villages or monasteries 
will probably not last the rough journey 
home.

Pop quiz – legendary Vikings
The Vikings were a bold people. They were great explorers and excellent sailors. 
They travelled throughout much of Europe by sea, and they conquered many of the 
lands they came across. They were brave and ruthless fighters, and their weapons 
were usually superior to those of the people they conquered. 
The Vikings were so legendary that, even today, most people have some idea of who 
they were, what they looked like and where they came from.

know – or think you know – about the Vikings.

(Hollywood / Australia / Scandinavia / Antarctica)

(ship / car / horse / foot)

●	 surrendered to other people
●	 were very peaceful and did not leave their own villages

searchText:
ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
23
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Social structure and honour 
Objectives
l	 Identify the three main Viking social classes
l	 Recognise the importance of honour in Viking 
culture
l	 Explore the role of Viking women in Viking 
society 
l	 Introduce students to ‘things’ as a form of 
governance
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required.
Background
Viking society was very ordered. There were clear 
class delineations and laws were strictly enforced. 
Honour was central to Viking culture. Roles and 
responsibilities were divided between men and 
women. For example, women took care of all 
matters related to the home and family, while men 
looked after the farms, boats and trade. However, 
when the men went away on long trips, the women 
were left in charge of everything. While not having 
as many rights as Viking men, Viking women 
certainly fared better than women in other parts of 
Europe at the time. 
Starter activity 
Discuss as a class how ‘outsiders’ might view our 
society. Imagine that a group of aliens were to come 
here. How would you describe our society to them? 
What would you say about the roles of men and 
women? How important are children in our society? 
What are the values that underpin our society? Do 
we have a class system? What does it look like?
Resource and Activity sheets
As a class, read the Resource sheet ‘Viking hierarchy’. 
Write the names of the social classes on the board and 
discuss the differences between them. Some students 
may need help pronouncing the class names and 
understanding the differences between the classes. 
Students can then complete the Activity sheet ‘In 
their place’.
After students have completed the Activity sheet 
‘The role of Viking women’, discuss as a class how 
women’s roles have changed since the Viking Age.
Before students attempt the Activity sheet ‘Honour’, 
spend some time discussing what honour means. 
The Activity sheet ‘Things – Viking meetings’ invites 
students to compare modern governments to the 
Viking meetings called ‘things’.
Extension activity
Honour was central to Viking life and society. As a 
class, create a definition of honour that is relevant to 
contemporary society. For example, behaving with 
honour is behaving in a way that respects yourself 
and other people; it can include sticking by your 
friends, not telling lies and taking responsibility for 
your actions. 
Is honour considered as important in our society 
today? Are there other personal characteristics or 
behaviours that are considered more important than 
honour in our society? Make a list. Can students think of 
how (through our behaviour, customs or social systems) 
we as a society reinforce the importance of these 
personal characteristics?

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
24
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Viking hierarchy
There were three classes of people in Viking society: jarls, karls and thralls.
Class
Who made up this class?
How did they live?
Interesting fact
Jarls
Jarls were wealthy 
nobles who owned large 
properties, ships and 
treasures.
The most important jarl 
was a king. Each region 
had a king.
Jarls lived in large, 
fancy halls. Their lives 
were comfortable 
compared with those 
of the other classes. 
Jarls were only as 
powerful as the people 
who supported them. 
A good jarl knew he 
had to take care of his 
followers so that he 
could remain in power. 
Karls
Karls were landowners, 
farmers and other 
freemen, such as 
carpenters and 
blacksmiths. 
Karl families tended to 
live close to other karls. 
They usually lived in 
longhouses and used 
other buildings (such 
as barns) as well. 
If a karl worked hard 
and became wealthy 
and famous enough, 
he could become a jarl.
Thralls
Thralls were slaves and 
bondsmen.
Slaves were used to 
help run farms, go 
on raids and row the 
Viking boats. They 
lived hard lives and 
had few rights. If they 
had a generous jarl 
and were able to save, 
they could buy their 
freedom. 
If a Viking could not 
pay his debt, he would 
be forced to become a 
bondsman. This meant 
he would have to work 
for someone else until 
he had cleared what he 
owed.
Some people – such as beggars and outlaws – did not belong to any of these classes. 
Beggars could not afford to own land and so they had no legal rights. They couldn’t 
pass on anything they owned to their children when they died, and they weren’t 
allowed to marry.

26
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012

The role of Viking women
+	 1	 Read the passage below, then match the underlined words in the passage with 
the correct definition below. 
Viking society was patriarchal. Men made the laws, spoke at important meetings 
called ‘things’ and could be elected kings. Women weren’t allowed to do any of these 
things. They did, however, have more rights than most women living in other parts of 
Europe at the time. 
Viking girls usually got married in their early teens. Before a girl married, her father 
had authority over her. After she was married, her husband had authority over her. 
Viking women were in charge of looking after their homes and their families. They 
were responsible for all the household chores. They also had to run the family farm or 
estate when their husbands were away. Wealthy Viking women had slaves to help them, 
but most Vikings were not wealthy. Viking women did not go on raids or sail away on 
trading trips.
Viking women were expected to behave with honour, just like Viking men. They were 
proud, generous and strong-willed. Viking men were expected to treat their women with 
respect.

b)	 ____________________   jobs that have to be done

e)	 ____________________   the power to control another person
	
f)	 ____________________   moral and respectful behaviour

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
27
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Honour
The Vikings had a very strict society with a strong code of honour. They believed that acting 
with honour was extremely important – even more important than living. They believed that 
if they did not live a life of honour, they would not enjoy a comfortable afterlife. 
Activity sheet – Social structure and honour

The first one has been done for you.
	
a)	 honesty	
Handing in a wallet to the police after you find it in a park
	
b)	 loyalty	
________________________________________________
	
c)	 courage	
________________________________________________

Loyalty
Vikings believed 
that loyalty to family, 
clan and king was 
important. 
Hospitality
Vikings were travellers. 
They understood the 
importance of shelter 
and food when on 
the move. Therefore, 
they were generous 
to their guests. 
Honesty 
Vikings were 
expected to speak 
the truth and to keep 
their word.
Courage
Vikings saw 
courage as a mix of 
determination and 
bravery. Once a Viking 
made up his mind, he 
stuck to it. 
Having honour
Honour wasn’t defined by  
the laws of the day; it was more 
a sign of Viking character.  
Honour was shown through  
honesty, loyalty, courage  
and hospitality.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
28
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Things – Viking meetings
The Vikings used a special system of law-making meetings, called ‘things’. There were 
local things and regional things. In Iceland, there was also a national thing called the 
Althing. At a thing, free Viking men would discuss laws and settle arguments. 
●
●First, at a local thing, the karls (freemen) of each region would select a chieftain that 
they wanted to support. The chieftain, called a godi, represented his people at regional 
things. He had to take as many supporters as possible to a thing, just in case a fight  
broke out. Also, the more supporters he had, the more powerful he would be. Chieftains 
knew they had to look after their followers if they wanted to keep their support. 
●
●All the chieftains from all the regions would attend the national things. Things could 
last several days. The Althing – held annually in summer – would last a couple of 
weeks. There would be much feasting and drinking during this time.
●
●Viking laws were not written down like our laws today. Instead, a Viking lawman 
would memorise the laws and recite them at the beginning of each thing. 
●
●Vikings would also elect their regional king at the regional thing. Viking kings had 
to be honourable, generous and brave fighters, and they had to be able to inspire 
other warriors.
Similar or different?
+	 1	 Below are some features of our modern-day system of government. Are these 
features similar or different to a Viking thing? Tick the correct box.
Similar to a 
Viking thing
Different to a 
Viking thing
In our modern governments, all laws must be 
written down.
In our modern governments, elected officials 
need to keep their followers happy otherwise 
the officials can be voted out.
In our modern governments, women can be 
elected to represent the people.
In our modern governments, we do not 
expect our leaders to be good warriors.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
53
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Trade and expansion
Objectives
l	 Understand what trade is and why studying it 
is an important part of historical studies
l	 Identify some of the items traded by Vikings 
l	 Identify key trading locations and routes
l	 Introduce students to Erik the Red, a Viking 
committed to the expansion of Viking trade 
Prior knowledge
Students should have some geographical 
knowledge and an understanding of where 
the Vikings came from. They should also know 
the location of key countries in Europe (such as 
England, France and Spain) and Russia. 
Background
Aided by their prowess as sailors and their success 
with raiding, the Vikings were exceptional traders 
who built extensive and complex trade networks. 
Many trade ports and cities were either founded 
or expanded by the Vikings, with the settlement 
of these ports and cities being one of the central 
factors in their dominance. 
Starter activity
Who do we trade with? Think about the various 
cities, states and countries we trade with. Do certain 
goods tend to be associated with a particular 
country? If so, which goods and which countries? Do 
trade relations matter? How well do you think your 
town/city/nation would survive if it didn’t trade with 
other people? Are there certain items you simply 
wouldn’t have were it not for trade?
Resource and Activity sheets
Students should work with a partner to complete 
the Activity sheet ‘Trade matters’. This Activity sheet 
encourages students to consider the role of trade in 
history as well as in their own time. 
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The Vikings as 
traders’ then complete the Activity sheet ‘Viking trade’. 
These sheets explore the role Viking trade played in 
expanding commodities throughout the world. 
Finally, students can read the Resource sheet ‘Erik the 
Red’ before completing the Activity sheet ‘Erik the Red 
expands Viking trade’. These sheets examine the role of 
Erik the Red in the colonisation of Greenland.
Extension activity
This activity is designed to show students how 
extensive modern trade routes are, and how we tend 
to take them for granted. The students are required to 
complete the first section as homework. 
Each student should select two items of food from 
their pantry at home. They should write down the name 
of each item, as well as the name of the country it came 
from (this information is on the label, but you might 
need to explain this to students first). 
In class, on a large map of the world, write all the 
food items recorded by the students and mark the 
countries that these items came from. 
How wide-ranging is global trade? How does it 
compare to trade during the Viking Age?

© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Erik the Red
Resource sheet – Trade and expansion
My name is Erik the Red. I was born in Norway in 950 CE. My full name is  
Erik Thorvaldsson. People call me ‘Red’ because I have red hair.
I moved from Norway to Iceland with my parents. When I was 32 years 
old, I killed several people. I was then exiled (barred) from Iceland for 
three years.
I decided to spend that time sailing and exploring other lands. I discovered a 
place I called Greenland. No Vikings or other Europeans lived there. I liked the 
idea of living away from all the people I had fought with back in Iceland.
Once my three-year exile was finished, I sailed back to Iceland. I told people 
how wonderful Greenland was. I figured the name ‘Greenland’ would make 
it sound like a nice place to live, and I was right. Lots of people decided to 
come back with me. In 986 CE we left Iceland and sailed to Greenland.
We started up two colonies in Greenland. Both were on the south-west 
coast, as the land there was better for farming. In summer, men from both 
colonies would travel north to hunt seals and whales for their meat, and 
walruses for their tusks. Life was tough. It was very cold and sea ice made 
sailing difficult. We also fought from time to time with the 
native Inuits.
My son, Leif Eriksson, eventually left Greenland and 
explored Vinland (North America). I was to have gone with 
him, but I changed my mind. I never saw my son again.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
54
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Trade matters
Trade refers to the buying and selling of goods and services between people. Trade can 
happen within a village, or it can take place between different countries. 
Throughout history, people have exchanged goods. Historians know, for example, that 
even in the Stone Age humans in different areas exchanged one type of rock (flint) for 
another (obsidian). As civilisations grew and people began to travel further, they traded 
with people from other cities and then other countries. 
Archaeologists and historians like to study the trading habits of people who lived long 
ago. It gives them information about a lot of things, such as:
●
●what items were considered valuable enough to trade with
●
●which peoples and countries traded with each other
●
●where trading took place (for example, in a market or in a port)
●
●how items that came from one culture ended up somewhere completely different
●
●what the most common land and sea trade routes were.
+	 Work with a partner to complete the following activity.
1	 Imagine you are historians from the future and you are writing a book about the 
trading habits of people who live in your city right now. 
What sort of things do they buy?
What do they use to buy things with? 
Are there special marketplaces where 
people get together to trade? Where 
are they? 
How do goods arrive at these 
marketplaces? How do people get 
these goods back to their homes?

searchText:
ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
55
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The Vikings as traders
The Vikings were great traders. Their skills as sailors made it possible for them to travel 
between countries, and their large boats helped them carry goods from one place to another. 
As the Vikings travelled further, to other countries throughout Europe and towards 
Asia, they traded with different peoples. They traded the furs they hunted as well as wood, 
wool, leather, honey and other items for silver, silk, jewellery, weapons and spices. 
The Vikings also bought and sold slaves. During Viking raids, local people were taken by 
the Vikings and enslaved. These slaves were then taken to Viking settlements to work or 
taken to other cities to be traded. Slave trading was common throughout most parts of 
Europe during the Viking Age.
Many cities and ports in Europe were created or expanded by the Vikings through 
trade. For example, the Vikings founded Dublin in Ireland and Birka in Sweden. They also 
traded with people as far east as Russia. 
The Vikings created a complex network of trade routes over land and sea. These 
routes covered Scandinavia, most of Europe, the northern part of the Atlantic Ocean and 
the Mediterranean area. Historians know where the Vikings traded because they have 
found Viking artefacts in these areas.

searchText:
ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
35
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Viking beliefs
Objectives
l	 Understand that beliefs influence behaviour 
and the study of belief systems is an important 
aspect of historical investigation 
l	 Identify the most significant aspects of Norse 
mythology (i.e. the three worlds of the universe, 
the Norse creation myth, Valhalla and the most 
important Norse gods) 
l	 Introduce students to Viking funerary customs
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required.
Background
The Vikings had a complex and interesting 
mythology. A mythology is a collection of stories 
used to explain the world, the creation and role of 
humans in the natural world, and the relationships 
between humans and gods. This mythology (and the 
beliefs that accompanied it) influenced the way the 
Vikings lived and fought, and underscored a host of 
their social behaviours.
Starter activity
When we study people from the past, it is important 
to think about the things they believed in. Belief 
systems influence laws and can shape the way 
people interact with each other. Use the following 
questions to encourage class discussion regarding 
the way present-day beliefs affect our society: 
l  Why do most people believe it is important to 
obey laws? How does this belief affect behaviour?
l  What do some people believe happens when they 
die? How might these beliefs affect the way they 
live their lives?
l  What are some positive effects of people having 
different belief systems?
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The Norse 
universe’ before completing the Activity sheet ‘A 
complex mythology’. You might like to search the 
internet for pictorial representations of the Norse 
universe so that students are able to visualise the 
three world levels.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Norse 
mythology’ before completing the Activity sheet 
‘Understanding Norse mythology’. These sheets 
introduce students to the Norse creation myth and a 
handful of important gods.
The Activity sheet ‘Valhalla’ examines Viking beliefs 
about the afterlife and Viking funerary customs. 
Extension activity
A society’s funerary customs are strongly influenced by 
its belief systems. What do the funerary customs of our 
society say about us? Take a poll within the class. How 
many funerals have students attended? How were the 
funerals conducted? For example, was the deceased 
person buried or cremated, and was the funeral a 
religious or secular event? Be aware that some students 
may find it upsetting to talk about funerals they have 
attended, so make sure all discussion is voluntary.

The Norse universe
Viking mythology is usually called Norse mythology. ‘Norse’ simply means that it came 
from Scandinavia during the Viking era.
Norse mythology was full of courage, hardship and larger-than-life characters. It 
contained magic, as well as elves, giants and dwarfs. Norse mythology was strongly based 
on the natural environment. Trees, the sky, forests and snow all featured in its stories.  
According to Norse mythology, there were three worlds that made up the universe:
●
●Asgard
●
●Midgard
●
●Niflheim.
The first world, Asgard, was where the gods of war and the gods of the sky lived. 
Asgard was full of wondrous halls and palaces made of silver and gold. The most brilliant 
of these halls was Valhalla. Elves and the Vanir (fertility gods who could see into the 
future) also lived here. 
The second world was Midgard (which means the Middle World). Human beings lived 
in Midgard. Midgard was a fortress built by the gods and given to the Vikings to help 
protect them from the giants. Giants, dark elves and dwarfs lived on the same level as 
human beings, but in separate lands. 
Between Asgard and Midgard was a huge 
and beautiful rainbow bridge called Bifrost. 
Anyone could use the bridge to travel between 
worlds but the journey was always very 
dangerous, even for the gods.
Finally, there was an underworld called 
Niflheim (which means land of the mists). 
Niflheim was also known as Hel, named after  
the goddess of the dead who ruled there.  
It was an icy, cold place and one that was  
feared by the Vikings.

Norse mythology
According to Norse mythology, there once lived a frightful giant made of frost, called 
Ymir. One day, the god Odin set out with his two brothers, Vili and Ve, to kill Ymir. They

and magic. He could create battles on Earth by throwing down his spear. He also liked to 
choose the winner of any war between humans. The Vikings did all they could to keep

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
47
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Viking conquests 
Objectives
l	 Recognise the links between the Viking raids 
and the Vikings’ expansion throughout Europe 
and beyond
l	 Understand the reasons why the Vikings raided 
villages, cities and monasteries, and why those 
raids were generally successful
l	 Consider the effects of raids on the people 
being raided
l	 Develop some skills at interpreting a primary 
source
Prior knowledge
Students should have basic map-reading skills, 
including an understanding of the location of 
Europe. 
Background
Throughout the three centuries that the Vikings 
dominated Europe, it was violence and the threat 
of violence that made their conquests possible. 
Viking raids were sudden, swift and destructive. 
People were killed or enslaved, items of value were 
stolen and many raided villages were left ablaze. 
The Danegeld evolved as a means of appeasing the 
Vikings and protecting people and property. 
Starter activity
What is a raid? Ask students to look up the word in a 
dictionary and write the definition in their workbooks. 
Invite students to brainstorm reasons why raids 
would have been an effective way of dominating a 
region. Write their responses on the board. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Viking raids’ and 
then complete the Activity sheet ‘Conquered by Vikings’. 
The Resource sheet emphasises the fact that Vikings 
saw raids as battles rather than acts of theft.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Lindisfarne 1’ 
and complete the Activity sheet ‘Lindisfarne 2’ in small 
groups. This Activity sheet may be difficult for some 
students; you may need to help them with interpreting 
the language used in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 
excerpt. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Danegeld – paying off the 
Vikings’, can be completed by students individually. 
This sheet combines grammatical knowledge with 
an understanding of the Danegeld. The final exercise 
invites students to consider the effect of the Danegeld 
on farmers at the time.
Extension activity
Play the game ‘Viking Quest’ on the BBC History 
website. This game invites students to build a ship, 
cross the seas, loot a monastery and return home to 
claim their prize. The village chieftain then determines 
whether the raid has been a success or not. The 
game lasts approximately 5–7 minutes per go and is 
designed as an educational resource. It can be accessed 
by visiting the BBC website at www.bbc.co.uk/history/
ancient/vikings/launch_gms_viking_quest.shtml 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
48
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Viking raids
For centuries, the Vikings sailed their way throughout much of Europe, attacking villages 
as they went. One of the first and most famous Viking raids took place at the monastery 
at Lindisfarne, in northern England. A monastery is a place where a community of monks 
or nuns lives. Vikings attacked monasteries because they were poorly defended and those 
who lived there had no weapons. Monasteries also often held lots of valuable things, such 
as gold, food, animals and jewels. 
During raids, the Vikings would burn buildings, kill people, take women and children 
as slaves, and steal any riches they found. The Vikings did not see raiding as stealing. They 
were very proud and honourable people. They believed that stealing was a terrible act 
and if you stole something you would have a horrible afterlife. Instead, they saw raids as 
honourable battles in which the victor (the winning side) was allowed to keep the spoils 
of war (all the valuable items that they took from the losing side). 
Viking raids were very successful for a few reasons. Firstly, the Vikings could sneak up 
quietly in their boats and take villages and monasteries by surprise. Secondly, raids were 
known to be fierce and bloody, so people often ran away or surrendered. The Vikings 
then moved on to the next place just as quickly as they had arrived.

Lindisfarne 1
In 793 CE, Vikings attacked a monastery at Lindisfarne. Lindisfarne is a small island off the 
north-eastern coast of England. The monastery contained many religious relics (historical 
objects). It was also an important centre of learning. 
The raid was swift and brutal. Many monks were killed, and some were taken as slaves. 
The monastery was burned and valuable items were stolen. After the raid, the remaining 
monks fled Lindisfarne with whatever relics they had managed to save.
The following account of the Viking raid at Lindisfarne was recorded in the Anglo-Saxon 
Chronicle. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a collection of historical records written in England 
between the 9th and 12th centuries. It is an example of a primary historical source, 
which means that it was created during the historical period that is being studied.

52
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Danegeld – paying off the Vikings
A proper noun refers to the name of a person, place, group, event or important object. 
Examples of proper nouns are ‘England’ and ‘Ingrid’. Proper nouns start with a capital 
letter. A common noun is the name given to a type of person, place or thing. Examples of 
common nouns are ‘chair’, ‘boat’ and ‘men’. 
+	
1   Identify whether the underlined words below are common nouns or proper 
nouns by circling the correct option. 
Viking raids were organised and brutal. Few cities survived a Viking raid and 
most people – including rulers (common noun / proper noun) – were scared 
of being attacked and killed. 
In 810 CE, more than 200 Viking ships (common noun / proper noun) 
attacked a place called Frisia (common noun / proper noun). The Vikings 
demanded a bounty (a lot of money) in return for not destroying the area. 
The people of Frisia gave them 45 kilograms of silver (common noun / 
proper noun). This payment came to be known as Danegeld (common 
noun / proper noun), which means ‘Danish gold’. Over time, the Danegeld 
became a way of paying off the Vikings so that they wouldn’t attack. To raise 
the money (common noun / proper noun) needed to pay the Vikings, kings 
(common noun / proper noun) charged their people a Danegeld tax. 
The Danegeld was commonly used as a way of avoiding Viking attacks for 
300 years. During that time (common noun / proper noun), many tonnes of 
silver were given to the Vikings. In return, the Vikings would agree to settle 
in an area (common noun / proper noun) and rule it fairly without violence. 
Sometimes the Vikings would take the silver and return to Scandinavia 
(common noun / proper noun). 
2	 Imagine you were a farmer living in England. How would you have felt about having to 
pay the Danegeld tax? Write your answer in your workbook.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
5
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Who were the Vikings?
Objectives
l	 Identify how the legend of the Vikings 
continues to permeate and influence the 
modern world
l	 Recognise relevant geographical locations 
and situate Europe – and in particular, 
Scandinavia – on a world map
l	 Identify the geographical spread of Viking 
influence 
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading 
skills and be able to identify at least their home 
country in an atlas. 
Background
The Vikings were a legendary people and, as such, 
the potential for misconceptions about who they 
were and how they lived is considerable. They came 
from Scandinavia, travelled throughout Europe and 
beyond, and dominated Europe from the late 8th 
to the 11th centuries. ‘Who were the Vikings?’ aims 
to clarify when the Vikings lived, where they came 
from and how far their influence spread, and to get 
students thinking about their own assumptions and 
how these are shaped. 
Starter activity
Ask students to pair up and, working with their 
partner, draw how they think a Viking looked. Ensure 
that students know that they do not need to worry 
about whether or not their representation is correct. 
Once everyone has drawn their Viking, invite each 
pair to share their picture with the class. On the 
board, make a list of any features that the pictures 
had in common. For example, how common were 
horned helmets? Are students aware that Vikings 
did not have horns on their helmets? From here, it is 
ideal to move straight on to the first Activity sheet 
‘Pop quiz – legendary Vikings’. 
Resource and Activity sheets
As a class, read the Activity sheet ‘Pop quiz – legendary 
Vikings’. Ask the students to write their answers 
individually, and then discuss the answers as a class.  
The aim is to generate discussion about the assumptions 
we make about the Vikings, as well as about other 
peoples and historic events. Discuss the use of reliable 
sources such as school texts, educational internet sites 
and documentaries. Remind students that ‘CE’ stands 
for ‘Common Era’.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The Viking 
Age’ before reading and completing the Activity sheet 
‘The Vikings travel far and wide’. Discuss the information 
in both sheets. Ensure that students understand where 
Scandinavia is in relation to where the students live. 
Students can then use the information they have 
gathered in both these sheets to complete the Activity 
sheet ‘Vikings’.
Finally, students can complete the Activity sheet 
‘Tracking the Vikings’. This sheet emphasises how far the 
Vikings travelled and their scope of influence. 
Extension activity
As a class, discuss the importance of how extensively 
the Vikings dominated Europe. Using an atlas, work out 
how far it is from Sweden to Spain. You will need to use 
the map scale to calculate this. Put this distance into a 
context the students can comprehend – for example, 
from their school to another city. How hard would it 
have been for the Vikings to cover that distance? How 
would students cover that distance without cars? 
Would climate have been a big factor for the Vikings? 
Remember, northern Europe is very cold and the seas 
can be very rough.

The Viking Age 
The Vikings ruled much of Europe for centuries. In fact, the years between c. 790 CE and  
c. 1066 CE became known as the Viking Age.
Scandinavia
The Vikings came from Scandinavia. Scandinavia is a region in northern Europe that 
is centred on the Scandinavian Peninsula. A peninsula is a piece of land that is mainly 
surrounded by water. The Scandinavian Peninsula is the largest peninsula in Europe.
Today, Scandinavia is made up of three countries:
●	 Denmark       
●	 Norway       
● Sweden.
Resource sheet – Who were the Vikings?
This map shows the Scandinavian Peninsula and the 
three countries that make up Scandinavia.
The people who lived in Scandinavia from c. 790 CE were exceptional boatbuilders 
and sailors, so they were able to raid and trade throughout the region. These people 
came to be known as Vikings. Before the Viking Age, many other peoples had lived in 
Scandinavia, such as the Goths, the Vandals, the Cimbri and the Angles.

searchText:
Energy and matter
18
© Chris Greef, Suada Bilali and Blake Education 2010
Assignments in Junior Science – Book 8 – Energy and matter
The term thermodynamics comes from the Greek language; thermo has to do with heat, a form of energy, and 
dynamics refers to movement. So thermodynamics is about how heat energy moves. Three important laws of 
thermodynamics were developed in the mid 19th century and the early 20th century. 
8a
The three laws of thermodynamics
The first law of thermodynamics: Conservation of energy
Energy changes from one form to another, it cannot be created or destroyed. Energy is always 
conserved. The total amount of energy in the universe stays constant.
When a bar heater gives off heat and also some light, these forms of energy have come from another 
energy form: electric energy. Neither the heat nor the light were created.
Einstein’s famous equation E = mc 2 broadened this law. The total amount of energy and matter in 
the universe stays the same. Therefore, people are able to change some matter into huge amounts of 
energy, like in a nuclear reactor. In this case, the energy did not come from another form of energy, it 
came from matter. The law of conservation of energy is only true when the amount of matter stays the 
same, which is most of the time.
The second law of thermodynamics: Entropy
The word entropy means messiness or disorder. Energy systems increase their entropy; that is, they 
become more and more messy. Look at your bedroom – after a few days, it can look really untidy. Its 
entropy has increased. If everything in your room ends up on the floor, the potential energy (here 
gravitational potential energy) has become less. Over time there is more entropy – that is, more 
chaos, more disorder, more mess – less orderliness and less potential energy.
Furthermore, heat travels from hotter objects to colder ones in order to make everything equally 
warm. Then it is no longer an ordered system, where heat would be ‘over here’ and cold

searchText:
Antibiotic resistance – news story
Read the article below which features a news item from 13 th January 2017.



    A superbug that could not be treated with 26
    different antibiotics has killed a woman in the
    USA
    The 70-year-old returned to the USA from India in August last year with
    an infected swelling in her pelvis. The infection arose after the woman
    broke her right leg. She was seriously ill when she arrived at the hospital
    in Nevada – her immune system was going into overdrive in an attempt
    to fight the infection causing inflammation throughout her body.

    Eventually, she died from septic shock.

    Samples of the infection taken from the wound were sent for testing to
    the Centre for Disease Control.

    They showed she was infected with a bacterium called Klebsiella
    pneumoniae – which normally lives in the gut without causing any
    problems. However this sample proved to be resistant to all 26 available
    antibiotics in the USA, including the group of drugs known as
    carbapenems used as a 'last resort' to treat drug-resistant infections.
    This superbug produces an enzyme which makes them resistant to
    carbapenems.

    The young and old are most at risk of antibiotic-resistant infections. This
    is because these two groups have low immunity, making them more
    susceptible to infection.

    Such resistant bacteria are primarily created in hospital conditions.
    Antibiotics are used to kill bacteria, but some antibiotic-resistant bacteria
    propagate, spreading throughout medical centres, and beyond.

    Each year in the United States, at least 2 million people become infected
    with bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics and at least 23 000 people
    die each year as a direct result of these infections.

    Prof Laura Piddock commented:

    "In circumstances such as this, where doctors are faced with the inability
    to treat a life-threatening infection, they need the flexibility to use
    antibiotics licensed for use in other countries and shown to be active in
    the laboratory against the patient's infecting bacterium."

    Dr David Brown, chief scientist at Antibiotic Research UK, said: "It is still
    quite unusual for a bacterial infection to be resistant to such a large

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017         28034                                Page 1 of 5
                                              Antibiotic resistance – news story

    number of antibiotics. However, the ease of global travel does mean that
    such cases will increase."




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017      28034                             Page 2 of 5
                                                Antibiotic resistance – news story

Task

Using the information above and your own understanding of how antibiotic-
resistant bacteria evolve, answer the following questions.

   1. Which people are most at risk to resistant infections and why?

   2. How many types of antibiotic are available in the USA?

   3. Why are some potentially useful antibiotics not available to doctors
      treating patients with infections?

   4. What do you know about Klebsiella pneumoniae?
       Extension: Why might doctors be particularly concerned about this
       bacterium?

   5. Describe how antibiotic-resistant bacteria might be 'created' and spread
      in a hospital environment.
       Extension: If you were in charge of infection management in your local
       hospital what procedures would you put in place to prevent the spread of
       resistant bacteria? What role can you play in helping to reduce antibiotic
       resistance?

   6. Using numbers with one significant figure, estimate the percentage of
      people who recover from infection by antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

   7. How might cases of infection by drug resistant bacteria be increased by
      global travel?
       Extension: How could this risk be reduced?

   8. Describe how the rise of antibiotic resistance provides evidence for the
      process of evolution.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017        28034                             Page 3 of 5
                                                            Antibiotic resistance – news story

Suggested answers
1. Young and elderly people are most at risk. They have low immunity to infection and disease.

2. 26 types

3. Prof Laura Piddock implies that different countries have different antibiotics available to
   doctors. Antibiotics have to be licensed for use. Perhaps if an antibiotic is available for use in
   one country doctors in other countries should also be free to use it.
   Some may be licensed to treat one or two specific infections only but they may have been
   shown to be effective against other bacteria in the lab. Perhaps these should be made
   available without going through all the stages in drug development.

4. It is a bacterium. It is found naturally in the gut. It is normally harmless. Some forms are
   resistant to antibiotics.
   Extension: It's a very ubiquitous bacterium which is found in lots of people. It could pose a
   serious risk to people if the ability to produce the enzyme which renders carbapenems
   ineffective, is passed on to other bacteria and becomes widespread.

5. The idea of mutation producing new strains some of which are resistant to antibiotics. These
   are not killed when exposed to antibiotics. They survive, reproduce and percentage of resistant
   bacteria in population increases.
   Extension: Possible answers might include – scrupulous hygiene management and cleaning
   routines; reduce number of visitors; treat cases that do not involve wounds, surgery etc. in a
   different hospital; reduce the number of operations e.g. no cosmetic surgery.
   Your role could include taking care not to spread infection; looking after your own health by
   cleaning teeth, eating well; not taking antibiotics for minor infections; taking the full course of
   prescribed antibiotics; deciding to become a research scientist in this field!

6. 2 000 000 cases

   (20 000 ÷ 2 000 000) x 100 = 1% deaths therefore 99% survive.
   23 000 deaths = 20 000 deaths (1 significant figure)


7. Cases such as the woman from Nevada introduce new, resistant forms of bacteria into a
   country and its hospital environment.
   Extension: Taking antibiotics to the patient rather than moving the infected person. Not allowing
   an infected person to travel if they have a resistant strain unknown in their destination country.
   Preventing infected people from travelling e.g. a person with TB unless they can prove
   themselves free of infection.

8. Bacteria reproduce at a fast rate. Mutations in bacteria produce new strains. Resistant strains
   are not killed by antibiotics so survive and reproduce – passing the resistant gene/ mutation to
   the next generation.

       resistance/

                                                  Antibiotic resistance – news story

BOOK 3; ECOLOGY

Bioaccumulation and biomagnification

In the same way that nutrients and other compounds can be cycled through an ecosystem, so can harmful
toxins and pollutants, The terms bioaccumulation and biomagnification are often interchanged but each has
a specific meaning. Both words refer to the effects of pollutants (or toxins) entering the food chain. The
difference lies in their effects once they are present.

Bioaccumulation describes how substances enter the food chain at the lowest trophic level, in other words,
from the grazer upward to the final trophic level, the top carnivore. Bioaccumulation describes the
accumulation of an undesirable substance within the tissues of an organism or a population of organisms.

Biomagnification (sometimes called bioconcentration) describes the magnified effects, or increasing levels of
concentration, of these compounds as they travel along the food chain (trophic levels). Consider the simplified
example below used to illustrate how the amount of toxin can become biomagnified within an ecosystem:

A certain water bug is considered a pest in Lake Perfect. The water is treated with a toxic chemical
compound that kills most of the bugs. One molecule of poison is sufficient to kill each bug, therefore each
dead bug contains one molecule of the toxin.

Ten ‘mini-fish’ come along and each fish eats 50 poisoned bugs, The tissues of each mini-fish then contain
50 molecules of toxin. A large ‘killer fish’ then eats 10 of the mini-fish (each of which contains 50 molecules
of toxin). The tissues of the killer fish then contain 500 molecules of toxin.

A predatory bird eats 5 of the killer fish. Its tissues will contain 2500 molecules of toxin. A land carnivore kills
and eats 3 of the predatory birds (each of which has eaten 5 killer fish). The tissues of the land predator will
contain 7500 molecules of toxin.

This is a domino style activity about the control of blood glucose. There are 32
cards, allowing it to be used with a whole class. The activity could also be done
individually, in pairs or in small groups to produce a complete ordered set of
cards.

card as all vowels are missing – this might be useful as a quick settling activity.
The domino activity can then begin.

To allow for differentiation, a few of the harder cards have been shaded
red/pink, whereas some of the simpler ones are shaded green.

When attempting this activity, students should have already studied
homeostasis (especially blood glucose control and including diabetes and its
types, risk factors and treatment). The last four cards focus on general aspects
of homeostasis and could be missed out if other aspects of homeostasis have
not been covered.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
46
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Cholera
In 1854 London was suffering from an outbreak of cholera, a deadly disease. Nobody 
knew how the disease was spread. At that time, people had to get their water from pumps 
in the street. John Snow wondered if cholera was being spread by contaminated water. 
He made a map showing where the cases of cholera were occurring, and discovered that 
most cases were around Broad Street. John Snow broke the handle off the Broad Street 
pump so nobody could pump drinking water from it. 
London’s drinking water came from pools in underground beds of gravel or from 
underground streams. Sewage had leaked into the water, spreading cholera. John Snow 
is now known as the Father of Epidemiology (the study of the spread of disease). He 
saved dozens of lives.
+ 1 How can natural disasters (for example, floods, cyclones, earthquakes, tsunamis) 
lead to cholera outbreaks? 
 
 
2 Military Response teams and organisations such as the Red Cross often rush to disaster 
zones with supplies of clean drinking water. Why? 
 
In modern times when a nation reports an epidemic, large scale international teamwork 
between doctors and governments takes place to control the disease. Disease outbreaks 
such as SARS are controlled by international cooperation.
+ 3 Write down four things you think governments might do to control an 
international disease outbreak.

©  Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008

Classifying diseases 
1
Disease is described as disorder in the normal, healthy functioning of a living organism. It is a condition that reduces 
health and well-being in some way. Diseases can be categorised into several groups. Two main classifications are 
acquired and congenital. 
Acquired diseases are those that people are not born with, but contract through other ways. While many of these are 
self-inflicted, such as smoking-related lung cancer and liver disease resulting from alcoholism, diseases can also be 
acquired through work and environmental conditions.
1 
Name a different disease that could be acquired, and describe how it is acquired. 
 
2 
Why do people put themselves at risk of contracting diseases? 
 
3 
Animals are not the only organisms that contract ‘illnesses’. Name a disease that affects the health of plants. 
 
Congenital conditions are those that people are born with. These conditions may be diseases or syndromes. A 
syndrome is a group of symptoms that occurs together to produce a particular disorder (Greek sundromē, meaning 
‘to run together’). Many people think that a syndrome, such as Down Syndrome (‘Trisomy 21’, the result of extra 
genetic material from chromosome 21), is not a disease. One argument for this is that individuals with Down 
Syndrome often display cheerful dispositions. However, individuals who have Down Syndrome show varying 
degrees of mental retardation and roughly 40% have serious heart defects. (The damage is determined by how 
much extra chromosome 21 the person carries and which genes are involved.) Some people argue that it should be 
classified as a disease condition because of this impairment to health.

     The heart has its own blood vessels which supply the heart muscle with
  glucose and oxygen. Blood vessels are like hose pipes with blood flowing through
  them. As people grow older, certain forms of cholesterol (a type of fat) carried
  in the blood may stick to the inside of the coronary artery. This forms a
  plaque which narrows the tube, slowing or even blocking the flow of blood to the
  heart. When this happens, the heart does not receive enough oxygen to work
  properly. The person may feel pain in their chest and this is one symptom of a
  heart attack.

     A device called a stent can be inserted into the coronary artery to open up the
  narrow part and make it wider. Although this involves an operation, it is not as
  serious as other operations on the heart. There is less risk of complications after
  the surgery and patients recover more quickly. Sometimes, a patient may have
  an allergic reaction to the stent but this is unusual and blood flow to the heart is
  fully restored alleviating the symptoms of a heart attack. Over time, scar tissue
  could grow inside the stent and a blood clot may form, putting the person at risk
  of a stroke. A drug called aspirin is taken to reduce the risk of a clot forming.




     Balloon angioplasty and stent insertion / Credit: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Inc. / Copyright © Encyclopaedia Britannica / For Education Use
              Only. This and millions of other educational images are available through Britannica Image Quest. For a free trial, please
                                                             visit www.britannica.co.uk/trial




     Reducing the amount of cholesterol carried in the blood, reduces the likelihood
  of a build up of fats in the coronary artery. This can be done by eating a healthy,
  low fat diet, stopping smoking and reducing the amount of alcohol consumed.
  Exercise is also very beneficial. A group of drugs known as statins can be taken
  to decrease the amount of harmful cholesterol in the blood. They do not cure
  cardiovascular disease but can prevent it getting worse. Some side effects
  have been reported including, muscle pain, dizziness, insomnia, tingling hands


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017                                       27201                                                            Page 1 of 5
                                                 Coronary heart disease - treatments


  and feet and inflammation of the liver or pancreas.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017         27201                              Page 2 of 5
                                                  Coronary heart disease - treatments

Information sheet 2 - heart valves


     The heart itself, which pumps blood continually around the body, may also
  suffer from disease as it is a very complicated structure. Valves inside the heart
  open to let blood flow into a chamber or artery and then close to prevent the
  blood from returning. Heart valves can become stiff and perforated over time.
  They do not close as well and do not prevent the back-flow of blood. This reduces
  the amount of blood reaching the brain and body.

     Heart valves can be replaced with artificial valves. The perfect artificial
  heart valve has yet to be designed. The ideal replacement valve should allow
  blood to flow in one direction only. It must be durable, opening and closing 40
  million times a year. It must not cause blood clots and should allow blood to flow
  smoothly with no turbulence. The valve needs to be designed to close without
  damaging any red blood cells. Finally, artificial valves need to work quietly!

     Inserting artificial valves into a heart involves major surgery. These valves
  keep working for 20 – 30 years but the patient must take drugs which reduce the
  risk of blood clots forming, for the rest of their lives.

     Replacement heart valves can also be biological in origin. They may use pig,
  cow or horse tissue or come from a human donor. This type of valve is usually
  given to older patients as the valve may only work well for 10 – 15 years. If the
  valve fails another operation will be needed. The patient does not have to take
  anticoagulant drugs but they will need medication to prevent the body rejecting
  the replacement valve.

‘The peregrine falcon is one of a number of predatory birds belonging to the raptor family. During the decade
from the mid-1950s to mid-1960s, the numbers of surviving falcon chicks dropped dramatically. Tests revealed

8
Fred Hollows (1929–1993): A man with a vision
Professor Fred Hollows is known and admired by many people for the incredible number of lives he improved by 
reducing blindness. Fewer people are aware that this New Zealand-born ophthalmologist (eye specialist) was the 
Head of a Sydney hospital’s Eye Surgery Department and a pioneer in the treatment of trachoma.
Fred Hollows was appalled by the number of Australian Aborigines suffering unnecessary blindness as a result 
of poor health and unclean living conditions. He set to work enlisting aid to save their sight. By the 1970s, he had 
reduced blindness in many Aboriginal communities by up to 50%. The cause of this blindness was Chlamydia 
trachomatis, a micro-organism with both viral and bacterial characteristics. C. trachomatis causes the condition 
trachoma, the main cause of human blindness around the world. The condition is extremely contagious, as the 
micro-organism is found in the runny ‘weeping’ discharge it creates as the eye becomes increasingly inflamed. The 
discharge is easily transferred to fingers, tissues and other surfaces. It also travels easily via flies as they move from 
person to person. 
This is an ancient condition, dating as far back as the Egyptian Pharaohs. It causes scarring on the fine membrane 
coating the inner eyelid and eye surface (conjunctiva). It is extremely painful and the inflammation and scarring 
continues until finally, if left unchecked, blindness results. Trachoma continues to be a problem in poor countries 
where sanitation, access to clean water and good hygiene are inadequate.

Task 1
Quickly skim read the text, to get the ‘gist’ of each paragraph. Write in the box above
each paragraph what you think it is about in 5 words or less!

 A
 Your liver is important for breaking down any potentially dangerous substances you
 consume.
 Within your liver, as within every tissue in the body, many chemical reactions occur.
 Often these reactions require "help" to happen at a faster speed, and this can be supplied
 by enzymes — types of proteins.
 Enzymes speed up the rate of a chemical reaction by acting as a catalyst.
 A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself
 undergoing any permanent chemical change.


 B
 All enzymes are made of proteins and have a specific shaped site where the chemical
 reaction can take place.
 This is known as the enzyme’s active site.
 Each enzyme has a different shape active site which explains why they only interact with
 specific reactants (which are known as substrates).
 We call the ‘fit’ between the active site and the substrate complementary.


 C
 Enzymes are very specific and need to be in certain environments or conditions to work well
 —or at all.
 If the temperature is too low, then the enzymes and substrates do not have very much
 kinetic energy, so they don’t collide very often.
 This means that the rate of reaction is slow.
 Increasing the temperature will increase the kinetic energy so will increase the rate of
 reaction.
 However, enzymes can be damaged (denatured), if exposed to too much heat.
 A denatured enzyme may no longer work to catalyze a chemical reaction because the heat
 will alter the shape of the active site.
 All enzymes have ‘optimum’ conditions – this means they each have a temperature and pH
 where they work at a maximum rate.


 D
 Catalase is an example of an enzyme in the liver that breaks down harmful hydrogen
 peroxide into oxygen and water.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
34
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Fred Hollows
Although he was originally a New Zealander, Fred Hollows is one of Australia’s most 
famous scientists – he was even named Australian of the Year in 1990.
In the 1960s Hollows helped to set up the first Aboriginal Medical Service. By 2005, 
there were more than 60 of them around Australia. As an eye specialist he was horrified 
to learn that many Indigenous Australians were blind from trachoma – a preventable and 
treatable eye disease. Hollows did many trachoma repair operations himself and started 
up the National Trachoma and Eye Health Program to inform Australians, to raise funds 
and to carry out operations.
Hollows didn’t stop there. He and his teams visited many poor countries to carry out 
operations; they even set up a lens factory in desperately poor Eritrea. When he became 
terminally sick with cancer he set up the Fred Hollows Foundation, an organisation that 
works to prevent avoidable blindness and to improve Indigenous Australians’ health. Since 
1992 the Foundation has worked in more than 30 countries in Asia, Africa, Australia and 
the Pacific. The one millionth intraocular lens (a device used to treat cataracts, which cause 
blindness) was inserted in 2003.
Fred Hollows helped millions of people, and his legacy continues to help millions more.
