harmless] eye diseases happen in places where people are very [poor/wealthy]. Hollows 
and his teams went to these places to help hundreds of thousands of people. He was a

Students could be given the game to play in small teams with one of them as
the question master. Each team will need 10 coloured counters or hexagons to
place on the grid when they get a question right.

The object of the game is to complete a path across the board. One team
should make a path from left to right and the other teams should go from top
to bottom. The original TV game pitted one contestant (on the shorter path (top
to bottom)) against a pair (going left to right).

they place a coloured counter over the hexagon. The team that wins is the one
that makes a complete path from one side to the other.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
32
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Immunisation and the media
We rely on the media to provide us with information. However, we need to be aware 
of how the information is being presented, and whether all the information is being 
reported. How often have you seen a news story saying that everything is all right? Good 
news stories are not very dramatic, so we don’t see them in the news very often. 
The topic of immunisation is one that people have different opinions about. 
Immunisation can save millions of lives by preventing the spread of disease. However, 
there have also been stories of immunisation having terrible consequences, such as brain 
damage, in children. These stories may sometimes be reported more widely than the 
success stories.
It is important to study the news and history while also asking questions such as:
 
l What is the risk of the vaccine?
 
l What is the risk of the disease it is trying to stop?
 
l Is the risk just to my child or others as well?
Reading the news in this way allows individuals to form a considered opinion.

Worksheet 10.1



Investigating neurons
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ...........................................

The nervous system is made up of billions and billions of neurons. A neuron is an individual nerve
cell that transmits information around the body, combining it with information from other sources.
     Neurons have specialised functions. Some neurons specialise in transmitting information from
the sense organs and muscles to the CNS. Other neurons specialise in sending information to the
organs, muscles or glands from the CNS. Some neurons carry information between neurons.
     The number of neurons in the human body is not known. However, estimates of the number of
neurons in the human brain alone range from 10 billion to about 100 billion neurons. The entire
nervous system that extends throughout the body is comprised of neurons that connect with many
other neurons to enable the continuous communication of information around the body. Unlike skin
cells, for example, the body does not replace neurons if they die. However, the function of a neuron,
if damaged, is often taken over by another neuron.
     Not all neurons look the same. They vary in shape and size depending on where they are located
in the body and on their specific function. However, most neurons have some features in common.
     The diagrams on this worksheet show the different types of neurons in the human body. They
also shows the various parts of each neuron.

Structure of the neuron
Soma: The soma is the large section located centrally in the neuron. The soma, or cell body, is the
structure that determines whether the neuron will be activated and thus transmit (send) messages to
other neurons.
    Within the soma is the nucleus of the neuron. The nucleus contains the biochemical information
that provides the energy to keep the neuron functioning. The soma has a number of extensions that
branch from it. There are two main types of extensions — dendrites and axons. Some neurons have
thousands of dendrites that extend from the soma, but most neurons have only one axon.
    Dendrite: A dendrite is a short, thin, widely branching nerve fibre that is specialised to detect
and receive neural information. Like an antenna, dendrites receive incoming information from other
neurons and transmit the information to the soma.
    Axon: An axon is a single, tubelike, fluid-filled extension that transmits messages from the soma
to other cells in the body including other neurons, muscles, organs and glands. Most neurons have
only one axon.
    Axons vary in length, for example, some axons extend over a metre from your spine to your big
toe, others are as small as the width of a single hair.
    At the end of each axon are branches called axon terminals. Each axon terminal has a small
knob-like swelling at the tip of it called a synaptic knob or terminal button.
    The synaptic knob is a small structure like a sack that stores chemicals called neurotransmitters
that assist in the transmission of neural information from one neuron to another. Axon terminals are
located physically close to dendrites of other neurons, enabling information to pass easily between
neurons as messages are transmitted to and from the CNS.

The role of neurons
There are three main types of neurons, each of which has a different role in the nervous system. The
three types of neurons are called sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons.
    Sensory neurons and motor neurons are found primarily in the peripheral nervous system,
whereas interneurons are primarily found in the CNS.

searchText:
BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Heavy metal pollution: the Minimata case

Mercury (chemical symbol Hq) is a ‘heavy metal’, one of a set of metal elements that are toxic. Mercury has
been used for thermometers, barometers, electrical switches, lighting, batteries and in the manufacture of
sodium hydroxide. The metal itself is moderately toxic, but becomes severely toxic when it forms compounds
with carbon.

Early last century, the people of the Japanese fishing village of Kumamoto, about 600 km from Tokyo, hoped
to expand their quiet little fishing village to a larger, more prosperous town. Consequently they welcomed
the arrival of the chemical producing company, Chisso Corporation. The Chisso plant produced, among other
forms of waste, mercury compounds that were freely dumped into Minimata Bay. The villagers depended on
this bay for fish. Almost immediately the deadly effects the chemicals had on the fish became evident. The
company recognised the damage and paid the villagers for permission to ruin their fishing industry. The
dumping of mercury compounds continued from the late 1920s up until 1968. Minimata Bay flowed out to
the Shiranui Sea (an inland sea), poisoning the aquatic species along its path.

By the 1950s rumours began to spread that the village was haunted by a spirit that took over the bodies of
Kumamoto residents, Many cats, and some dogs, began to do ‘weird dances’ on the streets before dropping
dead, Children were also behaving strangely and soon adults followed. People began to develop speech and
vision problems, others began screaming wildly, muscle spasms led to paralysis and suicides occurred. The
bizarre condition became known as ‘Minimata Disease’.

People then suspected some form of infectious disease was attacking the central nervous system. The corporation’s
doctor, Dr Hajim Hosokawa, discovered the connection between a fish diet and the condition. This led him to
analyse the fish and identify the heavy mercury contamination.

Microbes

Viruses

Viruses are even smaller than bacteria and are the cause of many diseases.
They are different from bacteria because they can only reproduce inside a
living cell. The common cold, chicken pox, measles, AIDS and glandular fever
are all caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not affect or harm viruses. Viruses
can be used to transfer genes into target cells.




Bacteria

Bacteria are so small we need a microscope to see them. They are single
celled organisms found in the soil, water and air around us. Harmful bacteria
can cause diseases such as scarlet fever, food poisoning and whooping cough.
Bacteria can reproduce and grow outside a living organism, and they can
reproduce very quickly: a small group invading the body does not take very
long to multiply into millions. They can be treated with antibiotics. Bacteria
have many uses, including the production of insulin and sewage treatment.




Fungi

These are simple organisms that feed off dead and rotting material. Organisms
that belong to this kingdom are moulds, yeasts and mushrooms. They used to
belong to the plant kingdom. Some fungi can cause rashes and often affect
nails, hair and mucous membranes. Ringworm, athlete’s foot and thrush are all
examples of fungal diseases. Fungi have many uses, e.g. yeasts are used in
brewing and baking; Penicillin is produced from the mold Penicillium.

Noise and Health

‘We don’t always realise that noise can be a danger to our health. A ‘noise’
is often defined as ‘a loud, disagreeable sound’. Yet the same sound can
be either pleasant or a nuisance — it depends on the person hearing it.

What you think is ‘music’ might be ‘noise’ to older people. HIGH
NOISE
Noise is a problem to people who live in busy cities — they are continually AREA

exposed to loud noises, This noise can be from ordinary traffic, airports,
trains and trams, building work and machinery. Such types of noise can
make life uncomfortable for people living near these sources of noise.
Exposure to loud noise, for example, loud discos and concerts, can damage hearing or even cause deafness.
People who have had prolonged exposure to loud noise may suffer from headaches, tiredness and stress.

Noises are measured in units called decibels (dB). Special sound meters are used to measure loudness.
Zero decibels is the threshold of audibility, that is, the weakest sound the human ear can hear. Sounds
above 140 decibels (‘the threshold of pain’) hurt your ears and can cause permanent damage. If you
whisper, this will give a sound level of about 20 decibels, talking normally will give about 60 decibels,
whereas loud rock music registers at about 120 decibels.

We try to keep unwelcome sounds to a minimum. Traffic noise can be a problem so, in the exhaust systems
of cars, mufflers (silencers) are included to quieten the noise made by the engine. Insulation can also be
used in machinery to reduce its noise level. People working with noisy machines wear ear protectors or
earmuffs to reduce the amount of noise entering their ears.

The biggest danger with organ and tissue transplants is rejection. A patient’s body 
will see a new organ as an invader and try to get rid of it. Transplant recipients 
must take anti-rejection drugs to stop this from happening. The drugs are called 
immunosuppressants, because their job is to suppress the immune system. 
Rejection is less likely to occur if the organ comes from a close relative. Identical  
twins are the best match, and a brother or sister may be the next best.

Chapter 3                                    Living systems
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1:                        Respiratory diseases
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING,                                                SCIENCE AS A HUMAN ENDEAVOUR
                                     VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________

Getting oxygen into your body is vital for our survival. Many different diseases of the
lungs and respiratory system prevent you from being able to breathe as deeply as
normal and breathing may cause you to cough or wheeze. Common diseases of the
lungs include asthma, emphysema, bronchitis and pneumonia. These diseases may
be chronic, which means they are long lasting or occur over and over again. Other
diseases are acute, which means they come on rapidly and last a short time.


Asthma
Asthma is a chronic disease in which the bronchi in the lungs are swollen and tender.
In this condition the bronchi react to factors in the environment, known as triggers.
Triggers such as tobacco smoke, dust and pollens cause muscles in the walls of the
bronchi to contract, making the airways narrow, as shown in Figure 3.1.1. The cell
lining of the bronchi produces extra mucus. The mucus reduces the space inside the
bronchi even more and the person has difficulty breathing.

When people with asthma feel an attack coming on, they use puffers. The puffer
contains chemicals that relax the muscles of the bronchi. This allows the bronchi to
open up and the person is able to breathe freely again.




      Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Figure 3.1.1
The passage through which air can pass is very narrow during an asthma attack.


Emphysema
Emphysema is a chronic lung disease in which the bronchi, alveoli and blood
capillaries are damaged. Emphysema is usually caused by smoking or long-term
exposure to air pollutants (chemicals) and dust.

The tissues of healthy bronchi and alveoli are elastic, which means that they are able
to stretch and then return to their original shape. When bronchi and alveoli are
exposed to pollutants and dust over long periods of time, they lose their ability to
stretch. The bronchi become narrow and the alveoli break. Damage to the alveoli
creates larger spaces within the lungs. Having large spaces reduces the surface area
for gas exchange. The blood capillaries surrounding the alveoli are also damaged
and less carbon dioxide and oxygen can be carried to the alveoli and away from
them.

Ross River virus
Many diseases are spread by contact between people but some are spread by vectors. 
Vectors are disease-carrying organisms. The mosquito is a common vector that can spread 
serious diseases such as malaria and dengue fever. In Australia the Ross River virus is 
spread by mosquitoes. The virus mostly infects people in rural areas, and causes a flu-like 
illness with a rash, joint pains and fever. Sometimes joints can become swollen. The illness 
can last for several weeks, making the patient feel weak and tired. Fortunately it is not fatal, 
but there is no specific treatment.

Taboo – stem cells and cloning

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any of the
additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.

1.    Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each team).

2.    Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto different coloured
      paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have all the cards back at the end
      of the activity in order to reuse them.

3.    The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

4.    An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile, and then
      describes the word at the top of the card without using the words below. The rest of
      their team must guess which word is described. Participants are not allowed to say
      ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

5.    Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the opposing team
      may challenge and the individual must move on to the next word.

6.    Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as possible to
      the players in their team (a longer time may be required to allow more descriptions
      to take place) before play passes to the next team. There are no penalties for
      wrong guesses.

7.    For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
      point. Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each
      group.

Understanding Biology – biotechnology and disease
35
For a person to be in good health, the heart must beat steadily and blood must flow continuously through it. At rest, 
the heart generally beats around 70 times a minute, governed by electrical stimuli generated by a region of the heart 
called the sinoatrial (SA) node. Sometimes these stimuli do not occur in the regular manner, and this can cause 
heart problems. Until about 40 years ago, major surgery was the only option for people with heart problems. The 
development of non-invasive and minimally invasive medical techniques has been of great benefit to patients.
1 
Outline some advantages of non-invasive and minimally invasive medical techniques over earlier methods. 
 
One of the most familiar biomedical devices is the artificial cardiac pacemaker. It consists of a corrosion-free lithium 
battery and a pulse generator that connects a wire to the heart. It works by sending an electrical charge from the site 
of the SA node. 
The pacemaker came about quite by accident in 1958. While building a device intended to amplify and record the 
sounds made by hearts, American scientist Wilson Greatbatch invented a pacemaker. Modifications were made to 
the original invention, and the pacemaker became a viable proposition. The earliest pacemakers were only partially 
implanted. They had wires that emitted the electrical charge connected to an exterior device. Within ten years, totally 
implantable pacemakers had replaced these versions. In the past, the functioning of pacemakers was affected by the 
wearer standing too close to microwaves, airport metal detectors or other radio-type devices. These difficulties have 
been addressed, leading to the development of the superior models currently in use. 
2

Treating heart disease
Task

Look at the information sheets about different methods for treating heart disease. Use the information to fill in the table.

           Method                     Description                         Advantages                        Disadvantages

                                                                      Treating heart disease

Information sheets


  Artificial valves - what are they?
  It’s a device implanted in the heart of a
  patient to replace their faulty valve.
  By Stif Komar (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0
  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia
  Commons


  Artificial valves - advantages
        No rejection

  Artificial valves: disadvantages
        Can damage red blood cells, so
         patients need to take anti-clotting
         drugs.


  Biological valves – what are they?
  They are based on valves taken from
  animals, such as pigs or cattle. They are
  treated with chemicals to stop your body
  rejecting them.
  By Stif Komar (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0
  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia
  Commons


  Biological valves – advantages
        No need for blood thinning drugs as
         they don’t damage red blood cells.

  Biological valves – disadvantages
        Valves can harden and need replacing.



  Stents – what are they?
  Stents are used to treat narrow coronary
  arteries. The stent is pushed into position
  using an x-ray, the balloon is inflated,
  expanding the stent, and then removed,
  leaving the stent to open up the artery.

  Stents – advantages
        Lowers risk of infection as major
         surgery
         not required.

  Stents – disadvantages


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016                              27263                Page 2 of 7
                                                  Treating heart disease

       Fatty deposits can build up again.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016          27263                Page 3 of 7
                                                     Treating heart disease


  Bypass surgery – what is it?
  A surgical procedure used to treat coronary
  heart disease.
  It transplants a vein from the leg to divert
  blood around narrowed or clogged parts of
  the major arteries to improve blood flow and
  oxygen supply to the heart.
  Around 20,000 coronary artery bypass
  grafts are carried out in England every year.

  Bypass surgery – advantages
       No rejection risks.
       Very effective treatment.

  Bypass surgery – disadvantages
       Major surgery, so involves risks.




  Statins – what are they?
  These are drugs which lower cholesterol
  levels by stopping the liver producing as
  much.
  Patients can also change their diet to help
  reduce cholesterol.

  Statins – advantages
       They reduce cholesterol which helps
        slow down the build-up of fatty layers
        in the arteries.

  Statins – disadvantages
       They have possible side effects, e.g.
        liver damage.
       Patient has to remember to take them
        regularly.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016             27263                Page 4 of 7
                                                   Treating heart disease


  Artificial pacemakers - what are
  they?
  Some people can’t control their heart rate.
  Artificial pacemakers can be fitted under the
  skin. A wire is passed from a vein to the
  right atrium. This sends electrical impulses
  to the heart to control the heartbeat.

  Artificial pacemakers – advantages
       Major surgery not required, so not very
        risky.

  Artificial pacemakers –
  disadvantages
       The immune system can reject the
        pacemaker and it will need replacing.
       The pacemaker may sometimes
        malfunction.


  Heart transplants – what are they?
  A heart transplant is an operation to
  replace a damaged or failing heart with a
  healthy human heart from a donor who
  has recently died.
  Heart transplants are rarely performed in
  the UK, mainly due to a lack of suitable
  donors.
  There were 197 heart transplants
  performed in the UK between 2012 and
  2013.

  Heart transplants – advantages
       A better quality of life (improved
        strength, energy & stamina).
       More normal lifestyle day to day
       An improved chance of a longer life.

  Heart transplants – disadvantages
       Major surgery (anaesthetic risks,
        bleeding, clotting, infection)
       Anti-rejection drugs needed for life
       A shortage of donors.

Vaccination and the prevention of disease
1
IntroductIon
Edward Jenner (1749–1823) introduced the term vaccination. He discovered that by infecting people with cowpox (a mild 
disease) it made them immune to smallpox (a fatal disease). We now know that this immunisation is due to antibodies 
(immunoglobins) that are produced by the body in response to pathogens (bacteria and viruses) or toxins entering the 
bloodstream. Antibodies attack these invaders and then disappear once the infection is over. A much more rapid 
response is triggered if the same pathogens or toxins infect the body at a later time. When this happens, large numbers 
of antibodies are speedily produced and home in on the foreign bodies and destroy them. 
Epidemiologists study the distribution, frequency, causes and controls of diseases in populations.
Aim
To improve our knowledge of how vaccines work and be able to understand the arguments for and against their use.
data
Evidence box 1
There are several types of vaccines currently in use:
• Inactivated – These are cultivated viruses (or bacteria) that have been killed and cannot replicate (e.g influenza vaccine). 
• Attenuated – These are active viruses or living bacteria but they have been weakened and can only reproduce very slowly. 
Booster injections are not usually needed for these.
• Virus-like particles – These particles are derived from a virus but are not infectious.
Evidence box 2
Since the introduction of vaccines, epidemiological studies have shown that the incidence of chicken pox, whooping cough, 
measles, mumps, polio, rubella and smallpox has declined to a fraction of their pre-vaccination rates. 
Evidence box 3
The symptoms of chicken pox (varicella) are an itchy rash and red spot (pox) blisters all over the body. There are few 
complications and a very low death rate for healthy children, but the illness can be much more severe in adolescents and

Vaccinations
Vaccines are liquids that contain either dead germ particles or harmless live germs. The 
germs used to make a vaccine are similar to the germs that cause the disease being 
vaccinated against. When a vaccine enters the bloodstream, the body reacts as if it were 
actually suffering from an infection and makes antibodies. The antibodies stay in the 
blood for a long time, making the body immune to a real infection. 
Scientists have produced vaccines for a range of deadly diseases such as tetanus, 
diphtheria and measles. Most vaccinations are injected but some, such as the polio 
vaccine, are swallowed.

Understanding Biology – biotechnology and disease
©  Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
6
The word disease comes from the Latin words dis meaning ‘lack of’ and aise meaning ‘ease’ or ‘comfort’. Whenever a 
virus or other micro-organism impairs (harms, spoils) our health we can be in a state of disease.  
1 
Write each of these terms beside the correct definition below: ailment, hypochondriac, pathogen, epidemiology, 
pandemic, contagious, epidemic.
a Widespread occurrence of disease in an area or country. 
b An illness that can be spread by contact with others. 
c A person who is overly concerned about their health, always thinks they are ill. 
d An illness or medical complaint. 
e Large scale spread of a given disease across the world (global). 
f Study of the spread of disease. 
g A disease-causing microbe. 
There are many causes of disease, including genetics, parasites, viruses, bacteria, sexual transmission and obesity.
Genetic diseases are inherited from one or both parents (who are called carriers). These diseases are ‘programmed’ 
to occur through information coded in our DNA (our genetic material). Most genetic diseases are recessive, 
meaning they require a ‘dose’ of the recessive gene from each parent. The fact that both parents need to donate a 
recessive gene makes many genetic diseases much rarer. Sickle-cell anaemia  is an example of a recessive, blood-
related condition that can be inherited. This disease causes the red blood cells to collapse into a sickle (crescent) 
shape, which reduces the amount of oxygen that can be carried through the body. The cells also tend to clog up the 
blood vascular system which can be dangerous. Genetic diseases are not contagious (not infectious, cannot spread to 
other people).
2

• Petri dish with nutrient agar
                                                         Cultures – possible bacterial
• Sterile cotton swabs                                   infection risk

• Coloured permanent marker pens                         Handle sealed Petri dishes only.
                                                         Dispose of in biohazard marked bags. Wash
• Ruler
                                                         hands after handling.
• Clear sticky tape
                                                         Glassware – risk of cuts if broken
• Incubator
                                                         Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
• Location class list                                    immediately.


Method:
Step 1: Your teacher will assign you a location from where to collect your sample.

Step 2: Without removing the lid, turn your Petri dish upside down and label the perimeter with your
name and the date.

Step 3: Using a ruler, carefully draw a line across the middle of the Petri dish to divide it into two
halves. On one half, write the name of the location from where you will collect your sample, and label
the other half as ‘control’.

Step 4: Remove the swab from the packaging, taking care not to touch the end. Gently rub the swab on
the assigned location.

Step 5: Quickly but carefully open the lid of the
Petri dish – just wide enough to fit the swab in –
and rub the swab over the agar in a zig-zag pattern
in the half labelled with your location. Take care
not to mark the agar, or to rub onto the half marked
as control.

Step 6: Replace the petri dish lid and secure on four
sides with sticky tape. Leave some gaps to prevent
anaerobic bacteria growing.

Step 7: Place your Petri dish, upside down, into
the incubator. This helps to prevent condensation
occurring, and allows easier identification of the
plates when checking them.


                                                 Page 1 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?

Step 8: Examine your Petri dish again after one day, two days and then five days. Record all observations
on your result sheet.

Step 9: Your teacher may also conduct a control* investigation to measure bacteria from the air.


 This could be done by simply leaving a Petri dish of agar open and exposed for a specified time
 length e.g. one hour, then sealing and incubating with the other Petri dishes.




                                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?

Teacher note: Suggested are several locations and space to add in your own. You may decide for students
to investigate a location each or to work in pairs, depending on your class size. We recommend assigning
the students to a location and them displaying the list to the class.

Results
Draw the bacterial colonies (if any) which have grown on your agar plate.




                After 1 day                   After 2 days                     After 5 days

Count the bacterial colonies that have grown on the agar and complete the table below.
Tips for counting the colonies:
•   Dot each colony with a coloured marker as you count.
•   Use a different colour each time you examine to count the additional colonies only. Add this amount
    to the previous count.
•   Place the Petri dish on a piece of graph paper and count the colonies row by row.
•   If there are many colonies to count, divide the area into 2 using a marker pen, count the colonies in
    ½ then multiply by 2 to find the total.



    Location:

                              Day                                    Number of colonies




Compare your results with the other locations. Your teacher may ask you to add your results to a
collective data table.
You may be given the opportunity to take photographs as a means of recording and comparing the
bacterial growth from difference locations.
                                                                                  Where Do Bacteria Live?

Questions


1. Which location has the most number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
2. Which location has the least number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
3. Why is it important to use sterile nutrient agar for the investigation?
4. Describe the common environmental conditions where the highest bacterial growth was found.
   (Think about temperature, light, moisture etc.)
5. What does the control Petri dish show? Explain why.
6. What measures can you take to reduce your exposure to bacteria?
                                                                                   Where Do Bacteria Live?

Answers

1. Which location has the most number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
   This will depend on the locations used and the results the students have obtained.

2. Which location has the least number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
   This will depend on the locations used and the results the students have obtained.

3. Why is it important to use sterile nutrient agar for the investigation?
   It ensures that the culture(s) which grow on the agar after incubation, are only the ones from the
   swab, and therefore ensure that the investigation is valid.

4. Describe the common environmental conditions where the highest bacterial growth was found.
   (Think about temperature, light, moisture etc.)
   Bacteria are likely to be found in abundance in areas which are moist, and contain traces of food
   for nutrition. Also high traffic items or locations, e.g. mobile phones and door handles may also
   show high levels of bacteria.

5. What does the control Petri dish show? Explain why.
   The control dish will likely show some growth of bacterial cultures. These cultures will have
   come from the air around the Petri dish whilst it was left open.

6. What measures can you take to reduce your exposure to bacteria?

    • Wash your handles before and after eating or preparing foods, suing hot water and soap.

    • Bleaching and disinfecting worktops and surfaces regularly.

    • Ensuring that mouths and noses are covered, and then hands are washed after coughing
    and sneezing.

    • Drying and removing excess moisture from areas such as the bath tub, shower head and
    kitchen sink.

    • Other sensible suggestions.

Baking soda is a chemical compound used when cooking cakes. The chemical name

Refining crude oil
Crude oil is a fossil fuel that formed millions of years ago from buried dead plant 
and animal matter. These remains were turned into fossil fuels by heat and pressure. 
Crude oil is a mixture of different compounds. Most of the compounds in crude oil are 
hydrocarbons. The only atoms they contain are carbon and hydrogen.
Some common hydrocarbons found in crude oil
Chemical formula
methane
CH4
ethane
C2H6
propane
C3H10
butane
C4H10
Crude oil is separated into a number of different parts, called fractions, using a process 
called fractional distillation. This involves heating the crude oil until it evaporates and 
then letting the gas condense. The different hydrocarbons can be separated because 
they have different boiling points. The fractions are then processed into more useful 
hydrocarbons. Crude oil provides useful substances such as petrol, waxes, plastics, 
detergents, bitumen and man-made fibres such as nylon. 
The diagram shows the different substances formed from fractional distillation. 
Substances with a high boiling point condense at the bottom and substances with lower 
boiling points condense at the top.

Fertilisers
+ 
1 Circle the correctly spelled word in each pair.
Fertilisers are chemicals/chemcials used to increase crop yield by putting essential 
eliments/elements such as phosphorus and potassium/potasium back into the soil. 
They also provide nitrogen, which increases plant growth. Fertilyzers/Fertilisers dissolve 
in water and are then absorbed by the plant. Fertilisers are salts that are made by 
neutralising different acids and bases.
The problem with fertilisers is that they can pollute/polute water supplies and cause the 
growth of algae/algee in waterways. This leads to a process called eutrophication. Lakes 
and rivers become ‘dead’ due to pollution from fertilisers.
2 What is the chemical symbol for each of the following essential elements?

fertiliser that help increase crop yield. The first one has been done for you.

  Other plants die. 
 
  Fertilisers run off into the waterways. 
 
  Algal bloom appears. 
 
  Most organisms in the water die. 
 
  Increase in amount of nitrate or phosphate in the water. 
 
  Extra algae blocks off light to other plants.

Flame Tests

What is the flame test?

The flame test is used to visually determine the identity of an
unknown metal of an ionic salt based on the characteristic colour
the salt turns the flame of a Bunsen burner.

What are the limitations of this test?

The value of the flame test is limited by interference from other
brighter colours and by ambiguities where certain different metals
cause the same flame colour.

What is happening?

When the salt is placed into the flame, the electrons from the metal
become excited and jump up energy levels. When they fall back to
their ground state they emit the energy they absorbed as photons of
light. Often these photons are in the visible spectrum and a colour
unique to that ion can be seen in the flame.


Method

  1. Light your Bunsen burners so that a hot flame is produced
  2. Collect a pop stick and dip it in distilled water. Place it in the
     blue flame, and then remove it. Observe the colour of the
     flame and record it in your table.
  3. Next using a fresh popstick, dip the stick into the distilled
     water and then into the Barium chloride. Record the colour in
     your table.
  4. Repeat for all of the metal chlorides, using a fresh popstick
     each time.

Atomic Theory

                                  Part One: Flame Tests
                                Part Two: Atomic Spectra
                      Part Three: Applications of Spectra (optional)

                                              C12-2-02 &03




This activity will focus on the visible portion of the electromagnetic spectrum.


Background Information:
About 300 years ago, Sir Isaac Newton saw a beam of sunlight through a glass prism. He discovered
that light is made up of a spectrum of seven distinct visible colors. This spectrum of colors always
appears in the same order. You can see this color spectrum (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo,
Violet and all the colors in between) when you look through a diffraction grating. There are two color
ranges that are not visible to our eyes in this spectrum: below red is infra-red and above violet is ultra-
violet. In a rainbow after a rainstorm this same color spectrum appears in the same order. Rainbows are
created when sunlight passes through rain drops that act as millions of tiny prisms.

The color of a solid object depends on the colors of light that it reflects. A red object looks red because it
reflects red light and absorbs all other colors. A blue object looks blue because it reflects blue light and
absorbs all other colors. A white object reflects all colors of light equally and appears white. A black
object absorbs all colors and reflects no visible light and appears black. Just like when you color with too
many colors in one area with crayons or markers, all colors are absorbed, none are reflected and it
appears black!


Explanation of visible light at the electronic level:

What do fireworks, lasers, and neon signs have in common? In each case, we see the brilliant colors because the
atoms and molecules are emitting energy in the form of visible light. The chemistry of an element strongly
depends on the arrangement of the electrons. Electrons in an atom are normally found in the lowest energy level
called the ground state. However, they can be "excited" to a higher energy level if given the right amount of
energy, usually in the form of heat or electricity. Once the electron is excited to a higher energy level, it quickly
 loses the energy and "relaxes" back to a more stable, lower energy level. If the energy released is the same
amount as the energy that makes up visible light, the element produces a color. The visible spectrum, showing the
wavelengths corresponding to each color, is shown below:




Note: [1 Å = 0.1 nm]


Is light a particle or a wave?

Is light composed of waves or of particles? If light is waves, then one can always reduce the amount of
light by making the waves weaker, while if light is particles, there is a minimum amount of light you can
have - a single ``particle'' of light. In 1905, Einstein found the answer: Light is both! In some situations it
behaves like waves, while in others it behaves like particles.

This may seem odd. How can light act like both a wave and a particle at the same time? Consider a
duck-billed platypus. It has some duck-like properties and some beaver-like properties, but it is neither.
Similarly, light has some wavelike properties and some particle like properties, but it is neither a pure
wave nor a pure particle.




A wave of light has a wavelength, defined as the distance from one crest of the wave to the next, and
written using the symbol . The wavelengths of visible light are quite small: between 400 mm and
650 nm, where 1 nm = 10-9 m is a ``nanometer'' - one billionth of a meter. Red light has long
wavelengths, while blue light has short wavelengths.

A particle of light, known as a photon, has an energy E. The energy of a single photon of visible light is
tiny, barely enough to disturb one atom; we use units of “electron-volts”, abbreviated as eV, to measure
the energy of photons. Photons of red light have low energies, while photons of blue light have high
energies.

The energy E of a photon is proportional to the wave frequency f,
                                  E=hf
where the constant of proportionality h is the Planck's Constant, h = 6.626 x 10-34 J s.

Also, the relationship between frequency and wavelength can be defined as:

                                 f=c
                                   λ

where c is the speed of light (3×108 metres per second).


So photons still have a wavelength. A famous result of quantum mechanics is that the wavelength
relates to the energy of the photon. The longer the wavelength, the smaller the energy. For instance,
ultraviolet photons have shorter wavelengths than visible photons, and thus more energy. This is why
they can give you sunburn, while ordinary light cannot.


Spectra can be simplified to one of three basic types. Simple examples in the visible wavebands are
shown below:

Decay (Method 1

{ Notes) Background

This investigation is a simulation of radioactive decay. Radioactive decay is a random
event. You will have noticed this by watching or listening to the uneven count rate on a
Geiger counter when it is detecting low intensity radiation. If, however, a large number of
atoms are disintegrating, the average number of disintegrations per second can be predicted
with reasonable accuracy.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time taken for its decay rate or activity to
decrease by one half. This is also the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei to

Nuclear chemistry studies the nucleus (centre) of atoms, In 1909, Ernest Rutherford was the first person
to come up with the idea that the nucleus of an atom was very small, dense and positively charged.
Rutherford calculated that the radius of an atom would be in the order of 10" m and the radius of the
nucleus would be approximately 10" m.

1 How does the size of the radius of the nucleus compare to that of the whole atom?

Shortly after this (1913) it was calculated that the protons of an individual atom made up about half of
the mass of the nucleus. Hence there must be some other (unknown) particles making up the ‘missing’
mass. The concept of atomic number (Z) came into use around this time. The atomic number of a
particular atom of an element shows:

* the number of electrons

¢ the number of protons

© the order in which the element is listed in the Periodic Table.
In 1932, James Chadwick discovered that inside atoms there were uncharged particles with a mass
approximately that of a proton. We now call this particle a neutron and know that it is located inside
the nucleus.

elements that have different masses are called isotopes. English physicist Francis Aston (1877-1945) was
awarded a Nobel Prize in 1922 for his invention of the mass spectrograph. This machine can show the
relative percentages present of different isotopes of the same element.

Chapter 6                          Sustainability
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1: Available nitrogen

The nitrogen cycle
Nitrogen (N) is an essential component of the molecules that carry genetic
information, and of proteins, the building blocks of life. All organisms require
nitrogen to live and grow. Seventy-eight per cent of air is nitrogen in the form
of N2 molecules. The two atoms of nitrogen are held together strongly making
the molecule relatively chemically inactive and therefore unavailable to living
things. For plants and animals to be able to use nitrogen, it must be in a
chemically available form such as ammonium (NH4+) or nitrate ions (NO3–), or
the compound urea (NH3)2CO. Nitrogen is often in short supply in natural
ecosystems and is a limiting factor for plant growth.

There are five main processes in the nitrogen cycle (see Figure 1):
   •   nitrogen fixing
   •   nitrification
   •   nitrogen uptake by plants
   •   decomposition
   •   denitrification.




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                  ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 Figure 1 The nitrogen cycle.


Nitrogen fixation
Some bacteria, for example those of the genus Rhizobium, can fix nitrogen
(convert nitrogen into a usable form) through metabolic processes. Many
nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in a symbiotic (depending on each other for
survival) relationship with host plants, especially leguminous plants. Other
nitrogen fixing bacteria are free-living in soils and in water.

Small, but significant amounts of nitrogen are fixed from the air by high-
energy natural events such as lightning, forest fires, and even hot lava flows.
The high energy involved in these natural occurrences breaks the bonds
between the nitrogen atoms in the N2 molecule, making individual atoms
available for nitrogen-fixing chemical reactions.


Human alteration of the nitrogen cycle
Early in the 20th century Fritz Haber, a German scientist, developed a way of
fixing nitrogen in a chemical reaction at high temperatures and pressures. He
created nitrogen-rich chemical fertilisers that could be applied directly to the
soil. By using nitrogen-rich fertilisers, the yield of crops has improved and
productivity of agricultural land has increased. The protein content of the
crops and the food value of the crops have also increased. This has helped
feed the rapidly increasing human population.

Burning fossil fuels, using chemical nitrogen-rich fertilisers and cultivation
(growing) of legumes all add fixed nitrogen to the biosphere. Within the last
century, through these activities, humans are greatly increasing the amount of
nitrogen cycling between the living world and the soil, water and atmosphere.
We have more than doubled the rate of nitrogen entering the land-based
nitrogen cycle.

Chapter 6                         Sustainability
EXTRA WORKSHEET 2: The phosphorus cycle

The phosphorus cycle
Phosphorus is an essential element of DNA, cell membranes, bones and
molecules important to the processes that release and use energy in the
body.

Phosphorus is like carbon and nitrogen in that it cycles through natural
ecosystems. However, unlike these other elements, phosphorus is not
present in the air. Phosphorus is found in sedimentary rocks. The
phosphorous cycle begins with phosphate ions (PO4) in sedimentary rocks
such as limestone.

Water percolating through the soil dissolves phosphate ions from the rock and
distributes them through the soil. Some of the phosphate ions remain in the
soil; others move into the ground water and into rivers and streams.

Phosphate ions in the soil are absorbed by plant roots and used and stored
within the plant. Animals then eat the plants and so the phosphorous passes
up the food chain. When dead plants and animals and their wastes are
decomposed, phosphorus is returned to the soil.

Once it gets into the soil the phosphorus is available to be taken up by plants
once again and so the cycle continues. However, some of the phosphorus
may move through the soil dissolved in rain water. It may be carried into rivers
and into oceans hundreds or thousands of kilometres away from where the
phosphorus was released. The phosphorus may circulate in the ocean,
entering the ocean food webs through algae. Alternatively, the phosphorus
may settle in the sediments at the bottom of a lake or the ocean. There it
becomes part of sedimentary rocks, such as limestone, and is lost to the
cycling process for hundreds of thousands or millions of years. The
phosphorous cycle is shown in Figure 1.




           Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 Figure 1 The phosphorus cycle.


In natural ecosystems, phosphorus is added to the soil when rocks are
weathered and when plant and animal wastes are decomposed. In urban
environments, phosphorus from sewage treatment plants goes out to the
ocean. In agricultural (farm) ecosystems, the plants and animals are taken to
market. The phosphorus is added to the urban ecosystem instead of being
recycled. The soils in agricultural ecosystem are therefore running out of
phosphorus. To maintain healthy crops, farmers have to add phosphorus to
soils through using fertilisers.

Pollution

A substance pollutes when its presence in air, water or soil harms living things.

The main cause of air pollution is the burning of fossil fuels, such as coal and oil. This happens in factories,
power stations, houses and the engines of cars, buses, and aeroplanes. Poisonous gases from chimneys are
quickly spread out in the air but, if there is not too much of them, they can change into less harmful
substances over time.

The smoke produced by burning contains tiny particles of dust, which are mainly carbon (C). This dust
settles on plant leaves, cutting out some of the light taken in by the plants and so reducing photosynthesis,
People also breathe in the dust and this can worsen illnesses such as asthma and bronchitis.

Sulfur dioxide (SO,) is a gas produced by burning fossil fuels. It can dissolve in water vapour, forming an
acid, which falls as acid rain. As well as damaging buildings, plants and wildlife this can affect people's lungs.

gather in city streets. As well as sulfur

can collect in the bodies of people living in

is soft, easily worked and lasts for a long
time. It has been replaced by copper (Cu) or

{_ RENEWABLE AND NON-RENEWABLE ~_)
7 RESOURCE DISCUSSION ep
Resources
Natural resources can be classified as either non-renewable or renewable.

Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced — once they are consumed they are gone
for ever. Resources such as coal, iron, natural gas, uranium, and crude oil are all non-
renewable. Some of these resources, such as coal and gas, can re-form. However, they
take millions of years to do so, and as such cannot be renewed in a suitable timeframe
to be considered renewable.

Renewable resources can be used, and within a few years or a few decades, they can be
replaced. Resources such as trees, oxygen, and fresh water are renewable resources.
Living things are often thought of as renewable resources because they reproduce.
They will continually be replaced, as long as we don’t over use them.

Energy
Natural resources are also used to provide energy.

Some non-renewable energy sources are called fossil fuels. Fossil fuels include coal,
crude oil and natural gas.

Fossil fuels are made from the remains of plant matter that died millions of years ago.
Swamps once covered large areas of the Earth and thick layers of dead plant material
built up and were buried and compressed. These layers eventually turned into coal,
crude oil or natural gas.

Renewable sources of energy, sometimes called alternative sources of energy, include
solar, tidal power, wind power and geothermal power.

searchText: WHAT IS NUCLEAR POWER? Nuclear power is an alternative power source that uses the nuclear fission of uranium to create heat and, thereby, through a heat transfer mechanism and turbines, create electricity. HOW DOES IT WORK? For a nuclear reactor to create energy it is necessary for nuclear fission to take place. Fission is when an atom is split into smaller particles and an enormous amount of ener gy is released in the process. The element U ranium is used as the fuel for the reaction because it is radioactive, so it is unstable enough to be broken down into smaller parts. The uranium atom absorbs a neutron and splits into two equal parts and energy is created. This kinetic energy becomes heat energy, which is used to produce electricity. APPLICATIONS OF NUCLEAR POWER About 440 nuclear reactors are used around the world to produce about 17% of the world's electricity but in theory nuclear fission can be used for much more. At the end of the Second World War the Allies secured victory by dropping the atomic bomb on Japan. The bomb uses the same principles of splitting the atom as the nuclear reactors do in creating electricity. On a smaller, less destructive scale, the theories of nuclear fission are used daily in medicine. Scanning devices and the treatment of cancer both use the radiation from splitting an atom. ADVANTAGES As an alternative to normal coal-based electricity p roduction nuclear power is favo rable as it is much more efficient than coal (250g of uranium produces 20000 times more electricity than 250g of coal) and is far less polluting, especially to our atmosphere, as no harmful greenhouse gases are emitted. ( ie . carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxide etc.). It is generally a reliable process that can be counted on to produce electricity for many years (average availability over three years is about 80%). The amount of waste produced each year would cover only your dining room table! The waste is stored in fire-, water-, and earthquake-proof capsules to ensure safety. DISADVANTAGES There is pollution in the form of radioactive waste but with new technologies the process is becoming cleaner and safer each year. The possibility of radiation leakage or plant meltdown. This is possible in theory and has happened in the past (Chernobyl in Russia) but nowadays there are procedures in place to ensure safety. There are problems and dangers, which could lead to accidents. The power stations are all manually run and human error could lead to possible accidents. The reactors also have a very expensive capital outlay in the beginning, although the costs are cheaper in the long run. The plants do require downtime for maintenance .

Total internal reflection and optical fibres
25
IntroductIon
Optical fibres are used increasingly in communications 
and medical procedures. 
Aim
To understand some principles used in these fibres which 
enables them to transmit wave motions as they do.
data 
The phenomenon of total internal reflection occurs in 
some situations when light travelling in one medium 
strikes a boundary with a second medium of lower 
refractive index. If the angle of incidence (i) is small, 
refraction occurs as the light pass into the second 
medium (Figure 1). As the angle of incidence is increased, 
a point is reached at which the refracted ray passes along 
the surface of separation of the two media (Figure 2).  
If the angle of incidence is increased beyond this point, 
the light cannot leave the original medium. Instead, it is 
totally reflected within this medium, with the reflection 
obeying the normal laws of reflection (Figure 3). The angle 
of incidence that results in refraction along the surface  
of separation is called the critical angle (θc). It is related  
to the refractive index (RI) of the original medium by 
the relationship:

searchText: right 0 GM back in the spotlight The West Australian Friday, 15 December 2017 7:35AM PGA grains committee chairman Gary McGill.Picture : Astrid Volzke WA farm lobby groups are concerned an inquiry into compensation for non-GM farmers will explode into a broader campaign against the gene technology. A new Senate committee parliamentary inquiry will examine potential compensation schemes for farmers who claim economic loss because of genetically modified material. The landmark inquiry was sparked by a 900-signature petition from European consumer rights organisation FOODwatch , tabled by Greens MLC Diane Evers earlier this year. It called for “farmer protection legislation to compensate any non-GM farmers who suffers economic loss form GM contamination”. But supporters of the technology this week flagged concerns about the inquiry. Both the Pastoralists and Graziers Association of WA and WAFarmers agreed there was “no need” for the examination and common law should cover what PGA labelled “very rare” instances of farm-to-farm contamination. PGA grains committee chairman Gary McGill said the inquiry was a “tactic by the anti-GM movement” designed to “intimidate the cautious GM farmer”. “If someone, through some incursion, suffers economic loss, for example through a crop over-spray... our public liability program looks after these things,” he said. “We will argue there is no need for any special legislation... common law, discussions over the fence - most people are reasonable - they have a yarn and work it out.” WA Agriculture Minister Alannah MacTiernan said she supported the inquiry, which comes almost two years after the Marsh versus Baxter case, in which Kojonup farmer Steve Marsh unsuccessfully sued his neighbour Michael Baxter over GM canola contamination. “We need to ensure that GM and non-GM farming can co-exist,” she said. “Growing GM crops makes financial sense for some, but if neighbouring farmers growing organic crops lose money as a result of contamination, we need to look at whether that financial burden should be shared.” “We will await the outcome of the committee’s inquiry and encourage stakeholders to make a submission.” Ms Evers said the rights of non-GM farmers were not sufficiently protected by law. “It is apparent from the case of Kojonup farmer Steve Marsh that the rights of non-GM farmers in WA, who outnumber farmers growing GM, are not sufficiently protected by law,” she said. “For as long as farmers want to meet demand from consumers for non-GM products, the risk of their fields being contaminated and them experiencing economic loss will remain. “WA farmers should not lose their right to sell non-GM crops at a higher price, due to the actions of another grower. This is an issue that cannot be ignored.” Hundreds of thousands of hectares of GM canola is grown in WA each year after the Barnett Government changed regulations in 2010. Previously, WA was classed a GM crops-free zone with just two exceptions, GM canola grown Statewide and GM cotton in the Kimberley’s Ord irrigation area. Study raises health concerns over GM crops Rebecca Dollery Updated 23 Sep 2012, 8:36am PHOTO: In 2010 the WA Government lifted a ban on GM crops.(User supplied) RELATED STORY: Cancer in rats reignites GM food debate The second study this month to link genetically modified crops with serious health problems has prompted calls for the WA government to ensure the State's GM crops are safe. The latest study, published in the journal of Food and Chemical Toxicology, shows rats fed a GM corn diet over their two year lifespan, suffered mammary tumours and severe liver and kidney damage. The corn, produced by the American multinational Monsanto, had been sprayed with the company's weedkiller, Roundup. The State Government controversially lifted a ban on GM crops in 2010. At least 10 per cent of WA's canola crop is now genetically modified and GM wheat trials have been conducted at locations around the State. The decision to lift the ban has since been the subject of international attention. Earlier this year a Kojonup farmer took his neighbour to the Supreme Court for allegedly allowing a GM canola crop to contaminate his organic farm. Anti-GM campaigners say the State Government could put farmers and consumers at risk if it doesn't instigate an urgent assessment of the use of GM and Roundup in WA. The director of Australia's Safe Food Foundation, Scott Kinnear, says the WA Government has a responsibility to pay attention to the latest study on rats. "The Government would be wise to have a look at this research and a lot of the other indicator research," he said. "There is now a plethora of research that is building to show harm from GM." Mr Kinnear said he did not think banning GM products altogether was the answer. "It's too early to call for a ban on GM, but what we should call for is a change in the way we regulate GM." Full confidence In a statement the WA Minister for Agriculture Terry Redman said the Government has full confidence in the Australian regulatory system for GM products. "Which includes both Food Standards Australia New Zealand and the Office of Gene Technology Regulator," he said.

X – Linked Problems

1. Red-green colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive trait. A woman with normal
   vision whose father was colour blind marries a man with normal vision. What is the
   genotype of each of these people? What can you predict about their children?

2. Haemophilia is a disease caused by a recessive trait on the X chromosome. You are
   a genetic counsellor. Bob and his sister Mary come to your office. Bob is 25 and has
   no children. Mary is 23 and engaged. Bob and Mary are both normal as are both
   their parents. However, they had a brother and an uncle who died of haemophilia.
   Bob and Mary both want to know what their chances are of having haemophiliac
   children. What would you say to them?

3. A certain form of muscular dystrophy is inherited as a sex-linked, recessive gene.
   Jack has muscular dystrophy. (Neither of his parents has this disease.) Jane, Jack’s
   wife, does not have muscular dystrophy, but her father does. What fraction of their
   daughters would you expect to have muscular dystrophy? What fraction of their
   sons would you expect to have muscular dystrophy?

4. Colour-blindness is a sex-linked recessive gene. A colour-blind woman marries a
   man with normal vision. She is pregnant. What is the chance that her child will be
   (a) a girl with normal vision? (b) a colour-blind girl? (c) a boy with normal vision? (d)
   a colour-blind boy?

5. (a) Why are men never heterozygous for an X-linked trait? (b) Why must men
   always inherit an X-linked trait from their mothers? (c) Can a colour-blind father
   pass this allele on to his sons? Explain. (d) Can a normal male ever have a daughter
   that is colour-blind? Explain.

6. Anthony, a colour-blind person got married, divorced, and remarried. He and his
   first wife, Linda, have a colour-blind son, a colour-blind daughter, a normal son and
   a normal daughter. He and his current wife, Mary, have
   four boys and two girls, none of whom are colour-blind. Give the genotype of each
   wife and state whether or not she is colour-blind.

Heat may be taken in or given out during a reaction. Sound, light, movement or
electrical energy may also be produced. When fuels are burnt they give out heat and
light energy. Explosive fuels give out movement and sound energy as well. The
chemical reaction that takes place inside a torch battery gives out electrical energy.

Energy from fuels.

Wood can be burnt asa fuel. Fossil fuels form over millions of years.

Burning of fuels makes carbon dioxide, water and heat energy :
FUEL + OXYGEN i) CARBON DIOXIDE + WATER +

The heat energy can be used to keep our houses warm and to cook food. It can also
be changed into movement energy to drive engines.

Effects on the environment.

Burning fuels release carbon dioxide into the air. This stops heat escaping from the
surface of the Earth back into space. This is called the GREENHOUSE EFFECT and it
may lead to GLOBAL WARMING.

Oil and coal release sulphur dioxide gas when they burn. This gas goes into the air and
dissolves in rain droplets to form ACID RAIN. In some parts of Europe acid rain has
destroyed plant and animal life in lakes and forests. Acid rain also causes corrosion of
buildings and statues.

The word organic is often used to imply that a product is ‘natural’ or better than other, similar goods. Organic 
vegetables are produced without the use of pesticides and cost more than other vegetables. Originally a compound 
was only considered to be organic if it was only produced by an organism. In chemistry, ‘organic’ has a different 
meaning – it applies to carbon-based compounds with the exception of oxides and carbonates. 
1 
All living things contain carbon compounds, but not all carbon compounds come from living things.  
Discuss this statement. 
Carbon is only the 14th most abundant element on Earth. However, there over 10 million organic compounds, many 
times more than in any other class of compounds. There is a huge variety in the size, shape, physical properties 
and chemical properties of these componds. This is due to a combination of factors. Carbon is in Group IV of the 
Periodic Table and is tetravalent.
2 What is meant by tetravalent? 
Figure 1 shows how carbon bonds are arranged in a tetrahedron  
around the central carbon atom. 
3 Which type of bonding is most likely to be involved with carbon atoms? 
Explain your answer.
Carbon’s ability to form up to four strong covalent bonds at different angles means it can form  
branching molecules. Carbon also exhibits concatenation – the formation of long chain molecules  
based on a ‘backbone’ of carbon atoms.
4 Silicon is the other element that can display concatenation.  
Give a possible reason for this.
Methane (natural gas) is the simplest organic molecule. Figure 2 shows three ways to represent the structure of 
methane. The conventional model (also known as the ‘structural formula’) gives less detail, but is much easier to 
draw. It gives the untrue impression that methane is a planar (flat) molecule.
5 Give the formula for methane.

                                           Station #1

                A Wellesley student’s nutritious breakfast…
The United States Recommended Daily Allowance of iron is 18mg. Iron-fortified cereals often
contain large amounts of iron to help people meet this dietary need (the demonstration in front of
you is the extracted iron from a box of cereal). Suppose you eat 2 servings of one of the cereals in
front of you for breakfast (choose one and write down which one you chose). How many iron atoms
have you just ingested?




Now suppose you had to eat each iron atom one at a time, at a rate of one atom per second. How
long would it take to ingest the above number of iron atoms? (For comparison, the age of the
universe is 13.7 billion years, according to the NASA Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe.)




People generally have approximately 3g of iron in their whole body. Most of the iron in the body is
used to transport oxygen (O2) through the bloodstream so oxygen can reach every cell in the body.
One iron binds to one oxygen molecule (this process is mediated by a protein called hemoglobin,
which you may have heard of). Assume that about 80% of the iron in your body is involved in
transporting oxygen at any given time. How many grams of oxygen are being transported in your
bloodstream at this moment?

Moles Galore: Quantitative Chemistry
Goals

       Establish a solid understanding of moles and Avogadro’s number
       Practice estimation skills
       Introduction to common ions used in chemical reactions
       Have fun and get to know your fellow students

Background

       Atoms, molecules, and ions: The atom is the smallest unit that can be
        identified as a specific element (e.g. a copper atom, containing one copper
        nucleus surrounded by electrons). Molecules contain many atoms bonded
        together. Ions are charge species, and can be either atoms or molecules.

       The mole is a unit that helps us answer the question "How much?" It makes
        numbers much more manageable. Just like donuts are measured in dozens,
        and paper is measured in reams, atoms and molecules are measured in
        moles. Mole is abbreviated "mol".

       Avogadro's number: NA= 6.022142 x 1023 mole-1 refers to the number of
        items in a collection containing 1 mole of that item. It is derived from the
        number of atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12 (e.g. a 60-carat diamond,
        or a 1.8 cm cube of graphite). For some interesting history and controversy
        regarding Avogadro's Number, read An Exact Value for Avogadro's
        Number.

       The mole in reactions:
        The mole is the common language in a chemical reaction. For example, for
        the reaction:

                                 Pb+2(aq) + 2OH¯(aq) → Pb(OH)2(s)

        You could say:
        1 Pb+2 ion reacts with 2 OH¯ ions to form 1 lead(II) hydroxide molecule, or
        1 mole of Pb+2 reacts with 2 moles of OH¯ to form 1 mole of lead(II)
        hydroxide

        However:
        1 gram of Pb+2 and 2 grams of OH¯ do NOT form 1 gram of lead(II)
        hydroxide
       Atomic/molar mass: Each cell in the periodic table contains a non-integer
       number. This represents the average mass of one atom of this element (in
       amu). It also represents the mass of one mole of an average sample of this
       element (a.k.a. "molar mass", in grams/mole). The molar mass of a
       compound is the sum of the molar masses of each atom in the compound.

      Converting grams to moles:
       Use dimensional analysis (i.e. set up the problem using just units):
         grams * (moles/gram) = moles
         grams / (grams/mole) = grams / (molar mass) = moles

      Converting molarity to moles for solutions:
       The unit M = moles/liter is used to refer to the concentration, or "molarity"
       or a solution. To convert from molarity to moles, you must know
       concentration and volume of a solution. Use dimensional analysis (i.e. set up
       the problem using just units):
          L * (moles/L) = moles

in aqueous chemical reactions:

We will be refering to these ions throughout the semester, so please download the
chart and make it easily accessible to you.

of copper(II)sulfate (CuSO4(aq), which dissociates in water to form Cu+2(aq) and SO4-
2                                                                   +2         +3
  (aq)). The iron and copper react to form iron ions in solution (Fe (aq) or Fe (aq) - you
will determine which one) and solid copper (Cu(s)). You will determine the number
of moles involved in the reaction.
 Figure 1 - Glassware and Vacuum Filtration Setup (you will not need watch glass)

Avoid contact with skin, eyes, and clothing.

CHAPTER 11: The Mole

In Science, as previously mentioned, the mass of single atoms is far too small to be of
practical value. However, masses must be used in calculations, hence masses based
on Atomic (and Formula) Masses are used.

Consider the elements aluminium and carbon —

Atomic mass of aluminium _ 27
Atomic mass of carbon 12

the mass of 10 atoms of carbon 10x12 ~ 12
the mass of N atoms of aluminium _ NX 27 _, 27

Whenever the number of aluminium and carbon atoms is the same the ratio of the
mass of aluminium to the mass of carbon will be 27:12.

Therefore, if we take 27g of aluminium and 12g of carbon, each sample must contain
the same number of atoms

Similarly, if we take 1g of hydrogen or 14g of nitrogen, we must have the same
number of atoms in each sample as there are atoms of carbon in a 12g sample of car-
bon.

That is, whenever we take a sample of an element which has a mass equal to its
Atomic Mass expressed in grams we have the same number of atoms in that sample
as there are atoms of carbon in a 12g sample of carbon.

The very large number of atoms contained in such a sample is called Avogadro's
Number.

Australian film industry
Resource sheet – Cinema and censorship
1900s–1920s: Innovation
In the 1900s, anyone could enter 
the film industry if they could buy 
the equipment. Most films were 
‘one-reelers’ which meant they 
were only about 12 minutes long. 
The Australian film The Story of the 
Kelly Gang (1906) was the first full-
length feature film in the world.
1940s–1960s: Imitation
Australian–British or Australian–American 
films such as The Sundowners (1960) were 
made in Australia. Uniquely Australian films 
were less common and often centred on 
stereotypical Australiana like the kangaroo in 
Skippy and the Intruders (1969). One exception 
was Jedda (1955) which was the first film to 
star two Indigenous Australian actors. Another 
was They’re a Weird Mob (1966). This was a 
comedy that explored the problems that Italian 
migrants encountered in Australian society.
1970s: Golden years
In the 1970s, the Australian 
government realised that the film 
industry needed their support. 
Many films made in the 1970s 
were ocker adventures like The 
Adventures of Barry McKenzie (1972) 
which relied on stereotypes and 
rude humour. Other films were 
more literary and artistic, like 
Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975). The 
critical success of these films paved 
the way for the funding of more 
popular films like Mad Max (1979).
1980s–1990s: Australia goes international
In the 1980s, Australian films like Mad Max 2 
(1981) and Crocodile Dundee (1986) became 
very popular overseas. Australia was idealised 
as an exciting, exotic location. This image of 
glamour extended into the 1990s with the 
ballroom dancing in Strictly Ballroom (1992), 
ABBA’s music in Muriel’s Wedding (1994) and the 
drag queens of The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen 
of the Desert (1994). These films showcased a 
very different version of Australia. 
Australia in the 21st century
Many films made in the Australia in the 2000s and 2010s focused on Australian 
criminality: serial killers, families of criminals and hitmen. These films included Chopper 
(2000), Wolf Creek (2005) and Animal Kingdom (2010). However, there have also been 
heart-warming stories about unlikely heroes and underdogs such as The Sapphires (2012), 
The Dressmaker (2015) and Lion (2017).

Censorship and classification
Censorship is when someone controls what you can read, write, listen to or watch. When you 
were a child, your parents may have stopped you from watching shows that were intended 
for adults. This is a kind of censorship.
+  1  Cross out the incorrect words in bold so that the information about censorship 
make sense.
Activity sheet – Cinema and censorship
The Australian government has censored / supported materials over the years, usually 
due to violence, sexuality or political views. Censored materials cannot / must be 
published or distributed. Some people approve of this as they believe it protects people 
from boring / dangerous material. Other people disapprove of censorship because it 
means they must / cannot make their own decisions about what they read, watch or play.
In 1929, Lady Chatterley’s Lover by D. H. Lawrence was censored / published because of its 
sexual content. 
In the 1969 case Crowe vs Graham, four men were fined for publishing / hiding parts of 
censored books. 
Because of the Graham case, in 1972 the government / cinemas began using a 
classification system instead of censoring / giving materials. This system tells you which 
materials are suitable for different audiences: G (General, suitable for everyone), PG 
(Parental Guidance recommended), M (Mature, recommended for people aged 15 and 
over), MA 15+ (restricted to people aged 15 and over), R18+ (Restricted to people aged 18 
and over) and RC (Refused Classification – banned).
In the 2000s, some gamers made compliments / complaints because games were being 
banned / sold due to extreme cuteness / violence, sexuality and other problematic 
content. Some games that were originally rated as RC and celebrated / banned were 
permitted under a R18+ rating in 2011. 
2 Answer these questions in your workbook. 
 
a  How does censorship affect popular culture?
 
b  When do you think books, movies or games should be censored?  
Give reasons for your opinion.

Bill Haley vs The Beatles
In 1957, Australia faced a huge rock’n’roll experience when American band Bill Haley & His 
Comets came to Australia. Many parents were concerned that bands like this would turn 
their children into rebels and criminals. In 1964, this fear was increased by the extreme 
Beatlemania of the fans when British band The Beatles came to Australia for the first time.
Source 1 
But Bill Haley who wants to see rock‘n’roll catch on in Australia, doesn’t want to see riots. 
‘I never HAVE seen riots,’ pronounced big smooth-faced Bill Haley who sports a C (for 
Comet) shaped lock of hair down the centre of his forehead. ‘Let me tell you about some 
so-called riots… Inside the Ballpark where we were playing were 11,000 kids, Outside 
because they didn’t have the money to go in were two teenagers. When the police asked 
the two kids to move off, these two kids smashed a soft drink bottle against a wall … 
All seven of the Comets are married – six out of the seven are fathers.’
Helen Frizell, ‘Please no riots says American Rock’n Roll King’, Australian Women’s Weekly, 
23 January 1957
Source 2 
In June 1964, The Beatles toured Australia. Huge numbers of fans turned up to their 
performances, flight arrivals and even their hotel rooms. This obsessional fan behaviour 
was labelled ‘Beatlemania’. Over 30,000 people waited to catch a glimpse of The Beatles 
when they performed at the Town Hall in Adelaide. At the time, the band said that this was 
the largest welcome they had ever received. When The Beatles performed, audiences were 
often so loud with their screaming, stamping and singing that many people could not 
actually hear the band playing.
Rachel Towns, Achieve History: Pop Culture 1945–present, Blake Education, 2018

remember that when they were young they listened to songs with titles like ‘Marsey Doats

Melbourne Olympics
In 1956, the Summer Olympics were held in Melbourne, Australia. This was an important time 
for Australia – for the first time, elite athletes travelled from all over the world to compete 
in Melbourne and Ballarat. Television was introduced to Australia that same year so people 
could watch the races instead of just listening to them on the radio.
+  1  Highlight the keywords in the source below. Keywords are the important words 
that tell you what a sentence is about. The first paragraph has been done for you. 
Women and Olympics
After almost four years of bickerings, recriminations and gloomy forebodings of one kind 
or another, the Olympic year has finally dawned – and peacefully at that.
It is now pretty certain, come what may, nothing can take the Olympic Games from 
Melbourne. For the first time in history, Australia in staging games with almost 3000 years 
of tradition behind them, is about to enjoy a spot of the glory that was Greece.
We suspect, though, that this glory as Melbourne will see it would cause a sharp shift of 
amazement to the classic eyebrow of any ancient Greek …
The Grecian village of Olympia was off-limits to women. On pain of death, no female 
dared show her nose inside Olympia even as a spectator, let alone as a competitor. 
It is true that one determined type, undoubtedly the spiritual ancestress of all feminists, did 
get herself not only into the village, but also into a chariot race which she had the tactlessness 
to win.
This finished the Games as far as Greek women were concerned. But obviously not as far 
as Australian women are concerned.
They are taking an almost 50–50 part in these Games as competitors, as organisers, as 
hostesses, as officials. 
That they will fully justify the responsibilities given them we have no doubts at all. And in 
doing so they’ll demonstrate one glory that Greece never knew – the equal rights of women.
‘Women and the Olympics,’ The Australian Women’s Weekly, 18 January 1956
2  Write a paragraph about how the involvement of women in the Olympics changed 
from Ancient Greece to Melbourne in 1956 to now. You could research the most recent

Parents and children often think differently and have very
