+  Read what Doreen and Michael have to say about conscription and the Vietnam War. 
Conscription: When the 
government needs soldiers 
and makes a law to say 
that if you can fight, you 
have to join the military.
I can’t go and fight. I just can’t. T hey sent me my draft card the 
other day. My numbers had come up in the lottery for National Service 
and suddenly I have to go to another country and kill people who have 
never done anything to me. I’m not afraid. I know I will go to jail 
for this and I am not afraid of that. But – I am afraid of not being 
a good man. Of going to another country and forcing those people to be 
something other than what they want to be. You don’t see the politicians 
going over to fight, but they tell us that we should go, and be proud. 
Well I am not proud. I cannot be proud of a country that does this.
Reading the newspaper, I can scarcely believe the world we are living 
in. When my father was a young man he fought for our country. He 
He was only 19 and fought in the jungles of Borneo. Now with the 
Vietnam War and the fight against communism, we have all these kids 
trying to tell us that it is a ‘dirty war’. T hey’re just cowards. You didn’t 
hear my dad complaining about being sent away to war. Now these boys 
are going around, burning their draft cards, saying they don’t have to 
go. Makes you ashamed to be an Australian.
Michael
Doreen

Changes in the home, changes in our world
In the past women were expected to stay at home to look after  
their family and to cook and clean. Over time, appliances such  
as vacuum cleaners, washing machines, ovens and microwaves  
became more advanced and quicker and easier to use.
Many women found it easier to get an education and a job  
outside the home when they did not have to spend so much  
time cooking and cleaning. They also had more time to  
consume popular culture in the form of films, books and music.

Entertainment
With the development of technology, 
entertainment activities moved from reading, 
writing and playing to listening to radio and 
finally to watching television.
Television was introduced in Australia at the 
same time as the Melbourne Olympics in 1956. 
This meant that people could now see the events 
as well as listen to them.

ABN), Nine (originally TCN-9) and Seven (HSV7). 
Channel Ten was introduced in 1964. In 1980, the 
SBS channel was created to broadcast content 
targeted at multicultural audiences. 
To support Australian culture and identity, the 
Postmaster General decided in 1960 that 40% of 
programs on Australian television channels had 
to be made in Australia.

searchText:
Albert Einstein: E = mc2 
Motion
19a
Albert was born in Ulm in south Germany in
1879 and spent his youth in Munich, where his
family owned a small shop that manufactured
electric machinery. He did not talk until the age
of three. As a youth he was curious about nature
and able to understand difficult mathematical
concepts. At the age of 12 he taught himself
geometry. 
However, Albert didn't enjoy school. After a
break from school when he was 15, he sat for the
entrance exam to a Swiss university. Sadly, he
failed the Arts section and so he had to finish
secondary school in Aarau, Switzerland. Finally,
in 1896, he entered the Swiss National
Polytechnic University in Zurich in order to
become a science teacher. After Einstein
graduated in 1900, he became a tutor. Einstein
had also renounced his German citizenship in
order to avoid military conscription and he
adopted Swiss nationality. In 1902 Einstein could
not get a position as a lecturer or teacher, so he
took a job at the Swiss Patent Office. Although
Einstein and Mileva Maric, another student, had
a baby (who was adopted) in 1901, they only
married in 1903. 
In 1905, Einstein published five papers. The first
(Generation and transformation of light)
suggested that light consisted of quanta, bundles
of energy which behaved sometimes like
particles (e.g. in reflection) and other times like
waves (e.g. in refraction). This contribution to
quantum mechanics eventually earned Einstein
a Nobel Prize in 1921. 
The second paper (Motion of suspended particles
and the kinetic theory) provided a mathematical
explanation that molecules in liquids moved
and a proof that atoms really did exist. 
The most famous paper (on the electrodynamics
of moving bodies) introduced the Special Theory
of Relativity. This was the basis for a new
physics: time, space and mass were all connected
with each other, no longer separate and fixed,
but different, relative to the observer. In a
supplement of 1907 Einstein included the
famous equation E

searchText: Navigational Vectors Distance 1. Imagine you live in a regional town in WA and you need to plot a flight path to fly your private plane to Perth. Locate your home town on the map of WA, and draw a line between your home town and Perth airport. 2. This line represents the distance between the two towns and is a scalar value. Use the scale on the map to calculate the actual distance in km. Length of line on map: ________________ Distance in km: ___________ Can you plot a flight path from your home to Perth if you know distance alone? Of course not, direction is also an important factor. 3. Using a compass rose on your map find the direction that a pilot would need to head the plane to go from your hometown to your state capital. Express your direction as a degree heading from North (0º). _________________ 4. Now express the distance and direction together (example: 10 km at 37 o ). Distance and d irection, together, is called displacement . Displacement is a vector . __________________ 5. Now check your answer online. __________________ Scalars and Vectors A scalar is just a regular number. You've been using scalars for a long time now. Your height, how many dollars you have, and how much time has gone by in this class so far -all of these are scalars. No big deal, right? The only information a scalar gets across is the size of something, which we call magnitude. Scalars only have a magnitude, or size. A vector is like an "enhanced" number. It also has a magnitude (size), but in addition, it contains a direction, which is usually given in degrees. Because of this, a vector is written differently than a scalar. The most common way of writing a vector is to draw it using an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction the arrow is pointing in represents...well, the direction. Here's an example: 1930400 98425 If you took out a ruler and measured the length of the arrow that would be the vector's magnitude. And the direction is due East . (If we set North as 0º, which is what pilots do, then the vector above has a direction of 90º.) So, now do you see why distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector? Distance is simply how far you have moved, while displacement is where you are in relation to where you started out from. Draw a vector on your map from your hometown to your state capital. Is the tail or the head of the vector at the state capital? ___________________________ The following information is important for pilots to know for any airplane flight. Which of these quantities are vectors and which are scalars? Why? Number of passengers Plane speed Plane velocity Distance travelled Flight displacement Flight duration Plane Altitude Acceleration of plane Deceleration of plane Amount of fuel needed Give examples of other vector and scalar quantities that you use or encounter every day. In what other areas other than flight would knowledge of vectors be useful? Imagine that you are a pilot ready to fly between two cities. You must first file a flight plan. What do you think should go in a flight plan? Choose any two cities, devise your own version of a flight plan for this trip, and share it with the rest of the class. Graphical Addition of Vectors Your Mission: Plan a flight from your state capital to Sydney, NSW with a stopover in Coober Pedy. Locate a map of the Australia and find your state capital on the map. Draw a vector from your state capital to Coober Pedy. Using a ruler, compass rose or protractor, and the map, determine the flight's: Distance (km) Directional heading in degrees (as measured from 0º North) Displacement Draw another vector from Coober Pedy to Sydney. Again using a ruler, compass rose or protractor, and the map, determine this flight's: Distance (km) Directional heading in degrees (as measured from 0º North) Displacement Check your displacements for each leg of the flight online. Displacement from state capital to Coober Pedy (km and degrees) Displacement from Coober Pedy to Sydney (km and degrees) B) How far has the plane travelled? 1. Find the total distance the plane travelled by adding the distance that each vector represents. 2. Does this value indicate how far the final destination is from the origin? How far is the plane from your state capital at the end of the trip? The value that you are looking for is the total displacement which is the distance and direction from the point of origin to your final destination. To determine this you must add the vectors: Vector Addition Instructions Draw the first vector on your map (your state capital to Coober Pedy). Draw the second vector on your map (Coober Pedy to Sydney) with the tail of this vector beginning at the head of the first vector. Draw a third vector called the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second v ector. Measure the length of the resultant vector (km) and its directional heading (degrees) from your state capital. This resultant represents the total displacement of the plane. What is the resultant displacement of the plane from your state capital to S ydney (as m easured from your vector diagram)? How did your measured displacement compare with the displacement found using the i nternet? Think of a situation (other than flying) where it would be preferable to know displacement rather than distance travelled. Think of a situation (other than flying) where it would be preferable to know distance t ravelled rather than displacement. Create a vector game or puzzle for your classmates to solve. It could be a board game, a maze, a riddle, a mystery, a treasure hunt or anything else that you wish. It should use 5 vectors. Trade games/puzzles with your classmates and see if they solve it correctly. Wind Velocity Flying in the w ind Imagine that you are walking in a cyclone with howling winds a ll around you. How will the w ind affect your movement if it is blowing: at your back directly towards you from the side Flying a plane in the wind can produce the same effect. A pilot generally wants to fly in the shortest path between two cities. Why? Well, it saves time and fuel. The wind, however, may prevent her from doing this. How can the wind affect a plane's flight? What does a pilot need to do to compensate for the wind? B) Determining Wind Velocity Winds in the northern hemisphere normally blow from west to east. This can change dramatically, however, when there is a front moving across the continent. Velocity is another example of a vector. Wind velocity is indicated by the wind speed and direction. Pilots use wind maps that show the wind velocity at the altitude of the plane. A special symbol on the map called a wind barb shows the both the speed and direction of the wind (wind velocity). Draw a vector to represent your plane's velocity. Make sure to draw it to scale. What was the wind velocity (speed in km/h and direction) over your home state at 14 ,000 f eet? Draw this wind velocity vector so that its tail is at the head of your plane's velocity vector. Make sure to draw it to scale. What is the plane's resultant velocity? Find examples of how wind affects sports activities, architectural designs, or other real world applications. D ) A captain is heading his boat directly across a river with a very strong current. Work and Power
Whenever a force moves something, work is done. It is a measure of
the amount of energy used in moving the object. Work is measured in
joules (J). If a force acts but nothing moves then no work is done.
Work can be calculated using the following equation:
    Work done = force applied x distance moved                   or     W =
F x d
where W is the work done (J), F is the force applied (N) and d is the
distance moved (m).

Power is the rate at which work is done, or how fast energy is used.
Power is measured in Watts (W), work in Joules (J) and time measured in
seconds (s).

searchText:
Work
Work done is defined as product of the force and the distance over which the force is applied.

Work is done when a force is applied to an object and the object is moved
through a distance.

For example, when you lift a load you are applying a force over a distance so
you are doing work.

When you push a shopping trolley around a supermarket you are applying a
force over a distance, therefore you are doing work.

When a car is moving on a motorway, a force is being applied over a distance
and work is being done.

Work done: = force x distance
W=Fxs

       W is measures in joules.
       F is measure in newtons.
       s is measured in metres.
       When work is done, energy is transferred.

Example questions:
Question 1
A fork lift moves 34m carrying a 1023N box across the warehouse floor. How
much work is done by the fork lift?

Answer:
W=Fxs
W = 1023N x 34m
W = 34,782 J                  The forklift does 34,782J of work.

Question 2
A crane operator on a building site slowly
raises a loaded crate of mass 1500 kg at a
steady speed.

a) What is the weight W of the crate?

b) What is the upwards pull P on the crate?

c) How much work is done by P in raising the crate to a height of 4 m?

d) What is the gain in gravitational potential energy of the crate when it is at a
height of 4 m.

e) What is the gravitational potential energy of the crate when it is a height of 9
m?
 Answer
a) The gravitational pull acting on a mass of 1 kg is 9.8 N.
So the gravitational pull on a mass of 1500 kg is 1500 x 9.8 = 14 700 N
Weight of loaded crate = 14 700 N
b) Upwards pull P = weight of crate = 14 700 N
c) Work done by P in raising crate to a height of 4 m
= force applied to crate x distance moved
= 15 000 x 4
= 60 000 J
d) Work done by P in raising crate to a height of 4 m
= gain in gravitational potential energy
So, gain in gravitational potential energy = 60 000 J
e) Gravitational potential energy, Ep= mgh
= 1500 x10 x 9
= 135 000 J
Gravitational potential energy of the crate at a height of 9 m = 135 000 J

Practice Problems:
1. Calculate the amount of work done when moving a 567N crate a distance of
20 meters.

2. A fallen tree of mass 700kg lifted 2.75 meters. How much work is done?

3. If it took a bulldozer 567.6 joules of work to push a mound of dirt 30.5 meters,
how much force did the bulldozer have to apply?

4. A frontend loader needed to apply 137 newtons of force to lift a rock. A total
of 223 joules of work was done. How far was the rock lifted?

5. A young boy applied a force of 2,550 newtons on his St. Bernard dog who is
sitting on the boy's tennis shoes. He was unable to move the dog. How much
work did he do trying to push the dog?

6. If it takes 68 joules of work to push a desk chair 3m across a floor, what force
would be needed?

7. If a long distance runner with a weight of 596.82 newtons does 35,674.7
joules of work during a portion of a race, what distance will she cover during that
portion?

8. If a weight lifter raises a barbell with a mass of 125.7 grams doing 5,023
joules of work, what distance did he move the barbells? Remember that you
need a force, not a mass. You must first calculate the force in order to complete
your solution. HINT: Weight is a force. Weight on earth is determined by
multiplying an object's mass times earth's gravitational pull (9.8m/s 2 ).

searchText: ﻿Specific Heat Capacity Activity 1: Heating Substances in the Sun The following table shows the temperature after 10g of four different substances have been in direct sunlight for 60 minutes. Time (mins) Air (⁰C) Water (⁰C) Sand (⁰C) Metal (⁰C) 0 25 25 25 25 15 29 26 30 35 30 33 28 35 45 45 36 29 40 55 60 40 30 45 65 Create a line graph for each substance on the grid below. Put the time on the x-axis (along the bottom) and the temperature on the y-axis (up the side). Don’t forget to give your graph a title. 1. Order the substances based on the time required to heat them from slowest to fastest. 2. Which do you think will cool the fastest? Explain your choice. 3. When you boil water in a pot on the stove, which heats up faster, the metal or the water? Explain your choice. 4. The specific heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1g of a substance by 1⁰C. A substance with a high specific heat capacity heats up more slowly than one with a low specific heat capacity because it needs to absorb more energy before it heats up. a. Which of the four substances has the highest heat capacity? Explain your choice. b. Which of the four substances has the lowest heat capacity? Explain your choice. 5. The specific heat capacities of the four substances are 4200J/kg/⁰C, 880J/kg/⁰C, 1000J/kg/⁰C and 400J/kg/⁰C. Match each specific heat capacity to one of the substances. a. Air = __________ b. Water = __________ c. Sand = __________ d. Metal = __________ 6. Assuming they both start at the same temperature, which will heat up faster in the sun, a bottle of water or a swimming pool full of water? Explain your choice. Activity 2: Calculate the amount of heat absorbed or released (show all working) 1. A pot is filled with 9kg of water at 10oC. Calculate how much heat energy would be needed to raise the temperature to 60oC. [ specific heat capacity of water = 4200J/kg/⁰C ] 2. A girl is hiking in the bush and has a 2litre bottle of water, which weighs 2kg, in her backpack. The water gets heated by the sun and its temperature increases by 5⁰C. How much energy has it absorbed? 3. If the temperature of 3.5kg of water increases from 50⁰C to 100⁰C, how much water has been absorbed by the water? 4. How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of a 2kg bar of gold from 25⁰C to 85⁰C? [ specific heat capacity of gold = 130J/kg/⁰C ] 5. Half a kilogram of water at room temperature (25⁰C) is put in the freezer until it freezes at 0⁰C. How much heat energy has it released? 6. An iron object weighing 4kg was accidentally left outside in the sun. When it was brought inside, its temperature was 45⁰C. How much energy will it lose once it has cooled to room temperature? [ specific heat capacity of iron = 440J/kg/⁰C ]

12 Moving day 
Moving to a new home can be a daunting task and requires some planning. You need to consider how 
you are going to move all your belongings to your new home. This will depend on:
•  the amount and size of your belongings
•  your transport options – you could:
 –  get help from family and friends who have vehicles to help transport your things 
 –  hire a van and organise people to help you 
 –  use a removalist. Note that some companies charge based on an hourly rate while others use  
a combination of time and distance travelled.
•  your budget. For example, if your budget allows for this, you may opt to have a removalist 
company do all the packing as well as the moving. 
Try to have a system.  
For example, pack  
one room at a time.
 
Label all boxes clearly, 
including contents, whether  
it is fragile or not, and  
which room it is for. 
Bubble wrap, towels, 
blankets and clothing 
all make good packing 
materials.
Use small boxes  
for heavy objects, 
such as books.
Tie electric cords 
in neat bundles so 
they don’t tangle. 
Leave your clothes on their 
hangers so you can rehang 
them as soon as you get to 
the new place.
Carry your valuables with 
you when you move, 
rather than packing  
them in a box.
Tips for packing

2 
Why is it important to start early when packing?
3

4 
What transport options do you have when moving? Explain the circumstances in which you might  
use each one.
5

6 
Read the story about Bill. What were his costs when he moved house? Should Bill have been  
better organised?
7 
Read Ally’s story. Do you think she should have asked friends and family to help her move, like Bill did? 
Why might this not have worked?
8 
Look at the packing equipment illustrated on the previous page. Can you think of anything else that 
you might need when packing?
9 
Study the tips for packing. Taking each tip in turn, explain why they are important.
Working in groups, imagine 
you share a house with friends 
and are about to move house. 
Decide which suburb you’re 
moving from, and where 
you are moving to, and then 
plan your move. Locate the 
websites of two removalists 
and compare their prices. How

 12 Moving day
Bill
Bill was moving out of home for the first time. 
He didn’t think he had much stuff, so he didn’t 
worry about packing until a couple of days 
before. Once he started to pack he realised he 
had a lot more than he’d thought – he ended 
up having to throw it all in boxes at the last 
minute! Bill borrowed his friend’s ute, and asked 
a few mates to help him with the move. Once he 
was all moved in, he bought everyone pizza as a 
thank you.
Ally
Ally was moving from a house into a unit. She 
had a busy, demanding job and didn’t have 
time to pack. She also knew it would be a tight 
squeeze to fit all her furniture into the new place, 
and she was worried that some of her things 
might get damaged in the move. Ally decided it 
was worth hiring removalists to pack and move 
all her things. It meant spending a bit more 
money, but it saved her a lot of stress and time.

Living and Work Literacy 7
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
15 Share houses 
Housemates
We are all different, so when choosing a housemate we need to be 
aware of the sort of person, or people we can live with. Differences 
in cultural, religious, social or political backgrounds can sometimes 
cause conflict. Differences can also exist between smokers and non- 
smokers, people who like their space tidy and people who don’t mind 
a bit of mess, meat eaters and vegetarians, morning people and night 
people, outgoing and shy people and pet lovers and pet haters. 
It may be a good idea to try and get to know the people you are 
sharing with before committing yourself. It is also important that 
everyone tries to be understanding and considerate of other people’s beliefs and cultures. 
Housemates and conflict
Read the following case studies to discover the kinds of problems people can have in share 
accommodation situations.
Mia 
I am currently living with a female housemate who pretty much does what she likes. 
She works at the local pub and comes home around 7 or 8 in the morning. When she 
gets home she’s incredibly noisy. This wouldn’t be a problem normally, but I’m doing 
shift work and I can’t sleep with all the noise she makes. Things have gone missing 
from my room, too – I think she might be stealing from me.
Daniel
I moved into a house with two 
other students and at first, all was 
well. After about three months 
a new girl moved in. As soon as 
she arrived she started cleaning 
and rearranging everything. She 
would clean practically every day. 
At first we didn’t mind too much 
– at least the house was clean – but then things 
started getting worse. She told us we shouldn’t 
use our dishwasher because it was dirty, so we 
had to wash everything by hand. She would 
leave a mess and then criticise others. It got to 
the point where she was constantly complaining 
and we were basically ignoring her. We are 
relatively clean, but I don’t see the need to clean 
every single day.
Nick
I had a really bad experience 
once. I moved into a house 
with two girls under a joint 
tenancy. They were an 
absolute nightmare to live 
with and wouldn’t pay any 
bills so I gave up after two 
months and moved out. However, the tenant 
who replaced me cleared out before signing the 
contract that the landlord had sent him. It turned 
out that both girls hadn’t paid any rent since 
we moved in. It had been four months, but I 
wasn’t aware until the landlord decided to throw 
them out. Because my name was left on the joint 
tenancy I’ve been dragged into the whole mess 
and am now being pursued for the rent they 
didn’t pay. 
Serap
I moved into a share house early last year with a few other people. Everything was 
fine until we realised one housemate didn’t know how to use a bar of soap or a 
washing machine. He smelt terrible! We tried to explain why it was a good idea  
to shower daily, and why you had to actually clean the kitchen, not just wave a  
damp cloth over it. We went to the landlord, but he didn’t want to get involved  
in personal disputes between tenants.

1 
Explain the importance of household organisation in a share situation.
2

Explain the reason for your first choice.
3

4

a What was Mia’s problem with her housemate?
b How would you advise Mia to handle her situation?
c Do you think Daniel was justified in his criticism of his housemate? Why/why not?
d If you were Daniel what would you say to the housemate?
e Imagine you are Daniel’s housemate. What would be your response to him?
f 
What was Serap’s objection to her new housemate?
g If you were Serap, what would you say to your housemate?
h What options might be available to Serap to resolve the  
conflict in their house?
i 
What problem did Natalie face when she moved into her flat?
j 
How did Natalie resolve the problem?
k What was the arrangement when Nick first moved in to a shared house?
l 
How did this arrangement backfire on Nick?
m What do you think Nick’s options were in resolving his position?
5 
Do the case studies have anything in common? How might house  
rules prevent these problems from occurring?
Working in groups 
or pairs, role play a 
conversation between 
the housemates in  
one of the case 
studies. See if you’re 
able to find a way to 
resolve the conflict in 
the house.

 15 Share houses
Natalie
I moved into a share house near my university that was occupied by a really shy guy. 
He seemed fine and helped me carry everything when I first moved in. Things seemed 
very normal – until my boyfriend came over one night. After he left, my flatmate 
said he wanted to have a ‘chat’. He told me he had wanted a flatmate who was single. 
He thought that once we had spent some time together, we could have a romantic 
relationship. It was very awkward – I had to move out.
Household organisation
Moving in with other people can be a great experience, but living with people can be tricky. To avoid 
conflict, it can help to make decisions about how you want to run things. Agreeing on the details up 
front can keep them from becoming big issues down the track. 
•  cleaning the house (How will you divide up the jobs? How often do they need to be done?)
•  washing the dishes (Will everyone wash their own dishes, or will you take it in turns?)
•  preparing the meals (Will you each cook separate meals or will you take it in turns to cook  
for everyone? Will you share food or buy your own?)
•  paying the bills (Who is in charge of the bills? How will they be split?) 
•  use of communal spaces/things, such as living areas, TV etc. (Will you have a timetable, or just 
consult one another?)

Living and Work Literacy 7
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
2 Moving out, moving back 
Not everyone wants to move out of home immediately – in fact, some people are moving back.  
Read the following newspaper article about a recent trend in society. 
JUDITH IRELAND 
January 9, 2010
Kippers, boomerang kids, rent-
free adults or freeloading lazy 
bums. 
Whatever 
the 
latest 
market 
research 
term, 
it’s 
become 
increasingly common for young 
people to live with their parents 
rather than spring off on their 
own.
Recent Australian Bureau of 
Statistics analysis indicates that 
young Australians are staying at 
home more than ever before. An 
estimated 23 per cent of 20- to 
34-year-olds are living in their 
parental home. And almost half 
of those who leave before their 
mid-30s end up rebounding back 
to their old bedrooms at least 
once over the next few years.
The Pew Research Centre 
recently found rising numbers of 
US graduates are returning to the 
family bosom, while the British 
Business and Skills Secretary, 
Lord Mandelson, has called 
on parents to be more forceful 
when ousting their little kippers 
(kids in parents’ pockets eroding 
retirement savings).
Naturally, the reasons behind 
the trend are more complex than 
just laziness or an undying love of 
mum’s lasagne. People marrying 
later, coupled with huge increases 
in tertiary study, the sky-high cost 
of housing and frosty economic 
climes are just some of the factors 
that have conspired to make it less 
necessary and more expensive to 
move out.
Yet for a significant proportion 
of young people there is also an 
element of choice in the matter. 
Those with full-time jobs in 
their 20s and even their 30s are 
staying put to save money for 
entertainment or investments 
rather than ‘’waste’’ it on rent. 
As 26-year-old labourer, Joe 
Singleton, who lives with his 
parents, recently told Britain’s 
Sun, “I could probably afford to 
live elsewhere if I didn’t go out but 
I want to buy rather than rent.’’
According to the ABS, the 
most common reasons for young 
Australians to stay at home 
are money issues along with 
convenience and enjoyment.
While the financial costs of 
moving out are widely recognised, 
the social costs of bunking down 
in the ‘burbs until the economy 
picks up or some babe pops the 
question are barely mentioned.
Share housing may still be the 
most common living arrangement 
for people in their early 20s 
but an increasing number are 
missing out on the experience. 
Unglorified by frat houses, Big 
Brother and John Birmingham’s 
horror tale, He Died with a Felafel 
in his Hand, the share house is 
also an important staging ground 
between 
childhood 
reliance 
on your family and something 
approaching adult independence, 
be it on your own or with 
someone you really love. Even 
your basic-model share house 
– with its inbuilt compromises, 
simmering disagreements, snarky 
estate agents and propensity for 
things to break - has the potential 
to teach you more about life 
than any Contiki trip through 
Thailand.
Moving out also exposes you to 
the rich tapestry that is humanity 
other than your family. Sure you 
meet some freaks but chances 
are some of your housemates will 
also drink beer with you.
In addition, up-close exposure 
to others provides an excellent 
opportunity to tinker with the 
less appealing aspects of your 
personality. When flatmates are 
not related to you by family or 
friendship, they won’t be as shy 
when pointing out that you have 
not cleaned the bathroom for 
three months.
It’s not all harsh reality. 
Flatmates inadvertently introduce 
you to new ways of seeing the 
world. From new brands of 
toothpaste to better bootleg DVDs, 
more obscure countercultures, 
a tastier way of making lasagne 
– maybe even different types of 
pasta altogether.
Life lessons lost for the 
stay-at-home generation 
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
7
Activities
1 
What is a kipper?
2 
Why is the term ‘boomerang’ used in the article?
3 
What did the Australian Bureau of Statistics analysis reveal about young Australians?
4 
What was the result of overseas research in this matter?
5 
Why are significant numbers of 20 and 30 year olds with full-time jobs staying at home?
6 
What are the advantages of share housing that the author was referring to?
7 
What are the so called ‘perks’ of living at home? Is it possible to enjoy these perks but still live 
independently? If so, how?
8 
What do you think the author meant by the phrase  
‘the rich tapestry that is humanity’? Give examples.
9 
In what context did the author use the term ‘style 
cramping’? How is it relevant even for those who get  
on with their parents?
10 What basic message do you think the author is trying to 
convey in the article? Do you agree with this message?
As a class, come up with a 
list of arguments for and 
against staying at home 
into your 20s or 30s. Hold  
a class debate on the topic. 
T
R
Y
 
T
H
I
S
!
 
 2 Moving out, moving back
Besides, no matter how well 
you and your parents get on, 
living at home through your 20s 
bears all the hallmarks of style-
cramping. Beyond your 21st 
birthday, how many house parties 
do you want with mum or dad 
around? The thought of carrying 
on romantic relationships at 
home into your 20s or 30s is even 
less appealing.
The debate about not moving 
out is dominated by financial costs 
with the holy grail of buying, not 
renting, lurking in the background. 
But surely independence, some life 
skills and fun are worth investing 
in, too, even if it means you don’t 
have that hefty house deposit 
at 25.
More important, there’s no 
need to live with mum and dad 
to take advantage of the perks. I 
boomeranged home for the day 
to write this article and use my 
parents’ cable TV, faster internet 
and better scotch. I don’t think 
they mind me freeloading once in 
a while, either. So long as I don’t 
stay past dinner.
Judith Ireland is a freelance writer.
© Judith Ireland, The Sydney 
Morning Herald, 9 January 2010

16 The household budget 
Managing the household’s finances is an important aspect of 
living in shared premises. Making a budget is an effective way 
to keep things under control. 
 The key to managing a household budget is working out:
•  household income – money coming in 
•  household expenses – money going out 
•  priorities – which expenses do you have to pay, and which can you avoid. 
Establishing priorities
There are some things you have to pay for on a regular basis. These include food, rent, electricity and 
telephone bills. There are other items which may also need to be allowed for. These can include medical 
expenses, train fares and car or bicycle repairs. Then there are luxury items such as new electronic 
gadgets, overseas holidays or weekends away. If you can manage the essential items and allow for 
occasional added expenses it may also be possible to indulge in some luxuries from time to time. If you 
are having problems paying for the essentials, however, it is the luxury items that need to be cut first.
Sharing expenses
Some expenses, such as rent and electricity, may be shared with your housemates, while others, such as 
mobile phones, will be separate. How landline costs are shared will depend on whether one housemate 
makes more calls to mobile or long distance numbers. You may need to devise a system of either 
recording telephone calls or monitoring the bill when it comes in to ensure costs are split fairly. 
Some share houses set up a combined fund or ‘kitty’ to manage shared expenses. Each housemate 
puts in an agreed amount of money each week to cover expenses. The kitty might be used to pay for 
rent and electricity, and sometimes also covers food and other household items such as dishcloths, tea 
towels and toilet paper. In other share houses people prefer to buy their own food, particularly if some 
housemates eat out a lot while others prefer to stay at home. However, this can lead to difficulties when 
it comes to keeping food separate, and remembering what belongs to each person. 
Managing bills 
Managing bills sometimes requires a bit of planning. Most bills arrive regularly – they are usually issued 
either monthly or quarterly. It is a good idea to make a note of when you expect bills to arrive, and 
when they will need to be paid. This will help you to ensure that you have enough money set aside to 
pay bills when they arrive.
It is important to stay on top of your expenses. Failure to pay the rent on time can lead to disputes with 
the landlord or agent and can have serious consequences. If you do run into trouble with any of your 
accounts, it is a good idea to contact the company first to see what arrangements you can make. Many 
companies will be willing to let you pay in instalments to help you get on top of your debts. 
Creating a budget 
A good way to plan for your expenses is to draw up a simple budget. Using two columns, write down 
how much you earn each week (or fortnight or month) in the left-hand column, and how much you 
spend on essentials on the right-hand column. The money that is left over after you subtract your 
expenses from your income represents your savings. This money can be set aside for unforeseen 
expenses, or perhaps spent on luxuries.
Definition: A budget is a plan 
outlining your expected income, 
spending and savings patterns 
over a period of time.

1 When can I leave home? 
Moving out of home is a big step. Different people have different ideas about how it will work, and 
when they are ready to do it. Ben and Jessica, in the above scenario, illustrate just a couple of these 
different viewpoints. It is natural for teenagers to want their independence, and many see moving out 
as a way to achieve this. In some cases the process is negotiated mutually between the person and 
their parents or guardians, while in other cases there may be disagreement or conflict. Whatever the 
situation, there are some important legal points to consider.
What the law says
• When you turn 18 you can legally leave home. If you are under 18 you are classified as a ‘minor’. 
Turning 18 means you achieve your ‘majority’.
• If you are under 18 years of age, you can still leave home under the following circumstances:
 – if your parents or carers agree to you leaving home, despite your age
 – if your safety and well-being is under threat in your home environment
 – if you have left school and wish to attend an educational institution (such as a TAFE college) 
that is located too far from home for you to be able to attend on a daily basis
 – if you have left school and have found a job located a long way from your home.
• At age 18 you can also enter into loan contracts, sign a lease for accommodation and make major 
purchases (such as a car or motorbike).
Things to consider before moving out
Moving out of home is a big step. It is important to consider the decision carefully and not rush into 
anything. Teenagers who are considering moving out may not be fully aware of the responsibilities  
that come with living out of home. They may not be prepared to manage their finances independently,  
or they may not be ready to handle living in a shared environment with people they don’t necessarily 
know very well.
Similarly, their parents may worry about who they will be living with, or how they might cope without 
the daily support of their family. Some parents may prefer their children to live at home until they  
get married. 
Scenario – two students having a conversation in the living room at Ben’s place
Ben: 
 I’m sick of living at home. I’m always fighting with my parents – I can’t wait to get out of here.
Jessica:  I’m thinking of moving out too, but not because I fight with my folks.
Ben:   
 What do you mean? Do you get along  
well with your parents?
Jessica:   Yep, always have. They’re great –  
that’s not why I want to move out.  
I just want some more independence  
and some freedom.
Ben:  
 Yeah, I just want to be able to do  
what I like.
Jessica:  I think there’s more to it than that.  
You have responsibilities.
Ben:  
Like what?
Jessica:   Oh, it’s late! I’ll tell you later –  
I have to get home!

Activities
1 
Read the scenario on the previous page and think about how Ben and Jessica’s parents might feel  
about their situations. Write conversations between:
a Ben’s parents, Graham and Betty, discussing their son‘s behaviour and attitude
b Jessica’s parents, Bill and Adele, discussing their daughter’s approach to moving out.
2 
When can you legally leave home? Why?
3 
Under what circumstances could you leave home before this?
4 
Why might some teenagers be worried about leaving home?
5 
Why might parents also worry when their child leaves home?
6 
After talking to Jessica, Ben had a huge fight with his parents. He decided to leave home straight away. 
Do you think Ben made the right decision? Which of the tips listed above did Ben fail to heed?
7 
What do you think Jessica would have said to Ben if she didn’t have to rush home?
8 
What skills do you think you need if you are moving out? Why do you need them and who is likely  
to be involved?
9 
Alicia left school and was offered a job in a restaurant quite a distance from her parents’ home.  
She was faced with either accepting the job and moving out, or rejecting the job offer. What factors do 
you think Alicia should consider in making her decision? If you were Alicia, what would you do? Why?
10 Omar was in his final year at school and wanted 
to study law at a university. He had applied to 
study at a university close to home and one in 
another state. What factors would Omar need to 
consider:
a if he was accepted into both universities
b if he failed to gain entry to the university 
close to home? 
In groups, discuss the advantages 
and disadvantages of leaving 
home before you are 18 years 
old. Consider things like rights 
and responsibilities. Record a 
summary of the discussion on  
a poster or display board.

 1 When can I leave home?
Tips for making the decision
Moving out can be a positive and even life-changing experience. These useful tips might help in  
the decision:
• Think it through – make sure you’ve really thought about whether you’re ready. Don’t act too 
hastily. Can you afford to move out? Is it the right time or are you rushing into it?
• Communicate effectively – discuss your decision with your parents and friends as well as  
potential flatmates. 
• Don’t be afraid to ask for help if you feel you need it – if you encounter difficulties there are other 
people willing to help you.

id: github:uploads/science/Periodic Properties of the Halogens.docx
title: Halogens - Periodic Properties and Redox
subject: Chemistry
searchText: Periodic Properties of the Halogens Reminder: Dilution Lab Practical due soon! Lab practicals will take place starting in this lab and continuing until your instructor's deadline. For more information, see Instructions for Pipetting/Dilution for Lab Practical in the lab manual appendix. Goals To explore periodic trends among the halogens (Group 17 (VIIA) elements). To design and use qualitative identification techniques. Improve observation skills To begin to learn how to balance redox reactions Background Periodic Trends The Periodic Table of the Elements is so named because of the periodic variation of many important elemental properties along a row ( Period ) or down a column ( Group or Family ) of the table. For example, atomic size decreases from left to right along a Period as well as from bottom to top within a Group, as can be seen in Figure 1 below. Figure 1: Trends in bonding atomic radii for periods 1-5 (Ref: Brown et. al.; Chemistry: the central science; 12th ed.; p. 255.) Ionization energy, electronegativity, and electron affinity also vary in similar manners (see the sections in your textbook). Oxidation-Reduction Reactions The effects of these periodic variations in properties are often expressed in the relative chemical reactivities of the members of a Period or Group. This experiment is designed to allow you to determine the relative reactivities of three (Cl, Br, and I) of the Group 17 elements ( i.e the halogens) in reduction - oxidation reactions (referred to as redox reactions). Redox reactions involve the exchange of electrons. In the example below, 'X' represents a halogen (e.g. F, Cl, Br, or I) and 'Y¯' denotes a halide ion. A reaction of halogen X 2 with halide Y¯ would be as follows: X 2 + 2 Y¯ → 2 X¯ + Y 2 Redox reactions are best understood when written in terms of two half reactions. A Redox Reaction can be divided into two half reactions: A half reaction that With a reactant that undergoes That reactant is defined as Loses Electron(s) Oxidation Reducing agent Gains Electron(s) Reduction Oxidizing Agent Viewed as a half reaction the reduction of X 2 would be: X 2 + 2 e¯ → 2 X¯ a gain of electrons And the oxidation half reaction of Y¯ would be: 2 Y¯ → Y 2 + 2 e¯ a loss of electrons In this reaction, X 2 is being reduced; it is called the oxidizing agent because it is taking electrons away from Y¯, causing Y¯ to be oxidized. Conversely, Y¯ is being oxidized; it is called the reducing agent because it is causing X 2 to be reduced. Upon successful completion of the exercise, you will be able to arrange these halogens in order of their relative reactivity as oxidizing agents. Likewise, you will be able to arrange the halides in order of their relative reactivity as reducing agents. Qualitative Analysis A chemical reaction may be analyzed quantitatively or qualitatively. In quantitative analysis , the amounts of reactants and products are carefully measured and those data are used to make precise interpretations about the reaction. In qualitative analysis , changes in a reaction mixture are observed and that information is used to determine whether or not a reaction ocurred . Qualitative changes include: the formation of a precipitate, the evolution of a gas, the release of energy as heat, the dissolution of a solid, and changes in the color or changes in clarity (clear vs . cloudy) of a solution. In this experiment, we will be observing color and clarity changes accompanying redox reactions, i.e. we will be doing qualitative analysis. Spectator Ions and Net Ionic Equations Many ionic compounds dissociate in water to form solvated ions, as can be seen in Common Ion Chart from Lab 1. With rare exceptions, salts containing Group 1 elements are water soluble. For example, NaCl dissociates to form Na + ( aq ) and Cl¯ ( aq ) , where ( aq ) means the ions are in an aqueous (water) solution. In addition to atomic ions, many polyatomic ions exist that remain as a unit when dissociated, e.g. potassium permanganate, KMnO 4 in water forms K + ( aq ) and MnO 4 ¯ ( aq ) . When we write a reaction, it can be written in terms of ionic compounds: NaOH + HCl → H 2 O + NaCl or in terms of solvated ions: Na + ( aq ) + OH¯ ( aq ) + H + ( aq ) + Cl¯ ( aq ) → H 2 O + Na + ( aq ) + Cl¯ ( aq ) You may notice that there are some species in the above equation that do not participate in the reaction. They show up as exactly the same ion/species on both sides of the equation. They are known as spectator ions . When a reaction is written in terms of solvated ions, the spectator ions should be removed, leaving the net ionic equation : OH¯ ( aq ) + H + ( aq ) → H 2 O This reaction is not a redox reaction. If it were, we might not be able to balance the reaction by inspection and would need to use the rules for balancing a redox reaction by the half-reaction method, as seen in our Appendix . Note, you will be balancing redox reactions using the half -reaction method in this lab and reporting any reactions that occur in lab in their final balanced net ionic reaction. Synopsis of the Experiment In Part I of this experiment, you will develop a qualitative identification scheme which you can use to identify the presence of each halogen/halide used in the lab. In Part II, you will mix each halide with each halogen to see which halogens are capable of oxidizing which halides. Using your identification scheme, you will be able to identify products if they form. In addition, you will combine each halogen with solid copper to see whether it can oxidize the copper. Using your results, you will be able to draw conclusions about the relative oxidizing strengths of the halogens. In Part III, you will mix each halide with CuSO 4 and with KMnO 4 . Using your qualitative identification scheme, you will be able to identify products if the halides are successful as reducing agents. You will be able to draw conclusions about the relative reducing strengths of the halides. Preparation Reading Assignment: Description of experiment —see below. The Group 7A Elements —Brown et al., Sec. 22.4, pp. 926–930. Periodic Properties —Brown et al. , Chapter 7, pp. 249-277. Review Oxidation-Reduction Reactions — Appendix & Brown et al. , Sec. 4.4, pp. 131-138. Prelab : Click here for Prelab worksheet : pdf or Word format Experiment To print instructions , select the portion that you with to print, choose File/Print, and choose "selection" to prevent printing the entire document. Safety ** Aqueous chlorine and bromine may produce vapors that cause eye irritation. Make sure to keep the caps on these solutions when they are not in use. Please rinse your eyes thoroughly with water if you experience the slightest eye irritation in lab. ** Copper sulfate solution is a skin and eye irritant. Please rinse any affected area with copious amounts of water. Wear safety glasses! Do not pour solutions down the drain! Collect all halogen/halide wastes in the appropriately labeled disposal containers provided. Materials and Equipment Test tubes (13 mm) Mineral oil Aqueous solutions of Cl 2 , Br 2 , and I 2 1 M aqueous solutions of NaCl , NaBr , and NaI 1 M CuSO 4 0.01 M KMnO 4 in 1 M H 2 SO 4 Cu turnings Parafilm Instructions Students will work in groups of 2 unless otherwise specified by your instructor. When preparing to perform an experiment, it is often advantageous to construct a chart or table in your notebook for recording observations and results. This not only guides your work while you are conducting the experiment but also makes review of the results easier after the work is complete. Please design an appropriate table for all 3 parts of this experiment. The data tables should make it easier for you to report your hypotheses (if applicable), observations, and conclusions for every test tube you create in lab. Before you perform Part 1 - prepare three solutions for use in Part 2 Obtain 3 test tubes. In each test tube, place a small piece of copper turning (approximately 2 to 3 cm in length). Fill each about half full with a different aqueous halogen solution. Cover the test tubes with Parafilm and then allow them to sit for a minimum of one hour while you perform the rest of the experiment. Part 1. Preliminary Study - Making a Qualitative Identification Scheme (i.e.-creating "controls" for Part 2) Before we can perform any reactions between various halides and halogens, we need a qualitative identification scheme which we can use to confirm the presence of the halogens and halides that will be reactants and products in our reactions. Begin by observing the provided aqueous halogen solutions and the aqueous halide solution in mineral oil (density of ~0.8g/mL) and without mineral oil (i.e.-in their own aqueous solutions where the aqueous solution's density is ~1.0 g/mL). In the elemental form, halogens (X 2 ) are neutral and preferentially dissolve in mineral oil because the molecules are nonpolar. Halides (X¯) are negatively charged and readily dissolve in water because the ions are polar and should be very hesitant to dissolve in mineral oil. Using test tubes, create your "controls" that show how all the halides and halogens appear in an aqueous environment and in the presence of mineral oil. Record your observations about each halogen and halides' appearence in the presence of water and mineral oil in a data table .. Make sure that you mix up any aqueous/mineral oil combinations to ensure that any halogen present finds it's way into the mineral oil. Save these test tube solutions to use them as your "controls" when trying to identify which halogen/halide are present in your reactions in Part 2. Part 1—Questions for thought: Are the solvents miscible (capable of being mixed)? If not, which solvent forms the top layer and which solvent the lower layer? What can you conclude about the solubilities of the halogens and halides in mineral oil? Explain the preference for one solvent or the other. Do halides or halogens possess a unique color defining their presence? Which solvent accentuates the halogen's presence in a solution? Part 2. Halogens as Oxidizing Agents When a halogen and halide from different elements are combined, (i.e.-Br 2 & Cl - ) two outcomes can occur: 1) nothing, or 2) the reaction will occur to produce the opposite halogen and halides (i.e.-Br - & Cl 2 ). You and your partner will be combining various halogens and halides and looking for indications of the presence of products (new halogens and halides from your starting materials) to determine whether or not a reaction occurred. In this way, the relative oxidizing strength of halogens can be determined. Another way of testing the strength of halogens is to look for products when they are combined with metals. If a halogen is introduced to elemental copper, Cu (s) , a reaction may occur in which the elemental copper disoolves and the Cu 2 + ( aq ) ion forms in the test tube (indicated by blue-green color ). Prior to performing any halogen/halide reactions in this part of the lab, prepare a data table that will allow you to report the following information: -- the specific halogen/halides you want to react in your test tubes -- the hypothesis before the reaction takes place in the test tubes as to whether you think a reaction will take place -- the observations after mixing the halogen/halide reaction -- the conclusion as to whether a reaction actually took place or not. Now, proceed with your experiment combining various halogens and halides in new test tubes. Combine the various halogens and halides in approximately equal volumes. Add ~1 cm of mineral oil to each test tube and mix vigorously. Allow the contents of the test tubes to settle a moment and then record your observations and conclusions in your data table. After approximately one hour, record observations of your Cu/halogen test tubes. id: github:uploads/science/Kinship- indig society.docx
title: Kinship- Indig Society
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Kinship is at the heart of Indigenous society . A person’s position in the kinship system establishes their relationship to others and to the universe, prescribing their responsibilities towards other people, the land and natural resources. Traditional kinship structures remain important in many Indigenous communities today. [1] There are over 500 Indigenous nations across Australia. Indigenous nations cover wide geographical areas, and have distinct borders. Within these nations there are clan groups, and within the clan groups there are family groups. Clan groups share a common language and kinship system, which is based on either patrilineal or matrilineal lines of descent. [2] There are three levels of kinship in Indigenous society: Moiety, Totem and Skin Names. Moiety The first level of kinship is Moiety. Moiety is a latin word meaning ‘half’. In Moiety systems, everything, including people and the environment, are split into two halves. Each half is a mirror of the other, and to understand the whole universe these two halves must come together. A person's Moiety can be determined by their mother's side (matrilineal) or their father's side (patrilineal). Moieties can also alternate between each generation (people of alternate generations are grouped together). [3] People who share the same Moiety are considered siblings, meaning they are forbidden to marry. They also have a reciprocal responsibility to support each other. [4] Each nation and language has its own term for Moiety. For example, the Yolngu people of north-eastern Arnhem Land are either Dhuwa or Yirritja . In the Yolngu worldview, ancestral beings assigned everything in the universe to either the Dhuwa or the Yirritja Moiety. For example, the black cockatoo is Dhuwa , while the white cockatoo is Yirritja . The two Moieties complement and balance each other in ceremonies, marriage, and daily life. Totems The second level of kinship is Totem. Each person has at least four Totems which represent their nation, clan and family group, as well as a personal Totem. Nation, clan and family Totems are preordained, whereas personal Totems recognise an individual’s strengths and weaknesses. Totems link a person to the universe - to land, air, water and geographical features. People don’t ‘own’ their Totems, rather they are accountable for them. Each person has a responsibility to ensure that their Totems are protected and passed on to the next generation. Totems are split between Moieties to create a balance of use and protection. For example, while members of one Moiety protect and conserve the animal, members of the other Moiety may eat and use the animal. [5] Skin Names The third level of kinship is the Skin Name. Similar to a surname, a Skin Name indicates a person’s blood line. It also conveys information about how generations are linked and how they should interact. Unlike surnames, husbands and wives don’t share the same Skin Name, and children don’t share their parents’ name. Rather, it is a sequential system, so Skin Names are given based on the preceding name (the mother’s name in a matrilineal system or the father’s name in a patrilineal system) and its level in the naming cycle. Each nation has its own Skin Names and each name has a prefix or suffix to indicate gender. There are 16-32 sets of names in each cycle. For example, in a matrilineal nation, if a woman with the first name in the cycle (One) has a baby, the child’s Skin Name will be the second name in the cycle (Two). All other ‘Twos’ in that community are now considered the sibling of that child, and all ‘Ones’ are considered their parents. When that child grows up and has children of their own, those children will be Threes. This sequential naming continues until the end of the number cycle is reached, then it begins again at One. [6]

id: github:uploads/science/Spice Worksheet answers.pdf
title: Planetary Atmospheres - Answer Key
subject: Science
searchText: Planetary atmospheres Worksheet answers 1. Which environment has the coldest average surface temperature? Titan (-180 °C) 2. Which environment has the greatest atmospheric pressure? Venus (about 90 bar) 3. Which solar system body has an average surface temperature that is most similar to Earth’s? Mars 4. Describe differences between the Earth’s atmosphere now and four billion years ago. The Earth’s atmosphere today is composed of 77% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 2% of other gases. The atmospheric composition of Earth 4 billion years ago shows higher amounts of carbon dioxide (45%) and less nitrogen (10%). 5. Titan contains compounds that scientists believe are similar to the building blocks of early life on Earth. What differences exist between Earth and Titan that prevent us from assuming there is life on Titan? Life on Earth exists in conditions that include an average surface temperature of 15 °C and an atmosphere which includes oxygen. Titan’s average surface temperature is -180 °C, which is too cold for most life forms on Earth. Titan also appears to have no oxygen, which is required by many life forms on Earth. One of the reasons for Titan’s very cold temperature is that it is much further away from the Sun than the Earth (it is one of Saturn’s moons). This means much less sunlight reaches the surface of Titan. This might affect the survival of life forms such as plants. 6. If found, what type of life is most likely to exist on Mars? Life on Mars would have to be well adapted to cold temperatures and high amounts of carbon dioxide. Perhaps a primitive form of plant life might exist on Mars, as conditions seem to be similar to those of Earth 4 billion years ago. 7. What challenges would humans be faced with if they decided to colonise: (a) Mars Temperature: it is very cold (-65 °C) and humans would need specialised living conditions, maybe similar to those used in Antarctica. A lack of breathable atmosphere would require some means of producing oxygen, and extracting water from ground-based frozen sources might be a challenge. (b) Titan Titan is extremely cold (-180 °C). This would require specialised living conditions because we don’t find conditions this extreme on Earth. The atmosphere is not breathable by humans and might contain poisonous gases. Water might be difficult to find, but perhaps not impossible (it could be frozen). Sunlight would be poor, and it might be difficult to cultivate plants for food as there is no carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. (c) Mercury Mercury’s average temperature is 180 °C, hotter than anywhere on Earth. Shielding humans from this extreme temperature and the solar radiation this close to the Sun would be a challenge. There is almost no atmospheric pressure on Mercury, so finding breathable air or water for drinking would probably be impossible. The temperature on Mercury means that there is probably no water to be found on the surface. © 2009 The University of Western Australia | for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage | ast0421 | version 1.0 Life in the Solar System 3: Planetary atmospheres 1 (worksheet answers) | page 1 secondary teachers’ enrichment program (science)

searchText:
Scientific Enquiry Skills 2

16
a close look at beetles
It has been suggested that one out of every four or five living animals on 
Earth is a beetle. Beetles belong to the order Coleoptera, the largest order of 
living things by number of species. Find out how many beetle species have 
been identified by scientists.
A distinguishing feature of beetles is their elytra – a hard exoskeletal covering over 
their wings. All beetles have four wings but only use one pair to fly. The other pair 
of ‘wings’ is a hard covering called an elytron. This is held up when the beetles fly.
Han and Charlotte collect two specimens from a 
garden that may be beetles.
1. How do you know if an insect is a beetle? 
2. Suggest some ways Han and Charlotte can find out if their specimens are beetles.
3. Observe the four beetles below and then describe their main features in your work 
book. Use the differences between the beetles to design a key to tell them apart.

The substance we commonly call alcohol is the chemical
ethyl alcohol or ethanol. Its chemical formula is
CH3COOH, and it is found in nature in fermented fruit.
Fermentation is where sugars in the fruit, combined with
natural fungi like yeast, cause a chemical reaction,
which produces ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide gas.
Alcohol is a depressant. It slows a person’s reaction time
and can distort his or her judgement of speed and
distance. It also reduces a driver’s ability to concentrate.
The more a person drinks, the greater the effect. For this reason, throughout Australia, if a person
has a full driver’s licence, the maximum blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is 0.05%. This means
that there is 0.05 gram of alcohol in every 100 millilitres of blood.
Once alcohol is in the body, it can only be removed by being broken down in the liver. This process
takes time. The liver can only break down about 8 grams of pure alcohol, or one standard drink, per
hour. Nothing, including drinking strong black coffee, cold showers or sleeping it off, can speed up
this process. This means that once a person has reached the legal limit, consuming one standard
drink per hour will keep them at that level.
A person’s level of alcohol is affected by both their weight and their sex. The lighter a person is, the
less alcohol is needed to put them over 0.05. Also, if the person has not eaten recently, because
alcohol is absorbed more quickly if the stomach is empty, the effect may be greater.
As a general guide, women should think carefully before their second drink, because two standard
drinks in the first hour may put many women over the legal limit. Men are likely to go over 0.05 if
they have a third drink in their first hour.

1 INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

Even the best experts in the world cannot solve a crime without evidence. Therefore, it is essential
that the scene of the crime be treated in the correct way.

A. Securing the crime scene

In most cases the first police officer on the
scene will be a uniformed police officer. They
are not usually trained as detectives and so
should touch as little as possible of the crime
scene and the area in the vicinity. All
precautions should be taken to avoid any
accidental destruction or contamination of
potential evidence.

The officer who arrives on the scene first will
ensure the safety of any injured people and of
the site itself. This may involve turning off gas,
water and electricity supplies. Ideally, the site
should be secured with a physical barrier, so
that no unauthorised people can enter. This will
leave the site as close as possible to the state it
was in at the time of the crime, preserving all
traces left by the criminals for the officers
tained in searching for evidence.

Where it is obvious that a person is dead, the body is not touched or moved in any way until it has
been carefully examined and photographed. Where there are injured people involved, the police officer
will see to their safety and call an ambulance before asking for the appropriate police backup. While
waiting, the uniformed officer may record the names and addresses of any eyewitnesses to the crime.

B. Examining the scene

If a major crime has been committed, then the next person on the scene will probably be the senior
detective in charge of the investigation. A police surgeon and/or a pathologist may be called in if
a body is involved. Specially trained crime scene investigators (CSIs), also called scene of crime
officers (SOCOs), who are experts at looking for evidence, are called in at an early stage of the

— N-3 | ASTRONOMY —
Astronomy and Australia

The view of stars and planets in the Southern hemisphere is different from the view in the Northern
hemisphere. In 1768, in command of the Endeavour, James Cook was sent to the South Pacific. He, with
a group of British astronomers, observed the transit of the planet Venus across the sun in June 1769.
Following this he charted the coasts of New Zealand, Australia and New Guinea.

The Astronomer Royal in England (Nevil Maskeleyne) expected a comet to reappear in 1789 and wanted
an observatory set up in the Southern hemisphere. He appointed Lieutenant William Dawes to travel with
the First Fleet to Australia. Dawes constructed his observatory in Sydney (at Maskeleyne Point, now known:
as Dawes Point) but the comet never appeared. His son (William Rutter Dawes) became a well-known
astronomer.

Sir Thomas Brisbane was a British soldier and astronomer who was appointed Governor of New South
Wales in 1821. His interest in astronomy began when he was nearly shipwrecked due to a navigational
error. He established an observatory in 1822 at Parramatta, near Sydney. He appointed two astronomers to
study the stars visible in the Southern hemisphere and, by 1835, they had described and classified
thousands of new stars.

Australia has had its share of famous astronomers. John Tebbutt was an amateur astronomer born in
Windsor, NSW. He started his observations in the 1850s and built his first observatory in 1863. He was the
most famous Australian astronomer of his time. He discovered two comets and was also interested in
meteorology (the atmosphere and weather).

Another notable Australian astronomer was Joseph Lade Pawsey who died in 1962. He specialised in
radioastronomy and worked for the CSIRO.

searchText:
No matter how hard you try, you can only do this one hand at a time.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Place a wooden ruler on top of your two hands so the ends
of the ruler are supported by your two index fingers.
2  Slowly slide your two index fingers towards the centre of
the ruler. (Only one finger at a time will move along the
ruler. The fingers will alternate until they meet at the
balance point of the ruler.)
3  Now try to move both fingers back to their original positions. (Only one finger will move along 
the ruler.)
EXPLANATION
The moving finger is whichever one has the least weight on it and, consequently, the least friction. At any
one time, the amount of weight on each finger will depend on its location relative to the ruler’s centre of
gravity and the turning moments at each finger.
TO INVESTIGATE 
Predict what would happen if you used an irregular object, such as an axe handle or a pool cue, instead 
of a ruler. 
Railway lines are very smooth, but they still do their work by friction. The train engines are so heavy
that there is enough friction between the wheel and the tracks to provide grip.
Friction heat ignites matches.

1  Feel the force of friction. Take two exercise books and interlock them by alternating at least 20 pages
from each book. Make sure they overlap over at least half their width. Hold the books at the bind and
try to pull them apart. (Friction between the pages will make them very hard to pull apart.)
2  Make a model hovercraft using a balloon, a cotton reel,
some glue and a small sheet of plywood with a hole in the
centre. Blow up the balloon then quickly push the
hovercraft over a smooth surface. (It will seem to glide
because the air from the balloon decreases the friction
between the plywood and the surface below.)

Balance in Nature

Ecosystem: a space containing organisms interacting with each other and their surroundings.

If an ecosystem has existed successfully for a long time, then the populations (members of a particular
species) are usually stable. This occurs when all of the organisms in an ecosystem are reasonably
compatible with each other and their environment. If numbers do change, this often happens at regular
intervals in a way that can be forecast, for example, in line with changes of seasons.

An ecosystem can be upset by the arrival of a new species or the loss of an existing one.

1 Apart from living creatures, what factors can change an ecosystem?

Cattle were first brought to Australia by sailing ships late in the eighteenth century. Due to the long voyages
many organisms were either left behind or died on the way. These included both beneficial and
pathogenic creatures. The dung beetle was one example. Dung beetles lay eggs in cattle dung. When the
larvae hatch out they eat the dung, This makes sure that the compounds present in the dung are returned
to the soil. It also keeps down the number of flies (which also breed in the dung) and increases the area
available for pasture. There are dung beetles native to Australia, but these tend to eat native wildlife dung
and do not eat the dung of introduced cattle.

2 Give meanings for the words shown in bold in the passage above. Choose from: disease causing
helpful excrement living creature indigenous grass young insects _ produce offspring
If cattle are introduced without dung beetles then they are likely to have an adverse (hostile) effect on their
new environment. Because flies tend to eat dung, their numbers will increase — with the obvious
consequences. Some environmental organisations monitor the number of dung beetles. Dung beetles are
killed by some cattle drenches (medicine). It has been suggested that different species of dung beetles
should be introduced from overseas.

Blood groups

Before the 1900s, it was well known that if blood from one person came in contact with the blood of
another person, very often the red blood cells would form clumps and so no longer be able to carry
out their role.
In 1901, Austrian biologist, Karl Landsteiner, discovered that some people had certain antigens that
could affect blood that did not have that antigen. The different blood types were named A (if it had
only antigen A), B (if it had only antigen B), AB (if it had both A and B antigens) and O (if it had
neither A nor B antigens). It was found that these blood types contain antibodies that react against
the antigens as shown in the table below.
Every living person belongs to one of these four blood groups; the group being decided at the
moment of conception and inherited from the parents. Hence the blood group is fixed for life and
does not change. This ABO system of blood grouping interests forensic scientists because even if
dried, the antigens can be detected and identified.
Nowadays the technique of DNA profiling can use blood to link a specific individual to a bloodstain.
However, even before this development, a blood sample was considered important evidence if found
at a crime scene.
Blood is a good example of a class characteristic because it is associated with a group of people all
having the same characteristic (ie the same blood group). It is not unique to only one individual, like
a fingerprint. Such evidence is still very important during investigations because it eliminates some
suspects and so decreases the number of people who need to be examined further.
This type of evidence allows the calculation of the probability that a sample of blood found at a crime
scene came from a particular person. To do this, the proportion of the population belonging to that
group or class needs to be known.

1-4
Examination of blood splashes and smears at a crime scene is an essential part of a murder
investigation. The position and appearance of blood marks on the body and surroundings will help
the investigator to reconstruct the crime.
For example, because blood cannot flow uphill against gravity, it may indicate to the investigator that
a body was moved after the victim was killed. French criminologist, Alexander Lacassagne, is
credited with linking the shape of blood spots with the position of the victim.
Blood dropped vertically, onto a stationary, flat surface forms
a circular mark with a serrated edge. (see right)
Drops of blood falling from a moving object hit a flat surface
at an angle, leaving a spot like an exclamation mark, with a
smaller spot showing the direction of movement. (see right)
The arrow shows the way the person was moving.
It is sometimes possible to make a rough
estimate of the height from which blood
fell by inspecting its edges. As the height
increases, so does the length of the spines
or serrations. (see right)
Examination of the shape of obliquely falling blood
splashes yields information about the direction and speed
of impact. Such evidence helps to determine the
positions of the victim and assailant at the time of the
assault and may indicate the degree of violence, the type
of weapon used and which person was the attacker and
who was in a position of self-defence.
The shape of the blood splashes is approximately related
to the steepness of the angle of fall. (see right) The
thickness of the blood, due to the degree of clotting, also
has some affect on the shape.
Blood smears tend to start as drops, which become
ragged at one edge, indicating direction of travel of the
smear. (see right) The arrow shows the direction in
which the blood was smeared.

clean surface a distinctive ‘swipe’ pattern results.

1

A classic murder case in which blood evidence played a major, if controversial, part occurred in 1954.
Dr Sam Sheppard’s wife was found dead on a bed in an upstairs room of their home in Ohio, USA.
She had been hit by over 30 blows with a blunt object. The room had been ransacked, and was
heavily spattered with blood. A trail of stains led down the stairs and onto a terrace.
Dr Sheppard, who had been awakened from sleep
on the living-room sofa by his wife’s screams,
claimed to have been knocked unconscious by an
intruder as he rushed up the stairs to help his wife.
His behaviour was thought to have been suspicious,
and so there was some doubt about his story. This
was partly due to his infidelity towards his wife.
The doctor was sent for trial and found guilty of
murder. The coroner made much of the bloodstains
found on the pillow in the murder room and a
bloody imprint, which he suggested, was made by a
surgical instrument.
The murder room was full of blood splash evidence which if properly examined would have led to
other conclusions. A forensic expert in blood splashes examined the room several months later and
came to the following conclusions. As the ceiling showed no traces of blood, the murder weapon
must have been used almost horizontally. This was supported by the state of the blood splashes on
the walls, some of which appeared to be cast offs flung from the weapon as it was moved backwards
and forwards on to the victim’s head.
The investigator carried out experiments which suggested that the most likely weapon to have caused
the pattern of blood splashes was a heavy torch. He concluded, having noticed blood drops that had
been smeared into streaks on the right side of the victim’s bed, that the murderer had stood between
the twin beds. This suggestion was supported by blood-free areas on two of the walls behind the
murderer, which had been protected from flying blood by t

searchText:
When you have your heels against the wall you cannot touch the floor.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Stand with the backs of your heels firmly against the wall.
2  Try to touch the floor in front of your feet without moving
your feet or bending your knees. (You will not be able to
touch the floor without falling over.)
EXPLANATION
A person’s centre of gravity is usually just above his/her hips.
When you try to touch the floor your centre of gravity moves
in front of both feet and you topple over. 
Tug-of-war teams try to achieve a low centre of gravity. The
five-man tug-of-war was an Olympic event up until 1920.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a tightrope walker. Insert two forks and a match 
into a potato so it balances on a tight string. (Using the
weight of the fork handles, the centre of gravity of the
system will be lowered to just below the string, so the 
potato will not fall off.)
2  Which senses are involved in balance? Close your eyes
then try to balance on one leg. (You will find it extremely
difficult to stay upright. The eyes and the semicircular
canals of the middle ear work together to give you
information about balance.)
Your brain makes you seasick. When your eyes and your middle ear send conflicting messages (as when
you are in a rolling ship), the brain gets confused and floods your body with stress hormones that
make you feel sick. This seems a pointless thing to do and scientists still don’t understand why the
brain does it.

Method:
Step 1: Label the tests tube 1, 2, 3 and 4

Step 5: In test tube 3, fill ¼ of the test tube with the salt solution you just made, and add a nail

    The results show that rusting occurs in the presence of water and air (test tubes 1 and 3). It
    should also show that salt increases the rate of rusting.

    The oxidation reaction of iron requires oxygen, which is in the air, and dissolved in the water.
