searchText:
When corn kernels are put in fizzy water they go up and down.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Put about a dozen kernels of popping corn in a 200mL
beaker of water. (They will sink.)
2  Put an antacid tablet in the water, wait for it to finish
fizzing and then observe the corn. (The corn kernels will
rise to the surface and then sink many times over the next
few minutes.)
EXPLANATION
The corn kernel by itself is more dense than water, so it sinks.
However, the surface of the kernel provides sites for bubbles
of carbon dioxide to form. The average density of the
corn–bubble unit is lower than that of water, so it rises to the
surface. The bubbles burst, and the process is repeated.
TO INVESTIGATE
Does this phenomenon apply only to corn and antacid? Try
‘hundreds and thousands’ and currants; and try other types of
carbonated drinks.
Pumice is a rock that floats, and ebony is a wood 
that sinks.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Do the rotten egg test. Let an egg go rotten, then place it in
a beaker of water with a fresh egg. (The fresh egg will sink,
but the rotten egg will float because gases are produced by
bacteria as they decompose the contents of the egg.)
2  Make an egg float in acid. Safety glasses and laboratory
coats should be worn. Place a fresh egg in a beaker and add
dilute hydrochloric acid until the beaker is almost full. (The
egg will initially sink, but will then rise to the surface as the
acid reacts with the calcium carbonate in the shell of the egg
to produce bubbles of carbon dioxide.)

The Development
of Astronomy

Astronomy: the study of planets, stars and other heavenly bodies.

Humans have always been interested in the skies, People have been frightened by comets, meteor showers,
eclipses of the sun and of the moon and so on. Many ancient civilisations came up with calendars based
‘on astronomical investigations, which they used to work out when it was time for planting, harvesting and
so on. A summary of advances in astronomy is given below.

© Almost 2000 years ago, an Egyptian astronomer named Claudius Ptolemy said the Earth was the
centre of the universe. He also stated that all objects in the sky were perfect spheres. For the next 13
centuries this idea (the Geocentric theory) was held by most people.

* A Polish monk, Nicolaus Copernicus (around 1530), came up with the idea that the sun, and not the
Earth, was the centre of our solar system. This suggestion (the Heliocentric theory) disagreed with
the beliefs of the Church at the time. His work was not published until just before his death in 1543.
It took a long time and the work of many scientists to prove that Copernicus was right.

© Tycho Brahe (1546 to 1601) was a Danish astronomer who, with the assistance of his sister Sofie,
gathered very accurate astronomical observations. He didn’t agree with all of the theories of
Copernicus. His work was used by his German assistant, Johannes Kepler (1571 to 1630), to prove
planets did not move in circular orbits, but in ellipses (ovals).

© Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) is credited with being the first person to
use the telescope to make astronomical observations, He saw the
Earth's moon had craters, Saturn had rings and that there were moons
orbiting Jupiter. The idea that other planets had satellites, contradicted
the idea that the Earth was the only object that had others orbiting it.

Investigating the Effects of Exercise
Aim: To describe how the body changes during exercising.

Equipment:
• A partner to work with

• A blood pressure monitor                                Safety Information
                                                          Exercise – possible injury
• A timer
                                                          Do not exercise more than you feel comfortable
                                                          with. Any sickness or dizziness inform the
                                                          teacher immediately.

                                                          Only exercise in a clear space.



Method:
Step 1: Decide who will be the ‘coach’ and who will be the ‘exerciser’

Step 2: Exerciser – find your pulse, either on your neck or wrist, and count
the number of ‘beats’ you can feel in 15 seconds. Multiply this by 4 to get
the BPM. Record your resting pulse rate

Step 3: Measure the exerciser’s blood pressure using an automatic monitor
and record the results

Step 4: Whilst resting, observe the amount of redness and sweat on the
exerciser’s face, as well as their breathing pattern. Record these observations

Step 5: Exerciser – perform some moderate exercise e.g. 50 jumping jacks or
jogging on the spot for 2 minutes

Step 6: Repeat steps 2 to 4 and record your measurements after exercise

Step 7: Swap roles and repeat for the other person



Questions:
 1. Describe how your pulse rate changed after exercising.

 2. Describe how your blood pressure changed after exercising.

 3. Describe how your appearance (redness and sweating), and your breathing changed
    after exercising.

 4. Explain why you think you saw the changes you observed.




                                                  Page 1 of 2
                                                  Investigating the Effects of Exercise



    Factor       Observations whilst resting   Observations after exercising



  Pulse rate



Blood pressure



   Redness



  Sweating



  Breathing




    Factor       Observations whilst resting   Observations after exercising



  Pulse rate



Blood pressure



   Redness

                                                                         Investigating the Effects of Exercise
Answers:

 1. Describe how your pulse rate changed after exercising.
    The pulse rate has increased.

 2. Describe how your blood pressure changed after exercising.
    The blood pressure has increased.

 3. Describe how your appearance (redness and sweating), and your breathing changed
    after exercising.
    The face will have become more red than before. There may be visible sweating. The breathing
    will have become deeper and more rapid.

 4. Explain why you think you saw the changes you observed.
    When the body is exercising there is a demand for more energy; and therefore more oxygen to
    release the energy.
    The pulse rate increases as the heart works faster to pump more blood, carrying oxygen, to the
    cells.
    The blood pressure increases as the heart is pumping faster and harder, so the blood is being
    moved at a higher pressure.
    The blood vessels move towards the surface, and sweating begins in order to transfer excess heat
    energy from the body (by evaporation of sweat).
    Breathing becomes deeper and more rapid in order to get more oxygen into the body, and to
    remove the increased production of carbon dioxide.

Understanding Biology – biotechnology and disease
19
How far is too far?
In biomedical research, ethics (moral values) must be considered. Ethics differ between individuals and groups 
of individuals. What one considers acceptable, another does not. Many cultures and religions do not approve of 
‘tampering with nature’, often arguing that humans were not designed to extend life unnaturally. Others argue that 
great minds are meant to be used – hence, if we can find a way to do it, then we should do it! No matter how far we 
progress with scientific research, ethical issues will always be nearby to remind us of other considerations involved 
with developing technology.
Animal Ethics committees are important groups that represent the welfare of animals. In the past, the welfare of 
animals in scientific research was not considered important, and many animals suffered horribly. Today, people 
generally respect the lives (and feelings) of animal subjects used for experimental purposes. Ethics committees are 
often made up of a variety of people, for example, a teacher, a clergyman, several scientists and a police officer. This 
is to ensure a ‘public’ opinion is reached.

own lives (humanely) when they are terminally ill. Discuss the ethics of this ‘right’, including reasons for and 
against.
 
 
‘Stolen body parts’
In mid-2006, newspapers reported that American firms had unknowingly been using products made from stolen 
body parts. Bones, ligaments, skin and other tissues were removed from corpses in funeral homes, without the 
knowledge of the relatives of the deceased. The body parts were sold onto other firms who used them a

© Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
Understanding Biology – human and plant life
31
The term ‘ethics’ is derived from the Greek word ethika, which can be loosely translated as ‘the proper conduct, 
customs, principles or standards of how humans should behave’. 
Stem cells are undifferentiated cells (cells that have not yet committed to developing into a specific tissue type). They 
are present in developing embryos. They also occur in adults, but in lesser numbers. If stem cells are removed before 
they follow specific growth patterns, researchers can direct their course of development. It is hoped that stem cell 
research will one day allow replacement organs to be grown for impaired individuals, and help sufferers of diabetes, 
Parkinson’s disease and many other conditions. 
Embryonic stem cell research is extremely controversial, because the cells can be obtained from aborted foetuses. 
Many people are concerned by the idea that our society could use ‘crops’ of embryos in order to help or save other 
people. They think that abortion rates may increase, justified ‘in the name of research’, and some believe that it takes 
away an embryo’s right to life. Those in favour of embryonic stem cell research point out the benefits to society in 
helping people who have potentially curable conditions.
1 
In your workbook, list arguments for and against embryonic stem cell research.

2 - 2 Fibres and fabrics

2 CONTACT TRACES

If loose fibres found at the crime scene have not come from the victim, they may have come from a
large number of sources—from the perpetrator's clothes, from carpet or curtains where the crime
occurred, or even from a rug or blanket in which the body was wrapped for transportation, if the body
was moved. Also, fibres from the victim may have been deposited on the perpetrator, and these will be
looked for on all suspects. Any such fibres found could connect the suspect with the crime scene.

Fibres can be either synthetic (man-made)—such as nylon, rayon, terylene, polyester—or they can be
natural, being made from either plants (cotton and linen) or from animals (wool, silk and mohair).
Generally, under the microscope, natural fibres have a rougher surface, taper from root to tip and appear

somewhat irregular. Cotton fibres are actually collapsed tubes, while wool fibres, like hair, have scales.
On the other hand, synthetic fibres are smooth and even and have a much longer length (staple).

Fibres of the same type may vary in thickness, depending on how they are made. Their strengths can
also vary. Often, both the strength and thickness of any fibres found at a crime scene are measured
in the forensic laboratory and compared with any found on a suspect. The melting point of a
synthetic fibre is usually measured and its colour analysed. If two fibres look the same under the
microscope, have the same thickness, strength, colour and melting point, then they probably both
came from the same source. If the fibres are uncommon, then two matching fibres are even more
likely to have come from the same garment,

Sometimes, CSIs are fortunate enough to find a piece of fabric instead of only a few fibres. Knitting

The force of attraction (cohesive force) between the molecules at the surface of the water is strong enough

Do other liquids have surface tension? Try salt water, warm water, cooking oil and methylated spirits.

Flossie Wong-Staal (s.7-) 10a]

Flossie Wong-Staal’s original name was Wong Yee Ching and she was born in China in 1947. In 1952 her
family settled in Hong Kong. While at school, she was given the English name Flossie after Typhoon Flossie,
which had struck Hong Kong the week before. Wong-Staal enjoyed studying science and maths and her
family was very supportive of Wong-Staal continuing her education, In 1965, she emigrated to the United
States to study at the University of California, where she specialised in molecular biology and continued as
a postgraduate student in bacteriology.

After completing her doctorate she took a position with the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda,
Maryland, where she was the first researcher to copy the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The
cloning of the virus that causes AIDS allowed Wong-Staal and other scientists to determine the structure of
HIV. She has continued to work in AIDS research, specifically gene therapy.

haemophiliacs, and some people who had been given blood transfusions. Today we know that specific
behaviours such as unsafe sex, the sharing of needles, or infection from blood, increases the risk of getting

| = 6 The forensic

science laboratory
1 INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE X

The forensic scientist, employed full-time by the police department, is the analyst back in the
laboratory. They usually do not attend the crime scene. Their main responsibility is to help the police
investigation by using their specialist knowledge and techniques. Forensic scientists usually have a
science degree from a university, with specialist training and experience on top of that. They are often
not police officers and they do not usually interview witnesses or suspects; interviewing is left to the
police officers.

Many forensic scientists specialise in a certain
area such as fingerprint identification, DNA
profiling or forgery detection. It is the forensic
scientist who can identify whether a hair is
human or animal and can identify from what
part of the body it came. A forensic scientist
who specialises in ballistics can often identify
the exact gun from which a bullet was fired.

The forensic laboratory houses many pieces of
expensive and specialised equipment to help
the scientist analyse the evidence.

Once an item arrives at the laboratory, the
forensic scientist decides what tests or analysis
it should undergo, and in what order. Some tests
will destroy part or all of the evidence, while
other tests will not affect the sample at all.
Obviously, all non-destructive tests should be
carried out first. The scientist needs to know the
information required by the investigating
officers in order to select the appropriate tests.

‘To prevent cross-contamination in the laboratory, all evidence from the crime scene is stored in a
different place to any items taken from a suspect's home or car. Items from the different scenes are
analysed by different forensic scientists where possible, and always on different days and in
different rooms.

— QT Eve )
Fuels

Fuels: substances that produce heat or power during combustion.

A fuel is a substance which gives out heat energy when it burns. Most fuels need to combine with oxygen
(©) in order to burn to release their energy. Another name for burning is combustion. When carbon-based
fuels burn they give out carbon dioxide (CO,) and water (H,0). Reactions giving out heat are called
exothermic reactions.

Many of the fuels we use are fossil fuels. They are the remains of organic (living) matter from millions of
years ago. They consist mainly of hydrocarbons — compounds containing the elements carbon (C) and
hydrogen (H) only. Coal, oil and natural gas (methane, CH,) are the major fossil fuels.

Coal is the remains of ferns, trees and other plants that lived about 300 million years ago, when most of
the Earth was covered in swamps or forests, These plants stored energy from the sun in making their food
via the process of photosynthesis, When trees died, they fell and gradually became covered by layers of
vegetation. As time went on, the layers were crushed into the Earth, often by earthquakes, volcanic
eruptions or layers of mud and sediment.

The dead trees were squashed by the layers above. This pressure and heat from inside the Earth changed
the trees which eventually turned into seams of coal. Much of this coal lies deep underground, covered by
layers of sediment. To mine these underground deposits of coal, deep shafts must be dug. Some coal seams
have been pushed to the surface by earth movements. This coal can be mined by open-cast mining, once
the surface rock has been bulldozed away.

Crude oil (petroleum) is thought to have been formed in a similar manner to coal. Millions of years ago,
life flourished in the warm, shallow seas and oceans of the time. As these marine creatures died, their
bodies fell to the bottom of the sea. Gradually the remains became covered with mud and silt. Decay
(rotting), heat and pressure turned this organic (living) matter in

2-10 Glass Q

2 CONTACT TRACES

Glass is a material that is made mostly from sand. For practical uses it is usually clear and
transparent. It can be made to be heat resistant, coloured, stronger, more brittle or more flexible by
just changing the amounts of the other chemicals that are added to the silica from the sand. The
mixture is heated to a very high temperature so that all the substances melt together. When forensic
scientists are asked to compare fragments of glass from a crime scene, there are a number of tests
which they may carry out. These include inspection under UV light, and a measurement of its
density and refractive index.

Some glass samples will fluoresce under UV light, so this test would be carried out first. Density is
a measure of how closely the particles of a material are packed together. If a type of glass contains
a lot of lead then it would tend to be denser than one with very little lead. The density of a sample
can be compared by finding in what liquids a sample will float. If the glass is placed in a liquid like
water or methylated spirits and sinks, we know it is denser than these liquids. If it floats on top of
a dense liquid like glycerine, then we know it is less dense than glycerine. If the glass neither sinks
nor floats in a certain liquid, or mixture of liquids, then its density must be exactly the same as the
liquid, Now, if two glass fragments were both suspended in the same liquid, then they would have
exactly the same density, and may have come from the same source. Comparison of densities is not
used as often in the forensic laboratory as in previous years, because glass manufacture today is more
automated and density characteristics do not vary as much as they did years ago when each factory
had its own ‘recipe’.

Glass

Glass has been used for over 4000 years to make containers and ornaments. More recently it has been used
for windows. Glass is a poor electrical and thermal conductor. Glass is neither a ‘proper’ solid nor a liquid
but is a ‘super cooled liquid’. Over hundreds of years, glass can very slowly flow and change shape. The
most commonly used glass (used in windows, jars, drinking vessels and so on) is soda glass. The raw
materials used in the manufacture of this type of glass are sand (silica, silicon dioxide), sodium carbonate
(‘soda’) and calcium carbonate (limestone).

‘Crystal’ glass contains lead oxide, is heavy and refracts (bends) light well, It is used in making ‘costume’
jewellery, lenses and prisms. Glasses containing lead are used to protect people working with radioactivity.

Laboratory glassware is made of borosilicate glass (Pyrex™) and contains borax. This
is also used to make cooking containers. It is strong, heat and chemical resistant.

Vehicle windshields are made of laminated glass. This consists of two sheets of thin
plate glass with a layer of plastic in between. The glass used to make lenses in
spectacles, cameras, microscopes, and telescopes needs to be very pure and free of
distortion, Although heavier than plastic, and more likely to shatter when dropped,
glass does not scratch as easily as plastic.

Fibre optics is the branch of optics (the study of light) dealing with the transmission of light through fibres
or thin rods of glass. Light can travel through the fibre over long distances with very low loss, even if the
fibre is curved. Optical fibres are used in medical instruments for viewing inside the human body and for
laser surgery, One growing application of optical fibres is in communication, where cables can carry much
more information than the equivalent copper cable.

I. 7 Going to trial

1_INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

In court the suspect, the person police believe carried out
the crime, is put on trial before a jury for major crimes, and
before a magistrate for less serious crimes. It is often the
quality of the police evidence that will influence the
opinion of both the jury and the magistrate.

In a jury trial, the judge is there to listen and pass sentence
if the jury decides that the accused is guilty. The
prosecution lawyer puts forward the police case and calls
any expert witnesses to give their opinion in order to
convince the jury of the facts of the case.

The defence lawyer must try to defend the person charged
with the crime by trying to point out any holes in the
prosecution's argument and to try to put doubt in the jury
members’ minds. Only the jury can decide if the accused is
guilty or not, beyond any reasonable doubt. An expert witness may also be called in by the defence
to discredit the case against a suspect.

The scientific evidence must be presented in a way that can be understood by the court, and not in
a way that may confuse it. Judges, lawyers and juries do not usually have a deep knowledge of
science, so all scientific results have to be presented in non-technical terms. This is why photographs,
videos, maps and plaster casts are so important.

Because of the court’s lack of scientific expertise, the forensic scientist or expert witness must be
prepared to give an expert opinion on what the evidence implies—that is, they must be able to say how
likely it is that the crime is linked to the suspect who has been charged. They may give an opinion of
the probability of the soil found on the suspect's shoe coming from the crime scene, or the suspect's
fingerprint matching one found on some stolen property, hence linking the suspect to the crime.

2-4 Hair

Although hair cannot usually identify a single individual as fingerprints can, hair found at a crime
scene can be very useful. Besides giving some indication of age, race and sex, hairs found at a crime
scene can strengthen the links between a suspect and that scene.

Human hair can be classified into six groups, according to its origin:

Hair from the scalp tends to have a circular cross-section, often with somewhat split ends.
Beard hair often has a more triangular cross-section.

Eyebrows and eyelashes also have a circular cross-section, but their ends are tapered.
Under-arm hair has a more oval cross-section than the other types.

Pubic hair is often short, curly and stiff, with an oval or triangular cross-section and short roots.
General body hair is finer and softer than pubic hair, but is also curly and either triangular or
oval in cross-section.

Hair is composed mainly of the protein keratin, which is very difficult to destroy except by fire and
certain chemicals. It will remain preserved in the grave longer than most of the body except for the
bones. Microscopic inspection of hair can also indicate whether hair was pulled out, cut off or
whether it just fell out naturally.

elements it contains. These chemicals reflect the
food you eat, your work and home
environment, any drugs and poisons you may
have consumed as well as the shampoos and
other chemicals like dyes and bleaches that you
may have put on your hair. In the 1960s, when
some of Napoleon’s hair was obtained and
analysed more than 100 years after his death, it
was found to contain many more times the
normal amount of arsenic. In his day arsenic Fig. 10
was thought to improve the complexion, but it

was also a favourite method of poisoning as its

taste was difficult to detect.

A
give us a clue – change agent
What you need
3 × 100 mL Erlenmeyer, Alka-Seltzer tablets, water (iced, hot and room temperature), plastic teaspoons, 
mortar and pestle, 50 mL measuring cylinder, 2 balloons
What to do
Carry out the following 4 experiments, which will provide you with useful information about chemical 
reactions. After each test, rinse the 3 flasks with fresh water.
1 Pour 50 mL of iced water into one flask, 50 mL of tap water into another, and 50 mL of hot water 
into the third. Add one Alka-Seltzer tablet to each flask and observe how fast the tablets dissolve. 
2 Take 3 Alka-Seltzer tablets. Keep one whole, break one into quarters and grind up the third in the 
mortar and pestle. Pour 50 mL of tap water into each of the 3 flasks. Add the whole tablet to one 
flask, the broken tablet to the second flask, and the ground-up tablet to the third flask. Observe 
which tablet dissolves the fastest.
3 Pour 50 mL of tap water into 2 flasks. To the first beaker, add 1 ground-up tablet; 
quickly pull a balloon over the mouth of the flask to catch the gas produced. To 
the other flask add 3 ground-up tablets all together and quickly attach a balloon. 
Observe how much gas is produced in each balloon. 
4 Pour 50 mL of tap water into 2 flasks. Add a whole Alka-Seltzer tablet to each 
one. Vigorously swirl one flask but not the other. Observe how fast each tablet 
dissolves.
Now answer these questions:
• At what temperature does the reaction go the fastest?
• Does the amount of substance affect the speed of the reaction?
• Does stirring increase or decrease the reaction rate? 
• Which of the factors you tested were important in determining how fast each reaction occurred?
What happens next?
After you have completed these experiments and answered the questions above, you will be asked to 
solve a problem. You will need to use the information learned from this experiment

If a dark stain is found at a crime scene, it may be blood belonging to either the victim or criminal.
Or it could be something else, like furniture polish or another dark stain. Before sending a sample to
the lab for testing, the Crime Scene Examiner must first establish that the stain is blood. For this
reason, a presumptive blood test is done. This is a test that is quick and simple to carry out at the

Fibres are classified as either synthetic (man-made), such as nylon and polyester, or
natural. If natural, they might come from plants such as cotton or from animals such

they are made of exactly the same substances. Strength comparisons can be made by

Natural fibres are far less uniform in their appearance. Their quality depends on the

This ink will only appear when it is heated.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY 
Safety warning: this activity requires a safe method of disposing
of sheets of paper that have accidentally ignited.
1  Dip the wooden end of a match stick into some lemon
juice then write with it onto a sheet of paper.
2  Let the lemon juice dry on the paper. (The writing will be
almost invisible.)
3  Hold the sheet of paper very close to an electric radiator,
but not so close that the paper burns. (The lemon juice will
darken and become visible.)
EXPLANATION
The lemon juice contains sugar and other carbon compounds. Upon heating, these begin to break down
and some of the carbon appears by itself. Pure carbon is black, so the colour of the lemon juice slowly gets
darker as more and more carbon appears.
The charcoal on barbecued meat contains a substance

acid. (The carbon will become separated from the hydrogen

Iron and Steel

With the exception of certain meteorites, iron (Fe) does not occur native (uncombined with other
elements) in the Earth’s crust. There are many compounds of iron, such as iron sulfide (iron pyrites, FeS,),
haematite (Fe,0,) and magnetite (Fe,O,). Iron is the second most abundant metal in the Earth’s crust,
Because it can be relatively easily extracted from its ores and because it has useful physical properties, it
has become a metal of considerable importance.

Iron is produced in a blast furnace. This is a tapered, cylindrical tower approximately 30 to 40 metres high.
It is constructed of steel and is lined with special heat resistant (refractory) bricks.

A blast furnace works continuously and can produce more than 1000 tonnes of iron every 24 hours. The
taw materials are iron ore (for example, haematite), coke (carbon, C), limestone (calcium carbonate,
CaCO,) and air, Coke is obtained from coal.

The molten iron formed flows to the bottom of the blast furnace, Impurities (mainly calcium silicate) form
as slag, floating on top of the molten iron. Slag and iron are tapped off, and allowed to cool and solidify. The
iron produced is still relatively impure and is known as cast iron or pig iron. It contains about 4% carbon. It
is very hard but brittle. This type of iron is only used for objects which are not likely to be bent when used.

Pure iron is not a good material for building things. It corrodes (rusts) very easily and is soft. Most iron
produced in blast furnaces is turned into steel, an alloy (mixture) of iron. There are thousands of types of
steel and their properties will depend on the other elements added. The impurities present are removed
from molten cast iron in a special furnace and other elements are added in careful proportions. Mild steel
is commonly used for car bodies. It is cheap, easily shaped and relatively strong.

What does ‘native’ mean?

List the names and formulae of all of the iron compounds mentioned

— =6hL-2 AUSTRALIAN ENVIRONMENT pe!
Kangaroos

Kangaroos are furry, marsupial mammals only found in mainland
Australia and bordering islands. There are over fifty species of kangaroos.
They hop on their hind (rear) legs. Their front legs are short and the five
digits (‘fingers’) are of different sizes. Their long, powerful hind legs have
tendons that act as springs for powerful leaping. A large kangaroo can
jump over six metres in one bound and reach a top speed of nearly 50
kilometres per hour. Kangaroos can jump nearly two metres high.

Kangaroos use their long, muscular tails for balance when hopping and support when walking or sitting.
They are not normally aggressive, but can cause harm when they feel threatened, hitting out with their
forepaws and kicking with their muscular rear legs. Apart from humans and dingos, kangaroos have no
natural enemies. They were once hunted extensively for their meat and coats. Kanagaroo hunting was once
a popular sport in Australia, with hundreds of thousands killed each year. Some are still hunted in areas
where they are abundant or are a nuisance.

Kangaroos are marsupials and females have abdominal pouches. A newly born kangaroo (2.5 cm long)
makes its way slowly into the pouch. It does this by tracing a path of fur licked by the mother kangaroo.
The ‘joey’ remains in the pouch until it is six to nine months old. This pouch usually contains four
mammary glands — only two of these at a time operate to give milk. When the joey permanently leaves
the pouch, it still stays with its mother and continues to obtain milk by putting its head into her pouch,
usually for another six to nine months. Kangaroos can live for up to seven or eight years.

Kangaroos as also described as macropods, meaning they have large feet. The best known and largest
kangaroos are the giant, or great grey, kangaroo (Macropus giganteus) and the red kangaroo (Macropus
rufus). Red kangaroos tend to be found in the deserts and dry grassland of central Australia

Radio astronomers use the term Jansky as the unit of

Structure of radio waves 
Light, X-rays, microwaves, infrared and radio 
waves are all electromagnetic waves with 
different wavelengths and frequencies.
1 Label the electromagnetic spectrum in figure 1 using these words:  
Radio, UHF, Microwaves, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-rays, Gamma rays.
 
 
Sound and radio waves
Sound waves and radio waves are not the same. Sound is a longitudinal wave and cannot travel through a vacuum. 
radio waves are electromagnetic waves and can travel through a vacuum.

Other Australians

The koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) is only found in Australia. It is an arboreal marsupial (not placental)
mammal. It feeds almost exclusively on the leaves and flowers of certain (about 20) species of eucalypts.
A koala will seldom drink. It obtains most of its water from the leaves it eats. It is lethargic and often stays
in the same tree for days at a time. The koala grows to about 75 cm in length and has a life span of
approximately 12 years in the wild, but can live for up to 20 years in captivity.

dingos started to prey on the introduced sheep and rabbits rather than on native wallabies and kangaroos.

searchText:
A floating match will suddenly spring away from your finger.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Fill a beaker with water and gently place half a
matchstick onto the surface of the water. (You will be
able to see water adhering to the matchstick.)
2  Put a small drop of liquid soap on the tip of your
finger and touch this ‘magic finger’ to the surface of
the water to one side of the match. (The matchstick
will suddenly spring away from your finger.) 
EXPLANATION
This activity demonstrates the tension in surface tension. The soap weakened the surface tension on one
side of the match. The match sprang away because the surface tension on the other side was stronger (like
a wire under tension will spring away from the point where you cut it).
TO INVESTIGATE
Is it possible to repeat this activity using the same water? (No, you will need to use fresh water and a new
match and remove all the soap in the beaker before you can repeat the activity.)
Some beetles (Stenus) walk slowly on the surface of
mountain streams. But when threatened, they dab the
end of their abdomen on the water and release a
chemical that lowers the surface tension so
dramatically they are whisked away almost faster
than the eye can see.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a soap-powered boat. Cut out a small boat shape
from light cardboard. Cut a notch in the back and fit a
small flake of soap into it, then put the boat in fresh tap
water. (The boat will move forward because the surface
tension is lowered at the back.) 
2  Design a big-bubble recipe. Try mixing different ratios of dishwashing liquid, water and either sugar or
glycerine or gelatine. (When surface tension is weakened, the distance between the water molecules can
be increased to form bubbles. Substances such as sugar, glycerine and gelatine help to make the bubbles
last longer because they form weak adhesive bonds with water. This helps to slow down the rate of
evaporation of the water from the large surface area of the bubbles. A good bubble mixture is one part
dish

Marie Curie
Marie Curie (1867 – 1934) biography A




                                  Maria Salomea Sklodowska was born in
                                  Warsaw, Poland, on November 7th 1867. She
                                  was the youngest of five children – three older
                                  sisters and a brother. Her mother was a
                                  headmistress and her father taught maths and
                                  physics. He introduced the subjects to Maria
                                  when she was a child. When Maria was young,
                                  Poland was ruled by Russia. Maria’s family
                                  didn’t like the rules the Russian government
                                  made, however. For example, it was against
                                  the law to speak Polish and it was illegal for
                                  girls to go to school. Maria was clever and
                                  curious so her parents decided to send her to a
                                  secret school, where she did extremely well.

 Unfortunately, however, not everything in Maria’s early life was easy. In
 1877, when Maria was just 10 years old, her oldest sister died from typhus
 and in 1979 her mother died of tuberculosis. Maria and her family were
 heartbroken. Maria finished school when she was 15. She and her sister,
 Bronya were both interested in scientific research and after school, they both
 desperately wanted to go to University. The University in Warsaw, however,
 only allowed men to attend at the time. Women were allowed to go to
 University in other countries, but that was very expensive. So Maria and
 Bronya promised each other that they would take turns working to pay for
 the other to travel abroad to study. Maria thought that every child should be
 educated, so for almost 5 years, she secretly worked as a governess and a
 tutor, illegally teaching poor children to read. She sent the money she earned

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019         34893                           Page 1 of 14
                                                                  Marie Curie
 to Bronya, who attended University and became a doctor, which was almost
 unheard of for women at the time.

 In 1891, Maria moved to Paris. She changed her name to Marie because it
 sounded more French. She studied at the Sorbonne, a famous University,
 where she earned a degree in physics, maths and chemistry. Later, she
 gained a master’s degree in physics and then yet another degree in maths.
 Marie was so poor while she was there
 that she had to live on bread and tea and she
 sometimes fainted from hunger!

 While she was in Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, a physics
 professor. They soon fell in love and were married in
 1895. Marie worked with her husband in scientific
 research to investigate x-rays, radioactivity, and how
 atoms work. In 1898 Marie and Pierre discovered two
 new substances, called polonium (named after Poland)
 and radium. In 1903, they won a joint Nobel Prize for
 their work in physics, making Marie the first woman ever
 to win the award.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019      34893                          Page 2 of 14
                                                                        Marie Curie
 Marie and Pierre had two children – Irene born in 1897 and Eve, born in 1904.
 Sadly, in 1906, when Eve was just 2 years old, Pierre was killed when he was
 knocked down in the street by a horse drawn carriage. Marie was devastated
 but she decided to take over Pierre’s work. She became the first ever female
 professor at the Sorbonne University, and she won a Nobel Prize of her own
 for her work in chemistry in 1911. Soon after this, doctors found that
 radiology could help with curing cancer.

 Then, in 1914, the First World War started. Marie realised if military doctors
 had access to x-ray machines, they could make better medical decisions and
 save more lives. She helped to develop mobile x-ray machines and put them
 into ambulances, which she herself drove to the wounded soldiers on the
 front line.




 These vehicles became known as ‘Little Curies’ in Marie’s honour and they
 helped over one million soldiers during the war. She trained doctors and
 taught them how to use this new life-saving equipment and in 1921, she set
 up the Curie Institute in Paris. It is still an important cancer research centre
 today.

 Marie didn’t realise it, but the radioactive substances she worked with were
 very dangerous. As a result of working with them for such a long time, Marie
 developed leukaemia, a blood disease, and died on 4th July 1934, aged 66.

 Marie’s discoveries of radium and polonium have changed science and
 medicine forever. Her work meant that x-ray machines became more useful
 and were used more by doctors. They continue to be used today to detect
 broken bones and other problems, helping doctors to treat and cure their
 patients.

Microscopes in the

forensic laboratory
1_ INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

Still one of the most commonly used and most important tools in the forensic laboratory is the

microscope, The simplest microscope is a magnifying lens which has been used for over 100 years
to examine anything from fingerprints to footprints. It can magnify objects x 10 to x 20.

The common compound microscope found in
all schools is another useful but relatively
inexpensive piece of equipment used regularly in
the forensic laboratory. It is used when a
magnification of up to x 1000 is needed. It has
two lenses, an eyepiece lens at the top through
which the scientist looks, and an objective lens
at the lower end of the barrel, near the object
being examined. Most compound microscopes
have three or four objective lenses of different Fig. 1. Magnifying lens
powers of magnification that can be selected by
rotating them. Hairs, fibres, glass fragments,
pollen grains and fingerprint samples are all
commonly examined under such a microscope.

If even greater magnification is required, then
an electron microscope may be used. Relying
on a beam of electrons rather than visible light,
this instrument can give images of molecules
and even atoms, It can magnify up to x 200 000
and can be used to examine soil bacteria or
pollen grains to show up the smallest
difference. Generally these instruments are not
found in a forensic laboratory so scientists must
send material away to be examined under an

electron microscope if they believe that this will
reveal important information. Fig. 2 A compound microscope

The stereoscopic microscope is also a very useful instrument in the forensic laboratory. It has two
eyepiece lenses that allow objects to be seen in three dimensions. It has a quite low magnification of
about x 100 to x 150, but allows specimens such as soil, hair and fibres that have been collected to
be sorted for closer inspection under other microscopes of higher magnification. Quite large obje

You can make mosquito wrigglers dive on command.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Collect some mosquito wrigglers from some stagnant
water (look in ponds, drains, puddles, old buckets, old 44
gallon drums etc.) and put about six in a beaker of fairly
clear water. 
2  Leave the wrigglers undisturbed until they come to the
surface and hang by their breathing tubes. 
3 Tap the beaker with a pencil. (The wrigglers will dive.)
EXPLANATION
Mosquito wrigglers respond to vibrations by diving, probably to avoid predators. However, after
continued stimulation, they do not respond as readily.
TO INVESTIGATE
What other stimuli will make wrigglers dive? (Try dipping a pencil into the water, a sharp clap, blowing on
the water or passing a shadow over the beaker.) Also, how deep can wrigglers dive?
If you get bitten by a mosquito, then you know it was a
female. Male mosquitoes feed only on flower nectar.
Butterflies look fragile, but they have existed in their
present form for millions of years longer than humans.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Resuscitate some ants. Put some large ants in a jar, cool
the jar until the ants are motionless, then place it on an
overhead projector. (All the chemical reactions in living
things are controlled by enzymes, which decrease in activity
as the temperature drops below their optimal level. As the
ants are warmed by the projector they will become active
again and can be observed on the screen.)
2  Observe predation. Place a praying mantis in a jar with
some small branches to climb on. Add a few small living
insects. (The mantis will readily strike at them.)
During mating, the female praying mantis usually kills and eats the male.

2 CONTACT TRACES

Small fragments of paint can be chipped off when a hard object strikes a painted surface. For
example, this may occur when a car strikes something or someone. If a thief tries to jemmy open a
window, the tool may remove some flakes of paint. These flakes can be unique if the building is an
older one that has been repainted several times. ‘

If such paint chips are found, they can be placed edge-on

under a stereoscopic microscope, and the different layers of

paint can be examined. It is not unusual for some older cars

to have up to ten layers of paint, including binding

materials. In each case, the colours and the order of these

colours are unique for different makes and models of cars.

The scientist is able to examine the flakes for colour, texture i Plasticine owed
and the sequence and thickness of the colour layers. ee i pplontadin pene dinld

These days, the colour layers for all models of cars are supplied by the car manufacturer, and are
recorded on a computer database. This allows the forensic scientist to quickly discover the colour,
make, model and year of manufacture of the car from a paint chip.

If the paint chips found at a crime scene match the paint on a suspect's car, then that car was
probably at the scene. Often dents or damage are further evidence that incriminates the suspect.

Some paints and binders used on the car body can be dissolved in some solvents such as acetone
(found in nail polish remover) or butane (cigarette lighter fuel). Paint chips can be placed in a
number of different solvents and examined to see if there is any seepage of colour from any of the
layers. If the same layer in two different chips dissolves in the same solvent, and the order of the
other layers is the same, it can be concluded that the two chips are probably from the same object.

Human beings have kept records since at least the last Ice Age, about 20 000 years ago. Many systems of
characters and symbols have been used. The Sumerians (who lived in a region similar to modern day Iraq)
pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay about 5000 years ago, using a language known as cuneiform.
Other civilisations have used marks on parchment (goat or sheep skin) or vellum (calfskin), The ancient
Egyptians wrote on papyrus, a plant-based material. Paper was invented by the Chinese nearly 2000 years
ago. Paper can be produced from almost any plant material fibre containing cellulose. Wood pulp is the most
common (95% of total production) but bamboo, cotton (and similar fibres) and straw can also be used.

Here is a simplified sequence for making paper:

wood is made into small wood chips

chips are turned to pulp by being ground and/or by being treated with chemicals

the pulp is bleached

substances are added to the pulp to give paper colour, texture and lustre

water is added

the pulp is passed through rollers, where the water is removed by squeezing and heating
the finished paper is wound on reels.

‘To make paper, a large amount of raw materials is needed. It also requires a large amount of energy and
generates a large amount of effluent (waste). Many people are concerned with the chemicals (often based
on chlorine) used to bleach paper. Environmentally friendly brands of paper have been produced which
are either not bleached or are bleached using oxygen,

Recycling paper can help cut down on the amount of wood needed for paper.
However, recycled paper cannot be used by itself to make high quality paper.
It needs to be either used to make packaging materials, or to be mixed with
new wood pulp. Before printed paper can be recycled it has to be ‘de-inked’.
Australian industry recycles a large quantity of the paper it uses.

The quality of drinking water

Introduction

Providing water to any population of people is critical. It is even more critical when a big city is involved. In
Sydney, for example, Sydney Water provides approximately 1500 million litres of water each day to more than
3.7 million people. An integrated network of 15 dams and storage reservoirs with associated catchments, eight

reservoirs are used to gather, store and transport water. In addition to supplying a large quantity of water, they
must also supply a high quality of water.

To understand how drinking water is monitored and treated to ensure that it is safe for human consumption.

Raw water is groundwater and water in rivers, streams and lakes that has not been treated to ensure that it is suitable for

Do you believe in science?
It is difficult to believe in science because the whole point of science is not to believe.

Scientific Method |

The word ‘Science’ comes from the Latin ‘scientia’, meaning ‘to know’. It is used to describe organised
knowledge. A scientist could be described as someone who studies a particular area of knowledge in a
methodical way. There are many areas of science, including astronomy, biology, chemistry, geology,
meteorology, paleontology and physics.

Scientists deal with problems in a certain way. They may notice something interesting and then try to
explain why it happens. The main way they do this is to gather more information (often by carrying out
experiments) and then make an educated guess. If this doesn’t work, they think again and perhaps try
different experiments, The following terms are often used to describe scientific method.

Observation: seeing, hearing, touching, smelling or tasting.
Inference: a judgement based on an observation.
Hypothesis: a possible explanation based on observation,
Experiment: to do something to test a hypothesis.

Results: observations/measurements from an experiment.
Conclusion: a final decision reached after doing experiments.

eee eee

Observations involve more than seeing — they can also involve hearing, smelling, touching and tasting.
Observations are quantitative when numbers are given (for example, 25°C) and qualitative when they
involve descriptions (for example, ‘hot’, ‘cold’). An hypothesis should be written as a statement which can
be proved or disproved by experiment.

Scientific Method II

In science experiments it is important to change only one thing (or variable) at a time.

In Australia we expend a lot of effort keeping hot drinks and food hot, and cold items cold, It is therefore
important to know the insulating properties of materials. A teacher gave a class a practical assignment to

Name

When a crime has been committed, there are specially trained police officers who are called out to search a
crime scene for clues. These officers are called crime scene examiners (CSEs). They look for evidence (evidence
is what the clues are called) that untrained people might not notice. These officers wear gloves, and overalls
made of a fabric that does not shed its fibres. Often they also wear elastic caps and overshoes, similar to those
worn in hospital operating theatres, so that they don’t leave any small particles (trace evidence) from
themselves at the scene.

The CSE will usually photograph the scene
first, then use a strong torch to inspect the
scene in more detail. Tweezers are used to
pick up small items that may have been left
behind by the criminal. If a smudge of
fingerprints is found on a hard surface, it
will be dusted using a special powder.

Any shoe prints or impressions left by tyres
at the scene are photographed, then a plaster
cast is made of each impression. These
photographs and casts can then be compared
to prints made from the suspect's shoes

or tyres.

Sometimes hairs or tiny fibres from a
criminal's clothes are found. These are
collected and sealed in specially labelled
bags, and then sent to the forensic laboratory
for further testing.

The police hope that this evidence will lead them to the person or people who carried out the crime, and will
provide enough information to convict the guilty person(s) ‘beyond all reasonable doubt’.

Name

Before the twentieth century, it was almost impossible for a criminal to be convicted of a crime unless he
or she was ‘caught in the act’ or identified by an eyewitness. However, in the early 1900s solving crimes
started to develop into a science, which involved police closely examining the place where a crime was
committed, They looked for clues or evidence that might lead them to discover who committed the crime.

For this to be successful, the crime scene must be as close as possible to the condition it was in when the
offender (the person who committed the crime) left. If the scene is interfered with, it is possible that clues
or evidence could be destroyed or accidentally carried away by innocent people. Extra evidence that has
nothing to do with the crime could also be left behind,

To avoid this, examining the site should be left to experts because they have been trained to look for the
smallest pieces of evidence without doing any damage. They look for hairs, fibres, fingerprints invisible to
the eye, small spots of blood and more obvious evidence, such as shoeprints or tyre impressions.

These experts wear special protective clothing that does not shed fibres. They stand on duckboards to avoid
touching the floor. They also wear hairnets, overshoes and gloves so that they don't leave anything of them-
selves behind, Small objects are picked up with tweezers and then placed into special bags. These bags are
sealed and labelled with the type of object, the date, where the item was found and by whom. This evidence
is then transported to the forensic laboratory where it is closely inspected or tested by experienced scientists.

The Ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle (AD 384–322) conducted thought

An object is balanced if its centre of gravity is on, or just

QED Cire Science y
The Skin

The skin (or cutis) is the largest organ of the body. It is a protective covering and holds other organs inside
the body. The thin outer part is called the epidermis, in which cells multiply continuously and push dead
cells outward. Cells (melanocytes) in the epidermis contain a pigment (colouring matter) called melanin,
which gives the skin its colour.

In the presence of sunlight the skin produces Vitamin D, an essential ingredient for healthy bones and
teeth. Although we need to be in the sun for a certain amount of time to maintain health, too much sun
is bad for us. It can cause sunburn, dry skin and, over a period of years, cancers can develop. The major
cause of this is ultraviolet (UV) rays.

A thicker, inner layer is the dermis, or true skin, The dermis contains
connective tissue which has blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands,
oil glands, hair follicles, muscles and fatty tissue. The skin has many
sensations, because the nerve endings that can detect touch, heat, cold,
pressure and pain are present in it. The ends of nails and hair are dead
cells, so it does not hurt to cut them,

Oil produced in the oil (sebaceous) glands help keep the skin smooth and
soft. Hair grows from follicles (tiny tubes) that extend into the dermis
where cells divide rapidly. The length of the hair depends on the location
in the body. For example, eyelashes only grow to a certain length.

Tiny openings or pores are in the skin. These allow us to rid ourselves of waste products through
perspiration (sweat). This also helps us to maintain a steady body temperature of 37°C, When your body
is cold, muscle fibres on either side of hair follicles contract. This gives you the feeling of ‘goose bumps’.
When this happens, air is trapped between the hairs. This provides insulation and helps to keep us warm.
Underneath the dermis is a layer of fatty (adipose) tissue which acts both as a fat store and an insulating
layer. Capillaries are tiny blood vessels wh

When sunlight passes through a prism, it separates into a whole series of different colours that we

in sunlight and they tan the skin; however, too much can cause sunburn. Radiation with even shorter
wavelengths than ultraviolet light includes X-rays and gamma rays used in medicine.

Water and Life:
Assignment

NAME QUE DATE

All living things contain water (usually being somewhere between 66% and 95% water). A typical male
human adult's body will be about two-thirds water.

1 Assuming that tomatoes are 94% water, calculate how much water there is in 1 kg of tomatoes, Show
your working.
Water transports many substances around the body. This is because it is such a good solvent, Water
represents a major constituent (over 80%) of blood, Blood carries nutrients and waste products around the
body. It carries oxygen from the lungs to cells and waste products, such as carbon dioxide, to the lungs.

When food is digested it is broken down into simpler, soluble products and these are carried by the blood
to cells to provide energy and raw materials.

2 Give the chemical formula for water,

3 Give the chemical symbol for oxygen.

4 Give the chemical formula for carbon dioxide.
Water is a chemical reactant in photosynthesis. In this process, green plants use sunlight to cause carbon
dioxide to react with water to form glucose (C,H,,0,) and oxygen.

Respiration occurs in animal cells, producing heat (and waste products). Water has a high specific heat,
which means it can store a large amount of heat. Blood can carry the heat from respiration around the
body. Water also helps the body to keep cool, When a person sweats, water evaporates from the skin,
taking heat from the body in the process.

Large bodies of water tend to have steadier temperatures than the land. Coastal regions have milder
climates than inland areas. This is because of water's great capacity to store heat. When layers of ice form
on the surface of water in very cold climates, the ice acts as an insulator for the water beneath.

Water provides a habitat for many organisms. It also contains dissolved oxygen for aquatic plants and fish
to breathe. Water also provides support (by displacement) for large mammals such as whales, who have
great problems with their body mass when out of the water

Wire mesh can hold water.
HOW TO DO IT
Hold a dry wire kitchen strainer over a sink. Carefully put 2 or
3 drops of water into it. (The water will stay in the strainer.)
EXPLANATION
Water is held in the mesh by adhesive forces between the wire
and water and cohesive forces within the water. A layer of
water forms in each hole in the mesh and the surface tension
stops the rest of the water from passing through. 
TO INVESTIGATE
What would happen if you put some detergent in the water? What would happen if you used oil or
methylated spirits instead of water? (Safety warning: be careful of methylated spirits’ fumes.)
If you hold a piece of canvas up to the light, you can see that it has lots of tiny holes in it, yet 
it still manages to keep the rain out. When it rains, the first drops of water seal the holes, so the rest
of the water runs off. But the Golden Rule of Canvas Tents is: don’t touch the inside of the tent when
it is raining. If you do, adhesive forces between the water and your finger will drag the water into 
the tent. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES

a sheet of fly wire. Gently lower it onto the surface of the
water in a beaker. (The raft will float because the water

the fly wire.) Quickly tip the bottle upside down.(The water
will not run out because the water has sealed the holes in
the fly wire and air pressure exerts a force that counters the
weight of the water.)

2 CONTACT TRACES

In 1910, the French criminologist Edmond Locard proposed his ‘Exchange Principle’. He stated that
“every contact leaves a trace’. The things he was talking about include fingerprints, hairs, fibres, glass
and paint fragments, even pollens.

We constantly drop hair from our bodies and shed fibres from our clothes. If there is a cat or a dog in
our home, its fur can be transferred on to our clothes and carried to a new location. Pollens from plants
around our home or workplace can land on our clothes and be carried away to be deposited at another
site. A burglar who breaks a window to enter a building is often showered with minute fragments of
glass which can get caught in the seams and pockets of clothing. All these very small items of evidence
are referred to as contact traces or trace evidence, and will be meticulously searched for by the crime
scene investigators (CSIs). It is almost impossible for a criminal and a victim to be in contact and not
exchange particles of some sort. This ‘exchange principle’ is the basis of all modern forensic science,
with the particles that are exchanged being the key to solving the crime.

Searching for trace evidence

At a crime scene, after the large, easily seen objects like weapons and clothes have been removed,
the area may be vacuumed so that all loose threads, hair and other small trace particles will be caught
in a special container called a vacuum trap. Before moving a dead body to the mortuary where the
post mortem will be carried out, the forensic pathologist wraps the head, hands and feet in separate
plastic bags, so that no small traces may drop off and be lost before a thorough inspection can be
made. Any debris under the fingernails from a possible struggle could also yield important evidence,
as could any foreign particles that have been breathed into the air passages.

Blood is probably the most important fluid that the forensic biologist has to deal with at a crime
scene. It makes up about 9% of a healthy person’s body weight, and the average adult has about
5 to 6 litres of blood in their body. When blood is spilt, it goes a long way and is extremely difficult
to remove completely. Murderers’ attempts to clean up usually fail because blood tends to stick to
clothing and the murder weapon, and is splashed around widely in a violent crime.
Blood found at crime scenes has trapped many killers who thought that they had removed all
incriminating traces. Tests for blood are so sensitive that they will show up the presence of blood
even after a surface has been wiped so that no blood is visible to the unaided eye. Blood that is many
years old can still be identified as blood and analysed for DNA.
Forensically, blood can yield a great deal of information. The first task for an investigator at a crime
scene is to determine whether any suspicious stains are blood by doing a presumptive blood test. If
the test is positive, then it must be determined if the blood is animal or human. Once this is
established, the stains can be further tested for approximate age, sex, blood group and now DNA.
Understanding how bloodstains and splashes appear under different circumstances can help
enormously in reconstructing the sequence of events in a violent crime. Bloody fingerprints, palm or
foot prints also tell their own story and may be very helpful in solving the crime.
Composition of blood
Blood is a very complex mixture. It consists of four main components: red blood cells, white blood
cells and platelets, all suspended in a pale yellow liquid called plasma.
Plasma consists of 90% water and 10% dissolved proteins, hormones salts, digested food materials
and waste products.
Red blood cells are a donut shape, and give blood its colour. They carry oxygen to the cells.

forensic science?
1 INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

The word ‘forensic’ comes from the Latin word
forensis meaning ‘connected with the forum’.
The forum was the Roman square where the
Court of Law and public discussions were held.
In some countries, such as Canada and the
United States, forensic science is also known as
criminalistics.

Forensic science is any science that is used to
solve crimes, and its results are used in the
courts of law. It is based on the belief that
whenever a contact is made, there is always
some exchange of material. This principle was
first suggested by the famous French
criminologist Edmond Locard who, in 1910,
said that a criminal always leaves something at
the scene of a crime, or takes something away.
In other words, when a person comes in contact
with an object or another person, there is
always some material transferred from one to
the other. This has been referred to as Locard’s
Exchange Principle. These pieces of evidence
are for the police to find and for the forensic
scientist to analyse.

Things left at a crime scene can include fingerprints, small fibres from clothes, body hair, saliva left
on a sealed envelope, or semen in the case of a sexual attack. A suspect can be incriminated if flakes
of their skin are found under the nails of a victim who has been attacked. A criminal may take away
drops of a victim's blood, some hair or fibres from the victim's clothes or soil from the crime scene
on the soles of their shoes. The expression used today for such exchanged materials is ‘contact
traces’ or ‘trace evidence’. Other evidence can include footprints, tyre prints from the get-away car,
tool marks from a forced entry, body fluids, ink, paint flakes and oil. In fact anything, no matter how
small, that has been altered by the crime can be called a contact trace.

A
give us a clue – fluids behaving badly 
What you need 
Experiment 1
5 test tubes, filled with the following fluids: milk, cooking oil, glycerine, honey, water; 15 paperclips; 
stopwatch; access to a hot water bath
Experiment 2
Ziploc bag; white PVA glue; food colouring; borax solution; 20 mL measuring cylinder; scissors
What to do
Experiment 1: Newtonian fluids
1 Drop a paperclip into each fluid (one at a time) and 
use the stopwatch to carefully time how long it takes 
to reach the bottom of the tube. 
2 Put your thumb over the end of each tube and shake 
vigorously. 
3 Repeat step 1, again noting the times.
4 Place the test tubes into the hot water bath for 5 
minutes, then take them out and repeat step 1 again. 
Experiment 2: Non-Newtonian fluid
1 Take a ziploc bag and add 20 mL of PVA glue, 20 mL 
of water and 4 drops of food colouring. Seal the bag 
firmly and mix by squishing and kneading the mixture 
in the bag.
2 Now add 15 mL of borax solution, close the bag firmly and knead the bag between your fingers for 
10–15 minutes. 
3 Take the fluid out of the bag and knead it some more in your fingers, forming it into a ball. Observe 
what happens when you: set it on a piece of paper, hit it hard, stretch it, walk over it slowly with your 
fingers, run over it with your fingers, bounce it, and cut it with scissors.
Now answer these questions:
• Which fluid in Experiment 1 is the most viscous and which is the least viscous?
• Did shaking or temperature cause any change in these fluids? 
• When you held the fluid in Experiment 2 in your hands, how did it behave? 
• Is it a solid or a liquid? 
• What are the properties of this non-Newtonian fluid?

China’s One Child Policy was introduced in 1979. Up until this time, the Chinese government had been
encouraging its population to have children. However, by the 1970s a realisation had come about that if the country was going to
develop and improve the economic circumstances of its people it would need to limit population growth.

Interpreting a population pyramid
In order to interpret a population pyramid there are a number of features of population pyramids that you should be aware of:
∑Population pyramids display information about the age and sex structure of a total population.

How does the One Child Policy work?
∑Each workplace has a quota of the number of women who can get pregnant in a given year. Before having a child a woman must
inform her work unit that she is planning on having a baby and will only be given permission if the yearly quota is not yet full.
∑Incentives are used to encourage women to sign the One Child pledge such as an extra month’s salary per year until the child is
14 or larger houses.
∑Penalties are used if a woman breaks the One Child pledge such as a demotion at work or job loss, enforced abortions and
sterilisations.
∑If people have a second child without permission, it cannot be registered and therefore cannot legally attend school and will have
difficulty in obtaining permission to marry in the future.
∑While in cities most couples are restricted to one child, in some rural areas if the first child is a girl couples can seek permission
to try a second time to have a son. The government accepts that in rural areas a son is needed to inherit the land and look after
elderly parents.
Effects of the One Child Policy
∑A significant drop in fertility. In the 1970s, China’s fertility rate was 5.8 babies per woman, but is now at 1.7 babies per woman.
Fertility has dropped to below the level to replace the population.
∑A huge gender imbalance. Due to a cultural preference for sons, parents have used ultrasound tests to detect and selectively
abort daughters. The latest census found 117 male newborns for every 100 females.
∑Female infanticide. There have been many reports of baby girls being starved, abandoned or dumped.
∑A generation of little emperors. Many people believe the One Child Policy has created a generation of pampered, over-indulged
only children.
∑The ageing of China’s population.
∑Human rights abuses. Many people feel that China’s One Child Policy is an abuse of human reproductive rights.

Introduction
Native Title is the recognition under Australian law that indigenous people prior to European settlement had
a system of law and ownership of their land. This recognition finally came about in 1992 as a result of the High Court’s Mabo
decision. Until this time the doctrine of terra nullius had prevailed.

resolve Native Title issues.

arrival.

Introduction
Australia’s pattern of vegetation is the result of it’s geologic history, past and present climate, location and
size, and the impacts of its inhabitants. Land clearing and vegetation modification have accelerated to the extent that we now
need replanting, pest eradication and forest protection programs. These programs are an acknowledgment of the value of our flora
to our environment, economy and society.

Australia’s biodiversity (the range of plant species found) is
relatively high with a world ranking of 17. The native genus

GNI – gross national income. The sum of the value added by all resident producers in an economy, plus receipts of primary

Introduction
International Aid comes from a variety of government and non-government sources and exists in a range of
forms from financial assistance at the national level to food and clothing in a disaster at the local level. However, it is a
controversial aspect of human development. Criticisms include concerns over the amount of aid being given by nations,
approaches to providing aid, lack of accountability, the donor benefiting more than the recipient and the imposition of a Western
model of development on developing nations.

technical assistance being provided.

Introduction
The traditional ‘demographic transition’ model of population considered only birth and deathrates. Initially,
populations were kept small by high birth and high deathrates, then falling deathrates led to rapid population growth. Birthrates
then began to fall until a final stage of low growth or stability was reached. Countries were seen to pass through these stages with

Introduction
Landform refers to the shape of the earth’s surface, and is the result of processes operating both beneath
the earth surface (tectonic forces) and those affecting the land from above (gradational forces). Tectonic forces usually force the
surface upwards or change its structure, while gradation forces usually break it down and even out the level of the land. Individual
landform features are often classified into residual, erosional or depositional by the way these gradational forces have affected the
initial surface.

searchText:
Spatial distribution of AIDS
These are some of the significant facts about the AIDS crisis:
∑At the end of 2002 the number of people living with
HIV/AIDS was 42 million. [UNAIDS]
∑At the end of 2001 more than 13 million children under the
age of 15 in Africa, Asia and Latin America had lost a
parent to AIDS. [UNICEF]
∑More than 11 million of these children live in Africa.
[UNICEF]
∑The number of children who have lost 2 parents to AIDS is
expected to increase from 3.8 million in 2001 to 6.9 million
in 2010. [UNICEF]
∑In 2002, average life expectancy in 16 African nations was
at least 10 years lower than it would have been without
AIDS. [UNAIDS]
∑In Africa only 1% of the 4.4 million people in need had
access to antiretroviral treatment. [WHO]

of the global AIDS crisis.

Introduction
Tropical rainforests are found in the warm wet climates of the tropics. They are vitally important, not only
for their biodiversity – over half the world’s plant and animal species live in rainforests – but for the role they play in regulating
global climate, as a source of plants to produce medicines, in providing homes for indigenous people and in acting as watersheds.
Despite their value the world’s tropical rainforests have experienced, and are continuing to experience, drastic rates of
deforestation.

Introduction
Freshwater is a universal necessity. It sustains all forms of life, allowing ecosystems to operate by providing
food, recycling energy and removing waste. For humans, water also promotes development. Without adequate supplies, living
standards decline, people suffer and economic growth declines. To focus the world’s attention on current and growing water-
related issues, the UN declared 2003 the International Year of Freshwater.
Definition
Term
1 Removal of freshwater for human use from any natural source or reservoir such as a lake,
river or aquifer
2 Freshwater that is regularly replenished by the hydrologic cycle for withdrawal within reasonable
time limits.
3 A layer or section of earth or rock that contains freshwater (groundwater)
4 A situation where a country has an annual per capita water supply of 1000 to 1700 cubic metres
and will experience temporary or limited water shortage
5 Water in aquifers or other natural sources that is not recharged or recharges so slowly by natural
processes that its withdrawal by humans causes depletion
6 A situation where a country has an annual per capita waster supply of less than 1000 cubic metres
and will experience chronic and widespread supply problems that hinder development
7 A term for water/systems that reduce health risk to humans, such as sewage disposal and drainage
aquifer, non-renewable water, renewable water, sanitation, water withdrawal, water scarcity, water stress
Global inequalities
The amount (and quality) of water available for human use
varies markedly due to natural availability from the water
cycle, population levels and availability of technology to
protect, treat and transport the available water.

The future
About 40% of the world’s population currently live in areas of
water stress. It is estimated that this will rise to about two
thirds by 2025 (5.5 billion people). Water use increased six-
fold during the last century, more than twice the rate of
population growth. Wetlands are being degraded, water
supplies polluted and ground water is being depleted. More
than 2 million people die each year from diseases related to
contaminated drinking water and poor sanitation. In 1999 the
world supported 6 billion people, which will grow to over
8 billion by 2025. [Source: UN 2003]

Introduction
Australia’s low rainfall and the distribution of water resources are the most important factors determining our
settlement pattern, landuse and rural production. A scarcity of both surface and groundwater resources places significant
limitations on our use of this continent that can only partially be overcome with modifications such as dams and reservoirs.
Although our main river system, the Murray–Darling, ranks as the world’s 15th longest, its discharge (the volume of water flowing
through it) is among the lowest for the world’s major river systems. Recent and current water shortages and restrictions on water
use in Australian towns and cities have highlighted our water resource problems.

Despite international efforts to reduce
poverty, hunger is on the rise again
after falling steadily during the first
half of the 1990s, according to the
annual FAO report, ‘State of Food
Insecurity in the World’.
Almost 850 million people go to
bed hungry every night, the vast
majority in Africa and Asia, while the
number of hungry people in the
developing world is climbing at a rate
of almost 5 million a year, according
to the UN.
At the UN World Food Summit in
1996, governments set a goal of
cutting in half the number of hungry
people by 2015, using 1990–2 as a
base-line. The FAO said it was time
nations examined why hundreds of
millions of people went hungry in a
world that produced more than
enough food for everyone. ‘Bluntly
stated, the problem is not so much a
lack of food as a lack of political will,’
the report says.
Except when wars or natural
disasters put a spotlight on
developing countries, ‘little is said and
less is done’ to end the plight of the
798 million people who suffer from
chronic hunger, the report says.
Another 11 million people in the
developed countries and 34 million in
countries in transition are hungry.
According to the FAO report,
during the first half of the 1990s, the
number of chronically hungry people
decreased by 37 million. But since
1995–7, the number has increased by
18 million. A closer analysis of the
figures revealed ‘an even more
alarming trend’ – that the number of
hungry people in the developing world
increased by 4.5 million a year
between 1995 and 2001.
About 19 countries reduced the
number of hungry people since
1990–2 by a total of over 80 million.
Twenty-two countries, including
Bangladesh, Haiti and Mozambique
‘turned the tide’ against hunger, in the
second half of the decade.
At the other end of the scale are
26 countries where hunger increased
by almost 60 million, including
Afghanistan, Congo, Burundi, North
Korea, Somalia, Tanzania,
Guatemala, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Case study: Alexandra
Alexandra was in a relationship with Robert. She liked him very much but did not feel 
ready to settle down with anybody just yet. When they discovered she was pregnant, 
Robert proposed. Alexandra was not ready for marriage and did not think Robert was the 
right person for her. However, she was afraid she would not be able to support herself and 
her baby, so she agreed to the marriage.
13 Legal requirements of marriage
Family law
Consent to marry
The Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) outlines circumstances where consent to a marriage may not be 
considered real. These are:
• where consent was forced
• where consent was obtained by fraud
• the party was mistaken as to the identity of the person they were marrying
• the party was mistaken as to the nature of the wedding ceremony
• the party did not have the mental capacity to understand the nature and consequences of the  
wedding ceremony.
1 
Apart from the issue of appropriate consent, the Marriage Act 1961 gives three 
requirements for a marriage to be valid. List them.
 
 
 
REMEMBER 
The Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) sets out the requirements for a marriage to be valid. It also 
states the conditions under which a marriage is void.
2 
a Identify which of the circumstances outlined in the Act is in issue here.
 
b Was Alexandra’s consent to the marriage real or not real? Give reasons for your answer.

Case study: Sanjit
Sanjit was born in Australia, and his Indian immigrant parents raised him according to 
the customs of their birth culture. Sanjit had dated several girls of different nationalities 
but showed no signs of settling down. When he turned 30, his parents arranged for an 
18-year-old girl from their village to come to Australia to marry Sanjit. He had never met 
her before. Sanjit was not happy but went along with his parents’ decision. He did not 
want to upset them, and none of the girls he had previously dated had been right for him 
anyway.

a Identify which of the circumstances outlined in the Act is in issue here.
